consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The union of a collegiate church cannot be made to any dignity unless the chapter of the said united church consents to such union.
2. Only the Pope can unite churches without requiring the consent of the chapter.
3. What touches all must be approved by all.
4. A simple church, not collegiate, can be united without requiring the consent of the chapter.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A certain collegiate church was united to a certain dignity for a reasonable cause by the diocesan bishop with the consent of its chapter, all solemnities being observed: except that the chapter of the said united church did not consent, but entirely contradicted, and continues to contradict. It is asked whether the said union is valid or not. And it seems that it is valid: because since the union was made for a reasonable cause, the affair of the united church was usefully managed; therefore it ought to be held as ratified: as in the Digest, On Negotiorum Gestio, the law Pomponius writes, if the affair. Thus the son is bound to ratify the act of the father, if he does not have a just cause for contradicting: as in the Digest, On the Dissolution of Marriage, law 2, § voluntatem; and law Dotem. Moreover, it is sufficient to serve the words of the canon; nor ought we to require more than the law or canon requires: as in the Digest, On the Military Profession, law 1, § si is qui navem; and in the Digest, On the Publician Action, law De precio; in the Digest, On Acquiring an Inheritance, law Si servum, § non dixerit. But the decretal Si una does not require the consent of the chapter of the united church; therefore the union is valid.

On the contrary, it seems that it is not valid, because by such a union the status of the united church is changed, and especially the status of the chapter of the united church: because it loses the right of electing a prelate; but wherever status is changed, it is necessary that he whose status is at issue consents. Hence it is that in adoption, to which union is similar, the consent of the person being adopted is required: as in the Digest, On Adoption, law Nam ita divus, even if it concerns his benefit; it is not valid unless consent intervenes: the law says that a son cannot be legitimated against his will. And yet legitimation increases status: as in the Authentic Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, § et qualiter, column 7. Similarly, the law says that no one is emancipated against his will, even though it often benefits the emancipated son: as in the Digest, On Adoption, law Non potest filius. And briefly, wherever status is changed by good will, or without fault, no one is ever compelled to change his status.

† Hence, since the chapter here would lose its right of election and its status, in this very right of election the consent of the chapter is required by necessity; unless such a union were made by the Pope, who can take away his own right against the will of the other, and change the status of churches: as is noted in c. Cum venisset, Extr. de iudicibus, in the Novella, and is proved in l. Quaeris, D. de naturalis restitutione. Moreover, to unite a chapter is to transfer it into another family. Therefore, the consent of him to whom it is transferred is required: as in D. de adoptionibus, l. In adoptionibus, and l. Quod nepos. The objection from l. 2, § Voluntas, Sol. Ma. Cum Si. does not hold, because there no change of status is involved. Furthermore, that case is rather an execution of natural law than a creation of new law. Nor does the objection from c. Si una hold, because that Clementine must be understood provided that the consent of those whose consent is necessary intervenes. It declares certain persons whose consent is not required, but it does not proceed further:

† by saying that if there were any persons whose prejudice would be at issue, they should not consent; for it is said in the law *quod id, quod omnes tangit, debet ab omnibus comprobari* [that that which touches all must be approved by all]; see C. de auctoritate praesentantium, l. si. To this effect also serves the Clementina *ne in agro*, § *ad haec*, de statutis. And thus it seems to me, saving the substance of the truth. The objection does not hold from the gloss which is in the Clementina *si una*, in the gloss beginning *vocatus*, which says that a bishop can unite churches without the consent of both churches, by the text of the said chapter *si una*; because that gloss does not speak of a collegiate church, but of another. And the reason for the distinction is that where there is a college, there is a dignity. But a bishop cannot suppress the dignity of a church; as is noted in c. *cum accessissent*, de constitutionibus.

† Moreover, where there is a collegiate church, there is jurisdiction, from which the chapter ought not to be deprived without its consent. But in a simple church, this reasoning ceases to apply: because neither is a dignity suppressed, nor is jurisdiction confused. And this is also held by certain doctors. Moder. in the said chapter *Si una*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a mother is bound to institute her daughter as heir, to such an extent that if she passes her over, the will is declared null. And no. 3.
2. A granddaughter does not come under the name of daughter. No. 5.
4. The statutes of places are equated to stipulations.
6. The dowry of the mother coming to the daughter arises not by the judgment of the grandfather, but by chance.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The words of the statute. We have enacted that if any daughter, or married daughters, or married and dowered daughters, or dowered daughters, have been dowered by the father, or by the mother, or jointly by the parents, upon the death of those parents she shall have no further recourse to claim inheritance, whether paternal or also maternal, against brothers, or the heirs of those deceased heirs: but they shall be silent and content with the dowries given to them, whatever their amount may be. Now it has happened in the case that the father dowered his daughter: and from the daughter a granddaughter was born: and when the daughter was removed from the scene by death, the grandfather died having made a will, passing over the granddaughter, except that he left her a legacy, yet not by way of institution [of heir], nor from his own goods, but from the goods of the girl’s mother: now the said granddaughter, a girl, wishes to invalidate the grandfather’s will. It is asked whether she can. And it seems that she cannot: and first,

† because the granddaughter is included under the term “daughter” by an explanatory interpretation of the word, drawn from the very nature of the matter, even if the word “son” appears to be taken more strictly, insofar as the word signifies: as in D. de verborum significatione, l. liberorum; D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. filium diffinimus. Moreover, the daughter being excluded, it seems that every descendant through the daughter is excluded, since she cannot succeed except by some aid of the mother. Argument: D. de collatione bonorum, l. dedit dotem; and C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si. And this doctrine is taught by the text in c. 1, § illud notandum, Qui feuda possideant, Collatio 10. Furthermore, three things produce one and the same legal effect: namely, the word, the reason, and the intent. For each person is presumed to have such an intent as is shown by the cause of the disposition: as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, § et si maxime; and noted in c. in argumento, D. de regulis iuris, lib. 6, according to Digestum. Hence we say that from the reason of the same law arises a direct aid; but from the reason of another law, by analogy throughout, arises a useful aid: as elegantly noted by Bartolus in l. 1, D. uti possidetis. But the reason which moved the legislator in the case of the daughter: the same reason moved, and ought to have moved, in the case of the granddaughter; therefore it is as if the statute had expressly mentioned the granddaughter: as in D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, § si; and noted by Nicolaus de Tudeschis and Cynus in C. quae sit longa consuetudo, l. 1.

† On the contrary, it seems that this statute contains a certain disinheritance of the daughter: as in D. de haereditate instituenda, l. qui volebat. Therefore, it is permissible to argue from the words of the law to the words of the testator, and vice versa: as in D. de manumissione testamento, l. si ita, §. si. But if the testator says, “I disinherit my sons,” granddaughters are not included; because these matters are of strict law: as in D. de venditionibus in possessionem mittendis, l. 1, §. quare; and in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. cum quidam. Therefore, the same should be said regarding the statute.

† Moreover, local statutes are equivalent to stipulations: as is noted in the rubric of C. de decretis; for they are formed by question and answer: as in ff. de legibus 1, l. 1. But stipulations are so strictly construed that we do not depart from the words, even if equity suggests an extension: as is read and noted in l. si, ff. de conditionibus ob turpem causam. And laws are general. ff. so. ma. l. si vero. §. de viro. ff. de verborum obligatione, quicquid astringendae. And this is stated in l. no, ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si servum. §. non dixit praetor. Moreover, the law provides that a prohibition made against a son is not extended to a grandson. This is the text and the singular gloss in Auth. de restitutione fideicommissi, §. manifestum. To this effect, ff. de excusatione tutorum, l. 2, where the jurist says that from the meaning taken from the word, it is not the same to be a son and a grandson; likewise, Inst. qui datis tutoribus possunt, §. si. Moreover, a privilege granted to sons is not extended to grandsons; therefore, neither is odium: as in C. ad Trebellianum, l. iubemus. Moreover, by the same reasoning, it would be extended to great-grandsons and all descendants: as in ff. de postulando, l. 1, in fine, with the following law, which is false: as in Auth. de non alienando, §. emphyteusim. Furthermore, a son is the first descending person; a grandson is the second; a great-grandson is the third, and so on, as the text there says. But that the first person is the second, and vice versa, involves a natural impossibility.

† Therefore, concluding from the first to the last point, it does not seem that the granddaughter is signified. But I hold that in this statute the granddaughter is signified, although the statute makes mention of the daughter; nevertheless, it also mentions “parents,” which is a general term, as in D. de in ius vocando, l. quinquibus, §. parentes. And thus the signification of “children” is extended by the annexation of “parents,” as in D. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. regula, §. si. Moreover, this is proven by the reason of avoiding absurdity. Suppose, for instance, that the paternal grandfather provided a dowry for the granddaughter. For the daughter, being dowried, does not break the will; yet the granddaughter, through her son, would break it if her son predeceased her, which is highly absurd, because greater rights should not be granted to more remote descendants than to nearer ones, as in C. de maioribus, l. si viua matre. Hence, by the mental necessity of the statute, the granddaughter is included. Furthermore, because the disposition of the law should not be imperfect, as in C. ad Sillanianam, l. pen. But here it must be observed that the woman is excluded on account of her femaleness, because she is a woman; as if the statute said that a female daughter does not succeed, and then it would include the granddaughter, which may be for the favor of those coming intestate. Also, for the favor of instituted heirs, so that they do not break the will. For greater favor is due to a will than to legitimate heirs, as noted in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. instituens. But sometimes the statute does not exclude the daughter simply, but only the dowried daughter. And then it does not exclude the undowered daughter, because the quality of being dowried is not present in the granddaughter; nor does she have any provision from her grandfather by which she can be said to succeed in place of the legitime. And therefore, according to what is proposed, the granddaughter has the right to break the will. Someone might say: this granddaughter succeeds to the maternal dowry; therefore she is dowried even against her mother’s will, because a filiafamilias cannot make a will and exclude her own daughter. Thus, according to Bartolus, this granddaughter must impute this dowry to herself in calculating her legitime to be deducted from her grandfather’s goods, as he notes in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in quarta.

† because certainly this does not arise from the judgment of the grandfather, but from a fortuitous event, as in the Digest, *de legatis*, l. 3, *sed si sic*. And therefore, regarding the aforementioned niece, I conclude that, since she was passed over, she can break the will. Although Bartolus says in a certain place that in the maternal line it is not required that she be left an inheritance by way of institution, so that the rights of the codicil in the maternal line remain unimpaired, because the mother is not said to pass over her own child, as in the Institutes, *de inofficioso testamento*, § *mater*. But the contrary is truer according to § *aliud quinque capitulum* in the Authenticum *ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur*, because now even today it is said that she is passed over, and the will is rendered null. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The stipulation for double damages, whether, when, and how it applies.
2. The seller is not bound to assume in himself the action arising from a lawsuit initiated by the buyer with the intent of renewing the action. And also on this point in opinion 23.
body: In the name of Christ. Titius sold a certain estate to Seius for a certain price, and promised said purchaser to defend and disencumber it at his own expense, under penalty of the double. A first dispute having been raised against the said purchaser by a certain creditor of the said vendor on a hypothecary claim, the said vendor stood by the lawsuit through his procurator; he did not, however, take the trial upon himself. And a judgment was rendered against the purchaser, following which rendered judgment the said vendor reached an agreement with the creditor so that the said estate might remain freely with the purchaser. The purchaser sues for the penalty of the double on account of the property not having been defended at the vendor's own expense.

† It is asked what the law is. I answer: the nature of the stipulation for the double is this, that the stipulation is not incurred if possession remains with the purchaser, as in ff. de euict. l. habere licere. To this point ff. de exce. doli. l. fideiussor euictionis and ff. mand. l. fi. apply exceedingly well. And therefore the double of the price cannot be sought by virtue of the said stipulation with reference to the sold property itself. But certainly, nor on account of expenses not supplied is the stipulation for the double incurred with respect to the whole property, as one reads and notes in ff. de procu. l. qui absentem and C. de euic. l. 1; for it would be unjust if a thing of great value, say one thousand, was sold and the expenses are ten, that the vendor should be held for two thousand, as in ff. de sen. quae pro eo. l. vnica. §. fi. Likewise, that vendor, considering the end result, is seen to have defended and disencumbered. And therefore on account of expenses alone the stipulation for the double is not incurred: by the argument of ff. de lib. leg. l. petitor. Likewise, although the expenses can be claimed under the name of damages (interesse), one cannot nevertheless sue for the double, because this is not of the nature of the contract, nor indeed of the intention of the contracting parties; for the stipulation for the double was drafted under the condition, ‘if he does not defend the property’. But here the property has been defended, because the hypothecary claim has been extinguished, as in ff. de pig. l. si fundus. §. si pluris. I say further that if the vendor had refused to appear for the defense, yet had freed the property for the purchaser by paying and satisfying the creditor, since it would not concern the purchaser’s interest except by reason of the expenses of the suit, the stipulation would not be incurred except as to the expenses, in accordance with the note on ff. de verb. ob. l. stipulatio ista, and on a similar subject matter, ff. de iureiu. l. nam et postea, and l. alias, in magna gl. From these things it appears that the stipulation for the double is not incurred unless the principal thing is evicted, in such a way that it has been recovered, because such is the case in the said l. habere licere. Likewise, no one doubts that a purchaser acts fraudulently who retains the property and seeks the double, as in ff. de conditio. sine causa. l. si fullo. To treat further here whether the vendor ought to take the lawsuit upon himself with the intention of novating, or not, is not expedient as far as the present matter is concerned; but the truth is that he is not bound, nor can he against the will of the plaintiff, as noted on ff. de sol. l. solutionem. et iudicium, except when from his own person he has a ground of exception, because then the plaintiff is bound to receive him as far as this effect is concerned, namely that he may raise the exception, as in ff. de peti. haere. in l. sed si lege. §. sed si res distraxerit. I speak of a peremptory exception, not of a declinatory exception to the forum, as in ff. de iud. l. venditor; and thus ought to be understood what is noted on ff. de neg. ge. l. liberto. §. fi., ff. de pac. l. si cum fundum, and C. vbi in rem actio. l. 1.

† From this it appears that the vendor is not bound to take the lawsuit upon himself with the intention of novating when he cannot do so because the plaintiff does not consent; and even if he could, he is still not bound, but it is enough that he assist the lawsuit and bear the expenses in the lawsuit, as in ff. de euict. l. si plus. §. mota and l. 1 C. vbi rei actio; and thus I have noted in many places in my lectures, both ancient and modern. And ff. de euic. l. si rem. §. quolibet and what is noted on ff. de ver. ob. l. venditores and ff. de pcu. l. si actor malit support this. Consider also that if he were bound to transfer the lawsuit onto himself with the intention of novating, he would be compelled to join issue (litem contestari), which is nowhere provided by law. The antecedent is proved by l. in iudicio. ff. fa. et c., and ff. de procu. l. licet. §. ea obligatio supports this. And because he does not have the right of declining the forum, he therefore does not appear in his own name only, but in the name of the purchaser, albeit for his own interest, as in l. 2. §. sed si alius. ff. quando ap. sit. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether sureties, by renouncing all benefits, are understood to renounce the benefit of the letter of the divine Adrian: And what effect a general renunciation of benefits accruing to them, or operating to the contrary, produces.
2. Special clauses are applied in practice, so that it may be understood that general clauses are not sufficient.
3. A concise general renunciation has as much force according to the strict law as a special renunciation.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked whether guarantors who have renounced generally all benefits may oppose the benefit of the letter of the Divine Adrian. It is also asked whether several debtors liable for the whole, by renouncing generally all benefits and not expressly specifying any particular benefit, are understood to have renounced the benefit of the new constitution concerning two debtors, and the benefit of the cession of actions. And it seems that such a most general renunciation is not valid: as in l. sed et si quis, §. quaesitum, D. si quis cautio. On the contrary, it seems that a genus operates with regard to a genus as much as a species operates with regard to a species: as in l. si duo, D. de administratione tutorum. Moreover, it is certain that one can renounce these benefits, as noted in l. pen. and l. nisi, D. de pactis, and in Auth. de fideiussoribus, in principio. For these benefits are sufficiently known to the contracting parties from the very beginning, so that they could well have foreseen them. And thus the aforementioned §. quaesitum does not apply, because there it speaks of exceptions which could not be foreseen from the beginning, but later emerged from fortuitous events. Moreover, there it speaks of trials in which equity is more leniently applied by the praetor. In that title, l. et si post tres, and l. si servus, and si plurium. It can be said that a general renunciation is valid, unless it is a minor or a woman, who must be specifically informed of their benefits; and they are not presumed to be informed unless it appears: as is read and noted in D. de verborum obligationibus, l. sciendum. And the following general rule applies to the above, that it is permitted for each person to renounce a right introduced for his benefit: as in C. de pactis, l. si quis in conscribendo. However, the contrary is supported by l. 1, D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, where the text seems to require that the quality of the benefit be expressed: for example, he renounced the benefit of forum, the benefit of guarantors, etc. For even that l. si quis in conscribendo holds the same view. Moreover, we have a similar case in C. quoniam mulier tutelae officio fungi potest, Auth. matri et aviae, and in Auth. ut sine prohibitione mariti debere et credi, §. quia vero. And the custom of notaries is such that in instruments special clauses are appended, and then general clauses are added. In response to l. si duo, it is answered that there is a special rule in the renunciation of benefits, that words entirely general are not sufficient, according to the matter of the aforementioned §. quaesitum, noted by Cy. in l. 1, C. communi. And this is the safer opinion, that some benefit must be specified, in order that the general clause may have any effect, and then it operates from similars to similars: not from greater things: as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, §. frumenta, and arg. D. de fundo instrato, l. si, §. qui dulcia. And this can be defended from the contrary sense of practical custom.

† Therefore, special clauses are practiced, so that it may be understood from the contrary sense that general clauses are not sufficient. Spec. in tit. de renunc. et conclusione, in 1. col. ver. pone ergo multa verba says, whether the said general renunciation is valid or not. And finally he inclines to the opinion that the renunciation is not valid: but the pact is valid. Afterwards in the same title ver. et qio. de renunciatione he says that daily in public instruments four benefits are renounced by naming them individually. namely, the benefit of the letter of divine Anianus: the benefit of the new constitution on suretyship; the benefit of the new constitution on several debtors; and the benefit of cession of actions. And because these renunciations are very prejudicial, therefore by custom it has been introduced that they be specified and declared: lest ambiguity and uncertainty of speech deceive simple people. arg. ff. de transa. l. cum aquiliana. and in c. 1. de noua forma libelli. col. 10. and ff. de mino d. illud. §. si talis: and ff. de proc. l. pomponius, in prin. and in d. l. sed et si quis. §. quesitum. cum si. supra alleg. this opinion is more equitable.

† But a brief and general renunciation operates according to the strictness of the law only to the extent that the species individually enumerated do. Arg. C. de praescrip. 30. anno. l. omnes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Poverty excuses a person who does not appeal, or does not pursue an appeal, to such an extent that he may appeal, or pursue the appeal.
2. Whether poverty is excusable or not is left to the discretion of the judge.
3. He who was not negligent is not prejudiced by the passage of time.
body: In the name of Christ.

It is asked whether the time limits for fatal appeals run against widows and the poor. And it seems that they do: because we are so much in debt to widows in justice, that we ought not to commit injustice against others: as is stated in the extrajudicial title *De foro competenti*, in the chapter *Ex tenore*. Although they have the prerogatives of judges: as in the Code, title *Quin imperator inter pupillos et viduas*, the sole law. Nevertheless, they do not have the prerogative of time limits: because no law says this. On the contrary, the laws state that a woman must be subject to the common law, except in the case of the *Senatusconsultum Velleianum*: as in the Code, title *De iure et facti ignorantia*, the law *Si*, where is the notable text. To the contrary, it seems on account of poverty: because he is not considered negligent who, on account of poverty, does not appeal or does not pursue the appeal. This is the notable text in the Digest, title *Mandati*, the law *Idem*, section *Si ignorans*. This is expressly held by Innocentius in the extrajudicial title *De appellationibus*, in the chapter *Ex ratione*, and by Guillaume de Cuggiat in the Authenticum *Hodie*, Code, title *De appellationibus*.

† solution. It is left to the discretion of the judge to determine which poverty excuses and which does not, as in D. de excus. tut. l. paupertas. Thus, in a case where destitution is established, relief shall be granted on account of poverty:

† because he is not prejudiced by the passage of time, who was not negligent: as is noted in the Authority on appeals, principal, collection 8; and it is established in the Digest, On the Status of Persons, title 1, law Cum heres, in the principal part; and in the Digest, On the Institution of Heirs, law Suus, section Puto; and in the Digest, On the Signification of Words, law Nepos Proculo; and what is noted in law Succurritur, together with the following law, in the Digest, Those Who Are Excluded from the Cause of Madness.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Holidays cause a compromise to lapse, provided there is a statute that holidays are observed in ordinary and extraordinary courts, and in any case exceeding a certain sum.
2. What effect the words "proceeding on holiday and non-holiday days" have.
3. One cannot renounce public law.
4. Before an arbitrator, all days are working days.
body: In the name of Christ. The statute of the city of Pavia states that there are holidays for harvests and vintage in certain months of the year in ordinary and extraordinary courts, and in any case exceeding a certain sum, whether it be ordinary or extraordinary. And it is proposed that the parties have submitted themselves to an arbitrator and an arbiter, specifically regarding a certain question and cause: adding that the arbiter may proceed, hear, and terminate on holiday and non-holiday days, even to the honor of God: wishing that the said submission should last 40 useful days computed from the day of acceptance.

† It is asked whether the time of harvests and vintage seasons ought to be deducted, so that in the meantime the period of forty days for the harvest does not run. And it seems that it should be so: because the time of holidays is not useful time: as in the Digest, On Holidays, l. 1, with its accompanying material. Moreover, although an arbitrator has authority on both holiday and non-holiday days for the benefit of men: as in the Digest, On Holidays, l. si feriatis; nevertheless, he cannot be compelled: because the parties could not waive holidays to the prejudice of the arbitrator: as noted in the Speculum, On Arbitration, §. fi, near the end, under the words "but whether he is bound"; and as noted in the chapter saepe, On the Verification of Signatures, in the Clementines, in the gloss on the Ordinary, under the word "may". Since, therefore, the arbitrator may plead holidays, they are indeed holidays; hence the time is not useful, and thus in the meantime the compromise lies dormant, and the time does not elapse.

† To the contrary it seems, because the arbitrator accepted the compromise with these clauses: therefore he consented to the renunciation of the holidays. And he who has consented cannot allege the holidays: since with such holidays one can renounce expressly and tacitly, in l. 1, ff. de feriis, in principio. This single reason suffices: as noted by Paulus de Leaza in the cited declaration. Moreover, it is certain that during the holiday period he could proceed: as noted by Speculum, where it says, but for the time to be useful, it suffices that one can proceed according to law: as l. 2, §. dies, ff. quis ordo in bonis possessoribus servetur. Moreover, the party whose interest it was should have required the arbitrator himself to proceed. And if he had proceeded, well indeed; if he had not proceeded, then the party was excused, but if he did not require him, he is not excused: as ff. qui ex causa maioris, l. sed et si per praetorem, §. 2. Moreover, if this arbitrator had jurisdiction by the form of the statute, it does not seem that he could allege holidays: because no law provides that he who presides over jurisdiction can allege the holidays of harvest or vintage: because this allegation is given to the litigant, not to the judge: since jurisdiction is a power introduced from the public with the necessity of exercising jurisdiction: as noted in l. 1, ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum. Although Speculum says the contrary in the cited words, it does not prove by any law nor by any reason. It says, namely, that this pact does not bind the arbitrator or judge, but this reason is of no value because this obligation is legal. For since he can say the law, he must say it: as extra de foro competenti, c. ex tenore.

† Moreover, he offers another reason: because public law cannot be renounced. But this is true only insofar as it is public law by authority and utility; yet this matter is private and concerns family affairs, as noted in the Authentica *Ut sine prohibitione*, *Matres debitrices*, § *Quia vero*. Otherwise, it would follow that one could not renounce the said holidays, which is absurd to say. Furthermore, the statute speaks of ordinary and extraordinary judicial proceedings. But here we are not in a judicial proceeding, but outside of it, and before an arbitrator, before whom the days are useful, except if someone were factually impeded by illness or another cause or accident, especially one occurring in the person of the judge. Since therefore holidays are not to be granted, there ought to be no deduction of holidays which do not exist. The case seems to be expressly stated in l. *Si*, C. *De feriis*, and there by Bartolus, and noted in the Speculum, *De arbitris*, § *Si*, under the words *Sed nunquid amicabilis compositor*, and there the friend ought to have seen. It must therefore be concluded, since we are speaking of an arbitrator, that the holiday days of the harvest did not cause the compromise to sleep; because these holidays are not holidays in compromises having the force of a transaction or quasi-transaction; because, as I said, there is no judicial proceeding there, nor are they reduced to the likeness of a judicial proceeding, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, *De iureiurando*, c. *Quintavallis*. And thus you, who have thundered against my opinion, did not understand. Although the gloss in l. 1, ff. *De feriis*, says that the reason of occupation is not a total reason of the gloss, nevertheless the following gloss, which begins *Libellus*, says that the judge is compelled against his will to receive the libel on a holiday. But to this it could be answered that the giving of the libel is a momentary act. Whatever it says, the truth is what I said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the dowry of the mother, upon the dissolution of the marriage by the death of the husband, and subsequently upon the death of the mother, is to be restored to the father or to the children of that woman.
2. The father is bound to preserve the dowry of his daughter, restored to him or remaining in his possession, for the case of her subsequent marriage.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Peter married off his daughter and promised her a thousand as dowry; this daughter bore sons; and upon the death of her husband, she returned to her father’s house, and there she died: the said sons, as heirs of their mother, claim this dowry from their grandfather: the grandfather says that he is not bound [to pay it], since even if he had paid it, he could recover it: on the contrary, custom is alleged, concerning which in l. dos a patre. It is answered that this custom applies when the daughter dies during the marriage: but here she survived her husband. Hence we are not within the scope of the custom, but within the common law; and according to the common law it is certain that the action for the dowry given by the father (dos profectitia) vests in the father upon the death of the daughter, and upon the death of the father it vests in the daughter: as l. 2 and l. post dotem, D. de iure dotium (so. mat.); and the aforementioned l. dos a patre, where the text says that a dowry proceeding from the father is given to revert to the father; and C. de rei uxoriae actione, auth. sed quamuis; and C. de coniugii dotium, l. si. Hence it must be said without doubt that, since the custom does not speak in our terms, because the daughter survived her husband, but in contrary terms, when the husband survived the wife: and the common law provides for the father: that the provision of the common law should be followed; because we must not extend the custom beyond its case, where the common law provides the contrary: as D. de legibus, l. de quibus; and arg. D. de iure dotium, l. si vero, § de viro; because just as a law correcting another law does not correct except in its own case: so neither does a custom derogating from the law derogate except in the case expressly stated by the custom itself, even if the same reason were thought to apply: as noted in C. de facultate sanctae ecclesiae, auth. quas actiones. Moreover, an omitted case is to be held as omitted. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. commodissime; and D. de conditione ob causam, l. si extraneus; and l. si cum dotem, in principio, D. de iure dotium; and to this point serves well D. pro socio, l. si socius pro filia, vers. verum in proposito; and D. de pactis dotalibus, l. 2, solutio. It must be admitted according to the common law that this dowry remains with the father: but considering the reason of the custom, which provides that the sons succeed to this dowry as heirs, it is more truly said that these sons succeed to their mother; because the reason of the custom must be considered. arg. C. de iudiciis viduarum, l. si; and l. de quibus, D. de legibus; and thus in this dowry the daughter will have her sons as heirs.

† Certainly, this is not without doubt: because the father is not bound to anything else, except to preserve this dowry of the daughter for a subsequent marriage; therefore, if no marriage follows, it remains with the father himself. Arg. dig. l. si extraneus, in fine. And this is useful to know for another question, namely whether these nephews are bound to impute this dowry to themselves in the legitime due from the goods of the maternal grandfather. And it must be said that they are not: because it does not pertain to them; nor do they succeed to it. These statements are true, even if it were said that the dowry is retained on account of the children: because that pact is not valid in the case where the woman survives the husband, unless the marriage is dissolved by divorce: as ff. de pactis dotalibus, l. inter socerum, §. vir dotem, and §. quomodo inter, and note in l. 1, and l. 1, ff. de dote prælegata. And these statements are true, unless the dowry had been stipulated to the daughter alone: because then her children would rightly succeed as heirs of the mother, although the mother had survived the husband, as if by a donation made to the mother: as ff. fa. hæred., l. pomponius philadelphus. Moreover, the duty of the father is to provide a dowry for the daughter, not to make a gift: as ff. de ritu nuptiarum, l. qui liberos, and ff. quæ in fraudem creditorum, l. si, in principio. Furthermore, it is not the duty of the maternal grandfather to provide for his nephews in any respect; and therefore the provision of the law is not extended to them, because they are of another family. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether expenses incurred for the recovery of a common thing ought to be contributed by the co-owners, and when.
2. Whether the deed prevails over the word.
body: In the name of Christ. There were five noble co-owners of a certain very strong tower, which was called Orco: two of these were expelled by the other two: the third also, wishing to return to that tower, was not admitted: yet the expulsion was not made out of hatred for the said third party: but out of hatred and enmity towards those two expelled: and therefore war arose between them: because those two expelled raised troops: on account of which they borrowed money, the third, or fifth, not consenting, but saying that he did not wish to contribute to the expenses, except insofar as he was bound by law: and finally, after many expenses had been incurred, the said tower could not be recovered. Now the said third, or fifth, is summoned to contribute to the expenses, who says that he is not bound to contribute.

† The question is what is the law. And in this matter, much time should not be wasted on words; rather, it must be concluded that he is not bound to contribute, for several reasons. First, because this undertaking was rashly begun, more rashly pursued, and unhappily abandoned. He who undertakes any business ought to undertake a possible business. Likewise, he ought to undertake a useful business. Likewise, he ought to undertake a business that will not overly burden the family estate. These points are proven textually in D. 3.5 (de negotiorum gestorum), sed an ultra, § 1; and § is; and § ego vero. But in the present case, it appears that this expense was incurred rashly, which is shown by the indefensible quality of the castle, as noted in D. 4.2 (qui satisfactionem cogantur), l. 2, in principio. Likewise, the rashness of the act, which was carried out by force of arms, as in C. 7.12 (ut armorum usus), l. 1. Likewise, the unhappy outcome, because, laboring all night, they captured nothing. And such an outcome was foreseeable by this prudent man, who ought not to have attempted matters greater than himself and too arduous. The law states that a negotiorum gestor who has undertaken even a just lawsuit cannot claim the costs of the lawsuit, as in D. 46.1 (iudicia soluta), l. iam tamen, § in hac. And if it is said that this business could not be expedited in part, considering the nature of the thing, and this is conceded in fact, nevertheless, since those who caused the enmity placed themselves in this necessity, it ought not to redound to another’s detriment; for inconveniences and damages bind their authors, especially passively, as in D. 9.2 (pro socio), l. cum duobus, § si cum; l. subsequent; and D. 46.1 (de fideiussoribus), l. si a reo, § si reo; D. 17.1 (solutis matrimonii), l. in his; D. 19.2 (de locato conducto), l. si mentes, § culpae; D. 46.1 (de fideiussoribus), l. exceptione; D. 20.1 (de pignoris actione), l. si, § si; D. 3.5 (de negotiorum gestorum), l. nam et servius, in principio; D. 24.2 (conubia divortia), l. is cum quo, with many others; and from D. 20.1 (de pignoris actione), C. ex literis. The third reason is that this third party objected, saying that he did not wish to contribute except insofar as he was bound by law; otherwise, he does not wish to. But it is so that he is not bound by law, and from the beginning of the management he declared his mind, as in C. 3.28 (de negotiorum gestorum), l. si, where it is expressly stated. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, it clearly appears that the contribution of expenses cannot be demanded, especially from those cited, who come into no judgment, as in D. 10.3 (communis dividundo), l. cum dividundo, § inter praedones. Although that third party, who was not admitted upon his return, was truly dispossessed of possession, as in D. 41.2 (de acquisitione possessionis), l. clam possidere, § si cum; l. subsequent.

† For whatever a protestation may assert, the fact prevails over the word: as in Extra, De constitutionibus, Cum M. Ferrariem; Codex, De institutionibus et substitutionibus, Reprehendenda; and note in Gratia, De rescriptis, in the Clementines, unless both can be saved, and is saved with effect. And thus it is understood, as noted in Si duo, Digest, Uti possidetis; and Codex, ibid., Law 1. Moreover, concerning this good faith, it would have to be proven, since the contrary fact induces it: Codex, De iniuriis, Si non convitiis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A fief alienated by the vassal passes by operation of law to the lord: nor is a judicial sentence required.
2. If a vassal commits felony against his lord, whether he loses the fief by operation of law, or whether a judicial sentence is indeed necessary.
3. Whether the alienation of a fief with reservation of the right of the direct lord is valid.
4. The possessor of a fief, when sued, may raise the defense of the right of a third party.
5. If a minor sells a fief without a decree, he does not lose his right.
6. Whether a custom regarding the alienation of a fief without the lord being summoned, while saving the direct right of the lord, is valid.
7. Whether the Church may invest someone with a fief possessed by another, which has devolved to it by operation of law.
8. How manyfold similarity is.
body: In the name of Christ. The facts are as follows. In the year of our Lord 1388, the Reverend Father, the Lord Bishop of Asti, made a certain investiture of a fief consisting of a certain castle and village in the person of Gandulf and Valencia, his wife; that is, in the name of the said Gandulf and of the said Valencia, namely in the person of the said Valencia, as if it were a paternal and ancient fief held by her ancestors from the said Church of Asti, namely for the said spouses and their legitimate and natural male and female children descending from them, etc. Finally, in the year of our Lord 1389, the said Gandulf and the said Valencia, his wife, and each of them jointly and severally, namely the said Valencia with the authority and consent of her said husband, she being moreover over the age of eighteen and under the age of twenty-five, renouncing the benefit of minority and restitution in integrum, under the condition that the said Lord Bishop of Asti, in his own name and on behalf of his Church of Asti, would consent to the alienation set forth below, and would provide counsel and authority in all and singular instruments, and would successively invest the noble man Bartholomew de Garretis, the purchaser set forth below, and make investiture to the said purchaser according to the form and tenor of the investiture made to the said Gandulf and his wife Valencia in their names, or another superior of the said Lord Bishop; if, however, the said Lord Bishop did not consent, and did not provide consent, authority, and license for the said alienation, and did not make, or refused to make, the investiture of the aforementioned things in the due manner and form, even while reserving the right of fief of the said Lord Bishop and the Church of Asti, they gave and sold to Bartholomew the said castle, etc., this being done, that the said Bartholomew should hold and possess the said place in the name of the said Gandulf and Valencia, until the said Bartholomew was lawfully invested by the said Lord Bishop or another superior having power to do so. The said vendors also, under the said condition, constituted themselves as holding precariously, etc. Afterwards, the said Bartholomew, thus invested only superficially, held the said castle against the will of the said Lord Bishop, who did not consent, although investiture had been requested from him; after which the said Lord Bishop invested another with the said castle, as having reverted to the Church of Asti; after which supplication was made to the Lord Pope that he ratify the said sale; the said Lord Pope committed the matter, however, he did not ratify it, and he died. Therefore, presupposing the said theme as true, and saving the terms of truth.

† It is asked whether the said fief of the said Church of Asti was opened, so that another could be invested, or not. On this point, some say that alienation without consent is void. But with consent, even if it is prejudicial to the alienation, it is not prejudicial to the lord. That consent is of the substance of alienation, and this is the cause of causes, is proven: D. de cond. ob cau. l. 3. §. subtilius; and D. si cer. pe. l. si ego. That it holds against the alienator is proven: Inst. de us. §. finitus; and the whole matter of fiefs sings nothing else. Immediately, it is noted that the vassal proceeds to the act and consent, so that two things intervene: namely, the act and the will, and the transfer of corporal possession, even if abusive and superficial; the fief reverts to the lord, and especially to the church by operation of law: as C. de iure emph. l. 2; and in c. imperialem, §. callidis, de prohib. alien. eccl. rer. per Fed. Nor is re-transfer of possession required, nor any other formality; because the force of direct dominion is always in the act of the preceding right by virtue of attraction. To this effect is D. ad trebell. l. si heres, where it says that direct actions suffice. And this is properly not a new dominion, but a consolidation; because direct dominion has the force of both direct and useful dominion, just as when emphyteusis ends, and when usufruct ends, and when the dowry reverts to the woman: so, max. as C. de iure dot. in l. rebus; and especially in the church, which also acquires new dominions without tradition: as ex de consue. c. ex parte; and C. de sac. san. eccl. l. ut inter diuinum. Thus, when the action of the father and daughter consolidates to one of them. Nor is cession of the right, which was with the deficient party, necessary; nor even any corporal tradition: as C. de rei ux. act. l. vnica, §. videamus. But when consent is not present in alienating, then alienation is not said to exist, neither in fact nor in name. So it is in the case at hand: for wherever a future condition is appended, which is properly a condition, until the condition exists, there is no consent: as D. de act. et ob. l. non solum; D. de ver. sig. l. cedere diem; D. de cond. indeb. l. sub conditione; and l. qui promisit; and noted, C. de rerum perm. l. ex placito. Likewise, if a vassal sells without requesting the lord, under the condition that a ship comes from Asia: and the ship does not come from Asia, he does not lose the fief; because nothing was contracted. But, D. si cer. pe. l. nonia; and l. proinde; and l. non omnis. So therefore in the case at hand. For there is no difference in saying, if a ship comes from Asia, or if the lord consents. For in both cases, the words and the intent of the contract fail when the condition fails: as D. de peric. et comm. rei vend. l. quod si pendente. For the condition existing in your act imposes the beginning of the cession of the day: as fully noted, C. de cad. tol. l. vnica, §. 1; D. de cond. et demon. l. meus. And in this a condition differs from a mode: as fully read and noted, D. de cond. et dem. in rub. dicit aliquis. And although the contract is conditional, yet if the tradition is pure, let it be said that alienation proceeds from a title which is in hope: as D. de sol. l. sub conditione; D. de usucap. pro dote. l. 1; D. de iure dot. l. sed nisi. And if you say that this tradition was not pure, because it was agreed that Bartholomew should hold and possess in the name of the said Gandulphus and Valentinus, I answer: tradition has three things in itself: namely, the effect of the contract, where the contract holds as to the transfer of dominion by transfer of the substance of possession, and a certain superficial act of some asinine detention. And this act, contrary to law, and in fact grave and damaging to the lord of the fief, intervened in the case proposed. And therefore the lord should not be defrauded with fictitious tergiversations: as d. §. callidis. To this asinine detention, the fact exists, which cannot be regarded as if it had not been done: as D. de capt. et postlim. rev. l. in bello, §. factae. Nor does protestation help; because it sings well and scrapes badly, as noted in c. gratia, de rescr. in cle. Whatever therefore we may say, certainly by the act of the word the fief did not fall into forfeiture; but by the true act of fact, that it fell into forfeiture. D. de ver. sig. l. alienatum. Likewise, how can the seller be excused from fraud, who received the price? Certainly not at all: as in l. si, C. de praed. curialium, lib. 10. Nor did fictions avail to excuse excuses in sins; rather, he sins more heavily who defrauds the law than he who expressly does the words of the law: as l. si libertus minorem, D. de iure patr.

† Because, for the understanding of the aforesaid, I form one question: if a vassal transfers a fief without title to the prejudice of the lord, whether he loses the fief by operation of law, or whether a sentence and the judgment of peers is necessary, and the rules in the matter of fiefs say that fraud must be proved before the peers, and that they by their sentence declare the feoffee deprived of the fief; nor is it opened to the lord except by sentence. Although, therefore, by alienation it returns to the lord by operation of law, yet by fraud it does not return by operation of law, but finally by sentence. And just as the petition for inheritance is not open before the complaint of an undutiful will is brought, as is fully stated and noted in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, law *qui de inofficioso*; so too the fief is not open to the lord before the complaint of the vassal’s fault is brought, as I will fully prove in law. And if it is asked, what is the reason regarding *res iudicata*, that by alienation it returns to the lord by operation of law, but not by fault or fraud, a twofold reason is given. The first is that, by alienating, although in fact, the vassal makes himself alien to the fief. Argument from the Digest, *de peculio legato*, law *cum dominus*, section *si*. It is otherwise where he does not intend to alienate, because he does not alienate who merely loses possession, as in the Digest, *de alienatione iudicio mutata causa faciente*, law *non solum*. The second reason is that the felony of the alienator is purged by the law *contractus*, and thus by the law *consensus*, as in the Digest, *de locato conducto*, law *quero*, section *inter emptorem*; and in the Code, *de sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, authentic *qui res iam dictas*. It is otherwise in the felony of a delict, because that is purged by a condition according to custom; which condition must be proposed, and a pronouncement made upon it; because the vassal ought not to lose the fief without certain and manifest fault, and approved by the judgment of the court or his peers; as in chapter 1, *de feudo sine culpa non amittendo*; and in chapter 2, *quo tempore miles investituram petere debeat*. For when that which concerns fault between the lord and the vassal, the peers of the court ought to judge, not the lord himself; because he would be judge in his own cause; as in the law and note cited from *de iudicibus*, chapter *ceterum*; and in chapter 1, section *ad hæc*, in the title *hic finitur lex*, then the customs of the kingdom begin: for it is one thing to have returned, another to ought to return. Just as it is one thing to be free, another to be freed, and one thing to have been provided for, another to be provided for; as in the Digest, *de iudicibus*, law *qui se dicit*. So it is in the present case: because before the thing is evicted from the feoffee, the fief is not open to the lord. Although it is most true that between the lord and the vassal no fraud, nor any evil intent, ought to intervene; nor any commerce be devised, by which the utility of the lords is diminished; as in chapter *imperialis benivolentiae*, at the end, in the beginning, *de prohibita feudorum alienatione per Lotharium*; and in the last chapter of the same title. Nevertheless, as I said above, it is necessary that the fief be evicted by sentence, or the vassal deprived of the fief; as in chapter 1, *de investitura in manu feuda*, with many others. But against the aforesaid it is objected, and truly, that this fraud was directly committed in the alienation; because either saying that no fraud was committed.

† because the right of the lord was reserved, according to what is stated in the law and noted in l. 1, C. de fundis patrimonialibus, lib. 11; and this is false in fiefs: for the right of the lord is not in the power of reservation of the vassal on account of personal, real, and mixed services, to which the new possessor cannot be compelled, as noted in the Speculum de feudis. Moreover, because a penalty is established in the matter of fiefs, that however the vassal may alienate without the will of the lord, the fief by operation of law reverts to the lord: as in c. 1, §. pen., Qui modis feudum amittatur; and this is what the text says “without the permission of the lords,” as in the cited chapter *Imperialis benignitatis*. If, however, it is said that this is due to a condition appended, namely “if he can sell according to law”: or if the lord has consented, as the aforementioned Jacobus Ardixone says in his Summa under the rubric which he calls: “if he sells under the condition that he can sell according to law,” now he loses the fief, which is noteworthy, and in black he uses such language. The vassal, however, if he is skilled, will be able to devise a fraud so that he sustains no danger of loss: for example, let him sell and transfer possession under the condition that he can sell and transfer according to law without loss of right and price. For this are the arguments in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. *Si me in vacuam*, at the end of the first response; and l. *Qui absenti*, §. 1. Or if he alienated under this condition, “if it pleases the lord”: for then he does not seem to act to the fraud of the lord. Argument in D. Qui et a quibus, s.v. *Primo responsio*. These are his words. For against this caution, indeed cavil, and fraud, there is a sufficiently open remedy by means of what has been said: because deceit and fraud ought not to aid the vassal. Indeed, feigned equity is double iniquity. Moreover, by another reason, because he did not reserve the will of the lord simply, but with a certain alternative: namely, or of another superior of his, since consent was not of the nature of the fief, although this power is proper, yet not without injury to the lord of the fief, as noted in Extravagantes de iudiciis, c. *Quum venisset*. In the Novels, therefore, because he anticipated the prejudice, he seems to despise the lord: hence they should know that they will deprive themselves of the benefit, as in c. *Ultima*, Quae fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi. But this must be observed, that when the text says “will deprive,” which is of the future tense, it seems that a sentence is required, as noted in Extravagantes de foro competenti, c. *Si diligenti*; and C. de iure omnium iudicum, l. *In criminali*. But against this stands the word “knows,” which is of the present tense. Godofredus in his Summa under the rubric “Whether the fief is lost by operation of law or by sentence,” conclusively says thus: “But I can say that it is lost by operation of law; nor does it hinder that certain guilt, and conviction, must cause loss. For interpreting the law, the judge must pronounce that it has been lost on account of the guilt. And thus it is known. Or say, that it must always be lost by sentence, unless he dies without an heir: for then it ought to come to the lord by operation of law.” These are the words of Godofredus. I have spoken more subtly, that in the case of alienation it reverts to the lord by operation of law. It finally seems to me that by any machination of alienation made with whatever fictions, the fief reverts to the lord by operation of law, as in the cited §. *Callidis*; and argument from C. de agris et censibus, l. *Quemadmodum*, lib. 11. Otherwise in the case of another fraud. It is true that the episcopal constitution declares this doubt, namely, that it is by operation of law. I hold that this episcopal constitution is valid, because it is just, and ought to be understood according to the law of fiefs; otherwise it would be unjust and not to be followed, as in Extravagantes de consuetudinibus, c. *Cum dilectum*. But it is strange if the aforementioned Bartolus holds without any right: can the lord of the fief not vindicate the thing by direct vindication of the thing, and can Bartolus not oppose the exception of the right of a third party?

I answer that the gloss is unique and singular in law, in that the possessor may oppose the emphyteutic right of a third party, and is not compelled by judgment to restore natural possession, because we do not consider what benefits the defendant, but rather what harms the plaintiff according to the law itself. For this is not properly to raise an exception, but to deny. Thus says the gloss in the Ordinary Gloss on the Digest, in the title "On Conditional Indebtedness," in the law "In the case of a debt," section "But if coins." This view is not acceptable, because it would amount to raising an exception based on the right of a third party. And this is clear from the following reasoning: the useful domain acquired by prescription is stronger than the feudal useful domain, and regarding it, no one can raise an exception except the one who has prescribed; as stated in the Code, title "On Prescriptions of Thirty Years," law "If anyone by purchase." In accordance with the principle that "what pertains to you, I hold free," as found in the Digest, title "If a slave is sold," law "The body of the place." Since there is no doubt that this question is disputable on both sides, nevertheless, because in our question it is established that the girl, to whom the fief pertained as paternal, or at least by favor of her father—which must be regarded as equivalent, as stated in the Digest, title "On the Law of Dower," law "Profectitious," in the beginning, and title "On Vulgar Substitution," law "But also if several," section "In the arrogated"—it seems certain to determine that the said girl did not lose the fief. And for the understanding of this statement, I premise the following question.

Whether a minor who sells a fief without a decree loses his right, and I say that he does not, because this sale is invalid by reason of age, so that it cannot be said to be an alienation of right or of fact: as in l. magis puto. §. j. ff. de reb. eorum. and C. de admi. tu l. lex quae tutores. and ff. de fideius. l. quum lex non obs. ff. de mino. l. si ex causa §. si in commissum. Indeed, it supports the affirmative, because fraud is not presumed. For in a woman ignorance of law is presumed, especially when she is also a minor. ff. de iur. et fac. igno. l. regula. And because she consulted those more expert, and by their advice she is not seen to have committed fraud knowingly, as noted in C. de his, quibus ut indi. l. polla. Moreover, the oath of a minor is not valid, because it is contrary to the law of fiefs, as in C. de legi. et consti. l. non dubium. and extra de fo. compe. c. si diligenti. §. fi. Moreover, because she was not informed of the custom of the fief, unless the instrument states this. arg. extra de consti. c. 1. and noted in ff. de uerbo obliga l. sciendum. per Dy. Moreover, because she sold in the same instrument with her husband. Indeed, the husband himself was the principal seller, with the name of the wife added: in which case, even with an oath, the woman is not bound, as in C. ad uelleia. l. antiquę. and noted in Spe. de obl. et sol. §. 1. Since therefore, even if it were in the matter, which is denied, nevertheless, because she was circumvented by the law of fiefs, the contract was null, she does not deserve the penalty, as in ff. quod quisque iur. in alterum statuerit. l. 1. §. haec uerba.

† A new doubt arises here, whether a custom is valid which dictates that a fief may be alienated without the lord being requested, the right of direct dominion being saved. And I say that it is so, if it is a universal custom of the churches of that diocese. The provision *extra de re iudicata*, chapter *Cum causam*, does not stand in the way, because this alienation does not partake of the alienation of the right of the church, but of the right of the fief itself. And thus it disposes not of the right of the church, but of another private person: as *extra de feudis*, chapter *Ex parte*. And this is true, provided that the church does not suffer damage therefrom, or does not lose a solid profit: for example, the *laudemium*, or some other benefit which is given by the license to alienate: as *Codex de iure emphyteutico*, law *Si*; and *Digestum de legatis tertio*, law *His verbis*, section *Alumno*. Now, a custom would not be valid by which the right of the church would be prejudiced: because it would be proximate to sacrilege. For it is quasi sacrilege to usurp the rights of churches: as *extra de foro competenti*, chapter *Conquestus*; and *extra de constitutionibus*, chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae*. And for the proving of this custom, a remission to the parties ought to be made, where perfect knowledge of the truth can be had, as *Codex ubi de crimine agi oportet*, law 2; and the arguments of those things which are read, and noted, *extra de iudicibus*, chapter *Cum deputati*. From which it is concluded that the said Bartholomew ought to be absolved, the right of direct dominion of the Church of Asti being saved. It suffices for the said Bartholomew that the useful dominion does not pertain to the agents, and especially if it pertains to his wife. For the husband in paraphernal property uses the assistance of his wife, as *Codex de pactis conventis*, law *Si*.

The last article is as follows: suppose that a fief is open to the church, but in fact it is possessed by another; whether the church can invest a certain third party in a real and effective manner, so that this third party acquires the useful domain. It seems that not, because a corporal, not an abusive, investiture is required: for example, by means of a staff or a biretta: as in c. 1, quid sit investitura, col. 10, and in C. sciendum, de consuetudine recti feudi. And the reason is that, just as direct dominions began from possession, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, in principio, so also do useful dominions, which are derived from direct ones. Argument from D. de usufructu, l. 3, § dare.

On the contrary, it seems that a fief which the church cannot recover on account of the power of the holder may be enfeoffed to another; and he will claim it by means of a useful rei vindicatio, as in Extravagantes de feudis, c. ex parte, lest the fraud of the intruder aid the intruder. Argument from D. de bonis autem iudicis possessis, l. quamvis; and what is noted in C. de surrogatione, l. subtracto, and l. si abducta. This is especially favored in favor of the church, as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. si; and as if by cession of right. For a useful rei vindicatio can be ceded even without possession, as in C. de hereditate vel actione vendita, l. si; and D. familiae erciscundae, l. plane; and what is noted in l. 1, in principio, of the great gloss, D. de edendo. For even actions which belong solely to the owner can nevertheless be ceded: as is clear in the condictio furtiva, as in D. de solutionibus, l. cum quis, § 1; and in the direct action of the Lex Aquilia, D. de contrahenda emptio, l. quod saepe, § si res.

† And for clearer understanding, it must be known that certain things have the semblance of being, yet are not beings, such as a chimera, a hypocrite, and a false prelate: as in D. 50.16.1 (Paulus). Others, however, are beings, that is, true, yet ordered, and again there is a more perfect one, as is the case with investiture, which is called abusive in comparison to perfect investiture; likewise, possession of goods for the purpose of recognizing a lawsuit is of this kind, as in D. 28.5.1 (Papinianus), § 1, in the gloss beginning "tres sunt." Certain things have in themselves both semblance and perfect essence: as when external acts signify the true habits of things, such as by tonsure a monk who has truly professed; by clerical habit a cleric; and by stigmata a knight. I therefore say that investiture, which is noted as abusive, stands in relation to full investiture as the way to the terminus, and the ship to the port, and obligation to dominion, as in C. 3.34.1 (Qui successores teneantur), col. 10. Although perhaps some would be said to adhere negatively, as the Bolognese Carotius, as noted in D. 50.17.1 (Omnis definitio), that without corporal investiture it is impossible for a vassal to pursue useful actions in his own name. And the aforementioned c. Ex parte should be understood to mean that he acts in a procuratorial capacity, as in D. 7.1.1 (Quem ad causam), in fine. And therefore, if he acts in his own person, he acts ineptly, as in C. 3.32.1 (Quae stipendia), which is perhaps more correct. And through these matters, now examined, those touched upon in the points become apparent. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When two statutes inducing a contradiction stand, to which one greater adherence should be given.
2. Whether a sentence pronounced without citing those who have an interest is valid.
3. Truth is regarded more than the solemnity of law.
body: In the name of Christ.

There are two statutes in the city of Lucca. The first provides that if any draft of a deed of any deceased notary, which was not public, or had some defect, and it could be objected that faith should not be given to such draft, and said draft can and must be examined by the vicar of the lord podestà, and the consuls of the college of judges of the city of Lucca, and four notaries of the city of Lucca to be elected by the lord vicar, and the consuls of the college of judges, each of whose notaries is at least thirty years of age. And thus, after diligent examination, it shall seem to them, or to the lord vicar, and two of the others, provided that the consent of at least one of the consuls of the judges accedes, that faith should be given to such draft: the notary having authority to reduce deeds into public form may and must take the protocols of such deceased notary from said internal draft, and reduce them into public form, and full faith shall be given to such draft thus approved, and to the instrument taken therefrom. And this statute is in the 3rd book of the statutes. Then in the 4th book of the statutes follows such a statute: and if any writing in public form is produced, which does not contain the day, or the month, faith shall not be given to it, except in the acts of the court, or of arbitrators, and public writings from the public archive, notwithstanding which faith shall be given to them. Now it happens that in a certain file of requests, or protocols, there is found a certain draft without day and month, in which file there was a preceding draft of another matter, in which the year, the day, the month, and the day were written by the hand of the same notary: after the said writing was examined by the lord vicar of the podestà of Lucca, and the consuls of the college of judges, and four notaries elected by them according to the form of the statute, and it was approved, and it was adjudged that faith should be given to said draft now and in the future, ordering it to be reduced into public form: to which judgment, and process made concerning said draft, the intestate heirs were cited, but not the poor heirs of Christ instituted. Finally, it is asked whether the instrument taken from said draft proves or not. And truly, that said instrument taken from said draft does not prove, because since said draft must be the foundation of the instrument, and said draft is void and empty due to defect, especially of the day and month, both by common law, as in Auth. ut praeponatur nomen Imperatoris § 1, and there noted, and C. de tabulis, l. generali, lib. 10, with its matter; and from the form of said statute, faith ought not to be given to said writing, because from the invalid cannot follow the valid, and because the force of the copy is from the original, as C. de edendo, Auth. si quis in aliquo documento. To the same effect is the later statute, of which I spoke. On the contrary, it seems that in deeds of a deceased notary having some defect, power was given to the aforementioned officials to approve such writing, and to impose upon it full and perpetual faith. Thus, the words say: "or had some defect, etc." Hence they speak indefinitely of any vice, and of all its substance not observed. For the indefinite is equivalent to the universal, as fully noted by Dy. in rub. de regulis iuris, lib. 6, with its common matter. Nor is it strange if, on account of the death of the notary, the statute introduces more abundant provision than for a living notary, because sudden deaths often befall men, who, if alive, could perform solemnities. Arg. C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. 3. Moreover, faith is sometimes given to a private writing, although it does not contain the day and the consul. As ff. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam, § idem quaeritur. Moreover, although this writing does not have the beginning of the day and the consul, because the draft of the file had no continuity, nor is it something concrete with this: nor is it also a Code having consequence, nor the same matter, but entirely different, and from one separated it is not argued to another, and thus we are outside. l. si quis ex argentariis, § si nuncium tabularum, ff. de edendo. Nevertheless, since it was adjudged, and no appeal was made, the judgment is held for truth, as ff. de regulis iuris, l. res iudicata.

And if it is true that the instituted heirs were not summoned, and therefore the aforementioned sentence does not prejudice them, as the Doctor teaches in the aforementioned Authentica *Si quis in aliquo*, although the ordinary Glossa states that citation is not required, C. *De re iudicata*, l. *Gesta*; yet this defect can be remedied by requesting anew that the aforementioned writing be examined as it was from the beginning, and by summoning the poor persons to all these matters, as in C. *Quoniam et quando iudex*, l. *Si ut proponis*, and C. *De accusationibus*, l. *Absente*. Hence, I am of the opinion that, by virtue of the aforementioned first statute, once these things have been done, faith should be given to the writing, the form of the aforementioned first statute being observed; so that

† truth is to be regarded more than the solemnity of law. arg. cited. §. idem, q. si it. Not against. according to the statute, because it fails in the case of the notarial writings of deceased persons, examined and approved, as they are. because it is proper that laws should agree with laws, as l. 1. C. de inoff. dotibus. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Having left a widow as usufructuary, and having instituted the poor of Christ as heirs, to whom he wished that the money exhibited from his goods sold and given to the executors, who ought to execute his testament within five years, be given, whether the five-year period begins to run from the time of the testator’s death or from the time of the wife’s death.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Ser Dinutius left his wife, Do. Francesca, as usufructuary of all his goods during her lifetime, so that whatever remains to her from her maintenance ought to be given to the poor of Christ. With this usufruct reserved, he instituted the poor of Christ as universal heirs, willing and ordering that, after the payment of the said legacies, all the goods be sold and given to the poor by certain executors appointed, to whom he assigned a term of five years for execution. It is asked, since when does the said time begin to run for the said executors: whether after the death of the said wife, or immediately upon the death of the testator? I answer: either we speak with respect to the usufruct left to the wife, and the time begins upon the wife’s death; or with respect to the sale of the ownership, and the time begins upon the testator’s death. Thus, indeed, the testator’s intention is preserved, and the usufruct is not derogated from, as in the Digest, On Usufruct, Law 1, *uxor usumfructum*. Although perhaps it was the testator’s mind that all the aforementioned things be done only after the wife’s death. But we do not have sufficient knowledge of this mind. And it is clear from the fact that the poor are instituted as pure heirs: and from the day of death the office of the said executors for pious causes begins immediately, without the inheritance being acquired in the name of the poor. For the executors themselves are heirs for the poor, as in the Code, On Bishops and Clerics, Law *si quis ad declinandam*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter instituted in a thing which the testator asserts, and which is not true, may bring an action of complaint of an undutiful will.
2. Whether a null institution, concerning which above whether it can be ratified tacitly or expressly, such as by leasing the goods of the inheritance itself, or by paying bonds in the name of another heir. nu. 3.
4. Whether prescription runs against the right of intermixture.
5. Whether an heir, who once possessed the goods after the death of the deceased, and afterwards ceased to possess, has a claim against the possessor for the vindication of the inheritance.
6. One who knows that a thing is alien cannot acquire it by usucaption.
7. Whether it can be established by statute or custom that a possessor in bad faith prescribes.
8. Prescription of thirty years to take possession does not run against a son ignorant of his father's death.
9. A negotiorum gestor, or his heir, never prescribes.
10. Prescription of thirty years runs against the vindication of the inheritance by a possessor in bad faith.
11. Whether a son possessing his father's goods is presumed to have continued possession until his death.
12. By ratifying a lease made by a third party in my name, whether it is presumed that said third party was a possessor for the times past.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A certain Lord Matthew died more than 35 years ago, having made a will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs his three male sons; he also instituted his daughter, Lady Agnes, as heir to 250 livres and for the giving of a dowry, as he stated. The said daughter claims the will is null on the grounds of her preterition, asserting that she was never dowered. The question is asked: whether, assuming that she was never dowered, she can claim the will is null, even if the time limits were to allow it, or whether she can claim it is null by way of exception, because the right to raise an exception is perpetual.

I answer: a false description added to a certain quantity does not invalidate the institution in that quantity, just as it does not invalidate a legacy; and therefore, if she was dowered, the matter is well settled; if not, the said quantity is owed to her, as established in the Code, on the false cause added to a legacy, in the law *Si non designata*; and fully noted in the Digest, on legacies, in the laws *Legaui* and *Cum scriptum*. But this is doubtful, because he did not testate with that intent, as when I bequeath to Titius 10 which I lent. For this legacy is for the purpose of raising an exception, not for bringing an action, as stated in the said law *Legaui*. Therefore, from this bequest no action is given to the daughter, as noted in the Digest, on the sale of things, in the law *Emptor*, § *Ancilla*, and in the Institutes, on legacies, § *Si debitori*.

Wherefore, since she is instituted in nothing, the complaint of preterition seems to have place, as noted in the Digest, on minors, in the law *Denique*, § *Sed utrum*. And this is true, because she was instituted in a false thing, which is not in the nature of things, just as if by right of institution a dead man, or one never born, were left to her. Hence, it is not only a false description, but one that is demonstrably false, because it is not in the nature of things, nor is it expected to be.

† However, it must be observed whether this daughter ratified or not, because if she ratified, she cannot claim it to be null, as stated in D. de inoff. test. l. filio praeterito and D. de leg. praest. l. si duo. Yet this point is still not free from scruple, because even if she ratified, the will does not become valid unless the instituted heirs petition for possession of the goods according to the will, since they cannot enter upon the inheritance due to the defect of omission, as stated in D. de lib. et posth. l. Gal. § in omnibus, as noted in C. de contr. l. posth., because the strictness of civil law opposes it, as in Inst. de exh. liber. in princ. Although the Speculum and ancient advocates, not proceeding so minutely according to the letter of the law, held that in this case the inheritance should be granted by the equity of civil law, as in the aforementioned l. si duo. Others should not do so, especially not in the case of children, so that in this case they may intervene according to civil law. And this opinion is quite equitable. But the common opinion is that the benefit of the praetor is necessary here, and the gloss confirms this in C. unde legit. l. certum. And thus, according to all, the case is one of intestacy.

† Another question follows, because the said Do. Agnes, as a person joined with Gabriel, one of her brothers, leased certain possessions formerly of their father, asserting that she did this as a procuratrix and in a procuratorial capacity. And it was established by the hand of a public notary named on a certain day and under a certain consul. Now it is asked, presupposing that from these words no delivery of the inheritance is founded, as in D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. pau., whether nevertheless by these words an intermixture is proved. And it seems that it is, because what she has clearly protested in her own voice, she cannot deny, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter.
