On the contrary, it seems that this confession was made in the absence of Gabriel; and thus it does not prove, as is fully read and noted in D. de interrogationibus actorum, l. 1., and in C. de confessionibus, l. unica, because although a confession does not require the express consent of both parties, it nevertheless requires presence and at least tacit consent. For presence, it is held that it is not directed by a messenger or by letter, as in D. de deposito, l. publica, §. si; otherwise, if a messenger or letter intervenes between absent parties, as in D. de legibus, l. aurel., §. si. And if it is said that here a negotiorum gestio was performed, which can be ratified, the adversaries will respond that the time for ratification does not avail, because thirty years have elapsed, during which the right of ratification, like other rights, is consumed, as in C. de prescriptione triginta annorum, l. sicut.

† Someone will say that the right of intermeddling is not subject to prescription, as the ordinary gloss in l. 1, C. quoniam non petuntur partes, states. And the reason is that a sui heres and a necessary heir is immediately intermingled, insofar as it concerns his own advantage. And thus, once he is an heir, he cannot cease to be so by the passage of time, as ff. de minoribus, l. et sine, §. et quod Papinianus. But goods could well be prescribed by a lawful possessor. However, this sister, concerning whom the question is asked, did not possess lawfully, because she possessed in another’s name, as she herself asserts, and her own intention is held against her, even in the absence of the adversary, in the very declaration of her intention, as ff. de negotiis gestis, l. Nescennius. But this passage, whether the right of intermeddling is subject to prescription, is doubtful. For although the first and legal intermeddling takes place instantly, and this initiatively, nevertheless completively it requires will and act: so that this second intermeddling, which is more perfect, can well be absorbed by prescription of the longest time, according to the opinion of the gloss and the commentators in l. licet, C. de iure deliberandi. Beyond the above, it is proposed that the said Agnes declared before the fisc that she would pay the taxes for the said inheritance and for the said Gabriele. And it is asked whether the said declaration harms her? And it seems that it does not, as ff. de acquirendo dominio, l. quam quisque, and C. de donationibus, l. censualis. On the contrary, it seems that it does, because a declaration made before public records cannot be corrected, as the commentators state in l. iura (alias rura), C. de omni agro deserto. Because the fisc is understood to be a public person, and its presence benefits those whose interest it is. Argument: ff. de usu, l. Caius, and ff. de magistratibus conventis, l. 1, §. exigere.

† Another case occurred: whether an heir, who once possessed the goods after the death of the deceased, and later ceased to possess them, has a claim for the recovery of the inheritance against the possessor? And it seems that he does not, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. et non tamen, §. quod si pro emptore. And according to this, the action for the recovery of the inheritance is an action for acquiring, and does not lie against a possessor who has acquired it: which is false, because it is of the nature of a real action that whenever anyone ceases to possess, he may bring an action, as in D. de iureiurando, l. sed et si possessori, in principio. Likewise we see this in the action for the recovery of a freedman, which imitates the nature of the action for the recovery of the inheritance: as in D. de fundo dotali, l. 1. The aforementioned §. quod si pro emptore does not stand in the way, because there the action for the recovery of the inheritance was altered and novated: just as the Publician action is novated by completed usucapion, and the action for the recovery of the thing lies. So the action for the recovery of the inheritance, which was available for the thing, which was not that of the deceased, but possessed by him, completed usucapion for the heir, passes from imperfect to perfect, and in the person of the heir the ownership is founded: which if the heir pursues, he does not bring the action for the recovery of the inheritance: but if he relies solely on the person of the deceased, he properly brings it, because the right of the heir is not made worse by the acquisition of ownership.

† Finally, it must be known that today, both by canon law and civil law—which does not disdain to imitate the sacred canons—one who has knowledge of the thing belonging to another from the very beginning, such that he never had good faith, does not prescribe even a mere exception: because the right to sin cannot be prescribed, as stated in Extra, de praescriptionibus, c. Quoniam omne; and in c. Malefidei, de regulis iuris, lib. 6; and note the gloss and Cynus in l. 1, § 1, C. de usucapione transformatione, whatever Bartolus says in ff. de usucapione, l. Sequitur, § Si viam. For he who knows that he is bound does not prescribe, as in c. Peccatum, de regulis iuris, lib. 6.

And this is the truth, unless the municipal law or custom expressly introduced this to the detriment of the negligent party; for it is not novel that one loses his right on account of negligence, as in l. non, n., ff. qui ex cau. ma., and l. pupillus, ff. quae in frau. credi. Or say that either prescription runs against a right in the process of being acquired, and then the good faith of the possessor is not required, as in C. de iure delibe., l. licet; or against a right already acquired, and the same applies if prescription runs for the strengthening of the dominion of the prescriber, as in the aforementioned § si viam, because the dominion itself serves as the cause. But if someone has neither any cause nor good faith, then he does not prescribe. And thus l. si quis emptionis, C. de praescri. 30. annorum, is corrected by canon law, for the Pope can do this by reason of sin, as argued in extra de iudic., c. noluit. Others say that each right must be observed in its own forum, because lay judges swear to observe the laws, not the canons, from which they have no jurisdiction; nor can they transgress the mandates of princes or statutes, from which they have no jurisdiction; and this can well be defended in municipal statutes, because they have among their effects the force of a pact, as noted in C. de dec., l. de decurionum, in ru.

† Another doubt follows, whether the period prescribed in § 30 of the *lex* runs for a son ignorant of his father’s death in order to accept the inheritance, and whether it does so, because that time is continuous. You should say that it does not run, because the case is covered by *C.* de captivis postliminio revertentibus, *l.* nec nos coniuncta; *l.* 1, in fine, *C.* de annalium exceptione. Moreover, the year for deliberation, which is preparatory to the right of acceptance, does not run; therefore, neither does the right of acceptance run, as in *C.* de iure deliberandi, *l.* cum antiquioribus. And even assuming that the time for acceptance were running, nevertheless the time for claiming possession of the estate, which is beneficial, would not run. In which case, one who accepts the inheritance before the praetor is deemed to be claiming possession of the estate; thus, conversely, as in *C.* de iure deliberandi, *l.* puberem, and *D.* de bonorum possessionibus, *l.* cum quidam, which law is very notable for this purpose.

† It is also doubted whether one who possesses as a manager of affairs, or his heir, prescribes at any time. And say that he does not, because he does not have true possession, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. etiam, § si quis absentis; and C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur.

† It is doubted whether prescription runs for thirty years against the action for the recovery of an inheritance by a possessor in bad faith. And it seems that it does, because it is a mixed action, and consequently personal, and against a personal action prescription runs by mere silence, as noted by Bartolus in the said § si viam. Hence also the inheritance of a debtor lying fallow prescribes, if not interrupted, and yet the inheritance does not have good faith, because it has none. But say that, as regards the corporeal assets of the inheritance, it is an action in rem, not in personam, as C. de petitione hereditatis, l. haereditatis. It is asked, 11

Whether a son, who possessed the goods after the death of his father, is presumed to have continued possession until the death of the son himself after the deceased. And say, as is noted in l. 1, C. de servis fugitivis, where the glossa says that unless interruption is proved, it is presumed that he continued possession for ten years, namely, civilly. The same is said by the aforementioned Doctor Dy. in the cited chapter Sine possessione, and it is proven in ff. de usucapione, l. Furtum, § Fundi, even if another held it corporally in the meantime, unknown to the son. Note this. C. de duodecim probationibus, l. Siue possideat.

† Finally, it is asked whether, if today you lease some thing in my name, and I ratify it, you are presumed to have possessed it retroactively in my name. And it must be said that no, because from a contingent matter, which relates to various outcomes, no inference follows, as in C. unde legitimi, l. non habet. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether prescription runs against a son ignorant of his father’s death for the purpose of entering upon or interpleading.
2. Prescription does not run against the right to claim possession of the estate.
3. Whether one who says before the judge “I enter” is understood to acknowledge possession of the estate.
4. Prescription is impeded by lease.
5. A petition for inheritance, once arisen, may be alleged against the possessor even after possession has subsequently been lost.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked whether the prescription of the longest time for the right to enter upon or to intermingle in the inheritance runs against a son dwelling far from his father and therefore ignorant of his father’s death. The affirmative is true, because the time for entering upon the inheritance is continuous, as noted in C. de iure deliberandi, l. licet. I state the contrary, that as long as he is ignorant of his father’s death and consequently believes him to be alive, as noted in l. 2, § si dubitetur, ff. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat, the prescription does not run, unless perhaps the ignorance were supine, because he is hindered by an impediment of law and of fact; and this is established by the law C. de captivis et postliminio revertentibus, l. nec nos. And it supports this what is noted in ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. illud.

Secondly, it is asked: assuming that there is a prescription against the ignorant person regarding the right to enter upon an inheritance, whether there is a prescription regarding the right to claim possession of the estate; and it must be said that there is not, because the time for accepting possession of the estate is beneficial, as stated in l. 2, ff. quis ordo in bonorum possessione seruetur.

Thirdly, it is asked, assuming that he cannot enter upon the inheritance but must petition for possession of the goods, whether, if he says before the judge that he enters upon it, he is understood to accept the possession of the goods? And I say that he is, by the law *Suum haeredem*, Codex, *De eo iure deliberandi*, and Digest, *De bonorum possessione*, law *Cum quidam*.

Fourthly, it is asked, because the sister, within the last thirty years, leased certain possessions in the name of her brother, which were paternal assets and ought to be common property by intestate succession; and the brother has now ratified them: whether this recognition, made by such a lease, interrupts the prescription of thirty years. And I say without doubt that it does, by the law *Male agitur* and the law *Cum notissimi*, on Prescription for thirty years. And it is the same as if she had done this by the mandate of her brother, because ratification, before the prescription is completed, is deemed to operate retroactively, as in the last paragraph of the law *Si*, § *Si*, in the Digest, *De rebus rationibus habendis*.

Fifthly, it is asked whether a petition for inheritance, once arising and having finally obtained possession, and then lost, can be brought against the possessor? And it is alleged that Spezzano says that it cannot; but the truth is that it can: because real actions can be brought as often as possession ceases, as in *l. sed et si possessori*, § 1, D. de iureiurando. This is also clear, because the *iudicium familiae herciscundae* has the same nature as the petition for inheritance, as in D. familiae herciscundae, *l. haeredes*, § *quod si cum tempore*. It is not excluded by former possession, because possession is not a mode of extinguishing a real action, but of strengthening it, as in *l. 1*, D. familiae herciscundae. It accords with what is said in D. de evictionibus, *l. si mancipium*, § 1. Therefore, the sister, notwithstanding the aforementioned allegation of prescription, ought to have her share, and the male his share; nor would it be equitable that the sister, or her heir, should exclude the absent brother on this pretext, especially since she knew, and ought to have known, that the brother was owner of his share of the paternal inheritance, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, *l. in suis*, and *l. 2*, D. de condictione furtiva. Moreover, the gloss sometimes says that a certain quasi-possession descends continuously to his heir, as in *l. cum miles*, in principio, D. quibus ex causis maiores. And not in D. de acquisitione possessionis, *l. cum haeredes*. This quasi-possession is a fictitious possession; nevertheless, the gloss in the said *l. cum miles* does not approve this. It may also be added that it is not believed that the said sister intended to possess the whole for herself; therefore she did not prescribe the brother’s portion, because she did not hold it with that intent, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, *l. qui iure familiaritatis*, and D. pro socio, *l. merito*. I therefore conclude that, notwithstanding the objection of prescription, what belongs to the brother shall be restored to the brother, and what belonged to the sister shall remain to her heirs. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A false procurator renders a release void and is punished for the crime of stellionatus; however, at times he is not punished for any crime when no damage ensues to anyone from his contract. And when his contract is void by the law itself, no action for fraud is granted.
2. When falsity harms no one, when is it punished?
3. Whether a son who assigns his father’s rights, when he cannot do so, is bound.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A son of the family released his father’s debtor, although he was not his father’s procurator: it is certain that the release was void by operation of law. For either he released him in his own name, and the release does not bind, as C. de cap. et postlim. reuoc. l. nec nos praeterit; or he released him in the procuratorial name of his father, although he was not procurator: and the release did not bind to the prejudice of the father, as C. de pactis l. filius. But if, knowing that he was not procurator, he falsely asserted that he was procurator, or on this occasion he was enriched in some way, and then he is to be punished on account of fraud, as ff. de furtis l. falsus procurator in princ. and C. de furtis l. falsus. And some say that he is liable for theft, and as a thief of that sum which he receives. Others say that even if he is not liable as a thief, he would be liable for the crime of stellionatus, because he is acting in fraud, and the title of the crime fails, as l. 2 ff. de pign. actio. Or he released him for a lucrative cause: or for one cause, and then he is in no way punished criminally, because he harms no one, because it is not understood to be a crime where no damage is inflicted on anyone, as noted in C. de falsis l. nec exemplum and l. damus. Although he does not act according to good morals, nevertheless there is no law that punishes him: and we blush to speak without a law, as in Auth. de triente et semisse §. consideremus.

† Now follows another point. A certain person formally released his debtor, and after this release, claiming to be a creditor, he assigned his rights to Sempronius. Sempronius sues him, alleging that he lied and made a false statement by assigning the rights as though he were a creditor, when in fact he was not. The question is whether he should be punished. The answer is the same as above. For if the assignee was deceived and gave something for the assignment, the assignor ought to be punished; otherwise not, because the assignee suffered no damage from a lucrative cause, as stated in the Digest, *De edicto*, edict, *Ad res donatas*.

† The third point concerns a son who assigned his father’s rights, although he could not do so; whether he is bound to the assignee, because he asserted that he could assign them. I answer: no; because the assignee ought not to have believed him, unless he showed a mandate, as in D. de deposito (16,3), l. si quis inficiatus; and D. de regulis iuris (50,17), l. qui cum alio. He knew, and ought to have known, that such an assignment was invalid, as in D. de solutionibus (46,3), l. qui hominem, § si nullo; and fraud is not imputed to one who knows. Hence, in this case, no crime is committed: neither the crime of falsity, nor the crime of stellionatus; nor is there any law that says otherwise. To this effect: C. de evictionibus (7,63), l. si fundum sciens. Moreover, fraud is not said to exist unless damage occurs or could occur. And therefore it must be considered whether the said assignment was gratuitous or not, as above, in other cases, as in l. 1, D. de statu liberorum (40,4); and D. de edicto edilitio (21,1), l. cum autem, § excipitur. That point is true, namely, that a false procurator, whose act has been verified by the ratification of the principal, is not considered to have committed true fraud, but rather to have contracted boldly in the hope of the principal’s ratification, as in D. de furtis (47,2), l. vendideto, § si titius. And it is also to be noted that fraud committed in a contract that can be purged by an action arising from that contract does not fall under the crime of stellionatus; because a civil action for fraud is not available, as is read and noted in D. de infamibus (3,2), l. furti, § si; and D. quod metus causa (4,2), l. si cum exceptione, § in causis; and l. eleganter, in principio, D. de dolo (4,3). And if the contract is null by law itself, an action for fraud is not given, nor an accusation of stellionatus, if the matter remained within the bounds of words: as appears there. And see concerning this matter what follows immediately below. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The crime of stellionatus (fraudulent deception) applies wherever falsehood intervenes in a contract.
2. Not every illicit act is punished, but only that which the law has established as a delict.
body: In the name of Christ.

† For the sake of clarity, I premise that there are certain offenses in which a title of the offense is found, i.e., a proper name of the offense, such as theft, forgery, and the like. There are other offenses which do not have a title of the offense: such as the crime of stellionatus, as in D. 48.10 (de crimine stellionatus), l. 3, in principio. That crime of stellionatus is of such a nature that it is not brought except on account of fraud (dolus): and a criminal accusation is available in a subsidiary capacity, just as an action for fraud (actio de dolo) is available in a subsidiary capacity. And from this follows such a conclusion, that wherever fraud can be purged by an action arising from contract, or quasi-contract, it is not purged by an action for fraud civilly, as in l. eleganter, in principio, D. 4.3 (de dolo), nor by an accusation of stellionatus criminally, if the fraud lies within the bounds of contracting. Unless one of two things intervenes: namely, perjury, as in D. 48.10 (de crimine stellionatus), l. de periurio; or the thing is delivered in a wrongful manner, with fraud committed in the delivery itself, for example in a pledge corporally delivered under the guise of false or falsified material, as in D. 13.7 (de pignoris actione), l. 1, and l. tutor, § 1, and l. si quis in pignore. There are other cases as well, even if the thing is not delivered, provided that someone is induced by fraud to enter into a contract detrimental to himself, and he would not otherwise have contracted, as in the aforementioned l. si quis in pignore, § si; or there it speaks of a pledge which does not require delivery, because a hypothec is contracted by consent alone, in which, if one deceives the other, the crime of stellionatus has place. In the case of a thing sold to two persons, the crime of forgery (falsum) would have place, as in D. 48.10 (de falso), qui duobus. And this is special in the contract of sale and purchase on account of the abundance of the contract of good faith; and outside these two contracts, namely sale and purchase, it does not apply. Likewise, from the contract of pledge, which is most frequent, we do not have certain accusations established for fraud giving rise to the contract or occurring within it, because the species of obligation of contract and of delict are different, as in Inst. 3.13, § sequens, and D. 2.14 (de pactis), l. si unus, § pactus ne peteret. And it would be very absurd to say that wherever any falsehood intervenes in a contract, one could be accused of the crime of stellionatus. Moreover, where the contract is null by law itself, so that no obligation arises from it by law itself, neither from the principal contract nor from the accessory, the action for fraud has no place, nor the accusation of stellionatus, nor any other remedy, if matters remain within the bounds of the contract, as in D. 21.1 (de edilitio edicto), l. ad res donatas. From which it is inferred, considering all arguments for and against, that according to what is proposed along with the matter on which action is taken, it is not suitable nor directed toward committing a crime, but rather toward contracting nullly; nor should fraud be understood without the effect of damage, as in l. 1, D. 4.4 (de statuliberis). And here there was nothing that was directed toward the damage of another, nor was there any damage that ensued, as is proposed; therefore, no criminal penalty can be imposed. Nor is it new that certain things are done dishonestly, and yet do not have punishment.

† Because not every illicit act is punished, but only that which the law has established as a delict, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De religiosis et sumptibus funerum*, in the law *At si quis*, § *Divus autem Marcus*, where there is a singular text that pertains to the matter; as is also read in the Digest, *De his qui non infamantur*, in the law *Furti*, § *Contraria*; and in the Proemium of the Institutes, in the beginning; and in the Institutes, *De poena temere litigantium*, § *Si*; and in the Digest, *De mandatis*, in the law *Fideiussor*, § *In omnibus*. This does not constitute an obstacle, because there the case demands it. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a fief can be alienated to closer relatives without the consent of the lord, and if it has been alienated, and the closer relative remained silent for a year and did not revoke it, whether he lost the right that he had. And number 2.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The evidence of the facts is set forth, as follows: Titius, having sons, and having Sempronius as his brother, Caius as his paternal uncle, and Damian as his full blood relative, alienated an ancient fief not for a price, but in another manner, to Seius, a more remote agnate, without the consent of the nearer relatives, who were indeed entirely absent. Caius, the paternal uncle of Titius, revoked that alienation within a year, protesting that he did not wish to consent to it, and that it ought to be entirely null; moreover, within the year he sought investiture, offering fidelity by oath to the lord for the thing, as promised, which had been alienated. Sempronius, the brother of Titius, remained silent for a year, although public voice and fame concerning the alienation made had continuously spread. When that year was completed, Caius died, leaving behind his sons and the agnates mentioned above. It is asked to which of them such a fief, even though it is a proavital fief, pertains, and this question arises: to whom does a fief devolve, when such a fief has been alienated by a vassal having sons to a more remote agnate, even while the nearer agnate is alive? Unless, knowing of it, he remained silent for a year, as stated in the Usus Feudorum, Title "If there is a dispute about a fief between the lord and the vassal," Chapter "Titius having sons," where it is expressly stated.

Therefore, it seems to follow that, since Sempronius, the brother, remained silent for the completed year and long beyond, and did not seek investiture, and thus by his own fault deprived himself of the fief devolved, that it devolved in order to Caius, the paternal uncle, who was then the nearer agnate; hence it is that he revoked that alienation, which was forbidden by law. A rule is given that the alienation of a fief is prohibited. The rule fails when the vassal sells to the nearest agnate, who is to succeed to the feudal thing, as in Chapter 1, § "But also the thing," of the Title "By whom investiture is made and by whom it is received." Furthermore, under the rule falls the provision that a fief cannot be sold to a more remote agnate even with the consent of the lord, unless the nearer agnate consents, as in Chapter 1, Title "Of alienation by a father." From these it is inferred that the alienation in question, unless perhaps it was made with the consent or knowledge of the lord, was made contrary to law; so that the prior agnate can revoke the thing alienated, insofar as it was in fact alienated, and by a useful vindication of the thing, or in the said chapters.

It now remains to be seen whether the prior agnate, having remained silent for a year from the time he knew that the revocation was not made, has lost the right which he had. And it must be said that he has, as in c. Titius, in the end, if there is a dispute about a fief. Here it must be observed that that period of a year seems to be fixed when the agnate in whom the alienation was made was the next in order after the one seeking revocation, for this is established in favor of the recipient, arg. C. de fideicommissis, l. Voluntas. But if the one in whom the alienation was made was an outsider, or a most remote agnate, whom several others preceded in degree, as is the case in our question—for I understand by “outsider” everyone who cannot hold the fief—then the gloss which is in the said §. Titius holds that the one who is next in order before all others is not excluded by the tacit passage of one year, because it would be unjust to exclude the prior agnate and admit the subsequent one to revoke. And the gloss says that this is done by the sentence, and by the passage of the year, and by the agnation of him who possesses; but if the possessor were an outsider altogether, to whom no right can be acquired by the passage of a year in the retention of the fief, then the prior agnate can revoke even after a year has elapsed; because this prescription of a year is introduced solely in favor of the possessor. Hence, if this favor cannot protect him, the annual prescription does not run against the next agnate. Briefly, therefore, I say also according to the mind of the gloss that if a vassal alienated to an agnate whom two perhaps precede in successive order, the right of revocation is first given to the next agnate; and he is excluded by the lapse of another year from the time he knew, so that after the second year has elapsed, possession will be confirmed to the latter, who is third in the order of agnates, and so on with the rest, as in ff. de successionibus edicto, l. 1, §. Largius, and §. Sed videndum. For the reason that these times endure is the favor of the possessing agnate, to whom the fief is confirmed by the negligence of those preceding him in order; for if the alienation were to an outsider, the third would have the right of revocation. Therefore, since the alienation was made to him, he has a stronger right of retention. Arg. ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Frater a fratre, in principio; ff. de superficiebus, l. 1, §. Quod ait; and ff. de regulis iuris, l. Inuitus, §. Cui damus. The successor right therefore has place in this time of the passing year, and this is the truth, for which reason, according to what they propose, he who is second in order, the prior being excluded, could seek investiture; otherwise, if he had sought it before the time of exclusion, for then the petition would not be valid, nor the agnation, as in C. qui ad bona possessionis possunt, l. Si; and ff. de bonis liberorum, l. Si filius; C. de causis, l. Nec nos; and de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Qui superstiti. Whether a feudatory can enfeoff another.

† Moreover, if the vassal, instead of alienating, has enfeoffed another under a similar law, then, as I have said, it might be doubted whether this subinfeudation was lawful or not. For a vassal can acquire another vassal from his fief, and because the first does not cease entirely to be a vassal, according to the authorities cited in the Digest, *ad Trebellianum*, and the law *Ex asse*, namely, the subinfeudation is valid, as can be said in the chapter *Imperiale*, § *Illud quoque*, *De prohibitione feudorum alienationis*, by Federicus. It can be said that if the vassal who enfeoffed another died with an heir, the agnate cannot revoke. For the son succeeded to the right of the father, namely, to the paternal vassalage, as in chapter 1, *An filius vel agnatus*, column 10. And whenever some remnants of the first degree remain, the subsequent degree is rejected, if those remnants have some effect, as in the law *Si*, Digest, *De successionibus per edictum*, and the law *Si duo patroni*, in the beginning, Digest, *De iureiurando*. Someone might say, what remnants can these be, since when the vassal alienates, all his right passes to the successor, when by way of fief, as noted in the Digest, *Communi dividundo*, law *Si ut certo*, § *Si duobus vehiculum*. Indeed, certain solutions are great remnants, because the vassal of my vassal is not my vassal with regard to personal obligation, but is bound immediately to his own enfeoffor for those things which come into the oath of fidelity. And the gloss on the said § *Si duobus* must be understood with regard to natural possession and common law rights. Hence it is concluded that he ceases to be a vassal who acquired another vassal, as in the Institutes, *De hereditatibus*, law *Tale*, § *Si*. But if the vassal had died without an heir, the fief would be open to the nearest agnate, in which case the right of succession from degree to degree would have place; but if there were no agnates, it would revert to the lord by strict law, because when the right of the grantor is resolved, the right of the grantee is resolved, as in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Lex vectigalis*, and in chapter 1, § *Rursus*, *Quibus modis feudum amittitur*. But by benign equity it has been received that then the second vassal, by recognizing the lord, must retain the fief, as in chapter 1, § *Si autem*, *Qualiter poterat olim feudum alienari*, and in the same title, § *Porro*. But this statement must be understood where there are no agnates, or there are, but they are excluded. But where there are nearer agnates, they are preferred to the more remote subinfeudated party, because an agnate cannot prejudice an agnate, as in the said chapter 1, *De alienatione feudorum patrimonialium*. And if one consents and another dissents, the whole accrues to the dissenting party, as in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Quoties*, and in the Digest, *De legatis secundis*, law *Cum pater*, § *Liberis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who is the judge in a case of usury.
2. How one is said to be a manifest usurer, and how his testament is to be annulled or pronounced valid.
body:
In the name of Christ. The facts, concerning which counsel is requested, are as follows. Titius made a will, in which he instituted certain universal heirs. After the death of the testator, collateral relatives coming in intestacy brought certain witnesses before the court for the eternal memory of the case, in order to prove that the said testator was a public and manifest usurer; these witnesses testified that the said testator had lent a certain sum of money at interest to certain persons. Finally, they filed a libel against the instituted heirs, claiming the intestate inheritance, and produced certain witnesses to prove that the testator was a public and manifest usurer up to the time of his death; these witnesses testified that they had seen the testator lend money at interest to certain persons. Against the articles produced, a declinatory exception of incompetent judge was raised, because the cognizance of usury cases belongs to the ecclesiastical judge. From the foregoing, it is asked, and first, whether the declinatory exception raised against the articles produced to prove that the testator was a public and manifest usurer should be upheld or not. Second, since it has not been proven that the said testator, during his lifetime, held a prepared altar [i.e., was a cleric in major orders], nor that he confessed before his judge, nor that he declared himself a usurer in his will, nor that a sentence was passed against him regarding usurious wickedness, nor that he was convicted during his lifetime of having practiced usury, but rather it has been proven after his death, against the instituted heirs, that during his lifetime he lent money at interest to certain persons: whether from these proofs the will should be annulled, or declared null as the will of a manifest usurer?

The cause of usury is sometimes so ecclesiastical that the secular judge cannot cognize it, but the ecclesiastical judge must cognize it, as when there is doubt about the quality of the person, with one party calling him a usurer and he denying it; for in this doubt the bishop cognizes, as noted in *Extra*, *De fidei instrumentis*, c. *Licet in suscepto*, and in *11 q. 1*. In summary, sometimes it is not a merely ecclesiastical cause, as when it is disputed whether someone is a usurer, because it is established that he is a usurer, if the matter concerns the quantity of usury extorted; then the secular judge can cognize. To this effect is what is noted in c. *Dispendiosam*, *De iudiciis*, in the Clementines. Nor is it found that civil law is corrected by canons in this regard, as in *Digestum*, *De conditione indebiti*, l. *Si non fortem*, in the beginning, according to Bartolus, who thus notes in l. *Titia*, *Digestum*, *De solutione matrimonii*. Sometimes the matter is not about the quality of a living person, but after death it is said that his will is invalid because it was made by a manifest usurer. And then the secular judge can principally cognize the invalidity of the will, and incidentally can cognize whether he was a manifest usurer or not; because the cause of usury is not a spiritual cause, as in *Codex*, *De iudiciis*, l. *Quotiens*, nor is it a cause of the validity of a will, since there is no doubt that the lay judge can cognize the validity and invalidity of a will, and pronounce the will to be null or valid, nor is it found by law that the secular judge cannot incidentally cognize usury, although he cannot principally do so, except according to the distinction aforementioned. Moreover, no decretal is found that reserves this incidental question to the bishop; therefore, one must adhere to the civil rule transmitted, as noted in c. *Quod clericus*, *Extra*, *De fidei instrumentis*, and in c. *Dispendiosam*, *De iudiciis*, in the Clementines. And this concludes the first point.

However, it would be more cautious, and thus I would advise beforehand, that the article of usury be remitted to the bishop for the removal of doubt. And thus I have often seen it observed.

I come to the second point, and I premise that there are three things, one of which is not the other. One is being a usurer by not appearing, whether he is manifest or not manifest; another is appearing, that he is not manifest; and the third is appearing, that he is manifest. For this, namely that he is manifest, is a certain adjectival quality, which has in itself the infamy of the act and the apparent nature of the delict. And to prove that he is manifest, it is required that he be publicly caught in the sin before the people, or before a great part of men. As in C. de accusationibus, l. ea quidem, and there by Cynus; and in l. 2, ff. de furtis, by Bartolus; and the argument in ff. de adulteriis, l. quod ait, §. si. Or that, by preceding proofs and infamy, the bishop has ordered him to be avoided as a usurer. As in Extra, de usuris, c. quia in omnibus; and c. cum tu; and in the same title, c. 1 and 2, lib. 6. Or that he himself has confessed in court, and thus publicly, or perhaps in a testament before a priest or notary, who are public persons, or in the presence of a multitude of men: according to the notes by Innocentius in Extra, de cohabe. cler. et mulier., c. tua; and in the Summa, that which is manifest is that which neither can be excused nor concealed, but has come to public knowledge. It is established what is noted in c. statuimus, de officio delegati, in 6, by Innocentius and others. Since, therefore, the weight of the invalidity of the testament rests on the quality of being manifest, and this quality is not proven, in doubt the testament shall stand, as is read and noted in C. de iure et facto igno., l. si post divisionem. It is rightly to be pronounced in favor of the testament and its force. And to this effect is what I fully said concerning the quality to be proven, in the said l. Titia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How, in what manner, when, and for what causes a donation may be revoked.
2. An agreement must not be one-sided.
3. A pact by which future fraud is remitted is not valid.
4. Whether a donation divided among several persons, so as not to exceed the sum requiring insinuation, is valid.
5. Whether one entering religion may give away his goods to defraud the religion he has entered.
6. The hope of future succession of living brothers cannot be donated.
7. A penalty appended in an award may be claimed.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is well known that donations may be revoked on account of ingratitude. Among the greatest causes of ingratitude is the failure to observe agreements, as stated in C. de revocanda donatione, l. si; and in c. 1, § item si id, propter quod, which was the first cause of loss of benefit, col. 10, where the text says: “Nor is there any more just cause for depriving someone of a benefit than if he refuses to do that for which it was given.” I understand this to apply whether the agreement is contained in the same instrument or in another. If it is in the first instrument, made immediately, and the first instrument itself contains the agreements in proper form: because things done immediately are deemed to be included, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. lecta, § dicebam. But what creates doubt in the instrument of agreements is that the donees promised to keep and observe the said agreements under penalty of damages, expenses, and interest, the donation always remaining valid. And therefore it does not seem that the donation can be revoked on this ground. It is not an obstacle that we have ff. de transactionibus, l. qui fidem, because there that clause was added for the stipulator; here it is for the promisor. However, it is necessary that the donee choose one of two options: because by virtue of this agreement it is converted to his election. That is, either he must fulfill the promises, or restore what was donated, as in C. de pactis, l. cum proponas; C. de transactionibus, l. sive apud acta; ff. locatio conductio, l. quaero, § inter locatorem. Even if an oath had been added: because an oath adds strength to the convention to be observed on both sides.

† Moreover, the agreement should not be defective, so that one party is bound to observe it and the other is not, because that which is defective is not just, as is stated in D. locato conducto, l. si socius, pro filia; and D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iulianus, § si quis a pupillo; and l. 1, C. de reputatis, quae fiunt in iudicio; D. de acceptilatione, l. si. Another doubt arises concerning other causes of ingratitude, namely whether a donation can be revoked on account of the other causes noted in the law, or any one of them. And here too there is no doubt that it can be revoked, which is established in the provisions regarding donations. But what if it has been stipulated that it cannot be revoked on account of some ingratitude, as is the case in our matter: here there are differing opinions. For some say that it cannot be revoked; others say that, on the contrary, it can, as is noted in Speculum, de donationibus, verso quid si actum est in donatione ne propter ingratitudinem. I say that either ingratitude is committed by wrongdoing with malicious intent, as is proven in our case, because they observe nothing of their promises and compromises, but rather deceive and mock: and it can be revoked, because

† A pact by which future fraud is remitted is not valid, as stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Si unus*, section *Illud Mela*; or ingratitude consists in something other than fraud and delict. And then one must adhere to the statement, as in the Digest, *De edilitio edicto*, law *Quaeritur*, section *Si venditor*; to this effect, in the Extravagant, *De donationibus*, chapter *Si*. For, since they inflict a heavy loss, they cannot be excused from the penalty of ingratitude with fraud.

Thirdly, it is doubted whether a donation exceeding five hundred gold coins is valid, if it has been arranged that it is not one donation, but several: namely, as many as can individually take the lawful sum. And on this point there are likewise opinions, as Speusippus states in the cited title on donations, in the section "What if someone gives." For some say that this precaution is valid. Others say that it is not valid. This second opinion is pleasing to Jacobus de Arena, so that the law is not circumvented, C. de don. l. sancimus. And this is the truth, because this is a kind of distributive agreement of a single sum, and it constitutes fraud against the law, whether done distributively or comprehensively. It is supported by D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fundi partem; and D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si sterilis, §. si tibi. For it is fraud if the donation is made individually at the same time, just as if it were made as a whole, because all taken together exceed the limit. Argument from that which is not, D. de legibus tertio, l. nomen, §. filio, since the donation itself in principle is universal and integral in its entirety, and under one principal structure of words.

Fourthly, it is doubted whether he who is bound to enter religion may donate all his goods to the prejudice of the religion he is about to enter. And it must be said that the religious order may revoke the donation of goods as a son for support, unless he expressly renounces it. See C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Si quando, §. Finis; and C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Auth. Si qua mulier. It is otherwise in a donation on account of a future cause: for that is an innominate contract and does not contain a merely gratuitous cause. See ff. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. Non usque adeo.

† It is further asked whether one can make a donation of the future succession of living brothers. And it must be said that no, as in C. de cap. l. nec nos, unless the brothers themselves consent and persist in their consent until death, as in C. de pac. l. si.

† Furthermore, it is asked, if compliance has not been rendered with the contents of the arbitral award regarding the quantity to be provided, whether the penalty can be claimed. And it seems that it cannot, because it is added to the quantity; hence it seems added in fraud of usury, as in C. de usuris, l. cum allegas. The contrary is true: because this penalty is added on account of contempt. And because we are not in the context of a loan for consumption (mutuum), and because where there is another presumption, the presumption of usurious fraud ceases. And briefly, it is an example from ff. de verb. oblig., l. 5, § si sororem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What kind of partnership is said to be contracted between brothers living together, and what division should be made among them of gifts and windfalls acquired by any one of them during the period of cohabitation.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: there are three brothers, A., B., and C., residing and living together in the same house, at one table for bread and wine, having all their goods common and undivided, and conducting all their affairs jointly. Now it happens that one of the said brothers, namely A., wishing to engage in trade and having the intent to trade, seeing that his own resources and those of his brothers were not sufficient or adequate for this purpose, because they lacked movable property, approached a certain friend of his and requested a loan of money from him. This friend, from whom he requested the loan, said, “Friend, I am willing to lend you the money that you ask of me on loan; but I wish to be secured for the said money to be granted.” Upon hearing this, A. returned to his brothers, namely B. and C., and narrated the aforementioned matters to them. Both brothers responded to their brother A. that they did not wish in any way to encumber their goods. Having returned to his friend, A. accepted the loan of money and secured the said friend with his own goods only, encumbering to the friend solely his own goods. It was agreed between these contracting parties that half of the profit that would accrue from the money lent to the said A. would belong to A., and the other half would belong to the friend who lent the money. Having done this, A. traded with this money, to the extent that he had borrowed on loan, and from that money he gained a certain quantity of coins as profit, namely one thousand. Having done this, A., the same debtor, and liable for the whole, approached his friend, from whom he had received the loan of money, and said to him, “Friend, it is true that I gained one thousand in profit from the money that you lent me; and therefore I wish to discharge myself towards you and give you what is owed, namely the principal of your money, and also half of the profit, namely one thousand.” The friend said, “I am content.” And so it was done, because he returned to the friend the entire principal and half of the profit, namely one thousand; of which one thousand, five hundred fell to each of them. Now A., the same brother, still traded with those which fell to him as his share, namely five hundred, and still gained very much in profit. And thus, by trading and proceeding in this manner from one profit to another, this man gained a great quantity of money in profit. Now the brothers wish to come to a division, A., B., and C. From the aforementioned, it is asked: whether, in the division of these brothers, that which A., the same brother, gained in profit from the aforementioned money, ought to be included; and if it ought to be included, whether the whole ought to be included, or a part.

† To understand this question, it must be known that sometimes brothers acquire something while their father is alive, and this is not our subject matter, but pertains to l. cum oportet, C. de bonis, quae libe. Certain things are acquired by brothers after the father’s death, and then four cases must be distinguished: for sometimes an express partnership is contracted between them, and then we adhere to the agreement, as in ff. pro socio, l. coiri, and l. 2 and 3, and Inst. pro socio, per totum, and ff. de pac., l. 1, §. conuentionis. Sometimes a tacit partnership is contracted: because a partnership is contracted even by tacit consent, which tacit consent is presumed from acts consonant with partnership: such as living together, sharing profits and gains, and bearing losses in common: and they are capable of contracting a partnership, and then there is no doubt that they are partners both actively and passively, because partners share actions and liabilities with each other, unless they arise from delict, as in ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. damna, and ff. si cer. pe., l. si socius. Sometimes it is certain that they are not partners, as when they live separately and conduct business separately, and then there is no doubt that they owe nothing to each other, as in ff. pro socio, l. itaque. The fourth case is when it is doubtful whether they are partners or not, as when they live together and dine together: for from the quality of affection, partnership is presumed or not presumed: but in doubt, since partnership is a matter of fact and intent, it is not presumed from mere cohabitation, or common habitation, or common paternal or maternal inheritance, because it is not proven that this exists, which easily and frequently is found to be present, as in ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. si fratres, with the saving that if one of the brothers buys something with common money, or with common property, it is presumed that, as far as this is concerned, they are partners: and it must be shared with the partners, as noted by Spe. in tit. de iudiciis, §. generalia. If therefore he does not seek from the common fund but seeks for himself through his own industry, just as conversely if he obligates himself, he alone is bound, as in ff. de mune. et hono., l. et qui originem, §. fi, and C. de decurionibus, l. licet in diuisa, li. 10. For it is not presumed that a brother, who alone profits through his own industry, wishes to squander his own and make a gift to his brothers, who contribute nothing to him, unless perhaps it were something small, and fraternal charity induced it, as in ff. de dona. inter uir. et uxo., l. si seruus communis. Nevertheless, this would be a gift, not a partnership. And therefore, returning to our question, I say that in the division among these brothers, that which A. gained in excess, which same brother acquired through his own labor and his own money, or acquired, in no way comes to be shared, unless it were proven that a partnership was contracted between them tacitly or expressly. For if things acquired during the father’s life are not shared, as in C. de colla., l. fi, ergo, much less are things acquired after the father’s death, when those acquiring are sui iuris, unless they were acquired in the common name, and this were proven, as in ff. de admi. tuto., l. titium uel meuium, §. altero, and l. qui negociationem in princi., and C. communia utriusque iudicii, l. si patruus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Once the time limit within which the appeal case was to be processed has elapsed, judgment shall not be rendered on the merits, but it shall simply be declared that the appeal has been abandoned, since the delay was not attributable to the judge.
body: In the name of Christ.

† In the decree of the illustrious Lord Marquis of Ferrara, it is provided. Furthermore, that the said civil questions be terminated by our said vicars and judges, or any one of them, by definitive sentence within six months from the day the petition was presented; whereas causes of appeal are to be decided and cognized in civil matters within three months from the day the petition was presented before the judge of appeals, counting from that day: but in criminal matters, etc. It is asked whether, after the lapse of the said three months, the appeal in the cause of appeal is considered deserted? And it must be said without doubt that it is so, because all terms for appeals are decisive and fatal, and therefore, once they have elapsed, the appeal is deserted, provided that the delay did not occur due to the judge, as is read and noted in D. de dolo, l. arbitrio, §. pen. Since in the decree of the Lord Marquis no mention is made of the restoration of the appeal, these three months succeed not only in place of the year, but also in place of the two years prescribed by the common law; nor is valid the protestation made after the appeal has been deserted; because the protestation must precede, not follow, as in C. de his, qui per metum iudicis non appellarunt, l. si, and C. de tempore appellationum, l. si, §. illud, there, in summa ope, etc. Nor ought the judge to pronounce whether the appeal or judgment was well or ill made, but only that the appeal is deserted, as in C. quo et quando iudex, l. si praeses quasi. From these things it appears that witnesses can no longer be received when the litigation is already dead, as in l. cum lite mortua, D. iudicium solui. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How expenses incurred by someone standing in communion, whether in study or otherwise, are to be compensated to him in the division.
body: In the Name of Christ.

Five questions are raised. First, concerning expenses consumed on a grandson through a son, whether they should be imputed to the father’s portion? And it must be said that they should not, if the expenses were consumed during the lifetime of the grandfather; but those which were consumed during the lifetime of the father must be imputed to the father’s portion, and consequently to the portion of the grandson himself succeeding in the person of the father: because while the grandfather was alive, the burden pertained to the grandfather, as in D. de collatione bonorum, l. dedit dotem. Upon the death of the grandfather, the burden returns to the father of the grandsons, as in D. familiae herciscundae, l. si maritus. And therefore the uncles are not bound to contribute to this burden, just as they are not bound to the burden of maintenance. The second doubt is concerning expenses made, but not consumed, such as expenses for books which still exist. And it must be said that the scholar, who is in study, does not acquire these books, because they are not like castrense peculium, but must be shared with the coheirs, even if they were strangers, as in D. familiae herciscundae, l. quae pater. The third doubt is concerning expenses made after the death of the grandfather and the father: and it must be said that, insofar as the scholar’s portion suffices, they must be made from his part, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. si, and D. familiae herciscundae, l. si filia, §. idem scribit, and §. se, and C. de decurionibus, l. licet indiuisa, lib. 10. The fourth doubt is concerning expenses for the doctorate after the death of the grandfather and the father, and for provisions. And here a distinction must be made: for modest expenses for provisions are presumed to have been made from the common fund, because this is the custom among those who live together at one bread and one wine; but other large expenses must be imputed to the one who assumes the doctorate. Argument to this distinction: D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si seruus communis. The fifth doubt is concerning expenses made in taking a wife: and in this the same must be said as in expenses for the doctorate, or for military service, as is read and noted in D. de muneribus et honoribus, l. e qui originem, §. si. And according to the foregoing, it must be understood what is customarily noted in l. 1, §. sed an id, quod, D. de collatione bonorum, and C. familiae herciscundae, l. filiae cuius, and by Speculum in title de iudiciis, fourth part, §. sequitur uidere, ver. quid si alter ex cohæredibus cum multis, ver. sequentib. What I said about the uncle is not to the questions asked, because here we inquire what is the law among the grandsons themselves. And it must be said that while the father was alive, consumed expenses are not computed against the said student, because they were disbursed from the father’s goods while he was alive, as I proved above regarding the grandfather. The last doubt is concerning the profits which this doctor made after the doctorate. And this is like castrense peculium, as in l. cum oportet. And of these there is no doubt that he is not bound to share with his brothers, neither by any law nor by written equity: but if, out of true charity and purse equity, he wished to render an equivalent to his uncles, he would be highly praiseworthy. The same if his uncles wished similarly to bear burdens in common: nevertheless, there is no obligation from either side to this effect, as in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. si fratres, and C. communi utriusque iudicii, l. si patruus, and D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium, et Mævium, §. altero. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testament made among children prevails over a prior one containing clauses stating that it cannot be revoked, even if the second testament does not mention said clauses.
2. Friars Preachers may serve as witnesses to what is bequeathed to the Order.
3. An oath does not prevent the revocation of a testament.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. A certain person made a will, in which he instituted the Friars Preachers, with the said Friars Preachers present as witnesses, along with certain others; and he instituted his daughter to a certain portion under a non-potestative condition, deliberately adding clauses that the will be irrevocable, and appending an oath not to revoke it; and if it should happen to be revoked, that the revocation would not be valid; and if the revocation were valid, that it would be a donation inter vivos; and if it were not valid as a donation, he requested the heirs to be instituted in a second will that they would restore the inheritance to the said Friars Preachers. Finally, the said testator made a second will, which he decreed to be the last, without adding other derogatory words; in which he instituted his said daughter as universal heir; and to the said Friars he left a certain estate. Now a matter of dispute has arisen between the said Friars Preachers and the daughter: because the Friars Preachers want the whole of the said inheritance by right of institution, or at least by right of donation, or at least by right of fideicommissum; but the daughter says that the first will, with all its safeguards, and with all its donations and fideicommissum, has been revoked; and they say that the second will prevails entirely; and she objects to the said Friars, first their incapacity, secondly she objects that a will cannot be made in such a way that it cannot be revoked; and just as a will is revoked, so too is the donation substituted in its place. Also, that the said fideicommissum left by those instituted in the second will is not owed as being attached indecently in default of the revocation of the first.

† The question is what is the law. And it seems that the statement according to the second testament is in no way valid on account of the derogatory clause appended in the first testament, which removes the testator’s intention from the second testament, as in l. si quis in principio testamenti, together with its common legal authorities. To the contrary is the truth: for that testament prevails which is last confirmed, as in C. de test. l. omnium. But the second testament is last confirmed by words and by intention. I say by words, because the testator expressed it. Also by intention, because among children indications of will suffice, so much so that what does not avail among strangers often avails among children, as in l. si, C. fam. her.; ff. de contrata. l. si duobus, §. si prius; and l. hac consultissima, in §. ex imperfecto; and §. si quis autem; and in Auth. de testa. imperfe. in prin.; and in §. nos omnia igitur clara. Moreover, the first testament was null by the law itself, considering the quality of the condition appended, as in l. filius, ff. de condi. insti.; and C. de instit. et substi. l. si pater. Moreover, whoever wishes to institute God and disinherit his son, let him seek someone other than Augustine. l. si quis ad declinandam, in the glossa similiter modo, C. de epis. et cle. Thus the matter easily returned to its natural state, and especially paternal piety. Moreover, these points are proved by l. stipulatio hoc modo, de ver. obl. Moreover, in place of a derogatory clause, those words suffice by which he wished it to be the last testament, as noted in c. 1, de consti., lib. 6, in the novella. And therefore, all things considered, I think the daughter upholds justice, notwithstanding the precautions of the said brothers. And I presuppose that the brothers are capable on account of their privilege, which is called mare magnum.
† I further presuppose that brothers may serve as witnesses in matters left to the order or convent, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on witnesses, chapter Cum nuncius.

† Nevertheless, I state, according to the true opinion, that an oath does not prevent the revocation of a will, although according to some one would be perjurious, which I do not admit: because the oath is not valid. Furthermore, I state that the said donation is not valid as being contrary to good morals, although D. says the contrary through the said l. stipulatio hoc modo, and there through Bartholus. That which, however, makes me doubt more is the fideicommissum left by the heirs of the second will: because it appears that the testator codicilled to the second will; but to this I respond that the testator of this codicillation is deemed to have repented, since he did not add derogatory words to this codicillary clause, for, by providing in the second will for his brothers regarding something, he appears to have receded from the promise concerning the whole. arg. ff. de usuris, l. in fideicommissi, §. cum Pollidius. From all of which it is concluded, saving the substance of the truth, that the said brothers, the Preachers, are fostering an unjust lawsuit both in law and against all natural equity, as l. cum ratio, ff. de bonis damnatorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the stipulation of double damages is incurred, and in what manner, and what those words "promised to defend and to free from encumbrances" import. And see on this matter above in this volume in the third counsel.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† In a certain instrument it is thus contained. Titius, the seller, promised to Seius, the buyer, to defend and to clear the title of the said possession, both in court and out of court, whether it should be evicted or not, under the penalty of double the agreed price. Now, a hypothecary action was brought, and the seller did not defend, so that judgment was rendered against the buyer; but after the judgment was given, he cleared the title to the possession, so that it remained with the buyer. The action for double the price is brought. The question is asked: what is the law? I answer that those words, “to defend” and “to clear the title,” are infinitives of mode. And therefore it suffices to defend and to clear the title before the thing is corporally evicted; nor is the penalty of double the price incurred; because since the said penalty takes the place of the price, and the price ought not to be restored to the buyer, because good faith does not permit that the buyer recover the price and possess the thing, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. bona fides, rightly and without doubt he is repelled from the petition for the penalty. Moreover, the penalty itself is for the simple formal price agreed upon, which cannot be recovered, as in the aforementioned l. bona fides, where the case is expressly stated; and to this reason, rather than to what might be answered, one should adhere. Furthermore, he acts in bad faith who possesses the thing and claims the penalty, as in D. de exceptionibus doli, l. apud Celsum, §. Labeo. Also, this is well supported by D. de pignoribus, l. si fundus, §. si plures; D. de legatis 1, l. si fundum per fideicommissum; D. de exceptionibus doli, l. si fideiussor evictionis; D. de evictionibus, l. habere sicere, where it appears that to have is permitted, therefore the thing is not evicted; moreover, it is not said to be undefended or uncleared of title, since the seller paid the judgment. Argument from D. de procuratoribus, l. sed hæc, §. defendere; and what is noted in the same title, l. non solum, §. si status. But also because the interest ceases, hence the action ceases to be available. Moreover, it is in vain to labor over the penalty when the matter is settled, as in l. 2, post principium, D. si quis cautionem. And I add this to the confirmation of the opinion given by me, which is the third in order, which was and is the truth itself and equity itself. Moreover, the stipulation would not be incurred for the expenses of the litigation, except for those expenses themselves, or for double the expenses, as is read and noted in D. de procuratoribus, l. qui absentem. Also, the aforementioned is supported by l. 1, C. si servus extero. Moreover, since the buyer ratifies the release and is bound to hold it as ratified, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Pomponius, rightly he cannot allege the contrary, directly or indirectly, as in l. 1, C. de furtis, and D. de solutionibus, l. qui hominem, §. si. Moreover, the stipulation of double is not incurred while the litigation is pending, D. de rei venditione. Certainly, the words of the contract are referred to the disposition of the law, D. de usuris, l. stipulatus. Moreover, one ought not to have both the price and the thing, D. de conditione sine causa, l. si fullo. Moreover, it is the same for someone to be absolved by payment and for someone to be absolved by the judgment of a judge, as noted in D. de exceptione rei iudicatæ, si quis cum totum, §. plane, and C. ad legem Aquiliam, l. ex morte. But if the buyer had been absolved by judgment, undoubtedly he could not claim double, because he claims in vain what he already has within himself, as in C. de re iudicata, l. 1. Nor even that which is added in the name of penalty, as happens in the stipulation of double.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Adoption is prohibited when one's own children exist; and if an adopted son is instituted as heir, the institution is voided.
2. A statute making mention of sons or brothers is not extended to adopted sons or brothers.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen.

† The statute of the city provides that a married and dowered woman shall not take a share with her brothers, nor with the sons of her brothers, in the paternal or maternal inheritance. Now, a certain man wishes to adopt a son for himself and to institute him as heir. It is asked whether this father can institute this son as sole heir, in such a way that the legitimate and natural married daughter cannot come to the succession of her father’s goods, and also exclude her from her legitime by virtue of the said statute.

I premise, for clarity, that one who has a legitimate and natural son, and especially if he has several children, is not permitted to arrogate an outsider, lest the hope of succession of those whom he begat in lawful marriage be diminished, a hope which each child ought to confirm for himself by obeying his father, as stated in the Digest, De adoptionibus, law Nec enim, section Praeterea, unless he did this by special authority of the prince, or by special commission of the latter.

Secondly, I premise that if such an arrogated person were instituted heir in fact as an arrogated or adopted son, the institution would be void by operation of law. The text is unique in the law: Codex, De fideicommissis, law Eam quam. But if he were not instituted as a son, but as an entirely outsider, the institution would be valid, saving the legitime of the children. For we can also institute our friends as heirs in this manner, provided we do not deprive our sons of their legitime, as stated in the Authentica, De triennio et semisse, section 1.

Thirdly, I premise that where a statute makes mention of sons or brothers, it is never understood to refer to adopted ones. For adopted sons are fictitious sons; and fiction has no place in statutes, as is noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, § haec verba. Moreover, if even natural sons are not comprehended, then all the more so are legitimate sons not included, as C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter; § si, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. fideicommissum; D. de legatis 2, l. Si ita quis, § is cui; C. de his qui vetantur ab imperio, l. si; C. de natura liberorum, l. legem Anastasii. And from these points the solution to the questions raised becomes clear: first, because adoption is prohibited; second, because if he were instituted as an adopted son, the institution would be voided; third, because the statute is not understood to apply to these fictitious and not true sons. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a libel alternatively conceived is valid.
2. Whether creditors who do not appear at the time of the proclamations, if anyone wishes to be satisfied, lose their right.
3. Whether excussion is necessary, when it is established that there are no assets.
4. Whether the second creditor can challenge the sale made by the first creditor.
5. Whether the name of the debtor comes into the mortgage of the goods: and whether, and when, it can be extinguished.
6. The understanding of l. omnes and l. bene a Zenone, C. de quadriennii pręscriptione.
7. Whether an obligation can be made to a procurator: and whether a verbal offer is sufficient. nume. 8.
body: In the Name of Christ, Amen. In the dispute arising between the learned Catherine de Fulgeriis, widow of the late Marcello, son of the late learned Gasparo de Brachifortis, or her lord procurator, on the one part, and Philip and Frederick, brothers of Brachifortis, on the other part, committed to the noble and prudent men Hector Angoxola, Corrado Letericorno, and William de Fornicibus, as three good men by the Lord Podesta of Piacenza, to whom the commission was made by the Magnificent Lord, the learned Galeazzo Visconti, Imperial Vicar General, the following doubts are raised. On which the learned men Paulus de Arzonibus and Ioannes de Carnago, doctors of laws, have given their counsel. And under the first doubt is whether the libel produced on behalf of the said Lady Catherine proceeds, or not: and without the allegations of the said lord consultants, they say and advise that

The petition proceeds, because the possessor of the pledge, by doing one of two things alternatively, namely by releasing the pledges or by paying the debt, obtains absolution, according to *l. si fundus*, § *in vendicatione*, D. de pignoribus. And the payment of money is not in the obligation, but in the performance, or in the faculty of paying, according to *l. Paulus*, in fine, D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca soluitur. And such a judgment is rendered, in which someone is condemned to pay what is in the obligation, or to do what is in the faculty of paying, as in *l. miles*, § 1, D. de re iudicata. Therefore, in the same way it can be demanded thus alternatively. To this it contributes that the text is noted in *c. ex literis*, de pignoribus, and that Bartolus notes it in the said § *in vendicatione*.

The second doubt is whether the said proceeding is valid notwithstanding the proceeding and lawsuit that ought to be pending between the said parties before Messer Bartholomew de Placentinis and Rizzardo de Villanis. And briefly, the said consultants say and advise that the said proceeding made before the said Lord Podestà of Piacenza and the said three good men is valid, notwithstanding the said exception of pending litigation: because it does not appear that any lawsuit is pending between the said parties before the said Messers Bartolomew and Rizzardo which would cause prejudice to this lawsuit, since nothing appears except a certain commission made by the aforementioned Magnificent Lord to the aforementioned lords, his counselors, containing that the aforementioned Lord committed to the said lords Bartholomew and Rizzardo, etc., the cognizance of the question arising between Lord Brancha de Fulgosii, grandfather and administrator of Catherine, wife of the late Marcello de Brachifortis, on one part, and Filippo and Federico, brothers de Brachifortis, on the other part, and a certain peremptory citation made by the said lords to hear the sentence. So that from these things nothing appears of the pendency of any lawsuit which would cause prejudice to the present lawsuit.

The third doubt is whether the said Lady Catherine has lost her right in the said goods, which are the subject of the dispute: because it appears that she remitted her right of pledge, inasmuch as she did not appear, as is said, at the time of the proclamations made by order of the Lord of the Podestà of Piacenza, in the execution of the letters of the late Magnificent Lord Galeazzo, Viscount, etc., according to the law *Si eo tempore*, Codex, *De remissione pignoris*. And certainly the said consultants say that she has not. And the reason is this: because in our case the law *Si eo tempore* does not apply. For there, at the instance of subsequent creditors wishing to sell the pledge, a general proclamation is made, so that if there were any creditors, they might appear, so that they might be paid. Hence there, rightly, lest the buyer be defrauded, creditors who do not appear are deemed to have remitted their right of pledge. But in our case, the proclamation was made solely for the purpose of making an estimation, so that the goods might be taken in satisfaction of the debt of the chamber of the aforementioned late Magnificent Lord Galeazzo, for which debt the aforementioned Lord wished to be preferred to others and to impose silence on other creditors regarding what is given in satisfaction. Thus, the law *Si eo tempore* does not apply. Moreover, a procurator of the said Lady Catherine was present at the certain act of estimation or giving in satisfaction. Moreover, the effect of the said letters of the aforementioned late Magnificent Lord ceases, as will be said below. Therefore, this doubt rightly ceases.

The fourth doubt is whether the aforementioned lady should prevail notwithstanding the exception of excussion: and regarding this doubt, the said consultants state and advise that if it were true that it were established that there are no other goods of the aforementioned late Marsilius upon which excussion may be made by the said lady, she should prevail notwithstanding the said exception, according to the number, by Bartolus in the law *decen.*, D. de verb. oblig. and the law *fi.*, D. si cert. pet. And granted that it were not established, they say that since the said brothers of Brachifortis would remain merely creditors, as will be declared below, the second creditor, namely the said lady Catherine, offering money to the said brothers, secures the pledge for herself; and the said brothers are bound to release the pledge and also to cede their rights to her; and consequently the said brothers cannot avail themselves of the exception of excussion.

The fifth doubt is whether the brothers themselves are secure, because the older creditor sells: according to l. 1, C. si antiquior creditor. And briefly, the said consultants say concerning this doubt that l. 1, the aforementioned, does not apply in our case, because there the creditor sells by virtue of the power granted to him by the debtor. Hence the thing appears to have left the debtor’s assets up to the time of the grant. Hence the aforementioned second creditor has no right of offer, because by legal fiction it does not fall within his obligation. But in our present case it is not so. For the aforementioned late lord, although he was a creditor of the late lord Gasparis de Brachifortis, and had a tacit hypothec on his goods, and ought to be preferred to the dowry of the said lady, according to l. 1, C. de privilegio fisci, nevertheless he does not have an agreement to sell from the debtor. And if, as the fisc, he could have done so, the solemnities of law set forth in l. 1, C. de fide instru. and iure astae fiscalis, lib. 10, ought to have been observed. And if it were said that the solemnities were supplied by the letters of the aforementioned late Magnificent lord, the said consultants say that the effect of the said letters is removed by the Magnificent lord, the Count, in the concession made to the lord Podestà of Placentia, in whose execution the process of the present question was made, as will be said below. The sixth doubt is whether the said lady, having the goods of the said Marsilius bound, can come to the said goods by virtue of the dowry of the mother of the said late Marsilius. And certainly the said consultants say that she cannot, the reason being that

† Although the name of the debtor falls under the obligation of goods, as stated in the law *Nomen*, Codex, *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*, nevertheless the name of the debtor may be extinguished to the prejudice of the creditor, before it has been paid by the creditor; yet the name is bound, as in the aforementioned law *Nomen*. Now, in our case, Marsilius, before he made the dowry for his wife, was the heir of his father, and consequently the right of the mother’s dowry was extinguished by confession; therefore, it does not fall under the obligation of the wife’s dowry.

† The seventh doubt is whether the aforementioned brothers of Brachifortis are secure by virtue of the sale and the *datio in solutum* made to them by the letters of the aforementioned late Magnificent Lord, according to the laws *Omnes* and *Bene a Zenone* in the Code on the four-year prescription. And the aforementioned consultants rightly state that on this account the said brothers are secure. The reason is this: although it is presupposed that the aforementioned Magnificent Lord could exercise or enjoy the right of the Empire or the right of the fisc, and thus that the laws *Omnes* and *Bene a Zenone* in the Code on the four-year prescription would apply to his alienations, nevertheless in our case the disposition of those laws does not apply. This is because, in our case, the aforementioned Magnificent Lord, by his letters, then commanded his power in Piacenza, in effect, to have the goods of the said Lord Gaspar appraised and given in *datio in solutum* to the said brothers of Brachifortis, etc., as is more fully contained in the letters themselves.
