Thus, from an inspection of those letters, and of those appraisals and *dationes in solutum*, it appears evident that the brothers of Brachifortis knew that those goods belonged to the aforementioned late Lord Gaspar and the aforementioned late Marsilius; and they did not acquire them as belonging to the aforementioned Lords, but rather wished to have them given in *datio in solutum* as goods of the aforementioned Brachifortis, in satisfaction of the debt which they had paid to the chamber of the aforementioned Magnificent Lord. And they wished to obtain a benefit from the aforementioned Lord, namely that they would be preferred to other creditors, and that silence would be imposed upon other creditors, and so it truly happened. Now, however, by the letters of the aforementioned Magnificent Lord, the Count, justice is to be done notwithstanding the letters of the aforementioned late Magnificent Lord, his father, nor his own; it must be seen whether the effect written by the virtue of those letters should remain firm. And certainly the aforementioned consultants state that every effect of the benefit of those letters has been removed, a benefit which the said brothers would not have had if the letters had been circumvented; for words must be understood with effect, as in the law *Si*, § *Dotem*, in the Digest under the title *Ne quis eum qui in ius vocatus non ierit*. Since therefore the Lord Count states that justice is to be done notwithstanding the letters, he even wishes to remove the effect of the letters insofar as they confer a benefit to one and take away the right of another. Thus, therefore, the said Lady Catherine, although a later creditor, can offer her credit to the said brothers and revoke the pledges; since the brothers, with the effect of the said letters circumvented, remain merely creditors; because the solemnities which must be observed by common law in *dationes in solutum* were not observed. And so the aforementioned consultants conclude that in our case the disposition of the said laws *Omnes* and *Bene a Zenone* does not apply.

† The eighth doubt is whether the offer made by the said lady, or by the procurator of the opposing party, suffices? And briefly, the consultants state that in court an offer may validly be made by a procurator ad litem, according to what is contained in the law *Si reus*, D. de procuratoribus; although payment cannot be made to the procurator ad litem, according to the law *Hoc iure*, D. de solutionibus.

† But because it does not appear that any offer was made on behalf of the said lady other than a verbal one, which is not sufficient in law, they say that the said commissioners should make an absolution, absolving the said brothers of Brachifortis, and those who appeared in court, from the bill served upon them on behalf of the said lady, and from the contents thereof. And this, because the said brothers have a right of retention of the said goods for the said quantity paid to the chamber of the aforementioned late Magnificent Lord for the debt of the said late Lord Gaspar of Brachifortis, and for improvements, and according to the contents of the said letters: and this in the case where only the said verbal offer appears. But if a real offer of the said quantity of the said debt appears, and in the case where the said brothers of Brachifortis refuse to receive the aforementioned money offered, and a consignation and deposit of the said quantity of the said debt is made on behalf of the said lady, then the said commissioners should condemn the said brothers of Brachifortis, and any person who appeared in court on their behalf, to release the said goods to the said procurator of the said lady, and to the said lady, after the said lady has first made payment, or is ready with effect to make payment, to the said brothers of the improvements made in the said goods. And this they say, the said consultants, for this reason, namely that in this case the said improvements have not been proven: hence it cannot be imputed to the aforementioned lady if she did not offer the quantity of the improvements, nor should the said brothers lose the improvements, since in the bill she offered to pay, and beyond that the said brothers never had need to make other defenses, since no real offer was made to them, either to pay, or to make the aforementioned payment to the said lady of the quantity of the dowry, and of the donation ante nuptias of the said lady: because although for the donation ante nuptias the said lady does not have the husband’s goods bound, unless perhaps by the form of the statute of Piacenza, nevertheless from the promise made in the dowry instrument this can be gathered, that she has an obligation. And thus I say, and I advise that it should be done by the said commissioners in each of the aforementioned cases, as is contained above: always reserving the better counsel. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When and how a judge may be challenged: and what effect the challenge itself produces, and no. 2.
3. If a delegated judge claims the benefit over which the dispute was pending before him, whether he may thereafter adjudicate upon it, and nos. 5 and 6.
4. If a judge is instituted as heir by one of the parties, he ceases to be a judge.
7. Solemn holidays do not impede the running of peremptory days.
body: In the name of Christ. While the lawsuit and question were being debated before the Lord Vicar of the Bishop of Piacenza between Lord William de la Silva, a cleric of Saint Odo in Piacenza, on one side, on account of a certain canonry and prebend, which the said William de la Silva claimed pertained to him by virtue of a certain exchange made by him of the aforementioned canonry with a certain Francischino de Macagnis, a cleric of Cremona, to whom the said canonry and prebend had belonged by canonical collation and provision made to him by apostolic executors; and Lord William de Zenariis, on the other side, claiming that the said canonry and prebend pertained to him by virtue of a certain operation duly made by him of the said canonry and prebend, sentence was passed by the said Lord Vicar against the said William de la Silva. From this sentence the said Lord William appealed to the Apostolic See, requesting that apostolic letters be granted to him. These not having been obtained, nor a term having been given to him by the said Lord Vicar to receive them, and notwithstanding the appeal, the said Lord William de Zenariis, in whose favor the sentence had been passed, took possession of the said canonry and prebend and received the fruits by mandate of the said Lord Vicar. These things having been done, at the petition of the said Lord William de la Silva, the cause of the said appeal was committed by the Apostolic See to Lord Uberto Deterano, Prepositus of the major church of Piacenza, of which commission there is proof by an apostolic rescript. The said Lord Uberto, as apostolic delegate, proceeded in the case at the instance of the said Lord William de la Silva, many exceptions being opposed, and especially those of suspicion and recusal against the said Uberto by the said Lord William Zenariis, the adversary. While these exceptions were pending and the litigation ongoing, the said Lord William Zenariis died. After whose death the said Lord delegate, a canon of the said church, opted for the said canonry and prebend insofar as they were due to him by right, which the said Florentinus de Saluis, a canon of Piacenza, older and prior in opting than the said Lord Uberto, the delegate, as above, also similarly opted for. Notwithstanding these things, the said Lord delegate cited by edict affixed on the doors of the church whomever he thought had an interest, until a certain term, to appear on account of the aforementioned delegation and commission in the case pending, or which had been pending, between the said Lord William de la Silva and the said Lord William Zenariis, the above-mentioned parties. Within which term certain persons appeared, asserting themselves to be the procurators of the said Lord Florentius, claiming that they did not have the said Lord Prepositus before the chapter of the major church of Piacenza, alleging the option made by the said Lord F. Upon this being done, the said Lord Prepositus, being in the university of Pavia, subdelegated at the instance of the said Lord William to two subdelegates, and to each one in solidum, the case pending between the said Lord William and Lord Florentius, which he asserted had been committed to him, and made no mention in the said subdelegation of the said Lord William Zenariis. It is asked,

Whether the aforementioned Lord Ubertus, either personally or through another, could intervene in the aforementioned case. And in effect, it is stated that he could not. Three arguments are alleged on behalf of the said Lord Florentius: first, the recusal made by the said William Zenarius, during which time the delegate cannot proceed, according to what is found and noted in chapter *Iudex*, *De officio delegati*, Book 6; second, that by the option made by the said delegate, he cannot be judge in the aforementioned case; third, because the said Lord Ubertus, assuming that he were a true delegate, did not subdelegate the case committed to him, but rather the case pending between the said William de la Silva and the said Florentius. To the matter serves chapter 2, *Ut lite pendente*, Book 6, which can be induced for and against. Whether a litigious benefice can be opted for or not while the litigation is pending, the response follows.

† To the first point, it is answered that the aforementioned recusal does not constitute an obstacle, because it was not properly made nor pursued: for the bill of recusal ought to have been offered in the presence of the person recused, and arbitrators ought to have been requested, and confidants ought to have been given in writing by the recuser, and the recuser himself ought to have offered, in the presence of the person recused, to prove the causes of suspicion alleged before non-lay arbitrators chosen from the confidants of those parties, which was by no means done. And thus it appears that a tacit renunciation was made of the recusal itself, especially given the failure of the recuser himself, as is noted by Johannes Andreae, Hostiensis, Archbishop, in the chapter *Legitima*, On Appeals, Book 6.

† To the second point, it is answered that the option made by the said delegate d. Vber. does not prejudice the matter: because another, who is older, is alleged to have proceeded, namely the said d. F., and because the said option was made under such a condition, which, failing, is not valid nor binding. See the argument from the law *Sub conditione*, in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*; and the law *Multum*, in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*. But neither do conditional betrothals induce public standing in justice, as in chapter 1, *De sponsalibus*, Book 6. In support of this, the major gloss at the end of chapter *Cum plures*, *De officio delegati*, in the same book. But those alleging the said option in this manner seem to contradict themselves, because either the option of the said delegate was valid, and the option of the said Lord Florentine, upon which they rely, is not valid: because two options are not valid with respect to the same prebend; or the option of the said Lord delegate was not valid. And how then can it be said that he lost jurisdiction by an option that was not valid? Nor does the law *Iulianus*, the second law, in the Digest, *De iudicibus*, stand in the way.

† Where it is said that if a judge is instituted heir by one of the parties, he ceases to be a judge, because no one is judge in his own case, this must be understood where the judge was instituted heir and accepted the inheritance in that matter in which he was judge; which appears from the reason of the law joined with the gloss, because he would have been judge of his own thing, as is said to you. And thus, notwithstanding the title that no one is judge in his own cause, he could no longer be judge. But in our case, the said lord delegate is not said, nor can he be said, to be judge of his own thing, because he does not pursue the option made by him, nor is any question made of it, since it is not valid; because if any question were made of it, it seems that the said law, moreover, the said Urban, acting properly, sent an edict at the instance of the said lord William, by which it sufficiently appears that he receded from the aforesaid option, and not being able to attend to the delegation, because he is occupied with study, he subdelegated the said cause, as above. And thus the second objection does not stand. The third objection does not stand, because from the form of the primary letters, namely of his delegation, and the authority of the secondary letters, namely of the subdelegation, the subdelegates, or either of them, have power to proceed, according to what is noted by Innocentius in the chapter Quia, title 5, extra de iudiciis, where there is a good text on this point, and in the chapter Ex parte, extra de arbitris. And also because the said lord Florentine, by the aforesaid comparison, in the case in which his asserted procurators are true procurators as to the litigation, seems to be substituted in the place of the said lord William Zenarius, by the Clementina 1, § Si vero alter moriatur, Ut lite pendente. And thus, by virtue of the said delegation, the said lord delegate, by himself or by his subdelegate, had power to proceed and to terminate between the said lords William de la Silva and William Zenarius, and anyone substituted for him in the aforesaid litigation.

† From all the aforementioned options, exchanges, petitions, recusations, delegations, and subdelegations, the question arises as to what the law appears to be: namely, whether, since it did not rest with the said Lord William de la Silva that his appeal was not concluded within the term for prosecuting it during the last Easter holidays, it may still be concluded notwithstanding the lapse of one or two years; and it seems that it may, according to the glossators in the chapter *Ex ratione*, and there by Innocentius, in the Extravagantes, *De appellationibus*. Furthermore, it should be considered whether any documents produced by the said Lord William de la Silva are prejudicial to him; and it seems that they are not in any way.

Without repeating the very prudently made allegations, but proceeding briefly to the points at issue, I premise that the jurisdiction of the delegated judge was not invalidated by the recusal of a suspect judge proposed in court, but was suspended until the cause of suspicion is resolved, either by the sentence of a person or by the sentence of the law. For if the recusal is circumscribed, the recused judge remains judge with effect. For if the jurisdiction were immediately invalidated upon the proposal of the cause of suspicion, there would be no need to examine the cause of suspicion. This is expressly clear in the chapter *Cum speciali*, in the verse *Causa*, in the Extravagantes, *De appellationibus*.

Since the matter now stands thus, that when Lord William Zenarius, who filed the libel of recusal, closed the final day, and the recusal of the judge is in personam and not in rem, the question of suspicion was immediately circumscribed, because the said recuser ceased to have an interest, as stated in the Digest, *De suspectis tutoribus*, law *Post finitam*. And from this it is concluded that, since the said recusal is laid to rest, the said subdelegation held good, because it was made by one who had resumed jurisdiction by operation of law.

† Furthermore, it is no objection that this delegate opted in his own favor, because one cannot administer justice in one’s own case. But if two third parties were litigating against each other, he could properly administer justice between them. See the chapter *Suborta*, § final, *de re iudicata*; and what is noted, *Digestum*, *de rei venditione*, law *Inter officium*; and *Institutes*, *de testamentis*, § *Legatariis*.

Moreover, by a more evident reason, because this option was abusive, and no right was acquired therefrom, and by an act that is null in law, jurisdiction is not terminated: since it is an external act, and does not pertain to the termination of jurisdiction; and jurisdiction itself is a necessary office. For this is the rule, that the useful is not vitiated by the useless. And that which is null does not take away that which is valid in law: especially when it contains a necessary right, as in the rule *utile per inutile non vitiatur*; and *Institutes*, *quibus modis testamentum infirmetur*, § *Posteriori*; and *Digestum*, *de legatis tertio*, law *Si iure*.

Furthermore, because an option which one has not pursued is considered as not done, as in *Digestum*, *de fideiussoribus*, law *Si stipulatus es opus*, where is the better text to be found in law. It is certain that the rescript endures, even if one of the litigants dies, regarding the benefit of the pending litigation, whether as suspect or substituted, he is to be remitted to the same judge, as in the said Clementina, § *Si vero*; and argument from *Digestum*, *de inofficioso testamento*, law *Filius non impeditur*; and *Extra*, *de iudicibus*, chapter *Quia*, 5; and *Digestum*, *de his qui notati sunt infamia*, law *Servus*. For the Florentine lord was substituted by law in a certain order, as he claims successively. This is proved by that law *Nota*, *Digestum*, *de re iudicata*, law *Ex contractu*. And yet, as I said, he was not substituted in the article of suspicion: because it is personal.

And thus I conclude briefly, that the subdelegation was valid and held. It remains to see regarding another point, whether the appeal is deserted. But in this point, let the acts speak: and this article is determined by law 2, at the end, § *Illud*, *Codex*, *de tempore appellationum*. See in the Authenticum *Ei qui*, in the same title.

It must be said, therefore, that solemn holidays do not interrupt the running of peremptory time periods, but a pending question of recusal does impede it, so that it does not run as long as it remains pending, as stated in the Digest, *De minoribus*, in the law *Intra utile tempus*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. We strictly prohibit the present letters from being sent by quaestuarii. What this entails.
2. Who are called quaestuarii.
3. Messengers truly sent are by no means called quaestuarii.
4. Those who purchase, not merely hire, quaestum from the Minor Friars, and likewise the friars themselves who sell or lease it to them, are to be considered quaestuarii.
5. To render the office of piety gratuitously and to manage one’s own affairs have a considerable distinction between them.
6. From the description in the law ff. de publicanis, l. quante, it is evident how great is the audacity, temerity, and avarice of the publicani.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: in a certain privilege granted by the Lord Pope for the repair and preservation of the fabric of the church and the house of Saint Francis of Assisi, and for the support of the brothers residing there, etc., the following is inserted:

† clause, but we more strictly forbid the present letters to be sent by questors, declaring them void if otherwise done. It is now asked whether brothers thus sent by their prelates, or to execute what is contained in the privilege, should directly be called questors. Questors
† those are called who bring profit to themselves, as in D. 17.2.32.1, *sed si adijciatur*, *nuntii*.

However, those who are truly sent and are suitable for pious works of almsgiving are not said to be consigned as questors; otherwise, how would the matter be expedited, unless perhaps some receiver were appointed by the local diocesan, who ought to receive and consign the alms: namely, a faithful and upright person approved by the authority of that diocesan, specifically the diocesan in whose diocese the alms are collected. But this is superfluous: for it suffices that the brothers themselves, the Minor Friars, specially elect this collector, especially with the authority of the General Minister or the Provincial. These points are proven in the Extravagant Decretals, De poenitentia et remissione, in the chapter Cum ex eo. In others than the Minor Friars, it would not be necessary to have a cause distinct from the contract of money; but regarding this matter and the customs of the said brothers, the brothers themselves are better informed. It suffices to say that these men are not questors. But
† those were the quaestuarii who purchased or leased the said quaestum from the brothers, and the brothers themselves coming or speaking. Another

For it is the duty of piety to bestow services gratuitously, whereas it is another matter to manage one’s own property; thus, in the Digest, under the title *De negotiorum gestione*, in the law *Qui sine usuris*, it is stated that they must certainly render a faith that is gratuitous, entire, and abstinent from all profit, as the text there elegantly says. Otherwise, they would be reduced to the status of publicans, who

† How great their audacity, temerity, and avarice are, is established by the description of the law. D. de publicis, l. quantae. And thus it is probable that the Pope understood it. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A deed of deposit, which contains these words: "in the presence of Titius, the depositor, Mevius confessed to having received a deposit, etc." — whether it can be said to be false, since in truth no actual deposit was made at that time; and whether such a deed proves anything, when the witnesses testify only about the confession.
body: In the name of Christ. In a certain instrument it is thus provided: at the instance of Titius, present there and deposing, Mevius was confessed by him, on account of a deposit, to have had and received from the said Titius one thousand five hundred gold florins, which the same [Mevius] promised to return and restore, etc. This very instrument is called into doubt as suspicious and not credible, and is alleged to be false. Witnesses having been produced on both sides, and certain presumptions having been proven against the instrument, and it being established that the notary was otherwise discredited for another forgery, nevertheless, for the confirmation of the said instrument to the contrary, three witnesses described in the said instrument state and depose that the said Mevius said that he had had and received from the said Titius, in deposit and safekeeping, one thousand five hundred gold florins of the money of the said Titius; they do not remember the year and month. When asked whether they saw any quantity of money being counted or given to the said Mevius, they answered that they did not; but that they heard the aforesaid confession.

† Now it is asked whether anything is proved by the said instrument. And it seems that it is: for the said instrument has two clauses: the first is an assertive clause of payment, when it says, at the instance of the said Titius, present and deposing. For this word, deposing, signifies a true and natural act of the time then present. And note, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. Si ex cautione; and C. si certum petatur, l. Si ex pretio. Although when these words are uttered by someone against himself in his own writing they are words of confession, as l. Publia, §. Si, ff. de poenis; nevertheless, when the notary utters these words, they are words of the sight and sense of the notary himself: just as when such words are uttered by a witness: for the notary and the witness are the same, that is, each testifies, as ff. de testibus, l. Domitius Labeo. And in testifying about a true act of a man, one cannot testify except by sight, as elegantly noted by Master Dy. in l. 1, ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae. The second clause of the said instrument is a clause of confession, and this confession is perceived by hearing, nor is the sight of any intervening payment required, as C. de non numerata pecunia, l. In contractibus, §. 1. Therefore, the said instrument, insofar as it refers to the natural act, testifies by sight, but insofar as it refers to the verbal act, testifies by hearing. Our question therefore stands on this: whether, one act being disproved, namely that of sight, the other act, namely that of hearing, is also disproved. And it seems that it is not, because these are different, and therefore one does not infer from one to the other, as in the whole title de non numerata pecunia and de dote causa non numerata, throughout. Moreover, that payment did not intervene is a mere negative, which by the nature of things does not seem to be able to be proved, as C. de probationibus, l. Actor quod asseverat; and fully noted, extra de renuntiatione, c. Super hoc, with its common material.

† Furthermore, in a deposit, it is superfluous and excessive to prove the actual payment, because a confession made in writing suffices, as stated in the law *in contractibus*, at the words *ideoque sancimus*. And when proof is superfluous, although it may be removed from the equation, it suffices that another valid species of proof remains, because the useful is not vitiated by the useless, as in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Certi conditio*, section *Quoniam*; and because superfluous omissions do not vitiate, as in the Code, title *De testamento*, law *Testamentum non ideo*. Furthermore, if it does not hold as proof of the instrument, namely as proof by witnesses, because they are different species of proof: and therefore, although the instrument is false, the obligation can nevertheless be proved by true witnesses, as in the Code, title *Si ex falsis instrumentis*, law *Falsas quidem*. But here, through witnesses confirming the instrument, the confession of the deposit appears; therefore, at least by the force of the witnesses, the debt is proved.

However, the contrary seems to be the case, because in this instrument three things must be weighed: namely, the obligation, its natural cause, i.e., the payment, and its civil cause, i.e., the confession, as noted in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law 2, section *Si*. Furthermore, it must be considered that the said confession presupposes as its foundation a natural act: and that natural act itself, intervening therein, i.e., in the instrument itself, as the words of the instrument state. Now, remove the natural act, and immediately an impediment to the civil act appears, because they cohere with one another, and when one, namely the more important one, is removed, the other must necessarily be removed, as in the Digest, title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Cum tale*, section *Falsum*. And thus the stipulation is annulled if the payment is disproved, as in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Qui pecuniam*. Furthermore, an instrument false in one part is rendered false in any part dependent on it; hence, false in the cause, it is rendered false in the effect, as fully read and noted above in the title *De transactionibus*, law *Si ex falsis*. For just as the deposition of witnesses must be pure, simple, and without blemish, so too must the deposition of the instrument, as fully noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, title *De haereticis*, chapter *Fraternitatis*. Therefore, the truth is that no faith should be given to the said instrument thus struck down. And so it should be reported to the Magnificent Count.

However, I do not say that the notary should be punished. For it also happens with witnesses that they are sometimes saved by distinction, supplementation, or an understood implication, although they do not prove, as in the Decretals, title *De testibus*, chapter *Cum tu fili*. And thus there is no objection to what is noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Singularia*, and in the Digest, title *De acquisitione possessionis*, law *Praedia*. Let us examine something regarding the statements of Bartolus, whether he speaks well or not. The words of Bartolus in law *Singularia* are these: "But how did the notary state in the instrument that such a person confessed to having received one hundred, and had and received it in the presence of me, the notary, and the witnesses: the debtor, to disprove the instrument, produced witnesses who say that the money was indeed there, etc." This statement of Bartolus is irrelevant to the proposition: because it does not appear that the money was here ready for payment; and even if it appears, it would operate for nothing here in a deposit, because this is special to a loan (*mutuum*); therefore, the common law is to the contrary, as noted in the gloss in the said law *Singularia*. Furthermore, Bartolus in another question says: if the notary says, such a person loaned, which is verified in a fictitious loan, even then this statement of Bartolus is irrelevant to the proposition: because a loan admits of fiction, a deposit does not. Furthermore, even in a loan, perhaps he does not speak the truth, because the notary cannot fabricate an instrument of an invisible act by asserting the act to be so, but rather that it is so said by the parties. Nevertheless, whatever it may be, the statements of Bartolus in the said law *Singularia* are irrelevant to our proposition.

The foregoing is supported by the fact that the notary and witnesses are understood to depose about a visible act, and not an invisible one, as noted in the Digest, title *De verbis obligationum*, law *Stipulatio ista*, section *Hi quoque*, where it is noted that a witness is understood to depose about a natural position, which is visible, not about a civil one, unless he also depose about the natural one. Therefore, neither the scribe nor the witness seems to speak of an invisible loan; otherwise, it would follow that the scribe or witness would fabricate an instrument that would be verified by the fiction of postliminy, and not by the nature of things, that the instrument of the scribe would be true, which no person of sound mind would say, as in the Digest, title *De captivis*, law *In bello*, section *Factae*.

I come to Bartolus in law *Praedia*, whose words are these: "The instrument states, he gave and sold to Titius a fund for a price of one hundred, which price he gave and paid to him: the witnesses who intervened in the instrument said that no money intervened: can the instrument be refuted as false? Jacobus Butriga disputed this question: and determined that these words are verified by a fictitious act just as by a true one. And therefore, although the act, namely true payment, did not intervene, nevertheless a fictitious act intervened, namely because he confessed to having had and received. And this is the case here, although he does not allege Bartolus. But Bartolus considers, or wishes to argue from the text with the gloss, and then either it is established that there was a prior giving, and the instrument could be sustained, unless the instrument said 'and then gave and paid,' or it said 'and there gave and paid'; because it would assert payment at the time of the instrument, and deny it by prior act. Hence, it is impossible that he speaks of any payment other than that which was then. But this is false: therefore, the notary speaks wrongly. And this is said by the ordinary gloss in the said law *Praedia*, in the second gloss. Otherwise, it would follow that if the instrument provides that such a person loaned and paid to Titius one hundred, and furthermore confessed to having had and received, that this instrument would prove nothing: because it is equivocal as to naturalness and fiction, and thus as to natural and civil loan: or that the civil would be proved, and not the natural: which is ridiculous to say, and very erroneous. Furthermore, because the words of the scribe must be understood according to common usage of speech, and according to how they fall into the understanding of the witnesses added to validate the instrument: therefore, the adverb 'there' (*ibi*), which is in the instrument, must be weighed: because it signifies 'then.' And that which is added regarding the confession does not refer to the natural act of payment: but signifies that the depositor, or lender, deposited, or loaned, his own money, which dominion is invisible. Hence, it is not proved by the scribe and witnesses. And therefore, the confession is useful and very effective, as noted in the Decretals, title *De testibus*, chapter *Cum causam*.

If, however, Bartolus argues from the disputation of Butriga, certainly Butriga speaks when the instrument says thus: 'Titius confessed to having had and received from Seius giving and paying by reason of a loan, etc.' For those ablatives, 'giving' and 'paying,' come in consequence of the confession, and are words of the party; otherwise, if they are not placed in dependence, but principally and by themselves, the notary asserts the payment or deposit. For Butriga never said that the notary could append these words unless he saw the payment or deposit, as in the Digest, title *De deposito*, law 1, section *Sic ista*.

Therefore, there are four cases: either the notary attests to the payment alone, or to the confession alone, or to both principally and equally; or he appends the ablative, 'giving' and 'paying,' in consequence of the confession. In the first and third case, the instrument lies, or is at least suspect. And this interpretation is more humane. But in the second and last case, the instrument suffers from no suspicion; and the same is to be said of witnesses, as in the Code, title *De fide instrumentorum*, law *In exercendis*, as he clearly states in the said law *Si ex cautione*, in the sixth opposition, which begins, 'Furthermore, I oppose from the division.'

I conclude therefore that the said instrument proves nothing, nor should faith be given to it. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation between husband and wife is confirmed by oath, and what is the reason for the prohibition between them.
2. In how many ways impossibility is said to occur.
3. How an oath must be observed where it can be kept without detriment to eternal salvation, and how it is to be understood.
4. If a compromise has been made regarding a donation between husband and wife, with the wife’s father being added, and if the said donation was declared confirmed or altered in some respect in the presence of the arbitrator and umpire, whether the said compromise and award shall hold.
body: In the name of Christ. Case. A husband donated to his wife the revenues of four thousand Genoese pounds, and he confirmed this donation with a solemn oath. Here, it is first asked whether a donation between husband and wife can be confirmed by an oath, so that it cannot be revoked? Or, if the donee dies before the donor, is the donation revoked?

† And it seems, in the first place, that this donation is confirmed by oath: because such an oath, if kept, does not lead to detriment to eternal salvation; therefore it must be kept, as in the chapter *Quamvis*, *De pactis*, Book 6; *De iureiurando*, chapter *Mulieres*; and chapter *Debitores*, with their similar provisions. Moreover, if it confirms the contract of an adult, as in the *Authenticum Sacramenta puberum*, then all the more it confirms the contract of a husband, who is of perfect age. Furthermore, because a donation between husband and wife, speaking properly, is not prohibited; for if it were prohibited, it would not be confirmed by death; but rather it is merely outside the law, as in the law *Nec enim tanquam inter infestos legibus huiusmodi donationes recipiendae sunt*, in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law 1; and the law *Cum hic*; and the law *Si praedia*. Hence it appears that this prohibition is not odious, but favorable. Favor is shown to the donor, lest he despoil himself through mutual love, not out of hatred for the donee, as in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *Haec ratio*. Therefore, the laws which seem to speak prohibitively do not signify a proper prohibition; but they mean that the law does not lend its favor to such donations, nor does it wish that a civil obligation arise, as in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *Papinianus*. Or, if we say broadly that it is prohibited, such a prohibition is in favor of the donor, not out of hatred for the recipient. For the recipient has committed no fault for which he deserves hatred. Then I argue thus: one may renounce with an oath a law introduced for one’s own benefit, even if otherwise one could not do so in order to avoid the danger of perjury, as is proven in the laws cited above, as fully in the law *Plene*, and noted in the Decretals, *De foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenti*. Therefore, concluding from the first point to the last, this oath makes this donation irrevocable: for the one who swears must be compelled to observe this oath, which is lawful according to natural and divine law, because it does not lead to the sin of the swearer, nor to any act whose execution would be a venial or mortal sin. This is held expressly by Bartolus in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, in the law *Cum lex*.

On the contrary, it seems that the said donation is not confirmed by the said oath, because if the said donation is against the law, the oath against the force and authority of the laws is not valid, as in the Digest, *De legibus*, law *Si quis inquilinos*, § *Finis*, especially because the authority of the laws has natural equity. First, lest poverty be induced between husband and wife through a certain luxury of body and mind. For from bodily luxury easily arises luxury, and the squandering and prodigality of goods, as noted in the Institutes, *De successionibus sublatis*. Moreover, it is against good morals that things which are venial in marriage should be given, and that occasion for divorce be provided, as in the Code, *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Reprehendenda*; and the said law 3, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*; and the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si ita*, § *Si tibi nupsero*. For if the donation to the husband and wife is denied, strife and hatred will intervene, and from this divorce will arise. Hence, considering that this could easily follow and would likely happen, although the said donation is not against good morals in substance, it is nevertheless against good morals in occasion and circumstances. For not only is something reproved for itself, but also for its accident. And one must abstain not only from principal evil, but also from incidental evil, as in the law 1, in the beginning, in the Digest, *Ad Macedonianam*. Then I argue: whether the donation is truly against good morals, or by interpretation of law—for we take good morals to mean the morals of our city, i.e., Rome—the oath is not validating nor obligatory, because the impossible is not validated, nor is it brought into obligation, as in the rule *Ius non est obligatorium*.

For there are four ways in which something is said to be impossible: by law, by nature, by fact, and against good morals; and none of the impossible can be possible, because just as, when a possibility is posited in being, no impossibility follows from it, so conversely, as stated in the Institutiones, De verbis obligationibus, § Impossibilis, and in the Digest, De actionibus et obligationibus, l. Non solum. Moreover, it is prohibited that sureties for dowries be given, lest perfidy arise between husband and wife, nor is it confirmed by oath, as noted in l. 2, Codex, Ne fideiussores dotium dentur. Therefore, the same applies in the present case. Furthermore, divorces appear to be contrary to the public utility, for a path would thereby be opened in fact if a donation could be made with an oath; therefore, it is not valid, as argued in l. 1, Digest, De solutione matrimonii. Moreover, if an oath could rescind all civil laws, such laws would be written down in vain. Moreover, it would follow that a donation exceeding the lawful sum would be valid without insinuation, if an oath were added; which is false, and therefore the law is greater than the oath, because the law can rescind the oath, but the oath cannot rescind the law, unless the law goes further by approving the oath itself. For just as in an oath the authority of a superior, namely the prince, is always understood to be excepted, so much more strongly is the authority of the law, as stated in the Digest, De iure patronatus, l. Adigere, § Finis, and in the Extravagantes, De iureiurando, c. Venientes.

† Notwithstanding the rule: an oath can be kept without detriment to eternal salvation; therefore it must be kept: because this rule should not be formulated thus, but should be formulated in this way: an oath can be kept without detriment to eternal salvation, and if not kept it leads to detriment to eternal salvation, therefore it must be kept. But if it can be kept without detriment to eternal salvation, yet if not kept it does not lead to detriment to eternal salvation, it is not necessary that it be kept, as C. de legibus, l. non dubium. And note C. de collationibus, l. pactum. And C. de iure dotium, l. si praedium. And ff. qui satisdare coguntur, l. qui iuramento. It is true that in certain cases the civil laws disagree with the text of the canonical law. And then the canonical law must be observed, not the civil law. But returning to our point, no text of the canonical law says that a donation between husband and wife is validated by an oath. Therefore in this we must adhere to the civil law. Solution: this question is determined by the said Cynus and Petrus de Bellapertis, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. 1. And it is said that either this donation is made by granting, or by promising: if by granting, it can be revoked; if by promising, because in the future one must comply with the oath, but in this distinction Cynus does not follow Petrus, nor does he speak clearly or intelligibly. Nor certainly does this distinction hold: because the same reason applies to validating a confession as to observing a provision, if it can be validated, therefore I firmly hold that a donation between husband and wife has the nature of a last will: because this nature is attributed to it by law, so that there is free will to revoke until death. And thus an oath cannot prevent a last will from being revocable. Likewise an oath cannot do this, so that this donation, which ought to be of free will, can be revoked, as C. de pactis, l. si, ver. nisi. For indeed this clause, to be irrevocable, is contrary to good morals, as noted C. de transactionibus, l. cum donationis. And contrary to the nature of the act itself: and if we were to say that the oath validates it, all the absurdities would follow which the legislator wished to avoid. Moreover, an argument from absurdity is most valid, as ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. Pomponius scribit, cum si. I therefore hold that the said donation is not validated by an oath, and that if the donee first dies, it expires, because it cannot pass into a tacit last will; the same if it is revoked expressly or tacitly. Otherwise this grant, or assignment, would be confirmed, because it would have the force of an incorporeal cession, as noted ff. de donationibus, l. penultima. And because annual revenues are counted among immovables, and their possession is quasi held, and quasi transferred: and especially if the donee at any time demanded the revenues. For immediately she is constituted in quasi possession, arg. extra de causa possessionis, c. cum ecclesia Sutrina. And de electione, c. querelam. And C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus nulli. And in Auth. de non alienando, §. vult enim.

† The second question is whether, if a compromise was made regarding the aforementioned matter, with the wife’s father also being involved, and by the sentence of the arbitrator and umpire the said donation was confirmed or in some way altered, whether the said compromise and the said award hold in law? It seems that they do: because every contract is permitted between husband and wife, except for the contract of donation, which is presumed to be invalid even if celebrated by another contract, insofar as this is shown by the nature of the thing. And then it is vitiated only to that extent, not in its entirety, as stated in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *Quod autem*, section *Si maritus*. But to compromise is to contract, because the compromitting parties obligate themselves mutually to obey the sentence of the arbitrator and umpire, as noted in the Authenticum *Ut differant*, in the gloss, column 9. Therefore, this contract is valid. Furthermore, between husband and wife, judgment or quasi-judgment is not prohibited by any law; indeed, they may sue each other regarding any matter except the dowry, which would not be the case in the instance of consignation to a guardian, as is proved here. Code, *De fundo dotali*, law *Manifestissimi*, section *Si*; and Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Non tamen*. Therefore, the compromise and the subsequent award were valid.

On the contrary, it seems that they are not valid, because if the principal is not valid, that which follows from it or on account of it is not valid. I say that that which follows immediately from it is not valid, nor that which follows mediately, as stated in the Code, *De legibus et constitutionibus*, law *Non dubium*. And therefore, if a transaction intervenes between husband and wife concerning a preceding donation, even with the authority of the praetor, the transaction is null by law itself. The first point is proved in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, section *Sed cum lex*. The second point is proved because the arbitrator, who succeeds to the place of the praetor, cannot decree that a donation contrary to law shall be valid, as stated in the Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Actiones quae non propriis viribus*. Thirdly, this is proved because a transaction is a kind of donation when liberality is present therein. The text is notable in law 1, section *Sed si rem*, Digest, *Ne quid in fraudem patroni*. The fourth and final reason is: it is absurd that the authority of the law could be circumvented by compromise; an argument from absurdity is drawn from natural discretion, which is immutable. And the legislator uses this argument in law *Pomponius scribit*, Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, and in innumerable places in the law. Nor does the involvement of the father’s person, even if the father had bound himself, accomplish anything, as stated in the Digest, *Quaere re actio non datur*, law 1, section *Exceptiones*. And because between fathers-in-law the same prohibition exists as between husband and wife, this supports the point. Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haeres meus*, section *Quod in fraudem*.

Therefore, concluding from the first to the last point, since we must return to the root and origin, and if that is vitious, the whole is vitious, as stated in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Tutor*; Digest, *De donationibus*, law *Qui id quod*. Furthermore, that which lacks validity must be extirpated, as the said decree and decretal state, that even an oath should not be informed by such agreements, as stated in the Extravagantes, *De foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenti*, section *Si*. And this is supported by the Digest, *De legibus*, law *Fraus*, with its entire subject matter. And thus I hold. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute stating that a dowried daughter does not succeed extends to the daughter of my son.
2. Whether a statute excluding dowried women in the presence of agnates applies when agnates are present; and thus, whether a statute of laymen benefits clerics.
3. Whether a statute speaking of uncles extends to nephews.
4. Whether a statute speaking of a brother extends to a uterine brother.
body: In the name of Christ. Given the statute that a daughter who has been endowed by her father shall not succeed to the endower, nor to any other descendant of his.

† It is asked whether, if I have dowered the daughter of my son, whether living or predeceased, the statute is understood to speak of her? And it seems that it is not, because in statutes it is permitted to speak from an enumeration of persons made by the statute; hence persons who are not enumerated appear to be neglected by the provision of the statute, and also conversely by the disfavor of the statute, as in D. 24.3.11 (Si vero), § De viro; and Inst. 2.20, col. 2; and C. 5.18.1; and C. 5.27.1, in fine; D. 28.5.1; D. 24.1.3. But the statute does not speak of one dowered by a grandfather; therefore it does not dispose concerning her: because that which is not changed is not prohibited from remaining, as in C. 6.23.1 (Sancimus). For in the correction of laws, the words of the municipal law are required; for correction of laws is not made from tacit conjectures which do not arise from the interpretation of words, as in C. 4.2.1 (Apud antiquos); and C. 1.13.1 (Quas actiones). To the contrary, for this part, it is made because, although a grandfather dowers a granddaughter in consideration of his son, as in D. 24.4.1 (Dedit dotem), nevertheless this is by a certain fiction, that what I do, I interpret as done by my son, as noted in D. 43.1.1, § Quotiens. But statutes do not receive fiction, whenever they can dispose over a true case, as noted in D. 15.3.3, § Haec actio; unless they expressly dispose over a fictitious case; and then all other laws which speak of a true case are drawn to the fictitious, as in D. 50.17.1 (Singularia); and D. 35.2.1, § Lex Falcidia; and D. 28.2.1 (Filio, quem pater); C. 4.18.1 (Si). To the contrary, it seems, because it matters not whether something is done by me or by someone for me, as in D. 50.16.1 (Cum servus). Hence, one dowered is understood to be dowered by someone in whose consideration she was dowered by whomever, as in D. 23.3.1 (Profectitia), in principio. I speak of immediate and proximate consideration, as in D. 28.6.1, § In arrogato. And this is effected by the understanding of the doer and the receiver, as in D. 28.5.1 (Quidam cum filium). For understanding transfers the act into right, and transfuses from person to person in those things which do not adhere to the person, but to the cause: as in the legal rule Qui per alium, as in C. 7.71, § Ne autem. This appears by such a demonstration: if I die first than my son, then his daughter dies, the action for the profectitious dowry consolidates to my son, as in D. 24.3.2. Therefore, truly and really, she is dowered by my son; because what I did has been transfused to him. Solution: if my son died while I was living, this one is not dowered by the father, nor does the statute have place, because understanding cannot take that she was dowered by one predeceased, as in D. 38.2.1, § Posthumus. But if I died first: this one is properly said to be dowered by my son, because the reality of the dower from the grandfather to the son, and from the son to his daughter, appears to have been transfused.

It is asked whether a statute that excludes a dowried daughter when agnates exist applies if the agnates are clerics? And it seems that it does not, because clerics are not included in the statutes of laymen, as in Extra, De constitutionibus, c. Ecclesia S. Mariae, because they are not part of the body of laymen. 12 q. 1, c. Duo sunt genera Christianorum. So much so that even statutes favorable to church property do not bind them, as in 91 dist., c. Bene quidem. To the contrary is the truth: because clerics are included in favors just as laymen are. 10 dist., c. Si in adiutorium. For where the reason is the same, as is the case here with agnation, clerical status should not hinder but benefit; hence clerics are included together with laymen, as in Legi and Nota, ff. De iure dotium, l. Promittendo, in principio. To this effect is Extra, De foro competenti, c. Dilecti, where it is expressly stated that a privilege granted to the people benefits clerics. Nor is it surprising if we can confer benefits upon those to whom we cannot impose burdens: as in Nota, Codex, Ubi senatus vel clerus, l. Quoties; and Nota, ff. De regulis iuris, l. Nemo qui condemnare. There is an excellent glossa there on clerics being included in the favors of statutes and not included in odia, although the glossa in that passage is not true in contentious judicial matters, as in Extra, De iudicibus, c. At si clerici; and Extra, De foro competenti, c. Si diligenti.

Secondly, it is asked: suppose that the statute provides that the brother of the dowry-giver excludes the dowried daughters; now there remains a brother and the son of another brother. It is asked whether the son of the brother succeeds together with his uncle, and it seems that he does, as in the Authentica "Ut fratrum filii" in the rubric and black letter, and in the Code, on Legacies and Inheritances, Authentica "Post fratres." Nor is it found that the statute says the contrary; but it seems that the son of the brother does not succeed, because the benefit of the statute is directed solely to the brother of the dowry-giver; and this brother is the one who calls the inheritance from the seed; and if the brother were not the son of the brother, he would not exclude them; therefore, the sons of the brother do not make the father from the uncle, since they are not called. The benefit of the statute speaks only of the brother, not of the sons of the brother, as in the Digest, on Inofficious Testaments, Law 1, and in the Code, on Inofficious Testaments, Law "Fratres." The statute has not only the force of excluding the daughters, but also the force of applying the inheritance to the brother; therefore, the brother alone succeeds in solidum. Moreover, the edict of the statute is not opened in the same way as the edict of the praetor is opened. For even that would not be opened unless the praetor had said so, as in the Digest, on Contracts, Law "Si post mortem," Section "Si." And to this effect is what is noted in the Digest, on Inofficious Testaments, Law "Pater filium," according to that reading, that the father comes through the querela inofficiosi testamenti; and thus, through the passed-over son, the contra tabulas action is not opened against the father. So I say in the case at hand that the intestate succession is not opened through the uncle to the nephews, concerning whom the statute does not speak, as in the Code, on Collations, Law "Illam," there, "because no constitution, etc." For that argument is valid: Law "Non cauetur." Therefore, it is not justly demanded, as in the Authentica, on the Triennium and Semis, Section "Consideremus." Also, what is granted to one is seen to be denied to others, as in the Code, on Military Testaments, Law "Sicut," certain.

Thirdly, it is asked, behold, that paternal collaterals are preferred in paternal goods, and maternal collaterals in maternal goods, as stated in the aforementioned authority *post fratres*. And thus, the goods which were united in the person of the deceased receive division in the persons of the heirs: which is contrary to the nature of union. D. de separatione bonorum, l. 1, § sciendum; D. de vulgari et substituta, l. sed et si plures, § filio. Suppose, therefore, that there remains a brother who is consanguineous to these dowried daughters, yet also uterine; does the uterine brother succeed in the uterine goods? I answer that if the statute spoke of a brother simply, division would be made in the manner aforesaid; but if it speaks of an agnate, only the consanguineous brother is an agnate, for the uterine brother is not an agnate, because rights of agnation do not arise through females, since neither do rights of family. I. de potestate, as D. de adoptionibus, l. qui in adoptionem datur. It is not objected, C. de legitimis heredibus, l. meminimus, § sed nec fratrem, because there it speaks of the common law. Here we are in municipal law. Moreover, it does not say there that the uterine brother is an agnate, although he sometimes has the rights of agnates. The statute, however, speaks of an agnate, and it does not follow: I have the right of an agnate, therefore I am an agnate. I therefore answer the question of this clerk, that this clerk succeeds in the benefit of the statute: and that he succeeds in all, excluding the dowried daughters according to the form of the statute, because statutes made by laymen benefit clerks. D. 10, c. si in adiutorium; and so advised Oldradus. And if these women, being dowried, are in possession, they do not possess justly, considering the municipal statute. And therefore they are bound by the petition of the heir to restore possession of the hereditary things. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute providing that every buyer and seller is bound to pay a certain sum applies when someone buys from a church; and what is the law when a church sells things for which it did not pay tolls, namely whether the buyer himself is bound to pay them. And number 2.
body: In the name of Christ. The civic statute of Asti provides that every seller and buyer is held liable in solidum to pay a certain tax. Now, a certain subject of the legislators has purchased from the church.

† It is asked whether the tax is due? And it is certain that the church is not bound: because it is not subject to those who enact statutes. For the making of statutes is a matter of jurisdiction, as appears from the definition of jurisdiction. D. de iurisdi. om. iu. l. 1. And a statute is sometimes by the right of the prince, and is called a constitution: as D. de consti. prin. in rubro, et nigro. Sometimes it is by the right of the people, and is called a municipal statute: as D. de decre. ab ord. fa. l. municipali. Sometimes it is by the right of the magistrate, and is called an edict of the praetor. Hence also the constitution of a bishop is an edict of the praetor, as C. quod quisque iu. l. 1. §. qui magistratum. Sometimes it is by the right of a lawful assembly, and is called the civil law of that body or college, as D. de consti. prin. l. 2. in fi. But whatever statute is valid, it is said to be made by the right of jurisdiction taken in general. Since therefore laymen have no jurisdiction or power over clerics, they cannot enact any statute against them or upon them, as Extr. de consti. c. ecclesia sanctae Mariae. libertas. The liberty of clerics is so great and such that it cannot be subjected to the laws of laymen: because it is written, "Touch not my anointed." S. neither in person nor in goods, as noted in Auth. de non alie. §. vult. This is also expressly proved by civil law. C. de sa. san. ec. l. placet. It is also proved by the latest constitutions of Emperor Frederick. C. de sa. san. ec. Auth. cassa, et irrita. And C. de epi. et cle. Auth. item nulla communitas.

† Now it remains to be seen, although the church is not bound, whether the layman is bound? And first let us inquire into the intent of the statute. Secondly, into the legal possibility, assuming the intent to be certain. And I return to the first point: namely, that the intent of the statute was not to bind anyone except the contracting parties, who can equally be bound, as in D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. hoc iure, §. sed si alter; and C. de impubibus et aliis sub tutela, l. quamvis. On the contrary, it is argued that if two persons are constituted as joint and several debtors, one validly and the other invalidly, or if there are two sureties, the valid obligation is not vitiated by the invalid one. Hence, he who can be bound is bound; and he who cannot be bound is not bound. As in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si Titius et Seia. It appears in the present case that the subject is bound, and the church is not bound.

Solution: At first glance, this question seems to be resolved by a case directly on point. D. de pupillis, l. licitatio, §. mercatores, where it is said that if someone buys from the fisc, although the fisc is not bound to pay the toll, the buyer himself is nevertheless bound. Here one must consider: either the burden of the toll is annexed to the contract, or it arises from a separate act; for example, buying grain from the church and exporting it through places where the toll is collected. In the first case, the statute does not seem to speak of contracts celebrated with the church; because indirectly it would be contrary to the liberty of the church, for the church would sell its property all the less to the extent of that burden; by many authorities. A free thing is sold more readily than a burdened thing; for this reason is subtly established by law or agreement, D. de servo exportando, in l. si venditor.

But if this burden arises from a separate act, which has nothing in common with the origin of the contract, then the buyer is bound to pay, although the church is not bound to pay; because the act of the buyer has nothing in common with the act of the church; as in the aforementioned §. mercatores. Although Bartolus says there that such a buyer is not bound to bear extraordinary imposts, since he has a title from the church. Therefore, if I buy a fund from the church, which did not pay tithes and extraordinary and arbitrary collections, neither shall I be bound to pay them even for the future time. Which, with due respect to my learned master, is not true; because when the statute changes the person, the thing subject to the statute must be changed accordingly, as in C. de impositione lucrativa descriptione, l. 1, lib. 10. And what is granted out of reverence for clerics or the church does not extend beyond them, as in D. de solutione et liberatione, l. alia, §. eleganter. Hence, a share-cropper will rightly pay tithes on his share, although the monastery from which he leased does not pay on its portion, because diversity of persons admits of separation, arguing from C. si unus ex pluribus, l. 1, in the literal sense.

Furthermore, in one case it could be maintained that where the church does not pay the toll, neither does the buyer; namely, when the buyer transports goods at the expense of the church by agreement. Arguing from D. de locato, l. penult., §. navem. From the foregoing it appears that even if the words of the statute were clear, speaking of both subject and non-subject persons, nevertheless no more and no less toll should be paid than as I have said above. And I highly commend the subtle opinion rendered in this matter by the learned doctor, my dear friend Manuel de Ast. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the right of patronage is included in the sale of a universitas, and at number 3.
2. Whether the right of patronage is included in the sale of goods.
4. How one is said to be in possession of the right of patronage.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain nobleman held the right of patronage over a church built by his predecessors; he was in possession of the right of patronage and of presenting to it a rector to be presented for the time being. This nobleman held a large territory and lands, within whose boundaries was said patronal church together with certain possessions assigned to said church by said founders, of which things said nobleman, along with his honors, was given a fourth part by a secular judge, or by an unpaid agreement, a fourth portion to another certain nobleman.

† It is now asked whether the right of patronage passed in any way to the said nobleman, who received the unsold property? And it seems that it did: because the right of patronage of the church appears to be a real right; and therefore it passes with the universality of the sold estates, within the boundaries of which the said church is located: according to that rule, and that certain things pass with the universality, which cannot be sold or exchanged by themselves, even if they are of sacred or religious law, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis; and l. quondam, D. de acquirenda re dominica. On the contrary, because the right of patronage is a right annexed to the spiritual aspect of the church; and therefore it cannot be transferred by a contract of laymen; nor by the giving of unsold property made by a secular judge: as in Extra de iudicibus, c. caeterum.

† It is asked whether the right of patronage is included under the term "goods." And I say that it is not, because it is more a burden than an honor: as is fully shown in the law and note 16, q. ult., c. piæ mentis. Or at least it is something mixed, which is included under the term "simple goods": as in ff. de leg. 3, l. hoc legatum.

† Solution: The right of patronage of the church passes with the universitas to the universal heir; because it passes by necessity, as stated in the aforementioned law *Quaedam*. But it passes to the universal buyer, who buys not only corporeal things, but also rights, as to the buyer of a castle and village with its rights and appurtenances, as in *Extra*, *De iure patronatus*, chapter *Ex literis*. But it does not pass to the buyer of corporeal things only; because the right of patronage is incorporeal: and although it adheres to the church, which is corporeal in a material sense, nevertheless the church is outside commerce, as in *Digest*, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Inter stipulantem*, § *Sacram*. And to the church, which is outside commerce, the right of patronage accedes. Hence, if the principal, i.e., the church, does not pass, neither does the accessory. I do not say that the church can in any way be sold or alienated; but the right of presentation itself, if the universitas were sold, passes with the universitas; because the universitas contains within itself both corporeal and incorporeal things: as in the law and note in *Digest*, *De verborum significatione*, law *Rei appellatione*; and *Digest*, *De hereditate vel actione vendita*, law 2, § *Sed si vendiderit hereditatem*; and law *Venditor ex hereditate*. Therefore, the words of the contract must be considered, whether the sale was made under the form of a universitas, in which corporeal and incorporeal things are contained; and then the right of patronage is included. Or if only corporeal things were sold, then the right of patronage is not included. I say, however, that if the sale was made under the name of a territory, jurisdictions are included, and therefore also incorporeal rights. But if under the name of described and bounded estates, then the right of patronage is not included, as noted by Innocentius in the aforementioned chapter *Ex literis*, *De iure patronatus*, and it is proven in *Digest*, *De actione empti*, law *Fundum nihil*. And therefore the reader of the instrument has the solution of the question from this: as in *Code*, *De probationibus*, law *Ad probationem*; *Digest*, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Fideiussores magistratuum*, § *Pro Aurelio*. And it supports what I wrote in chapter 1, *De capitulo qui cum vendit*, column 10; and what is noted by Dynus in law *Ergo*, *Digest*, *De acquirenda rerum dominium*. But if the bishop granted me a castle, it would not be understood that he granted me tithes, but temporalities, or things annexed to temporalities, according to Innocentius. Moreover, every universal is collective; for under one name it gathers into itself corporeal and incorporeal rights, as an inheritance, possession of goods, patrimony, peculium, territory, and a castle which has jurisdiction. But the names of corporeal things, which are circumscribed by their own boundaries, are not a universitas, nor anything universal, as in *Institutes*, *De fideicommissis hereditatibus*, § *Si quis una*; and fully in the law and note in *Digest*, *De transactionibus*, law *Controversia*.

† That also must not be omitted, that by a single act of presentation a quasi-possession of the right of presentation is acquired. On the cause, I ask: unless the presentation is rejected by the superior; for then the one expelled from the act cannot acquire possession by such an act, just as one expelled from a fund does not possess the fund. Likewise, in the same manner regarding corporeal things, since their quasi-possession is not acquired except through patience, as in D. de serv. l. quotiens. From which it follows that such a conclusion holds: if the presenter is neither admitted nor rejected, or if a condition is opposed, the truth of which is uncertain, then such a presenter does not begin to possess by such presentation, nor can he present thereafter as a possessor, unless he again acquires possession. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An agreement not to prove payment except by a public instrument, and one that brings the matter to an end, does not prevent it from also being proved by witnesses, and no. 4.
2. Poor grammar does not invalidate, when the intention of the contracting parties is clear.
3. When witnesses are said to be singular and various.
5. Set-off is not proof.
body: In the name of Christ. The words of the instrument: the aforementioned Nicolinus confessed to having received one thousand [units] from Titius, renouncing all proof of payment without this brief being incised, or another [instrument] making an end to all right and aid of the laws. And to observe this, the consul of justice condemned him, and he swore not to contravene it. It happened that, after the death of the said Nicolinus, the wife of the said Nicolinus and testamentary guardian of their common children received from the late debtor of the said Nicolinus the said one thousand pounds, which immediately came into the hands of the said creditor, and whom she carried away with her, as has been proven by witnesses. It is objected that the said witnesses should not be believed, because proof by witnesses has been renounced, and only proof by the said incised instrument or another similar instrument making an end has been reserved. The question is: what is the law?

And these are three points to be considered. First, whether a renunciation could have been made. The gloss in the Constitution *Ut maiores debiti et creditores*, § *Quia vero*, says that it could not. This gloss might be understood as applying when the contracted debt is proved by witnesses; but when it is proved by a public instrument, the renunciation or pact that payment cannot be proved except by the cut debt instrument or another public instrument seems valid: as in the Code, *De non numerata pecunia*, law *Generaliter*; and in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Prout quisque*; and *De re iudicata*, law *Nihil tam naturale*.

Second, it must be examined, because the writing does not seem to say this. For those words, "or by another end," are obscure. They do not, namely, say "or by another instrument of the end." Moreover, a debt is said to be "ended" when it is proved to have been paid by witnesses: as in the Code, *De transactionibus*, law *Fratris*. Furthermore, I see that although a sentence is rendered in writing, payment can nevertheless be proved by witnesses; for it suffices that this is not prohibited by law: as in the Code, *De fide instrumentorum*, law *In exercendis*. Also, witnesses are included under the term "instruments," unless "public instruments" is added: as in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Notionem*, § *Instrumentorum*. Also, this is supported by the fact that the woman made payment, and it is permissible for her to ignore the subtleties of the law, especially when the matter concerns avoiding damage: as in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Cum de indebito*. Also, because it was paid on behalf of the pupils, whose loss should not enrich the creditor. Nor does the oath stand in the way, because the one who swore was dead: as noted by Innocentius, *Extra*, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Veritatis*.

To the contrary, it seems that what was ordered and agreed upon with the deceased, and especially when established by an oath, must be observed, even if a pupil becomes heir: as fully stated in the law and notes in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Emilius Largianus*. Nor does the ignorance of the guardian or the pupil remove public right. Nor does it stand in the way that those words, "or by another," are imperfect; for they are imperfect in voice, but not in consent: as in the Digest, *De legatis*, book 2, law *Cum pater*, § *Cum imperfecta*. Also, words are to be drawn to the understanding, not the understanding to the words: as in the Code, *De libellis pretiis vel ex haereditate*, law 3. The sense will therefore be this: "or by another instrument, supplied, of the end," i.e., the end. And this is proved thus: the disjunctive conjunction "or" induces a tacit repetition: as fully noted in the Digest, *De legatis*, book 3, law *In repetendis*. Since therefore it was said above concerning an instrument, it is understood to repeat similarly concerning an instrument; and especially, since words must have some effect: as in the Digest, *De usu*, law *Si stipulatus*; and in law 1, *Ad municipium*; and *Ad Trebellianum*, law *Balista*; and *De legatis*, book 1, law *Si quando*, in the principal part. Also, the disjunctive is presumed to be placed between equals: as in the Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, law 1. And the conjunction between things of the same quality and reason: as in the Digest, *De vino legato*, law *Si*, § *Cui dulcia*; and *De penus legatis*, law *Nam quod liquide*, § *Si cui*. And if anyone were to say, "if you supply 'by another,' i.e., 'instrument'," it would be bad grammar. Against this: law *Plautius*, *De auro et argento legato*.

I answer that, when the intention of the contracting parties is established, poor grammar does not invalidate the agreement; for our laws are not subject to Priscian, as is stated in the Codex, Title "On Wills," Law "Since it is unworthy."

It is also alleged that the witnesses are diverse and singular. Regarding this, it should be known that either the witnesses refer to different terms or to one common term. In the first case, the witnesses are singular; in the second, they are not, as noted in the Digest, De testibus, l. Ob carmen, §. Si, in fine; and according to Bartolus in l. 1, in fine, Digest, Quemadmodum testamentum aperiri. And therefore this is our matter: because I presuppose that the witnesses are consistent.

† Therefore, our question must be resolved as follows: either you ask whether the witnesses prove the exception of payment, and they do not; or the exception of set-off, and they do, because the agreed pact does not speak of set-off, but only of a settlement and refutation. It is true that he who sets off pays. [See] the section *Facta compensatione*: but then a public instrument will be drawn up regarding it, just as it suffices for a debtor to offer money in court, so it suffices if set-off is offered in court, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. And it demonstrates that L. Iul. and L. item: set-off is not properly payment.

† and therefore an agreement to prove payment is not an agreement not to prove set-off: because they are different, although they ultimately converge on the same end, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. debitor. It must also be considered that a minor could be restored to his original position against the omission of an instrument: for by way of restitutio in integrum it sometimes follows that what was not done is treated as done, as in D. de minoribus, l. si ex causa, § nunc videndum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A person banned for six months may return without punishment once those months have elapsed; and one who has been punished with a lesser penalty, although he deserved a greater one, cannot be punished again with a greater penalty. And number 2.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: Guido was publicly inquired into by the Lord Vice-Count of Lucca, the magistrate of the territory of Sarzana; and he was found guilty, because it had come to his knowledge that his brother was plotting to betray Sarzana, since the said brother had disclosed the said plot to him. The said Guido did not consent to it, but rather rebuked him strongly, stating that no one from their house had ever been a traitor, and that he should desist entirely from such plans. However, because he did not reveal this to the officials and to the said Lord Vice-Count, he was banished from the territory for six months. From the foregoing, two questions are asked: first, whether the said Guido, after the term of six months, may freely return to the place from which he was temporarily interdicted; second, assuming that he may, whether he can be further punished and prosecuted for this offense, on the ground that he was punished with a lighter penalty. Although there is little doubt, indeed none, regarding this first question, nevertheless, because I am compelled to respond on the basis of the facts,

And I say that sometimes a person is banished simply, or in perpetuity with this expressly stated, and in this case the penalty is perpetual, as in D. de legibus, l. fin., and C. de poenis, l. seruus. And this is not our case. Sometimes a person is banished at the pleasure of the judge: for example, the judge said, “I banish you as long as I wish, or as long as it pleases me, or until I recall you.” And it is said, as noted by Bartolus in D. de verbis oblig., l. centesimis, §. si. Sometimes a person is banished for a time without the term being expressed, and the time is understood to be ten years. This is the unique case in law, and notable. D. de poenis, l. sine praefinito tempore. And similarly, this is not our case. Sometimes a person is banished for a time with it expressed and declared: for example, for two years, or three years, or five years. And this is our case, in which it must undoubtedly be said that, upon the expiration of the six-month period, the penalty is extinguished, and one may freely return to the place temporarily interdicted. For what is prohibited at one time is seen to be granted by law itself at another time, as in D. de legibus 2, l. statuliberum, §. stichum; and D. de postulando, l. imperator; and D. de iudicibus, l. cum prior, with similar authorities. For a temporal sentence is not extended to perpetuity, as in C. de his qui non infa., l. et si seuerior, where it is expressly stated, as we say elsewhere in the pact. D. de pactis, l. epistola, §. fin.

† Regarding the second doubt, whether the accused may be punished according to law, because the judge did not impose a penalty suitable to the crime, and it seems that he may: for it seems that the judge cannot reduce the legal penalty. L. 1, § calumniatoribus, D. ad turpil. Moreover, we see this in civil cases. For it is not permitted for the judge to change in the sentence what was demanded in the libel. Therefore, similarly, he cannot change the penalty arising from the crime. Moreover, the judge swore to observe the laws, as C. de iudi. L. rem non nouam. By these reasons, it seems that one should say that the judge could not reduce the penalty. On the contrary, I think it should be said according to law, namely, that the judge may reduce the penalty for cause, as D. de pę. L. hodie.
