And note the authorities in D. de his, qui notantur infamia, L. quid ergo, § poena grauior. The cause in our case could have been due to the non-occurrence of the result, although according to the strictness of the law the same penalty ought to have been imposed due to the attempt, as noted in D. de poenis, L. aut facta, § euentus, and there by Jacobus de Areti. And especially in our case: since this person, about whom the question is asked, perhaps and plausibly was the cause of the crime not being consummated, but the bond of blood led him to silence: and similarly, piety. From which I conclude that, by reason of this crime, he cannot be further punished or molested according to law. And we see this practiced daily according to law. Therefore, and the rest. Argument: D. de extraor. cri. L. saccularii, § sunt quaedam. And it is expressed where someone was exiled for a crime of majesty. D. de poenis, L. eorum. I, Baldus, and Jacobus de Isolanis.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It is understood that mention is made of the causes, by the very fact that mention is made of the proceedings.
body: In the name of Christ.

† If we are governed by the common law, and the judge’s sentence mentions the causes, and is rendered by way of a definitive judgment, I advise in all respects, and in every way, as is contained above: pursuant to the law and the reasons most prudently alleged: also considering the reason of blood. According to the notes in l. 1, ff. de receptoribus, together with similar authorities. And it is understood that mention is made of the causes, by the very fact that mention is made of the proceedings, and in the proceedings the causes appear, as in l. in summa, de re iudicata. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What the plaintiff in a hypothecary action must prove with regard to the petitory and possessory claims.
2. Who is presumed to be the possessor when the issue concerns presumed possession.
body: In the name of Christ. The facts appear to be as follows: A certain Bononius sold a certain house, which is the subject of the action, to a certain Peter of Losanna for one gold florin in the year of our Lord 1383. Finally, in the year of our Lord 1388, he sold it, together with John of Brescia, to another certain Peter of Fabriano for the price of 35 gold florins. And it is true, as appears from the records, that the said Peter of Fabriano, the second purchaser, sold the said house to a certain Francischino Malacharne for the price of 37 florins in the year 1388. Furthermore, it is true that a certain Lady Catherine, wife of the said Peter of Losanna, possessed it. It is also true that the other said Lady Catherine, wife of Francischino, as heir of the said Francischino, possesses the said house, against whom the said Lady Catherine, wife of the late said Peter of Losanna, brings a hypothecary action, alleging that the said house is mortgaged to her for the amount contained in the dotal instrument. Conversely, the said Catherine, the defendant, contends that the said house belongs to her. Now the question arises: what is the law? Having seen, considered, and examined the matters in the case, namely whether the said Lady Catherine, the defendant, ought to be condemned regarding the said hypothecary action, or absolved, and we shall not err if we lay the foundation upon the rule of law.

† For it is established that the plaintiff in a hypothecary action must prove that the debt subsists, that the thing is hypothecated by agreement or by law, and that the thing itself was in the debtor’s assets at the time of the obligation. And these matters are expressly proven. D. de probationibus, l. ante omnia. And note in the Speculum, de obligationibus et solutionibus, § 1, under the rubric “but what must the creditor prove in a hypothecary action.” Also, it must be premised that when a hypothecary action is brought against a third-party possessor, it must be proven that the thing was in the debtor’s assets in such a way that the debtor would have been entitled to a vindicatio, or a publiciana, or some other similar remedy to oust the possession: for example, a condictio under l. si coloni, C. de agris et censibus, Book 11; or an officium iudicis, as in D. de condictione furtiva, l. et ideo, § Neratius. For this rule regarding petitory actions is proven by the well-known l. si ab eo, D. de pignoribus. But as to possessory actions, it is proven by what is subtly noted by Jacobus de Aretino and Cynus in C. si res aliena pignori data sit, l. cum res. Also, for clarity, it must be premised that when a thing is sold to two persons by the same vendor, the thing becomes part of the assets of the person to whom it is first delivered, as in C. de rei venditione, l. Quotiens, which is fully stated in the law and noted in D. de publiciana, l. si autem, § si duobus. For delivery, or quasi-delivery, is regularly necessary to incorporate a thing into someone’s assets, as in D. de rei vindicatione, l. si ager; C. de pactis et traditionibus. And if it is delivered to no one, the thing is in no one’s assets; but there is only a personal action, which is not granted against a third-party possessor, because a personal action does not follow the land, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. 1, § haeres. And because I do not find it proven by the records of the case that the said Peter de Losana possessed the said house at any time, nor was it alleged that he possessed it by virtue of the said title, as in D. de publiciana, l. eum qui, § penultimo, for the presumption in Book 2, C. de acquisitione possessionis, exempts from proving but not from alleging; and especially it does not appear to be proven that the said house was in the assets of the said Peter de Losana before the said Francischinus possessed it, except by one witness, who is not sufficient in cases of grave prejudice, especially since an oath was not demanded in default of proof, as in C. de testamento, l. iureiurando, in fine. And that one witness is named Otinus, and he does not even testify to the priority of possession. It necessarily follows that it is not proven that the said house was in the assets of the said Peter de Losana. And consequently, the said Catherine, late wife of the said Peter, fails in proof regarding this article, that the thing was in the assets of the said Peter de Losana. And therefore, assuming that the said Catherine, the plaintiff, had a right in the inheritance—but this is not conceded, because it does not appear to me, since the proof does not appear—the rule of law applies that if the plaintiff does not prove, the defendant is absolved; and in costs, according to the strictness of the law, the loser would be condemned to pay the winner. Nevertheless, let the judge do what seems equitable to him. There are also many other matters which, as to the subtlety of the law, do not appear to be proven, which I do not pursue.

† Moreover, when we are dealing with possession, present possession is to be presumed stronger than past possession: because present possession is established by truth, whereas the other is not. It is what is noted in C. de edicto divi Adriani tollendo, l. Edicto. As for the expenses, I have assessed them at four florins, which I received as my fee from the nuncio of Catherine, who was summoned; as for the others, I have no knowledge of them. And therefore I leave their assessment to the discretion of the judge, who has the authority to judge. Nor was the decree of the lord presented to me. For if I had seen it, I would not have accepted such a commission: because I have never sworn in any counsel, and in the great commissions frequently made to me. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is more readily believed that an instrument was drawn up in ancient times, even when two witnesses contradict it. And at number 5.
2. Why witnesses are said to be singular.
3. Semi-full proof is not sufficient for torture.
4. A public and solemn instrument is presumed with great force.
6. Oblivion is presumed from the passage of ten years.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A certain notary drew up a certain instrument, or some writing on parchment, and in the form customarily observed in public instruments, in which such writing is contained, and therefore, that A. was alleged to have had, and received, sixty-eight ducats as the price of a certain sale, and that he had and received them in the presence of the said notary and witnesses. Four witnesses are described, two of whom are not alive. But the other two, who are alive, testify that they never attended the said instrument, nor the said sale, nor the said payment of money. Hence, since the said notary is accused of forgery, it is asked whether he ought to be condemned? Assuming that otherwise the said notary is of good reputation, and his other instruments are true and legal, and that the said alleged writing was made eighteen years ago, or thereabouts. And it seems that the said notary ought altogether to be condemned: since the crime appears fully proven by two witnesses, described in the instrument, as noted by Baldus in l. 1, at the end, ff. quemad. test. aperian.

† Nor does it matter if you say that the said witnesses are singular; for rather they are concurring witnesses tending to one end of the matter, namely, the very falsity of the instrument, as in C. de poenis, l. cum reis. And Bartolus says in the said l. 1 that these witnesses are not singular. Furthermore, indications do not avail the notary, for recourse is to be had to them in case of doubt, not when express falsity is proven, because truth excludes every presumption. For conjectures have place in uncertain, not certain, matters, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. continuus, § cum ita; and ff. de re militari, l. non omnes, § a barbaris. To the contrary, it seems that the said witnesses are singular; for they testify in such a way that one does not know of the other, each saying only of himself that he was not present. For it is so that whenever a witness testifies regarding a privation of sense—for example, I did not see, I did not hear—it necessarily follows that he is singular in his statement. For these witnesses do not testify regarding a negation of act, namely, that the contract was not celebrated; but only regarding a negation of sense, because they say that they were not present, that is, that they did not hear nor see. And that these witnesses are singular is expressed in extra de electione, c. cum dilecti, in fine.

It follows, therefore, since the said witnesses are singular, that we are only in half-proof. But it is so that half-proof can be rebutted by contrary indications, to such an extent that it does not even suffice for torture, as is usually noted. C. ad l. Iul. maiest. l. Si quis. What, however, here are strong indications in favor of the notary, appears from the continuous possession of the aforementioned purchaser from the day the said instrument was executed: because he who has possessed for so long a time, with the knowledge of the former owner, is presumed to have the alleged title, as fully stated in the law and noted in ff. de usu. l. Cum de in rem verso. and C. communi divi. l. Penult. And let the judge weigh these matters, who has the duty to judge. Likewise, this supports what is noted in Spec. de instru. edi. §. Nunc dicendum. ver. Quid si dominum attestationes publicantur.

† Moreover, for an instrument that is public and solemn in its form, there is a strong presumption in its favor, unless the contrary is fully proven. An affirmative claim is one that is fully proven, not a negative one, as is noted in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Diem proferre*, § *Si plures*, unless witnesses substantiate the negative and provide its cause, so that they are in agreement, as is noted in the Code, *De errore advocatorum*, in the final law. Furthermore, the remoteness of time contributes to this.

† For the jurist states that consideration must be given to the passage of time: for when an ancient matter or fact is being proved, more credence is to be given to a written instrument than to witnesses; otherwise, if the fact is recent, as is stated in the aforementioned verse, "What if one," at the end of the Digest title On Proof; the law Census; and according to Cynus, in the Code title On Written Instruments; the law Emancipation; and the law It is said.

† That oblivion is presumed from the passage of ten years. D. de usucap. l. furtum, §. si, together with the following law; and note Inst. de usucap. §. quod autem. Moreover, if we were to say that the instrument is suspect and that torture should be resorted to, if it so seemed to the judge, both parties and the said witnesses ought to be tortured: especially if they were persons of low status and suspect, and the notary is a man of known authority, as in D. de falsis, l. ubi nam testes. Those who testify against an instrument must be free from all suspicion and all exception, as in l. optimam, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione. Moreover, the accuser, who delayed for so long, is presumed to have delayed with malicious intent, in order to deprive his adversary of the opportunity to prove his case, and to await the death of the witnesses who could confirm the instrument, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. in Aquilia si deletum, and C. de usuris pupillorum, l. si. But tortures in some cases ought to be rather terrors with a certain affliction of the flesh. In some cases they ought to go up to, but not including, the destruction of the body, as in l. 1, D. de quaestionibus. Solution: This depends greatly on the discretion of the judge, although we say that the beginning [of proof] by two witnesses is regularly not rejected, when others are described who can corroborate the instrument. Extravagantes, de fide instrumentorum, c. cum Ioannes; and fully noted Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. item verborum; and C. de fide instrumentorum, l. in exercendis. The statutes concerning accusations of forgery should also be carefully examined, as well as the inscription of the accuser. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a fief can be alienated or divided by one of the co-owners to the prejudice of a third co-owner.
2. A fief is a usufruct attached to the person.
3. One having a right in a thing, or in expectation, cannot be prejudiced.
4. Whether the right of accretion applies to fiefs held jointly by legal connection.
5. One cannot confer a benefit from another’s property, but only from one’s own.
6. A verbal investiture suffices.
7. The passage of time does not harm one who is not negligent.
body: In the name of Christ. Lord Thomas de Scarampis of Asten. Three quarteria of the place of Montis Alti, which place is of the property and domain of the community: retaining the usufruct, and retaining the dominions, he handed over unpaid to Lord Matthew, his brother and co-participant of the fief, although the said Lord Thomas had other brothers similarly co-participants of the fief. This Lord Thomas died without sons.

† It is asked whether the said conveyance of the property to an insolvent party prejudices other agnates in the right of succession, given that it is an ancient fief, or in the right of accrual descending from the nature of the fief; and it seems that it does. For, just as a division of feudal things and of men holding fiefs can be made by dividing the territorial jurisdiction, and as jurisdiction adheres to the territory, as in c. Imperiale, § Praeterea, de prohibitione alienationis feudorum, by Federic, not only when it is by necessity: for example, when one is provoked to division by the other: as in l. Et ideo, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, but also when it is made by mere agreement and the will of the co-feudatories: because it would be unjust to compel anyone to perpetual co-ownership, as in ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Si non sortem, § Si centum, and ff. de communi dividundo, l. In hoc iudicio, § Si conveniant. Moreover, from the nature of co-ownership in act follows division in potentiality: therefore, just as co-ownership is of the nature of the fief among co-heirs, and the subsequent division, and thus is permitted, because it is of the nature, this is posited by the gloss in C. de familia erciscunda, l. Si familia. Hence, from a similar case, I will say that among co-heirs of fiefs, any alienation is permitted which is due to the necessity of litigation or of the household, as in ff. de legatis 1, l. Peto, § Praedium, and ff. de legatis 3, § 11, § Si rem. Moreover, this seems to be expressed in the title Per quos fiat investitura et per quos recipiatur, C. l. Sed et res, in the text there: "but also the thing whose alienation is prohibited is not granted even by benefit, unless to an agnate, the nearest; and the nearest agnate is said to be he whom no one precedes, even if there are others of the same degree." As in Inst. de legatis agnatorum successione, § Proximus, and l. Qui duos in principio, ff. de rebus dubiis. To the same effect is c. 1, de alienatione feudorum: a paternal fief cannot be alienated to any nearest agnate. And this, since it is done by the authority of custom, should not be retracted by a supervening case: what is lawful by law is valid, otherwise contracting parties would be deceived by the authority of the law: which is an inconvenience, as in C. de his qui velut aetatem impediunt, l. 1. Moreover, because the thing is made alienable, as in ff. de legatis 3, l. Pauper, § Quindecim. Moreover, in those having a symbol, the transfer is easy; to this effect is what is noted by Guil. de Cuneo, ff. de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, § Sed si pluribus. Moreover, and if some revocation were granted to other agnates, they should restore the price to that agnate who bought in good faith by right permitted, as in c. Titius, si de feudo fuerit controversia; nor should fruits received be imputed in that price, as in ff. de rei venditione, l. Emptor, in principio. To the contrary it is proved: it is manifestly certain that a good argument is from what is the case at a time. As in ff. de testamento militis, l. Miles in haeredem, § Ei, quia diximus. But he who has a part of the thing cannot transfer the whole thing, but only his part, as in ff. de legatis 1, l. Servi electione, § Cum fundus, and ff. de acquisitione haereditatis, l. Duo fratres, and ff. de acquisitione haereditatis, Doctor, l. Traditio. Therefore, the same if he has a part of the time, because after the time pertaining to himself he cannot dispose of the thing, as in C. de legatis, l. Penultima, and ff. de pignoratitia actione, l. Lex vectigali, and ff. de pactis, l. Epistola, § Si. Since, therefore, this alienator had no right except during his life, therefore after his death, when he died without children, he could not alienate. And this is what that vulgar rule said in the usages of fiefs: the right of the grantor ends, and the right of the successor is not extended. To this effect is the aforementioned l. Peto, § Praedium, and Inst. de usufructu, § Finitur. For

† A fief is a kind of usufruct, which adheres to the person and is not transmitted, except insofar as the custom of the fief provides. As stated in the Digest, *De nova*, l. *Si usufructus*. Moreover, if a more distant agnate, and not the nearest, had accepted this alienation, it would be revoked, as is clear in the aforementioned § *Sed et res*, from the contrary sense of the word *proximioris*. And in c. 1, *De alienatione feudi patris*.

And the reason is that the nearest agnate could not be prejudiced, neither in the thing itself nor in the hope thereof, since the hope is due by right of contract, as in l. 1, D. si quid in fraudem patroni. Likewise, the lord ought not to have any other vassal than the one to whom it is due by the nature of the fief. Likewise, the subjects ought not to have any other lord, as is read and noted in D. de fideicommissis libertatibus, l. inuitus.

† Moreover, the next agnate is united by a legal bond, from which alone, and not from a verbal one, the right of accretion in fiefs proceeds, as in c. Cum vero Corradus, Qui feudum dare possit. Although the contrary rule is stated in legacies, ff. De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Mulieri et Titio. And the reason for the difference is: because the legal bond in fiefs is called the nature of the fief; therefore, no feudatory can prejudice another in this right of accretion. For if Titius has the right of accretion, then Seius is in this respect more remote. Indeed, not so much more remote as none at all, because he is irrelevant with regard to this accreting portion. Hence, concluding from the first to the last, it necessarily seems that one must say that the act of the said D. Thomas could not prejudice the rights of others, nor does the argument from gratification hold.

† because one may confer a benefit from his own property, not from another’s, as stated in D. de legatis 2, l. si quis servum, § si inter duos; and D. ad Sillanum, l. si qui in gravi, § si cum omnes; and C. de secundis nuptiis, auth. lucrum hoc. Moreover, it is certain that no one may make a gift of another’s property. Nor does it matter that the act was done lawfully, for it was lawful only for the time being, not perpetually, as in D. locati conducti, l. si quis domum, § huic. Supporting the foregoing are the rules of law, which must be observed even in fiefs, unless a contrary provision is specifically established, as in c. Ubertus, § strenuus, de feudi cognitione. For the rules of law dictate that things subject to restitution by operation of law or by the testator’s disposition cannot be alienated to the prejudice of the person to whom restitution is due, as in Auth. de nuptiis, § quoniam infirmas, col. 3; and C. communia de legatis, auth. res quae. Thus it is with fiefs, insofar as they are subject to restitution in the person of the agnates. For each person ought to be content with his own right and not seek a thing belonging to another’s right, as in C. finium regundorum, l. si constiterit.

† Nor does the lapse of a year stand in the way, because he had himself invested within the year. For a verbal investiture suffices in this matter, so that he cannot be accused of negligence through silence. For

† He who is not negligent is not prejudiced by the passage of time, as is stated and noted in the Authentica de appellationibus, § 1, Collatio 8; and in the Extravagant de electione, chapter Eis quibus; and in the chapter Quia diversitatem, de concessione praebendarum. And even if no law or constitution were to say this, natural reason dictates it, which gives the correct response to all matters, as in the Digest, si certum petatur, law Si me et Titium. And scarcely is anything found contrary to natural reason and discretion that does not sting the conscience: as is noted in the Digest, de triticario, law In hac, in the great gloss. Moreover, form is nothing other than an impression in matter: just as the figure of Caesar impressed in iron, which the heir cannot alter, since it is derived from its origin in perpetuity. Argument from the Digest, ad legem Falcidiam, law In ratione, § Si filio; Digest, de verbis obligatis, law 2, § Ex his, with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The testator left five hundred to his daughter already born, and five hundred to the one yet to be born, on the condition that if it should happen that the said daughter already born and the one yet to be born should die before they were married or entered religion, then the said legacies should be distributed to the poor. The posthumous child is not born; the daughter already born dies while still a ward. It is asked whether the said legacies are due, and which ones, and in what amount.
2. Whether an institution in a certain sum, declared pro non scripto, is said to be pro non scripto of the inheritance, of the legacy, or of both.
3. Whether that which is declared pro non scripto accrues with the burden.
4. Whether a fideicommissum can be substituted for a ward.
5. Whether the father of a minor can leave a fideicommissum from the legitimate heir of the ward.
body: In the name of Christ. The testator, having a single daughter born as a minor, left her five hundred by way of institution; and believing his wife to be pregnant, he likewise left five hundred by way of institution to the posthumous child about to be born; and he instituted his natural brother as universal heir; and he appended this clause: “Furthermore, I wish, establish, and ordain that if it happens that the aforementioned Maffina, my daughter, and the child to be born from the womb of the aforementioned wife, if she is pregnant, as above, should die before they are married or enter religion, that then, and in that case, the aforementioned legacies made to them be distributed and disbursed to the poor of Christ by the undersigned distributors named below for the remedy and merit of my soul and of my deceased ones, etc., as is more fully contained in the will.” Now it has happened that the posthumous child was not born, and that the aforementioned Maffina, who was born, died in minority; it is asked whether the aforementioned one thousand florins are to be distributed and disbursed to the poor in whole, in part, or not at all?

† And it appears that they do not come under any dispensation for the poor: and this is derived from the force of the conjunction, and I argue thus: the putative posthumous child was conjoined to the said Maffina, already born, by these words, “if it should happen that the said Maffina, and the one to be born, should die, before they were married, or entered religion.” But it is of the nature of a conjunction that it requires the truth of the union. And the reason is, because it is taken from the whole conjoined, and not from any part, as in D. de cond. inst. l. si heredi plures. Moreover, in this substitution a condition was appended which, as far as the words are concerned, requires that both should die. But he who is not born cannot die, as is noted in D. de man. testa. l. qui duos. Therefore, at least as far as the legacy to the said posthumous child is concerned, the legacy fails as if not written. Then I argue thus: what is deemed not written goes to the conjoined, or substituted heir, without burden, as in C. de cad. tol. §. in primo. Therefore, the legacy to the said posthumous child accrued to the sister without burden, and consequently the heir of the sister, i.e., the uncle, is not bound to these five hundred. Nor does it obstruct if it is said that either the legacy goes as not written to the conjoined, or substituted heir, and then without burden: or it is not written as to the inheritance, and then with burden, as in D. de leg. 1. l. ciuitatibus. §. Lucius.

† And here it must be observed whether an institution of a certain quantity declared pro non scripto is to be considered pro non scripto as an inheritance, or as a legacy, or as something intermediate between these. And indeed, that it is to be considered pro non scripto as an inheritance, because it is by the law of institution. On the contrary, that it is pro non scripto as a legacy, as in C. de her. inst. l. quoties. On the contrary, that it is intermediate between these, or neither: and thus this case is not found determined in the law.

Whether the property is redeemed with the burden or not. And in case of doubt, one should adhere rather to the interpretation favoring liberation than to that favoring obligation, as stated in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Fauorabiliores*. Unless one argues against the favor of the last will and the pious cause. Argument from the law *Locum*, in the beginning, Digest, *De usufructu*; and Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *In testamentis*. But certainly, regarding this question, it appears to be a case covered by the law. For it must be known that the substitute was born, being born under the condition if she shall be born and shall die. But these words encompass the case even if she is not born, as in the Digest, *De ventre in possessionem*, law *Qui ventri*, where in the aforementioned legacy the one born succeeded to the posthumous child as if vulgarly substituted. But it is so that the one vulgarly substituted to the posthumous child must pay the legacies of the posthumous child. The case is found in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Ab hereditate*, section *Si*. Furthermore, it must be known that no legitime is owed to a posthumous child who is not born, as in the last law, Digest, *De adsignatione liberto*. Hence, from the person of the posthumous child, nothing can be deducted from the said legacy, but the whole must be distributed to the poor. Briefly, I consider this part true with regard to the testator’s will, as in the Digest, *Ad Trebellianam*, law *Heredes mei*, section *Cum ita*.

† However, it must be considered regarding the testator’s power, that he cannot substitute by fideicommissum to a son in his legitima, in which he does not hold any burden, even for pious causes, as C. de fideic. authen. hoc amplius; and ff. de vulg. substi. l. cohæredi, §. cum filii. And it is expressly clear in c. si pater, a contrario sensu, de test., lib. 6. And see the note in c. Rayn., §. in eo vero, extra de test., in the gloss which begins: “no. ergo.” Although a father may make a will for an impubes son, and make a pupillary substitution, as d. §. cum filio; and in the same title, l. sed et si plures, §. ad substitutos; yet here he did not make a pupillary substitution: because it was made by oblique words, and in a certain thing, namely in one thousand florins, as ff. ad Treb. l. cogi, §. generaliter; and there by Dy. and Bar. And that the said substitution, in the manner in which it was made, is fideicommissary, is a case in C. de insti. et substi. l. generaliter, in the beginning. The objection from ff. de vulg. et substi. l. cohæredum, §. si, where a constitution in a certain thing is drawn to the whole, and is direct, does not stand: because there he directly substituted pupillarily; here it is oblique, and by fideicommissum, since neither were the words direct, nor was the condition of pupillary substitution, which would expire at puberty, added. And therefore, if the said one thousand florins do not exceed the third part of all the goods, which is the legitima of the said Maffina, the said legacy ought not to be distributed among the poor. But if there were anything above the legitima, that ought to be distributed. But here there is doubt, because the law says that a fideicommissum ought to be substituted to a pupillus, as ff. de leg. primo, l. quod fideicommiss. Cyn. examines this passage in C. de inofficio. testamen. l. ex tribus. But I answer to the said l. quod fideicommissum: either a fideicommissum is imposed on an impubes, and it is not valid in the legitima; or on the heir of the impubes; and then it is so. But according to what is proposed by the heir, who had been substituted to the impubes, nothing is disposed. Hence the burden remains, which is not valid. And therefore he who succeeds the impubes intestate to the legitima of the impubes is not bound, because the legitima is due to the son, even against the testator’s will, as C. de inoffi. test. l. quoniam in prioribus. But this one, who succeeds the impubes, is the father’s brother, who is not burdened in the restitution of this legitima: for if he had been burdened, he would be bound in his own person, as d. l. quod fideicommiss. I demonstrate: if the said heir of the testator were understood to be requested, with another, for example the mother of the impubes, being heir, he is bound to the mother as heir of the pupilla in that right of transmission, and to the poor in the others, with no right of another fideicommissum. And thus, burdened in one thousand, he would be bound to two thousand, which is impossible. It will therefore be concluded that the said general heir is burdened to no one else than the pupilla; and the pupilla to the poor, whom she could not burden in the third part due by the law of nature. And therefore the aforementioned opinion is true by the necessity of law, and it holds. ff. de lega. 3, l. si fuerit; and l. si sit. It is certain that the daughter transmits the legitima bequeathed to her to her heir: because in transmitting she is considered a legatee, as noted by Bar. in l. ex facto, ff. de hære. inst. It supports what is noted in ff. de ac. et obli. l. is, cui. It does not obstruct c. cum tibi, extra de testi.: because there no other universal heir was instituted. Moreover, the word “distribuatur” (let it be distributed), added to a certain quantity, imports a legacy, not a pupillary substitution, as if the testator said: “if my son should die in pupillary age, I wish one thousand to be distributed to the poor.” For this is not a direct pupillary substitution.

And when it is asked whether a father of an underage child can leave a fideicommissum to the legitimate heir of the underage child, whether such heir is legitimate according to the form of the common law or according to the form of municipal law, it must be said that either the fideicommissum is left to him as the heir of the underage child, and under the appellative name of heir: and this is permitted, as stated in the aforementioned law *Quod fideicommissum* and in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Si sic*; or the fideicommissum is left by the underage child himself, and not by the heir of the underage child: and this is not permitted, as stated in the Code, *De inofficiosis testamentis*, law *Ex tribus*, according to Bartolus, because it is noted in the aforementioned law *Quod fideicommissum*; and the reason for the difference is that in the first case the heir of the underage child is found to be immediately burdened expressly in his own person, not in the person of the underage child; but in the second case he cannot be bound in his own person, but only in the person of the underage child. And therefore he cannot be said to be burdened in the legitime of the underage child, because he is burdened in nothing, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law 1, at the end, and in the Digest, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, law *Cohaeredi*, section *Cum filiae*. And this is the truth, omitting circumlocutions: I know this to be most evident to those who have to judge, because they are most expert in the law, as I believe. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a condemned man may restore the dowry to his wife after condemnation.
2. The defect of litigiousness has no place where a personal action is brought: and especially where an action is brought for vindicta.
3. The cause of the dowry takes precedence over obligations arising from delict.
4. A donation propter nuptias takes precedence over the fiscus.
5. The defect of litigiousness has no place where a personal action is brought, or by the office of the judge.
6. Whether a creditor from a delict may offer the dowry and demand that it be handed over to him, given that the husband condemned can restore the dowry itself?
7. Whether goods are tacitly obligated after the promulgation of the condemnation.
8. The estimation is made by the office of the judge.
body: not of the thing. In the name of Christ. A husband, condemned for a delict to a certain stranger in a large sum, which penalty would absorb all his patrimony, after the said condemnation gave to his wife, as unpaid dowry, certain estates: because he had begun to misuse his property.

† First, it is asked whether he can do this after condemnation: and it seems that he cannot, because his goods are affected in two ways: namely, by the defect of being a litigious person; and, what is stronger, by the condemnatory sentence: therefore, the administration of such goods does not belong to the aforementioned husband, and consequently he cannot contract regarding them, as in C. de litigiosis, auth. litigiosis, and l. chirographis, ff. de admi. tut. Moreover, the husband cannot impede the execution of the sentence pronounced against him: because the said sentence has ready execution; but the wife, for the dowry, does not have ready execution, but must offer a libellus, contest the litigation, and proceed to sentence, as in ff. solu. ma. l. si cum dotem, §. eo autem tempore, and C. de senten. quae sine certa quantitate, l. si. Moreover, that the husband misuses his substance must be proven before the restitution of the dowry is made, as in C. de col. auth. quod locum. Moreover, the judge, having omitted this proof, could not order the said dowry to be restored; therefore, neither could a private person, i.e., the husband. Furthermore, the law expressly states how this restitution to the condemned husband must be made by the fiscus, as in ff. so. ma. l. si marito publico iudi. damnato; therefore, not by the husband, because the obligation and payment have been transferred to the fiscus, as in ff. de fideiussor. l. inter eos, §. bonis, and C. ad l. iul. de vi, l. tutoris tui. Solution: it must be said that either the goods of this condemned person are confiscated universally: and then the fiscus must pay the dowry; and the husband cannot restore it, who is exiled naked and leaves no goods in the city, as in ff. de noua, l. quotiens, §. fi, ff. de capi. dimi. l. tutelas, §. si libertate; or the goods are not confiscated to the fiscus, but he is condemned only to a private person, or even to the fiscus in a certain quantity, not in the universality of his goods: and then the said husband could make the said payment in good faith according to the measure of the dowry, because he did not cease to be the debtor of the wife.

† Nor does the objection based on the vice of litigiousness hold, for it has no place where a personal action is brought; and especially where the action is brought for vindication, as is read and noted by Guillaume and others in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. abstinendi. Moreover, this alienation is necessary and therefore permitted, as in D. fam. haer., l. alienationes. Furthermore, it was not necessary to require proof on this point, namely that he would misuse his property, for proof ought to be given to the judge, not to a private party, as in C. de eden., l. is, apud quem. Moreover, this was notorious by virtue of the judgment, and thus did not require proof, as in D. de actionibus empt., l. emptorem. Moreover, a husband is not prohibited from acknowledging good faith, as in D. mandati, l. quintus; and in D. de admi. tu., l. quotiens, § sicut.

† Moreover, it is certain that, on account of the dowry, preference is given to obligations arising from delict, as in Extra de pignoribus, c. Ex literis; and Extra de consuetudine, c. Ex parte, as is read and noted in ff. de bonis damnatorum, l. Quinque legibus.

† Moreover, a donation propter nuptias takes precedence over the fisc, as stated in C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. res, and in D. eodem, l. sed interim. Furthermore, a husband may exchange the dowry with his wife for money in lieu of land, as provided in D. de iure dotium, l. si constante. In this donation, there is contained a certain exchange of what remains unpaid, if this is advantageous to the dowry, as in D. de solutionibus, l. qui res, in principio; or a certain tacit purchase and sale, as in D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur, l. si; or it is a title that accrues to the person who receives the thing alienated, rather than to the contract itself, as in D. pro soluto, l. 1, and throughout. And I do not care how we interpret this,

† Since the defect of the contract of the litigious person does not apply where there is a personal action or the office of the judge, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, *De consuetudine*, c. *Cum*; M. Ferrariensis. And this regarding the office of the judge is not found elsewhere except in Innocentius. Likewise, on account of the prerogative of the dowry. Codex, *De litigiosis*, l. 1, at the end.

The following question arises: assuming that the payment of an unsatisfied debt is valid, whether the aforementioned creditor, on account of a delict, may offer the said wife the dowry and the donation, and demand that they be delivered to him. It appears that he may, because goods are tacitly bound for a wrongful act after the condemnation of the defendant, according to the true opinion, as stated in D. de pactis, l. rescriptum; C. de poenis fiscalibus, creditores preferri, l. unica, lib. 10. Hence, a creditor who holds a mortgage has the right to make an offer, as stated in C. si antiquior creditor, l. final; and D. qui potiores in pignore habeantur, l. mulier.

It must be said that a private person’s goods are not tacitly bound on account of a delict; and therefore, if he does not possess them, he has no right of offer, as is noted in C. de solutionibus, l. obsignatione. This applies after the goods have become the creditor’s, except insofar as the value of the goods exceeds that of the dowry and donation, as in l. si, C. de iure dominii impetrando, and C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, §. licentia. But before the goods had become the woman’s, the right of offer would have had place. D. de solutionibus, l. qui dotem, §. 1. And it is at the woman’s election, when she has become owner, to make up the just price, or to receive the dowry and donation, and to relinquish the things, as in D. quae in fraudem patroni, l. 1, §. quis in fraudem. And thus the answer is given to all the questions asked.

† Moreover, the valuation shall not be made by option, nor by a third party sent by the father to the father, but at the discretion of the judge, as is fully known in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether partners in all property are bound to redeem one of them captured by the enemy from the common assets? And what if one captive is taken by a servant of the said brothers, if presented to only one, is he considered common to the other brothers?
2. Whether a ransom imposed by one who captures a prisoner and consigns him to another is to be shared with the other brothers.
body: In the name of Christ. There were three brothers, all

† Partners in goods and comrades-in-arms: one was captured and ransomed from the common patrimony; then the other brother was captured and agreed to a price for his release under oath, according to the custom of arms. They divided the goods; after the division, it is demanded that the other brothers contribute to paying said promise from the common patrimony. The question is what is the law: and it seems that they ought not to contribute, first, because said partnership does not seem lawful: for a partnership in shameful and wicked crimes is prohibited, as in D. pro socio, l. quod autem; and what is shameful is whatever is taken by force: for since it establishes a certain relationship among men, it is an abomination for a man to lie in wait for another man, as in l. ut vim, D. de iure et iur. On the contrary, it seems that they should contribute, because since both are men of arms, one cannot impute guilt to the other, as in C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. in aream, and C. de haereditate, l. quoniam, § inter se. There is another reason, because just as he desired to receive contribution for himself, so conversely he ought to contribute, as in D. pro socio, l. quod non. There is a third reason, because common error makes law; but if there is error in these matters of arms, it is a common error. There is another reason, because when we speak of arms, we must speak according to the usage of arms: and every day we see such partnerships contracted, and we ought not to assume with closed eyes that they are valid. Moreover, if the war were lawful, there would be no doubt of law or fact. For it would undoubtedly be valid, as fully noted by Innocentius, Extra, de iureiurando, c. sicuti. Therefore, assuming this, I say that said brothers are bound to contribute to paying said ransom, as in D. de conditione indebiti, l. frater a fratre, vers. idque maxime, and vers. igitur. Nor does it matter that this was not mentioned in the division, as in C. de collatione, l. si soror. The following question is: a certain familiar of said brothers, while he was with one of them, captured one

† a captive, whom he presented to one of them. The one to whom he was presented exacted the *talia*: whether he is bound to share it with his brothers, and it seems that he is not, because the one to whom he was presented and who imposed the *talia* ought to obtain the entire benefit. The contrary is true: because that which is acquired through a common slave or a common agent is acquired for both. And once the acquisition has been initiated, the slave cannot make the condition of the master worse, as C. *per quas personas*; l. *si*, C. *de acquisitione possessionis*; l. *si*, C. *de pace*; l. *servus*; and l. *ultima*, ff. *de stipulationibus servorum*. And this is the truth by reason of partnership, because they were partners, as is stated, in all goods. The objection in column 10, *de fratribus de novo bene investitis*, c. *si duo fratres*, vers. *quod si cum equis*, where it was asked concerning that which was acquired with common horses and arms, is not common, does not apply, because there it speaks of a fief, in which the will of the lord is considered, so that he may not have another vassal than the one he intended to have. Moreover, horses and arms lack sense, and therefore nothing is acquired through them, but a slave or a retainer has sense, and through his consent something is acquired for the masters. And thus it does not obstruct. I conclude that the said *talia* ought to be shared, just as I said on the contrary regarding expenses. For the same rule applies to opposites, as ff. *de regulis iuris*, l. *secundum naturam*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A compromise was made among three persons, with the stipulation that if two were in agreement, the third should have no place; now, all three have concurred in rendering judgment: whether the award is valid, and whether the useful is vitiated by the useless.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A compromise was made to three arbitrators, one of whom was a minor brother; this was done with the provision that the sentence of two should be valid, and that where two were in agreement, the third should have no place. All three pronounced in agreement. It is asked whether the award is valid, and it seems that it is not, because an incompetent person joined to a competent one vitiates the act, as in Extra, De officio delegati, c. Cum super abbatia. Moreover, because although the two had the power, they did not wish to use it, since two of them would not have pronounced otherwise without the third. For power which one does not wish to use does not confirm one’s act, as in Digest, De fideiussoribus, l. Si puer. And the sentence is not valid regarding the mind of the judging party, as in l. Qualem, in principio, Digest, De arbitris. To the contrary is the truth, because no one is presumed in doubt to choose a way to impugn his own judgments, as in l. 3, Digest, De militum testamento. And because a useful person is not vitiated by an useless person, unless something else intervenes, such as a defect of form, as in Digest, De arbitris, l. Pedius, § In seruum, together with the following law, and l. 1, § Idem Pomponius, Digest, De falsis tutoribus; Auth. Non obstat, c. Cum super, because there he would not have pronounced otherwise except with the incompetent colleague, and this appears clearly in the text. Moreover, because there it speaks of delegated judges who represent one person, namely the delegator, as in Digest, De officio eius cui mandata est iurisdictio, l. 1, § Qui mandata; and therefore there the useful is vitiated by the useless placed in the act, because it concerns one and the same person, as in Digest, De verbis obligatio, l. 1, § Cum adicit. Furthermore, here in the compromise it was expressly stated that where two were in agreement, the third should have no place; therefore, in fact, the compromise was made to the just brother, the minor; and thus he is not so much incompetent as nonexistent, because outside the compromise; whose statement or act does not vitiate, because it is irrelevant, extraneous, and remote from the act, as in Digest, De legibus, l. Si duobus, § Haeres. And so I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a document drawn up by a notary is considered public against the party himself when it is written in his own hand.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain document of a certain notary is found to have been made in the notary’s own matter, in the form that follows; and the sign of the said notary appears engraved at the beginning of the said document, the tenor of which, on the side, is as follows: namely, in the year 1285, indiction 6, on the 25th day of the month of April. I, John, son of the late Nicholas Jacobutii of Sarzana, have had and received, and confess to have had and received, from the persons written below the quantities of money written below, for the purpose of investing them, or having them invested, in one ship together with the officials necessary therein and their wages, in the presence of the witnesses written below. First, namely, from Master Peter, physician of the late Lord John of Sarzana, one hundred gold florins; from Franchinello, son of the late Peter of Sarzana, two hundred gold florins; and from the brothers of the late Ser James of Sarzana, two hundred gold florins. Renouncing the exception of money not had, not received, and not counted, regarding the above-mentioned quantity of money. Promising to invest the said quantities, or have them invested, in one ship; or to give and repay them to the said Master Peter, Franchinello, and Federico within the next coming month, under the penalty of double the whole amount, should I wish to contravene this, by express pact, that for the below-mentioned quantities, at the instance of the above-mentioned persons, if the promises are not kept, I may be sued both in rem and in personam, in Genoa, Pisa, Florence, Lucca, Savona, and in all places, and under any magistrate, both ecclesiastical and secular; removing from myself the authority to allege any place or judge as suspect; but I wish to be able to be sued both in rem and in personam under him and in that same place, as if that place had been specially appointed for payment, or if I had made this promise present there. Renouncing all law and aid of laws introduced against the below-written, or against any of the above-written. In testimony of all the above premises, I have here appended my customary sign of my notaryship. Done in Sarzana, in the apothecary’s shop held by James, son of the late Ser Thomas of Sarzana; in the presence of the said James, Franchinello Vande of Sarzana, James, son of the late Levinii of the Castle of Sarzana, witnesses called and requested for this purpose by Lord John, son of the late Cibaldini, judge, etc.

† It is asked whether the above-mentioned writing is valid or not, and it seems that it is not valid, because the notary must be requested, as in the Authentica de tabellio, §. nos. But no one can request himself: because no one gives a mandate to himself, as in D. de arbitris, l. pen. Also, because no one can act in the capacity of two persons, unless in another’s name, as in D. de pactis, l. si plures. Also, because no one can be judge in his own case, as in C. ne quis in sua causa iudex sit, l. vnica, and D. de iudiciis, omnes iudices, l. qui iurisdictioni. To the contrary is the truth: for in matters of voluntary jurisdiction, one may exercise both public and private office, as is fully read and noted in D. de adoptionibus, l. si consul. And one must abide by one’s own writing against oneself, as in D. de testamento tutelae, l. ex sententia, ver. nec admittendam, and D. de contrahendis tabulis, l. non putavit, §. si quis sua manu. Also, in this instrument all things are present which ought to be present, as appears in the instrument itself, as in the Authentica ut praeponatur, nomen imperatoris, in principio, and noted in Inst. de pupillis iudicibus, and C. de accessoribus, l. si. Nor does it matter that he was not requested: because rather he was requested by the contracting party with him: and it suffices sometimes that one of the contracting parties request the notary, as says the gloss, noted in the said §. nos autem. Also, since a writing intervenes, the presence of the parties is presumed: and all things are presumed to have been done solemnly, as in Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. si scriptum, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1, D. de verborum obligatione, l. sciendum, with its common material. From these it follows that the said instrument, as public, is to be followed and observed in its force. Nor does it matter that the said writing is not written on parchment, but on paper. For even on paper a public writing may be written, as says Speculum, and is proved in l. 1, in principio, D. de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas. I nevertheless advise that it be first inquired whether it is in his own hand or not. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The letters of the prince are not always to be executed, but a response must be written to the prince.
body: In the name of Christ. Lord Bailardin, with the support of the lords of La Scala, began to hold two villages, from which he exacted tithes by virtue of an investiture from the Bishop of Vicenza. On the other hand, the Bishop of Verona claims that the said tithes belong to his right and are within his territory. While the lawsuit concerning this matter was pending, letters were issued by the secular Prince against the peasants, ordering them to pay the said tithes to the heirs of the said Lord Bailardin, without any mention being made of the pendency of the lawsuit. By virtue of these letters, a command was issued to them to make payment. It is requested that this command be revoked as having been issued de facto and without proper cognizance of the case. The question is: what is the law? Assuming that the Prince has jurisdiction in this matter.

† And for clarity, it must be premised that sometimes the prince commands something to be ordered before the cause is cognized; and then, before the command is issued, the cause ought to be cognized, as in C. si contra ius, vel utilitatem publicam, l. si cognitio. And if it were contained in the prince’s letters that the cause should not be cognized, it would be presumed that the letters did not emanate from the prince’s conscience, as in c. 2, extra de rescri. Sometimes they emanate after the cause has been cognized; and then the prince’s letters must be obeyed, and execution carried out, since through the cognition of the cause it appears that execution is to be performed; otherwise the decrees would be illusory; and therefore the executor does not cognize the cause, because it has already been cognized, as in ff. de iudicibus, l. si prior, in principio, and ex de re iudicata, c. de caetero.

Furthermore, I premise that if no mention is made in the rescript of lis pendens, the rescript does not hold in effect, because it is presumed to have been obtained by concealment, as in C. ut lite pendente nulli liceat imperare supplicationem, l. 2, and extra de rescriptis, c. caeterum.

From these things it appears that, since it is not necessary, one ought not to command in writing that the order of law be disregarded; and such a command, without cause, is not to be executed, because the Pope says: either you reverently fulfill our mandate, or by your letters you allege a reasonable cause why you cannot fulfill it, because it is sustained that, if you do not, something false has been suggested to us by malicious insinuation, as in extra de rescriptis, s. quando facit, eo. tit., c. super literas, and c. plerunque, with many similar authorities.

Therefore, I advise that execution not be made without cognition of the cause; but rather that a reply be written to the prince, as in no. ff. de re iudicata, l. Neratius. But if, through cognition of the cause, it is established that the said Lord Bailardinus was in possession with a title obtained from a possessor, the peasants cannot subtract the pension from his heirs until judgment is rendered on the ownership, as in C. de agricolis et censitis, l. litibus, lib. 11, where this point is determined. And it supports this, Inst. de interdictis, § commodum; extra de electione, c. querelam. The same applies if these peasants had promised to pay, or had acknowledged themselves to be debtors, as in ff. de conditione indebiti, l. si urbana. But mere payment alone does not make one a debtor, especially if it is irregular, as in l. si certis annis, and l. cum de in rem verso, de exceptione doli, and ff. de officio proconsulis, l. observare, § si.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is not an injury to say, "You are lying," in one's own defense.
2. By statute, it may be provided that the oath of the accuser shall be believed.
body: In the name of Christ. The statute of Pavia provides that if anyone utters insulting words to the daciarii, namely on account of their office, he shall be punished with a fine of 25 pounds, and the daciarius’s oath shall be believed regarding the insulting words. Now, a daciarius said to a certain guest that he had defrauded the tax; the latter replied to the daciarius that the daciarius was lying through his throat. The daciarius seeks to have him punished for the fraud, and furthermore accuses him of insulting words. The fraud is not fully proven; the insulting words are proven by the oath of the accuser.

† Now it is asked what the law is, and it must be said that he ought to be absolved from the libel of fraud, as in C. de edendo, l. qui accusare; ff. de probat., l. quotiens, § qui dolo. For since the statute does not provide how fraud is to be proved, the common law must be followed, as in C. de noxalibus, l. 2; and extra de consuetud., c. cum dilectus.

But there is doubt concerning the libel of defamation. For a statute may provide that the oath of the accuser shall be believed, as noted by Jacobus de Arezzo and Cynus in l. 1, C. si adversus libertatem; see also C. unde vi, l. si quando; and what Innocentius notes in Extra, quod metus causa, c. fi. In which laws it is provided that in certain cases the oath shall be believed, having regard to the quality of the oath, and especially if there were two daciarii taking the oath. Argument: Extra, de probat., c. quoniam contra falsam. It therefore appears that the accused ought to be condemned for the defamatory words. On the contrary, it appears that these words are not defamatory words, but repel the defamation, because it is lawful for me to say, if anyone calls me a thief or a fraudster, "you lie," unless he proves that he is telling the truth. D. de procuratoribus, l. quae omnia vero responsum; and there by Butrinteus. The daciarius was he who uttered the defamatory words, as D. de iniuriis, l. item apud Labeonem, § conditione. And therefore the said causes are so connected that one must either be condemned in both or absolved in both. For the absolution from the fraud omitted requires that the daciarius lied, and therefore it was lawful to say to him, "you lie," as D. de iniuriis, l. eum qui nocentem, in principio; and D. de bonis libertorum, l. qui cum maior, § libertus. If it is not therefore defamation to speak the truth in defense of one's own innocence. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a substitution is said to lapse, and in the following opinion, number 1.
2. Whether one who repudiates an inheritance is deemed to repudiate the right to a universal fideicommissum, and in the following opinion, number 2.
3. A universal fideicommissum whose term has arrived may be renounced.
4. Whether an assignment of an action made by a person in the age of pupillary minority is valid?
5. Whether, when the nearest substitutes are excluded, the subsequent ones come into effect.
body: In the name of Christ. The words of the institution state thus: the lord Anastasius instituted and made his legitimate and natural sons, Tiberius and Macrobius, his universal heirs in equal shares; and if it should happen that one or any of his sons should die without legitimate and natural children, then, in that case occurring, he willed and bequeathed that the other, or others, surviving, or survivors, should succeed, or succeed, in equal share to such predeceased son or sons in all and each of the movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, and claims of the said testator. Furthermore, he bequeathed that in the case where all the said male sons of the testator should die leaving no legitimate and natural children, then, in that case occurring, he made and instituted as his universal heirs in all and each of his movable and immovable goods and claims two of the eldest of the house and progeny of those of the Calcanei. Then, after the death of the testator, all his sons died after having accepted the inheritance, and without issue.

† It is asked whether the said substitution has become void. And it seems that it has, because the said substitution was made using civil and direct words. For no word is more direct and more civil in law than the word “I institute as heir.” And this follows from the attribute assigned by the understanding of the law to the very word “I institute” and to the word “heir,” as is clear. D. and C. de heredibus instituendis, throughout; and Inst. eodem, throughout; and Inst. de bonis possidendis, §. quos autem. But then I argue: a substitution made by Paganus using civil and direct words is sometimes made to a minor, to whom a pupillary substitution can be made; sometimes it is made to a person who has reached puberty, and to a minor joined together under one sense of the words; sometimes it is made to a person who has reached puberty, however. In the first case, while in pupillary age, it is valid by pupillary right; afterwards, it is of no effect. In the second and third cases, after the inheritance has been accepted, it expires, as is read and noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. verbis civilibus. The objection based on the word “Moreover, he bequeathed” does not hold, because, by reason of the added word “he instituted as heirs,” if it generates an institution of heirs, as in D. de verborum significatione, l. verbis legis; and this is a singular gloss in C. de testamento, c. Rainaldus, in the gloss beginning “Moreover.” That the said substitution was purely direct, and thus expired, is argued. But Bartolus, in D. ad Trebellianum, l. recusare, §. Titius, and in l. Centurio, holds otherwise.

On the contrary, it seems that in the said testament there is the common word “shall have made,” which is understood as “by fideicommissum,” and “he instituted” is understood as “directly.” And thus there is a double substitution, so that the twofold wording is not in vain, D. de usuris, l. si stipulatus. Moreover, the term “heirs” is apt to be used improperly or obliquely. For in D. de fideicommissis universalibus, the universal fideicommissary is rightly called an heir by the testator; because that to which the definition and the defined thing apply: but the definition of inheritance applies to the universal fideicommissum, as in D. de petitione hereditatis fideicommissariae, l. 1. For the inheritance is applied to him; therefore, the said secondary heir, although not principal, is valid. Nor does the rigor of words vitiate the will of the deceased, because we ought rather to examine the weight of the will and the intention of the testator, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. pater Severinam, §. conditionum, and l. in conditionibus primum locum. We must not go by the apices [minute details] of words to overturn the fitting wills of testators; because the understanding is prior and more important than the words, as in D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo, §. nec mirum; and C. de liberis praeteritis vel exheredatis, l. 3. Hence, it did not become void by puberty. C. de fideicommissis, l. si frater. And this is true, as in c. si pater, de testibus, lib. 6. And this dictates natural discretion and the conscience of any one judging rightly. I therefore say that those words must be understood as they could be according to law, and also according to fact, i.e., according to the will of the testator, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. qui filium, in principio; and C. de heredibus instituendis, l. finalis. Hence, the words must be drawn to the quality of the act, so that certainly the act may be valid and not perish; because interpretations were invented for this reason, so that by them the act may be strengthened and not destroyed, as in D. de manumissione testamento, l. finalis. It follows, therefore, that the said substitution, as a fideicommissary one, having its condition, assumed validity. Moreover, that which the master began by the pupillary substitution of the brothers must be restored by the Trebellianic action, because first he substituted pupillarily, secondly he requested, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam. But to this it can be answered, because it is not true that he requested; but only that he substituted directly. Nor does the addition “without children” and the said law l. continue, whatever the gloss says in l. precibus, hold; for that gloss is rejected by all. And although this opinion is very rigorous and contrary to the mind of the testator due to the notary’s ignorance, who did not know how to compose the words better: nevertheless, the writing speaks thus: and although harsh, it must be observed. But because this bites the conscience and natural equity, and is also contrary to the truth of the law because of the general word “makes,” and especially because the daughter of the testator is in the middle, it seems that the said substitution should be interpreted as pupillary in age, and afterwards as fideicommissary.

Because the next question is: two older, closer relatives of the said house, the said inheritance having been devolved to them, as they asserted, as onerous, repudiated it upon the death of the said principal heirs, and then, after the space of a year, accepted it. It is asked what is the law, since the daughter of the testator survives, who claims that the said inheritance pertains to her as the closer relative of her said brothers intestate.

† This question turns on whether, by repudiating the inheritance, they are understood to have repudiated the right to a universal fideicommissum. And it seems that they did not, because they believed that the said inheritance had devolved upon them by direct succession; hence they would not seem to have renounced a right which they did not know pertained to them, as in D. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. Mater decedens, § Praeterea; and D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Clodianus. To the contrary it seems, because a simple renunciation harms all: and because one is presumed to know the law: from which it is known that the first will is proved, D. de pactis, l. Emptor, § Lucius; the second is proved in I. 1, D. de iure et facti ignorantia.

† It is certain, however, that a universal fideicommissum, the term of which has arrived, may be renounced, as is fully read and noted in C. de pac. l. 1. and ff. de ver. ob. l. romę. §. duos fratres. This is especially so before a notary receiving the act on behalf of those whose interest it is, as was the case here, as in ff. de adop. l. his verbis. From this, since the inheritance had been accepted and the condition of the fideicommissum had arisen, an action on the testament was available to compel the restitution of the inheritance. This action was acquired in a commutable manner, not in an incommutable manner. And therefore it could be repudiated. But to this I respond in the facts of the case that the repudiation was preceded by an acknowledgment; and therefore it could not be repudiated, because the fideicommissum was fixed. On the contrary, it is replied that it was not a simple renunciation, but a pactum de non petendo (agreement not to sue), which can be made even by one who has accepted or taken possession. C. de repu. haeredi. As in this case, one must look at the words of the instrument to see whether they contain a promise and an agreement, or not. And having viewed the instrument, it contains an agreement not to act against the renunciation, and therefore the renouncers are excluded; and this is the final conclusion: unless perhaps someone says that this was not the intention of the renouncers, who believed they had the right to accept, not the right to bring an action on the testament. But this is to divine, because in the instrument of repudiation mention is made of knowledge, which is to be understood as knowledge of law and fact. And this renunciation, in case of doubt, ought to have some effect; and he who speaks with loose words incurs immediate peril, as in l. fi. in fi. C. de dotis promissione. And because in the instrument of repudiation are these words: "they repudiated in every mode, way, right, and form, by which they could better do so." Hence, if what I do as such is not valid, let it be valid as it can be valid. But against this it is objected, because in the said renunciation a reservation was made for debts, deposits, and legacies contained in the testament mentioned above; therefore the right of the fideicommissum is reserved; because legacies and fideicommissa are synonymous, as in C. communia de le. l. j. and l. 2. Here one must see whether in the testament itself there are other legacies which are without burden, to which the said reservation can be referred, as in ff. mandati. l. hęreditatem. ff. de leg. 2. l. miles. §. pro parte. ff. de le. 1. l. et quidem totum. And l. legatum est. All these doubts cease by holding the common opinion that this substitution is so direct that it does not oblique; for then it would have expired with puberty; and outside of that the inheritance could neither be accepted nor repudiated, because it vanished with puberty. Third

† The article concerns a certain assignment of an action made by the said sister at the time when it was said that she was in pupillary age and could not have entered upon the inheritance of her brothers. If this is so, the assignment was invalid, nor was the entry upon the inheritance valid, as in D. de appell. l. cum in una §. tutor. and as noted by Dy. in l. potuit D. de auctor. tutor. Fourth doubt

† is, whether the next in line come after the closer relatives have been excluded. And it must be said that they do not, because at the time of death they were not the closest relatives, as in D. de rebus dubiis, l. si cognatus, and the argument in l. 1, in fine, D. de legatis tertio. I, Baldus.

In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: the said Andriolus de Calcagnis, having four male children and some female children, namely Anastasius, Tibur, and Macrobius, instituted the said males as his heirs, and if it should happen that one or any of the said sons should die without children, he willed and bequeathed that the other or others surviving should succeed the said predeceased ones in all and each of the goods, rights, and actions, etc. Then follows the substitution with these words: "I also bequeath that in the case where the said male children of the testator should die leaving no legitimate and natural children, then, and in that case occurring, he made and instituted as his universal heirs in all his goods the two eldest of his house and progeny of the Calcagnis, with this burden and encumbrance that the said eldest were bound, etc. He also left to the daughters a certain quantity by way of institution. The said testator died with the said sons still in pupillary age; then three of the said sons died in pupillary age, the said lord surviving, who afterwards died in the eighteenth year of his age or thereabouts without issue. Finally, those two of the Calcagnis, claiming that the inheritances of the said testator pertained to them, accepted the inheritance. Then they repudiated it as onerous, reserving to themselves the debts and legacies in the said testament, and promised not to act against the said renunciation. It is also true that one of the said daughters is alive, and she renounced every right that pertained to her, real and personal, in all goods, even in real and personal rights and actions, and also in paternal and maternal property. It is asked whether the said daughter has a right in the paternal, maternal, and fraternal goods or not? What is the law regarding the aforementioned substitution?"

And indeed, that the said substitution lapsed upon puberty, because it was made with merely civil and direct words. The case in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law *Centurio*, does not apply. The gloss in the law *Precibus* is also not applicable, for it is rejected by all the doctors, who say that a substitution made by the word "let him be heir" is drawn to a fideicommissum on account of the added condition of children. To the contrary, that this gloss is true, and that the word "I institute," with that condition inserted, is drawn to a fideicommissum, considering the mind of the testator, who, thinking of children, thought of puberty. And also, after the case of the newest law in the chapter *Si pater*, *de testibus*, book 6, the law *Centurio* does not apply, for it must be understood when it is established that the testator precisely wished to substitute directly, and not by fideicommissum. For this, the Code, *de fideicommissis*, law *Si frater*. Here too it was said, "he made and instituted," which I explain so that the words may not be superfluous: namely, by fideicommissum when he said "he made," and also directly when he said "he instituted"; for he added the word "instituted" to augment, not to diminish. And thus there was a double substitution, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Recusare*, section *Titius*. And I consider this part more equitable, so that the will of the testator may not fail, as in the Digest, *de verborum significatione*, law *Verbis legis*.

† But let us assume the premise and consider whether the said renunciation of the two aforementioned ancient [rights] has become void? And indeed, it has not, because to accept and to repudiate pertains properly to the heir, not to the universal fideicommissum. But I say the contrary: because even a fideicommissum is said to be repudiated. Someone might say, first they accepted, therefore they could not repudiate. I answer: rather, because it was not the voice of one repudiating, however, but of one contracting, as in C. de repu. haere. l. suus, because they promised not to come against the repudiation. Furthermore, someone might say, they reserved to themselves legacies; but I answer, these legacies are not found in the testament, but only a universal substitution is found; and reservation operates for nothing if there is nothing reservable, as in ff. de le. 1. l. si quis ita legauerit. Regarding the exception of the vineyards, someone might say, rather, it does not appear that the fideicommissum was renounced, because legacies and fideicommissa are synonymous; and I say that rather, because they wished to renounce the substitution, which had a burden attached, as is clear in those words, "considering the said inheritance to be rather burdensome," etc. For they did not wish to be entangled with burdens, but to enjoy only the benefits, as in ff. mandati. l. haereditatem. Again, someone might say, the daughter renounced her father's property; but I answer, that since they had been acquired by the brothers, they were no longer paternal goods, but fraternal; because they began to be commingled, as in ff. de vul. et pup. l. sed et si plures. §. filio, and C. de dona. l. si auia. And now the repudiation does not avail, ff. de transactio. l. qui cum tutoribus. in prin. and that not, C. vnde. lib. l. qui se patris, and ff. de acq. hae. l. Iul. and l. quaesitum. And therefore it must be concluded truly in favor of the said daughter. Moreover, because she was a ward, the oath is not valid as to the firmness of contracts and the alienation of immovable things. And this reason is clearer than the first. Furthermore, even if she had been of age, she was not informed of the benefit of restitution in integrum, of which singular mention must be made. ag. ff. de mino. l. illud. §. si talis. It supports what is not, Dy. in l. sciendum. ff. de ver. ob. And this is the common opinion, which Jo. An. holds, although some doctors are of the contrary opinion. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a prescription runs while the inheritance lies unclaimed?
body: In the name of Christ. Among other things

† It is asked whether this prescription runs during the period when the inheritance is lying open. And briefly, it must be said that either the prescription is conventional: and it runs, whether it began to run from the person of the deceased, for example because the debt was pure; or whether it did not, for example because during the lifetime of the deceased the condition or the day had not yet occurred, which occurred while the inheritance was lying open; because it was so agreed between the deceased and the prescriber, and the inheritance sustains the person of the deceased, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. ad diem; and D. de minor. l. emilius. The same applies to a prescription which takes its origin from a will; because a will and last will are equated. Thus it is understood in D. qui ex cau. maio. l. iulia; or there it began from the predecessor. The same applies if the time is appointed by law, yet in consequence of a contract, as in the two years or three years given to the emphyteuta to pay the canon, as in C. de iure emph. l. si. For this time is a certain tacit part of the contract itself, as in D. de eden. l. 1. §. diem. And therefore one does not depart from the contract, except by the benefit of restitution in integrum, by which the contract is not rescinded; but, so to speak, mercy is granted with indulgence of the penalty, where no fault is found.

But if we speak of a legal provision and penalty, or of a legal provision and prescription, which takes its origin purely from the law itself: and then either the prescription begins at the time of the deceased, and runs while the inheritance is lying open, but restitution in integrum is granted if a just cause intervenes; because the heir was in the womb, or was a minor, or an adult, as in D. de mino. l. etiam ei. lapicola; or it began from the inheritance lying open itself: and then it matters, or the delay in entering the inheritance cannot be imputed to the heir; and the prescription does not run, as is fully read and noted in C. de tempo. in integ. resti. l. ea, quae.
