Or the delay can be imputed, as to one who, knowing the right, did not avail himself of the time for deliberation: and then he is not restored, because by entering he is fictitiously considered to have been heir from the beginning; and thus against him the prescription begun by a true fiction of law, and the law does not aid those who are negligent regarding any temporal and extraordinary benefit, as in D. quib. ex cau. ma. l. non n. tempus. Therefore, negligence is to be imputed to the heir, as in C. ad vel leia. l. pe.

In one case, however, a conventional prescription does not run while the inheritance is lying open, namely, because from the form of the contract the prescription ought to begin from the heir, as in D. de stipu. ser. l. si seruus hęreditarius. Others say that the prescriptive period for the acquisition of ownership by the owner never begins while the inheritance is lying open; but where prescription is claimed, there is an exception, so much so that sometimes the prescription runs, and yet there is no one to prescribe, nor anyone against whom prescription is made, as if the debtor and creditor died without an heir; for only time prescribes and corrodes the efficacy of the action, which I do not believe to be true, because time is not a mode, etc., as in D. de act. et ob. l. actionum fere. §. placet.

Returning therefore to the question of my friend, it is clear whether the prescription effectively ran while the inheritance was lying open, or not? Although others say indiscriminately that, since negligence is always required in prescriptions, that against dominion or action prescription never begins while the inheritance is lying open; because an inheritance lying open can never be in delay, unless perhaps a curator was appointed for the inheritance lying open: in which case that prescription would run which runs against a minor, i.e., the prescription of the longest time; because the curator represents the inheritance as being adult. And therefore the prescription of the longest time would not run by the law itself. And it supports l. si seruus. de diuersis, et temporalibus praescrip. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Custom and privilege are equivalent, and both confer jurisdiction.
body: In the name of Christ. In the case of the abbot of Saint Christine, I say,

† That the privilege and the custom must be observed: because both custom and privilege confer jurisdiction, and also assign territory, and the rights of the territory are enlarged, as in c. Super quibusdam, §. Praeterea, de Verborum Significatione, and C. de Diversis Officiis, l. Viros, lib. 12, with countless others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a creditor, who offered his credit to the first creditor verbally and not effectively, and therefore succumbed, may sue again after the matter has been adjudicated, and by making an effective offer, may he obtain judgment?
2. Whether a defendant absolved because the condition did not exist may be sued anew when the condition exists, such that the plaintiff loses the case.
body: In the name of Christ. The second creditor, having the right of offer against the first, while the first creditor was in possession of the hypothec, proceeded in this manner: that either the debt be paid to him, or the pledge be released, since he was ready to pay the debt and to offer it to the first creditor together with certain expenses incurred by the creditor on the hypothecated property. And because he subsequently did not make the offer, the first creditor was definitively absolved from the libel and its contents. Now, after many years, the said second creditor offers the debt and the expenses; the exception of res iudicata is raised against him.

† The question is what is the law: and indeed, that the exception of res iudicata should be an obstacle; for we say that a definitive sentence having been rendered, because it was not proven, gives rise to a perpetual exception of res iudicata, so that there may be an end to litigation, as is fully noted in D. de condictione indebiti, l. Iul. But here the tender that was being asserted was not proven; therefore, the exception of perpetual res iudicata is an obstacle. On the contrary, however, it is argued that this case is similar to one who sues while a condition is pending: for if the defendant is absolved because the condition did not occur, he can be sued again when the condition exists, as in D. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. Si mater, §. Eandem. Although the glossa says that he loses his case in D. si certum petatur, l. Pecuniam, which glossa is not commonly approved by the doctors; but that glossa does not say that he loses his case ipso facto because he sues while the condition is pending. And in this it speaks incorrectly, as in l. Bouem, §. Si sub conditione, D. de edicto edilitio, and in l. Si rem, §. Finem, D. de pignoris actione. But it does not say that if the condition, which was potestative during the pendency of the trial, is not fulfilled, and therefore an acquittal follows, that one can sue again after the sentence. I consider that the term for tendering is until the sentence, as in the aforementioned l. Si rem, §. Finem. I also consider that the second creditor properly has a hypothecary action, although the prior creditor is preferred, yet his hypothecary action is not extinguished. I also consider that the right of tendering is an accessory annexed to the hypothecary action once born, and its executive remedy. Wherefore, the absolving judgment extinguishes the hypothecary action already born, and there is no longer room for the right of tendering. And when the principal is removed, the accessory is removed. And it is supported by D. de damno infecto, l. Si finita, §. Postea. Wherefore, I say, saving the advice of a sounder opinion, that after the aforementioned definitive sentence, there is no room for the right of tendering. Moreover, it is not surprising that potestative conditions are extinguished by the prescription of time, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Hæc conditio, Lapicola. Moreover, delay is harmful to everyone, and it is supported by D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Si quis instituatur. Moreover, because by tendering verbally he bound himself to tender in reality, which he did not do while the matter was intact, i.e., during the pendency of the trial and within a reasonable time. And therefore let him impute it to himself, as in l. Habebat, de institoria, cum si. Moreover, after the cause is concluded, tender has no place, as in Extr. de causa possessionis et proprietatis, c. Pastoralis, where it is said that nothing can be changed in the trial, nor can it even be alleged according to Innocentius. Therefore, much less after an absolving sentence which has passed into res iudicata: unless the right of tendering was reserved in the sentence, as in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. Cum eo, and C. de colonis, l. Si soror. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the seller is liable for eviction if the buyer has gained more than the price, even though the thing was later evicted.
body: In the name of Christ. Titus sold a certain estate for a price of one hundred pounds; which price is to be paid to A. and B., creditors of the said vendor, for the liberation of the said vendor, and otherwise the said vendor is not bound regarding eviction; provided that the said creditors have assigned their rights of credit to the said purchaser; finally, the said thing was evicted by a certain third party. It is asked,

Whether an action for eviction may be brought: and truly, that it may not; because the said debt was not paid to the creditors; and thus the condition under which the promise of eviction was conceived did not occur. He does not pay who is released gratuitously, as in D. 46.3, l. *solutam pecuniam*. And where the condition fails, the action does not lie, as in D. 5.1, l. *certi condici*, in the beginning; and D. 50.17, l. *cedere diem*. I say the contrary, because the debtor succeeding to the creditor truly pays him, although he succeeds gratuitously, if this is to his advantage, as in D. 46.3, l. *Stichum*, § *aditio*. Also, because satisfaction is said to have been made in whatever manner the creditor wished, as in D. 20.1, l. *solutum*, § *solutam*. Also, this pact that another shall pay is valid only to the extent that it is in the interest of the contracting party, as in D. 45.1, l. *liber honorum*, § *si*. Also, it does not matter which of equivalent things is done. And for this, l. *ultima*, D. 40.12, is most apt. Also, a donation made after merit takes the place of natural payment, as in D. 40.12, l. *si remunerandi gratia*, in the beginning, where there is almost the very case of the question. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the principal is liable for homicide committed by his agent, given a statute providing that no one shall be punished by death unless municipal law so provides; and in how many ways one is said to be a murderer?
2. Whether an indefinite term is equivalent to a universal one by interpretation.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows. The statute of the City provides that no one shall be punished corporally, unless it is provided by municipal law; but otherwise he shall be punished pecuniarily at the discretion of the authority. Another statute provides that if anyone commits homicide, he shall be punished by the head: so that he shall die. It happens that a certain person commanded another to commit homicide: and he committed it. It is asked,

Whether a person who orders a homicide to be committed should be punished by death, just as the one who committed the homicide? For clarity, I premise that a homicide was said in many ways. For there is one who is a causal homicide, and not formal: such as he who orders, and whose order is executed. He is the cause of the homicide: but he is not a formal homicide, because he did not kill with his own blow: hence he is not properly a murderer, but by interpretation, as noted in D. de vi, et viar. l. 1. §. quotiens. and this as far as the subtlety of words is concerned. But as far as the effect of law and fact is concerned, he is more than a homicide: because he sins against himself, and against another, whose mind he corrupts by ordering, as noted in D. de infa. l. athletas. §. Pompo. and D. ad leg. Aquil. l. qua actione. §. cellus ait. Moreover, the one who orders is said to be the principal of the crime, as in D. de seruo corrupto. l. in hoc iudicio. Therefore, he deserves to be punished, as in C. de accu. l. non ideo minus. Also, he who orders does not truly and properly do, but causally. And he who is the cause of the cause, is the true cause of the caused: although he is a mediated cause, as in X. de sent. excom. l. mulieres. and D. de re. iur. l. hoc iure. §. deiecit. Also, the decree expressly says that he who orders a homicide to be committed, when it is carried out, is truly and properly a homicide. D. de pe. dist. i. c. periculose. sed se decipiunt etc. Some, however, are a formal and causal homicide, such as he who kills someone with his own mind and his own hands. And this one is a homicide speaking most properly: and from this one begins to arise the obligation, as in C. si reus, vel accu. mor. fue. l. j. and in this respect, the one who orders is said to be an accessory, and the one who sheds blood is said to be principal. And this is the difference between the doer and the orderer: because the doer's crime stands by itself: but the orderer's crime does not stand by itself, as in D. de furt. l. si is, qui rem. §. si tutium. unless it were such a crime that is consummated by the order alone, as in D. de seruo corrupto. l. 1. §. persuadere. In the third way, one is a formal homicide, and not causal, such as if a madman, or an infant kills another, as in D. de off. praesi. l. diuus. Thus, therefore, someone is called a homicide in many ways naturally and truly. Some are not a homicide as far as punishment is concerned by interpretation of law: some, however, are not even as far as punishment, nor as far as interpretation of law, such as a madman, or one who kills justly. For justice removes the name of crime, because it is its contrary, as in D. quod me. cau. l. nec timorem. §. proinde. and D. de iust. et iu. l. vt vim. From these also it appears that homicide is sometimes said strictly, sometimes broadly, so that it includes by interpretation of the word even the one who orders, or advises.

I return to our case, and the decision will rest on this point: whether the indefinite is equivalent to the universal by interpretation or by the signification of the word. For, by interpretation, the penalty of death ceases in this statute, because whatever comes by interpretation is tacit, not express; as we say in the tacit vulgar and the tacit pupillary substitution, D. de vulg. et pupill. subst. l. iam hoc iure. But that which comes by the signification of the word is express. Now, on this point, some say that the indefinite is equivalent to the universal by interpretation; others say that it is so by signification, as in l. si seruitus, D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum. I say that all things of the same reason are totally included by signification; but if one thing is greater than another, and different from another, it is not included, as noted by Decius in the rubric D. de regulis iuris, unless this difference contained within itself a connection of the same equity; and then it is excluded by interpretation, not by signification. And therefore, extensive interpretation has no place in statutes, as in the statute about which we inquire, D. quod vi aut clam, l. autem qui aliter, §. si; and it is supported by D. de minoribus, l. auxilium, §. in delictis, where the adulterer and that which is punished as adultery by subtlety are set forth as different in fact. Therefore, speaking strictly according to law, the said commander is not subject to punishment by the penalty of death, because he is a homicide in a certain respect; see Decius in c. 1, X. de officio delegati. I, Baldus. See on this matter below in consilium 71.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a thing purchased with the money of a ward becomes the property of the ward, or of the purchaser in his own name?
2. Whether money succeeds in the place of any thing?
3. The uncle being alive, and the ward being in communion of all goods, whether the money, out of which many goods have been purchased, is presumed to have been derived from the common revenues.
4. Fruits are always understood to be after deduction of burdens and expenses.
body: In the name of Christ. The ward remaining in the community of her father's goods, and the uncle, who the uncle purchased many goods not intentionally, but presumably from the common fruits.

† It is asked whether the said purchased things are common to the uncle and the ward. And indeed, that they are, because the thing purchased with the ward’s money becomes the ward’s, unless he did not ratify it, as in C. de rei vend. l. si ex pecunia and l. si vt proponis. To the contrary is the truth, because the thing purchased with money derived from the ward’s property does not become the ward’s: because the purchaser buys in his own name, and the transferor transfers in his own name, as in ff. de admini. tut. l. titium, et meuium §. altero. And fully noted on this matter by Bartolus. The objection that we note in the said l. si vt proponis, there, is special when it is from the ward’s money, or of similar persons. For there are certain singularities in the ward’s money, which are not in other persons, nor in other things, as noted in ff. si cer. pe. l. singularia and l. si pecuniam militis. Moreover, it is established that if I sell your thing in my name, the price becomes mine, as in ff. de cond. ind. l. si vrbana; and I, by paying the price, acquire dominion, as in inst. de rerum diui. §. venditae. Furthermore, if we were to say the contrary, there would be two actions: one that the thing and the money are deemed the same; another that it is deemed purchased in the name of the ward; and two different fictions from different sources do not concur, as in l. 1. C. de dotis promis.

† Money succeeds in place of any thing, because it was artificially invented for this purpose; but not so in other things, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si ita fideiussorem accepero. Unless in universal actions, as in D. de hereditate vendita, l. Venditor ex hereditate; and D. de legatis 2, l. Idem servandum.

Secondly, it is asked whether the aforementioned money is presumed to have been derived from the common revenues? And indeed, it is so, by analogy with the church; but to the contrary, C. arbi. tute. l. si defunctus. This is the opinion of Bartolus in the said §. altero. However, this argument lacks force, because this manager is bound to render an exact account of the revenues that were probably collected, and of those that could probably have been collected; because he performed his duty with due diligence: although he is not liable for the slightest fault, as C. de neg. gest. l. tutori. Hence, according to the quality and the course of times, and according to the quality of the things, it is presumed that he collected the revenue and profits in accordance with the quality of the neighboring lands, as noted in l. 2. C. de rescin. ven. and C. vbi pupil. educ. debeat. l. fi. Therefore, that which a diligent head of household would have collected, the said uncle of the said ward is bound to hand over; nor is he less liable for negligence than for what was actually collected. And by this, all the questions raised have been answered.
† However, fruits are always understood to be calculated after deducting burdens and expenses. C. de fructibus, et litis expen. l. 1.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether two witnesses testifying against a document can be excused from perjury. And no. 4.
2. If one is placed in existence, the other is necessarily removed.
3. Whether an accusation of forgery proceeds where the place is not expressed.
5. A chapter false in part is rendered false in its entirety.
6. Witnesses are understood to testify upon the chapter and to refer themselves to the chapter.
7. One who challenges a document regarding that which concerns truth and falsity cannot draw proof from it, nor found his argument thereon.
8. Diversity of forms argues diversity of contracts.
9. The term "part" includes a half, even in a witness.
body: In the name of Christ. This case is brief and arduous. A certain instrument appears in the form of a sale of certain castles and jurisdictions, with a pact of repurchase; which instrument the heir of the seller claims was simulated and made in lieu of a pledge, and that the things sold were claimed by certain other possessors. To prove this, he produced two witnesses from among the said buyers: who testified that it was a true sale, and that no pact of repurchase had been made. They are accused of perjury: because the instrument, which is presumed to be true, states the contrary.

† It is asked whether the said witnesses can be excused from the charge of perjury. And the answer is that they cannot, because these statements are immediately contradictory: having promised to resell, and not having promised.

† and if one is posited in being, the other is necessarily removed. As in l. 1, D. de his qui sunt sui vel alieni iuris; and C. de furtis; l. 1, D. de condictione indebiti; Iulia. For between true and false there is no middle ground: because falsehood is nothing other than the alteration of truth, as in Auth. de tabellionibus, in principio. Truth, however, is nothing other than that the thing is as it is said to be. It is established naturally, and by a point of reasoning, that contradictory statements cannot both be true at the same time, as in D. pro socio, l. si ancillam. Moreover, if such witnesses were to testify to the truth, the instrument would be discredited, as in Extra, de fide instrumentorum, cap. cum Ioannes Heremita. Therefore, conversely, since the instrument is presumed true by virtue of the instrument itself, the witnesses are discredited as forgers: thus they are to be punished by the penalty of the Cornelian law on falsification: or by the penalty of the municipal statute. As in l. 1, D. ad legem Corneliam de falsis. Since their falsehood cannot be concealed by any evasion, as the acts themselves seem to speak expressly, and conjecture has no place in uncertain rather than certain matters, as in D. de verborum obligatione, l. continuus, § cum ita.

On the contrary: for the understanding of which two things must be premised. First, that there is a certain sale which has both existence and formal existence: similarly, a certain pact has both existence and formal existence. For example, if a true sale precedes, and a pact of repurchase is added, as in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. 2. Some have formal existence in appearance, yet do not have existence in substance. And this occurs in two ways: for example, a sale made in simulation in place of a pledge, as in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione; and consequently a pact made for repurchase. For this pact is simulated since the sale was simulated, because it is its consequent. And if the contract is simulated, the alienation is simulated. And because the simulated seller cannot truly buy back his own thing which remains his, because the purchase of one’s own thing which remains one’s own does not stand, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. suae rei. From this it follows that it is true to say that no pact of repurchase intervened. In the manner in which the accuser alleges, because he alleges a simulated pact. And the witness says that such a pact, i.e., a simulated one, never intervened: nor does he understand himself to be testifying outside the heading by testifying directly on the heading. Hence, if the heading is about a simulated pact, and he testifies the contrary, he is understood to be testifying by the contrary: but the contrary to simulated is simulated verging into the opposite, so that this is the sense: a simulated pact of repurchase never intervened; because such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate, as in D. de interrogationibus et actionibus, l. si defensor.

Secondly, it must be premised for clarity, that some things refer to the fact, some things refer to the mode: for to buy and to sell refers to the fact: but in this manner expressed, or tacit, which appears from the coherence of the acts, as in D. de pactis, l. item quia, § idem Iulianus. For acts that are subjunctive and continuous have a tacit repetition in themselves, as in D. de locato conducto, l. item quaeritur, § cum impleto; and D. de solutionibus, l. in his, § si inter. But to promise to resell refers to the mode, because mode is called whatever qualifies the act, Extra, de testibus, c. Pisanus. These witnesses, therefore, do not say against the instrument, but they say against the mode alleged by the adversary, who alleges a simulation concluding both the fact and the mode. By the force of this understanding, these witnesses are saved from the crime of falsity. l. 1, facie culpabiles videantur. For even if the party says the instrument is tacitly simulated, the witnesses nevertheless say the instrument is expressly false. Written which was falsely said when it was not said. And one thing is the simulation of words spoken, another is falsity and false fabrication of those not spoken, D. de edicto edilitio, l. sciendum, § dictum; D. de rescriptis, l. super literis, per Innocentius.

† Regarding the point in question, namely whether an accusation of perjury proceeds when the place is not specified, I say that this crime is committed in court, and the place of the court is notorious; hence, according to some, the expression of the place is not necessary, because it is included by necessity insofar as the place is concerned. Others say the contrary, because examinations may take place outside of court. Others distinguish: either the procedure is by accusation or by inquisition, as noted in the gloss, sine titulo, in the Institutes, De publicis iudiciis, in the beginning. Jacobus de Belvisi says that in both cases it is necessary to append the coherences of place and time, as he notes in the Institutes, De actionibus, in the beginning, in his lecture; which is the truer view, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, De accusationibus, in the law Libellorum, which makes a chapter with Abbatem sane, De re iudicata, Book 6. Hence, due to the defect, the libel would be abolished, as in the said law Libellorum, § Quod si libelli. Nor can the judge supply the defect of the libel, except by rejecting the libel, as in law 1, Digest, De officio assessoris; because drafting the libel pertains to the office of the party, not to the office of the judge, although inquisition pertains to the office of the judge. And this reason moves the gloss in the Institutes, De publicis iudiciis, and it supports what is noted in Decretum 1, quaestio 3, chapter Quia presulatus.

Let us dismiss these subtle and scrupulous allegations, and come to the clear defense of the witnesses. And because the witnesses testified upon the chapter, I will refer to the words of the chapter. The words of the chapter state that, in truth, the true alleged price of the sales was only one thousand florins, although in the instruments themselves the contrary appears at first sight, namely two thousand, which the said Lord Galvan, Nicholas, Bartolin, Gaimald, Blanca, Michael, and Jacopinus were obliged to lend or had lent to the said Lord Ubertino. And in truth it was a contract of pledge, and not of sale. And that the said Lord Galvan, Nicolin, and Bart., Gaimald, Blanca, Michal, and Jacopinus solemnly promised to the said Lord Ubertino, then present, stipulating and receiving, that whenever the same Lord Ubertino would give and pay to the above and often-named parties the said one thousand florins, that then, and in that case, the above and often-named parties would make a solemn re-sale and retro-dation to the said Lord Ubertino of all and each of the goods, of which mention is made in the two pretended writings in the manner of a sale, for his given and done amount only; although otherwise it may be found written, or according to which and as the witnesses will say in favor of the chapter, and let the aforementioned two pretended writings in the manner of a sale, or their exemplars, be read to the witnesses. These are the words of the chapter, as appears in the records.

And before I proceed further, I premise that this chapter concerning the re-sale sounds in the person of Lord Ugolino; however, because an external person is not understood, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus, in fine; but this is shown to be false by the instrument, because if any promise was made concerning the re-sale, it was conceived in the person of the father and son, who had sold by a colored or uncolored sale; I do not care about this. Hence, this chapter, so formed, lacks truth, because a conjunctive differs greatly from a simple statement. Hence, as it is chaptered, the chapter is not true; just as one debtor differs from several joint debtors. Moreover, those words, "to the said Lord Ubertino," are understood in their proper name, as in D. sol. matr. l. magis; but here it was in a common name, as in D. de usufr. eccles. l. si mulier cum liberis. Therefore, by the force of the voice and sense, the chapter is erroneous; therefore, the witnesses testifying against the chapter testify the truth, which

† If a clause is false in any respect, the whole is rendered false: because a little leaven corrupts the whole lump. Dist. 9, c. Et scripturas; C. de transig., l. Cum ex falsis; Inst. extra de haer., c. Fraternitatis. Hence the Speculum says in the title De deposito that a clause which is false in a substantial or qualifying part of the whole may be denied in its entirety; and the one who denies it speaks the truth, and not the one who pleads the clause. And this consideration pertains to the words “to Lord Ubertino.” The second consideration pertains to the words “to the above-mentioned and often-named persons.” For the clarity of this point, it must be known that when several persons are enumerated in a contract or promise, they are understood to be joined jointly and per capita, as C. si certum petatur, l. Si non singuli; ff. de duobus reis, l. Si reos, § Cum tabulis; C. si plures una sententia, l. 1. Therefore, the sense of the words is this: whenever the per capita shares have been paid to the said named persons; and this is false, because from the form of the instrument it appears that such distribution was not made per capita; therefore, the clause lacks truth; and the witnesses also speak the truth in stating that the said promise did not intervene.

And although the instruments were read to the witnesses, the witnesses are understood to testify regarding the chapter and to refer themselves to the chapter, not to the instruments in themselves, as noted in C. qui legitimam personam, l. momentarie. The third consideration is in the words "the said one thousand florins." For it does not appear that a promise of the said sales or writings was made for one thousand florins; hence the witnesses, who state that no such promise was made, speak the truth, because a lesser sum is not included under a greater; for there is no consensus in this matter, as in ff. locati, l. si decem.

† The fourth consideration is on those words, “although it is otherwise repeated in the writing.” Here it must be stated clearly that he who challenges an instrument on the ground of what concerns truth and falsehood cannot draw proof from it, nor base his case upon it, as in D. de his quibus ut ind. l. post legatum, in principio; and in Regula ex eodem, l. 6; and fully noted by Innocentius, Extra, de exceptionibus, c. Cum venerabilis; and C. de his quibus ut ind. l. Polla. Hence, to overthrow witnesses and accuse them, an instrument cannot be extorted against them, which the accuser himself endeavors to challenge by saying that it was written differently than stated; and consequently it followed that no faith ought to be given to instruments, as in the said l. Si ex falsis.

Now I come to the statement of the witness Gaimaldus, whose words are these: “And I also say that the said Lord Galuamus, Nicolinus, Bartolinus, I the witness, Blanca, Michael, and Iacopinus, nor any of us, where I was present, never promised, nor made any promise to the said Lord Ubertino by deed, nor without deed, of repurchasing from the said Lord Ubertino all those goods and rights concerning which mention is made in the said sales, for two thousand florins, nor even for any greater or lesser amount.”

For although this witness directly testifies against the tenor of the instrument, nevertheless he does not testify against the tenor of the chapter. And therefore he testifies without being sworn, nor having been interrogated.

Moreover, those words, “to the said Lord Ubertino,” must be weighed, as I said above, because not to him alone, but to him joined with the persons of his sons. For these are different matters: just as we say that one thing is when a father acts in his own name; another when he acts with the person of his son joined, as in D. sol. matr. l. 2; D. re am. l. Cum dos.

Again, one thing is when a father stipulates for himself; another when for himself and his son; another when it was for himself or his son.

† For the diversity of forms indicates a diversity of contracts, as in D. de verb. oblig. eum qui, § qui sibi; and D. de solut. l. stichum, § quæsitum. Moreover, the said witness can and ought to be upheld on another ground, because those very words “all goods and rights” signify one universal contract, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. scire debemus. Hence, it is true in a formal sense that these words were never uttered as the price, etc., of two thousand florins, as in D. de edict. edict. l. si plura. For ten and ten make twenty, as noted in D. de solut. l. ubi. Next follows Master Nicolinus de Laudo, another witness, whose words are these: “Nor was I ever requested by the said Master Ubert, nor by any other person in his name, to do so; nor did I ever make to the said Master Ubert, nor to any other in his name, any promise to resell or return to the said Master Ubert the said goods and rights sold to us, either in whole or in part.” And it is certain that the said promise was not made in whole, as appears from the instrument; for it would be unsound reasoning to hold that one who buys a part is bound to resell the whole; but it ought to be understood soundly, i.e., proportionally, as in l. 1, D. de rebus dubiis. Moreover, it is not true that each promised to resell for half, but according to the proportion of the price. Hence it must be known that he who denies or affirms a part speaks of the half, and not of the other part, as in D. de verb. sig. l. nomen filiarum, § portionis; and D. de rei vend. l. si in rem agat aliquis.

† Hence Bartolus advised in *Teste*, that when one testifies "de parte" [of a part], it is understood simply as testifying of a half-part; but in truth this witness could not truly or colorably sell the whole, because no similar prior act had preceded, nor could he sell a half-part for the same reason. Hence it must be noted that the witness said "a part," he did not say "some part"; and thus, according to the true intention, it is saved. That which must not be omitted, which is clear and evident, is that if the instrument speaks of a contract by way of condition, and the chapter by way of what denotes the purity of the contract, the witness may say that the chapter does not contain the truth. The case is literally *Extra de fide instrumentorum*, c. *Cum Ioannes heremita*. Since therefore the chapter is pure, and the contract conditional, the witness ought certainly to have denied the promise contained in the chapter; because the chapter departs from the substance of the truth: the case is literally in the said c. *Cum Ioannes heremita*. Now it remains to inquire whether they ought to be condemned to pay interest to the accuser, who says that she suffered loss in the case because of the said testimony, in which case she says she had the truth; for this was because it pleased the judge: for since these witnesses are not proven to have spoken falsely, it is established that they are not bound, by the law *Qui nomine*, with its material. That which must also be weighed is that although the accusation was general, it was nevertheless restricted by the first chapter of the accuser's own intention, and upon that chapter the witnesses swore, as appears in the records. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether greater credence should be given to witnesses testifying against an instrument than to the instrument itself, or to the notary; and whether such witnesses who contradict the instrument are to be subjected to torture. See no. 5.
2. Whether reliance should be placed on a witness who assigns a reason for his statement.
3. The statements of witnesses are to be reconciled.
4. Whether three witnesses prevail over an instrument? And whether, if they contradict the instrument, they are to be subjected to torture. See no. 5.
6. The witness is to be tortured first, together with the notary, and the witnesses are to be subjected to torture.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain record of testimony of the following tenor is found. Henry Roberti of Prato, a witness produced, constituted, and sworn, as above, on the first chapter which begins, “First, that the aforementioned,” etc., and on the second chapter, “Also, that the aforementioned site,” etc. Being interrogated, he responded that it is true, as contained in the said chapter. Being interrogated how he knows this, he responded: “Because he himself saw manifestly that the aforementioned site and house are contiguous to the said way, and that the said way is adjacent to the said site and the said house.” Also, how does he know that the said way is common or vicinal? He responded that he knows that the said way is vicinal, because he saw and sees that the said way does not belong to anyone except the neighbors having their sites and houses, to which and which it is necessary to go by the said way; and the said way has no flight or exit except only into the neighbors, as is said. Being interrogated what is the difference between the said ways? He responded that the difference is such, because a common way is that by which anyone wishing to go and return by it can go and return, whether going to the fields and to the gates, or elsewhere. And a vicinal way is that by which certain persons do not have the right to go or return, except the neighbors who have their lands, houses, possessions, and sites, through which they have entrance and exit. Being interrogated who are those neighbors who were accustomed to go by the said way? He responded: Nicholas of Prato, William Gala, Baldassare of Prato, Peter Gaiotus of Perugia, Tignolius of Prato, the witness himself, his brother, the aforementioned of the Qualeis, and the aforementioned of the Bande. Being interrogated whether the aforementioned Baltraminus and Antonius of the Qualeis, and their predecessors, were always accustomed to go and return by the said way as if it were their own proper way, and whether the said brothers of the Qualeis today go and return as if it were their own proper way? He responded, “Yes.” Being interrogated whether the said brothers of the Qualeis in past times had, held, and today have and hold wood, thorns, and other things, which they wished, in the said way as if it were their own proper way of the brothers of the Qualeis? He responded, “Yes.” From this record arose a question of falsity: because the witness says he never said that the way was proper, but only said that it was vicinal; whereas the notary says he wrote legally word for word as the witness said, but the witness says that the notary wrote falsely, insofar as he wrote that the witness said that the way was proper: and to prove this he introduces two witnesses, who, by consent of the parties, were present at the examination together with the notary; these witnesses deposed that the said witness said that the way was vicinal and not proper. Now the vicar of the Lord Marquis, cognizant of the case, commanded the said witnesses, present, hearing, and understanding, that within 8 days they must make all defense they wish. The question is asked: what is the law?

And it must be said that the aforementioned witnesses ought not to be tortured for three reasons. For behold, the principal witness, who is called Henry Roberti, ought not to be tortured because he stated a probable truth with the giving of a reason: because it is a neighborly path, through which access is open to neighbors, and not to others, and it leads to the lands of the neighbors, however, and not to the public way, as in D. 43.8.1.1, § viarum, and the following section.

† And in this manner the witnesses and the common people understand the vicinal way, and the said witness assigns the reason, which must be followed, as noted in C. de testibus, l. solam; even if afterwards the same witness had said that it was his own, it is understood as being his for his part. For what is common is mine for my part, as noted in l. 1, C. qui testamento facere non possunt. Whence

† It is fitting that statements be reconciled with one another, as stated in the extrajudicial chapter *Cum filii* on witnesses. Therefore, a witness should not be understood to waver, because the reasoning is common to the entire testimony, and that reasoning must be upheld, since reasoning carries more weight than mere statement, as I have proven above. The second reason is why witnesses

† they ought not to be tortured: because they fully prove the truth: since three witnesses prevail over an instrument, as is fully established in the Institutes, *de inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *item verborum*; and in the Extravagant Decretals, *de fide instrumentorum*, c. *cum Ioannes heremita*. And witnesses who fully prove are not to be tortured, but followed, as in the Extravagant Decretals, *de probationibus*, c. 2.

Thirdly, they should not be tortured, because they are superior to all exceptions, as stated in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam, and noted by Laurentius de Arena and Cynus in C. de falsis, l. si quis de curio. Where, however, a witness who has testified contradicts the instrument, and has no corroborating witnesses, the instrument should rather be believed, since it has the force of at least two witnesses, and even of several. The witness himself, however, is singular, as in c. bone, extra de electione, and fully noted in l. 1, in fine, ff. quemadmodum testes aperiantur, C. de fideicommissis, l. quoniam, and C. de fide instrumentorum, l. in exercendis. And then, if one were to begin with torture, it is true that the witness should first be tortured as the inferior person, since the notary is a person of authority. But when there are several witnesses against the notary, the witnesses should not be tortured, as I said above, and so it is in the question at hand. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

In the name of Christ. Petrutiolo of the castle of Castro Plebis solemnly made his will, in which, among other things, he thus disposed: furthermore, he left and ordered to be given to Ant., nephew of the testator, 60 gold florins, which, as he asserted, pertained to and were owed to the same Antonio by Ser Vane Manuchii, formerly chamberlain of the commune of Castro Plebis, and which were the subject of a case entered in the book of receipts and expenditures of the said Ser Vane. Furthermore, he left that 100 Perugian pounds be restored to the said Ant. from the goods of the said testator, for the restitution of the dowry of Lady Biblia, godmother of the said Antonio and former wife of the father of the said Antonio, for the restitution of which dowry the said Ant. was bound in the person of his said father, the former legitimate and natural son of the said testator. Furthermore, he left and bequeathed one piece of land, cultivated, vineyarded, and wooded, situated in the boundaries of Castro Plebis in the contract of Glauii, which adjoins on one side the property of Amodya Tactoli, on the other the property of Angelo Petrili, and at the head the road, and at the foot a ditch. And the said testator left to the same Antonio several other properties from his goods, as is contained in the said will written and published by the hand of Paul, formerly notary of Master Vincentio of Castro Plebis. And afterwards, the said testator in his said will by the words written below, namely in the aforementioned provisions, instituted the said Antonio as his heir, commanding him to be silent and content with the aforementioned things left to him, and not to be able to claim more from his goods. And if the said Ant. should die at any time without legitimate sons descending from him, he vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum substituted his brother Vanutio as universal heir. But in all his other movable and immovable goods, he instituted Vanutio, his son, as universal heir. After the aforementioned things, the said testator died, with the said Ant. and the said Vanutio surviving him. Then the said Ant. died, being more than 14 years old, with Lady Cecha, his mother, surviving him, who was the legitimate and natural heir and former wife of the son of the said testator, the father of the said Ant. Now it is asked: whether the said legacies of 60 florins in one hand, and 160 pounds of denarii in the other, pertain to the said Lady Cecha, mother and heir of the said Ant., and whether she ought to have these legacies claimed from the goods of the said testator? From whom, and what, and how much ought the said Lady Cecha, mother and heir of the said Ant., to have from the other legacies and things left in the said will by the said testator to the same Ant., and from the other goods of the said testator, and in the person of the said Ant., formerly the son, and the son of the said testator, and from whom?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether what the testator wishes to be deducted, such as debts, comes into the restitution of the fideicommissum? And whether it is imputed to the legitime.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Because that which the testator wishes to be deducted or provided as a debt in the restitution of a fideicommissum is not included, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law *cohaeredi*, section *cum filiae*, words *nec fideicommissum*, and in the Digest, *ad legem Falcidiam*, law *pater filium*, I say that the legacy made to the grandson, as to a creditor, the mother has free and preferential. And this is certain if the debt can be proven; but if it cannot be proven, it is doubtful, because by such a confession the debt is not proven, as in law *mater* at the end, *de liberis et posthumis legatis*. However, because the affection of the testator was that it should be possessed as a debt, I believe, as I said above, that it is not included in the fideicommissum according to the mind of the testator, arguing from the Digest, *de legatis primo*, law *quod in rerum*, section *si quis post*, and from the Digest, *de pactis et legatis*, law *cum domus*, section *filius*. Whether, however, it is imputed to the mother in her legitime, since the debt is not proven: truly, that it is, by the said law *Aurelio*, section *fi*, because it is presumed to be of the substance of the testator's goods, since the debt is not proven; but if it is proven, there is no doubt that it is not imputed. Code, *de inofficioso testamento*, law *scimus*, section *repletionem*. And therefore the mother must have her legitime from other goods, which are truly of the substance of the testator; which is the sixth part of the whole inheritance, considering the number of children, as in the *Authentica nouissima*, Code, *de inofficioso testamento*. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the crime of lèse-majesté is committed against the city of Florence, or other cities outside Rome. And whether. 3.
2. Whether a person conscious of the crime of disturbance, or sedition, committed against the city, ought to be punished on account of knowledge alone as a participant. Add the following Consilium.
body:
In the name of Christ. The point is as follows: instruments of condemnation are found, as contained below in each individual condemnation.

First, it is found that Lord Jac. was condemned by Lord Contem., then Captain of the People, etc., because the said Lord Jac., in the year 1379, in the month of June of the said year, while he was in the territory of Fabriano at the borders, in the market of the said territory, which is surrounded on all sides by public roads, there appeared [a man] sending arrows from Florence, and he said to the said Lord Jac.: "I have heard good news, that Benedetto di Simon Peruzzi has arranged to be able to enter Florence, and together with other exiles to lead up to twenty lances, and with other people, and it is believed for certain that he will come towards Florence, and re-enter for certain. And so that things may have effect, the method has been given, that all those who wish to hold this order make a written document in their own hand with their seal, so that it may be known whether those are capable or not. And therefore I beg you on behalf of Benedetto, and of those other exiles, that you wish to make this written document, which I have said, with the seal: and you will find that in court we will re-enter Florence, and if we cannot re-enter, we will make such war that we will have every agreement that we wish from the Florentines." And then the said Lord Jac. responded: "I am prepared, but I beg you, that you tell Benedetto, that he keep such a method, that I do not lose the grace of the Count of Florence, if this thing were not done, and give me notice in every way of wishing to make this written document." And then the said Matth. responded: "You have to write that you are content with every thing that Benedetto de Peruzzi does to re-enter Florence, he with the other exiles." And the said Lord Jac. made then the said writing, and sealed it with his seal, and handed it to the said Matth., and did not reveal the aforesaid to anyone, so that they might have effect to the grave damage and prejudice of the Guelph party, and the popular status of the arts and artisans of the city of Florence, etc. And it is known to us, and our court, that all and each of the above things are true, and were [true] by the free confession of the said Lord Jac. made spontaneously before us, and our court, as these, and other things are contained in our acts, and those of our court. Therefore we, Count, knight, defender, captain, governor, aforesaid, as above following, and wishing to follow the form of the statutes and ordinances of the commune of Florence, by the strength of our authority, that the said Lord Jac. be led to the customary place of justice, and there his head be amputated from his shoulders, in such a way and manner that he die completely, and his soul be separated from his body, in these writings we condemn him by sentence, as these, and other things appear more fully in the said condemnation, and sentence.

Also, it is found that Peter Philip of Florence was condemned by the said Lord Contem., because in the said year, and in the month of September just past, the said Pierus was returning from the city of Venice, where he had stayed at the borders, and was in a certain inn in a certain village near the castle of Saint Peter of the county of Bologna, there appeared Leonardus Lippicioni, and he said to the said Peter: "You are very well known. I see well that you have to ride in haste before you ride, I want you to hear several good news, it is true that we believe for certain to re-enter Florence, and all the exiles have given order to lead at our expense up to two hundred lances, and with these lances, and with other people that we will have together, we will go towards Florence, and we will go so provided, and warned, that within Florence a tumult will rise, and we will re-enter by force or truly we will be restored by the love of the people of Florence, and we have given order that one of these exiles go for this people, and you will find, that this will not have a long term: and therefore you will be warned, when you hear the fact, you will be prepared with all your power, one thing I beg you, that this be kept secret." And then the said Pierus responded: "Alas, woe, what have you said, that you have put me in a great dilemma, that if I reveal it to our lords, I will be a traitor to you, and I will put you all in danger, and if I do not reveal it, and if this were known, I am in danger that my head not be cut off. And therefore I beg you that you be disposed to do so that it be done so cautiously, that you, and I, not be in danger, I promise you to keep it secret, and in place and time I will do my just power." Which all he kept in secret, and did not reveal to anyone: to this end, that it might have effect better to the grave damage, and prejudice of the Guelph party, and the popular status of the artisans of the city of Flor., against the form of the law, statutes, and ordinances of the said city. As it is known to us, and our court, that all and each of the written things are true, and were [true] by the free confession of the said Perii made spontaneously before us, and our court, as these, and other things are contained more fully in our acts, and those of our court: therefore we, Count, knight, captain, and defender, and governor aforesaid, as above sitting, following, and wishing to follow the form of the statutes of the commune of Flor. and by the strength of our authority, that the said Perus be led to the place of justice, and there his head be amputated from his shoulders. in such a way and manner, that he die completely, and his soul be separated from his body, in these writings we condemn him by sentence, as these. and other things are contained more fully by the hand of the public notary, and in the said condemnation, and sentence.

Also, it is found that Ciprianus Lipposi of Florence was condemned by the said Contem., because in the said year, and in the month of September just past, the said Ciprianus was returning from the city of Milan, where he had stayed at the borders, he passed through the city of Bologna: and while he was in the inn of Felicis Admanatis, Nicolaus Bordonus of Flor. approached him, and he said to the said Ciprianus: "You return to Florence, that you have finished the borders of here, I am very content for your love," to whom the said Ciprianus responded: "I would wish, that you, and with others of Florence, could finally return, and I would not be less content for you, than for me, that suppose that you return, you make that we do not find anyone to hinder us." Which thing having heard, the said Nicolo responded to the said Cipria no, and "I see the love, and the faith that you have for the site of Florence. I want to make you content before you leave from here, that you will have very great pleasure, but I want that you count on faith, I promise you to keep it secret," to whom Cipria. responded: "On the faith of a merchant, what you tell me, no person will know it," to whom Nicolaus said to Ciprianus: "To return to Florence we have given order to have over two hundred lances at our expense, and to have other people of friendship, and with ours, and the others we will work in brief by war we will return to Florence with the name of God, you will be warned, that when the time will be, with all your power and knowledge you will do what you can, that the thing remains, that to return to state you and the others, who are out of flower, there is no other way than this, and stay well happy, that for the firm it cannot be, that it not be so." To whom Ciprianus responded: "Of this I am very content, and I know, that there is no other way for our fathers than that which you say, when it will be the time, I will do all my power, and knowledge of this, that you tell me, so that it have place." And it is said that the aforesaid Ciprianus kept in secret, and did not reveal to anyone, to this end, that the aforesaid might be more easily put into execution: to the grave damage, and prejudice of the Guelph party, peaceful, and the popular status of the arts, and artisans of the city of Flor. against the laws, statutes, ordinances of the said city. And it is known to us, and our court, that all, and each of the above things are true, and were [true] by the free confession of the said Cipria. made spontaneously before us, and our court, as these, and other things are contained more fully in the acts of our court. Therefore we, Count, knight, etc. as above following, and wishing to follow the form of the statutes of the commune of Flor. by the strength of our authority, that the said Ciprianus be led to the place of justice, and there his head be amputated from the shoulders. in such a way and manner, that he die completely, and his soul be separated from his body, in these writings we finally condemn him.

Also, it is found that Philippus Blaxii of Scrotis of Florence was condemned by the said Lord Contem., because the said Philippus in the said year, and in the month of May then just past, while Lord Philippus was staying at the borders in the city of Castello, and on a certain day of the said month Lord Philip. was standing in the church of Saint James of the said city of Castello, whose building adjoins on one side the said church, and on the other a road, and on the other Matthaeus Scieiti of Florence went to the said Philip. and he said to him: "Philip, I have to tell you the best news in the world, that Benedetto de Simon Peruzzi with other exiles staying in Bologna have given order to lead people for hire, and these people come to Florence and procure all their power to re-enter in Florence either by force, or by love, therefore Lord Benedetto has sent, if you wish to attend to these things, the method, which is this, that all the banished who stay in Bologna are gathered, and associated together, and each of them has a written document of his seal of never abandoning this business, until it be sent to execution. And therefore I beg you on his part that you wish to attend to it, and do not wait for the term of your borders, that God knows if you will be left to be taken out, and therefore make a written document in your hand with your seal as you consent to these things, and do not delay any more, and you will find for certain, that Benedetto with the other exiles, and banished of Florence will be sent to execution. from the fact suddenly." And then the said Philip. responded: "I am prepared, but I beg you, that this thing be kept secret, because if this were not done in time of my borders of returning to Florence, knowing this, you will never be able to re-enter, and return, and immediately he took a certain chart: and in it he wrote with his own hand, that he consented to all things that were done, and treated by the said Benedict re-entering the city of Flor. and he sealed his said writing with a certain seal of his, promising the aforesaid against the present peaceful, and tranquil status of the Guelph pupillary of the city of Flor. and to the grave damage, and prejudice of the artisans of the said city, and those wishing to live well in the said city, against the law, statutes, and ordinances of the said city. And it is known to us, and our court, that all and each of the above things are true, and were [true] by the legitimate confession of Lord Philip. made spontaneously before us, and our court in judgment, as these, and other things are contained more widely in our acts of our court. Therefore we, Count, knight, captain, Count, and defender aforesaid sitting on the tribunal, as above following, and wishing to follow in the aforesaid the form of the law, statutes, and ordinances of the city of Flor. and by the strength of our authority granted to us, that the said Phili. accused be led to the customary place of justice: and there his head be amputated from the shoulders in such, and such a way, that he die completely, and his soul be separated from the body. in these writings we condemn him by sentence, as these, and other things appear in the said sentence.

Also, it is found that Lord Donatus Glerutii of Barbados of Flor. was condemned by Ianinus Lutii of Cestulo, ordinary executor of the city of Flor., because Lord Donatus had been sent on behalf of the commune of Florence in an embassy to Lord Bartolus de Pace to the commune of Venice, and to Lord of Padua, he had made the journey through the city of Bon., and while he was staying in the said city, he found in the said city of Bonon. Barthola. Nicolini Cianis Rodulfi Beseondic. Cymonis Raynerii of Perusia, excommunicated of the said commune of Flor. and Ben. 12. other excommunicated of the commune of Florence aforesaid, of whose names he said he did not remember, in whom the said Donatus, excommunicated, inscribed, had a discussion, and conversation, namely that the aforesaid excommunicated said to Lord Donato, that they had ordered, that certain citizens of Florence, who dwell in Lono., excommunicated, and not excommunicated, who are called Litionipii, should come to the said city of Flor. with the said banners, signs of the Guelph father: which banners were made in the city of Bologna, and raise a tumult in the city of Flor. with the said banners in hand, and cry, "Long live the people, and the Guelph party:" and some should begin the said tumult at the gate of Saint Nic. and some others at the gate of Faentina, and in many places of the said city, and the tumult raised, they should draw to the said gate of Faentina, and the said gate they should break, and through the said gate the said excommunicated should enter with a great company of people, and the aforesaid should be done on the 20th day of the month of December then next future: and thus change the status of the city: to which all aforesaid, and each, the said Donatus responded. that it was well ordered, and for certain it will have the desired end. and that in necessary, and opportune time the said Donatus will give counsel and favor to the aforesaid. and by the said Donatus, and others it did not remain, that the aforesaid discussion had been brought to effect, but for the reason that those. who came to the said city of Flor. with the said banners were captured by the officials of the commune of Flor. and thus the said discussion was destroyed, and manifest. by which all aforesaid committed, and perpetrated by the said Lord Donatus, and others named, tumult, scandal, tumults were made in the said city of Flor. and the peaceful, and tranquil status of the said city was disturbed. And it is known to us, and our court, that the aforesaid, and all, and each contained in the aforesaid inquisition are true, and were [true] in place, and time contained in the said inquisition by the true, and legitimate confession of the aforesaid Lord Donati made spontaneously before us, and our court in judgment: to whom Lord Donatus etc. and he made no [defense] etc. as these, and other things are contained more widely in our acts, and our court. Therefore we, Ianinus, executor aforesaid, sitting on the tribunal, as above following, and wishing to follow the form of the law, statutes, and ordinances of the commune of Flor. and by the strength of our authority granted to us in this part specially, namely, that the said Lord Donatus be led to the customary place of justice, and there to the said Lord Donatus his head be amputated from the shoulders, in such, and such a way, that his soul be separated from his body, and he die completely, and in every way by the way of law, and form of authority, and cause by which we can, and ought, best, Lord Donatus in these writings we condemn him by sentence, and as these, and other things contain the aforesaid condemned, and sentence in the year 1379. on the 23rd day of the month of December.

Also, it is found among other things a certain statute placed. in book 3 of the Lord Podesta under the heading "On finding the goods of the condemned." The tenor of which, word for word, is as follows: The said Lord Podesta, and his judge, knight, and notary, and any of them, to whom the said Podesta would commit, and the Lord Captain of the People, and his judge, are bound, and ought to make a solemn, certain, and diligent inquisition of all goods of the condemned of Flor. or excommunicated, however, or condemned: however, and if anyone appears willing to defend certain goods, or things, in his own name, or another's, which were, or were said to be of the said excommunicated, or were said to be goods, and things belonging to him, or to another, by any right, or cause, before he be heard in anything, or his defense be admitted, he is bound to deposit with the officials, and lords of all tolls of the said commune 500 lib. or less, as it will seem to such official actor, considering the quality, and value of the said goods, and things, and the man exactor, or official is bound within the fifth day after the said deposit was made to notify in the council of the people of Flor. and the chapter of the arts. how such has made the said deposit for the defense of the goods of such condemned, or excommunicated, and moreover the instruments, by which he wishes to use for the defense of the said goods, and things, immediately assign, or to the official, before whom he will be, under this condition, and mode, if it appears that the said instruments are fictitious, or simulated, the said money come integrally to the commune of Flor. And the same rector, before whom such instruments were produced, is bound to punish, and condemn him producing, or using them, to the commune in the public general council in the quantity deposited: and nevertheless to cancel, and annul the instruments totally. And it be held for full proof, that such instruments are fictitious, or simulated, if such excommunicated, or condemned, or anyone of his family has used the goods, and things alienated: or held them, and possessed them after the contract of alienation made, or before such alienation for one year, or less: as is contained in the statute placed here under the heading "On alienation made by those committing maleficium etc." or otherwise of the simulation, or fiction it has been proved by four good, and legal witnesses proving public fame. In the aforesaid also it may be proceeded, or ought to be, at the petition, and instance of any public, or private denouncing, notwithstanding holidays, and without noise, and figure of judgment. And to remove all doubt it is added, that the res publica, and fisc of the city, and commune of Flor. be understood to have, and have the same privileges, honors, and prerogative, and immunity, which, and which, as, and so it has, or is understood to have the res publica of the Romans, and the fisc, and it enjoy all, and each of these in any case by right, and business etc.

Also, it is found a certain other statute placed in the said book 3 under the heading "On the penalty of one shouting, and making a contractation." The tenor of which, word for word, is as follows, namely: If anyone from wherever, and of whatever condition, and status he be, has presumed, or dared against the Lords Podesta, Captain, Priors of the Arts, and the Banner of Justice, or any, or some of them in council, parliament, or other congregation, or elsewhere wherever to shout, or make a tumult, or say any contemptuous, vile, or dishonest words, or offend any of them, or in any part of the city, boroughs, suburbs of Flor. to shout to arms, or to seram, or to any singular person, or house, or progeny of the city of Flor. to say, "Long live, long live." or "Die, die." or make a tumult, sedition, exclamation, or have made, for the time of any tumult without the will, and license of the Lords Priors of the Arts, and the Banner of Justice, or at least come to the city of Flor. with arms, or with a company of men, or without, or in the county, or city of Florem. or elsewhere create, order, make, or have made anything, for which scandal, tumult, or tumult arises, or may arise in the city, county, or district of Florence, or for which the peaceful, and tranquil status of the people, and commune aforesaid is disturbed, or may be disturbed, let him be punished, and condemned in person, and goods at the discretion of the Podesta, or Captain. And moreover in all, and each, the Lords Podesta, and Captain, and any of them have this cognition, and bailiwick, and also free authority inquiring, investigating, torturing, cognizing, punishing, and condemning with accusation, and condemnation, and without accusation. or from denunciation by his office, and inquisition secretly, and openly, and in every way, and mode also as it pleases, and seems convenient to the same, or either of them, considering. the person and persons committing against the aforesaid or any of the aforesaid things. and business, access, quality considered, provided that a lesser penalty, than that contained in the ordinances of justice in the commons, in which the said ordinances speak, in no way can be imposed against those doing the aforesaid, or any of the aforesaid, and the process, which the said Lords Podesta, Captain, or any of them has begun, he must, ought to terminate. within 20. days, after it has come to the knowledge of any of them, Podesta. Captain, that if they do not do so, they lose from the salary of the said contravening 50 lib. for which. in which the ordinary executor of justice, and the syndic, who will syndicate him, or syndics only, be condemned. And nevertheless they are bound, and ought. within other 15. days after the aforesaid 20. to do, and execute the aforesaid under similar penalty of statute. or ordinances, nothing else obstructing.

Also, it is found a certain other statute placed in the said third book under the heading "On the penalty of one making a congregation, or alteration by violation of the people, order of justice, or invading any city, or place," the tenor of which is as follows: Whatever person of the city, county, or district of Florence. or even another from the year of the Lord 1333. month of January until now has done, or will do in the future in the said city, district. or county, or elsewhere wherever, any alteration, or congregation of people, conventicle, conspiracy, or post for violating or subverting the people, or the order of justice of the said people, or any of them, or against the said people, or the liberty of the same for invading any city, or castle, especially of the province of Tuscany, or neighboring the county of Florence. or city, or district bordering with the county, and district of Florence. or goes, or is in the said contra-conventicle, conspiracy, or posture under penalty of the head, and publication of all goods, unless he made it for occupying, or invading etc.

Also, it is found a certain other statute in the ordinances of justice 323. under the heading "On the penalty of one shouting in council, or parliament, or coadjuvation, and making a contract without license of the commune:" the tenor of which, word for word, is as follows. Also, lest and which for the eviction of the people will be saved, found, cannot redound to the perniciousness of any, nor of any cunning, it is statuted and ordained, that no rector, or official of the commune of Florence. or any singular person of the city, county, or district of Florence dare, or presume in council, or parliament, or any coadjuvation, which happens to be made in any way, to make any incitation, or exclamation, or advise the populars, that they break out in any vociferation, or exclamation, unless perhaps he shouted, or said, "Long live the people," or "Long live justice," or "Long live the Guelphs," and that none even of the aforesaid dare, or presume to enter into any discussion, bargain, or treat with any lord, or with any whatever person of whatever status, or condition of those things that pertain to the commune of Florence. openly, or secretly, and secretly of any rebels of the commune of Florence to be reduced, or rebanned without the express license of the Lords Priors, and Banner of Justice, of which there ought to appear a public instrument: whoever however has contravened, immediately let the Podesta have him retained personally, and to him convicted let the head be amputated from the shoulders, in such a way that he die: which the executor shall procure to be done diligently, and if the Podesta has neglected to do this, let him be condemned by the executor in 1000 li. [Currency = parvorum?]. for which. and nevertheless the executor shall do, that which ought to be done, or was omitted by the said Podesta. and if at any time there were in the city any tumult, suspicion, the said executor may, and is bound to gather all the banner-bearers of the society, and from their counsel do etc.

Also, it is found a certain statute placed in the said ordinances 225. under the heading "On the penalty of a popular. who has been present, where something was treated against the people of Florence," the tenor of which is as follows, namely. Also, that traitors of the people, and supporters of the magnates be constrained by due discipline, it is provided, and deliberated, that if any popular of the city, county, or district of Florence. has been present at any conventicle, or has accessed the counsel of a magnate, where it was treated of the violation, or subversion of the people of Florence. or the ordinances of justice, or where it was treated of any tumult to be made in sedition, or where anywhere it is conspired against the liberty, or status of the people of Florence. and especially against the executor, or prior of the arts, and Banner of Justice, let him be punished, and condemned by the penalty of the head by the aforesaid executor: and nevertheless he, and his sons, and descendants by the male line be understood, and be magnates, and be had, and treated. saved that the aforesaid do not obstruct, nor prejudice in any way the partners, or blood relatives of such pupillary.

Also, it is found a certain other statute placed in book 3 of the Lord Captain under the heading "That the executor may inquire of maleficia, which are committed by magnates," the tenor of which is as follows: That maleficia, which are committed daily by magnates, and pupillaries, do not go unpunished, it is statuted. that the ordinary executor of justice etc. Also, it is statuted, and ordained to this end, that cities, and counties, or districts flourish in quiet, and tranquility, and conspiracies, and conventicles, which are said to be frequently made in the city of Florence. for the subversion of the Guelph father, and the Florentine people, be removed, that if anyone has dared, or presumed in the city, county, or district of the same to make, or have made any congregation, composition, or conventicle, or in council, or any congregation to say, or utter vile, or dishonest words against the Lords, Podesta, Captain, Priors of the Arts, and Banner of Justice, or any of them, or to make a tumult, or rumor, or anything else, or have ordered to be made, for which rumor, or scandal, or tumult, or incitation of arms would arise, or could arise in the city, or county, or district of Florence, or the present status of the peaceful, or tranquil people, or commune of Florence. be disturbed, or be disturbed, or be subverted. or be impeded in any way, let him be punished, and condemned in person, and goods by the ordinary executor of justice at his discretion. And in the aforesaid, and any of the aforesaid, let the aforesaid executor have cognition, bailiwick, and authority, inquiring, investigating, and proceeding, and condemning, and with accusation, and denunciation, and without, and by his office, and inquisition secretly, and openly, and in every way, mode, and as it seems, and pleases to the same, inspecting the condition, quality, and excess of the business, and persons, preceding indications, and not preceding.

† It is asked, having seen all and each of the aforesaid matters, whether the goods of those condemned should have been published and confiscated by the aforementioned rectors who issued the said sentences; and whether, assuming that in the said sentences they were not published or confiscated, they can or ought today to be published and confiscated, or incorporated, into the Commune of Florence, or not? What about the fruits received from the said goods after the said sentences? And it seems that they should have been published and confiscated by the aforementioned rectors; and assuming that in the said sentences they were not published, they can today be published and confiscated for the Commune of Florence; and consequently, the same applies to the fruits. And first, according to common law, even with all statutory law written down. Second, let it be assumed that not according to common law, because the contents of the aforementioned inquisition and condemnation seem to fall under the crime of lèse-majesté: because it is said that they solicited and incited that sedition and tumult against the public good should not occur. L. 1, D. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis. Also, because they seem to have incited and supported enemies, that is, those excommunicated and outlawed. L. 3, eod. tit. Also, they seem to have acted with malicious intent against the public good, or to have caused it to happen. L. 4 and L. 5, in fine, eod. tit. Also, it seems to be the text in L. 1, eod. tit., and the gloss holds this in L. fallit, C. de abolitione, in fine, gloss on the word "praedicta." Therefore, the aforementioned goods should have been published and confiscated, and can be, etc. L. in fine, eod. tit. Nor is anything innovated in this case, as is clear in Auth. bona condemnatorum, in fine. Also, it seems expressly stated in L. quisquis, C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis.

† Moreover, because one who is aware of the disturbance of his city, or of another offense committed in his city, is punished as a participant on the basis of knowledge alone, as stated in *l. utrum*, ad *l. Pompeiam*, de partibus, and as noted there by the doctors, especially against the prince, in *d. l. quisquis*. Secondly, let it be established that, if not by the common law, at least by the municipal law, this appears clear; and this in three ways. First, by the first statute, *Per quos res publica ciuitatis Florentiæ et c.*, without calling into doubt the power of the condemning authority in this regard. Secondly, let it be established that, in the city of Florence and so forth, yet in the aforementioned statutes placed under the rubric *De pœna facientium congregationem et c.*, in the aforementioned cases, the publication of goods is expressly imposed, as is evident from the form of the said inquisitions and condemnations, as stated in *l. municipali*. If so, therefore, the *Authentica bona damnatorum* has no application, and thus the goods ought to have been published by virtue of the said municipal laws. They ought to have been so treated under the old law, *Auth. bona damnatorum*, especially since, once the crime has been declared by sentence, the publication of goods follows, according to *l. 1, § 1*, ff. ad *leg. Iuliam de turpitudine*; *l. ordine*, in fine, ad *leg. Iuliam de municipalibus*. Thirdly, because even if the publication of goods is not expressly stated in the sentence, it is nevertheless understood to apply by right by virtue of the said municipal laws, according to *l. quod ad statutum* and *l. qui ultimo*, ff. de poenis; *l. 1*, ff. de bonis damnatorum; *l. deportatorum*, C. eodem titulo.

† To the contrary, and first: because under the common law, the goods of the aforementioned persons, or of any of them, circumscribed by statute, ought not to have been published, etc., because the matters contained in the aforementioned inquisition and condemnation, or any of them, did not fall under the crime of lèse-majesté. This crime applies only where someone acts against the prince, or those who stand on his side, or against the Roman Republic, not in other cities. L. quisquis, C. ad l. Iul. maiest.; and L. ob pecuniam, D. de furtis; L. 2, in fine, ad l. pecul.; and this is proven in the aforementioned L. fallaciter, §. si, C. de abolitis, where the crime of lèse-majesté and the attack on the fatherland are distinguished as different species. And this is the ordinary gloss and the note in L. 1, in principio, D. ad l. Iul. maiest. And thus all the laws cited above regarding this contrary part speak concerning the city, namely the Roman Republic, as is expressly clear in them. And so they do not act against [the present case], but rather for the place from the special: because thus specially in the city and Republic of the Romans, as there: therefore in others it is otherwise. D. de municipiis, L. 1.
