And this is most true in the proposition, where it was not a matter of oppressing or destroying the fatherland, but of mute defenses and partialities among citizens, as in L. si quis ingenua, §. in civibus, D. de captivis; and L. 2, §. iisdem temporibus, D. de origine iuris. And by this the gloss in the aforementioned L. fallaciter is clarified. For it seems to speak well, unless it was understood concerning the common fatherland. And if, therefore, on account of conscience, from mere knowledge he were to be punished as a participant in the crime from those things done against their city, as in the aforementioned L. utrum, nevertheless not as a principal in the crime of lèse-majesté, because it was not against the city or Republic of the Romans, as has been said. Secondly, I say that under municipal law, and if the Republic and the treasury of the common city of Florence are understood to have, and do have, the same privileges, benefits, and immunities which, and as which, as, and so as the Republic of the Romans has, or is understood to have, and suffers in all these and each one in any case, law, and matter, and without in any way calling into doubt the validity of the statute: nevertheless the Republic or treasury of the city of Florence is not the Republic or treasury of the Roman city; because the words of the municipal law do not sound, nor do they say this. S. that the Republic and treasury of the Roman city: therefore the offense committed against the Republic and treasury of the city of Florence is not the crime of lèse-majesté, because the terms cease. L. delictum, D. de levis inducentis. Nor do the words of this law make it so that an offense committed against one appears to be against another. Thus, therefore, one who offends against the Republic and treasury of the city of Florence does not offend against the Republic or treasury of the Roman city, nor is he deemed to offend. Therefore, they are not bound by the crime of lèse-majesté: because such a crime is not committed. For a disposition concerning actively or passively does not go beyond him, nor have place in another. L. si unus, §. omnia, D. de pactis. And if it is said that, although the Republic and treasury of the city of Florence is not, it is not necessary that it be deemed the Republic or treasury of the Roman city, nor that one is heard to offend against the Republic or treasury of the Roman city, who offends against the Republic or treasury of the city of Florence, publication of goods ought to follow, as for that committed against the Republic and treasury of the Roman city: because the Republic and treasury of the city of Florence has the same privileged benefits, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How manyfold majesty is.
2. Those who act against their own city, other than Rome, do not incur the crime of lèse-majesté, but rather the crime of sedition, no. 3.
3. By what punishment those committing the crime of sedition are to be punished.
4. The punishment must be imposed according to the municipal law, when the municipal law itself differs from the common law.
5. A statute concerning personal punishment is not extended to property; hence, confiscation of property does not follow as a consequence. Add the preceding opinion.
body: In the name of Christ. Although laws properly bearing on the matter and determining it have been elegantly adduced for and against, nevertheless, for fuller instruction, three points are to be reviewed. First, it is to be considered what is the title of this crime; second, how it is punished; third, by what penalty, and these have certain particular members: first, whether in such a penalty a judicial sentence is also required; but if a judicial sentence is required, whether a tacit sentence suffices regarding the confiscation of goods, or whether an express confiscation is required. I return to the first.

I premise, for the sake of clarity, that majesty is manifold. See the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Non distinguimus*, § *Sacerdotio Imperatoris*; as well as the Institutes, in the Proemium; and the Code, *Ad legem Iuliam maiestatis*, l. *Quisquis*; also the Digest, *Eodem titulo*, l. *1*, and the Code, *Ut nemo princeps*, title *De maiestate*. Secondly, there is the majesty of the praetor. See the Digest, *De iustitia et iure*, l. *Penultima*; and *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, l. *Si familia*. However, cities are not said to possess majesty, except those pertaining to the City [Rome], because cities are regarded in the place of private persons. See the Digest, *De furtis*, l. *Ob pecuniam*; and *De verbis significatis*, l. *Bona ciuitatis*, and l. *Eum, qui vectigal*. Likewise, the Guelph or Ghibelline factions are not said to possess majesty; for these are not names of the city, but names of partiality, as is noted in the Decretals, c. *Statutum*, § *Cum autem*, *De rescriptis*, Book 6.

From these it appears that such partialities, whether for or against, do not properly fall under the crime of lèse-majesté, since such partiality is not majesty: and from whom the name is removed, the effect is also removed. C. de feriis, l. nullo. And those who fight among themselves by reason of their offices or stations in common are not properly said to rebel against the public affairs of their city. ff. de cap., l. si quis ingenua, §. 1, in ciuilibus. Nor ought they properly to be said to rebel against the prince, who granted them magistracy and authority, as expressly noted by Bartolus in the Extravagant ad remp., on the word “rebellando,” in the question which begins, “sed an haec constitutio,” etc., and he cites for the case the saying in §. in ciuilibus. Since therefore municipalities, however distinguished, do not possess majesty, the crime of lèse-majesté is not properly committed against the city itself, as is the ordinary gloss in l. 1, ff. ad l. Iul. maie., unless there were a sedition such that the city itself would be withdrawn from the prince by whom it was immediately governed; for then the crime of lèse-majesté is committed with respect to the prince, not with respect to the city. And thus the gloss in l. 2, C. de aboli., should be understood, which can be seen from the laws it cites, in which mention of the res publica is often found, which refers to the res publica of the empire and the Roman people, not to other places, except insofar as they are part of that res publica in a subjective manner. Arg. from what is noted in l. 2, §. publicum, ff. de iust. et iure, in the ordinary gloss: for then he who offends a part, even if it be an ear, seems to have offended the whole. Arg. ff. de fur., l. vulgaris. Let it therefore be concluded first that the title of this crime is not properly lèse-majesté; but it is the crime of sedition. And even if it were lèse-majesté, it is under the special head of sedition. Sedition is when someone treats of making treason and innovation against the public and good state of the city, or makes war, or something similar, not by bare thought, but by proceeding to some act, such as making a conspiracy, or a rumor, or war, or occupying some land against his city or municipality.

† These persons are sometimes punished with death according to the common law. C. de sedi. l. 1. et 2. ff. de re mili. l. proditores. Sometimes they are punished more mildly, either on account of the dignity of the persons involved; or, for example, because they committed a lesser offense, in that they did not proceed to the act immediately following the preparatory acts, or because of wantonness rather than deliberate intent. ff. de pe. l. capitalium. §. solent. et l. si quis aliquid. §. fautores. Or, so that a massacre of many may not occur, eo. titu. l. aut facta. §. si. Or on account of extreme youth, as noted in §. pęna grauior, and this is according to the common law.

But we are now in the common law, for by municipal law one often departs from the common law, and the penalty ought to be imposed according to the municipal law. Therefore, this crime is to be punished by a new penalty. [This is the rule] of the municipal law, when the municipal law differs from the common law, as in D. de re militari, l. 3, § qui post discretionem, in the words "recessu" etc. From this it appears, according to the main point, that this crime is punished by the municipal law; and therefore we must adhere to the words of the statutes. D. qui et a quibus, l. prospexit. And we must be content with the penalties of the statute, not to be supplemented by the common law. D. de verb. oblig., l. si ita stipulatio facta. For a statute that detracts from the common law is not supplemented by the common law. D. de iust. et iur., l. ius civile. By what law, then, is this crime punished in Florence? I answer: by the law of the Florentines. From this it appears what the penalty is; because the penalty of the statutes, since the case, because the cases comprehended and named in the statute, the law in which we are, directs us in the way of knowing the penalty; because according to the law assumed in proceeding, it is necessary that the penalty be inflicted upon the condemned. And if several laws can be invoked, as noted in D. de confess., l. 2, in the gloss at the beginning, in case of doubt the way of the statute is assumed, because it is special at least with respect to place. D. de legibus, l. de hoc legatum. Therefore, let us follow the way of the statutes, neither adding nor detracting; because we ought not to add to penal and local statutes, as is fully noted in C. de temp. ord., l. 6. Although the common penal law, not being local, is sometimes extended by the word, but not by the meaning. C. de furtis, l. si quis servo. Likewise, we ought not to detract from the statutes; nevertheless, if the judge detracts, it is valid, because it is presumed by the sentence, and because he has power by the law today regarding penalties; and because if an absolving sentence is valid, therefore also a modifying sentence is valid. D. de in litem iuram., l. in actionibus, § 1; and l. videamus, § fin.; D. de iudicibus, l. si praetor; D. quando appellatio sit, l. 1, § biduum; D. de interdictis et relegationibus, l. relegatorum, § ad tempus. And certainly cities hold it of the greatest importance that their statutes and customs be observed by them. D. de officio proconsulis, l. observare, § ad tempus, and § pen. And therefore we will base ourselves on the statutes, not glossing them rashly, but serving the letter of the statutes and understanding them as they stand and lie. And I say, according to the truth, that the statute which begins "Si quis undecunque" speaks of an informal and arbitrary penalty, at the discretion of the authority; and the chapter, likewise, the statute which begins "Ut malitia quae per magna" speaks of the executive discretion of the ordinances of justice. And because an arbitrary penalty is uncertain until it is declared by the judge, in no way is a penalty not declared to be supplemented by legal implication; because it does not have uncertainty, except that which it cannot assume by the declaration of the judge, arg. D. de iure fisci, l. eius qui delatorem; and C. de contrahenda empt., l. fin. Hence it has in itself a condition, if the judge should arbitrate. And therefore if the judge declares a personal penalty, it is not understood to be such, because one penalty cannot exist without the other. C. de mulieribus quae servis propriis se iunxerunt, l. 1; C. de raptu virginum.

†Moreover, a statute imposing a personal penalty is not extended to goods, since it makes no mention of goods: because it is odious and of strict law, and local in nature; and because from one of the separated things, nothing is inferred to another, which is capable of being separated from it. C. de bonis praescrip. l. si filius: and de mino. l. 3. §. sed utrum. And because this procedure is not founded upon l. Iul. maie. but upon l. Flo. and it takes the form and observance of Imola. Hence, to argue from the Julian law is to argue from a law not intended, nor to be intended. Let us therefore remain content with the statute, and with the sentence fixing its foot in the personal penalty alone.

And from these it appears that the tacit confiscation of goods does not fall within the scope of corporal punishment in conscience: because the statute, which is of strict law, does not dictate this; therefore neither should we dictate nor supply it, as stated in the argument of the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the final law, at the end; and as noted in the final chapter of the Decretals, *De eo qui furtive ordinem suscepit*, according to Innocentius. In matters of discretion, we must simply hold firmly to what has been decided and presume that nothing further is to be adjudicated, especially to the exaggeration of the penalty. The objection based on the words "goods of the condemned" does not hold, because here there has been no proceeding under that law, nor that penalty, nor that crime, nor that fault. It supports what is noted in the Institutes, *De hereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur*, § *Per contrarium*; and in the Institutes, *De publicis iudiciis*, § *Penultimus*; and what is noted in the gloss on the Ordinance, etc. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus of Perugia, doctor of both laws. And to the truth I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made to a minor, whereby upon his death all his goods shall pass to another, excludes the mother: and if the woman is left as mistress, housekeeper, and usufructuary, so long as she lives honorably, such that she is bound to share the fruits of both the dowry and the other goods of the testator with his heirs, whether, upon the son’s death, the mother is required to share with the third substitute, etc.
body: In the name of Christ. Having seen the testament of Ser Jacopo of Csamario, in which he instituted as his heirs Ser John and Nico, his sons who were minors, and if both should die without sons, that all their goods should remain and be those of his grandson Cincitius, it is asked, if they die in minority, whether their mother succeeds in anything?

And it must be said that the answer is no; because, on account of the word “all,” the phrase “all their goods” constitutes an express pupillary substitution, in the event of their dying during minority. For, since the testator intended the goods of the minors to pass under the substitution, the substitution was therefore pupillary; for the goods of minors would not pass under a fideicommissum. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Haeredi, §. Cum filiae, ver. Nec fideicommissum. It follows that the mother is excluded entirely. L. Precibus, C. de impuberibus et aliis; D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, §. Sed nec impubes; and in c. Si pater, de testibus, lib. 6.

Secondly, it is asked: what if the same will contains a certain legacy, namely: “Furthermore, he left to his wife, the lady Vanutia, the dominium and the usufruct, so long as she maintains an honest and widowed life, provided that she shares and shall share the fruits of both the dowries and his other goods with the heirs of the said testator named below.” It is asked whether the said Cincius, the substitute, is included in these words, so that the legacy is due to the wife, where the wife shares the fruits with him. And it must be said that it is not due otherwise; for in a pupillary substitution, the heir is directly to the testator, with the knowledge of the testator, as noted by Bartolus, D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione; Baldus, l. Qui liberis, §. Haec verba.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a sum given as a reward for emancipation is to be counted toward the allowance.
2. Whether a son instituted for a single coin may declare the will null, or bring an action of complaint for an undutiful will.
3. Whether a son to whom the full legitimate portion has not been left may sue for the supplement, notwithstanding a prohibition or a paternal curse.
4. Whether daughters excluded by statute cause the legitimate portion to accrue to others.
body: Ser Lippus. Baldatimi died having made a will, which is shown to you in its form, in which he made mention of Franc., his son, as is more fully contained therein. Likewise, he made mention of his four daughters and two sons, as is more fully and clearly contained in the said will. Franc., the son, complains about the disposition of his said father as being made indiscreetly; because by it the portion due to him was not assigned, but rather was unduly denied or taken away. It is asked first, whether the said will, in which the said Franc. is instituted as a legatee in a certain thing, and in which no words are placed in his favor in the institution, but rather to his detriment, because he is instituted in the thing of Franc. himself by ambiguous words, such as “in gifts,” etc., and by rights held by me, and by precepts, etc., and then in a minimal quantity, s. in x. lib. cum dicta haereditas, or whether the remaining goods are one thousand florins, should it be annulled or declared null? Or, if it cannot be declared null, whether it can be challenged by a querela, or what remedies are granted to Franc. by law? And because the statute of Cortona excludes dowried daughters, what and how great is the license, whether it is half of the whole that remained in the goods, or a third, since the words of the law are verified. s. that five sons or more remained, and it is half: are these female daughters admitted to this half? Or are they repelled by the statutes, which repel dowried daughters, one of whom was dowried and married during the father’s lifetime? And because the father expressly wished that the dowries of the daughters be paid from the prelegacies made to the two sons usefully instituted, are they to be paid so much from the prelegacies that they should not be paid from the said half? And how should debts due by natural law be divided? Likewise, whether what was given as a reward for emancipation is computed in the legitima. In the name of Christ.

† On the point concerning the computation in the license, there are opinions. For Bartolus says that it is not to be imputed, unless it was done at the time of the donation that it should be computed. C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Si quando, §. 1. Nevertheless, according to him, it ought to be collated. C. de collatione, l. Ut liberis, §. 1, and l. Illud. But Richardus, Malumbra, Marinus, Sylvestrus, and most doctors say that what was truly had is to be imputed in the license, since it was given as a reward for emancipation, because it is the same as if the father were to say, I give to you for your share. And this is truer in our case, where it was said for alimony, for it takes the place of alimony. C. ad legem Iuliam de maritandis ordinibus, l. Quisquis, §. Ad filios; C. de nuptiis, l. Scimus, through Cynus. And therefore I say that it is to be imputed in the license, insofar as it was truly given. And this ought to be investigated by the subtlety of the law. D. de castrensi peculio, l. Si forte; C. de collatione, l. Si dona.

† On the first point, whether the aforementioned Fran can declare [the will] null or bring an action for an inofficious will, it must be said that an institution of an heir in a single coin suffices to validate the will, as noted in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Si quis priore; and C. de inofficioso testamento, Auth. Nouissima; and D. de minoribus, l. 3, § Sed utrum.

†Concerning the point, however, which is asked, namely whether, since the said Fran. does not have his full legitime, he can bring an action for the supplement notwithstanding the prohibition or malediction of his father, it must be said that he can, as in Auth. sed cum de appel. cog. §. caeterum, C. de inoffi. test., l. omnimodo, and l. sancimus.

But there remains one very difficult doubt, namely: what is the amount of this legitime? Is it one-third, considering only the males? Or is it one-half, considering the females? And there is no doubt under the *ius commune* that all sons and daughters are counted, as in the *Authentica Nouissima* and in the law *Maximum vitium*. But the statute, which excludes those who have received a dowry, creates a doubt. It seems, namely, that either the daughters are counted, and thus it is one-third; because he who is not admitted to succession is not counted among the successors, especially the useful ones, D. de contrah. emptione, l. 1, §. si. Or they are counted, and then, to the extent that their share is deducted by the statute, the share of the males is increased. For the provision of the law must benefit him in whose favor it is made. D. de pactis, l. Quod dictum; D. de legatis 3, l. Fideicommissum, §. Interdum. But this provision, which detracts from the right of women, was made for the sake of the males, as noted by Cynus, C. de adulteriis, l. Publico. Therefore, what is taken from the women is conferred upon the males. Moreover, to the extent that a share is lacking, it accrues to the others; if it is lacking in its entirety, it accrues in its entirety. Thus it should be in part with respect to part. D. quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Cum maiores; D. de rei venditione, l. Quae de tota. To this point contributes the reasoning noted by Bartolus, D. ad tertium, l. 2, §. Videndum.

On the contrary, it seems that the dowry succeeds in place of the full legitime, as noted, C. de nuptiis, l. Scimus. Therefore, daughters who have received a dowry have their full share; because the statute limits it only to what it can, as in the rule *Indultum*, according to Decius. Therefore, nothing accrues; because nothing is lacking; just as if the statute said that the daughter must have 10 for her share and no more, for that which would be more is corrected by the form of the statute according to the *ius commune*; and therefore that excess is not found, and thus it does not accrue, since the sons are counted with respect to themselves according to the *ius commune* and have a male share; but the females are counted with respect to themselves according to the municipal law and have only the dowry, or that which the statute provides. And to the extent that the statute derogates from the *ius commune*, that, as if it were non-existent, does not accrue, but remains at the discretion of the testator, whose freedom is increased to the extent that the share is diminished and prohibited by the municipal law. And thus I hold in the *Authentica Nouissima*. And this is the truth. And many other arguments could be alleged to this effect, which I omit for the present for the sake of brevity. And by these things the response is clear to the note by Decius in the law *Plane*, D. de legatis 1, because here there is nothing caducous. And because only the useful heir is burdened with the provision of dowries, and not the heir of a certain thing, therefore the benefit resulting from such provision of dowries ought to remain with the useful heir, not with another. D. familiae herciscundae, l. Si filia, §. pen. And the action for supplement, which is introduced in place of the complaint against a non-inofficious will, has no place here.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A release granted by a son to his father out of excessive reverence is invalid.
2. The expenses of the wedding feast pertain to the father, not to the son.
3. Whether gifts given to a wife remain with the husband or with the heirs of the woman.
4. No wages are owed to a son who is in the service of his father.
5. Heirs are not bound to a certain sum that has come to a woman of whom they are not heirs.
body:
The facts, upon which counsel is sought and requested, are these. And first, that a certain person named Ser Lippo Baldacchini of Cortona, in the year 1371, indiction ninth, on the 15th day of the month of November, promised, by way of emancipation, and as the price of his emancipation, to Franc., his legitimate and natural son, 200 gold florins, which 200 florins were to be held in the shop of the wool guild; and the same Ser Lippo wished and ordered that the said quantity of 200 gold florins, and all and every profit, advantage, and disadvantage that was then in the said shop, and that would be hoped for in the future in the said shop of the wool guild of the said Franc., be given as the price of the aforementioned emancipation. Finally, after the aforementioned premises and agreements, as appears from a public instrument drawn up by a public notary, the same Ser Lippo, wishing to attend to and observe the said premises and agreements with the said Franc., his son, but rather wishing to be released from the said obligations, bound and compelled the said Franc. to make, if he pleased, a discharge, release, and renunciation of the said quantity of 200 gold florins, and of the aforementioned profit, advantage, and disadvantage, together with a perpetual covenant not to sue further, with all those clauses which are customarily required in such instruments, as fully appears from the hand of Ser Lud., public notary. This was done because the same Ser Lippo stated that he had incurred many expenses during the time when the same Ser Franc. was under his power, for cloths and garments made for both the mother of the said Franc. and his wife, and for other expenses incurred by him, as is mentioned in the said instrument of release drawn up by the hand of the said Ser Lud. The said Ser Lippo, holding, possessing, and receiving the fruits from both the dowries of the mother of the said Franc. and those of his aforementioned wife, the said Franc., not wishing to contradict the will of his father, nor to contend with him, but rather out of fear and reverence, discharged and released him from the said 200 florins and the advantage, profit, and disadvantage derived therefrom, in the year 1372, on the 13th day of September.

It is asked whether the said discharge is binding? Whether it can be revoked by law, so that the said Franc. may claim the said quantity of 200 gold florins, and the aforementioned advantage and profit, from the heirs instituted in the will? Furthermore, it is asked whether the aforementioned heirs are bound to restore to the said Franc. the inheritance and the donation of his deceased mother? Furthermore, it is asked whether, after the emancipation granted to the said Franc. by his said father, the fruits received by the said Ser Lippo for two years from the dowries and dotal goods of the wife of the said Franc., then deceased, which dowries remained to Nico., the legitimate and natural son of the said Franc. and his said wife, who succeeded his said mother intestate, must the said heirs restore, if they exist, or if they do not exist, their value? The same is asked, because the said Franc., after the said emancipation granted to him, remained and exercised the wool trade for a period of three years and more for the said Ser Lippo, as his factor; whether he ought, or may, claim wages for the said time from his heirs? Furthermore, it is asked, since a certain person named Iunta Manuti of Cortona bequeathed and left in his will, by way of institution, to Dame Franc., formerly the wife of the said Ser Lippo and formerly the mother of the said Franc., 100 pounds of denari, which quantity was paid by the heir of the said Iunta to the said Dame Franc., wife at that time of the said Lippo; from which quantity of 100 pounds, by the order, presence, will, and consent of the said Ser Lippo, the aforementioned Franc., being under the power of the said Lippo, made a settlement, discharge, and release, and a covenant not to claim the said quantity of 100 pounds of denari from the aforementioned heirs of the said Iunta after the death of Iunta or of the mother; whether the said Franc. may claim restitution and satisfaction of the said 100 pounds of denari from the aforementioned heirs of Ser Lippo, formerly his father? In the name of Christ.

†On the first point, it must be said that if a son releases his father through fear or excessive reverence, such release is invalid; nevertheless, the son must prove this. C. de dolo, l. si superstitem; and ff. quarum rerum actio non datur, l. 1, §. que honorandę. But if fear or excessive reverence is not proven, then the repudiation is valid, provided that the final cause of the repudiation is a lawful cause for repudiating; but here there is no lawful cause, because the burdens of marriage pertain to the father-in-law, who received the dowry, not to the husband, who is under his power, as ff. so. ma., l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur; and what is noted eo. ti., l. si constante, in prin.; and ff. de mune. et hono., l. et qui originem, §. fi. sumptus.

† Therefore, the marriage does not pertain to the son; nor is he bound to the father on this account; nor is this a legitimate reason why the son should be required to make compensation to the father. And thus, the defense, which has a just cause, is overthrown by the replication of fraud.

† On the second point, Bartolus states that dowries given to the mother by the husband’s blood relatives remain with the husband; but if they were given on account of the wife’s blood relatives, they must be restored to the wife’s heirs. D. 35.2.12 § in arrogato (per Bartolus). But the better view is that, since the donation is complete and a right has vested in the wife, the wife transmits it to her heirs. C. 5.13.1. On the third point, it must be said that half of the usufruct remains with the mother, and the other half is due to the son. C. 5.55.1 § cum autem.
† On the fourth point, it must be said that no wage is due to a son who is in the service of his father, unless it has been agreed upon, i.e., promised. C. de negotiorum gestorum, l. obsequio.
† Regarding the last point, it must be said that the heirs are not bound by those [transactions] which came to the woman, of whom they are not heirs. 100. lib. C. de transac. l. nec intentio. cum si.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who, and in what manner, and through which persons property is acquired for a monastery, or for a church, see the three conclusions up to the end, with the distinction.
body: In the name of God. The facts are as follows: The said Nic. Herculanus, of the nobles of Castellio Stellio, of the city of Perugia, canon of the church of Saint Lawrence, the major church of Perugia, before he made profession in that church, drew up his testament; in which, among other things, he reserved for himself, and for the said church, the usufruct of all his paternal goods during the life of the said Lord Nic. Of this testament it appears from the mandate of Ser And. Nutii, notary; the fruits of which the said Lord Nic. always received during his life; which fruits could commonly amount, year by year, calculated from one year to another, to the value of 90 gold florins, or thereabouts. Finally, having made the testament, the said Lord Nic. made profession in the said church of Saint Lawrence according to the rule of Blessed Augustine, and remained in the cloister of the said church of Saint Lawrence for 13 years. Finally, the said Nic. was made archpriest of Saint Valentine, a manual member of the said church of Saint Lawrence; and he was instituted archpriest of the said church of Saint Valentine by the chapter of the said church of Saint Lawrence. Finally, within two years after the said Lord Nic. was instituted as the aforementioned archpriest, Nuptius Lelli bought certain houses, in truth from the funds of the said Lord Nic. and with the money of the said Lord Nic., although in the instruments of purchase it is stated for himself, Nuptius; and also, in the name of the aforementioned Francia Manutii, a certain part of the houses was bought, in truth for the said Lord Nic., although in the instrument it is stated for herself, Francia. Finally, the said Lord Nic. died, now 15 years ago. Finally, after the death of the said Lord Nic., the sons and heirs of the said Nuptius relinquished their right and renounced all possession and right which they had in the said houses by virtue of the said purchase, as appears from the hand of the public notary; and they said, and voluntarily confessed in court at the request and insistence of the syndic and procurator of the said chapter, that the said Nuptius paid nothing for the aforementioned properties; and if he had paid anything, he had been fully satisfied. Now the question arises, having seen the above, whether, according to law, the said houses belong, and ought to belong, to the said church of Saint Lawrence, or to the said church of Saint Valentine; and whether that which the said Lord Nic. acquired after he made the said profession belongs, and ought to belong, to the said church of Saint Lawrence, or to the said church of Saint Valentine, which church is, and was, a manual benefice of the said church of Saint Lawrence. In the name of Christ.

† It must be examined who, in what manner, and through which persons monasteries or churches acquire. Nevertheless, it is necessary to presuppose that those who are under the power of another acquire for those in whose power they are, with a distinction. For they are either under the power of another by reason of servitude, or by reason of profession, or by reason of paternal power. In the first case, whatever a slave lawfully acquires, he acquires for his master. D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Quod servus; D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 1, in principio; D. de acquisitione rei donatae, l. Etiam invitis. In the second case, whatever a professed religious acquires, he acquires for the monastery. De officio ordinantis, c. Quanto; and fully noted by Innocentius, De privilegiis, c. Cum olim; 12 q. 1, c. Non dicatis; 54 dist., c. Multos; and noted in c. Dudum, § Verum, De decimis, in the Clementines. And although a monk may hold a manual priory, or a regular canon a priory, or an archpriest a manual archpriestric, nevertheless it is not within his own power, but constitutes disobedience, since he can be recalled to the cloister; therefore, from all causes he acquires for the monastery, except if he acquires from the property of the priory or administration, and by virtue of the priory or administration something is given or left to him. And the reason in the first case is that the thing acquired succeeds in place of the thing from which it is acquired; hence this follows from the nature of subrogation, as is noted. C. de rei venditione, l. Si ut proponis. In the second case, the reason is derived from the nature of contemplation. D. de annuis legatis, l. Annuis viris verbis, § 1; D. de vulgari substitutione, l. Sed et si plures, § In arrogato. For the nature of contemplation is such that it produces upon request. De testamentis, c. Requisisti. It is held that contemplation has a representative force. D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Aditio, § Finis.
† And from these, set forth three conclusions. The first is that whatever the monks acquire, they acquire for him in whose power and obedience they are by right of power which is in him.

The second reason is that what he seeks from the priory or from the administration entrusted to him, he acquires for that priory or administration by virtue of a certain commutation made by him, which is done in three ways: from a thing to a thing; from money to a thing; from a thing to money. It could also be from money to money, as from carlins to florins.

The third conclusion is that what is sought by reason of the priory is sought for the priory, even if it is manual, since it has goods and a table for itself, as in c. 1 de rescriptis in the Clementines, and this is the nature of the relation in it.

† Moreover, it is necessary to know that sometimes the one who is in power passes from power to power; sometimes he passes from power to non-power; sometimes, while remaining in power, he is to attain a rank or administration; sometimes he passes from power into liberty. An example of the first is a religious person passing from one monastery to another, or to another religious order; and in such cases, the following rule is given in contracts: he acquires for that monastery in whose power he is at the time the contract is perfected. D. de verb. oblig. l. si filius; and l. ult. D. de stip. serv. An example of the second is an acephalous monk, who is expelled from the monastery on account of a crime and does not pass to another. And regarding this, a negative rule is given: since he is considered as having been abandoned, he no longer acquires for the monastery from which he was expelled, as noted by Innocentius in the cited chapter Cum olim, and by Federicus de Senis in his work, c. 20, c. 21. The same applies to a monk who becomes a Minor Friar; for after he has become incapable of acquiring, he acquires for no one, except insofar as the law permits, regarding which such a rule is given, beginning with a reference: “First, it must be said.” That is, the order is considered. D. de leg. 2, l. debitor, § servo. An example of the third is properly our case: in which, from the foregoing conclusions, it must be said that if it is established that the houses were purchased with the money of the chapter, they are acquired by the chapter; and the money of the chapter is that which was reduced together with the fruits of the former personal patrimony. Doc. Nicolaus, as noted in Auth. ingressi, C. de sacr. sanct. eccl. And what was purchased therewith belongs to the chapter of the major church of Perugia, because its name ought to have been inserted in the instrument. 12 q. 4, c. sacerdotes; and see Innocentius de testamentis, c. cum in officiis. It supports D. de haered. inst. l. quidam cum filium; D. de manum. l. 4, § ab ignoto. But if it is established that they were purchased with the money of the archpriest, then they are acquired by the archpriest; but if there is doubt, then recourse is had to presumptions; so, however, that each may acquire as much as the reason of the law permits and diligent inquiry indicates. D. de stip. servo, l. servus communis Menii, § si. And judgment must be rendered as if between the father, that is, the chapter, and the son, that is, the archpriest, the question arises, Inst. per quas pers., note after the beginning. And if this cannot be distinguished in any way, it may be judged in favor of the chapter, by the right of power, that in case of doubt concerning an uncertain quantity, power should yield; supra, n. alijs partibus nihil potestas operatur, si ea non praefertur: quod esset absurdum. And thus I hold and conclude, struggling with each other, and in certain cases preferring a certain power. And I conclude for the chapter against the archpriestal church. But the example of the fourth member of the transition is explained. 23 q. 1, c. si. And these are notable and true. Therefore, assuming that the money for expenses was verisimilarly made from the fruits of the patrimony and from the revenues of the canonry, and could be reduced, judgment must be given for the chapter, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If someone has promised to provide sureties subject to a certain penalty, to be approved by such and such persons, and if the sureties are provided but not yet approved, and the penalty is claimed, after which claim the approval subsequently occurs, whether the penalty can be claimed.
body: A certain person promised to provide two sureties under a specific penalty, by such and such persons; and such approval did not follow, the penalty was demanded: after the demand of the penalty, approval followed; it is asked, whether the said penalty can be effectively demanded or not: and it should be known: that between the said parties it was agreed to provide within 8 days two sureties customarily given in similar cases: and where they were not customarily given, they must be approved afterwards by such and such persons; which approval did not follow before the demand of the penalty but afterwards, therefore whether the penalty can be effectively demanded. In the name of Christ. It matters greatly,

Whether the sureties were given to the party present and receiving, or to the absent party and another subsequently receiving. In the first case, the promise has been satisfied; nor is any further approval required; therefore, the penalty cannot be claimed. D. 40.1.1 (Inter causas), § Abesse; D. 46.1.1 (Satisdare); D. 46.1.1 (Qui satisdare cogantur); C. 2.15.1 (Si ab arbitro), § Finis. In the second case, if indeed the party ratified with certain knowledge, the same result follows; but if he did not ratify, then the discussion concerning money arises, where it matters greatly whether a day was appointed for the giving of security, but not for the approval; and then it suffices that approval be given at any time, provided, however, that it be within such a time that it may have some effect. Arg. D. 21.2.1 (Si rem), § Quolibet; D. 18.1.1 (Qui fundum). Whether a day was appointed on which the party promised to cause and procure approval, or promised to give approval within so many days. And then, because there is a day and a penalty, the penalty can be claimed with effect. L. Magna, C. 4.33.1 (De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione). Because where the interest ceases, nevertheless the action does not cease to be available where there is a day and a penalty; otherwise, where there is a penalty but no day; and therefore then delay is purged by the action, by which the interest ceases before the joinder of issue concerning the penalty. D. 50.17.1 (Si insulam), according to the opinion of the Transmontane jurists. What, therefore, in our case, where those words are used, "and afterwards to be approved," what is said: does "afterwards" mean within a few days, as in L. Et si post tres, up to the joinder of issue concerning the penalty, as in L. Si ita quis, § Seia, D. 50.17.1, and the aforementioned L. Si insulam? I answer and say that words uttered by a person do not signify a certain time; and therefore they do not constitute interpellation, but interpellation by a person is necessary, after which, up to the joinder of issue concerning the penalty, that which is principally sued for can be fulfilled, not afterwards; and therefore if in our case suit is brought concerning the penalty, upon joinder of issue it is effectively due, notwithstanding the approval in question. D. 19.2.1 (Si in lege), § Colonus; D. 16.3.1 (Promissor); D. 50.17.1 (Si servum), § Sequitur; and L. Cum stipulatus sum mihi a Proculo, with its material. It should be noted that, according to the hypothesis, approval is entrusted to two persons simultaneously; hence one alone does not suffice, even if the penalty could not be avoided by the approval of one. D. 3.3.1 (Pro tribus); D. 4.8.1 (Pedius); D. 28.5.1 (Si ita fuerit). The words are conjunctive. S. Bart. and Antonius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a son or grandson can revoke the contract of his father or grandfather, and to what extent.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A contract is sometimes made to the fraud of a son or grandson; sometimes it is simulated as if made, yet it is not truly made. In the first case, either it is a true contract that is not lucrative, such as a sale, and it is not rescinded, because by such a contract an alienation is contracted which prejudices the legitime. D. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. non usque adeo; and l. 1, de inofficiosa donatione, according to the authorities. Or it is a contract of donation, and it is rescinded up to the amount of the legitime. C. de inofficioso testamento, Auth. Unde et si parens; D. de legatis 2, l. Titia, § Imperator, s. quando frater committitur pro liberis contra liberos. Otherwise, according to some, it is revoked beyond that, as stated in the aforementioned laws. But that it is rescinded up to the legitime is not in doubt according to all. Or the contract is simulated, because, intending to accomplish nothing, they feigned a sale; for then such property must be divided among the children, just like the other goods of the deceased. Nevertheless, here the grandson must be content with the legitime, as in l. omninodo and l. cum in prioribus; he cannot demand more than the legitime. Or there is doubt, and then recourse is had to presumptions; and sufficiently probable presumptions are proposed here, as noted by Bartolus in a similar case: D. de donationibus, l. post contractum; D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. emptor. Therefore, this grandson can claim his share in the legitime. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si quis filium. Baldus

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a sale or a donation between husband and wife is valid.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Between husband and wife a true sale may be celebrated; and between the same persons a true donation cannot be celebrated. If this is a donation, whereas it is a sale, it matters. Was it principally sold, or was something secondarily donated? And it is valid insofar as it is a sale, but not insofar as it is a donation. Or was it principally donated, otherwise he would not have bought it? And then it is not valid: and this is proved in l. si sponsus. §. certa. and l. quod autem. §. si maritus. D. 24.1. (de donationibus inter virum et uxorem). D. 18.1. (de contrahenda emptione). l. si quis donationis. If, however, the contract is not a true sale, but simulated, it is litigated, and nothing is valid, neither the contract, nor the precarium, nor any conventional clause. D. 9.3. (de aqua pluviali arcenda). l. emptor. If, however, it is doubtful whether it was a true sale, or a true donation: or whether it was neither sale nor donation, but simulation: those inquiring must first consider whether the instrument contains testimonies of the thing and of the price agreed upon and paid: and then a true sale is presumed: or whether it contains a confession of the price, and then either the confession can be aided by some supporting evidence, and the confessor is believed, or not: and then a donation is presumed on account of the judgment of the law, as D. 22.5. (de probationibus). l. qui testamentum. and D. 24.1. (de donationibus inter virum et uxorem). l. iure iurandi. D. 39.4. (si quis in fraudem patroni). l. 1. §. si quis in fraudem. An oath in a simulated contract is not valid, as C. 4.30. (de non numerata pecunia). l. final. In this uncertainty, however, while the case is sub iudice, whether the wife possesses, she must be protected, or whether the adversary possesses, he must be protected. l. final. D. 43.16. (si per vim vel alio modo). It supports what we have said D. 7.5. (de bonis quae liberis). l. cum oportet. §. 1. and in c. cum in officio. X. 3.26. (de testamentis). according to Innocentius. From this it is concluded that if the wife, during the lifetime of the husband, possessed corporally, by collecting fruits, leasing, and doing that which possessors do, which is done in many ways. D. 46.3. (de solutionibus). l. titia. then the benefit would belong to the heirs of the wife. l. edicto. And just as it belongs to the first heir, so he transmits it: and simulation cannot be opposed with regard to that maximum edict, because it requires a deeper investigation. Some also say that the condictio ex lege would belong when it was sought. as in Inst. 2.6. (de usucapionibus). §. quod autem. at least if the heir is a son. l. cum miles. in princ. D. 39.3. (quibus ex causis maioribus). The petition for inheritance also belongs: and he could justify possession by proving the simulation, or by proving that it was a donation, when it was revoked. I do not trust the statute, because it does not require a true purchase, unless the instrument could be aided by other proofs, then the statute would have place, because the heir has the title of the deceased, and his own proper title. D. 41.2. (de acquirenda possessione). l. 3. §. pluribus. Personally, even if the contract is true, an action could be brought for delivery, as fully noted D. 2.14. (de pactis). l. ab emptione. If corporal possession was not delivered, otherwise it is different, as D. 18.1. (de contrahenda emptione). l. si quis fundum. §. fere.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an institution is conditional if the instituted heir has not dissipated the estate, or if he has not alienated it.
2. Whether an institution of a spurious grandson is valid.
3. How a grandson is included under the term "son."
4. Whether a spurious grandson can inherit from his grandfather by virtue of legitimation occurring after the grandfather's death.
body: In the name of Christ.

† If the said institution of the said spurious grandson was conditional or pure, it appears to be conditional according to the proper nature of the words used; for those words, “if he does not dissipate” or “if he does not alienate,” expressly create a condition, as is stated in the Digest, De acquisitione possessionis, in the law Qui absenti, § 1, and in the law Si quis peregre. And there, Dyonisius seems to hold the contrary: because where words, according to their proper meaning, cannot achieve what is at issue, they are understood outside their proper meaning, as in the Digest, De usufructu, in the law Leg. and in the law Proculus. Moreover, because ultimately one must adhere to the final intent, as in the Digest, Si certum petatur, in the law Si tibi, at the end. But here, at the end of the institution, the testator declares his own intent: for by permitting alienation in a certain manner and form, he seems to make him heir. As stated in the law Factum esse praecedentibus declarare, and in the argument from the Decretals, De testibus, chapter Cum tibi. And this is the truth, considering the mind of the testator, as in the argument from the Digest, De manumissionibus testamento, in the law Mevia, § Quod testator vere voluit, namely, that he should be owner and heir, so long as he did not dissipate and lived frugally. If, however, he did dissipate, what the law would be is not our concern. Secondly, having considered the testator’s will, we must examine the power of his will, namely whether he could have instituted this person as heir. And if indeed he had instituted him as heir under the condition “if he can take,” the institution would be valid, but it would contain within itself a condition, as in the Digest, De hereditate instituenda, in the law In tempus. But the testator did not add this to the form of the institution.

† Therefore, two points must be considered: first, whether this spurious grandson can inherit by virtue of the will; second, whether he can inherit by means of imperial legitimation in the territories of the Church. This matter has been much debated. Speusippus also raises it in the title *De haereditatibus quae ab intestato deferuntur*. Roffredus disputed it, and Jacobus de Belvis disputed it, and he places this question in *l. 1, de natu. li.* They hold contrary opinions. Bartolus holds with Jacobus de Belvis that the institution is valid, as he himself states in *l. Gal.*, § *quid si his*, *de li. et posth.* The conclusive reason is that in the case of a grandson, no law prohibiting this is found, as noted in *C. de nat. li.* and *l. 1*. Nor is there a reason of the law, because the grandson was not conceived through the fault of his grandfather; nor is there fraud of the law, because through a spurious or natural grandson nothing is acquired by his father, since he is not under his father’s power; nor is there any indication from the wording of the law.

† because the term “son” does not signify “grandson” in a matter where a distinction is made between son and grandson. As stated in the aforementioned law *si*, for in those things which are inseparably inherent in the son and adhere to his bones, there is no extension to the grandson. Law 3, § *si emancipatus*, *de contrahenda*. Just as his own passion, such as curvature or pain thereof. I consider it most unworthy that a spurious grandson, born of a spurious son, can be instituted as heir, when he labors under both his own and his father’s baseness. And therefore, the aforementioned last law, speaking within certain permissive and limiting boundaries, refers to a spurious grandson: but only to a natural one, who is born of a legitimate concubinage. However, we have no express law permitting or prohibiting this, as Odoardus says in the aforementioned law *si*, gloss. Nevertheless, the gloss states in *Auth. qui monachos effici sui*, § *si*, column 7, that where no express prohibition is found, it is understood to be permitted. And that gloss greatly supports the opinion that this grandson is capable [of inheriting] with respect to his grandfather. To this effect, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *si is*, in the reasoning of *sui*. In my view, regarding this spurious grandson, in whom I find no permissive action, either for the whole or part, on his own person, the following distinction pleases me: either this grandson was instituted as a grandson, and the institution is invalid, by argument from *C. de fideicommissis*, law *eam quam*; *C. de haeredibus instituendis*, law *nec apud peregrinos*. Or as an outsider, because he merited it well, provided that the merits preceded: and then it is valid, by argument from *C. de inofficioso testamento*, law *unde et si parens*. Otherwise, there is doubt, and in doubt, natural affection induces a presumption that [he was instituted] as a grandson. And thus it is invalid. By argument from what is noted, *ff. de pactis*, law *si tibi*, § *si pactus*. For this affection is of bad and corrupt root: and the defect is not purged, but continued, by argument from *C. de haereditatibus*, *Auth. idem de Nestorianis*. And if we were to say the contrary, behold, the law could be perpetually defrauded: for no one would ever institute his own spurious son; but he would say, “I institute my descendants.” And if the spurious grandson were to succeed from these, it would give the father of the grandson an opportunity to adulterate and to establish, in whatever manner, the procreation of children, even of nefarious and incestuous origin: which I do not believe the supreme prince, lover of chastity, would have wished to permit. Therefore, in my judgment, this grandson, who appears not to have merited, but rather to have demerited due to the quality of his life, could not have obtained the inheritance solely by the power of institution or restitution. Thus I believe and advise, always saving the truer opinion.

But whether he could have acquired by virtue of imperial legitimation: I say that he could not, because at the time of the testator’s death he was not capable, and therefore he does not acquire under the will, as is noted in the last paragraph of the Digest, *De regulis iuris*. Moreover, because a spurious son exists in the intermediate position and does not consent, or because the son is dead, the grandson cannot become his own heir of the grandfather through the legitimation of the grandson made after the grandfather’s death, with neither of them consenting, as is noted in the Digest, *De legitimationibus*, in the law *Benignius*, by Guillaume. Furthermore, legitimation made by a count, once successions have been accepted by another, cannot be taken away. See the law *Gallus*, section *Et quid si tantum*, and there by Bartolus; in the chapter *Quamvis*, *De rescriptis*; law 6. Moreover, legitimation is properly said to be a gift of the prince, as in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, section *Si non his qui solummodo*. And therefore the count and imperial authorities cannot extend their gift in the lands of the Church to the prejudice of those who do not consent. This is supported by the Digest, *De naturalibus restitutionibus*, in the last law, by Jacobus de Arena; *De filiis qui sint legitimi*; the chapter *Per venerabilem*, by Innocentius. Although Jacobus de Belvis disputes against Cynus and Bartolus, he consulted the same opinion as Jacobus de Belvis. For neither can the Pope legitimize with regard to succession in the lands of the Empire where it would cause prejudice, for example by approving a marriage which does not subsist according to civil law. Just as the Emperor cannot give the goods of barbarians, so he cannot give the patrimony of those exempt. Furthermore, it must be concluded decisively that the said institution and legitimation were of no effect, and that the inheritance of the said testator pertains to the persons enumerated. See the Code, *De incestis nuptiis*, in the law *Si quis in testamento*. And if those persons do not exist, then it pertains to the fiscus, as in the said law *Si*, *Ad fiscum*. Although this is commonly known, it is not so, nor does it object that the capable substitute was incapable: which could have been done, Code, *De heredibus instituendis*, law 3. For this was done in fraud of the law, so that it might be restored to the capable person: which could have been done, Code, *De heredibus instituendis*, law 3. And therefore it is not valid, by argument from the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Haeres meus*, section *Quod in fraudem*. And this is clear from the express wording of the will. And therefore it does not require proof.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a dowried woman shall not succeed to her paternal grandfather, whether a granddaughter who was not yet conceived during the grandfather’s lifetime, although the grandfather left something for the dowry of women to be born, may succeed to the said grandfather.
2. Whether a grandson who was not born during the grandfather’s lifetime is to be considered a grandson.
3. A lesser amount ought not to be given for the purpose of providing a dowry than the legitime.
body: ... contains chapters of which

† Because the statute has three chapters so far as concerns the matter proposed—one chapter is concerning a grandfather dowering, another concerning any other person whomsoever dowering, and the undowered [girl] having to be dowered by the paternal uncle, and by this to be excluded from the remainder of the succession—let us consider each chapter by itself. The chapter concerning the grandfather does not apply here: because with regard to the subject matter and cause of successions,

† one is not called a grandfather if the granddaughter was not conceived during his lifetime; although with regard to a certain source of memory and the absolute reckoning of degrees she remains a granddaughter, as in ff. unde cog. l. 1, § si quis proximior, de suis, et legi. l. titius, insti. de hær. quæ ab inte. § cum autem, de bo. lib. l. paulus, § paulus, at the word responsum, n., ff. de iniust. testa. l. si quis exhæredato, § sed hoc, as is also noted in C. de inof. test. l. si quis filium, de ver. sig. l. pronuntiatio, in fin., de gradibus, l. iurisconsultus. Therefore, since words are to be understood according to the subject matter, whether they are conferred by the law or in contracts, as noted in l. fi. de condi. et demon., de in diem adiectio, l. Imperator, and in l. si uno, ff. lo., and we are in a treatise on successions, we understand "grandfather" according to the laws in which we are engaged, not of a grandfather in whom the rights of cognation never existed, de capi. dim. l. tutelas. The chapter concerning any other person whomsoever dowering does not prejudice this girl: for she can refuse to accept that legacy, namely the thing bequeathed; for this is the counsel of the law, when someone is excluded from the legitime on account of a bequest, that she not accept such bequest. And thus, since she is not said to be dowered when she does not consent, she succeeds to the legitime, as in ff. de bo. lib. l. si libertus patrono quod ad debitam, § quid ergo. Another statute does not stand in the way, namely that daughters and grandchildren are bound to observe the will of the father and grandfather: for that person is not to be regarded in the place of a grandfather, because by no natural bond, nor even by natural affection both perfected and caused could he yet be so called, as has been said; for through natural affection certain things are granted more generously, which ought not to be granted when that affection ceases, as in ff. de lib. le. l. aurelius, § titius testamento. And thus neither in fact nor in affection is he properly called a grandfather, but a stranger, as I have proved above. Therefore, although an ascendant can impose a law upon a descendant in whom acknowledgement is found by virtue of the form of the statute, it is otherwise with a stranger; because whatever is not permitted to parents is permitted to strangers, C. de impub. et aliis, l. humanitatis.

† The chapter concerning the paternal uncle is to be understood equally of the arbitrament of an upright man, l. 1, ff. de leg. 2, ff. de leg. 3, l. si filiæ, ff. de alimen. le. l. cum unus, § alimentis. For since she is the only girl, she is to be more richly dowered, so that at least she may have the legitime. For never will an upright man deem that the daughter's legitime ought to be taken away: because it is said to be a debt, and is owed by the law of nature necessarily, as natural, as in l. cum ratio, de bo. damna., C. de inof. test. l. si quis in suo, and it succeeds in the place of alimony, as noted in C. de nup. l. sancimus, by Cynus; indeed, where there is no one else to make a share, the entire inheritance of an intestate father who is entirely deceased—because he made neither a testament nor codicils—is owed by natural law to an only son or to several sons, de li. et post. l. in suis, C. de usuc. pro hære. nihil. Thus the paternal uncle, by giving a meager portion to the girl and retaining much for himself, would not be deemed to have arbitrated rightly, but rather unjustly, as in ff. pro so. l. casu si nervæ. Moreover, in the meantime, before the uncle dowers her by paying or effectively promising, the girl herself succeeds to the universality: hence up to the marriageable years she is the universal heir, because the statute says "let her be excluded henceforth, after she shall have been dowered." Therefore, in the meantime she is not excluded, because one excluded after a time is seen as included before that time, and vice versa, ff. de le. 2, l. statulib. § stichum; saving the fideicommissary substitution made by the grandfather among the sons. In conclusion, I say that, although concerning the Trebellian portion it is doubtful whether she ought to have it up to marriageable age, yet concerning the legitime and the fruits of the legitime I have no doubt that she ought to have them by abstaining from the legacy made by the grandfather, who is called grandfather in name, but is not so in reality, as was said. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A dowried daughter, excluded by statute due to the existence of males, if she was passed over by the death of a male, and subsequently survived, whether she can claim the will to be null.
body: In the name of Christ.

It is proposed that a father passed over his dowried daughter, instituted his son as heir, and after the father’s death the son survived, having possessed the paternal goods; then the said son died without male children. Now the said passed-over daughter claims that the said testament is null. It is asked whether the said testament is null today, and thus that it was not null retroactively, so that while the son was alive the testament was valid; or whether today the testament appears to have been null retroactively. This is to be considered in light of the words of the common statute of Perugia, which states that a dowried daughter could not come to, nor revert to, the goods of the donor, or of those descending from him, as long as a male survives. Regarding this, it must be said without doubt that the said testament is now null, and appears to have been null retroactively, which is proven by reasons and also by similar cases and their reasons.

First, if it is certain that this dowried daughter who was passed over can today declare it null, and this was the intent of the statute, which only intended to exclude her from the goods as long as a male survived, and thus admits her upon his death—because that which is prohibited for a time is considered permitted after that time, as the common laws say—then, etc. If, therefore, she is admitted today by the disposition of the statute, and it cannot be declared null today unless it is stated that it was null retroactively, I will therefore demonstrate from the intent of the statute that it was null retroactively. I prove this thus: he who was passed over cannot declare the testament null if he was not required to be instituted at the time of death, as in *l. si quis exhaeredato*, in the beginning, *ff. de inoff. test.* If, therefore, we were to say that the testament was something while the son was alive, and the son was not necessary to be instituted, then the testament would not be broken, as in the aforementioned *l. si quis exhaeredato*, in the beginning. Since, therefore, the daughter today declares it null, she necessarily has to presuppose that it appears today that she was of such a condition that at the time of death she ought to have been instituted. Moreover, this appears from *l. gallus*, § *et quid si tamen*, *de lib. et posth.*, where if a son deported after the father’s death is restored, the testament is not declared null unless he is restored for a cause that is drawn back retroactively, as is clear there in the gloss at the end. Either, therefore, this dowried daughter became capable of succeeding by a cause due to the son’s death, because it did not hold retroactively, and she can declare it null; or by a cause that is drawn back retroactively: and then it is established that the testament appears to have been null retroactively. And these reasons necessarily conclude.

Furthermore, from that testament which is expected to be broken on account of the omission, the inheritance cannot be entered upon, nor can one exist as a *sui heres* (*l. cum quidam*, § *quod deus*, *de acqu. haer.*). But that is of this kind; therefore, if it happens that the son dies without surviving children, the passed-over daughter being present, that testament is broken; therefore, the son could not be heir by the testament; therefore, it is concluded that the said testament was null, at least in that the inheritance was not entered upon by the said testament, nor did a *sui heres* exist.

Secondly, the aforementioned points are proven by similar cases, first regarding a posthumous child who was passed over, who cannot declare it null as long as he is among the enemies; when returned, he breaks it retroactively, as they say: and our case is of those who are drawn back retroactively, as has been proven, etc. It seems to be expressed in these very terms in *ff. de bon. poss. secund. tab.*, *l. aequissimum*, around the first part there, *expectandi ergo erunt*, where it is said that as long as anyone remains who can come against the tablets, if they are excluded by death or otherwise, certainly those instituted come by the second tablet. Just as here the statute says that as long as a male survives, the female shall not come. Now suppose that those who can come by *contra tabulas* are excluded by death or otherwise: certainly then the instituted would come by the second tablet, not as if the testament were confirmed from now on, but as if the testament had been valid retroactively, although they could not have come. So here the daughter must be able to come, as if the testament had been null retroactively, not as if it were annulled today; and this is what the meaning of the words imports, as is clear there.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter excluded by a statute through general words is not excluded from her legitime.
2. And such a statute is mixed of favor and of hatred.
2. Whether daughters excluded by a statute transmit the right to declare that no testament exists, in which they are passed over, following the death of those on account of whom they are excluded, to their own children.
3. Whether a statute excluding dowried daughters utterly destroys the existence of sui status, or merely suspends it.
4. Whenever a sui heres has an impediment arising from accident, or from legal or factual incapacity, dying in the interim, he transmits.
5. The interpretation of l. cum antiquioribus, C. de iure deli.
6. When genitives create a condition.
7. The right of accretion, even if conditional, is transmitted to the heir.
8. One thing is to suspend, another to remove.
9. The right of accretion has no place in the legitime.
10. When and in which successions the right of non-decrement has place.
body: In the name of Christ. Since the statute of the city of Perugia dictated that if any woman was, or shall be, endowed by her father, or by her maternal or paternal grandfather, or by her brother, she may not, nor ought she, to revert to the succession of the aforementioned persons, or of any of them, as long as any male son survives from her, or in that inheritance or succession to which she would wish to revert. And it adds, saving the testament and last will of the aforementioned persons, which shall be observed. And afterwards it adds, saving that women may come to the succession of parents, and brothers, and other persons: to successions according to our law, if male heirs do not survive, by remitting their dowries into the inheritance. Now the case has arisen that from a certain noble house of the Giacanis of Perugia, by the death of Lord Philip, the last surviving male, no male exists; nor do there exist any males who proceeded from the progenitors of the said house from the said agnation; but there remain from them certain sons, nephews, and descendants begotten in other agnations, or houses, who wish to come to claim the supplement of the legitime of the mothers, or grandmothers, of the said house of the Giacanis, formerly endowed there by their progenitors, and seek the said supplement. It is asked, whether they may?

† And first of all it must be considered whether this statute disposes of the legitime: and it seems that it does not, because by general words, that one cannot come to the inheritance or succession, the legitime is not excluded; thus it is stated in the law that a daughter who is excluded from universal succession by a general release made to her brothers is nevertheless not excluded from the legitime, unless this has been specially stated. C. de inoffic. testa. l. si quoniam. l. fin. Therefore, we ought to say the same, and much more strongly, regarding a statute: for if a liberatory pact, which is favorable, does not exclude the legitime, then neither do the general words of a statute, which is undoubtedly mixed of favor and odium. C. de libe. praete. l. maximum vitium. To this effect is what is noted by Guil. de Cu. ff. de trans. l. de his controuersiis. Bartolus seems to determine the contrary in expressae. ff. de condit. et demonst. l. titio centum. §. titio genero. in the question which begins, quaero statutum, where he seems to determine that this statute excludes a dowried daughter from the law [of succession] when males exist. For it seems that, by consideration of the dowry, she is disinherited per l. arg. ff. de haer. instit. l. qui volebat. or her legitime is diminished and reduced to the dowry itself, as is noted C. de nup. l. sancimus. per Cy. For the statute considers the dowry to be the congruous portion of a dowried woman, and a license is nothing other than a certain congruous portion fixed by the discretion of the law for those persons to whom succession is due by necessary right. C. de inoffi. test. Aut. nouissima. For it is called the debt of the subsidiary portion of goods, but dowried women have the subsidy of the dowry and of their husbands. C. vnde vir, et vx. l. 1. and it succeeds in place of alimony: but dowried women rarely lack alimony. Therefore, the statute rightly considers this dowry to be the legitime portion when males survive, not without cause. C. de adul. l. publico. per Iac. de Are. et Cy. Whether, therefore, they have the entire statutory legitime in the meantime, or whether they seem to be excluded from it by common law in the meantime, it seems that they cannot demand more in the meantime; and if they demand more in the meantime, the exception from the municipal law, which are considered peremptory on account of the uncertain time, stands against them, de condi. et demon. l. sufficit. Indeed, even without the exception, the municipal law itself stands in the way, because, since it excludes the beginning of succession, an exception is not necessary: for the action cannot be founded, according to what is read and noted C. de transact. l. vbi pactum.

To the contrary, it was consulted by the excellent doctors, Master Thomas de Tosinis, Master Francis de Bici, Master Antonio de Machiavellis, and the Florentine college. For they say that if the words of the statute are rightly considered, they do not exclude the daughter simply from the paternal inheritance, but rather, by the existence of certain persons and by consideration and favor of them, they impede her for a time. Which the words of the said statute openly state, namely, "as long as any male son survives." By which words time is signified, as C. de leg. l. 1. ff. de excusa. tut. l. titius. de condi. condi. et demon. l. si quis ita. But a temporal [condition] ought not to be drawn to a perpetual exclusion, as ff. de pac. l. epistola. §. fi. It is clear, therefore, that the daughter is not altogether excluded from the legitime, but that her claim is suspended for a time, namely, until the males survive. And this is the truth in this point. Nor does Bartolus say the contrary, if it is well observed; indeed, he says for [the affirmative], because he says that the statute diminishes the license in time, not in quantity: and thus it makes the right pure for a day. ff. ad l. Falcid. l. in lege falcidia. It is not held as pure, because the word which imports a temporal impediment is different from that which imports a perpetual and precise impediment: for the first impediment is removed by the course of time, either simple or qualified. But the second is not, as is noted in reg. non firmatur. lib. 6.

† Now it must be considered regarding the second point: whether these daughters, dying in the interim, transmit [their rights] to their children. And if we say they are excluded, it is clear that they do not transmit; if we say they are incapable, likewise they do not transmit; if we say they have a conditional right, as Bartolus holds in the said § Titio genero, they still do not transmit, because conditional rights of succession are not transmitted; if we say that the order of preference of males over females is given, or that, this order remaining, the one who dies later does not transmit, as these things are clearly proven. C. de iure delib. in l. cum antiquioribus, for he who cannot acknowledge does not transmit, as is evident there. But this daughter does not have the right of acknowledgment while the males are living; therefore she does not have the right of transmission. And this is held literally by Bartolus, descending. ff. ad Tert. l. fi. in q. which begins, quaero quid si filia decedat. But this inquiry is deeper, with due respect to my teacher, to be considered. It is necessary to consider the common law, which grants the legitime, as l. cum in prioribus, l. quoniam nouella, and l. sancimus, C. de inoffi. testam., and in Aut. de tri. et se. § 1, in Aut. de resti. et ea, quae parit. § quam ob rem, and grants ipso iure, as to the name of heir, in licentia; so that dominion continues from the father to the sons and daughters in power. ff. de lib. et post. l. in suis.

It is therefore necessary to examine whether this statute utterly invalidates the status of being one’s own heir, or merely suspends it; and it is certain that it does not eradicate it entirely, as I stated above in the first point, but rather suspends it. Then, furthermore, one must renounce [or determine] the nature of this suspension: whether it converts what is pure into conditional, or indeed into a day [dies]. And if we say that it converts it into conditional, it would follow that this is not a reduction in time, but a change of substance; because pure right and conditional right differ as contradictories; because in the one birth is found, in the other birth is not found. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Nam ad ea. But if we say that an uncertain day does not here create a condition, we overthrow the rules of law. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Dies incertus. If, however, we say that it creates a condition, therefore it is not transmitted in the meantime. D. l. Dies incertus, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; and l. Quibus diebus, §. Quidam Titio, eodem titulo, where it seems expressly stated. D. Quando dies legatorum cedat, l. Si Titio, uidetur. By the order of preference given by the statute, the male is to be regarded in the place of the instituted heir, the female, however, in the place of the substitute; therefore, dying in the meantime, she does not transmit. D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. Sed et si plures, in principio; D. de suis et legitimis heredibus, l. Si ex pluribus.

To the contrary it seems, for it must be known that when the person to whom the legitime is due is not impeded in it on account of an intrinsic defect of his own right, but on account of an extrinsic defect of another person, who suspends this right and defers it, dying in the meantime, he transmits. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quis filium, where it is expressly stated. But here, since the ordinance of the common law proceeds concerning legitimes, and defers it to the daughter, and the common law itself is not corrected by the statute in the substance of the legitime, nor in its quantity, but is deferred in time on account of the extrinsic person of the males, rightly this right, with its suspension, is transmitted to the children of the daughter. C. de his qui ante apertas tabulas, l. 1, Quotiescunque. There is no defect in the right of being awarded, but there is a suspension of the right of acknowledging or claiming; there the law dispenses so that an impediment to transmission may be made: which ought to be temporary and suspensive, becomes precise and perpetual, as D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Ventre, and there it is clear in the gloss, and in the first rule which Bartolus takes there, and in the rule of Jacobus de Belvis in the second rule, which is,

† That whenever one’s own heir has an impediment, whether arising from chance, or from an incapacity of law or of fact, which he transmits upon dying in the interim. And Bartolus holds this rule, for which it appears there that it is settled. To the same effect: D. ad Sill. l. si quis in graui, §. fin., together with the following law; D. de contrahenda hereditate l. illud, §. ultimo. And what is noted there to the same effect, because when by the death of another it is not sought for another, but what was acquired retroactively can be claimed, where the dying person transmits. C. quando dies legati ceperit l. ex his verbis.
