Thus it is here, because the death of males tends toward interpretation: nor does it differ from the legitime, but the common law has already conferred it; hence it can be said that the life of males causes the legitime of the daughters to sleep in the interim, but not to expire or be eradicated. Therefore, the daughters, dying in the interim, transmit the right which they have in habit, although not in act, arg. D. de militum testamento l. ex militibus, §. fin., together with l. Lucius praeterea. Bartolus, in the question where Bartholus was consulted, opined that, upon the removal of the impediment of the males by their death, this removal of the impediment fictions that the impediment had not existed retroactively, or that the passed-over daughter, according to him, could not succeed unless there were this fiction. Since therefore she succeeds, the law fictions it; and he himself posited this as a settled point. But then I argue: the subsequent death does not impede this fiction; rather, the law fictions it notwithstanding the death of him who, if he were alive, would succeed, and fictions the deceased to be retroactively owner and heir, as in D. ad Sill. l. si exhaeredatus. Therefore, upon the removal of the impediment, although the daughter died in the interim, since it is fictions retroactively, she transmitted, by the said l. si exhaeredatus, which is the unique authority for this, and noted.

It remains only to respond to the law *Cum antiquioribus*, which Bartolus cites for the case in the aforementioned law *Finis* to the *Senatusconsultum Tertullianum*. Certainly, that law states that a repudiated right is not transmitted; but this is not a repudiated right, but rather the right of a *sui heres*, which is transmitted with its own quality and nature. *Digestum*, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Si quis filium*. Moreover, that law speaks of regular transmission, whereas we are now dealing with an irregular and anomalous transmission.

† Moreover, the ablative phrases, such as “remittendo dotes” etc., do not stand in the way, as if they denoted a condition which cannot be fulfilled by the heir. See D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. a testatore. For I say that, in this case, the text does not establish a condition, as is expressly stated in l. pretor, in 1, D. de collatione bonorum, and C. eodem, l. si soror. Furthermore, let us consider that this dowry is imputed by operation of law to the legitime; therefore, the daughter has a share of the pure legitime. Moreover, in the other portion she has a hope arising from the death of the males who are to die; in the meantime, even if she dies at her appointed time, her share accrues to the others.

† For the right of accretion, even if conditional, is transmitted to the heir, as is fully read and noted in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatum*, in the law *Qui patri*, in the section *In propria*, number [unspecified]. The son of the daughter herself constitutes for her a share through concurrence, as long as the son lives; and he is, as it were, joined to the daughter in this legal conjunction of the legitime. And just as the son is joined to the grandchildren by the edict on joining, insofar as he takes away from the grandchildren the share existing as their heir’s portion due to them, by dividing with them and diminishing their shares. But in our case, this right of conjunction, or right of diminution, is subject to a certain temporality, namely, for as long as he lives. Hence, upon his death, the legitime is restored and consolidated. And this right of restoring and solidifying the legitime is transmitted to the heir; not, indeed, because the law burdens the daughter with the time of her own life,

† Therefore, it is private. Indeed, one thing is to suspend, and another is to revoke. D. de pactis, l. si unus, § 1; D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. cum hic status, § sive. In these rights having a cause for a time and an end, by the law itself and by time, and after concurrence, the right of accretion has place by reason of the contract being terminated. D. de usufructu accrescendi, l. 1, § interdum. And it is made by what is noted, D. de legatis 1, l. plane, § si duobus, according to Dy. Moreover, it does not object that the ancient statute speaks only of the daughter, because posteriors come from the person of the daughter, by the law of transmission, which is made from children to children. D. l. si quis filium, which specially makes for this. Moreover, as I said, the prior right of accretion of the legitima is the same in number to itself; hence it is not to extend the legitima of one to the legitima of another, but it is to its own nature according to a certain consolidation of the remainder. And it is made, D. de coniunctione cum emancipatis liberis, l. 1, § si quis ex nepotibus. Moreover, it does not object to the prescription of time, because in prescriptions the right is not considered as it is in habit, but as it is in exercise. L. cum notissimi, § illud, and § in his, D. de praescriptione triginta annorum. And since Lord Philip died recently, it is clear that the prescription has not run. But it objects to what I said about the right of accretion, which is noted by Bartolus, D. de inofficioso testamento, l. pater filium, in 2 and 3.

† where he says that in the legitime the right of accretion by legal convention has no place: because it is a singular succession, in l. quod proculo. ff. de legatis 2. For in the contrary opinion are Dyonisius and Jacobus de Belvisio in public disputation. And rightly, because the privilege of the legitime due by natural law is that the right of accretion has place, as all the doctors note in Auth. nouissima, nouissima, C. de inofficiosa testamento, and C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quotiens, perlac., and in Auth. ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, §. caeterum. Moreover, even in our case there is the right not to diminish, which the concurrence of males had taken away from the daughters of their legitime; the death of the males restored it.
† The right of non-decrementum, however, applies in any conjunction and in any succession, because it is rather the removal of a certain impediment than an extension of the succession.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a sale made by a person having a capital enmity, with a confession of the price, is presumed to be simulated, especially when there is a *factum conventum* (stipulated fact).
2. An argument drawn from what commonly occurs is valid.
3. He who possesses is not presumed to have sold.
4. A fictitious alienation is presumed if the buyer allows the seller to retain possession.
5. For how long it is required that the buyer allow the seller to possess, in order that simulation be presumed.
6. Whether a woman who purchases is presumed, and when, to have purchased with her husband's money.
7. A statute speaking of a seller applies to the heir of the seller.
body: In the name of Christ. Certain instruments appear sufficiently suspect of simulation to anyone possessing a keen understanding of the matter. And it must first be considered the instrument made in the form of a sale by Cecharellus of Spello to Vagnolus, lord of John of Assisi, concerning certain possessions for a certain price of one thousand florins, as the notary asserted, then confessed: who, however, Cecharellus lived for many years afterwards, until he possessed said things and peacefully collected their fruits; and after his death, for many years, said Vagnolus possessed them peacefully until he died, and after his death, lady Rigutia, his wife, possessed them peacefully and without controversy of any litigation raised in court for a period of ten years and more. And this Vagnolus made a certain instrument in the form of a sale of said things to the aforementioned lady Rigutia; and this Vagnolus finally bequeathed said things to said Rigutia, his wife, and to the stepmother of Guido, born of another wife. Now Guido brings an action against said Rigutia for half of other things, because another son of said lady remained, named Jacob, in whose inheritance said Rigutia succeeds by full right. The question is what is the law. And if men had a divine eye in knowing the truth, there would be no need to examine through arguments; however, our eyes are like the owl, dimmed in light, which is the truth; and therefore signs, arguments, and clear conjectures, and proofs require indications. L. illicitas, §. veritas, de officio praesidis; L. non omnes, §. a barbaris, ff. de re militari and de testibus; L. ob carmen, §. fin., there where it says, although truth may assist them, Greeks seek a sentence; Hebrews seek signs, when the apostle says, it is necessary for men to be Greeks and Hebrews, and especially judges, so that they may not be deceived by error of fact. Let us therefore consider the quality of the persons, the subsequent possession, the order of acts, and a certain circulation of stepmothers, the presumed ambush, and the presumption of law, and the disposition of the statute, from all of which we will come to the investigation of the truth. In the first place, said Cecharellus was the uncle of said lady Rigutia, and a relative and confidant of said Vagnolus. And he had enemies, and with them penal bonds of peace, as is narrated to me.

† Therefore, considering that the said instrument is founded upon a confession, not upon a true payment; and that penal bonds of obligations stood in the way; and that the person was related, it appears that there is a presumption of simulation. C. de don. ante nup. Auth. sed iam necesse. C. de do. l. data. alias lata iam pridem. He who, on account of enmity, is always in thought of wrongdoing, appears to make a simulated act concerning all his goods, or the greater part thereof; as is the case here, as is fully read and noted by Bartolus and others. ff. de do. l. post contractum. For natural reason urges us to consider relatives and very close friends. ff. de leg. 2. l. vnum ex familia. §. item Imperator Marcus. ff. de bon. libe. l. nihil. §. facilior. C. de natu. lib. l. si quis. C. de sac. sanc. eccl. Auth. quibuscunque modis. ff. de haered. institu. l. quidam cum filium. For we trust most in relatives; and we see this through the argument from what commonly happens. ff. de opti. leg. l. theopompu. in the word "my uncle," and "kinsmen" persuades the understanding, lest one forestall fortuitous events and guard oneself against the snares of fortune: not by squandering, because it would not be prudent, nor a cunning counsel, to sell everything; but by feigning to sell or to donate. And thus we see it commonly done, and argument from what commonly happens.
† is valid in the matter of presumptions and conjectures, as in the law and no. C. de prob. l. neque natales.
† On the second point, namely concerning possession, it must be considered that one who possesses is not presumed to have sold. D. qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur, l. sicut, § super vacuum.

† From which we have to note that if, after the sale, the buyer allows the seller to remain in possession, the alienation is presumed to be fictitious. So holds Dyonisius in the said law *Omnes*, § *Lucius*, *Digestum*, *De acquisitione hereditatis*; the law *Si is qui bonus*, *Codex*, *De naturalibus liberis*; law 3, *Codex*, *De re hereditaria*; law 2; and Bartolus, literally, in the said § *Superuacuum*.

But it is asked, for how long a time must the buyer be required to endure, in order that simulation be presumed? Some say for a long time, others for three years, as in *l. quicunque*, *de apostolis publicis*; others determine that it is at the discretion of the judge, according to the quality of the persons. Since, therefore, Cecharellus, after the aforementioned superficially apparent but not really existing sale, collected the fruits for many years and until he died, a good and equitable man ought to presume that the contract was fictitious and simulated.

On the third point, namely, on the order and sequence of the acts of purchase, it is established that if Cecharellus’s sale had been without simulation, fraud might perhaps be presumed in the others on account of the stepmother, *C. de secundis nuptiis*, *l. hac edictali*, *ff. de probationibus*, *l. qui testamentum*, and it would not prejudice the stepson; but because there is a defect in the first contract, which appears from the following, the stepson has no right. Rather, Vagnolus acted in good faith than committed fraud; for Cecharellus instituted as heir Do. Joanna, mother of the said Rigutia, and certain others, to whom Rigutia and Dom. Marchiola, her daughter, succeeded, to whom the goods of the said Cecharellus belonged in part. Therefore, in the person of Rigutia there was a resignation and an acknowledgment of good faith, not a plan of fraud; and perpetually Vagnolus in his will likewise wished to cleanse his conscience, as appears therein. And because effects are presumed from causes, and the order of causes is that which orders the whole for proving simulation, it is rightly presumed that Cecharellus’s sale was simulated. And if Guidus wishes to proceed by the superficial appearance of the instruments, certainly Rigutia has in her favor the instrument of purchase from Vagnolus.

And if it is said that it is presumed that she purchased with her husband's money, it is answered that this is true if the husband's resources are sufficient; but it is not probable that Vagnolus had so much ready money, as is alleged to me.

† Above, in the third section, regarding the statute, it must be considered the time during which Cecharellus possesses, and that during which the lady Rigutia possessed for ten years and more continuously: and although the statute speaks of a seller, feigning a simulation, so that proof to the contrary is not admitted: nevertheless, the same is to be said of the heir of the seller, who possessed for ten years after the death of the seller, that the contract is feigned to be simulated from such possession. D. de acquirenda possessione, l. Pomponius; D. qui ex causa maiestatis, l. cum miles. In those matters which pass to heirs, the same law applies to the heir as to the deceased. D. de rebus iudicatis, l. quod in ipsis; D. de probationibus, l. pactum, cum si. From all of which it is truly concluded that the sale by Cecharellus is presumed simulated by three presumptions: namely, the presumption of man, the presumption of common law, and the fiction of the statute. Hence, not only ought Guido to have a share of these goods, but he is bound to the restitution of one-half of all the goods and fruits which Vagnolus received under the pretext of the said simulated contract, proving by witnesses that which is narrated in the facts. §. narratur. Hence, regarding the possession of Cecharellus after the sale, and the succession of Rigutia, and the possession continued thereafter by her, public fame also is of great weight in this matter, because it confirms the credibility of the thing in question. Moreover, the said Rigutia holds from the coheirs, in the portion of the coheirs, titles and cases in the said goods, from which title, and good faith, which is presumed to exist in one holding title, undoubtedly at least prescribed both by common law, and more strongly by the form of the statute, if she possessed from those titles for ten years. Otherwise, she would have the Publician action, but not true ownership of the thing before the prescription was completed, if the sellers had not been owners. However, in this case, they were owners, and Cecharellus, by virtue of the simulated contract, never lost ownership. Thus, the said lady Rigutia has many ways by which she defends herself from injury.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a new mill may be constructed to the damage and detriment of another mill, because the influx of people who formerly resorted to the first mill will now resort to this second one.
2. If one inconvenience is posited, many follow.
3. A river is said to be public if it is perennial and flows continuously.
4. When account is to be taken of lost profit.
5. Interpretation of l. 2, §. merito, D. ne quid in loco publico fiat.
6. Interpretation of l. unica, C. de sententiis.
body:
In the name of Christ. The case is as follows. The commune and the inhabitants of Villa Francha on one side, and the commune and the inhabitants of Lusorio on the other side, hold in common the river Macra, which is situated near the boundaries of the aforementioned communes. Along this river, the aforementioned commune and inhabitants of Lusorio wish to build a certain mill on their own territory of the commune of Lusorio; the dam, or sluice, of which mill they wish to construct in the said river; which dam is claimed to extend and run from the bank of the river that faces the territory of Villa Francha to the bank of the river that faces the territory of Lusorio; which dam, or sluice, is accustomed to be maintained by the border guards, or inhabitants of Lusorio, although it has been broken by the flooding of the waters of the said river Macra.

On the contrary, the commune and inhabitants of Villa Francha prohibit that the dam, or sluice, be made in the aforementioned river, saying that, since the said river is common between the said parties, it is not permitted for either party to build or do anything in it that results, or could result, in damage or prejudice to the other party; and that by the construction of the aforementioned mill, the aforementioned commune and inhabitants of Villa Francha would be damaged in this respect, because the inhabitants of Lusorio, Trisana, Canosa, and Richo, when their own mills cease to grind due to a lack of water, are accustomed to go to grind at the mill of the commune of Villa Francha, which commune of Villa Francha has as a common mill over all others, which it has on the river Macra; these inhabitants, if the said mill with the aforementioned dam, which the said commune of Lusorio intends to build, were constructed, would cease from the use of the mill of Villa Francha, because the aforementioned mill to be built by the commune of Lusorio would be more nearby and suitable for grinding for the same inhabitants.

To the contrary, it is replied on behalf of the commune of Lusorio that the aforementioned inhabitants of Lusorio, Trisana, and Canosa, and also of Richo, are not obliged to go to the mills of Villa Francha if they do not wish to; and therefore it does not pertain to the commune and inhabitants of Villa Francha to say and allege that they suffer damage if the aforementioned inhabitants, accustomed at times to grind with them, cease from the use of their mills. From this use they can also cease if they wish, even if the aforementioned mill by the said commune of Lusorio is not built, and go to other mills, although more distant, than the mills of Villa Francha.

Regarding which river Macra, or along it, the aforementioned parties asserted that there are no mills. Furthermore, that the said river Macra is not common to those of Villa Francha and Lusorio, but is a public and perennial river; however, it is not navigable.
† Now the question arises: what is the law. In the above-mentioned case, the proposition of Aristotle may be assumed,

† namely, that once one inconvenience is posited, many follow, as in l. a testatore, ff. de cond. et demon.; and l. Gallus, C. de resc. ven.; and l. ex diuerso, §. j., ff. de rei ven. Since therefore in the case proposed it is presupposed that the said river Macra is common to the inhabitants of Villa Francha on one side and to the inhabitants of Lusorio on the other, as private persons: and this is absurd, since the said river is perennial and always flows:

† Therefore, if no other evidence is shown, it must be held to be public, as stated in l. 1, §. fluminum, D. de fluminibus; and in l. nemo, in fine, D. de rerum divisione; and in Inst. eo, §. flumina. It is therefore absurd to base an opinion on it as if it were common property of private individuals. From this it appears that the laws speaking of a thing common are absurdly alleged in the aforementioned case. The matter of the laws disposing concerning a public river must therefore be assumed: and thus it must be observed that by the mill, which the commune and the inhabitants of Lusorio strive to build, navigation is not impeded; since it is not navigable, nor does it thereby become navigable, as in l. quominus, D. de fluminibus; and l. si autem, in fine, D. de aqua pluviae arcendae. With this presupposition, it seems that one should say either that the mills of Villafranca, which are said to be in the river Bagnone, were not granted by the prince, nor was antiquity of time, of which there is no memory of the beginning, granted; or that something of the two aforementioned cases has occurred. In the first case, let it be that by the mill to be constructed by the commune of Lusorio, the mills of Villafranca would be harmed; nevertheless, the said commune and the inhabitants of Lusorio cannot be prohibited, as in l. 2, §. si quid in loco, D. ne quid in loco publico; and l. si alius, §. bellissime, D. quod vi aut clam; and what is usually noted by the doctors in the question of the mill touched upon by the gloss in l. si manifeste, C. de servitutibus et aqua; and in l. si quis, §. si initium, D. de ejectionibus. In the second case, since the mills of Villafranca are not harmed thereby, nor is there any public inconvenience, or of the neighbors, in use, it is to be granted plainly that the said commune of Lusorio can have the said mill built, as in l. 1, in principio; and §. quod autem, D. ne quid in loco publico; and l. si in publico, D. de aqua pluviae arcendae; and l. vim facit, §. fin., with the notes there, D. quod vi aut clam; and l. fi, D. de servitutibus; and l. impera, D. de servitutibus rusticarum praediorum. Nor let anyone say that the advantage of the mill of Villafranca is diminished if the said mill is built, because the concurrence of persons accustomed to go to grind at the said mills of Villafranca is diminished; and thus some would say that at least this advantage, which is thereby lost, causes the commune of Villafranca to suffer damage, as in l. 2, §. merito, D. ne quid in loco publico. Furthermore, because account is taken of profit, the consultant alleged l. 1, C. de sententiis quae pro eo quod interest. Which is of no effect, as will be said below.

And that the aforementioned matters do not constitute an obstacle is shown thus: no account is taken of lost profit, because it depended on the discretion of another, as in the law *Idemnitatis*, § 1, with the notes thereon, in the Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*. But such is the case in the present matter, that although the people of the contracted lands were accustomed to go to the mills of Villa Francha, that custom is not thereby attributed to necessity, as in the law *Solent*, § final, in the Digest, *De officio prætoris*, and in the law *In ea*, in the Digest, *De legibus*. And by this alone it appears that the commune of Villa Francha cannot complain.

† Moreover. The section *merito* speaks when the benefit was derived from the public domain; yet in the case at hand, although having mills in a public river constitutes receiving a benefit from the public, nevertheless, considering the milling activity, which derives from the grain of private persons coming to have it milled, the said benefit ought rather to be received from those private persons who contribute, and such contribution, by its operation, provided that no work is done with malicious intent, may be prohibited, as stated in l. 1, §. *denique*, D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, and l. *Proculus*, D. de damno infecto. Furthermore, the section *merito* speaks because a certain benefit was derived from the public domain; whereas in our case, it depends on the will of the cultivators.

† Moreover, the aforementioned unique law is irrelevant, for it speaks of a case where someone fails to fulfill the good faith promised in a contract. But in our case, the communities are not bound by a breach of faith. And from these points I conclude that, since the mills of Villa Francha are not harmed in any other way by the construction of the said mill of Lusorio, except insofar as it is alleged that the influx of individual persons going to grind grain at the said mills of Villa Francha will be diminished, this in no way ought to be grounds for saying that the community of Sosorio is prohibited by law from constructing the aforementioned mill. And thus it appears that the opinion mentioned above is founded on false premises and an absurd presumption, and therefore it is not surprising if other absurdities follow, in accordance with what I said first. Signorolus de Homodeis, knight and doctor of laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Certain things are common to all, which are said to be certain public things.
2. A river, insofar as it is within the territory of a certain city, belongs to that city; and the citizens may enact statutes concerning it.
3. How a river flowing between two cities pertains to them.
4. How waters springing up on the boundary of two private persons pertain to them.
5. Waters which originate in public land and subsequently flow through the fields of private persons: whether, once they are in private fields, the owners of the fields may use those waters as their own.
6. It is one thing to make anew, another to repair.
body: To the same. In the name of Christ. For clarity, it must be premised that

† because certain things are said to be common to all: such as the sea water, and a public river, and so forth, as in l. 1. §. fin. ff. de rerum diui. Certain things are public as to ownership, i.e., of the republic as to ownership, and common as to use: such as public rivers with their beds, as in insti. de re. diui. §. flumina. This is to be understood in such a way that, as to useful ownership, they may belong to the republics of cities and castles having, by custom, mere and mixed dominion. For in this they perform the role of the republic, having reason and jurisdiction over rivers, just as over the rest of the territory: because custom grants this jurisdiction.
† Hence, the river Tiber, insofar as it is within the territory of Pavia, belongs to the Papians, and they may enact statutes concerning it.

But here arises a doubt: what if a river flows between two cities, how does it pertain to them? I answer that the water is common in undivided shares, on account of the continuous motion of the water and its intermingling; but the riverbed is common in divided shares, as a place forming the boundary between two cities, by analogy to a stone situated on the boundary, and to an island born in the river, as in the Institutes, De rebus divisis, § Insula; and in the Digest, De communi dividendo, l. Auctor. And so it is in the case at hand regarding the river in question, because the water is common in undivided shares. Hence, each city may use the water for its own part in building on the soil of its own community; but it cannot appropriate the whole water, as in the Digest, De aqua pluviae arcendae, l. In concedendo; and De acquisitione hereditatis, l. Duo fratres; and in the Code, De finium regundorum, l. Si constiterit, in the reason of its own case. From this it follows that mills, whose dams and apparatus are fixed in the riverbed, if they extend beyond the middle of the river, cannot be constructed, not on the ground that they are made in common property, but because they are made on the adversary’s own soil, insofar as they extend beyond it. And thus it is not necessary here to allege l. Sabinus, De communi dividendo; nor Suam materiam. And if this is not permitted to the public, it will not be permitted to a private person either.

† And certain waters, which arise on the boundary of two private persons, must likewise be distinguished. There are also others, which originate in my land alone and extend into another’s land, and do not have their source in public property, whether they arise from a spring or are rainwaters. For as long as they adhere to my land, they are mine, and I may lead them away for the irrigation of my estates: and I may divert them to whatever place I wish, even if another’s meadows suffer dryness therefrom, provided that I do this for my own benefit, and not principally to the detriment of my neighbor, as is stated in D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. 1, § item aiunt.

There are also other waters which arise in public places and subsequently flow through private fields: concerning these, it is asked whether, once they are in private fields, the owners of the fields may use those waters as their own and divert them for the irrigation of their own estates wherever they wish: and it seems that they may, because water follows the soil, without which it cannot exist. Hence, just as it is impossible that the bed of a public river should not be public, as stated in the Digest, *De fluminibus*, law 1, § *si insula*, at the words *quia impossibile*; so, conversely, if the bed is mine, the water is mine. But to the contrary, it seems that if I draw water from a public river through a ditch to my field, it remains public. And therefore, if anything is done there, it is considered done in a public river, provided that the flow through that ditch is perennial, as stated in the Digest, *De fluminibus*, law 1, § *si fossa*. Navigable rivers, or those from which another navigable waterway is formed, even if vessels are drawn by ropes, are not our subject matter, but rather the law *quominus* in the Digest, *De fluminibus*. From these things therefore said above, the answer to the question is clear: because what one is not permitted to do anew, one is also not permitted to introduce into another’s property, as stated in the Digest, *Si servus vindicetur*, law *sicuti*, § *Aristo*.

† But ancient customary buildings, and those prescribed, may indeed be repaired, if they are very different, to be made anew and repaired. As in D. de itinere actuque privato, l. 3, § hoc autem. And the aforementioned are confirmed by what is read and noted in l. 1, in principio, D. de damno infecto; and C. de servitutibus et aqua, l. si manifestae; and l. praeses; and the said l. quo minus, D. de eodem; l. si quis ex argentariis, § si initium tabularum. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A judge delegated to execute a sentence, once he has declared it to be executed, cannot revoke it and declare it not to be executed.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Your judge, Bertus, in order to determine whether the sentence is to be executed or not, after he has pronounced that it is to be executed or not to be executed, has fulfilled the mandate for which he was appointed, so that he cannot revoke his sentence: because this judge was entrusted with the issue, not the entire case, and therefore, although the sentence is interlocutory, he cannot revoke it, because the limits of the mandate do not permit it: just as an arbitrator appointed on one issue cannot revoke his decision, as in D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. arbitro. And this is clear from the rule set forth in D. de arbitris, l. qualem, §. si. And therefore, the opinion of the excellent doctor, Master Signorino, pleases me. And I give the same opinion even if he had reserved to himself the right of revocation: because such reservation is impossible and contrary to law: because the limits of the mandate, as read in its text, do not permit it, as in l. iudex, D. de re iudicata; because a mandate to judge is understood to apply only once, not repeatedly on the same matter principally committed, as in D. de verbis significandis, l. boue, §. hoc sermone. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus. See in consilium ccxxxiiii.

The words of Master Cino, In the name of Christ. He began on the old Digest in the law "filium" etc. You will find this opinion in the fifth part, opinion 437, beginning, "Titius had a slave woman, and so forth."

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the property of a ward may be sold to satisfy a debt, when it is of greater value than the debt.
2. A grant made for a specific cause is deemed granted only to the extent that the cause requires.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A certain tutor of a certain ward, on account of a debt which amounted to the sum of 130 florins, sold a certain house of his ward, from which a perpetual annual rent of 12 florins was paid, for 375 florins; this sale was made with the decree of the judge and with the due formalities. Now it is in doubt whether the said sale is valid in law, because the thing, or house, sold was for a higher price than the debt.

† It must be stated for clarity that what is granted on account of a certain cause is considered granted only to the extent that the cause requires, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § in causa; C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, Auth. hoc ius porrectum; D. de exercitu, l. Lucius; D. de rebus eorum, l. magis puto, § idem praetor, where it says, “so that a large possession may not be broken up on account of a small debt.” Therefore, if that which ought not to be broken up is broken up, bad faith is presumed, because it is not done according to the judgment of a reasonable person, as noted by Bartolus in l. alio haerede, de alimentis et cibariis legatis. Hence, it ought to be rescinded, as in l. 1, C. si venditio pignoris agatur.

The solution is this: it must be said that either there was another thing that could have been sold up to the amount due, or approximately so, or the thing sold could have been conveniently and at a fair price sold in part up to the amount due; and in that case the decree does not hold, being obtained by concealment, rash, or ambitious. Or else it could not have been otherwise broken up, nor was there any other source from which payment could be made; and in that case, since the matter could not be otherwise resolved, the whole is valid, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si sponsus sponsae, § generaliter; and C. de bonis, Auth. iudicium possessorium, l. fin. And with this distinction the question is resolved, which cannot otherwise be resolved according to law. And so I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether legacies left by an instituted heir are considered to be repeated by the substitute, and vice versa.
2. An heir may not make a donation to the prejudice of legacies.
body: In the name of Christ. The facts are as follows: Lord Nicolinus de Riuola died having made his will, in which will he instituted his son William as sole heir; and in which will he stated, willed, and ordained that, in the event that the said William should die without legitimate and natural male heirs, his inheritance should pass to the community of Saint Mary of Major Pergami. In that will, he left many legacies; and among other things, he bequeathed fifty imperial pounds to each of the four daughters of Lord Gromerinus de Riuola, in the event of the aforementioned case occurring, whereby the said inheritance passes to the said community. Now, this William has died without legitimate and natural male heirs, having made his will; in which will he instituted his two legitimate and natural daughters as heirs, and after the death of the daughters, he donated this inheritance to the aforementioned community of Saint Mary of Major Pergami. Now comes Lord Gromerinus, as legitimate procurator and administrator of his daughters, and asks the aforementioned community whether it wishes to be the heir of Nicolinus; and the community responded that it does not, but that it is well pleased for this inheritance to pass to the said community by virtue of the donation made to it by William. Secondly, the said Lord Gromerinus asks the daughters of the said William to release, and ought to release, the possessions of the said Lord Nicolinus; because they are encumbered in favor of the daughters of Lord Gromerinus by virtue of the legacy left to them by the said Lord Nicolinus. The daughters of William say that they ought not to release the said possessions of Nicolinus; because the said inheritance did not pass to the said community by the will of the said Lord Nicolinus, since it has been renounced on that ground. The question is, what is the law? For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that when a testator

† He leaves a universal and a particular fideicommissum; after the former, the particular fideicommissum appears, or rather a legacy added as a burden to the universal fideicommissary, as in C. ad Trebellianam, l. si. And thus the universal fideicommissary is bound only if he accepts the fideicommissum, ff. de legatis tertio, l. haec verba. If he comes into it from another source, for example by contract, he is not bound by the fideicommissum, nor is he said to act in fraud of the fideicommissum, as in ff. si quis omiserit causam testamenti, l. penultima. On this basis, it seems to be said that the said legacies made to the daughters of Lord Gromerini are not due, as if the condition had failed. For those words, “if the said inheritance shall come into the consortium,” are understood to mean from that testament, and not from elsewhere, as in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. qui liberis, § haec verba.

To the contrary is the truth, because if the universal fideicommissary repudiates the universal fideicommissum, the inheritance remains with the heir, burdened with the legacies substituted by the fideicommissum, as in C. de caducis tollendis, § pro secundo. Moreover, those words, “if the inheritance shall come into the consortium,” do not constitute a condition; for just as when instituting and burdening an heir with the words “if he shall enter,” these words do not create a condition such that, upon his repudiation, the inheritance does not pass to the jointly instituted heir with the burden, so it is in the present case. For this condition is not attached to the substance of the legacy imposed, but to the person burdened, namely, the universal fideicommissary himself, so that he is not bound unless the fideicommissum comes to him; nevertheless, the inheritance itself is properly bound, as in ff. de acquisitione et obligatione hereditatis, l. hereditariarum.

I therefore say that when legacies are left by the universal fideicommissary, those words, “if the fideicommissum shall come to him,” refer to the person of the fideicommissary, so that he is not bound unless it comes to him; however, they do not refer to the person of the heir, with whom the inheritance remains, burdened with its own encumbrance, according to what we noted in l. finalis, C. ad Trebellianam.

But against this strongly stands the objection: for although legacies left by the instituted heir seem to be repeated by the substitute, yet the reverse is not true, as in D. de legatis, l. licet imperator, and l. si fundum per fideicommissum, § si pater. And I answer that here the legacies left are simply apt to comprehend both in the burden of the legacies. Moreover, those words, “if the said inheritance shall come,” could be explained as meaning: if it could have come, as in D. de statu liberorum, l. Labeo; or if the case of substitution has occurred, because there are no male children. And thus I think it was the testator’s intention. Furthermore, the heir could not make a donation to the prejudice of the legacies, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. fundo, and D. de hereditate instituenda, l. 3, § quid fideicommissariam. Hence here fraud would be committed by the heir, and it would be shared by the said consortium, which is inequitable and absurd, as in D. de bonis libertorum, l. liberta octoginta. And for this purpose it is most fitting, D. de legatis 1, l. si servus plurium, § si quis ante. Therefore, considering above all equity, and because deceit and fraud ought not to be supported, nor a title acquired in fraud, as in D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. his qui bonis, and elegantly noted in l. 2, C. de repudianda hereditate, I say that the said legacies are due and justly claimed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a settlement made with the principal debtor benefits the sureties.
2. Arbitrators may reserve the right to adjudicate, and by the award of the arbitrator a novation is effected.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain Lord Galeacius bought from Master Franciscus de Surdis a certain annual rent of seven modii of grain, to pay which rent a certain Lanzelotus was bound annually, under an added penalty that if the said Lanzelotus did not pay the said rent to the said Lord Galeacius, the said Master Franciscus would be bound to pay on his behalf. Thereafter the said Galeacius exchanged the said rent with a certain Lord Andreas and his brothers de Celis and formally ceded his rights. And it is true that the said Lanzelotus de la Rocha and his heirs defaulted in the payment of the said rent. Afterwards an action was brought for the payment of the said rent, and a compromise to arbitration was made, and the said Lanzelotus was condemned in a certain sum of money, with this reservation: that if the said money were not paid, the right of the former obligation would remain intact. Thereafter the said rent was not paid, either before joinder of issue (litis contestatio) or after. An action is brought against the sureties. It is asked, what is the law?
† And it seems that the sureties are released from the former obligation and are not bound under the new obligation, because they did not intervene in it. For it must be known that through the award

† of an arbitrator a voluntary novation is effected, because it is a species of compromise (transactio); and therefore the sureties are released by aid of an exception, as in ff. loca. l. cum in plures. §. lege dicta. and C. loca. l. cum hermes. And therefore, since the said obligation of the modii of grain has in effect been extinguished, a compromise made with the principal debtor benefits the sureties, to the extent that by the act of the debtor they cannot henceforth fall back into the obligation, as in ff. de pac. l. fi. The truth is to the contrary, and I premise that the said reservation could be made in the said arbitral award, as noted in ff. fa. her. l. Item Labeo. in gl. parua; whence it preserves the right of the old obligation in its own case, as is fully read and noted in C. de sent. et interlo. l. libera quidem Theodora. To this tends l. 1. in prin. ff. si quis cau. and what is customarily noted in l. fi. ff. de eo, quod cert. lo. And therefore, regarding the provision of the said rent, a new judgment could rightly be rendered, and ought to have been rendered, both against the principal and against the surety; nor is it a judgment contrary to a judgment, but rather in accordance with the reservation of the arbitral award. Likewise, another judgment is indeed valid against an arbitral award, just as against a compromise, as in ff. de cond. ind. l. eleganter §. si quis post. It is established, therefore, that it is valid and was lawfully rendered. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If two statutes are contrary, the more specific one prevails.
2. The son of a sister is said to derive from the agnatic root.
body: In the name of Christ. There are two statutes in the same city.

† In the first statute, which is placed under the rubric of brothers and sisters dying intestate, it is provided thus: it is enacted and ordained that upon the death of any man or woman intestate, whether they were able or unable to make a will, their brothers and sisters shall succeed; and if these do not exist, the children of brothers or sisters shall succeed, etc. In the second statute, which is placed under the rubric that a mother does not succeed to a son dying intestate when there are any persons of the father's house, and how agnates are preferred to cognates in intestate succession, it is provided that a mother does not succeed, etc., and that the aforesaid provisions concerning a mother shall take place in all ascendants, and descendants, and collaterals on the maternal line. The case arose that a certain man died leaving a sister's son and leaving agnates more remote in degree. It is asked whether, by virtue of the first statute, the sister's son succeeds, or whether, by virtue of the second statute, the agnates succeed, the sister's son being excluded? And it seems that the second statute ought to prevail, because it is the later one, as in ff. de leg. l. sed et posteriores, with its subject matter. I believe the contrary to be true, because the first statute is special, and most special regarding children of a sister; whereas the second statute is general regarding any collaterals on the maternal line. But it is certain that a species contrary to a genus—whether it precedes the genus in the same disposition or in another, or whether it follows—is exempted from the genus, and derogates from the genus, and restricts the genus, so that the genus is referred back to that species, since between the genus and the species there is an incompatibility or contrariety, as is fully noted in said l. sed et posteriores, and C. de lit. contes. Auth. offeratur, and ff. de leg. 2. l. legatorum. §. qui plures, ff. de verb. ob. l. doli clausula, and l. stipulationes commodissimum est ita componere, ff. de pe. l. sanctio legum, ff. de adim. le. l. alimenta. §. basilicae, and l. stichus, de vulga. substitu. l. coheredi. §. qui patrem, and §. qui discretam.

† Moreover, a sister's son is begotten of an agnatic root and has been brought into the right of agnates, as is the notable text in l. meminimus. §. 1. C. de leg. here. Hence it is that I am called 'patruus' (paternal uncle) to the children of my sister, according to Johannes, although others hold the contrary, as is noted in C. de successo. edicto. l. 1. Likewise, the sister's son enters the degree of the sister, because they are deemed one and the same person. He is therefore a cognate when his own person is considered; but when the person of his mother is considered, he has the right of agnates. However, one should not insist upon these subtleties of the civil law where there are statutes contrary to the common law. But as I have said, here, as regards the sister's son, I do not think the common law has been corrected; rather, I think it has been corroborated by force of the first statute. And this opinion is exceedingly equitable and agreeable to the common law, for the sake of avoiding absurdity and preserving the proper meaning of the words, and because the substance of mother and daughter is seen to be the same, as in C. de impu. et alijs substi. l. fin. But in my mind there remains a doubt, because the first statute is founded for the most part on the common law, and therefore in that part it is not a statute, but the common law, as is noted in ca. 1. de consti. in 6. But the common law expressed in special words is removed by municipal law expressed in general words, because a statute operates to derogate from the common law and removes it in that municipality, as in l. omnes populi. Since, therefore, the first statute concerning children of sisters is common law, it seems accordingly to be removed by the municipal law. And this must be carefully considered; but it can be said that it is not common law, because it differs in many things, as in ff. de iusti. et iu. l. ius ciuile. Consider: one statute is special with respect to agnates, etc., the other with respect to the children of a sister; yet the latter is more special, because its quality resides in fewer persons. Likewise, if any agnate whatsoever were to exclude the daughter of a sister, the statute would provide in vain that a brother of the whole or paternal blood should exclude [her]. And therefore no other agnate excludes the daughter of the deceased's sister, except the deceased's brother, arg. C. de procu. l. maritus, and ff. so. mat. l. si vero. §. de viro. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the fideicommissary heir, having restored the inheritance, since he is the useful heir of the one who requested it, not of the one who was requested, acts ineptly by acting as if he were the heir of the one who was requested.
2. A petition is rendered inept in many ways.
3. Whether a father can substitute for his daughter while the dowry stands, given a statute that the husband shall acquire half of the dowry, etc., and whether such a statute extends to a dowry bequeathed beyond the dowry given.
4. Whether a statute can deduct from a fideicommissary substitution.
5. Whether what is received from a pupillary substitution must be restored in full.
6. Whether a legacy made to a husband is to be computed in the profit that he must have according to the form of the statute.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: Zeno, coming to his death, made his will; and in it he disposed, among other things, as follows: "Furthermore, I leave to my daughters Camilla, Julia, and Isabella two thousand seven hundred gold ducats; namely, nine hundred for each for her marriage or dowry; in which I institute them, and each of them, as my heirs, etc. I further wish that if any of the said daughters should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without legitimate children, that the said portion of her nine hundred gold ducats ought to devolve equally upon the remaining survivors, and then in that case I substitute my surviving daughters as heirs to one another by vulgar, pupillary, and fideicommissary substitution. And the same is to be understood even if only one should survive." Now it happens that the said Isabella died in pupillary age; and those two, namely Camilla and Julia, succeeded equally. Then Camilla, who had already contracted marriage with Laurentio, having constituted a dowry from the goods which Camilla herself had, which were one thousand three hundred fifty-one gold ducats according to a certain quantity of ducats and certain plots of land, and immovable goods as if from donations and things coming to her by virtue of the said legacy, died having made a will, in which she left to the said Laurentio by right of legacy. And because a statute is in force in Verona providing that, if the wife predeceases, the husband shall gain half of the dowry, the said Laurentio wishes, from the goods of the late said lady Camilla, his wife, first half of the aforementioned dowry; furthermore, the entire quantity left to him in the will. It is now asked, what is the law? Furthermore, it is asked whether the legacy is to be imputed in the said portion which the husband must gain according to the form of the statute; furthermore, it is asked whether that which is taken by pupillary substitution comes to be restored in full by fideicommissum, or in no way, or in what manner; furthermore, it is asked whether the universal fideicommissary, acting as the heir of the one who made the request, acts ineptly? Furthermore, it is asked whether the statute can deduct or diminish the fideicommissary substitution? And I begin with the libel, and it seems that the libel is apt. This case seems to be according to the letter of the Digest, On Compromises, the law "He who with tutors" in the beginning, as it is understood there in fideicommissary substitution, in that word "who was heir."

† The contrary is true, because the universal fideicommissary, having restored the inheritance by the Trebellanian rule or by the new constitutions, is the useful heir of the one who requested (rogans), not of the one who was requested (rogatus); for if he were the heir of the one who was requested, he would not be permitted the Trebellanian deduction, as appears most clearly from D. de legibus 1, l. cum filio. This is especially evident because the fideicommissum is pure, since even during the lifetime of the one who was requested, he has useful rights. Therefore, he is not the heir of the one who was requested, because a living person does not have an heir, as C. de captivis, l. nec vos. Moreover, the one who was requested restores the inheritance as a debt (aes alienum) and as a debtor, and not as one leaving an inheritance, as C. de bonis autem iuvenum possidendis, l. 1. Furthermore, this is expressly stated in l. quae, which is commonly cited, D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohaeredi, § cum filiae. The objection from l. cum tutoribus does not hold, because according to its true meaning, it speaks there of a case where a brother became heir to a brother intestate, not by the right of a paternal fideicommissum; or, if you explain it by the right of fideicommissum, say that it is from a brother left actively, not from a brother left passively; for example, because the predeceasing brother instituted someone as heir and requested him to restore the inheritance to another brother, in which case the transaction does not obstruct, because no libellus was conceived upon it; therefore, it is invalid due to a false cause, because he is not the heir of the one who was requested, as was alleged. However, the libellus would proceed if implicit, because it is understood in that part which may subsist according to law, as D. de iudiciis, l. si quis intentione, and Extr. de causa possessionis et proprietatis, cap. cum super, and cap. cum ecclesia Sutrina.

For a libel is sometimes rendered defective on the part of the plaintiff, as when a patron of a church brings an action for the recovery of property on account of the right of patronage; sometimes on the part of the defendant, as when he who is not alleged to be in possession is sued for the recovery of property, as in the extrajudicial title *De iudiciis*, chapter *Examinata*; sometimes on account of the entire underlying matter. For just as the matter must correspond to the mandate, so must the cause correspond to the libel, as noted in the Digest, title *De exceptione doli*, law 2, section *Circa*.

I now come to the points that are substantial to the case, and first it is asked whether a father can substitute for his daughter in her dowry. Distinguish thus: either we are speaking of a dowry given between living persons upon the contracting of marriage, and say, as noted by Dynus in l. finalis § filiae, ff. de legatis 2, and more fully there by me. And this is not our case; or we are speaking of a dowry bequeathed by will, then without doubt a substitution can be made beyond the legitime. And the reason for the difference is: because a dowry given pertained to the burden of the father between living persons, whereas a dowry bequeathed does not, because the father is not bound to bequeath a dowry to his daughter, but between living persons he is bound to provide a dowry if the daughter contracts marriage, as in l. qui liberos, ff. de ritu nuptiarum, and ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligare § lege, and ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum § Titio genero, and in the Authentica de sanctis episcopis § sed hoc praesenti, col. 9.

But does the statutory portion in this case diminish the paternal fideicommissum? And it is argued subtly that it does; because since the father bequeathed in consideration of the dowry, therefore all statutes speaking of the dowry profit have effect in such a bequest; because the statute is drawn to the bequest by passive interpretation, as in D. ad l. Falcidiam, l. 1, § lex Falcidia. Moreover, since the principal thing, namely the endowment, is permitted, therefore also the accessory, namely the profit of law; for the accessory is understood to be included in the principal, as in D. de rei vend., l. ex diuerso.

To the contrary it seems. For either the testator expressly substituted in the dowry, and then the substitution is stronger than the tacit profit, which arises from the statute as from a tacit agreement; because the express restricts the tacit, as in D. de vulg. subst., l. ex facto, § item quæro. And thus it seems in our case; otherwise if he had substituted specially in the dowry. So notes Bartolus in the said § filiae.

A solution may be said probably, that the husband profits half of the said dowry notwithstanding the said substitution; because the substitution of restoring is understood to be of that which can be restored in law and in fact, as in D. ad trebell., l. mulier, § si hæres. But here in law the portion cannot be restored which the husband must profit in public, which here derogates from private utility, as the text says in Auth. res quæ, in fine, C. comm. de legibus; if in the body it speaks of the dowry profit at the end. And this has place especially in that which he takes from the substitution, which does not come into the fideicommissum, unless the first portion, as appears from these two: D. ad trebell., l. Marcellus, § quidam liberis.

Moreover, since the law disposes of the dowry profit, and the father disposed of the dowry, which is a certain universal, it is understood that he disposed of the profit, which is a burden of the dowry; for in universals burdens are always contained, as in l. 2, D. de hæred. vel act. vendita. Moreover, it is presumed that one wishes that laws and customs have effect in his disposition, as in D. de edili edicto, l. quæritur, § si venditor; and D. de pactis, l. item quia. Since therefore the father consented to the dowry profit, rightly it does not come to be restored, both by the disposition of the law and by the will and intention of the father opposing the restoration.

And the laws which speak of the fideicommissum speak in another case, namely when the right of fideicommissum is not diminished from another cause, as in C. de inst. et subst., l. generaliter, in principio. And these have place especially in the portion which happens from the pupillary substitution, as in D. ad trebell., l. Marcellus, § quidam liberis; and l. ita tamen, § qui suspectam.

† Regarding the matter in question, namely whether that which is received from the pupillary substitution must be restored in full under the fideicommissum, it is to be said that yes, according to the order of the one who imposed the charge, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, ad Trebellianam, l. ita tamen, §. qui suspectam, because he was charged as heir of the minor, not in his own person. Digest, de legatis 1, l. quod fideicommisso; and noted by Cynus, and by me after him, Codex, de inofficiosa testamento, l. ex tribus. And that the substitution was pupillary is clear from the case stated, where it says “pupillary” etc. For this alternative, “vulgarly and pupillary, and by fideicommissum,” gives the choice of remedy to the substitute, not to the one burdened, as in the Digest, ad Trebellianam, l. recusare, §. Titius. But according to others, a pupillary substitution does not fall within the paternal fideicommissum, because it is the inheritance of the minor, unless someone was compelled to enter upon it. And this seems to be what the text says in the aforementioned §. qui suspectam. But that is understood when he was charged with a certain portion, not with the whole, of the paternal goods, and not of the pupillary ones. The words of the will considered indicate that the said portion falls within the fideicommissum; it does not say “inheritance,” as noted in the Digest, ad Trebellianam, l. Marcellus, §. quidam liberis. Furthermore, considering that according to the mode of persons of honorable standing, both an agreement and a statute concerning gain could rescind the fideicommissum, as I said in the Authenticum, res quae, Codex, communia de legatis. Regarding the matter in question,

Whether a legacy is to be imputed to the gain of the statute, I do not extend myself, but I refer to those matters, namely, ff. 30, de mat. l. si cum dotem, §. si pater, and C. unde vir et uxor, Auth. praeterea. And the common opinion is that it is imputed, unless the words of the testament sound otherwise, so that several lucrative causes do not concur simultaneously. I disputed this in the said Auth. praeterea. For Lord Federicus de Senis held that it is not left with the intention of compensating, unless this is expressly stated, because the gain of the dowry is not mere gain, as noted in l. si donaturus, §. fin., ff. de cond. ob causam. It does not obstruct Ant. praeterea, because there he does not speak of the gain of the dowry, but of other goods. Likewise, it does not obstruct §. si pater, because there he speaks when the father made a legacy, whose goods the law does not intend to burden with a double charge: here the father does not make a legacy, but the wife; and if it appears that the legacy is made with the intention of compensating, it would be in a manner to bequeath a debt to a creditor uselessly. Observe, because this question ceases here, because it was expressly stated that compensation would be made. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Two witnesses testifying fully about the true payment, and two affirming, are more credible than those denying; and one who testifies to a negative of sense, if he does not also testify to a negative of act, does not prove.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Two witnesses alone, who ought to have been present at the counting, fully establish proof, as the gloss on the authenticum *Si quis vult caute deponere* in the penultimate paragraph states; and therefore one should not proceed by circuitous routes. And although a third person says that he did not see the counting, it is of no consequence: because he testifies to a negation of sense, not a negation of the act: for he says that he did not see, but he does not say that the counting could not have taken place, since he himself saw it, as is noted in the Digest, title *De itinere actuque privato*, law 1, § 1. Moreover, because those who affirm are more readily believed, as is noted in the Digest, title *De actione diei*, law *Si plures*. The text in the aforementioned authenticum *Si quis* is not to the contrary, because there it speaks of the case when the writing is not confirmed by witnesses proving the true counting, as appears there in the gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Legitimation is not valid by tacit acknowledgment of spuriousness, and an institution made in favor of such a legitimated person is not valid.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain Simoninus of Janua adhered to a certain Catherine of the Tartar race, formerly his servant, who had been absolved from the bond of marriage; yet he himself was married. From her he begot several children. Thereafter, by a rescript of the Count Palatine, he obtained their legitimation without mention of their spuriousness, because he did not state that they were born of a married man.

† It is asked whether the legitimation is valid. I answer that it is not, because the defect was not expressly stated, which at least ought to be expressed in general terms: for the genus of natural children is not the same as that of spurious children, although they differ in substance and quality; therefore, the legitimation was obtained by concealment (obreptitious). But if it had been expressed that he was spurious, the legitimation would be valid, even if the specific quality of the spuriousness had not been expressed. For, since a person can be spurious in various ways, it suffices to express spuriousness in general, because all the particulars comprehended under this genus have the same root and reason, although they are called by different names: for example, spurius and manzer, yet they have their tails tied together. It must therefore be said that the said legitimation does not hold. And thus Oldus advised, because legitimation is a certain dispensation, which is not valid when the defect is suppressed, as in c. 1, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6. Furthermore, know that a son cannot be legitimated: because where substance is lacking, quality is not found; and therefore the institution made concerning him is not valid, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. eam quam. And there I noted most fully on this matter. Furthermore, where there is no substance, there can be no quality, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. eius qui. It is also to be known that the clause "notwithstanding" does not increase the grace, but strengthens the intention therein, as is the text in c. 1, de prebendis, in the Clementines. And the reason is: because the impetration of the clauses "notwithstanding" is as obreptitious as the principal itself; and he who knows the defect ought not to keep it silent, nor to deceive the granting prince, as in extra de rescriptis, c. super literis; ff. de in ius vocando, l. sed si hac, §. patronum. And these things are true in law: although I think that simple people, by naming someone natural or bastard, believe they are speaking generally of all legitimacy, but it does not matter: because it is not a simple man who speaks, but a learned one, namely the Count of the Sacred Palace. And error of law does not benefit the spurious child, nor ought it to prejudice the legitimate heirs: and especially since spurious children deal in seeking gain to the injury of the legitimate, to whom succession is due by natural equity, as in C. de codicillis, l. finalis, §. ultim.; and C. de inofficioso lucro descriptione, l. 1, lib. 10; and l. si quis, C. qui testamento facere possint; and C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. humanitatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a bequest in a will, or a stipulation in a contract, made for the remedy of the soul of the testator or contracting party, or of a third party, may be converted to other uses by the authority of the prince or the pope; and, assuming that it may, whether certain persons must first be sought out before it is distributed to the poor. And number 2.
3. And whether the necessary steps have been taken by means of a general edict.
4. Whether usurious heirs ought to participate in the distribution and payment; and to whom it pertains that restitution of usury be made.
5. Inquiry may be made concerning usury as concerning theft, and below. See the following counsel, number 1. Add also the following counsel on the matter.
body: In the name of Christ. The following case is presented: a certain Michael, a money-changer, confessed that he had held in his custody and under his mandate from his brother Thomas, also a money-changer, six hundred florins. He promised to pay this sum to Thomas or his heirs, provided that Thomas or his heirs, upon receiving and taking possession of the said money, would convert and expend the remaining six hundred florins from the money that Thomas had and ought to have solely for the purpose of restoring usury and goods wrongfully taken by his late brother Gabriel, for the remedy of Gabriel’s soul, and not for any other uses; for so had the aforementioned Thomas and Michael agreed and willed by an express pact fortified with a solemn stipulation. Subsequently, the said Thomas died. Now the question arises: whether that money may be converted and expended for other uses than the restitution of usury and wrongfully taken goods, for example, for providing dowries for daughters by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff.

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that that which has been designated for the remedy of the soul of the testator contracting, or of a third party, ought not to be converted to other uses by the authority of the prince; because, speaking of reasonable power, neither the Apostolic See nor the Emperor can rescind a testament, or a contract, or another pious disposition. Regarding the testament, this is expressly stated in civil law, in l. si testamentum, C. de testibus; regarding the contract, it is expressly stated in civil law, C. de rescindenda venditione, l. ratas; ad hoc, ff. de usufructu legatorum, l. legatum. In canon law, it is expressly stated that it ought not to be exchanged for another use, if it can be converted to the use to which it was destined, in c. quia contingit, de religiosis domibus. From this, such a conclusion follows: first, because insofar as restitution is imminent on account of usury, therefore this cannot be converted to another use, as in C. de precibus imperatoris offerendis, l. rescripta; because such an exchange or alteration of will is contrary to natural reason and equity. Furthermore, once satisfaction has been made for usury, if anything remains to be expended on account of uncertain and ill-gotten gains, since such things ought to be distributed among the poor, as in Extra, de Iudaeis, c. cum sit, and therefore the father of the poor is the legitimate administrator of all the poor of the whole world: if he wished to give these to the rich, he could not do so according to law, nor would the execution of the contract thereby be impeded according to law. But if they are indigent, and especially on account of a dowry, he may well do so, whether they are blood relatives or others, as is read and noted singularly in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud, on the word "ad similem," in the principal part. And it supports what is read and noted by Bartolus in l. legatum, ff. de administratione rerum ad civitatem pertinentium; l. cum hi, §. si in annos, ff. de transactionibus; and ff. de conditione indebiti, l. cum his in ratione sui. And this concludes the first point, in which I also consider that the change of use was expressly prohibited, which is a matter of great weight in Auth. de alienationibus et emphyteusibus, §. sanctissimas.

Secondly, it is asked, presupposing that the Pope could do this at least by his absolute power, whether certain persons must first be identified before money is disbursed to the poor or applied to another pious cause? And it must be said that this inquiry ought to be made: because usuries are truly and properly a debt owed to another, which must be paid before all else, as in C. de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possidendis, l. 1. And therefore, without doubt, usuries must be paid first, after an inquiry has been made into who ought to receive the usuries first. Moreover, what is certain ought to be put into execution before what is uncertain, as in C. de iudiciis delatorum, l. si, §. si praefatam. Furthermore, this is evident from the order of Scripture: because Scripture places the restitution of usuries first, and postpones the restitution of things taken unjustly from uncertain persons, and the reasonable order of Scripture must be observed, as in ff. de usufructu, l. quotiens. And special provision takes precedence over general provision, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. cum ita legatur, §. in fideicommisso. And therefore, a division of the will does not occur, so that half of the quantity is for the restitution of usuries, and the other half for things taken unjustly from uncertain persons; because the conjunction denotes order, not simultaneity. To what I have said about the inquiry, the following is most apt: l. cum quidam, de legatis 2, together with the following law.

† These matters are to be carried out by means of a general edict, because there is no certain and determined person who can be summoned, according to the rule of Innocentius in *c. humilis*, *de maioritate et obedientia*. In the meantime, however, the money must be deposited in a safe place, so that it may be disbursed according to the form of the agreement or of the last will. Therefore, the depositary ought to expect no benefit, because he is a mere minister, as stated in the Digest, *de auro et argento legato*, law *l. medico*, § *si*.

Thirdly, it is asked whether the heirs of usurers ought to be present at the distribution and payment. I answer that everyone whose interest is involved must be present or summoned to this distribution, so that the contract may be observed, as stated in the law and noted in l. 1, § cum dicitur, D. si cui plus quam per l. Falc., and by Jacobus de Arena, D. de leg. 1, l. quidam testamento, § si scriptus. This also pertains to the office of the diocesan bishop, whether where the testator was born, or where he had his domicile, as C. de episc. et cler., Nulli, or where he extorted usury, because by reason of the delict he himself and his heir have become subject to the forum of canon law, as Extra, de sepulc., c. Patrochiano.

† It should be noted that an inquiry may be instituted civilly concerning these matters, and also in detestation of the crime of usury and of goods wrongfully extorted; for these are equated with theft according to divine law. This is elegantly held by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, De iureiurando, chapter Ad nostram. I, Daldus,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A usurer who voluntarily deposited money to satisfy those from whom he had extorted it cannot subsequently revoke the deposit; rather, satisfaction must be made to those very persons from whom he had extorted usuries, and this is to be done at the discretion of the bishop. See also no. 2.
3. Protestations made for the sake of the soul do not admit of delay in time.
4. The heirs of a usurer must participate in the distribution of the usuries. Add the preceding counsel.
body: In the name of Christ.

First, it must be considered whether the aforementioned deponent may repent of the said agreement by reclaiming the deposit, without restoring the usury or the ill-gotten gains; and it seems that he may, because from such an agreement no right is acquired by those paying usury, and even less by uncertain persons with regard to the clause concerning the ill-gotten. For neither a public nor a private person stipulated on their behalf; and thus, in their absence, no action is sought for them, as in c. *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, lib. 6; and according to Innocentius in c. *Dudum*, *De conversione coniugata*; and according to the ordinary gloss in C. *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, *Illud*, ff. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, l. *Consensu*, ff. *De contrahenda emptione*, l. 1, in fine. Moreover, it was not peculiarly in the interest of the depositaries to agree in this manner; hence no right is sought for the depositary, as in Inst. *De inutilibus stipulationibus*, § *Si quis alii*. Furthermore, in deposit, repentance is permitted, as noted in ff. *De conditione ob causam*, l. *Si pecuniam*. To the contrary, it appears that from an agreement made between the interposing party and the depositary, an action is sought even for the absent party, as in ff. *Depositii*, l. *Publia*, in principio. Especially where the salvation of the soul is at stake, as noted in 1 q. 7, c. *Quotiens cordis oculus*. Moreover, in cases of usury and ill-extracted goods, one may proceed by inquisition, even in civil matters, as elegantly noted by Innocentius in Extra *De iureiurando*, c. *Ad nostram*, el. 2. Since therefore it is established here by public confession of usurious and extortionate wickedness, it pertains to the bishop to carry out execution, as in Extra *De iudaeis*, c. *Cum sit*. And this is the very truth: and it is special in favor of the soul.

† To the second point, it is answered that the said moneys ought, at the discretion of the bishop, to be restored to those from whom they were extorted, if they are known; but if they are not known, they ought, at the discretion of the bishop, to be distributed to the poor, of whom he is the father and legitimate administrator, as is stated in C. de epis. et cler. l. id quod pauperibus, and l. si quis ad declinandam, and in Extra de testamen. cap. cum tibi, and the said cap. cum sit. To the third point, it is answered,

† that they are compelled to pay, because what is established today, let it be paid today: for these payments, which are made for the soul, do not admit of delay of time, as noted by Cynus, Codex, de iure delatorum, l. si, §. donec. But if the bishop wishes to grant a postponement, he may demand a surety bond: because it is within his discretion to impose a condition upon his own liberality, ad hoc, Digestum, solutione matrimonii, l. si constante, §. quotiens. And because it is a praetorian postponement, as Digestum, de iudiciis, l. si debitori, and Digestum, de praetoriis stipulationibus, l. praetoriae, unless the bishop were content with an oath-bound caution, as Digestum, de iudiciis, l. 2, §. si dubitetur.

† On the fourth article, it must be said that it is so, because it is in your interest, as noted by Ioannes de Andrea in the gloss on the law *Quidam testamento*, § *Si scriptus*, *De legatis* 1. I, Baldus. See below in Consilium 89.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a division of the property subject to a fideicommissum, made by arbitration award with a pact not to contravene said division, upon the occurrence of the condition, impedes the claim for the fideicommissum.
2. The long and steadfast memory of the people is held as proof of the truth.
body: In the name of Christ. The things prohibited from being alienated outside the male line in perpetuity finally came into the possession of two persons, who divided them among themselves; the division was also made by arbitration, and it was promised not to act against it, in law or in fact. Later, one of them died without male children, having instituted the husbands of his daughters as heirs.

† It is asked whether the survivor can claim by vindication. I answer that if the fideicommissum was renounced, he cannot claim it; otherwise, if it was not renounced, either tacitly or expressly, as in C. de fideic. l. quotiens; ff. de leg. 2. l. peto. §. fratre; and l. cum pater. §. libertus. In the first case, there is no one wishing to revoke; in the second, there is, as in ff. de leg. 3. §. quindecim. And because the division was made by compromise, it is not understood to have been made regarding the conditional fideicommissum, about which there could be no judgment, nor any judicial or arbitral proceeding: although an express agreement can be made, as in C. de pac. l. conditionis incertum; ff. de iudiciis. l. non quemadmodum. Moreover, since the words state that they will do nothing against the division, it is clear that, with the fideicommissum existing, the condition has its place, as in ff. de verbo. obli. l. qui Romae. §. duo fratres; and ff. de pac. l. tres fratres; ff. de trans. l. qui cum tutoribus. in princ. Nor is it necessary here to prolong the discourse, for it would be one great commentary: but this is the truth: however, it must be proven that the thing claimed was in the testator's estate: which is proven in the ancient fact by the longest voice and fame, as noted in ff. de neg. gest. l. aqui. nam. §. cum me absente; and C. de rei vendicatio.

† For the long-standing and persistent memory of the people or of the republic is held as truth, as in l. 2. in principio, ff. de aqua pluviali arcenda; and ff. de probationibus, l. si arbiter; and extra de verbis significandis, c. quid per novale; and de acquisitione hereditatis, l. cum quidam, §. fin.; and l. quod si dubitet, sic. And a strong opinion is held as truth, as noted in the same title, l. si is, ad quem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a fideicommissum for pious causes is excluded by one who does not enter the church by profession, or assume the title of the church, and incorporate the goods of the church, but merely bequeaths them.
2. The Falcidian deduction, which is to be deducted from what is left to the church.
