3. A fideicommissary substitution made to a son for pious causes, or to a church, on the condition that he dies without sons, is not excluded by entry, or accession, nor by the assumption of sacred orders.
4. Whether a son burdened with restitution can make a will in the Trebellianic and legitimate portions.
body: In the name of Christ.

It is asked whether he who does not enter the church by professing, or by assuming the title of the church, and by incorporating the goods of the church, but simply by bequeathing them, excludes the trust for pious causes? And it must be said that the trust does not fail, as is noted in the Authentica de sanctis episcopis, § sed hoc praesenti; and in the Extravagant de probationibus, chapter In praesentia; the Code de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Authentica Ingressi; and the Authentica Si qua mulier.

Secondly, it is asked, what falcidian deduction is to be made from legacies left to churches? I answer, only the legitima due to the sons by natural law, which is deducted as a debt. The Trebellianic deduction, however, is not deducted because it is not a debt. C. de episcop. et cleri. l. Si quis ad declinandam, where I have examined this most fully, although the Archdeacon says the contrary in cap. si pater, extra de testam., and wrongly according to Bartolus and all Baldus.

† To make the matter evident, it must be premised that a fideicommissary substitution made to a son for pious causes, or to a church, under the condition that he dies without children, is not excluded by entry into, or accession to, religion, nor by the assumption of holy orders, as stated in the Authentica *De sanctis episcopis*, § *Sed hoc praesenti*, at the end. Likewise, if the person burdened does not enter a monastery or church, but donates or bequeaths goods to it, the fideicommissum left to whomsoever does not expire; because no one can, by relinquishing and not entering, nor by offering himself and his goods, establish that the church is to be regarded in the place of a son born of him, as noted in the said § and in the Code *De sacris sanctisque ecclesiis*, Authentica *Ingressi*, and in the Extravagant *De probationibus*, chapter *In praesentia*. From this it follows that brothers substituted to a brother who died without children, and who bequeaths his goods to an oratory or church, can claim the fideicommissum from the father’s testament; because he died without true, fictitious, or equivalent children; and the substitution is fideicommissary, as in the Code *De institutione et substitutione*, law *Generaliter*, in the beginning; and in the Code *De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus*, law *Praecipue*; and in the Extravagant *De testamento*, chapter *Raynaldus* and chapter *Raynaldus* in the old collection; and chapter *Si pater*, book 6. And this concludes the first point.

But it must be considered whether the aforementioned son, having been asked to make restitution, could make a will; and it must be said that he could make a will regarding the legitime, as if it were his own patrimony: for he holds it by the benefit of the law, not by the benefit of the father, as in D. 40.1.1 (*Si arrogator*), § *Sed an impuberi*; and in C. 6.30.1 (*Si quis autem non implens*); and in D. 28.6.1 (*Cohaeredi*), § *Cum filiae*; D. 28.6.1 (*De vulgari substitutione*). Likewise, regarding the Trebellian portion, according to the common opinion canonized in the aforementioned chapters, because the fideicommissum was conditional, as in C. 6.37.1 (*Quamquam*); and C. 6.38.1 (*Iubemus*). For although if the principal testator had left the fideicommissum to the Church, the Trebellian portion would not be deducted; nevertheless, it is otherwise if the heir left it, because he could not leave more than his right allowed; hence, just as he himself could not deduct the Trebellian portion, so neither could his heir, and this is the truth. I, Baldus. See above in Consilium 53.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a daughter, to whom a legacy has been left by her father that she may come to reside in a house, can come by her own authority and choose whichever house she wishes. No. 2.
body: In the name of Christ. The testator provided that if any of his daughters should remain a widow, she shall have the right of return and may come to reside in the house of the said testator with her heirs.

† It is asked whether she may do this by her own authority? I answer that she may. For the words of execution are directed to herself; the text and gloss are to this effect in l. Titia cum testamento, § 1, D. de legatis 2.

Secondly, it is asked whether he may choose for himself any house he wishes for his habitation. I answer: no. Rather, it is understood to refer to the house in which the testator habitually resided, as in D. de cond. et demonst. l. quae conditio § si; and D. ad municip. l. eius § si; and l. 2 C. ubi senatus vel clarissimi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an uncle cohabiting with his niece and making a purchase is presumed to buy with the ward’s funds, and whether he acquires the property for the niece who is a ward.
body: In the name of Christ. An uncle purchased certain goods in the common name, certain in his own name, and certain simply: which goods the niece, as heir, demands be shared with her; yet this niece, on account of her age, the nature of the profit, and the provision of the statute, could not be a partner. The question is asked, what is the law.

† And doubt arises, because it is presumed that the purchase was made with the ward’s money, or from the common revenues of the estate, insofar as the revenues permit, always however deducting expenses incurred both for the property and for the person of the ward, as in D. de negotiorum gest. l. Nescius. Sol. If nothing else is established, judgment should be given in favor of the uncle regarding things purchased in his own name, or simply, as in C. de arb. tu. l. Defunctus; D. de probat. l. Si pactum; D. de pactis l. Tale pactum §. Si; D. de solutionibus l. Et magis. And it is expressly stated in D. de administratione tutorum l. Titium et Mevium §. Altero porro: those things which are purchased in a common name, but not with common money, are subject to the action of negotiorum gestorum for the common advantage, with restitution of the price for that share, as in D. de negotiorum gest. l. Si pupilli §. Sed si ego. It is also certain that dowries and the fruits of dowries should not be common, because the burdens of marriage fall upon the mother, as in D. de familia erciscunda l. Si maritus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person appointed to manage a certain business, who fully releases debtors, is understood to have released them only with respect to what was owed to him alone, or also with respect to the common debt, which he could release by virtue of his office.
2. Between two stipulators and those who stipulate, who has the stronger right and who ought to be preferred.
body: In the name of Christ. Due to the misfortune of fate, a bankrupt merchant deserved that certain creditors be appointed as heads of creditors over his goods with full mandate, who afterwards made a refutation in a certain name of the heads, whether and also in their own name.

It is asked whether the releases are understood to have been made both with respect to what was owed to them in their own name and with respect to what they could hold in the name of their office. It is alleged that this applies only to what is owed in their own name, as stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, in the law *Si ita stipulatus*, section *Gri*. But this is false, because the words state that they were entirely absolved; for "entire" means that no part is lacking, as noted in the law *Si quando*, Codex, *De bonis vacantibus*, book 10. Furthermore, because what is equitable in one's own person ought to be equitable in other creditors, and vice versa, as stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Cum in eo*. Also, consider the words of Cynus in the Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Si unus*, section *Finis*, which are these: "What if he stipulates under both names?" Some say it matters which one he proposes, according to the law *Si servus communis*, Digest, *De stipulationibus servorum*. But this is not so, as will be shown below in the same title, in the law *Tale peccatum*, section *Finis*. You, First Part of the Consilia, say,

†which will be valid, having regard to that name under which the thing can be valid, as in the law *Quo non obstat*, in the title *De rebus dubiis*. That distinction applies, because it then matters which name is placed first, when it can be valid under either; hence, in case of doubt, we revert to the name prefixed. And by these means is distinguished the rule that the name is preferred, according to Petrus and Gulielmus de Cuneis. Concerning this, it is said, as in the law *Tale*, at the end, in the same title, where Cynus concludes from these things that they appear to have made the liberation under both names, as in law 2, *De stipulationibus servorum*. And this is the gloss in the Digest, *De procuratoribus*, in the law *Quacumque ratione*, on the word *procurator*, where the gloss says: "under the name of procurator." And it is supported by the Digest, *De istis*, in the law *Lucius*, and in law 1, Code, *De precibus imperatori offerendis*. And therefore, the same is what I advise, through my associate. In the aforementioned law, *De II.*, I say and advise. I, Baldus. Let it be taken by itself, setting forth all the questions contained in this opinion. See also above, opinion 82.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. No one is presumed to be the owner or possessor wherever he asserts this, and proof of ownership is difficult.
2. How very ancient possession is to be proved.
3. Whether an heir may claim that the testator lied.
4. Whether anyone is presumed to possess from himself or from a preceding title.
5. Ancient reputation has the force of notoriety; and whether true ownership or possession is proved by reputation.
6. Whether an heir, who holds a title from the deceased and possession from himself, is presumed to have held both from the deceased.
7. A fideicommissary cannot transfer ownership of the thing to the heir unless he delivers the thing to the legatee.
8. A fideicommissary cannot prohibit the alienation of the heir’s thing; and why the heir is then bound.
9. When someone is said to renounce a fideicommissum, and whether he may do so.
10. Whether a father’s renunciation harms the son.
body: In the name of Christ. Thomas Asmarus of old established his testament, in which, among other things, he disposed that the castle of Camera should always remain and devolve upon the males of his progeny, as they were nearest in degree, excluding daughters and descent through the female line. After the testator died, his heir possessed that castle; and finally it came to Thomas and Michael, brothers, who were of the progeny of that ancient testator. These brothers indeed came to a division of the said castle, with the added clause that each party should have and hold the part adjudged to him, and do with it whatever he wished; promising to each other to observe that division and never to contravene it, etc. Afterwards, the said Thomas died, leaving two daughters claiming to be his heirs. Now the said Michael holds the said castle in its entirety. The daughters, however, wish to claim it for one-half, and they found their claim on the ground that their father held it for one-half, a possession which they justify by arbitral sentences and divisions made between them and other predecessors. It is opposed against them that they should not be admitted, notwithstanding the said testament. It is replied on behalf of the daughters that it is not established that that castle belonged to that ancient testator; and that the matter disposed of in the said testament was remitted by subsequent divisions, even if it were established that the castle belonged to that ancient testator. It is doubled on behalf of Michael that at least it is proven that the heir of that testator held the said castle. Hence, this is first asked: whether it is presumed that he held it as heir, and as a thing mentioned in the testament. Secondly, it is asked: whether, if it was his heir’s, the prohibition mentioned in the testament applies against the daughters, especially since those brothers, through their predecessors, were heirs of that ancient testator. Thirdly, it is asked: whether it suffices to prove by voice and fame that that castle belonged to that ancient testator; and whether this is aided or confirmed by the arbitral sentence passed between those brothers on one side and the heirs of Manuel Asmarus on the other. Lastly, it is asked: whether by those divisions it is said that the prohibitive disposition of that ancient testator was renounced; and if prejudice were caused to the said Michael, whether prejudice would be generated to the sons of that Michael, having seen and examined the words of the testament there, where it says, because the will of that testator is that the said castle remain with his heirs while they live, and afterwards with their sons, males, and other males descending through the male line, etc.

† It must be stated for clarity that no one is presumed to be the owner or possessor, even if he asserts this in a will, contract, or judgment, unless he proves it. Indeed, proof of recent possession is easy; but proof of possession that has lasted beyond a human lifetime is difficult. Proof of ownership, however, is always difficult, as is fully set forth in the law and notes, C. de probat.; l. cum res; and ff. de probat.; l. si arbiter. The reason is that ownership consists in law, as noted in the excerpt, de probat., c. cum causam. First, it is proved by a true act of man, as noted by Dynus in l. 1, in fine, and l. 2, de aqua pluviali arcenda.

† However, when possession is exceedingly ancient, witnesses cannot prove the true act of a man, namely that which they did not see nor know; because in proving possession, sight, memory, and act are required, just as in proving any other fact. D. de furtis, l. quidam tabularum; and C. de testibus, l. testium. Therefore, the mere instrument of a will is not sufficient to prove ownership or possession. As in X. de fide instrumentorum, c. inter dilectos, § si.

† Nevertheless, one point must be observed: if the testator disposed of something in his will as if it were his own property, the heir who has accepted the inheritance cannot claim that the testator was mistaken, provided that the testator based some legal claim on the aforementioned assertion, as is expressly noted in the aforementioned law *Cum res ad*, which supports this principle in the Digest under *De petitione hereditatis*, and in the law *Rem alienam* at the end, unless the heir had made an inventory and this is established; for then the assertion of the deceased does not prejudice the heir, if perhaps the property belonged to the heir, as is fully explained in the law and glosses in the Code under *De re vendicata*, in the law *Cum a matre*, and in the Code under *De iudiciis delatorum*, in the final section, § *In computatione*. Furthermore, it must be stated for clarity,

† Although it is true that he who has no title is presumed to possess as a possessor, and on his own behalf rather than on behalf of another, as is fully set forth in the law and notes in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. regulariter, and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. cogi; nevertheless, where a title precedes and possession follows, and that title is known to the possessor, it is presumed that he possesses by virtue of the preceding title, whether the title arises from contract or from last will, as in C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. minus instructus. And rightly so, because it is more reasonable to presume that he possesses in good faith than as a thief, according to the argument in D. pro socio, l. merito. The same rule applies if possession precedes and a title follows in the specific case, that is, in the thing possessed, as in D. de rei venditione, l. quaedam mulier.

Thirdly, it must be premised that although reputation does not prove true ownership, nor true possession, by its own force: for one thing is to be said, another to be, and one thing is opinion, another truth; for truth always remains in the same state, but opinion does not, as is noted in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, in the law *Qui bona*, § *Si quis stipulaturus*. Nevertheless, a very ancient reputation, one that transcends the memory of living persons, makes a matter notorious and proves it by the force of notoriety. This is the ordinary gloss in the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, in the law *At quaenam*, § *Cum me absente*. To this point, it is highly pertinent what is noted by Archidamus, Question 2, Question 7, Chapter *Beati*. And to this point, it is highly pertinent what is noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant Decretals, *De iuramento calumniae*, Chapter *Cum causam*. Moreover, from these three evident points it follows that the aforementioned ancient testator is presumed to have been possessor and owner; and especially because, as has been said, the heir cannot deny this, since the act of the deceased is regarded as the act of the heir; and because the most ancient reputation bears this meaning. And also by a new reason,

†because if these things had a title from the deceased, and possession from himself, it is presumed that he had both from the deceased, as in D. de don. causa mort. l. si alienam, and l. qui alienam, although there is an argument to the contrary in D. de pet. haer. l. item veniunt, §. quod si pro emptore, and D. de condi. indebiti, l. indebiti, §. sed si nummi. To this also contributes the arbitral sentence passed between the brothers themselves and the heirs of the said Manuel, which is presumed true between the compromitting parties themselves and their heirs, as noted in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. 1, and by Dynus in c. quod quis mandato, de reg. iur., lib. 6, and more clearly in his consilia, in the consilium beginning Tholomaeus. And to this the law l. si duo patroni, in princ., D. de iureiur., with its gloss, is most apt. And by this the first point is sufficiently answered: and that males, until they come of age, are preferred to females in the said castle.

† To make the second point evident, it must be premised that a testator cannot transfer ownership of the heir’s property, even if the heir, by accepting the inheritance, consents, unless the heir delivers possession to the legatee, as stated in D. de legatis 1, l. si heredi servus; and D. de servis, l. Papinia. Although the singular gloss states that, on the contrary, ownership passes upon acceptance of the inheritance, as noted in l. 2, C. communia de legatis, just as if the testator had bequeathed subject to the heir’s will—a unique case in law, D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur, l. sicut § venditoris—and touched upon by Bartolus in l. cum quis decedens, in principio, D. de legatis 3; nevertheless, the truth is, as I have said, that the testator cannot by operation of law transfer ownership in the heir’s property. And the reason is that in the acceptance of the inheritance a contract is formed, and by contract, or quasi-contract, ownership does not pass by operation of law, as in D. de rei venditione, l. si ager.

And from this it follows that, although the testator prohibits the alienation of the thing, so that it may not be alienated by the heir, nevertheless he cannot [effectively prohibit it], as is stated in C. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. ea lege, and in D. de pactis, l. penultima. Nevertheless, the heir is bound by an action arising from the will towards those to whom the testator wished the thing to pass. Moreover, he is bound by a hypothecary action, as in l. 1 and l. 2, C. communia de legatis. The will prevails, unless error induced the testator to make the legacy, which he would not have made otherwise; but such error is not presumed in case of doubt, as in D. de legatis, l. unum ex familia, l. si rem, § cum filius, and § heres meus, and fully noted in D. de legatis 1, l. si domus, § de evictione. Furthermore, retention would be granted to the possessor, and the question arises whether restitution should be made in the case of alienation, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. filiam fratribus. And by this means the second point has been satisfied. As for the third point, it has already been answered.

† Regarding the fourth point, it must be known that there is a difference between dividing [the inheritance] and the parties granting each other license to alienate at their own will, with knowledge that this will overturn the burden of the fideicommissum. In the first case, a renunciation of the fideicommissum is not induced, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Cum pater*, § *Haereditate*. In the second case, although a renunciation is not induced, nevertheless, by reason of the pact, that which would otherwise not be permitted is lawful. Thus is understood what is noted by Dynus in § *Duo fratres*. Therefore, the fideicommissum endures by the law itself, but not its effect, because the exception does not apply. Moreover, in doubt, no one is presumed to renounce such a hope, which was not placed in the natural order, but in the adverse fortune of a free man, which the contracting parties ought not to have considered, as stated in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, *Inter stipulantem*, § *Sacramentum*, and as is noted in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*.
† l. Mutiana. And this as to the fourth point.

† Regarding the last point, it must be said that the father’s renunciation does not prejudice the son in those matters which the son acquires by virtue of his own person, as stated in l. 3, ff. de interdictis et relegatis; just as we say in the matter of fiefs. Although the renunciation does not prejudice him, the obligation could prejudice him if the son is the father’s heir, because he would be bound by the father’s obligation, as in C. de pactis, l. conditionis incertum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether arbitrators elected according to the statutory form are to be called judges of the legate or ordinary judges, and what power they have.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked whether arbitrators and arbiters, who are chosen according to the form of the statute by the parties and have the power to define and decide, are ordinary judges or delegated judges? I answer: either you ask about the truth, and they are neither, but sound in themselves; or about similarity, and then because they have power immediately from the law, they seem to be ordinary, as in D. de iudiciis omnium iudicum, l. more maiorum. But the contrary seems to be said, because they are not judges appointed for the universality of cases, but only for one case, namely, the compromise. Also, because they do not preside over a territory, which has jurisdiction, as in C. ubi et apud quos, l. si. Also, because they do not execute their sentence, as in C. de episcopis audiendis, l. episcopale. Also, because the ordinary judge compels the parties to compromise; and if an appeal were made from them, it would be as if from a delegated judge, or quasi, as in C. de iudiciis, l. cum specialis. However, considering the truth, as I said, they are not properly judges, but certain good men. This is held by Speculum. But Jacobus de Arena says that they are true arbitrators, D. de solutionibus, l. quod si forte, § 1, and the same in the third, who is chosen by them, or by the judge, where they do not wish to choose: the end of their discord is the election of a third. Nor would they have performed their office, which is to choose a third and judge with him, unless the time of the compromise had elapsed, because there is no repair of such time, as in D. locata, l. si in lege, in principio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the executors of a will, in distributing goods to the poor, may choose the testator’s illegitimate son as a poor person and give him some of the goods that belonged to the testator.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Hence, that the election made concerning the said spurious son Anton. was valid: for according to the equity of canon law, the father could leave him maintenance, as in the extrajudicial title *De eo qui duxit in matrimonium quam polluit per adulterium*, chapter *Cum haberet*. Therefore, the executor of the paternal testament can do so, because what the executor does is considered to have been done by the testator himself, as in the Digest, title *De re dubia*, law *Vtrum*, section *Cum quid*. Moreover, the said lady Soptana could, out of her own liberality, give, donate, and distribute to the said spurious son, because the prohibition of the law does not apply except between ascendants and descendants, as in the Digest, title *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Si is qui*, and noted in the Authentic *Quibus modis naturales et sui*, section *Si*, column 7. Nor is it presumed that she did this by any tacit fideicommissum for restoring to one incapable, because a tacit fideicommissum contrary to law for restoring to one incapable is not presumed to have been imposed unless it is proven, as in the Digest, title *De legatis primo*, law *Lucius*, section *In testamento*; Digest, title *De iure fisci*, law *Non intelligitur*, section *Tacite*; Digest, title *De probationibus*, law *Cum tacitum* and law *Qui testamentum*. And this was advised by Bartolus, that a wife instituted as heir by her husband can exercise liberality; therefore, the spurious son of the testator [can receive] those things which freely pertain to the wife, because he is not prohibited by any law, therefore it is permitted, as in the Digest, title *De procuratoribus*, law *Ab ea parte*. Moreover, the cause of maintenance is pious, and therefore it seems that it could rightly be distributed for the soul of the testator, as in the Digest, title *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, section *Si cui*, note *n.*; [he receives] not as a spurious son, but as any person, as in the Digest, title *De adoptionibus*, law *Si pater*, section *Qui duos*. From which it follows that the said spurious son could encumber the said goods; and thus the creditor could bring a hypothecary action. Moreover, the authority of the bishop contributes to this: for the bishop is not prohibited from distributing to a spurious son, nor is this guarded against by any law. Moreover, the prohibition of alienation in the contract does not prevent the hypothec or alienation from being valid, as fully in the Code, title *De conditionibus ob causam*, law *Ea lege*; Digest, title *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si ita quis*, section *Ea lege*. From which it seems to be concluded on the part of the creditor.

To the contrary is the truth itself, for the understanding of which it must be premised that one who is asked to restore after his death cannot restore before death to the prejudice of those others who are honored after death, as fully in the Code, title *De fideicommissis*, law *Post mortem*, and Digest, title *De legatis secundo*, law *Cum pater*, section *A filia*. Also, that goods which are subject to restoration after the death of the heir cannot in the meantime be alienated by the heir, without the alienation being rendered void by the law itself, given the existence of the condictio of the fideicommissum, as in the Code, title *Communi de legatis*, law *Si*, section *Si autem ob avaritiae cupidinem*. Since therefore there remain poor persons who have the right of revocation to their prejudice, otherwise the restoration could not be made, and the right of the obligor being extinguished, the hypothecary right of the creditor is extinguished, as in the Digest, title *De pignoris*, law *Lex vectigal*. Nor let anyone say that the poor are uncertain persons: for the congregation of the poor acts in the place of a person, as in the Code, title *De episcopis et clericis*, law *Nulli*. Also, the bishop himself is held in the place of a person, as in chapter *Contingit*, title *De religiosis*, doctor in *Clericis*. And therefore the opinion of the eminent doctors Peter and Angelus of Ubaldo of Terni is the truth itself, as noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De legatis*, law *Filius*, section *Divi*, and by Cynus and Butrius and all in the said law *Post mortem*.

The authority of the bishop does not obstruct: for authority is accessory, and ends when the principal ends. Also, the bishop prohibited alienation: and alienation or hypothecation made against the decree of a judge was not valid, as in the Digest, title *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Si quis sciens*. That which is also to be weighed is that the said spurious son died while the said lady was alive; hence, what had been done could not be confirmed by the death of the lady; because the person in whom the act could be confirmed was not in existence. And nothing done at an improper time is confirmed at a proper time, nor can it become valid by the passage of time, as in the Digest, title *De legatis secundo*, law *Unum ex familia*, section *Et in regula non firmatur*; and Code, title *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law *A marito* and law *Non omnis*; Digest, title *Si certum petatur*. Also, those words "for maintenance" must be considered, which in the case of a spurious son are in the place of a final cause, because the spurious son is not otherwise capable by the disposition of the father; and therefore, the final cause being finished, the effect is finished, although it would be otherwise if the said words were added to one capable, as noted in the Digest, title *De transactionibus*, law *Cum his*, section *Si cui*. Furthermore, the son of one receiving maintenance does not succeed in the maintenance, because they are personal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment may be retracted on the pretext of newly discovered instruments: and the time for seeking restitution in integrum lasts for four years from the time the judgment was rendered.
2. Whether what has been paid by virtue of a judgment may be recovered.
3. Whether a judgment rendered within an excessively short time is void by operation of law, and whether it may be appealed.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain judgment was rendered in the following form: And because we have seen the oath in lieu of proof, likewise the oath against calumny, and the oath as to the truth, and due to the lack of proof insofar as it was not fully proven, but only half-proven in the said case, therefore we pronounce him to be a usurer, and condemn him, etc. This judgment was rendered six years ago and more. Now instruments are discovered, by which it appears that the said condemnation was not just, because it was made after a general and most complete discharge arising from the cause of payment, as appears in the instrument. It is asked whether the said judgment can be retracted. Secondly, it is asked whether, if it cannot be retracted, what was previously paid can be reclaimed by virtue of the said instrument of discharge. Thirdly, it is asked whether the said judgment, rendered within an excessively short term, is null by operation of law:

† And it seems, with regard to the first point, that the said sentence was valid and cannot be retracted: because a sentence is not retracted on the pretext of new instruments, as in C. de iudic. l. sub praetextu (which otherwise begins sub specie). The contrary is true, because when two things concur, namely, that the sentence is rendered based on an oath administered due to a lack of proof, and that oath subsequently appears false by virtue of instruments newly discovered, such a sentence is rescinded by restitution in integrum, as in ff. de iureiurando l. admonendi. Someone might say that the time for seeking restitution in integrum has lapsed, because the four-year period has passed from the day he knew the sentence was rendered, as in C. de tempore in integrum restitutionis l. supervacuam. But this does not avail, because rather the period begins to run only from the day the instruments were newly discovered, because this period is useful with respect to its commencement, and it does not begin to run against one who is ignorant, from whom the substance of the restitution in integrum depends, as is fully noted in the aforementioned l. supervacuam. Moreover, the ignorant person could not seek restitution, because he could not even allege what he was ignorant of; therefore, the useful period does not begin to run, because it is not such a period in which knowledge is not required, as is sometimes the case. ff. de infantibus exheredatis l. generosa. And this is proven by ff. de excusatione tutorum l. quinquaginta, and ff. quis ordo in bonis possidendis servetur l. 2 §. dies. And this is the truth, if the instruments are newly discovered, which allegation, as if alleged through ignorance, is proven by oath, unless the contrary is proven. ff. de probationibus l. verius. And in the rule of law, ignorance is presumed. And this concludes the first point.

† Regarding the second point, it appears that recovery would not be possible if payment has been made by virtue of a judgment, as stated in D. de man. l. Fideiussor, § In omnibus, and C. de cond. indebit. l. 1. However, the contrary is true, because the initial payment reverts to having no cause; and the glossa ordinaria expressly determines this in D. de cond. indebit. l. Iulianus, in the first gloss. I add further that, if payment had not yet been made by judgment, set-off could be pleaded, as in D. de compens. l. Si cum militi, § Cum intra, because the instrument of refutation and confession, although general, constitutes a liquidated claim, as in D. de solut. l. Si ex pluribus, and D. de pact. l. Emptor, § Lucius.

† On the third point I do not insist, because it is a case outside of the matter of delay. c. 1. For unless there is such a restriction of time as induces impossibility, a delay is valid, although it could be called excessive brevity of the term; but here no appeal was made. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the right to denounce passes to successors.
2. Whether successors are to be believed in the same manner as the principals were believed.
3. Whether a denunciation made before the vicar, given a statute that denunciations ought to be made before the Lord Podesta, is valid.
body: In the name of Christ. In a certain contract for the sale of the fruits and revenues of certain mills, it is stipulated that if at any time the water should cease to flow due to a defect in the sluice gate or for any other reason, that from the time it ceases until it begins to run and flow again, a certain period of the said term of purchase shall not run against the said buyers. Regarding this cessation, the said buyers, and each of them, are to be believed if they have notified the lord of the Podesta and the Elders; and such notification was placed in the archive, which notification, thus made, is to be considered true unless the contrary is legitimately proven. Finally, the said buyers sold their said right to Titius, and Titius, upon the occurrence of the event, notified the Vicar of the Podesta and the Elders. Three questions are asked: first, whether the right to notify passes to the buyer of the buyer; second, whether the buyer of the buyer is to be believed? Third, since the notification was not made to the Podesta, but to his Vicar, whether it is valid?

† Regarding the first point, the words of Baldus of Arezzo in *l. si sic*, D. de legibus, *l. hic*, are as follows: That the action which accrues to someone by reason of a contract passes to any successor, even a singular successor; as here, and below, D. de verbis oblig., *l. si stipulatus fuerit*, and *l. si*, § 1. But suppose that a certain village promised Titius to cleanse a certain stream at the discretion of that same Titius, who sold the stream to me; I ask whether they are bound to cleanse it at my discretion? It seems that they are not. D. locato, *l. si merces*, in the beginning; and D. de procuratoribus, *l. si is, qui stichum*; and by this, below, D. de verbis oblig., *l. si stipulatus sim*. Nor does it matter that these laws speak of a universal successor; for the same applies to a singular successor, by argument from above, D. de iureiurando, *l. etiam si in rem*; D. de damno infecto, *l. fluminum*, § *adiicitur*. Likewise, the laws cited do not obstruct, because they speak when someone is chosen as a minister. But was this done on account of the thing? And the same applies when someone promised to restore damages at my discretion, and I assigned the rights to another; others must grant this on account of persons and causes, for this, below, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, *l. si*. From these, Jacobus de Arena shows that a pact to give notice passes to a singular successor.

But it is doubtful whether he ought to be believed: and it seems that he ought not, because the faith of a certain person has been chosen for this purpose. D. de dote praelata, l. Theopompus; and C. de rebus creditis, l. Generaliter, in principio. But the contrary seems more correct: because this is not entrusted to the person by reason of the person, but by reason of the contract. Hence it suffices if the person is equally suitable, which is presumed in doubt, as is noted. D. de procuratoribus, l. Si actor malitiose. And this is the second point.

† Regarding the third point, there is no room for doubt, because that which is done before the vicar is deemed to be done before the presiding judge himself, as stated in the Code, *De officio eius qui vicem alterius gerit*, l. *Suggestente*. And it is the same tribunal, as in c. 2, *De consuetudine*, Book 6. Nor should a distinction be made in the name of the official, but rather in the quality of the office, as in l. 2, § *Pe*, D. *Ad tertullianum*. And according to the foregoing, the opinion previously rendered by me should be understood. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a husband may claim maintenance from an unpaid dowry.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Whether a husband who sustains the burdens of marriage can claim maintenance [derived] from a dowry not paid within the conventional or legal term. Some say no, because the action concerning a dowry is of strict law, except insofar as it is available to the wife, and therefore such accessions are not due except from the time of joinder of issue (litis contestatio); and this opinion is posited in the gloss on soluto matrimonio l. de diuisione. But the contrary opinion is also touched upon there: for since the husband sustains the burdens of marriage, he fulfills with proper affection on his part; therefore it ought also to be fulfilled on an equal footing, at least by compensating him for the burdens of marriage, by argument of C. de ac. emp. l. curabit, because it is not equitable that a woman be enriched to the loss of another. Just as, on the other hand, if he did not sustain the burdens of marriage, he ought not to have the fruits, as in l. pater, ff. de ex. do., and it seems to be the case that after a two-year period any third party is bound, C. de iu. do. l. fina. Moreover, because the two-year period succeeds in place of joinder of issue according to dominus Raynerius de Forlivio, and the law assesses it there; nevertheless, he does not believe that there is room for that assessment today, but rather that maintenance ought to be provided according to the custom of the region, or according to the correspondence of the burdens of marriage to the extent that it is to be paid from the dowry, and thus proportionally; and this opinion is held by Iacobus de Rauenna and Petrus in the said l. de diuisione. And it is a very equitable opinion when they are claimed as damages (interesse), by argument of ff. de in litem iuran. l. numis. And therefore I conclude that according to the measure of the arbitrament of a good man, taking into consideration the burdens of marriage, and the amount of the dowry, and the practices customary in the region, the said interesse, which we call maintenance, can undoubtedly be claimed: for if, the restitution of the dowry not having been made, maintenance is due because, the marriage having been dissolved, the dowry is deemed the woman's own estate, as noted in C. de rei vxo. ac. l. unica. §. exactio. in the Great Gloss; so, conversely, while the marriage endures, the dowry is the husband's own estate, and therefore its maintenance is owed to the husband, that is, wherewithal to support himself, his wife, and his children, as in C. de iure do. l. vbi adhuc. at the verse ita tamen, ff. de uentre in pos. mitten. l. curator, and extra de vsuris. l. salubriter, and ff. fa. herciscun. l. si matris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person who has confessed a crime against himself ought not to be interrogated regarding the conscience of others; this rule fails in certain cases, but whether such a confession constitutes evidence.
2. Those who believe that by the power of demons some good can be done are heretics and apostates.
3. He who says that God is not God is the chief of heretics.
4. To whom the articles of accusation and the statements of witnesses are to be given in an inquisition.
5. Indicia, or infamy, must precede torture.
6. What indications are sufficient for torture.
7. To which confession regard shall be had: whether to one made under torture or outside of it, or to one made in court or outside of it.
body: In the name of Christ. The rule of law is,

† That one who has confessed a crime against himself ought not to be interrogated regarding the conscience of others. Nor is this surprising, for he is an infamous criminal, a base person, and suspect. Hence, he is not believed, as in C. de accusat. l. si. Nevertheless, this must be understood as meaning that he is not believed with regard to full or half-proof, but he is properly interrogated with regard to inquisition, as in ff. de poenis l. quis ultimo in fine, according to Oldradus. And it constitutes an indication for the purpose of inquiring, not for condemnation, nor for corroborating other proofs. The exception fails in certain crimes, as in the crime of heresy; for this is a crime of lèse-majesté divine, as in Auth. Gazaros C. de haereticis. Likewise, it fails if one is accused of magical and witchcraft arts, as noted in the aforementioned l. si C. de accusat. and C. de maleficiis et mathematicis l. si. For there, considering the quality of the person who is defamed, one may proceed to torture upon preceding infamy or other probable conjecture concerning the deed of the one who is tortured. I believe, however, that this is committed to the discretion of the judge, having weighed the indications and conjectures nearest to the truth, as in ff. de quaestionibus l. 1 §. cum quis latrones; and extra de simonia c. per tuas; and el grande §. nos vero; and noted in spec. de inquisitione §. 1 ver. et scias, quod ubi verba. Johannes de Andrea, ff. de edictis edictorum l. quod si nolit §. qui mancipia: one is presumed good or bad on account of his associates. Likewise from his conversation. Likewise from the master whom one has, whether good or bad. 2 q. 7 c. pervenit ad nos; 28 q. 1 c. saepe; de edictis edictorum l. ediles etiam §. Pedius, where the gloss of Accursius cites that saying of the wise man: "Walk with the good"; for morals are formed by association, as in C. de cohortalibus lib. 12 l. si cohors. And it is supported by ff. de re militari l. non omnes §. a Barbaris; and de praesumptionibus c. literas. By this it is clear that the Bishop, who has this cleric as vehemently suspect due to preceding infamy, may torture him and extract the truth from him, so that the province may be purged of such pestilent men, as in ff. de officiis praetoris l. congruit.
† It is certainly not ambiguous that those who believe that something good can be done through the power of demons are heretics and apostates. 2 6. q. ult. c. non observetur.

† Moreover, there is no doubt that he who says that God is not God is the chief of heretics. C. de sum. Tri. l. epistola inter claras. And in the Psalm it is said, "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God." And in the Creed: "I believe in one God." And in the Athanasian Creed: "Whosoever will be saved." And of this there is no doubt.

† Moreover, if it is asked whether the accused ought to be given the charges and the statements of the witnesses, it must be said that yes. [This is established] in the cited chapter *Per tuas* and chapter *Licet Heli* in the title *De sententia et re iudicata*, and chapter *Qualiter et quando* in the second book of the *Extravagantes*, § *Debet*, in the title *De accusationibus*, and in the title *De accusationibus*, chapter *Qualiter et quando*. And note the gloss of Bartolus in the law *Si*, in the Digest, title *De quaestionibus*, in the part *De poenis*, unless this is done through subterfuges, and there is notoriety of the offense, and it publicly serves more to proceed to punishment than to delay. And [see] the Code, title *De feriis*, law *Provincialium* (otherwise beginning *Procons

† It is certain that indications or infamy must precede torture, as stated in the Digest, *De quaestionibus*, law *Maritus*. However, as I have said, in this crime, with regard to torture, the confession of another coheretic in the same act of heresy constitutes an indication. Otherwise, if the aforementioned confession had no effect, the interrogation would be futile. Therefore, it may be said that the bishop, if the opinion of the infamous person is weighed heavily, may subject him to torture unless he purges himself. This is supported by what is noted in the Extravagant Decretals, *De iudiciis*, chapter *At si clerici*.

† Lord Bartolus, in the last paragraph of the law *De quaestionibus*, states: suppose that proceedings are brought against someone for a crime, and there are indications sufficient for torture; the doctors commonly hold, and rightly so, that no certain rule can be given on this matter, but it is left to the discretion of the judge. I say, however, that the bishop could exercise his discretion, because a confession made voluntarily, together with joint association, constitute indications sufficient for torture, if the bishop’s conscience so dictates. Moreover, the mind of the judging authority is greatly moved by frequent association and cohabitation with a heretic, because those who associate with one another are presumed to know each other’s condition and actions, as in the Digest, title *De locato*, law *Dominus horreorum*; and in the Code, title *De repudiis*, law *Consensu*, section *Super*; and in the Decretals, title *De testimonio*, chapter *Veniens*.

† Another doubt arises from the contradiction in the response, which gives rise to suspicion, as in c. Ut nostrum, Ut ecclesiastica beneficia. Because the heretic, when first questioned, denied the charge, but subsequently confessed. The doctors say that against another person, greater weight is given to a confession made under torture than to a voluntary one; but against oneself, greater weight is given to a voluntary confession: as in D. De quaestionibus, l. 1, § Quoniam, and there by Bartolus. But sometimes weight is given to a confession made under torture applied, where the laws command that torture be resorted to, provided that the confession is maintained in court, not in prison, because a retraction of a confession made in prison has no effect, since it is made outside the court, not in court, as in C. De custodia rei, l. 2. On the contrary, even the maintenance of the confession must be made in court, so it is practiced, and this is held by Bartolus in l. 1, § Divus, D. De quaestionibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute, etc., as here in the principal part, whether the respondent is said to have responded appropriately when he answers inappropriately or ambiguously.
2. If the lady promises to ratify whatever the procurator has lawfully done, the mandate is not valid.
3. An oath is indivisible, and therefore it cannot be approved in part and not in part.
4. Given the statute that the lawsuit is to be contested with all exceptions reserved at the time of disputation, so that the proceedings are not thereby delayed, if an exception impeding the proceedings has been raised, and despite this witnesses were received, etc., whether such witnesses are valid in another judgment.
body: In the name of Christ. The Decree provides that after the publication of the testimony, the party who produced the witnesses, when asked whether he wishes to avail himself of their statements, if he answers in the affirmative, and if the witnesses have given false testimony, is deemed to have knowingly produced them. And if he does not answer within the time limit set by the judge, he is deemed not to wish to avail himself thereof. In the present case, the party, when asked, answered in this manner, that he wishes to avail himself of those passages and points tending in his favor; and he declares himself in no other way.

† It is now asked whether he is to be understood as having responded appropriately, or whether he is to be regarded as having failed to respond: and it seems to me that he does not respond appropriately who responds obscurely, because by his response the judge or the adversary is not made certain, since the matter remains still subject to dispute in court.

†. The wife, however, regarding what we say about the procurator: if the principal promises to ratify whatever the procurator has lawfully done, the mandate is not valid, as is stated in c. 1, *De procuratoribus*, in the Clementine.

† Moreover, the statement of the witness is based on an oath, which is a single indivisible entity according to Oldradus; and therefore it cannot be approved in part and rejected in part. Argument: Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *In causa*; 60th Distinction, chapter *Si ad scriptas*; and by Bartolus, Digest, *De liberatione legis*, law *Aurelius*, section *Idem quaesivit*. The third reason is that the response does not correspond to the question, as in Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law 1, section *Cum adicitur*. He ought to have answered regarding the whole matter. For this question implies whether he wishes to avail himself of the witness’s oath, because the deposition is founded on the oath, and the person questioned regarding the disposition appears to be principally questioned regarding the oath, which is indivisible, as I have said above. Therefore, it is equivalent to answering improperly, as in Digest, *De interrogationibus et responsionibus*, law *De aetate*, section *Nihil*; and Digest, *De iure fisci*, law *Ita fidei*; and Digest, *De iniuriis*, law *Praetor edixit*.

The following question arises: a statute provides that the litigation is to be contested with all exceptions reserved at the time of the disputation, and that the proceedings are not to be delayed thereby. Now, an exception impeding the proceedings was raised; notwithstanding this, witnesses were received and their testimony published; subsequently, it was pronounced that the exception was an obstacle. It is asked whether the said testimonies are valid in another trial. I answer: no, because they appear to have been received when the litigation was not legitimately contested. I prove this by the following reason: to reserve exceptions is nothing other than to reserve their effect. L. si fideiussor, in principio, ff. qui satisdare cogantur. But the effect and proper nature of these exceptions was to impede the contestation of the litigation; hence, it appears from the subsequent fact that the litigation ought not to have been contested; and consequently, that the witnesses were not duly received, because a contestation not duly made is held as void, as in C. de litis contestatione, Auth. offeratur. Moreover, because this exception impedes the judgment by its very nature, and easily reverts to its nature, since if the judgment does not hold, the testimonies do not hold, which are part of the judgment, as noted by Innocentius, extra de testibus, r. cum causam. For the protestation appears to be repeated in every act, and the reservation has the force of a protestation; otherwise, the exceptions would certainly not be preserved if they lost their due vigor, which is contrary to the words of the statute. And thus I hold regarding the said doubts, saving the substance of the truth. I, Baldus. CON.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. It was asked by one of the brothers whether it should be communicated.
body: A certain John of In Christi nomine, of Genoa, acquired certain goods, not from common funds, as appears, but simply in his own right; although a certain instrument had been made for him by his mother, who was the guardian of his other brothers, stating that the said John took nothing from the paternal and common goods; and although afterwards for two years he held the proceeds from the sale of a certain mill, nevertheless he always conducted business in his own name. The question is whether he is bound to share the acquired goods with his brothers?

† Regarding this, it must be said that the aforementioned goods purchased by the said John were acquired for the said John himself and are not to be shared with his brothers or sisters, for several reasons. First, because each person is understood to intend to acquire for himself and his heir, not for his brother; the text is literal. D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. si. This is also proven by D. de probationibus, l. si pactum, and D. de verbis oblig., l. si ita stipulatus, §. grisogonus. The second reason is that there was no certain partnership among these persons; therefore, each conducts business for himself, and not for his brother or sister, as in D. pro socio, l. cum duobus, §. papinianus, also beginning l. si fratres, and C. comm. utriusque iudicii, l. si patruus, and C. de decurionibus, l. licet indivisa, lib. 10. The third reason is the wisely cited law: D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. altero. The fourth reason is that the same reasoning and nature apply to contraries. Hence, just as if he sold, it does not harm his brothers, so if he bought or acquired, it does not benefit another; this is proven by C. de furtis, l. manifestissimi, §. cum in secunda. The fifth reason is that what is acquired through effort is acquired solely for the one who exerts the effort, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. si haeres. From these it appears that the said John, because he conducted the business for himself, acquired it for himself alone, and ought not to share it with others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute, which provides that one is called an assassin who, having received a price or a promise, has killed someone, and likewise one who, having given or promised a price, has caused someone to be killed: how this is to be understood and interpreted.
2. Price properly refers to money counted out.
3. To give signifies the transfer of ownership.
4. How a promise is to be understood.
5. The word "or" partakes of the nature of a conjunction.
6. A confession made against oneself is not believed when it implicates another.
7. A mandate to commit a delict is not presumed unless it is proven.
body: Betonus de Couo, inhabitant of the land of Cadagnano, district of Brescia, consul of the commune, and the men of the said land of Cadagnano, in excuse of themselves and their said commune, notified and denounced that it had come to their ears and knowledge that, when a certain Tempesta went to the courtyard of the habitation of a certain Betinus, in order to tell him that he ought to vacate and clear out the said courtyard for the said Tempesta, and in this matter Matthew of Verona, corporal, Aldrigo de Homis, natural son of Lord John, and Iacopinus, natural son of Lord Iacobinus, behold, the said Betinus, with a pitchfork which he held in his hands, struck and wounded the said Tempesta in the person of the said Tempesta with one wound passing from one side to the other in the chest on the left side, and the aforementioned others with so many wounds, that the said Tempesta died immediately, specifying the wounding parties and the wounds, etc. Who, James of Iseo, in effect, testified concerning the said homicide, adding about two horses sent, etc., as is contained in the records. Afterwards, however, on the same day, he testified how Aldrigo de Homis called the said Iacopinus and secretly told him that he ought to be with the said Vinciguerra and Matthew at the said place in the said courtyard, and that he ought to join and commit with the aforementioned Vinciguerra and Matthew that deed which they wished to commit; because the said Aldrigo would send a horse to meet the said Iacopinus, just as he would send for the aforementioned Vinciguerra and Matthew; and afterwards, when the said business was completed, he would attend to and give to the said Iacopus those things which he promised and wished to give to the aforementioned Vinciguerra and Matthew. Given this order, the deed followed, etc. But it is provided by municipal law that if anyone assassinates, or causes another to be assassinated, he shall be dragged by the tail of a horse to the gallows; and there he shall be hanged, in such a way that the assassin dies; and it is understood that he who, having accepted a price or promise, has caused another to be attacked on his journey, is similarly an assassin; and it is understood that he who, having given a price or made a promise, has caused another to be killed, is an assassin.

† Now it is asked, granted but not conceded, rather entirely denied in the fact, that the said Aldriginus committed and did the aforementioned homicides: whether the assassin ought to be judged or not. And it seems that he ought to be, for the words state that the said Aldriginus would send a horse to meet the said Jacob, just as he would send for the said Vinciguerra and Matthew, for whom it is established that he did send; therefore, something was promised, indeed even executed, for the purpose of committing this homicide, because horses were sent, as in ff. de calumniatori, l. quin etiam. Furthermore, it was promised that he would give to the same Jacob those things which he had promised and wished to give to the said Vinciguerra and Matthew. And thus it was promised to give, and from the conjunction of the words it appears that it was promised to give and to do; therefore, the assassin ought rightly to be judged, as in c. 1. de homicidio, lib. 6. To the contrary is the plain truth by several reasons. First, because to him to whom the words of the law do not apply, neither does the law apply, as in ff. sol. ma., l. si vero, §. de viro. But the words of the statute do not apply nor pertain to our case; therefore, the statute ceases, and I principally take three words.

† For a statute must be referred, properly and strictly, to ready money, as in l. si, C. de praediis curialium, lib. 10. The words of this statute are to be taken in their most proper and strictest sense: because this statute is most penal and most odious, and therefore one must adhere to the proper meaning of the words, as in c. odia, de reg. iur., lib. 6, and there by Dy. according to the word is the word, given.

† but this word signifies the transfer of ownership: for to give is to make for the recipient, as in l. j. C. de fundo dotali; ff. de usuris; l. si stipulatus; ff. de condi. ob causam; l. fi; ff. de verb. ob.; l. ubi autem non apparet, §. fi. But here no ownership was transferred. The third word is the word "promised": where it must be considered that there are four things, one of which is not another, namely: said, pledged, promised, and stipulated. Now, the words which are not said to have been uttered here, which were enunciative words, were not words of promising: for it does not appear that any agreement intervened on this point, as in ff. de pac., l. 1, §. conventionis; and ff. de edil., l. sciendum, §. dictum; and ff. de pollicitationibus, l. 1, where it is clear that what is merely pledged by bare voice is improperly called promised.

† Moreover, that which is certain is said to be promised; namely, that which is uncertain in substance and in kind is not called a promise nor a stipulation, as in C. mand. l. Salarium and D. de verb. oblig. l. triticum. Hence, Lord Frederick of Siena in his consilia holds that he who confesses himself to be a usurer in general confesses nothing. To this effect is what is noted in D. de leg. 1, l. turpia and l. Titiae textores, and where it is said that what is obscure is regarded as void. And this is confirmed by what is read and noted in D. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei and l. in facti, D. de leg. Furthermore, those words, "given" or "promised," are understood thus: namely, promised to be given.

† because the word "or" has the nature of a conjunction, as is noted in l. repetendis, D. de legibus; l. per Bartolus and C. de servis fugitivis; l. si fugitivi; and l. 1, D. de rebus dubiis; and l. j. and l. fi., §. cui dulcia, D. de pignoribus et legatis. Behold, therefore, that in our case there was no price, there was no delivery, there was no promise to give, nor anything else. And if it is said that this person stated he would send the horse, it does not follow that he promised to give the horse; because these words imply a loan for use (commodatum), not a transfer of ownership, as is noted in l. cum quid, D. si certum petatur. Moreover, such sending is usually done by a friend to a friend, as is noted from de simonia, c. et si quaestiones. Furthermore, it must be observed that the words of the statute say "shall have caused someone to be killed": for certainly nothing has been proven that the said Aldriginus caused the killing, because it has not been proven that Vinciguerra and Matthew had a mandate to kill the said Tempesta; nor could they have had a specific mandate. For the fact that the said Tempesta approached the said Curtius was due to chance and fortune; rather, it was due to the fault of Tempesta himself, which the said Aldriginus could not foresee, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Item si putasset. And if he had this in his premeditated mind, because perhaps the said Tempesta had boasted of expelling the said Bethinellus, this mandate could be understood in the case where the said Tempesta could have expelled him legally, and also repelled him with arms: for a mandate that can be exercised according to law and justice should not be understood as involving fraud, as in D. de conditione indebiti, l. si procurator, §. Celsus. It is a most grave crime to assassinate, as is noted by Bartolus in D. de iniuriis, l. non solum, §. si mandato. And therefore it is not included in the mandate unless it is specifically stated. Now, having considered the words of the law, let us consider the words and deeds of the said Aldriginus. It is said that he called Jacopinus and secretly said to him, etc. Thus it appears that this witness is singular, due to this adverb "secretly."

† Moreover, Jacobino should not be believed, because a person confessing against himself is not believed when implicating another, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on confessions, chapter 1, on accusations, law 1. And thus it does not constitute evidence sufficient for torture, because he is a rejected witness. Furthermore, the following words are added, that he himself ought to do and commit what Vinciguerra and Matthew wished to commit. For what intention Vinciguerra and Matthew then had is unknown, as noted in the Digest, on damage inflicted, law "Whoever has good faith," section "If one intending to stipulate." Moreover, those words, that he would give to the said Jacob what Vinciguerra had promised and wished to give, and similarly to Matthew, are of no effect, because they are most uncertain, as noted in the Digest, on legacies, book 1, law "Legacy generally." From all these points, and each one individually, concluding from the first to the last, and also because assassination has not been alleged, it is clear that the said Aldrigo cannot and ought not to be condemned of assassination; because neither do the words of the statute allow it, nor do the words of the said Aldrigo imply it. Furthermore, regarding the secrets of secrets, which are in no way proven, judgment does not pertain to the Court of the Militia, and this is what is said: that the Emperor and the Church judge concerning hidden matters; the heart of man only God knows. Nor does mere mental contemplation suffice in crimes.

† It is certain that a mandate is not presumed unless it is proven, even if the offense is committed by a servant or a friend; the text is found in the Digest, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Cum ad sedem*. And note this through Bartolus in *L. 1, §. Familiae*, D. *De publiciana*. It is also established that assassination is a certain quality; and therefore, unless the mandate is proven, it cannot be proven that the mandator committed assassination, because no quality can be proven where the subject is not proven, as noted in the Digest, *De probationibus*, *L. Si arbiter*, at the end. Furthermore, even here, prior enmity is not proven, from which material for so great a crime would arise; therefore, the intent to commit a delict is not presumed, as noted in the Digest, *Ad legem Corneli de sicariis*, *L. 1*. Moreover, even if the mandate were proven, standing on the defense of a friend, it is presumed to be given with the moderation of blameless protection: because this befits an honest man, as in *L. 1*, C. *Unde vi*; and *L. Ut vim*, D. *De iustitia et iure*; and D. *Ad legem Aquiliam*, *L. Scientiam*, §. *Qui cum aliter*. The confession of Aldrigo, which he later appears to have made, does not obstruct, granted but not conceded, that it was made voluntarily, because it does not include assassination or anything similar, and in this matter one should not argue from analogy. Furthermore, if we were to say that he who sends his mercenaries to his friend for his defense is an assassin, it would follow that all lords of Italy, who send their mercenaries to the aid of other nobles, are assassins, which is absurd to say and contrary to law, as in *C. Domino guerram*, in the title *Hic finit lex*, then the customs of the kingdom begin, column 10, where it is expressly stated. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a false statement of time invalidates a legacy.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain Ioannolus made his nuncupative will, of which a public instrument appears: in which he bequeathed to a certain Marchesio all the right which the testator himself had in certain goods and things lying in the place and territory of Romantini, acquired by the testator from the above-mentioned legatee: as it was said to be established by a public instrument drawn up by the hand of Gulielmus Langnidus on the 1300th day of the month. It is objected that the legacy is not valid because in the year 1300, etc., no acquisition made by the said testator in any things or goods appears.

† It is asked, what is the law: and it seems that the said bequest is not valid, because the thing is not specified, and a false description of time vitiates an uncertain legacy: because the corpus is not established. But the contrary is true: because the things are certain by reference to a certain instrument, as C. de sen. quae sine certa quanti, l. hęc sententia; and ff. de ver. obl., l. ubi autem non apparet, §. qui vero a titio. For when only one purchase appears to have been made, the description is rendered certain, as ff. de libe. et posthu., l. 1 and 2, ad hoc; ff. de fundo inst., l. fundus, qui locatus; and ff. de leg. 3, l. patronus, §. 1. Moreover, this writing of this legacy is not erroneous, but imperfect, as is evident from the space left between the letters and the letters. And this imperfection is not substantial, and therefore it does not vitiate, as ff. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. cum imperfecta. Likewise, ambiguity, which is certified by another, does not have to harm, as C. de test., l. ambiguitates, where is the case; and ff. de leg. 2, l. cum pater, §. vicos; and C. de insti. et sub., l. pe. Likewise, one writing is supplied by another, as ff. de hęred. insti., l. asse toto; and ff. de condi. insti., l. illa substitutio; and ff. de re iud., l. in summa. To the same effect is what we [say] in l. fi., C. de erro. aduoca. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Reservations of rights in the judgment, if any are applicable, do not impede the execution of the judgment.
body: In the name of Christ. Most excellent and honorable Master, since a certain judgment was rendered by me in a dispute between Monium de Reteigno on one side and Beatrisina de la Curte on the other, and in favor of the said marriage; from which judgment an appeal was taken on behalf of the said Beatrisina, alleging nullity; upon which appeal it was pronounced that the first judgment should remain firm and that the said appeal was abandoned, reserving, however, to the said Beatrisina all exceptions and defenses against the said judgment that may be applicable, as appears from the form of the said judgment. Now, execution of the said judgment is sought, but the opposing party objects, claiming that the said judgment is null and void in the same manner as was alleged in the appeal, due to the aforementioned reservation. From these facts, it is asked: what are my duties in executing the said judgment? And regarding this, please transmit your written opinion after first having examined the said judgments and all pleadings in the said case. I, Thomasius de Cumis, licentiate in civil law. Given at Viterbo on the 13th day of September.

I answer that no exceptions are available, nor can they be available: since the sentence has passed into the force of res judicata, execution of the said sentence must be carried out; and the reservation is invalid, because it finds nothing to reserve, and so the statute determines. Moreover, impossible reservations are of no effect, as noted in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Authent. ingressi; and C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. terminato; and ff. de legatis, l. R. si quis ita legauerit. And thus the objection that we note in l. Labeo, ff. de familia erciscunda, does not prevail.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When it is doubtful whether there is one road or several, contrary witnesses cannot be accused of perjury, and when witnesses are to be rejected.
2. If some witnesses say that they saw the water being cleared, and others say that they did not, whether such witnesses are to be called false.
3. When there is doubt about the location of a place, whether the judge may commit the matter to two experts in the art, who shall examine it: and whether their report shall be followed.
4. Whether the judge may resort to torture, so that the truth may be elicited from witnesses.
5. A witness who gave false testimony, which did not benefit the party producing him, whether he may be punished for perjury.
6. A witness who said one thing falsely in one instance, and something else in another, whether he may be punished for perjury.
body: In Christ's name. Certain witnesses testified that a certain road was so destroyed that at certain times it could not be traveled with carts and oxen; others say that it could not be traveled conveniently, but for the greater part they say that it was so spoiled that it could not be traveled with carts and oxen at certain times. The witnesses were accused of falsehood; these witnesses say that at the said time several people went, and they saw many persons going with oxen, and with laden and unladen carts. Likewise, it is doubted whether there is one road or several. Likewise, it is doubted how many witnesses disprove witnesses.

† I respond: if it is doubtful whether there is one road or several, falsehood is not proven, as in extra de testibus, c. cum tu filii, and de fi. insti., c. cum lo. hęre. Likewise, if it is certain that there is only one road, nevertheless these witnesses are not contradictory, because it does not follow that because some went, therefore all, or the greater part, were able to go, as in ff. de verb. ob., l. continuus, §. 1. And what is noted by Iaco. But. in l. 2, C. de erro. aduocatorum, supports this very well, as does Bar. in l. insulam, ff. so. mat., and ff. si cer. pe., l. 2, §. item mutui, and Iaco. But. in l. sed si possessori, §. et si iurauero, ff. de iureiur., and by Bar., ff. de noui ope. num., l. non solum, §. sed vt probari. Likewise, from the fact that it was spoiled, it could not be traveled conveniently, as in ff. quemadm. serui. ami., l. si locus, §. fi., and ff. de reli., l. si quis sepulchra. Likewise, that which cannot be done conveniently is not properly said to be able to be done, as in ff. de uerb. sig., l. nepos proculo. But concerning the number of witnesses, it must be said that one witness is disproved by two, and two by four; four, as noted in inst. de inuti. stip., §. item verborum, and noted in the said c. Io., and C. de fi. inst. by Cy. and others.

† Likewise, certain witnesses said that they saw water overflowing upon a certain vineyard; others, who were neighbors, say that it never overflowed, and that it could never have overflowed without their seeing it. It is asked what the law is: whether those who say they saw it overflow are false. Consider here that the latter depose to a negative, which they strive to prove also by nature and also by the site of the place, because the water could run down through the flat land, and therefore could not descend to the said vineyard.

† And concerning this it is asked, whether the judge can commission two experts in the art to view this, and whether their report should be relied upon? I respond: if witnesses depose negatively in the manner that these have deposed, they do not provide proof, because their statement is somewhat suspect unless it is aided by visual inspection and by the nature of the place, as noted after the gl. or. by Dy. in l. 1, §. 1, ff. de iti. actuque priua. But because they add a natural reason, the judge ought to go to the place with experienced men and subject the matter to their eyes, as in l. si irruptione, §. ad officium, ff. finium reg., and l. semel, C. de re mil., and in Auth. de non alie., §. quod autem, col. 2, C. de admi. tut., in l. lex quae tutores, ff. de offi. procom., l. si in aliquam. But the witnesses could not be re-examined, nor could they clarify anything once dispute has begun concerning the testimonies, as noted in Auth. de testi., §. quia vero; they could, however, clarify words if the fitness or uncertainty of the words permitted it, as noted by Inno., extra de test., c. cum clamor, provided that they work no prejudice to either party, as in ff. de prob., c. in praesentia, and exr de accu., c. cum dilecti, although they might be effective for excusing falsehood; and in doubt, favor ought to be shown to affirming witnesses rather than to denying ones, as noted in ff. de arbi., l. diem proferre, §. si plures.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether in the aforementioned cases recourse may be had to torture in order that the truth may be found? I respond: this is sufficiently discretionary, because you are better able to know, as in ff. de testibus, l. 3, §. tu magis, and C. de falsis, l. ubi, ff. de quaestionibus, l. quęstionis modum, and l. edic. diui. Nevertheless, the judge may well abstain from torture where some natural reason can excuse the witness; and the confession of a witness ought to accord with natural facts, as in ff. de interro. act., l. confessionibus.

† Likewise, it is asked whether, if a witness has deposed something false that helps the party producing him, he can be punished for falsehood. I respond: yes, if it is relevant to the cause, as in ff. de falsis, l. si quis legatum, provided it is not void from a defect of form, as noted in l. 1, C. de sepul. vio., and Bar. in the said l. si quis legatum.

† Lastly, it is asked, if a witness in one instance said one thing and in another instance another, whether he can be punished for falsehood? I respond: yes, as in ff. de testi., l. qui falsa, vel varia; and he is presumed to have spoken falsely in the second testimony as if suborned, as in Auth. de test., §. qui vero; and even if it should not be apparent, it follows of necessity that he is false in the first statement or the second, although it is not established in which of them, as noted in ff. de iureiu., l. duobus, §. fi. Yet on account of that doubt he does not escape a penalty to be imposed at the discretion of the judge, because he offended the ears of the judge, as noted in C. de tes., l. nullum; what is noted in l. 2, C. de spor. supports this; and he shall be punished by the second judge whose ears he offended, ff. de falsis, l. eos. And although the acts in one case do not establish proof in another among different persons, as noted in C. de eden., l. 2, nevertheless they establish proof against the testifying witness himself, as noted by Inno., extra de testi., c. ueniens; and in different instances this, as a vacillation, is punished by an arbitrary penalty and under the ius commune from the mere office of the judge, rather than by a statutory judicial penalty, as in C. de testi., l. nullum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the defendant is to be condemned in costs, and when not, and when the judge condemning a party in costs is to be punished. Number 2.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The statute, which states that the victor is to be condemned in costs in those cases in which he ought to be condemned according to law, even if he has a just cause for litigating, appears to contradict itself: for if he has a just cause for litigating, therefore he ought not to be condemned in costs: the laws are well known. Solution: this statute is not self-contradictory, because although the rule is that the victor is not condemned in costs if he has a just cause for litigating, nevertheless sometimes, even if he has a just cause for litigating, he ought to be condemned, as is fully noted in the Speculum de expensis, §. nunc uidendum restat, through the whole of that title, §. si ante litem, ver. sunt autem. This statute therefore regards both cases jointly, not disjunctively. Where, therefore, costs are to be reimbursed according to law, let them be reimbursed; where, however, they are not, let them not be.

But let us see: the defendant obtained the first judgment in his favor, the second against him, in which he was condemned to pay costs; the third in his favor. The judge who condemned him to pay costs is sued, on the ground that he made the litigation his own, because he ought not to have condemned him; and to prove this, the first and third judgments are produced. I say that these judgments do not prejudice him, because a matter acted upon between others does not prejudice another; but recourse should have been had to the records.
