For if it appears from the records of the second case that he ought not to have condemned him, he made the litigation his own. But if he ought to have condemned him, or if it is doubtful whether he ought to have condemned him or not, he did not make the litigation his own, because only then does he make the litigation his own if the judge sat [in error]; otherwise not. This is noted in the Authentica de iudicibus, § oportet, column 6. The decree of the Lord does not contradict this, because it refers to the law, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How much bare ownership is valued: and how much a perpetual emphyteusis.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked, how bare ownership should be valued, and how perpetual emphyteusis? I answer that bare ownership should be valued at what emphyteutae would commonly purchase the bare ownership for, who could be examined on this point: nor is this testimony singular, but common to many emphyteutae, as noted by Cynus in the sole law, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo, quod interest, at the end. Emphyteusis, however, will be valued at what it could commonly be sold for: which is easy to know, and especially through public auctions: because a thing is worth only what it can be sold for, its condition being known, as fully read and noted in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione. Some, however, make this estimation in a rustic manner, namely, that bare ownership is worth one-third. But this method is in no way approved: the first method, however, is juridical. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Six things are required to validate a contract.
2. That which pertains solely to the Prince is deemed impossible.
3. A deposit made for a dishonorable purpose to be carried out is not valid: and it must be restored to the depositor.
4. The subsequent wording.
body: In the name of Christ.

There are six elements that constitute a solid contract: namely, the creditor, the debtor, the subject matter, the cause, the existence of the condition, and the fulfillment of the mode, or of the final cause. For the creditor and the debtor are correlative terms, and one cannot exist without the other, as stated in l. 1, D. si certum petatur. The subject matter must be such that it can be the object of a stipulation; it cannot be sacred property, a free person, or anything else excluded from commerce, as stated in D. de verbis oblig., l. inter stipulantem, §. sacram. The cause must be possible, as stated in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non solum; and it must be honest and reasonable, as stated in D. de exceptione doli, l. 2, §. circa; and it must be a final cause, not merely perfunctory or impulsive, as stated in D. de donationibus, l. 2, §. fi. Furthermore, it must not be dishonest, as stated in D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. si ob maleficium; D. de verbis obligationibus, l. si plagii; D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. fi; D. de conditione ob turpem causam, l. 1, together with the following laws. The existence of the condition is required, because otherwise the obligation does not arise if the condition fails; this occurs whether the condition is contradicted by facts or it is certain in law that it cannot exist, as stated in D. de verbis significationibus, l. cedere diem; D. si certum petatur, l. proinde. The mode must be fulfilled, as stated in D. de locato conducto, l. quaero, §. inter locatores; C. de transactionibus, l. cum mota and l. siue apud acta; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quibus diebus, §. fi; D. de legatis tertio, l. si tibi.

I say, however, that the contract in question lacks all these elements. First, with regard to the creditor and the debtor, because no one contracted or stipulated in the name of A., as stated in Inst. de verbis obligationibus, §. alteri; and see the note in l. 1, D. de pactis non obligatoriis; l. Publia, in principio, D. de deposito. For there, the right of repentance of the depositor applies; but if he does not repent, then the principle applies, as noted by the gloss in l. si pecuniam, in principio, in the major gloss, D. de conditione ob causam. For this was not a deposit made by the consent of both parties, as discussed in D. de dolo, l. sed oleum. Rather, it was made by the consent of the depositor alone, which can be revoked while the matter remains intact, even if it was made for the purpose of giving to another. The text is explicit: C. de usuris, l. acceptam, in fine.

Moreover, when something is to be performed on both sides, if it does not appear who has performed, the innominate contract is not binding, as stated in D. pro socio, l. si Margarita. This does not contradict the note in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. si quis ante, where it is said that there is no innominate contract unless this is the intent; for that statement is true when the act naturally falls under a nominate contract. And it supports what is noted by Jacobus de Arena in l. 1, C. de iure emphyteutico. But in innominate contracts that tend to create an obligation, the right of repentance applies, even if the other party offers to perform and nothing prevents them from doing so, as noted in D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. 1. Although the rule is different when the contract tends to release from an obligation, as stated in D. de pactis, l. si cum fundum. And although the contract has been performed in some respect, if not in that which is more principal to the contract, the right of repentance applies, as stated in the aforementioned l. si pecunia, D. de conditione ob causam, under the words "sed cum liceat."

And so it is in our case, because the withdrawal is a preamble to the intended end, namely, the acquisition of ownership; but this end is impossible. Hence, once the opportunity to acquire ownership is removed, it is futile to discuss the preambles. I have said that the existence of the condition is required; and a major foundation must be laid on this point, because the words state that possession, ownership, and lordship will be accepted. But this is impossible, because ownership cannot be acquired without the command of the Emperor, as stated in c. 1, de notis feudorum, col. 10; and in c. 1, de pace constantiae, col. 11. Indeed, high jurisdiction is not in the commerce of private individuals.

† because that which pertains to the Prince alone is considered impossible, as in D. de legibus 1, l. apud Iulianum, §. si. Or, if we wish to speak otherwise, we can say thus, that the said contract contains within itself this tacit condition, if it shall please the Emperor: because in every contract which touches the right of empire, the power of the Emperor is always understood to be reserved, as in c. si, de prohibitione alienationis feudi, by Fedine. But the Emperor prohibited this, after it came to his knowledge; therefore, the condition tacitly fails. Moreover, the Emperor, by prohibiting anyone from acquiring, is understood to prohibit the other party from transferring, as is singularly proven in l. 1, C. de cupressis ex lucris damnis, lib. 11. Since, therefore, the prohibition supervened in the person of the one who ought to transfer, he cannot fulfill the contract on his part, because he is perpetually prohibited. And a supervening case before delivery harms the possessor, as in D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. necessario. Therefore, since he is impeded by the act of Caesar, he cannot bring an action, because he cannot transfer. Furthermore, a promise is understood to be made with things being thus: but not when the prohibition of a superior intervenes, as in D. de conditione ob causam, l. quod servus; D. de lege commissaria, l. mulier fundos.

From all of the above, each and every one, it appears clearly that the said deposit must be returned to the depositor; and furthermore, in confirmation of the foregoing, it is added that the final cause is lacking, as stated in the Digest, *De conditione indebiti*, law *Damus*. And this conclusion is most certain and true. Moreover, I note that I weigh those words: "accepted possession, dominion, and lordship by virtue of the said agreements"; I weigh this word, "by virtue." But this is impossible, unless the common council of Genoa does this with certain knowledge; for what is done by fact is not truly done by virtue of agreements, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Praeterea*. The said agreements have no force; therefore, those words "concluded," etc., create a condition which cannot exist. Nor can the same instrument be made, as in the cited chapter *Imperiale*, *De prohibita alienatione feudorum*, and in the Authenticum *De non alienando*, section *Quia vero Leonis*. I, Baldus.

In the name of Christ. The words state that, should the ambassadors withdraw in discord, and subsequently it should happen that A. withdraws and is replaced, and G. is placed in his stead, the said withdrawing person from the Signoria ought to have fifty from a certain deposit. Now, a condition existed regarding the first withdrawal of the ambassadors; regarding the second, not yet, but he is in possession of the Signoria, as before; nor has anything been notified to the citizens concerning his intention. It is asked whether the said deposit ought to be returned to the depositor? And it must be said that yes: because it is not true that he subsequently withdrew from the Signoria.

† For the term “subsequently” immediately or forthwith signifies, as argued from the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Haec conditio*, § *Si capitulum*. For he who retains possession is not presumed to have the intent to transfer it, but rather the intent to continue holding it, as in the Code, *De probationibus*, law *Sive possidetis*; and in the Digest, *Quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur*, law *Sicut*, § *Supervacuum*; and in the Decretals, *De renuntiationibus*, chapter *G.*, through this. Thus, therefore, four things are necessary: namely, to cede or withdraw, to substitute, and to notify. And I do not believe this to be necessary, because perhaps he could not do this without danger to his life. Nevertheless, it must be done in some manner such that it is valid in law, as noted in the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Huiusmodi*, in the beginning; and in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Quidam cum filium*; and that these things be done within a short time, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si ita quis*, § *Ea lege*; and in the Decretals, *De electione*, chapter *Si alicuius*. Moreover, this pact is not lawful, but rather is punished by the Julian Law on Extortion, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Iuliam de repetundis*, law *Eadem*, I, § *Lex Iulia*, where the gloss says that he who receives money to bribe in the Council of Bologna is bound by this law. And in this case, the wrongdoing is proven by the instrument, and for a shameful gain there is no action, as in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Si aere*, § *Id quod vulgo*; Digest, *Fa.*, *De hereditatibus*, law *Caeterae*; Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Nec quicquam*. From which, concluding from the first to the last, it is clear that the said deposit, as having been made without cause, ought to be restored to the depositor, to whom the exception of turpitude does not hinder, because it does not hinder the owner of the thing, to whom the vindication of the thing belongs; and the deposit remains in the ownership and possession of the depositor. Hence, considering that he is the possessor thereof, the condition of the possessor is stronger, as in the Digest, *Communi*, law *Si ita ut si fur*; and noted in law *Nam et si fur*, Digest, *Si certum petatur*. And the conclusion is most certain and true. And it supports the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, law *Qui sine usuris*, where it says that they ought to provide entire, certain faith, and assist in all profit. And for this reason the gloss elsewhere attacks the prefect of the district. That also which is certainly to be considered in this second head of the deposit is that, on account of the continuation of contracts, the same final motive is understood to exist; because those things which are ordered to an end are regulated according to the nature of the end, as in the Digest, *De sponsalibus*, law *Oratio*. And therefore this second head is tainted and wounded by the first head; because those things said in prior matters are believed to continue in posterior ones, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Titia*, § *Idem respondit*; Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Cum tactum*; Digest, *De pactis*, law *Item quia*, § *Idem Iuliano*; and in the Decretals, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Secundo requiris*. And therefore, since it appears that he who wishes to profit from the deposit by a detestable profit is improper, and thus the exception of fraud perpetually hinders him, the deposit ought rightly to be restored to the depositor for the reasons and causes expressed above. For law cannot be acquired for another from a contract which is informed by illicit pacts, even if an oath had been interposed, as in the Decretals, *De foro competenti*, chapter *Si diligenti*, § *Ultimo*; Code, *De legibus et constitutionibus*, law *Non dubium*; Code, *De agris et censibus*, law *Quemadmodum*, book 11; Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Si quis inquilinos*, § *Ultimo*. Moreover, it is to be known that in this article of law, in which the time of the Signoria is consumed by the course, as that decretal says, the notable rule in the Decretals, *De iudicibus*, chapter *Si*, does not have place in the purification of delay. Moreover, ratification after the fact does not reconcile, as in law *Si*, § 1, Digest, *Rem ramm haberi*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A witness who testifies outside the chapter, provided that he tells a falsehood, by what penalty is he punished; and what is required in a witness.
2. Purge of delay is not admitted where there is a fixed day and a penalty.
3. The word "ut" signifies the final cause.
body: In the name of Christ. When a certain penalty was sought from a promisor of an act, who had promised to perform a certain work within a fixed time, and he claimed that he had completed the work within the time, and produced a certain witness named A. to prove this, the latter, in testifying, said that the promisor had caused the promised work to be completed, yet he did not clearly remember whether it was within the term; but he stated that, even if it had not been within the term, it had been completed and consummated shortly thereafter. He is accused of perjury, and it is proven that the work was neither completed before nor after.

It is asked by what penalty this false witness ought to be punished, presupposing that in the place of judgment there is a certain municipal decree of the lord, which provides that whoever shall give false testimony so that someone may be condemned or absolved in a criminal or civil case, shall be punished with the penalty of the tongue. And by another municipal statute it is provided that if anyone commits falsehood otherwise than as is provided by the municipal law, he shall be punished in money or in person at the discretion of the authority. And it seems that this man ought to be punished with the penalty of the tongue, because he spoke falsehood in either disjunctive part; and thus he is necessarily false, because this statement, "that or that," is necessarily false if neither this nor that is the case, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. si is, cui ducenta, § cum ita, and § vtrum.

To the contrary, it seems to me that truth is given: for whenever a written instrument has two parts, we must distinguish it by those parts, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haec scriptura; and D. de arbitris, l. Celsus, § idem ait; and Ex de dolo et contumacia, c. dilecti; and D. de legibus, l. quidam testamento in principio; and C. quoniam dies legati cedunt, l. ex verbis. Now, let us take the individual parts of this testimony: first, the part concerning the work completed within the term; and in this regard the witness is not false, because he does not wish to testify upon this point; he testifies nothing of a certain sense of the body, nor by memory, which is required in a witness. For, as the text elegantly states in D. de furtis, l. quidam tabularum, presence is required in a witness, behold the sense, and memory, behold recollection. Hence, if a witness says that he does not remember, or does not remember well, he therefore does not speak falsely, because he does not testify falsely, nor does he wish to testify falsely. And this applies to that particular part which refers to the act done at the proper time.

There follows another part, which speaks of the act done after the term; where two things are to be considered. The first is that when time is of the substance of the action or defense, the act must be proven to have occurred at the proper time, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. eum actum; C. de probationibus, l. matrem tuam; C. de petitione hereditatis, l. si post motam; and fully noted by Bartolus in D. de novo operis nuntiatione, l. solum, § sed ut probari; and c. ultimo de rescriptis, Clementinae. Secondly, it is to be considered that this witness does not testify falsely in the case; because the case is founded upon the term, not upon what is outside the term, as in D. de fideicommissis, liber, l. Thais ancilla, § intra. The case upon which he was testifying was a case of penalty:

And because there was a fixed day and a penalty, purification of delay was not admitted, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. magnam; and ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Traiectitiae, § de illo. Although the jurists of the chair sometimes hold the contrary opinion, nevertheless in practice we must observe the opinion always approved and that of the transmontane jurists; otherwise the expression of the term would effect nothing, which is false, as in l. 1, ff. de poena legis, omnis. He who appends an express term binds himself to it; for the equity of the praetor does not avail, except in praetorian stipulations, as in ff. si quis cautionem, l. et si post tres. Therefore, this being premised as evidently true, it follows of necessity that the witness testified outside the article and outside the cause; and consequently it follows that he testified without having sworn, and without the cause being joined, regarding that on which he testifies. Wherefore this is not properly testimony, but certain enunciative words. And in a witness, falsehood is the same as perjury, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. presbyter. Hence, concluding from the first to the last, the words of the decree do not apply here, because he did not testify in the cause. Moreover, because he did not testify so that someone might be condemned or absolved.

And the word "ut," insofar as it signifies the final cause, is evident in all four innominate contracts, as appears in D. de praescriptis verbis, l. naturalis; and in the case of witnesses, as in D. de adimendis legatis, l. alumnae, §. seya. And this is true when it is appended with the force of a cause apt to produce its effect; otherwise it would be an impulsive cause, as in D. de donationibus, l. 2, §. si; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. generaliter. But sometimes it is placed with the force of a similitude, and this does not serve the purpose at hand, as in D. de legatis 2, l. ut hæredibus. Moreover, this testimony is evidently defective in form according to the records, and in offenses which require a certain form, the omission of the form at least diminishes the offense, as in D. de furtis, l. si is qui, §. si tu Titium, unless the law expressly extends further, as in C. de furtis, l. si quis servo. The statement of Bartolus in l. si quis leg. does not obstruct this, where he says that a witness is not excused, even though his statement does not favor the party, as in a testament in which a son is passed over or wholly disinherited: for that testament is not wholly null, since it can be confirmed, as in l. filio præterito, with the related material. It therefore appears that the witness cannot be punished by the penalty of the tongue, but by an extraordinary penalty at the discretion of the authority. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that no one shall grant credit to soldiers, otherwise they shall not be able to demand payment from them; and that a proclamation concerning this matter shall be made every month, if for one month such proclamation is omitted, the Captain shall be liable only for debts incurred during that same month.
body: In the name of Christ. The Magnificent Lord Mala testa of Mala testis, General Captain of the armed forces of the commune of Bologna, had in his brigade a certain Spanish soldier, who contracted certain debts with individual citizens of the City of Bologna: and then, having not paid the said debts, he departed secretly; but before his departure, the aforementioned Lord Captain had proclamations and public cries made each month, according to the tenor of the statutes and agreements: except that for the month of July last past, no proclamation appears in writing, and this because the official, who was required to have the proclamations made, when requested, refused to have them made.

† It is asked, what is the law: the words of the lease are such that if he caused a proclamation to be made through the city of Bologna, no one ought to lend or make credits to anyone from his Brigade without the license of the said person, then he is not bound for those of the Brigade: of whose commission of the proclamation, or report, there appears writing, etc. Also, if the said Captain sent and caused proclamations and cries to be made every month, of which it is established with the officials of the lease, retentions cannot be made at the instance of anyone, etc., as is more seriously contained in the statutes and pacts. To which question I answer that the said Magnificent one is not bound, except for that month in which the cry does not appear, and not for other months in which the statute and pact have been observed, and this by l. si sterilis. §. fi. ff. de act. empt. notwithstanding those words, every month: because for this, that he be bound in nothing, it is required that every month, but for this, that he be not bound, except proportionally for the time of delay, particular diligence from the excuse of that time suffices, as ff. quorum leg. l. si duae res. and ff. de his, quibs vt indig. l. rescriptum. and l. in singulis. ff. ad l. Fal. and in l. vlti. ff. de eo, quod cer. loco. and ff. de pig. act. l. si necessarias. §. si annua. and ff. de penu lega. l. 1. in fi. and ff. de reb. dub. l. si is, qui ducenta. §. cum ita, because in those laws cumulative diligence and observance of all clauses and times were required. And it makes. ff. si cer. pe. l. lecta. But here it must be noted: because it must be established that the said debts were contracted in that month in which the cry was not made, because that month only is under obligation, as ff. de neg. gest. l. eum actum. From which month the said Magnificent one is not excused, although he committed to another, as ff. mandati. l. idemque. §. si tutores. But from other months he is immune, as ff. nau. cau. stabu. l. fi. §. item si praedixerit. and ff. de institoria. l. sed et si pupillus. §. proscribere. From these it appears that when the said debts are produced so that the said fugitive may be detained in prison, it is required that before the power of Bologna by commission of the Illustrious and Serene Prince, Lord Duke of Milan, or his officials, the Potestans of Bologna transmit writings proving: signs also themselves with the writings of merchants, which writings make faith in Bologna at least half-full, as no. ff. de iureiu. l. admonendi. and in Aut. de exhib. reis. § etiam quidam officiales. And whoever did not want to make cries be made, undoubtedly is bound to the said Magnificent one, as C. de magistrati. conueniendis. l. fi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman of full age may make an augmentation of dowry in immovable property.
2. Whether a gift may be made by a sister to a sister.
3. Whether feudal goods may be given in dowry for another.
4. Whether law 2, Codex, de rescindenda venditione, has application in a contract of hire.
body: In the name of Christ. It is asked whether an adult woman may make an augmentation of dowry in immovable property without a judicial decree: and it seems that she may not, by the general rule, which provides that the immovable property of adults may not be alienated without a judicial decree, as in l. 1, D. de reb. eorum, with its entire subject matter. For alienation is every act by which ownership is transferred, as in l. 1, C. de fundo dotali. Moreover, it is expressly stated in l. lex quae tutores, in princ., C. de admi. tut., where it says, or to give in dowry, as in D. de iure dotium, l. siue generalis, in fine. To the contrary it seems, because the cause of dowry is considered accepted, not only when an adult woman gives a dowry for herself, but also if an adult brother gives a dowry for her, born of the same father, as noted in C. de admini. tu., l. non omni, and D. de amit. tu., l. cum plures, §. in primis. This opinion seems to be approved by the ordinary gloss in C. de praediis mino., l. prędia, and it is supported by D. de tutel. et rationibus distrahendis, l. 1, §. sed nonnullos. The solution: the first part is true, because a decree is required; for if a minor cannot expressly bind property without a decree, much less can he alienate ownership, as noted in l. vl., C. de legi. tute. But in this matter others say the contrary: since this mortgage is legal and necessary. However, the constitution of a dowry is not legal and necessary, but voluntary; therefore, considering the reason of the law, it cannot be done without a decree. There is also another reason, because knowledge of the cause is required, as in D. de minoribus, l. si ex causae, §. dotis, whether the means are sufficient, and whether the husband is worthy of such a large dowry. And this knowledge of the cause pertains to the judge, as in l. magis puto, §. ne tamen, D. de rebus eorum. And it is supported by what is noted in l. 1, C. si aduersus dotem. The gloss in the aforementioned l. predia does not stand in the way, because those who cite it do not have the meaning of that gloss; for that gloss permits a donation propter nuptias with a decree, not a simple donation, even if made by spousal largess; because a decree cannot be interposed over the donation of a minor’s property, as in C. si maior factus sine decreto, l. fi, §. cum autem.
† Moreover, he cannot make a donation to his sister when they are adults, because in this case to provide a dowry is to make a donation, as stated in the Codex, Title "On Donations," Law "If."

† Moreover, feudal goods cannot be given in dowry for another than for oneself; nor is the alienation strengthened by any passage of time, as in c. 1, *de prohibita alienatione feudi* by Frederick. Nor does the ratification of the vassal hold, because consent is prohibited. That it is a fief appears from the privilege of Conrad, which has the power to renew and to supersede the privilege of the preceding Emperor, as in D. *de acquisitione possessionis*, l. *si quis ante*. And therefore I conclude from the aforementioned reasons that the said augmentation of dowry could not have been made: and this is true as regards the validity of the alienation. However, he is liable for eviction or for damages, if the contract was concluded with an ignorant party, as in D. *de contrahenda emptione*, l. *et liberi hominis*. Otherwise, if with a knowing party, as noted in C. *familiae herciscundae*, l. *si cum familia*.

† Finally, it is doubted whether law 2, Codex, *de rescindenda venditione*, applies when someone is deceived, that is, by error exceeding half the just price; and it must be said that it does, because law 2, Codex, *de rescindenda venditione*, applies to all contracts of good faith. Codex, *de locato*, law *si olei*; Codex, *de communibus utriusque iudicii*, law *maioribus*; Codex, *quibus ex causis maiores*; law *in contractibus*, Digest, *de verbis obligatorum*; law *si quis cum aliter*. And I confirm the beautiful arguments made above by the excellent doctor Raphael Fulgosius, my colleague and friend. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter, to whom only a dowry has been left by her father, is said to be passed over: and whether she has the right of accretion.
2. Whether a substitute instituted in such a way that he may enjoy the property for the entire period is a substitute in ownership, or in usufruct.
3. Whether she herself is bound to deliver the deed to the heir requesting the deed offered by the said daughter for the said legacy.
body: ...ed for a dowry, not...ed for a dowry, not

† Although it was left to the daughter for a dowry, nevertheless she is not thereby instituted heir, nor does she have the right of accrual if the instituted heir renounces, on the argument of ff. de iure dotium. l. mulier bona. and ff. de haere. insti. l. qui nolebat. C. de haere. insti. l. quotiens. And thus the daughter is understood to be omitted; nor is the will valid by the strictness of the civil law. And this as to the first point.

† Secondly it is asked, when a daughter was substituted to a male under this form: that she should succeed in such a manner that during the entire time of the life of the daughter herself she ought to enjoy the said goods, and once the said daughter is dead the aforesaid goods ought to devolve upon the brother, save that the said daughter may make a will concerning the fruits of the interim: now it is asked, whether the said daughter was substituted in the usufruct alone, or in the ownership? And it must be said that as long as she lives, she is the owner and mistress, as in ff. de dona. l. in concubinam. §. species. and there literally by Iaco. de Aret. Thirdly,

† it is asked whether the heir of the said daughter is bound to restore possession without a libel, when he asks that a libel be offered to him: and it must be said that he is not, even if the edict of the divine Hadrian is brought. For even in that edict a libel must be offered to the holder, nor is he bound to justify his possession before a libel has been offered: because it would be proceeding preposterously, as in C. de edicto diui Adria. l. fi. §. 1. This is expressly held by Innocen. and all the doctors in extra de libel. obla. c. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a procurator may confess that his principal incurs the penalty for perjury on account of the oath taken by him: and whether he appears to have a mandate from his principal that contains injustice and fraud: and when he appears to have a sufficient mandate: and a protestation does not harm those who protest.
body:
In the name of Christ. The decree of the Lord provides that whenever anyone, claiming to be a creditor and to have a right by reason of some credit over certain goods seized in the name of the aforementioned Lord’s chamber, appears in respect of his rights: that such appearing person, proving his rights in his appearance, and in the production and exhibition of his rights, is bound to swear personally, or through a procurator having a special and singular mandate to swear, namely, that in truth he did not make, nor does he make, such appearance, production, and exhibition of rights out of malice or fraud; but believing with certainty to satisfy justice, and that the instruments and rights mentioned in that appearance, and in the written submission and production, are true and not simulated or fictitious; and that such appearing person is the true creditor on account thereof, in whole or in part: he may also swear for a part. And if he wishes to swear for a part, he is bound to clearly specify and declare that part. And it adds, saying furthermore, that if anyone knowingly swears falsely or untruthfully on the occasion of the aforementioned matters, or any of them, that for such perjury he shall fall, and be understood to have fallen, from every right which he had or claimed to have in the goods on account of which he appeared, as above. Moreover, by the law itself and by fact, and without other process, he incurs the penalty of four times the value or estimation of those goods, or of the part which he seemed to defend unduly; the half of whose penalty goes to the chamber, and the other half to the accuser or notifier of the aforementioned matters. And he is also to be reputed always and everywhere a perjurer and forger.

Now, certain merchants appointed as their procurator a certain J., and specially for appearing in the procuratorial name of the said merchants before the masters of the intrate of the said Lord, and for giving in writing and exhibiting before them any instruments and rights competent to the said constituents against a certain confiscated person and his goods seized in the name of the said chamber; and for stating and protesting that those goods belong to and pertain to the said constituents by virtue of their rights; and that they have stronger rights therein than the aforementioned chamber of the Lord; and for swearing upon the souls of their constituents that they do not make the said appearance, written submission, and exhibition in fraud or out of malice, but with the intention of preserving their right. And in all things and in every respect, and word for word, according to the form of the decrees of the aforementioned Lord, they ought and are bound to swear; and to perform any other necessary oath on account of the aforementioned matters. And it should be noted that they do not specify in the said procuratorial instrument what quality the instruments ought to have, nor which instrument they ought to produce; but they delivered to the said procurator a certain instrument for 1300 florins, in which appears the obligation of the confiscated person against the said appearing parties; which quantity was not truly due in full, but only in part, which procurator swore according to the form of the decree. From which it is objected to the said merchants that they committed mendacity and falsity. It is asked, what is the law?

And it seems indubitable that the said merchants are liable to punishment, at least by the penalty of quadruple damages, as contained in the decree of the Lord. And this for three reasons. The first is that, after a reasonable delay had been granted for deliberation, they appointed a procurator and handed over the instrument to him; this handing over of the instrument has the force of a singular mandate, as in C. de pac. conuen. l. si. For he who hands over an instrument to a procurator seems to instruct him, or render him instructed, to produce the instrument and use it. Nor is it for the procurator to distinguish, because in another’s affair he has no other certainty of the truth, as in ff. de iniuriis. l. sed si vnus. §. procuratore. And see ff. de leg. 1. l. seruum filii. §. eum qui chirographum. And what is noted by Guillaume de Cuyac in ff. de pac. l. postquam. And it is noted that, without preceding deliberation, it is done with certain knowledge, as in ff. de iureiu. l. iusiurandum. et ad pecunias. And not in de diuortiis. c. ex literis.

The second reason is presumed from the words of the mandate there, when it is said, “and in all things, and in every way, and word for word,” as according to the form of the decrees of the said Lord they ought and are bound to swear. For these words seem individually specified, as contained in the decree of the Lord, as in C. de sententiis, quam sine certa quantitate. l. hęc scientia. And ff. de re iudi. l. in summa. C. de pręscrip. 30. an. l. omnes. ff. de ver. obl. l. vbi autem non apparet. §. si id, quod a seyo. ff. de hęre. instituen. l. asse roto.

Moreover, in the crime of falsehood, one proceeds from indications to inquire into the truth, as in C. de falsis. l. vbi. But this is a crime of falsehood, says the decree; therefore, at least by way of torture, the truth ought to be inquired into from the said merchants, namely, whether they acted with malice and whether they acted with fraud in having the aforementioned things done. For certainly in a creditor who claims a debt paid to him, fraud is presumed, as in ff. mandati. l. si fideiussor. §. in omnibus. It is presumed that he holds the memory of what he did, as in C. de contrah. et com. stipu. l. magnam.

Moreover, if they were not in fraud, they were in gross negligence, because they ought to have informed the procurator and sent him instructed to the case, so that he might know that he acts in the name of the procurator, as in l. 1. §. 1. ff. de edendo. Moreover, if notice of what the procurator did came to them, they ought to have immediately contradicted it, as in ff. de adulteriis. l. si adulterium cum incestu. C. de incest. nup. l. cum ancillis. And noted in l. 2. C. de erogatione militaris annonae. lib. 12. Otherwise, they seem to have ratified it, as noted in l. qui. n. §. 1. rem ratam haberi.

But notwithstanding these things, it seems to me, saving the substance of the truth, that the said merchants did not fall under the decree of the Lord: and this first by general rules. For the rule is that a procurator cannot cause the principal to incur a penalty unless he has a special mandate, or the principal, having been informed thereof, ratifies it. This is the text in ff. quod quisque iuris in alterum statu. eo. lib. 3. §. si procurator. Moreover, one does not seem to have a mandate to commit falsehood, or quasi-falsehood, as in ff. de falsis. l. diuus. §. nec generalem. Also, a mandate does not seem to exist unless it is something that can be mandated by law, as in ff. de condi. inde. l. si procurator. §. celsu. Also, the law is express to the letter that that which one does in fraud is not seen as mandated; rather, it seems prohibited, as in l. si pater. ff. quae in frau. cre.

Moreover, this procurator did not have a sufficient mandate according to the form of the decree: for it must be considered that sometimes a mandate is general, sometimes special, sometimes singular: and that which is singular is that which is issued singularly, i.e., which excludes all plurality from itself, as in c. 1. de noua forma fidelitatis. colla. 10. Hence, whenever a mandate is equivocal, which can be interpreted in many ways, that mandate is not singular. Hence, it is necessary that in a singular mandate the cause, the person, the quantity, and all things that demonstrate the quality of the future litigation to the letter be expressed, as noted by Guillaume de Cuyac in ff. si quis caut. l. sed et si quis. §. quaesitum. And in c. vt citra. de elec. li. 6. in the word, omnia et singula. On which word the Archdeacon says, i.e., singularly and specially specified with all the circumstances of each, as in c. const. de elec. in cle. The same is said by Paulus de Leaza. But this mandate was not singular, because singular mention was not made of the production of the instrument in question, nor of when it was executed, nor of the quantity.

Furthermore, a procurator is called one who does nothing from his own mind, but from the mind of the principal alone, as in ff. de manu. vindicta. l. pater nec prouincia. Nor do those words “and in all things, and in every way, etc.” stand in the way, because this captious formula and artfully composed words are broken by the interpretation of the decree, as in ff. de transa. l. cum aquilia. Moreover, in the mandate are placed juridical words, there, “instruments, and rights”: and therefore it does not seem a mandate that commits lying and fraud, nor would such a procurator have accepted, nor did he accept, a mandate pertaining to injury to the Camera, as in ff. de re milit. l. non omnes. §. a barbaris.

Moreover, this appearance was made not for the end of obtaining something, but for the preservation of a certain protestation of their right: and for this alone, so that silence would not harm the said merchants; which protestation does not harm those who protest, as appears there, when it says “with the mind of preserving their right.” as in ff. de procurato. l. per procuratorem non semper. And ff. de religiosis. l. Sed et si quis. §. plerunque non semper.

Moreover, there is no doubt that the procurator acted in good faith; otherwise he would not have acted. He was led by the writing, which writing has the beginning of truth, as in ff. de interro. act. l. de aetate. §. ex causa. So that here there was no malice, nor fraud, but good faith, which does not deserve punishment, as in ff. depositi. l. bona fides. And ff. de condi. et demons. l. quamuis. Moreover, this is expressed in the words of the decree, there it says: “If anyone knowingly swore falsely, or not truly”: but here there is no knowledge, nor fraud, as in C. de falsis. l. nec exemplum. And l. 1. in fi. ff. de abigeis. And l. illud. ff. de liberali causa.

From all of which it is concluded that one must adhere to the truth without incurring any penalty, as in ff. de iure dotium. l. siue generalis. And what is noted in Auth. de iudicibus. §. oportet. colum. 6. And l. filii. ff. pro suo. And this I say, subject to the correction of experts and the fiscal advocate, to whose corrections I submit.

Someone might say, by all means, the said Thomasius, one of the said principals, is not excused, who appeared before the said masters in his own name and in the name of his brothers and nephews, saying that he had hypothecated and obligated the said goods for the quantity of one thousand gold florins by instruments drawn up in the City of Venice or Ancona, which he lacked. And it is asked, because he could not produce them in so short a time due to the distance of the journey, why he asked for a reasonable delay to be granted to him, within which he could produce the said instruments: and he adds, swearing moreover in his own and the said names, that he does not make this appearance in fraud, nor with malice, but for the cause of preserving his right: and in all things, and in every way, and word for word, as according to the form of the decrees and orders of the said Lordship disposing on this matter he is bound and ought to swear. To this, it is answered that the penalty of the decree has no place unless the oath is given in the production and showing of rights or instruments. For the words of the decree say this clearly, where namely, that in truth the appearance itself, and the production of rights, and the showing, etc. But here no production or showing of rights or instruments was made in the appearance of the said Thomasius: hence we are outside the case of the statute, because it is one thing to produce instruments, another to allege them verbally, as in ff. de edendo. l. 1. §. edenda sunt omnia. And ff. de testibus. l. produci. And ff. de arbitris. l. non ex omnibus. Hence, when the statute ceases, the penalty of the statute also ceases. For even if one attempts by alleging, the delict is nevertheless not consummated, as in ff. quod quisque iuris. l. 3. §. haec verba. And it is a rule of law that where the law requires a fact, an attempt is not sufficient, especially when the attempt is not proximate to the fact, as fully noted in l. si quis non dicam rapere with its material.

Also, in attempts and non-consummated acts, repentance has place, which intervenes here, and especially in extraordinary crimes, as in ff. de in ius vocando. l. quamuis. ff. de falsis. l. qui falsam. And noted in l. ex hoc edicto. §. fi. ff. de alie. iudicii. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, because the words of the decree cease, the penalty also ceases, as in ff. de adquihęre. l. Si seruum. §. auo dixit prętor.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who has entered religion but has not made profession, yet has remained in religion for a long time in doubt as to whether he ought to remain or depart, may remain in the secular world; and if he cannot, whether he may at least enter another religion. And number 2.
3. Whether a Friar Minor may transfer to a regular canonry.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain youth, in his seventeenth year, entered religion, having assumed the habit of the professed, which was indistinguishable from the habit of novices or non-professed, with slight deliberation, with the mind and intention of leaving the world, and there hoping and intending to remain perpetually, who nevertheless did not believe, nor intend, to bind himself; indeed, he always considered himself not to be bound; and while he was in the aforementioned religion, he never had the intention of binding himself, nor of not binding himself; but he simply remained there: who, after two months had elapsed, having laid aside the habit, returned to the secular world; after a certain time, however, he deliberated with great maturity to return again to that same religion, and had a long discussion with the brothers about returning; nevertheless, he did not return.

† It is asked whether, according to law, he may return to the secular world. I answer that within the year of probation one freely returns to the secular world, unless he has made profession tacitly or expressly; or it appears that he wished to change his life absolutely, as in Extra, De regularibus et transeuntibus ad religionem, c. Statuimus. I therefore say that he should examine himself in his conscience, and if he had the intention entirely to abandon the secular world, and assumed the habit, as stated above, he cannot return to the secular world. But if he does not have this conscience, or if we are not in a contradictory judicial proceeding, but in the penitential forum, and then his word is believed, as noted by Innocentius in Extra, De iudiciis, c. Novit. Or if we are in the contest of the judicial forum, it is not presumed in doubt that he wished to bind himself to religion, but rather to deliberate. For the year is given for deliberation, and it is not presumed that anyone renounces a delay introduced for his benefit, as in the cited c. Statuimus, in the word “nisi” (unless) it appears evidently. But it may appear evidently, first, if he assumed the habit of a professed religious, different from the habit of novices; second, if he made a testament or another disposition of his goods, as one dying to the world; third, if other clear, manifest, and certain indications appear, as noted by Goffredus in the cited title De regulis, in his Summa, in the third column, there: “Moreover, one who has entered religion without profession, etc.” For by an undistinguished habit no distinction or quality is proved, unless there intervened some other declaration of words, as in Digestum, De religiosis et sumptibus funerum, l. Ac si quis, §. Plerique. And especially in this boy, who did not have a stable mind, but to whom the facility of his age provided a motive for changing; for as appears from the case, first he was of the opinion of remaining perpetually, second he was not of the opinion of binding himself, and thus his mind wavered. And although he later had the intention, nevertheless that intention was not joined with the act. For the treatment of words does not consummate an obligation, unless a response has followed, as noted in Digestum, De conditionibus indebiti, l. Eleganter, in the beginning, on the word “puto.” Wherefore, if conscience does not oppose, I think that this person can return to the secular world. Otherwise, however, if he had a guilty conscience: for no one knows his own conscience except God and himself, as noted in Digestum, De pactis, l. Iuris gentium, §. Pactorum, in the first gloss.

† Another doubt arises concerning the aforementioned Innocentius in c. Significatum, Extra, De regularibus, who states that a bishop may dispense with a minor under twenty-five years of age so that he may transfer to a stricter profession. For I say that the statement of Innocentius is true, although a minor cannot seek restitution in integrum against his profession. This is because he has changed his status, as in D. De minoribus, l. Si ex causa, § Papinianus; because he has usefully conducted the affairs of his soul, as noted in the same title, l. Aut praetor, in principio, in the gloss Nunquid ergo; and because an adult is considered as one who has reached twenty-five years, as in Extra, De iudicibus, c. Si, and on this point in Speculum, De restitutione in integrum, § Qualiter, vers. Quid si maior, and according to Petrus and Cynus, C. De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Auth. Ingressi. Finally, concerning that which is asked,

Whether a Minor Brother may transfer to a regular canonry, it must be said that he cannot, because the rule of canons is broader: unless by the disposition of the Pope, on account of the loftiness and singularity of the privilege of the said rule of the Minor Brothers and of other mendicants. That which Goffredus notes in the said title *De regularibus* in his *Summa*, § *Si*, which begins, “In summa notandum est,” etc., supports this. And that which is said in *Caput unicum*, *De voto*, Book 6, and in the *Extra*, *De regularibus et transeuntibus ad religionem*, *Caput 1*, Book 6, supports the foregoing. Moreover, although it is established that Preachers and Minor Brothers cannot receive anyone into the profession of their order within the year of probation, according to the said title, *Caput Non solum*, Book 6, the glossa there states, however, that such profession does not bind to the order, but binds to religion in general. And therefore, in effect, it comes to what I said above in the beginning. And then it is most certain that he can become a regular canon, since he is bound to religion and not to the order. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who are called continuous inhabitants and laborers, but you should see in volume 6 the same opinion, but more extensive: and with its position, the case begins, the fact is such, the truth is, that when formerly the magnificient etc.
2. Whether the immunity granted to the lord and sons extends to grandsons and other descendants.
3. How these words, from angaries and perangaries, and from all burdens, appended in the immunity, are to be understood.
4. Whether the immunity mentioned above extends to goods subsequently acquired.
5. The substituted thing succeeds in the place of the thing in whose place it is substituted.
6. Whether the immunity granted to inhabitants extends to inhabitants subsequently arriving.
7. Whether the immunity granted by one prince passes to his successors.
8. Words of declaration uttered from a long time ago create a presumption.
9. Words in immunities are to be understood strictly and rigorously.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked, who are to be understood as continuous laborers and inhabitants? I answer, those who serve by continuous labor and farming for a year, as in D. de publicanis, l. si, §. quotiens, in the word "continuous year"; not those who hire out their services daily, from day to day; because these are not called continuous laborers and inhabitants, as in D. de his qui deiecerunt vel effuderunt, l. 1, §. habitare, and in l. 1, D. furti adversus nautas, cauponas, stabularios, and D. de conditione indebita, l. si non sortem, §. libertas. But this privilege in the person of the inhabitants and laborers does not endure, except as long as they labor and inhabit, as in D. de legatis 3, l. qui concubinam, §. uxori meae, and C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. qui sub prætextu; and it is pertinent, D. de funerariis instructionibus, l. si ita, §. mulier, and l. cum quidam, duos, and D. de pignoribus, l. debitor. Secondly, it is asked.

† Whether an immunity granted to the lord and to his sons, because Lord Francis transferred the Empire which he held in the city of Piacenza together with the body of the city, to the illustrious Viscounts of Milan, extends to the grandsons and other descendants succeeding by hereditary right. And it seems that it does not pass, by the nature of a privilege, considering the reason of correct speech: because a privilege is personal, as in c. Privilegium personale, de regulis iuris, lib. 6; and as there by Dyonisius, and in the Digest, de excusationibus tutorum, l. 2. Moreover, immunity tends to exempt, and consists in fact, and in exceptions and pacts one may provide for one heir, and the provision does not extend to another heir, as is read and noted in the Digest, de pactis, l. Annus. But certainly in our case it seems that the contrary can be said, because we do not follow the figure of the words, but the intent, as in the Digest, de verborum significatione, l. Quisquis mihi. For this is not properly a privilege, but a pact, in which one seems to have stipulated for the son as heir, as noted in the Digest, de pactis, l. Si tibi, § Pactus, and l. Tale pactum, § Si fuit. It is an innominate contract, facio ut facias. And it was not a donation, nor liberality, arguing from the Digest, de donationibus, l. Si pater. And thus it does not obstruct the Digest, de aqua quotidiana et aestiva, l. 1, § Permittitur. Moreover, it does not obstruct the Authenticum, de non alienando, § Emphyteusim; because there it speaks of an emphyteutic contract, which in some way partakes of the nature of usufruct. Moreover, it does not obstruct the Digest, de donationibus, l. Aquilius regulus; because there the concession adhered to the person, but here it did not adhere to the person; nor is it presumed to adhere in doubt, as noted by Bartolus, de servitutibus legatis, l. Pater. Thirdly, it is asked,

† In order that these words may be understood, namely, “from angariae and perangariae, and from all burdens of the commune of Piacenza?” Answer: What angariae and perangariae are, is noted in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. neminem, and in ff. de verborum significatione, l. ferri. For neither are they to be subjected to angariae in their person, nor in their carts, nor in their expenses; hence neither in the levies which would be imposed in place of labor, as is noted by Bartolus in l. 4, § actor, ff. de re iudicata. But that which follows, “and from all burdens of the commune of Piacenza,” is thus explained: since the specific kinds, namely angariae and perangariae, which are species of burdens, have been set forth, the general clause follows, “and from all burdens of the city of Piacenza.” Hence it contains all burdens that can be enumerated, which other citizens of Piacenza bear, as in ff. si quis cautionem, l. sed et si quis, § quaesitum. It is otherwise if they were imposed by the prince by the absolute power of the prince, because that which is done by the plenitude of power is not included in this immunity, since the person of the prince is always understood to be excepted, as in c. Imperialem, § fin., de prohibitione feudi alienandi, according to Federicus.

Fourthly, it is asked whether the said immunity extends to property subsequently acquired? And it seems that it does, as in D. de serv. urb. praed. l. si servitus and D. de fund. instr. l. Lutius. To the contrary it seems, and this is the more correct view, by l. si ita D. de aur. et arg. leg. For the matter concerns a great prejudice to the public; therefore, future things are not included, as noted in C. quae res pign. oblig. poss. l. si, non oblig. l. si servitus: because there it speaks of future things concerning the present thing, i.e., of future lights concerning the servient and the dominant thing. Nor is this surprising, because the accessory follows the nature of the principal, as in D. de fund. instr. l. Seiae § Tyrannae and D. de leg. 3 l. praediis § balneas and C. de serv. urb. praed. l. Olimpico, and as noted in C. de serv. l. non modus and C. de sac. sanct. ecc. l. 1, and according to Cynus.

† And the aforesaid are true, unless new things have succeeded the old ones, i.e., purchased with money derived from the former assets, or through exchange; because in universalities, the substituted thing succeeds to the place of the thing in whose place it is substituted, as in D. de haereditate vendita, l. venditor haereditatis; and D. de petitione hereditatis, l. si rem, et precium; and fully noted in C. de rei venditione, l. mater; D. de legato 2, l. Imperator, §. si, together with the following law; D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. si donatae, §. si sponsus; D. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filiae, §. 1; and noted in D. de verbis significandis, l. Labeo. Nevertheless, this requires proof of the fact.

† Fifth, it is asked whether the provision is to be understood as applying to the continuous inhabitants who were then in place, or to any persons whatsoever? I answer that these words are appellative and granted to a class of persons; and therefore they extend to anyone whatsoever, as noted by Dyonisius in the cited chapter *privilegium personale*. And thus, if certain laborers have died or been dismissed, and others have been appointed in their stead, these new ones enjoy the immunity of the former tenants, by argument from *Digestum*, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, l. *Si donatae*, § *Si sponsus*; *Digestum*, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, l. *Filiae*, § *A Titia*; *Codex*, *De episcopis et clericis*, l. 1; *Codex*, *Ne filius pro patre*, auth. *Habita*; *Digestum*, *De iudiciis*, l. *Non alias*, § *Primo*. 5

Sixthly, it is asked, since this immunity was granted by the illustrious Lord Marcus, whether it passes to his successors? I answer: yes, if he has a successor in the Empire entrusted to him, because it appears that a contract is made under an appellative name. D. de pace, l. iure gentium, § pactorum; and D. de probationibus, l. si pactum. Nevertheless, I advise these nobles to have the immunity renewed for themselves by each individual successor. For it is a favor if it is granted to them, and an injury if it is denied to them. Yet this ultimately rests in the breast of the lords, who are to be moved by devotion and merits, not bound by promises.

† It is further asked whether the compromise must be shown? And it is to be said that, since it has been executed, it is presumed to have preceded for a very long time, those who make faith for it. For from the remoteness of time it is presumed for enunciative words, as noted by Cy. C. de prob. Otherwise, it is necessary to make faith of the compromise as of a mandate, as is read and noted in extra de off. dele. c. cum in iure. Finally, it is asked,

†How are words to be interpreted in this matter? I answer that in privileges, which are contrary to the public utility, they are interpreted very strictly and rigorously, as noted by Guillaume in *l. beneficium*, D. de constitutionibus principum. But we are here in the realm of contract, in which good faith and natural equity must be observed, in accordance with the words or the common understanding of those who speak, as in D. de verborum significatione, *l. nepos proculo*, "nam qui ambigue loquitur"; and *l. ut alphemus*, D. de legatis tertio; *l. librorum*, § *quod tamen Cassius*, D. de uso et habitatio; *l. plenum*, § *Aequitii*, D. de auro et argento legato; *l. pediculis*, § *argento potorio*; and *l. Plautius*, D. de supellectili legato; *l. Labeo*, § *idem Tubero* and § *nec mirum*; and *l. 1*, eodem titulo, cum materia sua; and D. de pactis, *l. veteribus*; and Extra, de auctoritate et usu pallii, c. *ex tuarum*; and de privilegiis, c. *porro*; D. de legatis tertio, *l. Offilius*, and the rest. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A donation causa mortis may be revoked; and if it has been made with an agreement that it cannot be revoked, it becomes a species of inter vivos donation; and therefore it must be insinuated, and the laws of insinuation cannot be waived.
2. An heir may renounce the fourth shares without insinuation, because it is a fuller restitution. See also in consilium 115.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain lady Brolia of Campograndi wishes to donate all her goods to lords I. and A. secretly, so that her blood relatives may not know; and therefore she does not wish it to be insinuated.

† It is asked whether it is possible? I answer that, if it is causa mortis, nevertheless it could be revoked, as in l. si, C. de donationibus causa mortis. But if he donates with the pact that he cannot revoke, it passes into the species of a donation inter vivos, as in ff. de donationibus causa mortis, l. ubi ita donatur, and it is noted in C. de pactis, l. si; and therefore, without insinuation, it is not valid beyond the legitimate sum. But it is asked, what if there has been a renunciation of the laws speaking of insinuation? I answer that, one cannot renounce, since they regard public utility, lest frauds be committed, and lest anyone use his substance prodigally. And because insinuation is a certain form and a certain solemnity, to which one cannot renounce, as in ff. de legibus, l. nemo potest, and C. de iure calumniae, l. 2, §. sed quia veremur. And I believe that even if it were made with an oath, it would not be valid beyond the legitimate sum, as noted by Bartolus in ff. de fideiussionibus, l. cum lex. But suppose that I donate all possessions, which are worth two thousand florins, and in the contract of donation specifically I stipulate this pact, that there be as many donations as there are things, and that each thing be understood to be donated by itself: is insinuation required? And it seems that it is not, as in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. scire debemus, and ff. de edicto edicti, l. si plura. To the contrary, it seems that these words were added in fraud of the law, as in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus, §. si quis. This opinion is held by Jacobus de Arena in Speculum de donationibus, §. quinimmo; the same applies if separate instruments were made for each thing, simultaneously or even separately, in fraud of the law, as in ff. de legibus, l. nomen, §. filio. For fraud is presumed on account of the immensity of the donation; and therefore Lord Raynerius of Forlì concludes that no counsel against l. sancimus can be found, and if any fraud could be found, this does not pertain to a perfect man, as you are; nevertheless, I will consider whether, with a clear conscience, a mode could be seen.

† However, an heir may renounce the fourth without insinuation, because it is not properly a donation, but a fuller restitution, as stated in the Digest, title "Those who are instituted as heirs," law "Father," and law "If a betrothed," § last, Digest, on donations between husband and wife; and even if the fourth is due by natural law, according to that law "Not," which is not found elsewhere, Code, on inofficious wills, law "If at any time," § "If." I, Baldus

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given an investiture of a fief for oneself, one’s heirs, and those to whom one has transferred one’s rights, whether a mother can succeed her son in fiefs.
2. Who are called heirs.
3. This term, *affictus*, is rarely found in the law.
body: In the name of Christ. Certain nuns made an investiture of a certain house to a certain Master Jacob, so that henceforth the said Master Jacob and his heirs, and son, and anyone to whom they shall have transferred their right, shall have, hold, enjoy, and possess, by renewing the ancient investiture of the same house made to a certain Facinus and Zaninus for a fictitious fee of two solidi each year; but for the renewal of the investiture in the person of the purchaser a certain sum was to be paid. It happened that the said Master Jacob died, after which there remained descendants, and descendants of descendants; finally the last one died, leaving a mother.
† It is asked whether the said mother succeeds to the said house, just as she succeeds to the other goods of her said son, or not? And it seems that she does succeed, because the investiture is said

† concerning Master James and his heirs. For heirs are called in infinitum, even if they be strangers, as in the Digest, De probationibus, l. Si pater; in the Code, De hereditatibus instituendis, l. Si; and in the Digest, De locato, l. Viam veritatis. Moreover, those words, “and to whom he shall have given his right,” seem to imply this: because he who dies intestate is deemed to leave his goods to the intestate successors, as in l. 2, Digest, De iure codicilli. But I believe the contrary to be more correct; for the truth is that this son, who last died, was an infant, who could neither tacitly nor expressly grant anything to his mother; hence that clause, “and to whom he shall have given his right,” has no application in the case of an infant. Furthermore, an infant is not said to die intestate, but intestabilis, as in l. 1, Digest, De suis et legitimis heredibus. Therefore, we must base our argument on the word “heirs,” if we wish to say that the mother succeeds; but this is impossible, because in ecclesiastical emphyteusis, the word “heirs” does not stand for anyone except descendants, as in the Authenticum, De non alienando, § Emphyteusim. And this is the ordinary gloss on the text in l. Etiam, in principio, Digest, Soluto matrimonio; and note this through Dyonisius in l. Ex facto, § Si, Digest, Ad Trebellianum. But that this contract was emphyteutic, the common interpretation holds,

And the nature of pacts, although this term, *affictus*, is rarely found in law, is nevertheless found in c. Pisanis, Extra, de restitutione spoliorum. Moreover, if this contract were an innominate contract, it ought to be judged according to the nature of the emphyteutic contract, because it is more similar to that than to any other contract, as in ff. depositi, l. 1, § si quis seruum. From which it is evidently concluded that the said house has reverted to the monastery. And this is true, unless the custom of the country is otherwise: concerning which custom it must be established. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made to brothers is real, such that it passes to the heirs of the said brothers.
2. Whether renunciation may be made of insinuation.
3. Whether a donation may be made of the goods of a living father.
4. The dowry is understood according to the father's means.
5. An oath does not supply the defect of insinuation.
body: In the name of Christ. The words are: “Lady Antonia gave, donated, renounced, and refused to Matteo and Samparino, her brothers and sons of the late Lord Jacopo and Lady Lucia, all rights and actions which she has, or will have, or may have in any case, during life and after death, by will or intestacy, or in any other way, in, upon, and to the paternal and maternal goods, present and future, her own and emphyteutic; promising not to revoke for cause of ingratitude or any other cause, and promising not to allege that they ought to have been insinuated in the form of the law and the statute of the commune of Cesena concerning donations to be insinuated; expressly renouncing, having been certified by me, the notary written below, of the said laws and statutes of the commune of Cesena, and every other aid; and she did this, being satisfied with her paternal dowry, and with the consent of her father, mother, and blood relatives.” It happened that the said Matteo and Samparino died while their father and mother and sisters were still living. Then the father and mother died, with the said Lady Antonia and the sisters surviving. The sisters wish to exclude her. And it is presupposed that all the aforementioned matters were secured by oath. The question is: what is the law, both regarding the personal goods and the emphyteutic goods, of which express mention was made in the aforementioned renunciation? Therefore, it is asked first, whether the said donation was real, so that it passes to the heirs of the said brothers? Second, concerning the force of the renunciation, given the statute concerning the insinuation of donations. Third, whether the said donation could have been made regarding the goods of the father and mother, who were then living, and also because the said donees died?

† And it seems, with regard to the first point, that this was a real [right], as in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Si pactum*. To the contrary, it seems that here the final cause makes the donation personal, not the expression of the name; for the final cause was the favor of the brothers, which ceases in this case, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Tale pactum*, § *Si*, and law *Quod dictum*. And this is dictated by natural reason, which is held as law, as noted by Cynus, according to Petrus, in the Code, *De legibus et constitutionibus*, law *Non dubium*, and by fraternal charity. Moreover, the real or personal nature of pacts consists in the mind, and the mind is proven by reason, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Iuris gentium*, § *Pactorum*. Moreover, it seems expressly stated in the Tenth Collection, *Si de funere fuerit controversia*, chapter *Titius cum Sempronio fratre suo*. And because the consent of the father and mother was directed toward the brothers, not toward others, see the argument in the Authenticum, *De restitutione fideicommissorum*, § *Manifestum*, and what is noted there.

† As to the second point, it appears that the said renunciation is valid, because municipal law is private law, and one may renounce it according to the general rule. C. de pac. l. si quis in conscribendo. and C. eo. l. pacisci. To the contrary, it appears that one cannot renounce the common law, which provides for insinuations; therefore, neither can one renounce municipal law, because the same reason moves municipal law. Or, because it is not credible that anyone would throw away his own right. Also, because it ought not to be permitted that anyone abuses his own property, and especially in the case of women, who are easily deceived.

† As to the third point, it appears that the said donation could have been made, as C. de pact. l. si. On the contrary, it appears that, since the donees had died, the consent of the father and mother, whose inheritance is in question, could not endure until the time when the donees were dead, as ff. de iure codicillorum. l. Quidam referunt. Solution: all things considered, the said refutation and donation do not prevent the said Lady Antonia from succeeding with her sisters in a per capita share, upon making collation of the dowry; which must be made because she immediately succeeds to the father and mother, notwithstanding the said refutation. And this is because the brothers predeceased; hence she cannot come to the succession of the father and mother through the succession of the brothers, but comes in her own right; and therefore she must collate the dowry, as C. de inoff. testam. l. Quoniam nouella. And although she confessed to having received a dowry, if the quantity of the dowry, or quasi-dowry, does not appear, as is customary when they enter a monastery, this uncertain confession cannot induce computation or compensation, as ff. de castrensi pecu. l. si forte. and l. certam. in prin. ff. de confessis.

† unless it is said, and it is sufficiently reasonable, that the confession of the dowry is understood to refer to the dowry according to the father’s means, as in D. 35.1.3 (*Si filiae*) and D. 23.3.10 (*Cum post*), § *Generi*. Therefore, the collation ought to be made in accordance with that amount, and so I hold. As for the oath, I do not place weight on it here.

† because an oath does not supply the defect of insinuation, and because an oath does not operate beyond the intention of the contracting parties, and because if the principal obligation becomes void, the oath is annulled, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. si; and ff. de legibus, l. si quis inquilinos, §. ult.; ff. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. si; C. de legibus, l. non dubium, in fine; ff. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. praetor ait; and Extra de foro competenti, l. si diligenti, §. si. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether two emphyteuticaries invested in a single instrument are said to be bound jointly and severally, or for a half share: and if one of them subsequently purchased the entire direct domain of this emphyteutic thing, the emphyteutic thing was destroyed, and rebuilt by only one, whether he can recover the expenses from his associate, who had already purchased the entire direct domain. And number 4.
2. Whether, if it appears from a written document that fictitious payments were made, although not regarding the investiture, the preceding fact is proved, namely, that the written document of investiture preceded.
3. Whenever one and the same act can signify alienation and non-alienation, alienation ought not to be presumed.
4. Whether an emphyteutary can bring the condictio indebiti for the census which he paid without being indebted.
body: In the name of Christ. Columbinus granted in emphyteusis two parts of one castle, and of certain possessions, to Marsilius and Clauellus, in the same instrument, for an annual *fictum* of 63 Piacentine pounds and 10 solidi. Finally, after some time, the said Columbinus sold his ownership of the said *fictum* in solidum to the said Clauellus, ceding to him all his real and personal rights, and specifically the right to the said *fictum*. Afterwards it happened that the said Marsilius, while he lived, and afterwards his heirs, possessed and enjoyed the entire two parts of the castle and lands, and every year for a long time and beyond, paid the said entire *fictum*, i.e., the said 63 pounds and 10 solidi of Piacentine denarii, to the said Clauellus. Finally, during this intervening time, the castle was destroyed in time of war; and finally it was restored and repaired at great expense by the said Marsilius or his heirs. From this case arise doubts: First, whether the heirs of the said Marsilius are bound in the future to pay the said 63 pounds and 10 solidi to the heirs of the said Clauellus? Second, what is the law regarding the said expenses, whether they can be recovered for half by the heirs of the said Marsilius from the heirs of the said Clauellus? Third, whether by the heirs of the said Marsilius, offering to restore the estimation of half the fruits, an action on the ground of undue payment (*condictio indebiti*) can be brought for half of the said census, as having been unduly paid, against the heirs of the said Clauellus? And that these matters may appear, it is necessary to begin with the contract of the *fictum*.

And it is certain that the aforementioned Marsil. and Clauellus were each bound for their respective share to the said *fictum*. For the said emphyteusis, for the sake of which the obligation of the *fictum* was contracted, came to each of them for their respective share. Moreover, because when several persons bind themselves in the same contract simply, each is held liable for his virile share, as C. si certum petatur, l. si non singuli; C. de locato et conducto, l. si diuisa; D. eodem, l. cum apparebit; D. de duobus rebus, l. reos, §. cum in tabulis; C. eodem, l. 1, no. ff. ad Velleianam, l. vir uxori, §. fi. Since, therefore, the obligation was divided from the very beginning, both by the nature of the thing acquired for a share and by the nature of the obligation contracted simultaneously, such is the derivative obligation as was the primitive one, as l. 2, §. Ex his, D. de verbis obligatorum. The status of the primordial obligation always follows it; nor is it changed by the passage of time, nor by the person of the successor, as C. de locato et conducto, l. viam veritatis; and D. de verbis obligatorum, l. insulam intra biennium. From this it necessarily follows that, if the matter were at the end of the said emphyteusis, the said *fictum* could be recovered pro parte as unduly paid, since it is presumed that there is at least an error of law, when the one recovering deals with avoiding damage, and the nature of the business is somewhat confused, as D. de probationibus, l. cum de indebito; and arg. D. de condictione sine causa, l. fullo.

† Let us now see whether another transaction has been carried out besides the first. And it seems that it has, namely, that the clauellus reconveyed his share in emphyteusis to the said Marsi and his heirs. And this is proved as follows. It is certain that a certain contract results from the relation of the pension to the thing for which the pension is paid: but this resulting contract seems to be an emphyteutic contract, as if descending from the first, and if it is said that it cannot be an emphyteutic contract because no writing intervenes, which is of the substance of the proof of that contract, as C. de iu. emph. l. 1. Moreover, no investiture intervenes, which is of the substance of perfecting the said contract, as C. de iu. emph. l. fi. I answer to the first, that it is sufficient that the payments of the fictum, or ficta, appear by writing: for whenever the consequent is proved by writing, and the antecedent seems proved by the same writing, as C. de apocis publicis. l. quicunque. li. 10. Furthermore, the presumption of the law is held as writing, but here it is presumed to be so from long time, if it is alleged to be present, as expressly read, and noted, de contractu emph. ff. de vsu. l. cum de in rem verso. And thus neither he who pays the fictum can deny it, nor can it be denied, as C. de agr. et cen. l. litib. li. 11. and in c. querelam. de elec. Moreover, it does not matter that no investiture appears, because since the cause of the author's patience precedes, it is held as a solemn investiture, as C. de acq. pos. l. minus instructus. The same is also to be said in fiefs, so that the effect of investiture arises from patience with a preceding title, and in c. sciendum. de consuet. recti feudi. And because this is a presumption of law, it should be held as writing. C. de peti. hęre. l. si filius. C. communi. diui. l. pe. in gl. For even possession of goods must be acknowledged in the records: and thus writing is required, yet it is proved by long patience, as noted in l. 1. C. qui admi. in bo. pos. On the contrary, it seems that the said tacitly resulting contract is not considered an emphyteutic contract, but a simple lease, which in rural properties is presumed from year to year: not in perpetuity, as ff. loca. l. Item quaeritur. §. qui impleta.

† and this if it is proved. Whenever one and the same act can signify both alienation and non-alienation, alienation is never presumed, as noted in *l. cum quid.*, D. *si certum petatur*. But this act, relative to a pension existing in cash and intended for the enjoyment of fruits, can truly and properly signify a simple lease, as in D. *de praescriptionibus*, *l. naturalis*. Therefore, if it does not signify an alienation made by an emphyteutic contract or a perpetual lease, as in Inst. *locatio conductio*, § *adeo*, this serves the purpose excellently. C. *de praescriptione triginta annorum*, *l. male agitur*. This is the truth here: that a simple lease is presumed, which was consummated in the past, but has not been commenced nor is to be consummated in the future. In the said § *qui impleto*.
