From this follow two conclusions. The first is that the condition does not cease with respect to past events. The second is that past fruits are not subject to restitution. As stated in D. de furtis, l. si servus, § locavi, one might say: “This Marsilius received fruits from the common property; therefore, he is bound by the action for division of common property to restore his share.” I answer that here the situation has not remained within the limits of co-ownership, but has proceeded further to a tacit simple lease, and the rent has been paid. And know that this term “fictitious” is a general and indefinite name, as in X. de restitutione spoliorum, c. Pisanis.

From the foregoing it appears what the law is regarding expenses: for expenses of repair and of permanent utility do not fall upon the tenant; and insofar as he has usefully incurred them, he has a right of retention of the thing, as in D. de vi et vi armata, l. colonus, provided, however, that he does not burden the owner with money; because that which imposes an unbearable burden is not considered to have been done usefully, as in D. de negotiorum gestione, l. sed an ultro, § pen., and D. communis dividundo, l. in rebus. This is left to the discretion of a good man, considering the quality of the thing and of the persons, as in D. de re vendicata, l. in fundo. And in the case where expenses cannot be recovered, nevertheless what has been built may be demolished and removed, the cement being saved, the original form of the thing remaining intact and its substance not impaired. Nor does it seem that he who made the expense as if in a leased thing donated the expense; because he had no occasion for donation. We say the same of the usufructuary, as in D. de usufructu, l. ad tempus. And this response addresses all these very beautiful and useful doubts.

Consider, however, if the instrument states that the emphyteusis was granted to two persons simply, and the rent was likewise promised: then, by enumeration of the persons, the grant and the rent appear to be divided. There is no doubt about the grant, because the parties make themselves co-obligors by concurrence, since useful dominion cannot be held by several persons in solidum. Similarly, there is no doubt about the rent, as in l. reos, § cum tabulis, D. de duobus reis, and C. si plures una sententia, l. 1. But if the grant was made to each in solidum, and the rent was promised by each in solidum, then it is impossible that the parties do not make themselves co-obligors by concurrence in the grant; but in the promise of the rent, since it consists in a generic thing, two persons are debtors in solidum. Nevertheless, observe that, lest the obligation for the other’s part be without cause, it must be understood that they mutually act as sureties. Hence, for that part for which you stood surety for me, it is impossible that, since I am the principal debtor and you the surety, I can sue you in solidum; because although from the person of the assignor it may seem that I have a right of action, nevertheless from my own person I am repelled. Hence, that I have purchased the entire ownership is of no consequence, because I act fraudulently in demanding what I am bound to restore by the useful action of mandate or negotiorum gestio, as in the rule “dolo facit.” Therefore, the opinion is true and just. Nor can anything else be said, saving the reason of right speech.

In doubt, one is rather to be considered as promising on account of a tacit suretyship, or more truly as constituting himself principal for the other, as in Auth. de fideiussoribus, in principio, than without cause, because it would imply a donation; or the promise would be invalid, as in D. de exceptione doli, l. 2, § circa, and D. de probationibus, l. cum de indebito. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an immunity granted to one having twelve children has effect, if he once had them, even though they have died.
body: The words *debet* are thus stated, we say, that in the name of Christ, according to our orders, those having immunity. 12. of freeborn persons, namely, let there be at least ten freeborn persons arriving subsequently, in whose number are not to be counted those born of daughters of those having such immunity or descending from the female line, let them be and ought to be exempt from burdens or purely personal charges, and from extraordinary ones only; but to ordinary ones, namely to duties and tolls and other ordinary charges, they are bound and constrained, the said immunities in no way obstructing this. In which said ordinary charges are understood to be included the collections or taxes which come to the chamber of our God-given treasury; wishing this order to be observed by all having immunity. 10. of freeborn persons, given, etc.

† It is asked whether this immunity continues for the children after their death? And it seems that it does, because a benefit granted by the prince ought to endure, as in c. Decet, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. The objection you raise, that the text says "superusnientes" [those who come after], does not hold; for rather the text says "superuiuentes" [survivors]. Hence, it suffices to have had them once. 12. children, even if they subsequently died, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. Si quis haeredem. To the contrary, it seems that the cause of the immunity is the number of children; therefore, when the number ceases, although the grace endures with respect to past matters which have achieved their effect, nevertheless the prince's benefit ceases with respect to new occurrences after the death of the children, as ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. 2; and ff. de iure patriae, l. Vel adigere, §. Quamuis; and ff. de bonis liberorum, l. Qui libertinus, §. Posthumus. Solution: it must be said that either these taxes and tolls were ordered and completed in the past, or ordered but not completed, because the day of the term had passed for part but not for the other part; or neither ordered nor completed previously, but after the death of the children. In the first case, because the immunity is completed, it endures. In the second case, the same seems to apply upon inspection of the beginning, upon which inspection the immunity begins to have its force, arg. ff. ad municipalia, l. Incola. In the third case, the immunity does not endure, because it arrives at a case from which it cannot begin, as ff. de legatis 2, l. Titia Seio, c. Usuras. And because the true text should be "superuenientes" [those who come after]; for the text "superuenientes" cannot be adapted according to the reason of correct speech, as ff. de auro et argento, l. Plautius. Therefore, erroneous writing is overcome, and truth is substituted in its place, as ff. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, §. Cum imperfecta; and C. de testamento, l. Error. To the aforementioned pertains the entire brocard: "No fact is given which does not endure," as ff. de in rem verso, l. Si pro parte, §. Versum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an illicit contract and one involving usury are termed, and when fruits are to be imputed to the principal.
2. Although the action on pledge is personal, in a usurious contract it is framed as an action in rem.
3. Whether buyers in good faith are bound to account for consumed fruits.
body: Benedictus, and Co. In the name of Christ. A certain Laurentius was granted a concession (condictionem) of certain lands for a price of 8,000 florins, on this condition, that within the term of 8 years they may redeem them, the fruits not being computed into the principal; and if they do not redeem within the said term, that the said buyer is bound to pay to the said sellers 310 florins for the complete payment of the aforesaid sum; and oaths were interposed. And it is alleged that the said buyer was accustomed to practice usury, however not in the same type of contract, but in tolls (gabellas).

It is asked whether the said contract should be judged as usurious or not; and whether an action may be brought on a pledge with fruits computed into the principal; and what if these goods were alienated by the said buyer. And it seems that the said contract ought to be considered lawful, and not usurious, but rather a certain sale made under certain conditions and at certain times. For these agreements can be lawful; therefore, they are not presumed to have been made in fraud, as in l. 2, C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem; because we ought rather to presume good than evil, as in ff. pro socio, l. merito. To the contrary it seems, for these agreements cannot be suitably adapted except to a pledge contract, and one made in fraud of usury. And this is the case expressly stated in extra de emptionibus et venditionibus, c. ad nostram; and extra de pignoribus, c. illa vos. And this is the truth. It is no objection that he did not practice usury in the same kind of contract, because it suffices that he was accustomed to be evil in the same kind of usurious wickedness, as in the rule semel malus. And there, according to Dy, it is not considered in what manner he practices usury, provided that he practices it; because a sin which is not deleted by penance, by its own weight draws one to another.

And know that, although the action arising from a pledge is personal, it fails in the case of a usurious contract, where it is drafted as an action in rem, according to Hostiensis and others. Although Innocentius says the contrary, whose opinion is not followed in canon law equity, namely so that usurers and rectors may not be given grounds for fraud, cf. Extra de iudicibus, c. Quia veritas. If the contract was a pledge contract, upon rescission of the contract as having been celebrated in fraud of the canons, the hypothec is also rescinded, as in D. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. Non omnium. And where there is a pledge, the fruits of the pledge are counted toward the principal; and this is true with respect to the lender:

† But those who purchased in good faith are not bound to restore the natural fruits consumed, which they gain in compensation for cultivation, as stated in D. de rei vend. l. fructus, and there by many. Pensions, however, are understood to be industrial fruits, as stated in D. de rei vend. l. si navis. But they are more properly called acquisitions, as noted in D. de cond. ind. l. et quia bona. If he receives them in good faith by his own foresight, he profits from them. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A marriage between blood relatives is not contracted by words in the present tense. And if it has been consummated by carnal intercourse knowingly, the dowry is confiscated by the son.
2. Whether one who first contracted illicit marriages, and afterwards lawful ones, or vice versa, ought to be punished.
3. In delicts, the consummation of the act, not of the law, is examined.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Words of marriage do not create a marriage between consanguineous relatives or affines up to the fourth degree, as stated in the extrajudicial title On Consanguinity and Affinity, chapter *Non debet*. And if the matter has reached the stage of verbal agreement, but carnal copulation has not intervened, such a marriage is considered void, as provided in the Code, title On Laws and Constitutions, law *Non dubium*. However, if carnal copulation has intervened and they knowingly contracted incestuous marriages, the dowry is confiscated by operation of law: if there are no children, and the dowry ought not to be returned to the giver, but rather to the treasury, as is fully read and noted in the Authenticum, title On Incestuous Marriages, in the principal part, column 3, and in the Digest, title On Conditions Without Cause, law *Si fullo*. But if the marriages were contracted through error of law or due to the facility of youth, penalties do not apply, as noted there. From the part of the minor, even though from the part of the major, penalties do apply. For instance, if the boy was fifteen years old, at which age ignorance of law is tolerated: he does not incur penalties; for this is expressly stated by the gloss in the aforementioned Authenticum. But the woman, being of older age, properly incurs the penalty, and no leniency is shown to her on account of her sex, because she sins against natural law, as stated in the Digest, title On Adultery, law *Si adulterium cum incestu*, and in the Code, title On Being Called to Court, law *Veniat*.

† Further, it is asked whether this young man, having taken another wife without the judgment of the Church, ought to be punished corporally or by some other penalty, or not. It seems that he ought to be punished corporally, because he took two wives at the same time, as is stated in Codex, De adulteriis, l. Eum qui duas. Nor does he seem to be excused on account of his age, because he is acting in bad faith, as is stated in Digestum, De minoribus, l. Auxilium, § In delictis; and l. 1, Codex, Si adversus delictum.

I hold the contrary, because it matters greatly whether one first contracts lawful marriage and then, at the same time, contracts unlawful marriage; in that case, because he has sinned in multiple ways, he must be punished with the penalty contained in the aforementioned l. Eum qui duas, or with another penalty according to custom and the statutes of the places. Or whether, on the other hand, he first contracts unlawful marriage and then contracts lawful marriage; in that case, he is not punished, because a lawful act does not deserve punishment, as is stated in Codex, De adulteriis, l. Gracchus. And because he did well and laudably corrected his error, as is stated in the aforementioned l. Si adulterium cum incestu. Nor is it necessary here to approach the bishop for permission, as is stated in Digestum, De conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Quam sub conditione, § Si; because it is in vain to implore by prayers that which is granted by common law, as is stated in l. 1, Codex, De thesauris, Book 10. For the nature of this matter was open and notorious; and that which is notorious is equivalent to a sentence, as is stated in l. Emptorem, in principio, Digestum, De actione empti.

From these things it is concluded that the sum given in the name of the first dowry, if it was actually paid, is owed to the Chamber of the Lord. However, this young man, concerning whom the question is asked, is not to be punished in any way on the ground that he is said to have contracted two marriages, unless it appears that carnal intercourse was continued with the person of each of the two women, such that he knew the first even after the second lawful marriage.

†because in delicts, the consummation of the fact, not of the law, is considered, as noted in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium; and in the aforementioned l. eum, qui duas; and it is established in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. qui contra, and what is fully noted there. Nor does the aforementioned § in delictis object to what I have said, that this minor is excused entirely, because there the whole was illicit, whereas here the second marriage was licit. And thus the gloss seems to understand it in the aforementioned l. eum, qui duas. It is also understood in l. 1, ff. de his, qui non infamantur, when the first betrothal held. Otherwise, if they were prohibited: for then infamy would not be imposed on account of the second betrothals, which were licit and honest. And thus I opine on these points, saving the substance of the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who promises to keep the sluice gate shut by hand, and who assumes upon himself the risk and all peril, if indeed a flood should occur, is not bound, because the promise is understood to apply only if it is possible. And what effect the renunciation of fortuitous case has at the end of the opinion.
body: In the name of Christ. The words state that the miller is bound to clear and purge all obstructions that might occur in the river, so that the water of the river may flow sufficiently, and to maintain the banks, and to keep the mill in its same condition, provided that he is not bound to do so during time of war. And he is bound to restore the dam to a good condition and state at the time the lease ends: provided that if the water changes its bed, he assumes all risk, danger, and expense, promising to maintain the said dam in good and firm condition until the time of 10 years, which was the duration of the said lease or contract. Now a great flood has occurred, and has destroyed the said dam to such an extent that it is difficult and very costly to rebuild. It is asked,

† What is the law: whether he is bound to pay the annual fictitious rent and to repair the said dam and mill, or to both, or to one, and in sum, what is the law regarding all these matters? And it seems that he is bound indiscriminately to all risks of fortuitous events, whether fortunate or unfortunate. And first, because this person bought or leased the fruits in hope, therefore the risk pertains to him, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si iactum retis. Second, because he who excepts one fortuitous case, e.g., enemies, seems to have provided against himself in another case: for the exception confirms the rule in cases under the same genus of fortuitous events not excepted, and if the cases are similar, as noted in l. 1, de regulis iuris. Also, because this person assumed the risk upon himself, which signifies a fortuitous event, when this term is used in contracts, as noted in l. 1, C. communi; D. si quis cautionem, l. sed et si quis, §. quaesitum; and l. periculi, D. de nautico foenore; and l. periculum, D. si certum petatur. Also, because of this agreement, it is leased for a lower price, D. de servis exponendis, l. si venditor; therefore, conversely, he must be subjected to greater risk. C. de furtis, l. pe., §. fi. Also, the risk occurred imprudently, because it is a fault to bind oneself thus, and thus fault precedes the event, fault, i.e., in contracting, arg. C. de dote promissa, l. fi. Also, the word "reschium" signifies unfortunate events according to common usage of speech, to which one must adhere, as in D. de legibus 3, l. liberorum, §. quod tamen. Therefore, let the lessee or buyer impute it to himself, because it is not new nor unthought-of that rivers bring danger of flooding, as in D. de minio, l. verum, §. sciendum, with the following §.

On the contrary, it seems that this is a case more than fortuitous, because it exceeds the usual limits of water inundation, and is in a manner a miracle: and of such a case it does not seem to have been thought, because to those things which rarely happen, neither the will of the law nor of man seems to be adapted, as in D. de legibus, l. 4, and fi. Also, this supports it, for he who accepts risk upon himself against the nature of the contract seems to accept usual risks, not unusual ones, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, §. frumenta. Also, this agreement injures beyond half the just price, therefore it must be reduced to equity and proportion, as in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione, and no. C. locati, l. si olei. Also, because it does not seem that anyone wishes to precipitate himself and squander his patrimony, arg. D. de probationibus, l. cum de indebito. Also, this case is in a manner a "casmia," as in C. de iure emphiteutico, l. 1. Also, because the lessee seems to have assumed rather the work upon himself than the defect of heaven or soil, as in D. locati, l. opus, and there by Bartolus. Also, because a promise of a fact has a tacit condition, i.e., of possibility, as by Bartolus, no. D. de verbis obligatorum, l. Stipulatio ista, post principium; and D. de publicanis, l. caesar. Also, because the promisor promises his own act, not the act of nature, as in D. de damno infecto, l. fluminum, §. uicium, and §. seruius. Also, because the promisor made the preparatory things possible, therefore the impossible is not imputed to him, as in C. qui petunt tutelam, l. cum a matribus; and D. locati, l. si merces, §. uis maior. Also, because the words "reschii" and "periculi" signify in this contract the slightest fault, which did not arise from the simple nature of the contract celebrated for the benefit of both parties. Also, just as the slightest negligence causes the case to arise, so by the argument from the contrary, the utmost diligence causes it not to arise. But our case is in the greatest fortuitous event, and intolerable, and beyond all human power, and not reparable with customary expense, or equally great, but with maximum and unsustainable expense, and against the nature of the contract, and against natural equity: therefore, by these words, the aforementioned case does not arise, as noted in the said §. quaesitum, in the ordinary gloss at the end of the great gloss, and by the final conclusion; therefore, on the contrary, I hold that the said lessee is not bound to repair, nor to the pension in the meantime, until it is repaired: but a new agreement is needed between the aforementioned parties, as if the place had perished by "casmata" or incursion of enemies, or almost so: so that it was deteriorated beyond half the perception of revenues, arg. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. domum. For when fishing rights are bought at double, beyond what another would buy them for, the law l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione, has place; and thus it must be understood, as noted by Bartolus, D. de publicanis, l. quotiens, §. qui maximos. Also, because the exception of fortuitous event was not renounced, as in the said §. quaesitum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What a partnership is.
2. Whether a partnership is presumed to have been contracted between brothers who hold property in undivided co-ownership, so that whatever they acquire from external sources must be shared.
3. A partnership is contracted not only expressly, but also tacitly.
body: In the name of Christ. Certain Antonius Zaninus and Francis, brothers, stood in communion of their paternal inheritance for many years, living together familiarly in the same house; and they traded for a period of twenty-four years, crossing the sea and exercising the trade of wool, as well as of various other goods; which wool, transported during the said times, was for the greater part purchased in the land of Viterbo and other places by the said Zaninus, and was placed or caused to be placed in the common house of the said brothers by the said Zaninus; and also the said Zaninus for the greater part managed all the other goods, and the said common wool of the said brothers was deposited or caused to be deposited, hired by the said Ant. outside Viterbo, and in various other places; and sold by the said Ant. for the greater part, and the price of the said wool was received by the same Ant., and creditors by reason of the said wool were constituted in his name. Now, however, the aforementioned Ant. and Zaninus wish to come to the division of all goods; it is requested by Zaninus that the said Ant. ought to give one-third part of the entire price of the said wool sold by him, together with one-third part of all the profit derived therefrom, and that creditors by reason of the aforementioned matter be assigned for one-third part, and that all subsequent matters ought to be communicated and divided. And to the same Zaninus ought to be assigned, before the dowries of the late mother and of the wife of the said Io. which accrued in the house, and to give him one-third part of the money expended by the said Ant. on account of one son of the said Ant., both in the purchase of books and of other things which arose for his said son; and those things ought to be given which are contained in the petition presented by the said Io. And it is opposed by the said Ant. that the profit of the said wool ought not to be communicated, and that it arose from his own industry and from money borrowed at his own risk. And the said Zaninus says that the said profits arose from the industry of both, since the said wool was traded by both of them in the manner stated above. And from the common money of the said brothers, although certain moneys were borrowed, they were repaid from the common money of the said brothers. From these things it is asked, what is the office of the arbitrators in pronouncing and proceeding, having seen the petitions; and whether the said Ant. is bound to render an account of the things managed by him; and whether the said goods ought to be communicated, etc., and the said dowries deducted before the share.

† It must be premised for the sake of clarity that partnership is a contract binding both parties, involving the sharing and division of profits and losses, as equity dictates. For example, if one contributes more to the partnership than the other, which I do not pursue here, because this is a matter treated in l. 1, C. pro socio. Furthermore, some partnership is express: and this is established by an express agreement or pact. Some partnership is tacit: and this presupposes, if it is indeed a commercial partnership, that both parties practice the trade, and not only one; however, it is not required that in this practice both contribute equal industry, because there is a great difference among artisans, as stated in ff. de solutionibus, l. inter artifices. It suffices that each contributes the diligence he knows how to apply, and avoids the fault from which he ought to refrain, as noted in ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. si negotia.

From these premises, I say that although the brothers hold undivided property, whatever they acquire from external sources accrues to the acquirer and not to the other brothers, because it is adventitious gain, as we say when they conduct business while the father is alive, as in D. 17.2.1 (*Cum duobus*), § *Si fratres*; C. 10.32.1 (*Licet indiuisa*). And this is true unless it is proven that a partnership was contracted among them. For if that partnership was contracted for certain trades, the profits and losses of those trades must be shared. If, however, it was contracted for universal business, then the sharing is universal; and the same applies to location, as fully noted by Bartolus in D. 26.7.1 (*Titium et Meuium*), § *Altero*. Now it must be seen whether a trading partnership is presumed to have been contracted here. For then whatever follows from that business must be shared among the brothers, whether it be profit or loss, as in D. 33.2.1 (*Si totius*), and whatever happens is apportioned per capita, as in D. 17.2.1 (*Si non fuerit*). Now let us see whether a trading partnership was contracted between them, and then whatever follows from it, under whatever name it was conducted, must be shared.

† It must be known, namely, that a partnership is contracted not only expressly, but also by tacit consent, which is presumed from the quality of the acts: as when all engage in business and there is a sharing of profits and participation in losses. For a partnership is proven by joint acts. If, therefore, all the said three brothers were engaged in the art of weaving, even though the said Antonio contributed more labor than the others, and greater industry, because perhaps he was more industrious, nevertheless, from the very quality of the facts, a tacit partnership appears to have been contracted. For by engaging in business together, the will is understood to be given by the very act itself, as argued from the Digest, *ad municipalia*, law *Si quis instructus*; and the Code, *de institutionibus et substitutionibus*, law *Reprehendenda*; and especially due to the length of time, as in the Digest, *de usuris*, law *Cum de in rem verso*; and due to the presumption of fraternal charity, as in the Digest, *de probationibus*, law 1, § *Procurator*. And if it is said that the said Antonio alone bore the risks, because he borrowed money at his own risk, it is answered that, since they were partners, this loss must be common, namely, to be shared through the action *pro socio*. And if it is said that the said Antonio conducted business in his own name, unknown to his brothers, this rather argues his bad faith, because he ought to have conducted business in the common name, since a partnership preceded. A partnership has the nature of a mandate; for they appear to mandate to one another that whatever is done in the course of business be done in the common name, as argued from the Digest, *de procuratoribus*, law *Licet*, § *Ea obligatio*. Although this mandate does not give rise to an action on mandate, because it is not gratuitous, as in law *Quaedam*, in the beginning, Digest, *de edendo*. Hence, if what is proposed is true, namely, that all the brothers engaged in business reciprocally and in turn, they must be judged to have been business partners: I do not say partners in other matters, for example, in providing dowries for the daughters of one of them, unless there had been an express or tacit agreement to this effect: as because all had daughters dowried from the common fund, as in the Digest, *pro socio*, law *Si socius pro filio*. And the reason is that this act of providing a dowry is not a business act, but a burden incumbent upon the person; and a partnership is not presumed to be contracted except in business matters, as in the Digest, *pro socio*, law *Si adiciatur*. And therefore each acknowledges the burden of providing a dowry for his own daughter from his own share, because this burden does not arise from any business transaction, but by natural law, as in law *Qui liberos*, Digest, *de ritu nuptiarum*. And this is the answer to the questions asked. Let it also be concluded that a partnership contracted in a certain matter, since the contract is one of good faith, excludes any bad faith of one of the partners. Moreover, a partnership contracted in a certain matter appears to be contracted in all matters that follow from it during the partnership, as argued from the Digest, *de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, law *Servitutes*, § *Domo*. Dowries, namely, of the mother received by the father, and of the wife received by them, bound by the same instrument, are due to the son, when the father received them to be set aside for the burdens of marriage, as in the Digest, *familiae erciscundae*, law *Si maritus*. However, those brothers who gave the obligation must be indemnified. Books also bought with common money for the son of one of these must be counted in the father’s share, at least such as they are today, as in the Digest, *familiae erciscundae*, law *Si filia*, unless it were proven that another agreement had intervened between the brothers, for then that agreement must be followed, as in the aforementioned law *Si socius pro filia*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a rescript of the prince is valid against a statute.
2. The clause in a rescript that justice must be done notwithstanding his contumacy: what effect it produces and how it is to be understood.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that, according to the wording of the statute, a true contumacious party who fails to respond to the allegations is deemed by operation of law to have confessed. However, a rescript has now been issued by the prince, stating that since defense must not be denied to anyone, justice ought to be administered to the parties notwithstanding such contumacy.

† First, it is asked whether the rescript is valid. And it seems that it is not, as in C. ut lite pendente, in rubro et nigro, and in Authen. in medio litis non fieri sacras formas. But he descends from the father both naturally and with regard to paternal affection, as in ff. de inofficiosa testamento, l. posthumus, and l. quod dicitur, de liberis et posthumis; ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. cum pater. If, however, reference is made to the mother, then either the mother herself utters the words, or some third party does so: in the first case it is said that she gave birth, even though the child saw the light after the womb was opened, as in C. de inofficiosa testamento, l. 3. And the reason is natural, because the affection is the same according to nature, and the same intention to make a will, and the necessity that the will not be broken, as in C. de posthumis heredibus instituendis, l. fin. The third reason is that, since the matter concerns the benefit of the posthumous child and his favor, the posthumous child is considered as already born, even while still in the womb, with regard to obtaining the effect of the institution, and especially on account of the favor of the will, as noted in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. a primo herede and l. Gal. §. instituens, and l. qui in utero, ff. de statu hominum. And thus, considering the benevolence of the law, he is first deemed born before the mother died: this is expressly held by Odofredus in d. l. anniculus, §. falsum, on the word extractus. Odofredus says that is, cut and extracted from the womb, and the son is considered as already born, as in ff. de inofficiosa testamento, l. posthumus. Odofredus in his lecture, which I have, and if it is expedient I will send it: however, it should not be necessary, because I ought to be believed when citing authoritative doctors. Since therefore we are dealing with a son, he is considered as born, and it clearly follows from this that he was instituted, and consequently it follows that the substitution is valid. The aforementioned §. falsum in the text does not obstruct this, because that §. must be understood in the case of a stranger, not in the case of a son. For example, when the testator left something to the mother if she gave birth, or to his friend under the same condition. But when he instituted a son, then that §. does not apply. Moreover, there the testator did not dispose in favor of the womb, here he did. And this response is very clear. But one might doubt, because the male was not an immediate birth, but a mediated one from a second pregnancy, whether he is included in the words of the will? And I say that he is, first by the case of l. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. placet. Second, by the case of the will, because there the testator said, one or more. For more rarely are born from one womb, but rarely: hence, considering what commonly happens, the words should be referred to successive pregnancies: nor should they be restricted to one and the same, because the mind should conform to natural things, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutis, and ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum auus, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter. Also, even in one womb one is born first, another later: and yet each is instituted, as in l. 1 §. quare, ff. de ventre in possessionem mittendo. Nor does it matter that the daughter was the firstborn, because she was mentioned separately. Moreover, separate cases include the disposition that results from the conjunction of the members of the disposition, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. si ita scriptum, and ff. de heredibus instituendis, l. Clemens patronus.

† My beloved [client] asks me whether a substitution made by these words, “if it should happen that my son dies before the legitimate age of testating,” is a compendious substitution limited by time, which encompasses both a true pupillary substitution and a true vulgar substitution, and both as if expressly stated, or whether it is merely a pupillary substitution. I am accustomed to saying, and it is the truth, that it is a compendious substitution limited by time. Hence, if the ward dies while the father is alive, the substitution does not vanish; for it is not a tacit vulgar substitution, but an express vulgar substitution. And thus, it is no obstacle that in the Digest, in the title *De captivis*, the law *Quod filius*, and in the Digest, in the title *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, the law *Lex Cornelia*, hold the opinion of Dyonisius. For that is true when the testator would say thus: “My son shall be heir.” For that word can be understood to mean, unless he survives his father. For while the father is alive, it is certain that he is not the heir of his father, as in the Code, in the title *De captivis et postliminio reversis*, the law *Nec nos*; and in the Code, in the title *De pace*, the law *Si*; and in the Code, in the title *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, the Authentica *Si qua mulier*. And this applies if he dies while the father is alive. But if he dies after the father’s death, then, the father’s inheritance having been accepted by the ward, the compendious substitution turns into a mere pupillary substitution, by the general form of the substitution itself and the nature of its words, as I said in the first consultation. To this also contributes the common opinion, that a substitute appointed to the universality of goods, with mention of the pupillary age, or what is held to be the same, is a substitute appointed by the direct path, i.e., directly; because the pupillary age is appended as a time and as a term of the substitution; which is not of the nature of a fideicommissary substitution, unless it were an express fideicommissary substitution, as in the Code, in the title *De institutionibus et substitutionibus*, the law *Generaliter*; and in the Digest, in the title *Ad Trebellianum*, the law *Scaevola*; and in the Digest, in the title *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, the law *Qui habebat*, rendering each thing to its respective members. But if the testator did not express these words, “if heir,” but said, “if he should die in pupillary age,” it is certain that if he dies while the father is alive, the condition is nevertheless fulfilled, and the substitution is purified. In this substitution, the contrary is true, when the prince writes by rescript with certain knowledge, in the case of litis motae et pendentes, and thus the custom of princes is observed, even if the clause “notwithstanding” is not appended. See the law *Ut lite pendente* and the said title in the middle of the section on litis motae. And this is true, unless something was concealed from the prince in the matter of fact; for then the rescript would not be valid, as in the Digest, in the title *De tutoribus et curatoribus dandis ab his*, the law *Tutor si petitus*; and in the Extravagantes, in the title *De rescriptis*, the chapter *Super literis*. Having seen the validity of the rescript, presupposing that it is valid,

It is asked how the said rescript is to be understood, namely, that justice be done notwithstanding contumacy. And it seems that contumacy does not harm in any way, because the prince pardons it; thus the burden of proof remains upon the parties, as from the beginning, because the prince appears to have established this by his benevolence, as is permitted. See *extra de dolo, et contumacia*, c. 1. To the contrary it seems, because fraud ought not to remain unpunished; at least the burden of proof ought to be transferred back to the adversary, as in *ff. de novo operis nuntiatio*, l. *si is prius*. Moreover, the prince is not understood to intend, nor to will, that which he ought not to will by law or written equity, as in *extra de restitutione spoliorum*, c. *audita*. Nevertheless, although the plaintiff does not prove his case, the fisc cannot demand anything from him, because the fisc, or the lord, deprived him of the opportunity to prove, as in *C. de probationibus*, l. *de possessione*. Moreover, the adversary cannot object contumacy against him, because whatever right one establishes for another, he himself shall use the same right, as in l. 1, *ff. quod quisque iuris in alterum statuerit*, and *de constitutionibus*, cum *accessissent*. Moreover, because equality ought to be observed in judicial proceedings, as in l. *fin.*, *C. de fructibus et litis expensis*. Therefore, since the prince granted pardon, and by pardoning abolished contumacy, a term ought to be fixed for the plaintiff to prove his case; and if he does not prove, the defendant has sufficiently made his defense, as in *C. de edendo*, l. *qui accusare*. Unless, as I said above, something was concealed from the prince, for then the rescript would not be valid, and the defendant ought to be condemned as contumacious and confessing. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the womb is instituted in this manner, namely, if she were to bear a son, and the child is extracted from the mother’s body after the pregnant mother has died, whether such an institution or substitution takes effect, because he is not properly born, but cut from the womb. And see below, consilium 128.
2. A substitution made by these words, if it should happen that my son dies before the legitimate age for making a will, whether it is pupillary or compendious.
body: In the name of Christ. The words of the testator say thus: he instituted the womb of his wife, if she were pregnant, and if she bore, or should bear, one or more male children, he instituted them as his heirs in equal shares. But if she were not pregnant, or if she bore, and should bear, as is stated above, and it should happen that they die before the legitimate age for making a will, and do not reach that age, etc. The residue of all his other goods he left to the works of the church of Saint Michael: and he appointed executors. It happened that the wife of the testator first bore a daughter, then in another pregnancy died in childbirth, and a male child was extracted from the womb, who lived for only one day or less. Hence it is asked whether there is place for the said substitution.

† And it seems to be a case according to the letter of the law that the answer is no, because it is false to say that she gave birth, who died before childbirth, as in D. 50.17.1 (de verborum significatione), l. Anniculus, §. Eum. To the contrary, it seems expressly stated that she is said to have given birth who died in the puerperium, as in D. 1.5.1 (de statu hominum), l. Aretusa, together with the following law. On this point, the advocates of the city of Lucca are in doubt. I have previously advised that the said substitution applies: my opinion is the very truth, notwithstanding any contrary opinions, because they are frivolous. And it must be considered that when the testator says, “I institute the womb,” he who is in the womb is instituted, whether he is born with the mother alive or is expelled from the womb. For when the testator says “the womb,” the sentence is complete; and whatever is added is a certain demonstration, which does not invalidate, even if we have true knowledge in another way than by way of demonstration. This is the case: D. 28.5.1 (de liberis et posthumis), l. Titius, §. Lucius. Secondly, this is proven because sometimes mention is made of the birth with respect to the man who begets, sometimes with respect to the woman who conceives. In the first case, it is most true to say that the child was produced from the seed: hence, whether the wife dies in the puerperium or after childbirth, the substitution cannot be other than vulgar, since it is direct in the case when she dies during the father’s lifetime; but a fideicommissary substitution cannot be made pro parte if the son dies during the father’s lifetime, as in D. 36.1.1 (de vulgari substitutione), l. Cohaeredi, §. Cum filiae. Moreover, this seems evident by the clearest reason, for it is the same to say “if he should die in pupillary age” as to say “if he should die at any time in pupillary age”; because the word “at any time” is understood, as in D. 36.1.1, l. Centurio. For no one doubts that the word “at any time” pertains to the compendious form, as in c. Si pater, de testibus, lib. 6. And it should be known that this vulgar substitution can also be made in a legacy; and it could have been made to the daughter, a female, in our case, if the testator had so wished, as in D. 35.2.1 (de legatis secundis), l. Ut haeredibus. For a vulgar substitution can also be made in the legitime, as in D. 28.5.1, l. Si posthumus a primo, §. Quod vulgo perpendat. Therefore, I believe I advised faithfully for the work of the church of Saint Michael, first out of reverence for God, secondly out of respect for the majesty of the truth. The principal doubt, which concerns l. Anniculus, §. Falsum, is in no way doubtful, because that §. in no way touches our case; and thus I advised for the work, and whoever would advise the contrary would depart from the truth and fail in the true understanding of the laws. For as the ordinary gloss says, because laws often seem to will something other than what they will, masters and students are often deceived, and especially when they do not weigh the words of the testaments, which have great weight in themselves for ascertaining what is meant. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the creditor’s hypothec is extinguished if he himself purchases from his debtor, and subsequently resells to him the goods which were previously pledged to him.
2. Whether a creditor, who is prior in rank, having purchased from the debtor the pledged goods, is bound to the subsequent creditors.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain Alexander bound himself for a certain sum to a certain Augustine and his brother, pledging all his present and future goods, as well as to several other creditors, who ultimately assigned their rights to the said brothers. Finally, the said Alexander made a sale of certain things to the said brothers. And note that this was not a *datio in solutum* (payment in kind) for the prior credits, but a simple sale. Finally, the said Alexander and the said brothers made a compromise before a certain arbitrator on account of the said sale; who, the arbitrator, ordered that, if the said Alexander gave and paid the price of the said sale within a certain term, the said brothers were bound to resell the said things to the said Alexander. And having made the said sale, immediately the said brothers leased the said houses and lands to the said Alexander; and afterwards they made a resale of the said things to the said Alexander, with the saving and reservation that by the said resale no prejudice should arise to the said brothers regarding any of their rights competent over the said things returned to the said brothers by obligation and hypothec, as above, but that the said right should remain safe. After the aforesaid, the said Alexander made a sale and *datio in solutum* of the said things to the said brothers for the prior portions owed; which things the said brothers hold. Now a certain other creditor of the said Alexander, however posterior in time to the said brothers, brings a hypothecary action against the said brothers. The question is whether the said brothers, for the said ancient debt, in which they are prior in time, can defend themselves against the new creditor bringing a hypothecary action. And the question rests on this: whether the hypothec of the said brothers is extinguished, because they purchased the hypothecated things and became owners, or because they again resold them, or because they again and finally purchased them once more and received them in *solutum*, or not.

And it seems that one should say that the ancient hypothec was extinguished, and this can be proven by several reasons. First, because the creditor, by purchasing from the debtor, appears to consent to the debtor selling the pledge, and thus the pledge is discharged, as in D. 20.5.1 (*Sicut*), § *venditionis* (Who and in what manner pledges or hypothecs are discharged). Second, because by such a purchase they became owners, and therefore they cannot hold their own property as hypothecated, as in D. 50.17.107 (*Neque pignus*) (On the rules of law). Third, because the said hypothec has reached a case from which it cannot begin, and therefore it is overcome, as in D. 50.16.107 (*Pluribus*), § *et si placet*, and D. 50.16.110 (*Existimo*) (On verbal obligations). Fourth, because once the thing has been released from the bond of the pledge, and therefore it never falls back into it, as in C. 8.13.1 (*Solita providem*) (On things pledged). Fifth, it seems that the law expressly determines this: for when the creditor has received what was unpaid, the personal obligation is extinguished, and therefore also its accessory hypothecary obligation, as is read and noted in D. 2.15.1 (*Si tibi*), § *de pignore* (On pacts). To the contrary, it seems that the said brothers, who were also the creditors, reserved to themselves the rights of the hypothec, which reservation is valid, as in D. 20.5.1 (*Si debitor*), § *si in venditione* (Who and in what manner pledges or hypothecs are discharged), and there the ordinary gloss seems to determine this question literally.

† Question. If the prior creditor purchases from the debtor, is he bound to the subsequent creditors? And it seems that he is not, since the bond of the pledge is now dissolved. To the contrary, because it appears that he would have wished to be released from the bond of the pledge if the transfer made by the debtor had been irrevocable, as in the argument from the title *De separatione bonorum*, law *Debitor*, and it is expressly stated in the Code, title *Si antiquior creditor*, law 1, at the end, and in the Digest, title *De exceptione rei iudicatae*, law *Ex sextante*, section *Latius*. Thus says the very notable gloss in the Digest, title *Qui potioribus in pignore habentur*, law *Qui a debitore suo*. And especially because here the transfer was not initially *in solutum* (in satisfaction of the debt), but a simple sale, and thus we are not in the controversy discussed in the law *Libera quidem Theodora*, title *De senatu et interlocutionibus*, and in the Digest, title *De pignoris actione*, law *Eleganter*, in the beginning, and law *Qui res*, in the beginning, title *De solutionibus*. And although the final transfer was *in solutum*, it was made with reservation and protestation; and thus the right of the protesting party remained safe, as in the aforementioned law *Si debitor*. To understand the truth, distinguish four cases. For sometimes one possesses the thing first pledged to himself, then to another; sometimes, on the contrary, first pledged to another, then pledged only to himself. In the first case, it is certain that he defends his hypothecary right if he possesses. In the second case, he does not defend his hypothecary right unless the debt is offered to him. And thus speaks that famous gloss cited above. In the third case, his hypothec still endures on account of the right of offer, until the prior creditor is dismissed; for once he is dismissed, his hypothec would endure in vain, since he has full and irrevocable dominion; and a thing irrevocably made his own cannot be hypothecated to himself, as in the Digest, title *De captivis*, law *In libello*, section *Si quis servum*. In the fourth and final case, when the thing was pledged to himself as the purchaser, the right of pledge is dissolved, so that no one can evict him. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The archpriest has jurisdiction over his subordinates and may issue commands to them; and on account of such exercise of jurisdiction, he cannot be mulcted by his bishop.
body: In the name of Christ.

† An archpriest who has canons under him has jurisdiction, and the power even to excommunicate, since he is in full administration, *de officio ordinario*, c. *Cum ab ecclesiarum praesulibus*; and *de maioribus et obedientia*, c. *Cum in ecclesiis*, according to Innocentius and Hostiensis, and *eo titulo*, *Quanto*, *de officio archipresbyteri*, with what is said *de iudicibus*, *Decernimus*; and there by Bartolus, where he says that all prelates who are in possession of their prelature are ordinary judges of their subjects. Hence, this archpriest undoubtedly has jurisdiction. Nevertheless, a matter which cannot be exercised without cognition of the cause, if it exists outside the territory, he cannot exercise, as in l. 2, ff. *de officio proconsulis et legati*; and ff. *de iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, l. *Extra territorium*; and in c. *Ut animarum*, with its material. For whether one is outside the territory or judging strangers, it is said that he proceeds illicitly, as C. *de decurionibus*, l. *Duumviri*, lib. 10. But where cognition of the cause is not required, as in those matters which are of voluntary jurisdiction, such jurisdiction can be exercised anywhere in an honest place, as in the said l. 2, *de officio proconsulis*; the same applies to mandates, which superiors issue to their subjects in those matters which can be mandated without judgment: namely, in those which pertain to observance, or constitution, or rule; especially because no one’s prejudice is at stake, arg. ff. *de arbitris*, l. *Diem proferre*, in the beginning; and what is noted by Innocentius in c. 1, *de iudicibus*, lib. 6.

Therefore, these things being considered, because he mandated what was just, and because he justified his precept in two ways, namely, that he could do so by law, and that he could not come to the place, it must be said that by the mandate he justifies himself: he has not incurred any penalty, because in the case where it could not be done by law, or by place, or by time, the act appears not to have been done, as ff. *de actionibus et obligationibus*, l. *Non solum*; and ff. *de manumissionibus testamento*, l. *Si quis locupletior*, in the end.

Moreover, a fine could not be imposed without cognition, and without assigning a term to the archpriest himself for making his defense, as C. *communia episcoporum*, l. *Praeses*; and l. *Inter locutionem*; and it is expressly stated, ff. *de re militari*, l. 3, § *Si ad diem*. Moreover, by the swiftness of correction, it is understood that he has purged any fault there may have been, as ff. *de adulteriis*, l. *Si adulterium cum incestu*, § *Fratres*; and § *Idem Pollioni*; and *de officio praesidis*, l. *Illicitas*, § *Finis*; ff. *de in ius vocando*, l. *Quamvis*. For in extraordinary crimes, repentance has place while the matter is entire, let alone here, where there was no crime, as noted in l. *Et hoc edicto*, § *Pe*, ff. *de aliena indicii mutata causa facta*; and there the gloss *ordinaria*, on account of which it is openly concluded that the said fine cannot be exacted from the said archpriest; especially since the severe penalties of fines are not accustomed to be extorted except on account of contumacy, as ff. *de verborum significatione*, l. *Aliud*, inter *mulctam*; and C. *de modo mulctarum*, d. *Eos*, non obstantibus c. *Sacro*, *de sententia excommunicationis*, because another case is there.

I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. From what presumptions is a contract presumed to be simulated, usurious, and illicit.
2. A transaction may be made concerning fraud, provided that the fraud itself is not contained therein.
body: In the name of Christ.

† There were three contracts: one for three hundred florins, on the ground of a loan; another of sale for a certain price for the said three hundred florins and additionally for three florins. The third contract was a transaction between the aforementioned parties, and in the name of the transaction a similar sale was made for the said three hundred florins, and the said debtor confessed that, in addition to the said three hundred florins, he had received from the aforementioned lender, as above, one hundred seventy-four livres of tertioli, by reason of the said transaction. And for the confirmation of the said instrument of sale, the debtor therefore states that all these contracts were made in fraud of usury; and he seeks to have them rescinded and judged illicit and usurious. And it was proven that the said creditor was a manifest usurer; and this also appears from his caution. However, it does not seem to have been specially proven that the said first contract was usurious; but I presuppose that it was so in truth, and that no doubt remains except concerning the said transaction. The question is therefore: what is the law? I answer: if the obligation of three hundred florins was usurious, whatever followed from it or by it must be revoked as void, as in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium, §. si. For from the beginning the subsequent event is shaped by the title, as in C. de imponendis lucrativis descriptionibus, l. 1, lib. 10. And not the title of the contract, but the origin must be examined, as in D. de donationibus, l. qui id quod; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. tutor. And this appears manifestly, because in every subsequent contract usury was tacitly included, and whatever exceeds the principal by any colored contract is usury, as noted in D. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, §. si tibi. And a confession made against a usurer is suspect of fraud of usury, as noted by Guillaume and Cynus expressly in D. de pactis, l. si tibi, 10 milia, in principio. Moreover, fraud is presumed from successive cautions, as noted in l. 6, D. de conditione instituta, in the gloss, noted. Moreover, this was not a transaction, but a sordid concession; and this appears from the order of the titles or contracts, and from the vacillation or variety of them. That the purchase was not free from pure fraud appears, because it does not accord nor confront the truth. For in vain would the price of one hundred seventy-four livres have been added in the subsequent contract of transaction, unless because the first sale was tainted with usurious depravity. And fraud is presumed from the variety of contracts, as in C. de mandato, l. ab Anastasio.

† I do not say that a good-faith settlement cannot be made concerning a usurious dispute, since a settlement can be made concerning any fraud, unless a defect is found in the settlement, as in C. de plus petendo, l. 1. But here a defect was repeated, because a usurious amount was included under the sum of three hundred and three florins and another sum of one hundred and seventy-four pounds, as in D. de rebus dubiis, l. Si is qui ducenta, § 1, propter fermentum. Therefore, the entire mass of usury is corrupted, according to the principle that a little leaven corrupts the whole mass, as noted in D. de pactis, l. Si unus, § pactus. This also appears from natural and civil reason. For no one who has once bought something purely and freely can buy it again and add a new price; since no new purchase can exist for a thing already sold and transferred, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. Neque pignus, and D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Rei suae. But if true payment had appeared, the pawn contract could have been converted into a sale contract through a release from the pledge and an acquisition of ownership, as in l. Ex sextante, § Lucius, D. de exceptione rei iudicatae. But in our case, true payment does not appear. Moreover, a settlement made in fraud of the canons is not valid, as in l. Non dubium, with similar authorities. From these, it is concluded that the said Vicar can take cognizance of the said petitions, or rather has in a sense already taken cognizance; furthermore, the order, connection, and sequence of the events clearly declare this to anyone who rightly considers them, as in D. de transactionibus, l. Cum hi, § ex causa, and § si praetor, and it is done excellently. C. de transactionibus, l. Cum ea est; C. de fidei instrumentis, l. Scriptura; and C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 2. And from the coherence and successive origin of the contracts, fraud between prohibited parties is detected, as in D. de probationibus, l. Qui testamentum. I, Baldus. See below in consilium 137, where some matters are placed at the end that are not placed here.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a posthumous child, or the womb of a son under paternal power who had acquired many goods from his military estate, shall be put in possession of the military goods upon the mother’s request, or whether the grandfather himself shall hold possession; and whether a curator ought to be appointed for the womb; and whether the mother or the grandfather shall be the curator; and whether the child, once born, shall be raised with the mother for three years even against the grandfather’s will.
2. The grandfather may make a pupillary substitution for the posthumous child.
3. We ought not to consider what may happen, but the present state of affairs.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain noble son of a family acquired much from his military pay through his prowess in arms, and other things by roaming about the whole country with other armed retainers, committing violence and extorting goods, as is the custom in Italy. This man died, his father being still alive, under whose power he was; and he left behind a pregnant wife, who seeks to be admitted in the name of the unborn child to possession of the good estate of her late husband. But the father, under whose power the said noble armed retainer had been, objects.

† Now it is asked, what is the law regarding castrense and quasi-castrense property; for there is no doubt concerning adventitious property, that the sole father of the said nobleman has the usufruct, as C. de bonis quae liberis l. cum oportet. And it is argued first in favor of the father: for if a posthumous child, who is in utero, is considered as born, therefore administration pertains to the father, just as it would pertain to a born impubes, since he is born in his power, arg. ff. de negotiorum gestorum l. cum pater. Likewise, just as he would be the legitimate administrator of the goods of his grandson, as C. de bonis matri l. 1, so he ought to be the legitimate administrator according to the ancient reason of the species of one to be born: for either the child will not be born, and the goods pertain to the said nobleman’s father himself, because he succeeds his son intestate; or he will be born, and administration and usufruct even of the castrense goods of the son pertain to the grandfather himself, as ff. de acquisitione hereditatis l. Paulus §. si. Since therefore, in every event, the right of paternal power is certain, taking into consideration the son or grandson, therefore the mother cannot reclaim possession for herself. And thus she ought not to be put in such possession as in the name of the womb. Moreover, she ought not to be given license or capacity to administer or touch [the property], because in this there could be danger to the father, as ff. qui satisdare coguntur l. si fideiussor §. fin.

† Moreover, a grandfather may make a pupillary substitution in favor of a posthumous child, and entirely exclude the mother, should it happen that the boy is born and dies while still in pupillary age, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari et pupillari substitutione*, law *Moribus*, § 1, and law *Sed et si plures*, § *Ad substitutos*.

And briefly, the contrary view seems more correct, because we ought not to consider what may come to pass, but the present state; once that state is fulfilled, the one in the womb is part of the mother’s viscera, and the mother’s right is stronger over him, as stated in the Digest, *De ventre in possessionem mittendo*, l. 1, and noted in the same law *Cum pater*. And this applies not only while he is in the womb, but until the age of three years, while he is at the breast. Hence, the grandfather could not in the meantime take the grandson away from the mother, unless she were to enter into second vows, as in c. *Ultima*, Extra, *De conversione infidelium*, with the very notable gloss. It therefore seems to be said that the mother ought to be put in possession of the womb to obtain certain effects which such possession of the womb produces, which the law does not otherwise grant; however, so that a curator be appointed to the womb or to the goods, who shall perform those acts which pertain to the office of said curator; provided, however, that movable property and money remain in safekeeping with the same church, as in l. *Ita autem*, in the beginning, Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, so that they do not come into the hands of either said father or said woman, until nature reveals the end of the birth. The revenues of said moneys, however, come to be disposed of and administered by said curator, according to what is said in l. 1, § *Curator*, Digest, *De ventre in possessionem mittendo*, with the *si*. I nevertheless advise said mother, and those who have counsel for her, that they rather treat this matter amicably than contentiously with the father-in-law, because much can be done in this matter, as is clear from the above; and perhaps in this case said grandfather ought to be appointed curator, and not the mother, nor another. On the matter of this curatorship, see the notable points in the Speculum, *De successione ab intestato*. And I said this in the preceding counsel, which is cited below in counsel 137. Therefore, without doubt, said noble lady can demand three things: first, that she be put in possession of the womb in name; second, that a curator be appointed to the goods or to neither, as in l. 2, § *Sed si mater*, Digest, *Ad Tertullianum*, although the Speculum says that it never saw a curator appointed to the womb. But whether a curator be appointed to the goods or to the womb, he must make an inventory and ensure that movables, and especially money, are not concealed nor can be squandered even by the paternal grandfather, because he is not yet the legitimate administrator, since he does not have the un-born womb in his power, as in l. *Ultima*, Digest, *De assignandis libertis*, and l. *Si*, Digest, *De collatione bonorum*. Thirdly, she can demand that, when the womb is born, she may have the boy with her for three years, even against the will of the grandfather, as is fully noted in Extra, *De conversione infidelium*, c. *Si*, unless she contracted second marriages, as in the Authenticum, *De nuptiis*, § *Omnes quoque*. But he will be born into the power of the paternal grandfather, and the curatorship will cease when he begins to be in the power of the grandfather; and the grandfather will be the legitimate administrator, as in l. 1, Code, *De bonis matri*, in l. *Cum oportet*, and l. *Cum non solum*, *De bonis quae liberis*. However, so that neither the grandfather, if he is ill-behaved or suspect, can squander them, Digest, *Ad Trebellianum*, l. *Imperator*, Code, *De senatus consulto Pegasiano*, l. *Si*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A fief granted for renewal must be renewed, so that the church may obtain its due relief; otherwise, the vassal falls into penalties.
body: In the name of Christ. Certain nobles received certain estates in fief with the condition attached that they could lease and let them for a fixed term, or for ten years renewable; these nobles thus leased them, namely, for ten years renewable.

† It is asked, if the renewal has not followed nor been made, whether these properties have reverted to the monastery or to the said nobles. And it seems that they revert to the monastery. Because the pact was appended with the monastery and was not observed. It is established that from this pact the right of the monastery is acquired, as in C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2, in principio, and in column 10 of quibus modis feudum amittitur, §. est et alia. And this is due to the breach of contract; for the church ought to have vengeance for its injury. Since the emphyteuta did not care to have the pact observed, nor did he interpellate the subtenants, he fell from his right on account of his own fault, because he is bound not only for his own act, but for the act of those who derive their title from him, as in ff. de verbis obligatis, l. si servum, §. de illo, and l. stipulatio ista habere licere, §. 1. And therefore, the law is committed against him, from whom the pact is not observed. For he would not complain of the right of a third party, but of his own interest, as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, Auth. qui res iam dictas, and ff. locati conducti, l. quaero, §. inter locatorem. That he ought to do this and take care of it is proved by what is said and noted in ff. de verbis obligatis, l. si ita quis, §. ea, and l. et ff. de pactis, l. non impossibile puto. And this is especially so if a laudemium ought to be paid to the church for the renewal, just as if a fictum ought to have been paid and was not paid, and several years had elapsed; for the penalty is incurred even if the least thing is not paid, as in ff. familiae herciscundae, l. haeredes, §. idem iuris.

To the contrary, it seems that this lease was not tacitly renewed for renewal. For a fief requires writing, unless there are equal witnesses, as in c. 1, de feudo guardiae et castaldiae. And where writing is required, the thing does not seem to be tacitly re-leased. The text is noted in ff. locati conducti, l. item quaeritur, §. qui impleto, in fine. If, therefore, the said sublease was terminated by time, as in C. locati conducti, l. si cum haereditas, but not reverted, because it was not granted: therefore, when the time is finished, it returns by operation of law to its first state, and thus the church has no right of claiming it.

Solution: If nothing has been done to the prejudice of the church, it does not return to the church, because there is no fault; but if something had been done to the prejudice of the church, for example because the church ought to receive a laudemium for renewals to be made, then it would revert to the church, because the vassal did not keep the church indemnified in this matter; rather, through his own fault, the church suffered injury. And this is clear expressly from the laws cited above. Moreover, the thing was subleased contrary to the pact, considering the outcome; therefore, the church has the right of revocation, as in the said §. Est et alia, and §. finis, in the title quae fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi, and in ca. Imperialem, §. illud, de prohibita feudi alienatione, per Federicum.

From these things it follows that the vassal can not only renew, but must renew, so that the church may obtain the laudemium, if it is customary to pay it, because he is bound to manage the thing of his lord faithfully with regard to the fief itself. But if there is no custom that a laudemium be paid to the lord for a renewal made by the vassals to their subtenant, then the lord cannot complain of the right of the vassal, as is noted in l. 1, §. 1, and in l. 2, ff. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticarius petatur.

I, Baldus de Ubaldis. This following opinion tends to the same thing as was consulted above in consilium 122.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a testament in which a posthumous son has been passed over becomes valid under civil law or praetorian law.
2. Whether a substitution made to the womb, if she bore a male and died before the age of legal capacity to make a will, is valid and comprehends only the womb that existed at the time of the testament; and what kind of substitution this is.
body: In the name of Christ. For the understanding of two doubts, it must be premised,

† that the said testament was null: because the daughter, who was in the power of the testator, was passed over, to whom nothing was left by way of institution, as in the Authent. Ut cum de appel. cogno. §. aliud quoque capitulum. unless the local statute provided that it would suffice if left under any title whatsoever, as was the case under the codified law, as C. de inof. test. l. omni modo. And although the daughter died during the lifetime of her father, nevertheless it seems that the testament does not become valid, as ff. de li. et posth. l. filius, qui in potestate. and Inst. de exhaereda. libe. in prin. But nevertheless the contrary is true in this case, when the son of the testator was instituted heir, as ff. de iniu. test. l. posthumus. ver. idem et circa. for then it becomes valid by praetorian law as regards the first degree of institution: however, because the son died immediately, and did not claim possession of the goods according to the will, the institution of the son seems to be in the category of a lapsed legacy. since possession is not transmitted to heirs if it has not been claimed, as ff. de bo. pos. l. 3. §. et acquirere. But by civil law the testament does not become valid, as ff. si tabulae testa. nullae exta. l. 1. in fi. and no. ff. de in iu. test. l. cum in secundo. and C. de contrata. l. posthu. It follows therefore, that if the testament is null due to the passing over of the posthumous child, the vulgar substitution made to the male son does not hold. It is, namely, vulgar: because the testator said, if she were not born, as ff. de ven. inspi. l. qui ventri.

But a doubt remains, whether a substitution made to the womb, if it bears a male, and he dies before the lawful age of testating, has effect: and before I come to this, it is necessary to premise such a question, namely, whether the aforesaid testament is understood to refer only to the womb that existed at the time of the testator’s act, as in D. de legatis 2, l. si ita scripsisset. The contrary is true, because the testator did not say, “if she is pregnant,” but said, “if she were pregnant”: which is understood to mean whenever, from the testator’s words, she might be pregnant, by argument from C. de posthumis heredibus instituendis, l. si, and D. de liberis et posthumis, l. patet. For in doubt we must interpret that the testament is valid, and that the testator intended necessary cases, as noted in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § videndum. Hence, when different pregnancies produced a daughter and a son, I understand the testator to have intended both, namely, the daughter by legacy, and the son by institution; and I say that it was a pupillary substitution, because those words, “if he should die before the lawful age of testating,” express this sense, i.e., if he should die in pupillary age, because that is the age of not testating, as in D. de testamentis, l. qua aetate. Hence there was an express condition, if he should die in pupillary age: wherefore the substitution is formally and figuratively pupillary. But then immediately the question arises, whether the said substitution vanishes on account of the omission of the said female: and the glossa says that a pupillary substitution is not vitiated by reason of omission, as noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. 1. And the same is held by Bartolus, although Dino del Garbo holds the contrary opinion to the glossa. I consider the glossa’s opinion true when the pupillary substitution is made to an instituted heir, and not to an omitted one: as is the case in our instance. But if it were made to an omitted impubes, then Dino’s opinion would be true, by argument from D. de legatis 3, l. ex filio, and C. de fideicommissis, l. pene. And therefore, in the question proposed, for the work of the church of Saint Michael, I opine both as to the paternal inheritance, which is entirely devolved to the posthumous child, because the sister died during the father’s lifetime; and also as to the maternal inheritance, because only the male survived; and although he was born in the eighth month, which according to physicians cannot truly live, nevertheless it suffices that he lived for a moment, as in C. de posthumis heredibus instituendis, l. uxoris abortu, and l. quod certarum. And so I opine on these points, and on the codicillary clause, if it is expedient to treat it, since the pupillary substitution is valid by direct law. Moreover, know that institution and pupillary substitution are valid by direct law. Moreover, know that institution and substitution comprehend similar cases, i.e., where there is the same intention and reason, although there is some diversity in fact, because we must look to the reality of the intention, as in C. de posthumis heredibus instituendis, l. si, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. si, and l. si mater. But extraction from the womb in reality differs nothing from being born, nor is it to be imputed to the testator if he did not consider an unusual case, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. si mater. Moreover, in confirmation of my opinion in the preceding, it serves that a substitution under the condition, if he dies while the testator lives, is vulgar. And the same if it is a case that can be conceived from the words, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, in principio, and § 1. Moreover, it serves from de ventre inspiciendo, l. qui ventri, and de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thais ancilla, § splendidus forus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made by a mother, both pupillary and direct, in favor of her son is invalid or valid by the law of the fideicommissum; and whether, if the son dies during his pupillary age while the mother who made the will is still living, the substitution lapses.
body: In the name of Christ. Lady Francisca, formerly of Odo, made a will, in which, among other things, she instituted Conrad, her son, as her universal heir; and if by chance the said Conrad, her son, should die within fourteen years, namely in pupillary age, she substituted Peter, her brother, or his heirs, as heir to herself; and she asserts that this is her last will, which she wished to be valid by the law of wills; and if it were not valid by the law of wills, at least let it be valid by the law of codicils, or of another last will, by which it may better be valid and hold according to law. Finally, the said Conrad, the instituted heir, died, with the said Lady Francisca, his mother, and the said Peter, his uncle, surviving; finally, the said Peter died, with the said Lady Francisca surviving, and with Michael and Margaret, his children, surviving; afterwards, the said Lady Francisca, the testatrix, died; finally, the said Michael and Margaret died; to whom Benedict succeeded, who says that the inheritance of the said testatrix pertains to him. Now the question is, what is the law: presupposing two statutes of the city of Genoa, one of which provides that if anyone capable of making a will, or last will, or other disposition in contemplation of last will, has made it, although the institutions or substitutions were not made according to the laws, nevertheless the disposition made in contemplation of last will shall be firm, if there are five competent witnesses, etc. The other statute, or chapter of the statutes, contains the following: "Also, if the father or grandfather of a pupil, male or female, having made a will, shall die, let it be observed according as he ordered; so much so that if he was silent in substitution for the said pupil, male or female, and did not make a pupillary substitution according to the laws, nevertheless let it be understood that an express vulgar and pupillary substitution was made; so that neither the mother nor any other person may claim anything, except according as they could claim by law, if a pupillary substitution had been made by the father or grandfather; but after the time of puberty, let it be understood and be such as it would have been by law." And of this second statute I shall say nothing, because it does not bear on the case, since it speaks only of fathers or paternal grandfathers making substitutions.
