† I therefore answer the question asked, and first I inquire whether, if Conrad died in pupillary age while the said testatrix was still alive, the said substitution has entirely failed? And it seems that it has, for the words of the said substitution are formally words of a pupillary substitution, save that the condition "if he shall be heir" was not added; for from the mention of age, it is understood to be pupillary, as noted in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. precibus, and in D. eodem, l. et l. institutis, de pupillari substitutione, in principio. Although a pupillary substitution made by a mother does not hold, as noted in l. si mater, D. de vulgari substitutione, because she does not have the pupillus in her power, as is read and noted in the same title, l. moribus, this pupillary substitution therefore did not hold as a pupillary one, nor as a tacit vulgar one, because the pupillus died while the testatrix was alive, as is read and noted in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. lex Cornelia, de privilegiis creditorum, l. pater, and it is expressly stated in D. de captivis, l. quod si filius.

On the contrary, it seems, first, from the ordinary gloss which is in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. verbis civilibus, a gloss which all doctors commonly hold, that if a mother substitutes for her son pupillarily and directly, the substitution is not altogether useless, but rather it is valid by the law of fideicommissum. And thus hold Guillaume de Coucy, Decius, Raymond, and Bartolus. And this is proven by natural reason, because the ignorance of a woman, who does not know what a pupillary substitution or a vulgar one is, should not prejudice her true and real intention, arg. D. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, § fin., and C. de testamento, l. quam indignum. For even the judge should be compelled by the power granted to him by law to uphold the last will, so that it may be valid and not perish, as C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas, and l. si, D. de manumissione testamento, crudelis est. For an interpretation which is directed towards overturning the judgments of the deceased is entirely alien to law and truth. Hence, even if the words of the fideicommissum were lacking, we must nevertheless take that speech as a fideicommissum, arg. D. de legatis 2, l. unum ex familia, § Item Imperator Marcus. And this is confirmed because the testator wished it to be valid even by the law of codicils or another last will, by which it could better be valid according to law. By these words, even a direct substitution is turned into an oblique one, if it could not be valid at any time by direct law, as D. ad Trebellianam, l. Scevola. Although that clause, that it be valid by the law of codicils, placed absolutely, is not referred to, according to the gloss which is in Auth. ex causa, unless due to a defect of solemnity of witnesses; which gloss has no place here, because the testator proceeded further: for he wished it to be valid in any way in which it could be better valid. Moreover, that gloss is not commonly held according to Decius and Cynus.

But here it must be observed, because I hold in l. precibus that a substitution made by these words, "if he shall die within such age," comprehends all time during which he dies within pupillary age; for no reason restricting the time runs, whether he dies during her life or after. Hence, as it adapts to the time, and the quality of the persons, and the case by which the way of substitution is opened, such a substitution is considered to have been made by compendium of time, as if the testator had said: "But certainly if it is a fideicommissary substitution, this cannot be made to an instituted heir dying during the life of the testatrix; for the instituted heir cannot enter upon the inheritance, as C. de fideicommissis, l. eam quam. Hence, if this substitution is fideicommissary, it has undoubtedly failed, as l. si nemo, D. de regulis iuris. But my opinion is that this substitution is compendious, similar in that respect, and contains a vulgar one, by l. qui ventri, D. de ventre in possessionem, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. si. And I believe that my opinion is the very truth: however, if he who has to judge wished to adhere to the common opinion of law, that this substitution made by a mother was fideicommissary, it would undoubtedly be in the case of caducity, unless we said that it was transferred by the codicillary clause to the clause of intestacy. But from this head I do not see that anything was done or disputed in court, and therefore from this head the defendant could not be condemned. Nor does the statute of Genoa stand in the way, because it can and should be understood according to the common law, as C. de noxali actione, l. 2, and Extra de consuetudinibus, c. cum dilectus. Indeed, the said statute supports this opinion, that it be valid by the law of fideicommissum, since it could be valid uniformly in every case of testacy and intestacy. And this by the doctrine placed in l. precibus, cum si. And thus this substitution made by a mother will not be considered compendious, but merely fideicommissary in every case of testacy and intestacy; for since it is one, it should not be divided; and this following the common opinion. The matter therefore came to the case of intestacy, because the instituted heir died together with the testatrix. And thus the inheritance was not entered upon by the will. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What effect does a privilege confirming that they possessed as before have?
2. Custom and prescription are the best means of acquiring privileges among the present ones.
body: In the name of Christ. The words properly say: We confirm to you, by apostolic authority, the church of Saint Mary of the Hill, the church of Saint Lawrence with its court, and the lands and persons residing there, and its other appurtenances, just as you previously held them reasonably.

† It is asked whether by these words spiritual jurisdiction is understood to have been granted. And the opinion is that it is so, because the grantor did not have any temporal jurisdiction there; therefore, it appears that he granted spiritual jurisdiction, so that the privilege might have some effect, as was prudently alleged above, in the argument to this point. On contracting purchase, ff., l. qui tabernas; and on funeral instruments, ff., fundus, qui locatus; and what is noted, ff., if anyone is cautious, l. sed et si quia, § quaesitum, at the end, the great gloss.

On the contrary, it seems that it is not so, because no word signifying jurisdiction is added here, as in c. 1, de capitulo, who with sold, col. 10; and extra, de restitutione spoliorum, c. cum ad sedem; and C., de servitutibus, l. si. For our men are called those who serve us, even without any jurisdiction, as ff., de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. qui iurisdictioni. Moreover, this was a confirmation in common form, and therefore it confers no new right; and if it did confer anything, it would pertain to honors and other dues which the inhabitants of places make by reason of persons or things, but this word does not pertain to anything spiritual. Also, ver. hoc, C., de emancipatione liberorum, l. ne auus; and ff., ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, § si quis a principe; and extra, de auro et usu pallii, c. ex tuarum. Solution: from the foregoing we presume in the present case.

† For custom and prescription are the best interpreters of privileges, and therefore one must depart from that which has long been considered equitable and just, as stated in the Digest, *De constitutionibus principum*, in the laws *Beneficium* and *In rebus*. Hence, the custom of most faithful antiquity must be observed, and those things which have always had a certain interpretation must not be changed. It seems reasonable that prelates should have a moderate coercive power over their men, by which they can compel them to render the customary services to the Church. And it is clear that, in this regard, the Church is the competent judge, which would be beyond doubt if they performed homage. I, Baldus. See in Consilium 205 and Consilium 199.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether it suffices for a lessor, who promised to deliver to the lessee sown possessions, if he gives the lessee grain to sow in the threshing floor.
2. If the lessor stated that he is not bound to pay the tithe except for such a one, are the lessees understood to be released from the fiscal authority? Especially since in the lease instrument there are these words, that they are not bound to pay to any person.
3. If the lessor were to sell the leased possession by his own authority, because the rent has not been paid, does he forfeit any of his rights?
4. Whether fruits collected diminish the principal sum.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: a certain nobleman of Magnano leased to P. de Summaria certain possessions for a fixed term, with this express stipulation, namely, that the said lessor is bound and ought to deliver to the said lessee at the beginning of the present lease the sown lands. It is asked: if he delivers grain in the granary, and not the sown lands, and the said P. confesses that he received the grain, can he claim damages? Secondly, it is asked: if the instrument contains a provision that the said P. de Summaria is not bound to pay anything to any person, except what is limited in the present lease to the said de Murana, excluding the water of Muzi; nor is it the case that the lesseors themselves, nor their farm managers, are bound to pay any tithe by virtue of the said possessions; it is asked whether, by virtue of this stipulation, the said lessee is absolved from the tax on the fruits to be gathered? Thirdly, it is asked: if the said lessor, by his own authority, re-entered into possession of the leased thing, because the lessee ceased from the payment of the annuity for two years and more, has he forfeited any right? And if he has not forfeited it, if the fruits were on the leased property, do the said fruits reduce the principal sum?

† On the first point, it appears that the lessor has not performed on his part, because he did not deliver the sown lands as he promised; and thus he cannot be said to be discharged by performance, since one thing cannot be given in satisfaction of another, as stated in l. 2, § 1, D. si certum petatur. To the contrary, it is argued that the obligation to deliver the grain, which is the principal obligation, has been removed; therefore, the accessory obligation for damages has also been removed, as in D. de eo quod certo loco, l. centum Capuae and l. final. This latter view seems more correct, not on account of this reasoning, but because the lessee, by receiving the grain for sowing, is deemed to have relaxed something of the obligation, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. stipulatus opus. And the reason is evident, because the lessor could not sow, since the seed was in the possession of the lessee, arg. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Iulii.

† On the second point, it seems to be said that an exception made in one case appears to dispose contrary in other cases, as is noted in l. 1, ff. de regulis iuris. For the function of an exception is to confirm the rule in cases not excepted; likewise, to declare the rule, as in ff. de penus leg., l. nam quod liquidae, §. si qui penus. Although the rule does not have the power to expand so as to include things which are not of the genus of the rule, as in ff. de usufructu legato, l. generali. The solution is to say that either for the said fruits it was due to pay the fisc and the tithes, and not others: and by the name of the fisc I understand the tax collectors, and then the lessor is bound to pay, so that the words may have some effect, as in ff. de usuris, l. si stipulatus, and ff. de fundo instrato, l. fundus qui locatus. Or it was due to pay other persons besides the fisc and the tithe: and then in those words, "to any person," the fisc is not included, because it would be a contract, as in ff. de pactis, l. inter debitorem; ff. de impensis, l. neque stipendium; ff. de legatis 1, l. apud Iulium, l. haeres; ff. de legatis 3, l. qui concubinam; ff. de usufructu, l. sed et si quis, §. si quid cloacariorum.

† On the third point, it must be said that the owner does not lose his right, because the tenant does not possess, but the owner himself does, as is stated in C. de praescrip. 30. anno., l. male agitur, and l. colonus, ff. de vi, et vi armata.

† On the fourth point, it must be said that if the two-year period had elapsed, the fruits still attached, which were part of the soil, reverted together with the soil itself to the owner, as stated in the Digest, *De usufructu legato*, law *In fructu*. It is otherwise if they had been separated from the soil before the two-year period: for then the owner must impute this to his own possession. This is according to the strict law; but in equity, I hold that in any case the owner must compensate himself, and indeed he cannot demand the pension, since he expels the lessee from the present use of the thing, as in the Code, *De locato*, law *Eodem*, and in the Digest, *De locato*, law *Habitores*. Otherwise, a pension would be paid for non-fruits, which is absurd, as in the Digest, *De usufructu*, in law *Defuncta*, because it is unjust that one should have both the thing and its price, i.e., the fruits and the rent, as in law *I*, Code, *Si servus extero*, and in the Digest, *De actione empti*, law *Bona fides*. Although we say otherwise regarding the emphyteusis of the Church, because that statute is established as a pure penalty, as in the Code, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, Authenticum *Qui res iam dictas*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Alms given to churches, or the fruits of the said churches, how they are to be distributed.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Assuming that the mother church, or baptismal church, ought to have three parts of the tithes, one of which belongs to it, another to the fabric of that same church, and the third to the poor, while the fourth part belongs to the Bishop of Palazzolo and the canons, the following factual situation is proposed: by custom, the bishop appropriates three parts for himself and leaves only the fourth part to the baptismal church. The question therefore arises: since, by custom, the baptismal church has only the single fourth part, should that fourth part be divided into three parts, so that one part goes to the church for the fabric, another to the clerics of that church, and the third to needy and miserable persons? And it seems that this fourth part should not be divided, because it is the legitimate portion of the rector and the clerics of that baptismal church. Therefore, this legitimate portion ought not to be deducted or diminished. For, since the mother church has only its own portion and share according to the common law, it is not bound to others for what it does not have beyond its own share, as stated in C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Sancimus. Moreover, the injury done by custom to the fabric and the poor ought not to redound to the detriment of the baptismal church, according to the argument in ff. de evictionibus, l. Si per imprudentiam.

The contrary view seems correct: for this injury is common to the rector, the fabric, and the poor. I call it an injury, although it is fortified by custom, having regard to the common law. Furthermore, an injury common to several partners or a consortium, since it is done to the society and not to the individual person, tends to the detriment of each partner pro rata, as stated in ff. pro socio, l. Cum duobus, §. Si, and l. Si unus. Moreover, although the benefit is divisible, the burden ought likewise to be diminished pro rata, as stated in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Plautius, §. 1. Moreover, it is divided. It would be equitable that if the bishop appropriates for himself that which ought to be applied to the fabric, he should contribute, because this portion, burdened by canon law, ought to pass with its burden, according to the argument in C. de causis tollendis, §. Pro secundo. Just as the peculium passes with the burden of collation, as stated in ff. de condictione indebiti, l. Frater a fratre. Since we are in customary law, that which has been observed in past times should be observed thus, as stated in ff. de pollicitationibus, l. Totiens. For a new question cannot arise regarding what was defined long ago by custom, as stated in extra de sepulturis, c. Certificati. And if any transaction has been made concerning these matters with the parishioners, the same law applies to the sum of the transaction as to the principal sum, as stated in ff. de mandato, l. Si, and ff. de transactionibus, l. Controversia.

Solution: The rector of the church is bound to repair the roof and walls, since he is a usufructuary. Similarly, he must bear necessary expenses, according to the revenues he receives, after deducting what he needs so as not to be in want, as stated in ff. de usufructu, l. Hactenus, and extra de prebendis, c. Cum secundum appellationem. And if the fruits were very meager, the parishioners are bound to make up the difference, just as they did in ancient times when the curates were poor. For since they receive spiritual benefits, it is reasonable that they should assist, especially in food, as the Apostle says. However, those who attend the canonical hours, which are assigned to them by law, ought to have their daily distributions. If, however, the church were in danger of ruin, then, on account of necessity, the daily distributions ought to be reduced, and the remainder spent on repairs, according to the argument in l. 1, in the end, where a pupil ought to be educated. And if the archpriest receives any fruits unduly by reason of the vacancy of any prebend, he ought to consign them, especially for the repair of the church, according to the argument in l. Si aliquam, ff. de officio procuratoris et legati. And it is supported by ii. q. 2, c. Quatuor, where it is said that four parts are made from the oblations of the faithful: one is for the pontiff, i.e., the rector; another for the clerics, i.e., the college; the third for the poor; the fourth for the fabric. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the first oath not to alienate takes precedence over the second oath not to contravene an alienation subsequently made, or vice versa.
2. Usurious malice is presumed from the stipulations appended in the instrument.
3. Likewise, it is presumed if he is accustomed to lending at interest.
3. If a pact of repurchase was made with two persons, whether an offer of the price, or a deposit made by only one of them alone, suffices.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain woman, a daughter of the family, having maternal property, swore not to alienate it, nor to consent to its alienation by her father, and this in the presence and with the understanding of Titius. Finally, the father, with the consent of the swearing daughter not to contravene, sold the said property to the said Titius; and this woman was under 25 years of age, or if older, wishes to proceed against the said sale, on the ground that she could not sell the first adventitious goods, nor could she consent, notwithstanding the said first oath. It is alleged to the contrary that, since she contracted solemnly with an oath given, by such an oath strength is given to the contract and to her age; for what we say, that the oath represents majority of age, is nothing other than to say that the oath lends strength and firmness to her age, as if the swearing person were of legitimate age by the course of nature, as in the Authentica sacramenta, and fully noted in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione.

† It is therefore asked, what is the law? I answer: the jurist says that the first oath was lawful and honest, and therefore the second oath was unlawful: for the first can be observed without the loss of eternal salvation; but the second cannot, and therefore the second oath is not valid, but the first is valid. And the same is held by Johannes Andreae in the Extravagantes, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Mulieris*. For the first oath was not clandestine or deceptive to the adversary, because it was given with his knowledge and understanding, and without his objection. Moreover, he could have had a just motive or impelling cause for the first oath, because perhaps the girl believed or suspected that her father intended to disinherit her, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatum*, law *Celsus*; and *De quarum rerum actio non datur*, law 1, § *Quae onerandae*. Furthermore, the first rule does not apply, because an oath is made to God, and therefore it cannot be remitted except by the mystery of God, as in the Extravagantes, *De iureiurando*, chapter *Debitores*. And certainly in this case I believe the opinion of the jurist to be true. Otherwise, if the oath had not come to the knowledge of the contracting party, as in law 1, at the end, Digest, *De actione empti*. Also, it must be considered whether he swore not to sell, or not to consent, or not to do either, as in the Digest, *De manumissione vindicanda*, law *Si pater*, § *Finis*; and *De re iudicata*, law *Aliud est vendere*. Or say that, however he swore, he can neither sell nor consent regarding his own property. The aforementioned law *Si pater*, § *Finis*, and *De regulis iuris*, law *Aliud est vendere*, are not to the contrary, because there it speaks of consenting in another’s property, and to confirm the contract of another owner, as in the Digest, *Quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur*, law *Sicut*, § *Venditionis*; and law *Si consensit*. Concluding, therefore, I say that in the case proposed the second oath does not hold, because it cannot be observed without the loss of eternal salvation. And let him blame himself who contracted with such a person: and this is on the first point. And add, when the first oath is given in fraud, i.e., to defraud one’s neighbor, that first oath cannot be observed without detriment to eternal salvation, because it is written, “You shall not defraud your neighbor.” Therefore, the first oath does not bind. The second oath is therefore valid and must be observed. As for the first, penance is to be imposed, as in law *De periurio*, Digest, *De crimine stellionatus*; *De falsis*, law *Qui duobus*, law.

† On another point, I say that from the pacts appended, according to the matter of usurious wickedness, it is presumed that usurious wickedness has intervened, as in Extra de pignoribus, chapter *Illa vos*, and Extra de emptione et venditione, chapter *Ad nostram*, especially if the quality of the person accords with the acts, as in *L. Nomen omnes*, § *A barbaris*, D. de re militari; D. de transactionibus, *L. Cum hi*, § *In causae*; and noted by the doctors in C. plus valere quod agitur, *L. Emptore*. Moreover, certain things appear honest at first sight, which tacitly contain turpitude, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, *L. Si*. Moreover, the law assists the deceived, and not the deceivers. Moreover, in a contract of loan, usury is more easily presumed than in other contracts, because it is not presumed that the lender wishes to squander the interest of the intervening time, as in C. de usuris, *L. Cum allegans*. In other contracts, usurious wickedness is accustomed to be exercised in this way, and therefore it matters greatly whether a loan contract preceded, and it suffices to prove those two things which are set forth in chapter *Ad nostram*, de pignoribus; or whether another contract preceded, and then it must be proven that he is accustomed to practice usury. In the third case, when no other contract preceded, but he began with a contract of sale with deception and the aforementioned pacts, and usury is not presumed, it must be proven that he is accustomed to lend at interest, or to exercise similar contracts in fraud, as stated by Cynus in the said *L. Emptione*, and C. de probationibus, *L. I*.

† Regarding the third doubt, which asks whether the aforementioned deposit is valid, and whether he is bound to make the retro-date in the hands of the said Balzerela, in whose name the said deposit was made, notwithstanding that in the pact it is stated that he promised to make the sale, or re-sale, in the hands of the said father and daughter, if the price of the asserted sale were given or offered to him. It seems to be said that the offer of one suffices, because they are two persons to be credited, as in C. de duobus reis, l. si. And because it is considered as a solution, which can not only be made by the obligor, but also by another, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. qui personam utriusque. So that the pact may be observed: and then the father is bound, or his heir, to restore the part of the money deposited on behalf of the daughter, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. fundus ille. And C. si certum petatur, l. si absentis. And l. cum quaeritur, de administratione tutorum. But if the father consented that the re-sale should be made only to the daughter, there is no doubt, as in l. sicut, §. venditionis, ff. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur. And it applies, ff. de verbis obligatis, l. si ita quis, §. Seya. I, Baldus. See in counsel 74.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. 1. A dishonorable institution is rather an omission, when it has not been made with a title of honor, and therefore the will is rendered void.
2. How filiation is presumed.
body: In the name of Christ. In the first will, Titius instituted Seius as heir by these words: “I institute Seius, my legitimate natural son, as my universal heir.” Similarly, the mother made the same institution. Finally, the said Titius made a second will, in which he said: “I institute Seius, whom I previously made heir as a son, as heir to such a fund. But in my other goods, I institute my brother Gaius as universal heir.” Now, it is provided by the statute of the city of Milan that the heir acquires possession of the deceased’s goods by operation of law. In the execution of this statute, the said Gaius petitioned to be put in possession of the testator’s goods at the time of death. Seius objected, because according to the form of the second will he was not instituted as a son, and thus was passed over. Therefore, the judge declared the will null according to its form, and ruled in favor of the said Gaius, ordering him to be put in possession and maintained in the execution of the said statute in all the goods, and also according to common law, saving the legitime of the said Seius, whom he declared to be a son.

And it must be known that it was disputed concerning this Seyus whether he was a substituted child or not; and proofs were received on both sides; nor does it appear that the substitution of the child was most fully proven. For, since he was born to the husband and wife in their home, with the neighbors aware, he is presumed to be the son, as stated in the law *Filius diffinimus*, even if the mother asserts the contrary. And there, the doctors note fully in the reading of Cynus, whose words are as follows: "It is opposed first." Furthermore, from the fact that he was instituted as a son in the first will, he is presumed to be a son and a legitimate son, as in the Code, *De naturalibus liberis*, Authentica *Item si quis*. Moreover, because he was always held and treated as a son, as in the Digest, *De manumissionibus testamento*, law *Uxorem*; and *De verbis obligatis*, law *Quidam cum filium*; and in the Extravagant, *De probatibus*, chapter *Per tuas*. And the gloss on the Decretum states that if anyone has been publicly held as the son of someone, this is held as notorious, as noted in Question 2, Cause 1, chapter *Manifesta*. Furthermore, this son is named in the last will, as in the Extravagant, *De probatibus*, chapter *Per tuas*. And the gloss on the Decretum states that if anyone has been publicly held as the son of someone, this is held as notorious, as noted in Question 2, Cause 1, chapter *Manifesta*. Moreover, this son, named in the last will, appears to have been instituted with ignominy, as if it had been said that he was a substituted child or a false son; and this is evident from what follows: because for that reason he made another person universal heir. But an ignominious institution is rather an omission, and therefore the will is null, as noted in the penultimate law of the Code, *Quemadmodum testamentum aperiri debeat*; and in the law *Turpia* of the Digest, *De legatis primo*; and in the law *Et si pepercerit* of the Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*. Moreover, the law states that a son must be instituted in honor of himself, as in the law *Filius* in the beginning of the Digest, *De legatis praestantibus*. But here he was instituted in infamy, because by remaining silent about him being a son, he tacitly accused him of substitution; for he remained silent in order to make the offense understood, as in the Authentica *Quibus modis naturalis effectus legitime*, section 1. Moreover, it is not probable that he would have preferred a brother to a son, unless he had been deceived in the matter of filiation, as in the Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Lucius*.

† or because, in case of doubt, he applied his opinion to that opinion which was later declared false by judgment: and error in filiation renders a will null, as in l. 1, D. de car. edict.; C. de haer. inst.; l. si pater, C. de fideic.; l. ea quam, C. de test. mil.; l. sicut certi; and l. si cum vel in utero. For this is such a case as if the testator believed he had no son, when he did have one, as in D. de test. tut., l. si quis ita. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, weighing the words of the said judgment, which state that he is a true legitimate and natural son, and that if the testator had believed this, he would by no means have instituted his brother, as stated in l. illa not., D. de pact.; l. tale pactum, §. si, I presume that the testator erred in filiation, or, being in doubt, inclined toward the untrue part: which is the same as erring, as in C. de furtis, l. manifestissimi, §. si autem dubius. The doctors say so in d. l. et si pepercerit, above, on the word "and whether he believed," or it is doubtful that he believed: and thus it is proven above in l. here cited, below, l. si posthumus, §. 1. Fran. de Arbergotis says, I believe the will is invalid, because he was not instituted by paternal thought and charity, nor by pious affection, but with disgrace, and with ignominy, and contrary to the usual order of nature recognizing its own. For no one is so mad as to use these words concerning him whom he would consider a true son: nor would any prudent man be of this understanding or interpretation. For true interpretations agree with all, or with the majority, or at least with the wise. Moreover, my brother is not my offspring, but my son is so; and no one seems to prefer another’s offspring to his own, as in c. 1, §. si cum vero, Corradus, qui fev. da. pos., col. 10; and C. de fideic., l. cum acutissimi. Furthermore, if the father had spoken thus in bad faith, the exception of fraud would stand in the way, as in D. de doli except., l. 1, in fin. And I say this having seen the said judgment: for if filiation were not held as constant unless the contrary were in doubt, the will would not be rescinded: and it is provided in C. de test., Auth. hoc inter liberos, namely, that the first will be valid, and the second will be null for the reasons stated above; for it cannot accrue as if instituted in a certain thing, because the institution was vitiated, inasmuch as he was not named as a son, nor with a title of honor, but rather with reproach, although tacit, yet not so tacit that it cannot be gathered from the words. Moreover, often we say one thing and signify many, which have a cause mutually connected. Otherwise, I had disposed not to speak on this matter. Nor did I wish to say anything for or against before the said judgment. Not because I was bound to anyone, but because it pleased me so by my gratuitous promise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Perishing does not release the debtor, unless the specific thing owed perishes, or a subordinate corporeal genus. And therefore the fideicommissum is due in the state it was in at the time of the testator’s death, not at the time of the fideicommissary’s death:
body: In the name of Christ. Father divided the houses, i.e., those assigned to the public loan, together with the money and merchandise, among his children, having provided but not observed a guarantee for the restitution of the shares. He requested that the one dying without children restore to the others the house which had fallen to him in his portion. It happened that the house which had fallen to one of the sons, say Titius, after many years, and after many mixtures of assets, and after new pledges and new sums of money, was stolen by robbers by force. Finally, the said Titius died without children. It is demanded that he restore the house with the valuation of the merchandise and money which existed at the time of the testator’s death; or with an equal number, or the same amount. The objection of fortuitous event is raised. The question is: what is the law?

† I shall premise for the sake of clarity that the following must be considered here: whether the genus or the quantity within the genus is included in the fideicommissum, or whether it appears to be a specific species, and whether the money found in that chest at the time of the death of the said Titius, the legatee, is included, or whether money at any time is included, such that the fideicommissum increases and decreases like a peculium. And it seems that the things and money pertaining to that chest at the time of the testator’s death came into the fideicommissum, and not other things, as in D. de auro et argento legato, l. Si ita; and D. de liberis legatis, l. Aurelius, §. Testamento; and D. de legato 2, l. Si ita scripsisset. And this is well supported by C. de secundis nuptiis, l. Hac edictali, §. Mobilium. Those things and money were not stolen, but were converted to the benefit of the burdened heir; and it suffices that this occurred once, even if subsequently a fortuitous event happened, as in D. quod metus causa, l. Si ipsa, and l. Quod diximus. Moreover, this Titius lent for his own benefit, therefore also at his own risk, as in D. pro socio, l. Si socius, §. 1; and C. de furtis, l. Manifestissimi, §. Sed cum in secunda; and D. de administratione tutorum, l. Titium et Mevium, §. Altero. Furthermore, this case does not occur with things comprehended in the fideicommissum, but with things of the legatee himself; which things do not come into the fideicommissum, and consequently are not at the risk of the fideicommissary, arg. C. locati conducti, l. Si damnum. Moreover, since this art of usury is condemned by divine and human law, and all usury is called fraud, it does not come into the restitution of the fideicommissum, namely that which the heir acquired to the peril of his soul from usurious wickedness, as in D. pro socio, l. Quod autem; and arg. D. ad Trebellianam, l. Debitor, §. Si; D. familiae herciscundae, l. Ceterae. That which, however, was in the goods of the deceased at the time of death was properly subject to the fideicommissum, just like the earnings of a testating prostitute, D. de peculio haereditario, l. Et non tantum; D. ad Trebellianam, l. Sed et qui magna. Because the burdened heir cannot allege the turpitude of the deceased, as in C. de communi servo manumisso, l. Si creditoribus.

To the contrary, it seems that the said fideicommissum was universal, as in D. de legato 2, l. Cum pater, §. Mense. And in universals, one thing and one quantity succeed in place of another thing or quantity, as in D. de legato 2, l. Imperator, §. Si, cum l. seq.; and D. de pignoribus, l. Cum tabernam; and D. de funerariis impensis, l. Lucius. And note by Jacobus de Arena, C. de iure dotis, l. Ubi adhuc.

Solution: The father, by providing caution, seems to have prohibited that usury be further exercised with his things and money; because to provide caution and subsequently to lend at interest are contrary acts. Therefore, it seems that the testator disposed of the chests in the state in which they were at the time of his death. Moreover, this act of usury contains in itself a delict, hence the said Titius was at fault in lending at interest, which should not harm the universal fideicommissary. He ought to have completely ceased from usury and the chest. Also, in illicit commerce there is no legitimate consequence, and therefore one thing does not succeed in place of another, and consequently the said Titius is not released from the fideicommissum, because the things contained in the fideicommissum were not perished, but were intentionally converted to the benefit of the burdened heir. Hence, concluding from the first to the last, because perishing does not release the debtor unless the specific species due perishes, or the genus under an alternative corporeal obligation, as in D. locati conducti, l. In nave saupheli, and l. Quod, D. si certum petatur; but an intellectual genus cannot perish, because it is eternal, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. In ratione, §. Incertae. It follows and is concluded that the said fideicommissum must be restored in the amount of goods and money that were present at the time of the testator’s death, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. In quantitate, §. Magnae.

Notwithstanding D. ad Trebellianam, l. Mulier, §. Si haeres, because there the primary species perished by destruction, but were not converted to the benefit of the burdened heir. Moreover, the reason is the same for diminution and increase, but increase would not pertain to the universal fideicommissary, because the burdened heir is not bound to procure the fideicommissary’s gains; therefore neither is he bound for loss, by argument from the contrary, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Postulante Sticho.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Two statutes being in force, one of which provides that possession is to be transferred by judgment, and the other provides that execution is to be carried out, it is asked whether the party who obtained the judgment is bound to carry out the execution.
2. Exceptions that could not be raised before judgment may be raised afterwards, when the cause begins from the condemnation; reasonable exceptions are not understood to be removed.
3. The custom of practice is to be observed.
4. Execution is twofold.
body: In the name of Christ. Given the two aforementioned statutes, by one of which it is provided that a public instrument shall be regarded as a judgment, and also as a transfer of possession; and by the other, that execution shall be carried out through whatever hands the property may have passed; it is assumed that the creditor brings a hypothecary action against an alien possessor.

It is asked whether the exception of non-exhaustion of remedies (non factae excussionis) is an obstacle; and it seems that it is, because the action on the stipulation (condictio) has not been brought, as per the law *sed hypothecaria*; and he must blame himself if he did not propose a better action, as noted in the law *quidam*, Digest, *de in rem verso*. On the contrary, it seems that it is not an obstacle, because execution is not necessary against the possessor; hence, by the hypothecary action here, possession is not taken away from him, but is confirmed to the creditor. Also, because by statute the judgment is understood to be rendered not only against the debtor, but against any possessor; and the exception of exhaustion of remedies cannot be raised after judgment, because it is an exception of order, as in the Digest, *de fideiussoribus*, law *si fideiussores*, section *idem tamen dicit*. The solution is that, although by the benefit of the statute the creditor is deemed to possess, nevertheless, since he brings the hypothecary action, he makes his adversary the possessor, because he is seen to have tacitly renounced possession, as is proved from the conjunction of two laws, Digest, *de pignere*, law *si fundus*, section *in vendicatione*; and what is noted in the Digest, *de acquisitione possessionis*, law *naturaliter*, section *nihil commune*. Also, it does not follow that he is considered condemned, because by this fiction legitimate exceptions are not removed.

† Moreover, when the case begins with a condemnation, and thus exceptions could not be raised before the sentence of the statute, they may be raised after the sentence, as in Extra, de iureiurando, c. Debitores; and see also in l. Neratius, ff. de condictione indebiti. And therefore, unless something else has been observed in the practice of these statutes, I hold that the exception of excussion obstructs the proceeding, especially because the statute does not mention this matter; hence it is not understood to remove reasonable exceptions. See l. Ita pudor and l. 1, § 1, ff. quod vi aut clam; and in c. 3, Extra, de rescriptis; and Extra, de consuetudinibus, c. Cum dilectus; and Codex, de noxa, l. Si servi vestri. Otherwise it would follow that no exception could be raised, neither dilatory nor peremptory, as in Codex, de probationibus, l. Exceptionem; Codex, senatus consultum rescindendum non posse, l. Peremptorias. Which is false and inequitable, as in Codex, si contra ius vel utilitatem publicam, l. Et si non cognitio.
† however, as I have said, the customary practice should be observed, if it is evident, as in the Digest, on laws, l. minime.

† Moreover, there are two kinds of excussion: one for proceeding to the names of the debtors by way of execution, and then first movable property is subjected to excussion; secondly, immovable property; thirdly, recourse is had to the names [of the debtors], as in D. de re iudicata, l. a diuo pio. The other is excussion, which is made of movable and immovable property and of the names of the debtors, before recourse is had against an alien possessor by means of a hypothecary action, as in Auth. de fideiussoribus, §. sed neque. And it is this second excussion that is in question in the aforementioned point. Furthermore, it must be considered that, since the statute speaks of possession jointly with the contract itself, it necessarily speaks of the goods possessed by the debtor at the time of the contract, not of those acquired afterwards, unless they are transferred by a new delivery, as in D. si certum petatur, l. si socius, and l. 3, D. pro socio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. See above, almost word for word, but here more copiously, and some more elegant points are added in counsel 136.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain noble son, through his prowess in arms, acquired much from his military pay, and also obtained some goods by roaming throughout the world with other men-at-arms, violating and extorting, as is the custom in Italy. This man died, his father being still alive, in whose power he was, and leaving behind a pregnant wife, who sought to be appointed, in the name of the unborn child, to the possession of her husband’s goods; but the father, in whose power the said noble man-at-arms had been, objects.

† It is asked, what is the law? And it seems that [the mother] should not be put in possession, for the reins of control appear to pertain solely to the paternal grandfather, as in C. de bonis matri et filiis rel. l. 1, because since the posthumous child is considered as born, as in ff. de statu hominum l. qui in utero, it is therefore feigned to be in the power of the paternal grandfather, and a curator cannot be appointed for one existing in the power of another, as in C. de bonis quae liberis l. si. Therefore, the paternal grandfather appears to be the curator of the womb, and as curator would possess in the name of the curatorship, and thus possession should not be handed over into the hands of the mother, because the father does not have the right of legitimate administration, as in ff. de solutionibus l. filiae, and ff. de negotiis gestis l. qui aliena §. quamquam. Furthermore, one argues from the testamentary tutor, who administers the goods of the womb, just as also of the born, as in ff. de negotiis gestis l. cum pater curator. But briefly, the truth seems to be to the contrary, namely, that the mother should be put in possession in the name of the womb, because the edict of the praetor does not distinguish, therefore neither should we distinguish, as in ff. de ventre in possessionem mittendo l. 1, for the posthumous child is part of the mother’s viscera: and just as the mother is not in the power of her parent, as in ff. de collatione bonorum l. si, ff. de adsignatione lib. l. ult., hence it is that the interim omission does not break the will, as in l. posthumi per virilem §. ex his apparet ff. de iniuriis testamenti et nuncupativi, ff. de liberis et posthumis l. posthumus. And first, l. cum pater does not obstruct, because there he administered de facto, as noted there. I conclude therefore that the mother should be put in possession to obtain the effects which follow from such admission. And if it is asked, what are these effects, I answer, because she must nourish in the name of the womb, l. 3 §. antepen. ff. de iure iurandi, and ff. de ventre in possessionem mittendo l. curator. The second effect is that the mother herself will petition for a curator for the womb, as in ff. ad legem Terentiam l. 2 §. sed. However, the Speculum says that he never saw a curator appointed for the womb, and therefore does not set forth the form of this curatorship. But whether a curator is given to the womb or to the goods, the piety of the mother ought to provide for this, and an inventory should be made, so that movables, and especially money, cannot be concealed: but they should be placed in a safe location until the birth of the child, and upon the child being born the curatorship will vanish, and administration will pertain to the paternal grandfather by reason of usufruct, as noted in C. de bonis quae liberis Auth. excipitur. And although the father or paternal grandfather should not give security, nevertheless a description [inventory] should be made, because upon his death the goods having come to him must be restored to the child, or to the child if emancipated, as in C. de bonis quae liberis l. cum oportet §. si. And because this description benefits and harms no one, as in C. de iudiciis facultas lib. 10, and there by Andreas de Barulo. Furthermore, a curator suspect to the mother should not be appointed, to whom the succession of the child might devolve with the order of mortality disturbed; and because one suspect to the mother is considered suspect to the child, as in C. si contra matris voluntatem tutor datus fuerit l. 1. But if the grandfather were suspect, an assistant could be appointed to him, arguing from ff. de suspectis tutoribus l. si tutor aliquo. For the grandfather should not be tolerated if he wishes to squander or conceal, C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano l. si, and ff. ad legem Trebellianam l. imperator, or deny, as in ff. ad legem Falcidiam l. haereditatum §. si. For in honor of the blood he should not be removed, but another trustworthy person should be associated with him in administering, as in ff. de suspectis tutoribus l. si tutor aliquo. Furthermore, a very significant effect is that justice is satisfied, arguing from ff. de minoribus l. ait praetor §. permittitur. Another effect is that the mother, who is found to be diligent and pious, must nourish the child for up to three years, whether the grandfather wishes it or not; because while the child is unborn, he differs in nothing from one who is in the womb. This is fully and clearly noted in Extra de conversione infidelium c. si, unless the mother passes to second vows, for then she ceases to be the legitimate educator, as in Auth. de nuptiis §. eiusdem quam principis coll. 3. However, by the foregoing I do not deny that the maternal grandfather may substitute pupillarily in the territory, and exercise other equal rights. Furthermore, although goods acquired through the probity of arms are castrense in the acquirer, nevertheless upon change of person they cease to be castrense, and for the grandfather having [the child] in power usufruct is sought, and quasi, as in ff. de acquisitione hereditatis l. Paulus respondit per procuratorem §. 1, because the condition of the person and thing having changed, it is fitting that the status and quality change, as in C. de impositione lucrativae descriptionis l. 1 lib. 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person created a citizen on the condition that no damage be thereby inflicted upon the village from which he originated, if he subsequently purchases property in the said village, is bound to pay the *collectae* (taxes), as if he had not been created a citizen. And number 4.
2. Where *collectae*, or *taleae* (taxes), are to be paid.
3. Emancipation creates two families, yet it does not remove public law status, nor origin, nor domicile.
body: In the name of Christ. Petrinus of Iseo, assessed in the said castle of Iseo, emancipated his son Francischinus. Finally, the said Francischinus obtained letters of citizenship of the city of Brescia, in whose district the said castle of Iseo is located, from the Magnificent Lord B., with the clause that, therefore, the commune of Iseo should not suffer any damage from the said grace. Subsequently, the Magnificent and Illustrious Lord Count of Virtues likewise granted the rights of citizenship to the said Francischinus, the petitioner, with the added clause that the commune of Iseo be exonerated by the city of Brescia by such amount as is the sum of the assessment which the said petitioner bore. Most recently, however, at the petition of the commune of Iseo, the aforementioned prince confirmed the letters of citizenship, as they stood, by the letters of the said first Magnificent Lord, other letters of the same Illustrious Lord being shown, wherein it appears that Petrus, after the emancipation, acquired several properties in the castle and territory of Iseo. It is asked whether the said Petrus and the said Francischinus are bound to pay the *factiones* for the said properties acquired in the land and territory of Iseo?

I answer that the said Francischinus is bound, because there are two households in the assessment, as stated in the Digest, title *Ad municipalia*, law *Incola*. Petrinus is not bound, because he has no interest in the said properties; for an emancipated son acquires for himself and not for his father, as stated in law 1 of the Digest, title *De his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt*, and in law *Cum oportet* of the Code, title *De bonis quae liberis*. For after emancipation there are two households, because there are two heads of household. But if the son were under paternal power, there is one household and one assessment is reckoned, as is elegantly noted in law 1 of the Code, title *Qui aetate*, book 10. Moreover, nothing is alleged from which the emancipation should be presumed to be simulated and made in fraud of the assessment; since by this the condition of the common community of Isei is not made worse, because the said Francischinus is bound to pay, as stated in the Code, title *Sine censu*, law *Ultima*, and law *Omnes*.

Secondly, it is asked whether, if the commune incurred expenses for the purpose of collecting factional dues, it ought to be reimbursed. I answer that it should, according to the aforementioned Francischino, who was bound to pay, as stated in l. 1, C. sumptus iniuncti muneris, lib. 11.

Thirdly, it is asked whether, while this question is pending, the said community of Isei can compel the aforementioned Petrinus and Franciscinus to bear the burdens? I answer that the judge should order the said Franciscinus to assume the said burdens, notwithstanding any cavil, as in the Authentica de mandatis principum, § coges, col. 4.

Fourthly, it is asked whether the said Francischinus is bound to pay after the aforementioned grace. I answer in the affirmative, because the first grace of the illustrious lord was revoked by subsequent and more just letters, as stated in the extrajudicial provisions on restitution of spoliation, chapter *Audita*, section *Si vero post*. For each person is bound to pay for the goods which he possesses in the place where the goods are valued and encumbered by obligations, as provided in the Code on immunities not to be granted to anyone, law *Per Bithiniam*; and in the Code on the burdens of patrimonies, law 1; and in the Code on burdens and in which place, law *Unica*. There, the matter is fully noted in Book 10. The points were not well formulated, because this Francischinus, after emancipation, acquired goods outside the territory of Isei, in the territory of Brescia. Nevertheless, it is true that he resides in a certain third village within the district of Brescia. It is asked in which place he ought to be compelled to pay for the said goods. I, Baldus.

In the name of Christ. It is customary in the land of Iseo, within the district of Brescia, that the inhabitants of the said land pay tolls, levies, and burdens imposed upon the universitas of the said place, which are subsequently distributed among them according to the amount of the estimated value for which they pay for their goods located in any place within the district of Brescia. Now, a certain son of a family of the said place of Iseo was emancipated by his father and obtained citizenship of the city of Brescia, saving the right of the community of Iseo; and he purchased certain immovable goods in the district of Brescia, outside the said Iseo, and resides elsewhere, not in the district of Iseo. Now the community of Iseo wishes to compel him to make an estimate for the said goods in the estimate of Iseo; he has objected.

† It is asked, what is the law: and it seems that he is not bound, because he has nothing in the district of Isei, nor does he reside there, nor did he make an assessment there. And if it is said that when the father made the assessment, the son also appears to have been assessed, and he has favors, and contilitates, and similarly offices, just as other assessed persons, as is noted individually in l. 2. C. qui aetate. lib. 10. It is answered that this is true when he is under the power of his father, but he is emancipated and is a head of household in his own right, nor is he now understood to be of the same family as his father, as ff. de verb. sig. l. pronunciatio. §. familiae. For emancipated sons are independent and conducting business, and are the head of their own family, and heads of households; indeed, under ancient law they are considered as dead with respect to the father, as ff. de lib. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. et quid sit tantum. Moreover, either these collections succeed in place of real burdens, and then, because they are rendered for the territory, they should be borne in the place where the property is, as C. de immunitate nemini concedenda. l. fi. where it seems expressly stated, and fully noted in l. 1. C. de mulie. et in quo loco. lib. 10. Or they succeed in place of personal burdens, for example in place of guard duty or angaria: and they must be rendered in the place where they reside; otherwise they would be forced to change their domicile every third day: which is absurd. On the contrary, however, it seems so, both from the common law and from the form of the custom. Behold, from the common law, collections are imposed on citizens and natives, and mere possession does not make one a citizen or native; therefore it is necessary that they make an assessment, and pay as debtors of public functions in the place from which they are, not in the place where the property is, because the person draws the property to itself, not the contrary, as ff. de aedi. edi. l. iustissimae. This is the ordinary gloss, not the vulgar one. ff. de mune. et ho. l. rescripto. §. fi. Moreover, even if this were not true according to the common law, because perhaps the property is in the territory of another province or city, which has a statute or custom that payment be made there for the property of its territory: nevertheless in our case it is not so, because both territories are under the city of Brescia, and that city is under one lord, our magnificent lord, and therefore the said custom is not less reasonable, since everything is referred to one principal treasury, as in Auth. qui. mo. na. §. si quis igitur ex qualibet and ff. ad municip. l. qui ex vico. and C. de epi. et cle. l. nulli. §. quod si ex vico. Hence finally it is one and the same fiscal purse: therefore the custom is valid, and also the statute, if it were confirmed by a superior. Nor certainly does emancipation avail anything, because by it public right is not removed, but only paternal power, nor by it is origin or domicile dissolved, as ff. de muni. l. assumptio. in prin. And especially if the statute of the place provided that such emancipation should be considered as simulated, and made in fraud of the treasury of that place, as is said to be the case in the said town or village of Isei. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made to a ward for a determined quantity in general terms is to be called pupillary; and whether the mother or the substitute is bound to request a guardian for the son; and whether the son, to whom a legacy is given by right of institution, is to be called a legatee or an heir; and whether the mother, if she does not request a guardian, is deprived of all the son’s inheritance, and even of the legitime?
2. Whether the legitime can be abolished by statute in descendants as well as in ascendants.
body: In the name of Christ. Having examined the will of Henry of Pontremoli, and the institution and substitutions made therein, as well as the legacy left to his daughter, a ward, by right of institution, and assuming that the said testator died while his mother was still alive, and also while his wife, named Contesina, was still alive, and also while Lady Petra, a ward, legitimate and natural daughter of the said Henry and Lady Contesina, was still alive, and that the said ward survived her father for a period of several years, and that the said Contesina did not assume the guardianship of the said ward.

It is asked whether the said Lady Contesina succeeds to the said ward in the legacy, or in the legitimate portion due, or owed by the said ward in the goods of the said Henry, her father? And it seems that she does, because the father substituted the said daughter, who was a ward, in that certain quantity which he had left to her by way of institution under the condition that she should die before entering into marriage: which substitution, by reason of her age as a ward, appears to be a pupillary substitution, as in the Institution *de pupillari substitutione* in the beginning. Then I argue thus: when a father makes a pupillary substitution of his underage son, the burden of requesting a guardian does not fall upon the mother, who does not expect the succession of the underage child; but it falls upon the pupillary substitute. And if he does not request a guardian, he is deprived of the substitution, and the inheritance devolves to the mother, as in the Code *de legitimis haeredibus*, law *Sciant*, where it seems expressly stated. And it is noted by Bartolus in law 2, Digest *qui petant tutores*, and by me in law *Precibus*, where it is examined at length in my lecture.

To the contrary is the truth, because this substitution was not pupillary, since it was made in a determined quantity, and in common words not directed, as noted by Decius and Bartolus and all, in the Digest *ad Trebellianum*, law *Cogi*, section *Generaliter*. The objection from the Digest *de vulgari substitutione*, law *Cohaeredes*, section *Finis*, does not hold, because there the substitution was made in civil and direct words, which are drawn to the universal, but it is not so when the son is not instituted in the universal, but only in a thing or a fixed quantity: and another is the heir instituted universally; for such a person has in all respects the place of a legatee, the inheritance having been accepted by the universal heir, with this single exception, that he cannot break the will as one passed over, as noted in the Digest *ad Trebellianum*, law *Si quis priore*. And therefore such a substitution in the legitimate portion would not be valid as a fideicommissum: and this is the truth.

Then it appears that, given that there is no pupillary substitute, the mother expects the succession of the ward, and therefore she is bound to request a guardian within a year, and according to Bartolus, even within a year as soon as she can: which does not please me upon inspection of the law of the Code and the Institutions, and of the Authentics, such as *Ad Orficinum*, section *Nouissime*. For that law *Sciant* always grants a year for requesting, thus the custom observes. This mother, therefore, by not requesting a guardian, succeeds neither in the legitimate portion of the son nor in anything else to the son, as in the Authentic *de nuptiis*, section *Si autem tutelam*, and the Code *ad Trebellianum*, law *Omnem*. For since she is repelled from succession altogether by the law itself as unworthy, and deprived of the right, as in the Code *ad Tertullianam*, law *Matres*, she rightly succeeds in nothing, and therefore I hold thus.

Beyond the aforesaid, there is the statute of Pontremoli, which excludes her, whether she requests or not, when agnates exist up to the degree limited in the statute, who exist, as is proposed to me.

And although Dynus says that the legitime cannot be taken away from children by statute, unless perhaps they have something in place of the legitime, such as a dowry, nevertheless it is otherwise with ascendants, to whom the legitime is due, unless a statute stands in the way, because it is not due to parents as much as to children, and this is also practiced and observed everywhere every day: and therefore they are by no means to be changed, which have always had a certain interpretation, as in D. de legibus, l. minime. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an appeal lies from a possessory action and from execution.
2. The exception of ownership prevails to exclude the possessory action.
3. By the appeal of an heir is understood the true heir in the statute, not the abusive one.
4. The eye of the law sees all things, considers all things.
5. Every article of usury must be resolved according to canon law.
6. Whether an appeal lies from a decree, and from the execution of a sentence in a possessory action.
7. Whether an appeal lies from mixed causes, and from a null sentence.
8. Whether an appeal lies from a sentence passed on the condition of l. si quis in tantam.
9. C. unde vi, and from the Carbonian interdict, and in the name of the womb, and from a decree, or if it is a null sentence.
body:
In the name of Christ. Premised are the words of a certain statute of Milan stating that upon the death of any person, possession of goods shall pass to his heir by operation of law without any apprehension. And if anyone, who is not an heir, enters into possession of hereditary goods, such entry shall be of no effect, etc. Also premised are the words of a certain statute stating: If anyone henceforth wishes to make a disposition in a last will, or to institute an heir, this may be done, unless otherwise prohibited by law from making a will or making a disposition, provided that five witnesses and three notaries are present and requested, etc. Also presupposed is another certain statute, that filiation and other proximity of blood may be proved by an instrument, or instruments, made and drawn up within the last ten years, or by proof of voice and reputation made by three witnesses of good fame and opinion, etc. Also presupposed is a certain episcopal constitution, which is observed to the letter, or fully: it is found in the city of Milan that wills made by manifest usurers are not valid, but are void by operation of law, if they are usurers with usuries not restituted according to the ability of their faculties, and without security being given; and in which these words are placed: "For we declare those to be manifest usurers concerning the aforesaid, of whom public fame in the parish in which they have dwelt, or where they die, shall have been that they extorted usuries, from which, even in the absence of the usurer, before the vicar himself, or the priest, it shall appear that they were usurers, or of whom it shall appear that they received usuries by inspection of them, or by suitable arguments, or by another legitimate mode, etc."

Now the case is as follows: A. of the city of Milan, and Lady Berta were husband and wife; from the legitimate marriage contracted between them, they held and treated C., their legitimate and natural son, by nourishing and rearing him from the day of his birth in the house of their conjugal habitation, and educating him as a legitimate son, providing all necessary sustenance to him, always calling him legitimate and natural son, and treating him as true and legitimate parents treat their legitimate and natural sons; thus he was publicly treated and reputed by those who knew him. Now A., after many years had elapsed, in the city of Milan, where he was known, made his solemn will, in which, after legacies disposed by him therein, he instituted the said C. as universal heir as his legitimate and natural son descending, by these words: "I institute the said C., my legitimate and natural son, in all my other goods." Then the said B., being sick in body but sound in mind, doubting of death, made her solemn will in the presence, with the will and express consent of the said A., her husband; in which she instituted the said C. as her heir as her legitimate and natural son by these words: "In the residue of the goods of the said testatrix, she instituted as her universal heir C., legitimate and natural son of the said Lady testatrix, and of the said A.," and it is added in the will, and with the said A., husband of the testatrix, always present and urging, and he obligated himself to distribute the aforesaid. Then the said A., in the month of February or March 1385, having gone beyond the mountains for certain of his affairs, died and passed away there. Now, after it was certain of his death, a certain person named D. appeared, asserting himself to be the brother of the said A., and produced a certain will made outside the territory of the said testator in the month of February on the 25th day of the month, which he asserts was made by the said A. in solemn form; and in which, revoking all other wills made by him, it appears that the said D. is the universal heir of the said A., and it appears that a legacy was made to the said C. by these words: "Also I judge, will, and leave by right of institution, that C., whom I, the testator, have hitherto nourished and reared and caused to be nourished in my house, after my death shall have and ought to have my possession and all my goods which I have and possess in such place, and otherwise naming him in the said will; and not otherwise instituting him."

After these things, the said D., while the said C. was in tenure or possession of the testator's goods, asserts as follows, namely: because it is proved that before the death of the said A., the said C. held and possessed the goods of the said A. in the name of the said A., his father, and after death held and possessed the said goods, until the said D. entered the aforesaid goods in this manner: because a certain person of his name appeared before the vicar of the podestà of Milan, asserting the said A. dead, and proving his death by two witnesses, and obtained a sentence, showing the said second will for the execution of the said statute disposing of the continuation of possession, etc., without citing the said C. in any of the aforesaid regarding entering possession of the said goods. By virtue of whose sentence he went with a messenger of the commune to the said goods. And the messenger, as he reported in the said goods, introduced him. And afterwards command was given to the tenants that they should answer to him, who tenants contradicted, naming the said C. as lord; and the said C. said, contradicting that the aforesaid should not be done for many reasons and causes; and especially because he was not cited. And finally, it was committed by the will of the parties to three arbitrators, of whom two pronounced in this form, namely: "We declare, knowing from the proofs made before us, that the said C. was and is the son of the late said A., and therefore the legitime is due to him by right of nature by the aforesaid sentence. And from this occasion following, we concede that the said D. was and is null; but in the other goods, the legitime ascending, we say that the said sentence and what followed therefrom is valid and holds; and in those goods the said D. was and is possessor. Also we absolve both parties from expenses." The other, however, pronounced in effect that the aforesaid sentence was not juridical, from which sentence appeal was taken by the other party, it being said that one could not appeal in a possessory action, especially in this case. It is replied that rather one could, especially considering that the said testator was a manifest usurer. Now it is asked, what is the law?

† And it must be premised first, for the sake of clarity, that according to canon law, an appeal may be brought from any possessory judgment: although formerly there was a question on this point, which is fully noted in the Extravagantes, in the title *De restitutione spoliorum*, chapter *Cum ad sedem*, nevertheless this question has today been determined by the first Clementine Constitution, in the title *De causa possessionis et proprietatis*, and therefore, namely, that an appeal may be brought from a sentence rendered in a possessory action, and as if from a definitive sentence; for if it were appealed as if from an interlocutory sentence, it would be necessary to appeal in writing, on account of legitimate causes: and this applies to other possessory actions, which are regulated by the common law. But so that an heir in writing may not be put into possession in favor of the execution of wills, whether this putting into possession is called interlocutory or definitive according to civil law, no appeal lies therefrom according to civil law; but according to canon law, an appeal lies, if the grievance is manifest or notorious, that is, known of itself. Hence, if the judge put the heir into possession on the basis of a will that does not stand up to legal reasoning, and if this was clearly proven before the sentence, and appears from the records, an appeal may be brought, as is noted in chapter *Romana*, section *Si autem post*, in the title *De appellationibus*, Book 6. Consider that an appeal from a definitive sentence always holds good; nor is it necessary that the law expressly permit it; it suffices if the law does not expressly prohibit it, as is singularly noted in the Digest, in the title *De re vendita*, law *Qui restituere*, section *Quo ergo*, where it says that the judge to whom the appeal is made ought to take cognizance, even when the appeal is prohibited. I answer that the appellant alleged such a cause which, if true, would allow the appeal to proceed: for example, if he said that he had confessed under duress, or if the other party claimed that a fact was notorious against the appellant, but the appellant denied that it was notorious, that is, known of itself, or clearly evident beyond doubt from the records. Since therefore the cause giving rise to the appeal, and conversely that which would invalidate it, are in doubt, jurisdiction is always to be deferred in favor of the appellant, and even according to civil law, rescission of the contrary order of a superior could be sought, if someone were ordered to be put into possession on the basis of a will that appears null at first sight. For this recourse is rather a remedy than an appeal, according to what is read and noted in the Digest, in the title *Qui satisdare coguntur*, law *Arbitro*, and in the Code, in the title *De accusationibus*, law *Absente*, and according to Bartolus in the Digest, in the title *De appellationibus*, law *Si expressum*. For the said putting into possession requires that the will be at least apparent, and existing at first sight on the surface, even if it does not exist in the marrow without the root of solemnity and validity. For those matters which require a deeper future investigation do not prejudice this possessory action, because it is a possessory action akin to the recovery of possession, as if we were to say that the inheritance was as if dispossessed in the person of the heir, to be restored and reintegrated: although the inheritance is not properly possessed, as in the Digest, in the title *Si quis testamento liberum esse iussus fuerit*, law 1, section *Scaevola*. For the possession of the deceased contained a certain right, as in the Digest, in the title *Uti possidetis*, law 1, at the end, which right the inheritance has, considering the right itself in the abstract understanding of the intellect, and not in the concrete act of the body, as in the Digest, in the title *De usucapionibus*, law *Ceptam*, and law *Nunquam*, section *Vacuum temporis*, and in the Digest, in the title *De acquisitione possessionis*, law *Cum heredes*. Thus it is concluded that the benefit of the edict is similar to the benefit of the interdict for recovering quasi-possession. And therefore, in the edict, the true hereditary right is not to be fully disputed, but only the first appearance, or apparent form, as in the Digest, in the title *De falsis*, law *Si quis legatum*, and in the Digest, in the title *De poenis*, law *Si quis aliquid*, section *Testamento*.

Secondly, I premise that although in a possessory action for recovery one should not dispute ownership, nevertheless if ownership has been disputed and proven, the exception of ownership prevails to exclude the possessory claim. This is the case noted and unique in law, Extra, de restitutione spoliati, cap. 1. And thus it is understood, as noted in the Digest, de iudiciis, l. si deui, in fine, Magna Glossa.

Thirdly, it must be premised that, whatever may be the case in the simple edict of the divine Adrian or Justinian, nevertheless in the edict of Milan, i.e., in the municipal law, if a named heir wishes to claim possession as continued by him by virtue and by the fiction of the statute, he must prove the truth, namely that he is truly an heir; and every exception which pertains to the petition for inheritance has the effect of destroying the fiction and the benefit of the statute. For the statute speaks of an heir, therefore of a true heir existing, and not of an abusive one, as in l. 2, ff. quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur, and ff. de verborum significatione, l. Paulus, l. unde. Concerning every hereditary right, true, and even concerning the slightest points of law, there ought to be dispute if anyone relies on the said statute. And if it is said that the said statute comes to the aid of common law, and therefore in the same cases it is as in the Authentica de filiis ante dotalia instrumenta natis, §. si, it is answered that rather it is contrary to common law, and is a fiction contrary to the truth, and it makes no possession fictitiously. And because it is contrary to common law, it cannot be regulated according to common law. Furthermore, if it is said that this statute was made for execution, i.e., in the edict, so that execution, which ought to be carried out by the judge, is carried out by the municipal law: which seems to be said with sufficient probability. Nevertheless, it seems here to be considered subtly that the law does not execute something unjust or void,

† because the eye of the law, just as the eye of God, sees all things and beholds all things, as is stated in that law, ff. de cond. ob causam, l. si pecuniam, § si seruum. And therefore I concede that the said statute is for edictal execution, where a decree was required in the person of the true heir: but not in the person of an abusive heir, and prima facie, however. And therefore the statute prudently made mention of an heir, such an heir as he is, but in its primary meaning, i.e., of a true heir. Otherwise, if the testator had said, "whoever shall be my heir, let him be heir to my son." For by these substantive words the efficacy of the heir is demonstrated, as in ff. de vulg. sub., l. qui liberis, § hęc verba. For an heir is one who is the same person as the deceased, which cannot happen except through truth.

Fourthly, it must be premised that every article concerning usury must be adjudicated according to canon law, both in the ecclesiastical forum and in the secular forum; and both in the principal cause and in the cause of appeal; because an appeal changes the forum and the judge, while the quality of the case is retained. And since the laws in the matter of usuries are subject to the canons, nor do they disdain to imitate the sacred canons in this regard, as is fully noted in C. de usuris, Auth. ad haec, and in Auth. de ecclesiasticis titulis, in the beginning, it is clear that the canons must be observed in any forum and in any cause, as in c. quamquam, §. si, de usuris, lib. 6, no. extra de foro competenti, c. quod clericus. For no one would say that the testament of a manifest usurer deserves execution, when the decretal not only condemns the testament of the mind, but also removes the presence of witnesses; so that his testament is said to lack witnesses, unless a confirming cause supervenes, namely, a solemn caution, which in this case fakes retroactivity, as in c. quamquam in the text, and in the novella.

From the foregoing premises, it is evident that the said appeal, with respect to the chapter on usury, proceeds according to both canon law and civil law, which imitates canon law. Furthermore, it is evident that it proceeds with respect to the statute of Milan, since that statute requires a cause of ownership. It also appears to proceed with respect to the law *edicto*, because although the merits of the testament should not have been disputed, yet if they were disputed and the nullity was established, the judge cannot, against his conscience, put the actor in possession, presupposing the opinion of many who say that the second testament is null due to the omission of the son. For this omission is established by writing, from the conjunction of two writings of the first and second testaments; for it is sufficiently clear that from the conjunction of two writings matters become clear, as stated in the argument of the Code, *de fidei instrumentis*, law *comparationes*. I willingly pass over this point, because it is not now to be disputed, but only whether the appeal should be admitted or not.
