Moreover, every appeal that can be justified and does not err in matter or form in its introduction is, as it were, a new certainty for the actor, who is to be favored in the principal cause rather than the defendant; the laws are common. But I do say this: because it has been known promiscuously and implicitly concerning that which pertains to the cause of ownership and possession, and the cause of usury, undoubtedly the appeal must be admitted, and then scrutinized and decided according to the nature of the appeal. I will not omit that the son, who was detained and held by his father during his lifetime, is fully presumed to possess immediately after the father’s death, as noted in the law *cum heredes* and in the Institution *de haereditatum qualitate et differentia*, section *sui*. And since he was not cited, the judge’s decree was null by the law itself: partly because he is presumed to be the heir, partly because he is presumed to be the possessor, as in the Digest, *de ventre in utero*, law 1, section *denunciari*, where it is expressly stated, and also by the rule of both civil and canon law, as well stated in the law *meminerint* and in the Code, *si per vim*, law *fi*, and in the canon *licet episcopus*, *de praebendis*, book 6. It is also worthy of consideration that the first testament was valid, solemn, and favorable to the son; but the second testament did not make express mention of the first, but only in a general clause, which does not seem sufficient to revoke the first testament, as in the Code, *de testamentis*, Authentic *hoc inter liberos*. Since the first testament was made before many notaries and witnesses, and in which writing is necessary according to the form of the statute of Milan, it ought to be regarded as made in writing, as in the Code, *de fidei instrumentis*, law *contractus*. These matters, therefore, are to be speculated upon and all considered, saving the sentence of the more weighty counsel, as in the law *Claudius Felix*. On this matter, I have noted something by way of discussion in the law 1 of the Code, *de secundis tabulis*, after Cynus.

I also do not omit that point, namely that when two causes are joined together, one of which rejects an appeal and the other admits it, and a sentence is passed simultaneously on both, an appeal may be taken from both, especially on the grounds expressly stated in the law; or when the sentence is notoriously unjust: in which case the appeal is considered as a recourse. For this defect in the judge’s mere office must be remedied by a superior. This is the text and the ordinary gloss, according to one interpretation, which is commonly approved by the learned authorities. D. qui satis cogantur, l. arbitro.

† And to the aforesaid it contributes that we have said, that from a sentence passed on a condition under the law *Si quis in tantam*, Codex, *Unde vi*, an appeal may be taken, because it exceeds the most well-known limits of a simple possessory action. Moreover, it is inequitable for anyone to be enriched at another’s loss, and from another’s goods; and this is the equity written in the law *Si me et Titium*, Digest, *Si certum petatur*. Hence it follows that the judge, by virtue of his office, even if the strictness of the law is lacking, ought to supply from equity, as in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Plane*, in the end. And that also is the reason which moved the gloss in the said law *Arbitro*. Moreover, when inequity is detected, especially by the substantial instruments of the litigation, then, on account of notorious injustice, since the notorious is equivalent to a judicial declaration, an appeal may be taken from the sentence, notwithstanding that otherwise the appeal has been removed. This is stated by the ordinary gloss in the Decretals, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Ex quaestione*, in the penultimate gloss, *Quis non debent iniuriae procedere, unde iura nascuntur*, hence the laws arise, as in the Codex, *Unde vi*, law *Meminerint*. Indeed, from the first decree, which is detentory, an appeal is taken, because it establishes a right in the thing, that is, a praetorian pledge. Moreover, from the Carbonian and the *ventris* [interdicts], because the petitory action is deferred in the meantime, and it is not momentary, but has a determined period of time, as in the law *Si*, Codex, *De Carbonario edicto*. The cause of filiation is also to be decided by canon law, both principally and incidentally, as in the Decretals, *De ordine cognitionis*, chapter *Tua*, and chapter *Lata*, Decretals, *Qui filii sint legitimi*, both in the first instance and on appeal, as there it is clear. I, Baldus. CON.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a compromise between two territories, by order of the prince, is valid when one of the said territories has protested that it acted out of fear of the prince; and whether an award rendered immediately after the appointment of arbitrators is valid or not: and no. 3.
2. For 40 years, the way of saying that no award is valid is closed.
3. When there is a question of territory, etc., whether such a controversy can be compromised.
body: In the name of Christ. To the most powerful and illustrious lords, Lord Luchino of the Gloriosi, Viscount of Milan in the city of Vercelli, and the illustrious prince and lord, Lord John, Marquis of Montferrat in the territory of Casale. Behold, that a lawsuit and dispute concerning the territory and boundaries of the said lands was pending between them and the inhabitants of those places; therefore, so that no further brawls and contentions might arise between the aforementioned parties, the said Lord Marquis commanded, under penalty of two thousand florins and his indignation, the power, council, and county of the said territory of Casale that they appoint a certain syndic to compromise the said cause both in law and in fact, which likewise did Lord Luchino in the community of Vercelli: and syndics were appointed on both sides, however those from Casale, prior to the appointment of the said syndic and subsequently, protested that they were making the said syndic out of fear of the said Lord Marquis, otherwise they would not have done so. Finally, during the same fear, the said syndics made a compromise in law and in fact, and the arbitrators chosen immediately judged and pronounced. And the aforementioned events occurred already more than forty years ago.

† Now the inhabitants and the community of the castle of Casale wish to assert that the said syndicate, award, and compromise were null by operation of law, because the appointment of the syndic was oppressive and made under the fear of a superior. Conversely, it is conceded that the fear was just, since the aforementioned lords had jurisdiction and the power to command, so that recourse to brawls and arms might be avoided, and also for the sake of peace. Certain things are not only permitted but also commanded, as in D. de usufructu, l. aequissimo; and Extr. de praebendis, c. nisi esset; and D. de novo operis nuntio, l. 1, § et post operis. Moreover, these compromitting parties did not compromise regarding their jurisdiction, because jurisdiction does not reside in cities, but in the lords of the cities, according to Innocentius. Hence, those who caused the matter to be compromised were those who had the principal interest. It was not for the subjects to object, but to obey; for whenever jurisdiction is in question, status is at issue; and status pertains to the superior, not to the subjects, as noted by Innocentius in Extr. de iudiciis, c. cum deputati; and in c. olim; and in D. de restitutione spoliatorum. Unless it were alleged that the dominion was tyrannical, because it was not by permission of the Emperor. But this allegation should not be pursued, because the whole world observes the contrary. Hence, I turn to another allegation on the other side, namely, that the said syndicate did not hold good; and this by D. qui in aliena, § si, D. de acquisitione hereditatis; or by the gloss placed there. But to the other gloss it may be answered, because it speaks of that which depends on the will of one person, whereas compromising depends on the will of two. Likewise, an act by a revoked procurator is valid if the revocation did not come to notice; so by similar reasoning it ought to be valid here, lest a fraudulent device avail those who protest, because fraud ought not to aid anyone, nor deception, which properly concerns the authority of a superior, as in c. 1, de renuntiationibus, in the Clementines. Likewise, an act contrary to a protestation, as in Extr. de constitutionibus, c. cum M. Ferrarien. Moreover, the award was observed for so long a time after the death of the said lords, and after the oppression ceased, because all things are deemed ratified, as noted in D. de conditionibus ob turpem causam, l. si obturpem; and by Cynus in l. 2, C. quod metus causa.

† Moreover, forty years have elapsed. By this prescription, the way of saying "null" is closed, which way is the office of the judge, as is stated in the Digest, On Prescriptions, 30 years, l. sicut. Indeed, even the complaint of falsity is removed by such a long time, as is read and noted in the Code, On Falsity, l. querela. To solve for the conclusion, it must be said that the transaction which is impositive is not valid, and that which is impositive is one made under compelling imperial authority; the text is in the Code, On Transactions, l. si quis maior.

† It must also not be omitted that, since nothing regarding the rights of the transacting parties was ascertained, but judgment was rendered abruptly and on the same day, the pronouncement does not appear to have been valid, unless the rights of the parties were notorious to the arbitrators; which is not presumed, unless it is established, as noted in *l. sed et si per praetorem*, § *quotiens*, D. *qui ex causa matrimonii*. And this is true, unless the parties were prepared for brawls and arms; for then all things are valid on account of public utility. For these civil disputes are accustomed to produce all evils; and therefore they ought to be restrained by the authority of a superior, as noted by Innocentius, Extravagant, *de probat.*, c. *in praesentia*. This is to be proved or presupposed simply, because it consists in fact. Moreover, he who deceives so that he may not be deceived is said to use prudence, not calumny, as in D. *de legibus*, 2, *l. cum pater*, § *Titio*; and C. *de ponderibus auri*, *l. fin.*; and D. *de dolo*, *l. 1*, § *non fuit*, where this matter is discussed.

† That also must not be omitted, that when it concerns territory, in which resides the jurisdiction to exercise jurisdiction, to interpose decrees, and the power of the sword, such a controversy cannot be submitted to arbitration, as is stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, l. *Non distinguimus*, §. *De liberali*, unless such an arbitration agreement were confirmed by the authority of a superior holding both mere and mixed empire; and then it would be valid by the power of the confirmation, and not otherwise, as in the Digest, *De officio proconsulis*, l. *Observare*, §. *Finis*, and in the Authentica *De defensoribus civitatum*, §. *Interim*. For one cannot grant nor take away private jurisdiction, and especially not perpetual jurisdiction, as in the Code, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, l. *Priuatorum*, and there the note. It makes no difference what is noted in the Decretals, *De constitutionibus*, c. *Cum omnes*, and c. *Cum accessissent*. Moreover, jurisdiction granted under fear is null by the law itself, as in the Digest, *De iure*, l. 1, §. *Nec mirum*, because there is involved a change in the natural status of a free person, and that is the reason, l. 1, §. *Quae honorandae*, Digest, *Quarum rerum actio non datur*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Although statutes are made by inferiors, they are not valid unless confirmed by superiors. And statutes are abrogated by contrary disuse.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows. A certain man named Antonius took Bertha as his wife, who remained with him in marriage for ten years; after the ten years she died without children. The brother of the aforementioned Bertha demands that the dowry be returned to him according to the common custom of that place. The husband opposes, stating that the dowry belongs to him by virtue of a certain ancient statute enacted by the commune of that place without the authority of its superior, which provides that if the wife dies after ten years, the dowry shall belong to the husband. That statute was never alleged until now; indeed, the common custom in the said place has always been that if the wife is found to have died without children at any time, the dowry was always recovered by the relatives. There are also new statutes, in which no mention is made of this matter; nor was there ever any lawsuit or controversy concerning this; indeed, the dowry was always restored to the relatives. On this point it is asked: what is the law?

† According to the foregoing, the said statute was invalid, because a statute of those who enact it is valid only when it pertains to them to enact and confirm it; but since confirmation of statutes did not pertain to those concerning whom the question arises, the statute was ineffective from the very beginning, as in C. de iur. om. iu. l. priuatorum, and as noted on both sides in ff. de ius. et iu. l. omnes populi. For there it is not said that every people can make a statute. Rather, it is said that that people which is governed by its own laws or customs, partly by its own, etc. For that word “which” is placed restrictively, as in C. de sum. trinita. l. 1. To this effect also serves Auth. de defen. ciuit. §. interim. And although making statutes is sometimes a matter of low jurisdiction, nevertheless confirming statutes is always a matter of mere empire. And statutes cannot be confirmed except by a magistrate having mere empire, as noted in l. 1. §. 1. ff. quod quisque iuris, and C. de sen. et interlocuto. l. nulli. Moreover, when a superior confirms certain statutes, whatever is not found to have been confirmed appears to have been derogated, as in l. tribunus. §. vltimo. ff. de milit. testa., and as noted by Dyn. in ff. de lega. 1. l. legata inutiliter, and C. de emenda. Iustin. C. l. 1. Furthermore, contrary custom prevails, as in ff. de legibus. §. fin., and especially when it accords with the common law, because it easily returns to its nature, which the law of action for dowry gave, as in ff. de pact. l. si vnus. §. pactus, vers. quid in specie dotis. It is therefore clear from the above that the said dowry does not pass to the husband’s profit, but must be returned to the heirs of the woman. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether lessors of a lease for the cutting of a certain wood by a third party are bound to name the lessee himself, or whether the lessee himself is bound to confess. And see in counsel 264.
2. Fault in omitting does not give rise to an action under the Lex Aquilia. And no one is ever punished criminally or pecuniarily for the slightest fault.
3. One is not said to disturb who does not have the intention of disturbing.
4. A statute granting discretion to punish is understood to apply where there is a delict.
body: In the name of Christ. Given the common statute of Pavia, which imposes a certain monetary penalty on those who disturb anyone in the possession of a thing which he truly possessed, it is proposed that A. and B. were hired by C. to cut down a certain forest truly possessed by D., adjacent to another wood of the said D. The said hirers of laborers and the said hirer of laborers were thereupon accused. Now the question arises, without calling into doubt the possession of the said D., whether the said hirers or the said hirer are therefore liable to the penalty of the statute, or rather to a simple action under the Lex Aquilia, or to the interdict *quod vi aut clam*.

And it appears that they are liable to the penalty of the said statute, because the statute does not distinguish whether fraud intervened or not; therefore, we ought not to distinguish either, as in D. de publicanis, l. de precibus. Moreover, injury should not be done to another under the pretext of error, lest one of better condition be more foolish than one who is expert, as in l. servus, D. quod vi aut clam. Furthermore, because they ought to have inquired, at least by domestic inquiry, and among neighboring inhabitants, whose said wood it was and who possessed it; for if they had inquired, they would easily have known, as in C. de ingenuis et manumissis, l. si aviam, and D. de fluminibus, l. 1, § 1. And not to inquire about that which one is accustomed and ought to inquire about is a species of gross negligence, as in D. de nova operis nuntiatione, l. doli mali, § fin. Moreover, he who causes damage in another’s property is liable not only civilly by the action of the Lex Aquilia, but also criminally to the penalty imposed on the fisc; this is the singular gloss in l. fin., D. de privatis delictis.

To the contrary, it appears that no damage was given if the coppice was intact, provided, however, that the wood was not carried away by them. It would be otherwise if the wood were not coppice, because then some damage would have been given, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si servus servum, § si oliva, and D. quod vi aut clam, l. nam et si ramos. Moreover, in the interdict quod vi aut clam, no distinction is made between damage and no damage, because the very disturbance of possession is held as damage given, as fully noted in D. quod metus causa, extat.

To the contrary is the ordinary gloss on the text in D. de rei vindicatione, l. in rem, § signum. For these hirers of labor are excused, because they are accustomed to work in such matters and to hire out their labor, as in D. de iniuriis, l. item apud, § si quis astrologus, and having regard to their art, they applied their labor to a lawful thing.

† Moreover, if any fault could be imputed to the said workmen, it would lie in their failure to inquire; but such fault by omission does not give rise to an action under the Lex Aquilia, because it is the most slight, as states the text of the law *Si cuius*, § *De praeteritis*, in the Digest, under the title *De usufructu*. Furthermore, no one is ever punished criminally by ordinary penalty, such as this one, even if it be a pecuniary penalty, for the most slight fault. This is noted singularly by Cynus in the Code, under the title *De episcopis et clericis*, in the law *Si quis non dicam rapere*. And by this reasoning, the lessors are excused; however, the contractor of labor is not excused, because he ought to have known the boundaries and limits of his property, and ought not to have erred in his own conduct, as stated in the Code, under the title *De finium regundorum*, in the law *Si constiterit*, and in the Digest, under the title *Pro socio*, and under the title *De acquisitione hereditatis*, in the law *Duo fratres*. From these authorities it appears that the most slight fault has a certain latitude, the minimum degree or least appreciable aspect of which lies in non-feasance; and therefore one need not concern oneself with trifles, because when one transgresses only slightly, one is not censured, as stated in the Digest, under the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Quamvis*. If, therefore, the most slight fault is not the same thing, as stated in § *De praeteritis*, if it be understood subtly. Moreover, these lessors of manual labor are rustic persons, and leniency is shown toward rusticity, except in natural law, as stated in the Code, under the title *De in ius vocando*, in the law *Venia*. But to trust a good man who hires their labor, since everyone is presumed to be good, is not to do anything contrary to natural law, as noted in the Digest, under the title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Titio*. And it supports this what is noted in the Code, under the title *De servis fugitivis*, in the law *Quicunque*, § *Pe.*, where a lawful contract excuses the one who errs, and there I said. It supports the foregoing, because the law says "let him know," [meaning] we do not wish to bind [one] through ignorance, as stated in the Code, under the title *De tabulariis*, in the law *Generali*. For those deceived are not fully held liable due to the slippery nature of ignorance, as stated in the Digest, under the title *De decretis ab ordine faciendis*, in the law *Si*.

† Moreover, one does not disturb who lacks the intention of disturbing, as is elegantly noted in *l. si duo*, in the beginning, D. *uti possidetis*, unless they were neighbors, because they are presumed to be at fault, as in *l. si ita*, D. *de suntu inst.*, and *l. 1*, § 1, D. *de flum.*, and as noted in *l. 2*, C. *quoniam fiscus, vel priv.*, and *l. dominus horreorum*, D. *loc.*, and *l. 1*, C. *ubi de ratiociniis agi oportet*, and according to Bartolus in *l. 1*, D. *si cert. pet.* That which must not be omitted is that if these workers exceeded the limits of the mandate by sending a sickle into another’s harvest, the master is not liable, because he did not order it, nor did he ratify it, as in *extra de rest. spol.*, c. *cum ad sedem*. Nor does c. *ult.*, *de homicidio*, lib. 6, stand in the way, because there the mandatary exceeded the limit in a personal offense, here in a real one. Moreover, there the limit could not be set in the entry of the sword, because the sword obeys the body more than the soul, and other things are usually deadly to others: and death is connected with and inseparable from the atrocity of the wounds; and therefore that which harms is considered, because fraud precedes accident: otherwise it would be different, as in D. *ad Sil.*, *l. qui posthumos*. Nor are the workers themselves liable on account of ignorance, as I have said above; and if it is said that rather they should be punished by an arbitrary penalty, because

† A statute grants discretion. I answer that discretion to punish is never understood to be granted where there is absolutely no offense. For discretions apply to the selection of penalties between one penalty and another, as in D. de poenis, l. hodie. But where there is an offense, there is no penalty at all, and therefore no selection or discretion applies between penalties: since the accused is protected by his own innocence: and the credibility of innocence affords the greatest security, as in C. de iniuriis, l. si non conuicii. However, where the type of crime does not correspond to the quality of the penalty, it is necessary to deviate from the ordinary penalty to an arbitrary penalty, either ascending or descending to or from the penalty, as befits the degrees of culpability. Likewise, a substitution occurs on account of the status of the person involved, as in C. vt infra certum tempus crimi. quaestio termini, l. 2; and D. de poenis, l. hodie; and D. de his, qui non infa., l. quid ergo, §. poena grauior. And see what is noted by Bartolus in l. 1, §. 1, D. si quis testamento liberum esse iussit. Furthermore, it would be absurd to say that one who hires out his labor for one day or fewer would be required to investigate the owner, because the investigation would take more time than the labor itself, as in D. de damno infecto, l. inter quos, §. si dominus. The one who gave the order would also be excused if he did not specify the location with certainty, because he is not understood to have ordered what is contrary to law, as in l. si pater, D. quae in fraudem creditorum; and l. si procurator, D. de conditione indebiti. And there, note. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitute who dies before the fulfillment of the condition transmits the substitutions to his heirs.
body: In the name of Christ. Albert, a citizen of Verona, of the parish of Saint Mary in the alley, died having made a will, and in his will he instituted his legitimate son Antonio, who was underage, as universal heir, and he substituted to him Lord Cansegno della Scala, then lord of the city of Verona, by these words, namely: “If my legitimate son and universal heir, the aforementioned Antonio, should die without children born of a legitimate marriage, then, and in that case, I institute the aforementioned Cansegno as my universal heir.” Now it is the case that the aforementioned Lord Cansegno, the substitute as above, died twelve years before the death of the aforementioned Antonio, the instituted heir, who was then still underage; finally, the aforementioned Antonio died without legitimate children. Now the question arises: whether the aforementioned Antonio could have made a will regarding the aforementioned inheritance, or whether the inheritance, by right of the aforementioned substitution, belongs to the heirs of the aforementioned Lord Cansegno, the substitute as above?

† Because this question is determined by that solemn and notable law, *Qui patri*, in the Digest under *De acquisitione hereditatis*, together with its gloss, I therefore decide as follows: there are two cases. For sometimes a coheir is substituted to an impubes; and then, although he dies while the impubes is still alive, he transmits the right of pupillary substitution, if the pupillus subsequently dies during his pupillary age. This results from the union of the pupillary substitution and the right of accretion, which draws the substitution toward its own more favorable nature, because there is favor in transmission. Or, the substitute was not given as a coheir to the impubes, or the instituted heir died after reaching majority; and then no transmission takes place, because the substitution has become void, as stated in the Code, *De caducis tollendis*, § *Pro secundo*, and in the Digest, *De vulgaribus substitutionibus*, *Sed et si plures*. From these it appears that the said Lord Cansegnorius did not transmit the said substitution to his heir, as is fully set forth in Law 2 of the Code, *De his qui ante apertionem tabularum*. The objection from the second book of Legacies, *Quod principi*, does not hold, because this is not the prince spoken of there, since his [substitution] does not endure by any perpetuity. Likewise, it appears from the foregoing that if the said pupillus died after reaching majority, he could freely make a will, because the substitution had vanished, as stated in the aforementioned § *Pro secundo*, together with its material. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legitimated child fully acquires the rights of legitimate children, and whether legitimation is tied to territory.
2. Whether a son, whether present or absent, can be legitimated by the will of his father, whether present or absent.
3. A spurious child can be instituted heir subject to the condition that he shall be able to take.
4. A vulgar substitution can be made in favor of a spurious child.
5. Whether a grandfather can institute as heir or substitute a grandson legitimately born of a spurious son; and the precaution for this.
6. The precaution by which one having spurious children can exclude odious collaterals.
7. What form the institution of legitimated spurious children ought to take.
8. Whether an absent and unaware person can be legitimated.
9. Whether legitimation is valid if the testator has two spurious sons of the same name, born of different concubines, and it does not appear from the legitimation privilege which one he intended.
body:
In the name of Christ. Title of the Prince of Achaea. Amadeus of Savoy, Prince of Achaea, etc. The inscription, or title, by which the Count of Savoy styles himself is as follows: namely, Amadeus, Count of Savoy, Duke of Chablais and of Vaud in Italy, Marquis and Prince, and Imperial Vicar General.

Assuming that the Lord Count of Savoy and Prince of Achaea have, as they do have, effective privileges for legitimizing natural children, bastards, manzeres, those born of incest, adulterers, or adulterine offspring, or those conceived from any other incestuous or condemned intercourse, and that the legitimizations have been made in due form:

It is asked first, whether the institutions and substitutions made in the drafting of the will are valid and proceed according to law, or not.

Secondly, it is asked, whether the testator, in the case where all the aforementioned matters should fail, could institute and substitute as his universal heirs the sons of another bastard, whomsoever he wished, or not.

Thirdly, it is asked, whether the testator himself, for those causes for which a father can disinherit his son, or for any of the same, or for another cause, could in his will, or codicil, or otherwise, disinherit and totally deprive his sister and the sons of his sister of all succession and inheritance, and of his goods, in such a way and manner that whether the will is valid or is revoked to an intestate estate, the said sister and the son of the sister could not claim or demand anything in the goods and inheritance of the testator.

Fourthly, it is asked, whether the legitimized sons of the testator could be legitimized by another, for example by the said Duke of Milan, or the Count Palatine, or another having full power over legitimizing from the Imperial throne, etc.? And whether by a second legitimization the first legitimization is vitiated, or not? And whether one is strengthened and validated by the other?

Fifthly, it is asked, what, or what kind of way is the better, safer, and clearer path and mode of proceeding, by which the testator and his bastard sons, because he lacks legitimate and natural sons, and even natural sons only, could have and obtain what they intend? Because the father wishes absolutely that all his goods should come to the said bastard sons after his death.

Sixthly, and lastly, it seems to be asked, if the testator has two bastard sons of the same name, born of different concubines, acting in different parts, and it does not appear in the privilege of legitimization which one was intended, whether such uncertainty vitiates the legitimization? Also, whether the declaration of the father wishing to declare which one he intended is admitted, or can be received?

I answer the doubts, or points, formed above, and to be better formed, considering them. I premise for clarity that sometimes the status of a person arises from nothing, as in an adopted son, for adoption does not find any son, but makes one anew civilly and fictitiously, with nature cooperating: and this has nothing to do with our case. Sometimes the status of a person is transferred to the opposite status, as from a bastard to a legitimate: and this is our case,

† Where I consider that such legitimation, if made solemnly and by imperial privilege or by custom permitting it, of which custom there is no contrary memory, the person thus legitimated fully acquires the rights of legitimate children: yet with this distinction, that either the one legitimating has legitimate power by reason of territory circumscribed within his own boundaries, and cannot legitimize outside his territory, neither personally nor in rem, so that those who are legitimate outside [his territory] are not so. Cap. Per venerabilem. Hence the Count of Savoy could not legitimize a Florentine for the succession to the property of another Florentine existing outside the principality of Savoy; or he has the authority to legitimize by simple imperial privilege: and then he can legitimize throughout the whole Roman Empire, because the authority to legitimize does not adhere to the territory of Savoy, but exists by itself and in general. To this effect it is noted by Lord Dynus in l. Ergo, § 1, ff. de acquirenda rerum dominium.

† Furthermore, it must be premised that a son, whether present or absent, may be legitimated by the will of his father, whether present or absent; provided, however, that there is consent, as stated in the Authentico *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, §. *et generaliter*. For legitimation, insofar as it is a petition to the prince, is a certain type of supplication, which may be made on behalf of an absent person, even without a mandate, provided that it is subsequently ratified. But insofar as it resides in the prince who legitimates, the true reality of legitimation properly consists there, which is of mere imperial power, and more than mere imperial power, if anything greater can be said, because it cannot be effected without derogation from the common laws, as stated in the Authentico *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, §. *si*, column 7.

†Furthermore, consider that if an institution may be made to several persons under a condition, although it will be effective, with respect to excluding the intestate successors in the meantime, once the condition is fulfilled, nevertheless the instituted heir will not be able to enter upon the inheritance until there exists the capacity to succeed, as in D. de legatis 2, l. si ita quis.

† Furthermore, it is premised for the sake of clarity that a vulgar substitution may be made in favor of a spurious child, as established by the text and gloss, which is not contrary to the law, C. de her. inst. l. 2.

† Moreover, although there are diverse opinions on whether a grandfather may institute or substitute as heir his grandson, born legitimate through his own spurious son, some say that he may not, because the grandson lacks a legitimate root and an orderly sequence, being born from an abominable and condemned root, as stated in C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si. However, that reasoning pertains to intestate succession. Hence, others say that he may be instituted and substituted, because although the father is spurious, the grandson himself is legitimate and capable of holding honors and successions, and of all things; for there is no stain upon him, and rather the immediate person should be considered than the mediate person, because the proximate cause adheres more closely to the effect than the remote cause, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum tale, §. pen., and noted in l. si mulier, ff. rerum amotarum. It is not an objection that the grandson is loved on account of the father, as in ff. de verborum significatione, l. liberorum; for what is natural cannot be eradicated, and it ought not to prejudice the grandson. Moreover, it is established that anything is permitted unless a law prohibits it or a compelling reason for prohibition exists. This question is briefly touched upon in the gloss in the aforementioned l. si, and was disputed by Rosfred. The truth is that the force of marriage is permitted, and therefore the grandson may be instituted and substituted, because the grandson ought not to be excluded or rendered incapable on account of paternal hatred, as in ff. de contractis nuptiis, l. non tantum, §. si emancipatus, according to Bartolus. It was good counsel to add a clause that no usufruct should accrue to the father of this grandson; and I approve of this counsel, so that every presumption of fraud may be avoided; and I cite what is noted similarly in l. 1, in fine, ff. de auctoritate tutorum. From the foregoing it appears that it is not necessary to disinherit the sister of the grandson in the grandfather’s will, because the person instituted or substituted is not a person of ill repute.

† Moreover, a certain precaution appears, namely how one having bastards may exclude odious collateral relatives, provided that the bastard is subsequently legitimated; otherwise, they would not be excluded upon the death of the bastard while still in his state of bastardy. Furthermore, a time limit may be assigned to the bastard to effect his legitimation, by argument from the Digest, *De heredibus instituendis*, law *Si quis instituatur*. Moreover, he who appends a condition seems to consent and to wish it to come into existence, as noted in law 2 of the Code, *De conditionibus incertis*; the said testator, who appends that clause, “when he shall be able to take,” seems to consent to the principle of legitimation at any time, because the said clause does not have a determination of a certain time, as the text is noted in the said law *Si ita quis*. However, those effecting legitimation should beware of suppressing the truth and expressing falsehood, as in the final law of the Code, *De his qui a non domino manumittuntur*. In accordance with that saying: “If you expect the care of the healer, you must reveal your wound.” And the laws provide for legal affairs what medicines provide for the sick, as the text says in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturalis efficacia sui*. However, testators should beware for themselves who append this clause, because legacies left in such a form would not be valid, nor would they deserve any execution before the legitimation of the son, even for pious causes, as in the Digest, *De legatis primum*, law *Haec verba*. Where it is said that a condition appended to an institution seems to be repeated in legacies, and therefore legacies likewise should not be due at a term on account of a pending condition, not on account of an inheritance not entered upon. But, omitting all the above-mentioned matters, I shall now begin a new opinion, and I shall respond more fittingly and in an orderly manner to certain new points formulated for me by the party.

And first, what should be the form of the institution, whether the father ought to say "my such natural sons." I answer that he ought not to speak in this manner, first because they are not spurious, since they have been legitimated; and therefore they ought not to be instituted with ignominy. Moreover, he ought not to say "natural," because they have now changed their status, nor are they henceforth persons of base condition, as C. de nuptiis, l. Imperialis. But he ought to speak as the truth lies: saying "I institute my such legitimated sons as heirs": and I highly approve that, for caution, he also leaves a small portion by way of institution: although this is done for caution. Moreover, I approve that the father substitutes to the said spurious children their born and unborn grandchildren, both vulgarly and by fideicommissum: and that the aforesaid are true, is evident from what I have written above.

† And observe that an absent and ignorant person may be legitimated by the authority of the prince; because the absence of the party, in that which is beneficial to the absent party, is supplied by the presence of the law, as C. de emancip. lib. l. si, which states that an infant may be emancipated by the authority of the prince for his own benefit. To this effect, ff. de iureiur. l. Labeo, and what is noted there. Similarly, I say that he may be legitimated, and yet the infant cannot consent, but the authority of the father and of the prince removes every defect; or it may be said that he becomes legitimate: nevertheless, not in power, unless he consents. It may also be said that the son is understood to have tacitly ratified, arg. ff. sol. matr. l. 2, § voluntate. For the matter concerns his own mere benefit. Hence it is concluded that whether he expressly ratifies or tacitly, he is capable, and it is not necessary that the consent of a sister or another collateral relative intervene in the legitimation, as fully noted by Bartolus and by me, ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus, especially since he is not a person of infamous origin by virtue of the legitimation, as C. de nupt. l. Imperialis. And it is expressly stated in de ritu nupt. l. Quia in provincia, § Divus. Nevertheless, I advise that public instruments be made concerning these ratifications, both by the father and by the sons, and it would be better if they were again legitimated with the consent of the father and the sons before the said magnific and illustrious lords, to remove all doubt; and after the legitimations, a new testament shall be made.

If a father has two spurious sons of the same name, such that uncertainty arises from the name as to which one he intended, the legitimation is not valid, nor is his declaration given effect, because it is not an act of his alone, but of him and the prince. D. de test. tut. l. Duo sunt Titii. Therefore, it is necessary that the first be legitimated clearly and openly: or he should say “my two sons, each of whom is called John,” so that no doubt arises from the name as to what he or the prince intended in the legitimation. For legitimation is a certain dispensation, which must be clear and unambiguous, as in c. 2, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6, and in c. Quia nonnulli, X, de rescriptis. But if they were born of different concubines, and the name of the concubine is expressed, it is sufficiently clear, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Et si pepercerit, in principio. And therefore it does not hinder us from discussing our doubt, having seen the instrument of legitimation, where the name of the mother is expressed, which makes the legitimation as certain as the name of the father, and even more so, because it is more certain, for the mother is always certain, as in D. de statu hominum, l. Vulgo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute prohibiting the administration of an oath to a minor, and providing that if administered it shall not be observed, is valid.
2. An oath is personal and does not extend to the heir.
body:
In the name of Christ. The statute, which is assumed in the facts of the question, follows, being in force in Pavia. Heading: That an oath shall not be administered to those under 18 years of age, and concerning penalties against those who do so. We also decree that no person shall administer an oath to anyone under 18 years of age in any contract or alienation; and that no notary shall draw up or issue an instrument regarding any act performed or done by such a minor in any contract or alienation. And if this is contravened, whoever shall have administered the said oath, or caused the aforementioned minor to swear, and the notary who drew up the instrument, and each of them, shall be punished in the amount of 25 Pavesi for each of them and for each offense; and the oath thus given and made shall be void. Moreover, anyone who notifies, or causes to be notified, to the ecclesiastical judge the said oath in order to compel the aforementioned minor to observe the oath, shall be punished for each offense in the amount of 25 Pavesi, and furthermore shall be liable to the minor for restitution of the damage suffered by the said minor because he was harassed by the ecclesiastical judge, or by his command, to observe the oath. This statute shall not apply to an oath of peace made in a capital war. And that henceforth the authority *sacramenta puberum* shall have no place in the city of Pavia and its district; nor shall any other provision of law that disposes similarly or to the same effect.

Assuming the said statute, the following case arises. A certain Sianninus died several years ago, survived by his legitimate and natural son Jacob, who was under 18 years of age, heir of his said father, and by his mother Francischina, and his paternal grandmother Antonia. Lacking a tutor and curator, he held the said goods for a certain time, and in the year 1395 he was brought to the territory of Stratella, which is within the district of Pavia, but in temporal and spiritual matters belongs to the Lord Bishop of Pavia. And there, in the presence of the magistrate of that territory, he repudiated the said paternal and grandpaternal inheritances; and he swore to hold and keep that repudiation and abstention valid and firm perpetually, under the prejudice of his soul and the obligation of his goods, protesting that he was a pubescent minor under 14 years of age. And in that repudiation, the same magistrate pronounced that the said minor was of that age. After that pronouncement, he donated the said inheritances, having first taken a corporal oath not to go against it. Then he entered the religion of the Order of the Friars Hermits. Now the brothers say that the said oath is not valid, and that all the aforementioned acts are null, or at least invalid. They also say that the said successions belong to their order, and they wish to claim those successions.

† It is asked, what is the law? I answer that the said oath does not bind, nor are the said brothers bound to observe the said oath, nor does the *auth. sacramenta puberum* have application in this case. And for the true understanding of the aforesaid, I consider three cases: for sometimes an oath is prohibited from being made, sometimes it is prohibited from being received, and sometimes it is prohibited both from being made and from being received. And we consider either civil law, or canon law, or both civil and canon law together. Indeed, if we consider civil law indiscriminately, an oath which is prohibited by public law is not valid, as in D. de legibus 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. si. Otherwise, if it were permitted by public law, and thus speaks the *auth. sacramenta puberum*. And the reason is that, when an oath is prohibited, natural age is considered; nor does it represent the minor as being of age, because this fiction of age has been removed by statute, as in C. de his, qui vel quae aetate impediti sunt, l. si. But if we speak of canon law, or if the statute wishes to derogate entirely from the oaths of minors by cancelling the said *auth. sacramenta puberum* in its entirety, it cannot do so, because an oath is of natural law, to which divine law cooperates, as in Inst. de iure naturali, §. naturalium. And because the law of the prince is more powerful than a municipal statute, and more reasonable in its kind. But if the statute distinguishes that *auth.* but does not abolish it, for example by distinguishing adult age, because it limits that *auth.* by distinguishing between full puberty at 8 years or 20 years, and not full, then from there onwards the statute is valid, so that minors may not misuse their substance, and especially all of it, or the greater part thereof; and particularly in making donations, for to donate is the same as to lose; and it is in the interest of the republic that no one misuse his substance; and then without doubt the said statute is valid, because it is good and equitable. Hence it properly fits the definition of a law, as in l. 1, in principio, D. de iustitia et iure. And fully noted by Bartolus in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo. And by me in C. de legibus, l. non dubium. To this effect serves D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana, in the reason thereof, where it says, "the interpretation of the prudent has broken captious liberality."

Moreover, an oath has two extremes, one on the part of the one swearing, and this pertains to religion; the other on the part of him to whom the oath is sworn; and this is merely temporal, and a statute can prohibit it from being received, as in l. 2, C. ne fideiussores dentur. It can also prohibit it from being reduced into a public instrument, which cannot be drawn up unless both parties command it; and the mandate does not bind, as in Auth. de non alienando, §. quia vero Leonis. Certainly, it does nothing that the minor goes to another place, and if it were not within the penitential district, nor jurisdictional, i.e., neither of the soil nor of the Empire, because the place is not considered here, but the person and the age; and because a statute is favorable, the favor of minors extends everywhere, as noted by Bartolus in l. cunctos populos. And perhaps also for another reason the said brothers are not bound to observe the said oath as inducing upon them some bond of spirituality, because entry into the mendicant religion is held as being dead, and his brothers succeed in his place more by the indulgence of the prince than by the consequence of legitimate succession, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. arrogator, §. sed an impuberi.
† An oath is against the persons involved on the part of the one swearing; nor does it affect the heir, as stated in the extrajudicial collection on oaths, chapter *Veritatis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A promise to institute someone as heir is invalid even if accompanied by an oath, and number 8.
2. Whether a promise and renunciation of not succeeding is valid, even if accompanied by an oath.
3. The edict on account of fear was not so much the word of man as the word of God.
4. Whether fear is presumed in a son.
5. It is not presumed that one has renounced the benefit of restitution in integrum, unless one expressly renounces it.
6. When an agreement concerning the division of a future succession is valid.
7. Whether a son, content with a dowry, or a donation propter nuptias, or a legitime assigned to him, can release his father from the burden of leaving him something.
9. Whether a statute can invalidate an oath.
10. No appeal lies from an award, nor from a sentence confirming an award.
11. A statute providing that no appeal, complaint, supplication, or allegation of nullity may be made: whether nevertheless restitution in integrum may be sought.
12. Whether clandestine betrothals are valid.
13. What are called clandestine betrothals.
14. On whom the burden of proof of age lies.
15. How a statute prohibiting a minor from contracting is to be understood.
body: In the name of Christ. In the case proposed, it must be premised for the sake of clarity,

† That sometimes a pact is made concerning the future succession of a living person to be promised, sometimes to be remitted, sometimes to be divided, sometimes something is taken from the present for the legitimate portion, and a pact is made not to claim more. In the first case, the promise is not valid: as if I promise by pact to institute someone as heir, because it tends directly to the wish and motive of capturing the death of another, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulatio hoc modo. And this promise cannot be validated by an oath, because an oath should not be the occasion of sinning, as in C. de indicta vidui. tol. l. 1. C. de legi. l. non dubium. §. fi. Although Speculator says that the testator can bind himself not to revoke the testament with an oath, and the same is said by d. Dyn. in l. hęredes palam. and in c. quod semel placuit. Nevertheless, this is not true, because this would be nothing other than promising future succession and depriving oneself of public right, i.e., the freedom of testating, as noted in C. de transa. l. cum donationis. And in the aforementioned l. stipulatio hoc modo, as interpreted by Bart., and in D. pro so. l. cum duobus. §. item respondit. It does not object in D. de act. empt. i. si quis seruum, because there something was promised after death by right established between the living: here, however, there was no right established between the living. And by this, it is answered to Coria, which speaks of the patron emancipator, who holds the place of manumission, and this first member does not pertain to the article of the question.

† The second member follows. Where a promise of non-succession has intervened: and then either an oath confirming the renunciation has intervened, which oath indeed was given freely, not by force or fraud: and the person swearing is of adult age, which age is suitable for taking an oath. For the oath of an adult has the same effect as the age of 25 years and more: because it adds the bond of religion, as noted in l. 2, C. de rescindenda venditione. Therefore, the oath must be upheld, as in c. 2, de pace, lib. 6. But if fear or fraud has intervened, then it must not be upheld, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si quis maior, and in Auth. sacramenta puberum. And this is by natural reason, because when the recipient of such an oath sins, the absolution of sins cannot be extorted either by force or by fraud, and therefore the recipient of the oath sins, and must not be heard, even speaking of mere natural justice.
† Hence Master Raymond says in his Summa that the edict of the praetor, stating that what was done out of fear he will not uphold, was not so much the word of a man as the word of God.

But it is asked whether this fear is presumed? And say that, as a rule, it does not fail where the contract is celebrated with one who has the power to obtain [the thing], and where there intervenes enormous lesion, for example concerning status, or liberty, or the loss of the greater part of the patrimony, as in D. 44.2.1.1, § quae honorandae. The gloss there calls this fear "excessive reverence." [It is] not daring to contradict, as in D. 47.2.ult. And the same is said by the gloss in the Decretals. But here it is doubted: the instrument appears, that the daughter was dowered, and that she renounced future succession, or, as it is better to say, any kind of hope, and all future succession: and she swore, etc. Nor is the oath otherwise extended. Now it is doubted concerning the understanding of this brief speech, and how it ought to be interpreted by the equity of the judge: and I say that it ought to be interpreted in this way: she swore, i.e., not to come against. Therefore, can she come against by reason of age? And it seems that she cannot, so that the thing may rather stand than perish. On the contrary, it seems that these words ought to be understood that she does not come against, i.e., by reason of the contract, but by common law.

† But the singular right of restitution in integrum has not been taken away, unless she has been informed of the benefit of restitution and has expressly renounced it: because a minor is not understood to have sworn under this head, since it is presumed that she was ignorant, as in D. de cond. indeb. l. si and l. idem quaesivit. And because the singular benefit of restitution in integrum must be removed by special words, as in D. de mil. l. illud § si talis. So, if mention of age is made in any part of the instrument, it is understood to have been sworn over the whole, as in l. 1 § 1 D. quarum rerum actio non datur. For such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate, as in D. de interrog. act. l. si defensor § 1, and noted in d. l. 2 C. de rescind. vend. Otherwise, I do not understand that the benefit of restitution in integrum has been renounced. Notwithstanding the authority Sacramenta puberum, because there she had contracted as an adult, and thus the oath was expressly added to supply the age. Now follows the third member.

†. s. since it is a promise concerning a future succession to be divided, and then say, as in C. de pac. l. si. For either that condition is appended, if the succession is deferred, we shall divide, and then it acts concerning the inheritance of a certain person, as it speaks there: or of an uncertain person, and it speaks in l. 3. ff. pro soc. But if no condition is appended, then the pact is entirely rejected: and thus whatever profit would follow therefrom is applied to the fisc, as in l. 3. ff. de his, quibus vt indig. But in fiefs there is one very special thing, that if marriage is contracted ad morganaticam with the consent of the lord of the fief on account of the authority of the lord interposed, whose death would not be in any way profitable to the vassal: and therefore the vow of seeking death ceases there, as in 10. col. de mino. ad morganaticam contracto. c. 1. And thus is understood what is in C. de coll. l. pactum. And there I said.

The fourth member follows, namely, in what cases a son, content with the dowry, or with the donation propter nuptias, or with the legitime assigned to him, releases his father from the burden of leaving anything to said son. And certainly it appears that this contract is lawful, as in C. de inofficiosa testatione, l. Si quando, §. Si; similarly, if something is given as a reward for emancipation, and a renunciation is made, and that which is given is according to law, in proportion to the father’s means: for the son has been satisfied inter vivos, and the father may anticipate the satisfaction of the natural debt, by argument to l. Falcidiam, l. Cum quo, de peculio, §. Si; C. de fideicommissis, l. Post mortem; ff. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. Patrem; C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. Aut si qua mulier. And if it is said that the amount of the legitime cannot be certain except at the time of the father’s death, I concede this; nevertheless, a transaction may be made regarding this doubt, i.e., a composition may be effected between father and son. For there is agreement according to natural law among those who are not devoid of reason, even if it does not correspond to the strict points of civil obligation, as in ff. de conditionibus indebitis, l. Frater a fratre. If, therefore, to this natural bond there is added an oath, which is the simple supplement of a natural obligation, and if no fear or fraud intervenes, the sacrament must be upheld, as in the cited c. 2, de pace, lib. 6.

† Now, reducing the matter to the points of the question, I say that if the amount of the dowry ascends to the legitimate portions of both parents, the renunciation and the oath must be upheld on account of the equity of the renunciation itself; and if they do not ascend to such an amount, the same result follows on account of the authority of the oath, and also on account of the authority of the statute, if the dowry is appropriate. For the statute and custom bind minors as well as adults, because the law is universal, as is stated in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, fragmentum leges, and in D. de administratione tutorum, l. sine haerede, § interposito. As for the oath, it must be established by proof; otherwise, no one is presumed to have sworn if it is not proven.

† It is doubted, if a statute disapproves an oath, what is the law. I answer: either it disapproves it formally, that is, with cause and reason, namely, a good and equitable one, or a general or pious one; then the oath is not valid. An example of a general one: D. de legibus 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. fin. An example of a pious one: in the case of minors and those lacking discretion, who do not possess the solidity of counsel, as reported by Cynus in the constitution sacramenta puberum. It is also in the interest of the republic that minors not be oppressed in their affairs, arg. D. de legibus 1, l. ciuitatibus. Hence, the said statute is commendable, because it is pious, removing the traps of those under age, and it is good and holy, arg. D. de iure patronatus, l. adigere, §. fin., and there note. I take a point regarding statutes on arbitrations: one provides that between blood relatives and affines one must strictly abide by the award; another provides that between strangers, after a certain time, the arbitral awards shall be binding. Now, a guardian made a compromise according to the form of the statute between blood relatives; an award was rendered; an action was brought for nullity and inequity; the judge confirmed the award. Against the confirming judgment, the minor seeks restitution in integrum. The question is whether he may do so? And I say,

† And if restitution cannot be granted against the award, in that manner it cannot be granted against the sentence confirming the award; otherwise it would follow that the definitive confirmation would harm the prevailing party, which is false, as is evident in D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. euidenter. And if you ask whether, by the said statutes, restitution in integrum has been abolished, it must be said that it has not, having regard to the statute concerning compromises between blood relatives, because in the said statute there is mention only of the remedies of the common law, namely those of inequity and nullity, and not of the remedies of the singular law, namely restitution in integrum. For these remedies are distinct, as is noted in D. de conditione indebiti, l. si.

† Moreover, the statute provides that no complaint may be lodged against the judgment; rather, a minor seeking restitution in integrum complains of himself or of the fraud of the adversary, and does not complain of the judge or arbitrator, as stated in D. de minoribus, l. praesens and l. praefecti. This applies when restitution in integrum is sought by the right of minority. It is otherwise with adults, where one alleges the injustice of the judge or a gross error, which is considered fraud on the part of the judge, as noted in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. seruo inuito, § cum praetor. Observe that the statute states that no appeal may be taken on grounds of nullity, nor may supplication be made. Hence, it closes off the avenues of judicial recourse. And if something cannot be declared null, it therefore cannot be reduced to the effect of nullity through restitution in integrum, because restitution in integrum induces nullity once granted, as stated in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si plures, in principio. Therefore, I hold that restitution in integrum cannot be sought, especially because it is a certain species of supplication, as stated in D. de minoribus, l. minor autem magistratus, and a certain species of appealing, as stated in C. de transactionibus, l. si causa cognita. And because, when one similar thing is removed, another similar thing is understood to be removed, hence it could not even be raised as an exception. And the aforementioned Cynus states that where an exception is removed by statute, restitution in integrum is also removed, because through it one would arrive at the right to raise the exception. Thus it is noted in D. de minoribus, l. si in causa ipse secunda, in his additions. But against an arbitration agreement, if one had been harmed because he compromised with his enemy or with a foolish man, restitution could well be sought, and the award would be rescinded indirectly, as stated in l. si ex causa, § 1 and § nunc videndum, D. de minoribus. But if an error were evident according to written law, restitution could also be sought, as stated in D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. seruo inuito, § si praetor. From these things it appears that the said inheritance belongs, according to what was declared in the award, unless fraud or gross negligence can be reproached in the arbitrator himself, as stated in the aforementioned § cum praetor. However, I fear that this gross negligence would be concealed by the confirmatory judgment. And this applies if the question concerns judgments. But if the question concerns succession, assuming that no judgment had been rendered, it must be said that the daughter of the son ought to succeed universally; but not to those who renounced, nor to their children, because the mother excludes them, since they are survivors, and in the dowry, which is in place of the legitime, the successor. Hence, no right to succeed is opened to their children, nor can it be opened. Inst. de legatis et agris successione, § proximos; and Inst. de hereditatibus ab intestato, § cum filius. Moreover, this was not properly a renunciation, but was a certain satisfaction, as stated in D. de pactis, l. intra, and C. de pactis, l. 1.

† Now I come to the chapter on betrothals: and I say that clandestine betrothals are valid, unless there is some legitimate impediment, in which case they would not be valid; indeed, knowledge of the impediment and fraud are presumed, as in the chapter *Ut ecclesiastica*, Extra, and the chapter *Cum inhibitio*, Extra, on clandestine betrothals, and in the Digest, on the administration of tutors, *Non existimo*. I do not consider it true that a betrothed woman, upon reaching adulthood, can marry another by sending a letter of repudiation, thereby losing her dowry, as in the Code, on betrothals, law 1. And therefore it is expedient for her to marry another with the license of the bishop, so that she may not lose her dowry, as in the chapter *Ex parte*, Extra, on the restitution of betrothals. This license the bishop ought not to grant before she is of marriageable age, unless the betrothal was null, or unless the girl had been deceived.

And clandestine betrothals are understood to be those which are made before a smaller number, namely five persons, or before secret witnesses; whereas those which are made with the festivities of betrothal and a crowd of friends assembled are called public and solemn, especially if they take place in church, as in l. 1, C. de lat. lib. tol. It is for the judge to inquire into the nature of the betrothals, as in the case of those of girls, and to approve them. And this pertains properly to the bishop; and therefore I consider it good counsel if this is requested by the second betrothed man and the girl, and he should remain in a place where he cannot suffer ambushes, as in extra de rest. sp. c. ex conquestione and c. literas in fine. And these have usually been ill-disputed and great controversies, as I have sometimes seen.

† As to another chapter, when age is in question, the burden of proof lies upon him who seeks restitution, i.e., rescission, of any contract or possession, because the other party has a well-founded claim by reason of consent, and thus according to the law of nations; and therefore the burden of proving pertains to the adversary, as in D. de probat. l. ab ea parte and l. cum de ætate; C. de in integr. restit. l. minorum and l. si minorem te; and there I noted fully. D. 15 de arbitris l. 3, gloss. cum si.

† Regarding the statute which provides that a minor cannot contract, I answer that this is understood when he contracts without solemnity; otherwise it is with solemnity, and therefore the said compromise was valid in light of the statute on compromises, which imposes the necessity upon the compromitter. Hence, the minor is not to be considered injured, because he makes use of the common law of statutes, as in C. de in integrum restitutione, l. non videro; as in ff. de minoribus, l. ait prætor, § permittitur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a hypothec arises from a receipt.
2. The counsel of fraud is proved in three ways.
3. The rule, "He who is prior in time," how it is to be understood.
4. There are three kinds of writings.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that, by reason of a deposit, loan, partnership, and other commercial dealings or transactions according to the common saying, a certain merchant was bound to receive from Titius and others of the said partnership one thousand florins, or more or less, which is of no consequence; and concerning this, the said creditor had an apodissa, or a writing of the said merchant written in his own hand, and the same recognized in court and lawfully confessed; nevertheless, in the said apodissa there is no mention of a hypothecation of goods. It happened that afterwards, by a public instrument, the said promise was made, the said apodissa was confessed, and the goods were therefore hypothecated.

The aforementioned creditor brought a hypothecary action against the alien possessors of the goods of the said debtors, having made excussion according to the form of the law, which the possessors state and allege that they purchased the said goods before they were hypothecated; and therefore the said hypothec does not extend to the said goods to be hypothecated, since they had previously passed out of the goods of the said debtor before they were hypothecated; hence neither in a general obligation, by which one obligates the goods that he has and will have, are these included, for they did not come within it, as in D. de pignoribus, l. et quae nondum sunt, §. quod dicitur; nor could they have come within a special one, since they were not in the debtor’s goods. There, title, l. 3, §. 1; D. de probationibus, l. ante omnia; Inst. de actionibus, §. item Severina; C. de Salviana interdicto, l. 1; C. si res aliena pignori data sit, l. cum res. And especially because the said possessors also have a hypothec for the defense of the things themselves, as is contained in their public instruments, and he who is prior in time is stronger in right: as in the rule Qui prior est tempore potior est iure; which hypothec is valid even for defense, as in D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. ex sexaginta, §. Latinus. And especially because a public instrument prevails over the said private acknowledgment in priority of time, as in C. qui potiores in pignore habent, l. scripturas; and D. ad legem Velleiam, l. Seia mancipia; and C. de falsis, l. si creditor colludens.

On the contrary, it seems that fraud is deemed to have intervened on account of the alienation of all the goods, or the greater and better part. Hence a revocatory action is granted, as in Inst. de actionibus, §. item si quis in fraudem. But there is excussion, as is proposed to have been made; for even if the alienations were made at different times, nevertheless from the conjunction of the alienations itself, premeditated malice, deceit, and fraud are presumed, as is notably stated in D. de legibus tertio, l. nomen, §. 1. If fraud is established, a revocatory action may be brought; and if it may be brought therefrom, it may also be pleaded by way of replication. Therefore, the intention of the aforementioned creditor, who brought a hypothecary action with a replication of fraud, ought to be upheld and strengthened; and hence not only is fraud presumed, but simulation is also presumed. And this for a twofold reason: first, because in the instrument of the alleged sales no price intervened, but rather a concession of price; second, because the thing was sold and partly donated, as is contained in the instrument, as in C. de mandato, l. per diversas and l. ab Anastasio; and notably in l. 1, C. ne liceat potentibus. And if you say that there it speaks of the cession of actions, I answer that the same applies in our case according to Guillaume de Cuggione and Doctor Cynus, D. de pactis, l. si tibi decem millia, in principio. It is not doubtful that, insofar as the thing was donated in fraud of creditors, it ought to be revoked by the Paulian action in factum, as in Inst. de actionibus, §. item si quis in fraudem, upon fraud being discovered through the discussion of the debtor’s goods.

† Moreover, it is not to be doubted that fraudulent intent is proven in three ways: namely, by the inventory of all goods; by the majority of the goods; and because the debtor was publicly beginning to fall into poverty. Furthermore, fraud is presumed from clandestine contracts. D. de restitutione bonorum, l. Non existimo. Moreover, the testimony of Ser Jacopo is supported by the light of truth, as D. de testibus, l. Ob carmen, § Si. Moreover, we ought to love the truth, as D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Hoc modo. Moreover, Lippi and the barbers should consider that there is fraud here, and therefore Ser Jacopo ought to be assisted by legal remedies: and this is the truth of law and fact.

† Notwithstanding the rule *qui prior* and the like. This must be understood as applying to one who is prior in an effective manner, not to one whose priority is absorbed due to intervening fraud. How fraud is to be proven is set forth in *l. qui se bonis*, D. de acquisitione hereditatis, and C. de repudiato herede, *l. 2*, and D. quae in fraudem creditorum, *l. omnes*, § *Lucius*. Fraud is also proven if, after the sale and the acknowledgment of the price, a person remains in possession and uses and enjoys the property as before. For such a title is presumed to be colorable and celebrated to the fraud of another, as in D. qui in rem suam, vel hypothecam solvere possunt, *l. sicut*, § *superuacuum*. There are many other valid indications of fraud and simulation to be presumed, as in C. de donationibus, *l. data iam pridem*, as noted by Bartolus in D. de donationibus, *l. post contractum*. And these matters are largely discretionary, depending on the quality of the facts and the persons involved, as in D. de transactionibus, *l. cum hi*, § *in causae*, because it is sufficiently difficult to prove fraud clearly. And therefore, those things which cannot be determined by a certain rule are committed to the subtlety of judicial discretion, as in C. de sententiis quae pro eo, *l. vnica*, § *in alijs*, and D. de usu, *l. mora*, according to the saying of the philosopher that it is necessary for well-established laws to determine all things, and to commit as few as possible to those who judge. *I.* difficult matters, as in Extr. de restitutione spoliorum, c. *cum ad sedem*, § *fi*, and C. de quaestionibus, *l. milites*, § *oportet*, and *l. non omnes*, § *a barbaris*, D. de re militari.

That which I said above, namely that fraud can be raised by way of replication, is sufficiently proven by what is read and noted in *l. nam postea*, § *si minor*, and the following §, D. de iureiurando. Furthermore, the hypothecary action, of which I spoke, does not arise from the *apodissa*, because it is not contained therein. And because a personal obligation does not follow the land, as in D. de iudiciis, *l. si fideicommissum*, § *tractatum*, but arises from the instrument in which the hypothecary clause is contained, which is *in rem*, as in D. de pignoribus, *l. si fundus*, § *in vendicatione*. Furthermore, I do not say that a personal obligation is proven by the *apodissa* alone, except to the prejudice of the writer, or unless the statute of the city dictated otherwise, because there are usually statutes concerning the *apodissae* of merchants, that they have the force of public instruments; but I say that this is proven from the account books, as noted by Bartolus in D. de donationibus, *l. nuda ratio*. However, the glossators say that account books do not make faith among others who did not order the writing to be made, unless perhaps in a certain manner, as noted in D. de iureiurando, *l. admonendi*, and D. de edendo, *l. quaedam*, § *nummularios*. And therefore, according to the gloss, it is necessary that the truth be proven by public instruments made from the origin of the transaction, not made after alienations, or by witnesses who were present at the truth.

† Moreover, there are three kinds of writings: public, solemn, and private. A public writing is one executed by a public hand, which proves the act of the contracting parties against all, as in C. de deposito, l. desiderium. A solemn writing is one attested by three witnesses, C. qui potest in pignus habere, l. scripturas, provided that the hand of the writer and of those granting the obligation is established. A private writing, however, is threefold: one is extraneous, which is called an apodissa or apoca, as in C. de fidei instrumentis, l. plures apocis; another is that which is contained within the body of the account book. And this latter is twofold: one holding a middle position, as it were, between public and private, such as the writings of money-changers and bankers; another holding the extreme position, i.e., entirely private, which was not made by reason of any office, as in C. de probationibus, l. rationes, and C. de conuentionibus fisci debitorum, l. inter cartulas, lib. 10. But this distinction is not necessary in our case, for all these are presumed to be true and legitimate; the question is solely concerning the hypothec, which I have clearly determined above. And to this effect is ff. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam, §. item quaesivit. Furthermore, if there were a custom that merchants’ apodissae were to be enforced against all, they would thereby be regarded as public instruments, as in extra de fidei instrumentis, c. cum dilectus. And although several partners may seem to have given surety for one another, it is not necessary to exhaust all of them, as in ff. de exercitoria actione, and as stated there by Jacobus de Arena. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a stipulation made for another in this manner, namely, "I lend to you for the benefit and utility of the person whom I shall name," is valid; and within what time he is bound to name that person; and whether the action is acquired by the person whom he ought to name at the time of the stipulation, or at the time of the nomination.
2. The exception may always and at any time be pleaded against the intention and the fact.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: Vagnolus of Cassisio confessed that he had received and taken from Martin three thousand pounds as a loan from the personal funds of the said Martin, for the benefit and advantage of the person whom the said Martin designated, whom he could designate at any time, with the stipulation added that the said Martin could not be paid nor released by him, but rather by him and from him who would be declared the creditor in the said amount. It happened that, after the death of the said Vagnolus, the said Martin declared that the said payment had been made for the benefit and advantage of Guido, who at the time of the said contract was under the paternal power of the said Vagnolus, his father. The question is whether the said Guido, by virtue of the said contract, designation, and declaration, has the right to bring an action or not.

† And it seems that he may bring an action, because in a loan for consumption (mutuum) it is a special rule that an action is acquired for one person by another, as in *l. Certi condicio*, § *Si nummos*, D. *Si certum petatur*. Moreover, the notary, as a public person, had stipulated, as in D. *De actionibus*, *l. His verbis*, by whom at least a useful action is acquired without any cession. And if it is said that an action cannot be acquired for a son in power against his father, as is read and noted in D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, *l. Actiones cedi*, that must be understood according to the old law; but according to the new law, from an adventitious cause, an action can well be acquired for the son, as in C. *De bonis, quae liberi*, *l. Cum oportet* and *l. Non solum*. Even if the exercise [of the action] were competent due to paternal power, as in D. *De iudiciis*, *l. Lis nulla*, yet after the paternal power has ended, the exercise competes well, as in the laws cited above. Furthermore, this Vagnolus was already dead when the said declaration was made, and consequently the time from which it could begin had arrived. Hence, it does not seem that the impediment of paternal power is to be considered here, neither with regard to the capacity to sue nor with regard to actual exercise, as in C. *De collationibus*, *l. Si*.

To the contrary, it seems that the said contract was not valid, for it seems to contain contradictory terms: for it says that the money was Martin’s, and it says that no right is acquired to the said Martin. For these seem to contradict each other, since this contract was not a natural loan for consumption, but a civil one, from which it follows that an action must first be acquired directly for the stipulator, otherwise the contract is not valid, as in D. *De actionibus et obligationibus*, *l. Quaecunque gerimus*: “Unless it begins in our person, they make our act void.” Moreover, this pact was added with the consent of Vagnolus, by whom he could not bind himself civilly to a son in his power, as in D. *De conditione indebiti*, *l. Frater a fratre*.
