For it is certain that either the loan for consumption did not intervene, and the contract is simulated, and no action can be brought; or it truly intervened, and then Vagnolus immediately became owner of the money lent to him, as in D. *Si certum petatur*, *l. 2*, § *Appellata*, and immediately the money was profectitious of the father himself, and did not exit from his domain; and it is certain that profectitious property cannot be owed by the father to the son in power, so that any action arises, because the case is in the aforementioned *l. Frater a fratre*. And this reason seems demonstrative. And if it is said that that money is not owed, but only the same amount in kind, I answer: the same amount in kind is not owed, except because that specific thing is represented in the generic, and acts in its place, as in the aforementioned *l. 2* and *l. 1*, in the same title. For even in the aforementioned *l. Frater a fratre*, an obligation in kind is contracted, because it is an obligation of a loan for consumption; and yet an obligation is contracted, if only a natural one.

The third reason is that this declaration committed has the force of a kind of compromise, which expires with the death of the compromitter while the matter is still intact, as in D. *De arbitris*, *l. Non distinguimus*, in the principle. The words “by himself and his heirs” do not stand in the way, for they refer to the word “promised,” not to the word “compromised.” Hence, the sense is that if it is declared at a suitable time, he himself and his heir are bound to observe the declaration; not that this declaration can be made after death, as in D. *De pueris et libertis*, *l. Qui libertinus*, § *Posthumus*, and *l. Bonorum*, D. *Rem ratam haberi*.

The fourth reason is that this declaration is of the substance of the contract: for it is of the substance that the person to whom it is acquired be certain; but when there is some commission, or when someone is given discretion regarding the substance of the contract, this person must arbitrate or declare within a year. After a year, however, the declaration pertains to the adversary; hence, after a year has elapsed, Vagnolus ought to declare the person for whom the instrument was received, as in C. *Communia de legatis*, *l. Si*, § 1. But Martin could not declare this after the power had been transferred to another, according to Bartolus, who elegantly notes this in *l. Si*, § 1, C. *Communia de legatis*, and D. *De verbis obligatis*, *l. Si quis arbitratu*. And if you say that the aforementioned *l. Si* speaks of a last will, and otherwise in contracts, I answer: this distinction is false, for the law is not proven, for the law says that contracts and testaments are equated, as in D. *De legatis 1*, *l. Servum filii*, § *Eum, qui chirographum*. Moreover, the discretion should last longer after a year in a last will than in a contract, because it is a matter of greater favor; therefore, the authority to declare and choose should be extended more; but it is so that in a last will it is not extended; therefore, neither in contracts. Moreover, the heir is bound by a quasi-contract; therefore, we come to the contract, D. *De iudiciis*, *l. Omnem*. Wherefore, the opinion of Bartolus is the very truth. But here a year and years have lapsed, and Vagnolus has died, and he declared nothing; therefore, the contract falls into nullity, as in C. *De contrahenda emptione*, *l. Si*.

Moreover, it must also be observed here: either the said money lent was not the lender’s, but Guido’s, and this is contrary to the tenor of the instrument, and thus no action could be brought from the instrument, because it would be alleging contradictory things, as in *l. 1*, C. *De furtis*; or the money was the lender’s, and then either Guido wishes to sue as a simple person added to receive payment, and as a bare minister, and he cannot sue to obtain the said quantity and to reimburse himself, but finally for the benefit of the heirs of the said lender, and with their consent, as in D. *De verbis obligatis*, *l. Iulianus*, § 1; or he wishes to sue as a person added for a donation, and then the donation was null by law itself beyond the sum of the law or statute, because insinuation is of the substantial form of the donation, or at least accidental; and therefore, if rights are ceded with the intent of donating, the cession is not valid by law itself beyond the legitimate sum. The objection from D. *De donationibus*, *l. Ut mihi donares*, does not stand, because there the added person did not have a lucrative cause. And that this is a donation is more certain than anything certain, because no other cause appears, as is fully read and noted in D. *Solutis matrimonii*, *l. Quae dotis*. Someone will say that this Martin did all this as a negotiorum gestor of the one to be named. I answer: if so, nevertheless, upon this supposition, a donation results, which requires insinuation; for here it had not come to tradition, but the matter had remained at the limits of obligation. Hence, the defendant can raise the exception of the nullity of the contract, because he does not except on the right of a third party, but on the non-right of the plaintiff, and properly it is not an exception, but a nullity.

† Moreover, the exception of fact and of intent can always be raised by anyone, as is read and noted by Cynus and others in the Code, *De servis fugitivis*, in the law *Cum servum*, because it uproots and weakens the foundations of the plaintiff’s claim and renders it at least less true. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the law that it is not permitted for the more powerful applies to the chancellor, notary, or knight.
2. Whether a simple procurator is to be admitted.
body: In the name of Christ. The case: A certain widowed and elderly woman, having certain rights against certain adversaries of hers, assigned them to the chancellor of the Illustrious Prince, Lord Marquis of Montferrat. The chancellor, fearing to fall under Laws 1 and 2 of the Codex, *Ne liceat potentioribus*, did not bring a useful action, nor did he act in his own right by virtue of a mandate, but rather as a friend and simple procurator. The question is: What is the law? And the issue turns on two points,

† First, whether the chancellor is called more powerful by reason of his office, since his office does not extend beyond that of a scribe of the lord, nor can he be a terror to the subjects of the same lord, because before the lord there is no exception of persons: therefore, since he is not more powerful on account of the quality of his office, nor can he inflict threatening terrors, the cession holds, and even a simple mandate, as noted in the laws cited above. And in Extra, de alienatione iudicii, c. Si. On the contrary, it seems, since it is alleged in the facts that the said chancellor, both by reason of his chancellorship and also by reason of his power, can deter the adversaries of the said woman, and in fact we see that it is very harsh to litigate with these officials, according to the saying, "We cannot be equal to the more powerful." And this opinion is more equitable by reason of the said l. 1, C. ne liceat potentioribus, provided that the power is established: for that law does not apply to anyone having jurisdiction, because it does not apply to a cartulary judge, but to one who has mere imperium. Otherwise it would follow that notaries, who by the form of their privileges are cartulary judges, could not receive any cession: especially since they cannot exercise jurisdiction except between willing parties, as noted in ff. de iudicibus, l. 1. This question depends greatly on the facts and on the discretion of the judge, who must observe not only the words of that law but also its intent: for soldiers, because they are soldiers, have no jurisdiction: and by reason of whose dignity and power the intent of that law is encompassed.

The second doubt follows, because a simple procurator, but for this reason he should not be admitted, lest fraud be committed against the law. This is the gloss. or. to the letter. ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium. §. praetor. And therefore I think that the said chancellor should be barred from the said procuration and removed for the sake of honesty. However, I do not say that the said old woman, who is permitted to ignore laws and disputable passages, should lose her right, because ignorance of the law benefits women in avoiding harm, and especially miserable persons. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether witnesses may be recalled after their testimony has been published.
2. The testimony of a person of low repute does not establish the credibility of another person of low repute.
3. When threats give rise to enmity.
4. One who blasphemes against God is not infamous under civil law.
5. How it is to be proven that blood was present in the blow of a battery.
6. In matters that cannot be clearly proven, arguments suffice.
body: In the name of Christ. Many matters are touched upon, yet I return to the point of truth.

† For the fact that the blow was struck with a sword on the left arm appears to be proven by two eyewitnesses: and although one of them deposed regarding the time based on belief, nevertheless, having been recalled by the judge ex officio before the testimony was considered fully given, even though after publication made solely by the word of the judge they spoke with certainty about the truth, I hold that this declaration could have been made, as noted in the Authentica de testibus, §. quia vero, where there is the original gloss. And I confirm this because this is an inquisitorial proceeding, where witnesses published to the judge, and not read out by the parties, may be recalled: and if they do not contradict what they first said, but rather clarify it, the testimony is valid, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes de testibus, chapter Cum clamor. Moreover, the publication of a witness is twofold: one is declaratory, when the judge says, “we publish”; and if the matter stands at the end of this, where the production of witnesses is not impeded, the other is intimation, when the words of the witnesses are read and intimated to the parties: and this latter is the one that imposes an end to new testimony, because it constitutes the testimony as fully given. And thus it is determined by the learned Bartolus in his consilia. And this is the truth itself, especially when they are examined without an interval of time, because the text in this matter weighs more heavily the testimony as fully given than the interlocutory decision of the judge. It therefore appears that the blow is proven, and the time of the blow. Nor do I care that it is objected against the witness that he is a person of low status.
† for here he had a co-witness of no small importance, who strengthens his credibility, as in D. de fidei. l. si quis ex argentariis. § 1, where it is the third number.

† Moreover, I do not care about the threats, because the quality of the persons is not such, nor of such a kind, that the threats would induce capital enmity. Furthermore, this is a matter of discretion, as stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, in the law *Licet*. And in matters of discretion, the judge must always strive for the punishment of wrongdoers, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, in the law *Ita vulneratus*; and above, *De publicanis*, in the law *Licitatio*, § *Quod illicite*. Even sometimes by transgressing the laws, as elegantly noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant Decretals, *De constitutionibus*, chapter 1. Moreover,

† If he blasphemed God, it is of no consequence in civil law, because he does not thereby become infamous, as is taught by the authorities in the Code, On the Holy Trinity, in the law *Cunctos populos*; hence there is no doubt that the assault has been proven, but because bloodshed was threatened.

Two doubts remain. The first is whether the blood has been proven: and it seems that it has not, because the witnesses did not see blood present in the blow of the assailant; moreover, because the darkness of the night is an impediment to sight, as noted in ff. quod metus causa, l. si cum exceptione, §. haec autem actio; and in C. de sicariis, l. furem. However, due to the covering of the garments, which did not allow the blood to be seen from the outside, [one might argue otherwise], but this seems absurd to me: for it would follow that if the victim had died, the assailant would not be punished for the death. Furthermore, from the quality of the instrument, the infliction of a wound is presumed, as the text notes in extra de homicidiis, cap. significasti; and in C. de sicariis, l. is, qui cum telo. Moreover, when a malicious act is committed at night, it is not necessary to prove it to the letter, but conjectures suffice, as in ff. de adulteriis, l. capite quinto, where it is noted that adultery is not proven by sight; but because the wrongdoer was caught in the flagrant crime, adultery is presumed.

† Moreover, in those matters which cannot be clearly proven, arguments suffice, and especially when accompanied by reputation. The gloss is ordinary in l. 2, § 1, ff. de excus. tuto. and is established in l. non omnes, § a barbaris, ff. de re mili. This is also referred to by natural consequence. For if there is a wound, then there is a blow. But the blow was only once, therefore from it this conclusion is proven, which is outside de fide instru. c. cum Iohannes Heremita. To this effect, what we noted, Cyn. in l. dolum, C. de dolo, where not only from the blow but also from the preceding threats is the crime presumed, which later appears to have been executed. Moved by these reasons, I think punishment should be made of blood; and if not of blood, it should at least be made of simple assault, because the inquisitor is not constrained to the proof of quality, nor can he bind himself to this to the prejudice of the public, as I said. C. de prob. l. possessiones. in my old reports, and new reading. Which opinion of mine all good assessors follow, and in fact it is so, that inquisitors do not bind themselves to all things, but inquire about each one, so that crimes do not remain unpunished in any way. And thus I say on the points above, consulted by the noble man Jacobus de Martiano, honorable podestà of Cumae. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the possessor is called in the possessory action: and what is the law when the libel is mixed.
2. Whether the judge may make a reservation: and if he does, whether an appeal may be taken.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A new doubt is raised in the case of the nobleman Lord Iohannoli de la Porta, in these words: it is doubted that an appeal could not be taken from the sentence pronounced against Phebus. To this doubt I respond, premising that, peace being preserved, this doubt did not deserve to be raised. For a sentence is said to be rendered on the mere possessory when it is delivered upon a purely possessory libel; but when the libel is intertwined with the petitory, there is no force in how the judge pronounces. For either he pronounces according to the form and nature of the libel, and an appeal may be taken; or the sentence is not conformable to the libel, and then it is null by operation of law. The laws are so common that I do not cite them; therefore, the reservation made by the judge, which was a certain precaution of the judge and an entanglement of the litigation, does not alter the nature of the case.

† Moreover, it is manifest that the judge ought to have absolved the defendant from the whole, and not reserved [any part]; and therefore, by reserving, he prejudiced the party. Hence, without doubt, he may appeal. Furthermore, concerning the matter of which he took cognizance, he ought to pronounce judgment; nor is it found that a judge could reserve what ought not to be reserved, unless he immediately declared it, as in D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, § nunc de officio. Since, therefore, the judge ought to have pronounced judgment with respect to the statute, the crime being principally alleged, and to have absolved [the defendant], and he did not do this, there is no doubt that [the party] may appeal, because he did not observe the form of law, as in X. de restitutione spoliorum, c. Pisanis. There are also many other reasons assigned by me in the opinion, which I do not repeat. This opinion also has natural equity approved and written in canon law, as in X. de restitutione spoliorum, cap. Cum ad sedem, and in Clem. 1, X. de sequestro possessionum et fructuum. Moreover, as I said in another opinion, the foundation of this case touches the matter of usury; therefore, canon law must be observed. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Where a delict is to be punished, whether in the place where it was committed or in the place where it was discussed for the purpose of committing it.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that certain wicked accomplices, of ill repute, remained for some days in the land of the Marquis of Montferrat; and then, departing, they went to commit robbery in another territory; after the plunder, and certain thefts, albeit small, they returned to the territory of the Marquis, where they were captured.

It is asked whether they can be punished there. And it seems that they can, because it is written: “Where I find you, there I will judge you.” Moreover, crimes should not remain unpunished. But if they are released, they will go their own ways and will never be punished. Moreover, these men can be called vagabonds, as noted in l. 1 and 2, C. de crimine agi oportet. Moreover, if they are punished, it is a matter of good example, so that the punishment of one may be the fear of many, as in C. ad l. Iul. repetundarum, l. 1. Moreover, if they made an agreement in the land of the Marquis, it is certain that they began to commit the offense there; therefore, they ought to be punished there, as in ff. de adulteriis, l. si amicus, and there by Bartolus. To the contrary, it seems that these preparatory acts are merged with the final and ultimate offense, as in ff. ad l. Aquiliam, l. illud, §. fina., and noted in C. de accusationibus, l. quae de crimine. Hence, it suffices that they are condemned or punished in the territory where they committed the theft and plunder. Furthermore, it is not the concern of the officials of the Lord Marquis regarding what was committed outside their territory, because by this their territory has not been offended, as in l. extra territorium, with its material. Moreover, in crimes, the place where the offense ends is considered, not where it began, as fully noted by Bartolus in ff. de adulteriis, l. quod ait, §. fina. We also have an example of one who kills a man with a crossbow, because the place where he draws the bow is not considered, but where he wounds, and this agrees with what is noted in l. 1, C. de possessione agi oportet.

Solution: If the theft committed outside the territory of the Marquis is carried and brought within the territory, then it can be punished by the officials of the Lord Marquis in the very territory of the Marquis, according to the opinion of Bartolus, because a new territory means a new dominion, as in ff. de proditoribus et furibus, l. nec legatarius, and by the same Bartolus in l. si dominium, ff. de furtis, although Baldus seems to hold otherwise in l. si alumnam, C. de nuptiis. Otherwise, it would follow that thefts committed outside the territory could be received with impunity, which is false, as in l. 1, C. de his qui latrones. And if other receivers are punished, much more so the principal author and leader of the crime. Although this is rarely observed in fact, it is true in law.

However, if the goods were not transported to the territory of the Marquis, there is neither law nor custom that they be punished there as for theft fully perpetrated, namely by hanging; but because they ought not to have been able to negotiate with impunity in the territory of the Marquis, if it is true that they negotiated and arranged matters there, they are punished for the negotiation by an arbitrary penalty, since they have not been punished elsewhere, even if they were outlawed elsewhere. They can therefore be punished by beating with rods or by a monetary penalty, but I advise that this be done after consulting the Lord Marquis on these matters; and it is well to consult his superior, as in ff. de iudicibus, l. eum quem, §. fina.

What supports the above is that an attempted offense is not punished as severely as a completed offense, as noted by Cynus in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis non dicam rapere. The objection that the preliminary acts are merged does not stand against the above, because this is true only when they concern the same territory; but when there are two presidents, each ought to punish the offense committed in his own jurisdiction, by argument from C. de sportulis, l. 2, because the offender has done injury to each, which ought not to remain unpunished, as in ff. ad l. Aquiliam, l. ita vulneratus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether butchers of meat, who are required to maintain certain weights, are to be punished if they maintain greater weights.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is asked: behold, sellers of meat ought to keep certain weights. It is certain that those who keep smaller weights are punished, as in the Digest, *De dolo*, l. *arbitrio*, § *de eo*. But what if they keep larger weights? I answer: it is not likely that they always weigh with larger weights, because they are not bestial men who would throw away their own profit. Hence, they are suspected of having other, smaller weights which they do not show to the official. Therefore, the official ought to inquire into the truth, and at least administer oaths to them, if they are of good repute; and not to punish these for the greater offense, and, to avoid all fraud, to act in such a manner that in the future there could be no sinister suspicion. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an exempt abbot may alienate a thing of the church that is entirely useless.
2. Whether a third party may raise the defense of invalidity.
body: In the name of Christ. An exempt abbot, with the consent of his entire chapter and having conducted negotiations as is customary, leased a certain piece of land converted into a water-filled pond and nearly unproductive in perpetual emphyteusis for an annual census, without consulting the Roman Pontiff. It is asked whether the lease is valid. Secondly, without prejudice to the truth that it would not be valid, whether a third party may raise the objection of invalidity. And

It appears that it is not valid for three reasons. First, there is a general conclusion that church property cannot be granted in emphyteusis in perpetuity, as stated in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. iubemus nulli; 12 q. 2, c. sine exceptione; and c. abbatibus. Second, for a special reason, because exempt abbots swear not to alienate without consulting the Roman Pontiff, as in Extra de rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, c. nulli liceat. Since the oath binds them, they cannot alienate without papal license. The third reason is most special, because monastery property cannot be alienated without just cause and the license of the superior, as in c. monasterium, de rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, lib. 6.

On the contrary, it appears that this flooded land, reduced to a pond, was not possessed by the monastery due to the impediment of the flooding, as in ff. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 3, § labeo. Although a pond, as a pond, can be possessed, as in ff. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. lacus, § stagnum, if the water is useful for something, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. rutilia. Hence, it is said more accurately that the species was rather leased than the thing itself, which is not prohibited if done for the utility of the monastery, as in Extra de feudis, c. ex parte.

Furthermore, there are three cases: either it is established that it is to the detriment of the church, and thus it is not valid; or it is doubtful, and similarly the contract is not valid, as noted in ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § eam, and § cum praetor. Moreover, this land was not only sterile, which signifies scantiness of revenues, as in l. si fundus, ff. de rebus eorum, but it was also useless in fact and in hope. And it is permitted for churches to lease useless things even in perpetuity, by receiving some annual utility, as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, auth. si quas ruinas; and Extra de rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, c. ad aures. And even this alienation was necessary for the church, i.e., for the utility of the church. Hence, the oath not to alienate does not extend to this case, as argued in ff. de manumissionibus testamento, l. qui non potuerunt; and ff. de fideicommissis, lib. 1, l. cum fidei; and because the matter is minor, 12 q. 2, c. cerrulas. Hence, it is concluded that the said lease held and should not be rescinded, although the lessees diligently removed the water and improved the property. The text is notable in l. 1, C. de alluvionibus et paludibus. Nor should it be imputed to the abbot and others that they did not consult the Pope, because the cost of consultation would have exceeded the revenues of the pond, as argued in C. de annona et tributo, l. mediterraneae, lib. 10; and l. pro locis; and C. de appellationibus, l. cum post sententiam discussoris.

† Hence I conclude that the said lease was valid; and even if it had not been valid, no one could have raised an objection except in the name of the church, as noted in l. 2, § qui in perpetuum, si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticarius petatur; and as noted by Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution made in a second will prevails over a substitution made in the first.
2. Whether a substitution made by the words "if he should die without children" is fiduciary, and excludes those coming by intestate succession.
body: In the name of Christ. A father made a will, in which he instituted as his heirs Matthew and Tibald, sons of Francis, formerly his son; and if the said Matthew and Tibald, and the womb, should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without sons, he substituted his granddaughters from Lucia, his daughter; and also instituting Lucia as his heir in two hundred and fifty pounds, the said testator added that if the said substituted granddaughters should die without sons, then he substituted the nearest male relatives of the said testator. And it is true that Simon, named below, was the nearest in the male line of the said testator, and also a certain Gabriel in the same degree. Then after a short time the said testator made another will, in which he instituted as his universal heirs the above-mentioned Matthew and the womb. And because Tibald had already died, he also instituted his said daughter Lucia as his heir in 200 and fifty pounds of denarii, as above. Adding that if the said Matthew and the womb should die without children, he substituted Simon and Gabriel, his brothers of the same parents; although the said Gabriel died before the said womb: nevertheless, after the death of the said Matthew, finally the said womb, later called Nicholas, died in pupillary age, leaving behind the aforementioned Simon, substituted in the last will; and also leaving behind the aforementioned Lucia, heir in the first will, and a certain Francischina, daughter of Lucia, substituted in all goods in the first will.

† Now it is asked, which substitution is stronger, whether the substitution of the first testator or of the second. And the solution is brief, because by the second solemn will the first was revoked together with all its substitutions and clauses. Only the second will is the last will, because it was made last and made solemnly, as in Inst. Qui modis test. infirm. §. posteriore. Therefore, by the second will, together with the substitution, the aforementioned first substitute in the first will, along with her mother, can claim nothing, nor is there any doubt here whether the substitution made in the last will excludes the aforementioned Lucia from the intestate succession of the impubes. For I consider the words of the substitution lastly spoken indefinitely and confusedly, if he says, "if they die without children," and the testator did not distinguish the clauses, nor did he distribute the qualities of ages or times, which are specific notes of the qualities of substitutions.

† Hence, according to the true and common opinion, where the words state “if he should die without children,” the substitution is at all times fideicommissary, or compendious not taken in the proper sense, but in this case obtained as fideicommissary. And this is especially so since the aforementioned Lucia, who is among the nearest descendants, is in the middle, whose favor suggests interpreting a doubtful substitution as oblique. For if the mother is favored in this matter, then all the more so are the children, as in the law *Precibus* with its subject matter. And thus I have often advised. Nor does the chapter *Si pater*, *De testibus*, lib. 6, oppose this, because there the word “direct” was added, instituting, which, being appropriate to the time, makes the substitution direct. Also, there was no person in the middle whose favor would suggest making the substitution oblique, although Lord Cynus and Johannes Andreas speak otherwise: nevertheless, I do not depart from the customary opinion, which I have seen observed everywhere. And from this it follows that the said pupil died intestate, and the one succeeding him intestate deducts the legitime and the trebellianic portion on his behalf. The other half belongs to the substitute, partly by express legal right and partly by tacit legal right, namely, by the right of accretion: and this, in my judgment, is the truth. Therefore, the substitute must seek restitution under the Trebellian rule of the half portion, as in the extrajudicial decisions *De testibus*, chapter *Raynutius* and chapter *Raynaldus*. But if the testator had made a distinction of the substitution, then the pupillary substitution of the last testament would exclude all those coming intestate, as in the Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Papinianus*, § *Sed nec impuberis*. So that they could not succeed intestate, because we are in the case and circumstance of having made a will; nor by the right of substitution of the first testament, which was entirely nullified by the second through the aforementioned legal rule, which states that a pagan cannot die with two wills, but the last prevails, as in the Digest, *De adimendis legatis*, law *Quod iterum*, and law 1, Code, *De sacrosancta ecclesia*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How a negative is to be proved, and whether those who affirm are to be believed more than those who deny.
body: In the name of Christ. Three hermit brothers testify against a certain brother, alleging that he struck their prior with a staff. The latter, against whom they testify, proves by five brothers that he did not strike him. Hence, against the affirmative witnesses, he proves the negative against the affirmative, restricted as to place and time, in this manner: because they state that within the said period of time in which the witnesses affirmatively claim the striking occurred, the truth of the matter is that he was not struck, nor could he have been struck without them having seen it.

It is asked whether the said witnesses prove the innocence of the said accused brother. And it seems that they do not, because more credit is given to two affirming witnesses than to denying ones, as noted in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Diem proferre*, section *Si plures*. And the reason is that an affirmative statement is subject to the eyes, but a negative one is not seen by sight, but is perceived only by the intellect, even when accompanied by bodily presence. Moreover, these negative witnesses speak as if knowing the disposition of the affirmative witnesses; but it is certain according to the strict law that, after testimony has been given, witnesses cannot directly testify again, unless they are said to have been corrupted and to have spoken falsely, because then, on account of a new chapter of corruption, new witnesses are admitted, as in the Extravagant, *De probat.*, chapter *Licet causam*, and in chapter *Testibus*, *De testibus*, in the Clementines. Indirectly, however, they can well be impeached, because indirect impeachment, insofar as it is a matter of fact, consists in the diversity of facts, as in the Code, *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, law *Optimam*, at the end.

I do not believe that regulars, who proceed according to their constitutions, observe these subtleties of the law concerning what is good and equitable, but they go only to the naked and open truth, which God loves above all things, as in the Psalm, *Miserere mei Deus*, and in many other psalms. And because it is established by many witnesses that the accused is innocent, which is more than fully proven, and by almost double the majority of witnesses, the said accused ought to be absolved. And if it is said that a negative cannot be directly proven by the sense of the body, this is false, as is fully noted by Cynus in law 2, Code, *De errore advocatorum*. For the sense that perceives a determined object thereby understands that it does not perceive beyond or outside of it, as in the Code, *De rebus creditis*, law 2, and in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Fideiussores magistratuum*, section *Pro Aurelio*, and in the Code, *De probat.*, law *Approbatonem uti*. Furthermore, innocence, however it may have become clear, must be upheld, as in the Digest, *De poenis*, law *Si non defendatur*, and in the Digest, *De quaestionibus*, law 1, section *Si quis ultro*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The nature of devolution of power is such that it devolves to the superior, not to the inferior.
body: In the name of Christ.

† If the person to whom the collation of a benefice pertains does not confer it within the half-year period, the power devolves to the superior, and it never returns to the inferior, because this is the nature of devolving power, that it devolves to the superior: and once devolved, it does not return. And this is proven by the argument from the special case. For if it is special in c. Statutum, de praebendis, lib. 6, that the power descends to the inferior, therefore in the contrary case it is the common law, as noted there. And it is supported by ff. Qui modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Si cum vel in annos, where it is said that once admitted, it never returns to the same person, as in C. De liberis et eorum liberis, l. 2, where it says that he who has once fallen never returns to the same position, which is to be understood as meaning in that instance, not in another call. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether correlatives always have the same rule, and whether in pacts interpretation is made of leases.
body: In the name of Christ. An investiture was made of a certain mountain of Rochetis with a pact, because they promised to give and assign to the investor a fourth part of the entire price that could be obtained in any way or by any means from the quarrying of stones: provided that they might quarry by themselves and by others of their household, and not be bound to pay anything, nor to hand over the said fourth part of the price that might be derived therefrom: yet in such a way that the investor himself might quarry stones for himself and for his own work.

† It is asked whether, having examined the intention of the contracting parties, it should be understood that the investees also could not quarry except for their own work? And it seems that it is so, because statements in the subsequent clauses seem to be repeated in the preceding ones, as in l. 1, C. de li. praete., and conversely, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. titia. §. idem respondit, and ff. de iur. et fac. igno. l. regula. §. fi. Likewise, buyer and seller are correlatives, and the rule for correlatives is the same, as in C. de indi. vidui. l. fi. To the contrary, it seems that the buyer can be subject to one condition and the seller to another: for diverse extremes admit diverse pacts, and favors, and burdens, as in ff. de pac. l. qui in futurum. §. si ex altera. Likewise, these pacts are clear, and therefore they do not require extraneous aids of interpretation, as in ff. de fidei. l. fideiussores magistratuum. §. 1; and even if they were ambiguous, they are interpreted against him who dictates the condition to the other, upon whom he wishes to impose some burden, especially outside the nature of the contract, as in ff. de pac. l. veteribus. And if it is said that the intention of the contracting parties was to the contrary, I answer that it is not true, because such is the intention understood to be in the heart as is the word that is uttered by the mouth. For the trumpet of the heart is the tongue of the speaker; and there is no greater testimony of the intention than the examined quality of the words, as in ff. de suppel. leg. l. labeo. §. idem tubero. The resolution: that which the word sounds is to be observed; and that which the word does not sound is regarded as nothing, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. quicquid astringendae, C. de fide instr. l. contractus. And therefore the said investee can quarry by himself and his household, and sell to whomever he wishes without the burden of the fourth part: because it was so conceded to him, as in ff. de dona. l. qui saxum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. By positing the case itself, the law in this edictal constitution, C. de secun. nup., is to be understood, and what its observance is, and that which is in fraud of the law does not take effect. And no. 2.
body:
In the name of Christ. A certain noble lady, Agnesina, had two husbands. From the first, named M., she had two children, namely A., a male, and B., a female. From the second husband, however, she had three children. Upon approaching death, she made a will, in which she left one hundred to the daughter of the first marriage by way of institution. In all her other goods, she instituted as heirs John, the son from the first marriage, and her other children from the second marriage, for one half in equal shares; and she instituted her second husband for the other half, with this addition: that if the said second husband could not take the entirety of the said half, that surplus which the said Malatesta could not take from the said half, she left by way of legacy to the said children of the second marriage, in every manner, way, right, and form by which it might be done more effectively.

It is now established that, by the law *Hac edictali* in the Code on Second Marriages, more cannot be left to the second husband than is left to one of the children of the first marriage to whom the lesser amount is left. Hence, the children of the first marriage argue that the second husband ought to have no more than that amount, namely one hundred. The remainder, they claim, pertains to them, the children of the first marriage. Conversely, the children of the second marriage allege that in that surplus, they, the children of the second marriage, ought to succeed by virtue of the legacy expressly made to them. The question now arises: what is the law?

† And it appears that the children of the second marriage uphold justice, because the testatrix could have provided for those children unequally, although she would have acted more equitably if she had provided for them equally, as in Auth. de nuptiis §. disponat. and §. pe. col. 4. sufficit. It suffices that the legitimate portion is left to the children of the first marriage, so that it may be supplied by law, as in Auth. de triennio et semis. §. 1. col. 3. Moreover, that which is left to the son by the mother appears to have been left solely out of piety and consideration of natural cause, as in D. de liberis et posthumis l. filio quam pater; and D. de excusationibus tutorum l. a tutore §. quae tutoribus; and D. de bonis liberis l. nihil §. facilior; D. unde liberi l. scripto haerede; D. de bonis damnatorum l. cum rato. On the contrary, however, that the children of the first marriage have clear justice: and this for three reasons, and first, because this testament appears to have been made in fraud and in derogation, l. hac edictali, and to exclude the legal provision regarding the children of the first marriage, which is impossible, and especially because no one can act against whom the laws have effect in his testament, D. de legibus l. nemo potest, and expressed in the said l. hac edictali in the final part of the principle. Also, that which is done in fraud of the laws is held as not disposed, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. haeres meus §. quod in fraudem, whence it does not attain effect: and yet it deserves legal penalty, as is fully discussed and noted, C. de legibus et constitutionibus l. non dubium. Also, when mention is made of the father and paternal power: because that which was bequeathed to him under the name of legitimate children appears to have been left rather out of marital affection than under the pretext of filiation, as in D. de vulgari substitutione l. sed et si plures §. in arrogato; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. filio.

The second reason is that the law *hac edictali* has two heads: the law prohibiting more to be left, and also devolving to the children of the first marriage as a penalty against the one leaving it, which penalties, tending to the provision of the children of the first patrimony, have not been abolished, as noted by Innocentius in chapter *pe* on second marriages; and this opinion, so to speak, has been baptized among all experts. Now it must be known that what is left over to the second husband is taken from him, and the law proceeds further, because it applies to the children of the first marriage, who ought in no way to share in this with the children of the second marriage, as is expressly read and noted in the Authenticum *de nuptiis*, § *optime*. Hence, the children of the first marriage come in their own right, and alone. And this is the very truth: and it is confirmed in our case by a third, irrefutable reason. For either the children of the second marriage wish to obtain their legacy from the father, and they cannot, because the words of the testament are contrary, and because in a part that is impossible in law there is no heir; or they wish to obtain it for the children of the first marriage, and they cannot, because the children of the first marriage are not honored in this by the testator, but are provided for by law as a penalty against the testator, as in the aforementioned law *si arrogator*. Moreover, because here the penalty is the proper patrimony of the children of the first marriage, and this portion is separated from the rest of the inheritance, by argument from the Digest, *de administratione tutorum*, law *impuberi filio centurio*. And there was a question of fact in the city of Cortona, and there should be consilia, even in the simultaneous case, namely that if the second husband stipulates for the dowry profit for his children, that the stipulation is not valid, because it is in fraud of the law *hac edictali*, although I then tried to defend the contrary; nevertheless, it was so judged, and formally observed on the advice of most powerful doctors, namely Lord Francesco de Albergotis of Arezzo, and finally Lord Riccardo de Saliceto. And if you send for their consilia to a certain Bertolus, if he is alive, you will have it firmly. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the substitute in the first degree to the unborn child dies before the birth of the posthumous child, and the posthumous child subsequently dies, do those who would succeed intestate come into the inheritance, or does the second substitute?
body: In the name of Christ. A certain person was instituted as a vulgar substitute in the first degree of vulgar substitution, and another person was instituted as a substitute in the second degree of vulgar substitution; and these substitutions were made to the womb. Now the first substitute died before the posthumous child was born, and then the posthumous child died.

† It is asked whether those who come as intestate heirs or the vulgar substitute come into the inheritance, when he has also been substituted pupillarily. I answer that the case of substitution is [discussed in] ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. quandiu institutus; ff. de venditionibus insipientium, l. qui ventri; and ff. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thais, §. Splendophorus. And it is established by l. 1, ff. de vulgari substitutione. The objection from l. si mater, §. 1, de vulgari et pupillari substitutione does not hold, because there the second substitute is repelled because the instituted heir had survived, who is preferred to all subsequent degrees, as [stated in] ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. cum in testamento, in principio. The objection from l. penultima, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione does not hold, because there the condition had failed, by which [the heir] was bound to the first [substitute], for there the wife and sister of the testator, through the substitution made to the daughter, should have come to the goods of the impubes; but that substitution fails because the daughter had died after reaching puberty. And this is the true understanding of that law. Nor do the third and fourth reasons stand in the way, as is gathered from the notes of Bartolus in the said l. quandiu, under the rubric "Is autem," de acquisitione hereditatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that the husband shall acquire all the fruits of the wife, does he acquire the fruits that the wife had in the property of her son born from a first marriage, and does the term "property" include usufruct?
body: In the name of Christ.

† The statute provides that the husband shall acquire all fruits, even those of paraphernal property. The question arises: if the mother had a usufruct over the goods of one of her sons from her first marriage, who had predeceased her, whether the husband can claim that usufruct according to the wording of the statute. It seems that he can, because the term "goods" also includes usufruct, since it is a part of ownership. On the contrary, it seems that he cannot, because a servitude cannot be subject to another servitude, as stated in l. 1, ff. de usufr. leg. But to this it is responded that the term "usufruct" here is used for the benefit, not for the formal right, as in l. necessario, §. si, ff. de peric. et comm. rei vend.

Solution: This husband can neither claim the right nor the benefit of the usufruct. And the reason is that his wife could not claim the usufruct before she had provided security for using and enjoying it according to the discretion of a good man, since she was not in possession; therefore, neither can the husband. Although the benefit of possessing may belong to the possessor without providing the aforementioned security, the right to claim does not belong, as in C. de sec. nup. l. hac edictali, §. is illud, C. ut in pos. leg. l. scire, and ff. de usucap. l. si homo, and fully noted in l. unica, C. de usufructu, and ff. de usufr. leg. l. uxori. And this seems to me to be the truth, because the security is of the substance of claiming, although it is not of the substance of possessing, if the usufructuary is in corporeal possession, which pertains to the acquisition of fruits, as subtly read and noted in ff. de acq. pos. l. 3, §. ex contrario. Also, because the usufructuary does not acquire fruits unless they are separated from the soil by him or another in his name, as in ff. qui mod. usus fr. amit. l. si usufructuarius messem. For enjoyment and use require an act, as in ff. de usufr. l. si fur decerpserit, and arg. ff. de fur. l. si servus communis uni, §. locavi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the benefices of a person who has been created a bishop, but cannot take possession of the episcopate, are vacant.
2. Whether another bishop may commend a parish church to himself.
3. Within what time he may make the said commendam.
4. And whether the said commendam may be revoked, and whether the limited time begins to run. No. 5.
6. Of two presentees, who is prior.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain person was created an overseas bishop by the Pope.
† It is asked, since he cannot have possession, whether the benefices which he originally possessed are vacant. And it must be said that they are not, as in c. Cum in cunctis, de electione.

† Secondly, it is asked whether another bishop may commend a parish church to himself. I answer: yes, because his honor has been increased by the episcopate, but his condition has not become worse than it was during the time of simple priesthood, as in D. de cond. et de. l. falsa § 1.
Thirdly, it is asked, for how long may the said commendam of the parish church be granted? I answer, for up to six months, as in c. Nemo deinceps, de electione, 6.

Fourthly, it is asked whether a term of six months can be renewed for another six months. I answer that, before the first six months have elapsed, it cannot be extended, because this would amount to extending one and the same commission beyond its appointed time, as stated in the Digest, *De precibus*, in the law *Sed si manente*. However, once the half-year has expired, if one wishes to renew it continuously, this is not permitted, lest fraud be committed against the decree; but if renewed with some interval in between, it is permitted, according to the argument in the Digest, *Qui et a quibus*, in the law *Matrimonii*. Although the gloss distinguishes otherwise in the cited chapter *Nemo deinceps*, and holds without distinction that such renewal may be made for the utility of the Church or out of necessity, this view could sufficiently be sustained if the Church could not find an equally suitable candidate, as stated in the Digest, *De decuriis*, in the law *Generaliter*, section *Spurios*.

† Fifth, it is asked whether the time period of the Lateran Council runs in the meantime, and it must be said that it does not, as noted there. For although commendam is not a full title, it nevertheless causes the benefice not to be vacant in the meantime, since the commendatary in the meantime collects the revenues, as noted there by Ioan. mon. Now the question arises in another point, in another matter. Presented

† There was a certain person presented by a lay patron, who requested to be instituted by the bishop; finally, another was presented and instituted. Who is preferred? I answer that a lay patron may vary his choice, and therefore the second is preferred, as in Extra, De iure patronatus, cap. Pastoralis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a third party can prohibit a new work being carried out on a common thing.
body: In the name of Christ. There were three vassals, or noble feudatories, of a certain castle and territory, who divided the territory and the men among themselves, with the jurisdiction alone remaining undivided. Now two of them wish to build two fortifications, each in the territory of his own men, while the third objects.

† The question is asked: what is the law? I answer: if the jurisdiction is common and undivided, the condition of the party prohibiting is the stronger, even if he has no personal interest in the matter, as stated in the Digest, title *De communi diviso*, law *Sabinus*. For although one person cannot prevent the natural use of a common thing, such as the exercise of jurisdiction, as in the Code, title *De usufructu*, law *Arboribus*, section *Navis*; nevertheless, he may prohibit the construction of a new work, because it does not pertain to the ancient use. But if the jurisdiction is divided with respect to territory: then it is lawful for each to build a castle or fortification in his own proper place, as noted in the Digest, title *De uti possidetis*, law *Si duo*, section 2, with this distinction being applied: for either he builds it for his own defense, and he may do so; or principally for the emulation of another, and he may not, as in the Digest, title *De operibus publicis*, law *Opus et ple.*, and in the Decretals, title *De restitutione spoliatorum*, chapter *Pisanis*, and in the Novels. And although the prince permits it, nevertheless this is understood to be valid only on the condition that he who has the right consents, and not otherwise, as in the Digest, title *De coniunctione praediorum*, law *Receptum*, and law 1, section *Si quis a principe*, and in the Digest, title *Ne quid in loco publico*, and law *Si*, Digest, title *Communia praediorum*. From these it appears that each is the master and judge of his own property, provided he does not act against the law; but of a common thing, there is only one master and judge, as in the Digest, title *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*, law *Per fundum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute providing that only interest is to be paid from the day on which the delay in making the payment occurs is valid; and how and in what manner such interest may be claimed. nu. 3 and 4.
2. A statute providing that for every hundred imperiali, how it is to be understood.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The statute provides that interest to the creditor is to be deemed due at the rate of two soldi per pound, payable from the time of the debtor’s default. The question arises whether this statute is valid. It appears that it is not, because whatever accrues to the principal constitutes usury, as stated in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, and in the law *Rogasti*, section *Si tibi*. On the contrary, it appears that it is valid, because interest may be assessed by a judge, and is owed both under civil and canon law, as in the Digest, title *De in litis iurando*, law *Nummis*. Therefore, it may also be established by law, since the law is not of lesser power than the minister of the law. Moreover, a statute may introduce a legal fiction, especially when there is a cause; and it suffices that the cause exists in the mind of the legislators, as in law 1, in the word *ratus*, Digest, title *De postulando*. One might distinguish between a loan for consumption (*mutuum*) and other contracts: thus, in the case of a *mutuum*, the statute would not be valid, just as an agreement by which something is provided under the name of fictitious interest would not be valid, as noted by Cynus in his additions to the old Digest and in the Digest, title *De servitute exponenda*, in one of his excellent additions. But in other contracts, it would be valid, for there is a difference between contracts, as noted by Cynus in the Code, title *De usuris*, law *Cum allegas*. I believe the statute to be valid: for this fiction is close to the truth, since, according to the common course of the world, interest is commonly due; and because sin is not presumed in the lawmaker.

Secondly, it is asked whether the statute, which states "for every hundred Imperiali," is to be understood as referring to florins, of equal value. And it must be said that it is so, as in l. 1, D. de auro et argento legato, and noted in C. de donationibus, l. si quis argentum, in principio, and it is expressly stated in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. quae extrinsecus, §. si.

Thirdly, it is asked whether the aforementioned interest can be claimed after judgment has been rendered on the principal. I answer: not by virtue of the same instance, as stated in C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. terminato. But if the principal were again claimed, interest could be claimed together with it, unless the principal had been discharged, as in l. centum capita and l. si, de eo quod certum creditur. For this statute does not introduce a new right of obligation, but only a right of proof, as is clear from the words of the statute. Fourthly, it is asked whether interest that has accrued after judgment can be claimed. I answer: yes, by bringing an action on the judgment for the principal, and an officium iudicis for the interest, by argument from l. ordo, C. de executione rei iudicatae, and from l. 1, § 1, ff. de usuris, by contrary reasoning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person who promises to resell a fund, and does not wish to be bound except for what has been given and done, may at the time of the sale to be made demand improvements and expenses made in the fund, and to what he is bound. nu. 3.
2. Whether a hypothecary right may be assigned.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Titius sold a fund to Sempronius, which was encumbered for the restitution of the dowry of the wife of the said Titius; and the said Sempronius immediately promised to sell the said fund, and within five years did so to Martin, on the condition that the said Sempronius should not be liable for eviction, except for his own giving and doing. In the meantime, this Sempronius incurred many expenses and improved the said fund, because where there was a marsh, it is now fertile. Moreover, he had the rights of the said dowry and of the hypothecs assigned to him. Now Martin demanded that the fund be sold to him, offering the agreed price. Sempronius says that he has a right of retention for the said dowry and for the expenses incurred in the improvement of the fund. Martin says that he is not bound to this. The question is, what is the law?

It seems that the said Martin has the right, because if he to whom one sold, or promised to sell, acquires any rights after the contract, such rights benefit the buyer, as in D. de rei vend. l. si a Titio; D. de except. rei iud. and the glossators generally note, per Bartolus, D. de usuc. l. cum vir. §. prœmium. And it is a rule that when the right of the grantor, or of him who is to give, is augmented, the right of the buyer, and of any successor, is augmented, as in D. de leg. 1. l. seruum filii, in principio. Nor ought the buyer to pay two prices, one for the principal purchase and another for free delivery. For he is bound to deliver the thing free to the buyer, especially if he can deliver the thing free, as is the case here, as noted in C. de evict. l. ex prœdiis. Furthermore, for another reason it seems that the said assignment of the hypothec did not hold, because it was made to the owner of the estate, and no one can have his own thing encumbered by the right of hypothec, as in D. de re iur. l. neque pignus.

Also, regarding that doubt about the expenses, it seems that he cannot claim them, nor retain the thing on that account, because they were made for the sake of the fruits, and he received the fruits; therefore they are merged with the fruits, as in D. sol. mat. l. diuortio. §. quod in sent.; D. comm. l. in rebus.

On the contrary, the truth seems to be so. And first I come to the first point, and I consider that sometimes one sells, or promises to sell, the right which he has; sometimes one promises to sell the thing for the right which he has. And in these two cases, only the right which he had at the time of the contract is transferred, as noted in l. fin. C. quæ res pig. obl. pos. and argued in D. diuer. et temp. prœscr. l. an vicio. §. ex facto. And it is well stated in C. ad Vell. l. iubemus. And argued in C. de pet. hæred. l. hæreditas materteræ; C. de except. rei iud. l. si a te. §. Iulianus. Sometimes one sells the thing simply; and then I admit that he is bound to deliver the thing free. But this is not our case, because he promised to sell the thing only for his own giving and doing. But this thing is subject to eviction not for his own act, but for the act of the woman and the man. That is, the woman actively and the man passively, and from the act of the woman or her heirs we measure the right. Hence Sempronius comes as a new person; and therefore the replication of the contract does not hinder him, because on that ground he is not liable for eviction.

Moreover, this Martin is placed in the same right in which Titius was, by the continuation of the said possessions and by the true intention of the contracting parties. Just as the hypothec has force against Titius, so it has force over the said fund. To this it contributes that when two rights concur in the person of one, it is the same as if they pertained to the persons of different individuals, as in D. de his qui vt indig. l. tutorem; and D. de adop. l. si consul. and noted in D. de pac. l. si plures. Nor does the objection hold.

† That a hypothecary action cannot be assigned to the owner of the thing with respect to the same thing: for this is true when the thing is not subject to restitution, and [the action] can lie with respect to the same thing, as in D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. In bello, § Si quis servum; and D. de executione rei iudicatae, l. Ex sextante, § Latinus.

† Regarding the question of expenses, I state that improvements are to be awarded, as in D. de minoribus, l. intra utile, § vendentibus. For the quality of the thing has been altered and its value increased, whence they ceased to exist for the perpetual utility of the thing, as in C. de alluvione et palude, l. 1; and what is noteworthy, C. de iure dotis, l. si inter virum. These points are proven by what is read and noted in D. de legibus, l. quod si domus and l. domos; and D. de condictione indebiti, l. qui exceptionem, § si pars; and D. de rei vindicatione, l. emptor. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A general disposition is not restricted by a specific case when it proceeds from different laws.
body: In the name of Christ. There are two statutes in the City of Pavia: one provides for necessary compromises, the other speaks of compromises simply and generally, under the heading "which arbitrations cannot be called unjust." I say generally, that is, without distinguishing between a necessary compromise and a voluntary one, there is no connection, but rather they are different. This also appears from the heading "to which one must adhere," as in the Digest, *de iure et facto ignorato*, law *Regula*, § *Si*; and also as in *chirographariam pecuniam*, law *Unica*, and in the prologue, book 6 of the Decretals. Furthermore, it appears from the text, or black letter, which provides for the precepts of arbitrators, etc. And where the case of the law applies, there is no doubt, as in the Code, *de furtis*, law *Ancillae*. It also appears from the identity of reason, as in the Digest, *de novo operis nuntiatione*, law *Prima*, § *Et post operis*. Moreover, where the law does not distinguish, neither do we distinguish, as in the Digest, *de publicaniis*, law *Precio*, with its subject matter. The objection regarding the statute on necessary compromises does not hold: because there are two statutes, each dealing with its own matter, and one does not follow consecutively or relatively from the other. And therefore, a general provision is not restricted by a specific one when they proceed from different laws, as is read and noted in the Digest, *de poenis*, law *Sanctio legum*, according to Bartolus. And this was a question disputed by the learned Raynerius of Forlì. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the opinion of a wise man, or a judgment rendered, or rendered outside the limited time, is void by operation of law. See also below, consilium 172.
body: In the name of Christ. The statute of the City of Genoa provides that an appeal may be taken from a definitive sentence, or that a consultation of a learned man may be requested, and that new proofs may not be made by means of instruments. That very question is to be consulted upon, determined, and defined by that judge to whom the said question has been committed, within 20 days after the said question has been committed to him and he has accepted it; unless an instrument or writing to the contrary is exhibited. In which case the 20 days shall run, and be understood to run, from the day of the expiration of the term of the said proofs, and upon the expiration of the said 20 days he shall be compelled by the magistrate and by the syndics to deposit his consultation, during, however, the pendency of the aforementioned appeal according to the form of the common law. Now it has happened that the said learned man, who is also the judge of the appeal, after many months had elapsed beyond the time prescribed by the statute, yet within the time for prosecuting the appeal according to the common law, voluntarily rendered his consultation, and it was published; and according to the form of the consultation a sentence was pronounced.

It is asked whether the said sentence is null by operation of law. And it seems that it is, because when something is null, likewise whatever follows from it is null, as in C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium. But the said opinion was null by operation of law. First, by the nature of its own limited term, as in ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. consequens; and ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. qui fundum. Second, because that which is permitted for a certain time, i.e., which has a certain beginning and a certain end, seems to be prohibited after the time, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. statuliberum, §. Stichum. Third, because the time limit seems to be of a certain form, from which the consultant cannot depart, as in extra de electione, c. cum in veteri. And therefore it seems undoubtedly to be said that the power and office of giving an opinion expired with time. And because this opinion came to the sentence by way of form and foundation, the foundation being destroyed, whatever proceeds from it is destroyed, as in l. nam et si sub conditione, §. rumpendo, ff. de in iustis testamentis.

On the contrary, it seems that this term of 20 days, etc., is not attached to the instance; which appears from those words, "during, however, the instance." Moreover, the jurisdiction of the one exercising jurisdiction endures; therefore the sentence is valid, as noted in C. de iudicibus, l. properandum, in principio, by Cynus and others; and C. ut omnes tam civiles, l. 1; and arg. extra de officio delegati, c. consuluit. Consider that if a new command to give an opinion had been made by the magistrate, so that the form of the statute was observed, then without doubt the sentence would be valid, as in ff. de arbitris, l. si de meis, §. si. But because the form of the statute was not observed, but the consultant of his own accord issued the opinion after the lapse of the term, it seems rather to be said that the sentence is null, because the consultant did not observe the form of his commission in time for giving the opinion. Moreover, he did not wait to be compelled, which is of the order of the statute. Moreover, before the consultant there is properly no instance. And thus the argument from "during the instance" does not hold, C. de dilationibus, l. cum a nobis. Moreover, Bartolus determines expressly that the sentence is valid while the commission for the opinion is pending, and I note this in ff. de appellationibus, l. ad principem.

But to that I respond, that this is true, unless the opinion is required as a substantial form of the sentence itself, which is when the statute says that the judge is bound to follow the opinion. And to this I allege the same Bartolus in what he notes in ff. de re iudicata, l. si convenerit. Briefly, it is reduced to this point: whether the expectation of judicial compulsion is of the necessary order for exhibiting the opinion after the time of 20 days, which is mentioned in the aforementioned statute. And I believe that it is of the substance, arg. ff. de his qui notati sunt infamia, l. furti, §. si iussu. For the authority and mandate of a superior makes certain things valid which otherwise are invalid, as in ff. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, §. permittitur. And therefore, concluding, I think, adhering as we must to the words of the statute, that the said opinion and the subsequent sentence were invalid by operation of law, because, excluded from the authority and power of giving an opinion, he cannot reassume it by his own authority, to which he tacitly renounced by the lapse of the term, but he ought to wait for the command of the judge, arg. C. ad Trebellianam, l. non iustam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution can be made by a father in the legitime of his son: and whether a substitution made in a certain thing has the force of a fideicommissum.
body: In the name of Christ. The father instituted his daughters in certain amounts, and thus substituted them by these words, vulgarly, pupillarily, and by fideicommissum. After the death of the testator, one of these died in pupillary age.

† It is asked whether a sister who has been substituted succeeds to the legitime of the deceased. And it seems that she does not, because a substitution made in a certain thing has the force of a fideicommissum, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. cogi, §. et generaliter. But a fideicommissary substitution cannot be made in the legitime, as is fully stated in l. et no., C. de inofficiosis testamentis, from the three aforementioned cases, if it is made to the son himself to whom the legitime is due. But if a pupillary substitution were made for him, it would be valid, if the son died in pupillary age, as in D. de legatis 1, l. quod fideicommissum. And the reason is that it appears that the heir is burdened by the impubes, who could burden him with his own goods. On the contrary, it seems that an express pupillary substitution can be made for an impubes who is instituted in a certain thing, as in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohæredi, §. si, provided that this person substituted in a certain thing does not have another who is universally substituted for the impubes, because then he would be regarded as a legatee: and yet this legatee must receive this legacy from the universal coheir. Solution: because the testator said, “I substitute pupillarily,” and the pupillary substitution is made by express civil words, so that it does not conflict with pupillary age. And thus it is in our case. But if he had simply said, “I substitute,” it would be fideicommissary, even if he had added the condition “if in pupillary age,” also on account of the rule of the Doctor in the aforementioned §. generaliter. Otherwise an inconvenience would follow, because if the testator had said, “If my son dies in pupillary age, I leave ten for the sake of my soul,” the entire inheritance would be due: which is contrary to the entire intention of the testator, and contrary to the truth of the law, although some say that this is not absurd, and especially in favor of the soul. From this it is inferred that a substitution made by a common word can be made in the legitime, which is pupillary. But I do not see by what law, or by what civil or canonical reason, this is proven. l. legitima, n. detrahitur, as if it were alien, as in Extra, de testibus, c. Rayn., and c. Ravnal., and c. si pater, and in §. quarta, cum si. And if the testator had expressly said, “I substitute to my son in the legitime,” the substitution would not be valid, as in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. quodam in prioribus, l. omnimodo, and l. sancimus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The dowry and the legitime take precedence over the fisc; nevertheless, the fisc may sell the entire common property together with the dowry and the legitime.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain person was condemned to pay one thousand florins to the chamber of the lord duke, for which one thousand florins the chamber received a certain castle in full satisfaction; subsequently, the said castle was sold. The wife of the said condemned person holds the said castle, and also his sons for their legitimate portion.

† The question is asked: what is the law? I answer: First, the dowry must be assigned to the wife, as stated in the Decretals, *De dignitatibus*, chapter *Ex litteris*. Second, the legitime must be deducted according to the form of the statute, because the condemnation was criminal and nearly exhausts the assets, and the portion that falls to the children must be assigned to them. However, it should be known that, by reason of the fiscal share, the fisc may sell the whole, as stated in the Codex, *De alienationibus rerum fiscalium cum privato coniunctis*, law 1, book 10. Nevertheless, the wife may remain in possession of her hypothecary right until the assignment of the dowry is made to her, as stated in the Decretals, *De pignoribus*, chapter *Ex litteris*. Similarly, the children may remain in possession until the legitime is assigned to them in money or in kind, as stated in the Digest, *De bonis damnatorum*, law *Cum ratio*. Furthermore, the said women did not incur any other penalty, because they do not appear to have contemptuously defied the Duke or the imperial magistrates with malice, as stated in the Digest, *De iure omnium iudiciorum*, law *Si quis id*, especially since they had a just cause for not leaving their right undiscussed, as stated in the Digest, *De petitione hereditatis*, law *Illud*; and in the Codex, *Ne uxor pro marito*, law *Ob maritorum*; and as noted in law *Quinque legibus*, Digest, *De bonis damnatorum*. And thus it is to be said according to the law. I, Baldus. See also above, Consilium 169. CONSI

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a judge who has confirmed the opinion of a learned jurist may inquire into its nullity.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The statute provides that a sentence must be rendered according to the advice of a wise person who ought to have given counsel within twenty days. In the case where the appointed advisor gave his counsel after the term had expired, and the magistrate judged according to that counsel, it is now said that the sentence is null. The question arises whether the said magistrate can cognize the nullity of his own sentence. I answer that there is no doubt that the ordinary judge can regularly cognize the nullity of a sentence, both incidentally and principally, as stated in C. quomodo et quando iudex, l. si ut proponis, unless the nullity had been devolved to a superior by appeal, as in C. de accusationibus, l. absentem, and ff. de appellationibus, l. si expressim. And therefore, if you ask whether he can cognize it, it must be said that he can. But if you ask what he ought to pronounce, namely whether the sentence is valid or null, it must be said that, once the term for giving counsel has elapsed, counsel could not be given, as in ff. rem ratam habere, l. bonorum; ff. de contrahenda emptione, qui fundum; ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. consequens. And therefore, since by the form of the statute the sentence must be founded upon the counsel, it follows necessarily that if the counsel is null, then also the sentence which follows from it is null, as in ff. de iniusta rupture et irrita testamento, l. nam et si sub conditione, §. rumpendo, and C. de legibus et constitutionibus, l. non dubium. But if you were to posit that the advisor could have given counsel, then he could not cognize the nullity, unless perhaps on account of holidays or not being in the place of the major courts, as in l. 1, in principio, ff. de feriis, with its material. For this does not concern whether the counsel is just or unjust, but he cannot pronounce against the counsel, because his power is bound by the form of the statute, as in ff. de exercitu, l. 1, §. si plures, and extra de electione, c. cum in veteri, and l. Titium et Mevium, ff. de administratione tutorum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a dowry given to one of brothers who are cohabiting and partners in all their property is to be restored from the common fund or solely from the share of that husband.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: there were four brothers, heirs of their father, holding the estate in undivided common ownership. One of them took a wife and received a dowry, as well as other jewels from his wife, and a dowry instrument was drawn up according to common usage. Finally, the brothers came to a division of the estate. After the division had been made, the brother who had taken a wife died after some interval. Since his share was insufficient for the restitution of the dowry, nor even for the other goods of the wife, the said woman wishes to have recourse against the goods of the other brothers, stating that she gave that dowry at a time when all were in communion of goods, and consequently that every particular item of goods was hypothecated to her. The question now arises: what is the law, both regarding the dowry and the other goods? This question is a daily one, and the truth is that only that brother who received the dowry is bound to restore it to his wife. The reason is that, just as the said dowry is not acquired by his brothers, but pertains to the husband in its entirety, as stated in the Digest, *Familiae erciscundae*, law *Si maritus*; so too, he alone is bound to restore it, since he alone could not bind his brothers along with himself, as stated in the Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Cum duobus*, section *Si fratres*. This is expressly stated in the Code, *De decurionibus*, Book 10, law *Licet indivisam*. Someone might say: suppose that these brothers were partners in all their goods; in this case, are the other brothers bound to the woman? And similarly, I say that they are not, because she did not contract with them, nor did she intend to bind them to herself. For the rule of law is that one cannot bind another when conducting one’s own business, as is the case with the business of marriage and dowry, as stated in the Digest, *De duobus rebus iudicatis*, law *Si id, quod ego*; and in the Digest, *De muneribus et honoribus*, law *Et quia originem*, section final. Furthermore, the woman did not intend to bind the brothers with whom she had not contracted, nor quasi-contracted, as stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Si unus*, section *Ante omnia*. To this effect, it is noted by Doctor Dynerius in the Digest, *Solutis matrimoniis*, law *Si cum dotem*, section *Transgrediamur*. And these statements are true, unless this dowry had been converted to the common utility of the brothers, for then they are bound to share, or contribute, in the restitution of the dowry, either by an action *pro socio* or by an action *negotiorum gestorum*, as stated in the Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Si socius pro filia*. This action would be granted to the woman as useful, as if for a name bound to her by tacit hypothec, which would be competent against the brothers as against the husband’s debtors, after the excussion of the husband’s faculties, namely those which he possessed. Code, *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*, law *Nomen*.
