Although others say that excussion is not required, because a useful personal action is brought, which was competent to the principal debtor against his debtor, and this is not provided for in this law, that excussion is required, since he acts as a procurator in his own right in the name of the principally obligated party; but I believe the contrary to be truer, because this useful action partakes of the nature of a hypothecary action, and is substituted in its place; hence, I consider the excussion of the other goods to be necessary. On this point, it is sufficiently noted by Cynus in the said law *Nomen*. Concluding, therefore, I say that the said husband did not bind his brothers, either in dowry or in paraphernalia, neither by law itself nor in effect, unless it is proven that something else was done. And therefore, the said dowry and paraphernalia, things being thus situated, cannot be recovered from the said brothers. On the matter, it is noted in the *Speculum*, *De iudiciis*, fourth part, section *Generalia*. Furthermore, the general matter is treated in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Si Titium et Mevium*, section *Altero*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a legacy made to two granddaughters for the purpose of marrying them accrues to the other granddaughter upon the death of one.
body: In the name of Christ. Facinus sold a house to Secundonus for the price of five hundred florins. Then the said Facinus sold the said five hundred florins to the said Secundonus for an annual rent of forty ducats per year. Then the said Facinus, coming to death, made his will in this manner: "To my two nieces, the daughters of my brother, for their marriage, I leave fifty florins in undivided shares, and I institute my heirs, to whom Secundonus shall be bound." Then one of the said girls died before reaching marriageable age.

It is asked whether the surviving legatee can demand the entire said amount, or a part, or nothing. And it seems that she can demand the whole, on account of the right of accretion, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. pro secundo. For it was left to the said girls jointly, and jointness gives rise to the right of accretion, as in ff. de legatis 3, l. ei coniunctim, with its material. To the contrary it seems, because a legacy left to a certain person for a dowry is a legacy ob causam, just like a legacy of alimony, in which the right of accretion has no place, as in leg. et no. ff. de usufructu, l. dominus. Moreover, one girl died before the age of marriage, hence, the condition of the legacy failing, the legacy vanished, as in C. de nuptiis, l. sancimus; in Auth. de sancta episcoporum synodo, §. sed hoc presenti; and no. per Bartolus, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, §. Titio genero; and thus nothing is due except half of the said legacy in the person of the surviving girl. But certainly, it seems even more strongly that nothing is due, because the testator seems to have bequeathed the name of a false debtor already released by novation of the contract, as in ff. de liberatione, l. legaui.

Solution: There should be no doubt among experts regarding the part of the living girl, that the heirs are bound to pay from the hereditary purse, because this is not a legacy of a claim, but rather a certain demonstration of wherefrom payment is to be made, as in ff. de legatis 1, l. quidam testamento, where the case seems to apply literally. But regarding the other half, whether it accrues, there is considerable doubt. Nevertheless, it seems more probable to say that it does accrue, because there is no person remaining who would make a part with the dead girl, who is admitted to the part; or, if we were to say that those words, "for them to be married," do not constitute a condition, but a demonstration, as some hold in the aforementioned §. Titio genero, the surviving girl would come as heir to the predeceased, and that the right of accretion has place, as expressly held by Petrus and Cynus, C. de conditionibus insertis, l. si plures, in 2. q. It is certain that a dowry admits of increase; and therefore this is not similar to alimony, in which the right of accretion ceases. And thus the aforementioned l. dominus does not object. To this also contribute the words of the testament, because the testator had the intention of joining the legatees, namely, by words of appellative and comprehensive name: because he said, "to two nieces." Also by the thing: because he said "undivided." And thus, by a double reason, the right of accretion has place, and the death of one impugns the legacy of the other. This is also supported by the charity of the persons and the piety of the dowry; and because she who has a better dowry marries better, it is to be believed that the will of the testator proceeded thus, arg. ff. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredes mei, §. cum ita. Both the right of jointness and natural reason suggest that the portion of the ward who predeceased accrues to the survivor, in whose person the quality of marriage is fulfilled. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. From the formation of the case itself, it is gathered how a hypothec is to be proved, and what is the law when a third witness disagrees with the other two.
2. Writing is not a mode of creating an obligation, but a mode of proving it.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is presented in this form: during the pendency of the litigation, on the occasion of a claim of priority of hypothec, a guarantee is alleged based on a single private document, subscribed by the hand of the debtor and by three witnesses. And because the authenticity of the document was brought into doubt, it was stipulated that the document itself, the tenor of which had been described word for word in the chapter, was written and subscribed in the year, day, and month contained therein, by the debtor’s own hand; and that the witnesses subscribed thereto were present at the said document and subscribed as witnesses. And according as the witnesses shall say, so it may be proved, and the truth will appear. And upon the examination of the witnesses, two of them deposed that the writing of the tenor described in the chapter was shown to them as good and true; and that the money contained in the writing was counted. Furthermore, that the writing was written and subscribed by the debtor’s own hand, and subscribed by the hands of the said three witnesses in the year, month, and day contained in the chapter. The third witness, however, deposes that he did not see the debtor write or subscribe at the time he subscribed, nor did he see any money counted, but only heard the writing read by the debtor. Now, from the foregoing, it is asked: whether the hypothec of the goods, mentioned in the said document, is proved. And it is alleged that it is not. First, not by the force of the document, because it is required for the document to be solemn that all three witnesses were present, at least at the subscription of the debtor. And the third witness deposes that he was not present at the document nor at the subscription; therefore, the document is not proved. Furthermore, not by the attestation of those two witnesses, because the witnesses were produced to prove the hypothec by the force and solemnity of the document; which solemnity, as is stated, is not proved. But they were not produced principally to prove the hypothec by the form of the contract celebrated between the parties in the presence of witnesses, because then it would have been expedient for them to have given the reason for their statement by an act corresponding to the sense of that which is in question, in which case they would prove, or not. And that they append that the document is good and true, because it would stand that the document, with respect to the writing which they saw being written and subscribed, is good and true; nevertheless, they would not know to depose the truth of the contents therein, nor to give the reason by a sense corresponding to the act in question. Now, it is asked, what is the law?

† It must be premised for clarity that there are two things, namely, the container, i.e., the writing, and the content. And this is twofold, namely, the visible, i.e., the form of the contract set down in writing, and the indivisible, i.e., the obligation and the action arising therefrom, and whatever follows from the understanding of the law, such as delivery or quasi-intellectual delivery. And these are distinct, because the writing is distinct in itself, the contract is distinct in itself, the obligation is distinct in itself, and the action is distinct in itself.

† Writing in itself is not a mode of creating an obligation, but is a mode of proving the obligation itself, as is fully stated in the law and noted in the Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Non figura*. Moreover, although one thing is the container and another the contained, nevertheless the contained is included under the container; for example, under a chirograph (private writing) the obligation is included, as in the Digest, *De deposito*, law *Publia*, § *Si*. Likewise, release, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Postquam*. Likewise, delivery, from which it appears that possession is delivered by instrument, as in the Code, *De donationibus*, law 1.

Furthermore, I premise that the subscription is the final part of the writing, which presupposes its preceding parts as true, without which it cannot be effective. We say the same regarding the seal; hence, the subscriber appears to confess that all things are true, as in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Si fideiussor*, § *Pater*. Likewise, the one who seals, as in the Code, *De rebus alienis non alienandis*, law 2, and there noted. Moreover, the subscriber appears to approve all things, as in the Digest, *De testamento militis*, law *Tribunus*, § *Ultimo*. Hence, a witness who subscribed appears to assert that all things which could have been done at that place and time are true, just as we say regarding witnesses who are written into a written will, even though they are ignorant of what is written in the body of the will. For it is not necessary that the witness explicitly know and have memorized the things done in the writing, but it is sufficient that he recognizes his own writing, as in the Digest, *De testibus*, law *Haeredes palam*, in the principle, and law *Qui testamento*, § *Si*. For the subscription is the exit and conclusion of the entire act in question, as in the Code, *De fide instrumentorum*, law *Contractus*.

From these things it appears that, since the subscription is proven by three witnesses, that subscription deserves the effect of a subscription, and the testimony of a witness who says he read part and heard part should not be admitted: both because there is no force in the claim that he ought to have heard and seen, and because the substance is nothing other than the subscription, and a single witness proves his own subscription with one other witness as a con-testator; because the fact that the solemnity of three witnesses was present can be proven by two, since the light of truth is presumed to assist, as in the law and noted in law 2 of the Code, *De secundis tabulis*, and noted in law 1 of the Code, *De testibus*, and law 1, § *Si* of the Digest, *Quemadmodum testamentum aperiri*.

From these things follows also another conclusion: for, the subscription being proven, that subscription proves the other things contained in the subscribed chirograph, at least by way of confession; because the whole is one writing and tends to one final end, as in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Non est ferendus*. Although, therefore, one solemnity is that of the paper or chirograph, and another is that of the contract or business, as noted in the Digest, *De edendo*, law 1, § *Editiones*, nevertheless they are connected and both are presumed true from the fact that they are found written; and not only are they presumed true, but also solemn, as noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Iuris gentium*, § *Quod fere*, and *De verborum obligationibus*, law *Sciendum*. Moreover, since the obligation is true, the hypothec (mortgage/lien) is presumed true, as noted in the Code, *De falsis*, law *Satis aperte*, and especially because by customary condition a hypothec is appended. Therefore, etc., as in the Digest, *De edicto edilitio*, law *Quaeritur*, § *Si venditor*.

Moreover, certainly it is not an objection that it is said that the witnesses were not sworn regarding the hypothec. For, since they were interrogated regarding the truth of the cause, i.e., the chirograph, they could also be examined regarding the hypothec, as expressly noted in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Si quis intentione*. And conversely, if the principal question is regarding the hypothec, they can be examined regarding the principal obligation, by which one arrives at the hypothecary one; because these are mutually connected, and one arises from the other. Moreover, the oath receives an extensive interpretation necessary for its performance. Moreover, he who swears to one thing can be examined regarding that thing and its appendages, as expressly noted in the Code, *Qui legibus personis*, law *Momentariae*, and in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter *Licet causam*. Moreover, as I said, the oath is implicitly resolved explicitly into all articles which can be enumerated under that implicit oath, as in the Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, law *Omnes*, in the principle; Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Si chorus*; Digest, *De servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, law *Si servitus*; Digest, *Qui et a quibus*, law *Si optio*; Digest, *De legatis secundo*, law *Meuius*, § *Duobus*.

Wherefore, then, on account of the generality, then on account of the conjunction of the cause, then from the nature of the container and the contained, then from the fact that it is customary to do so: I say that, the subscription being proven as it is proven, everything contained in the subscriptions would be sufficiently proven. And this applies to heirs as to living voice, regarding what is contained in the subscription, as in the Code, *De non numero pecuniae*, law *Generaliter*, and in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter *Per tuas*. Nor can a witness recede, since he confesses that the subscription was made by his own hand, as in the Digest, *De falsis*, law 1, and law *Filius*, § 1, and in the Code, *De non numero pecuniae*, authentic *Contra qui proprias*. Even if one of three witnesses varies from the other two, credit is given to the two, and to the subscription of three and the living voice of two, rather than to the vacillation of one witness, because the voice of one contrary to his own writing is the voice of no one, even as regards simple presumption, as in the Code, *De testibus*, law *Iusiurandi*, and in the Extravagant, *De testibus*, chapter *In nomine Domini*.

Moreover, since two prove the truth of the hypothec, we are not in the matter of the authentic *Si quis vult caute deponere*, but we are in the matter of proof by living voice, by which, in doubt, the hypothec and its priority are proven, if two witnesses testify regarding the hypothec from the time which the subscribers are understood to testify from, according to the time when they subscribed, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagant, *De probationibus*, chapter *Quum contra falsum*.

It is not an objection if it is alleged that they do not give the reason for their statement regarding the hypothec; for rather they do give it, for the reason is that it is so contained in the instrument, as in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Fideiussores magistratuum*, § 1.

Concluding therefore from the first to the last, it is established that the hypothec with its time and priority is proven, and therefore judgment should be given for the said exceptor claiming the priority of the said hypothec, because he who is prior in time in personal and hypothecary matters is stronger in law, as in the rule *Qui prior*. For there are two foundations of the hypothecary right: the debt and the hypothec; and there is one foundation of priority, namely time, as in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Ante omnia*, and in the Code, *Qui potior in pignore habeat*, law *Assiduis*, with its material.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman who has fled from her husband can, and when, demand that he provide security, and whether in the meantime she is to be maintained. See also nos. 4 and 5.
2. What are the just causes on the basis of which a judge may determine whether sureties are to be given or not.
3. Whether one who has once been an enemy is presumed to remain an enemy forever.
body: In the name of Christ. Caecilia separated from her husband, Francisco, a man of work, and from the children she had borne by him; and she remained outside the household for many years. She wishes to return to her husband, provided that he furnishes her with good security that he will do her no harm.

It is asked whether, and what kind of security is to be provided; and it seems that it is not to be provided, because either she departed without fault on the part of the woman, and she ought not reasonably to fear, because he who possesses the faith of innocence has the greatest security, as in C. de iniuriis, l. si non convicii; or she departed with her own fault, and then it would be unjust that the husband be bound to the burden of caution on account of the wife’s fault. Moreover, it would be unjust that her own fault should be to her advantage, as in ff. de negotiorum gestione, l. sive hereditaria. Furthermore, the husband must and may correct his wife with a fitting correction, as in l. 1, C. de emendatione propinquorum; nor can he be compelled to give security for not correcting her bad morals, and if he expressly promised this, the promise would not be valid, because it would be contrary to good morals, and it would give the wife an opportunity to sin. See ff. de verbis obligatis, l. si plagii.

† The solution is that the laws and canons state that security must be provided if there is a just cause for fear, that is, if it is just, i.e., if it is legitimate or probable. This is what it means to fear justly, namely, that which even steadfast persons fear, as in D. 46.10.1 (Metum non vani timoris), which is left entirely to the discretion of the judge, who must consider the quality of the persons and the grounds for suspicion, as noted at the end of D. 43.12.1 § Idem ait (De ripa munienda). Therefore, the judge ought to interrogate the woman who fears, asking why she fears, so that she may specifically explain the causes by which she is oppressed. The argument is drawn from C. 3.31.1 (De praed. curia), lib. 10. Many things can occur; for sometimes the severity of the husband occurs, as in D. 24.2.1 § Si autem in sevissimo (Si cum dotem). And this severity can exist in greater or lesser degrees, like species of madness. Furthermore, it can arise from the bad custom of the husband, because he is accustomed to treat her ill, regarding which the reputation of the neighbors is considered, as argued in D. 48.18.1 § Tormenta (De minore) and D. 48.18.2 (Non omnes). And it is rarely corrected when it has passed into custom, as in D. 47.2.1 § Abarbaris (Non omnes, De re militari). Sometimes this happens because the husband is jealous and vainly suspicious; nevertheless, he beats his wife. But whatever the case may be, a good judge will determine the matter according to the various persons and causes, as argued in D. 47.2.1 (In fundo, De rei venditione), and will apply that remedy which can probably cure this malady, as in X. 2.27.12 (Ex transmissa, De restitutione spoliorum) and X. 2.27.13 § Finis (Literas), and in Auth. 10.42.1 § Si vero intra terminum, col. 1 (De moribus). Hence, this is sufficiently discretionary, as noted by Guillaume de Coucy generally in the matter of these securities against offending in D. 4.1.1 (Illicitas, De officio praesidis), C. 9.45.1 (De his qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt, Denunciamus), and C. 9.45.2 § Finis (Praesenti). And if it seems to the judge that an oath-bound security with the addition of a penalty is sufficient, the husband should not be compelled to provide security with sureties; because it is burdensome to find sureties, as stated and noted in D. 24.3.2 § Si dubitetur (De iudiciis, et ne inter virum et uxorem qui male secum vivunt), lest a matter of greater hatred arise between husband and wife, C. 4.20.1 and 2 (Ne fideiussores darentur), and C. 9.13.1 § Finis (Manifestissimi, De furtis). But if the nature of the case requires sureties, and the husband can provide security, he is bound to give a surety; but if he swears that he cannot provide a surety, his oath shall be believed, as above regarding the oath-bound security, as noted in D. 46.1.1 (Qui satisdare cogantur). Furthermore, if the husband is a discreet man and of amended life, I believe his oath to be sufficient, by argument from that noted gloss which is in D. 46.1.1 cited above. For securities which are not interposed by the edict of the praetor, but extra ordinem from various figures of causes, i.e., their quality and the mode of providing security, are committed to the discretion of the judge, as in C. 3.38.1 (Cui relictum, De indicibus viduis). And according to the foregoing, I understand the glosses of canon law prudently alleged by other consultants, 17. qo 4. c. G. (Uxor fecit), and D. 4.1.1 (Omnes, De in integrum restitutione), where the justice and truth of the causes are inquired into.

It must be known, however, that grave enmity is presumed to be continued and not abandoned; for in matters having the root of capital hatred, one presumes from the past into the present. Hence, once an enemy, always presumed an enemy, unless reconciliation is proved, as in l. 3, ff. de adim. lega.; and ff. de arbit., l. licet; and extra de accu., c. cum per Mantellam; C. fam. erci., l. in omnes; C. de inoff. testa., l. omnimodo. But enmities arising from light causes are not presumed to endure, because they have no origin nor foundation, having proceeded from levity of mind, as in l. 1, C. si quis imperat. maledic.; and they are not of great weight. For this dictates natural discretion, which is presumed to be in every man; otherwise man would not be man, but a certain beast, as says the gloss in Auth. de mon., in princ., on the word dicentem. For enmities proceeding from levity of mind are rather a certain momentary impulse of the mind than enduring, because reasonably it ought not to endure; and man, by his very nature, is a rational animal. And therefore the laws do not care for slight enmity, as in the laws cited above. I say this for so much, because if the woman had sinned against her own body, this would be capital, radical, and enduring enmity, as in ff. de leg. 2, l. codicillis, § poenam. From this cause there arises vehement indignation and hatred more than capital, and more afflictive than the death of children, as says the text there, and Jacobus de Arena. But if [the cause] were from morals much remote from sexual intercourse, it would not be capital enmity, nevertheless bad morals would be to be corrected. Arg. in l. 1, C. de sec. nup.; and it supports what is noted in c. tua nos., extra de spons., by Bartolus. And if the woman says that she was beaten once in ten years, this was not cruelty, but correction, as is noted in 7 q. 1, c. sicut alterius; and 23 q. 1, duo ista, sicut, which another consulting jurist also prudently alleged. Indeed, certainly a wise man ought daily to correct bad morals, lest they pass into a custom of sinning. Moreover, a vice hardly ceases which takes root by custom; hence it is written: Principiis obsta, sero medicina paratur. And Aristotle says in the Oeconomica that a wife ought always to be under the fear and reverence of her husband. This, therefore, I have said concerning the caution and its quality.

But it is asked, what is to be said concerning the dowry and the fruits of the dowry? Behold, the woman does not trust that she will return to her husband, because she knows his capital hatred and that his nature is without mercy; for often nature supplies the vices of the mind, as in D. ad Maced. l. 1. in principio. And briefly, regarding the fruits of the dowry, it must be considered thus: the husband must bear the burdens of marriage which pertain to the husband, as in C. de iure dot. l. pro oneribus; and conversely, the wife must undergo the burdens which pertain to the wife, as in c. ultima, Extr. de conversione in fidei; C. qui potior in pignore habenda est, l. assiduis. And even if the wife had committed adultery, she must be maintained by the husband from the fruits of the dowry until she is condemned, as in l. rei iudicatae, § 1, D. sol. matr.; and D. de inofficioso testamento, l. si instituta. But after she has been condemned, as one set aside, she ought not to receive fruits nor alimony, for she is declared unworthy by sentence. Argumentum, Extr. de dolo et contumacia, c. veritatis. Nevertheless, one thing must be observed: that she ought to work for her husband in servile and domestic tasks, as is noted in l. sicut, D. de operis liberto. Hence, if through her own fault she is outside her husband’s house, just as she does not labor, so she does not eat. I say that she works, or that it does not stand by her. It is said to stand by her if she gave cause for the edict, as is written concerning Calpurnia, as in l. illa, D. de postulando. But if the fault began with the husband, it is said to stand by the husband, argumentum, C. de servis fugitivis, l. quicunque, § si. Likewise, it is said to stand by the husband if cruelty is found in him without cause; nor does he wish to give security; indeed, the same applies if he cannot find a surety, for she should not impute this to herself, because she placed herself in necessity, argumentum, C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, § et quod; and as noted in l. 1, in fine, C. de natis liberis. But in the case of a widow, because she is released from the law of service and from the law of the husband, as the Apostle says, we say that she must be maintained from her own dowry, as is noted in C. rem in praesenti, § exactio; and D. de venditionibus in possessione missis, l. curator. Let us therefore conclude briefly in all the above matters. For if it is asked whether the husband is bound to give security by a simple caution, it must be said that yes; but if it is asked whether with a surety, it must be said that no, unless the judge, from the quality of the facts, has deemed it otherwise to be decided, as I said above. And this dictates equity, for by giving a simple caution he is not harmed, because it is in his power to keep his promises, and it benefits the other party, D. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. 2, § item Varrus. But to give a surety is difficult and outside the nature of marriage.

† Concerning the fruits of the dowry, whether she ought to be maintained, the conclusion is as follows: while the marriage remains in its status, she ought to be maintained, insofar as the resources of the dowry permit, by dividing the fruits between herself and her husband alone. However, the burden of maintaining the children does not fall upon the wife, because the mother is not bound to maintain a legitimate child after the term [of nursing], provided the husband’s resources are sufficient. D. 10.2.12 (Si maritus). I therefore advise that they reconcile with each other amicably, and that all things be arranged as noted in D. 2.11.1 (Furti) § Pactus. And if the said woman, having received adequate security, refuses to return to the household of a good man, she renders herself alien to the benefit of alimony, according to the argument in D. 36.1.1 (Si legatario) § 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A prebendary who does not expect appointment, provision, or any other disposition by the bishop, whether under a customary practice held jointly or separately, etc., is not included under a papal rescript issued by the Pope, etc.
2. Whether a derogatory clause derogates from custom.
3. Whether a son may deduct his legitime from a single asset.
4. Arbitration, even if granted freely to someone, is understood to be exercised with equity preserved.
body: In the name of Christ. In the Church of Regina and a reasonable statute, which states that the older canon who is making residence and is in sacred orders may accept a vacant prebend. And this statute being in force, a certain person obtained a canonry of the said Church with a prebend, if any was then vacant, or when it shall become vacant, by mandate of the Pope's executor, who reserved it to himself, prohibiting the bishop and chapter, or to whomsoever the collation, provision, presentation, or any other disposition of the said prebends pertains, jointly or severally, that they presume in no way to dispose of the said prebend.

It is asked whether, from these letters, prejudice is caused to the older canonist, so that he may not validly opt for a prebend according to the aforementioned statute of the Church and the custom prevailing in the said Church for the execution of the said statute. And it seems that prejudice is caused, because the older canonist has no right from any other source, except from the statute or custom. But derogation has been made to this statute and custom both by the reservation and by the derogatory clause "non obstante." For that custom does not seem to have place in prebends reserved by mandate of the Pope.

† Moreover, because the derogatory clause applies to custom: nor is it necessary that the Pope make mention of the form of the custom, but rather of custom in general. For the Pope cannot formally know the words of the statute or custom. All this is proved in c. Licet Romanus, De constitutionibus, Book 6, and in c. Finis, De consuetudinibus, same Book. The contrary seems to me, because the Pope does not write except concerning prebends pertaining to collation or provision; but this prebend does not pertain to collation or provision, or to any other disposition of the bishop or chapter, jointly or severally; because they cannot provide for it, notwithstanding the said custom, which binds their hands; so that collation, provision, or disposition is not open to them. Hence, since this case is not comprehended by the letters, the papal grace does not touch this case, as in c. Susceptu, De reservationibus; and in the Digest, De liberationibus et posthumis, l. Commodissime; and in the Digest, Solutis matrimonii, l. Si cum dotem, in principio; and in the Digest, De legatis tertio, l. Hoc legatum and l. Nuper; in the Digest, De vino legato, l. Finis, § Cui dulcia; in the Digest, De pignoribus legatis, l. Nam quod liquide, § Si quis penus; and in c. 1, De prebendis in clericiis. Those words “to collation” and similar in c. Declarant declare that the Pope’s intention in the preceding was to speak only of benefices pertaining to collation, etc., because species enumerated after a genus have the effect of restricting it, as in the Digest, De verborum significatione, l. Cum fundum; and most fully noted in l. Quaesitum, § Ultimo, Digest, De funerariis instrumentis; it is made clear in the Code, Familiae erciscundae, l. Quotiens; and in the Digest, De legatis secundo, l. Legatorum, § Qui plures; in the Digest, De hereditatibus institutis, l. Qui non militabat, § Lutio.

† Note that I equate the son with the master, as in D. de lib. et posth. l. in suis. And therefore, just as the master may deduct everything owed to him from the peculium in a single item, so too may the son deduct his legitime from a single item not bequeathed to another, since the legitime consists in genus or quantity; on this point, see no. in D. si peculium § 1 de pec. leg. in the words pro rata. For only the text argues to the contrary.

† And regarding this equivalence, although free discretion is granted to someone, it is nevertheless understood to be exercised with equity preserved; and therefore, if the middle course is equitable and the extremes are vitious, the middle course must be observed, as noted in l. cum certum, in l. ulti. gl. ff. de uino leg. Likewise, if arbitrators are bound to agree, a futile disagreement does not prevent them from being able and obliged to reach agreement, to which they must be compelled, or they will be condemned to pay damages, as in ff. de adopt. lega. l. seruo. Generally, the enumeration of things induces plurality, as in ff. de pec. leg. l. si peculium. §. plane. And pertinent to the question is that, in the donation of individual assets, the individual items are considered, not aggregated, with respect to insinuation; nor can it increase or decrease beyond the nature or definition of the thing itself, as in the aforementioned l. si peculium. §. 1. Therefore, the Roman Empire cannot increase or decrease with regard to the disposition of law: the specific prevails over the general, unless its declaration consists in the same species, as in ff. de lega. 1. l. si dominus Sticho. because it does not appear to be within the intention of the disposer, nor to be included under the general category, that which is specifically and precisely determined, as in ff. de optio. leg. l. cum ita. §. quaesitum. and ff. de fun. instruc. l. cum delanionis. §. cui spes. Nevertheless, it does not seem useless if something is taken away from the general category, as in ff. de aur. et arg. leg. l. medico. §. mulier. unless it is taken away by the person to whom the general disposition was conferred, as in ff. de pec. leg. l. cum dominus. §. filius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The question is whether a claim will be defeated if some of its allegations are false and others true, and whether it is void due to uncertainty of place.
2. It is credible to the judge that which the people believe.
3. Only he who asserts a claim is bound to prove it; otherwise, he will fail in his case.
4. A statute provides that the authority is liable for the delict of its household if the household commits theft in the village of Saint Mark, and this was so proven; however, there were two villages of the same name, and it was not proven in which one the theft occurred. The question is whether the authority is liable.
body: In the name of Christ. Given the statute concerning the conduct of inquisitions, especially regarding clandestine offenses, such as arson, nocturnal crimes, and certain daytime offenses, it is proposed, though not conceded, that the local authority conducted an inquiry against certain individuals, against whom there was then no infamy, nor did clamorous accusations reach the ears of the inquisitor. Finally, the chaplain of the village, or the syndic, denounced the same individuals for the aforementioned felony. Subsequently, the said inquired persons were absolved as innocent. An action is brought against the said inquisitor for damage and fault, and it is requested that he be punished criminally and civilly for injury and interest.

† The question is: what is the law? I answer that malice is not presumed in an inquisitor when he is bound to inquire, for the necessity of his office excuses him, as is fully noted in the Digest, in the title "De his qui notati sunt infamia" (Concerning those who are noted with infamy), in the law "Athletas" (Athletes), section "Calumniator" (Calumniator). Nor does he appear to have proceeded improperly, who is assisted by those pursuing the matter, as in the Code, in the title "De iudiciis" (Concerning judges), in the law "Rem non novam" (Not a new matter), section "Si" (If). For when his own motion concurs with that of many others, and the inquisitor asserts nothing himself, but rather public fame, which suffices to verify

† For it is credible to the judge. What is believed by the people is credited, as in c. Qualiter et quando, de accusationibus; in c. Licet Heli, de simonia; argument from C. ad Macedoniam, l. Zenodorus; and D. eodem, l. 4; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Cum quidam, quod dicitur. Nor does it obstruct the case if it is said that the judge asserted a falsehood, namely, that public fame had preceded, when in fact it had not; for this negative, that it had not preceded, is not proven: and since a delict arises from a negative, it must be proven, as noted by Innocentius, Extra, de accusationibus, c. Super his; and by Cynus, C. de iure emphyteutici, l. 2. Moreover, even if infamy did not precede in court, it could nevertheless have preceded outside of court; although infamy not brought to the ears of the judge is not promotive of an inquisition. Furthermore, what is predicted by private persons is verified by subsequent events, and the time of judging the matter must be inspected, to determine whether anyone is to be punished for calumny or not, as in D. ad Turpilium, l. 1, § Calumniatoribus. Moreover, civil and criminal actions cannot be cumulated, unless perhaps one says that this rule fails in the extraordinary scrutiny of officials, where one need not concern oneself with the subtleties of law, but, looking solely at the truth, one must proceed and expedite the case in the shortest time, as from unwritten law, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, de officio iudicis. The solution is that, unless fraud is proven, acquittal should follow, because conjectures are not sufficient in this case to prove fraud: for the conjecture that is in favor of the judge is greater than the conjecture that is against him; and because the judge is compelled, and therefore fraud is not consumed, as in l. 3, D. quod falsum aut turpiter auctum. Moreover, it is not very difficult to prove the fraud of a judge: since many things concur for the excuse of the judge; among which is the possibility that he has clean hands, as in Auth. Ut iudices fine quoquo suffragio, § Necessitatem. Hatred is also not presumed: because all hatreds are contrary to nature, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. Ut vim.

† I do not omit the point that he who alleges fraud is bound to prove the fraud: and he must succumb if he does not prove it. Which I prove by this reasoning: because fraud is a species of fault. For it is predicated of fraud and of non-fraud, and he who binds himself to a species must prove the species, not the genus, as is stated in l. igitur, ff. de lib. causa. It is also said that every fraud is fault, but the converse does not hold. Furthermore, know that a general inquiry is similar to the action for management of affairs (negotiorum gestorum), which is brought against the manager of affairs of some lord. Hence the republic seems to offer a general bill, rather criminal than civil, for itself and its subjects. And in a general bill specification of the particulars is not necessary, nor restriction of place and time: because if the species is not necessary, therefore neither are the individuals of the species. However, if the individuals were deduced in the form of a difference, they would have to be proved, as noted in C. de iud., l. licet, and l. sicum tibi. From these it appears that in the audits of officials, which are called the digestion of the office—because then the official digests what he previously swallowed—a general bill of inquiry concerning the genera of the particulars suffices, if afterwards a special proof follows for each genus: and especially if certain special chapters are placed in the inquiry. The case is expressly stated regarding fraud and contumacy of truth in the word "and other crimes." I saw this doubted when I was a boy in school.

The statute states that the magistrate is liable for the delict of his household, provided that the household of the magistrate committed theft in the village of Marci; and this was indeed proven. However, there were two villages of the same name, and it was not proven in which one the magistrate was absolved by Bartolus due to the uncertainty of the place. And perhaps this was wrongly decided, because in a general libel a general proof suffices, which, when distinguished by species, does not operate more in one species than in another, as argued from the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Qui si dubitet*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A mother is bound to institute her children as heirs, and she cannot deprive them of their legitime; nor does the codicillary clause have any effect in this regard.
2. Whether the preterition of a mother was valid in the past, and whether it is valid today.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Certain matters concerning the household. Catherine made a will, in which she passed over her children and instituted her mother, Dame Richadonna, as her universal heir in the said will by these words: “in all my other goods, and movable and immovable things, present and future, rights, and names of debts, and especially and particularly in my paraphernal goods, clothes, portions, and money to be converted into clothes for her to wear, and brought by her to her husband, and whatever is owed to her in any manner and cause: and all these things beyond the dowry brought to the husband, I institute Dame Richadonna, my mother and widow of the late Master Francis, as my universal heir, etc.” And the said testatrix appended to the said will a codicillary clause in the form which follows, namely: “But the said testatrix asserts that this is her will, which she wished to be valid, and ordered, and wishes it ought to be valid by the law of a nuncupative will; and if it should not be valid by the law of a nuncupative will, she wishes that it be valid and hold by the law of codicils; and if it could not be valid by the law of codicils, she wishes that it be valid and hold by the law of any last will, and in every manner, way, law, and form by which it may be better, etc.” Now the question is asked, what is the law regarding the aforementioned will?

† It must be known that the preterition of a mother is regarded as disinheritance: and formerly the testament of a mother preteriting her son was valid; but a complaint [querela] was necessary, as is stated in the Institutes, *de inofficioso testamento*, § *mater*. And all legacies and fideicommissa were thereby rescinded. And even the codicillary clause was rescinded, made by whatever words, as if made by one of unsound mind, as in the Digest, *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *Titia*. But today, according to the newest law of the Authentics, a testament in which a mother preterits her son without cause is null by the law itself, as is most fully noted in the Authentic *de hereditatibus et falsis*, § *exheredatos*. And according to Dynus in l. *Gallus* in the great distinction, hence without doubt the testament in question, as regards the institution of the heir, is null by the law itself. And therefore the said mother, instituted by her daughter as universal heir, is not the universal heir, but the sons of the testatrix are heirs ab intestato. But it is doubtful whether the sons of the testatrix are bound to restore the inheritance of their grandmother? And the doubt arises on account of the codicillary clause. And on this point there are two opinions of our elders. For the ordinary gloss in the Authentic *ex causa*, Codex *de libris preteritis vel exheredatis*, holds that the said clause has no effect if the institution of the heir is null on account of preterition or disinheritance, because the judgment of the testator is unjust; but where the institution is invalid on account of a defect of some other solemnity, then the said clause would be valid. And the gloss of the said Authentic *ex causa* confirms this. And thus all the ancient doctors and advocates held. And thus holds Modus. This opinion is held by Guillaume de Cuisse in l. *ultima*, *de codicillis*. Although Lord Dynus holds the contrary, namely that restitution of the inheritance may be demanded on account of the fideicommissum, as is fully reported by Cynus in the said Authentic, and he notes this in l. 2, Digest *de legatis tertio*. Nor does l. *Titia*, cited above, object, because that law is corrected as regards legacies and fideicommissa, even universal ones, as in the Digest *ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, l. *ita tamen*, § *quotiens*, according to Dynus and others. And this appears from the fact that the reason of the said l. *Titia* is corrected, namely that reason that the testament is feigned to be made by one of unsound mind, and where the reason of the law is corrected, the substance of the law is corrected. This opinion is held by Bartolus and many moderns, and therefore this question is very doubtful. I consider that the tacit disinheritance of a mother is vitiated and contrary to natural equity, and therefore that which is denied by one way ought not to be granted by another way. Moreover, I say that no law provides that the said law is corrected in its case, and even the correction of laws is to be avoided. Nor does § *aliud quoque capitulum* in the Authentic *ut cum de appellatione cogitur* object, because there it speaks of other chapters of the testament, not of the chapter of the institution to be transferred into a universal fideicommissum by a codicillary clause. Moreover, because that clause is interpreted by the glossators when there is a defect of external solemnity, for example of witnesses; or when the inheritance is not entered upon from the testament for some other cause than that of preterition or disinheritance; for since the said institution is odious, it ought not to be aided by interpretation, whatever opinion you hold, you have many illustrious men supporting you. But if we consider authority, the authority of the glossator is greater in such a conflict of opinions, a good agreement of the parties would be best. Argument, Extra *de probationibus*, c. *si*. What if the said mother had been instituted in a certain thing? I answer, the said institution cannot be extended to the whole on account of the vice of preterition, and therefore she is regarded as a simple legatee: and it is valid only in that thing, as is noted in l. *liberis*, Digest *de exceptione doli*. It is not doubtful that the said sons must have their legitime, whatever the case may be regarding the codicillary clause, as in the Codex *de inofficioso testamento*, l. *omnimodo* and l. *sancimus*, and in the Authentic *de triennio et semis*, § 1, column 3, Extra *de testamento*, c. *Raynaldus* and c. *si pater*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the interpretation of the following two statutes of Milan in the matter of prescription.
2. For how long a time tithes may be prescribed.
3. Whether, in prescription, one may avail oneself of the accession of one's author both under civil law and under municipal statute, etc., and number 4.
body: In the name of Christ. Given the words of a certain statute of the City of Milan, which provides, as follows, namely: that by the common law, prescription of ten or twenty years runs in immovable and corporeal things with possession, title, and good faith; but by our municipal law, only a prescription of thirty years shall claim its place. And given the words of a certain other statute in the form which follows the disposition: "Also, if any tithe possessed, or quasi-possessed, or held by anyone for thirty years continuously, his time being joined with that of his donors or predecessors, it shall be presumed to be his, and he shall be held and considered a legitimate possessor with regard to the defense of the property and all effects of the possession, or quasi-possession, of the said tithe, etc." The following case ensues: a certain Antoniolus of Lampugnano proved that he had possessed, or quasi-possessed, for forty years continuously, computing the time of his donor, or author, and predecessor, a certain tithe, or the right of tithing competent to him, on the occasion of a certain sale made to him of the said tithe by certain brothers of Birago, to whom the right of the said tithe had first belonged in full right. Now a certain Nicola of Landriano demands before the competent judge that it be declared that the right of the said tithe does not pertain to the said Antoniolus; and this on the pretext of a certain eviction made of certain rights from the said brothers of Birago by the predecessor of the said Nicola, and it is presupposed that the rights from which the said eviction followed were created before the sale made to the said Antoniolus of the said tithe. The question arises from these matters: what is the law? namely, whether the said Antoniolus ought to be disturbed in his possession, or quasi-possession, and rights of the said tithe,

† And for the evidence of the aforesaid, the First Part of the Consilia is submitted. It must be premised regarding the intention of the said first statute, which reduces the ten-year prescription to a prescription of 30 years: whether the hypothecary prescription is contained in this statute? And it seems that the said prescription applies to corporeal immovable things, for the hypothecary [claim] invokes bare possession of the hypothecated thing, as in D. de evictionibus, l. cum venditor, in principio. Moreover, the words of the statute are broad in regard to movable and corporeal things. Hence it follows that one does not prescribe against the hypothecary [claim] in a lesser time than 25 years, but here 30 years have not elapsed, but only 16 or so; therefore, the prescription is not complete according to municipal law, although it would be complete according to common law, as fully stated and noted in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, in principio.

On the contrary, it seems that he who prescribes against the hypothecary [claim] does not prescribe the thing, because he is the owner, as in D. de usucapione, l. sequitur, § lana; D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. in bello, § si quis servum; and as noted in l. 2, C. quod meo nomine cautum est. But an exception is against a personal action; hence it is not in the thing, but in the right, which is incorporeal, as in D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. ex sextante, § Latinus. And this is clear from the definition of an exception: since an exception is the exclusion of an action, therefore this exception pertains to a certain incorporeal right, namely, the right to sue on account of the hypothecary claim. But in this prescription of an incorporeal right, the statute does not speak; therefore, we are governed by common law, as in D. ad municipalia, l. constitutionibus; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum, § non dixit. And just as one prescribes against the hypothecary [claim], so one prescribes against a pact of entry, because that pact is accessory to the hypothec, as in C. de pignorationibus, l. 3; and D. de pignoris actione, l. qui ratione; D. de furtis, l. si creditor rem. And if one prescribes against the accessory, as in C. de usuris, l. eos, in principio.

Someone will say that this hypothecary [claim] could not have been brought before the right to sue hypothecarily was opened, as noted in D. de solutione matrimonii, in l. facere posse, by Jacobus de Arezzo and others; for when action is impeded, prescription does not run, as in C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, in fine; and C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. cum notissimi, § in his. For he is not harmed by the delay of time who was not negligent, as noted in Authentica de appellationibus, post principio, non obstantibus D. de servis rusticis praedialibus, l. et athilicinus. For a spring that dries up is equated to a debtor who is insolvent; but it is not equated to a debtor who is not bound. Whether a debtor, although insolvent, can prescribe, even though the action is futile, so that the prescriber is similar to one who pays, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. si pupillus; and l. finalis, § finalis, D. rem ratam habere.

Furthermore, this argument does not hold, because although this is true in fact, nevertheless in law the ten-year prescription having elapsed suffices, after which the hypothecary [claim] could purely and freely be brought; and it suffices that it is prescribed, although he who prescribes is not greater; as noted in l. 2, C. de servis fugitivis. For to add perfection to a perfect thing is in vain, as noted in l. pater, D. de causa peculii; and D. de verbis obligatorum, l. quibus idem.

The solution in this first point seems to be that he who prescribes against the hypothecary [claim] does not prescribe an immovable thing, because one thing is the res, another is the exception, unless by the custom of the wise men of Milan the statute was otherwise interpreted, as in D. de legibus, l. si de interpretatione. Now I come to the following statute concerning the prescription of tithes, and I premise for the evidence,

† Either the question arises concerning prescription against the Church, or it arises concerning prescription against a private person who holds this right by privilege or custom, without calling into doubt the validity of custom. In the first case, under the common law, a prescription of thirty years with title and good faith would suffice. In the second case, a prescription of thirty years would be required, as this distinction is sufficiently gathered from what is noted by Innocentius in c. Bonae, de postul. praelat., and by Bartolus in ff. de publicanis, l. Si publicanus, §. In vectigalibus. Hence it follows that, without prejudice to the Church, a private person can prescribe tithes against another private person over a period of thirty years, as C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. Sicut. But here two doubts arise.

† The first point concerns the common law: whether, if one avails oneself of the accession of time from the author, one must do so with the cause and its defects, that is, with the bad faith of the author. I answer that if one wishes to commence the prescription from the author, the origin of the prescription is examined, as in *l. clam possidere* in the beginning, *de acquirenda possessione*; and *l. Pomp.* § *cum quis*. But if one wishes to commence the prescription from one’s own person on account of one’s own good faith, then the author’s conscience does not obstruct, provided that the prescriber himself has good faith, as noted by the Doctors in *c. malefidei*, *de regulis iuris*, book 6, *de praescriptione longi temporis*; *auth. malaefidei*; and *D. de diversis et longis praescriptionibus*, *l. an victum* § *ex facto*; and *l. cum haeres*, in the same title; and *D. de regulis iuris*, *l. quod ipsis*. Hence, in our question, according to the common law, the intention of the prescriber for thirty years is well founded.

The second doubt concerns municipal law, which seems to provide that forty years are required for the prescription of tithes. For a special statute derogates from the general one, just as an exception derogates from the rule, as in the chapter *Generi* with its common subject matter. On the contrary, it seems that this statute regarding tithes was not enacted out of hostility toward those prescribing, but rather in their favor; therefore, it ought not to be turned to their detriment, namely, by depriving them of the common law, but rather it tends to augment it and to grant more remedies than the common law confers. Hence, the effect is increased, not diminished, as appears from the wording of the statute, as in the Code, *De legibus*, law *Quod favore*; and in the Digest, there, law *Nullum*; there, law *Tertia*, in the beginning; Digest, *De militum testamento*. Moreover, if several prescriptions are established regarding the same matter, one as general and another as special, it is within the power of the prescriber to choose whichever he wishes, by argument from the Digest, *De rerum divisione*, law *Quotiens duplici*. Furthermore, this statute does not state that forty years are required by necessity. Hence, by the form of another statute, thirty years suffice to obtain the effects arising from the simple prescription of thirty years, as in the Code, *De praescriptione triginta annorum*, law *Si quis emptionis*, in the beginning. For a statute that is not altered is not prohibited from standing, because the correction of laws is to be avoided, as in law *Praecipimus* with similar authorities. Moreover, the ordinary gloss of the Decretals determines this question, as below. But against this is what is read in the Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Pomponius*, § *Ultimo*, where it is said that vitious possession is not continued to non-vicious possession. I answer that this is true in long prescription, but otherwise in the longest prescription. Question 16, Cause 2, § *Hæc* concerning prescriptions of ten years. This gloss is very singular, and the conclusion here is that, both by civil law and by canon law, if he who has completed the prescription of the longest time is in good faith, the possession of his predecessors benefits him, even if it was vitious. And by this, as I said, our question seems to be resolved, because, calculating his own time and that of his predecessors, the tithes were possessed for a period exceeding forty years. And I consider this opinion to be true, saving the reason of right speech, as in law *Claudius Felix*, notwithstanding the aforementioned mortgage, mentioned above in the discussion of eviction. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a *missio in possessionem* is void when a party has not been cited.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: A statute of a certain city provides that possession of hereditary goods passes by operation of law to the heir without any other corporal apprehension. Now, a certain person made a will, in which he instituted his son as heir to the legitime, and as to the remainder of the goods, after the death of the testator, the said brother petitioned before the competent judge in these words: “That, by every right, office, and action by which he may and ought to do so according to law, he place and induce the petitioner, who asserts himself to be the heir, to be placed and induced, and that he preserve and defend him, once placed and induced, in the possession of the things and goods which belonged to the said deceased at the time of his death. And although possession of the hereditary goods passes to the heir according to the form of the statute, nevertheless, for caution, for the protection, defense, and preservation of the said possession of his rights, and for every other end and effect which may better benefit him, he requested the aforesaid.” The judge, having seen the will and heard the aforesaid petition, with knowledge of the cause, as I said, pronounced interlocutorily, committed, and imposed upon a certain public notary that he place and induce, by decree of the said judge, the aforementioned petitioner into incorporeal possession of the goods of the said deceased, and that he defend and preserve him once placed. And the said judge used the aforesaid words. Afterwards, a controversy arose between the aforementioned brother and son concerning the said putting into possession, which was sought to be revoked. And it is true that the said son was not cited to the aforesaid interlocutory judgment or putting into possession, who judge finally pronounced that the aforesaid license, of which mention was made, and what followed therefrom, should stand and hold insofar as the said license was granted for the protection and defense of the said petitioner, to protect himself in the possession transferred to him by operation of law by virtue of the statute of the said territory; but insofar as it was granted otherwise than for the protection and defense of the possession transferred to him by virtue of the said statute, he annulled the said license. From these facts, it is asked whether, the matter being thus situated, the said license is revoked or rather confirmed.

And it appears that it is confirmed, because confirmation rather refers to something confirmable, insofar as it is established regarding the thing confirmed and the confirmer, and they mutually accord. It is certain that confirmation has the effect of confirmation, as in D. de pactis, l. legitima; and D. de liberis legatis, l. Aurelius, § testato. But here it is established regarding the confirmable thing and the confirmer; therefore, there is no doubt that such confirmation is valid, as in C. de decurionibus, l. si quos spontaneos, lib. 10.

To the contrary, it appears that neither under common law nor by virtue of the statute was the first *missio* [grant of possession] capable of being confirmed, since it was void by law itself. And that which is void cannot be confirmed, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationis, [concerning those] which do not subsist by their own force. And it is read and noted in X. de electionibus, c. in causis. Briefly, this is true, because the words so say, "by virtue of the statute." Note this word "by virtue": but the *missio* could not have been made by virtue of the statute without the party being cited; the son ought to have been cited, since possession continues in him by common law, as noted in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. cum haeredes. And if you do not wish to say "possession," say "the effect of possession," as is read and noted in l. cum miles, in principio, D. qui ex causa mortis; and C. de usucapione, l. pro haerede; and l. nihil. Moreover, the son is a certain and legitimate adversary, therefore he must be cited, as in D. de venditionibus rescindendis, l. 1, § denunciari. Moreover, remission into corporal possession is an act of contentious jurisdiction, and it cannot be expedited without citation, even peremptory, as in C. de his qui ad ecclesias confugiunt, l. praesenti, § 1; and C. si per vim vel alio modo, l. si. Nor can it be confirmed; rather, it ought to be revoked, insofar as it proceeded as a matter of fact, as noted in D. de evictionibus, l. minor, in principio; and C. unde vi, l. meminerint. And the judge who was lenient in granting [possession] ought to be lenient in withdrawing it, as in l. 1, § 1, D. si mulier vendiderit, noted.

Since, therefore, by virtue of the statute there is no possessory effect unless this is done legitimately with the party cited, it follows that the said *missio* is not aided by the authority of the statute; and especially, because, as I said in another opinion, this statute speaks of the true heir, and the son existing; but it is not established that the brother is the true heir, unless the son is cited in the production of the will, as in X. de probationibus, c. quam contra falsam. Moreover, in the said sentence are these words: "transferred by law itself." But this transfer is not established; nor can it be established, unless it was established from the beginning; because an interlocutory judgment made without legal order can never be confirmed by subsequent acts, as in c. appellanti, C. de appellationibus, in the Clementines.

Wherefore, it necessarily follows that the said license was not granted for the protection and defense, I say, of the defense and protection of right, not of the protection of a reasonable fact. D. de re iudicata, l. 3, § condemnatum, and noted; D. de acquirenda possessione, l. iuste prius. Therefore, whatever was not done properly ought to be revoked; so that the said brother does not enjoy the benefit of the *missio*, as in c. eum qui de prebenda, lib. 6; and c. licet episcopus, 2 q. 1; c. in primis; and C. si per publicam pensionem, l. si deserta.

Wherefore, if the conditional words of the said last pronouncement are rightly and correctly understood, they sound not to the advantage of the said brother, but to the contrary. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A lessor leased a thing with an agreement that, if he alienated it, he would be liable for the damages of the lessee; upon the occurrence of the case of alienation, it is asked which damages are to be included: and this is a golden opinion.
2. What damage and profit properly are.
3. Whether one who hinders profit is said to cause damage.
4. Whether the estimation of fruits ought to be made according to the present time or according to the future. And no. 5. And
6. We must have recourse to the nature of the contract and the disposition when we are in doubt about the intention of the contracting parties.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain possession was leased to Titius for a period of eight years, for an annual rent to be paid. In this lease, among other things, two pacts were included: namely, first, that if the said lessor were to donate the said possession, in whole or in part, to anyone, he must ensure that the said lessee retains the said possession until the end of the said term, the said lessee paying the rent to the person to whom the said possession had been donated; and if otherwise done, that the damage to the said lessee be estimated by estimators and restored to the said lessee. Another pact followed subsequently, namely, that if the said lessor were to donate, alienate, or diminish part of the said possession, the said lessor is bound to remit to the said lessee the rent, or pension, pro rata. The case occurred that the said lessor, after certain years following the said lease, donated the entire possession to one of his soldiers. The said lessee, however, claims his damage and interest, even in lost profits, asserting that if he had held the said possession until the end of his term, he would have gained, every year beyond the rent, one thousand florins, let us say, or a certain sum, etc.
† The question is, what is the law? In this question, it must be considered,

† That damage, strictly and properly speaking, is said to be a diminution of patrimony, as in C. de cond. l. si, and C. de impon. lucr. descript. l. 1, lib. 10; hence in the definition of interest, emerging damage is placed on its own, and lost profit on the other side: for these two elements are very different, as is fully read and noted in l. 1, C. de sen. quae pro eo; and therefore one term does not contain the other, as if distinct in voice and meaning, by agreement and obligation, as is read and noted in ff. de re iud. l. in eo quod universalis, quod petit amplius. It should be known that it is not understood that one gives damage to him who uses his right in good faith and without fraud, as in ff. de aqua pluv. arc. l. 2, § item Varus; and ff. de damno infecto l. Proculus; and ff. de re iud. l. non fraudantur; and no one causes damage unless he does that which he has no right to do.

† And so that we may know whether he who prevents profit is said to inflict damage, it must be said that either he takes away profit due from a public source, and he appears to inflict damage, as in l. 2, §. me, ver. damnum, D. ne quid in loco publico fiat. And the reason is that he who illicitly causes someone to lose profit appears to give damage, because damage is said to occur in two ways: in respect of the thing itself and in respect of expectation; as is clear in the action under the Lex Aquilia, in which damage adhering to the body by way of expectation is included, as in D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. proinde, §. 1, and l. inde Neratius, and l. in legem Aquiliam, §. si deletum. For it is not lawful for a private person to take away from anyone rights arising from the public. And this is the reason for the aforementioned words. But damage is profit arising from a private source, and then either from the thing itself of him who suffers the damage, or from a thing owed to him by full right. And this is so because such profit was in preparation and in the order of acquiring, as in D. de bonis libertorum, l. liberto octuaginta, and D. de eo quod certo loco, l. 3, §. si, and C. de senatusconsulto quod pro eo quod interest, l. unica, in fine. Or it is profit arising from a contract celebrated together with the impeding party; and then either the impeding party acts with deceit and fraud, and this is not lawful, especially in a contract of good faith, because all deceit and fraud is contrary to nature; and remedies are therefore provided, as in l. 1, D. si quid in fraudem patroni, and l. 1 and l. 1, D. quae in fraudem creditorum. Or he acts by lawful right according to the tenor of the contract, and there is no doubt that he is not liable, since it is lawful to do so by agreement; and contracts receive their law from agreement, as in D. de deposito, l. 1, §. si convenerit. Or the intention of the contracting parties is doubtful, and then it matters whether the profit was already made or was in the process of being made. In the first case, he who loses the profit suffers damage, because the profit was already in his assets and rooted therein; and it was one and the same patrimony. D. de separatione bonorum, l. 1, §. illud sciendum; and D. de vulgari substitutione, l. sed et si plures, §. ad substitutos. Or the profit was not made, but was in the process of being made; and then, although preparation for the profit preceded, this is not called damage. This is the case expressly and notably stated in l. si pecuniam, in principio, D. de conditione ob causam, by which our case for our Prince is determined.

† One must consider that the species could have been sold for more, unless the species was formed in the present: for example, because the grain was still in the ear. For then, however much it was worth in the ear, it would be estimated: and not more. Moreover, many things could happen which prevent the fruits from reaching maturity and producing their effect: for example, snows, hailstorms, incursions of enemies, and similar things, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Fistulas, §. Frumenta. And therefore, one cannot judge with certainty about things entirely future, as is expressly stated. C. de usuris, l. Si a pactione; and D. de actionibus empti, l. Si iactum retis. And most fully, note this through the said Bartolus, D. de publicanis, l. Coten, §. Qui maximos. Furthermore, the estimation of past damage cannot increase from the future, as the text elegantly states, D. de re iudicata, l. Omnis hereditas, §. Nunquam crescit. From these things it appears that these terms, damage and profit, are distinctive and quasi-adversative terms. And therefore, what is established in one, by argument from the contrary sense, which has place in contracts, seems to be denied in the other, and the contrary is established, as in D. de pactis dotalibus, l. Inter socerum, §. Cum inter. For interpretation, which sometimes is based on good faith in contracts, has place from similars to similars. But extension to contraries cannot be made, because two contraries cannot stand together, argument from D. pro socio, l. Si ancillam; and note in l. Si cum dotem, in principio, D. de solutione matrimonii. It does not object, D. de condictione ob causam, l. Si extra; l. Si extraneus. For there, in the case of a marriage not contracted, the action is not brought by virtue of the stipulation, but by the defect of the final cause. And this is the true understanding of that law. From the aforementioned things, therefore, summarizing as it were, I say that there are four things: namely, profit per se. And this is either placed in form, or in patrimony, or is in hope of the future, or neither in form nor in certain hope. The second is damage per se, which is the loss of things already acquired, not subject to chances, but in the present thing. The third is neither profit nor damage. The fourth is damage mixed with profit. For this member clearly appears in the contract of partnership, as in D. pro socio, l. Mutuis; and l. De illo; and l. Sed si adijciantur. Where it is expressly clear that gain from a business not yet made, but future, is called profit: and not damage. So it is in the case at hand: for if it is said, it could have been sold for more, this is to take an argument from future business, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Si heres. And it is in a way to divine, unless

† As I said, the fruits were to be estimated as already rooted in the field according to their quality at that present time, not according to their future quality, which was not apparent at that time, as is argued in the Digest, On Contracting Sale, in the law *In lege*. And the rule of law states that what is pending is not considered as if it were certain, as in the Digest, On Rules of Law, in the law *Is qui damnum*, § *Quod pendet*. Furthermore, to make my conclusion clearer, I consider that although the contract of lease is named, nevertheless it is reduced by agreement to the nature of an innominate contract, in which, according to the tenor of the agreement, repentance has place in one case, namely if the said lessor were to donate the entire thing to another: but it is so that in innominate contracts, when repentance has place, only the interest of damage comes into question, i.e., expenses incurred, and the restitution of the rent paid to the lord. The case is literally in the said law *Si pecuniam*. Moreover, it must not be omitted that that clause, "and if it had been done otherwise, etc.," is conditional: and in conditionals, the form is rather considered than the general nature of the disposition, as in the Digest, On Conditions and Demonstrations, in the law *Meuius* and the law *Qui heredi*. And nothing is included in a condition except what is expressed in words. Notwithstanding the objection to the above: the law *Si fundus*, Digest, On Lease, where it is said that the lessor who can prohibit and does not prohibit is liable for all interest: because that is true unless he is permitted by agreement to rescind the lease, because, as has been said, the special convention is rather inspected than the general one. Also, because the agreement informs the contract and limits it, as in the Digest, On Contracting Sale, in the law *Pacta conventa*; and in the Code, On Agreements, in the law *In bonae fidei*; and in the Digest, If a Certain Thing is Demanded, in the law *Lecta*. And this is commonly said and held as a rule. I therefore conclude that profits do not come to be restored by the lord, but expenses pertaining to the utility of the leased things ought rightly to be reimbursed, because they are a utility of the estates actually remaining, as in the Digest, On Minors, in the law *Intra utile*, § *Vendentibus*. Let the lessees therefore impute it to themselves, who did not state the law more clearly, as in the Digest, On Agreements, in the law *Vete*. Nor is this contrary to reason, because on account of agreements a thing is sometimes sold and leased for less, as is said in the law *Illa notabilis*, Digest, On Servants Exported; and in the law *Si venditor ab emptore*, § *Finis*. Also, the said lessee ought to have considered that what could happen according to the form of the agreements. For this reason nature gives prudence to men, so that they may foresee the future, as in the Digest, On Lease, in the law *Si quis domum*, § 1; and in the law *Servius*, above, On What is Done by Force or Secretly; and in the Digest, On Negotiorum Gestio, in the law *Divortio*.

† Someone will say that the pact must be understood according to the nature of the contract. D. de usuris, l. si stipulatus; D. de damno infecto, l. damni, vers. et quod in stipulatione. For we must have recourse to the nature of the contract and of the disposition where we are in doubt about the intention of the contracting parties, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. interdum; and l. inter stipulantem, §. sacramentum; and l. ita stipulatus, in the words “propter ipsius rei natura.” But I answer that this is true if the words allow it. Otherwise, if the words do not allow it, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. quicquid astringendae; resp. D. de fideiuss., l. fidei, magistratuum, §. pro Aurelio. But these words do not allow it, because damage and profit are distinguished as opposites. Therefore, what is predicated of one is removed from the other, as in D. de verbis sign., l. si cum fundum; D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio commodissimum. For we do not have recourse to the genus where we have a specific disposition, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. doli, clausula; D. de vulgari substitutione, l. ex facto, §. item quaero; and l. cohors, §. qui patrem. And just as words added above must operate in increasing, as in the aforementioned l. si stipulatus; and D. ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum, l. balista. So, on the contrary, words taken away must detract and diminish, as in D. de contrahenda empt., l. pacta conventa; and arg. in l. tribunus, §. fin., D. de minorum testamentis.

† Therefore, reiterating my conclusion, I say that future cases which have no principle in the matter are not to be considered, nor are cases of commerce which depend also on an external contracting party. And they are not in a potestative condition, but a mixed one, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. si sterilis, §. cum per venditorem. Therefore, fruits not sown are not to be considered by reason of hope, because it is fallible. Nor by reason of nature: because they are not in the nature of things, and although sometimes they are not considered as fruits, but as interest, and this is shown both theoretically and practically by Bartolus in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. si filia, §. cum fundum, nevertheless in the contract interest was not promised, but damage. Hence we must be content with the limits of the words, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. quidam recte, where it says, which can be conceived from the words. For limiting words are exclusive of extension, as in D. de negotiorum gestorum, l. qui aliena, §. libertos; C. de procuratoribus, l. maritus; C. de pactis conventis, l. si; C. de transactionibus, l. si de certa; D. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. qui sella, §. qui actum, and l. inter actum, and l. certo generi, and l. Lucius, in the word digitum unum; and D. quod ad servitutes amittendas, l. si sic, and l. si quis alia; and D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si prius, §. aqua; D. de aqua quotidiana, l. 1, §. quaesitum. Therefore, a limited disposition does not allow its effect to be extended, nor can anything be added to it, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. Lucius, §. quae habebat; and D. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. lacus, et stagnum, and l. in agris limitatis; and Extravagantes de censibus, c. cum apostol; and de privilegiis, c. porro. Furthermore, it is not an objection if it is said that the pact was added in favor of the lessee; because rather it was in favor of the lessor, since it is restrictive of the nature of the action arising from lease, as has been fully proven in the above allegations; and it is expressly clear in its own reason, D. de locato, l. videamus, §. 1, because it matters greatly whether something is said generally or restricted to a certain species, as in cap. susceptum, de rescriptis, lib. 6, Baldus.

In the name of Christ.
