The case is presented that a certain Michael Asinarius confessed to having held in custody and on loan, etc. You will find this opinion above, opinion 82, beginning: “The case is presented,” etc. Given the statute of the City of Trivisano in the third treatise of the second book, chapter 2, under the heading “On the succession of males, with nieces and daughters excluded,” which begins: “Add on the contrary,” etc. The case is as follows: Titius died, leaving one male son by his first wife, and two daughters by his second wife; and likewise the said second wife died, intestate, having constituted no dowry for her said daughters, nor assigned anything to them, either as a dowry or in the name of a legitime. Finally, the said daughters died in pupillary age, and thus below the age of marriage, while their said mother survived, who makes herself heir to her said daughters. Now it is asked whether the said mother, as heir, has any right to claim something from the goods of their said father by virtue of the said statute, or by any other law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a compromise expires by law upon the death of one of the parties, just as does a compromissory agreement.
2. Whether a commission is reduced to the likeness of a last will.
body: In the name of Christ. Taking for granted that the statute is valid, one must see what the statute intends. And I consider, first, that the statute provides for male descendants by admitting them to the universal succession in full, to the exclusion of the daughters, and this up to the clause filiabus autem. Second, it provides for the daughters themselves, and this under a threefold heading and case: first, when they are endowed, by decreeing that the dowry remains in their hands; second, when they are not endowed, by providing for them according to the arbitrament of relatives; third, by laying down a special case when they wish to enter a monastery. The first case runs up to the clause caeterum; the second case runs from the said caeterum up to the clause semper consideratione. Our question concerns the clause caeterum: whether the provision of this clause is conditional, so that if the daughter dies before this arbitrament is rendered, the daughter herself transmits nothing; or whether the disposition is not conditional, but merely an obscure portion.

† Whether a submission to arbitration made by law expires with the death of one party, just as a submission made by man does. And for clarity, three cases must be distinguished. Sometimes a submission is made to the arbitrament of someone between living persons, and thus it contains an implied condition if the submission is made concerning substantial matters, namely, if the arbitrament should be made; C. de contrahen. emp. l. fi.; ff. de ver. ob. l. si quis arbitratus. Sometimes it is made in a last will, and then either there is an express condition, 'if he shall arbitrate', and who and how much is conditional; or there is no express conditional disposition, but an uncertain quantity at first sight; yet according to the interpretation of the law there is no uncertainty, because it is as much as it ought to be by the arbitrament of an upright man; de lega. 2. l. 1.

† Sometimes the commission is made by law, and here it must be considered whether this commission is to be assimilated to a last will or to a disposition between living persons. On this point, I state for certain that a statute disposing of successions is brought under the understanding of a last will and not on the model of a contract; ff. de iur. cond. l. si quis tamen; de leg. 1. l. si fundum per fideicommissum. §. Iulianus; de leg. 2. l. codicillis. §. pe. For one who does not expressly make a testament also seems tacitly to ordain that which the law ordains concerning his succession, as noted in ff. de col. bono. l. 1. §. vel maxime. From this it is concluded in the proposed question that the statute's ordination is not conditional, because it is not in the arbitrary power of the relatives, that is, neither the 'which' nor the 'how much', but the legal theory is in the power of upright men; therefore, although at first sight it may be an obscure portion, it is nevertheless not a conditional disposition, and therefore it is transmissible to the heir. There is no obstacle in de verb. ob. l. qui ratione. §. augerius, where it cannot be declared after death, because it speaks there of a contract and an express condition, whereas here there is no condition at all. Likewise, it is no objection if it is said that the final cause of providing for the girl by the arbitrament of the kinsmen has ended, since the girl has died; because the nature of these transactions, since it is owed in place of the legitime, succeeds by the authority of the ius commune, and it must be of the same nature. But it is certain that the owed support of goods is transmitted; C. de inoffic. test. l. si quis filii; by the argument of C. de suis, et le. l. apud hostes; for if an inheritance is transmitted to a mother, then all the more so the legitime owed by natural law. For the final cause is nature itself, not an accident outside nature; and thus de condi. et de. l. titio centum. §. titio genero and in Aut. de sanctis. episcopis. §. sed hoc pręsenti are no obstacle. Likewise, the clause semper consideratione habita is no obstacle, because it speaks of another case, namely when the girl wishes to enter a monastery; for if there is such a case or condition, that clause has its place, but we are not in that heading of the statute, but in the general heading, in which the statute also speaks conditionally; for the substance of an act with a condition inserted is one thing, and to commit the declaration of the quantity or portion to arbitrament is another. The case is found in the said l. 1. de leg. 2. And the aforesaid matters are confirmed because it is permissible to argue from the words of a statute to the words of a testator, as in ff. de ma. te. l. si ita fuerit. §. conditionem autem, which text is very adaptable to our purpose. And thus I state and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that the husband acquires a certain portion of the dowry, namely, if the wife leaves him the usufruct of the dowry for the entire duration of her life, and thereafter it is to be restored in its entirety, whether, after her death, the heirs of the wife are bound to restore the entire dowry.
body: In Christ's name.

† That after the death of the said Lord Ugolino the dowry ought to be restored in its entirety, notwithstanding the profit of a third part by virtue of the statute, is proved from the disposition of the said testament. For the said testatrix, as is set forth, ordained that the dowry was not to be reclaimed during the entire lifetime of the said Lord Ugolino, by which it appears that she left to the said Lord Ugolino the interim interest of the intervening time, as in ff. ad l. fal. in l. lege falcidia, which is not held to be true, as in ff. sol. ma. l. si constan. §. quotiens, and on the argument of ff. de leg. 2. l. debitor, and ff. de dote praelega. l. cum quis uxori; to this makes extra de do. inter ui. et ux. c. per uestras. Likewise she ordained that after the time of the life of Lord Ugolino the said eight hundred pounds should be restored; and thus it manifestly appears that she burdened her husband, who was also the legatee, and intended that the interim interest of the intervening time be set off against the profit of the said third part of the dowry. Thus, therefore, since the said Lord Ugolino recognized the said legacy up to the concurrent quantity of the aforesaid interim interest, once the set-off with the said profit of the dowry has been admitted, the claim of the heirs of the said lady is most just, on the argument of C. unde uir, et uxo. Auth. preterea, ff. ad l. fal. l. si debitor, C. de hę. actio. l. si adulta, and to this makes excellently l. 2. in fi. C. de iure dot. and l. cum patrem. §. si uero. eo. titu. and ff. de le. 1. l. filius familias. §. apud Marcellum. and after the express one, de leg. 2. l. Imperator. §. si tertium. 2. respon.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a daughter is included in the general institution of children, and if she is not included, whether she is included in the general and negative condition; and the number. 2.
3. On the conjunction "and," and what it repeats.
4. Whether a substitute appointed in movable goods is understood to be substituted in goods that are now immovable. If the substitution is uncertain, who is ordered to be content with the father's property.
5. The word "instituted" signifies the first degree.
6. Whether the benefit of the law *Edicto* is available to a universal substitute.
7. Whether the benefit of the law *Edicto* is transmitted to heirs, and whether it pertains to possession of goods or the office of the judge.
8. Whether the benefit of the law *Edicto* is available to one who was irregularly admitted to possession.
9. The exception of falsity cannot be raised conditionally.
body: In the name of Christ. Although the matters have been most subtly established, it would not be necessary to speak further, but merely to assert that what has been concluded is true; nevertheless, because the ancients, by good example, are accustomed to believe nothing without reason, and indeed to hold as known only that which they have established by reason, I shall add a few words.

† And in the first and second point, it appears from a fourfold rule that the daughter is not included in the general institution of sons. The first rule of law is that the legal inclusion of one person, sex, or quality in another does not take place if the contrary intention of the testator appears. Hence, under the appellative name of the masculine gender, for example under the name of sons, the appellative name of the feminine gender, for example the name of daughters, is not included, if the testator shows greater affection towards males than towards females, as in D. 35,1,3, l. Lucretia, § quaesitum, ver. nisi. But this reading of the will shows that the testator had greater affection towards males, as in D. 35,1, l. Paulo Calimaco, § Pomp. Orumpus. The second rule is that whenever several things are disposed of more distinctly, one is not contained under another, even if the reason for the distinction is not stated, it would be believed to be included. D. 28,5, l. cohors, § qui patrem; and l. ex testamento, § item quaero; and l. cum ex filio, § filio. To this is added the third rule, that a distinguishing species is not included under the genus, as in D. 37,15, l. alimenta, § basilicae; and l. stichus nutritius, in principio; D. 35,1, l. uxorem, § felicissimo. For that which is specially ordained seems to be exempted from the general ordination. D. 50,17, l. doli clausula; and l. stipulationes commodissimam. And thus it is opposed. D. 48,19, l. sanctio legum. But the testator ordained concerning the daughters distinctly, restrictively, and specially; therefore, he did not admit her under the tacit and general interpretation of the masculine gender, as the fourth rule accedes, that the expressed makes the tacit and conjectured cease. C. 4,34, l. maritus; C. 8,38, l. si; D. 28,5, l. Cornelia; D. 35,1, l. si ita legatum, § si illi nollet. And thus I hold regarding the first point and the second, as far as this passage is concerned.

† Having assumed this, it follows that we must consider, assuming that daughters are not included in the universal institution, whether they are included in that general and negative condition, namely, "if the testator himself had no sons, etc." For when a condition is taken negatively from something, neither alternative is required. D. de rebus dubiis, l. si is, qui ducenta, § cum ita; and especially if, from the contrary interpretation, the exclusion of children would follow. C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter, in principio. And thus it appears that a female daughter totally excludes an extraneous substitute, by the argument of the said § Papiam erumpit. For the natural impulse urges the father to leave something to his children, as noted there; likewise D. de conditionibus, l. cum auus; C. de fideicommissis, l. acutissimi. But I answer that, by the nature of the conjunction, females are not included; for if they are not included in the institution of the former part, therefore neither are they included in the condition of the substitution.

For the conjunction "and" repeats the same persons, not others; for the preceding and immediately adjacent conjunction joins persons who are not foreign or remote. See D. de fun. instr. l. cum delationis §. asinam, and l. seye §. gay. And this is evident, because he did not substitute for the female in this clause, but in another; therefore, the condition is not referred to the females, to whom, by these words, he did not make a vulgar substitution. See D. de vend. inspi. l. pe; D. de leg. 1. l. ab exhered.; C. de elucistol. §. et cum triplici, and §. seq. Therefore, the daughter, being female, does not exclude the lord Vampus, who was substituted, from his substitution.

† Next, it remains to consider the third point, namely whether Vampus is understood to have been instituted as a vulgar substitute only in the movable goods, or in the entire inheritance. It appears that he was substituted only in the movable goods, because the text so states, and we ought not to extend it, especially to the prejudice of the daughter, to whom her father’s inheritance is due by natural law. For a tacit or implied interpretation should not be admitted against children, especially when the words are repugnant, to which we must adhere. D. de legibus 3, l. Ille, aut ille, s. Cum in verbis; and D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo, §. Idem Tubero.

To the contrary, it seems that whenever in the same statement, which can be valid according to direct law, one universal term is inserted alongside a certain thing, the certain thing is not considered, but rather the universality itself without direct institutions, as in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. 1, §. Si ex fundo; and l. Quotiens, §. Si duo; and l. Si alterius; and l. Ex facto, sine institutionibus directis, such as vulgar and pupillary substitution. D. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. Coheredi, §. Si. And therefore, upon correct consideration, the addition of a certain thing does not diminish the meaning of the universal word. Thus, it comes to the whole rather by the right of not diminishing than by the right of accretion. But in our case, the testator tripled the direct and universal words. For first he said “heir,” second he said “universal,” third he said “instituted.” Hence, he did not wish to die intestate, for he died having instituted an heir, as in C. de testamentis, l. Non codicillum. There, the word “universal” is very worthy of consideration, because it designates the universality by law. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Quoties, §. Heredes.

Furthermore, the word “instituted” must be weighed more heavily: for by founding the institution in the very person of Vampus, he is reduced to the first degree, and he is made the head of his testament. D. de his quae in testamento delecta sunt, l. Proxima. And all legacies appear to have been left by him as by an heir; hence, female daughters are not preferred to him, but are subordinate to him, and they await his acceptance regarding their legacies, as in l. Eam, quam, C. de fideicommissis.

† For the word “instituted” is accustomed to signify the first degree, from which all else depends. L. 1, D. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione. And in this writing of the testament, if any word is superfluous, we ought rather to say that it is superfluous which diminishes a favorable disposition, than that which increases it. D. de auro et argento legatis, L. pediculis, §. Labeo. For useless words do not restrict the disposition, as appears there, all the more so if it were not drawn to the whole. D. Should Vampus be obliged to take from another? Because he is vainly said to take from himself, but it is certain that the instituted heir does not take from another, but from himself. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, L. sed si in conditione, §. fin. Someone will say, how can there be a first degree of Vampus, rather of the sons? I answer, you speak truly as regards the order of the words, although little to the point, as in the aforementioned L. cohaeredi, §. fin. However, considering the efficacy, when he instituted in the first order one who is not, nor will be, since this degree is as if unwritten, it is properly not a degree; but he who follows in the order of the words is the sole degree, therefore the first, whom no one precedes. Hence, whether we are in §. si ex fundo or in L. cohaeredi, §. fin., Vampus was the universal heir. Someone will say that the daughter was instituted in a certain thing, just as he was; therefore both are heirs. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, L. quotiens, §. si duo. I answer, the daughter was ordered to be content; hence she has no right of accrual, as in the aforementioned §. si quo, in fine. For unless she has a coheir, no institution can be drawn to the whole; the right of accrual can be applied to one instituted in a certain thing or quantity. §. si duo, in fine. Otherwise, it could not be prohibited in the son, arg. in Auth. ut cum appellatio cognoscitur, §. ceterum. In an outsider it is so; therefore, since in the chapter of the institution or substitution of Vampus it was not said that Vampus should not ask for more, he asks for the whole. Let laymen not wonder that it is most truly the case that more is said and less is written. D. de legatis secundis, L. cum pater, §. cum imperfecta. I conclude that Vampus was instituted or substituted as universal heir, this being presupposed

† It remains to consider the fourth point, namely whether the benefit of the edict was available to the lord Vampo. It must be said that it was, as noted in l. edicto, § 1, and in l. 1, eodem titulo, because he is not advanced to a degree, since none of those named is a degree; from a non-degree, no order is fixed to a degree. This being presupposed

It follows that we must consider the fifth point, namely whether the benefit of the law is transmitted to the heir by edict: and it must be said that it is, just as the interdict *quorum bonorum*. And any persecutory action can be assigned, just as any interdict, and any possessory action. D. de petitione hereditatis, l. *quod si in diem*, § *Iulianus*; D. ne quid in loco publico, in l. 2, § *idem Nerva*. Someone might say that possession of goods is not assigned, nor transmitted. D. de bonorum possessione, l. 3, § *acquirere*. I answer that one thing is in a possessory right, and another in a possessory fact. For possession of goods is not recognized as an imperfect right, and therefore it is not regularly transmitted. But to have an action, or the office of a judge, is a perfect right: and therefore it is transmitted, and assigned. This is confirmed by Speculum in the title *de testamento*, § *sequitur*, and by the notes in l. 2 and 3, D. de petitione hereditatis, and it is supported by D. quod metus causa, l. *videamus* in the reason of its own. And this being presupposed

† The sixth point follows: when Lord Vampus had possessed, and was sent away by the praetor because he had proceeded irregularly, whether the benefit of the edict is due to him. The truth is that it is not, because once removed, it cannot be reborn from a subsequent case. On obligations, *l. qui res.*, § *aream*. For this is the nature of acquiring possessory actions, that what one has once possessed does not further belong to him. And this is held by Speculum in the said § *sequitur*. But certainly that must be understood regarding effective possession once obtained. But here it was not effective, but void: hence it does not seem that what was immediately evicted was possessed; rather, it was annulled. D. *de arboribus*, *l. inter castellianum*. Moreover, it does not seem that the benefit of *l. edicto* is for acquiring possession only, but also for confirming and continuing it. C. *de carbonaria*, edict, *l. 1*. Hence it does not lose its force from the deprivation of possession, which the heir made by his own authority. This is also supported by the statute of the commune of Treviso: because it does not mention possession to be acquired, but simply speaks of effective possession, not of superficiality; in possession it must be understood. Moreover, that is the true nature of possession, to which the aid of law concurs. D. *de acquisitione possessionis*, *l. 1*, in the principle, in the gloss. For this, which was pronounced null, presupposing this, one office must be seen, insofar as the said dismissal ought to be made: since by statute it cannot be left to an outsider, unless a third part. And it is a prohibitory statute, to which one cannot renounce. Against this goes the sworn renunciation of the daughter. C. 2, *de pace*, lib. 6. Therefore it seems that what Lord Vampus does not receive by mere right of institution, he receives by the right of accrual. C. *de secundis nuptiis*, *l. 1*, in the gloss. But this passage is doubtful, and therefore on this it must be considered: understanding that the statute, with effect, also seems to prohibit the right of accrual in favor of the children: and thus two parts seem to belong to the daughter, the third to the late Lord Vampus, and now to his heirs. But from this an absurdity would seem to follow, namely, that the renunciation of the daughter would operate nothing against the said C. 2. For he who has renounced as to the right, which is excluded by renunciation, is held as dead, just as if disinherited, and therefore does not make a part. As D. *de contrahenda*, *l. 1*, at the end; D. *de inofficioso testamento*, *l. si is*. It supports what is noted, C. *de inofficioso testamento*, *l. si quando*, § *fi*. Because the statute resists the act and will of the father, supposing that the brother is an outsider using the legal vocabulary, as Inst. *de hereditatum qualitate et differentia*, § 1 and § seq. It seems to be concluded for the daughter in two parts, in which the dowry left to her is imputed. But against this, because the renunciation resists the daughter: and canon law, or perfectly concluded. But it can be said that the statute makes two parts be the legitimate portion of the children: and thus it amplifies the common law, as if therefore the legitimate is due to the daughter, because the statute does not want it to be taken away. And therefore those words, that the daughter cannot ask for or have more, do not impede the legitimate, because they are added in favor of the outsider heir, to whom the statute does not permit the legitimate to be left: but that which is beyond, namely the third part. And in doubt, one must stand by the words of the statute, according to the laws. D. *de exercitu*, *l. 1*, § *si is, qui autem*. But to this it is answered, as above, because she renounced, and thus she cannot oppose against the judgment of the father.

† It must be considered here subsequently regarding the exception of falsity: and because it was proposed under a condition, and the condition was false, it does not appear that the exception itself is valid by the law itself. D. de except. bsi quidem. Moreover, I do not believe that the exception of falsity cannot be proposed conditionally, nor can one raising such an objection waver in so grave a crime. C. de fide instru. l. si. in princ. And an exception which is inaptly opposed is not considered to have been proposed. D. de f. l. 1. §. labeo. And it does not harm the one who raises it, arg. D. de interrog. act. l. si filius. and l. 2. Nor does an inapt exception bind the one raising it to pursue the matter, as is shown by arg. D. ad turpil. l. 1. §. accusatio. On the question of Vernem. cum simi.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pronouncement on the exception may be sought by way of exception.
2. The exception of pending litigation is regulated by the exception of concluded litigation.
3. A judgment rendered on the exception excludes the right to bring an action.
4. While the exception of payment is pending, an action cannot be cumulated with the exception.
5. When the defendant may deny the plaintiff’s claim by means of the exception raised.
6. When the plaintiff’s libel impedes the defendant’s libel.
7. An action is sometimes cumulated with an action, sometimes with an exception, and vice versa.
body: In the name of Christ. There was a dispute between Philip de Marinis, in his own name, and his brother Benedict, on one side, and Lady Petra de Marinis, on the other, in that the said Philip, in the aforementioned names, first brought a hypothecary action on the occasion of certain instruments and debts contracted by the late Julian de Marinis for a certain house, as it is said, hypothecated by virtue of the said instruments. Finally, an exception of payment was raised by Lady Petra and in her name, and finally, on the occasion of the same alleged payment, it was requested on behalf of the said Lady that the said instruments be declared discharged.

And it is called into doubt whether the said petition causes the hypothecary judgment to be stayed, and whether judgment ought to be pronounced according to what was requested on behalf of the said Lady Vigor, by virtue of the statutes of Genoa: it was alleged both for and against with such subtlety, and with as much acumen of intellect as the most learned men are accustomed to employ in discussing the fine points and subtleties of the law; for which reason they are worthy of praise on account of the profundity of their intellect. Nevertheless, since in every contradictory dispute one side is true, it is necessary to choose that part which is more true in law, first by establishing and demonstrating it, and second by responding to the objections. And the libel of the parties is not called into doubt as to its form, for the libel of Philip has proper form; and similarly the libel of Lady Petra has the due form, concluding from the solution to the nullity of the instruments of obligation, as in C. de cond. sine causa, l. dissolvuntur; ff. de fideiussoribus, l. si contendat; ff. de legatis, l. Aurelius, § centum, in the gloss; C. qui bonis cedere possunt, l. pater tuus. By which laws one may principally demand to be pronounced not bound, according to Bartolus, who thus notes, ff. de damno infecto, l. si finita, § eleganter, although the argument is to the contrary, ff. de exceptione doli, l. pure, in fine; ff. de conditionibus ob causam datam, l. dedi, in principio. But that which I call into doubt contains three points: first, whether this petition can be cumulated with an exception; second, whether this petition operates more than an exception; third, whether it can be ventilated before a different judge.

† It must therefore be considered that the exception of lis pendens is regulated by the exception of res judicata: and that what ought to be decided by the sentence of the prior judgment cannot, in the meantime, be brought before a new court. That which depends on another matter must, in the meantime, remain silent, as is proved by the law of statutes and canons. D. de exceptionibus, l. Fundum Titianum; and l. Fundi; and in c. 2, de restitutione in integrum. For a doubtful cause of exclusion, while the doubt is pending, has the force of a perpetual exclusion. D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. Diximus; D. de noxalibus actionibus, l. Si ad libertatem; and D. de condictione indebiti, l. Sufficit; D. si certum petatur, l. Si pecuniam; D. ad Macedonianam, l. 1, § Si pendeat; D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Si quis libertatem.

Secondly, it must be considered that a judgment rendered on an exception sometimes excludes the right to bring an action on the same cause, and sometimes does not, provided that two conditions concur: namely, that there is full cognizance of the exception, and that the exception has the same effect as the action would have. Therefore, if the action and the exception arise from the same subject matter, are of the same nature in procedure, and of the same efficacy in deciding the case, and if the exception is raised first and judgment is pronounced against the exception, an action may not subsequently be brought. For, just as the genus is absorbed when the species is absorbed, because the cause being absorbed, the entire genus of the caused is absorbed; and since the material being consumed, the thing made from the material is consumed, as stated in D. de exceptionibus, l. An eandem, §. Actiones; l. Cum quaeritur; and l. Cum de hoc; and in C. de conditionibus, l. Si; and in D. de tributoria actione, l. Quod in hereditatem, §. Eligere; so too, when the exception and the action arise from the same equity, or the judge’s office regarding the mode of the action, which has once been included in the judgment and absorbed by the sentence, cannot be raised again. We have an example of this: if the exception of non-payment of money is raised and judgment is pronounced against the party raising the exception, he may not subsequently bring the complaint of non-payment of money, which he could otherwise have done, as stated in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. Autem hanc querelam. This is also clear in the exception of compensation, in which the party who succumbs may not subsequently bring an action on the same cause; namely, he has definitively succumbed, therefore a limit has been imposed on the litigation, as stated in D. de compensatione, l. Quod in diem, §. Si rationem. Likewise, this is clear in the exception of repudiation, so to speak; for if someone brings an action against a tutor, and the tutor, by way of exception, seeks to recover what he has expended, and the judge, having cognizance of the exception, rejects it, such a tutor may not subsequently bring an action in a contradictory proceeding, as stated in D. de contraria actione tutelae, l. 1, §. Penes; and in D. de negotiis gestis, l. Si autem, §. Si. Likewise, this is clear in the exception of falsity. For if judgment has been pronounced on it, an action for falsity may not subsequently be brought, as stated in C. de fidei instrumentis, l. Si, in fine. Likewise, this is clear in the exception of priority or superiority. For he who succumbs in the exception may not bring an action, as stated in D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. Duobus. These things having been premised, I come to the solution of the question.

† And I say that, while the exception of payment is pending, the action cannot be cumulated with the exception: because the pendency of the litigation stands in the way, just as the termination of the litigation would stand in the way. Therefore, whatever he chooses to raise by way of exception, he cannot meanwhile bring an action. The law speaks alternatively: either he must plead the exception, or he must bring the action; as is stated in the aforementioned § 1, where it says that it will be at his discretion whether he wishes to choose to set off or to claim; therefore, he ought not to cumulate them for the same purpose. D. de pactis, l. rescriptum, § si pacto. And this is confirmed, for he who pleads an exception tacitly requests that silence be imposed upon the plaintiff, as is noted in D. de in ius vocando, l. libertus; and in D. de rerum amissione, l. amplius. And therefore, in exceptions, an express conclusion is not necessary, because it is tacitly understood to conclude to the imposition of silence. D. de familia erciscunda, l. 1; D. de executione rei iudicatae, l. 2. If, therefore, he has once requested that silence be imposed by pleading the exception, and afterwards requests the same thing by bringing an action, the exception of duplicity stands in his way in the meantime. For, since the effect is not increased by the petition, he vainly requests expressly in the meantime what he had previously requested tacitly for the same end. Let him therefore pursue the exception opposed; because he cannot pursue the petition newly proposed. It is often said that no one can repeat and re-litigate the same cause. D. de compensatione, l. quod Labeo. If the cumulation of one cause with another cause is proven on account of prejudiciality, as in l. fundi and l. fundum, much more so does the cumulation of the same cause with itself lead to the same result. C. de assertionis tollenda, l. 1, in fine. Which I openly conclude concerning the petition of Lady Petra, that it should not be proceeded upon, but rather upon the exception. But if Lady Petra had not pleaded the exception of payment, it would also seem that she could bring an action, and that proceedings should be had on her petition. And in this case, the allegations made on behalf of Lady Petra would proceed, and the judgment rendered in her favor. But because the defendant pleaded the exception of payment, and this has been debated and the litigation is pending, the outcome of the controversy concerning the exception must be awaited; and in the meantime, an action cannot be brought on the same payment to invalidate the instruments. From these things it appears that, because the effect which is obtained by the petition can be obtained by the exception against the said Lady Petra, namely, that her petition does not proceed, but the exception proceeds well, provided it is proven, as in D. de probationibus, l. quinquaginta. From these things it appears that it is not expedient to proceed to the third point of diversity of judgment, of which in C. de iudiciis, l. nulli; D. de quibus rebus inter alios, l. 1 and 2; D. de sententiis, l. cum Papiam; and the authority there placed; D. de rescriptis, § dispendia, lib. 6; and D. de constitutionibus, c. cum, M. Ferraria, per Innocentius; and it supports the aforementioned, which is fully noted in Extra, de restitutione integrā, c. cum quaestione, per Innocentius and Hostiensis; and which is noted in D. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. si quis rem a non domino.

† It must be considered. Note that sometimes the defendant wishes to have something adjudged to himself, or to be done, which he cannot obtain through the mere raising of an exception. And then he is not prohibited from denying the plaintiff’s claim by way of exception in order to repel the plaintiff: and nevertheless, in the meantime, he may bring an action to obtain a fuller effect, as in D. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. Si inter mortem. Indeed, it is my counsel that the defendant should act thus. Sometimes the defendant does not wish to obtain anything except that the plaintiff be repelled: then it suffices to have and to plead the exception itself, as in D. de eo per quem factum erit, l. 1, § Si reus; D. ut in possessionem legatur, l. 1, § Si debito ei. Contrary to this, note that a judgment, which can be moved by itself, has no place except in cases expressly stated in the law. D. de contrario iudicio tutelae, l. 3, § Idem; D. communia, l. In rabis, in fine; and note D. de impensis in rebus, l. Dotali; Fac. C. ut nemo inuitus, l. 1. And the defendant could not demand before litis contestatio that witnesses be received, since he could bring an action: for the reason of the laws and canons would cease. C. de usu pupillari, l. Finis; D. de testibus, l. Curent; in Auth. de testibus, § Pe; Extr. eo, c. Significavit. To this effect serves what is noted by Innocentius, Extr. de officio delegati, c. Sanxit, n. 6, in his gloss, under the word “sed nunquid”; and c. Cum in substitutione non contingat. It would also follow that it would be within the power of the defendant to bring an action: and thus prescription would run against the defendant: and all these things are false, nor does it avail D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si contentat, because there is a special case, since on account of the delay of time the benefit of the thing could be lost, i.e., the approval of the right. Simul

Furthermore, it must be known that when the libelli are contrary and do not differ in any other respect, except that what the plaintiff affirms the defendant denies, the plaintiff’s libellus prevents the defendant’s libellus, so that contrary sentences cannot be rendered on the excess and the exceeded; then both libelli proceed. See the aforementioned law *Si inter me et te*. Unless the contrary cause were prejudicial and greater, in which case the first would be stayed. Codex, *De ordine iudiciorum*, law *Quam*. Unless sentence has already been passed on the first, as in the Codex, *De ordine cognitionis*, law *Si*. And noted by Innocentius, *De officio delegati*, chapter *Cum in iure*, in the principal part. And this is the matter of the contrariety of libelli offered by opposing parties; and it is not the matter of cumulation.

† In the matter of cumulation touched upon here, it should be known that sometimes an action is cumulated with an action; sometimes an exception with an exception; sometimes an action with an exception; and sometimes an exception with an action. In the first case, either a principal action is cumulated with a principal action: and the doctrine of Dy. in c. nullus pluribus and in l. edicta, according to Cyn., applies. Or an accessory action is cumulated with a principal action previously brought: and l. fundum and l. fundi apply. This fails in Auth. de fideiussoribus, § sed neque, because the hypothecary action is so closely attendant that it follows the principal action, just as its companion, and as one serving in a sort of mercenary capacity, as is clear in the first constitution of ff. similitudinarie loquor. Or a principal action is cumulated with an accessory action previously brought: and this can be done, because the accessory, by its own nature, does not regulate the principal; rather, it is regulated by the principal itself. de exceptionibus, l. sed si ante. In the second case, l. nemo ex his and Inst. de excusationibus tutorum, l. si plures, apply. In the third case, if they are of the same effect and nature, cumulation does not proceed, because it would be repetition, not true cumulation: and this is the case in our question. In the fourth case, an exception arises from the pending litigation: and this can be opposed, because it is by the nature of the judgment invoked. ff. qui ex causa maioris, l. nec non, § exceptio; ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. penultima; C. de transactionibus, l. si ad cognita; C. si ex falsis, l. fi. cum simil. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a paternal uncle related on both sides is to be preferred to a paternal uncle related on only one side, just as with brothers. And number 4.
2. Correlatives do not always have the same reasoning and nature.
3. It is equitable to expand successions.
body:
In the name of Christ. The double bond of kinship is considered, but the tenor and the ordering of the testament are considered: as in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*, §. *Quia igitur*, Codex. And therefore this question does not proceed with respect to substitution, but also with respect to intestate succession. And the question stands on this: whether, just as among brothers and the children of brothers, one united on both sides is preferred to one united on only one side, because a double reason and a stronger cause is greater than a single one; and one using double right excludes him who could use only a single right, as is said in the text in the said Authentica, where it says: "and those using double right exclude those who could use only one." So it is done among uncles. For that a double reason is stronger than a single one, this seems to be a natural reason, which seems to be extended from similar cases to similar cases. Therefore, from the nature of similarity, it seems to be so. For I find that what is tacitly computed, in which there is the same reason, is included. Codex, *De revocandis donationibus*, l. *His solis*. For the mind of the legislator always seems to consider reason, as in Digest, *De excusationibus tutorum*, l. *Scire oportet*, §. *Et si maxime*; Digest, *Ad legem Aquiliam*, l. *Illud*. Secondly, this seems to be true from the nature of correlatives. For just as a collateral nephew stands in relation to an uncle and his successors, conversely the uncle ought to stand correlatively in relation to the succession of the nephew. But in the nephew towards the uncle, the double bond of kinship is considered in the active succession of the nephew to the uncle; therefore, the same applies conversely in the passive succession to be made to the nephew. For correlatives cannot be separated, even where the correction of laws is concerned. Codex, *De indicio dividundo*, l. *Si*. And it is confirmed by a third reason, because it is inequitable for one to succeed to another in one way, and for that other to succeed to him in another way: since the laws of intestate succession ought to be reciprocal, as in Codex, *De legatis hereditatibus*, l. *Legem*, 12, tit., vers. *Et cum alia*. For equality must be observed, as there, in the same title, l. *Meuius*, after the beginning.

To the contrary it seems, for the said uncles are in the same degree, therefore they succeed equally, according to the ancient rule of law, as in Digest, *De suis et legitimis hereditatibus*, l. *Post consanguineos*, §. *Haereditas*. In the response, where it says: "if there are several of the same degree, it is competent to all." But these are in the same degree of agnation and cognation; the agnate of the question is a cognate, therefore they succeed equally. Although the one united on both sides is an agnate, and consequently a cognate on the paternal line; and also a cognate on the maternal line, nevertheless the effect is not increased by the double reason of cognation. For it is sufficient for someone to have a quality which is substantially required: although it inheres in one by one reason, and in another by several causes and reasons. For one reason alone suffices as much as several, argumentum Digest, *De successione edicti*, l. 1, §. *Sed videndum*, vers. *Et post hos*. And this is proved by clear reason. For it is special in brothers and the children of brothers that a distinction is made, when they succeed, whether they are united on both sides or not. Therefore, the common law is to the contrary. And that it is special in them appears from the text in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis fratribus*, before the end, where it says: "this law therefore is placed in a mixed case," etc., and below where it says: "and thus in such cases," etc. And it speaks there of a brother, but of the children of brothers another Authentica, *Ut fratrum filii*. In these, namely brothers and the children of brothers, when they are called to succession, the law did not neglect to place its distinction, whether they are united on both sides, and are preferred to those united on only one side. And it goes further, establishing that this distinction is not considered in others. In others, I say, namely more remote ones, as below, *De legitimis hereditatibus*, Authentica *Post fratres*. And in the Authentica *De hereditatibus ab intestato*, §. *Si igitur defunctus*, vers. *Si vero neque facto*, where it says that the deceased has no brothers, nor children of brothers. Therefore cognates succeed according to the prerogative of degrees. But in our case the deceased has no brothers, nor children; and the uncles are in the same degree, namely the third, therefore they are called equally. Moreover, that an uncle is more remote than a brother's son appears, because a brother's son excludes an uncle, as in the Authentica *Post fratres*, vers. *Hi autem si sunt remotiores*. Therefore only degree is considered. And on this reason Bartolus bases himself, who holds this opinion in the said *Post consanguineos*, where they determine and confirm for this part: because this distinction of those united on both sides was not known in the old law; but it began to be recognized by Justinian, as he openly says in the Authentica *De consanguineis et uterinis*, in §. *Quia igitur considerantes*. And Justinian established a new law, which has no place except in the cases expressed therein. Argumentum Codex, *De colonis*, l. *Illam*. Since the law does not extend such a distinction, but rather restricts and confines itself to brothers and the children of brothers succeeding, it is not to be drawn further, as in Digest, *De legibus*, l. *Ius singulariter*. Only the legislator can extend those things which are constituted as privileges. Digest, *De institutione et substitutione*, l. *Generaliter*, §. *Si*; Codex, *De fideicommissis*, l. *Cum acutissimi*.

Someone will say: if one united on both sides succeeds to a brother, excluding one united on only one side; and thus one united on only one side is repelled, lest he succeed to a brother who is nearer, therefore much less does he succeed to a brother's son, who is even more remote. But I answer: this argument does not proceed. For by this reason we would say that he does not succeed even to a son of a brother's son, who is even more remote: which is false, for he undoubtedly succeeds equally with another great-uncle united on both sides, as in the said Authentica *Post fratres*. Since therefore we do not have this distinction and preference in uncles by law, we will stand by the old law as uncorrected; rather as confirmed, because the old law is expressly confirmed in those more remote from a brother and from the children of a brother. But an uncle is more remote, although not by the enumeration of degrees, yet by the disposition of law. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, it follows that the said uncles succeed equally intestate, nor is there found any law which says the contrary. For which law makes this distinction among uncles? Certainly no law says this. The objection from similarity does not hold, because there is no similarity where there is not an equal disposition of law.

† Likewise, the argument from correlatives does not apply, because correlatives do not always share the same reason and nature. Hence, we say that a will is valid between children in the presence of two witnesses, but not between parents. C. de test. l. hac consultissima. §. ex imperfecto. and §. pe.
† Moreover, the argument based on inequity does not hold, because it is not inequitable, but rather equitable, to expand successions. Institutes, On the Acquisition of Property, § Quos autem.

From which I conclude and hold that both uncles shall succeed, following in this the opinion of Bartolus, fortified and declared, as appears above. Moreover, the objection from the Codex, *Communia de successionibus*, aut. *Itaque*, and what is said there by Cynus, does not avail; for it must be understood that those related on both sides are preferred in the cases expressly set forth in the most recent law of the Authenticae. For we cannot extend the most recent law to the correction of ancient law, unless in such cases. The case is this: Peter. The case is this: Who [is] in the cases expressly provided by law; for the correction of laws is of the strictest law, as is noted in the Codex, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, aut. *Quas actiones*, with similar authorities. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the substitute is the heir of the person to whom he is substituted, or of the substitutor, so that he is not liable for the delicts contracted by the latter.
body: In the name of Christ. M. instituted his wife as his heir during her lifetime, and after her death, he instituted his son Paul and Paul’s heirs as his heirs. However, if the said Paul were to die without male or female children, he instituted A. and B. as his heirs, and he willed that his son Paul should be his own master. Now it has happened that the testator Peter dies, and after him his wife dies while the said Paul, their son, is alive and without children. Finally, Paul himself incurs debts and has children. Paul dies, with the said children surviving him. The creditors of the aforementioned Paul demand satisfaction from his aforementioned goods. The children of the said Paul refuse, stating that they are not heirs of their father, but of their paternal grandfather, by virtue of his will, as stated above. It is asked, what is the law? In the name of Christ.

The institution of Paul, and of his heirs, is to be understood in this manner: that first Paul, and after Paul’s death, his sons, are called as sons, and not as heirs of Paul. This is due to what follows, namely, “and if Paul should die without sons.” D. de leg. 1, l. filius; § cum quis erit, D. ad trebellianam; l. ex facto, § si, and the note by Jacobus de Arena and Oldradus. C. de conditionibus insertis, l. 1, which supports the point. D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius; D. de legatis, l. Titia cum testamento, § seya; D. de liberis et postumis, l. Galus, § 1. And therefore, the grandchildren are not bound by paternal burdens, if they wish to accept the fideicommissum from the paternal grandfather’s testament, having repudiated the paternal inheritance. In this fideicommissum, however, the legitima and the trebellianica are not included with effect. De testibus, c. Raymundus, and c. Raymundus. And thus, the legitima and the trebellianica are bound to the creditors of the son. C. ad legem Falcidiam, l. in ritum, and l. quamquam. The son was not instituted; rather, the wife is to be considered as usufructuary, on account of the last word of the testament, there, “and he wished that Paul should be the owner.” D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. his verbis. For that which is said at the end determines all the preceding, as in D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. qui non militabat, § filiis, and l. cum te, § si; and D. si certum petatur, l. si tibi, at the end of the law, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a woman is bound by a confession made to her husband during the subsistence of the marriage.
body:
In the name of Christ. A certain man made a will, in which, among other things, he said: “I wish that the following goods, of the value specified below, which are in my house and with my wife, Lady Benevenuta, and under her custody, be sold by my fideicommissary named below.” Lady Benevenuta, summoned at that very moment to the place, in the presence of the witnesses named in the will and the notary present, and questioned by the said testator whether the said goods and things were with her, Lady Benevenuta, and under her custody, responded and said that they were, and that they were with her and under her custody, as she held and possessed the aforementioned things. After some days had passed, the aforementioned testator died. Now the heirs of the said testator demand the said things from the said Lady Benevenuta, wife of the said testator, on the basis of the said confession. The said lady says that she did not have, nor does she have, the said things, even assuming that she made the confession. Now it is asked: can she, by virtue of the said confession made by the said Lady Benevenuta, wife of the said testator, and written in his will, be condemned and compelled to deliver and pay the said things to the heirs of the said testator? It does not appear otherwise that she had the said things except through her confession. And assuming that she can be condemned to restore the said things, is she bound to restore the said things of such value as was expressed by the said testator by virtue of those words, “the said things and goods”?

It seems at first that she can, by reason of the said confession. For even if a donation is prohibited between husband and wife, a contract is not prohibited; and the contract entered into between the aforementioned parties appears to be a contract of deposit. And it seems that the confession of the said woman extends even to the value expressed by the said testator, because by saying “the said things,” it seems to comprehend not only the thing itself but also the quality attached to it.

On the contrary, it seems that by virtue of such a confession she cannot be condemned, since such a confession has the appearance of a donation, since it does not appear otherwise that the said woman had the said things from the husband’s goods except through her confession, and especially since it is presumed that the said woman made such a confession out of fear or reverence. And even assuming that such a confession binds her, she should not be bound to the value of the said things, according to what is noted and by Bartolus in the law *Si cui*, § *A filio*, *De legatis* 1. For if an accuser knew Bartola, the wife of Titius, and confesses that he knew the said Bartola, he does not thereby seem to confess that she was his wife.

It is asked: what is the law? Write the true truth, etc. In the name of Christ.

† To the negative part, that the confession is not valid, serves: D. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum; and D. de liberis et legatis, l. Aurelius, §. ult. Nevertheless, the truth is that such a confession between husband and wife is valid, as the text states: D. de iure dotium, l. si ego, §. plane si rerum. But whether it appears that he confesses to the extermination of the things, or to the bodies and substance of the things by nature of the relation, because he says “said,” it can be said that this is rather indicative of the substance than of the value of the things, because value is an extrinsic goodness, to which it cannot be properly applied to truly hold and possess. And to this I add the gloss: C. de sententiis quae pro iudicio habentur, l. 1, which begins “ex conventione,” at the end of the gloss, there: “Nevertheless, the words ‘hold’ and ‘possess.’” Unless, however, he exhibits those things with a probable estimation by the oath of the plaintiff: D. de in iurando, l. 2, through the gloss, and more elegantly by Jacobus Butrigarius: Inst. de verbis oblig., §. pe., in the ordinary gloss, and in C. quod metus causa, through Innocentius. And these are true, unless the wife proves that the matter is otherwise, as argued: D. de legatis 2, l. Titia, §. Gayus; and serves: D. de possessionibus, l. Publia, with similar cases. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In the name of the Lord. The case is as follows:
1. Whether it can be prescribed that a certain church be visited by the bishop, and thus whether episcopal rights are prescribed.
body: The prior, or the Abbot of Saint Cyprian of Murano in the Diocese of Torcello, built a certain church in honor of Saint John in his place called Costa. By reason of religion and out of reverence for the holy Baptist, the Bishop of Adria granted to that place one-third of the tithe, reserving for himself and his successors one-third for the defense of the three parts granted to that pious place. Moreover, the said Bishop granted to the said church the baptism of the people of that land; and in the said grant he reserved for himself and his uncle the Bishop that every year on the feast of Saint Peter the clerics of the above-mentioned church must place one candle with two Veronese coins on the Altar of Adria; he also reserved for himself that on Holy Thursday a cleric of the church must go to the bishopric for the Chrism, as other clerics used to do. Afterwards it is added in the privilege, narrating that when it happens that the Bishop of Adria makes a passage from there, or that his envoys ought to be received honorably according to the quality of the place and treated honestly. It is added in the privilege that if a monk or professed religious dwells in the said church, he shall be under the correction of the prior, but if he is of another condition, he shall remain under the power of the Bishop. Now the said Bishop seeks visitation from the said priest, or lay brother; it is asked whether he can do this by right, presupposing that the said Abbot is exempt, as appears from the privileges given to us. In the name of Christ.

† Although the church and the clerics are exempt, the people are nevertheless not understood to be exempt, as in c. Per emptionem, De privilegiis, lib. 6. Exemplum, De privilegiis, c. Cum capella. However, custom and prescription may extend to something else to which the privilege does not extend. For although a subject cannot prescribe that he not be visited, nor that he not give the procuratio annexed to a prescribable visitation, as in Extra, De praescriptionibus, c. Cum ex officii, nevertheless an exempt abbot can prescribe against the people of his non-exempt chapel the right of visitation and the procuratio; because the exempt can prescribe episcopal rights, as in Extra, De praescriptionibus, c. Cum. The case is such as in c. Casus talis, Serolimi, where it is said that the Abbot can prescribe episcopal rights in the chapel, and thus where a privilege is lacking, prescription supplies it. Since therefore the Abbot himself was always in possession, i.e., his predecessors in the name of the monastery always held that chapel, and visited it and its people, and he likewise exercised episcopal rights in the chapel and the people: what prescription has taken away from the bishop and granted to the abbot, the bishop cannot demand, ff. De lege prima, l. Quod in rerum, § Si quis, and there noted by Jacobus de Arena. Although it seems that the inusitatio [long-standing non-use] is denied to any abbot by the bishop, it nevertheless seems harsh to me that this prescription can be founded, yet the abbot did not have title; I speak with regard to the people. Furthermore, I say another thing, that if it were proven that the bishop was accustomed to receive something in the name of the procuratio, and no more, he ought to be content with that, arg. ff. De usuris, l. Qui semisses, and noted by Bartolus and Ioannes Andreae in the said c. Cum ex officii, on the word "procuratio." In our case, the bishop received nothing, as is alleged, other than candles every year. The visitation and everything else are said to have been done by the ancient and new abbots. From antiquity, good faith is presumed; hence if these things are proven, prescription has preceded, according to the note by Innocentius in c. Cura, De iure patronatus. For he is presumed to be in good faith who proves that some of his predecessors were in possession, according to Innocentius. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a legacy made by the testator to his daughters, if one of them dies during the testator’s lifetime, devolves to the other. And whether. 2.
3. Whether a substitution by compendium can be made in a legacy.
4. The vulgar substitute succeeds in caduc and quasi-caduc portions.
5. Refutation does not prejudice the substitution, nor the last will.
body: In the name of Christ. Leonard of Porto, having in his assets five hundred ducats and more, and having his two daughters hereinafter named, made his will: in which will, among other legacies which he left, he said thus. Item, he left to Marg. and Bar., his sister daughters, and to any other legitimate or natural or posthumous daughter or daughters to be born, £250 for each, for the purpose of providing dowries for marrying them at that time, since they will be at the time of marrying them; in which he instituted them, and each of them, as his heirs, and wished them to be tacit and content for their legitimes and portions by right of institution, in the manner, right, and form by which he could best do so, with this condition, that if one or any of them should die in pupillary age, or at any time before the time of contracted marriage, that the survivor should succeed the deceased, and have the said £250 which the deceased ought to have had for her dowry. And if both said sisters should die before the time of contracted marriage, that the said £250 should be given and distributed by his hereinafter named commissioners to poor and miserable persons, according to the discretion of his fideicommissaries, for his soul and those of his family. And if the sisters, and one of them, having contracted and consummated marriage, should die without legitimate children born from them: that the survivor ought to succeed the deceased, and ought to have the portion of the dowry of the deceased, which ought to come to her nearest relatives, or be restored. And if both, having contracted and consummated marriage, should die without legitimate children born from them, that the said portions to be restored of the said dowries should be given and distributed to the poor of Christ and miserable persons for his soul and the said daughters. And so forth. Now, thus, in the course of time, the father and aforementioned testator married one of the said daughters, namely Mar., and gave her £250 in dowry, and had her make a settlement and remission by instrument, as is read in it. And afterwards, his other aforementioned daughter, namely Bartholomew, before nubile age, and being in pupillary age, and while the aforementioned testator was living, died. Finally, afterwards, the said testator died, having instituted Fran., his brother, as universal heir in the said will. From the premises, it is asked, having inspected the words and intent of the said testator and legacy, and the said instrument of settlement, whether the said legacy of the said £250 left to the said lady Bartholomew in the manner aforesaid ought to remain to the universal heir, or whether it ought to accrue to the other daughter, namely Margaret, by virtue of some conjunction or substitution: and let the tenor of the instrument of settlement and remission be placed here, the tenor of which is namely: Margaret, daughter of Ser Leonard of Porto, for £250, by which the said Leonard, her father, constituted for the dowry of the said Margaret, to be given to Tardinello, her future husband, before my betrothal made by the said Tardinello, saying, confessing herself to be over 12 years of age, spontaneously, and with exercised knowledge, not coerced, nor by error, made the same Ser Leonard, her father, for herself and her heirs, a settlement, and remission, and acquittance of all paternal inheritance, and of all and singular paternal goods, and of all and that whole which to the same Ser Leonard, her father, for herself and her heirs, she received on account of paternal inheritance and paternal goods in the present and in the future whenever she could say or ask, which settlement, and remission, and all and singular aforesaid Margaret promised to her said father for herself and her heirs, received, and also swore on the holy gospels of God, touching the scriptures, always henceforth to hold firm and ratify, and to observe and fulfill, and not to contravene, or come on account of minority of age, or any reason, cause, or device in law or in fact, and never to say or oppose anything against the aforesaid, or any of the said things: nor to say herself injured or deceived in the aforesaid, or in any of the aforesaid. And so forth. Opinion of Alberico.

† And briefly, it is alleged and established on behalf of Margaret, because the legacy to Bartholomew, due to her death occurring after the will was made and before the death of the testator, fell into the category of a lapsed legacy, as the text states in C. de caducis tollendis, §. et triplici, at the words "ea, cui vel viuo testatore." And therefore, it passes to Margaret by a double right, or by either one, whichever she wishes and chooses. However, according to our opinion, for the gloss and doctrine in l. si quis haeres, in the first case, ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, it was said that there is a double right, and this Margaret and the aforementioned legatee Bartholomew were joined, at least verbally, as joint legatees, due to the conjunction placed above in the said legacy left to them, as in l. si ita quis haeres, ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, and noted ordinarily in §. interdum, as Raymundus de usage, l. adire, and Bartolus in l. coniunctim, de legatis 3, and some extraordinary cases, in l. simplici, de verbis significandis. Therefore, the said legacy accrues to the said Margaret as one joined at least verbally, by the aforementioned §. et triplici, C. de caducis tollendis, rejecting the opinion of Johannes, as fully recited by Raymundus in the aforementioned §. interdum, near the end of his repetition of that section. Furthermore, because the said Margaret was substituted for the said Bartholomew, therefore, etc., as in the aforementioned §. pro secundo, without regard to, nor citing, §. sin autem aliquid sub conditione, and extra, in the same title, since perhaps the legacy left to Bartholomew ought to be considered pure, by l. quam, in fine, C. de inofficioso testamento, l. et sic iste, §. sin autem, which does not apply.

To the contrary, l. quidam, ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, applies. Furthermore, because by the instrument of settlement the right of the said Margaret was extinguished, therefore, etc., l. postquam, cum si, C. de pactis, especially when fortified by an oath: therefore, etc., as in c. quamvis, extra de pactis, lib. 6, and fully by Bartolus in l. si quis pro eo, ff. de fideiussoribus, and it applies extra de iureiurando, c. cum contingit, and c. licet, in the same title.

One point I do not wish to omit against her: first, that perhaps the said Margaret cannot be called a co-legatee at the time of Bartholomew’s death, since she had already received from her father in dowry that which had first been left to her, as in l. filia, C. de legatis, and fully noted by Dyacinus and Raymundus in l. huiusmodi, §. cum pater, de legatis 1. And thus, the aforementioned aid of the right of accrual, of which I spoke at the beginning, has no place. Furthermore, because the instrument of settlement operates, because by it, speaking in a certain way, the right of the said substitution is not remitted; then, because the said Margaret, ignorant of the said substitution and legacies, remitted them, which ignorance is presumed, as in l. verius, de probationibus, and especially this remission occurred while her father was still living, and thus before the words of the will had been examined, as in l. si, §. si, de legatis 2. Therefore, etc., as in l. hec ignorans, de donationibus, and l. mater decedens, de inofficioso testamento, ff., and it applies, l. de his, and what is there said by Guillelmus, ff. de transactionibus, and Bartolus in §. duo fratres. Furthermore, even if it is opposed that she perhaps knew of it, as recited there by Bartolus, etc., and Albericus.

In the name of Christ.

† It is here to be treated of the law of substitution rather than of the law of accretion. For when a testator institutes his daughters in one hundred, and assigns to each of them a certain sum, there is no place for the right of accretion; he who assigns a separate and distinct quantity to each does not allow the right of accretion to arise in adverse cases, as is stated in the Digest, *De legatis*, title 3, in the law *Huiusmodi*, section *Quibus*. Thus, Bartolus formally posits this point there. We therefore see that the matter concerns substitution. And it must be known,

† That a compendious substitution may be made in a legacy, just as in an inheritance, as is stated in the Digest, De legatis 2, l. Ut hereditas, which includes within itself the vulgar substitution. And therefore, although the person to whom the substitution was made dies during the lifetime of the testator, the substitute is nevertheless called upon: as noted in the Code, De impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. Precibus, according to Cynus and Doctor Nicolaus de Tudeschis in the Digest, De ventre in possessionem missa, l. Qui ventri. From which it appears in our case that, with respect to the said legacy made to that girl who died during her father’s lifetime, the sister who was substituted shall succeed; for, as wisely alleged

† is in the caduca, and as if caduca, the vulgar substitute succeeds; indeed, even if he were a substitute by fideicommissum, because it remains with the heir with the honor of the fideicommissum. C. de caducis tollendis §. pro secundo and §. in novissimo. In our case, however, the vulgar substitution is this,

† From which the pearl is noted. This is the very truth. The objection raised on behalf of the pearl against her father does not stand: because such an objection does not prejudice the substitution; for the father, to whom the renunciation was made, may still leave a legacy to the one who renounced, since what is acquired by the father’s judgment is not included in a general renunciation, as in l. si, C. de pactis, where it is said that the father’s last will must be observed, nor should the freedom of testation be impeded. ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. stipulatio hoc modo concepta. And I speak more at length. C. de colonis, l. pactum. I say on this matter, although Bartolus in the said l. stipulatio hoc modo suggests that if the renunciation is made to the father, [the heir] is excluded in every way, but if it is made to the brother, he is prevented from acting under the father’s testament, so that the father’s free faculty of testation is not taken away. But I say that the right of substitution does not appear to have been waived. ff. de legibus tertio, l. Paulo Calimaco, § Pomponius. Nor does it appear that the father imposed a law upon himself, nor can he leave a legacy to his daughter. ff. de fideicommissis, l. Lucius, § Lucius.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an executor of a fideicommissum, tasked with dividing the estate among the poor, may make dispositions in the last will.
body:
In the name of Christ. He made a will, in which he instituted his son, Lord Aulivierius, as his heir in movable goods, and his nephew Nicolaus, son of his predeceased son, as his heir in immovable goods; and he left Lord Aulivierius, his son, as tutor and administrator of the said nephew Nicolaus, under the following condition: that if one should die before the other without legitimate heirs, the share of the deceased should pass to the surviving one, or to his heirs, saving what he may have wished to be done for his soul. Finally, the said Nicolaus, the instituted heir, having come of age, at the time of his death ordered his will thus. And among other things he said that in all his movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, he instituted his uncle, Ser Aulivierius, as heir, with this condition: that if it should happen that the said Ser Aulivierius should die without heirs descending from a legitimate marriage, the undersigned fideicommissaries should be bound and ought to distribute half of the said inheritance to the poor of Christ, and for masses to be sung and celebrated for his soul, etc. As his commissioners for carrying out the aforesaid, he chose Brother Simon of Parma, Prior of Saint Nicholas of the Order of Preachers of Trivisio, during his lifetime; and if he should have died, the Prior of the said monastery who shall be for the time being; and Ser Aulivierius, his uncle; and Ser John of Mandico; and each of them jointly and severally.

The said Ser John of Mandico, the aforementioned commissioner, died before anything had been executed from the said will. Afterwards, the said Ser Aulivierius, the other commissioner, ordered his will thus: namely, that the School of Saint Mary of Batutis of Trivisio should be instituted by him as universal heir, and he wished it to be so, with this condition: that the said School, or the castellans of the said School, should distribute the said goods among the poor of Christ, as is contained in his will, without expressing anything regarding the will of the said Nicolaus, his nephew.

Now, the current Prior of Saint Nicholas, who alone remains as commissioner and jointly and severally liable, demands half of the said goods of the said Nicolaus, saying that he wishes to distribute the said goods according to the form of the said will of Nicolaus, since, as he asserts, the said goods have not been distributed by the other commissioners, nor by himself. On the other hand, the School says that the goods have already been distributed by the said Ser Aulivierius, commissioner, also jointly and severally liable, because the said Ser Aulivierius instituted his School as universal heir with the condition that the said School, or the castellans of the same School, distribute the said goods to the poor of Christ, as is contained in the will of the said Ser Aulivierius.

The Prior replies that the said Ser Aulivierius could not have done this, because the condition of the legacy had not yet occurred at the time when, and in the pending case, the said Ser Aulivierius made the said will. On this point, the School asks for your counsel: whether the aforementioned Prior ought to distribute half of the said goods of the inheritance of the said Nicolaus, or whether the School itself, or its castellans, ought to do so. In the name of Christ.

† At first sight it seemed to me that this execution pertained to this prior of Saint Nicholas, even though the said Brother Aulivierius could not have carried out the execution of that which, having been requested to restore after his death, he was to restore, as in D. de legatis 1, l. filius, §. diuus. Moreover, because Brother Aulivierius spoke and made his will not in the name of an executor, but as a testator concerning his own property. See D. de solutionibus, l. et magis. For the increase is considered in those things which can be done in several ways. D. de adoptionibus, l. si pater; D. de locato conducto, l. si quis domum. Furthermore, the day of the executor’s office does not pass before the day of the legacy passes, since the legacy is principal and the office is accessory. But the day of this legacy did not pass except after the death of Brother Aulivierius; therefore, neither did the day of the office pass. And thus, before Brother Aulivierius was in office in this regard, he could not carry out the execution, nor choose the school. Moreover, the office of executor is terminated by death, and it could not be conferred for a time in which it is terminated. D. de curatore furiosi, l. cuius bona; D. de tutoribus, l. pe. For these reasons, it seemed so at first sight. But to one who looks closely, the truth appears to the contrary. For Aulivierius was not a mere executor, but a mixed one: because he was heir and executor. Now the law says that an heir requested to restore to the poor after his death, by instituting the poor, seems to choose them and to perform simultaneously the office of executors of the restoration, as in D. de legatis 1, l. vnum ex familia, §. si duos. And there Bartolus formally states this. Therefore, it is so in the case at hand, for Brother Aulivierius, knowing the testament of his nephew, seems to have chosen those poor whom he instituted as heirs, as in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. si quis prioris, §. illud. This also appears from the reason for the institution: because for the sake of his own soul and those of his predecessors, he said that he left it thus. From this, the movement of the mind and the reason are declared, which is compensatory, or inclusive of the execution and satisfaction of all preceding testators. Since, therefore, one executor was liable in solidum, and this one was not only executor but also heir: rightly there is no longer need to speak of another execution, because it has already been made. Thus, the school has the right in this matter, and not the said prior of Saint Nicholas. And so I hold, and this is the truth. Just as the bishop, if no other executor is appointed, is the legitimate executor, and yet is excluded by the aforementioned election: so too is another testamentary executor appointed with the clause that each is liable in solidum, for the condition of the one who takes possession is better among several constituted in solidum, and the first choice consumes the entire right of choosing, as in D. de procuratoribus, l. si is, qui stichum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a custom in the church that the useful right over a certain fund may be granted, if it has been granted, and that it is ceded to the archpriest, whether it could have been granted to another by the said church.
body: In the name of Christ. Between the noble and honorable man, Lord John, canon of Padua, on one part; and the noble and honorable men, Lords Mirum of Siena, and Daniel of Sala, Antonius Torquatus, etc., on the other part: on account of a certain possession and its revenues, and of certain houses, committed to me by the magnificient and excellent Lord of Padua. My arguments against Lord John are these. First, since it is said that the Lord Archpriest and the canons residing in the said church sold to the said Lord John a house of the Chapter of Padua situated next to the portico of the said church of Padua, which was formerly said to have belonged to Lord Nicholas of Vicolo, and afterwards to Lord James of Leone, canon of the said church of Padua, for a certain price, as is contained in the public instrument written by the hand of the notary on the 5th day of the month of January, 1373. The location of his house is afterwards said to be the said possession, concerning which there is contention between the aforementioned parties. And I do not find that the said house situated next to the said portico was then vacant, or belonged to the said Chapter, but rather to the said Lord James of Leone. Thus it appears from the public instruments written by the hand of the said Mundus, under the date of the 8th day of the month of December, 1373. It is manifestly apparent that, on account of the said John of Hensemel, it could not be leased: and consequently, nor could it be sold to him, according to the custom of the church of Padua. And from this follows another point, that if the lease nor the sale of the house did not hold, consequently, nor could the land, or estate, succeed in its place. And because almost the entire force of the question depends on the major premise, namely, whether it was held from the said Lord James of Leone, or not. It appears that this must be clarified, for when the facts are clear, knowledge of the law is easily attained. And truly this question is more one of fact than of law. And out of the reverence which I owe and have to both parties, it is very burdensome to me. For this reason, I have delayed for a long time, so that the parties might have material for reconciling, and would not make such a great thunder about proving. Now I return to the point.

† And I presuppose, from the instruments of both parties, that this house formerly belonged to Lord Jacob de Leohe, as a canon of Padua; and according to the custom of the Paduan church, this appears from the instruments, because it is proved by instruments, provided they are produced regarding title and perfect possession, as stated above in *de rei vend.*, l. *cum super verius*; and *C. de prob.*, l. *proprieta*; *ff. de acqui. pos.*, l. *praedia cum seruis*; *de rei vend.*, l. *quaedam mulier*; and what is noted by the doctors in *extra de fid. instr.*, c. *inter dilectos*, at the end, in the second point, that he who formerly was lord is always presumed to be lord, unless the contrary is proved, as in *C. de prob.*, l. *siue posside*.
