Thirdly, I premise that a vendor, who receives the price, or has security for the price, cannot rescind the contract by any authority of his own, assuming the validity of the contract, nor can a college, nor a city, nor a prince, unless this is done by one who has jurisdiction; and he who does not have jurisdiction could not do this even for a just cause, as is proved in the college and city in *ff. de decretis ab ordi. fa.*, l. *quod semel*; and in the prince it is noted by Cynus in l. *digna vox*, *C. de legi.*; and in private matters it is certain that repentance has no place in named contracts, as in *C. de rescin. ven.*, l. *de contractu*; *C. de act. et ob.*, l. *sicut*, with its material. Fourthly, I premise that by simple renunciation of dominion, dominion is not lost, as in *C. de acqui. pos.*, l. *si quis vi*, § *deria*; and *C. qui bo. ced. pos.*, l. *si quantitatem*, especially since the words were spoken rashly by an angry man, and in the heat of anger, as the text there says literally. Fifthly, I premise that it must be considered whether the purchase made by Lord John is founded on the occasion and custom of the Paduan church, or whether this contract is null according to common law, as in *C. de sac. san. eccl.*, l. *iubemus*; for it contains at least an alienation of usufruct, which is prohibited, as in § *fi* of the same law. Sixthly, I premise that when someone in an instrument says something enunciatively, although not dispositively, if nevertheless it is of the substance of the act, or qualifies the act, he cannot afterwards allege or confess the contrary, as in *C. de contra. stipu.*, l. *optimam*; for what one has clearly protested with his own voice, he cannot afterwards deny, as in *C. de non nu. pec.*, l. *generaliter*; *C. arbitrium tute.*, l. *fin*. Having premised these things, the following conclusion follows: that the said Paduan, as long as he was a canon of Padua, and consequently could not be opted for by another, since another possession proceeds, which follows, he cannot receive, as in *ff. de bo. lib.*, l. *qui filius*, § *cum filius*, ver. *et sine dubio*, where the text says this formally. And if it is said that Lord Jacob renounced, I answer that this is not clear to me, because by a public instrument made after the time when it was said he had renounced, written by the hand of the said notary, dated 1364, the first day of January, it appears how the Lord Archpriest ceded certain rights as then and previously competent to him against Lord Jacob de Leone, on the occasion of part of the price of the said house, which the said instrument also asserts at that time belonged to the said Lord Jacob de Leone. For if the renunciation had been made, the contract would have been resolved, as in *ff. de pac.*, l. *ab emptione*; and l. 1 and 2, *quando licet ab emp. discedere*; and thus he could not have ceded the right of the property. Hence, cession and renunciation imply a contradiction. Moreover, assuming that the said renunciation had been made, from the above premises it appears that the said sale and delivery made to the said Lord Jacob could not be revoked. Moreover, in the hands of the said Lord Archpriest alone, renunciation could not be made, because it is not true that the authority of the whole chapter resided in him, and especially it appears from the instruments: since there was someone having a voice in the chapter at that time, constituted in sacred orders; if Lord Jacob was forced, as appears in the said instrument of 1374, the first day of January, who also now ratified the aforesaid. And also it must be considered that the custom, which speaks of houses, since it is against common law, does not seem to extend to the aforementioned rustic lands. The point is such, that it can be transferred, arguing from *ff. de re milita.*, l. *milites a graui*; and thus from permitted things to prohibited things, no translation or pronouncement has place, but rather repetition of the price, as in *ff. loc.*, l. *si fundus*; and *ff. de lega. 2.*, l. *qui solidum*, § *cum post mortem*. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a sequestration by the hand of a third party, who confesses himself to be the debtor of another, is valid.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain lady Anto. was the heir of a certain Catharina by will, believing that the said lady Catharina ought to be the heir of a certain Gualuanus ab Insti., and as the closer relative, she began to bring an action for the recovery of the inheritance of the said Gualuanus. A certain Graucius, alleging himself to be the heir by will of the said Gualuanus, opposed the said lady Catharina and contradicted her, saying that he was the heir by will. Finally, it was pronounced by the award of an arbitrator, or the arbitrator himself, that Fran. was the heir of the said Gualuanus. This arbitrator condemned him, as heir, to give to the said lady Anto. 4 Palerminan pounds, or to her heirs, up to a certain time, under a certain penalty. Before the said time, a certain creditor of a certain Io. Marci, who was the husband of the said lady Catharina, for 200 ducats, caused the said Fran., the debtor, to be summoned before a certain judge, saying that the said Fran. was a debtor of the said Anto., the heir, and in the hereditary name of the said lady Catharina, the heir, and in the hereditary name of Io., her husband, through the person of Nico., her son, whom Fran. confessed to have 4 Palerminan pounds in his possession as belonging to the goods of the said lady Anto. in the hereditary name of the aforementioned persons. And thus he requested that a sequestration of the said money should be made. And the judge, having heard the aforementioned parties, ordered the said sequestration. Afterwards, when the term for payment to be made by the said Fran. to the said lady Anto. had elapsed, the said lady Anto. took possession of the goods of the said Fran. before a certain judge. After this taking of possession had been made, the said Fran. appeared to contradict, raising the exception that a sequestration had been made in his possession by order of the judge. It was replied that the sequestration could not have been made, since it is regularly prohibited. And even assuming that this did not stand in the way, the sequestration had been made on account of another debt, as is evident. The question is asked: what is the law? First, whether the sequestration was valid, so much so that the writ of execution subsequently obtained, made, and ordered should be revoked or not, and whether the penalty has been incurred. Second, whether there are two debts or only one. In the name of Christ.

† The said sequestration does not impede the execution of the said award, and therefore the said intrusion of the said Lady Ant. was valid, and the said sequestration was null for the reasons, especially those written below. And first, from the general prohibition of sequestrations. C. de prohib. sequestr. l. 1. And it is prohibited by interdiction that a debt be paid to a creditor, because this is prohibited. Nor ought the judge to have done it, except in cases expressly stated in the law. And if he did it outside the aforementioned cases, one ought not, nor need, act concerning the remission of the renunciation. C. de deposito. l. pen. and note per Innocentius de officio delegati c. sane. And from the disordered interlocution. And this appears in many ways, and first, because the debtor, even of the debtor, could not confess that his creditor was an heir, or was not. For no one can confess concerning another’s right to the prejudice of another. ff. de mandato. l. quamvis. C. de re vel inter alios acta. per totum. Second, because one cannot proceed to the names [of heirs] after the excussion of the goods which the principal debtor possesses. For the thing owed, which is in the name, is as if it were the thing of a third possessor, although obligated. And therefore it comes last to it. de re iudicata. l. a diuo. §. sic quoque. C. quoniam fiscus, vel privatus. l. non prius. Because at the time of the sequestration it did not appear that Lady Catharina was the heir of Nic. and Nic. was the heir of Io., his father. For this ought to have been proved above all. ff. de interrogatione actionis. l. 1. and ff. de solutione matrimonii. l. cum dotem. §. transgrediamur. and there the ordinary gloss. Fourth, because the rights of an heir, even a true one, let alone a pretended one, do not come into the obligation of the deceased. ff. de pignoribus. l. Paulus. Fifth, because to a judge, to whom nothing was duly proved, nothing could be commanded. de sententia excommunicationis. c. solet. per Innocentius. Also, because a judge can do nothing unless he first has clarity concerning the cause of fact and law. l. haec autem. in principio, quibus ex causis in possessionem eatur. Seventh, because what is done un-civilly is to be revoked as to fact, nor does it impede what is done afterwards according to law. ff. de re iudicata. l. si cum nulla. From which it is concluded that the said intrusion is null. Moreover, I say that this sequestration is not caused by a penalty, because it was made at the will of the debtor, who ought not to have confessed concerning the fact of a third party. And therefore the act procured against oneself does not help: for otherwise it would help him, ff. de lege Iulia. l. si servus plurium. per Iacobs. ff. de lege commissoria. l. fi. ff. de stipulationibus. l. si stipulatus. §. si Lancem. With this distinction it ought to be understood, which is noted in c. quicquid mandato perditur. Moreover, the confession of Fran., confessing himself debtor to Lady Ant., as I said, heir of Io. through the person of Lady Catharina, and Nico., her son, does not regard the tenure of the said Lady Anto., because I see a different cause from the diversity of inheritances. For one inheritance is that of Gualvanus, and another that of Io. Hence the cause is inequitable, the sequestration was made. It seems another cause from the cause from which the tenure was accepted. As C. de petitione hereditatis. l. hereditas materterae. with its distinctions. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a substitution made in default of natural children has effect upon entry into a monastery.
body: The testament of Puciarello of Ventimiglia. Moreover, he left to his wife, Francisca, one-quarter part of all his goods, or 12, and that it be at the election of his heirs. In all his movable and immovable goods, present and future, and wherever they are and may be found, he instituted Simon and Marin, his sons, as his universal heirs in equal shares. Moreover, he willed that if his son and daughter should die at any time without legitimate and natural children, the goods of the deceased should pass to the survivor, or their heirs. And if the said his sons should die without legitimate and natural [children], that one-half of all the goods of the said testator should come, and ought to come, by full right, to the Hospital of Mercy of the Gate of Saint Peter. And the other half should come, in the said case, to Vaguarrello and Peter, his brothers, during their lifetime, and after their death, they should be given for the soul of the testator and of his heirs, by his trustees. In the name of Christ. In this question, contrary opinions are held. For Lade Bel., in disputing...

He stated that where the testator made mention of natural children, sons: the monastery is not included under the term "sons," nor does the monastery exclude the substitute. And thus it is posited in his public disputation in the said §. sed hoc praesenti. And thus the ancient advocates held, because the monastery, since it excludes the substitute, excludes it solely on the ground that it is regarded in the place of an heir, and [see] Filiis, extra de probat., c. In praesentia. But this reason ceases where the testator has spoken of a true and natural son. And although regularly the civil son is not contained under the name of son, this fails in the case of the monastery. Nevertheless, this exception regarding the monastery fails where the testator has expressly stated the contrary: for in words, etc., as in §. Cum in verbis. But Ricardus, Decius, Cynus, and Bartolus say that the burden of the fideicommissum is remitted to one entering the monastery: so that, fearing the burden, he may be drawn back to the contemplative life, just as the condition of marriage is remitted: as in Auth. Nisi rogati, ad Trebellianam, through Cynus. And thus Bartolus advised in a counsel which begins, "It is asked whether the monastery." And most recently the same was advised by a certain powerful doctor from Bologna in a certain arduous case in the city of Florence. It seems to me that one must consider that here the testator substituted the legitimate and natural son to the brother, whence here the natural reason favors the substitute. For two reasons overcome one. The civil [reason], lest the truth be broken by the image of nature, ar. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. Filio. And thus I say that the brother of the deceased and the son of the testator are to be preferred to the monastery. Nor [are they subject to] the legitima and the Trebellianica, because [of] prudent counsel and c. ar. ff. de haereditatibus institutis, l. Lucius. And thus Franciscus held. There is also another reason, because in our case there remains a person who, by presumption of law, excludes the substitute: because the testator preferred the children of his soul, i.e., the poor; therefore the children exclude the poor, and the poor exclude the monastery. §. Sed hoc praesenti. And therefore the sons argue: If I overcome him who overcomes you, I overcome you also; for the testator's will and the authority of the law are for the sons. And the day before I advised thus in Trivigno, and thus it was judged: because the charity of one's own is greater than the tacit interpretation of the law. And note, ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. Lucius. And in l. Precibus, in the last gloss. I, Baldus. Certain one having, for the understanding of

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a debtor may make payment to the guardian of a ward against the wishes of the ward’s substitutes.
body: In the name of Christ. A debtor died owing a thousand, leaving one underage daughter as heir, and two other blood relatives as substitute heirs; and leaving his wife, the mother of the said girl, as guardian of the said girl, his daughter. The said debtor wishes to pay the said guardian by authority of the judge; the substitute heirs of the girl object. The question is whether the said debtor can pay the said mother, guardian of the girl, so that he may be released and secure. In the name of Christ.

† Neither by any color nor by any device can the heir or heirs named deduct anything from the payment of the said one thousand florins to the said guardian, by order of the judge; for by such payment they are perpetually and fully discharged, even if the guardian were to consume or squander such money. As stated in the Digest, *De minoribus*, in the law *Ait praetor*, § *Permittitur*; and in the Code, *De administratione tutorum*, in the law *Sanxi*, and noted in the Code, *Si adversus solutionem*, law 1. And those who delay payment are bound to pay interest to the girl. Code, *In quibus causis in integrum restitui potest*, law *In minoribus*; Digest, *De legatis secundis*, law *Titia Seio*, § *Usuras*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether and when a private writing, subscribed by three witnesses, proves a hypothec.
2. When fraud is presumed in a hypothec contained in a private writing. See also no. 8.
3. If a private writing contains a hypothec, four matters are to be considered.
4. Which writing prevails in a hypothec, and concerning the force of writings.
5. A public writing has the effect that a private writing is not believed.
6. Whether excussion is always necessary in a hypothec.
7. In contracts involving two debtors, whether excussion must be made against one or against both.
9. If it is notorious that the assets do not exist, whether excussion is necessary.
10. Whether a hypothec constituted by a procurator is drawn back to the date of the mandate.
11. Whether two debtors are considered to have provided mutual surety.
body: In the name of Christ. It is necessary to premise the understanding of the law, the scriptural passages, and the authentic texts cited therein. C. qui pot. in pig. habe.

† Distinguishing, for either a private writing is produced against the writer sued in a personal or hypothecary action: and it has its own solid strength, as it had under the old law. For it is taken as established that it was valid and sufficient for proof, if the debtor confessed that he had written it, even if he denied the rest, as in D. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam, §. idem quaesitum; and l. fideiussor, §. pater; and l. si his, qui bona, §. 1. Hence, from such a writing arises against the writer valid proof of those things which are written in it, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. generaliter; D. de constituta pecunia, l. quidam; D. de deposito, l. publica, §. si; and when it is made between persons present: all things are presumed to be both true and solemnly executed, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. sciendum; D. si certum petatur, l. lecta; and in §. scriptum; and C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. 1; and note in l. 1, C. de usu. Therefore, the judge rightly pronounced against the writer in favor of Ser. Lac. Mani, and properly, and finally the discussion proceeded: because it had in itself the order and truth of law and fact. And this is determined in the said l. scripturas, in the first part. Sometimes a private writing of the debtor is produced against the contrary debtor, who likewise relies on a private writing. And because this is not our case, we do not discuss it. Sometimes it is produced against an extraneous possessor, or another creditor, who has a public instrument in his favor, and then either the private writing does not contain a hypothec, or it contains a hypothec. In the first case, either an alienation or a new obligation is contracted in fraud, although a hypothecary action cannot be brought: because there is no hypothec, nevertheless it can be revoked by an action in factum with the distinction, of which see and note Inst. de actionibus, §. item si quis in fraudem.

† However, it is necessary to prove the counsel of fraud: if an outsider possessor, or a creditor, holds possession on account of an onerous cause, because fraud is not regularly presumed: as in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Quotiens*, § *Qui dolo*.

† If, however, the private writing contains a hypothec, then four matters are to be considered. The first is the form of the letters. The second is the substance of the personal obligation. The third is the hypothec. The fourth is the time. I say that the first examination is the form of the letters. D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. Non figura. For the form is the written statement itself. And regarding this, I do not believe that the defendant denies that it was written by the hand of the writer. And thus it is presupposed by me. The second examination is that of the personal obligation, as in D. de probationibus, l. Ante omnia. And this is also not denied by the adversary, because he cannot deny it without shame: since it appears from the account books, and especially because, according to the custom of merchants, their account books are held to be public instruments, as noted by Bartolus in D. de donationibus, l. Nuda ratio. The third examination is that of the hypothec, and here too I presuppose that the hypothec is not denied, but rather the time at which it existed. Fourthly, the time must be examined. The time, however, can be denied in two ways: first, because it appears that the property was sold and delivered before it was encumbered, and thus in the obligation that which was previously alienated cannot be included, because it is not among the goods of the obligor. As in D. de pignori actione, l. Si his qui, §. Quod dicitur. And this buyer has a public instrument of sale and precarial delivery, which suffices for transferring dominion and for preference. As in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Quod meo. And fully noted in D. de pactis, l. Ab emptore.

Secondly, because the purchaser has an express hypothec derived from a public instrument, which takes precedence over a hypothec derived from a private instrument, since a public instrument is more credible than a private one: this was established by excellent reasoning for two reasons. First, because more certain proof must be preferred, as stated in Extra de probationibus, chapter Licet causam. Second, so that it not be within the power of the debtor to deprive the creditor of his right by prior placement, as stated in Digestum de fideiussoribus instrumentis, law Repetita; Codex de falsis, law Si creditor; Digestum ad Velleianam, law Seia mancipia; Digestum de fideiussoribus, law 1, section Editiones; Codex de probationibus, law Exemplo. And there is a third reason, so that a transaction between others does not cause prejudice, as stated in Codex Res inter alios acta, throughout; and Digestum de iuris et facti ignorantia, law Iniquissimum. And it appears expressly stated in the aforementioned law Scripturas, section Finis; and Authentica Ibi posita. That is, unless the private writing is subscribed, or written by the hand of the debtor, and subscribed by three witnesses as true, and executed in the presence of the subscribers: for a public writing derogates from the faith of a private writing, and renders it invalid both in terms of probative force and in terms of essence, and especially regarding the prerogative of time. For if a public writing is greater than any exception, it is excepted from the exceptions of falsity, simulation, and failure of cause. But a private writing is not greater than any exception, because it can easily be colluded, just as we say that due to fear of subornation, the proof of truth is sometimes impeded, as in Authentica de testibus, section Quia vero. But notwithstanding these points, in our case it seems another consideration should be applied. For if the purchaser relies on some title from the vendor regarding ownership, he must use his title with its own defects, and with subsequent positive acts of time, as noted in Codex Si aliena res pignori data sit, law Cum res; and Digestum de Publiciana, law Sive autem, section Si duobus. For I ought not to be in a better condition than my author, as stated in Digestum de regulis iuris, law In his, section Non debeo. Likewise, it ought not to be within the power of the debtor to make the creditor’s proof more difficult and worse, as stated in Digestum de iuris et facti ignorantia, law Iniquissimum; and Digestum de pactis, law Si unus, section Et in summa. Hence Jacobus de Belvis says that it is against the purpose of the grantor that the said private writing proves, just as against the debtor himself who wrote it: as he places in the aforementioned law Scripturas. Therefore, the writing that made faith against the debtor makes faith against any successor, whether universal or particular. Argument from Digestum de usucapione, law Id tempus, section 1; Digestum de acquisitione possessionis, law Pomponius, section Cum quis; and Digestum de pignoribus, law Si separatus, section 1; and Digestum de exceptione rei iudicatae, law Si a te, section Iulianus.

† It is no objection if you say, and public writing establishes, that private writing is not to be believed: for this is true, unless it is established that the private writing is true. For the law *scripturas* is founded on the presumption that public writing is considered more credible. But presumptions cease where the truth appears to the contrary, as in D. de in integrum restitutione, l. *diuus*. Here, however, the truth appears: for the strength of the truth, i.e., the validity of the private writing, is not called into doubt. For the buyer does not say that the private writing is not true; but he says that the private writing is not valid, which is false, and indeed it is valid if it is true. D. de pignoribus, l. *contrahitur*; and C. de fide instrumentorum, l. *in exercendis*. For here the writing is not one of substance, since the truth can easily be proven, as I will say below in the conclusion which I put forward. Moreover, what does not avail singly, avails in multitude, when collected together they make faith, as in X. de probat., c. *causam*. Moreover, in cases of merchants, where good faith is at issue, it is not fitting to dispute on the points of law, as in D. de mandato, l. *si fideiussor*, § *quaedam*. And from this I draw such a conclusion, that if the said writing of Ser Jacopo, before the contract of sale and purchase, had been seen and read by three literate and understanding witnesses, and knowing the writing, before the sale was made, that such writing is verified, it would suffice against the buyer and any possessor, as noted by Cynus, C. de edendo, Auth. *si quis in aliquo*. And it is proven in X. de censibus, c. *cum olim*. Nor is it an objection if you say that the witnesses must be subscribed, for that is true in the testimony of the dead voice, but it is not necessary in the testimony of the living voice, as in D. de testibus, l. *ubi numerus*. And it is very fitting that which is read and noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. *si actum est*, l. *atqui natura*, § *Scaevola*, and in c. *ultima* de rescriptis in C. And it is likely that Ser Jacopo has many witnesses by whom it can be proven. Moreover, by the writer himself brought in as a witness, as in D. de finium regundorum, l. *eos*, and D. de procuratoribus, l. *si actor malitiose*. But also that which is not to be omitted is that here there is no question of two hypothecs, because the buyer has no hypothec on the thing bought. Hence the question is between the present hypothec and the private writing, and having no hypothec: and thus the one having a hypothec is preferred. Which is proven by three reasons. First, because one's own thing is not regularly bound to anyone, as in l. *neque pignus*. Second, because the thing bought is not here bound for delivery: for the thing was delivered, as in D. de solutionibus, l. *in numerationibus*. Third, because it is not bound for eviction, for in that obligation the day does not pass before the thing is evicted and possession is claimed, as in D. de evictionibus, l. *habere licere*. And it is proven by Jacobus de Arena, D. soluto matrimonio, l. *facere posse*. Hence unless Ser Jacopo evicts the thing and has possession, the buyer does not have a hypothecary right: for the condition has not yet occurred. And this is most certainly true, that here there are not two hypothecs, things being so situated, and to this reason no answer can be made. Having seen the force of writings, it must be seen regarding discussion, whether it is necessary.

† And for the sake of understanding, it must be known that in contracts involving two co-obligors who are partners, each is bound for his share; because the partnership, which is created by such a contract, is divided into equal shares, just as an inheritance is divided into shares of the inheritance, as stated in the Digest, *Pro socio*, law *Si non fuerit*. Therefore, partners are bound through the medium of the partnership, and thus in shares; because there cannot be a partnership without the concept of division, except in the case of a leonine partnership. And this appears to be the rule, unless it has been agreed that each shall be bound for the whole (*insolidum*), or unless they are administered by one person, as stated in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law *In l. Falcidia*, if this is to be observed; and in the Digest, *De exercitoria*, law *Ne in plures*. For when one person is the agent of several, and the matter is conducted as undivided, and the partnership is administered by that agent in the name of each for the whole, he can bind each for the whole. Consider, therefore, either we are in a case where each is bound for his share, and no prior action against the other is required; because action is not taken, nor can it be taken, for the share of the other. As stated in the Digest, *De duobus reis*, law *Reos*, section *Cum in tabulis*. Or we are in a case where each is bound for the whole; and then, either insofar as one does not guarantee for the other, but promises for himself, and the same applies; or insofar as he does guarantee: and then there are differing opinions.

† One opinion holds that excussion is necessary to the extent that: another holds that excussion is not necessary; because they are not properly said to be sureties, since they are equally principal debtors, but among themselves several persons bound jointly and severally can almost perform the mutual offices of sureties. Thus, he to whom the business principally pertains is called the principal debtor, and the other the surety. As in C. si cert. pet. l. si non singuli. And subtly noted in ff. ad Velle. l. vir vxori. §. fin. and ff. de his, qui no. infa. l. furti. §. qui alieno. and ff. de pactis. l. fideiussore. and l. si vnus. in prin. and l. 1. C. de duobus reis. and C. de transac. l. 1. and in Auth. de duobus reis. §. 1. Therefore, the hypothec of one has nothing in common with the hypothec of the other when there are two equally principal debtors. And the obligations themselves are distinct from one another. As in l. si plures. ff. de pac. And therefore, from one of the separated debtors, no impediment arises against the other, since the creditor may choose. As in ff. man. l. creditor. in prin. and noted in C. de pa. l. si creditores. And this opinion is held by la. de bel. 1Authem. de fidei. And the reason is manifest: because since the plaintiff is bound to assign his rights, if he must first exhaust the surety, he would never be bound to assign the action, unless it were empty due to the debtor’s insolvency; for it is ridiculous to say that only an empty action is to be assigned, and not a full and valid one. Which is ridiculous to say. C. de col. Auth. quod locum. and ff. de pa. l. nisi. and ff. de sol. l. stichum. §. si mandato. Excussion therefore pertains to the possessor to whom the rights have been assigned, because the benefit of assignment of actions should suffice for him to whom the rights are to be assigned, not for the assignor. As in ff. qui po. in pig. ha. l. mulier. Finally, it may be said that in this case discussion is not necessary: because it is not provided for by any law. And on this point is the original gloss in Auth. de fideius. in prin. in the gloss noted de iam in fi. gl. where it thus says, this end of the gloss applies when one is bound after another, otherwise if several are bound simultaneously and jointly and severally: because then they would be two principal debtors. For no one is compelled to sue two principal debtors before reaching the possessors of the pledges of one. Since it is free for the creditor to sue one, and to sue none. And the end of that gloss was an addition. This opinion is also proven by the text: because the text says that accessories, sureties, mandataries, or those who promise for another, are to be exhausted. As in ff. de pac. l. in personam. §. qui. pecuniam. But the debtor who is principally and jointly and severally bound for himself is not an accessory: since he is principal for himself jointly and severally towards the creditor, as in d. l. generaliter. And therefore he is not among those three persons enumerated, nor among similar ones. But he is bound by a more abundant caution, and especially in contracts of money-lenders, in which there is execution against clerics and more prompt execution. As is the noted text in d. Auth. de fideiusso. §. argentorum. Whose writings also, as private ones, are regarded by general custom as quasi-authentic and credible, on account of the particular fidelity of merchants, and partly by legal provision, as in ff. de eden. l. quaedam. §. nummularios. And especially since they are aided by supports for the public utility. Hence I conclude that excussion of equally principal debtors is not necessary, arg. ff. de condi. indi. l. dominus testamento. and ff. si cer. pe. l. cum fundus. §. 1. so that circuitous proceedings may be avoided, and the creditor may be assisted without so many windings.

† Furthermore, regarding another point, namely concerning the article of presumed fraud, no certain doctrine can be given; and therefore we resort to arguments, as in D. de re militari, l. non omnes, § a Barbaris; of which we note in l. omnes, § Lucius, quae in fraudem creditorum; D. de legibus 3, l. nomen, § 1; D. de donationibus, l. post contractum; and the arguments in D. de manumissionibus, l. per diversas and l. ab Anastasio; and D. qui in rem potestatem vel hypothecam solvere possunt, l. sicut, § supervacuum; C. de pignoribus, l. si; C. de donationibus ante nuptias, l. sed iam necesse; C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptor; D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. emptor; C. de pignoribus, l. si; C. de donationibus, l. data iam pridem; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si is; C. de repudianda hereditate, l. 2; and what is said there by Cynus in Auth. de aequalitate, do. § illud. And concerning this last point I have written most fully in another of my opinions; and therefore I do not repeat it, but I conjecture with certainty that fraud has intervened, and especially from the unusual and sudden alienation prima facie of all goods. And because in such cases with fraudulent merchants fraud is to be presumed, as in the rule semel malus; and from the outcome the intent is presumed, as in C. de adulteriis, l. si quis. That also concerning the aforesaid is not to be omitted,

† That excussion is not required where the assets are notoriously insufficient for payment and the debtor is in hiding, as is read and noted in D. de verb. oblig. l. decem and D. si cert. pet. l. si §. sed si cum Seyo, because excussion is futile, which is excluded by the debtor’s insolvency; and in D. de dolo l. nam is; and note C. quando fiscus vel privat. l. non patet. And this person, concerning whom the question arises, according to what I have asserted, left the city naked [i.e., penniless], and it is well known among the people that he is unable to pay. D. de act. empt. l. emptorem in princ. and note in l. 1 C. qui et adversus quos qui satisdare cog. l. si vero §. qui pro rei qualitate. Furthermore, consider that these excussions, concerning which the new law speaks, correct the old law, as appears in the text of the aforementioned Authentica de fideiuss. And where the correction of laws is at issue, we must be content with the words of the correcting law and not extend ourselves further, as is noted in C. de sacr. sanct. eccles. Auth. quas actiones.

† Another point, which may be raised for discussion, is whether a hypothec constituted by a procurator is drawn back to the date of the mandate. And it seems that it is, because the substance of this obligation consists in the mandate. Moreover, this obligation was made on account of a past cause, as argued from the Digest, *De pignoratitia actione*, law *Si rem*, § *Si*. Furthermore, the mandate perhaps could not be revoked, because it was necessary, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Fundum*, § 1. Moreover, this serves both for and against, as in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, law *Si ut proponitur*. To the contrary, that it is not drawn back, is because the time of the contract is considered. Moreover, because then, and not before, the consent of the procurator intervened, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, law *Qui absenti*, § 1. Moreover, because it concerns the prejudice of a third party, to whom in the meantime a sale and delivery had been made, as in the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Cum decem*, and law *Si offerenti*, and law *Fin.*, and in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Habe*. Moreover, because this fiction would have no limit, from which the thing was then not in the debtor’s possession, as in the Digest, *Qui potiores in pignore habent*, law *Pontio*, and law *Qui balneum*. Moreover, ratification, which is equivalent to a mandate, is drawn back to the day of the contract; therefore also the mandate, as in the Digest, *De pignoratitia actione*, law *Solutum*, § *Solutam*. Because in my own obligation, a true numeration having been made to me, partly from an impetrative cause, as in the Digest, *De conductori certi territorii dicti Pe.*, to consign a certain quantity, I am bound alone and in solidum, and the other in his own part; although one obligation is true, a numeration having been made to me, partly from an impetrative cause, as in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, because principally, and in my name only, I am bound, partly from my own action ceded to me, suing in solidum against the promisor, I do not have the benefit of the fideiussors. Nor can I demand that if you were to pay me, you should pay another at my will, and therefore it is paid to you at my will, it seems to me paid, if not: therefore because I promise for you, rather for myself alone. But because they say, because they say that a useful action of *negotiorum gestio* competes to the one who pays on behalf of another, the action of mandate would compete to the one paying. Which gloss says: the question is difficult, for if this were for the part of the other, I would be bound for your part. I answer, because they say that a useful action of *negotiorum gestio* competes.

† I ask whether two parties are regarded as equally principal in mutual suretyship, and especially when it is notorious that excussion has taken place. Let the hypothec be held by the creditor, and not by the buyer: and let it not be necessary in every event, according to what was promised, since I do not determine this point, because Ser Jac. has the right that final payment suffices for both obligations. And this serves to clarify the first point concerning excussion. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A confession made that one had possessed grain, yet under the hope of obtaining it, indeed with a promise made to oneself to deliver the grain after the confession: what action does this induce, and what contract? See above, counsel 131.
body: In the name of Christ. [It is alleged that] Perono [received] from the said Peter the land for sowing in that territory. But since the said Peter had in truth not made the said consignation, nevertheless, by certain knowledge, afterwards, from this new promise, and also from the old one, the said Perotus, the said Perono, confessed that the said consignation had been made to him, under the pretext, however, that he would not have done otherwise, except because the said Peter promised to compensate the said Perono for the interest both before the said confession and afterwards. [The defendant] wishes to act, [and it is] opposed.

† That this pact is naked, from which no action arises. It is replied that this pact is clothed, because, upon relating the confession to the interest promised, there results a named contract, namely: I make confession so that you may give interest. And in confessing, performance has been rendered; therefore, it is a pact clothed by the intervention of a thing, as in D. de praescriptis verbis, l. naturalis, and l. not. D. de pactis, l. si intra. Furthermore, it is alleged that the aforementioned words, “if you promise interest, I confess the payment,” have the character of a stipulation; because there is a certain interrogation, so that the sense is: you promise interest so that I may make confession; and the other says, “I promise”; as if all things were presumed to have been solemnly performed between those present. Furthermore, a confession accompanied by writing appears to be a certain solemn contract: as in Inst. de litteris oblig. and l. in contractibus D. de non numerata pecunia. Hence, the appended pact is clothed by the coherence of the contract, as fully noted after the gloss by Petrus and Cynus in C. de pactis, l. petens.

To the contrary, it is alleged that the said confession was fortified by an oath, against which it is not permitted to go, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si quis maior. Furthermore, even if no oath had been appended, it is not permitted to contravene it after thirty days, as in the aforementioned l. in contractibus.

Solution: It matters greatly whether the said confession was made in hope of future performance or not. In the first case, since there is an express pact regarding performance, one may plead the exception even after thirty days, because such an express promise is not terminated by the period of thirty days: as in D. si certum petatur, l. qui pecuniam, and C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. sicut. But if the confession was made not in hope of future performance, then it must be considered what words were appended in the said confession. For if indeed a simple confession was made, it gives rise to an exception of pact, and does not release by operation of law, as in D. de pactis, l. tale pactum, in the principal part, and singularly noted in D. de solutionibus, l. si ex pluribus. And therefore, since the first obligation is not extinguished by operation of law, but by means of an exception, the exception is overcome by a pact not to sue, and a replication is allowed, although it is a naked pact, as Barta, knowing the father, states in D. de pactis, l. si unus, § pactus ne peteret. And this is most certain in law. But if the words are such that they release by operation of law, it must now be considered that, although it is true that no action arises from a naked pact, nevertheless, because the other party does not observe the pact, the confession is overcome by the exception of fraud, because it appears that he who confessed was circumvented: D. de pactis, l. si cum te, and the following law, where it is almost expressly stated; and D. de locato, l. quaero, § inter locatorem; D. de rescissione venditionis, l. fi.

Furthermore, it must be considered that two pacts are alleged to have been made, one before the confession, the other after. And although the first was naked, the second pact falls under constituted money, because a natural debt precedes. In which case, action lies on a naked pact, clothed by the protection of the praetor, as in Inst. de actionibus, § si constituta. But certainly, what is said about the clothing by performance has been sufficiently stated, because the foundation of innominate contracts is performance, as in C. de rerum permutatione, l. ex placito, and D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, § 1, and § quinimmo, and the aforementioned l. naturalis D. de praescriptis verbis. And if it is said that these pacts are not proven, I answer: rather, they are clearly proven, and in this regard, let the records speak. And what is said that the witnesses are not competent, let the reverence of the alleging party spare us, because these allegations are frivolous and not worthy of any other response; since the witnesses are not prohibited by law, and are persons not suspect, and mindful of eternal salvation, as in l. ultima C. ad legem Iuliam de repetundis, and l. 1 D. de testibus. Furthermore, the allegation regarding the oath does not obstruct, as it has a tacit condition: C. de non numerata pecunia, l. fi, and there is the proper case of this point.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the acceptance of an inheritance is presumed, because the son appointed a procurator to bring inheritance actions.
body: In the name of Christ. A deceased person appoints a certain procurator to bring hereditary actions.

It is asked whether by this it is understood that he enters upon the paternal inheritance, or mixes himself with it: and it is said that yes, as the law and notes in ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Paulus, and Inst. de rerum qualitate et differentia, §. si. For this act cannot be performed without the right and name of heir: hence it implies not only presumptively, but necessarily, the acceptance of the inheritance: as ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. pro herede, in principio, and §. Papius. To the contrary it seems that although he had knowledge of the death, it is not established that he knew whether the father died testate or intestate, nor is such knowledge presumed in his own and necessary heirs: as ff. si certum petatur, l. eius qui in provinciam, and the notes by Bartolus in l. cum haeres, ff. de liberatione legatorum. Moreover, even if it appeared that he knew he died testate or intestate, nevertheless because he did not express from which title he accepts or mixes himself, and therefore the acceptance or mixing is not valid: as noted in l. illud, ff. si pars hereditatis petatur, and ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. gerit. Solution: either the father made a will, and the acceptance is not valid, because he does not state from which title; and because knowledge is not presumed; or he did not make a will, and the acceptance is valid, because it is certain that the inheritance was devolved to him from one title. Hence his will cannot be alternated between two alternatives, because there is only one remedy for money. Or it is doubtful: and in doubt no one is presumed to have died testate, because facts are not presumed, and thus in the case of doubt such acceptance should be considered valid. And thus distinguishing, the contrary opinions are solved. Or say that although these words are doubtful, since it is possible that the testator died both testate and intestate, nevertheless unless he declares by which title and from which head he accepted, this acceptance, being uncertain and obscure, should not be admitted, because it is not established that he acquired a right from it, he who speaks generally and is compelled confusedly, unless he declares when the adversary opposes. Moreover, the judge can supply this ex officio, by interrogating so that he does not proceed on an equivocation, as ff. de interrogatione actionis, l. ubicunque; Cod. de annona exceptione, l. si. It is similar to what the law says, that an obscure exception is held for none, ff. de legibus, l. Titiae textores. Also, an obscure petition does not proceed unless it is clarified, when the obscurity depends on the cause of fact, as ff. de re vendita, l. item Pomponius writes, si frumentum, §. fin. Also, it is fitting to observe with what mind something is said, as ff. ad exhibendum, l. penultima. Also, this supports the above, ff. de re vendita, l. si in rem, and ff. de iure fisci, l. ita fidei, and l. certum, in principio, ff. de confessionibus. The above are also proven by l. si is ad quem, and l. Clodianus, ff. de acquirenda hereditate, with the notes there. And this last opinion pleases me more, because it is free from all calumny and duplicity without captiousness. For the acceptance of an inheritance must be such and in such a way that the one accepting the inheritance can be sued from it just as he can sue, as noted in l. si cum dotem, §. transgrediamur, soluto matrimonio. And therefore it should not be alternative or conditional. The text is ff. de regulis iuris, l. actus legitimi. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an alienation is valid if a minor, prohibited from alienating without the consent of two of his closest relatives, alienates with the consent of two who are not so closely related, while the closer relatives were absent; and what effect an oath has in such alienations. See numbers 2 and 4.
3. Whether the masculine gender comprehends the feminine.
5. A judge sometimes supplies the place of an absent person.
body: In the name of Christ. There is a general constitution of the Church, which contains that donations, alienations, cessions, and releases of any persons, things, actions, and rights, made under any form of contracts or words by persons who have reached puberty or are adults, without a bodily oath being sworn, and also without the consent of two or three of the nearest blood relatives, if they exist, or at least of affines, if blood relatives do not exist, and without the decree of a competent judge, and without insinuation to be made in the records, are not valid, and are presumed and deemed to have been fraudulently extorted, and obtain no firmness. Likewise, in the territory of Fabriano of the said province, a certain statute is in force, which reads as follows: wishing to provide for the utility of minors, and lest such minors misuse their substance, we statuate and ordain that it shall not be lawful for any minor under 18 years of age to sell or alienate any immovable possession to anyone without the presence of the curator of the said minor, and without the presence and will of the nearest blood relatives of the said minor, nor to make any contract concerning any thing without the presence and consent of the aforementioned persons. And if anyone has contravened this, that which was done shall be of no value. Now, such a fact has occurred. Peter, aged 24, and being under 25, appeared before the common judge of Fabriano, with the consent and authority of his curator, and of two of his nearest blood relatives from among those who were then found and could be had in the territory of Fabriano, as he and the contracting party asserted; and with the authority and decree of the judge, and the insinuation of the contract, and the oath of the said adult, he made a contract of transaction, release, ratification, and remission with Martin concerning certain plots of land, rights, and actions, debts, and credits, under a certain form. And the said Peter received by way of transaction from the said Martin in the same contract a release and absolution from certain debts owed by the said Martin to the said Peter. Now the said Peter, being over 30 years of age, wishes to declare the said contract null, because the uncle of the said Peter did not consent, nor did the mother of the said Peter. But to this it is answered that the said uncle was absent from the territory of Fabriano by 40 miles, and had been absent for a long time as being suspect on account of partiality, nor was it safe for him to return. Likewise, it is said that the mother was also absent from the said district.

† The question is asked, what is the law. And it appears that the said contract was, and is, null by operation of law, because it was initiated contrary to the general custom of the Roman Church: as in C. de legibus, and const. l. non dubium; and C. de pac. l. pecta, quae contra; and ff. eod. l. iurisgentium, §. et generaliter; and ff. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos, §. fin. For just as an oath against good morals is not valid, so too is one not valid against good and equitable laws and constitutions, as in ff. de iu. pa. l. adigere, §. fin.; and C. de arbitris, Auth. decernimus; and C. quoniam mulier tutelae officium fungi potest, Auth. sacramentum; and C. de nup., Auth. quod eis; and in c. non est obligatorium, de reg. iu., lib. 6. But the constitution of the Church is good and equitable; therefore, it must be observed: because public law cannot be overturned, changed, or altered by the agreements of private parties, as in ff. de fideiusso. l. cum lex; and ff. de pactis, l. ius publicum; and l. inter debitorem. That both the constitution and the statute are in force with equity is apparent from their proemium, by which the final reason is proved, as in ff. de haered. insti. l. Pacumeius Androtenes; and as noted by Cyn. in Auth. sacramenta puberum.

The objection is not valid if it is said that two closer blood relatives were absent, because they ought to have been required and awaited: ff. de dam. infe. l. 4, §. totiens. For it is read in the Usus feudorum that a new investiture of fiefs cannot be made unless the peers, i.e., the vassals of the same lord, are present. Now the text says that if they are not present, they are to be awaited; and otherwise the investiture cannot be made. But if they were not in existence, then it could be made in the presence of other witnesses: in 10. colla., de consuetudine recti feudi, c. sciendum, §. quod autem dictum ibi, where it says, "they are to be awaited." By which text, however, this question is determined. Moreover, even in the case of an exile, the authority of consenting remains, as in ff. ad Treb. l. ex facto, §. ex scom., where it is expressly stated. And they can give their consent through a procurator: as in ff. de mino. l. Papiniana. Therefore, if this solemnity is omitted, the contract is not valid.

† Nor does the oath validate the contract, because an oath never validates a contract where there is a defect of solemnity. Although it is said that it represents one as being of age, it nevertheless does not supply other solemnities. Likewise, it does not supply for age, when age is required by way of solemnity: because all solemnities are of public law. And therefore they cannot be removed by private act. As stated in D. de legibus 1, l. nemo potest. Also, because the oath representing one as of age is a certain fiction, just as is the grace of age (venia aetatis), as C. de his, qui vel aetatem impetrant, l. si. And such is the force and power of law, and especially of canon law, that it can remove this fiction, as C. de his, qui vel aetatem impetrant, l. eos.

To the contrary, it seems that this transaction and agreement was valid for many evident reasons. First, I consider the special statute in the place, which must be observed more than the general constitution of the province. The text is in l. si, C. de testamentis. Therefore, the statute must be observed. And this in two ways: first, with regard to the time of age. For since it speaks of one under 18 years and one over 18 years, it does not speak by way of prohibition or annulment, as D. de postulando, l. 1, §. pueritiam. Second, because by prohibiting up to the age of 18, it seems, by contrary reasoning, to permit after the age of 18; the gloss is ordinary in l. 2, D. de eo quod certo loco. Also, by the argument from contrary reasoning, that which is valid in the status, as D. de testamentis, l. qui testamento, §. mulier, and noted in C. de surrogatione, l. apud antiquos, and the argument in D. de legibus 2, l. statuliberum, §. stichum. Also, because after the said age, one returns to the common law of the aforementioned auth. sacramenta pubertatis. Also, to the natural law of the oath itself, as Extra de probationibus, c. in praesentia. And easily a thing returns to its nature and to the common law, which is called nature. As D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. pactus, versi. quod et specie doctores.

Furthermore, it must be considered that the said statute requires presence, and therefore consent cannot be given between absent parties. As l. 1, in fine, D. de auctoritate tutorum. Also, presence is understood as possible, not impossible or less difficult, as Extra de rescriptis, c. sciscitatus; as in c. prudentiam, de officio delegati; argument D. de verbis significatis, l. nepos proculo. I say this speaking of the person of the uncle: because he is not said to be able to appear, whom he dreads the power of the adversaries. Especially since he has a perpetual cause for dread and fear, as Extra de rescriptis, c. statutum, §. 1, and there by Lotharius and Angelus in the Novella, and Extra ut lite non contestata, c. accedens, and what is noted in D. ad legem Trebellianam, l. de aetate. Even if he were cited, the citation would not bind him, but would be held as null. Therefore, it must be said that the uncle is similar to a dead man with regard to this article of presence. For one is not said to be present, nor living, who is held as dead, as D. de verborum obligationibus, l. ex ea parte.

† Furthermore, regarding the article concerning the mother, it seems to be said that no woman is included in the aforementioned statute, since it speaks in words of the masculine gender. For women do not have full capacity for judgment, and therefore the same reasoning does not apply to them as to men. And when the masculine and feminine differ in reason, then the masculine does not comprehend the feminine, as in l. 1, § si ea, ff. de ven. inpos. mit. And this is a matter of difference, as in l. quidam decedens, in prin., and l. Titium, et Meuium, in prin., ff. de adm. tu., ff. de neg. gest., l. qui aliena, § quamquam, ff. de procu., l. fęminis, ff. de sol. It thus appears clearly from the foregoing that the statute of Fabriano does not hinder the said contract; rather, it favors it by contrary reasoning, and the general constitution of the Church ceases to apply, according to what has been said.

† Let us now suppose that the general constitution of the Church ought to be observed in the territory of Fabriano; nevertheless, it is argued that the said contract is valid, because it is true that consanguineous relatives do not exist [in this case], but they cannot assist with respect to the matter in question, as in l. 2, D. de vi bonorum raptorum. But the paternal uncle could not assist with respect to this matter; therefore, he does not seem to exist [as a relevant party], as in D. de tutela, l. Quaesitum. And if you say that he ought to have been cited, because he could have given consent through a procurator—for the general constitution of the Church makes no mention of presence, but only of consent, which can be expressed through a procurator, as in l. Et licet, D. de constitutionibus pecuniarum, and l. 1, §. Usus, D. de procuratoribus—I answer that an absent person, who has only an interest outside the territory of that jurisdiction, ought not to be cited. This is the glossa ordinaria in l. Haec autem, §. 1, and l. 2, D. qui ex causa in possessionem eant, and it is expressly proven in C. de decurionibus, l. Pater legavit filiae, presupposing the statute to be observed, lib. 10, and it is supported by D. de iudicibus, l. Si longius, §. fin., and C. de collatione, Auth. Quod locum, and what is read and noted in C. de bonis quae liberis, l. Si, §. Necessitate.

† Moreover, the judge supplies the place of the absent party who is unable to appear, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. si infanti, §. si; for the absence of that person is filled by the presence of the deity, as in C. de iudicibus, l. properandum; l. si autem; C. qui admitteri ad bona possint, bonorum; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. tam dementis; ff. de iure dotium, l. profectitia, in principio. This is not obstructed by the cited chapter de usibus, feud., because that provision is understood to apply when the parties are equally capable and not absent from the territory. Furthermore, the rule in l. ultra applies there, but not here. From these considerations, it is clearly concluded that the said transaction is valid, since, especially through the intervention of so many honorable persons and of the judge, it is presumed to have been made for the benefit of the minor, as in C. de transactionibus, l. transactionem, quae; and note C. de his qui ut indigni, l. post haec. What I have said appears to be proven by l. multa non committitur, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A daughter, to whom a thousand were left by her father in the event of her marriage, if she later received five hundred from him, renouncing with an oath any further claim, whether she can nevertheless demand the entire amount in full. And whether the renunciation made regarding the contents of the will is valid.
body: In the name of Christ. A thousand [ducats] were given in marriage. Then he endowed her with five hundred, and received from her, under the bond of an oath, a general renunciation of any further claim, whether from a will or intestate succession. Now, the father having died, she wishes to recover the remaining five hundred.

† The question is, what is the law. And it appears that she may [sue], because a will is deemed to have been made at the time of death, whenever it was actually made, as in l. 2, C. de testamento. unless it had been revoked, as in C. de testamento, l. sancimus. But if the father first made a donation and afterwards made a legacy, she could bring an action for the entire amount, as fully stated in leg. and no. C. de legato, l. filia legatorum. Note that this does not appear to be true when the legacy is given on the condition of marriage; because the condition cannot be fulfilled except in a second marriage, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. si iam facta. But if the legacy were given simply, then the matter of the aforementioned l. filia applies. The same holds if the legacy were given as a dowry, for a dowry can be constituted even for a past marriage, as noted in l. obligamur, § 1, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus. Furthermore, even assuming that the testator accepted a repudiation [of the legacy], nevertheless, by this he does not appear to have imposed upon himself a rule of not being bound, as in ff. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Lucius, since he neither wished nor could deprive himself of the free faculty of making a will. Hence, the said repudiation does not hinder the daughter from bringing an action based on her father’s will, as I said, C. de collatione, l. pactum. To the contrary: for the father, who accepted the said repudiation, appears to have tacitly revoked and annulled the legacy. Hence, the exception of fraud stands in the way of the daughter, as in Inst. de adimendis legatorum, and C. de legatis, l. datum, and C. de fideicommissis, l. fideicommissarium, and C. de pactis, l. fin. But if there were no such repudiation accompanied by an oath, the daughter, who received a smaller dowry, would not be prevented from claiming the remainder from her father’s heirs, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. Lucius, l. prima. Nor is a legacy of a certain quantity diminished by the insertion of a cause, as in ff. de alio legato, l. Lucius. Solution: If the daughter knew of the will, the oath prejudices her; the same applies if she ought to have known. Otherwise, no agreement or compromise can be made regarding those controversies which arise from a will, as in ff. de transactionibus, l. de his controversiis, and most fully noted by Bartolus in ff. de verbis obligatorum, l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that the thing is to be repaired for the damage, from the damage given, individuals were cited, and finally condemned, whether the sentence is valid, and if after the sentence the depopulator was captured, and hanged on the gallows, whether the village is released: and this, because the thief is not only hanged, but the damage is to be repaired. And no. 4.
2. Whether a civil complaint can be brought before a judge of malefice.
3. Whether a citation made to the house is valid in the case of a university.
body: In the name of Christ. To the question, by which it is provided, whether the village is bound to repair the damages given and the thefts committed in its territory, without distinguishing whether it was by day or by night. Likewise, no distinction is made as to whether the village was at fault or not. The following case is proposed: Certain vines were cut down at night by a certain ravager of fields, and whether this person was known or unknown. A complaint was brought against the village in a civil action before the judge of malefices. The inhabitants of the village were summoned to their individual homes; they appointed a syndic, who appeared for the defense of the village. Finally, the authority of the city of the said village, with the advice of the said judge of malefices, condemned the said village to one hundred [units]. And there is a statute in the said city that from the said sentence no appeal may be taken, nor may it be declared null. Finally, the said ravager was captured and died in prison; and because his body was deemed to belong to the republic, he was hanged by the rope. Lastly, execution of the said condemnation is sought against the said village. The question is: what is the law?

And I premise for the sake of clarity that, if the said statute did not exist, the said village, which has committed no fault and, due to justifiable ignorance, could not have provided against the harm, would not be liable for the said damage. For, although it is bound to the custody of its locality, it is not bound in this case to prohibit what it could not prohibit, since it was unaware. Hence, the text states: "We wish knowledge, not ignorance, to be binding," as in C. de tabulariis, l. generali; ff. de decretis ab ordinariis faciendis, l. si. For even lords are not liable for the acts of their subjects, unless they themselves commit a fault in the service in which the lords employ their labor, as in ff. de publicanis, l. 1, § familiae. Hence, the judge, by virtue of his jurisdiction, if there were no statute, could not condemn the village on this account. The text with the glossa ordinaria is in Auth. ut nulli iudicum, § quam vero, Collatio 9. But since the statute of the city dictates this, such a statute is valid, because, although not equitable, it is beneficial for the security of the territory. The text is in l. hec quid, ff. de incendio, ruina et naufragio. And it must be presupposed that that statute is valid in the case and form of which it expressly speaks. For all statutes, with their modes and times, signify to act or to suffer; nor should they be extended further. ff. de solutione matrimonii, l. si vero, § de viro. Having therefore presupposed that the said statute is valid.

† It is asked, as below. First, whether a civil complaint could have been brought before the judge of maleficia. And it seems that it could not, as in D. de iudicibus, l. solemus, § latrunculator. To the contrary, it seems that it could, because this complaint is criminal, since it arises from a crime, even though it aims at a pecuniary condemnation. For with respect to the village, it contains mere vindicta. Moreover, the judge of latrocinium may adjudicate interest arising by reason of the delict, or quasi-delict, as in D. de furtis, l. interdum, § qui furem; and l. pen. D. de calumniatoribus; and l. agraria, de termino moto. But it is doubted, because the sentence was not pronounced by a judge, but by the potestas, whether it is valid. And it seems that it is not, as in l. 1, D. de officio consulis. To the contrary, it seems that it is valid, because the same is the auditorium, as in c. 2, de consuetudinibus, lib. 6.

† Furthermore, it is doubted whether a citation made individually at the houses is valid. And the ordinary gloss determines that in the case of a universitas, as is elegantly and fully noted in the Digest, De re iudicata, in the law Non potest dolo carere. And this is true, that the citation held, especially because the statute provides that the banishment be proclaimed in the public square, as is noted in the chapter Causam, De electionibus, in the Decretals. And there the citation was not duly made: although it was made in some manner, the sentence is null by operation of law. The gloss is ordinary in the Code, De accusationibus, in the law Si accusatoribus. Hence, if the said village were condemned in absentia, it is null by operation of law. But there is doubt, because the syndicus was present; and certainly this also does not seem sufficient, because the syndicus could not waive the declinatory citation, since he could not alone be cited for the conscience of the universitas. Therefore, he could not alone appear: being perhaps less instructed by the universitas, as the gloss says in the aforementioned rule of law.

But assuming that all the aforementioned points were to fail: this depopulator came into the power of the community and into the custody of the creditor. It therefore seems sufficiently satisfied, since the crime has been fully punished, and the obligation of the village is extraordinary, as in D. 14.3.1 (Licet), § Possumus; and as noted in I. 4.15.13 (Si quadrupedans), in fine. For by the leniency of the law, the village is discharged by handing over the malefactor, as in D. 47.10.1 (1), § Quod novissime certe. It does not matter by whom they are handed over, for it would be the same if they went to their punishment of their own accord. Argument from D. 41.1.3 (Qui fundum) and D. 45.1.10 (Cum servus). Moreover, the party who suffered the damage ought to be content, since the malefactor has paid with his body. The case appears in the aforementioned § Qui furem. For it seems satisfaction has been made to him in the body in place of money, as in D. 47.10.1 (Sed si unius), § Si ante. And just as one who is absolved is discharged, so too is he who has paid the penalty with his own body with the effect of execution, as in D. 48.8.1 (Divus Vespasianus), in the word "absolvitur." And this defense supervenes after the condemnation of the village. And it is established that the exception of satisfaction made can be raised after sentence, as in C. 7.45.1 (1). That too must be considered, that the party who suffered the damage, by procuring the death of his enemy, acted in such a way that the laws cannot effectively operate against him, as in D. 46.1.56 (Si debitori deportatio). This last reason does not please me much: because he may cede his rights to the extent that he can against the goods, and against the fisc, which is liable for the interest of the party who suffered the damage, if there are any goods; and if there are no goods, it would suffice to cede, in Auth. 9.3.1 (Actionem). Argument from C. 10.10.1 (Quod locum), in the word "maneat." This question is small in respect to the sum, but it is not small in the disposition of the law, and finally, all things considered, it seems that the village is immune from the said condemnation: either because it was not legitimately cited, or because the ordinary remedy executed against the delinquent causes the extraordinary remedy against the village to cease. And this opinion seems to me natural and equitable, although the words of the statute do not distinguish. And although it is not said that satisfaction is made by the sentence alone, as in D. 43.1.1 (Nepoti), nevertheless here satisfaction was made, because he died in prison, and his body, although dead, endured the infamy of the gallows. But this should not have been done according to law, because a dead body does not feel the penalty, nor can a dead man be corrected, as in D. 48.19.1 (Si poena alicui). Someone will say, we see that a thief is hanged, and nevertheless the theft is compensated, either by compensation from his goods, as is noted in C. 9.27.1 (Quoniam civilis actio praeiudicet criminali), in the rubric and black letter, and in Auth. 3.1.1 (Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio), § Eos. Indeed, even the penal action for theft concurs with these, as in D. 13.2.1 (Si pro fure), § Furti actio. Nor does one consume the other, because they do not apply to the same thing, as in Auth. 3.1.1 (Ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio), § Oportet. To this I respond: because you object regarding actions, one of which is for vengeance, the other not, but in our case, both are for vengeance: because nothing accrues to the village. And whenever several actions tend to mere vengeance, one extinguishes the other, as in D. 47.10.1 (Quod senatus). And if you say, that is true because they apply against the same person. I respond, it seems the same if against different persons, when action is brought on quasi-delict. For the village is liable on quasi-delict, although the depopulator is liable on true delict. Hence, milder treatment is accorded to the village than to the depopulator, as in D. 9.3.1 (Perceptione) and there noted, D. 2.1.1 (Si quis id, quod), § Si melior. Nevertheless, consideration must be given that the village is discharged by prohibiting the delinquent, just as if it had caught the malefactor in the crime and handed him over, argument from C. 9.18.1 (Si) and in Auth. 3.1.1 (Ut nulli iudicum), § Si quis vero comprehensorum. And for this, the treatise on prohibited alienation of fiefs by Federicus, c. Imperialem, § Insuper, and on keeping the peace and its violators, cap. Si clericus, § Si iudex clamorem, are most apt. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that no legacy may be left to a woman except for 15 [units] annually, and the testator has bequeathed certain goods to one person and the usufruct of those goods to his wife, burdening the heir with respect to said wife in the said legacy, which legacy, however, exceeds the sum of 15, the question is asked: what is the law? See further below, in opinion 230.
body: In the name of Christ. Benigno left a certain plot of land and certain houses, and then, in the same will, he bequeathed the usufruct of the same plot of land and houses to his wife, on condition that she conduct herself as a widow and live chastely. Finally, he added these words directly addressed to the heir: that my heirs, the monks, may not molest or harass the said lady in the said legacies, or any part thereof; but they must allow her to have, hold, and enjoy in peace, use, and possess the aforementioned judgments and legacies. It is presupposed that there is a certain Pisan statute, which does not permit leaving to a wife more than 15 pounds of denarii annually. Now the question arises between the said legatee of the things, the legatee of the usufruct, and the universal heir.

† The question is asked to whom the usufruct pertains, whether to the said legatee of the lands and houses, or to the said legatee [the wife], or indeed to the universal heir. And it is argued that that which the woman cannot take pertains to the legatee of the things. For he who is not admitted to a share from the beginning does not make a share, as in D. de leg. 1, l. plane, § si duobus. To the contrary it seems, because he who cannot take makes a share. D. de leg. 2, l. si Titio, et ei. And thus half of the usufruct pertains to the legatee of the things, and insofar as the wife cannot take, it pertains to the universal heir; but rather it seems that nothing of the said usufruct pertains to the legatee of the things: because the said usufruct, considering the judgment of the testator, seems to have been entirely adempted from him and conferred upon the wife. And although the collation does not hold, nevertheless the ademption holds. The first is proven. D. de adim. leg. l. sicut, and arg. D. de pecul. leg. l. cum dominus, § fin. The second is proven. D. de adim. leg. l. licet transferan, where it is said that an invalid transfer extinguishes the legacy. The objection D. de haer. inst. l. Iulianus does not hold, because one thing is an invalid institution of an heir, which does not remove a valid one, since from the invalid one the inheritance cannot be entered into. As D. de lib. et posth. l. si filius, qui potestate. Another thing is a legacy, which is admitted by bare will, as fully noted. D. de adim. leg. l. ex parte. This difference is proven. D. de testa. mili. l. militi, codicillis, § veteranis. The objection to this D. de leg. 3, l. si iure facto testamento, does not hold, because here there was an express transfer, and consequently an express ademption is deemed, noted there; but there it was tacit, which does not arise from an invalid will. And therefore it seems prima facie to be concluded thus, that the said legatee of the things has the entire ownership and half of the usufruct. But the other half he would not have as adempted, as D. de usufructu leg. l. si alii fundum, and l. semper, no. in princ. eo. tit. and there noted. Moreover, the said half, which is not due to the wife, does not accrue to the legatee of the ownership: because it is due to another, namely the universal heir, while the woman lives. Arg. D. de usufr. leg. l. uxor usumfructum villae, and D. communia praedio. l. si in venditione. And if that which is left to the wife exceeds what is permitted by statute, it is deemed not written: it remains with the heir, insofar as it can be adapted to the heir, and as the limits of the legacy permit: as C. de cad. tollen. § et cum triplici, and no. D. de leg. 1, l. ciuitatibus, § Lucius, and D. de haeredi. inst. l. 2, and D. de do. l. pe. The legatee of the things therefore ought not to have more than is assigned to him. It is understood that only half is assigned to him. Furthermore, although by strict law this legacy is not due to the wife, nevertheless out of the kindness of the heir he may provide it to her, dictated by natural equity, as C. de necessa. seruis. l. quidam, § ille. Which natural equity prevents the right of accrual, as D. de leg. 1, l. plane, § si coniunctim. Moreover, this statute ought not to be followed by the Monks instituted as heirs. For from their conscience they ought to fulfill the vow of the testator, as appears in the legend of Saint Sylvester. Also because they are not subject to the laws of laymen, but to the law of God, according to which this legacy is valid, and rightly, because chastity is to be rewarded, as in Auth. de non eli. se. nu. § Gregoria. And certain things ought to be done de facto, although they do not hold de iure, as D. de ver. ob. l. quidam cum filium, D. de cap. dimi. l. legatum, D. de adim. leg. l. seruos ad custodiam templi. The objection l. 1, C. de secundis nup. does not hold, because that is on account of the immodesty of the marrying woman within the year. But this one, who fulfills the mandate of the testator and guards his honor, is worthy of reward, arg. D. de manu. test. l. meuia. The solution of this question does not rest in any of these allegations: but something else is to be considered. And it must be premised that formerly there were four kinds of legacies, among which was one kind, which was called by the mode of allowing. These kinds have not been abolished, but the differences of the kinds have been abolished, as Inst. de leg. in princ. And therefore if the testator commands the heir to allow Titius to have, possess, or enjoy peacefully: it is understood that he leaves it to him, in whole or in part, as the writing sounds: as C. communia de leg. l. 1. And for him all actions are available which are available for legacies. Because now we are in the very legacy which is called by the mode of allowing. Because the heir is bound to allow the legatee to have and hold the said usufruct in whole, and to enjoy, use, and possess in peace, and in whole or in part not to hinder the said legatee. By which it is designated by express words that the said woman is left legatee in the entire and solid usufruct by that kind of legacy which is called by the mode of allowing. From which follows such a conclusion, that whether this legacy is called a transfer, or is called a declaration of the will not to leave the usufruct to the said legatee of the things, nothing is due to the said legatee of the usufruct aforesaid while the woman lives. Either because it is adempted, or because it does not seem to be left to the said legatee. The objection D. de condi. et demon. l. nam ad ea does not hold, because there it speaks when there are several forms of leaving to the same legatee. And the forms are compatible by alternation, hence the Instrument says, the election falls.
