But in our case it is not so, because there are different legatees: and since the entire usufruct is left to the woman, and the testator considered the effect of perception, rightly nothing of the said usufruct is due to the said owner, because the testator does not seem to have burdened the heir with double performance, as C. de cad. tol. § si autem disiunctim, and D. de leg. 2, l. Titia, § qui in vita. Repeating the conclusion, I conclude that the fruits of the said things while the said woman lives do not in any way pertain to the said owner of the naked ownership, diligently inspecting and knowing the words of the said testament, as D. de transac. l. de his controuersiis. But that which I would not think to be rightly said is that the legatee of the things seems to be burdened with providing the said usufruct: because the burden of a legacy in doubt seems to be attached and imposed on the heir, arg. D. de leg. 1, l. si seruus, § qui Margaritam. The objection C. ad tre. l. fi does not hold, because there it speaks of a universal fideicommissary: when the testator, in making his will, preserved this order, because first he instituted, second he burdened the whole, third he made singular legacies. But here it is not so, and therefore they do not obstruct. I commend the consilia rendered in this matter, because they are subtle and good: for by what I have said the truth becomes clearer. On other points it is no longer expedient to advise, because the sword is placed at the root. I, Bal.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. This matter was consulted on in consilium 131, and therefore it is not taken otherwise, although here he speaks more subtly and with greater ingenuity. See also above, consilium 199.
body: In the name of Christ. That the lessor delivered into the field one basket of wheat sown; this basket was delivered in a certain salary [or loft], and consequently was not sown in the field, because it is impossible, for wheat cannot be sown in a salary [or loft]. There follows the confession of the tenant, that the lessor delivered the said wheat in the loft, which was afterwards sown. These are the words of the confession. The witnesses say, as if wishing to prove, that it was not delivered, nor sown; but the other party subtly argues, in order to evade the promise of damages, or to declare a lesser interest, that granted that it was not delivered, nor sown, it is possible that it was first delivered, and afterwards sown. For such [witness] deposes nothing regarding whether it was sown afterwards or not. But the instrumental confession divides time, because first it says that it was delivered, secondly that it was sown. Distinguish the times, and you will reconcile the writing, as in C. de fur. l. apud antiquos. and extra de testi. c. cum tu filii. The question is what is the law. For the lessor rightly wishes to offer damages: because he himself did not sow, but not because it was not sown by someone. For by whomever it is sown, total damages cease, and particular damages for expenses remain. Similar. ff. rem ra. ha. l. si sine. and ff. de procu. l. qui absente. The question is what is the law. I answer, the opposition is strong. And in the first opinion which he gave, it was said to me verbally, that the question stood solely on a bare pact. And therefore I did not consider it further to advise. It is therefore necessary to consider anew: because those things which newly emerge, etc. I therefore consider that a witness is not understood to speak foolishly, but according to how a natural and discrete man speaks. It is therefore necessary to inspect the nature of things. The witness therefore says that he did not deliver into the salary [or loft] sown [wheat]. Either the witness intends regarding that which was sown previously, and he speaks foolishly: because that which is sown is in the field, which cannot be delivered in the loft. It is therefore necessary that the witness speak by negation of sowing in the field. I.e., that that which was delivered in the loft was not then sown in the loft, which is impossible: nor afterwards sown in the field. For this negative proposition the text can best prove: because it can be seen. Thus, it appears to act unsown, just as sown: and especially by rustics. And therefore from great necessity, which is the mistress of truth, it appears that the witness expressly proves that the field was not sown at the time of the instrumental confession, nor afterwards. And that necessity is the mistress of truth, the text says, C. de epis. et cle. l. omnes, qui ubique. §. fi. Furthermore, the said confession is uncertain, because it does not say by whom it was sown. Hence by this it is not proved that the interest of the lessee ceased: because a certain third party could have sown, who would have an action of negotiorum gestorum against the lessee on account of the seed and labor. This reason does not please me. By l. vltimam. C. de alimen. pupillo. and by no. per Bart. ff. de verbo. oblig. l. cum seruus. But the first reason pleases: because it is friendly to the truth of fact and law. Since the said confession of the lessees was made under the hope of performance of damages for the wheat not delivered. Because it concerns the principal, but not the expenses, which come incidentally; otherwise the contracting parties would have expressly stated regarding the expenses. Hence general wording in such a case draws the peril, as C. de don. promis. l. fi. in fi. and words are to be referred to the probable. Also, this indefinite [phrase] "not sown" is equivalent to a universal negative. I.e., never or in no way sown. And these words were words uttered by the lessor, who promised damages on the occasion of seeds not delivered. I.e., in no way delivered, nor in any way sown. For if they were delivered only, or sown only, this negative, which is taken from the universal, would be false, as ff. de re. du. l. si is, qui ducenta. §. utrum. Also, they could not have been delivered and sown, if they were not delivered. For the first is delivery. The second is sowing. And if you begin by denying the first, the second is inferred of necessity. Namely, that they were not delivered, therefore neither delivered nor sown cannot be referred to the same place: because not to the loft, and not sown. Hence those words, "delivered sown to the field." Hence neither in the loft nor in the field was faith kept. And otherwise, by explaining, it would seem a foolish disposition, as I declared above. The confession of the instrument says that the lessee confessed to himself that it was delivered in the house. The witnesses repudiate this first step, namely, that delivery was not made in the house. And only one delivery is alleged, not several: nor is plurality presumed, as in capitu. cum Ioan. Haeremi. de fide instrumento. Therefore this confession is repudiated as not true. And this first foundation being presupposed, it is impossible that this wheat, of which the confession speaks, was sown: because that which is not, cannot be sown. Then I argue thus. It was not delivered, nor sown, therefore he who ought to deliver and sow is bound to total damages. Moreover, the confession does not say that it was sown wholly, or in part, nor at the time of sowing, nor afterwards. Hence it does not appear that the interest ceased. He must prove this conclusively and necessarily, just as anyone who has to prove his intention or exception: as extra de proba. capi. in praesentia. It is not an obstacle that it is subtly said, that the witnesses say that it was not delivered, sown: because the words of the witness must be understood sanely, and to good understanding. I.e., that it was not delivered in the house, nor sown in the land. For these two adjectives, delivered and sown, are resolved into two substantives, because one cannot inhere in the other by mode of quality, nor of place, or time. Also it sufficiently appears, if it was not delivered, therefore neither sown. This they also expressly say there, and afterwards it was found that they lacked regarding the sum of the said blandum [wheat], it does not say regarding the sowing of the said blandum, but regarding the sum. And this diction "to the sum" signifies substance and measure, as ff. de verbo. obligationi. l. triticum. ff. si cer. peta. l. certum. It is therefore manifest that on account of the defect of sum and measure, the grain was not delivered, sown, nor not sown: because the principle being denied, all things which are after the principle are denied. And the truth of the fact is thus, which truth is to be aided by interpretation of wisdom. And in doubtful cases we must embrace that which is more probable. Also, no one sows wind, but wheat, as C. de alimen. pupillorum. l. fina. and ff. de actio. emptio. l. si sterilis. §. cum per venditorem. And I say this with due reverence. Also, let it please to consider, that the confession of one of joint debtors does not harm the other, when it is made by mode of voluntary jurisdiction: because confession operates no more than a pact, as ff. de pac. l. tale pactum. in princi. and l. si vnus. in prin. and it is expressed in confession. C. de noua. l. non abstulit. For without mandate no one can prejudice another by confessing: although he confesses payment. Although he can prejudice by receiving true payment. And the reason of the difference is, because payment comes from the nature of the obligation, but confession comes outside the nature of the obligation. Hence in confessing there are not two debtors to yield for the reason aforesaid. And it makes what fully no. Bar. ff. de duo. reis. l. ex duobus. in 9. q. and more fully in 6. quęstione. where he determines that when they are joint debtors from an onerous cause, the confession of one of the joint debtors to yield does not prejudice the other: nor a pact in his portion. And in this I do not think it necessary to insist. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Allegations on behalf of the Minor Brothers.
1. A cleric cannot be dragged before a secular judge, even if he himself consents.
2. Whether a public way can be acquired by prescription.
3. From patience over forty years, a grant of public use is presumed.
4. On the interpretation of the law *Viam* in the Digest, title *De via publica*.
body: In the name of Christ. It was enjoined upon the Friars Minor by Lord Gerardo de Bobio, vicar of the Bon. lord Giovanni de Repusano, vicar of the Illustrious and Magnificent Prince, our Lord the Duke, that he ought within 10 days to have opened a certain lane or pathway, which is said to belong to the commune of Pavia, etc.

† The question arises whether the said precept could emanate or not. And it is briefly answered that it could not, because the aforesaid Lord Gerardo and Lord Giovanni possess concerning this neither ordinary jurisdiction, since they are secular judges, nor delegated jurisdiction, since they lack a special mandate from our Illustrious Lord. For although they might have a general commission—which is nonetheless not established—our Lord is not understood to commit that religious persons and monasteries be drawn to a forbidden forum, as in C. de iuris. om. iudi. l. in criminali; for only that is deemed to be commanded which can lawfully be commanded, ff. de condi. indebi. l. si procurator. §. celsus. Likewise, the community of Pavia has no jurisdiction against the said friars, even if the said friars wished to submit themselves to its jurisdiction; for they could not do this, but rather would be punished by law, as in extra de iudi. c. at si clerici; extra de foro compe. c. si diligenti; and they state this with reverence as far as jurisdiction is concerned. Regarding the principal matter, however, the said friars state that they possess justice and truth, which they will demonstrate before a competent judge, or before whomever our Lord shall commission. And from now on they protest that all their exceptions and rights remain, and shall remain, intact. And the said friars protest with reverence, but under canonical penalties and cautions, that no innovation be made against the friars themselves, who have possessed for an exceedingly long time by just title and in good faith.

† It is necessary to reply to l. viam publicam, ff. de uia publica, which says that the people does not lose a public way by non-use, just as it does not lose the right of going to the Holy Sepulchre or to Saint James; and thus it seems to say expressly that a public way is prescribed by no lapse of time, even by the space of one hundred years, as the gl. says there. And I say that that law does not stand in the way, for several reasons. First, because this is not prescription, but custom. For the Friars Minor cannot prescribe any property, since they cannot have property; but it can well be introduced by custom that the people do not use a way in which base acts and crimes are committed, which are against God, the honor of the blessed Francis, and the state of the Friars Minor. For such a custom is reasonable. Indeed, furthermore, the people itself seems to prescribe that custom, or at least to approve it, on account of the justice of public decency, and indeed of public utility: because what is publicly decent is publicly useful. For formerly so many base and abominable things were done in the said alleyway that it was just and lawful that the said alleyway, or pathway, should be closed. For brothels ought not to stand in the midst of the gardens of the Friars Minor, as they formerly were, as in C. de re mili. l. cum supra virentes, lib. 12; whence the custom of enclosing the said alleyway, which was then not a way, but the contempt and disgrace of the city, had a just and godly origin.

† Furthermore, the said alleyway has remained thus closed off for a time of 40 years and more by concession of the people of Pavia, and this is notorious in the city of Pavia, and also notorious in law: because a concession is presumed from such great patience and such long desuetude of the people, as noted in ff. de vsu. l. cum de in rem verso, and it is the ordinary gloss also of canon law, 16. q. 3. c. dilecto. Furthermore, when the reason of the law ceases, and a contrary reason supervenes, the law ceases, as in l. adigere. §. quamuis. ff. de iure patron.; but the reason of l. viam publicam is public utility, therefore, since public utility is not involved here, nor the reason of public utility, the disposition of that law ceases. And this seems express in ff. de diuer. et tempo. praescri. l. si quisque and ff. de vsuca. l. fi.

† Furthermore, l. viam publicam ought to be understood so long as it is public; but when, by express or tacit consent of the people, it has been reduced to the form of a private way, certainly such a way can well be acquired by use, at least in favor of religion, as in ff. de relig. l. si quis Sepulchrum, in princi., and ff. de vsufructu. l. locum, and what is noted there. Furthermore, the said friars name the Lord Pope in judgment, whose are all the possessions of the Friars Minor. And they protest lest anything be done in this matter alone without his being consulted, as in extra vt lite non contesta. c. quoniam frequenter, and C. vbi in rem actio. l. 2. And although these allegations are clear in law and in fact, nevertheless they petition and humbly pray for the sake of God—since it does not befit the servants of God to litigate, as in extra de iudi. c. cum deputati—that you do not hinder them, especially because to take away the property of churches and monasteries is a kind of sacrilege, as in extra de foro compe. c. cum sit generale. These allegations are submitted to the venerable and holy council of justice of our Lord. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the father's domicile passes to the son.
2. Whether the son, by residing in the father's house, is deemed to have accepted his inheritance.
3. A written will requires that the name of the heir be written by the testator.
body: In the name of Christ. The father's domicile.

† It is asked whether it passes to the son. I answer: yes, as regards obtaining forum from the person of the father, as in ff. de iudi. l. haeres absens. in princ. Likewise as regards the burdens to which the father obligated himself, as in ff. ad muni. l. incola. iam. and C. de inco. l. ciues. As to other matters, the son can change the accidental paternal domicile by transferring it, and the paternal household gods, in reality, as in ff. ad municipa. l. domicilium. cum si., very prudently cited by dominus Signorius. The conclusion is: when a domicile has been contracted by his own will and that of another, to which an obligation is attached, such a paternal domicile does not follow the son.

† It is asked, moreover, whether the son, by inhabiting the paternal house, is presumed to intermeddle in the paternal inheritance. I answer: yes, because the fruit of a house is habitation; but he who gathers the fruits of an estate property is deemed to enter upon the inheritance, as in insti. de hęredum quali. et diffe. §. fi. and l. 1. C. de repu. hęre. Likewise, one is presumed to possess by virtue of a preceding title, as in C. de acq. pos. l. 2., unless something else appears from a paternal entry continued by the son; an intermeddling is presumed, if no other reason for possessing underlies it.

† Concerning the third question, the case is in C. de testa. l. iubemus. and l. cum antiquitas. and auth. quod sententiae subscriptione, if we speak of a written testament properly and strictly speaking, and l. hac consultissima. A written testament, that is, one not made by nuncupation, requires that the name of the heir be written by the testator or by another at his mandate, as in C. de testa. l. iubemus. and the authentica ‘et eo non obseruato’. It does not, however, require that the witnesses who subscribe know the name of the heir, as in C. de test. l. hac consultissima. It is necessary, however, that the witnesses who subscribe express the name of the testator, since they must have been requested by him, as in insti. de test. §. testes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statutes concerning the making of compromises, and that no appeal may be taken from the sentence of an arbitrator, whether one may at least petition for restitutio in integrum.
2. A place is presumed to have been appended to the instrument on account of the connection of the cause.
3. Whether a sentence confirming an arbitral award is vitiated by the fault of the arbitrators.
body: In the name of Christ. For the praise of the secure city.

First, that no appeal or complaint may be brought on grounds of nullity or inequity from precepts, arbitrations, and arbitral awards rendered between agnates or cognates. Second, generally, that if, in the case of arbitral awards from which an appeal may be taken, it is pronounced in favor of such precepts or arbitral awards, no appeal or complaint may be brought. Third, it is provided that all arbitrations, precepts, and arbitral awards rendered by whomsoever shall be ordered to be executed, although one may have five useful days to state and allege that such arbitrations and arbitral awards are unjust and inequitable.

The case is as follows: A certain guardian, acting in the name of her ward, together with her friends, declared that an arbitral award rendered against her was inequitable. However, because she did not prove the inequity, or even if she did prove it, the judge did not take heed, as in the Digest, *De edendo*, law *Argentarius*, section *Cum autem*, the arbitral award was confirmed. An appeal was taken from this confirmation. The question is: what is the law?

I answer that, by the third and final statute, the aforementioned appeal appears to be precluded. The reason is that the ward, who failed to prove her case, may prove it through restitution in integrum, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Minor viginti quinque annis*, section *Omissam*. Moreover, if she proved that the judge did not heed the witnesses produced, she may still prove her case more clearly and evidently. And the judge of the appeal, upon invoking the remedy of restitution in integrum, may restore the minor to full rights even after the testimony has been heard, as in the Code, *De appellationibus*, law *Praeses*; and in the Digest, *De non obtemperando operis novi nuntio*, law 1, section *Adversus*.

Furthermore, the statute makes no mention of restitution in integrum sought against omitted proof, and thus against the falsity of the minor’s claim, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, law *Si ex causa*, section *Nunc videndum*. Moreover, a judgment is rendered in one manner when restitution to prove is sought, and in another manner when restitution against a matter adjudicated or arbitrated is sought. For regarding restitution to prove, even if one prevails, one does not thereby win the case unless one subsequently proves it, as in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, law *Nam postea*, section *Si minor*. And therefore the statute does not stand in the way, because nothing is directly asserted against the arbitral award. Moreover, restitution in integrum is not extinguished, because it was not even attempted.

In support of this, see the Digest, *Ad Senatusconsultum Trebellianum*, law *Servo invito*, section *Cum prior*; and the Digest, *Mandati*, law *Creditor*, section *Lucius*, in the final part; and the Digest, *De in integrum restitutione*, law *Divus*, section *Nec intra has*. And by this, the response to the statute is clear, because the statute does not speak to this case. It is similar to what we say, that no appeal lies from a judgment rendered in a possessory action, and yet an appeal may well be taken from omitted proof and the expiration of a time limit, as is clear from the Code, *De iudicibus*, law *Properandum*, joined with the beginning and the end. Moreover, the equity of truth moves me.

† On another point, because it is said that a certain place is not stated in the notarial instrument, it must be said that, on the contrary, a certain place is tacitly added by the connection of the cause and the connection of the instruments, as in D. 42.1.1 (*Si quis ex argentariis*), § *Si initium tabularum*; and because things done immediately are presumed to have been done in the same place and time, as in D. 40.12.1 (*Lecta*); and because even imperfect writings are supplied by preceding ones which possess clarity, as in D. 35.1.1 (*Si servus plurium*), § *Si*, and D. 35.2.1 (*Cum pater*), § *Cum imperfecta*.

† On the third point, whether by a confirmatory sentence the gross negligence of the arbitrators is concealed. I answer that, if it is established, it appears that both will judge through gross negligence, and one negligence does not validate the other, as in D. de appellatione, l. si expressum. And by this, where in another opinion I spoke dubiously, I now declare, because that which appears manifestly from the records is not said to be concealed, or concealable, as in D. de re iudicata, l. in summa, and fully noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de errore calculi. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether letters are said to be obtained by concealment by remaining silent about the fact that another person had long been in possession of the said benefice after the letters had been obtained, and that the right of election pertains to the chapter.
2. Whether benefices can be acquired by prescription through the longest period of time, and without title.
body: In the name of Christ. Titius obtained from the Legate a latere in those parts the archpriestry of the collegiate and parish church of Saint Marcellus, as being vacant in those parts and devolved to the Apostolic See, which was accustomed to be conferred by the election of the canons of the said church. Titius omitted to make mention in his said petition that the said archpriestry was accustomed to be conferred by election; but he merely stated that the said benefice was collegiate, parochial, and devolved. And since the said archpriestry had for a long time been de facto detained and occupied by Gaius, and was also being detained by the same Gaius at the time of the said petition, the above-mentioned Titius omitted to mention for how long the said Gaius had detained the aforementioned archpriestry. But the case is such that he simply made mention of the present detention, which existed at the time of the above-mentioned petition, saying, “although Gaius de facto detains the said archpriestry, etc.” From the foregoing, it is asked whether the petition of Titius can be said to be defective, because it does not mention that the said archpriestry was accustomed to be conferred by the election of the canons of the said church, notwithstanding that he stated that the benefice was collegiate, parochial, and devolved.

† Furthermore, it is asked whether the said petition may be deemed subreptive, because it does not mention that the aforementioned Gaius held the said archpriestry for so long a time, notwithstanding that in the said petition he stated that the above-named Gaius in fact held the said archpriestry at the time of the aforementioned petition. Moreover, that which is tacit and included by the nature of the express, and even more so, is not a matter of legal distinction, as in D. si certum petatur, l. cum quid; and C. de fideiussoribus, l. non recte; and D. de legatis 1, l. haec verba. But that which is tacit and not included by the nature of the express causes the letters to be considered subreptive, or such a cause to be considered not included in the letters, as in X. de praebendis, c. cum in illis, § in illis vero, and § se, lib. 6. Having premised this, the question arises here as to whether, by making mention that the benefice is collegiate and curate, the election is included. And I say that either the election was made according to the common law, and it is included, as in X. de electione, c. 1; or it was not made according to the common law but by custom, and it is not included. Hence, according to what is proposed, I do not consider the letters subreptive. For the benefice being collegiate is like the faculty of election, or to elect is like the act. And mention having been made of the faculty, mention is understood to have been made of the act; just as mention having been made of the form, mention is understood to have been made of its operation, as in D. de legatis 1, l. Titiae textores. And from the fact that he administered before confirmation, deprivation is induced, but it is not properly called vacancy, because he had not yet acquired the benefice. And therefore, even from this omission, the letters should not be considered subreptive; because this is not a mode of vacancy, but an impediment to an imperfect benefice. As to the second point, the letters are not considered subreptive; because the longer one possesses without having canonical admission, the more one is a usurper.

† Nor is he aided by the long duration of possession in the case of benefices, because they cannot be acquired by prescription, as is stated in the extrajudicial collection on witnesses, chapter *Ex parte*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Statutes are abrogated by contrary custom. A similar opinion.
body: In the name of Christ. Dam A. took as his wife a certain woman named B., who remained with him in marriage for ten years; after ten years, however, the said wife B. died without children. Wherefore the brother of the said B. demands that the dowry be returned to him according to the common custom of that place. The husband, named A., opposes, saying that the said dowry pertains to him by virtue of a certain ancient statute enacted by the commune of that place, which provides that if a wife has lived with her husband for ten years, and then, upon the husband’s subsequent death, dies without children, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry; a statute which was never alleged except at that time. Indeed, the common custom in the aforementioned place was always that if a wife was found to have died without children, whenever the dowry was always recovered by the nearest relatives. That statute, although it was in the volume of statutes of that place, was not affirmed, nor read, and published in the public assembly of the men of that land. Nor does this appear, except that in 1381, on June 5, at which time the Illustrious Lord of Milan held that place, the aforementioned statute was confirmed. However, it does not appear that it was read and published. From this two doubts arise: first, whether the aforementioned statute is valid, which at the time it was enacted was not read and published in the public assembly of the people, although it was later confirmed by the superior; second, if it was not read and published at the time of confirmation, whether the aforementioned statute is valid, which at the time it was enacted was not read and published, although at the time of confirmation it was read and published in the public assembly of the people.

† A custom, by which one returns to the common law, is prescribed. That is, it is established by time and the public use of the citizens: even if it has not been obtained in a contradictory judicial proceeding; because a thing easily returns to its nature. Indeed, it is tacitly considered to have been obtained in a contradictory judicial proceeding, precisely because judgments were pronounced according to the common law. Nor do I care whether mention was made of the municipal statute in the sentences, or not, as in D. de legibus, l. de quibus, with its subject matter. For certain matters are not debated in a contradictory judicial proceeding, and yet a custom is prescribed, for example, the custom of making a will. In the same way, therefore, the custom of restoring a dowry. Likewise, the custom of succeeding intestate, or in certain things: because these are of voluntary power, and arise and are done outside of court; nor do they pertain to the judge by any necessity of law, as in D. de legibus 3, l. 3, § si rem posito. Therefore, although interlocutory or definitive sentences are sometimes required to prescribe a judicial custom, they are not required for an extra-judicial custom. Wherefore, in the question proposed, the said statute was abrogated by a contrary custom, proved and confirmed by the common law. Moreover, the said statute was invalid, because it was not published, as in Auth. ut factae novae constitutiones, in the rubric, and in Nigro. Moreover, its confirmation was also invalid, because the statute did not precede it. For where there is no publication, there is no statute; and where that which is to be confirmed does not proceed, the confirmation does not hold, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationes, quae propriis viribus non subsistunt; as in D. de legibus 2, l. cum ita legatur quicquid. Moreover, the said confirmation was obtained by concealment, because the contrary custom was not expressed in the confirmation; for if it had been expressed, the statute would certainly not have been confirmed, being abolished. It appears, therefore, that the custom should be followed, which has the force of custom with regard to the derogation of municipal law. Moreover, it has the force of common law with regard to its formal essence. And thus should be understood what is read and noted in c. 1, de constitutionibus, lib. 6. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A bona fide purchaser is protected by the forty-year prescription, unless the seller was a church, to which such prescription does not prejudice.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The case is as follows: P. killed L. while under ban in the year 1359, and in that same year the said P. was condemned on account of the said homicide to beheading, and his goods were confiscated, saving the right of creditors and of descendants according to the form of the city's statutes; and it was declared by the sentence then rendered concerning the said homicide that half of the aforesaid goods belonged to the heir of the slain person. Afterward, while the said slayer was still alive and under the ban for the aforesaid homicide, A., B., and C., the sisters of that slayer—who were married and likewise dowered—seized the said goods on their own authority and without any title, and divided them in the year 1350 [sic], and later sold them in the year 1362, in which same year the heir of the slain person died, who left all his goods, both movable and immovable, and whatsoever actions and rights belonged to him, by testament to two chapels then established by him. Now it is asked whether the said division and sale could be made or not to the prejudice of the said chapels; and whether the rectors of those chapels, who were ignorant and unaware of the said goods acquired for them by virtue of the said sentence, except recently, namely in the year 1364, can claim those goods notwithstanding the lapse of the aforesaid time; or whether the said sisters, about whom the question is raised, could not sell the share adjudicated to the heirs of the slain person because it did not belong to them, yet the purchasers, who bought in good faith, had good faith and possessed for an exceedingly long time in good faith—whence, if there were a dispute concerning the things and it were not with a church, they would be protected by prescription, especially that of the longest time, as in C. de pręscriptione 30. annorum l. si quis emptionis. Because these things passed to churches or chapels, against which a prescription of less than 40 years—to be computed at least from the day of purchase—does not run; which time indeed has not elapsed against the chapels or churches: as in C. de sacrosanc. eccle. authen. quas actiones. and de pręscrip. cap. de quarta. And therefore the chapels have the right. And although the church succeeds without privilege, nevertheless for the future time of prescription it enjoys its privilege: argument from C. de pręscrip. lon. tempo. authen. si autem quibusdam; ff. de vsur. l. cum quidam. §. fiscus; and most fully noted on the said authen. quas actiones by Pe., Cyn., and others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. On account of its brevity, it is not taken as a summary. And the understanding is placed in l. bene a Zenone.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Just as it was pronounced in favor of lady Beltramina, or her heirs, so original justice truly stood, as in ff. de inoffi. testa. l. nam et si parentibus. But because that Magnificent and glorious man reserved to himself the castle with the custody and honorances, and afterwards gave or granted in fief the said castle with its dignity and lordship to certain persons, who possessed it for a period of thirty years, as is alleged, a doubt arises for me, and especially on account of l. bene a Zenone, since I equate or identify that lordship with the fiscus; and in this matter I do not wish to set my mouth against heaven. Regarding, however, the prescription of the longest period of time, I have less doubt, because it would have been interrupted, provided we were outside the case of l. bene a Zenone. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A partnership contracted by a minor and sworn to is, insofar as he was prejudiced, invalid, unenforceable, and subject to rescission.
2. An oath that attaches to a contract of good faith is one of good faith; whereas one that attaches to a contract of strict law is one of strict law.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The point is as follows: A., B., C., and D. formed a partnership of all goods among themselves to last for up to 10 years, on the condition, however, that any one of them could withdraw from the partnership with impunity. In this partnership, A. contributed more than the others by more than half. However, because he was nonetheless an adolescent, he swore not to contravene it, either on the occasion of minority or on any other occasion, nor on the ground of deception beyond half the just price, and without any other solemnity of law. From this partnership they subsequently withdrew immediately—namely, after two years or thereabouts—by a machination devised from the very beginning by the other partners, who were of full age and shrewd. Hence it is asked whether, notwithstanding the oath, A. may contravene it and return to his former legal standing.

† I premise for clarity that an oath attached to a good-faith contract is of good faith, and that which is attached to a contract of strict law is of strict law; and this I prove by the analogy of a pact added immediately. For if it is attached to a good-faith contract, it gives rise to an action praescriptis verbis, which is of good faith, as in C. de pactis inter empto. et ven. l. nisi; if, however, it is attached to a contract of strict law, it is of strict law, as noted in ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium. §. quinimmo. And the reason is that the principal imparts to the accessory its own quality which it has from the beginning, as noted in ff. si cer. pe. l. certi conditio. in prin. From this it is thus inferred that, since the contract of partnership is a contract of good faith, if fraud gave cause to it, the partnership does not hold ipso iure, nor does the oath, nor is it necessary that that be done through the bishop which has been done—that is, remitted—ipso iure, as in l. quae sub conditione. §. vlt. ff. de cond. insti. and l. adigere. §. fi. ff. de iure patronatus. Moreover, the enormity of the lesion, the minor age, and the proximity of the persons testify that fraud gave cause to the partnership here, as in C. de in integrum resti. mino. l. de Tutela; and where the enormity of lesion is in propatulo—that is, open—to those of full age themselves, there fraud is presumed, as Bar. elegantly noted in alia man. s. in l. poenul. ff. de praeto. sti. Wherefore I say that the said partnership, full of fraud, did not hold, nor did any obligation arise from the pacts, nor was ownership transferred by fictitious delivery, since the property was that of a minor, because possession does not pass immediately from an invalid contract without bodily delivery, as in ff. de pollicit. l. si quis rem. §. voto. As for what is customarily said in ff. de dolo. l. eleganter. in prin., that the contract proceeds as invalid: delivery must be invalidated through the action de dolo and criminally by the crime of stellionate. This is to be understood of bodily delivery, not of civil and fictitious delivery, which does not arise from an invalid contract, because fictions of law require a factual subsistence. For the nature of fictions is to supply where the fact is lacking, and in that which is not contrary to law, as uniquely noted in ff. de leg. 1. l. talis scriptura. I say therefore that, since open fraud was present in the said partnership contracted with the said minor relative by those older in age who reaped the fruits, the said partnership was ipso iure void, exceedingly limping, and fraudulent; and therefore the oath did not hold, as in auth. Sacramenta. from the contrary sense. Furthermore, an oath is never observed except on account of the bond of equity, but here it would be a bond of iniquity and fraudulence, as in l. illicite. in prin. ff. de offi. praesidis. Nor does the gloss in l. 2. de rescin. vend. stand in the way, because there the fraud had not preceded the oath, but here it did. It must also be considered that the said partnership was contracted for up to ten years, and therefore the goods were not pooled except up to the ten-year period; and therefore, the partnership being ended, the capital ought to be preserved safe for each party, as is fully read and noted in l. 1. C. pro socio. Nor does profit extend beyond the pre-established time, since it is a limited time, as in ff. de pac. l. episcopali. §. fi. and l. si vnus. §. 1. eo. ti.; and although the ten years had not elapsed, nevertheless the ten-year period was renounced because the partnership was dissolved. To this the reply seems to be that the instrument states that he was certified concerning the benefit; but another reason underlies this, because he was not certified concerning the amount of the loss, and in the case of a minor, if ignorance is presumed, all the more is ignorance of fact presumed; and for greater certainty of the said consilium, consider the words of the instrument where it says, 'renouncing the defense of fraud.' For here we do not ask about a defense, but about nullity; and it does not follow that they cannot say or allege that they were deceived in any part of that contract. For by thus renouncing, the minor is harmed all the more, and greater fraud is shown, as uniquely noted in ff. de con. insti. l. sub conditione. la picola. and ff. de nou. l. doli mali. and ff. de mino. l. si iudex circunuento. And it follows in the instrument: 'and they swore to observe and not to contravene for any reason or cause in law or in fact, by reason of minor age.' Ioan. And. and Di. state that this does not prejudice him, since the minor was not certified concerning the benefit of minority. It follows in the instrument: 'and of modest or enormous loss.' For the same reason this does not prejudice him, because he was not certified concerning this, as in ff. de iuris, et fac. igno. l. regula; and because, as I have said, the adult is deemed to have been induced by fraud by his relatives, as in ff. vnde cognati. l. octaui. and the said l. de tutela; and because the bishop ought subsidiarily to cause the said oath to be relaxed on account of the enormity, as in l. illicitas. in princip. and by the argument of ff. de transac. l. cum aquiliana. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the risk of the thing sold before it is delivered pertains to the buyer or to the seller: and similarly whether the action lies with the buyer or with the seller.
body: In the name of Christ. The Cartusians of Saint James near Asti sold to Bartholomew and James de Socino, citizens of Asti, the share they held in a certain shop located in Asti, which share amounts to seven parts out of twelve, minus one thirtieth part of one twelfth. Upon this being done, they ordered Niccolino Beinerii, who previously held that share by lease, to deliver the aforementioned share to the said buyers and to hand over to them the keys of the said share. He promised to do this in the presence of the witnesses below within ten days. And then, there and then, the said Cartusians introduced the said buyers into possession of the said share by bringing them into the said shop and having them manually grasp the lock. Now, however, the said Niccolino, who previously held the said share by lease, does not wish to deliver it, but in fact holds and occupies it, and he violently threw out into the street the goods of the buyers, which they had placed in the said shop, and does not allow them to possess it. Hence, the question arises: what legal action should and may the sellers or the buyers bring against the said Niccolino, and whether the said sellers can bring any action against him.

I premise, for the sake of clarity, that all damage, all risk, and all injury occurring before the sold thing is delivered pertains to the seller, who is bound to act for the benefit of the buyer, as stated in D. 43.16.1 (*Is qui in puteum*), § *Si postea*; D. 19.2.1 (*In plures*), § *Vestimenta*; D. 14.2.2, § *Si res*; and D. 13.6.1 (*Si sic*), § *Si*. But if, after the thing has been sold and fully delivered, an injury is done to the buyer, the seller cannot bring an action on this matter, because the risk is that of the buyer, as stated in D. 18.1.1 (*Quod si neque*), in the beginning and § *Si*; D. 18.1.1 (*Id quod*); and D. 21.2.1 (*Lucius*). Therefore, in our case, it must be considered whether, after full delivery, the lessee used force against the buyer. If so, the seller cannot act before full delivery; but if so, as stated in D. 43.16.1 (*Colonus*), action may be brought in two ways: one by interdict, the other by action on lease, so that possession be restored to the buyer. Four words of the testament, as they say, or others, to whom the lessor wishes, as stated in D. 41.2.1 (*Si procuratorem*), § *Si quis*; and D. 41.2.1 (*Idemque*), § *Si cui mandauero, ut a Titio*. It is also not doubtful that the buyer himself may act on his own injury after fictitious delivery. And therefore, according to what is proposed, the said lodger may be sued in multiple ways, both by the sellers and by the buyer, to whom it was fictitiously but not fully restored; because the lessees had not withdrawn from detention, and thus had not left the thing vacant as they ought, because although a tenant farmer is understood to lease for a year, a lodger is not understood to lease except for as long as he dwells there, unless something else is expressly or tacitly agreed, as stated in D. 19.2.1 (*Item quaeritur*), § *Qui impleto*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In conditions, the mere existence of the fact suffices. And a compromise made prohibits one from bringing an action for eviction: because the arbitral award has the force of a settlement.
body: In the name of Christ. Principally, certain individuals were bound as sureties to a certain Lord Peter for 1005 florins on account of a commercial transaction, namely Georgius, Thomasius, Moschinus, and Fidelolus, of whom Georgius preserved the rights of the other three, because he alone was the true principal, or the more principal debtor. Then this Georgius made a certain sale to Antoniolo; and a certain third creditor evicted the said sold goods. Then the said Lord Peter assigned his rights to the said Antoniolo for 1300 livres, the said quantity owed to the said Lord Peter, under this form of assignment, which is equivalent, namely, for the defense of the said goods purchased by the said Antoniolo, and also for claiming and acting in case of eviction. Finally, the said Antoniolo, or his heirs, brought an action for eviction against the said Georgius, his author, and made a compromise with him without the consent of the said Thomasius, Moschinus, and Fidelolus. And an arbitral sentence was rendered against the said Georgius for a certain sum on account of the eviction of the said lands. Now the heirs of Antoniolo, by virtue of the said assigned right, wish to sue the said Thomasius, Moschinus, and Fidelolus. What is the law?

† However, this question turns on whether a condition was added in the aforementioned cession or not. The condition "if eviction should occur" is valid, and indeed it is so; for in conditions, the mere existence of the fact suffices, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui haeredi, and l. meus; and D. de verbis oblig., l. quidam cum filium. To the contrary, it appears that the condition "if eviction should occur" is not understood to refer to that which arises from a compromissory arbitration chosen without the consent of future obligors, nor are they bound to be cited to appear before alien arbitrators. D. de evictionibus, l. si ad dictum, § si compromisero. But this reason does not seem to hold: for this thing was evicted by a hypothecary action before a judge, and thus the condition of eviction exists, and after that eviction the compromise was made, by which the action was not novated; therefore, neither was its substance. Consider that an arbitral award has the force of a transaction; therefore, a creditor who transacts seems to have prejudiced himself with regard to others, because by transaction the obligation is novated, as in C. de transactionibus, l. ut responso. And it no longer seems that action can be brought by the old action, because the contract has been novated, as in D. de minoribus, l. minor 20 annis, cui fideicommissum in contrarium facit, l. ultima, C. de novatione, cogitabis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. By positing the case in itself.
2. A conditional fideicommissum is not transmitted.
body: In the name of Christ. The words of the will state as follows: Ioannes Antonius instituted as his universal heir in all his movable goods, rights, and actions, and in the right of debts wherever they may exist and be found, Francischina, sister of the testator himself and wife of Petrus de Valle, with this condition: that if the said Francischina should depart this life at any time without children descending from her, then and in that case he substituted in the said inheritance Antonieta, daughter of the said Francischina and of the said Petrus; and if the said Antonieta should depart without children descending from her, the same testator willed and ordained that then and in that case all the goods of the testator himself be distributed, and ought to be distributed, by Petrolus Albatorum and Francischinus Saxus among poor girls to be married, and as seems best to them. The above-written Antonieta, daughter of the said Francischina, has died, leaving two sons and two daughters, who are alive. But the aforesaid Francischina, mother of the said Antonieta, is alive, and has made a donation to a certain person of a certain part of the goods of the said testator Ioannes. Now it is asked whether, with respect to the children of the said Antonieta, who are substituted to the said Francischina, the said Francischina can by law make such a donation. In the name of Christ.

† It is questioned how many degrees the testator made, and there is no doubt that the first degree was of the institution of Francischina, the second of the substitution of Antonieta, and the third of the substitution of the poor. Likewise, the second degree had the condition "if without children, etc."; likewise, the third degree regarding the poor had a similar condition, "if without children, etc."; and this as far as pertains to the surface of the words. But as to the order of meaning, it seems that there were more degrees in the words "if without children." Silently or covertly, it is included that if with children, the children themselves are understood to be substituted, as in ff. de le. 2. l. Titia seio. §. seia. And Dynus so determines in a fideicommissary substitution; he says otherwise in a direct substitution, namely, that that condition does not create a tacit degree, as noted in ff. de hęred. insti. l. Luc. But Petrus indistinctly holds that a condition does not create a degree, because it is not of the nature of a condition to dispose, but to be joined to the thing disposed, as in l. si quis sub conditione. ff. si quis omis. cau. test. Now these contrary opinions have contrary final conclusions. For if the opinion of dominus Dynus is true, the substitution made of Antonieta vanished through non-transmission; nevertheless, her children are subrogated through a tacit substitution in the place of Antonieta. And thus, upon the occurrence of the case of the death of the said Francischina without children, they would come in their own person, not by benefit of transmission:

† because a conditional fideicommissum is not transmitted, as noted in l. vnica. C. de his, qui ante apertas tabulas. But if the opinion of Petrus is true, since the children of Antonieta do not come as substitutes, nor by transmission, therefore the substitution is consumed—except with respect to the poor in the case where the condition of the poor should occur, which is the final one, and the poor cannot die, because it is written, "the poor you will always have with you." Just as man in general does not die so long as the constitution of the world lasts—because generation passes into generation, and man remains, although individuals are corrupted through their own frailty, as in Aut. de nup. §. disponat. What, therefore, is to be said among such great doctors? And I do not doubt that if a testator said, "if my son departs without children, I substitute Seius," the children born of the son are preferred to Seius, yet not as substitutes, but they free their father from the burden of the fideicommissum, so that their father dying with children has the full power of alienating and testating concerning the said goods; but when the testator subjoins another substitution after those words—for instance, because he says, "and if the said Seius departs without children, I substitute Gaius, or the poor"—I do not care then, because he could not substitute through a fideicommissum for the children of Seius unless he had tacitly substituted the children themselves, ff. de le. 3., and he is seen to have tacitly substituted them so that the will of the testator does not perish, and because he seems to have observed the natural order of affection. And Dynus speaks better on this than Petrus. Nevertheless, that question hangs as a matter of fact in which I am an advocate, and therefore it behooves me to remain silent; you, however, may choose that which seems to you more just. Furthermore, concerning the goods donated by domina Francischina, the law is the same as for the rest of the goods, because during the life of domina Francischina nothing can be claimed, as in ff. ad treb. l. sed si ante. and C. de fideicom. l. post mortem. with its subject matter; and about this last point there is no dispute nor need for deliberation, because it is clear, and the safer path for the soul and for natural justice is always to uphold testaments as far as possible, and especially in pious causes, in which one must not dispute over the niceties of the law. And so I say and counsel, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the legitime may be deducted by a son in respect of a single item only: and what is the law regarding the Trebellian portion, and what regarding the Falcidian portion.
body: In Christ's name.

† It is asked whether a son requested to restore the inheritance after his death may sell paternal possessions up to the equivalent value of the legitime, and choose the entire legitime in a single thing. And this question is an ancient one, and the glosses commonly state that he cannot, unless the universal fideicommissary ratifies the alienation, because the legitime looks to the entire patrimony and not to a single thing, just like a debt; and therefore from each singular thing the universal corpus of the legitime is deducted from each corpus pro rata, because there is no reason why more ought to be deducted from one thing than from another. Whence the text states that the filling up of the legitime must come from the father's very substance; it does not say from a single thing of the father's substance itself, but from the integral substance of all the paternal goods, as in C. de inof. testa. l. scimus. §. repletionem. Therefore, on his own authority, the son cannot supply to himself or deduct in one thing that which is owed out of many things, unless this has been granted to him through the praetor's equity upon cause shown, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. potest haeres. To the contrary, it seems that this is a privilege of the legitime, that it may be deducted in a single thing, since the son can choose for himself. The doctors state: provided that this choice by the son is not excessively burdensome to the fideicommissum; and for this they bring in §. quamobrem in Aut. de rest. et ea quae parit. Dominus Iacobus Butrigarius in l. 2. C. ad l. Falc. says that either the deduction is made against one person, and then it can be made in one thing, or against several, and then it ought to be made in the individual things. But the ordinary gloss states the opposite there: because without distinction it cannot be made in a single thing, since it does not concern a specific corpus of the patrimony, but the universal corpus. Nor does C. fami. her. l. filium, quem habentem stand in the way, because that is on account of the presumed intention of the father, who had designated one thing for the son. Likewise, de le. 1. l. potest haer. does not stand in the way, because that is understood to be with judicial authority and cause shown, not on one's own authority; likewise, there the heir was not requested to restore the whole, but a certain quantity, and therefore a universal corpus had not been effected. Dominus Oldradus says that the principle of the Falcidian law requires that it be deducted pro rata from every thing; nonetheless, if that minute division would result in loss to the burdened heir, by permission of the judge it can be deducted in a single thing. Others say that since all the goods belong to the son pending the condition of the fideicommissum, he can separate the legitime in a single thing from the other goods, since he ought to have it immediately, and without the burden of any delay or contingency. On this there are diverse opinions: for some permit this to the son because he is equated to a true creditor, as in ff. de distra. pig. l. creditoris arbitrio; others say that out of the necessity of the household he can choose in a single thing, but when the necessity ceases he cannot; others say that if the estate is intact, that is, the goods have not been alienated, he cannot, but if the estate is not intact, because an alienation has been made in good faith, then he can deduct it in a single thing; and this opinion seems fair enough, and judgments now seem to be rendered according to this opinion. And this I maintain in l. potest haeres, de le. 1. and l. 2. C. ad l. Fal.; otherwise, it would follow that the son could not even alienate any small particle, because minute parts would not find a buyer, which is exceedingly absurd. Nonetheless, it would be good counsel that this be done with the tacit consent of the universal fideicommissary, whose prejudice is in question, as in ff. de leg. 2. l. si tamen quibusdam. However, in the legitime I speak of the Trebellian; there are opinions and it can be disputed pro and contra, for no one gives a person the power of dividing with a co-owner against his will, as in ff. de vsufru. le. l. is, qui fundum, where it is express, and which what is noted in ff. de ver. ob. l. qui Romae. §. duo fratres supports. Furthermore, as to the Trebellianic portion, I think without distinction that it cannot be chosen in a single thing, because it is not owed in a single thing unless the testator had granted the power of retaining the Trebellianic portion to the burdened party himself, because then he could retain it in a single thing. And these matters I have set out more extensively in l. filium, quem habentem, and in said l. 2. C. ad l. Fal. And let this be the conclusion: that if it can be conveniently deducted from all things, let it be done in all things; but if not from all, let it be done from the more convenient thing. For this is natural equity conforming to the judgment of a good man, as in said l. potest haeres; and the said Raynerius also seems to hold this view. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pledge or a mortgage falls under the term of alienation.
2. Where a sale is prohibited, everything by which one arrives at it is considered prohibited.
3. How the comparison of writings is to be proved.
4. A hypothecary action cannot be brought unless excussion has been made.
5. How a deposit is to be proved.
body: In the name of Christ. Presupposing a statute voiding every alienation of an improvement of an emphyteutic property, unless preceded by a certain notification to be made to the lord by the emphyteuta.

† It is asked whether under these words of alienation a pledge or a hypothec is contained. The words say all goods, even those which otherwise do not fall under a general obligation. And I shall see that it is not, because a pledge is not properly an alienation. For the hypothecary action takes away bare possession, as in ff. de euic. l. si cum venditor. in prin. l. vlt. C. de re. ali. non alie. does not stand in the way, because there it speaks of a broad interpretation, not of the proper meaning. Furthermore, an emphyteuta can be bound by pledge for so long, with the hypothec enduring, as long as the emphytheosis endures, as in ff. de pi l. lex. vecti. And therefore I do not think that the said statute includes the case of a hypothec, since it ought to be strictly interpreted, especially where it is contrary to the ius commune.

† Consider: the statute prohibits a sale, therefore everything through which one arrives at it: therefore also a pledge by a certain consequence, as noted in l. 2. C. de vsuca. and l. pro emptore. ff. de pig. In whose limits it can be said that if it is obligated for a great quantity, so that there is scarcely any hope of redemption, the prohibition is understood to have been made: because next to this pledging is to hold the thing as abandoned, otherwise it is different. In favor of this is that notable law ff. de le. 3. l. qui habebat. Or more truly it can be said that in such a general obligation things that are prohibited from being alienated are not included. Those words of the writing do not stand in the way which say, he obligated also all his goods, even those which otherwise do not fall under a general obligation: because those words refer to things purchased, but not to prohibited things. For a prohibitive law cannot be renounced. And therefore I conclude that the said libellary things do not fall into the hypothec, the statute standing in the way, or entirely by reason of the statute: because the statute was, or ought to have been, known to each contracting party.

† Another article follows, whether an effective subscription and comparison of hands (letters) has been proved by witnesses. I respond: comparison of hands is not proved, because it requires two writings, the comparing and the compared: as in C. de fide instru. l. comparationes. But the subscription well seems to be proved, because not every singularity makes witnesses singular, but that which differs in substance, as in extra de uer. sig. c. nihil obstat. and fully noted in extra de testi. c. cum tu filii.

† The third article is concerning discussion: and I say that since discussion was not made, which ought to be made both of the heir and of the curator of the estate, and of any universal possessor, the hypothecary action cannot be brought when the goods have not been lawfully discussed, as in Aut. de fideiusso. §. sed neque.

† The fourth article is: behold, the chapter says that a certain true deposit was made, for which he obligated himself; concerning this true deposit the witnesses do not prove, but concerning the subscription and verbal obligation. It is asked whether the chapter of deposit is proved. Speculum in the title de teste frames this question in a contract of mutuum, and says that it is not proved: because a mutuum that is counted out is one thing, and a mutuum that is confessed is another. By which reasoning the same seems to apply in a deposit: because the true act of counting out is not proved, although against this makes l. publica. in fi. ff. depositi. And there is a reason for the difference: because a mutuum is contracted in three ways, but a deposit is not contracted except in one way only, namely by the thing. This reason seems to be removed, and is removed by l. in contractibus. §. 1. C. de non nu. pe. And because the said chapter, as I said, speaks of true counting out, and of confession, supposing true counting out, it does not seem to me that the chapter is proved while preserving the substance of truth, arg. ff. de so.lu. l. si ex pluribus. And because the confession refers to then, and the witnesses do not speak of then, nay rather they say the contrary, therefore simulated, and not true, as in C. de dona. inter ui. et uxo. l. si non uerum. For the words of the chapter most clearly exceed the simple terms of a confession, or of a writing, and thus C. de non nume. pecunia. l. si ex cautione does not stand in the way. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the benefit of inventory, although raised, still applies when the judge has pronounced a sentence to be executed, which has become res judicata.
2. Whether a statute extends to alien territories.
3. Whether an heir omitting one item in the inventory loses only that item or the entire estate.
4. Whether it suffices to allege the inventory, or whether it must be formally pleaded.
5. Domicile is considered in a personal obligation.
body: In the name of Christ. It is prudently provided that judges, at the instance of him who has appeared prima facie to have a right to a debt by virtue of a written instrument, and who has demanded execution of said debt, are bound to order the debtor to pay the creditor within ten useful days, or to prove whatever he wishes as to why he is not bound to pay: if, after the expiration of this term, he has not proved it, he shall be compelled. And since execution was sought against an heir, who produced an instrument of acceptance with the benefit of inventory, the judge pronounced the instrument to be executed, nor did he reserve

† The benefit of inventory. The question is what is the law when the aforementioned judgment has become res iudicata, and the hereditary assets are insufficient. I answer: either the aforementioned exception was proven, or it was not. In the first case, it appears to be disproven. D. de compensatione, quod in diem, § 1. In the second case, let him blame himself. It is proposed that A.
† First, it is asked: although he did not prove, nevertheless after the sentence he cannot be opposed on the effect of the benefit. D. 50.17. l. etiam. §. si.

The second point is: since in the city of Pavia the benefit of inventory cannot be opposed, whether this statute is to be understood with respect to things that are outside the Pavia territory. I answer in the affirmative, because by the acceptance of the inheritance made in Pavia there arises a solid obligation by contract, which begins from the quasi-contract celebrated in Pavia by the acceptance of the inheritance, as noted by Jacobus Butrigarius in *l. cunctos populos* in his reading.

Thirdly, it is asked whether an heir who knowingly concealed certain items that he did not include in the inventory loses the benefit of the entire inventory, or only with respect to those items? I answer that he loses it with respect to the whole, because the inventory was not made in good faith. And this is provided for by the most recent law, as in the Authentica *De hereditate et falcidia*, § *Sancimus*, column 1, although the Civil Law had otherwise provided.
† It is added in the point in 1. c. that the heir did not raise the exception of the inventory, but nevertheless alleged it. I answer that he is excluded by the term of the statute.

† Furthermore, another point is raised, namely that the heir who made the inventory did so not in this city; therefore, it should benefit him, because the statute of Pavia does not bind outside its territory. I answer: rather, the personal obligation arising from the acceptance of the inheritance binds him for the whole amount, because he is a native and has his domicile in Pavia. And in personal obligations, the domicile is considered. D. de iudiciis, l. fideicommissum, § tractatum. Moreover, execution is sought in Pavia, and therefore the Pavia forum must be considered, as in C. de exactoribus tributorum, l. missi opinatores, lib. 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the payment of the annual pension is proven by two witnesses stating that the lord says, "I am satisfied."
body: In the name of Christ. B. granted a certain thing in perpetual emphyteusis for a fixed annual canon. When a dispute arose between him and the emphyteuta regarding the payment of the canon, namely whether it had been made, the emphyteuta produced two witnesses who testified similarly to the following effect: one stated that in his presence he saw the emphyteuta count out a certain quantity of money, and immediately thereafter the emphyteuta himself asked the lord whether he was satisfied for all and the whole of what he ought to have received up to that point; to which the lord replied that he was satisfied. The other witness omitted mention of the counting, but concurred with the former in the effect of the other matters. The question therefore arises whether the payment is thereby considered proven.

† It must be considered that certain contracts are executed in writing by agreement of the parties, because the parties would not have contracted otherwise, as in C. de side instru. l. contractus. And then payment, or a pact not to sue, cannot be proved except by written instrument or by five witnesses, as in C. de testi. l. testium. But certain contracts are executed in writing by disposition of law, such as the emphyteutic contract in perpetual emphyteusis, as in C. de iure emphyteo. l. 1. Likewise, a perpetual census contract is executed. And it seems that the same rule applies, for the same solemnity ought to be observed in contracting and in discharging: as in ff. de solu. l. prout quisque. And therefore in our case it seems probable to say that proof by two witnesses is not sufficient. And especially because those words, “you are satisfied,” do not necessarily include a confession of payment, or a pact not to sue; but rather some general and uncertain mental satisfaction: just as we say “satisfied, as the creditor wished,” as in ff. de pi. act. l. solutum. §. solutam. Moreover, the said witnesses are in a sense singular: because one speaks of a certain payment, the other does not; hence they prove neither in law nor in fact. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What is required in a perpetual ecclesiastical emphyteutic lease that is alienable.
2. And whether one treatise suffices, or whether several are required.
3. The decrees and consent are presumed to have intervened, and all things to have been done with due solemnity.
4. Whether the ratification of the bishop, or consent subsequently given, suffices.
5. Concerning the wording, and what it imports.
6. Whether a just title for prescription arises from ancient instruments.
body: In the name of Christ. Whether the agreement of the prelate and the chapter is required in the perpetual conversion of ecclesiastical emphyteusis: and it must be said that either the thing is customarily subject to emphyteusis, and no agreement is required; because this is not a new alienation but an observance of custom: as we say in fiefs, as in c. 1, Qui feuda dare possunt, where it says, abbot, abbess. For custom opens the way, as in l. 1, § permittit, ff. De aqua pluviali arcenda, and Extra, De feudis, c. 2 and 3, and c. 1, Episcopum vel abbatem, col. 10. Or it is a new emphyteusis, or a contract proper, such as a sale or exchange: and then the agreement must intervene, as in the chapter Dudum, De rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, and Codex, De sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Authentica Hoc ius porrectum.

Secondly, it is asked whether one hearing suffices, or whether several are required: some say that several are required, namely three. Others say that one solemn hearing suffices, as is noted in the chapter *Dudum*, *De rebus ecclesiae non aliendis*, Book 6. Speculator, in his *Speculum*, under *Delegato*, § *Sequitur*, verse *Et nota*, states that this hearing should be conducted thus. And note that this hearing ought to be held several times, at least three times. Some say that for each occasion a public instrument may be drawn up, which seems harsh, especially because he says that it seems harsh; thus, he holds that one hearing suffices. For it suffices that the causes by which they are strangled are once named and approved, as in the Code, *De praediis curialium*, Law 1, Book 10. This is true when necessity or utility is imminent, which is presumed to be imminent from the fact that it was concluded in the hearing, by argument from the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, Law 11, § *Si rem*. For in cases of necessity, no one is considered liberal, as in the Digest, *De probationibus*, Law *Cum de indebito*, and *De adimendis legatis*, Law *Rem legatam*. Therefore, since the superior subsequently interposed a decree or consent, everything is presumed to have been done solemnly and legitimately, as noted in Law 1 of the Code, *De fide instrumentorum et iure hastae fiscalis*, Book 10, and specifically in *De emptione et venditione*, § *Tunc dicendum*, verse *Et breviter scias*. Furthermore, it suffices that the causes were known once, as in the Digest, *De rebus eorum*, Law *Magis puto*, § *Ne passim*. And these statements are especially true in ancient cases, for which there is a stronger presumption, as elegantly noted by Innocentius in the Extravagants, *De testibus capiendo*, Chapter *Albericus*, and by Cynus in *De fide instrumentorum*, Law *Emancipatione*.

† Moreover, these decrees or consents are interposed by way of voluntary jurisdiction and between consenting parties; for they are not rendered against an unwilling party, even if cited. And therefore solemnity is presumed to have intervened, as noted by Innocentius in the Decretals, *De probat.*, c. *Quoniam*, and in the Decretals, *De eo qui fornicationem ordinem suscepit*, c. *Innotuit*. And it supports this what is noted in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, l. *Actor*, and in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, l. *Cum hi*, § *Si praetor*. Furthermore, the contracting parties themselves are not presumed to be forgetful of eternal salvation, especially since they are religious, as in l. *Si*, Cod., *Ad legem Iuliam de repetundis*. And it supports the aforementioned what is noted in Decretum 12, q. 2, c. *Sine exceptione*.

Thirdly, it is asked, since the consent of the prelate and of the chapter, and the authority of the diocesan bishop, or his decree, are required, whether the ratification of the bishop, or his consent ensuing afterwards, suffices. And it seems that it does not. For Speculum says that a license is required in the aforementioned §. sequitur, in the verse Porro. But a license must precede, or at least concur, just as authority and mandate, as in l. 1, ff. de auctoritate tutoris, and ff. de mandato, l. si vero non remunerandi, §. si post creditam. And the reason is, because it tends to render the contracting person capable, which capacity is required from the beginning, as in ff. de servis exportandis, l. si minor. Moreover, the church is similar to a minor, in whose case it is required that the decree of the judge either precede or be interposed immediately, as is noted in ff. de minoribus, l. ait praetor, §. pe. Moreover, this is the meaning conveyed by the force of the word.

† For the syllable "de" has the force of augmenting and signifying a completed act, as is held in l. 1, in principio, ff. de deposito. This is the opinion of Innocentius, the Archdeacon. I, however, hold that if a contract is subsequently confirmed by judicial authority with the consent of the parties, it shall be valid not as a decree, but as a confirmation, as provided in C. de decurionibus, l. si quos, lib. 10, and in ca. Cura, de iure patronatus. For that which is invalid from the beginning may acquire force through the authority of a confirmation made with the will of the parties. This is stated by Bartolus in a similar case. For a donation, which ought to be insinuated before a judge, if not insinuated from the beginning, may be approved by the judge with the consent of the parties, as he notes in ff. de donationibus, l. Modestinus. And these statements are true, especially if custom so provides. Furthermore, this is supported by what is noted in l. 2, C. de communi utriusque iudicii.

Fourthly, it is asked whether a cause for prescription has arisen from ancient contracts which are not shown to have been made with due formality; and it seems that it has not, because an error of law does not avail in prescriptions. Solution: That is true in prescription of long time. Otherwise in prescription of longer time, in which no sentence and authority is provided for by statute,

† First, the prior statute provides the cause for prescription. And the reason is: because a title is not required as a title, but only to exclude bad faith. And this is held by the gloss on the Decree, 16 q. 3, c. Si sacerdotes. Because whatever title suffices in prescription of long time, without it being necessary to dispute over the subtleties of the law. Also, because it is a just error, which the prior upholds, as in D. de nox. l. Et generaliter. Which makes the best point, and thus I hold regarding the aforementioned points, saving the substance of the truth. And thus I say, and I advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When responses to positions are to be given.
2. Whether poverty or excussion is proved by reputation.
body: In the name of Christ. It is provided by statute,

† that one must respond to positions in person, and not through a procurator. Now, a certain party appointed a procurator to respond in this manner. The judge, however, ordered him to respond personally. It is asked whether he ought to be held as confessed as being contumacious. I answer in the affirmative, because he obeyed neither the statute nor the judge's mandate, unless he were such a person as did not know how to respond by himself, as in extra de iud. c. pastor. Nevertheless, in our case, since he knows how to respond through another, he therefore also knows how to respond by himself, whether he be male or female. And therefore he ought to be reputed contumacious and held as confessed, because the statute so determines; ff. qui, et a quib. l. prospexit; C. de procu. l. fi.; extra de elec. c. vt circa. lib. 6.; and extra de iudi. c. 1. eo. lib.; for one must not depart from the form of the words and the precepts of the law, nor from the person whose trustworthiness and diligence were chosen, as in C. de cadu. tollen. §. ne autem; ff. de cur. fur. l. cuius bonis; and what is noted in ff. de arbit. l. sicuti.

† Subsequently it was asked whether poverty or exhaustion of assets is proved by common report. And say that it is, if the common report is conjoined with belief, that is, with the knowledge of those who speak, because they say and believe the same thing; ff. de excu. tut. l. paupertas, according to Iac. de Aret.; C. quando fiscus, vel priua. l. 2; C. de iu. do. where this is adduced; and according to Bar. in l. si constante. in prin. ff. so. ma. I had not properly examined the statute, for the statute, when it says that no other may respond on his behalf, states 'unless it be a woman or one illiterate.' And therefore, since a woman is expressly excepted by the statute, it is sufficiently clear that she can respond through a procurator; nor is she contumacious, and therefore the positions ought not to be held as confessed. And this exception is very reasonable, equitable, and consonant with the common law, as in l. 1. in prin. ff. de postulan. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Later statutes have greater force than earlier ones.
2. Later laws derogate earlier ones, to such an extent that the rationale of the earlier ones cannot even be alleged.
3. Decrees or rescripts, with regard to the power of revocation, are equivalent to last wills.
4. When two contrary statutes exist, that which is less absurd is considered; likewise, that which is less contrary to the common law.
5. A statute is said to be more specific when it provides for the fisc.
