6. A suretyship obligation is not found without a principal obligation: although the contrary holds for a hypothecary obligation introduced by the authority of law.
body: In Christ's name.

† First, it is provided by the Statute of Asti that in a cause of loan (mutuum) and deposit—concerning which a confession appears by a public instrument, a certain tax (gabella) having been paid to the commune—proceedings shall be conducted by a certain summary and expedited route, nor may any exceptions be raised except certain ones. But by a later statute—which does not come as a continuation of the first, but independently, and was enacted at a much later time—it is provided that all lawsuits and controversies between consanguines and affines must be submitted to arbitration (compromissum), and that it cannot be proceeded otherwise, and it nullifies any proceeding conducted otherwise. Hence it is first asked: if a cause of loan or deposit confessed by instrument is brought between consanguines and affines, must it be submitted to arbitration? And it seems that it must, first by reason of time:

† because later laws derogate from earlier ones, whether we speak of laws and statutes, as is commonly read in ff. de legi. l. sed et posteriores, and in the second constitution of the Code § fi., and C. de lati. lib. tol. l. 1 in prin., and C. de edi. di. Adr. toll. l. 1 in prin., and C. de edic. di. Adr. tol. l. edicto in prin., with countless similar passages, to such a degree that the old law cannot be alleged, nor its reasoning, which is noteworthy; or whether we speak of contracts, as in ff. loc. l. cum in plures § lege dicta, ff. de fideius. l. stipulatus es opus, ff. de pręto. stip. l. Valerianus, ff. de acque pos. l. si quis ante, C. de pac. l. pacta nouissima, ff. si cer. pe. l. lecta, with countless similar texts; or whether we speak of interlocutory sentences of judges, as in l. quod iussit de re iud.; or whether we speak of praetorian stipulations, as in ff. de pręto. stipul. l. 1 in fin.;

† or whether we speak of decrees or rescripts of princes—for with respect to the power of revocation and corrective interpretation they are equated to last wills, as in c. cunctis de conces. pręb. lib. 6 and fully noted in c. 1 de rescri. in the ancients—or whether we speak strictly of last wills, as in C. de sac. san. ecc. l. 1, ff. de adi. leg. l. quod iterum, ff. de leg. 1 l. si mihi, et tibi § in leg., Instit. qui. mod. testa. infir. § posteriore, with countless similar texts. Therefore, by an argument from a posterior ground, the latest statute must be observed, and not the first. Nor does it stand in the way if it is said that the first statute is special regarding contracts of loan and deposit; for certainly the second statute is also special regarding consanguines and affines. And whenever there are two special provisions, one in favor and the other against, the specialty by reason of the person seems to prevail, especially where a law of the judicial forum is concerned, as in C. quoniam Imperator inter pupill. et vi. l. 1; for the consideration of persons must be looked to before the consideration of the contract and obligation, as in ff. de iu. cod. l. quidam referunt and fully noted by the moderns in ff. de re iu. l. quidam consulebat. Thus I see that a woman in an action for dowry—namely, the person of the woman herself—is preferred to other causes of other creditors, as in C. qui pot. in pig. hab. l. assiduis and Instit. de act. § fuerat, ff. sol. ma. l. 1. Likewise, I see that the privilege of a ward is preferred to the privilege of the contract of deposit, as in ff. de priu. cre. l. si ventri § in bonis. Moreover, the rule is that whenever two parties are privileged by law or statute, the one who is more privileged is preferred, as is singularly noted in ff. de priu. cred. l. priuilegia; but that the agnates here are more privileged, I prove because they are defendants, whereas the adversary is the plaintiff, and we favor the defendant more than the plaintiff, as in ff. de doli exce. l. apud celsum § Marcellus, ff. de ver. ob. l. si seruum § sequitur. Whence, concluding from first to last, it seems that the cause must be submitted to arbitration, because natural reason dictates this among consanguines and affines, so that matters may be settled by amicable composition rather than by the severity of court judgments, by the argument in ff. de vsufru. leg. l. generali in prin. and ff. de lega. 2 l. cum pater § dulcissime. And so the forum of the judge ought to be transferred to the forum of the arbitrator. To the contrary, it seems that we should look to the privilege of the obligation rather than to a declinatory exception of the forum. And this I show first by reason of time, for the contract is later in time than the agnation, since agnation is from the very beginning of birth, while the contract occurred long afterward at full age. Then I argue thus: he who contracts is considered to consent to the law and custom of the contract rather than to the origin of the contracting party, as in extra de fo. compe. c. dilecti; nay rather, he seems to renounce the privilege of his origin if such privilege cannot stand together with the privilege of the contract, because one is always considered to choose the way to confirm his own act, as in l. 3 ff. de mil. testa. Moreover, two reasons overcome one, and three overcome two, as in Auth. de consangui. et vte. fratribus in the rubric and the text, and noted in ff. de min. l. Aemilius and ff. ad Treb. l. qui filium § Sabinus. But here multiple reasons work in favor of the instrument: for one reason is deposit, as in C. de non nu. pec. l. in contractibus § 1; another reason is the notoriety that arises from a public instrument, as in C. de edic. diui Adri. toll. l. si tertia, because by the form of the statute all declinatory exceptions are removed except those that go to the foundation, since where good faith is at stake, it is not fitting to dispute over legal niceties, ff. mand. l. si fideiussor § quaedam; likewise where good and expedited justice is concerned, as in C. de adul. l. ita pudor. But for consanguines and affines only one reason works, namely, the common good of agnation and peace.

† The solution: when there are two contrary provisions, one in favor and the other against, that which has less absurdity is looked to; likewise, that which is less contrary to the ius commune, and that prevails, as the rule of law states. But a statute on the execution of public instruments that are beyond every exception is less contrary to civil law than a statute on compulsory arbitrations, because no one is compelled to settle or make a pact under the ius gentium or civil law, as in C. de lib. l. nec emere and C. de transa. l. si quis maior. Likewise, submissions to arbitration are, by reason of the penalty, somewhat odious, as in ff. de mi. l. minor § minores, and are therefore to be restricted; but a statute on summary executions is favorable and equitable, even though it is contrary to the rigorous order of law; and written equity prevails over written rigor when both are in the genus, or both in an equal species, as noted in C. de iud. l. placuit. Indeed, certainly here the opposing species are not equal, because one—namely that regarding execution—is more special than the other, whether we consider the cases possible to be included or the greater degree of specialty based on reasoning. Likewise, where the interpretation of words is at issue, the consideration of persons is not attended to, as in ff. de leg. 3 l. item in legato § parui. Moreover—and this is the final reason—by the form of the statute, from a confession made in a contract of loan and deposit an actio in factum arises, for it is rendered akin to a confession made in court; and this is evident by an argument from the executive effect, as noted by Cynus in l. vnica C. de confessis. From these points it is therefore concluded that one must not submit such a cause to arbitration, but rather the statute must be observed that speaks properly in the case of loan and deposit, because it is more consonant with good faith and natural reason, as in ff. de consti. pecu. l. 1 in prin. Furthermore, no one would say that one must submit to arbitration regarding an actio iudicati, as in ff. de condi. ind. l. eleganter § si post and ff. de transa. l. post rem, because that would be to go backward, as in ff. de min. l. minor 25. ann. § cui fideicommissum. And note that those who hold that there are two statutes here, one earlier and the other later, speak improvidently, since our case is not included in the statute on arbitrations; therefore it appears unique, not second—that is, not merely preferable, but the only one, as in ff. qui po. in pig. ha. l. 2; and by this an answer is given to the brocard on genus to species, concerning which see Dynus in c. generi with his common commentary. Nor should it be omitted

† that a statute that provides for the fiscus is understood to be more special than a statute in which the fiscus is bypassed, because statutes are not to be interpreted against the fiscus; and this is determined by Iacobus de Arena in ff. de pec. leg. l. si peculium. Thus on the other points it is not expedient to advise, because instruments of conservation prove nothing against creditors with whom they were not transacted, as noted by Cynus in ff. deposi. l. desiderium, and it is a common rule of both laws. Likewise it is expressly evident in C. si cer. pe. l. si non singuli.

† Likewise, it is never found in law that one can find from the beginning a surety obligation of the principal, although it is found in a hypothecary obligation introduced by the authority of the law, as is the singular gloss in ff. ad Treb. l. si haeres pecuniam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Guardianships are regularly conferred according to the order of intestate succession.
2. Who is to be preferred in guardianships permitted by law, and number 3.
4. Whether a statute disposing of an inheritance also disposes of a guardianship.
body: In the name of Christ. The paternal grandmother and the mother of the ward: the grandmother wishes to assume guardianship jointly with the mother. But the mother says that she alone is the guardian, and that the grandmother is excluded from the guardianship by the mother herself. The question is: what is the law?

† And for the sake of clarity, it must be premised that certain guardianships are imposed by law, namely, those which are conferred by right of agnatic or male cognatic relationship; and in such guardianships, as in inheritances, he who is prior in degree is preferred in law, as in the Authentica *De haereditatibus ab intestato*, § *Ex his*; and in the Authentica *Defuncto*; and in the Corpus, from which this is derived. This is the rule: that guardianships are conferred according to the order of intestate succession, as in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Quo tutela*.

† Certain guardianships are permitted, but not commanded, such as the guardianship of the mother, likewise that of the grandmother. Nor is this commanded, but permitted, as in Auth. *matri et aviae*, in the word *permittimus*. And in these cases the same rule applies: because he who is prior in degree is stronger in right; this is the text in the said Auth. *matri et aviae*, where it says, “according to the order of degrees, we permit [them] to undertake guardianship.” But sometimes one guardianship is commanded, and another permitted: for example, when an agnate or an ascending cognate remains on one side, and the mother or grandmother on the other line, and there is doubt concerning these: for it seems that agnates and cognates are preferred; because immediately upon the death of the father, guardianship is attached to them by the mere existence of agnation or cognation: as in D. *de leg. tutor.*, l. *legitimos*. Therefore, since the ward immediately has a guardian, he cannot have another while the first remains in guardianship. And this reasoning moved the prince to say that the mother is not preferred to the legitimate guardians by rescript: C. *quando mulier tutelae officio fungi potest.*, l. 1, § *his illud*. For with the guardian lies the fullness of power. And therefore he rejects a new associate, although he does not reject an equal, as noted in D. *de app.*, l. *cum in una*, § *tutor*, and Inst. *de curat.*, § *interdum*. On this point, the gloss says: If they are in unequal degree, as father and mother, the father is preferred; but if they are in unequal degree, as grandfather and grandmother, if there is room for guardianship—because the ward is *sui iuris*—both are admitted, because the law does not provide that the grandmother is repelled by the legitimate guardians. And thus, in equal degree, the grandmother is more privileged than the mother, because the grandmother is not excluded by the grandfather, and the mother is excluded by the grandfather, because the mother is expressly excluded by the said l. 2, § *his illud*. Since that section speaks of the mother, it should not be extended to the grandmother, as in D. *sol. ma.*, l. *si ve*, 10, § *de viro*. And to confirm this, consider that today permission by Auth. *matri et aviae* operates the same as the rescript operated by the medium of legal prudence. For the law succeeds in place of the rescript, as in l. 1, C. *de thesauris*, lib. 10, and l. *quae sub conditione*, § *ult.*, D. *de condi. insti.* But, with due respect to the gloss, that the grandmother is more privileged than the mother is contrary to natural reason, as in C. *de bonis matern.*, l. *si viva matre*, and C. *de coll.*, l. *illam*. And therefore say that, in unequal lines, they are admitted equally, although one by one law, the other by another; and thus, by different laws, considering only the natural cause. Hence it appears that the mother, and the father, and the grandfather, and the grandmother, provided the woman is suitable for administration, are admitted equally. The objection that “they have a guardian, etc.” does not hold, because here he had a guardian with the hope of an associate, and not without hope. For if that reasoning were true, in the same way the grandfather would exclude the grandmother, which is false according to all. Sometimes there is a mother and a paternal grandfather. And then some say that the paternal grandfather is preferred, because he is legitimate. But observe, this reasoning is not good. For the mother is also a legitimate guardian, although voluntary. Hence a legitimate guardian does not exclude a legitimate one. I say that the mother is a legitimate guardian by dispensation, and voluntary: as in C. *ad Tert.*, l. *omnem*. And thus holds Speculum in the title *de anomala tutela*. And therefore, if there is a mother and a paternal grandfather, the mother is stronger in guardianship, if she accepts the guardianship solemnly, as is required by law, and we have a similar case in successions. For today the emancipated son is preferred to his grandson. For although the emancipated son is not properly legitimate, he nevertheless has the rights of legitimate heirs, as noted in C. *unde lib.*, l. *qui se patris*, and it is expressly stated in C. *de leg. haeredibus*, l. *defunctis*. Sometimes there is a father and a grandmother; and then the gloss, inferring from its preceding conclusions, seems to say that they are admitted together to guardianship; because the father does not exclude the grandmother, since a legitimate guardian does not exclude her, as no provision is found in law. Likewise, the mother does not exclude the paternal grandfather; because the paternal grandfather is a legitimate guardian. And no law provides that anomalous guardianship excludes an ascending legitimate guardian; but the law provides that it excludes a transverse legitimate guardian. But ancient and modern doctors do not depart from the letter, which says that the order of degrees must be observed. And therefore the gloss speaks dubiously; but if it spoke affirmatively, it would be false.

† Now follows our case, which is the subject of the question, namely, concerning two guardianships in neither of which the right of legitimate guardianship is found, as in the case of the mother and the paternal grandmother. For whether we say that both are anomalous, or broadly speaking both are legitimate, since all other things are equal, the nearer degree is preferred: and this is shown by the following reason. Formerly, the mother was required to petition for a guardian: as in D. ad Tertullianam, l. 2, § si mater. And if she did not petition, she was deprived of the inheritance by operation of law. Today, if she does not wish to petition, but rather to administer, she herself succeeds to the place of that guardian formerly petitioned for. But this is not expressly stated in the law regarding the grandmother when the mother is in the middle, as she is the guardian. This also appears from the fact that if they can jointly exercise guardianship, they could therefore jointly petition for different guardians. For example, the mother one, and the grandmother another. Moreover, if neither petitions within the same year, both would be excluded from succession, which is false, because the grandmother is not excluded, although the mother is excluded if, within the first year, she neither petitions for a guardian nor accepts guardianship, as noted in D. qui petant tutores, l. nepotibus, where there is a singular gloss. And thus I hold in my lectures, C. de impuberis et alijs substitutione, l. precibus. Nor do I omit the true opinion, but rather confirm it.

† As to the second point, if a statute disposes of an inheritance, whether it disposes of guardianship. Bartolus says that it does, in l. prima, ff. de leg. tut. But this must be understood when it disposes by way of universal succession; otherwise, if by way of succession to a specific thing or quantity; because such a person is not a successor in law, as C. de her. inst. l. quotiens; ff. de trans. l. controversia; ff. de eden. l. quaedam, §. is autem. Moreover, I do not believe that the question is found regarding the three things, that if a statute corrects the common law in succession, that it corrects it in guardianship; nor conversely, because by similarity of cases a correction of laws is not induced, as the common and vulgar gloss says, although very notable, C. de sac. san. eccl. Auth. quas actiones. All things therefore being considered for and against, it appears that the mother, concerning whom the question is asked, is to be preferred in guardianship, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The emphyteuta of the church is bound to answer to the church as to which goods are emphyteutic and which are not; and if he does not answer the allegations by word of mouth, whether he believes or does not believe them, they are deemed confessed.
body: In the name of Christ. The matter concerns the boundaries or abutting lands between the church on one side and the heirs of the emphyteuta on the other. On behalf of the church, a position is made regarding certain lands with their designations and abutting boundaries. The heir of the emphyteuta states that there are several estates, some emphyteutic and some not; and that unless they are shown to him visibly, he is not bound to respond to the position unless the properties are demonstrated to him visibly. The rector of the church says that the heir of the emphyteuta ought to be certain about this; because, having paid the canon for a long time, it is probable that he knows from whom and for what he paid, and that his position ought to be certified by the response of the emphyteuta, at least by saying "I believe" or "I do not believe." But the emphyteuta says that an uncertain position ought not to be answered; furthermore, that in another's matter ignorance is probable. As stated in the last law, Digest, "Pro suo."

† The question is asked: what is the law? I answer: first, it must be seen whether, in facts of great antiquity, this burden of declaration pertains to the emphyteuta or to the church. The specification raises this question as if in the terms of the title *De locato*, § *Nunc aliqua*, with the following glosses. And it speaks quite ambiguously, sometimes arguing for the church, sometimes arguing for the emphyteuta. But the gloss of Accursius says expressly that such uncertainty has the force of an alternative, and it is necessary that the emphyteuta choose and designate, as it were by choosing, what, how much, and of what kind. This is the gloss in the Digest, *De rei venditione*, l. *Si in rem agat aliquis*. And I add that he must choose according to what is probable, by the reasons of the specification and by l. 1, *De rebus dubiis*. Indeed, he is bound to know what is his own and what is emphyteutic, and to declare for the latter. L. *Notum*, Codex, *De rescindenda venditione*; l. *Quisquis*. Moreover, when he pays the canon, he must confess and acknowledge, as in the Codex, *De fidei instrumentis*, *Plures apocrisiarii*, l. 1, lib. 10; and Codex, *De donationibus*, l. *Censualis*. Likewise, he is bound to produce instruments speaking of this matter, especially in favor of the church, as in the Digest, *De actione empti*, l. *Titius*, since the church is equated with the fisc, unless he swears that he does not have nor has he ever had the instruments, as in the Codex, *De fidei instrumentis*, l. *Si*. Which, however, is not credible. And briefly, whatever the law may be regarding the decision of the lawsuit, yet regarding the response by "I believe" or "I do not believe," there is no doubt, because not only concerning the fact of the deceased, which is considered the heir's own, but even concerning a fact entirely alien, if the position pertains to the cause, he must respond by "I believe" or "I do not believe." If, given a term for deliberation, he persists in contumacy, he is held as confessing by the word "I believe." I do not say that he appears to confess the truth, but that he believes it to be so; which has the same effect regarding this article, as in the Digest, *De iureiurando*, l. *Iusiurandum*, and l. *Ad pecunias*, in the beginning. On the matter, it is noted in § *Quod observari*, with similar commonplaces. And it supports what is noted in the Extravagantes, *De testamento*, c. *Ultra tertia*. And thus I conclude that he must respond by "I believe" or "I do not believe," otherwise he incurs the penalty of being held as confessing, as in c. *Si post praestitutum*, *De confessis*, Book Six. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether derogatory words in the will cause codicils to be invalid, and whether codicils prejudice the derogatory words themselves, such that one should not adhere to the codicils, but rather to the last will.
2. What is the import of that clause, "in every manner, right, way, and form."
body: In the name of Christ. Dam A. made a will, in which he left certain legacies by the hand of B., notary. It is also said that he later made another will by the hand of C., notary, in which he revoked the first and derogated from any will made until the last; adding that by said will he did not intend to add or change anything; and that it could not derogate from it in any way; and that if he did so, he did not wish it to be valid in any manner; nor is it his intention that it be valid. Finally, he made codicils, in which he confirmed the heirs instituted in the first will; but he reduced certain legacies from ownership to usufruct; and he made these codicils by the hand of the aforementioned B., notary, referring to the will written by the hand of the aforementioned B., codicilling as if to that will; from which arises a certain modification of the contents of the second will with regard to the legacies.

† It is asked whether the said codicils are valid and must be observed, or not. And it seems that they are not, because the second will contains derogatory words. And from this it is argued thus: derogatory words expressed in a will invalidate codicils, because a will is a more solemn expression of will, as in D. de legatis 1, l. si mihi, et tibi; § in legato, D. de institutione et substitutione codicillorum, l. diui, § licet; D. de legatis 3, l. si quis in principio. Moreover, an equal will derogates from an equal one, as a will from a will, and codicils from codicils, by reason of derogatory words expressing the testator’s will to be absent in future acts. As is clear in the aforementioned laws, as in D. de legatis 1, l. si ita scriptum, where it is said: “It does not seem that what was written later, which was not considered in mind, is valid.” And therefore that which is not so much last as null is found, as in D. de supellectili legato, l. Labeo. And see also D. de testamento militis, l. Diuus.

To the contrary, it seems: and it must be considered that either the testator uses derogatory words of power, and such derogation is not valid, because it is impossible by law. For no one can deprive himself of public right, because public right cannot be conferred nor taken away by private agreements; and among these is the making of a will, as noted in D. de testamento, l. si fiscus, and l. testamenti factio; C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. senium, and there I said. It is therefore concluded regarding this point that no one can deprive himself of the faculty of making a will, because it is of public right. Also, because it is a matter of law, and to written law no derogation can be made, as in D. de legatis 1, l. nemo potest; D. de legatis 2, l. codicillis, § si.

Or if the testator uses derogatory words of future will: and here consider that such derogations derogate from enunciative words, not dispositive ones. I declare what I mean: namely, that what beyond the writing is not valid, this is because the testator by enunciative and protestative words wished it not to be valid; and it is presumed that he persists in the same will of mind; because that which is not changed is not prohibited from standing, as in C. de testamento, l. sancimus; D. de probationibus, l. quinquaginta, and l. cum tacitis. For even if the testator gives his will to oblivion, he does not thereby lose the force which depends on pre-established things, as in C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, § at cum humana fragilitas.

But if the last will contains disposition of words and mind, so that there is an intention to dispose, and this is established, the truth itself derogates from the presumption; and true disposition removes enunciative words and their effect; just as a protestation is removed by a contrary act; because since no one can deprive himself of power, the will is mutable notwithstanding any ingenuity or art of words, as in D. locati conducti, l. cum in plures, § locator horrei; and C. de pactis, l. pacta nouissima. From which it is concluded that that which is free and absolute in revoking cannot be made not free, as in C. de pactis, l. si; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. stipulatio hoc modo; C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1, and there by Cynus and me.

From these it is inferred another conclusion, that if it is certain from the mind that the testator wishes to stand by the last writing, derogatory words do not prejudice the last will. This was held by disputing by Johannes Andreas and Ioannes Calderinus after him, who was a man of great virtue and learning, and finally called Dom. Ioannes Andreas, the fountain and trumpet of canon law, concluding likewise in c. 1, de constitutionibus, lib. 6.

Now consider diligently the words of the codicils. For the codicillator says: “He willed, ordained, and ordered, and wills, ordains, and orders in every way, manner, right, and form, by which he could and can better, etc.” And he adds that all other things in the said will delivered and requested by the said B. shall take effect and be put into execution, as they lie. From which words briefly two things are elicited. First, the choice of solemn modes and forms:

† because he said, in every way and form. These words are precise, as in l. quae iure, ff. de milit. testa. Hence it is the same as if he had said, notwithstanding any words ordered to the contrary. Secondly, by reason of efficacy: which the testator wished his codicils to have in being; hence he certainly considered the effect, as in ff. quod quis iur. l. 1. §. Honestus vir frater, these words, and therefore to wish to infringe the pious last will under the pretext of certain little reasons, which are not worth one obol, seems to be of a perverted mind: and not to agree with the judgment of sound intellect. And thus I think that effect should be given to the said codicils: which codicils produce by their nature, as in instit. de ademp. leg. and no. C. de leg. l. datum. ff. ad Treb. l. si quis priore. and l. scævola. ff. de iu. codic. quod per manus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a person has acted as a minister and conducted himself as the minister of a hospital, and has litigated, he cannot claim that what he did was void by alleging that he was not a minister; because no one is heard to allege his own turpitude.
2. In a transaction, a certain kind of donation is somehow involved.
3. Whether a prelate can alone compromise.
4. A cleric must follow the statutes of laymen where he uses them for himself.
5. It is presumed in favor of the arbitrator’s sentence.
body: In the name of Christ. John de Cauatiis, minister and rector of the Hospital of Saint Peter of Siena in the diocese of Laude, made a compromise with certain lay nobles regarding a dispute pending between the said hospital and certain nobles concerning certain woods, and their ownership and possession. Finally, with the presence, authority, and decree of the diocesan bishop, the cause being known, the said Brother John, in his own name and that of the hospital, the chapter of brothers, and the convent thereof—which entire chapter the aforementioned minister states he fully represents—on one part, and the said nobles on the other, made a full and most complete compromise into certain common friends and good men, as into arbitrators and amicable composers; and they renounced appeals and recourses, etc. These arbitrators rendered their award and arbitration in favor of the said nobles. Subsequently, before the podestà of Laude, it was requested that the said award be reduced to the arbitration of a good man; and in the meantime, judgment was pronounced in favor of the said nobles.

† Now, however, the said minister and rector of the hospital, joined with the person of a certain Brother Francis, a brother, as he says, of the said hospital, opposes that all the aforesaid matters are null by the law itself: on the ground that since the said hospital is a collegiate or, so to speak, a capitular place, and the consent of the chapter has not intervened, the prelate alone cannot compromise, nor does the fraud of the prelate alone, who is lying, prejudice the hospital, as in the rule *delictum personae*. On the contrary, by reason of the falsehood, the prelate ought to be considered false as regards the validity of the compromise. Moreover, he deceived the praetor, i.e., the diocesan bishop, by falsely claiming to have full authority, when he had only half authority, and by alleging his own turpitude under the name of the Church, which does not prejudice the Church. Furthermore, it appears that the prelate alone could not compromise, because he could not even transact to the prejudice of the Church, the hospital, or the chapter, as in *Extra, de transactionibus*, c. *Cum contingit*, and I said. *Codex, de transactionibus*, l. *Praeses*.

† And especially in a transaction there is involved, in a certain sense, a kind of donation, as in l. 1, § quod si in lite, D. si quid fraud. patr., and there by Jacobus de Arena. It is certain, however, that a prelate cannot make a donation, neither directly nor indirectly, as in l. prohibere, § plane, D. quod vi aut clam; D. de pact.; l. inter debitorem; and C. de pac.; l. pactum curatoris. Moreover, it is most unjust that the condition of one should be made worse through another, as in D. de iur. et fact. ign., l. iniquissimum. To the contrary it seems, for administration appears to concern only the prelate, because he represents the legitimate person, as noted in C. de iur. calum., l. 2, § quod observari; in cap. praesentium, de testibus, lib. 6, Extr.; de rescriptis, c. decor.

† Solution: One should not persist in this point, because if the place is collegiate both in act and in habit, the prior cannot compromise without the chapter; but if the place is collegiate in habit, but not in act, because there is no one there besides the prelate, then all administration is consolidated in the prelate, and he is the entire corporate body, and he can compromise in good faith, and with the authority and decree of his superior. For the decree of the praetor validates that which would otherwise be null, as that noted text says in the Digest, title *Quod fallit tutorem*, law 1, section *Idem Pomponius*. But here observe that a hospital is said to be collegiate in habit, and not in act, in two ways: either because only the orphanotrophus resides there, and no one else is in possession. In the case of Lord Gudando, the voice is excluded because no one else has the will, because he is instituted in the hospital; but he is in work and quasi-possession. For in these ecclesiastical colleges, he who is not in possession has no voice, as in the chapter *Consultationibus*, on the right of patronage; and fully noted by Innocentius in the chapter *In literis*, on restitution of spoliation. Nor should dealings be had with those who are not in possession. And it is proven that he is not in possession, because he is not accustomed to attend, he does not dwell in the hospital as a conventual; he acts by himself, he negotiates by himself. Since therefore this is so in the truth of the facts and in the proofs regarding this brother, who claims to be a brother of the hospital, his consent or voice was rightly not necessary; and therefore the award and judgment should stand. Moreover, if this person, who says he is of the confraternity, knew what was being done by his prelate and remained silent, he is deemed to have consented. Furthermore, this rector of the hospital, who compromised in his own name, by coming against in his own name and another’s, incurs the penalty of the compromise, as in the Digest, title *De verbis obligatis*, law *Qui Romae*, section final; title *De transactionibus*, law *Pacto convento*. And especially by his own fraud, because he is lying, as he himself asserts. Hence he should not pass without penalty, who circumvents the judge and the party; nor should fraud benefit him, as in the aforementioned law 1, Digest, title *Quod fallit tutorem*. Furthermore, the said brother of Francis, by appealing, seems to ratify the person litigating, as in law *Cum minor*, section *Fallit*, Digest, title *Rem ratam habere*.

† Moreover, a cleric must follow the statutes of laymen where he makes use of them for himself and action is brought on their basis; because he who follows the whole is bound to follow the rules of the forum, as is noted in the singular in cap. quod clericus, de foro competenti, and in cap. caeterum, de iudicibus, and in l. secunda, ff. de eo quod certo loco, where there is a notable gloss. From all of which it seems sufficiently to be concluded that one ought not to depart from matters twice adjudicated by arbitrators,

† For whom it is presumed that they judged justly, as noted by Dynus in the consultation beginning *Tholomeus manentis*. However, I weigh more heavily the fact that nothing has been alleged regarding the said possession of the fraternity: hence, with respect to the possession upon which the right of voice depends, nothing has been alleged or proved concerning the possession; therefore, the right to demand annulment does not proceed. This has been done without prejudice, as states the Compostolanus and other great learned doctors of canon law in many places, and especially in the aforementioned chapters. And it should be noted that although the consultant was chosen by the will of the parties, he is nevertheless presumed to have been chosen as a legal expert. And therefore, if he advised through ignorance, his advice should not be followed. This is stated fully and clearly by Bartolus in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, in the law *Si convenit*. And therefore, although there was a colloquy with the consultant, prejudice was not thereby generated for the parties, as in the law *Titium et Mevium*, in the beginning, in the Digest, *De administratione tutorum*; and especially because of the proofs made afterwards, which the consultant did not see, nor could he see. I, Baldus. Addition to consultation 211, above.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The narrative words in a judgment give rise to the presumption that the judgment was rendered justly and with due deliberation.
2. Whether, while a criminal case is pending, a person may be promoted to a benefice by letters that do not mention the pendency of the litigation.
body: In the name of Christ. The words of the instrument of Helmi are these. And since a careful deliberation and discussion has been held once, twice, and many times between the said prior and the convent, and also counsel has been taken from faithful friends, and it has been determined that the aforementioned exchange was of great utility, etc.

† From these words it clearly appears that the said exchange is presumed valid, because it is declared valid by the judge. Therefore, it is valid, at least by the authority of the confirmer, as is noted. D. de transact. l. Cum hi. §. Eam. And to this point the following is most apt: D. de iure dot. l. Ultima. Likewise, the words “once, twice, and more often” clearly signify that several separate and independent transactions intervened, as is noted. D. de pign. act. l. Si convenerit; and D. quibus ex caus. mai. l. Necnon. §. Si quis saepius; and C. ad Vell. l. Si mulier; and D. ad Treb. l. Iulius. Phebus. And because that which can be valid or invalid is presumed valid on account of the judge’s decree, as D. de trans. l. Cum hi. §. Si praetor; and there the ordinary gloss. And therefore, without doubt, or at least in case of doubt, we must presume in the First Doubt that the exchange was valid, because where there is solemnity, there is validity, as is noted. Extr. de rest. in integ. c. 1; and 12 q. 2 c. Sine exceptione; and c. Abbatibus; and D. de aqua pluv. arc. l. Iuste.

† Another article is whether, while a criminal case is pending, one may be promoted to a benefice by letters that do not mention the pending litigation. And it must be said that he may not, as is fully read and noted in Extra, De solutione compendiaria, c. Si; and an executor appointed cannot execute, because a favor is added which is of no effect, as in Digest, De re iudicata, l. 4, § Condemnatum. And what is noted by Innocentius in Extra, De re iudicata, c. De testamento. And the reason is that a favor granted to the prejudice of an absent person by obreption is null by the law itself, nor can it be executed by execution of law or fact. The text is in Digest, De iudicibus, l. Si praetor, § Marcellus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether that sentence, “I condemn those who are to be condemned, and I absolve those who are to be absolved,” is valid.
2. The word *siue* (or), namely whether it is copulative, disjunctive, or explanatory.
3. How a petition should be drafted in summary proceedings.
4. Whether one who had a debtor imprisoned is said to have made a collection.
5. Whether a notorious fact requires proof.
6. Whether credence is given to an example taken from the archive.
body: In the name of Christ. It is.

Whether this sentence is valid, condemning the one who ought to be condemned, and absolving the one who ought to be absolved, as appears from the records. Regarding which I say that Jacobus Butrigarius first found this caution, that the judge is bound himself to pronounce: and he does not have full counsel for deliberation: and he said this sentence to be valid. For this sentence is certain by reference to the records. And although it appears to be rendered under a condition, it is an intrinsic condition, and of the present: hence it is not properly a condition. Thus he posits it. C. de sen. qui sine cer. quan. l. hęc sententia. Here it must be considered, because this sentence seems to introduce ambiguity, since it is rendered conditionally in either direction. i.e. I absolve, if he is to be absolved, and I condemn, if he is to be condemned. For the matter of the question still remains, since this is the sense: if it shall appear that you are to be condemned, I condemn; if to be absolved, I absolve; therefore the case is still sub iudice, according to that of the grammarian, they contend, and the case is still sub iudice. For since there is still dispute to be had on this, both in law and in fact, because those words, as they appear, are understood in law and in fact, therefore such a sentence is not definitive, because it does not decide the case, but rather involves a new case, and thus it is not valid, as in Inst. de act. §. curare. The solution of this point depends on the quality of the records, for if the records contain so liquid proof that it cannot be broken by any tergiversation, or probable disputation, or brought into doubt, the sentence is valid, otherwise not. And therefore it would not be valid on implicit reasons, but on explicit ones it would be. Hence the records speak, because reference is made to the records, as in ff. de fideius. l. fideiussores magistratuum. §. pro aurelio. and ff. de condit. indeb. l. eleganter. §. si post.

† The second point concerns the word "or," namely, whether it is a copulative, disjunctive, or explanatory conjunction. I answer that this depends on the intention of the speaker, just as with other conjunctions, as noted in the Digest, *de conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *has causas*. And we are instructed on this by the subject matter at hand, as in the law *si quis*, *de aureo et argenteo legato*.
†. The third chapter is what is required in the libel when proceeding summarily: I answer, whatever is required when proceeding ordinarily, as in l. 1. in prin. de eden.

The fourth point is that the decree of the Lord dictates that a judge who has carried out both real and personal execution must have a certain sum in hand. The question arises whether it suffices for him that he has had the debtor imprisoned, which is certain to be collected, since the debtor cannot leave prison unless he pays? I answer that it does not suffice, because what is still owed is not considered to have been collected, as stated in l. hi. §. si rem. ff. de leg. 3.

† The fifth doubt is: suppose it is manifest that someone is a treasurer; is it necessary to prove that he is a treasurer? I answer: if it is a notorious fact of a permanent nature, it is not necessary, since he is in possession of the office; otherwise, yes, as stated in l. 1, C. qu. et adversus quos, and from the argument in ff. de off. praetoris, l. Barbarius.

The sixth doubt is whether credit should be given to an example taken from a public archive? I answer: no, unless it has been taken by the authority of a judge or by the hand of a notary. D. de iure fisci, l. in fraudem; X. de fide instrumentorum, c. 1; and thus it ought to be understood. C. de fide instrumentorum, auth. ad hæc. I, Baldus. See in counsel 204. He repeats his counsel 174 and again confirms it. What I wrote in the case. Assuming the state

In the name of Christ. Benigni of Pisa, having again seen, read, and considered the matter. Moreover, I have seen your most subtle arguments, which I had also touched upon for the most part in my opinion; nevertheless, justice and the judgment of the vindicatory action always being reserved, I do not recede from my opinion. Indeed, I confirm it, because it appears expressly that the testator intended the entire usufruct to belong to the wife: and it is assigned to one indivisibly, such that no part may validly pertain to another, as is certain here, that it does not seem to have been taken away from the other, or does not seem to be included, as in D. de legatis 1, l. quod in rerum, §. siquis post. Since, therefore, only the ownership of the estate is bequeathed to the legatee, and only the usufruct to the woman, insofar as the bequeathed usufruct is concerned, it remains as if not written for the burdened party without burden, according to the general rule. C. de caducis tollendis, §. et cum triplici. The heir was indeed burdened; and therefore, as long as the heir wishes, the legatee of the estate ought not to have the usufruct, unless perhaps after the death of the wife, whose consideration the testator had in mind when disposing of the formal usufruct. And thus I write to your prudence. Notwithstanding D. de usufructu legato, l. si alij. Indeed, this is a case for this side, because here it appears expressly that the testator intended that the legatee of the ownership and the legatee of the usufruct should not concur in that manner, neither in whole nor in part. Hence, an exception stands against the owner acting against the will of the testator, as in D. de adimendis legatis, l. ex parte, with its material. D. de militum testamento, l. militis, codicillis, §. veteranus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the release from a debt is called a donation, such that insinuation is necessary.
body: In the name of Christ. To the point that a donation is not valid by law beyond a certain sum, whether given once or multiple times under a single deed of donation, but the sums must be aggregated.

† It is asked whether, if a creditor remits a debt on two grounds, and one of them is paid, insinuation is required in such remission; and it seems that it is not, for two reasons. The first is that it is not a donation, but an innominate contract, as in D. 2.14.10 (*Si intra*), and there noted. For this appears to be a kind of compromise, just as when several years’ wages are remitted in place of one year’s wage, as in D. 19.2.13 (*Si uno*), in the principal part. The second reason is that a tacit donation made to release someone does not require insinuation, as elegantly noted in D. 20.5.1 (*Qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur*), in the gloss there, where it says “or when it was not insinuated.”

On the contrary, it seems that this is not an innominate contract, but the execution of one named contract and the gratuitous release of another. And therefore this matter is mixed with a donation, as in D. 39.5.1 (*Aristo*). And thus the reason given above does not stand. Moreover, that a tacit donation made out of pure liberality to release someone must be insinuated is the ordinary gloss in D. 50.17.128 (*Si quis obligationum*). Also, this release, insofar as what has been paid is concerned, has no cause other than pure liberality; therefore it is a pure and simple donation. For liberality and donation are one and the same thing, as in D. 39.5.1 (*Hoc iure*). To this effect is D. 6.1.65 (*Rogasti*), § *Si tibi*, and what is noted there.

Solution: If the debt was effective and no exception barred it, it is a true donation and requires insinuation; and it is not an innominate contract. This is clear because it does not clothe the plaintiff with an action, although performance of payment follows from the said debts. The case is in the aforementioned D. 2.14.10 (*Si intra*), and Bartolus there holds that this is a simple pact and not an innominate contract. Some have very often advised that gratuitous release requires insinuation if the debt is liquid; because he who remits is deemed to give, as in D. 12.3.1 (*Si mulier*), D. 24.1.50 (*Si sponsalibus*), § *Fin.*, D. 38.6.1 (*Si quid in fraudem patroni*), D. 39.2.2 and D. 39.2.1 in the final part, D. 47.6.1 (*Quin etiam*), and D. 24.1.51 (*Si sponsus*), § *Fin.* From all these laws it is clear that gratuitous release is a true donation; therefore it requires insinuation. Also, the statute does not distinguish whether a donation is made by promising, by delivering, or by releasing. Therefore we ought not to distinguish either, as in D. 4.4.1 (*De precio*), because this determination is general, as in D. 49.16.1 (*In fraudem*).

The objection from D. 2.14.1 (*Tale pactum*), in the principal part, does not hold. The Preachers, in their commentary on instruments, say that this pact is valid as a simple will, without it being a donation; for in a pact to release, no cause is required; rather, there is a tacit cause, namely, liberality itself, which is the same as a donation according to Bartolus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Friars Preachers, who are privileged, are bound to pay the canonical portion.
2. An unreasonable custom, prohibited in the past, appears to be prohibited also for the future.
body: In the name of Christ. The matters in question possess the privilege of Boniface VIII, and, following the example thereof, of the subsequent pontiffs after the constitution *Dudum*, § *Verum*. Furthermore, they hold the privilege of the present Pope, albeit modeled on the aforementioned with a derogatory clause, namely adding that it may be left to them for perpetual alms, and that they may enjoy it, and the rest notwithstanding any provisions issued to the contrary.

† It is asked whether the said brothers are bound to pay the canonical portion. And the answer is that they are not, because a privilege granted by a prince with certain knowledge derogates from the common law: as is evident from the definition of the term, since a privilege is a private law; it prevails over the common law, as in c. 1 and c. Cum ordinem, de rescriptis, and as noted in c. Decurionibus, C. de silentiariis, lib. 12. To the contrary it seems, because this privilege is obtained through ambition and is contrary to natural equity: therefore it is not valid, as in C. de precibus imperatoribus offerendis, l. Rescriptum. Moreover, that section Verum derogates to preceding and future customs, and also to pacts. Therefore, by identity of reason, it also derogates to privileges, because they are presumed to have been obtained through importunity, as in l. 1, C. de bonis sublatis, lib. 10. To the contrary it seems, because that decretal derogates to past matters, therefore it permits future ones, just as conversely an indulgence of past matters is a prohibition of future ones, as in ff. de legibus, l. Cum lex, and by argument from ff. de legibus 2, l. Statuliberum, §. Stichum.

But to this it is answered that an unreasonable custom, prohibited in the past, is deemed also prohibited for the future, as in l. 3, §. diuus, D. de sepul. vio. And because custom and privileges, when coupled together, operate to prohibit, it is understood that both are equally disposed prohibitively, as in D. de lib. et posth., l. si ita, §. regula; and C. de nup., l. si liber; and C. de ind. vid., l. fi. Moreover, it is against the brothers, because all these privileges have the clause “ad instar,” i.e., “ad similitudinem”; but that which is abrogated has no similitude, nor “ad instar,” as in C. de lat. liber. toll., l. 1, in princ. Nor does the rescript of the present Pope avail, because the clause “non obstanti” is not placed to derogate from the common law, but from contrary privileges. In this question it is difficult to determine against the clergy, nor against the brothers; although the clergy supports greater equity, as in Extr. de pręb., c. cum secundum apostolum. Similarly, the law says that the fruits of the dowry should not be separated from the burdens of marriage. And thus the rescript of the prince should be interpreted, so that it does not oppose this reason, D. de pac. dot., l. cum pater dotem, in princ. Solution: Whatever may be said about the privileges of other supreme pontiffs, the privilege of the present Lord Boniface must be observed according to its letter, Extr. de priui., c. porro; and C. de legi., l. digna vox. In these ambiguities and dangers to souls, without prejudice to the peace of the supreme pontiffs, they themselves place in this question a great doubt both of science and of exception, except that there is no doubt about the power of the Pope, as in C. de crimine sacrilegii, l. 2. Furthermore, it suffices for the brothers that they are in possession in a doubtful matter, as in Inst. de interdi., §. commodum; and especially because the testators who today leave large sums to the said brothers would not have left them to priests. Hence, the priests, who would be equally deprived, could not complain. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When one may build upon a common wall.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Through instruments or witnesses it will be able to appear whether the wall and its front facade are common in undivided shares; it is lawful to build in common property by extending oneself toward the front without damage to the common wall, as in ff. de seru. vr. pręd. l. quidam Hiberus, ff. comuni diui. l. Sabinus, because the property tends toward this benefit, as in l. arbor. ff. communi diui. and ff. de vsufru. l. arboribus. §. nauis. If, however, it can be established through instruments or witnesses concerning the imposition of a servitude, those very testimonies or instruments ought to be preserved within their boundaries, because instruments have the force of a definitive determination, as in ff. finium reg. l. eos, C. de probat. l. cum precib., ff. ne fideius. l. magistra tuu. §. i. But if other proofs do not appear, but only the physical condition of the thing and long possession circumscribed within its boundaries, those things that have always had a certain state are by no means to be changed, as in C. de aedifi. priua. l. cum in totum; for whether that be custom or prescription, that very prescription seems to be its form, and it reveals how great and of what kind the thing is. Except that the aptitude [or capacity] ought also to be considered, not merely the act, by the argument of those things that are noted in l. 2. ff. si cert. pet.; and concerning that aptitude, and also the custom, one ought to stand by the judgment of experts in the art, to whom the thing ought to be shown, so that they may make a report with ocular faith [by eyewitness verification], as in ff. de off. procons. l. si in aliquam and ff. fin. reg. l. si irruptione. §. ad officia. If, however, all things are in doubt, it must be considered that he who introduces an innovation holds the role of the plaintiff, and therefore he must prove that it is lawful for him; otherwise he is bound to demolish the work according to the general rule, C. de eden. l. qui accusare and ff. quod vi aut clam. l. aut qui aliter. And if it should be said that two signs are made by the one building, namely that that little wall is contiguous and inserted, which ought not to be regarded by a different legal status, by the argument of ff. de vsucap. l. eum, qui ędes; likewise because the wall is not crowned or corniced: I respond, that which happens to be absent from this does not prove that it is so. Likewise, those beams sometimes do not show ownership any more than servitude, because beams of a servitude are accustomed to be inserted into another's wall, as in ff. de seru. vrb. praed. l. haec autem iura; and at times the law presumes a servitude rather than ownership, because less prejudice is involved, as in ff. de lega. 1. l. si fiendum. §. qui fundum. I, Baldus. See in consilium 213.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How manyfold habitation is said to be, and who is said to inhabit.
2. One may have two habitations at the same time, and be summoned to both,
body:
In the name of Christ. It is established that all and each of our household members or officials residing and living in our city of Pavia, who hold houses for their use and habitation from any citizen or native of our city and district of Pavia for a rent, cannot nor ought to be deprived in any way against their will of the possession and habitation of said houses and dwellings; nor can they be compelled in any manner to surrender them by the lords and proprietors thereof, or by those to whom they may pertain in any respect or for any cause, provided that our said household members and officials pay the due rent for said houses to those to whom they belong or pertain, do not cause damage therein, but inhabit them as is fitting.

Now it has happened that a certain Michilinus, a household member and apothecary of the lord, acknowledged and acknowledges by title of lease from a certain John a certain house or premises for a certain annual rent, which house is separate from Michilinus’s dwelling house; and in said house he had an apothecary shop constructed; and there reside and live the household members of said Michilinus, as well as his son and the rest of his family, who practice the art of apothecary; and there the servants sleep at night. For said John claims said house to be necessary for his own use and that of his family; and therefore he wishes to expel said Michilinus. But said Michilinus says that he cannot be expelled, since he is ready to pay the rent and to inhabit said premises in the manner aforesaid. The question is: what is the law?

† And for the clarity of what is to be said, it must be premised that "habitation" is said in three ways. In one way, for the right or servitude of habitation: as in D. de usu et habitatione, in the rubric and in the black letter; and C. de usufructu, l. Cum antiquitas. In another way, for a certain faculty of dwelling: as in D. de donationibus, l. Aquilius regulus. This faculty is possessed by a tenant: as in D. de locato conducto, l. Habitatores. In a third way, for the very bodily act, that is, for the very act of dwelling: as in D. de his qui de se vel de aliis noxam dederint, l. 1, §. Habitare; and D. de iniuriis, l. Lex Cornelia, §. Domum. For if habitation is taken in the first and second sense, there is no doubt, because he is said to dwell who receives persons pertaining to himself: as in D. de usu et habitatione, l. 2, §. Domus; and l. Ceterum in principio and §. Mulier; and l. Si habitatio legetur. And this is true when he dwells promiscuously with his household. However, if he dwells separately, and entirely separately, he is not properly said to dwell: as in D. de usu et habitatione, l. Sed neque in principio, unless the one who dwells is a joined person, and as it were the same body, such as a wife, or a son, or his own household: as in D. de dolo malo, l. Cum quis. For father and son are one identity, and there is one domicile for both: as is the sole gloss in l. 2, C. qui aetate, lib. 10; and it appears expressly in C. de agris et censibus, l. Cum sumus, §. Illud, where the golden text thus says: "Since a part, as it were, of their body remained in the estate through kinship, they were not considered to be absent." To this effect is C. communi utriusque iudicio, l. Possessionum; and D. de legatis 1, l. Si domus, §. Qui confitetur. For in such closely joined persons, separation is as harsh as death, as is clear from the said laws. But if habitation is taken in the third sense, for the very act of dwelling, that is, for the very bodily act: because there he dines, there he lies down, there he sleeps, the same must still be said, that by the extensive interpretation, which has place in stipulations and statutes, when it has in itself a natural cause: as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. Si stipulatus fuero, per non fieri, quo minus. Hence, the same immunity which is granted to the master is granted to the son, wife, and household: D. de iureiurando, l. Non alias; and C. ne filius pro patre, auth. Habita; C. de episcopis et clericis, l. 1. And in sum, whatever person is tacitly understood in the stipulation is included in the benefit of the statute: because such benefit proceeds from the contract through the decree, or from the decree through the contract, I do not care. But if it is such a person who is not understood, the contract does not extend to him: as in D. de verbis obligatis, l. Si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus, in fine. What does the decree of the lord say beyond this, namely, who hold houses for their use and habitation? For it does not require continuous dwelling: because the word "for" signifies the mode of the mind and the final cause, not however continuous in every way, but at the discretion of the judge: as in the law and note, D. de legatis 3, l. Qui concubinam, §. Uxori. And there is no doubt for anyone that this person dwells there during the day, converses for himself: and thus for part of the time. For although Labeo said that one cannot dwell simultaneously in different places, adhering more to the sense than to the reason, nevertheless the contrary is true:

† because one can have two dwellings and two domiciles at the same time: one in which he resides more, another in which he resides less, as stated in the Digest, *ad municipalia*, law *eius*, section *Celsus*. And he may be summoned to either house, as if to the house of his dwelling, as noted in the chapter *Causam*, *de electione*, in the Clementines. From which it is clearly concluded that the said Michilin cannot be expelled. Especially because the houses are so connected that from one there is a view to the other, and thus the dwelling is retained by use and by the capacity for dwelling when joined together. Argument from the Digest, *de contrahenda emptione*, law *Clauibus*; and the Digest, *de aqua pluviae arcendae*, law 1, section *Si iusserim*; and the Digest, *de solutionibus*, law *Si pecuniam*. Which, upon subtle and useful consideration, appears to me to be the truth. It is supported by chapter 1, *extra*, *de locato*. Moreover, it is manifest that one can have the same house as a dwelling for the day, however; and I say that from that dwelling he cannot be expelled; because it suffices that he dwells there for any amount of time, in order that he have the place of the lord’s decree; because the words of the decree are taken from something particular, not from the whole. But there is no doubt that during the day the lessee had full possession of the dwelling; because he performed all acts that are done by a dweller, nor is this said to be merely mercenary, because it is mercenary when one exercises some trade there during the day, and at night, with doors closed, departs, neither dining nor sleeping there, as are the stalls of cloth sellers. And this is clear from the similar case placed there regarding the stables of cloth sellers. But this shop was not only designated for the sale of spices, but there were also provisions and upper rooms with beds, which without doubt are not mercenary; and furthermore, above the attic there was a continuous passage from the house of the said Michilin to the leased house. From which it is manifestly shown that it was leased for full dwelling, and thus consequently taken and held. On this point is the case in the said section *Domum*. Also, he who dwells through another is considered to dwell by himself, when the other dwells for his benefit. Indeed, it is not a fiction, but the very truth, as in law *Certe*, section *Procurator*, Digest, *de praecariis*; Code, *de praescriptionibus*, 30 years; law *Male agitur*; Code, *si per vim vel alio modo*; law 1, *de aqua pluviae arcendae*; law *Peregrinus*, section *Si*; Code, *eodem*; law *Ultima*, Digest, *de contrahenda emptione*; law *Fistulas*, section 1, Digest, *de dolo*; law *Cum quis*; and many other laws are common and infinite: and it cannot be denied, neither in fact nor in law, that the household of the said Michilin dwelt in the said house for the said Michilin; and that it is the house of dwelling is clear, because it is the safest refuge, as in law *Plerique*, *de in ius vocando*. Notwithstanding section *Domum*, because there it speaks of one who did not reside in the stall except insofar as he exercised his trade: not on feast days, nor continuously, as in law *eius*, section *Celsus*, Digest, *ad municipalia*. Bartholomew. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A legacy made to one poor person annually for his necessities, if he shall request it, and this legacy remained concealed for 25 years: whether, when he later requests it, it is due for all the past years, or only for the year in which he requests it.
body: In the name of Christ. He bequeathed to Brother Andrew of the Order of Servants of Saint Mary, for as long as the said Brother Andrew shall live naturally, the entire sum of money that the said Brother Andrew shall wish to have for his necessities and shall request from the heirs of the said testator; provided, however, that he shall not request or receive more than the sum of 33 pounds of Bonenine currency in a year. This legacy remained hidden from the said Brother Andrew for 25 years and more; now he claims the said legacy. It is asked,

Whether it ought to be paid for the time from which he began to demand it, or from the time of the acceptance of the inheritance. And it seems that it ought to be paid from the time from which he began to demand it, and wished to have it for his necessities: and not before, because this legacy is conditional, as in the Digest, *De legatis*, book 1, law *Si ita legatum*, section *Ille si volet*. This condition is potestative: and therefore it is not drawn back, as in law 1, section *Servi*, in the Digest, *Ad Sillenum*. Moreover, because there are as many legacies as there are years, and since he lived and subsisted without this legacy, it appears that he did not have the necessity. Therefore, the final cause of the legacy fails: and thus the legacy is not due, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Illis libertis*.

To the contrary, it seems: because these words, "for his necessities," added to a certain quantity, do not diminish the legacy, as in the Digest, *De alimentis et cibariis legatis*, law *Lucius*. Moreover, in what is added, "and he demanded from the heirs," similarly these words do not create a condition: but a safeguard, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Si decem cum petiero*. And what is noted in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo*. Furthermore, this condition is feigned to operate retroactively, as noted in chapter 1, *De regulis iuris*, book 6, by Dynus. Furthermore, the heir was in bad faith by not notifying this legacy: but rather by concealing it, from which I infer in favor of the legatee for three reasons. First, because bad faith ought not to aid anyone; second, because it was through the heir that the matter stood: hence the condition seems fulfilled, as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Iure civili*. Third, if all these were lacking, it seems that restitution in integrum would be available under the general clause on account of this error, as noted by Dynus in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Ad diem*.

And if it be said that the four-year period has elapsed with respect to the old payments from four years back? I answer that this four-year period does not run against one who is ignorant, as noted in the Code, *De temporibus in integrum restitutionibus*, law *Supervacuam*. Moreover, even if this legacy were considered by some to be captatory, which I do not believe, nevertheless it would be valid for pious causes, as in the Extravagant, *De testamentis*, chapter *Cum tibi*. And if the testator had considered this case, he would undoubtedly have disposed of it in the same way.

This question is sufficiently doubtful, considering the force of the words and the nature of conditions; nevertheless, considering equity, because it is for pious causes and for the soul of the testator, since it is sought for the church and the Blessed Virgin, I believe and hold that it suffices to demand once, so that it is due for all years, as in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law 1, and the argument in the Digest, *De usuris*, law *Mora*. It would also be very inequitable that a pious disposition of the testament, which was left for necessities, should perish on account of the bad faith of the heir concealing it.

Now a great doubt arises for me, because it is certain that this brother did not have property of his own, and that many necessities intervened during the time: and that a poor person, who depends on alimony, always lacks in successive days and hours. Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, in the word *obsequiorum vitae*. And there noted. And Digest, *De operibus libertorum*, law *Suo victu*. And with these persuasions I am briefly content, and especially on account of conscience, because God ought not to be defrauded, and it is so. Digest, *Quibus ex causis maiores*, law *Si quis Titio*. And law *Si quis stipulatus*. Digest, *De acquirenda hereditate*, law *Cum quidam*, in the principal part. Code, *De restitutione militum*, law *Si Valerianus*. Digest, *Ad Sillenum*, law *Qui posthumos*. Digest, *De militum testamento*, law *Ex militari*, section *Si*, with the following law.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a statute prohibiting appeals, exceptions, and nullity from sentences also prohibits restitution in integrum.
2. Whether a statute that does not distinguish is said to correct the common law, so that it must be understood indiscriminately.
body: In the name of Christ. The statute of the city of Titus provides in the testament of Lau. that if the arbitrations or arbitral awards have been declared unjust or inequitable within the time period set forth in the statutes of the commune of Laudę, and a sentence has been pronounced in favor of the arbitrator, no appeal, supplication, or action for nullity may be brought against such pronouncement, nor may any exception be raised, if execution is carried out: as is contained in the statutes of the commune of Laudę. Now, a certain arbitral award was rendered against a minor; subsequently, it was declared unjust and inequitable; finally, the judge approved it by judicial sentence. Now the minor seeks restitution in integrum against the omitted proofs, which he did not produce before the arbitrator or the judge; and he proves this, as well as enormous lesion.

† It is asked, what is the law? And it appears that restitution in integrum cannot be sought: because from whom the end is removed, the beginning is understood to be removed, and every mode of punishing is directed to the end, as in D. de sponsalibus, l. oratio. But here it is prohibited that the judge’s sentence be retracted in any way: therefore, restitution in integrum cannot be sought, since by means of it the sentence would be retracted. Moreover, not only is it prohibited to bring an action, but also to raise an exception: therefore, every defense against the sentence itself is removed, as noted in C. de transactionibus, l. nec intentio. To the contrary, it appears that this minor, whose rights were not produced, was undefended: and according to the common law, without doubt, he ought to be restored in integrum, as in l. minor 25 annis omissam, D. de minoribus.

† Hence, nothing remains to be examined here except whether the statute in this article corrects the common law. And it seems that it does, because it speaks indiscriminately, as in D. de publicanis (50.12), l. de pretio. For where the statute does not distinguish, neither should we distinguish, as in l. in fraudem, D. de militum testamento (29.1). On the contrary, it seems that the common law of the City never appears to abolish the singular benefit of restitution in integrum, as is most fully noted in l. 1, C. si de momento possessoris (7.71). Moreover, the statute makes no mention of age, nor of the benefit of age; hence it does not appear to derogate from it, as in l. cum minor, §. si, D. rem ratam habere (50.17). Furthermore, this petition pertains to the benefit of age, not to the injustice of the sentence, as in D. de minoribus (4.4), l. si praeses. Moreover, natural equity dictates this, as in D. de dolo malo (4.3), l. doli mali. Moreover, in a general pact, the benefit of restitution in integrum is not deemed to have been renounced; therefore, the same applies to a statute, since a statute is said to be a certain agreement of the citizens, as in D. de regulis iuris (50.17), l. nec ex praetorio. And see C. de decretis decurionum (10.32), l. 1; D. de legibus (1.14), l. de quibus, in fine; and l. sed ea, quae. I have often doubted on this point: but now, inclining toward the more humane and more probable opinion in law, I hold that this case is not comprehended in the statute; and therefore the common law should be observed, and restitution in integrum ought to be granted to the minor. D. de iureiurando (12.2), l. nam postea, §. si minor; and D. de in integrum restitutione (4.1), l. si; and C. si adversus rem iudicatam (7.62), l. cum et minores. I, Baldus. Add in consilium 239.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether legacies made to a wife concerning the entire usufruct, and that she be clothed and provided with sustenance from the husband's goods, merge into one another.
2. Whether debts diminish legacies.
3. Whether one ought to pay the debts of the inheritance, or whether the heirs, legatees, or the usufructuary should do so.
4. Whether a legacy made to a daughter for the purpose of marriage is to be claimed immediately or not; and whether in the meantime she is entitled to sustenance, or to the usufruct arising from such a legacy of dowry. And add the counsel beginning "It is asked concerning legacies," and chapter in the sixth part.
5. How the words "on account of the dowry" are to be understood.
6. A burden does not attach to the legitime, nor to the fruits of the legitime.
body: In the name of Christ. He wished it to be his will, and it is his right, that Seya, his wife, shall have the usufruct of all the goods of the said testator, and may dispose of them as she pleases, and shall have food, clothing, and alms from the goods of the said testator, without being required to render any account of the said usufructs, and without being required to give any security, and without taking any oath: having done this, he instituted two strangers as his universal heirs.

† To make the matter evident, it must be premised that one thing is a legacy of usufruct, another is a legacy of alimony: for the usufructuary must give security for using and enjoying according to the discretion of a good man; and he must have full usufruct, as is noted in l. 1, c. Si secundo nup. mul. and the Authentica posita there, and in D. de usufr. leg. l. Uxori. But the legatee of alimony is not bound to give security. Moreover, he does not spare except for the necessities of life. Furthermore, they said in the name [of the law], moreover, that no transaction can be made regarding alimony without the praetor; but so it can be regarding usufruct, because it is a part of ownership, unless the usufruct is expressly bequeathed as alimony, as in D. de trans. l. Cum hi, §. Qui transigit, and §. Si uni, with the following §. And therefore it seems to be said that these, as distinct legacies, are not merged one into the other, but that alimony and, furthermore, usufruct are due, as in the said l. Cum hi, §. Si idem. Moreover, the conjunction placed between different things has the effect of amplifying, as in D. de leg. 3, l. Hoc legatum. Wherefore it seems that both should be obtained, as in D. de usufr. leg. l. Sempronio.

On the contrary, it seems that alimony bequeathed from goods must be provided from the fruits of the goods, if the fruits suffice, as in D. ad Treb. l. Imperator, and by Jacobus de Arena to this effect in D. de usufr. l. Si in pendentes, §. Si quid cloacarii; to this effect in D. de iud. l. Si fideicommissum, §. Qui tamen. For if the testator had wished to burden the heir with double performance, he would have said so, as in D. de leg. 2, l. Titia, §. Qui invita. He will therefore have alimony from the usufruct, not from the sale of the properties: so that the container, i.e., usufruct, embraces its content, i.e., alimony, so that the species does not enlarge the genus, since it comes after the genus, as in D. de leg. 2, l. In legatorum, §. Qui plures, and D. de vino leg. l. Si, §. Cui dulcia, and D. de pen. leg. l. Nam quod liquide, §. Si cui penus. One can therefore sue on two heads, namely, usufruct and alimony; but one cannot obtain full usufruct and full alimony, because this does not seem to have been the intention of the testator.

Solution: Strictly speaking, according to the rigor of the words, it must be said that both should be obtained, just as if they had been bequeathed to different legatees, they would not make parts for themselves by concurrence, as if they were legatees of different things, as in l. Si alii, §. Rerum, D. de usufr. And that one should not depart from the rigor of the words is clear from D. de usufr. leg. l. Si alii. Otherwise it would follow that if the usufruct of one estate were bequeathed, it would be imputed to the legacy of alimony, which is false. Moreover, it would follow that the legatee would seem to be burdened with respect to himself, which also lacks truth, because legacies are understood to be imposed as a burden on the heir, as in C. ad Treb. l. Si.

Secondly, it is asked whether debts diminish these legacies. And it must be said that they do: because a legacy is not due unless the debts have been paid, as stated in C. de leg. l. si universae; ff. de inoff. testa. l. Papinian. §. quarta. And this is expressly provided in ff. de iudi. l. fideicommissum. §. tractatum. Hence, only the heir is bound to pay the legacies by an action arising from the will, and not the legatee; because a quasi-contract is formed between the legatee and the heir, and not between legatees. Moreover, because property cleared of debts is not called the inheritance, as stated in ff. de lega. mino. l. non amplius. §. cum bonorum. And by this I say that, although debts diminish legacies, nevertheless they diminish and ought to diminish them in effect to the prejudice of the heir: since the heir is bound to keep the legatee and legatees indemnified; otherwise, if the assets are solvent, all loss falls entirely upon him, especially if he did not make an inventory or does not have the benefit thereof.

Thirdly, it is asked through whose hands the alien debt ought to be paid, whether through the hands of the heir or through the hands of the usufructuary: and it must be said that through the hands of the heir, who is bound; since the usufructuary of the goods is not bound to the creditors, but the usufructuary of the inheritance would indeed be bound to the creditors together with the universal heir, not alone, because it is not a burden of the fruits, but a burden of the entire patrimony, as in D. de usufr. lega. l. si. On the other hand, the burden of the fruits is borne solely by the legatee of the estates. Arg. D. de impen. in re. dota. fac. l. neque stipendium.
