† Furthermore, it is asked: if a legacy has been left to a daughter, and the words of the will state that it is on account of constituting a dowry, whether she can demand the legacy immediately or not, in such a way, however, that in the meantime she receives maintenance according to the measure of the legacy, as it seems the law *Cum unus*, §. final, *de alimentis legatis*, says. For if she could demand the dowry immediately, she would not have maintenance, but rather the legacy itself; but where the testator said, “to the daughter when she marries.”

† In the matter at hand, he said, on account of the dowry. These words signify a remote cause, as in l. si mulier, ff. rerum amotarum. They also signify an impulsive cause, or a certain demonstration, and a paternal counsel made in favor of the daughter alone. arg. ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Titio centum, in principio. For the testator did not say "in dowry" or "for the dowry," and thus it does not sound as a condition or a final cause for the future, and this I hold. Hence, it does not avail against the Authentica de sanctissimis episcopis, §. sed hoc praesenti; and the aforementioned l. Titio, §. Titio. And sometimes it even pleases parents to marry off their children prematurely for the utility of the children, as in ff. quod falsum tutor, auth. l. an etiam in patrem. In the same way, it does not avail against C. de nuptiis, l. sancimus. Nor does it avail against ff. de usuris, l. in fideicommissi, §. cum Pollidius, because there another minister was elected going to the truth in the interim.

† Regarding the legitime and the fruits of the legitime, there is no doubt, because it must be received free of burden, as stated in the Novella *Quoniam*. Moreover, this dowry, destined for the fruits, will meanwhile be in fruit: and from the alimentary support the girl will marry better, which accords with the father's wishes, as in D. ad Trebellianum, l. *Mulier*, § *Cum proponeretur*. And if the fiancé would not otherwise take her in marriage unless he profited from the fruits of the destined dowry: and in this case they do not increase the dowry, otherwise they do. D. de solutione matrimonii, l. *Si ante*. And this last statement does not bear on the point at issue: nevertheless it is true and noteworthy. I, Baldus. Allegations on behalf of those of Palantia,

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Public functions are demanded with the veil removed, and no petition is given.
2. The assignor of rights may act for the benefit of the assignee.
3. Statutes do not require proof, nor production in the place where they are in force.
4. A debt is satisfied by the longest performance.
5. A mandate may begin with execution.
body: In the name of Christ. It is so both in law and in fact.

† And it must be premised that a libellus (formal written complaint) is not necessary, nor is the litis contestatio (joinder of issue), when public functions are sought; rather, the procedure is coercive, with the veil lifted, both by common law and by general custom, as is stated in Auth. de mandato principis § coges; ff. de publicis iudiciis l. commissa; C. de exactionibus tributorum l. 2; and l. missi opinatores li. 10; and this is expressly noted by Innocentius in Extra de officio in c. j. And of this there has never been any doubt, because if publicans were required to offer a libellus in every case, collectors of taxes would not be found. Hence, in place of a libellus, they offer seizure, imprisonment, and retention of goods, as in ff. locati l. pen. § nauem. And therefore, if coercion is sought, it is rightly sought, because it is expressly stated in the aforementioned § coges. Moreover, this fact is notorious. Hence, on the statute of the law, a libellus ought not to be offered, because in notorious matters the order of judicial proceedings is not required, as in Extra de iureiurando c. ad nostram noueris. And by this it is clear that the allegation concerning the libellus, or that condemnation has not been requested, is irrelevant, because one may begin with execution and coercion; and although the judge is approached, the condition of the one approaching is not made worse, as noted in l. 2 C. de iure emphyteutici. And by this it is clear that the allegation of the inadequacy of the libellus is irrelevant, together with all its consequences, which I consider entirely frivolous.

† To that which is alleged, namely, that the common syndic does not have a mandate from the tax farmers, and that the matter is one acted upon between others, it is also answered that he acted in the name of the community and of the tax farmers, and the tax farmers have ratified it, as in the law *Licet*, with its subject matter. Moreover, it is common that the assignor of rights is the assignor, and the tax farmers are the assignees; and it is most certain that the assignor of rights can sue for the benefit of the assignee, because the rights remained with him to be asserted and executed for the benefit of the assignee, as in the Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Si actor malitiose*; as in the Code, *De nova*, law 3; and fully noted in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Si cum emptore*. Nor is it said that the matter is one acted upon between others, as in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Si superatus*, because one is the owner, the other the procurator for his own interest, who are considered the same person, as in law 1, at the end, Digest, *De usufructu*, *Quemadmodum cautio fiat*.

† To the further point that it is said the statute has not been produced, it is replied that, on the contrary, the original has been produced. Moreover, statutes are notorious in the place where they are in force; nor do they require production, just as it is not necessary to produce the Code or the old Digest, as in C. de legit. l. leges sanctissimae, and in Auth. ut factae novae constitu. post prin., and in Auth. ut cum de appel. cog. in prin. and pleno no. in proem. clemen. Furthermore, no allegation is made regarding written law; therefore, proof is not necessary. no. ff. de aur. et arg. leg. l. ornamentorum.

† To the other point, which is said and which is not proven, I answer that, on the contrary, it is proven to be exigible by law and its effect is to be obtained through long-standing performance, by which the debt is proven by condition from custom, or by the office of the judge from prescribed custom, as in D. de usuris, l. cum de in rem verso, and there note that all the Moderns hold this; D. de publ., l. si publicanis. For if the territory prescribes this jurisdiction, as in C. de agri. et censi., l. domini praediorum, lib. 11, and such revenues are counted among movables, C. de sac. san. eccl., l. iubemus, and for them a possessory action is also available, as in X. de elec., c. quaerelam. Moreover, to the letters of the lord, no reply should be given again, even if disguised or colored, whence the right of the client of the Testator thus said: it is certain of our palantia: because it accords with the rescript, as in D. de pecu. leg., l. si peculium, § sicut, in fi. §, and this is the very truth. To the other point, which is said, because execution is sought from a null sentence, nor were the parties cited.

† It is answered that this is not properly a sentence, but rather a certain mandate, in which one may begin with execution, as noted in the Digest, *De novo operis nuntiando*, in the law *De pupillo*, § *Meminisse*. Moreover, mandates which are justified in themselves by the clear nature of the business do not require other proof, nor a hearing of the case, according to Innocentius. I, Baldus. The same counsel contains the same thing as counsel 237, although through different words and different allegations.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The conjunction "and" is sometimes placed between a genus and a species; sometimes between two genera; sometimes between two species; sometimes between two significates; sometimes between a fund and a usufruct; sometimes between substance and quality; sometimes between predicate and subject; and in these cases, what effect it produces.
2. Differences between usufruct and alimony.
3. A universal legatee of a usufruct is bound to contribute with the heir towards a legacy of alimony left to another.
body: In the name of Christ. Having instituted an alien heir, who had no children except a certain married daughter, whom he ordered to be content with her dowry, and having made a refutation to the father, I leave to Beatrice, my sister, or to my wife, the usufruct of all my goods, and the maintenance of the said goods, or in the said goods, provided that the said wife claims the entire usufruct; and furthermore, so much more from the heir out of the heir’s purse, or of the inheritance’s properties, whereby she may have maintenance. On the contrary, it is said that maintenance, as a lesser thing, is said to be torn from the greater thing, namely, the entire usufruct, and is merged therein; so that if she has the entire usufruct, which suffices for maintenance, she cannot claim maintenance separately.

† It is asked, what is the law: and for clarity it must be premised that sometimes the conjunction "and" is placed between a genus and a species; sometimes it is placed between two genera; sometimes it is placed between two species. Sometimes it is placed between two significates which can be separated from the same body. Sometimes it is placed between a fund and a usufruct; sometimes it is placed between substance and quality. In the first case, the conjunction is placed between the predicate and the subject, concerning which I refer to the Glossator on the Codex, *De legatis*, l. *Cum quaestio*; and to Bartolus on the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Doli clausula*; and to the Glossator on the Decretals, c. *Generi*. And this is not our case, for here there is no genus and species, which is apparent from the definition, for the name "usufruct" is not placed in the definition of "aliments"; but the genus is placed in the definition of any species, and any species is represented in its genus, as in l. 1, D. *Si certum petatur*. But it could rather be said that these two legacies stand to each other as exceeding and exceeded. For sometimes usufruct is broader than aliments: as in large estates; sometimes it is less inclusive: as in small ones. The second and third cases of the principal text are clear: because the conjunction serves to enlarge the legacy; I do not say to double it, for doubling would occur when the same thing is given by the same title, as in D. *De funerariis instrumentis*, l. *Si cui*; and l. *Seiæ*, § *Caio*, D. *De legatis tertio*; l. *Hoc legatum*; and l. *Ea tamen adiectio*, D. *De legatis secundo*; l. *Sed ex duobus*. In the fourth case, when the conjunction is placed between two bodies, or universal terms, one of which is naturally apt to be separated from the body of the other, and also not to be separated, then the question is very doubtful as to what the testator intended: and if the sense of the testator has been proved to the judge, the declaration of the witnesses shall be followed, as in C. *De fideicommissis*, l. *Voluntas*. But if nothing is proved extrinsically, so that we have no basis to judge except according to the words, the nature of the words shall be followed: and because the nature of the conjunction is enlarging, and also because in wills a broader interpretation is made, I say that both are due according to the strictness of the words; nor is one confused into the other by way of confusion. Just as if the testator said, "I bequeath to Peter one hundred and fifty, or half and a quarter of such a thing," so that the conjunction is expressed, as this article is fully examined in the aforementioned l. *Cum quaestio*. Now it is thus in our case: because aliments can be understood as part of the body of the usufruct, and they can be understood as existing in themselves. And that they are two legacies is apparent, because one can be accepted and the other repudiated.

† Moreover, a donation made because the usufruct ends upon the alteration of the thing, but maintenance does not. Moreover, the right of accretion applies in a simple usufruct, but not in maintenance, as in the Digest, On Usufruct, l. dominus. Moreover, in a usufruct, security must be given for proper use, etc., but not in maintenance. Moreover, in a usufruct, the usufructuary is seized of the usufruct by his own hand, but maintenance by the hand of the heir, as in the Digest, On Usufruct, l. si quis ita, and l. solent, Digest, On Adjudication and Legacies. Here, however, it must be considered,

† That the universal legatee of the usufruct is bound to collate with the heir regarding a legacy of alimony left to another, as in D. de usufr. leg. l. si; although others say that, on the contrary, he is bound in full, because alimony is to be provided from the fruits, as in D. ad Treb. l. Imperator, in fine. But the more probable opinion is that the heir also collates: and if this applies to legatees who are different persons, the same must be said regarding the same person, by argument from D. si cert. pe. l. singularia. Namely, that the legatee of alimony receives half from himself out of his own usufruct, and the other half from the heir, by analogy to two debtors, as in D. ad Treb. l. nonnunquam, and by argument from D. de duob. reis. l. reos, § cum tabulis. For this obligation of alimony appears to be hereditary; and therefore it is to be divided among universal successors, namely the heir and the universal legatee, by argument from D. de act. et obl. l. hereditariarum. Moreover, if there were children from the first marriage, or even from the second, in favor of the children the word "usufruct" would be used improperly, as is fully noted in C. si secundo nup. mul. autem, there placed. Therefore, if there are no children, the word "usufruct" is used properly, and the word "alimony" properly; and one is not torn from the body of the other by way of resection, but by way of discharging, the general usufructuary of all goods must participate in discharging this burden together with the heir. Unless we say that only the heir is bound to discharge the legacies by an action on the will, and not the legatee, because a quasi-contract is celebrated between the legatee and the heir, not between legatees. Also, because goods purged of debt are not called the inheritance, as in D. de leg. 1. l. non amplius, § cum bonorum. Others say that there it is not all the goods, but a part, as in D. de leg. 2. l. si quis servum, § si. Finally, this doubt rests in the aforementioned l. ult. de usufr. leg. And it seems to me finally that the testator did not burden the usufructuary with respect to himself in any way; hence the heir is not released by confusion, because he is alone, and not for a part. And thus the objection from D. de leg. 2. l. miles, § pro parte, does not hold, because we are not in the case of that law, but rather in the reasoning of l. legatum, § heredi, D. de leg. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made in prison and subsequently ratified is valid.
2. Arbitrators must follow the truth, however it may be brought forward.
body: In the name of Christ. A transaction was made by Antonio, son of Francesco, at the time when the said Antonio was detained in prison; and it was made by persons of good repute; and it was ratified after his release from prison; and the said house had been possessed for many years.

It is not doubtful that the said donation was valid, as established in the Digest, title *Quod metus causa*, law *Metum*, section *Sed licet*; and in the Digest, title *De donationibus*, law *Si pater*; and in the Code, title *Quod metus*, law 2. The only point to be considered is whether the said donation has been proved or not: and it is undoubtedly proved by one witness as to the truth, namely Andrew, who attests to the said donation made in the presence of the said witness. Furthermore, the confession is proved, although made in absence, by many witnesses. Furthermore, the reputation is proved; from all of which the witnesses ought to be believed as providing strong corroboration, or at least an oath ought to be administered to the donee in supplement of proof: which I believe to be more correct, considering that the price of the said house is not large, and that the said Antonius is a person worthy of credit, as stated in the Extravagant, title *De successionibus ab intestato*, chapter *Cum dilectus*; and in the Digest, title *De iureiurando*, law *Admonendi*; and in chapter 1, section *Sacramentum*, of the title *De consuetudine recti feudi*. And

† especially before arbitrators, who ought to follow the truth as known to them in any manner, as noted by Innocentius in the extrajudicial decretals on oaths, chapter Quintauallis. And thus it may be defended according to law; and much more so, by natural equity, may this oath be demanded in any part of the litigation, as in the extrajudicial decretals on oaths, chapter Ex litteris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. These words, and in the case in which the said inheritance comes into the aforementioned joint ownership, create an express condition: if this condition fails, the legacy fails, and the codicillary clause sometimes has no application.
body: Because truth stands in one thing, in the name of Christ. The case is as follows, see the document. A in his solemn will instituted B, his natural and legitimate son, as heir, to whom he substituted the pious and legally approved community of Saint Bernardin in the event that B should die without male children: in the event that the said inheritance of the testator A should come to the said community, the said A left a legacy of one hundred to Titius. Now, after the death of the said A, the inheritance having been taken possession of by the said B, the said B died, having instituted as his heirs his two legitimate and natural daughters, namely I. and N., and having left no male children: these daughters accepted the inheritance of the said B, having repudiated the fideicommissum substituted by the said community of the testator A; who in his will added this clause: if it is not valid, or will be valid by the law of wills, let it be valid by the law of codicils, or by the law of any other donation. Now, the aforementioned Titius demands the one hundred from the said daughters by right of legacy: the daughters oppose him, saying that the legacy is not due to him, because the fideicommissum was repudiated by the said substitute, and the inheritance was not restored to the said community: and because the legacy was left by the aforementioned community, and not by the said daughters themselves. Now it is asked, whether the said legacy is due in the manner aforesaid, or not? I presuppose that the said community has formally repudiated the fideicommissum.

† It is therefore asked concerning the said legacy of one hundred, whether it is due, and I say that it is not: because those words, and in the case where the said inheritance comes to the said consortium, create an express condition, which, if lacking, causes the legacy to fail, as in C. de caducis tollendis § pro secundo. Nor does it remain with the heir subject to a burden: because the condition fails, as I have stated above. Moreover, that clause, if it is not valid by the law of wills, does not apply here, because the said legacy is not valid either by the law of wills or by the law of codicils: since it was attached as a burden on the consortium only: and the condition has failed, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus l. quae legata; C. de caducis tollendis Sub conditione; D. de verbis significatis l. cedere diem. Someone might say, rather, this condition is tacit, which does not make the legacy conditional, as in D. de legatis 1 l. haec verba. I answer, there the condition, if he shall be heir, is attached to the institution: and it is a necessary condition; here it was attached to a fideicommissum: and it is a voluntary condition, because the testator could have effectively made a simple legacy without that condition. But the words of the will must be carefully examined, whether they accord with the point formulated. For as Scævola says, everyone who gives counsel advises according to what is proposed. I, Baldus. See on this in consilium 234.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the purpose of a lease of a house does not appear, it is presumed to have been made for full use and habitation.
2. † Given a statute providing that the friends and household members of the lord, who have leased houses for their habitation, cannot be evicted by their respective lords, whether this applies to stalls and spice shops leased by such household members.
3. When a part is retained, the whole is said to be retained.
4. What the word "hold" imports.
5. What a house is.
6. What the term "for" imports. And no. 10.
7. What use is.
8. What habitation is.
9. He who dwells through another dwells by himself.
11. These words, "for use and habitation," do not require a conjunction, because one suffices.
body: In the name of Christ. In a word, without going into much talk.

It must be premised for clarity that where a lease of a house is evident, but the purpose is not apparent, it is presumed to have been made for full use and habitation; nor does it matter whether the lessee resides there himself or sublets it to others, because it suffices that he can reside and use it at his will; nor can the lessor prohibit habitation under the common law except in certain cases. But under the law of the rescript of the great lord, in no case [can he prohibit it] to household members and the like.

† Since it appears that he leased the premises for dwelling and for use, and since everything is established from the beginning of the lease based on that initial principle, it follows that, because Michilinus leased the property simply and without qualification, the lessor conveyed to him all his rights, both for dwelling and for any other manner of use. For no specific rule was imposed upon him other than the obligation to use the property properly; nor was the quality of use specified in a particular way, for example, for the spice trade and not for dwelling, or vice versa. This is because the rent stands in place of full habitation and full use; it is not paid for one specific purpose alone, given that the lessee is in possession of the right to use and enjoy the property in any manner.

† because by partition the whole is retained. These are proven literally. D. de usufr. l. item si feudum. §. si. D. de usufr. de pig. ac. l. solutio. §. unde si domum. D. quae ad feud. amit. l. is, cui via. Wherefore here a right arises from the faculty and a right of habitation is born, and having been born, the rescript of the lord is verified literally without any other interpretation. It is not an obstacle, §. domum, in that it speaks there of meritorious services. Because there it speaks when habitation is not joined to meritorious services by a preceding lease: which appears, since it says there, or stabling. Moreover, there it speaks of servants who stand there for wages, not of one who has hired habitation, as D. de iud. l. heres ab sens. §. at si quis. and §. at si quo consistat. where it is expressed that there he can be cited as to the house of habitation: indeed he has domicile there: since he has the greater part of his fortunes. And these are, in my judgment, undoubted on account of the many reasons assigned in my counsel. And on account of the case. l. cum servus. there alleged. The words of the decree of our lord the prince

They say, "who hold houses for their use and habitation": in which words each individual element must be weighed. First, the word "hold" must be weighed. And there is no doubt that he holds who holds through another for his own benefit and convenience: hence it is that he names his lord in court, as in l. 2. C. ubi in rem actio. Solution. The word "houses" must be weighed.
† But a house is a building consisting of a plot of land, a roof, and walls. D. 7.1.1
Third is the word "for," which signifies the mind, the cause, and the movement of the mind, as noted in the Digest, On Usufruct, Legacies, in the law "The master to Stichus."
The fourth is the word "use," i.e., for any kind of use; because it does not matter how one uses, provided that one uses without injury to another, as in D. de usufructu, l. hactenus, §. si.

Fifthly, habitation is a safe refuge and the repose of the inhabitant, where he makes his place, keeps his bed, eats, and drinks whenever he pleases. For habitation consists in faculty, not in necessity, as stated in the law *Habitationum*, in the title *De periculo et commodo rei venditae*. And he who causes another to inhabit for him and for his own utility, himself inhabits. Otherwise, no one would inhabit a single house except to the extent that he occupies the space of his feet and body, which is ridiculous. And our lord would not inhabit a castle except to the extent that he sleeps in one chamber, which is foolish to say. And if it is said that in contiguous buildings it is true that one inhabits through another, I say the same regarding non-contiguous buildings, because his household is part of his own body. Nobles have several habitations not contained within one enclosure: one in the city, another in the country. See the Digest, title *De acquirenda possessione*, law 4, section *Saltus*. And it suffices that they inhabit by aptitude and the faculty of power; for that which is in aptitude represents the act, as stated in the Digest, title *De dolo*, law *Cum quis*.

† Since, therefore, he who dwells through another dwells through himself, just as he who possesses through another: as in the Digest, on precarium, l. certe, § procurator, so it is in the case at hand.

† Moreover, this term, *pro*, signifies power; hence, one who hires a house for the purpose of possessing and inhabiting it is said to have hired it *pro habitando* (for inhabiting). But Michelinus hired a house, in which lease is contained the power to inhabit; therefore, habitation is included. The adversaries place weight on the statement of Bartolus, which does not merit citation, because he speaks of a station, in which there is no habitation. For nothing prevents a station from existing without habitation, and conversely, nor does it prevent a station and habitation from being joined together; just as nothing prevents one from inhabiting and weaving, as in D. 39.4.1 (*duorum libertus*). It is therefore apparent that the same house can pertain to and serve both habitation and a trade. Nor is it said to be merely for trade, but rather for trade and habitation; for this is manifest, such that it ought not to be placed in dispute what is evident to the eyes.

† Moreover, those words, "for their use and habitation," do not require a conjunction; for one suffices, as in the Institution on legacies, § If anyone [gives] maidservants. And especially because one is inherent in the other, as in the Code on usufruct, law When antiquity. Let the intellect, which appears most acute and discerning, supply the rest. I, Baldus. A certain noble

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A person outlawed for the crime of lèse-majesté made a will, and died while the condemnation was pending. Finally, peace having been made between the lords at war, on account of which he had been outlawed, all condemnations previously made were remitted and annulled; it is asked whether the will revives. And no. 2.
3. How it is to be understood that the person making a will must be certain of his status.
4. In a criminally prosecuted case, the heir of the deceased cannot be condemned.
5. Whether a will made during a time of incapacity to make a will revives upon the subsequent occurrence of capacity to make a will. And no. 2.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain nobleman named Antonius of Piacenza was condemned for the crime of lèse-majesté by the podestà of the said land, because he had rebelled a certain castle against the exalted lord, lord Galeas. While this condemnation was pending, he passed away, having made a testament; but after his death a peace was made, and their goods were remitted, as well as the condemnations of those, namely, who would be named as ought to come into the said peace. Here

† it is first asked whether the said testament was valid? And on this it must be said that it was not valid: because he had been condemned for the crime of high treason (perduellio). For if the memory of a deceased person can be condemned, much more strongly can an absent person be condemned. And this is expressly stated in the Extravagans of Henry; and it is clear in Inst. de haeredi. abintestato. §. per contrarium, and ff. de acu. l. ex iudiciorum.

† But it is doubted whether the said testament became valid through the restitution of goods and of memory made after death. And it must be said that it did, for just as memory can be condemned after death, so conversely, and more strongly, because more favorably, it can be restored after death: because the rule for contraries is the same, as in l. et si contra. ff. de vul. substi. But two doubts arise here: one by reason of the goods, because that condemned man left no goods in the city, whence he cannot have an heir, as the text notably says in ff. de vul. substit l. lex Cornelia. But to this the answer is that by the fiction of the restitution of peace reintegrating everything from the beginning, he is feigned to have left goods in the city, as in ff. de iniu. testa. l. si quis filio. §. pen. And so I saw it observed in the City of Perugia at the time of the war between the Church and the Perugians.

† The second doubt is because he who makes a testament ought to be certain of his status. But to this the answer is that that rule fails here by virtue of restitution in integrum. A third doubt can also be raised: because this deceased man was neither named nor accepted among the others; therefore he is not included in the benefit of the peace, because not even in the form of words, and when this form ceases no one recovers goods after death—just as Lazarus did not, as in ff. de capti. l. non vt a patre, and l. qui libertinus. §. posthumus. ff. de ope. liber. Unless we say that this restriction of naming does not apply to the deceased, because it would be held as not written, as in C. de caduc. tol. l. 1. in princ., and ff. de iure cod. l. quidam refert, and ff. de leg. 1. l. ciuitatibus. §. Lucius; nor is the useful vitiated by the useless, because it was not added with the intention of vitiating, ff. de haere. insti. l. si mihi meuia.

† Another case follows, because while the same war was pending, the said Antonius, by his counsel, brought it about that certain others took another castle from a certain Bartholomaeus, an adherent of the said magnificent lord; and on that account they were later condemned to ten thousand florins, each in solidum. This condemnation, however, was made after the death of the said Antonius, and execution of this condemnation is sought against the possessors of the goods of the said Antonius, namely against a certain Bernardus, who possesses certain goods left to him. It is asked, what is the law? I answer: the said condemnation was null by operation of law, and therefore does not warrant execution, as in ff. de re iudic. l. 4. §. condemnatum, and ff. de iudic. l. de qua re. §. 1, ff. qui satisd. cog. l. si decesserit, ff. quę sententia sine ap. rescin. l. Paulus. Likewise because the heir of a deceased person cannot be condemned on account of a crime prosecuted criminally, as in C. si reus, uel accu. mor. fue. l. defunctis, and ff. de poenis. l. si poenae, and the reasoning is stated there in the text, and C. si pend. appel. mors interuenerit. l. 4. Nor does C. si ex delictis defunctorum. l. 1 stand in the way, because there an action was brought civilly from a crime, principally and secondarily, whereas here it was brought criminally.

† But it seems that, on the contrary, a testament made during a time of lack of testable capacity does not become valid when testable capacity supervenes, because the testament itself did not take its beginning in the city, nor was it made by a Roman citizen, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. 1. §. 1. in the words haec vtique; nor can a fiction operate where the subject of the fiction, that is, the person, has been extinguished, as in ff. ad l. aquil. l. huic scripturae, and as subtly noted by Pe. and Cy. in l. fi. C. de senten. pas., for fictions cannot be drawn to things impossible in law, as is noted in ff. de leg. 1. l. talis scriptura. But to these points the answer is that there is a special rule in this lawful agreement which is made for the sake of peace: for whatever pleases the contracting parties between themselves has the force of law, as in ff. de pac. l. legitima; and this is derived from the ius gentium, namely as to the capacity which is retroactive through the fiction of the peace, not to the beginning, that is, to the preamble hour of the war, to which both the Pope and the said illustrious lord referred themselves, as in l. quid ergo. in princ. ff. de his, qui notantur infamia. For where the Pope interposes his authority, there the fullness of all power intervenes. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A notary who committed falsification not out of malice is to be absolved, and see number 4.
2. Where the parlatorium is said to be.
3. One thing is a tractatus, and another is a conclusio.
4. Fiction excuses from the penalty for falsification.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A doubt is raised concerning a certain young notary, of little practice in the art, who, having been called to draw up an instrument of syndicship, stated that the act was done in the parlor, whereas the nuns were assembled in a place other than the customary parlor, yet within the enclosure of the monastery: whether the instrument is false on this account.

† And it must be said that it is not, because the parlor is wherever the nuns determine to make a parlor within the precincts of the monastery, even in the church or the cloister; for this place is not so of the essence that another place cannot be chosen for a parlor, as in ff. de iudi. l. si locus coniuncta; ff. de arbitris. l. si cum dies. §. qui tamen; and de offi. ord. c. cum episcopus. li. 6; and C. de sen. quę sine certa quanti. pro. l. quamquam. in the final gloss. It is doubted, secondly, and this is the greater doubt: because, when there were seven nuns present at the discussion which was taking place concerning the appointing of a syndic, before the instrument of syndicship was requested, three nuns withdrew, saying, "we are content with the syndic whom the abbess shall make, and you may write it down"; and the notary wrote down as witnesses those three nuns who were not present at the completion—which he indeed could not do, as in C. de te. l. cum antiquitas. §. si tamen—should this notary be punished for forgery? And it seems that he should, because forgery is nothing other than an alteration of the truth. But this man seems to have altered the truth, because although those three nuns were present at the discussion, they were nevertheless not present at the completion.
† For the discussion is one thing, and the conclusion is another, as is noted in l. eleganter. in prin. ff. de cond. inde.

† The solution: in forgery, fraudulent intent (dolus) is required, as in C. de fal. l. nec exemplum; and therefore it is proper to consider with what age and with what mind something is done, as in ff. ad exhibendum. l. pen.; C. ad l. Cor. de sica. l. 1; C. si quis impera. maledixe. l. vnica. All things that ought to be considered having thus been considered, I say that which the text says elsewhere: "the penalty of the Lex Cornelia shall be remitted to you, into which I believe you fell more by error than by malice," C. de his, qui sibi scribunt. l. quod adhibitus; especially because the legal effect was not increased by those three, since the syndicship stood validly by the abbess together with the other three nuns who remained standing by, because here not merely the greater part, but rather the greatest part constitutes the chapter.

† Likewise, those three who withdrew committed their authority to the abbess; whence, by a fiction of law, they are understood to have been present, which fiction excuses from the penalty of forgery, as Bartolus elegantly notes in ff. si cer. pet. l. singularia. From which it is concluded that he must be entirely acquitted from the accusation, insofar as it is grounded in dolus, and from the penalty of forgery. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. One acting in another’s name cannot make a will.
2. Given a statute providing that a woman who enters a second marriage shall not succeed to her son, may the son institute her as heir, at least with respect to property situated outside the territory of the enacting authority? And is the word “succeed” understood to apply to succession by will, or only to intestate succession? And what if,
1. the statute speaks of a mother who is from the territory of the enacting authority, yet the mother is of foreign origin but married there. And see no. 3.
body: † A nun, when she

† It is asked whether he who publicly exercises usury in another’s name may make a testament without having furnished security. And it is to be said briefly that he may not. The case is [found in] Distinction 46, chapter *Nec suo coniuncto*; chapter *Quamquam*, On Usuries, Book 6.

Secondly, it is asked: since the statute provides that a woman who enters into a second marriage cannot in any way or by any device succeed to her son, whether the son can institute her as his heir, assuming that he was not a manifest usurer. And it seems that he can, as in the Authentica *De nuptiis*, § *Disponat*. The contrary is true: because the words of the statute are precise and admit of no distinction, as in the law *In fraudem*, D. *De militum testamento*. Here the statute is not only in favor of the son who made the will, but also in favor of the other sons, as in the Code, *De testamento militis*, law *Si*.

Thirdly, it is asked, because the statute speaks of a mother who is of the *masia* [estate/lineage]. Now, the woman was not originally from the *masia*, although she was married there; therefore, she is not included in the statute, and thus she can succeed to the intestate son together with his sisters in a male portion, as in the Authentica *Defuncto* and in § 1 of the Authentica *De haeredibus ab intestato*. To the contrary, it seems, because the statute does not only consider origin, but also dwelling and residence: but she dwelt and resided in the land of the *masia*, and there she married her second husband; therefore, she could not be instituted heir in the goods and lands of the *masia*: but in goods existing in Asti, or in another territory, when she could be instituted. Although there are opinions on this matter, nevertheless this opinion of Jacobus de Ravenna is commonly practiced and observed, which is cited by Cynus in the law *Cunctos populos*, *De summa Trinitate*. And thus the case occurs against the rule, that someone dies partly testate and partly intestate. For just as a soldier can do this, so can laws and statutes. It is therefore concluded that, by the will, the said woman succeeds in nothing, because the husband was a public usurer; but intestate she succeeds in a male portion of all the goods, except the goods of the *masia*, in which she succeeds in nothing on account of the statute of the said land. And this is the conclusion according to one opinion, sufficiently equitable, considering also that the said will was made in the land of the *masia*. Another statute concerning wills and last wills to be executed does not obstruct this: because it speaks of those made by a legitimate testator, but he does not testate legitimately who testates in favor of a person not capable, as is the case here. This passage is sufficiently doubtful: because the prohibiting statute does not make mention of a will; nevertheless, what I have said, I believe to be more correct, arguing from law 1, Code, *De secundis nuptiis*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a nun may cede her paternal dwelling to her brother.
2. Whether a statute may provide otherwise for those entering a monastery.
3. Whether one who makes a null will is said to be intestate.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A nun, with the authority of the abbess and convent, ceded to her brother all goods and rights that she possessed in her paternal or maternal inheritance: it is asked whether the cession is valid? I answer, immovable goods cannot be alienated without a decree of a superior, as in c. monasteriorum. de reb. eccle. non alie., although if she had not entered upon the inheritance, she could repudiate it with the authority of the aforesaid; just as an adult with the authority of a curator, as in C. de iure delib. l. potuit. What the lord Dinus noted in l. potuit. de auto. tuto. supports the aforesaid, and thus Bartolus advised.

† Secondly, it is asked whether a statute can make disposition against those entering monasteries by depriving or altering their succession? It must be said that it cannot, because such a statute is contrary to the liberty of religion, as in the Auth. de san epi. §. sed hoc praesenti; for those who are moved by the Spirit of God are not under worldly law, as the Apostle says. Others say that either the statute speaks of a woman about to enter, or of one entering, or of one who has entered. In the first and second cases the statute applies, because it speaks among subjects; in the third case it does not. I say that it is not valid even in the first and second cases, because that statute is then condemned not by reason of the persons, but by reason of the final cause, which is considered base and impossible, and tends against the salvation of souls, and this is the truth.

† Thirdly, it is asked, if the brother or son repudiated the aforesaid inheritance, whether it accrues to the nun. And it must be said that it does, and this is clear under the ius commune, as in C. de ca. tol. §. his ita; nor does the statute stand in the way, because he declared that it is not valid in favor of religion.

† Fourthly, it is doubted, because the father substituted the females for the males in one half of the goods if the males should die without children and intestate; he substituted the sisters of the deceased for one half; the last died having made a testament, which was nevertheless null because he was a manifest usurer. It is asked, what is the law? I answer, this substitution requires two things conjunctively, namely without children and intestate, as in C. de insti. et substi. l. generaliter; both of which are true, and therefore the substitution takes place, because the statute requires that in this case the testament be valid. I, Baldus. Unto that same thing which is in the consilium immediately preceding.

In the name of Christ. Premising the statute, wherein it provides that if any person shall have entered any regular house, and in the future should enter, or otherwise dedicate herself to God, or had been dedicated to God, and has made profession, neither she herself nor the house which she should enter or had entered may seek anything from her parents, or brothers, or sisters, or agnates beyond what was given or promised to her for her reception made of her, and that no law shall be administered to her by the Podestà of Como, nor by his judges, nor by the consuls of justice of Como, nor shall they be heard against the aforesaid; and if a certain quantity was not promised, or specially given, that she cannot have from the inheritance and paternal goods beyond 200 lire of tertioli; and if she should possess and hold beyond the aforesaid inheritance, that the male heirs or coparceners may without authority, without any ban, or penalty of crime, enter into possession and hold the aforesaid. Now a case occurred where a certain Lady Filippina, a nun, assigned to her brother with the consent of the nuns and the minister, without however the authority of the diocesan. It is asked whether it is valid, because it does not appear to have been contracted profitably for the monastery itself, on the ground that the entire money was remitted by the nuns and the minister to the said Lady Filippina. Secondly, it is asked whether the said assignment could have been effectively made notwithstanding the statute in force in the City of Como for the corresponding part, and especially the statute providing concerning those entering a monastery and dedicating themselves to God thenceforth, presupposing that that statute is not contrary to ecclesiastical liberty, and also that the said statute was never practiced because no case arose. Thirdly, it is asked, since the said nun had in the inheritance of her mother as co-heir her brother, who died leaving surviving him his father, which father renounced the inheritance deferred to him through his son, the said Lady Filippina having already entered [the monastery], whether the said portion repudiated by the father accrued to the portion of the Lady Filippina? These points consist principally in two matters: first, in succession; second, in the assignment of rights. As far as pertains to the succession, it is certain that this nun succeeds by the ius commune, as in C. de epis. et cle. l. deo nobis and extra de proba. c. in praesentia. It remains to respond to the statute, and without disputing whether the said statute is valid—because in the stated point it is presupposed that the statute is valid—one must merely consider what the statute means, and what the words of the statute import. And indeed the statute has two parts: the first part is when a certain quantity is given or promised for the reception made of her, and that part is general; the second is when nothing was given or promised for the reception, and this does not speak except of the paternal inheritance; whence in maternal inheritance we stand upon the ius commune. Therefore, she succeeds to the mother by the ius commune; for if she did not succeed, she could not seek two hundred lire in the goods of the mother and would be excluded in whole; for the statute does not speak of seeking two hundred lire upon the goods of the mother, but upon the goods of the father. Since therefore she cannot have the aid of the statute, consequently she does not have the burden of the statute; because whom I do not honor, I do not burden, as in C. de fideicom. l. ab eo. Likewise, it is certain that a statute does not amend the law except in an express case, as in C. de colla. l. illam, at the word eo quod vlla constitutio etc. To this effect make the common laws: because what is not amended is not prohibited from standing. Likewise because one does not proceed by analogy to the amendment of laws. Likewise because the law speaks of a man. Likewise because this nun was capable at the three relevant times; therefore neither the statute nor the ius commune stands in her way. Likewise she, before entry into the monastery, had acquired the maternal inheritance; whence once an heir, one cannot cease to be an heir, as in ff. de mino. l. et si siue. §. sed quid Papinianus, and ff. hęre. insti. l. ei, qui soluendo; and this regarding the first point. I come to the second point regarding the assignment: and I say that the said assignment is valid, because rights consisting in money, and money itself, can be alienated without a judicial decree with the authority of the prelate, just as a minor can with the authority of the curator, as noted in ff. ad Treb. l. 1. §. fuit quaesitum and l. potest. de auto. tut. by the Gloss and Dinus; it would be otherwise in the assignment of immovable things, because a decree is required, as in C. de prędiis min. l. si ad resoluendam and noted in l. 1. C. si ad uer. transac.; for what is in a claim is understood to be such as it is in the substance of the thing owed, as noted in l. mouentium. ff. de ver. sig. The witnesses do not stand in the way, who seem to wish to challenge the instrument by saying that the actual counting of money did not intervene; because their statement is not of necessity conclusive. For by the posit of a lesser sum, a greater is not excluded unless a taxative word is added, as noted in C. de prob. l. rationes. Likewise, because between related persons a simulated assignment is not presumed, as noted by Lord Dinus in l. patrem. ff. quę in frau. cred. Likewise, because money can be paid in a purse; and it is said to be counted if the parties confess it, although a notary would act more cautiously if he saw the act of counting and the money itself, as in ff. de vsufru. l. sed et siquis stipuletur, otherwise beginning, adhuc iterest, at the verse si vero simul in sacculo. With all these things therefore attended to and considered, I say that the said assignment was valid, and action can be brought upon it. Concerning the right of accrual, moreover, there is no doubt, because the repudiated portion accrues to that which has been accepted, even of necessity in inheritances, although in legacies it accrues by will, unless an addition was made that rendered the portions inseparable, as noted in ff. de acqui. haere. l. si seruus communis ab extero and C. de cad. tollen. §. is itaque, with the following paragraph, and the laws are common. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a donation made by a soldier and the Duke of Milan to his concubine is valid. And note that he later consulted on this in Consilium 456 in the fifth part, and see below Consilium 267.
2. A contract concluded with one who has the power to enact law has the force of law.
3. The exception that no one has supreme origin of power over the Caesar and the sons of kings.
4. Laws speaking of soldiers do not apply to the soldiers of our time.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The question is whether the gift formerly made by the Magnificent Prince and Lord, the lord Bernabò, unto the person of the lady, his concubine, and whatever followed by virtue of the said gift, were valid or not? For it seems that the said gift was invalid by operation of law: because it is notorious that the said lord Bernabò was a knight, and indeed an illustrious one, and the said lady was his concubine during his wife's lifetime. Likewise, it is certain that a knight of armed warfare cannot make a gift to a concubine, as in C. de don. inter vi. et exo. l. 2, so much so that the thing given remains by operation of law with the donor, as is clear there. To this contributes ff. de test. mili. l. miles. §. mulier, where it is said that where a dishonorable suspicion can fall, such a woman cannot take. To the contrary makes the fact that the said Magnificent knight was not only a simple knight, but was also a prince and lord of the city, and acted and did all things as lord, at least in effect. It is also said that he held a privileged imperial vicariate from the Emperor. From all of which it seems established that he was able to enact law.

† Now I argue thus: a contract entered into with one who can make law has the force of a contract and of law; whence nothing can be objected, as in C. de quadr. pręscrip. l. bene a Zenone, ff. de publi. l. Cęsar, and it is express in l. pe. C. de dona. inter vi. et vx. Likewise, since the said gift was made from sure [knowledge] of law and of fact, and from the certain knowledge of the prince, it has the force of a dispensation, as in l. quidam consulebat. de re iu.; whence if a prince who had supreme power were to institute his bastard as heir, the institution would be valid, because it is introduced by positive law that it is invalid, but the prince himself is above all positive law. But to this it is replied,

† that with the exception of the Emperor and free kings or the like, no one seems to have the supreme origin of power, as in l. 2. in princ. §. nouissime. ff. de origi. iur., in Aut. qui. mo. na. effi. sui. §. si. col. 7; and illustrious persons transgress more grievously than others, as in C. de natu. lib. l. 1. and C. ad orfi. l. si qua illustris. But

† certainly by another reason it seems that the gift is valid, because according to the common opinion, the laws that speak of soldiers have no application to the knights of our time, because they do not swear that they will not avoid death for the commonwealth of the Roman people, ff. ex quibus cau. maiores. l. pe. To this contributes the letter of the said l. 2. de don. inter vi. et uxorem, in the word 'milites tamen in eos', where it speaks of soldiers created for the service of the Emperor. And others are not created in due form according to Roman law, therefore they are not Roman soldiers; and consequently they are contained neither in the favors nor in the prohibitions under the designation of soldiers. Nor does it stand in the way that they are commonly called 'knights' (milites), because the usage of speech does not confer privileges. It would seem to me that it would be a good safeguard that first a decree be made that it could be given, and secondly the gift should follow; or if the gift were made first, a confirmatory gift by way of law should follow secondly. We nevertheless see daily that princes and lords do with their property whatever pleases them, and that their will is observed as law by general custom; l. j. ff. de cons. prin. contributes to this. Likewise, also having considered the course of time during which the property was possessed by bona fide possessors, and partly by the fisc, it seems sufficiently appropriate to say that the wife may retain for her dowry, as in ff. de bo. damn. l. quinque legibus, extra de pigno. c. ex literis. Nor do I dare, nor would I dare, to set my mouth against heaven to advise against the power of princes, because many very evil and dangerous things, which must be guarded against, could follow from this opinion, since they would generate very great scandal, as in extra de pręscrip. c. 2. Finally, I conclude that the gift is valid on account of the preeminent power of the Prince, and consequently that the hypothecary action is available to the wife concerning whom inquiry is made. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a true or fictitious novation from one creditor to another is said to occur; and from which presumptions it is assumed to be simulated, and from which it is assumed to be true. And no. 3.
2. Who is to be preferred among several creditors.
body: In the name of Christ. First, Antonius was found described in a document for one thousand; then that document was transferred to Bernardus for five hundred; finally, the said Bernardus committed fraud. And for two days before he committed the fraud, he had that document, which was for five hundred, retranscribed from himself back to the said Antonius. Now the creditors of the said defrauder say that the amount of that document should be divided and shared among them, and this according to the form of the statute of merchants approved by the decree of the lord, which provides that whatever is found, or whatever can be obtained and acquired from the goods of any fugitive, or which he held and possessed at the time of his flight, or within six months before, shall be shared equally among his creditors, whether they are creditors or appear to be so by public deed or condemnation, as regards the goods of fugitives, and among such creditors there shall be no privilege of cause or time.

It is asked whether the aforementioned transcript, prepared in anticipation of flight two days before, benefits Antonio in its entirety, or whether it should be shared among the other creditors. It is alleged on behalf of the creditors of this bankrupt debtor that it ought to be shared among the creditors, for the law provides that the peculium, which is to be shared among particular creditors, contains not only the corporeal things of the peculium, but also the claims against debtors, as is expressly stated in the text. D. de peculio, l. quam Tuberonis, §. in peculio. Moreover, the treasury record is presumed true, and not simulated. This holds both under the general law of all public records, as noted in C. plus valere quod agitur, l. emptione, and also under the special law of the public archive and authentic register, as in C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus; C. de apocryphis publicis, l. 1, lib. 10; C. de instrumentis authenticis, ad haec, and in the Corpus from which it is derived. Furthermore, by this transfer of the record, a novation by delegation was effected, whereby the treasury was released from Antonio and bound to Bernardo, as in D. de novatione, l. 1. Indeed, more so, because it appears that Antonio was discharged, as in D. de manumis, l. inter causas, §. abesse; and D. ad Velleiam, l. quamvis, §. interdum; and D. de novatione, l. delegare; D. de donationibus, l. ut mihi donarem. And an obligation once extinguished by payment never revives, as in D. de solutionibus, l. Quites, §. aream. Furthermore, this re-transfer from Bernardo to Antonio is a new contract, which ought not to prejudice other creditors, by argument from D. de pactis, l. si; and C. de locato, l. si cum Hermene, whence the beginning of the last agreement must be examined. For a new pact makes a new contract. Hence, Antonio is found not to be the first, but the third creditor, as in D. qui potiora in pignore habeant, l. creditor, §. si primus and §. si tecum. Moreover, if the re-transfer of the transfer of the record had not been made, the other creditors would undoubtedly have a right, because, as I said, one must not depart from the treasury record, to which recourse is had as to a mirror and as to the fountain of truth, as in l. 1, C. de exactoribus tributorum, as in Auth. de manumis, principium, §. publicorum, col. 3. Therefore, by these and other reasons, it seems that such a re-transfer should not hold to the prejudice of other creditors, as in D. de iureiurando, l. nam postea, §. sed et si quis in fraudem creditorum. Likewise, from the short interval before the flight, fraud appears to have been premeditated; for what is done immediately is deemed inherent, by argument from D. de privilegiis creditorum, l. si neutri, §. si, and fully noted by Bartolus in D. de donationibus, l. post contractum. Furthermore, color is not presumed to have been sought in writing, unless it is proven by clear indications, as in D. ad Velleiam, l. vir uexori. Nor does anything else appear to have been done than what is written, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum, §. pro Aurelio; C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus; D. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, §. quod ferre, and §. pactorum quaedam. These are the arguments that can be alleged for the body and universality of creditors. Natural equity also seems to persuade this, because these parties could lie by setting a prior date, as in C. de falsis, l. si creditor colludens; D. ad Velleiam, l. scia; D. de edicto, l. 1, §. editiones; C. qui potiora in pignore habeant, l. scripturas. For these bankrupt debtors are prone to lying, and especially because they can collude, which is absurd. For since they cannot testify solemnly in court regarding this matter, all the more so in a contract. Otherwise, they could agree upon a share, and certainly material for delinquency ought not to be given. Moreover, because they are infamous and infamious, who according to the custom of the most ancient law ought to be handed over to creditors to be torn apart, as noted in l. 1, C. qui bona cessisse possunt, so much so that on account of their fraud they do not seem to have the benefit of cession, which is a relief for the more wretched, but not a shield for glossators, as in l. si, §. fin., D. quae in fraudem creditorum, and by argument in l. pe., D. de iudicis dolo. Moreover, when the state has changed, good faith may not be acknowledged to the prejudice of a third party, much less when faith is suspect. D. de edicto, l. si quis ex argentariis, in the words humilis and deploratus; and D. de manumis, l. quintus. Moreover, what the word of the instrument signifies, that must be held as truth, and it ought to prevail without calumny, as in Extra, de privilegiis, c. porro; C. de libellis praetextatis vel exheredationibus, l. 3; D. de iudicatum solvi, l. iudicatum solvi. For instrumental stipulations bear witness to the truth, as in D. de pignoribus, l. contrahitur. For behold how we have consecrated both the bankrupt debtor and this Antonio. But on the contrary, let us turn our gaze for greater clarity. And it is shown by consideration that Antonio has a right to the entire aforementioned transcript, not to be shared in any way with the other creditors. And this is shown by many reasons, and laws, and also by natural justice and equity favoring it. And for the sake of evidence, I premise,

† that sometimes something is simulated to be done, and nothing is done: and this is properly a simulated contract, or a simulated chirograph; nevertheless, one cannot allege this by alleging one’s own turpitude, as in l. si creditoribus, C. de servo pignori dato manumisso, and l. transactio, C. de transactionibus. Sometimes one contract is simulated, and another is celebrated, and then the simulated contract is not valid, but the true contract is valid. If such is the genus of simulated contract, which is perfected by consent, otherwise if by words, because the words did not intervene, or writing: because the chirograph did not intervene, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. quicquid astringendae, and C. de fideiussoribus instrumentis, l. contractus. It also fails when an obligation is contracted by thing: and the thing did not intervene, as in C. si certum petatur, l. si ex pretio, because where there is a defect of substantial form, or quality of matter, that rule has no place, that what is done prevails over what is simulated to be conceived. But the rule must be drawn in this way, that nothing prevails that is done, because it is simulated to be conceived. Sometimes there is no simulation with respect to the obligation: but concerning the person of the stipulator, or chirographer: and this can be in several ways. In the first way, because from the beginning someone does not wish to be named in the stipulation, or chirograph, but makes the stipulation, or chirograph, be sung in the person of a friend. This is very often done even in good faith, fraud or deceit being absent, ff. de haereditate instituenda, l. quidam cum filium, and it is expressed, C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam; however, sometimes it is done with fraud, when namely fraud is committed against the law: as in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, or against creditors, who had previously contracted, even under a condition, whom the gloss calls future creditors, as noted in C. de donationibus ante nuptias, aut. Sed iam necesse est; or when something is contravened against the mandates of the laws, as in ff. de legibus, l. fraus; C. de naturalibus liberis, l. 1; ff. de auctoritate tutorum, l. pupillus, §. per interpositam; l. 1; ff. de aqua pluviali arcenda, l. emptor. Sometimes the name of another is inserted into the contract, or chirograph, afterwards: and this can be in several ways. In the first way, that it is added to the payment, and this added person obtains the place of procurators: and between the adding person, and him, an action of mandate arises, as in ff. de verbis oblig., l. Iulianus, §. qui fundum, in which case this procurator is bound, if the owner wishes to transfer the rights to the owner, or to whomever the owner wishes. This says that notable law, ff. mandati, l. idem quae, §. si cui. Sometimes a third person is added to stipulate, or chirograph, and then either he stipulates uselessly, and it has the same force as a simple mandate, this law, that unique one in the law, ff. de solutionibus, l. cum si Cornelius. Sometimes the obligation, or chirograph, is transferred to him usefully, and effectively. And this in three ways. For sometimes it happens, so that he succeeds to the right of the obligation: and he alone intervenes in the debt, or credit, and then novation occurs: as in ff. de novatione, l. aliam. Sometimes so that he is added in the debt, or credit: and novation does not occur, hence the first creditor still remains creditor, until the other of them is paid: sometimes it is doubtful, and in doubt novation does not occur: but aggregation. Hence, although you, what you owe me, make it be promised by a money-lender, you are not immediately released from me: but after satisfaction, as noted by Bartolus, although under doubt perhaps, ff. de novatione, in l. delegare, and ff. de solutionibus, l. si debitor. When therefore novation, or delegation, occurs, and this can be done in several ways. Namely, apparently, and effectively, and then the new obligation is in the goods of the latter creditor, and not of the first creditor: as in ff. de lege 2, l. si, §. filia, where is the usual case. Sometimes the transfer is apparent, but not effective, as because this is done between the first, and latter stipulator, and then in the same way the benefit remains with the first creditor, as when a pure procurator is employed. For example, a wife, who fears that her husband will compel her to testify, makes the obligation of the dowry to be restored be transferred to a certain friend of that woman: for by this she does not cease to be endowed, as is read, and noted, ff. soluto matrimonio, l. 2, §. nec cogitur. If therefore the transmutation of the chirograph can be done according to different intentions, and it operates differently according to the diversity of the minds of the actors, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. non omnis, sometimes it is doubtful, with what mind the chirograph, or stipulation, is transferred, then it matters, whether when the second creditor begins, the first ceases, or does not cease. If indeed he ceases, novation has been made between the first creditor, and the debtor. If however he does not cease, novation has been made, as in C. de novatione, l. si. But nevertheless in that case, where he ceases, it is asked, to whom the final benefit of the contract belongs, whether to the new creditor, or to the old one: so that if the new one demands anything, he is bound to restore it. On which it seems to me that this should be said, that when the chirograph is fulfilled by payment, or no new payment intervenes, and then it belongs to that creditor, who first paid, because to him principally belongs the thing, and the foundation of the credit, nor is it presumed that he donated his right, but that he agreed, as is fully read, and noted, ff. soluto matrimonio, l. quae dotis. If however a new payment intervenes, which is not to be presumed: as in extra de fideiussoribus instrumentis, c. cum Iannes heremita, then the second caution would not be second: alone, nor would it be descending, but by itself. Since therefore our question asks about the obligation descending from the source of the first payment, and that appears to be transferred to another, nevertheless not with the intention of donating. This second caution is affected, and subjected to the burden of transferring back the chirograph, or releasing, as it can be better adapted to that first creditor, Anthony, and it is in his goods, and always remained. Also, the universality of creditors could not come to share, and divide, except with its vices, and burdens, as in ff. de actione emptoris, l. in venditione; ff. de manumissionibus, l. Gayus. Also, to be bound to cede the action is to be bound to a fact, and perhaps the statute does not speak of actions of fact. Also it is an argument to this effect, ff. de iure dotium, l. si mulier, §. ex asse.

Furthermore, it must be premised for the sake of clarity, that either what is owed to Bernard is paid to Anthony, and nothing is owed to Anthony, or not; and then Bernard’s creditors can reclaim it, since they alone are creditors, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. si, §. licentia. Or all are found to be creditors, and then it matters. Or among them there is a right of priority, or a right of order, or they claim simple equality: in the first two cases, he who has priority is preferred, as in ff. de privilegiis creditorum, l. privilegium. Therefore, it is said that one is superior to others, because without prior designation no priority could be assigned. In the third case, however, when they simply claim equality, and equality is established, then either he to whom payment was made first claims gratification: or he extorted the money or the debt by force or fraud; and it must be shared, or divided among the other creditors pro rata. Or it was legitimately collected by a judge, and then either the goods were previously possessed by judicial decree, and the same applies, as in ff. de bonis autem iudicis possidendis, l. cum unus, because the praetor wishes his benefit to be open to all, arg. ff. de contrahenda tutela, l. si post mortem, §. si. Or the goods are not possessed, because the merchant confesses plainly, and thus by command, and then this person is not bound to share, because he received nothing of another’s, but only what was owed to him, as in ff. quae in fraudem creditorum, l. pupillus, and there by Jacobus de Arena and Bartolus. Sometimes the body of creditors claims equality. But someone is there who claims solidarity and priority: and this is directly the case of our question. For if indeed all things are equal, equality is presumed. If, however, they are unequal, because for him who claims solidarity there are vehement indications from a vehement presumption, and the treasurer testifies, who is a very solemn witness, then the case is decided from vehement supports, arg. extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. cum dilectus. If therefore for Anthony are those things which are supposed in the theme, and the judge’s motion concurs, as it ought to concur with him, nor is it directly against the tenor of the writing, but rather a certain interpretation and declaration thereof, judgment should be given for Anthony himself; because the said name is not in the goods of fugitives, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. fugitivus. And especially among merchants, among whom it is not fitting to dispute on the points of law, but on mere truth and the custom of commerce, as in ff. de mandato, l. si fideiussor, §. quaedam. But I also do not omit that if Anthony, after this transcription, receives from the treasurer the benefits of the credit, and not the said Bernard, that the said transcription is presumed to have been made deceitfully, and not really; because Anthony was always in quasi-possession, as in ff. qui in rem suam pignus vel hypothecam solvunt, l. sicut, §. supervacuum. The account books must also be diligently scrutinized, and consequently the writings; because the antecedent demonstrates the consequent, and conversely, as in ff. de legibus 1, l. si servus plurium, §. si, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. penultima. Also, whence are these 10,000 florins for this Bernard? Do they come from the wind? as in C. ubi pupillus educari debet, l. sin, and nec obstat C. si certum petatur, l. unde originem, because there appeared the counting, and the possession of the counter, as in C. arbitrium tutoris, l. si defunctus. And in sum, this pertains greatly to the discussion of the judge and the good man, whether we look to the common law or the municipal law. Indeed, what and how much is in each person’s goods can also be inquired into through household servants, as noted in l. 2, C. quoniam et quibus partibus debet, lib. 10. Moreover, if the said Bernard did not have such assets that he could verisimilarly support the said quantity, this is a great judgment that it is not from his goods, but Anthony’s, who is solvent and capable; and this is notorious, as in l. si vero, §. 1, ff. qui satisdare coguntur, and noted in l. facultas, C. de iure fisci, lib. 10. Therefore, it seems to me that according to the premises, it should be concluded for the said Anthony. And for him I conclude, and hold, summarizing my motives in brief. The first motive is the truth of the principle and origin. ff. de donationibus, l. Qui id, quod; ff. de solutionibus, l. Tutor. The second motive is: because the first named in writings is presumed to be the principal, and more principal, as in ff. de stipulationibus servorum, l. si, §. servus communis. The third is, that from the beginning of the title the subsequent event is formed, as in C. de impositione lucrativa descriptionis, l. 1, lib. 10. The fourth is: because by new law, and newest, novation does not occur, even if what is owed to one is transcribed to another for more abundant caution, as in ff. de novatione, l. delegare, per Bartolus; and today it is presumed that tacitly it is agreed that novation does not take place, but rather the addition of new caution, as in C. de novatione, l. si, although formerly it was otherwise, because the rule of ancient law was, where there is novelty, there is novation, as in ff. de solutionibus, l. si debitor, and Inst. quibus modis tollitur obligatio, §. Praeterea. And thus is understood the said Bartolus in the said l. si debitor, s. de iure fisci. The fourth reason is, because the one added is presumed to be added for the benefit of the one adding, not for his own benefit; which is shown by the obligation which exists between them, as in ff. solutione matrimonii, l. quae dotis. The fifth reason is, because it is not presumed that the one adding wishes to throw away his own, especially in a large sum, as in ff. de probationibus, l. cum de in debito. The sixth reason is: because although the chirograph in question was made at home, nevertheless the truth of the matter is not abolished, as in C. de donationibus, l. in rebus. The seventh reason is the natural consideration itself, which has the force of law, as in ff. de excusationibus tutorum, l. scire oportet, §. Et si maxime. For from natural indications truth is proven. For all things agree with truth: and nothing disagrees with it for him who beholds the true light, as in ff. de testibus, l. ob carmen, §. si testes. But here all supports support Anthony, and not only supportively, but also impressively, so that the contrary cannot be persuaded to the mind of the judge: nor could the intellect be turned to the opposite conscience. For that is called a vehement support, as in extra de successionibus ab intestato, c. si. Eighthly, and conclusively, it follows that the effective substance of this business always remained in Anthony’s goods, and that this name is to be considered as from Anthony’s goods: and separation is to be made from Bernard’s goods. And although it may be said of a public writing, “touch me not,” yet certainly nothing is objected to the writing; because to know a writing is not merely to read its words, but to hold its force and power, as in ff. de legibus, l. scire leges. Just as the writing of Zopyrus and Fulgentius is true, but the fable is not true. So often the writing is true: and true is what is asserted as the cause, yet the enunciation of the cause has another meaning, as noted in ff. de pace, l. iuris gentium, §. quod ferre. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a malicious counsel is presumed to have been given in conversation.
2. Whether the giver of malicious counsel is to be punished, if the offender was otherwise going to commit the act.
3. Whether advising flight amounts to advising a wrongful act.
4. By what penalty one who aids a wrongful act is to be punished, and when one is said to aid.
5. Whether one who knowingly conceals another’s debtor makes himself a partner in the same danger.
6. What is the penalty of a receiver of goods from a fugitive, and no. 11.
7. When an act is said to be committed immediately.
8. Who is said to be a fugitive.
9. How the value of a ledger of accounts is to be estimated.
10. Who is said to be a receiver.
11. Whether one who receives account books is to be punished by any penalty.
12. Whether the penalty of a statute abrogates the penalty of the common law.
13. How the statute that usurious merchants are not to be considered as merchants is to be understood.
14. Whether the penalty is to be mitigated, if someone deceived out of poverty.
15. Poverty excused in perjury.
16. The preamble of a statute is regarded as the final cause restricting it.
17. A reason founded solely on presumption restricts a general statute.
body: In the name of Christ. Concerning Milan, who is said to have given counsel to Vinciguerra of Siena regarding his flight and the bankruptcy of the said Vinciguerra, a merchant who defrauded creditors and fled the city of Milan, to the prejudice of certain creditors and merchants. In the first place, it must be examined under the common law whether, because the said Vinciguerra was a friend of the said Milan, and having had a secret conversation with the said Milan a few days prior, he immediately thereafter fled and took to flight, and because account books were subsequently brought into the house of the said Milan, and because the said Milan’s wife and servant were present, it is presumed that Milan gave him fraudulent counsel to the detriment of the creditors, indeed even aid and assistance, and whether the said Milan is therefore liable, especially considering the form of the ordinances of commerce of the City of Milan, wherein the aforementioned acts are described: or whether he is not liable in any respect; and especially since the said Vinciguerra later returned under a guarantee, and wished to pay up to the interim amount, and to settle the remainder. If he is liable in any respect, in what and to what extent, it will be advised in the name of God. What is the law: since the said Milan says that he gave no counsel for the flight, nor for any harm or damage to the creditors: but rather for good, and with good intent: as appears from the confession of the said Milan. Therefore, in the name of God, on the aforementioned matters, and on each of the aforementioned points, counsel is given supported by reasons, presupposing that the said Vinciguerra would have done otherwise, and was determined to flee, even if Saint Francis had given him contrary counsel: because he did not wish to die in prison, and considered it more feasible for him to flee than to die: although it was more dishonorable, as he also made understandable by his very act.

† First, it must be considered whether counsel given for an evil purpose is presumed from the conversation. And it seems that it is, because whose end is evil, his premeditation is presumed to be fraudulent, as in C. de adulteriis, l. Si qui adulterii. Moreover, the end demonstrates the beginning, as in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. Reprehendenda. Also contributing to this is Bartolus, de privilegiis creditorum, l. Si neutri, § Si cuius, where the words "adsunt" are found, as will be seen below. A certain person was accused of having given counsel for homicide: and the homicide is proven.
