Also, that he had spoken with the murderer: and the latter immediately went and killed, but it was not known what he had said to him. Certainly, from the brevity of the time interval, it is presumed that he gave counsel. Bartolus seems to hold the contrary: because counsel is not established. However, one thing is counsel, another is conversation; for conversation can be good or evil, and in doubt it is presumed good, if with a good man, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si auam; ff. de re militari, l. Non omnes, § A barbaris. Moreover, no one is presumed to commit fraud or deceit, as in ff. de probationibus, l. Quotiens, § Qui dolo, unless it is proven by clear indications: and clear indications are said to be those which are almost perfectly effective, as in C. de dolo, l. Dolum. Also, in doubt, good is presumed, and not evil. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Omni modo; ff. pro socio, l. Merito. Also, it does not prove that this is the case, which frequently and easily happens to be absent from this, as in C. de probationibus, l. Neque natales; C. unde legitimi, l. Non hoc. Nor does the objection hold against the statement of Bartolus, because it should not be understood so indiscriminately: but in that case, when causes and indications of hatred have proceeded; otherwise he would be saying something false.

Secondly, it must be considered whether, assuming that the evil and wicked counsel is established, yet the said Vinciguerra would have done it anyway, the said Milanus is to be punished in any way. And it seems that he is, because when counsel is given to commit a wrong, he who counseled is liable, upon the commission of the wrong, by an action arising from that fraud, as one concurring in the wrong, as noted in the rule *Nullus ex consilio*, D. 50.17.1, and there Lord Dyonisius holds that he is punished indiscriminately if the counsel was given to commit a wrong, even if the principal would have done it anyway. The same seems to be held by the gloss in D. 47.10, *Non solum*, § *Proculus*, and § *Si mandato*. But the contrary is held expressly by the gloss in Inst. 4.3, § *Ope*, and in D. 42.1, *Saepe*, at the end, which glosses expressly decide that where the principal would have done it anyway, regardless of the counsel for or against, the counselor is not liable, and the reason is that the principal did not follow the counsel, but rather the movement of his own mind. Therefore, it seems to be said that either the principal had the intention of doing it, but had not carried his will into action without the counsel, in which case the counselor is liable; or he had carried it into action in any way, and then he is not liable. Because, since he was about to act in full fraud, it cannot be said that the counselor, by approving, increased the malice; for that which is full does not need addition. And this opinion seems true according to equity: because the delinquent regarded this counsel as nothing, and consequently did not follow the counsel. And this is the reason on which the gloss of the said § *Ope* bases itself. This is also held by Paulus de Leaza in c. 1, *De poenis*, in the Clementines, and especially when we judge of counsel from presumptions; because then one should act more mildly, according to Innocentius, who thus elegantly notes in X. 2.20, *Quia verisimiliter*.

It remains to be seen whether advising flight constitutes advising a felony. Here it must be considered whether flight is a felony. And I say that either the fugitive is a slave, or one tainted with servile status, and it is a felony, as in l. 1, C. de servis fugitivis, and l. si, C. de operis liberto; or he is freeborn, and then either he flees with another’s property: and it is a felony by reason of the thing, because by carrying it away he commits theft. The same applies if he flees with a thing which at some time was another’s, and with money deposited for counting, although there is not properly theft there, as in l. ait praetor, §. si debitorem, ff. quae in fraudem creditorum. Or he flees without the removal of another’s property, or quasi-property. And this flight is not a felony: but it is a certain kind of concealment, as in ff. qui ex causa in possessionem, l. Fulcinius, §. quid sit latitare. Hence, even if someone summoned flees and is condemned, he is not said to be condemned for a felony, but for contumacy, as in l. 1, ff. si quis ius dicenti non obtemperaverit. Hence the doctors say that flight is not imposed on anyone as a felony, but as a suspicion, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de raptu virginum. And this is clear in Auth. de exhibendis reis, §. si non, and commonly by all the doctors in ff. de iureiurando, l. admonendi.

It remains to be considered regarding the action on work done, and I say that if my friend flees with my horses or my servant without my knowledge, I am not bound to provide assistance. For one is not punished for the act or ignorance of another, as in C. de incest. nup. l. cum ancillis; C. de tab. l. generali, § 10; and note in l. 1, ff. de recepta; and C. de seruis fugitiuis, l. quicunque; and in l. 1 and 2, C. de his, qui. And Longobarda says that if anyone has presumed to take another’s weapons and has done harm with them, it is not the fault of the owner of the weapons, but of the one who did the harm with them, as in Longobarda, in the title de his, qui cum armis alterius damnum fece, c. fi. But more is said in that title, c. 1: if anyone has simply provided weapons to someone, and the recipient has committed some harm with them, the fault is not imputed to the one who provided them, but to the one who perpetrated the harm with them.

It remains to be seen whether he who knowingly conceals another’s debtor makes himself a successor or a partner in the same danger; and it seems that he does, as in l. si, C. de operis liberto. But the contrary must be said: because the laws which provide for this speak of special cases; and there is one special case, another is in the debtor of tributes, as in C. de auctoribus tributorum, l. quo. Another is when someone by force removes a debtor. ff. ne quis eum, qui in ius vocatus est, vi eximat, l. pen. The fifth is when someone prevents a defendant or plaintiff from coming to court, whereby prescription runs against the creditor, as in ff. de eo, per quem factum erit, l. si. Since therefore in these cases there is something special and specifically provided, it follows that the common law is to the contrary, as in ff. de legibus, l. ius singulare. This is held by Innocentius, namely, that those edicts do not apply outside their own cases. extra de officio delegati, in c. pastoralis, in fine; and something touches on this in eodem titulo, c. 1. Moreover, just as I could receive common codices, as I will say below, so also a common debtor, so that he may not escape my custody; and by this also a clear answer is given to the aforementioned l. ultimam de operis liberto. Therefore, it is necessary that aid be provided for this purpose, as in l. 2, § homines coactos, ff. de vi bonorum raptorum. And if someone, having taken a knife from a butcher’s shop, killed his daughter, he himself is the parricide, not the butcher, as in l. 2, ff. de origine iuris. From these it appears that the said Milan is bound neither by counsel nor by aid; because neither was obligatory nor true. And this I say with certainty according to the common law, in accordance with what is proposed in its theme. Now let us come to the statute of merchants.

† And I premise that nothing can be imputed to Milan on account of the exception of the valisae, because he neither saw nor consented. Moreover, a sleeping person does not commit a delict, unless there had preceded a cause for which he ought to have kept watch, as in D. ad leg. Aquil. l. si seruus seruum, § si fornicatius. And if it is said that he was in subsequent fault by retaining the account books with a certain intent, for he ought immediately to have restored them to the creditors, as in D. de adulteriis l. si adulterium cum incestu, § incestum autem, and C. de incestis nuptiis l. cum ancillis.

I answer that an act is said to be committed *incontinenti* (immediately) if it was committed within three days, as stated in l. 3, C. de errore aduoca., or if it was done for one’s own caution with only a short interval of time intervening, as in ff. de usuris, l. sciendum. Moreover, since the creditors have received and accepted the books and account ledgers, even if Milan had incurred some penalty under the law or statute, he would immediately be released from the penalty of the law or statute, because one who has obtained the thing labors in vain regarding the penalty, as in l. 2 post prin., ff. si quis cau. This is especially true because this obligation, which arises from the decree of the merchants, is a praetorian obligation and consequently arbitrary, in which the aforementioned rule is most certainly true, as in ff. de publica, l. hoc edicto; and ff. quod met. cau., l. si cum exceptione, §. satis clementer. And that it is praetorian law is apparent because it descends from the jurisdiction of the consuls, who are praetors, just as are the curule aediles and similar officials, as in l. 1, ff. de offic. consulis; and ff. de verbo oblig., l. stipulationum aliae, §. pretoriae. Or at least it is modeled on praetorian obligations, from which an *actio in factum* arises. Furthermore, when the genus is specified in an obligation with respect to the species, the obligation is extinguished by the delivery of the species, as in ff. de pi., l. si fundus, §. si plures; ff. de excep. doli, l. fideiussor; ff. de lega. 1, l. si fundum per fideicommissum; de peti. haeredi., l. Item veniunt, §. idem recte. But because some might perhaps object to this, since this action is penal from the beginning, or perhaps argue that this penalty should be applied to the fisc, I turn to the interpretation of the statutes to remove this doubt. The words of the statute are as follows, as set out below: “Furthermore, no one from the city or county of Milan, or from elsewhere, shall dare or presume to harbor or receive such fugitives, nor their fathers, brothers, male sons, brothers’ agents, nor their ascendants or descendants, as contained in the preceding statutes, either in person or in property, in their own houses or others, nor give to them or any of them, in person or in property, counsel, aid, or favor, nor harbor them, nor advocate for them. Whoever violates this shall be punished in the sum of two hundred *tertioli* for each offense. And nevertheless, such receiver and perpetrator shall be liable for the restitution of the value of the received goods in double. And the aforementioned power, etc. The judges of the causal justice of the merchants of Milan may and must, under the aforementioned penalty of two hundred *tertioli* of their salary, inquire into the aforementioned matters, as above, and proceed against them, knowing them to be fugitives.” And first it must be observed that the statute speaks of receiving fugitives.

† Nevertheless, a fugitive is one who is caught in the act of flight, such that he has moved at least one foot, as stated in the Digest, *De edicto*, edict, law *Quis sit fugitivus*, § *Item Iulianus*. However, he who has not in any way reached the beginning of the act, even though he has mentally conceived the plan of flight, is not a fugitive; because the statute must be understood as referring to an act at least commenced, as in law *Cedere*, § *Subsequare*, Digest, *Vi bonorum raptorum*, and Digest, *De verbis significatis*, law *Fugitivus*. Therefore, it must first appear that there was an act, or a beginning of flight, at the time of the reception of the person or things.

But it is asked, since the statute says that he is bound to the restitution of the price, whether the account books should be appraised according to the names contained in the books, or materially: and it seems that [they should be appraised] for as much as the book of certain [accounts] could be sold, not for what the names are worth: because those consist in a legal fiction, as in D. 22.3.1 (Qui chirographum). But statutes, and especially penal ones, deviating from the common law as disposing new law, do not admit fiction, as noted in D. 3.5.3 (Haec verba) in the common and vulgar [interpretation], which is approved by all. To the contrary it seems that [they should be appraised] signifiatively, i.e., according to the names contained in the books, D. 35.1.1 (Servum filii); D. 22.3.1 (Eum, qui chirographum). For the words of the statute are to be referred to the effect, but the effect of the chirograph consists in the names, as in D. 2.15.1 (Postquam). Indeed, the papyrus itself is of little value: and thus it would be a small penalty for so great a delict. And for this [position], D. 47.2.1 (Quidam tabularum) and D. 47.2.2 (Qui tabulas); and D. 9.2.1 (In l. Aquilia si delictum). From which it follows that he is bound for as much as that name could be sold, provided it is proved that with fraud and with certain knowledge, knowing the quality of the chirographs, he received them with the intent of intercepting them, and not with the intent of resigning them to the creditors and meanwhile preserving them; and since the interpretation can be turned to either intent, the movement of the mind is to be judged according to the quality of the person, as in D. 11.7.1 (Atsi quis) § Interdum and the following §. And if any benefit would have come to him from the receipt, a bad intent is presumed, otherwise the contrary, as in D. 4.3.1 (Quod si cum scires). Moreover, the said statute must be understood as applying to the receiver, because he provides aid, counsel, or favor by the very act of receiving: because that clause, concerning aid and favor, which follows, declares the quality of the preceding [terms], as in D. 19.3.1 (Si) § Cui dulcia. But this last point I do not put as certain: but I leave it in doubt. I believe, however, that it is understood as applying to odious receipt, i.e., that which can be fraudulent against creditors, not to that which is done out of good grace, so that the account books are not subtracted from the creditors. For this person has the thought of managing the business for the creditors, so that if any case might happen to them, they may be able to instruct [themselves] with the subtracted [books]. Or [he holds them] for the cause of proof, lest the books be lost. But this is to be presumed from the quality of the persons, and also from the oath of the receiver: indeed, since even the merchants themselves can deposit the books with some trustworthy person: and such a depositary sins in no way, as in D. 2.13.1 (Quaedam) § His autem; and D. 37.11.1 (Si quae); and D. 12.1.1 (Quis aliquid) § Instrumenta, where it is expressly stated. For the books themselves are [held] with regard to their ownership: and although they go their own ways through fraud, nevertheless in depositing with a trustworthy person fraud does not intervene. Also, where an act is indifferent to good and evil, and injures no one, good is rather presumed than evil; but this deposit is an indifferent act, and insofar as the deposit injures no one, indeed it advocates [for them], D. 43.16.1 (Si alius) § Bellissime with the following §. Unless it is expressly proved that the books were hidden so that the truth might be concealed, or not easily become apparent, as noted by Bartolus in D. 47.11.1 (Locum) § Si quis dolo, where he says that then the intent of concealing is presumed, when it is concealed in such a way that it is apparent to no one. Otherwise, therefore, if it is apparent to a good man, who would likely denounce it to the creditors, as this one does, whom experience of things has shown to be a good man, and [who has] uncorrupted faith, and the supreme office of the treasury entrusted to him by our Illustrious Lord. Just as to any other, whom our Lord has chosen; for these things do not happen except on account of virtue; indeed, every great office is a proclamation of virtue, as in C. 4.49.1 (Si). Furthermore, the receiver, according to the etymology of the word, is nothing other than an acceptor of the thing. But this Milanese accepted nothing from the fugitive, because he was entirely ignorant. And although the household previously received [the books] through imprudence, indeed even if through fraud, it does not prejudice Milan, as in X. 6.1.1 (Cum ad sedem). For the household was not appointed for this, as in D. 47.10.1 (1) § Familiae, and there by Bartolus.

† and therefore the statute concerning the receiver of stolen goods does not apply, because three things are required in a receiver, namely, that he be a receiver of the person bringing the thing, the act of bringing, and the thing received, as noted in D. de verb. signif. l. Marcellus. Moreover, this Milanese did not receive from anyone, but found it in a house, as argued in D. de furt. l. si quid ex domo. For he was not present, nor aware, as argued in D. naut. caup. stabul. l. 1. in princ. For thus finding is rather a case of chance than a human transaction. Since therefore no fault is found in Milan, neither is there punishment. The ancients indeed took fraud for punishment, as in D. de edict. edict. l. cum autem. §. excipitur. And the reason is, because the quality of the crime is named from the genus of punishment, and conversely the genus, as appears there. Let therefore the common rule be added, that where no fault is found, there is no punishment, as in D. de fideicomm. libertat. l. sed si non data. §. fin. And it is made in D. ad leg. Aquil. l. qui occidit. in fin. and D. de fer. fug. l. 1. §. 1. and the following. Nor is it presumed to have the intent of receiving, he who within a few days made it public, as appears in the said l. 1. §. dies autem. and §. fin. Furthermore, for the clarification of the truth, and to stop the mouths of those speaking against justice and truth, although no one can be silenced: for as the wise man says, it is not of our will that each should speak, yet truth conquers all, and imposes silence on those who speak. It must be known in fact, and then concluded in law not persuasively, but demonstratively to the eye,

† That nothing can be imputed to Milan concerning the receipt of the books, and this is demonstrated as follows. In the aforementioned account books there were many accounts, and receipts and payments of large quantities, calculated between the said Milan and the said Vinciguerra. Hence it cannot be denied, since the said accounts were common, as in D. de edendo, l. 1, § rationes; and l. si quis ex argentariis; and fully noted in § editiones; and l. 1, C. eod.; and l. fin. On account of the aforementioned accounts, even the account book itself was common: nor could it be dissolved by quires, and separated, and kept in part, and not in part. Hence, with respect to this, this body was indivisible: and especially because the beginning of the accounts, which is contained in the book, is common to all, as in D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, § si initium tabularum; and by reason of the part, the whole can be kept, as in D. communi dividundo, l. Sabinus. I do not say that the whole can be contracted, D. pro socio, l. merito; and D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. duo fratres. And custody is something indivisible, as in D. commodati, l. si ut certo, § si duobus vehiculum. And if there are two who have a common book, it is lawful and just for either to keep it, and to hold it in custody with himself, until a common custodian is appointed by a superior, as in D. familiae herciscundae, l. si quae cautiones; and D. de fideiussoribus, l. fin. For indeed one ought not to suffer that accounts come into the hands of an unknown person, who might disturb them, as in D. de in rem verso, l. quidam; lest perhaps erasures, or cancellations, or additions be easily made, as in D. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. 1; D. de falsis, l. 1, § qui rationibus; C. de testamento, l. si unus. And therefore it is necessary that writings be under faithful custody, as in Extr. de praescriptionibus, c. ad audientiam. Since therefore these books are common, and it concerns Milan, and since he is a faithful person, and master of the accounts of the lord, he undoubtedly could receive the books pertaining to himself: and keep them diligently. For even if there are two lords of the same castle, and one departs, the other can keep it, as in D. de fundo instrato, l. si ita, § ville custos. For no one is bound to neglect his right, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. illud. And what is offered to him, he ought not to refuse, as in D. de feriis, l. more Romano; and C. de transactionibus, l. non minorem. Someone will say, these accounts were many and cancelled: therefore the book was not common. I answer, this argument is false: because accounts even when cancelled are common, because by them it is proved that a debt previously existed on both sides. Hence it is in the interest of both parties that they appear. The text is notable in l. fullo, D. de furtis; it makes C. de condictione sine causa, l. dissolutae; C. de fideiussoribus, l. plures apocis; in Auth. de mandato Principum, § publicorum; C. de apocis publicis, l. 1; C. de discussionibus, l. ne casu, lib. 10. And this is the very truth. Let therefore the objectors be silent. And although many powerful men are said to have advised the contrary, this is because they did not note the facts, nor was the truth explained to them. But that the account books were well kept, it appears from their reading: which first figure is without all suspicion, as in C. de edicto divi Adriani, l. fin. For the face of the writing shows ocular faith, and legality. Which is expressly clear, it is not necessary to prove, as in C. de fideiussoribus, l. comparationes; and D. finium regundorum, l. si irruptione, § ad officium. And to leave sense, and go by little reasons, is weakness of intellect, as say the two luminaries of philosophy, Aristotle and Averroes. And by these things the innocence of Milan appears most clearly, and more than clearly, against the biters, who sometimes applaud with voices, but bite with teeth with a curved sting, as says Blessed Jerome. But the decretal says, that it is not to be cared for what is oblique to the unjust, but what the equitable arbiter feels. Which twelve other things were asked by me.

And first, whether the penalty of the statute removes the penalty of the common law. And on this point I say that either it comes derogatively, and it removes it, as in *l. qui cum uno*, §. *qui post.*, D. de re iudicata, where there is a singular and unique text in the law. In all corporal penalties, and for the sake of humanity and equity, it seems that a departure is made from the harsher penalty: because a harsher penalty is equivalent to rigor; a lesser one is equivalent to truth; and equity, being written last, is preferred to rigor. Or, if the law disposes cumulatively, and then it does not seem that a departure is made, as in C. de sepulchro violato, *l. qui sepulchra*. Or it disposes disjunctively, and then in the same law it seems that the disjunctive is taken for the conjunctive, but in different statutes otherwise. But you say that, out of hatred for penalties, it is not taken for the conjunctive even in the same statute, but the last section is to be followed, as in D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, *l. Si idem cum eodem*, §. *finis*. For even if two legacies, which are favorable, are left to be paid for the same cause, only the later one is due, as noted in D. de probationibus, *l. quinquaginta*. Therefore, much more strongly, in penalties there should be no duplication. Moreover, we ought to be content with the penalties comprehended in the statute, as in D. de verbis obligandis, *l. huiusmodi stipulationi*, especially because magistrates swear to observe the statutes, as in Extr. de iureiurando, c. *Venientes*. Some, however, say that it is not true that one law is derogated by another, because the correction of laws is to be avoided, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, *l. quotiens*. But if execution of one penalty were carried out, the other penalty would cease: unless it were found to be for the supplement of the first; because a delict that is not fully purged ought to be purged, as noted in Extr. de iudicibus, c. *At si clerici*; C. de sportulis, *l. 2*; D. de accusationibus, *l. senatus censuit*. For even God does not judge twice for the same thing, as the Decretum says. 13

† Subsequently, I was asked, since the statute says that usurious merchants are not to be regarded as merchants, how this is to be understood. I answer that, in privileges and favors, they are not regarded as merchants, because guilt excludes all honor, as in C. ubi senato. vel cla. l. 1. and C. de digni. l. iudices. lib. 12. Hence, this is a kind of removal from the roll, which takes away privileges; nevertheless, it does not remove penalties, as in ff. de infami. l. 2. §. ignominiae. and §. miles, because no one by committing a crime makes his condition better. Therefore, when a merchant practices usury, he loses his privilege, as in ff. de priuilegiis credi. l. si uentri. §. in bonis; but he does not evade the penalties imposed on merchants, ff. de ne. gel. l. siue hęreditaria. Just as we see in the case of an excommunicated person, who is repelled actively, but may be sued passively, as in extra de iudi. c. Intelleximus. Moreover, an abominable merchant is one who practices usury; because the wickedness and voracity of usury do not befit a good man; since it is a disgraceful gain, as Aristotle says, and the whole school of theologians. And what I said later is for the satisfaction of the fourteenth question of the inquirer.

But there remains one fragment, or doubt, arising from the aforementioned matter: the statute concerning commerce speaks preliminarily of defrauders, but speaks definitively and dispositively on the point. Suppose, therefore, that a merchant defrauded due to poverty, not by design, but by chance; whether the rigor of the statutes ought to be mitigated on account of poverty.

† And it seems that this is so: because poverty excuses from perjury, as Innocentius holds in the Extravagant Decretals, De officio delegati, chapter G. Moreover, to allege poverty is a kind of raising an exception, as in the Digest, De procuratoribus, law Titius. Furthermore, it does not matter to the creditors that he fled, because the action is futile, as in the Digest, De dote, law Nam is. Also, because that which does not benefit the creditors and harms another ought not to be done; and Jacobus de Belvisis agrees in the aforementioned § Illud, where the gloss concludes. Quaerula’s pious prayers seem to hold otherwise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A rescript obtained through falsehood is void, even if the truth is merely concealed.
2. After three judgments, there is no remedy.
3. Clauses inserted in compromises, namely, "the agreement remaining ratified" and the penalty: what effect they produce.
body: In the name of Christ. The mind of the prince was moved.

It appears that, notwithstanding the legitimate arbitration and arbitral award, which provided for the restoration of the parties to the same status and rank in which they stood before the compromise and the sentence were made, and although this should not be done according to the strict letter of the law, as in C. sen. rescin. non pos., l. si; ff. de iureiu., l. admonendi, in fine; C. de trans., l. causas, vel lites; nevertheless, by virtue of the full power of the Prince, when some motive urges it, it is valid in law that what the Prince does is law, as the text states in c. cum olim, de dolo, et contumacia. And therefore, in the said arbitral award and sentence, no foundation can be drawn from them per se, unless it is proven that something was concealed from the Prince. But because it is established, according to what is alleged, that the rescript was obtained through fraud and falsehood, such a rescript is null by operation of law; and therefore the sentence and transaction remain firm. Just as, for example, if no mention is made of the proceedings, the rescript is null by operation of law, as in c. inter monasterium, de re iudicata, and is noted in c. super literis, de rescriptis, in the gloss magistra, which begins "ex hoc patet." So too, if mention is made of the proceedings by calumniating proceedings that ought not to be calumniated: because mention of the proceedings was not made in the manner in which it ought to be made; for it is the same not to recite them, or to recite them vitiously. Indeed, it is worse to recite them vitiously than not to recite them at all, as in ff. de edendo, l. ubi exigere, 2, where it is expressly stated in the response. And from this first true and most true foundation in law, the following are also founded; for, as appears from the facts, an appeal was taken from the sentence again rendered in favor of the community of Ponzanelli: and the appeal was abandoned by the adversaries; and the abandonment of the appeal passes into res iudicata, so that it is not a new sentence. This is elegantly noted in C. de appellationibus, l. eos, in principio. Hence, the first sentence remained confirmed by a confirmation of law, and subsequently another sentence expressly confirming the said arbitrator and arbitral award was removed by law. Hence, it can be said that three sentences were rendered in favor of the community of Ponzanelli: two by man, and one by law.

† And after three sentences, there is no remedy, except that the sentence must be committed to execution, as in c. Ut calumniis, De re iudicata, in the Clementines. And I say that even if they were sentences of mere arbitrium, at least by the form of the statute wishing arbitrations and arbitral awards to be committed to execution; for if it is committed to execution, an actio in factum is generated, and it has the force of a judge’s sentence, according to the doctrine of the gloss which is in l. 1, C. De arbitris; for this arbitrium is not naked, but is clothed with the aid of municipal law, as in ff. De pactis, l. Legitima. And therefore it is not necessary here to dispute whether the compromise is with a penalty or without one, and whether, once the penalty is paid, one can recede from the award or not; because we are not merely in the ius commune, but in municipal law. And thus the objection from no. in c. Quandiu, De appellationibus, in the Clementines, does not hold.

† Moreover, even in the common case where the conjunctive clause “the agreement remaining valid” is present, the arbitrator exercises two powers: one with a penalty, the other without a penalty; the latter power may be ratified, as noted in l. 2, ff. de arbitris. Furthermore, when this clause is appended, the penalty and the award do not refer to the same thing: because the penalty appears to be added on account of contempt, and not in place of the matter brought into the award. And therefore it does not prevent ratification, even tacit ratification. And although a stipulation to abide by the outcome (stare et perire) has been interposed, the arbitrator’s power does not arise from this stipulation, but from the compromise, which in itself is neither an agreement nor a stipulation, but is a certain grant of power, from which arises the award and its ratification. I always speak of cases where the said clause is appended to enlarge the power and effect. And this is the truth. And this is what Speculator means when he says that there are two compromises, i.e., two powers, which are not extinguished by election, as noted by Innocentius, extra de praescriptionibus, c. Cum ex officio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the hypothecary action lies against the person to whom the property was donated by the Prince with many full clauses, with certain knowledge, and with the fullness of power.
2. On the right of a third party. L. bene a Zenone.
3. For what period of time a hypothec is prescribed.
4. What effect the clause of the fullness of power and certain knowledge produces.
body: In the name of Christ. Our illustrious lord donated to Benentone a house, which had been seized from Thomasius under the name of the camera for 5,300 florins, for which amount Thomasius was liable to the camera at that time, and in the said donation the following words are contained: "in such and such a manner, that the said Benentone, etc., may hold, enjoy, and derive usufruct from the said house with all its rights and appurtenances belonging and pertaining to the said lord, and may sell and alienate it, and transfer it to another or others, freely enjoy it, and dispose of and do with it in all respects and in every way at his pleasure, just as the said lord could have done before the aforementioned donation, believing and firmly granting to the said Benentone, with the complete transfer of dominion and possession, all actions, both real and personal, competent to the said lord in the aforementioned house: placing him in the place of the lord himself, so that he may henceforth receive and have, use, enjoy, and derive benefit from the utilities and advantages, just as the lord himself could have done before the said donation, which he wished to be valid as law and decree, with all solemnity waived, which would otherwise be required. And this by certain knowledge and from the fullness of power." The said house was possessed by the said Benentone for a long time, and in good faith, in law and in fact, a creditor appears who has a prior hypothec, and he says that the property is hypothecated to him, and he brings a hypothecary action. Furthermore, he says that the said Benentone received large pensions, which diminish the quantity that was given to the donor. It is asked first, whether the said house can be defeated by the hypothecary action; secondly, whether the pensions diminish the debt that was owed to the camera.

And I do not doubt that the said lord did not donate anything other than his own right, as is stated in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Qui tabernas*; Digest, *De lege prima*, law *Si domus*, section *Si*; Extra, *De donationibus*, chapter *Cum dilecti*. Furthermore, it does not seem doubtful that the said pensions diminish the principal of eight hundred florins, because if he who has a claim from the creditor receives the fruits, those fruits diminish the principal, as is expressed in Extra, *De pignoribus*, chapter *Cum contra*. And thus Benentonus is bound to the restitution of the said house. Moreover, even if he had the right of the donor, since the creditor bringing the action is prior in time, it is established that he is stronger in law, according to the rule *Qui prior*; Extra, *De pignoribus*, chapter *Ex literis*; Code, *De privilegiis fisci*, law *Quivis*; Code, *Qui potiores in pignore habendi*, law *Assiduis*.

† not to the contrary. C. de quadrienni prae. l. bene a Zenone. because that law applies when the fisc has no right: but when it has some right, it seems to have granted only that, as C. de lega. l. vxor patrui. moreover, here the fisc contracted as a creditor, not as Emperor. hence in this case the common law must be observed: and not the privilege of the Augustus: as C. si aduersus fiscum. l. edicto.

† To the contrary it seems, for a hypothec is extinguished by prescription of ten years when a third party has possessed in good faith and with title, as is noted in l. cum notissimi, in the beginning, C. de praescriptionibus, 30 years. But Benentonus himself possessed in good faith and with a decree of the Prince; indeed, it seems even more correct to say that where a decree intervenes, good faith is not required; hence one prescribes even with bad faith and acquires the fruits, as in ff. de noxa, l. et generaliter, and there noted, and from de praescriptionibus, c. vigilanti. Moreover, the words of the Prince indicate, with the complete transfer of ownership and possession; therefore, ownership and possession have been transferred in perpetuity. d. l. bene a Zenone. Furthermore, in the said concession there are these words: “We wish all and each to be valid and inviolably observed as law”; but the Prince can, for cause, remove ownership; therefore, all the more so a hypothec, as in ff. de legibus, 2, l. peto, § praedium.

† Moreover, in the donation there are these words: "ex certa scientia" and "de plenitudine potestatis." And when these words are appended, it is akin to sacrilege to infringe upon the power assumed by the grantor. Nor is any other clause of "non obstante" necessary, according to all the authorities. Nor can it be said that the Prince restored a thing bound to another on account of that word "ex certa scientia." And because it appears from the words of the Prince that he wished the donation to be entirely valid, and the donee to become perpetual owner, and to have the fruits of the donated thing effectively: therefore they do not come into restitution, as in the Institutes, De rerum divisione, § Si quis non domino; and as we note in the Digest, De rei venditione, L. Fructus. For money is consumed by use; and consumed fruits do not come into restitution. Yet this is said, as we note in the said L. Fructus. But returning to the point, this Benentonus seems to be not only a possessor in good faith, but a full owner, made so by the will of the donor, and joined together. This question is doubtful; for the first part equity argues; for the second, supreme power. Also, in the donation it is said that the house was apprehended in the name of the camera, which words can signify by right of ownership for 5,300 florins, as in the Digest, De publicianis actionibus, L. Eleganter, in the beginning. I advise otherwise in this case: because it touches the interest of the Magnificent Doctor Notary, and its determination pertains to the counsel of justice, not to me, although the decision of the question is gathered from what is noted in the said L. Edicto, considering the words placed in the said instrument of donation. Digest, De evictione, L. Lucius; Digest, De rei venditione, L. Item si verberatum. And the question is common, about which by the doctors in the proemium of the Digests. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A perplex substitution involving impossibility is invalid.
2. A conditional fideicommissum is not transmissible.
3. Whether a substitution of this kind, namely, if my said sister should die without children descending from her, to the substitute, etc., is to be called a perplex substitution.
body: In the name of Christ. She, from whom Berta, her daughter, was then living among the living, made such a substitution by these words: and if my said sister should die at any time without children descending from her, I substitute the said Berta: and if the said Berta should die without children: I wish my goods to be distributed by my executors among girls to be married. First the testator died, secondly Berta died with children, thirdly the said sister died without children. Now there is a dispute between the children of Berta and the girls to be married, or the executors in their name. It is asked, what is the law regarding the said will and substitution.

† And it appears that the substitution made in favor of Berta was impossible: for either the sister dies while Berta survives, and the substitution lapses, because a daughter exists, and thus the condition fails, as in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. Luci; or Berta predeceased.

† and then the substitution is void, nor is it transmitted to the heir of the substitute: because a conditional fideicommissum is not transmitted, even to children, as is fully read and noted in l. 1, C. de his, qui ante apertas tabulas. Although a certain glossa says that a substitution made to agnates or cognates under a condition is transmitted to their children by the presumed intention of the testator, as is noted in ff. de act. et obl. l. his qui, and in C. de fideicom. l. cum acutissimi. But that glossa is not approved by Dyonisius, nor commonly by the doctors. Therefore, concluding from the first to the last, the substitution of Berta was a perplexed substitution, and involving an impossibility.

† Nevertheless, the truth is that the aforementioned substitution is not perplexed, because it is understood as "without children," i.e., without other children besides Berta; or it is understood as "without children and descendants," i.e., males: and in this case, the masculine does not comprehend the feminine, because it would be contrary to the testator's intent. Behold, therefore, that the substitution made in favor of Berta was valid from the beginning: but it became caducous, and was not transmitted to Berta's children: so that Berta's children cannot come by right of transmission, as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. pro secundo. But there remains the question whether they come in their own person by the presumed will of the substitutor, and on this point there are opinions: because the gloss and Petrus say that they do not; Dynus says the contrary, in ff. de legatis 2, l. Titia seio, §. seia. Solution: even if they do not come by substitution, because neither expressly nor tacitly, nevertheless they would exclude the girls to be married, because the condition of their being married fails; and this for a twofold reason. First, because the said sister did not die without children descending from herself: since the children of the daughter exist. The case is in l. 1, C. de conditionibus insertis. Although if Berta were alive, Berta's daughters would not exclude Berta, because the testator loved her more: and he placed before her only the sister, and her immediate male children. For the order of words is to be understood according to the order of affection, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredes mei, §. cum ita, and §. finalis, and it is expressed in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. quidam recte, according to which the gloss explains the text. Moreover, it must be considered that the testator preferred three persons to those to be married, i.e., ordered to marry. First, he preferred the sister. Second, he preferred the sister's daughter, Berta. Thirdly, the children of the daughter, as in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. verbis civilibus, and ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Publius, §. 1. Hence, the order of intention does not allow the girls to be married to come, to whom the testator wished his own blood to be preferred, as in l. 1, ff. de donationibus causa mortis. And thus I think that the marriage portion of the said girls from the goods of the said testator has no place, although this bequest is pious, as in l. cum, §. si mulier, ff. de conditionibus indebitis. For the inheritance is due to those who are up to the fifth degree, but the girls are seeking to gain a profit, and it is not equal to suffer losses and not to receive profits, as in C. de conditionibus, l. si quis agere, §. finalis. And thus I believe. Nevertheless, for the other party, it seems almost expressly stated in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. qui habebat, where it is said that when there are several degrees of substitutes, if the first degree is broken by death, the second degree fails. But that law certainly proves more that the girls to be married would not be admitted: because the anterior degree was consumed by Berta's predeceasing; so much so that even if Berta's children did not exist, the girls would not come, because if Berta's children did not exist, there would be no one who could exclude the girls to be married, since finally no one of the children existed. And from this it is concluded that by circumventing the second degree, the condition of the children is not circumvented. This is a difficult question proceeding by the pact of reason. And it supports ff. de fideicommissis liberis, l. Thais, §. Splendophorus. Because I fear God, because my conscience has never withdrawn itself from works of piety concerning the good of souls: but nevertheless I cannot depart from the reasons of the laws, and I submit myself to the sounder judgment, and especially of theologians and discreet men: because here the salvation of the soul is at stake. For someone might say that the testator preferred only two persons, namely the mother and the daughter: but now I ask, to what purpose would the mention of the daughter's children have been made, if such an addition effected nothing, as in ff. de legatis 1, l. filius, §. cum quis, and C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter, and ff. ad Trebellianum, l. haeredibus, §. finalis, and ff. de haeredibus institutis, l. Lucius, there "prudens" etc. Also, perhaps someone would say, the substitution of Berta vanished: therefore the condition annexed to it also vanished. But I answer, it does not follow: because the substitution remained with the heir with its burden, as in the said §. pro secundo. Or because, as I said, even if the daughter's children did not come by tacit substitution, they nevertheless have the right to exclude more remote persons. I see nothing else to be said in law: but nevertheless in the matter of excluding that which pertains to the good of souls, I never consulted without compunction of soul. And it would be good to reduce the parties to concord by composition, both for the good of peace, and for the good of conscience.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the successor of a prelate is bound to honor the tenant, and whether a lease contract made with the predecessor prelate is valid.
body: In the name of Christ. An abbot made a certain lease for 9 years for a fixed annual rent; and although he received the rent for 5 years before the time elapsed, he was removed from the abbey, or resigned.

† It is asked whether the following successor is bound to abide by the contract, or by the receipt of payment? It is alleged that he is not, through the gloss on c. querelam, ne prelati vices suas. To the contrary it is alleged that he is: because a prelate with the chapter can lease for a modest period of time, since it is not an alienation, but administration, just as a husband can also lease and the wife is bound to abide by the tenant, as noted in ff. sol. matr. l. divortio; not standing in the way l. defuncta, de usufruct. and ff. locati l. si quis domum, §. j., and there it speaks of a usufructuary who leases in his own name. And the same in the case of a prebendary, because he leases in his own name, not in the name of the prebend; and therefore the contract does not pass to his successor, because he is not a successor to the right, but to the thing, as in ff. de aedilic. ed. l. quaedam, §. his autem; but the revenues of the prebend do not pertain to the prebend, but to the prebendary, and therefore the prebendary can make a will and codicils regarding what has been received, nor is he bound to reserve it for his successor, as noted in c. praesenti, de offi. ord. But a prelate leases in the name of the church, and the church is bound to reserve it, and therefore he can contract; and the successor is bound to hold it ratified, just as a ward is bound by what was legitimately done by a guardian, as in ff. de minor. l. et si sine, §. 1, C. de admin. tutor. l. lex, quae tutores; for one does not contract badly with guardians and prelates, as in ff. de evict. l. illud quaeritur, §. 1; on this matter see extra de solut. c. 1, depositi c. gravis through Ch., C. locati l. emptorem through Barto., ff. de confess. l. certum, §. sed an ipsos. It is asked therefore what the law is. I shall speak according to the words of the Archdeacon, and conclude the same with him. The words of the Archdeacon on 12 q. 2 c. alienationes are these: suppose that a person has died who leased for a fixed time, will the successor be bound to abide by this contract? I answer: if that lease was made solemnly and beneficially, I think that he is; because not even a precarium is ended by the death of the grantor, extra de precario c. ult.; nor does C. locati l. emptorem stand in the way, for that speaks of a singular successor, not of a prelate, who is a universal successor, who by special favor ought to embrace those whom he knows to have faithfully obeyed his predecessor, eadem causa et quaestione c. hoc ius porrectum. But what if the lessor received the rent or price of the lease for several years, and dies beforehand? I say that his heir, if he has an heir, is bound to the successor pro rata temporis. If he does not have one, then the lessee is bound, who ought to have foreseen that this could happen, ff. locati l. si quis domum, §. 1, according to Goffredus, who thus notes extra ne praelati vices suas c. fi., and there this is stated by Bernardus. These are the literal words of the lord Archdeacon, and I hold the same in chapter 1, quis successor teneatur, col. 10. Since therefore the abbot has no heir, as in auth. ingressi, it follows that he who paid is not discharged for the future time. This is proved by evident reason: because the rent succeeds in the place of the fruits; but the fruits for that time do not pertain to him, since in the meantime he was removed from the administration. Whence, if he had not leased, he could not gather the fruits; therefore neither can he collect the rents. Very well to this point serves ff. de stipul. serv. l. si servus communis Maevii, §. fi. From these things it is concluded that the contract holds, but the one paying is not discharged. This is true unless it were openly proved that it was converted to the utility of the church; because then the successor ought to hold ratified what was beneficially done, ff. de negot. gest. l. Pomponius scribit si negotium. And from the things narrated to me in the case, having considered the character of the prelate, and because it does not appear that the entire chapter consented, I presume it was not so converted, through what is noted in ff. de novat. l. doli mali and in the said auth. hoc ius porrectum; for this abbot, as if having a guilty conscience, seems to have yielded the administration, ar. ff. de minor. l. Aemilius Largianus, in fi.; for one whose life is despised, his administration is held suspect, as is clear there and in C. de sentent. pass. l. in testamento. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a plaintiff suing on a deposit of money, if he proves only a confession, will succeed; and likewise, what is the law in the case of a loan.
2. A confession does not apply except in a contract evidenced by writing.
3. Whether a stipulation novates a contract of another kind.
body: In the name of Christ.

† An action of deposit was brought under this form: that he delivered 10 in deposit to a certain Albert, and that the said Albert confessed to having had and received them by stipulation, and promised. Only the confession was proved. It is asked, what is the law? And indeed, that the defendant ought to be acquitted, because a natural deposit was principally intended; and whatever follows afterward comes into conflict; therefore, since the principal foundation is not proved, the defendant ought to be acquitted. For we say this in a loan (mutuum), that he who claims counting (numeratio) does not prevail if he proves a confession, because he did not prove what he alleged, as in l. 2. §. verbis quoque. ff. si cer. pe., and in the case of a loan Speculator expressly holds this in ti. de test. §. videndum. ver. sed pone egi. Nor let anyone say that the counting was novated by the confession, because such a confession contains enunciative, not dispositive words; and novation does not take place by enunciative words, as in ff. deposi. l. publica. §. fi. Moreover, that the defendant ought to be acquitted is proved thus: a stipulation was claimed, therefore a transfer of the counting into an act of stipulation was claimed, as in ff. de noua. l. si ita stipulatus fuero. §. fi. cum. l. se.; for when one sues upon a stipulation, one is deemed to sue by the general condictio certi, as in l. certi conditio. in prin. ff. si cer. pet. But that action has not been proved; therefore, neither has the obligation, and thus acquittal ought to follow. Furthermore, that plaintiff bound himself to multiple elements, and therefore it is not enough to prove some of them: because whenever multiple elements are joined together toward one conclusion, they say that all must be proved; whence a quality inherent in the substance must be proved together with the subject, as in ff. de adul. l. denuntiasse. §. quid ergo. ff. de instito. l. habebat. For let him impute it to himself, because he restricted himself to an action that he could not prove, as noted in ff. de in rem verso. l. quidam. To the contrary is the truth. For it must be considered that in deposit one does not contract by a confession, but it is proved to have been contracted, as in d. l. publica. §. fi., and especially where no writing intervenes.

† Furthermore, a confession does not enter into any contract in the world except into a literal contract, as in inst. de lite. oblig. and noted in ff. de act. et obli. l. non figura., and by Guillelmus de Cuneo in ff. si cer. pe. l. qui pecuniam., and by Cynus in C. si cer. pe. l. Si non singuli. Whence it is clear that this confession was not claimed as an action, but as proof, as in ff. de solu. l. si ex pluribus. Whence it follows that once the confession is proved, the true counting is proved by it: because by a civil act the numerical act is proved, that is, by the confession, which is of the civil law, the counting, which is of the ius gentium, is proved. Nor is it novel that by the enunciative words of a confession the truth of what was disposed is proved, when the confession does not dispose, but finds what was disposed; otherwise a confession could bring something into being that never was, as in ff. de do. l. ex hac scriptura. Therefore, out of these two things claimed, namely the counting and the confession, the confession results as proving, and the counting as proved; and thus condemnation ought to follow from the counting, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. certi condictio. §. quam, and l. lecta. de ver. ob., and l. Si ita stipulatus. §. Grisogonus. And the aforesaid are confirmed: because, as I have said, a deposit is not contracted except in one way, namely re; but a loan in three ways, namely re, by chirograph, and by words. Whence in deposit there is one contract, one obligation: which having been proved, condemnation follows of necessity, as in extra de succes. abintest. c. cum dilectus.

† Someone will say: a stipulation was claimed. I answer in two ways: first, the stipulation does not novate a contract of another kind, that is, of counting, because it could have been added after an interval, as in C. de noua. l. fi. Likewise, even if it were added immediately, no novation would occur unless the counting had been done for the purpose of fulfilling the stipulation, as in d. l. si ita. 2. responso. That point is very clear, because the defendant denied the stipulation, and on the basis of an assumption denied by the plaintiff and by the defendant A., the defendant cannot plead an exception; therefore, since the stipulation comes as an exception of a certain novation, the defendant who denies the stipulation cannot establish a claim. Wherefore it is necessary that he succumb on the basis of the counting. To this, what Bartolus notes in ff. de excep. l. nemo. around the end, where it may be seen, applies exceedingly well. And this opinion I hold, especially because we ought to aid truth rather than legal subtleties, especially in the causes of miserable persons; indeed, from the nature of deposit, which is a contract of supreme good faith, as in ff. depositi. l. bona fides, whence in it it is not fitting to dispute over the subtleties of the law, but to protect the good and equitable, as in ff. mandati. l. si fideiussor. §. quaedam. And thus I hold in this quite fine and useful matter. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether improvements made to an evicted thing are owed by the victor to the vanquished.
2. Whether a possessor is presumed to be in good faith or in bad faith.
3. Whether one who purchases against a protestation is said to purchase in bad faith.
4. Whether one who refused to swear against calumny may appeal.
body: In the name of Christ. From Sempronius: then, after two months, it was denounced to him that he should not receive investiture, because the said fund belonged to the protester. By this deed, this buyer possessed it for many years, and with the knowledge and tolerance of the owner, he made improvements and buildings there. The owner brought an action for the recovery of the property; and, as owner of the fund and the buildings, the buyer, before delivering to the judicial officer, asked that his expenses be restored to him, insofar as the thing had been improved.

† The question is, what is the law: I premise, for clarity, that a bona fide possessor can recover such expenses by raising an exception before judgment, or by invoking the judge’s office after judgment, as in C. de rei vend. l. quis sciens; and l. si in area; ff. de peti. hęred. l. plane, §. doli exce.; and l. Paulus; ff. de cond. ind. l. si in area; ff. de nego. gest. l. ex duobus; ff. de rei vendi. l. emptor. But a mala fide possessor, if indeed in bad faith: because against the prohibition of the owner he can obtain nothing; because he is deemed to make a donation, as in C. de neg. gest. l. fi; because the robber improperly seeks aid for himself. And this expenditure is for the permanent benefit of the property, which passes to the owner, as in d. l. si in area; and ff. man. l. si parte; and especially when the thing is emphyteutic: because improvements are not owed to one who has fallen from the emphyteusis through his own fault, nor to one having a title derived from him, as in C. de iure emph. l. 2; and C. de sa. san. ecc. auth. qui rem huiusmodi, in fi.

† The question therefore stands on this point: whether the possessor is to be considered in bad faith or not? And it appears that he is to be considered in good faith: because good faith is presumed rather than bad faith, as is known from C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. pen. For, as the glossa says there, every possessor is presumed to be ignorant that the thing belongs to another. Moreover, good faith is presumed by reason of title, as in ff. de re iudicata, l. nemo praedo est, qui pretium numeravit. And note: There were three brothers, according to Jacobus de Arena, C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. improb.

† To the contrary it seems, for he who buys against a protestation is deemed to buy in bad faith; indeed, the warning harms him, even if he is truly in good faith, as C. de rei vend. l. si fundum, and there fully noted. For gross negligence cannot be excused in one who has disregarded a just protestation, as ff. de lega. praestan. l. virilis, §. si adierit. He ought to have been a curious investigator, not a presumptuous buyer, as ff. de re. iu. l. cum alio. Nor does it avail if it is said that he ought to have been given assurance regarding the right of the protesting party, as ff. depo. l. si quis inficiatus; C. quae res pi. oblig pos. in l. nomen, in the version certior factus. For in the cases of those laws, the one to whom the protestation was made does nothing rashly, whereas here he does. Moreover, proof must be made to the judge in court, not to the adversary outside of court, C. de eden l. 2, and fully noted in the said l. si fundum, and l. ait praetor, §. si quis particeps, ff. quae in fraudem credi., and l. 1, in the beginning, ff. de no. ope. nun., and ff. de l. commisso. l. fi., and ff. ad Tre. l. haeredes.

Solution: I consider that this denunciation was made to the buyer long after the purchase and the delivery made to him; and therefore it did not place him in bad faith regarding the purchase, because the beginning of possession is examined, as l. 1, §. 1, C. de vsucap. transfor. However, it rightly places him in bad faith regarding expenditures, because he ought not rashly to have made expenditures on another’s land after the protestation, arg. ff. pro suo. l. si ancillam, and ex de praesc. c. quam omne.

Solution: If the plaintiff had full ownership, this defendant would have lost his expenditures. But because the plaintiff has only the dominium directum (ownership), and this defendant has the useful dominium as an emphyteuta, because the owner consented to this, if the woman has useful dominium in the buildings, just as in the land. Hence it is concluded that the buildings pertain by right of ownership to the owner, by right of the leasehold to the emphyteuta. And this was not narrated to me from the beginning, as ff. de contrahem. emp. l. qui tabernas, and l. si domus, §. fi., ff. de leg. 1. Nor can he truly claim expenditures with respect to ownership, because he is in bad faith; nor with respect to the emphyteusis, because he claims in vain what he already holds. Furthermore, he has natural possession and the benefits of the emphyteutic right, both of the land and of the buildings. And this is the case in which, with respect to ownership, he is in bad faith, and with respect to useful dominium, he is in good faith. Therefore, I hold that he has lost his expenditures, because he knowingly threw away what was his own, as ff. de prob. l. cum de indebit8. Nor does the action for negotiorum gestio lie, because nothing was managed in consideration of and out of affection for the true owner; but rather in contempt of him, as ff. de negge. l. si pupilli, §. 2. He did not have the intention of obligating another, as ff. communi di. l. in hoc iudicium.

Secondly, it is asked whether he who refuses to swear the oath against calumny may appeal. And it seems that he may not, because he is deemed to have confessed by legal fiction, as in C. de iur. cal. l. 2. §. pe. To the contrary, it seems that he may, because a person who has confessed may appeal, since in the case of appeal he may prove a just excuse, as noted in ff. de appel. l. creditor. §. fin. and C. de rebus creditis. l. generaliter. §. 2; however, if the excuse is not proven, he will fail in the appeal. And this is true, and thus holds Jacobus de Arena in the said l. 2. C. de iura. calum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Bastards born from illicit intercourse do not succeed to a fief.
2. Whether bastards ought to be maintained and whether they ought to be provided with a dowry.
body: In the name of Christ. Both parents, and the vassal of one lord of an ancient fief, one being over 14 years of age, by his own free will and with the consent of his brothers, entered a certain monastery, in which he remained for a year and several months. While he was in the said monastery, one of his brothers died, another took a wife, and the said monk went to the wedding; and gradually he abandoned the habit; and with the consent of his brother he took a wife, whom the wife had seen in the habit of monks. Now from these two sons and one daughter were born.

† It is asked, what is the law regarding the succession to a fief, and regarding the maternal inheritance, and regarding alimony? I answer that the aforementioned bastards do not succeed to the fief, and especially because they were born from illicit intercourse. C. de incest. nup. l. si quis incest. and in c. naturales. si de feu. fue. controu. col. 10. Furthermore, they do not

† They succeed their mother on account of their incestuous origin, who could be accused, as in Inst. ad officia § nouissime and C. ad officia l. si qua illustris, and in both places the commentators note. However, they ought to receive at least maintenance from the maternal dowry, if they have no other means of support, according to canonical equity, as in c. cum haberet, extra de eo, qui duxit in matrimonium, quam polluit per adulterium. For by the equity of that chapter, any successor to paternal goods is bound to provide maintenance out of the clemency of canon law and divine law. But they ought not to be endowed, except insofar as the piety, compassion, and nobility of the uncle dictate: for this is his duty to God, because it is his honor. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An inquisitorial proceeding does not take place unless legitimate indications or half-proof precede it.
2. An uncertain inquisitorial proceeding does not take place.
3. Affirmative proof in a purgation is only as valid as negative proof.
4. Whether an indication is sufficient for torture is left to the discretion of the judge.
5. Whether one witness constitutes an indication for torture.
6. If witnesses do not prove the homicide, they cannot prove its accessory.
7. A maleficium against the instigator is not proven by the contumacy of the principal offender.
body: In the name of Christ. They ought to, who, having been named in it, when they found the matter explained by certain of their adversaries, that they had dined with Albert at the house of residence of the said Albert, armed, went to the said house, and made there an assault, and aggression, crying out against the traitors to death, certainly you cannot escape: and when one was fleeing, and wished to cross a moat of the said house of the said Albert, a certain John, one of them, with a lance killed the said crossing person, and a certain Peter, equally inquired of, and armed with a sword, standing on the public road through the middle of the aforementioned moat, in which that one was killed, went along the said road, and said to the said John, give to the traitor, give to the traitor. giving, and rendering to each other aid, counsel, and favor. The said Pe. appeared, and denied: against him Zaninus testifies saying in effect, that the said Pe. then cried out, and said, strike the traitor. standing armed on the said way: but Peter himself sought to purge himself by contrary evidence: because two witnesses say, that the thing was without it, that the said Pe. had cried out, and said the said words. Now it is asked, whether the said Pet. should be subjected to torture.

And briefly, it must be said, according to the matters proposed, first, that the said inquisition was not formed in due order: because there is no appearance of preceding indicia, or of half-proof, as the statute requires: for although a confessor could not allege this, a denier could: as in c. 1, de homicidiis, lib. 6, to which C. de senatus consulto et interludis, l. prolatam, with its material, contributes. And thus the said inquisition does not proceed on account of defective order. Second, it does not proceed: because by those words, “give to the traitor,” a mandate to commit homicide is not proved, nor a mandate to inflict a wound from which homicide could follow: because the said words are general and obscure: and they are to be understood in the lesser sense: for one can give [a blow] with a fist, and with a spear: as ff. ad legem Corneli de sicariis, l. 1, § sed si clava; as extra de homicidiis, c. significasti; and noted in l. 1, C. unde vi. And thus neither a mandate nor counsel to perpetrate homicide is alleged: but rather a striking in general, from which a specific condemnation for homicide by mandate, counsel, or aid cannot follow. Fourth reason: because here there were many: the words speak in the singular, “one to another,” which is a phrase of the singular number: hence the inquisition ought to have said, “and one to another, and all among themselves gave and provided aid, etc.” For when it says, “one to another,” it does not appear who was [the actor].

And an uncertain inquiry does not proceed, as in D. de iniuriis, l. Praetor edixit. To this effect is what is noted in C. de furtis, l. Ancillae, in the word "alteri." Although by that gloss the contrary might be argued, yet it is of its proper meaning that I have said. The fifth reason is, because, assuming that the said Zanino made a judgment, nevertheless he is one single witness, and solitary, as he himself asserts. But he does not seem to have told the truth, according to what is alleged. Because others saw, and saw the exact opposite; for if he had been the sole witness, therefore he would have been the sole observer. But this is false: therefore his testimony is suspect. I say more strongly, not only suspect, that is, weakened, but totally eradicated, because a negative, which can be perceived from a witness, operates in denying just as an affirmative does in affirming, as noted by Cynus in l. 2, C. de errore advocatorum.

† Moreover, in expurgation, negative proof is as valid as affirmative proof, because expurgation is the elimination of conjectural contrary proof: and conjectures are more easily eliminated than proofs made fully. As stated in l. licet imperator, ff. de leg. j., and l. diuus, ff. de in integrum restit., and this is held by Azo in a certain place sufficiently noted. The sixth reason is that the aforementioned Pe. did not act with the intent to commit evil, but rather with the intent to make peace: and this he had foretold at the beginning, and peace followed at the end; because neither did Peter know of the death, nor did any other pretor consider him a murderer. If, however, he had known, he certainly would not have treated of peace, nor would he have consented to be injured, if one turns the intellect to the wisdom and discretion of the mind, as stated in extra de accusatione, c. cum P. manconella.

The seventh reason is that whether a judgment is sufficient for torture depends greatly on the equity of the judge, since no certain rule can be given, as argued in D. de usu, l. mora, and D. de testamento, l. 3, § tu magis. Indeed, even more so, because certain, probable, and likely indications are required, as stated in C. de quaestione, l. milites, § oportet; not slight, nor perfunctory, nor those which can be interpreted in many ways, since the life of a person is at stake, and therefore the indications for torture must be clearer than light within their own category of indications. But in the present case, there is neither an indication nor half-proof, as is evident from the reasons and laws cited above.

† It is certain that when a single witness provides evidence sufficient to justify torture, that witness must be invulnerable, i.e., above all exceptions; for torture is a certain supplementary proof, not standing by itself, as in D. de quaestionibus, l. Minore, §. Tormenta; and l. Vnius, §. Cogniturum; and l. Edictum diui. It is also known that either a single witness testifies about the fact itself or about the circumstances. In the first case, if the witness is above all exceptions, he provides evidence sufficient for torture. In the second case, although he provides half-proof of an indication, he does not provide evidence sufficient for torture; and therefore one does not proceed to torture, nor would the accused be pressed, except to confess the indication; because no one is tortured in order to create an indication, but rather in order to manifest the crime principally alleged.

† And furthermore, it must not be omitted that unless witnesses prove the homicide, they cannot prove anything accessory thereto, such as aid and assistance, or a command, as stated in the Digest, *De furtis*, law *Si is qui rem*, section *Si tu Titium*. But here the homicide has not been proven, from which it follows consequently, because the murderer is not named, but is considered uncertain with respect to this witness, who states that he does not know him; hence, he does not prove the formal inquisition regarding a certain murderer. Moreover, it is necessary that the act of a certain person be alleged, so that if a witness gives false testimony, it may be properly refuted, as stated in the Digest, *De accusationibus*, law *Libellorum*, and law *Licet*, section *Possumus*; Digest, *De nauticis, cautionibus, et stabulariis*, and law *Si exhibuisset*, *De publiciis*. Hence, since this witness had no knowledge of the murderer, he cannot prove the homicide, and consequently neither its accessory, and especially because the crime of the doer and the commander is one in number, speaking realistically; and therefore one cannot be proven without the other, as noted by Cynus in law 1, Code, *Si reus vel accusator mortuus fuerit*.

† Moreover, the principal defendant’s contumacy does not prove the offense against the instigator, as stated in the Digest, *De adulteriis*, law *Denuntiasse*, section *Quaeritur*. This point must be carefully considered in the present question, where you will find many things usefully, subtly, and truly stated.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a partnership between brothers is said to have been contracted, and how things are to be shared in common, and which are not. The partnership that is said to have been contracted between brothers, and which profits are to be shared in common, and which are not, and whether properties purchased with common funds by one brother are to be shared with the other, or whether only the money is to be compensated by offsetting the fruits against the profits that could have arisen from the money: and two opinions are set forth, especially those of Bartolus and the Speculator. See also in consilium 304, where the same was advised between the same persons.
2. Whether household expenses are to be shared between brothers.
3. Whether a brother acquires for his brother, if they are not partners.
4. One who has money in a partnership must first withdraw his capital, and only the profits are to be divided.
5. How the division of acquisitions made before the partnership and after is to be made, and what is to be done with the money of paternal things. And no. 6.
7. Aliments are not shared in common.
body: In the name of Christ. One, namely John, of five brothers, by the will of their common mother and guardian of some of them who were minors, sold a certain mill formerly belonging to their father for 110 florins and actually received the price. Afterwards, after an interval, the said mother and guardian of the three youngest brothers confessed by petition that she held the said paternal goods in her possession, and that the said John held nothing of the said goods in his possession. Finally, after a lapse of time, the said John sold another estate for 310 florins and likewise received the price, and placed it in a certain apothecary’s shop, and the said brothers worked in it and remained in partnership and community, each working and exercising his person at different times. And when one of them, named Raphael, who was younger than the others, had reached puberty, he worked greatly in the said apothecary’s shop, operating there, and also sailing to various parts of the world, and he consigned his profits to the said John, his elder brother. And the said other brothers came to a division with the said John and sold him their share of the paternal goods. But the said Raphael, who did not divide, claims from the said John a half share in the said goods by right of partnership.

† The question is asked: what is the law? I answer: the words of the *Speculum* are these. When a father has died and several sons remain in the paternal home, some of whom are of age and others profit, while others do not, and when those wishing to proceed to division, the minors demand that the profits of the adults be shared with them. Either the goods among these brothers have been divided, or they have not. In the first case, each acquires for himself what he profits, and no sharing can be demanded by the other brothers, unless this was specifically stipulated in the division. If, however, the goods are undivided, and some brothers profit, either it is certain from where they acquire, or it is not, or it is doubtful. In the first case, each acquires for himself, especially from his own works and labor, and ought not to share, provided they are not partners in all goods. If, however, it is not certain, nor can it be, either the doubt lies in fact or in law. If in fact, for example, he acquires from his own works, because perhaps he is a scribe or artisan, then he acquires for himself, so that what has accrued to him through his labors and good fortune does not become burdensome to him by passing to his brothers. But if he is a man of bad conduct and no craft, it is presumed that he has everything from the common goods or from the paternal estate, etc. In doubt, however, it is presumed that he acquires from the common fund, other presumptions being absent. Thus it is noted in the *Speculum de iudiciis*, Part 4, § *Sequitur videre*, verse *Ut autem*. But Bartolus examines this matter more clearly and fully in *Digestum*, *De administratione tutorum*, law *Titium et Mevium*, § *Altero*, whose words, insofar as they pertain to the proposal, are these: Wherefore, when no partnership is expressly contracted, and one of the brothers buys a fund for himself, he is not bound to share the fund; but he is bound to share the money which he acquired from the business in which they were partners, and he wishes to say that things acquired from the partnership are not shared, nor are they common. The other things said by the aforementioned Bartolus are not necessary at present, but nevertheless I conclude thus: that the said lands bought are presumed to have been bought from the common profits of both said brothers; and that according to the *Speculum*, the said purchases should be shared. But according to Bartolus, the lands should not be shared, but rather the money itself should be contributed to the common fund. It is true that, because the said Raphael was sometimes at an age when he could not be a partner, they cannot make a division of profits according to times, because I do not know how much they profited after these two became partners, and how much before; but this ought to be examined by a common arbitrator according to the conscience of truth. And the profits made before are the property of the one who profited, unless he prohibited the use of Raphael’s money, and then account is taken of interest for the time during which he was a minor; but the profits made afterwards are to be shared, because by virtue of the partnership, the things bought succeed in place of the money commonly held, by argument from *Digestum*, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si socius*; *Digestum*, *Pro socio*, law *Si fratres* and law *Cum duobus*, § *Si in coeunda*. And this opinion is specific and sufficiently equitable. And these things are true if it appears that the said Raphael placed his profits in common in good faith.

† As for the expenses of the household, speaking generally, if they lived together on one bread and one wine, no compensation ought to be made; for perhaps the labor of the children compensates for such minor expenses. But if the partners were separate in their business dealings, and also in their table, each one ought to recognize the burden of his own household, and not that of another, as is argued from ff. de familia herciscunda, l. si maritus. This question, and similar questions, depend greatly on the discretion of the judge; because partners, and brothers, ought to treat each other in such a way that neither deceives nor is deceived. As is argued from l. ultima, C. de ponderationibus auri. So that equality between them is preserved, as far as it can be preserved.
