Moreover, if there were no partnership between them, brotherhood alone is not a cause for sharing profits: as C. de communibus utriusque iudicii, l. si patruus; and the aforementioned l. cum duobus, §. si fratres; and the aforementioned §. altero, where this matter is sufficiently and notably examined by Bartolus. And for a clearer understanding of the foregoing, say,

† If the brothers are not partners, one does not acquire for the other, nor is he bound to share: as in C. de bonis, quae liber, l. cum oportet. But if they are partners, one must share the profit with the other, both according to Speculator and according to Bartolus. However, if from those profits one buys something in his own name, that thing is to be shared according to Speculator, because a partner must conduct business in good faith, and not convert common money to his own uses. And on account of this fault he is liable to share, if the partner demands it. For he must not intercept and supplant his partner, but must seek the utility of the partner as his own, and do for the partner what he considers useful for himself, as in ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. si negotia. And this is dictated by natural equity. But according to Bartolus, although the profits of the business are common, because the business itself is common, nevertheless the thing bought, because the purchase is from the business of the partnership, and could not be bought in the name of the partnership, because no partnership was contracted for buying real estate, this contracting party is liable for the interest. For he ought not to have converted the merchandise to common utility, but into the purchase of real estate for his own convenience. From which it follows that, for the share that falls to the said Raphael, he is liable for all that he could have gained with the said money from the spice trade. And if it is said that the said Raphael put nothing into the said partnership, I answer: it is not true; since the said business was conducted with common money, which, considering the number of brothers proportionally, belonged to the said Raphael from things sold in common name. Moreover, the said Raphael contributed his labor, and therefore, as far as John is concerned, a partnership was contracted with him.

† But one thing must be considered: because he who contributes money to a partnership must first withdraw his capital, and only the profits are to be divided. As is noted in l. 1, C. pro socio, according to one opinion. Another opinion holds that, just as labor expended cannot be withdrawn by the laborer, so too money converted into merchandise cannot be withdrawn, lest the contract be defective. But the first opinion is fairer and more common; therefore, the arbiter ought more equitably to consider whether the said lands were purchased from the common money placed in the partnership, representing the price of labor. Raphael says, in reckoning the money, whether it came from the mere profit of the business. For if it is true that the lands were purchased from 300 florins out of a thousand, which were common to all the brothers, then compensation should be made to Raphael pro rata; because he ought not to have more than his hereditary portion of the uncertain common money. But if they came from the mere profit of the spice trade or another form of partnership gain, then Raphael would have a right to one-half, not because the lands were common by law, but because they are to be shared and divided according to the agreement. But according to Bartolus, they are neither common nor to be shared, because the purchase of lands is entirely outside the scope of the partnership. ff. pro socio, l. sed si adijciatur.

† From the aforementioned, it is also decided what the law is if certain profits were acquired before the partnership and others after, as in no. ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. Pomponius. In negotio. For the time before the partnership, there is no question of sharing; for the time after, there is.

Furthermore, it must be considered that this Raphael is entitled to a share of the money from the paternal estate, according to the number of children of the said John, to whom the said money came, as it is said to have been proven: this share subsequently entered the body of the partnership, which partnership was contracted between two persons, namely between John and Raphael. From one partnership, the profits arising must be distributed equally between these two. It is therefore concluded that there is a double distribution, namely an original and primary distribution of the price itself, and this is among four. Another secondary distribution of profits, and this is made between only two, namely John and Raphael, each for a half. However, what I said regarding the primary obligation with respect to John is true, unless John himself had resigned the price to the mother, who was the guardian of Raphael; because then John would be released to the extent that he had consigned it: as stated in the law *Sancimus*, Codex, *De administratione tutorum*. But if the mother were not the guardian, it would not prejudice the said Raphael: as stated in the law *Filiae*, Digest, *De solutionibus*. Finally, I conclude that the matter is very complex; because the account of the administration of the partnership must be rendered by the said John to the said Raphael, and conversely, if the said John has more in his share, even if he had converted it into the purchase of real estate, he is bound to restore it; because it is not asked whether the first [party] should remain enriched to the injury of his brother: as stated in the Digest, *Si certum petatur*, law *Si me et Titium*, and Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, law *Qui sine usuris*. Because a partner must owe full faith to his partner, all fraud being removed. As for the partnership, it does not appear to me through the proofs; but it is asserted to me that the arbitrator knows: I leave this to the conscience of the arbitrator, who can decide this case, even considering the points of law for the sake of peace and concord; especially because the partnership can sufficiently be gathered from presumptions even in the discretion of the arbitrator. For example, he may choose thus: thus he wishes, according to the opinion of Speculator. If it is possible, a division of the purchased things can be made. Otherwise, let him choose the opinion of Bartolus.

† However, the father must provide the maintenance of his children, as stated in the Digest, title *De familia erciscunda*, law *Si maritus*, because maintenance is not included in the partnership; nor is it a partnership asset, or a commodity for sale, concerning which the question is raised. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who cannot raise an exception may anticipate by bringing an action.
2. A liquidated matter is not delayed by an unliquidated one.
3. Whether a release is to be called a donation.
4. Mere liberality is a donation.
5. What a donation is properly speaking.
6. Whether one who is bound to give security is bound to obligate himself.
7. If a fideiussory obligation is found, whether it is presumed that the principal debtor has also been primarily obligated.
8. Whether a gratuitous pact of obligation is a donation, and whether it requires insinuation.
9. If I were to lend you a thousand gold coins on the condition that you restore five hundred, insinuation would be required for the other five hundred.
10. A penalty is not included under the name of donation. Add above consilium 231.
body: In the name of Christ. It is safely provided that instruments must be put into execution, notwithstanding any exception which is not proved by the instrument; however, if execution has been carried out and it can be proved that the creditor had already been paid, the debtor himself ought to be condemned to pay double. Another statute provides that a donation within five hundred gold coins is null if it has not been insinuated. Another statute provides that he who appeals must give security for the reimbursement of expenses; otherwise, he shall not be heard. Now, a certain man named Andreas was the creditor of Benedict in three hundred gold coins, for which Benedict, P. and Io. stood as sureties, and also constituted themselves principal debtors in the said amount. It eventually happened that the said creditor released the said Pet. for 25 florins; there is no instrument showing this. Finally, the said Pet. petitioned against the said A. to be released from the entire said obligation. After this, the said A. petitioned for execution of the said instrument; a sentence was rendered, and an appeal was taken, and it is found in the records that Sempronius stood surety for the expenses, but it is not otherwise found written that the appellant promised anything. From this case arise three questions.

First, whether he who cannot raise an exception may prevent the other party by bringing a prejudicial action: and thus it seems that he may, because the statute omits a just case; and sometimes an exception is denied, but an action is not denied, as in Extra, De iureiurando, c. Debitores. And this occurs wherever this order is established, that first execution takes place, and secondly one may sue and retract, as noted in Digest, De conditione indebiti, l. Neratius. The contrary is true: because where an exception is removed, since execution is ready, execution is not impeded, even if the defendant proceeds to file a libel, as in l. Si, Codex, De ordine cognitionum; and Extra, De restitutione in integrum, c. Suscitata; and Codex, De precibus imperatoris offerentibus, aut. Quae supplicatio. Also in favor of this is the general rule: to whom an exception is denied, an action is denied for him at that instant time, as noted in Codex, De transactionibus, l. Nec intentio. Moreover, an action is liquid, an exception is not.
† and that which is not liquid does not delay that which is liquid. As in C. de compensatione, l. si. And noted by Bartolus in l. 4, § condemnatum, ff. de re iudicata.

The second doubt is whether the aforementioned release granted to the surety for three hundred, in respect of twenty-five, constitutes a donation in that which exceeds the sum of twenty-five; and it seems that it does: because the money is partly paid, partly donated; as in C. de donat. inter vir. et ux. l. per diversas and l. ab Anastasio. To the contrary it seems, because the release of a surety or pledge is not said to be a donation, nor does it require insinuation; as in ff. qui pot. in pign. l. 1, § 1. Moreover, not every pact not to sue is a donation; because in a pact not to sue a cause is not required; as in ff. de pactis l. tale pactum in princ. The gloss in l. si quis obligatione ff. de re iudicata says that a gratuitous release is a donation and requires insinuation. But this release, above twenty-five gold coins, is mere liberality.

† And mere liberality is a donation, as in D. de donat. l. hoc iure; and this is noted by Bartolus in l. 2, § circa, D. de except. dot. solut., from which the solution of this question is gathered. D. de pactis, l. si intra, in the text with the gloss. For if it were a donation, it would today be a named contract; but there it is said that it is an unnamed contract, since the action is brought by prescribed words: therefore it does not require insinuation. Moreover, it is certain that a transaction does not require insinuation: as in C. de transact. l. sive apud acta; nor is it rescinded on account of enormous lesion, out of hatred for litigation, as in D. ad Trebell. l. Lucius, § fin., according to the true opinion, whatever Bartolus may say there, unless fraud intervened, as in l. in sum., in princ., D. de cond. indeb. But this contract is a kind of transaction, in which only so much is given for the whole of what remains to the creditor, namely the action against the principal debtor, as in D. de fideiuss. l. si ex duobus, § 1; and there could have been litigation between the creditor and the surety on account of the benefit of cession: therefore it is a transaction, or a contract similar to it; in which the same rule must be applied, as in D. de dep. l. 1, § si quis servum. Moreover, since it is doubtful what contract this is, in case of doubt as to the name we presume it to be a named contract, as is noted in D. pro socio, l. si margaritam. And this opinion is true, namely that it does not require insinuation; which also appears,

† For a donation properly so called occurs when the donor becomes poorer and the donee becomes richer, as stated in l. 1, ff. de donat. inter vir. et vxor., which is not the case here; this point is supported by C. de pact., l. si creditores, l. liberum, and l. reos. For it is clear from those laws that this is rather a division of a performance made by agreement than a liberality of donation. Moreover, it is rather a remission of a certain caution than a release of a debt, as in l. si pignus, ff. quae in fraud. cred., and therefore insinuation is not required, as in C. de pac., l. pactum, quod bona fide, since certainly no written instrument is required. And even if it were required, it would be required only for amounts exceeding fifty pounds, up to the male portion of three debtors, because there were three here.

† The third doubt is whether satisfaction has been rendered to the aforementioned statute concerning the giving of security. This question has been raised elsewhere, namely whether he who is bound to give security is required to bind himself by obligation; and there are opinions, as noted by Cynus in l. 1, C. de satisdando. Some say that, since the creditor was content with the mere promise of a surety, it is understood that security has been given, just as the creditor wished, as stated in D. de fideiussoribus, l. qui satisdare. And if you ask how one can act as a surety where the principal does not promise, I answer that this surety accedes to the office of the judge, by which the principal is bound to costs, and it suffices that the principal defendant is bound in some manner. For a surety may accede to the office of the judge, as l. 1, D. de fideiussoribus; and l. pecuniae, § 1, D. de verborum significatione; and D. de eo quod certo loco, l. centum capuae; and l. fin.; and l. 1, D. de in litem iurando. Moreover, in judicial proceedings there is not properly a suretyship, as D. de in ius vocando, l. eum, pro quo. On the contrary, it appears that the law is express that he who must give security must principally bind himself. D. de usufructu earum rerum, quae usu consumuntur, l. tribus. For, as the gloss elegantly states in D. ad Trebellianum, l. si haeres pecuniam, a hypothecary obligation is found without a personal one, but a suretyship obligation is not found without a principal one.

But here it may be doubted whether it is presumed that the defendant bound himself principally. And it must be said that it is not, since the records do not state this. And the ordinary glossa says that although the procurator’s obligation of a surety is not produced, the principal obligation of the defendant is not sufficient. This is the glossa which I always cite in D. 50.16.53 (De verbis oblig.). Sciendum. Having considered all things, I distinguish thus: either he promised principally as an expromissor, and the statute is satisfied; as in D. 9.2.27.1 (De dolo). Eleganter. § Servus pactionis, provided this is done with the adversary’s acquiescence; as in D. 46.1.11.2 (De fideiussoribus). Tuto. Cum ostendimus. § Ult. Or he intervened as a simple surety; and then the statute is not satisfied; because, as I said, he who must give security and provide a surety, so that the suretyship obligation has something to attach to; as in D. 46.1.1.1 (De fideiussoribus). Graece. § Illud commune, and the aforementioned law Tribus. The contrary argument, which is quite strong, does not prevail. To the contrary, because a surety can accede by the office of the judge. For I say that this has no place in the reimbursement of expenses; because expenses which come by the office of the judge do not apply where someone has a just cause for litigation; otherwise, where they come by stipulation, as noted in Auth. 3.1.1 (De iudicibus). § Oportet. From this it would follow that the surety would be bound in a harsher case, and to more than the principal, which is impossible. Nor does D. 19.2.1 (De locato). Quaero prevail, because there it is the effect of the office and the obligation; here it is not. Bartolus says that either the remission is made on account of a donation, and it must be insinuated, as he notes in D. 39.5.1 (De donationibus). Modestinus, and as noted in D. 50.17.128 (De regulis iuris). Si quis ob. Therefore, if insinuation were not required in another case.

† Now it must be seen whether this is a donation or another cause: and it seems that it is a donation: because from the fulfillment of part of the contract nothing is acquired by the creditor. For that which is paid was otherwise due, and liquid, and part of the same debt, and therefore such payment does not clothe the pact, as D. de pactis, l. si inter. Moreover, it does not seem to have been done with the intention of donating: because it is not done gratuitously. Moreover, let it be the cause of fulfilling a condition: and the condition is held as another, as if of donation, as D. de verbis oblig., l. a Titio. Although therefore the creditor is content with a lesser quantity, this is not a donation properly and purely, but certainly, rather it seems that it is a donation: because that which is the law of the whole with respect to the whole, the same law is of the part with respect to the part, as D. de rei vend., l. quae de tota. But if the remission were made in whole, insinuation would be required, because it is gratuitous according to Bartolus. Therefore the same applies to the part with respect to the part: otherwise an inconvenience would follow, namely that a remission could be made for one coin, and insinuation would not be required: which is false, holding the opinion of Bartolus, according to which I otherwise advised. And if I were to say the contrary, it would follow that if I hand over to you a thing worth a thousand without cause, and afterwards I free you gratuitously, that insinuation is not required. And thus a way would be found to defraud the precept of the law, which speaks of insinuation. It is concluded from these things that a gratuitous pact of obligation, and which could not be repelled by exception, would require insinuation according to Bartolus. Although on this point there are contrary glosses, as in l. patet, 1. §. 1. D. qui modis pignus vel hypotheca solvatur. Nor does it avail that the creditor has recourse against others: and thus nothing seems to be lacking to him, because in the person of the one released purely, liberality has been conferred with respect to his person. This question is sufficiently doubtful, but the opinion of Bartolus is very probable, as appears from the urgent reasons made above. However, I do not deny that the said contract is a mixed contract, partly donation and partly not, as D. de donationibus, l. hoc iure, §. Ariston. and D. de exceptione doli, l. 2, §. circa, per Bartolus. For no other title can be inscribed to it, unless donation, or liberality, or even that such renunciation of obligation was altogether a donation. In former times it was an innominate contract, as d. l. si inter. or an innominate pact, which is made by itself, as noted in l. si quis cum debitorem, de iureiurando. Someone will say, this donation contains nothing but interest: therefore it only requires insinuation, insofar as its interest is concerned, namely to be freed gratuitously: but insofar as he could recover from the principal debtor, his interest is not concerned. This opposition is subtle and doubtful: and saving always the truth, I answer that it is more of an interest not to pay, than to recover what has been paid. Moreover, because interest is not considered: but the quantity which comes into the contract, arg. D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, §. alteri. And therefore if a poor man promises me a thousand on account of donation, who cannot pay more than ten, nevertheless this donation requires insinuation, which severs the obligation without regard to interest: and with respect to interest, insinuation ought, or ought not, to be made, arg. D. de verbis oblig., l. stipulationes non dividuntur, §. Celsus. But it seems that insinuation is not required: because the obligation or contract does not extend further than the parties wish, as D. si certum petatur, l. rogasti, §. si tibi. Moreover, just as an unformed tradition is not always a donation, if the conjectures are different, as D. de solutionibus, l. si cum, as when it is handed over with the intention of deceiving, that which was handed over can be recovered by the condictio sine causa, or, so to speak, ex praetensa causa. Also when it can be recovered by a subaudita causa, as noted in l. cum quis, si certum petatur. So it seems to be said of an unformed liberation, that is, made without cause. Consider, deprivation must be proportioned to the habit, just as the price of a thing, as D. de exercitoria, l. Lucius. Insofar therefore there is more in the gratuitous, whether liberation, or whether there is proportion: as if someone is released for a thousand for five, to that extent it is a donation, as D. de contrahenda empt., l. si donationis. and D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. cum hic status, §. si maritus.

For even if I were to lend you a thousand gold coins, so that you were to restore only five hundred, the other five hundred would require insinuation, because they constitute a donation, since whatever is added to the principal is a donation; but that which has occurred is not a donation, but interest, in those things which are contained by weight, number, or measure; in other things, however, it would be a donation, unless it occurred in the place of a penalty.

† For a penalty is never contained under the name of fraud of my connation, as in D. de regulis iuris, l. quod a quo quam; D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. 1, § item si ita; D. pro socio, l. si quis a socio; D. de actione empti, l. praedia. Finally, consider whether the representation of part of the debt induces a just cause for remitting the whole: because if there were a just cause, the pact would not be known; which is false, because a necessary payment does not clothe the pact: as noted in D. de pactis, l. in traditionibus. And it is established in D. si quid in fraudem patroni, l. 1, § in caeteris, ver. sic si transeat. Nor does it move me that there are several debtors: for even in one person liberality occurs, as in l. 1, § nunc de effectu, de liberalitate legatorum. And what is said, that insinuation is required, is true if the pact was gratuitous; otherwise, if it was a transaction or a confession of receipt, because then insinuation is not required, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a knight and a prince may make a gift to his concubine.
2. Whether a knight and a prince may provide a dowry for daughters whom he had by a concubine.
3. If a knight and a prince made a gift to a concubine who subsequently married another, with the addition that no right shall be sought by anyone else than the woman herself, whether such right is sought by the daughters of the said concubine and the donor upon the death of the concubine.
4. On the interpretation of l. cum acutissimi, C. de fideicommissis.
5. Restrictive words also limit a favorable act.
body: In the name of Christ.

† I recall having advised that the formerly magnificent soldier and lord, the lord Bernabò, was able, by the plenitude of power—in whose quasi-power it then was—to make a donation to a concubine, but a simple soldier cannot make a donation. And the reason was and is: first, because the prohibiting law speaks of a soldier of the Roman people who is on the muster-roll of soldiers; otherwise he is not deemed a soldier under Roman law, as noted in C. de off. magi. mili. l. eos. Likewise, concerning a soldier marked with a brand (stigma), as noted in C. de fabricen. l. stigmata, ff. quibus ex cau. ma. l. pe. Likewise, concerning a soldier who has sworn not to evade death for the sake of the republic, as Vegetius says in De re militari. Likewise, concerning a soldier who is subject to the laws and military discipline, and who is constituted under the law. But the lord Bernabò was not one of those, nor was he under military law, but above the law; because he was able to derogate from the laws, just as the glorious princes of the House of Visconti do daily. Therefore, he was able to derogate from that law which says that a soldier cannot donate to a concubine; especially because that law does not contain necessary law, but voluntary and positive law. For natural laws are those that are immutable, whereas voluntary laws are abolished by a contrary will, as in ff. de legi. l. non est nouum and l. sed et posteriores; for whatever is bound can be unbound, in Aut. de nup. §. deinceps. Furthermore, the contract of a prince possesses two subordinate forces: namely, a tacit antecedent promise and an express subsequent promise, as noted in C. de dona. inter vir. et vxo. l. pen. Furthermore, that law which says that a donation cannot be made to a concubine assimilates the concubine to a wife. For it is similar in the rationale of the prohibition, namely lest he fall into poverty through unbridled love. But in relation to that magnificent lord, that donation was less than if an ordinary man were to donate one silver groschen. Thus, therefore, by comparing the act to the person and the person to the act, the prohibitive rationale ceases; and most especially because other merits concurred in that lady—where in other contexts we say that an agreement is reformed on another ground; I say conversely that another ground forms the contract, one that is honorable or at least causary and not disgraceful, arg. ff. de dona. l. si pater and l. aquilius regulus. And if I were to say the contrary, I would incur the hatred both of the said concubines and of their sons; and to strive in vain and to wear oneself out for no other purpose than to seek hatred is utter madness. Furthermore, when a prince donates to an infamous person, he is deemed tacitly first to restore their reputation and afterwards to donate, as in C. de nup. l. imperialis; whence it cannot be said that this donation was infamous. Furthermore, this donation ought rather to be called a privilege than a donation; and it is nowhere provided by law that an emperor or a king or another prince cannot grant privileges to a concubine; and since such incapacity is penal, it is sufficient that the prohibiting law ceases, as in ff. de procu. l. mutus. §. 1, and arg. ff. solu. matr. l. si vero. §. de viro, ff. de iurepatr. l. adigere. §. quamuis, ff. de diuor. l. quod ait lex. I conclude therefore, always saving the substance of the truth, that the said donation held good, presupposing that the said lord Bernabò had been a vicar of the Emperor, because he wrote letters to him as vicar, etc.

† The following question is whether the said then-exalted lord and prince was able to dower his daughters whom he had by that concubine. And it seems that he could not, as in C. de natur. Auth. licet, and l. 1, and l. fi.; for we can neither donate nor bequeath to spurii: not through their fault, because they have not sinned, but through ours. For they suffer from another’s disease, as in ff. de natu. libe. l. legem anastasii, where it says 'mercy moving him': because they are not unworthy who suffer from another’s fault. Solution: on the same grounds on which I said the donation to the concubine was valid, on those same and much stronger grounds I say that dowries could be given to the husbands of the said maidens; because the husbands committed no offense, and nevertheless upon dissolution of marriage the dowry reverts to the maidens, because the goods once left the estate of the giver, as in l. fi. in prin. ff. quae in frau. cre., and arg. ff. de leg. 3. l. pater. §. quindecim. Furthermore, a dowry succeeds in place of maintenance, as noted by Cynus on C. de nup. l. sancimus; therefore, what is the law regarding maintenance is the same regarding a dowry, arg. extra de bap. c. maiores. But maintenance can be donated to spurii, and bequeathed under canon law in view of natural affection; because although he is a spurius, he is nonetheless a child, because nature is common, ff. de accus. l. hos accusare. §. omnibus; this is stated by the text of extra de eo, qui duxit in matri. c. cum haberet; and the civil law, in providing the contrary, so loved chastity that it destroyed paternal affection. Whence on this point of law the canon law causes natural law to revive with respect to this kind of affection, by which law all were born legitimate, as in the double Auth. quibus mo. na. in prin. colla. 6 and 7. Furthermore, what cruelty this would be: for if the maidens could not be dowered, they would be forced into prostitution to the shame of their forebears, which is properly infamy. Likewise, there are few women who are true and natural [concubines] because of the many requirements for lawful concubinage, as in ff. de concubi. l. in concubinatu. I conclude therefore that, since so great a prince could establish and interpret laws, and since the cause of a dowry is exceedingly pious and favorable, ff. de condi. indeb. l. cum is. §. si mulier, both according to God and according to the world the said maidens could be dowered, the strict constitution of the civil law notwithstanding. Likewise, if anyone wished to call the power of lords into doubt, he would void all their efficacy, and I would not be of that opinion, wishing to throw the world into confusion.

† There follows another doubt: that the said magnificent lord donated by plenitude of power and by right of full ownership certain estates to a certain concubine of his who was in marital paternal power, with this added condition: that a right be acquired for no other person unless it is acquired for the woman herself. Whether any right is acquired for the daughters of the said donor begotten of the said concubine upon her death? And I state briefly that it is not: because the donation is personal and restricted to her lifetime, as in ff. de pactis. l. epistola. §. fi., and in Auth. de non alie. §. emphyteosim. And if it is said that it seems tacitly meant for the children, as in C. de fideicom. l. cum acutissimi,

† I say that this is not true: because that law has no place in the case of spurii, as in C. de insti. et substitu. l. generaliter. §. fin. Furthermore, this donation is odious because it is contrary to the ius commune and in a certain manner contrary to good morals, as in C. de natu. lib. l. 1 and l. fi., ff. de acti. et obli.; and it is rather a kind of odious dispensation, which ought to be restricted and not enlarged, as in c. 1. de filiis presby. lib. 6. What Bartolus notes in l. pater. ff. de serui. leg. is not an obstacle, because there there were no restrictive words, and because there the act held good under the ius commune, as in ff. de probat. l. si pactum. It is plausible, however, that the said magnificent lord did not think of the exclusion of the children, but of the exclusion of the parents, as in ff. ad Tre. l. haeredib. §. fi.; for that plausibility is very bare, completely stripped of legal supports, as in ff. de usufruc. lega. l. si alij.

† Furthermore, restrictive words restrict even a favorable act, as in C. de leg. l. penulti., and as noted in Authen. de restitutio. fideicommiss. §. manifestum. Likewise, in doubt one must adhere to the words, ff. soluto matrimo. l. si uero. §. de uiro, with similar texts. Likewise, because every cause of transmission to another was excluded, therefore, just as it does not pass to the father, so it does not pass to the heir, because these are equivalent, argumen. ff. de uulga. substitu. l. qui liberis. §. haec uerba, and C. de haere. institu. l. cum proponas; and this I hold, compelled by the strict force of the words, in which the intention of the donor is also expressed in writing. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the acceptance of an inheritance is brought about by enunciative words.
2. Which words are said to be, or are presumed to be, those of the notary, and which those of the party; and how they are to be ascertained; and no. 4.
3. Whether enunciative words have dispositive effect.
5. What presumption applies in the case of a soldier, whether of error or of knowledge, and whether he is to be favored.
6. Whether anything done in the name of the heir brings about the acceptance of the inheritance.
7. Whether error is presumed in the notary or in the party.
body: The words of the instrument, In the name of Christ, concerning the power of attorney, thus state: for the purpose of seizing goods and collecting debts; and the notary adds, which all things now pertain to such lord heir, and in the hereditary name of the said deceased.

† It is asked, since the said constitutor can claim under a will, and under a donation causa mortis, and inter vivos, whether by the said enunciative words the acceptance of the inheritance has been induced. And it seems that not: because the said words are the words of the notary: but they are not the words of the constitutor. And it is certain that one cannot accept an inheritance with another’s mind, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Paulus. To the contrary it seems, because rather these are the words of the heir, who requested the notary to write these words: as appears in the notary’s subscription: and it is the glossa ordinaria, D. de verbis obligantibus, l. Sciendum. It supports this, C. qui testamento facere possunt, l. hac consultissima, §. at cum humana. Moreover, these terms clearly express that the constitutor gave this mandate according to the law and the name of heir: therefore these words are dispositive with respect to the acceptance of the inheritance: because in the acceptance of the inheritance it suffices that the will alone be declared by act, as in C. de iure deliberandi, l. potuit; D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. gerit; Inst. de rerum qualitate et differentia, §. fin. For it suffices for accepting the inheritance any evidence of will, even if there is nothing in the inheritance that is corporeal or incorporeal, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. hereditas.

† On the contrary, it must be considered in the first place whether the words in question were the words of the notary or the words of the constituent; and what is to be presumed, and how we may know, and by what reasoning we may know, whether they are the words of the notary or the words of the party. I answer that there are certain matters which pertain to the office of the notary and not to the office of the party, such as writing the indiction, the year, the day, the place, and the witnesses. For the writing of the notary is not valid without these, as in the Authenticum, "Let the name of the emperor be prefixed," in the red and black, because this part of the instrument is [required]; but they are not part of the contract, as noted in D. de edendo, l. 1, § editiones. And this is clear, because without these aids the contract is valid, as in D. de pignoribus, l. cum tabernam, § idem quaesivit. But those matters which concern the contract itself or its clauses pertain to the contracting parties as regards disposing and ordering. The office of the notary, however, is to report and write down these matters; but he cannot add or subtract, because he would commit falsification. This is gathered from the noted authorities in D. 23, c. In nomine Domini. Hence, referring to the matter at hand, if these are the words of the notary and are false, the instrument would be false, and therefore it is not to be presumed that they are the words of the notary in speaking; but only in writing. From this it follows that this allegation, that they are the words of the notary, is not reasonable; certainly the notary could not have divined another’s act, as in l. 1, D. pro suo.

† Another consideration follows, namely whether the said words are words of enunciation, words of confession, or words of disposition? Enunciation sometimes refers to the past, sometimes to the present, sometimes to the future. Moreover, with regard to the past, it is either joined with the present, as in D. de donat. l. ex hac scriptura; or it is already completed and separated from the present, as in C. de testam. milit. l. ex his verbis Fortunato. But words of enunciation concerning the present are sometimes uttered principally for their own sake, when, namely, they do not terminate in something else, nor look to any other end, except for their own sake. And the nature of these words is to dispose, if such is the act that can be performed at that time by will alone: as in D. si certum petatur l. certae condictio § fin. and the aforementioned l. ex hac scriptura. But if they cannot then dispose, but are beyond the principal purpose, and are a certain addition of words: because then they are not called dispositive, since they cannot dispose, but are indicative of the mind, as in D. de pactis l. epistola in principio. And both members are proved in l. Aurelius § fin. D. de legatis liberis. For there the contracts do not have legal effect: because the contracts were not in the process of being made, but were in the process of being made by the law of last will, and were uttered by the testator. But if those words were uttered between living persons, that is, in the consent of the living, then those words would be a certain confession, as in D. de possessionibus l. publica § fin. But sometimes words are enunciative, that is, indicative of the future. And then they are either directed to the burdened party or to the favored party. D. de legatis secundis l. peto in principio; and D. de usufructu legato l. generali in principio.

† Let us now return to our case. For it is expedient to know whether the aforementioned words are words of one confessing, or words of one accepting. For if they are words of one confessing, those uttered through error of fact or of law do not prejudice: because we are dealing with an obligation to be avoided. And thus error of law does not prejudice, as in the law *Regula*, *De iuris et facti ignorantia*, and the last law of the Digest, *De constituto pecuniae*. But if they are words of one accepting, then error of fact would prejudice the acceptance, that is, it would render it invalid; but error of law would not hinder, as in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Filium*, and law *Clodianus*; and in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Multum interest*. And because the aforementioned words were uttered between living persons, they appear rather to be a confession than an acceptance: as in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Filium*, law *Clodianus*. And therefore error of law would hinder the acceptance by the heir.

It remains, therefore, to consider whether error intervened here, or certain knowledge, or inconsiderate speech, which is a third adjacent factor, or accident. And it appears that there was certain knowledge: because he knew the fact, therefore he also knew the law. For it is said that soldiers are presumed to ignore the subtleties and niceties of the law: as in C. de iure delib. l. si, in the beginning; for from soldiers no scrupulous inquiry into the law is required: as in C. de iur. et fac. ignor. l. 1; and C. de his, qui sibi ascri. l. eodem adhibitus; and C. quando prouo. non estne, l. veteranus; ff. de testa. mili. l. 1, especially since the act can be interpreted in multiple ways. For it ought to be interpreted favorably for the soldier, as in C. de rei vend. l. si ex pecunia. But against this it is argued that in acts of will, no greater presumption is made for the soldier than for another, nor is he favored more: as in ff. ad Trebel. l. sed et qui magis. But let us see whether this can be called error. For this soldier, who appointed a procurator, could have come forward under two headings: because he was an heir by testamentary right, and a donee inter vivos, or causa mortis, by succeeding to the heir. He burdened himself more, because he acted in solidum, than if he had come forward under the title of donation: because under that title he is not bound beyond the heir’s capacity. As noted in ff. de pact. l. fin. Therefore, it seems he erred in law by choosing the less secure and more burdensome path. But to this it is thus answered: because personal actions do not pass by donation, unless they are assigned; but here they had not been assigned, as in ff. de iur. dot. l. mulier bona, unless we say that there is a special rule in donation that assignment is not required, or that useful actions are transferred by donation causa mortis, just as in a legacy, as noted in ff. de publ. l. sunt et aliae. It could also be said that these words were uttered without deliberation, and that this soldier must blame himself for not having thought about what he ought to have thought about, as in ff. de don. promis. l. fin. For he is not excused who says, “I did not believe,” when he ought to have believed. For he ought either to have consulted those more expert: as in C. de inge. et manu. l. si auiam; and ff. de bono. poss. l. in bonorum quid plena. And if this soldier had had viriles in his own name, nevertheless he appointed a procurator to institute direct heirs in name. As in l. quotiens, in the beginning, ff. de admini. tuto.

† Moreover, whatever is done in the name of the heir induces acceptance of the inheritance, even without touching the hereditary property: for example, by burying the deceased, as in D. de relig. l. at si quis. §. plerique. And therefore l. requirit states that neither the right nor the name of the heir should intervene, as in D. de acquirenda hereditate l. pro haerede. §. Papinia. I do not see how I can safely say that the heir has not accepted the inheritance, since all the elements necessary for acceptance concur, as noted in D. de petitione hereditatis illud etiam, even if the respect or regard, on account of which the inheritance is accepted, does not follow.

† One single point remains: whether the error is presumed to be that of the notary or that of the lord Antonio; for in his own act, Lord Antonio is not presumed to have considered his own prejudice. The doubt is increased because the antecedent, namely “to demand,” seems to imply this consequent, namely that he is an heir. Also, because one seems to appoint a procurator rather to bring direct actions than useful ones. Also, because when a useful action and a direct action are available to the same person, the useful action is merged. As stated in D. ad Trebellianum, l. si haec res; and especially if the useful action arises from tacit cession, because the express is stronger and more worthy. It supports this what the noted jurist Dyonisius says in D. de solutionibus, l. si duo; and in D. tam in hereditatibus, l. plane. If it could be defended in law that the said words were the words of the notary, the acceptance would not have been induced; yet, as the Statute provides, which I have cited, it is harsh to say this; because the cause of doing, just like the act itself, adheres to the doer, and not to the writer. Hence, the notary does not signify the contract, but writes the contract; nor does it matter whether we speak in the first person or in the third; because the signification of the third person passes into the first, and conversely. Hence, these writings are synonymous: as noted in Extr. de conversione coniugiorum, c. dudum. All casual words, and not formal ones, are the words of the parties. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statutes referred to herein, and the rule that no interpretation of statutes shall be made, how is the word *intestatus* (intestate) to be interpreted? See also no. 4.
2. There are three species of those who die.
3. The word *sine* (without) creates a condition.
5. An inheritance once accepted is said to belong to the heir: and constitutes a single patrimonial entity.
body: In the name of Christ. When a person dies intestate without legitimate children, and without ascendants in the paternal line, and with no surviving brother or sister, or son or daughter of a brother or sister of the deceased from the same father at the time of his death, the mother, grandfather, or grandmother of such deceased person shall not be permitted to take more than one-fourth part of the legitimate intestate succession of all movable and immovable goods, and those that move, excluding houses and castels formerly belonging to such deceased person. The remaining goods of such deceased person shall belong to the male relatives on the father’s side, and of the paternal grandfather, up to the fourth degree commonly understood, according to the order of the nearest degree. And if there survive to such deceased person a brother or sister, or sons or daughters of a brother or sister, then the mother, or grandfather, or grandmother on the mother’s side succeed in no way. And this applies to women of the city of Siena, etc. Another statute provides as follows: It is also provided and ordained that no interpretation shall be made, nor admitted, concerning any chapter of the statutes, but as the words lie, so they shall be understood simply and commonly, without any interpretation. Now, the said statutes being posited, the case follows thus. A certain lady Fran., wife of a certain P., to whom said Fran. had given a dowry of one thousand, coming to death, instituted as her heirs in her will A., B., and C., her sons begotten by her and the said Pet., her husband: with this condition, that the said heirs could not alter the said will except from one to another. Then, after the death of the said F., one of the aforementioned sons and heirs, namely A., died intestate without legitimate children, or other descendants from him, with his other brothers B. and C., and P., his father, surviving him. Then B. died intestate, leaving a pregnant wife named M., and the said C., his brother, and P., his father, also without other children or descendants. Finally, the said M., no longer pregnant, gave birth to a posthumous daughter named Catherine; this posthumous Catherine died within a few days from the day of her birth, with her mother, C., her uncle, and P., her paternal grandfather, surviving her. Then the said uncle died intestate without children or other descendants, with P., the grandfather of the posthumous child, surviving him. Then the aforementioned grandfather died, leaving to him two legitimate, natural, and pupillary daughters from another wife, and his heirs, namely Magdalena and Petra. Now there is a dispute between the mother of the posthumous child and the daughters of the said grandfather. For the mother says that she ought to succeed, since she holds the first place in succeeding intestate. On the other hand, the said daughters claim the succession through the person of their father, the grandfather of the posthumous child. It is asked, what is the law, considering the said statutes.

† Because the statute provides that no interpretation of statutes shall be made, but that the words are to be understood as they stand, it seems that, in common parlance, one should say that a restrictive interpretation of the word “ab intestato” ought not to be made; for the common people do not follow this subtle scrupulosity of words, of which l. 1, ff. de suis et leg. speaks, nor do they understand it; but they speak indiscriminately and in a broad manner. And therefore the common understanding prevails over the subtlety of the law; because the statute so expressly provides, as in ff. de legibus, l. librorum, § quod tamen Cassius; and ff. de funerariis instrumentis, l. cum de lanionis, § asinam; ff. de verborum significatione, l. quisquis mihi; and l. Alphenus. However, by the subtlety of this word, “intestatus,” one who is “intestabilis” is not comprehended.

† Because there are three kinds of intestacy, and one is not the other, namely: testate, intestate, and intestabilis, as is noted in C. de iure deliberandi, l. cum antiquioribus. Moreover, that law l. 1. de suis et legitimis says that a pupillus must be considered as intestate; but it is one thing to be such, and another to be considered as such, as in ff. de verbis significandis, l. mortis. Also, that l. 1. speaks of succession being deferred to the mother, to whom it is owed as if by natural right. And thus in a pious and favorable disposition of the law, which ought rightly to be extended, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. placet. But in our case we are dealing with succession being taken away or restricted; and thus the disposition of the law is rather odious than favorable, as in C. de libris praeteritis, l. maximum vitium. And therefore the words must be interpreted so as to contain less absurdity, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. cum quaedam. Although the statute weighs the favor of agnates and the honor of families, nevertheless this favor is mixed with odium with respect to the opposite extreme, and by these and other reasons I was previously moved in advising, following the ultramontane doctors and Lord Rayne. And after I was in Lombardy, I found the man of excellent memory, Lord Signorinus of Milan, having determined thus in advising. Nevertheless, in our present matter I do not adhere to this subtlety, assuming however the common usage of speaking and interpreting. And therefore I also think the same statute applies to an infant as to an adult or major, and especially because of the word "sine liberis" which is in the statute, which signifies all ages indiscriminately, as is noted in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutis, l. precibus. Having considered the proper interpretation of this term "intestate," because interpretation must be fitting, as in l. 1. and l. 1. ff. de originibus iuris and ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. item veniunt, § aptanda, I descend to that which is principally asked, and I divide the statute into two parts: namely, the exclusive and the inclusive. The exclusive part is noted here: "non permittatur matri secunda," and here: "alia vero bona." Also, the first exclusive part is divided into three parts, namely: into the condition, the statute, and the modification. The first part lasts until "non permittatur," the second until "secunda," the third at "nisi." Also, the second principal part, namely the inclusive, is subdivided into two, namely: into the express conclusion at "Alia vero," and the tacit inclusion. For if male ascendants and the mother are excluded, and because sometimes a statute has two heads or two opposite extremes, the exclusion of one is the inclusion of the other. Hence, since the father is opposed to the mother, the mother is excluded and the father is admitted, as is noted by Bartolus in l. 2. ff. ad Tertullianum, and I said in l. maximum vitium. Someone will say, by what do you prove that the father is opposed to the mother? I answer first, because he is an agnate; second, because the mother is not called to the fourth part unless a male parent does not exist. This is gathered from the necessary understanding of the words: because the words say "sine parentibus masculis," which words would be placed in vain if male parents were not preferred to the mother. And on this point it is most elegantly alleged by those advising.

† For this word, "without," creates a condition, as in D. de haereditatibus instituendis, l. Lucius; and where there is a condition, I say that it is signified: the tacit meaning of which is called an argument from the contrary sense, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. si quis locuples; unless the same statute were found in the contrary case, as in C. de conditionibus insertis, l. 2.

† Returning therefore to the conclusion, I say thus: either the paternal grandfather did not accept the inheritance of his granddaughter, nor did he transmit it, and I hold the opinion of my venerable and most excellent brother, Lord Angelus; because the succession is reduced to the case of the fourth part. For the grandfather, who did not accept, did not obstruct the mother, because he did not avail himself of the privilege of the statute. And therefore the succession began to commence from the collateral agnates, as in the *Institutes*, *De legatis agnatorum successione*, § *proximus*. Or the grandfather acknowledged the inheritance devolved upon the infant, or transmitted it, and then the mother is entirely excluded:

† And the inheritance devolving upon the infant became united with the goods of the grandfather, and was reduced into one body of patrimony, as in l. 1, § sciendum, D. de separatione bonorum; and l. sed et si plures, § ad substitutos, D. de vulgari substitutione; and by argument from C. de donationibus; l. si auia, D. de legatis 2; l. pater, § quindecim, C. de inofficioso lucro descriptione; l. 1, D. de acquirenda hereditate; l. Paulus, § 1, D. de publiciana; l. licitatio, § fin. In this point, therefore, namely, regarding the inheritance accepted by the paternal grandfather, I hold precisely the opinion of the noble and eminent doctor, Lord Raynerius de Copollis, as well founded in law and reason, and moreover proved by the respectable doctors, my most beloved sons, Lord Honorius and Lord Marcus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the writing of the treasurer proves.
2. General words are understood according to the preceding special ones, from which they are derived.
3. The beginning of the truth indicates the following.
4. What conscience is.
5. That something has been paid is not presumed in two ways.
6. It is not probable that a large quantity, attributed to a poor merchant, has come out of his purse.
body: In the name of Christ. A creditor had 20 written in the books of the treasury in the person of Titius, with a monthly provision according to the custom of the treasury; and two writings are found: one, that the said creditor made himself debtor in the said books for 20; in the other writing, the treasurer says that he called himself satisfied of the above-mentioned amount by the said treasurer. Now the said creditor says that the debt of 20,000 was never paid to him; but only the merit of the said quantity. On the contrary, it will be said that rather he was satisfied, as appears from the said writing.

† The question is, what is the law: and it appears that the said writings must be strictly adhered to, as C. de non numerata pecunia, l. in contractibus, § 1; C. de apostolis publicis, l. 1, lib. 10; ff. de probationibus, l. centum. For a written record should be held as the truth itself, just as certain public and authentic writings, as extra de fide instrumentorum, c. 1 and 2; C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus; ff. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratum, § pro Aurelio. Moreover, the word “satisfactum” [satisfied] must be understood naturally and properly, i.e., “solutum” [paid], as ff. de pignoribus acceptis, l. solutum, § solutam; ff. de solutionibus, l. si ex pluribus. To the contrary, it seems that “satisfactum” should be understood as satisfied by delegation: because the creditor delegated his debtor to the said Titius, as ff. de manumis, l. inter causas, § abesse. For this term “satisfactum” is general, as ff. qui satisdare cogantur, l. 1.

† And general words are understood according to the preceding special words, from which they are derived and arise, as in D. de haered. inst. l. qui non militabat §. Lucio; C. fam. herc. l. quotiens; D. de leg. 1. l. si seruus plurium §. fin. For such are the subjects as the predicates demonstrate, and vice versa. D. de interro. actio. l. si defensor; D. de vino leg. l. fi §. cui dulcia; de pe. leg. l. nam quod liquide §. si cui. For we say that recourse must be had to the beginning of the records, as in D. de eden. l. si quis ex argentariis §. si nuntium; and that the action is formed from the head of the writing, and the sentence is moderated thereby. For this is what is said in l. quod ratio a capite est reddenda, as in D. de eden. l. argentariis §. edum; and that the outcome is formed from the beginning of the cause. D. de dona. l. qui id, quod; D. de fideiusso. l. tutor; C. de impo. lucra. descri. l. vnica lib. 10.

† The solution is that the truth is that which the beginning of the truth indicates in the subsequent matters, which are doubtful; and that which comes into the reckoning is that which comes into the reckoner. For reasons are explained in this manner implicitly, by observing from where and to where the computation has proceeded, and what the intention of the speaker or writer ought to have been, as in D. de pactis, l. emptor, § Lucius; and the aforementioned l. si ex pluribus, D. de solutionibus. Concerning this truth, however, which is to be investigated, the treasurer himself is to be examined, as in X. de testibus, c. cum clamor; C. de falsis, l. si quis decurio, because he knows the truth better. Therefore, once the truth has been ascertained, judgment is to be rendered according to it. And when the truth cannot in any way be made manifest, judgment may be rendered according to conscience, as in D. de officiis praesidis, l. illicitas, § veritas; and the argument in c. cum aeterni, de re iudicata, lib. 6.

† because conscience is the shield of the rational soul. Moreover, if nothing else appears except the aforementioned text, I hold that it ought not to be understood as referring to anything other than a single satisfaction. S. Delegationis: so that satisfaction is not understood to be rendered twice:

† which would be absurd, and not credible, nor reasonable: because from the books of the treasury, which are made with great and weighed solemnity, every absurdity and duplicity should be excluded, by which we would fall into an inconvenience, as in l. ne casu. C. de discusso. lib. 10. Also, recourse must be had to the quality of the persons, for no one becomes very rich by chance, as in C. de alimentis pupil. l. fi.

† and therefore, if such a large amount was assigned to the poor merchant, it is not likely that he paid it out of his own purse, as is stated in the Digest, *De statu liberorum*, in the law *Cum haeres*, at the beginning; and see the argument in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, in the law *Cum hi*, § *Modus*; and what is noted in the Code, *De bonis, quae liberis*, in the law *Cum oportet*, after the beginning. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether novation is said to be effected by the accession of a new surety, or of a co-obligor of equal rank.
2. A judge of accounts, or a notary, cannot effect novation to the prejudice of the public treasury.
3. Whether the culpable debtor ought to be sued first, before the other co-debtors.
4. Whether co-debtors who have been sued have a right of recourse against the culpable debtor.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that Antonius, together with certain partners, purchased the office of custodian of the prisons of a certain city, with the stipulation of a penalty, and in the event of the escape of any of the prisoners. Finally, after the passage of time, one of the said partners, on his own behalf, promised the judge of the offices and the public notary, who were receiving and stipulating on behalf of the said city and the partners of the said custody, and of anyone who has or may have an interest in the future, to keep the said prisons in custody and to pay the office fee, provided that he is not disturbed by the said partners, etc. And for the aforementioned obligations, he provided a surety. After this second obligation, certain prisoners escaped.

† It is asked whether an action for the penalty may be brought against those partners who were originally bound, and their sureties; and it seems that it may not, for it appears that a certain novation is presumed from the new agreements, as in D. 10, l. cum in plures, § lege dicta, and D. de praetoria stipulatione, l. Valerianus, in which laws the case seems to be presented; but the truth is to the contrary. For the partners are not released in any respect, nor are their sureties, even though new sureties have acceded; and this for a twofold reason. First, because novation is not presumed, even if a suretyship or an equal obligation is added, as in C. de novatione, l. si.

Secondly, because the judge of accounts or the notary cannot novate to the prejudice of the public interest: for he may improve the condition of the public interest, but he cannot worsen it, since he has no mandate to do so, as is stated in C. de nov. l. non abstulit; C. de trans. l. praeses; ff. quod vi, aut clam l. prohibere § plane. Hence it is concluded that the added obligation does not have the effect of novating the substantive obligation.

But it is asked secondly, whether this one who has newly given a guarantee, and his sureties, ought to be sued first, rather than the remaining partners. And it seems that this is so, because whenever someone is sued on account of another’s fault, the person at fault ought first to be pursued, by analogy to a certain surety who ought not to be sued if the principal debtor is solvent. This appears to be the case. D. de comm. l. Unde quaeritur. On the contrary, it seems that these persons are sued by virtue of their own and express provision, not by the mere foresight of the law. And therefore it is lawful for the republic to begin with whomever it wishes and to demand payment, presupposing that they are bound jointly and severally and have waived the benefit of the new constitution concerning the obligation of multiple debtors; because it is customary to insert such clauses into public instruments, as noted in Auth. de fideiuss. in principio and D. de pactis l. Nisi. And this is the truth, if the instrument is so worded.

† Thirdly, it is asked whether the partners may have recourse against him who subsequently bound himself and assumed the burden of custody, and what is the case with his sureties. I answer in the affirmative, for two reasons: first, because a partner is liable to another partner for fault, which arises in the action pro socio; second, because a formal stipulation intervened on this point, by which the promisor and his sureties are bound; for the words of the instrument expressly state: from which words one must not depart, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae; and D. de fidejuss. l. blandinis. And in this matter I say that the official may be strict or lenient: strict if he begins with whom he wishes, but lenient and discreet if he begins with the offender. Let him do what is more useful to the commonwealth by first having recourse against those who can pay first. But it seems to him that he is not compelled to do so. I do not omit that if he compels one for another, he must by the same authority have seized the person for whom the other is seized, until he keeps him indemnified, as in C. ubi causae fiscales l. cum vendente, according to Jacobus de Belvisi; and cf. D. de in ius voc. l. eum, pro quo. For these matters are connected, and one depends on the other; and therefore they must be explained together, because the whole constitutes one effect, or one structure, although consisting of different parts, according to Jacobus de Belvisi. To this effect serves C. de usu rei iud. l. si, in fine. I, Baldus. On this case he advised in consilia 268 and 262, although here he also advises with other words and arguments. It is added, moreover, whether the city of Milan may enact a statute that donations and legacies may be made to and left to bastards, from number 12 to number 15.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What concubinage properly is.
2. Whether a donation made to a concubine by a soldier is valid, and at no. †.
3. When a woman is said to have suffered violence.
4. Intent and will are of the very essence of a crime; hence, when will is removed from the equation, every act is indifferent.
5. A father may make donations to the children he had with a woman who suffered violence.
6. A father may provide a dowry for his natural daughter.
8. Soldiers of our time do not enjoy the privileges of soldiers.
9. Except for the Emperor and kings, one who wishes to exercise plenitude of power must demonstrate a privilege or an ancient custom.
10. Whether spurious children succeed to their mother.
11. The Prince dispenses with an incestuous person.
12. Whether the City of Milan may enact a statute allowing it to make donations to spurious children? and at no. 15.
13. Citizens are not properly those who cannot name their father.
14. A father cannot arrogate his spurious son, unless and c.
body: In the name of Christ.

† For clarity, I premise that concubinage is properly so called only when it exists between a man and a woman who are both unmarried; for, since the term has been adopted by law, as in D. de concubinis, l. In concubinatu, that which is prohibited and punished by law cannot be called concubinage, because a name contrary to law is not a name adopted by law. For the names of contrary qualities must themselves be contrary. And if indeed the man is married and the woman is not, or both are married, or some other cause renders the marriage detestable, this is called a fornicatory, adulterous, or incestuous embrace; nor is it necessary here to discuss the laws which speak of a donation made to a concubine.

But regarding those matters which speak of adulteries, incests, or the defilement of males, between which persons, when such donations are made on account of a most shameful or detestable cause, no liberality, donation, or affection arises, because this is not properly affection, but rather defection. And because it is made on account of a shameful cause while the act remains, as in C. de nat. lib. l. 1 and l. si quis incesti, and ar. ff. de act. et ob. l. fi. Secondly, it is proven by reason, for children begotten from such unions are said to be incapable and nameless, because they are deprived of the right to be named, as in Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, §. fi., col. 7; it is supported by extra de electione, c. innotuit, and no. C. quemadmodum testamentum aperiri, l. pe. And certainly these boys, who have not sinned on their own account, but on account of the practice of unchastity and to the hatred and reproach of their parents, are not prohibited, as in C. de nat. lib. l. legem Anastasii. Then I argue: on account of which one thing is such, that one is even more so; but bastards are prohibited on account of their parents, therefore all the more so the parents. C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, Auth. multo magis.
† And this is true, unless the woman had suffered violence, and from that bore children; and it is said that she suffered violence even if she could have been restrained by threats.

† For the will and the intention constitute the very essence of the sin. Hence, Lord Azo said, as cited by Cynus: "Remove the will from the equation, and every act will be indifferent," as in D. 5.1.1.1 (de postul.), D. 47.2.1 (de furt.), D. 48.5.1 (de adul.). In my own conscience, I would rather consider such an act good than evil; because such women can be compelled in fact, as in D. 4.6.1.1 (quae re actio non datur) and D. 26.7.1 (quod falsus tutor). This holds unless the contrary appears through acts and signs manifesting joy. From this, I draw two conclusions.

The first reason is that, in the case at hand, the children born from such intercourse may be manumitted by the mother, because they cannot be accused by the father. The second reason is that there was no consent in the intercourse on the part of either party: for such intercourse could be prosecuted, as is stated in the Code, in the title *Ad Legem Iuliam de adulteriis*, in the law *Si qua illustris*; and in the Institutes, in the same title, in the section *Novissime*; and in the Digest, in the title *Unde cognoscitur*, in the law *Si spuriis*.

† Moreover, another conclusion arises: for it is certain that a father may provide a dowry for his natural daughter, if he wishes, although he is not compelled to do so. D. 35.1.1 (*Uxorem*), § *Pater naturalis*. But he may not provide a dowry for a spurious daughter, except up to the amount of her maintenance, so that she may have perpetual maintenance according to the quality of her status; for that which is permitted on account of a cause is limited and moderated by that same cause, and is left to the discretion of the judge. And thus the canonical and civil law are reconciled, as in X. 4.17 (*De eo qui duxit in matrimonium*), c. *Cum haberet*. And cf. D. 43.1.1 (*Lucius*). From the foregoing it also appears that what I cannot do as I, or as a father, I cannot do as any other person, because the law prohibits it.

From these it is sufficiently clear that one need not inquire whether a soldier may make a gift to his concubine, as in D. de testamento militis, l. miles, § mulier. For if she were a true and mere concubine, such a prince could have made the gift, because the term “soldier” does not properly include a prince, due to the difference in names, even though the words “his soldiers” and “his comrades-in-arms” are used. And it is similar to the case where the term “benefice” does not include a dignity.

† Moreover, as I fully noted in another opinion, the knights of our time are not included in privileges; therefore, they are not included in odia either, because where a privilege does not extend, neither does an odium extend, as stated in the Digest, De testamento tutorum, l. Si quis ita. Nevertheless, another reason seems to remove the donation, because if it is not permitted between spouses, it is not permitted between lovers. But I respond that it would be confirmed by the death of the donor, since it was supported by delivery: as stated in the Digest, De donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Papinianus. Secondly, I premise for clarity that having the plenitude of power in temporal matters pertains solely to the Emperor, or to a free king in his kingdom, as stated in the Digest, De captivis, l. Hostes. It does not pertain to inferiors by right of ordinary power, but they can indeed have it by special privilege: for example, if a vicariate has been granted to them with the plenitude of power. For what a prince can do by himself, he can do through another: as we see daily in the case of the counts palatine; nor is he considered another, but the very same person, as stated in the Digest, De manumissionibus vindicta, l. Pater ex provincia, and in the Digest, De servis legatis, according to Bartolus.

† Since, therefore, the plenitude of power consists in a privilege outside all territorial jurisdiction, it is necessary that such privilege be established by a privilege of the prince or by ancient custom, as in Extra, de verborum significatione, l. Super quibusdam, § Praeterea; and in Digestum, de diversis officiis, l. Probatorias, lib. 12; Distinctiones 96, c. Nobilissimus; Codex, de manumissionibus principum, l. 1; de officio delegati, c. Cum in iure; and notably in c. Innotuit, de eo qui furti ordinariam susceperit, according to Innocentius. Nevertheless, because all the lords of Lombardy, by usual custom and as it were by a certain theory and practice, place here the words “plenitude of power,” and are in quasi-possession of the word and the fact, I think that, saving the substance of the truth, their speech should be believed; for it is not likely that they would use false language. Argument from Codex, ad legem Iuliam de repetundis, l. Si. Otherwise, many past matters could give rise to lawsuits, and whatever and however many settled goods could be reopened: which is inequitable, as in Codex, de summa Trinitate, l. 3; and the decrees of so many lords would become illusory, as in Digestum, de iudicibus, l. Si praetor, in principio.

The third conclusion, namely, that, assuming the plenitude of power, the acts done in favor of women and children held without doubt; for nothing resists the plenitude of power except two things only, namely, divine law and immutable, necessary natural law, as in Institutiones, de iure naturali, § Sed naturalia; and l. 2, Digestum, de usufructu earum rerum quae usu consumuntur. For these prohibitions, mentioned above concerning giving and bequeathing, are not of natural law, but of positive law, and thus do not bind the prince, as in Codex, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Penultima. And if the prince legitimizes the act that is celebrated, he legitimizes the person for the act; and conversely, as in Codex, de nuptiis, l. Imperialis.

From these, all the questions asked appear resolved, because the plenitude of power supplies all things; unless it were established that there was not plenitude, but limited power, for every jurisdiction is terminated by its limits, as in Digestum, de iure omnium iudicum, l. Finis. I recall that I have already given another opinion in different words, yet with the same effective conclusion. Hence it is the same in effect, as in Extra, de conversione coniugiorum, c. Dudum. For I always presupposed the plenitude of power, considering the words of so great a lord to be juridical, argument from c. 1, de probationibus, in Clementina; and what is noted there.

† Furthermore, it must be known that natural children succeed their mother, unless she is of illustrious rank; but spurious children, who are born from a condemned union, such that the participants can be accused of rape, adultery, or incest, cannot acquire anything from the father or the mother, as stated in the Authentica *Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui*, column 7, because that section speaks indiscriminately regarding any parent, whether mother or father. Nor does it avail to object that, on the contrary, they can acquire from the mother, unless the mother is of illustrious rank, because that distinction applies to natural children, not to the aforementioned spurious children. For there are other spurious children, for instance, if the father kept several concubines; for such children, born of a free man and a free woman, can acquire from the mother, unless the mother is of illustrious rank. This is noted in the aforementioned law *Si qua illustris*. And this is the truth, unless the prince, in whom there resides fullness of power by right, not merely in fact, had interposed his authority, as noted in the aforementioned Authentica and in § *I* cited above.

† For the prince even dispenses with an incestuous person; this is a unique case in the law. D. de ritu nuptiarum, qui in provincia, §. divus. Thus it is clear that a true and truthful answer has been given to all points of law, saving, however, the judgment of anyone who may think better. But dowries ought to be with the husband, as long as the marriage subsists, because women ought not to be without dowries. Yet we are still not free from the difficulty of the points, for a scrupulous doubt remains in the mind: granted that it were not established by the plenitude of power, and to this doctrine one thus arrives.

† Because I ask whether the people of Milan, not to speak of the Emperor, could make a statute whereby bastards could be given gifts and legacies, even with the peace of Constantia being observed. And truly, that so, as regards goods which are in their territory: and also as regards sums of money in general, which are circumscribed by place. And truly, that so, because all things which are in the territory are subject to the statute of that territory: and if they are not in the territory, nor outside the territory, as a sum in general, they are subject to the statute of the place of origin and domicile, as in D. de iudiciis, l. fideicommissum, §. tractatum; D. de foro competenti, c. postulasti; D. de bonis auctoris iudicis possessis, l. cum unus, §. is qui. Hence, those making statutes can impose a general law upon their own things or their domiciliaries, as in l. omnes populi and l. cunctos populos; and C. de edictis privatis, l. an in totum. Moreover, this is not to make new law: but rather it is to cease disputing about the tips of nativities, and to return to the primeval statute of nature, as if reins had been put on chastity, as in Auth. qui modo nati; and c. collata 6 and 7, in the beginnings. And things easily turn back to nature, as in D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. pactus, ver. quod est in specie. Moreover, just as it is not permitted to a father to kill a bastard, so neither is it permitted to deny him alimony, arg. D. de liberis agnoscendis, l. necare, because nature is common, D. de accusationibus, l. hos accusare, §. omnibus. And to kill a son is to sin against nature by the whole species, as in l. 1 ad l. Pompeiam, infra de parricidiis. And the city is held in the place of a parent, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. veluti; and D. de captivis et postliminio reversis, l. postliminium, §. filius. And if this is permitted to the people, much more so to its prince: as in D. de officio praetoris, l. Barbarius, in fine. For the people consents fictitiously, the prince truly: and truth is greater than fiction, as in D. de origine iuris, l. 2, §. nouissime; and D. de liberis et posthumis, l. filio, quem pater. Someone will say, this is true if the prince has enacted this concerning another; otherwise if concerning himself: because no one declares law for himself, as in C. ne quis in sua causa iudex sit, l. 1; D. de verborum significatione, l. ex parte. But I answer, that rule fails in the case of the prince and the fisc, as in D. de his quae in testamento delentur, l. proxime. Likewise it fails in voluntary jurisdiction, as in D. de adoptionibus, l. si consul. Moreover, to enact statutes concerning voluntary jurisdiction is of voluntary jurisdiction; concerning contentious jurisdiction, of contentious jurisdiction: but we are in voluntary jurisdiction. Moreover, he does not so much make it himself as the people, from whom jurisdiction proceeds. D. de officio eius cui mandata est iurisdictio, l. et si praetor; D. de legatis 2, l. unum ex familia, §. 1.

To the contrary it seems. First, by the text of l. omnes populi, if the text is understood there, for there it is permitted to peoples to make a statute whereby they are reduced to laws or customs. But in this article the people does not use law, because it acts against the law: as in the said Auth. qui modo; and c. §. si, collata 7. Nor customs: because these unions are against good morals, and fruits springing from a bad tree and infected root suffer from the same defect, as in C. de naturalibus liberis, l. si. Since therefore in this article the people does not live by laws nor by customs, it cannot make a statute whereby one lives shamelessly, as in the epistle Rex pacificus. Likewise a statute is not valid by which crimes are nourished or fostered. 4. distinctio, c. erit lex. For the law must be holy and honest. Hence it is defined in this way: law is a holy sanction commanding honest things and prohibiting contrary ones. D. de legibus, l. 2 and 3. Likewise among all precepts of the law, this is the first and most important, to live honestly, as in the said c. rex pacificus; and D. de iustitia et iure, l. iustitia, §. iuris praecepta. 13
