† Moreover, naturally and properly, those are not citizens who are born in such a way that they cannot name their father: as are spurious children, as noted in the Authenticum *De nuptiis*, in the beginning, column 4. Furthermore, the city does not have the power to legitimize spurious children; therefore, it does not have the power to make them capable [of citizenship], as noted.

† Innocentius, Extra, de fide instrumentorum, cap. Cum P. tabellio. Nor can a father arrogate a spurious son, even with the authority of the Emperor, unless there were a clause of plenitude of power and from a certain sentence. As in Codex, de natu. lib., l. Legem Anastasii. For arrogation is a legitimate act, by which one does not become a son as if a son, and in the power of punishment, i.e., almost imitating nature: but it cannot be as if imitating nature an adulterine, nefarious, or incestuous embrace. As Extra, de renuntiationibus, cap. Nisi cum pridem. Moreover, I fully examined this question after Jacobus Butrigarius in l. 1 and 2, Codex, de iure annui aurei. And although regarding the truth of the law it could more strongly be defended that the statute is invalid, nevertheless the eminent doctors, who were on the contrary side, rendered opinions to certain ones asserting that this is not a gift of the father, but such a benefit; you add: and conceding the condition from the law, not from contract; others saying that this is impossible, that a condition from the law arises from prohibited things. By the counsel of discreet friends it was composed between the parties, and thus the arguments for and against were resolved. Argumentum, Digesta, de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Si pater, and l. Et hic Tiberius, whenever it seems to me praiseworthy.

† Nevertheless, the more correct opinion in law is that the people cannot [act] unless by the specific authority of the prince. My lord commanded me to advise him as to what I thought in law. And this is useful and necessary to know on account of the case, which is tacit, to which my lord intends to provide. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a citation ordering the parties to appear on any day and at any hour to hear the sentence is valid; and, assuming it is, if neither party appears as soon as they were able, whether the edict is thereby circumvented. And number 2.
3. Whether the delay of judgment is purged by a subsequent compromise.
body: In the name of Christ. By means of an *instantia* summoned on behalf of the judge delegated in the appeal case, the appellant is cited to the extent that on the nearest coming Monday before the third hour, and successively from hour to hour until the twenty-fourth hour, and successively from day to day and hour to hour during the time of the *instantia*, the said case ought to appear in the court of the commune of Pavia before the above-named lord commissioner to hear the definitive sentence, which the said delegate wishes to pronounce. On that certain day, no sentence is rendered, nor does the plaintiff appear on that day and hour before the judge. Rather, on the following day, there is a compromise of right and of fact in the very delegated judge by the appellant. Finally, upon the expiration of the term of the compromise, the judge himself rendered a sentence against the appellee, the latter having been cited no further. It is asked whether such citation was sufficient, to such an extent that the sentence cannot be declared null.

Whether this citation is valid, so that someone must appear on each day and at every hour throughout the entire course of the proceedings to hear the sentence, it must be said that it is not: because it does not have the proper period of time required between one postponement and another: since for the term a moment of an hour is assigned, as in D. de publicis iudiciis, l. pen. Although the decretal seems to say that a short postponement does not render the postponement null: but it may be appealed, as in X. de dilationibus, c. 1. But there the postponement had the form of a postponement, here it does not: because a moment does not have the form of a postponement, etc. Because this postponement is implicit and uncertain: and those things which are uncertain do not pertain to the office of the judge, as in D. de iudicibus, l. non quemadmodum. Moreover, in no way is such a mode of citing permitted by civil or canon law: especially because such a citation is captious: and because it burdens liberty, and would in some way bind to a kind of servitude, not leaving the place of the causes, as in l. 2, D. de libero homine exhibendo. But let us suppose that this mode of citing were permitted.

† It is asked, if neither party appeared as soon as they could, whether the edict is circumducted, i.e., the citation abolished: and it seems that it is not: because it extends into the future. And because there are multiple citations, although one is circumducted, another remains. D. 43.2.1 (*Praetor*), § *Si aliquando*. Sol. It must be said that this delay is totally circumducted by the delay of both parties, and there is no place for awaiting the arbitrator’s decision, when both parties are in delay, as in D. 22.2.1, § 1. But if only one party were in delay, if indeed the one citing, the same applies, because the edict is circumducted. D. 2.1.1 (*Et post edictum*). The objection from X. 2.1.14 (*Consuluit*) does not hold, because I say that the judge may await the cited party, but not the citing party, as in D. 43.26.1 (*Si vitem*), § *Si*, and there by Dy. and Bar. For in the law *Si vitem*, the protesting party obtains the place of the citer: because he has already consented to the fixed term, which he himself appointed, the term should not be extended for him, as in X. 2.28.1 (*Ob lates*). Thirdly, it is asked, assuming without prejudice to the truth, that the judge may await,

Whether the subsequent delay in rendering judgment is purged by the compromise, I do not say the delay in paying the debt: and it seems that it is not, because upon the expiration of the compromise, the instance of judgment returns to its former state, and therefore the citation of the judge resumes its effect, as in C. de tempore appellationum, Auth. item; and in c. quandiu, de appellationibus, in the Clementine. To the contrary it seems, because in the compromise a new postponement is granted to a certain person by name, and from the arbitrator himself, who is substituted in place of the judge; therefore, there has been a departure from the old postponement, as in ff. loc. l. cum et in plures; and l. lege dicta, ff. de praetoria stipulatione; l. Valerianus, ff. de verbis obligationum; l. cum stipulatus, §. si mihi a Proculo. The contrary authorities do not stand in the way, because they speak of things remaining in the same state. And thus I hold. And consequently it follows that the sentence in question was null by the law itself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute that a clear and unambiguous allegation must be answered without condition, otherwise the allegation is deemed confessed, and given another statute that proof is not valid for amounts above 10 pounds unless proven by three witnesses, whether the said allegation is considered proven and confessed because it was not clearly answered. And number 4.
2. A legal fiction is equivalent to three witnesses, or as many as are necessary to prove the act.
3. An interlocutory judgment of the judge precludes the way of proving custom.
5. An oath in supplement of proof adds nothing, where the statute does not permit it to be administered, and in which cases it is not administered.
6. Whether a natural act is proven by confession.
body: In Christ’s name. A certain man named I. set forth in his libel against Guarinus, saying that the said I. gave to the said G. 85 carts of wine to sell; and that the said G. sold 77 carts and a half for 621 pounds, which the said I. claims back from the said Guarinus; he made a position in court concerning the delivery against the said Guarinus. The judge admonished the said Guarinus that he ought to respond to the aforesaid position fully, clearly, and sufficiently, and without any addition, within a certain term and peremptorily. Likewise, it is provided by statute that one must respond to positions within the term of one available day; otherwise the judge is bound to hold and pronounce the positions as confessed. To which position the said G. responded within the term in this manner: namely, that he believed the aforesaid position to that extent, insofar as it should be lawfully established that the matters contained in that position were true, and if otherwise and in another manner, he did not believe the aforesaid position nor the matters contained in it.

† Here it is first asked whether the said position ought to be held as confessed purely and simply, just as it lies. And indeed, [it seems] not, because the said confession was not pure, but suspensive through words concerning the future; whence it is not a confession, because it is not to what was asked, just as they are asked, as in ff. de verb. oblig. l. 1. §. cum adiicit, and extra de fid. instr. c. cum Ioannes heremita. The contrary is true, because although this man does not consent when considering the form of words of the response, nevertheless, when considering the power of the law and of the judge, he ought to be held as confessed. For concerning one's own act and concerning a past matter, a condition cannot be added in the response, as in ff. rer. amot. l. Marcellus. Furthermore, those words, 'if it shall be proved,' or the like, make a condition, and not a potestative one, but a mixed one, as in ff. de cond. et demon. l. Lucius. Moreover, he who responds to a position ought so to respond that the adversary is relieved by the confession from the burden of proving, as noted in c. 1. de iuramen. calu. l. 2. §. quod obseruari; but here he is not relieved from the burden of proving; therefore the response is neither sufficient nor good. Moreover, that response is captious because of the adverb 'legitimately,' as is noted on a similar point in c. 1. de procu. and in cle. Moreover, that response is neither a confession nor a denial, because it is made through enunciative words concerning the future, which prove nothing concerning the present. Likewise, from such a confession no actio in factum arises at the time of the response; and thus it does not dispose, and thus they do not have those things that belong to a confession. [A confession] must be such as to be held as the truth, not ambiguous, not uncertain, as is fully noted in l. 1. C. de confes. and l. certum. in prin. ff. eo. C. de interro. acti. l. de aetate. §. nihil. And that this response is not a response is clear, because it was not made to what was asked according to what was asked. The case is in d. §. cui adiicit. Whence, whether you look at the form of the answer, or the nature of the trial, or the mandate of the judge, or the tenor of the statute, the judge who judged the said position to be held as confessed pronounced justly and juridically: as in C. de iuramen. calum. l. 2. §. pen. and extra de confes. c. sed praestitum. lib. 6. From which pronouncement no appeal was taken, and perhaps it cannot be appealed: because it is a sentence delivered upon an article of law and accords with it: as in ff. de appel. reci. l. fi. Nevertheless, whether it can be appealed or not, at least it passed into a matter adjudged (res judicata) as to contumacy: as in ff. de appellatio. l. cum cessante. and ff. de mino. l. ait praetor. §. permittitur. But here it is doubted, what if the statute requires witnesses to prove? I answer,

† a fiction of law is equated to three witnesses, and to as many witnesses as are necessary to prove the act, as in C. de apo. publ. l. quicunque. lib. 16. and noted there. Furthermore, a statute concerning three witnesses is understood when the type of proof is made through witnesses; not when it is made through other types of proof, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. licet Imperator. and singularly noted in l. tutor. C. de peri. tutorum. Consider: this confession was conditional; whence, insofar as it is proved by witnesses, to that extent it is proved by the confession of the party and the witnesses. Furthermore, where it is proved by the confession of the party, the quality of the libel is not attended to, but the quality of the confession, as in extra de restitut. spoli. c. Pisanis. And therefore the judge can render and pass sentence of restitution as against one who has confessed, since the management of affairs is proved. This question requires many eyes to see the truth. But to all these things the adversaries respond and say that such responses are admitted by custom, whatever the law may be. I answer, custom is a matter of fact, and therefore it is necessary that it be proved, as in c. 1. de consti. lib. 6.

† It could also be said that the interlocutory sentence of the judge forecloses the way of proving this custom, as if it could not be proved after the interlocutory sentence passed into res judicata, lest the pronouncement of the judge be illusory, as in ff. de iudic. l. si praetor. in princip.; unless it were said that it ought to be revoked by contrary authority (contrario imperio), as having been delivered through an error regarding the custom. But the doctors say that this cannot be sought after ten days, granting that the judge might sometimes do so out of mere office, if the time limits permit. And this is what is said, that it passes into res judicata with respect to the party, not with respect to the judge; nevertheless, if the judge does not revoke it, the pronouncement stands. Because a sentence delivered against a custom that does not appear from the records is legally valid, as in ff. de re iudi. l. cum prola., because it contains no express error, and especially since it is a consequence of the common law; unless the custom were notorious to the judge as judge, and so I hold. And what is noted in ff. de regu. iur. l. nemo. §. temporalis supports this. I believe, however, that if anyone, having fallen into an error concerning custom, responded according to custom, that allowance must be made for custom (mos ei gerendus est), as in ff. de probatio. l. circa eum, and that custom excuses him from contumacy. And therefore the pronouncement that he be held as confessed was unjust. Either, therefore, the said custom is notorious, and the pronouncement causes no prejudice; or the said custom is not true, or true yet uncertain, and then the said interlocutory decree causes prejudice, because in doubt one must stand by the sentence; and let him who did not allege the custom blame himself, as in C. de re iudi. l. sub specie. and l. post rem. ff. de re iudic.

† But posited that he ought not to be held as confessed, whether anything has been proved through witnesses. And it seems not, because the statute requires, for amounts from 10 pounds and above, the proof of three witnesses, which is understood as three witnesses in number, as in C. de test. l. sancimus, so that this number is formal and of the substance of the proof, so that the supplementary proof of an oath has no place, eo. tit. l. si vnus; which is true, because that statute is not to be interpreted otherwise than as it lies. Whence in no case exceeding 10 pounds can an oath be tendered in defect of proof, because it is not proof of the same kind.

† Whence the oath provides no support, because it does not agree with the municipal statute, as in ff. de excu. tuto. l. 2. §. 1. and l. 1. C. qui nume. tutelarum. l. admonendi, de iure iuran., does not stand in the way, because that law speaks of where two witnesses suffice and more are not required; because when a plurality is of the solemnity of the proof, that law ceases. Likewise, it ceases where the witnesses are discrepant, because one collides with the other. Likewise, it ceases in large sums. Likewise, it ceases if that witness were suspect or of weak credibility, as I have fully noted there; for a slight defect of the witness repels the providence of that law. And therefore I say for certain that an oath in defect of proof has no place in our case; and especially because the witnesses here are not only singular, but discrepant, because one witness says that he sold 75 carts for 122 pounds; others say about 77 carts and a half for 622 pounds. Whence, a comparison and collation of the merchandise to the money having been made, a disproportion and inequality in the price arises, as in ff. loc. l. Si 10. and ff. de adi. leg. l. translatio. For they cannot in any way be reduced to concord. And therefore they destroy one another, because an adversative result arises between them.

† Another question is whether a natural act is proved through a confession. I answer: either it is such an act as cannot be performed except naturally, and then the natural act is proved indirectly, that is, through confession, as in ff. depositi. l. publica. §. fi.; or it is such an act as can be performed civilly, and then through confession nothing is proved except the confession itself, as in C. de non nu. pe. l. 1. and l. si ex cautione. cum si. And therefore a contract of sale is proved through confession according to the first rule, naturally and truly. However, a confession made in court has this special characteristic, that through it a natural act is proved without distinction, as noted in ff. de interro. act. l. cum sim. Because you, my friends, have failed in proving, you have no right, unless perhaps from the contumacy of the adversary. But let this remain in the breast of the judge. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Any plaintiff must prove the thing, the cause, and the action.
2. The testimony of witnesses is singular wherever they do not concur toward the same end.
3. The judge cannot apply his mind to only one species of proof.
4. Discrepancy and contrariety operate so that the lesser is not comprehended in the greater sum.
5. The agreed price is called formal interest.
6. If you managed my affairs concerning oil, and that one hundred casks of oil came into your hands, and that you sold them, I prove a thousand [units of currency], if I prove all things except the sale, whether you ought to be condemned to pay something.
7. The price of a thing is proved by presumptions.
8. The judge, in matters of interest, must have equity before his eyes, and must judge according to presumptions.
9. Against the contracting party, the estimation is proved by oath.
10. The judge must supply [the deficiency] so that the defendant does not become richer at another’s loss.
12. The judge may inquire about the quantity of value according to the common course. And this is one of the cases in which the judge may follow his conscience.
12. How it is to be proved, and what is to be proved, when the agreed price and that received from the quantity of wine are claimed. And what witnesses ought to testify. And nos. 14 and 16.
13. The thing and the price are correlative: and one cannot be proved without the other.
15. The appellation of simple [proof] does not include mixed proof.
body: In the name of Christ.

† For clarity, it must first be laid down that any plaintiff must prove the thing, the cause, and the action; and in these three consists the weight of the trial and of victory, or the contrary if any of these three is not proved, or proved less than legitimately, as in C. de eden. l. qui accusare and C. de prob. l. actor, with similar laws, which are commonplace. Now, in our question, the thing sought is the formal price—that is, the agreed and received price arising from a newly harvested quantity of wine—in which three matters must be considered: whether it has been proved, namely the quantity of wine, the quantity of the price, and whether regarding that quantity and amount the witnesses deposed harmoniously and concordantly, or indeed discordantly, discrepantly, or singularly.

† For singularity occurs wherever the witnesses do not concur toward the same end, as if one says that a basket of wine was sold for five, another for ten. For if the mode of testifying is considered, there is singularity; but if the mode of reference is considered—namely, reference being made to a true sale, not to the price—proof results. But grant that it has not been proved by witnesses, but is proved by fictitious confession and by the said interlocutory decree. The question is asked, first, concerning the simple proof of witnesses; second, concerning mixed proof and several other concurrent proofs,

† because the judge ought not to bind his mind to only one species of proof, but must investigate everything. I come therefore first to mere witnesses; then I shall come to this ordinary semi-full proof of an unconfessed private writing—because a confessed one would produce full proof, but a plausible one produces semi-full proof, which relates to another subsidiary semi-full proof, namely the supplementary oath in aid and assistance of proof, as in ff. de iureiu. l. admonendi, concerning which see below.

† And for clarity, I premise discrepancy and contrariety, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. pacta conuenta, §. paulus: because one supposes the thing to be worth less, the other to be worth more, which discrepancy vitiates, as in ff. loc. l. si decem; nor does the greater sum in this case encompass the lesser, because they tend toward different contracts.

† Likewise, I premise that the agreed price is called the formal interest; but unagreed interest in things to which no idiosyncratic affection attaches, as in things for sale or merchandise, is called common interest, as in ff. ad l. fal. l. pretia rerum.

† Likewise, I premise such a question: I say that you managed my affairs in oil, and that one hundred jars of oil came into your hands, and that you sold them for a thousand. I prove everything except the sale. Ought you to be condemned to anything in my favor? And it seems not, because the conclusion of the libel is not proved as to the formal or agreed price, which is the price stated in the libel; and thus the conclusion of the libel is not proved, whence an absolution will be made from the conclusion of the libel, not from the other narrated facts, as in ff. de pac. dot. l. bebius; and the judge will say, although the quantity of oil is proved, the amount of the price is not proved, whence a certain sentence cannot be rendered, as in Inst. de ac. §. curare. To the contrary, it seems that oil is a thing that has a certain quality and nature, l. cum quis, ff. si cer. pet.; likewise, it has a certain quantity, namely one hundred jars, as in l. certum, ff. si cer. pe. Therefore, a circumspect and equitable judge ought to consider how much it would plausibly have been worth and would have been sold for, as in C. de sent. quae pro eo, quod interest, l. vnica, §. in aliis.

† For the price of a thing is proved by conjectures, as noted in l. 2, C. de rescin. vendi.; and it is established that it came to you from my property; therefore it is good and equitable that it be restored to me, as in l. si Me. et Titium, ff. si cer. pe.

† Likewise, a judge in the matter of interest ought to keep equity before his eyes and can judge from conjectures, as in ff. eo, quod cer. loc. l. quod si ephesi; otherwise, an occasion would be given for misappropriating another's oil,

† and against the misappropriator the valuation is proved by an oath, as in C. vnde vi, l. si quando, and as noted in Inst. de ver. ob. §. pe. Likewise, it would be exceedingly unjust to say that the defendant should be acquitted of the whole because that specific amount was not proved,

† because the judge of his own office ought to supply what is missing lest the defendant become enriched at another's loss, as in ff. de peti. hęre. l. plane, and l. fi., and l. vlt., C. de alim. pup., and as noted by Bar. in ff. de ver. ob. l. cum seruus. 11

† The judge can also, and ought to, interrogate the defendant concerning the amount of value according to the common market rate, as in ff. de interro. act. l. vbicunque; and this seems to be one of the cases in which the judge can follow his own conscience, as in other discretionary matters. Therefore, the one judging must investigate everything and consequently render an equitable sentence. For the conscience of the judge must supply many things, as in ff. de testi. l. scio. Someone will say: here nothing has been proved naturally, but only by confession, as the Speculator says. 12

† I respond: even the confession itself has a certain quantity of wine and a certain nature, for instance Milanese wine, because the natural quality is contracted from the place in things born of the soil, ff. de ver. ob. l. vbi autem. Whence the confession is held for the truth, because the act could not be performed except in one way only, namely naturally, as in ff. depo. l. publ. §. fi. And although the statute speaks of the proof of three witnesses, that statute seems to be understood of the proof of the foundation, not of those things that follow consequentially: arg. C. de eden. l. fi. and ff. de testa. l. haeres palam, §. sed si notam. Solution: I believe that even if under the subtlety of the law it was perhaps not proved to the full, namely by witnesses alone, 13

† because the thing and the price are correlatives, and one cannot be proved without the other, ar. ff. de excep. l. fi. and C. de contrahen. et comm. stipu. per Cy.; nevertheless, in equity the defendant should be condemned up to the plausible and fitting interest. And this especially by such reasoning: because here the action on mandate is brought for business conducted, or its equivalent, namely the actio aestimatoria, in which two clauses are contained, namely the rendering of an account and the payment of the balance, ff. de condi. et dem. l. cum seruus; whence at least under the first clause the defendant ought to be condemned to render an account and a plausible calculation, as in ff. de nego. gest. l. eum actum and l. noui, et antiqui, §. Scaeuola. 14

† Consider the words of the statute: for the statute says that if anyone wishes to prove by witnesses above 10 pounds, he must prove by three witnesses; which statute ought to be understood when he wishes to establish proof from witnesses alone. But in our question, it is not only from witnesses, but from a private writing that has not been denied, nor could it be denied, because it is established—or if not yet established, it will be established—that it was made by the debtor's own hand. Whence that proof is not simple proof from witnesses, but is mixed proof; 15
† and under the designation of simple things in this case, mixed things are not included, as says Jac. But. in l. certi condictio, ff. si cer. pe. 16

† All things considered, therefore, I deem that the truth must be followed, especially upon an oath being tendered to the plaintiff and taken by him, as in l. 3, §. pe., ff. de iureiu. and ff. de pig. l. cum tabernam, §. idem quę siit; and these can be produced not only in the principal case, but also in the case of appeal, as in C. de temp. appell. l. per hanc. Likewise, the law says that things which do not avail individually help when combined; and there is a case in Extra, de succes. ab intest. c. cum dilectus. Likewise, since the witnesses make mention of the said writing and refer themselves to it, by which reference the said witnesses and their statements are saved, if there was any singularity or dissonance among them, as in C. de senten. quae sine cer. quantita. l. hęc sententia, and ff. de re iud. l. ait praetor, and the glossators thereon. The judge therefore has to examine the aforesaid writing, and once it is established that it is in the debtor's hand, he ought to render a condemnatory sentence according to what is contained therein; and especially because through a private writing a calculation of accounts is rendered, as in ff. de pac. l. emptor, §. Lucius, and ff. de neg. ge. l. Nesenn. §. apollinaris. For even though the witnesses do not agree on the measure of that same quantity owed, namely in the measurement, they nevertheless clearly agree on the same quantity, namely of money; but that dissonance, as I have said, is reduced to harmony through the writing to which they refer. And that which is derived from something refers back to its original, and in it and through it is saved, as proved above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether agreements made by a certain prince with a certain city are to be observed by his successor.
2. Whether the king can bind the republic of his kingdom, or the treasury.
3. Whether the republic and the treasury are the same.
4. Whether the kingdom passes to sons, and male and female successors.
5. Whether the successor of the prince is liable for his delict.
6. If the king has certain goods individually from his own purchase, or succession, whether his successor, who did not succeed in these, is liable for his debts and delicts.
body: In the name of Christ. Lord Ferdinand, King of Portugal, had a certain ship laden with goods and property of Oberto and Luciano de Spinola, which had been patronized by Stephen de Auria, seized. This King Ferdinand died, leaving a sole daughter married to the King of Castile, without other issue, according to law. This King of Castile, on behalf of his said wife and by right of inheritance, occupied the said Kingdom of Portugal. After the kingdom was thus occupied, a certain natural brother of the said King Ferdinand, named John, with the aid and favor of the people of the said kingdom, rose in arms against the said King of Castile, so that he might occupy the schismatics in his own name and that of the said kingdom; and by force of arms he attacked and conquered the said kingdom, expelling all the Castilians and those who held the said kingdom in the name of the said King of Castile, who was then a schismatic. After the kingdom was subdued, the people of the said Kingdom of Portugal, seeing that the said John was an upright and virtuous man, and that he was of the natural lineage of the said King Ferdinand, elected and wished to have him as King of the said Kingdom of Portugal; and he is King, and as King holds and presides over the said kingdom. From this King John, the said Oberto and Luciano demand and seek compensation and satisfaction for the said goods and merchandise. To which it is responded on behalf of King John that, since he does not hold the said kingdom as heir, nor as such, nor by hereditary right of the said King Ferdinand, he is not bound. But the said O. and L. say that, since the said King J. holds and possesses the said kingdom and the entire substance of his debtor, namely the said F., who was King of the said O. and L., he is bound to satisfy them for the said merchandise. The question is asked: what is the law? The words of Cynus in his Golden Commentary, Codex, De legibus, l. digna vox, are as follows: Finally, it must be known that Guido de Suzaria formulates this question.

Whether, if the Emperor enters into certain pacts with a certain city or baron, he and his successors are bound to observe them; and it seems that they are not, as stated in *l. princeps*, Digest, *ibidem*; and in *Digest, de legibus*, *l. si quis*, in the beginning; and because an equal has no authority over an equal, as in *l. nam magistratus*, Digest, *de arbitris*; and *l. ille a quo*, § *tempestiuum*, Digest, *ad Trebellianum*. For this part, it is argued from *Codex, de liberali causa*, *l. cum affirmes*; and *infra, de transactionibus*, *l. interpositas*; and *Codex, de curatore*, *l. euacua*, Book 10. On the contrary, it seems that they are bound, for it is a serious matter to break faith, as in *Digest, de constituto pecuniae*, *l. 1*; and the laws of nature urge that pacts be observed; and faith must even be kept with enemies, as in *Digest, de legibus*, *l. vltima*; *de censibus*, *l. 1*. Moreover, this is supported here by *l. quia honestas ligat etiam principem*, as is evident here from what I have said below; and nothing is more owed to a man than to keep pacts, as in *l. 1*, Digest, *de pactis*. For this, it is argued from *Codex, qui testamento facere possunt*, *l. ex imperfecto*; and *Digest, de legatis tertio*, *l. ex imperfecto*; and *Digest, de testamento militaris*, *l. quae a patre*. Moreover, the contract of the prince is law, as *infra, de donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, *l. vltima*. Therefore, etc. And this opinion is held by Guido himself. For which, it is argued from *Extrauagantes, de probationibus*, *c. 1*. Others distinguish: whether there was justice on the other side, or whether there was injustice and fraud there; so that in the first case the pact and composition are valid; in the second, they are not. Argument from those things noted *infra, de transactionibus*, *l. 2*; and *Digest, de conditione indebiti*, *l. in summa*, in the beginning. And it can be just for subjects to resist, if on the part of the lord there is unjust and notorious violence, as in *Codex, de iure fisci*, *l. prohibitum*, Book 10. Lord Ferrandus, King of Portugal, etc., as will be set forth below. Therefore, responding to the question, let us first examine the matter more deeply, beginning from its origins.

† And first I ask, whether the King can bind the public entity of his Kingdom, or the treasury, which belongs to the Republic of Portugal and is contained within the Republic as the content within the container: and, so to speak, it is the very soul and support of the Republic.

† And although it is an ancient question whether the Republic and the fisc are the same thing, and the true solution appears from the foregoing, because a part is not the whole, but is of the whole, as in D. de usufructu, l. si alij, I answer that this matter is proposed too generally, and therefore must be clarified by particular questions. For in the first place it is commonly asked concerning contracts, whether the contract of the King or Prince can bind the Republic or the fisc; because if it can bind, since the Republic and the fisc are something eternal and perpetual as regards their essence, although dispositions often change, as in D. de fisco, l. nunquam moritur, as noted in l. unica, §. si, D. si quis iurisdictio non obtemperet, it immediately follows that from a royal contract the Republic of the Kingdom and the fisc are once bound, always bound; especially because personal obligations by their nature are perpetual, as in Inst. de perpetuis et temporalibus actionibus, in the rubric, and in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationum fere, §. placet, and it is clear in c. 1, qui successores teneantur, column 10. On which point it must be said that the King can bind the fisc of his Kingdom, not only because he is the legitimate administrator, but also because he is regarded in the place of the owner, as in C. de quadrien. praescriptione, l. bene a Zenone, and in D. de publicanis, l. Caesar, and in C. de nauiculariis et navi, l. quod nauiculariorum, lib. 11, provided that he does not make any contract by which the Monarchy of the Kingdom and the honor of the crown might be diminished, as in Extr. de iureiurando, c. intellecto; it is relevant in Extr. de supplendis negligentia praeparatorum, c. grandi, lib. 6. And this is true, not only when doing what is customary, but also when undertaking what is unusual,

† because the Kingdom is more akin to dominion than to simple governance. This is evident from the law regarding the transmission of the Kingdom to legitimate sons and male successors, and sometimes to females, if this is the custom of the Kingdom, as in Extra, De voto, cap. Licet. And it is evident that the Emperor may, by way of contract, indirectly bind a successor, namely by obligating the fisc, which fisc is the same in the successor; so holds Cynus, according to Guidon de Suzaria, Codex, De legibus, l. Digna vox, in the last question, on contracts. Therefore, I premise this, because wrongdoings are sometimes considered under the law of contracts, as in Digest, De iudicibus, l. Eum quem. However, since the rule of civil law is that the dignity or successor is not bound by the delict of the ruler or prelate, as in cap. Delictum personae, De regulis iuris, lib. 6, and in cap. Damnamus, De summo Trinitate, at the end, it is necessary to explain this point more clearly. I therefore ask,

Whether the successor of a king is liable for the king’s delict: and I premise that the King possesses both patrimonial assets, i.e., those of the Republic, such as castles or mills of the Republic, as are the mills of the City of Bologna. Also fiscal goods, when the fisc succeeds, or when it proceeds from condemnation, as in the Digest and the Code, on the right of the fisc. Also his own and singular patrimony, which he either acquired by his own merit or which accrued to him by prosperous fortune. Now, as regards the first and second kind of goods, I say that either he committed a wrong in the form of a delict, for example by theft or robbery, and the Republic or the fisc is not bound: this does not depend on the administration of the kingdom, nor is the public person involved here, but the private person, and indeed a tyrant, as appears from the Code, On forcible entry, l. Meminerint. Every power to bind derives from law: and no obligation arises from prohibited acts, except against the wrongdoer or his universal successor, who is called the successor in law: as in the Digest, On the edict, l. Quaedam, §. is autem; Code, On the delicts of the deceased, l. 1; Extra, On restitution of spoliation, c. cum ad sedem. Notwithstanding, Code, On sacred churches, l. iubemus nullam, because there all consented to the delict, and therefore all are punished, as noted in the Digest, On the rules of law, l. Aliud, §. refertur. I say that there the reason is that all ships ought to pay tribute to Caesar for the successful embarkation. And therefore, because the tribute is withheld, the ship is confiscated. Or the king commits a wrong in the form of a contract, for example by committing fraud in a contract, whereupon the fraud must be purged by an action on the contract, and then he binds the Republic and the fisc, just as when an action is brought on a contract for a contract made without any fraud, according to Cynus in the said l. digna vox. Although perhaps the contrary could be said if nothing came to the Republic or the fisc: because one ought not to be pledged for another, where they can be separated from each other, as in the Digest, On common division, l. si is, cum quo; and in the Authentica, Ut non fiant pignorationes, in the rubric, and in the black, col. 5. To this is added that the delict of King Robert did not harm the Kingdom: because the kingdom was not enriched by the immediate cause of the delict: although it was defended from the Barbarian people, as in c. pastor, On judicial matters, in the Clementines. But sometimes the king commits a wrong in judging, and under the guise of pretended justice: and then it seems that he may prejudice his Republic and fisc, as in the Code, On those who are to be treated as indigent, l. polla. Now I come to our case: in which I say thus, that either the king committed a wrong by the open nature of a delict, or by one included under the guise of a contract or judgment. In the first case, if indeed the captured goods were sold by an official of the chamber of the fisc, the fisc is liable: because it is enriched. And the new king is liable, not as a debtor bound by the delict of his predecessor, but as a judge bound to do justice from his own fisc, as in l. proxime, Digest, On those who have committed a delict in a will. But if those goods were not sold for the chamber of the fisc, nor misappropriated in the name of the fisc, but in the name of the king as a simple person, then the successor is not liable: because he is not a successor in law, nor in the goods, from which an obligation could descend upon him. For, as has been said, the rule of law dictates that no one ought to be burdened by the enmity of another. Also, there are certain rules by which successors are bound. And this case is not under the rule, nor even under the obligatory exceptions. And where the subject matter ceases, the obligation ceases, as in the Digest, On peace, l. iurisgentium, §. 1; and Institutes, On obligations, §. sequens.

† Now remains the third member, namely: if the king had certain goods singularly his own by purchase, or succession, or any other right of his own, not as king, but as a man and rational animal, if indeed the successor does not possess these goods, he is not bound in any way; but if he does possess them: although the action ought to be directed against the daughter and the inheritance of the said King, nevertheless, since she has been dispossessed, the new king is bound by the office of the judge to consign those goods to the creditors so that he may thereby satisfy them, as in D. de bonis auctoritatis iudicis possidendis, l. cum unus, § is qui; and D. de officio praesidis, l. illicitas, in principio. From these things the solution of the question is clear, with this addition, that pignoration is prohibited; hence the said king acted very badly. It would be otherwise if he had done this with the law permitting, on account of defrauded revenue, or omitted profession of census, as in C. de nautico foenore, l. cum proponas; and D. de locato conducto, l. penultima, § navem. One thing must not be omitted, but rather diligently observed, lest these nobles, who were exacted for another’s debt, fall into the vice which they themselves condemn. That is, they must take care not to make pignorations for a true or pretended debt of the said deceased King without an heir who exists today; because if they were to pignorate one for another, or what is worst, exercise piracy, they would fall from their right, as in the said Authent. ut non fiant pignorationes, in principio, and there noted. But they must observe the due modes and with the order of reason. And pertinent to the above is l. providendum, C. de decurionibus, libro decimo. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Third Order of Saint Francis is an ecclesiastical order.
2. Whether persons of the Third Order of Saint Francis are called ecclesiastical persons, to such an extent that they are not bound to pay tithes or burdens.
3. Whether persons of the Third Order of Saint Francis fall under the appellation of clerics.
4. Whether persons of the Third Order of Saint Francis are subject to the forum of the bishop, both in criminal and civil matters.
5. A statute does not make something a testament which is null according to civil law.
6. Whether a grandmother is excluded from the succession of her grandson on account of not having requested guardians, when legitimate heirs exist.
body: In Christ’s name. Regarding that which is asked,

† whether the Third Order of the Blessed Francis is an ecclesiastical order, and whether the persons of that order are ecclesiastical persons, and whether they belong to the forum of the Church or to the forum of the laity: it cannot be denied, I think, that although the said order does not imprint a character, and is an order of habit rather than of tonsure, it is nevertheless termed in a general sense an ecclesiastical order. And I prove this as follows: for it receives its nature and form from the Church, therefore also its denomination. The reasoning is proved through what is fully read and noted in ff. de iusti. et iu. l. ius ciuile in the gloss there, iure naturali impositione exemplorum. It is therefore an ecclesiastical order from its material and formal cause. Likewise from its efficient and confirming cause: because it is an order specially approved and specially privileged by the Church; whence it must deservedly be called an ecclesiastical order, in Auth. de defenso. ciuitatis § interim, C. de vet. iu. enu. l. 1 § omnia. Likewise it is clear from the name itself, because it is called the Third Order of the Blessed Francis, arg. Instit. de do. § est et aliud; C. de offi. praefe. vrbis l. 1, where it says vt sciant ex ipso nomine, etc.; for it received its name through the Blessed Francis, as in ff. vt concubi. l. in concubin.; who would say that a fellowship distinguished by that most sacred name should be designated anything other than ecclesiastical? For they bear the sign of the Blessed Francis and his habit; whence they can deservedly be called signed with the sign of the Blessed Francis, arg. C. de aquae duc. l. decernimus lib. 11. And that collegium has the title of its name from the Blessed Francis—a title with which other collegia are not adorned, nor can they usurp such a title, because it is an alien title; and arg. C. de muta. not. l. 1; C. vt nemo priua. tit. l. 1; ff. de falsis l. eos § qui se; ff. ad munic. l. Titio cum esset in prin. And it is also an ecclesiastical order from the final cause: because it is a spiritual collegium ordered to the end of the spirit and of blessed fruition, like the other ecclesiastical collegia, and it proceeded by divine inspiration for the salvation of souls, and it possesses a spiritual rule. Moreover, it is just that all things be denominated from their end, according to Aristotle; ff. de reg. iu. l. cuius effectus supports this. I conclude, therefore, that this ordinance of this order, and the order itself, is ecclesiastical, and that an effect is denominated from its causes.

† But whether the persons are said to be ecclesiastical persons, so that they are not held to collectae or ecclesiastical and mixed burdens, as is noted in ff. ad mun. l. incola, because they are not imposed except upon subjects, as in l. rescri. § fi. de mun. et hono., whereas persons are so subject, C. de mulieribus, et in quo loco l. 1, de mun. et hono. l. munerum § mixtam; and Auth. item nulla conmunitas, C. de cler. et episc., supports this. Yet these members of the Third Order are held to collectae and mixed burdens on account of the goods they possess: therefore, these members of the Third Order ought not to be called ecclesiastical persons. And I prove the aforesaid through a certain saying of Dominus Federico of Siena, who says that in the privilege of Alexander IV concerning them it is contained thus: 'We command your fraternity by Apostolic words that you ensure that penitents of this kind, provided they acknowledge the burdens to which they are bound by reason of their goods, are not compelled to public offices or to discharge personal burdens.' Therefore, it seems that they ought not simply to be called ecclesiastical persons.

† How this same point is proved through the ordinary glosses, which say that these persons are not contained under the appellation of clerics, nor of religious, as is noted in Clem. de religio. do. c. 1 in the gloss, and see also de sententia excom. ca. cum ex eo in the gloss primus fuit of the same compilation. For they do not possess holy orders: because they have neither a sacrament nor that which is not holy; therefore none at all. Nor have they renounced the world, although they assume certain rules of ecclesiastical discipline, just as the disciplinati of the confraternity of the Blessed Francis do, who nevertheless are not ecclesiastical persons according to all, unless some among them happen to be clerics. What is noted in Extra, de locato c. 1 supports this; what is noted by the Archdeacon in dist. 42 c. si quis fideliter supports this; as well as Innocent in de off. or. c. cum ab ecclesiarum and de excess. pręlatorum c. dilecta. For such collegia are indeed licit and pious, yet the persons are not ecclesiastical strictly speaking; nor is their temple, that is, the place of assembly, a sacred place, but profane, like any other simple place; and nevertheless a legacy can be made to it, and it has capacity, ff. de annuis lega. l. annus § a Titia; ff. de legatis tertio l. pater § Tusculanus. And on the contrary it seems it must be said that the said penitents are called ecclesiastical persons. And this is proved, first, by reason, for their collegium is ecclesiastical; therefore the persons belonging to that collegium are as well. For a collegium is nothing other than the persons, with the added meaning that is taken universally, ff. de vsuc. l. rerum mixtura and ff. quod cuiusque vniuersitatis nomine l. sicut § 1 in the gloss sed si dissoluatur at the end. Of what nature the corporate whole is, therefore, of such nature are its subjects: because just as the genus is represented in each of its species, l. 1, ff. si cer. pe. Secondly, it is proved by the said privilege of Alexander, in which they are exempted from personal factions: therefore they are not purely secular persons, but either ecclesiastical, or it is a genus unto itself; just as the law elsewhere speaks of a contract, so do I speak of persons, C. de iu. emphyt. l. 1. And the example of persons in whom neither is found, like a third genus, is more properly applicable, ff. de iust. et iur. l. manu.; C. de iure aur. annul. l. 2; C. de lat. li. tol. l. 1; ff. de iu. fis. l. sed si accepto. What is noted in Instit. de iure personarum in the gloss sed quid de statu liberi supports this, or that a mixed kind of men will partake of both qualities of its extremes, as in ff. de iur. om. iu. l. improprium § mixtum. Why, then, may it be denominated in either manner, though not simply? Now let us see

† concerning the forum, whether persons of this kind belong to the bishop’s forum, such that they cannot be constrained under a lay judge, as in Extra, de fo. comp. c. si diligenti. And it seems at first that they are not of the forum of the Church. And I argue thus: they are bound by the statutes of the laity on account of the goods they possess, as is contained in the said privilege; therefore they are subject to secular jurisdiction, because making statutes belongs to jurisdiction, as is clear in the definition of jurisdiction noted in de iu. om. iu. l. 1 in the gloss and necessarily on the word statuendae. Since, therefore, those who are under the jurisdiction belong to the forum, C. de iur. om. iud. l. nemo and l. fi., therefore etc., unless a privilege of another forum were shown; which nevertheless does not seem to be contained in the law, ff. si quis cau. l. qui autem. But in their privileges it is contained thus: 'If, however, the brothers or sisters are harassed contrary to law or their privileges by the podestàs or rulers of the places where they maintain their domicile, their ministers shall approach the local bishops, etc.' They do not, therefore, seem to be subject to the bishop’s forum except for defect of justice on the part of the secular judge, because jurisdiction seems to be attributed to the bishop conditionally, not primarily, in Auth. vt diffe. iud. § 1, C. de anna. exce., as is more perfectly seen in de fo. comp. c. licet with its like. The bishop, therefore, is as it were a judge of intermediate appeals, not the judge of the principal cause. For since jurisdiction is granted to the bishop in certain cases, it is therefore seen to be denied in others, ff. de iud. l. cum praetor. If, however, the words of the privilege say, 'if anything unjust be suffered from a party, the bishop should be approached,' C. vbi de crim. agi oport. auth. qua in prouincia; but they say, 'if anything unjust be suffered from a judge': whence the first degree of jurisdiction rests with the lay magistrates, but through their injustice it spreads to the clerics, whether they cry out or are themselves aggrieved. For since by contemplation of those who are aggrieved this has been granted to the aggrieved themselves, it is seen to have been granted by name, as in ff. de leg. 3 l. fideic. § interdum, arg. de leg. 2 l. peto § iure. It seems clear from the aforesaid that by reason of possession and by reason of obligation they could be convened before a secular judge; but if something be done to them contrary to law, they can appeal, and have recourse to the bishops concerning the nullity of this. Therefore, after being attributed to the laity, this was granted to them in honor of the name of the Blessed Francis and of the Third Order, arg. de leg. 2 l. cum filius § petere, not because by reason of their profession they are truly persons of the Church, since they live in matrimony, although they are called exempting themselves, as Cino notes in l. rem in praesenti and in Auth. sed quamuis hoc. Whence I think that they have this prerogative in a criminal cause just as in a civil cause, and all the more strongly so: because the law speaks generally, and because one who is exempt in a civil cause would appear to be exempt in a criminal cause when he is exempt not by reason of the person, but of the order, as in C. de agen. in reb. l. ex eo lib. 12. There are certain other orders which have more and less immunity. But this is at the discretion of the Pope, who even makes something out of nothing, and who is living law on earth, as in Auth. de consulibus. But what these or others have remains in them, and is not to be drawn to consequential extensions, de leg. 2 l. cum patronis. Although a certain worthy doctor holds strictly that these members of the Third Order are not of the secular forum in any way, because their order is called a Religion, and because they are of the perpetual household of the Blessed Francis. But certainly it would be called a religion only in a broad sense, C. de sum. Tri. l. 1, and in a broad sense they are said to be of the household, as in the said c. ex eo. I, however, adhere to the words of the privilege as to the words of the law concerning privileges throughout. And therefore I think that in the said condition episcopal cognition is not in the first degree, but that this is a relief for those who have suffered injustice, as in Auth. de man. princ. § et non permittentur, and as in Auth. de quaestore § super hoc. And therefore, my most illustrious Giovanni, that professed lady of the Third Order was able to appeal from the first, sufficiently unjust sentence to the bishop, and all the more so to the Supreme Pontiff. And another was not the judge of appeal by force of the privilege, which transfers and revokes the appellate jurisdiction to him; nor by force of an erroneous appeal and of a sentence rendered therefrom can she suffer prejudice, C. si a non compe. iudi. l. fi. But she could have suffered loss from the fact that she had not appealed, and thus the sentence would have passed into res judicata. You should examine, therefore, the form of the appeal, whether it is an appeal to any competent judge; and then, notwithstanding the acts already performed, the appeal can be introduced in the ecclesiastical court; or whether it is an appeal to Lucius Titius, in which case the error is harmful, ff. de app. l. 1 § pen. et fi., because it was appealed to an inferior, since a bishop is greater than a secular judge, as noted in ff. de postu. l. ex ea causa. That we have the law on our side in the principal cause has been sufficiently revealed in another consilium; and although a certain beast has advised the contrary, as I believe, either out of supine ignorance or seeking to please the eyes of those present, he nevertheless advised wretchedly. For the inheritance of the four grandsons belongs to the grandmother, as I have proved at length, and the passed-over daughter must be content with the legacy. And although the words are of the present tense, if the condition is not valid, it was true in the present: because the passed-over daughter made the will null, as in l. Gall. § in omnibus and l. inter caetera, and Instit. de exhaered. liber. in prin., and de vulgi. substi. l. si quis with its like, and in § aliud quoque capitulum, and noted in Auth. ea causa.

† Nor does a statute cause that to be a will which fails under civil law, although the statute precludes the daughter from seeking more by intestacy: because one does not depart further from the common law than the statute expressly says, as noted in Auth. quas actiones, and C. de iu. delib. l. fi. § in computa. in the final gloss; and that fool was not capable of understanding. Likewise, to say that that woman, ignorant of the law, believed by means of an arbitration agreement that she was renouncing her right, which she did not know belonged to her because she presupposed it was in the hands of another, is an error against the spirit of truth, as was fully proved elsewhere.

† Likewise, on account of guardians not having been requested, the grandmother is not repelled: especially because there was a legitimate guardian, who is preferred to those requested by the grandmother, who had not undertaken the guardianship; whence she did not have the right of requesting, as noted in C. ad Tertul. l. matres. Although certain moderns, not grasping this reason, contradict the truth that is in the gloss. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Regarding a pact made by the husband concerning the acquisition of the dowry in the event of children, if the wife dies, then immediately the husband, and afterwards the sons, to whom such dowry pertains. And no. 8.
2. To whom does the dowry of a deceased woman belong? And what concerning paraphernal goods. And no. 3.
4. Whether a ward transmits the right of deliberation: and whether the mere knowledge of the ward is sufficient for the transmission of the inheritance. And no. 6.
5. Credit is given to the statement of a witness, because it is presumed true.
7. It is presumed in favor of the statement of a witness regarding fact, although not regarding law.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: Lady Catherine of Fogiano gave in dowry to Francis a certain piece of land, estimated according to certain agreements inserted regarding the gain of dowry. Finally, from the marriage contracted between them were born Christopher, Angelo, and Rosa. Then the said Lady Catherine died first; secondly, her husband Francis died on the following day; then the said Christopher, Angelo, and Rosa died before any of them had reached the age of ten years. Then Lady Lucia, the full sister of the aforesaid Lady Catherine, claimed back the said dowry as the intestate heir of her sister. To whom it was objected by the heirs of the said Francis that the said Francis, for his aforementioned sons, and the said Angelo, had accepted the inheritance of the said Lady Catherine, which, as having been accepted, was transmitted to them, and the sister was excluded. Proofs were produced on both sides: for the heirs of the said Francis strove to prove that the said Francis accepted the inheritance of his wife by possessing the dotal property as his own, and as one possesses his own thing; not only so, but also by possessing certain paraphernal goods, just as one has, holds, and possesses his own property. Also that the said Angelo accepted the said inheritance by possessing it as an heir. On the contrary, it is said that Francis, at the time of his wife's death, was at the point of death, and did not make any sign indicative of the acceptance of the inheritance; and that the said Angelo died at such an age that he could not accept without a tutor. Now the question arises, having seen the records, what are the duties of the judge wishing to adhere to the truth. In the name of Christ. Because

† The husband, in the case concerning the inheritance of the children, had contracted on their behalf regarding the dowry to be acquired for the children themselves; he upheld the contract, and the children acquired the dowry as children by virtue of the contract, not as heirs of law, as stated in the Digest, On Dowry Agreements, law *Inter socerum*, section *Vir dotem*. In this case, the woman, having become sui iuris, cannot make a will regarding the dowry, nor can she have an heir in it, by argument from the Code, On Inofficious Donations, law 1. Nevertheless, this is not called a dowry acquisition, because the husband does not acquire it, but the children do, as stated in the aforementioned section *Vir dotem*. Therefore, the issue of transmission of inheritance is not to be discussed here, because the children do not come as heirs, but by contract, that is, by virtue of the agreement, as stated in the Institutes, On Verbal Obligations, section *Ex conditionali*.

† Four cases are noted: sometimes the father stipulates for the profit of the children; then, if the wife predeceases him, the children come by right of the pact, as is noted in the Digest, *De dote praelegata*, law 1, § 1. Sometimes he stipulates for himself; and then he profits, without prejudice to the children’s complaint of an undutiful dowry. Code, *De inofficiosa donatione*, law 1. Sometimes he does not expressly stipulate, but promises to restore the dowry if the children do not survive; then the text says that, from the contrary sense, which has place in conditional contracts, as the pact to retain for the children, it is not said that [the father] profits for the children by a tacit pact, but rather that he retains for the children. Therefore, some say that it is not a pact for profit, insofar as the children come as heirs. Others say that it is by right of the pact, because under the old law the daughter did not have an heir in the profectitious dowry; rather, it was restored to the father upon the daughter’s death. Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law 2. Hence, the pact prevents consolidation; and it provides an exception by virtue of the pact. It supports this that it is noted in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, law *Filiae meae*, and law *Auus*. But today she could well have an heir in the profectitious dowry, since she is capable of full right. Argument from the Digest, *Familiae herciscundae*, law *Pompeius*. For the same reason seems to apply as in adventitious dowries, since ownership and the fullness of the entire right reside in the daughter. It supports this that it is noted in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Post dotem*, according to Dyachenko. I do not say that the daughter should make a will regarding the dowry, but that she should have an heir intestate. It supports this that it is noted in the Authenticum *Matri et aviae*, § 1, *Cum si*. Whatever may be the case regarding the written law, nevertheless there is a custom that the dowry for the children be retained; I hold that a tacit pact according to custom is to be presumed, so that it remains with them as with heirs. Argument from the Code, *De locato*, law *Excepto*. For just as it would be in the fourth case, when in the stipulation of the dowry to be returned no mention is made of the children, whereby the woman, having become sui iuris, cannot make a will regarding such dowry, because that condition does not seem to have been added by the father to the prejudice of the daughter, but rather in her favor, so that she alone has the right on account of the children, as in the Digest, *De statu hominum*, law *Aretusa*; Code, *Qui potiores in pignore habeantur*, law *Assiduus*, § *Exceptio*; Digest, *De excusationibus tutorum*, law *Amicissimus*, § *Lucius*. Sometimes no mention of the children is made in the promise; and then the custom has place, noted in law *Dos a patre*, that the dowry remains with the sons as with the heirs of the woman, according to Jacobus de Belvisio, even if the words are broad, for example, in every case of restoring the dowry. For by this it does not seem that the benefit of the custom is renounced. Digest, *Si quis cautio*, law *Sed et si quis*, § *Quaesitum*. For the word “restoring the dowry” restricts the pact to the case of restitution; but this is not a case of restitution, therefore, etc. Argument from the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, law *Quae Romae*, § *Augerius*. When it appears simply that there was a pact for the children to profit, this pact must be removed; for this dowry is imputed to the legitime. Law *Quam nouella*, Code, *De inofficioso testamento*. Therefore, the burden is rejected. Law *Quam in prioribus*, Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*. Solution: there, when the burden is imposed by way of last will; otherwise if by way of contract. Digest, *De legatis tertio*, law *Uxor*, § *Pater*, according to Jacobus and noted in the Code, *De re vendicata*, law *Cum a matre*. It supports this that it is noted in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si cum dotem*, § *Si pater*, according to Jacobus. And this is as far as the dowry is concerned.

But let us consider the paraphernal goods, which belong to the woman herself and which pass to her heirs, since the inheritance of the said lady was not accepted by the sons due to their minority, because they were minors. D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. pupillus si fieri possit, and l. impuberibus. C. de iure deliberandi.

† One could say that, although a ward cannot accept an inheritance, he can nevertheless transmit the right of deliberation: for in the transmission of the right of deliberation, the ward’s mere knowledge suffices; for the law states that knowledge suffices. C. de iure deliberando, l. Cum antiquior. But a ward who is older than an infant is understood to know at least his own perfect interest: and he can acquire for himself the right of transmission. For by this he is not bound to anyone, and he himself becomes richer, arg. Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, § Pupillus. Moreover, the witnesses testify directly concerning the mixing and management on behalf of the owner, or on behalf of this inheritance: because there is no proper mixing in the maternal inheritance; and mixing properly applies to one who has notice through an external act. Inst. de haereditatibus qualiter et quibus differant, § Si. And the statements of the witnesses must be upheld, unless the contrary is proven, as in Extra de testibus, c. In omnium; unless it were obscure, de probat., c. In praesentia, cum si.

† And their statement is presumed true, unless it is proven false, just as an instrument, C. de probat. l. cum precibus; yet it is not presumed beyond or otherwise than what they depose, C. de usur. l. 1; nor is a simple statement presumed conditional, as modal, or vice versa, Extra de fide instr. c. cum Ioanne heremita.

But it is answered that the knowledge of the minor who is near infancy is not sufficient for the transmission of the inheritance: because the law says that the minor does not understand the cause of acquiring the inheritance, d. I. pupilli si fari. Therefore, he does not have knowledge of the law, and he does not know what an inheritance, or succession, or acceptance of inheritance is; therefore, he does not have such knowledge as is required. Someone might say that knowledge of the laws is not required, but knowledge of the fact, ff. de cond. et demon. l. multum interest. But in his knowledge, this rightly falls, that he is dead in law, although he does not know that the law defers succession to him; this is not an impediment to succession. arg. l. multum. But it is answered: the text says that such age does not decide; therefore, he is said to be ignorant. d. l. pupillus non transmittit. Otherwise, even an infant would transmit, that knowledge of the mother's death falls on some infant, ar. ff. de acque poss. l. donatarum. Which is false: as l. infanti. §. si vero non sic tutor. Although knowledge of the law, i.e., of the constitution, is not required, yet true and effective knowledge that the inheritance pertains to him is required. ff. de bon. poss. l. in bonorum. And although the minor can acquire for himself by himself without a tutor, it is true when the acquisition falls within his understanding: but the deliberative and conservative act to accept or repudiate the inheritance does not fall within the pubescent, ar. l. fi. C. de mili. testa. Which I think is true in the case of one near infancy for §. si vero non sit tutor. And to say that this §. is corrected by l. cum antiquioribus is captious and not of sound intellect: because neither the text nor the gloss says this, nor does reason convince. Also, the statement of the witnesses does not obstruct:

† because testimony is presumed to be given regarding facts, and not regarding law, as noted by Innocentius in the chapter *Cum causam* on witnesses. For if the law opposes it, and also age, the testimony of a witness is not believed, as argued from the Digest, title *De interrogationibus et responsionibus actorum*, law *Confessio*; and from the Digest, title *De testibus*, law *Ob causam*, section *Si sicut*. For example, if one were to say that a stipulation was made between absent parties, or that a madman made a testament, regarding succession from an intestate, see the chapter *Cum dilectus* on witnesses, with the chapter *Si quaeratur*; and from the Digest, title *De probationibus*, law *Si ab ea parte*. For thereafter, the testimony of a witness must be consistent with fact, law, and nature; the testimony of impossibilities can be removed, because there is no knowledge, nor sense, nor any causes of non-existent things.

But someone will say that the husband aided the inheritance by possessing it, yet it is not established that the children were infants, from which it follows that the father alone could not enter upon the inheritance: because the infancy, which founds the entry, has not been proved, and therefore the burden of proof and justification of the entry lies upon him who alleges the entry. Nevertheless, it is not established that the husband used a new possession, nor that he changed the cause of his possession in his mind. C. de acquirenda possessione, l. Cum nemo. For, when the old possession is weakened, entry is not presumed; especially from the possession of one person. Arg. ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. Duo fratres; ff. si quis hereditatem petat, l. Finis; and the argument of what is read and noted in ff. si certum petatur, l. Certi condictio, §. Finis; and l. Eius, in fine; and C. de petitione hereditatis, l. Si filius. The husband and wife were dying, and he was at his last gasp and afflicted with mortal sickness; nor is it likely that, disturbed by death, he thought of acquiring a new possession. C. qui testamento facere possint, l. Hac consultissima, §. At cum humana fragilitas. And therefore a just judge, who had considered the nature of the fact, ought to have judged for the sister in the paraphernalia according to the truth and the quality of the fact, overthrowing the attempt of the witnesses; and if the arbitrator decided otherwise, he did so in good faith; nevertheless, his award was unjust in this respect, and a reduction to the judgment of a good man may be sought in another judgment, in the manner of an appeal. ff. de arbitris, l. Non distinguemus, §. Cum quidam, in fine, where the inequity may be better declared. And these things seem to me to be directly according to judgment, and what any good man ought to follow: it is presumed that the paraphernal goods, in which the wife has title and right of detention, are hers, as is noted in de iure dotium, l. Mulier; l. Si ego, §. Finis, with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a just impediment excuses in judicial proceedings, so that one does not incur a penalty on account of the delay of the contract.
body: The facts are as follows: In the name of Christ. John Cuigloti of Perugia was extracted from the Sacchetto [ballot bag] into the office of the City of Castello for a term of six months, who, according to the form of the agreements, ought to have arrived at the said city four days before the beginning of his office; and if he did not go, that he ought thereafter to remain during the time of the syndicate for five additional days. Now it happened that the city of Perugia, at the time when this Bailiff was to come to the said City of Castello, and even before, while he was still in the city of Perugia, was besieged on all sides by the pestilent White Company; so that he could not safely go to the said City of Castello; on account of which he did not arrive within the term of one day. The question is now whether he is excused on account of the said impediment, so that he ought not to remain during the time of the syndicate for those five additional days, or not? etc. In the name of God.

† Because the matter begins from the disposition in this manner: it states that the agreement is that the power must arrive four days beforehand, not from the condition if he does not go four days beforehand. I say that if, due to an impediment, he could not go within the term, he ought not for that reason to be punished, so that he remains as if in place of a penalty for five additional days, since neither delay nor default can be imputed to this power: because the narrowness of time prevented him from setting out earlier, as these matters are proven. D. si quis cautio, l. 2, § quod diximus; D. de publicaniis, l. Caesar; and to the Rhodian law on jettison, l. pen., § idem iuris est si prior nauta. Otherwise, if he had been in delay or at fault. D. locatio conductio, l. colonus, § si navem; and note in § cum quidam. The distinction is proven, whether the act begins from a condition, or from a disposition, or command. D. de verbis oblig., l. illa stipulatio; l. si Kalendas, where by conjunction; l. si ex legati causa, in the same title, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute and the like, whether one who introduces foreign wine into the county, upon payment of the toll, is subject to punishment.
2. A temporary suspension, once the time has elapsed, effects nothing.
3. What the term "perpetually" signifies.
4. Whether multiple pronouncements in a judicial proceeding are required to establish or declare a custom.
5. Whether a person may be accused multiple times for the same offense.
body: In the name of Christ. Tus, formerly of Nicoluccio of Arezzo, accused, among others, Feus Bon. John of Immissio, regarding the importation and bringing in of wine by a foreign Jew, and by the community of Arezzo, etc. Finally, having joined issue, the accuser withdrew from the lawsuit, seeing that he was supporting a weak case: and the judge, by interlocutory order and acquittal, pronounced judgment, as is contained in this folio. Then another of the tax farmers re-accused this same Feus for the very same act. Now two questions arise: first, whether one who imports foreign wine into the county of Arezzo, upon payment of the toll prescribed by ordinance, is subject to punishment, considering the wording of the municipal law? Second, whether the said Feus can be accused anew.

And regarding the first point, it seems that one should first say that it is so, firstly on account of the statute promulgated in 44 under the heading "Concerning Foreign Wine." For that statute must be observed. D. de publicanis, l. Caesar; D. de verborum significatione, l. censoria; C. de nautico feneratione, l. cum proponas; D. de decretis ab ordine facienda, l. si; D. locato, l. 1, §. nautae, cum si. Secondly, on account of the reform promulgated in l. 2. For that reform speaks of the sale to be made for the time of one year, promising to introduce foreign wine for the time of those buyers; therefore, for another time the statute remains in force, which is merely suspended for that time.

† For a temporary suspension, once the time has elapsed, operates to no effect, as shown by the authorities: ff. de legibus, l. cum; ff. de legibus 2, l. statu libe., §. si; ff. de poenis, l. si; Inn. de consuetudinibus, c. cum inter. The reform issued in the 40th [year], which restricts it to a certain time, and thus, where it would otherwise be perpetual, renders it temporary. ff. de militibus testibus, l. si certarum, §. ult.; ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. 2, §. post missionem; ff. de legibus 1, l. talis scriptura. This supports what is noted in §. poena gravior and l. ordine. However, the contrary view seems to me to be correct for two reasons. First, by the force of the reform issued in the 50th [year]; second, because it permits [something] perpetually, as is clear from the aforementioned Doctor Jacobus, who in his consultation there states that it is limited and declared to be validly and firmly established for perpetuity, since that entire reform is perpetual and will be valid at all times.

† For that adverb, “perpetually,” has such a meaning, as is noted in D. 17, 2, l. 1 and 2, § qui in perpetuum; D. 39, 1, si ager vectigalis; D. 43, 7, de servitutibus urbanis prœdiorum, l. eum debere, columna. Therefore, the preceding statute has been derogated in its entirety, to such an extent that nothing should be argued from it, nor should it be alleged in court in this respect. C. 4, 20, de latina liberatione, l. 1, in principio; C. 10, 50, et de veteri iure enucleando, l. 2, § sed quia. Nor does the objection hold regarding the reform made in l. uno, because that reform was made for one effect, namely, the promise. Therefore, it ought not to produce the contrary effect. Arg. D. 35, 1, de legatis, l. legata inutiliter; D. 28, 5, de hereditatibus instituendis, l. ex facto; and l. hereditas ad statutum. For the mind of the legislator, in derogating the old statute, was not in revoking it, and the acts of those who act, etc. D. 13, 6, si certum petatur, l. non omnis; D. 44, 7, de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationum substantia. And this is confirmed by D. 2, 14, de pactis, l. scimus, § 1, and what is noted there. Furthermore, the objection does not hold for another reason, for the said last reform speaks temporally, with regard to the new tax which is imposed there. L. 12, domini personaliter. Moreover, it speaks locally, extending itself as to whether within the city. Now I concede that such new law is temporary, and when the time has ended, one returns to the perpetual law, i.e., to the said reform made in l. 2, for I do not find it repealed either in form or in substance. Therefore, etc. C. 7, 62, de appellationibus, l. precipimus; and l. 1, C. 6, 59, de inofficiosa donatione, unless according to the letter of the reform issued in 56, non incapi.

Moreover, it will be said to me that custom has thus interpreted the said reform; therefore, one must adhere to it, because the interpretation of custom is probable and necessary. D. 50, 17, de legibus, l. si interpretatur. Added to this is the fact that this custom was alleged by the accuser, and the judge pronounced judgment; therefore, it appears that he pronounced judgment based on the allegation, as in D. 48, 18, de poenis, l. si prœses; D. 26, 10, de suspectis tutoribus, l. hæc, n. and no. D. 44, 2, de exceptionibus rei iudicatæ, l. si ad exhibendum; and l. si ex testamento.

† And although several pronouncements by judges are required to establish a custom, nevertheless, to declare a custom already established regarding a matter, one judgment rendered after full discussion suffices, according to other doctors, ff. de legib. l. de quibus.

† As to the second point, I say that this appears to be an obstacle for this accuser, because otherwise the action is based on a fact and has been adjudicated: and although the fact may be repeatable, nevertheless the repetition is not presumed otherwise. And see: D. 12.2.1 (*Eum qui*), § *In popularibus*; D. 44.2.1 (*Si a te*), in the beginning; and if it is said that there was a renunciation, others do not object. D. 48.5.1 (*Maritus*), § *Negavit*.
