I answer: here the process went beyond to an acquittal: and the same person should not be repeatedly prosecuted for the same delict, especially against the same individual. D. 4.8.11 (*Si nauiganti*), § *Passum*; D. 47.1.1 (*Si cui*), § *Hisdem*. And this is especially so when the first plaintiff was a partner of the second, as argued from C. 4.44.1 (*Si*). I speak presupposing the validity of the notification. Finally, I conclude that the accusation does not proceed in effect. To this effect contributes the reform made in law 17. For, since that reform accepts the toll, the denounced party is tacitly permitted, as argued from C. 8.38.1 (*Commissoriae*) and D. 21.2.1 (*Quidem*). And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In which goods does the substitute succeed by virtue of the substitution? And whether in the Trebellian portion.
body: In the name of God. The fact, concerning which counsel is sought, is as follows: Vannuccio, Puccio, and Cecio, natural brothers and sons of Giulio Putti, made a testament drawn up in a single document by the hand of Ser Francesco Andrioli, our notary of Alsel. In which testament they made such institution and substitution: in all their other movable and immovable goods, rights, and claims, present and future, wherever they may be and could be found, one instituted and made the other, and the other the one, of those surviving, universal heir to himself; and if any of them should die, they substituted the survivor of them; and if all should die, they substituted to them and to each of them Tommasello Loli: which testament is transmitted to you. After the aforementioned testament, Vannuccio, one of the said testators, died, with the said Puccio, Cecio, and Tommasello surviving him; who Puccio did not accept the inheritance of the deceased Vannuccio; after the said Puccio died, with the said Cecio and Tommasello surviving him; who Cecio accepted the inheritance of the said Vannuccio and Puccio; after which the said Cecio made his last testament: in which he instituted as his heir a certain niece of his and his wife. Now it is asked from the above regarding the rights of the said testament of the said Cecio, Puccio, and Vannuccio. And what, in quantity, the said Tommasello, as substitute, ought to have of the inheritances of the said Puccio and Vannuccio. Having seen the underwritten. Furthermore, it is asked, since the said Vannuccio at the time of the making of the testament had a daughter named Clara, to whom he left certain goods by right of institution in the said testament, whether the said Clara can further claim anything in the inheritance of the said Vannuccio, her father. In the name of Christ. On the first point

It seems that it must be said that, since all these three brothers have died, Thomassellus, by virtue of the substitution, comes to the goods of Vanucius and Pucius, after deduction of the Trebellian portion, if an inventory was made. For Cæcilius, who died last, appears to have been requested to restore what he acquired by title of institution or vulgar substitution as a fideicommissary, having regard to the order of the will, as noted in ff. ad Trebellianam, l. Marcellus, §. quidam; and in ff. ad legem Falcidiam, l. Titia facit; ff. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si tu, §. ex parte; and l. si totam. Provided, however, that if the daughter of Vanucius did not have what equals her legitime, she may, according to the common law, demand a supplement to be applied to her. C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnino; l. quam in prioribus; l. scimus, with similar authorities. And by this the answer to the second point is clear.

Furthermore, it seems that in the goods of Cæcilius, who died last, that is, in his own goods and not those inherited from his brothers, Thomassellus has no right. For either he wishes to come by the substitution made by Vanucius and Pucius, and he cannot: because in that substitution the heir’s own goods are not included. ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. cohæredi, §. cum filiae. Or by the will of Cæcilius, and this he cannot do: because Cæcilius, after the first will, made a second. Hence there was a revocation of the first and of its contents. ff. de legatis 1, l. si mihi et tibi, §. in legatis; de legatis 3, l. si quis, in principio; testamenti; and l. quod interim; de aditione legatorum; C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1, with similar authorities. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the judges of a certain society may adjudicate a case concerning a deposit made to the society itself, given a statute providing that no one other than their own judges may adjudicate cases of the society.
2. The interpretation of *l. si quis ex aliena*, D. de iudiciis.
3. A judgment on the incompetence of a judge becomes res judicata if no appeal was taken from it.
body: In the name of Christ. The acts having been examined, and the statute of the commune of Arezzo concerning those who speak out of turn having been viewed, because this question seems to have been debated for a long time, it is necessary to consider briefly whether the consuls were judges or not; and whether the pronouncement was valid, since they pronounced themselves to be judges, or not; and what is the law regarding the exception requested; and what is the law regarding the cause of nullity, and regarding the appeal interposed.

† And it appears first, that the sentence of the consuls was null due to the incompetence of the judge. C. si a non compe. iud. l. si. First, because the consuls were not judges of this lawsuit: because the statute makes them judges in certain cases, therefore it forbids it in others. ff. de iud. l. cum praetor. But among the enumerated cases, this case, namely, of money deposited or loaned to the partnership, is not included. For it is one thing to lend money, another to conduct commerce, especially since the statute speaks of movable goods. For he who lends or exposes [goods] is not said to exercise commerce, nor a market, which is derived from merchandise. C. de nundi. l. 1. C. de continentiis, et mercan. l. mercatus. And money is one thing, and merchandise another. ff. de contrahen. emp. l. 1. ff. de rer. perm. l. 1. de admi. tu. l. Titium §. altero. Nor does it seem that a loan or deposit descends from commerce: because it does not have its origin elsewhere, from which it does not depend on another contract or cause. C. si cer. pe. l. si exceptio. Nor does it seem that they could have pronounced upon the competence of judges against the tenor of the statute. ff. de excu. tu. l. qui testa. de tut. et cura. l. Seie egressae. Nor does it seem that the definitive sentence was valid: because it lacks the foundation of jurisdiction. de iniusto testa. l. si filio. §. quod si quis. C. de iur. om. iu. l. magistratus. in fi. and l. 1. cum si.

† Nor does it seem that one can say that he held [the case] on account of doubt. D. de iudicibus, l. Si quis ex aliena: because there was a doubt of fact, here there is not; rather, there was a fact, and it pertained to the jurisdiction of the consuls, because it arose from the case of the statute; and the ordered jurisdiction is certain. And when a judge exceeds the bounds of his jurisdiction, whether in person, place, time, or matter, the sentence is void by the law itself, as in the law Extra territorium, D. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum; C. de appellationibus, l. Ampliorem, §. Si; C. quando provocare non est necessarium, l. Cum cetera ratione, cum si. Since, therefore, the visible defect of nullity appears from the records, and through inspection of the statute, and such a visible defect is one that hinders execution, as in l. 2 and l. Edictum, D. de edicto; D. de appellationibus, l. Si expressum.

To the contrary, it seems that whether it be considered a loan or a deposit, as noted in D. si certum petatur, l. Cum quid, it was done as among merchants, and under its appellative name of merchants. Hence, the cause of the commerce exercised by this person, who bound himself with the faith of partnership, seems to have invalidated the entire transaction. C. ad Macedonianam, l. Si. For having accounts of receipts and payments with a certain merchant is a part and act of their commerce and trade. D. de instructionibus, l. Habebat; D. de exercitoribus, l. Si; D. quod cum eo, l. Si. Hence, this act pertains to commerce, in that it was done in contemplation of commerce and of the act itself. As in D. pro socio, l. Socium, qui in eo, §. Si; D. de fideiussoribus, l. Quaedam, §. Nummularios, and what is noted there; and in Auth. de fideiussoribus, §. Argentorum, and what is noted there. Moreover, the aforementioned money is contained under the name of movables, D. de verborum significatione, l. Mouentium. Otherwise it would follow that the said consuls could not have cognizance of the exchange of money, which is not true, unless another statute determines otherwise.

† Moreover, the judgment rendered on the competence of the judge has become res iudicata, because no appeal was taken from it, although it could have been appealed, as noted in the Authentica Habita, Codex, Ne filius pro patre. Therefore, the judgment cannot now be declared null, because the judge could have pronounced himself competent on account of the doubt, as stated in Digestum, Si quis in ius vocatus non ierit, l. 2. And such a judgment cannot be retracted by an appeal from the definitive sentence, as provided in Codex, De procuratoribus, l. Ita demum, because it is separated from the principal matter, as in Caput Ultimum, De appellationibus, Liber Sextus. Furthermore, I find that the parties consented to the judges and consented to the election of the merchants, which induces either a confession of jurisdiction or a tacit prorogation, as appears from the act performed on May 9. Hence, since the judgment subsequently followed, it must be held valid, according to Digestum, De iudicibus, l. 1, and Codex, Communia utriusque iudicii, l. 2. Furthermore, the matter was frequently and repeatedly examined and adjudicated by the consuls of the merchants, and it is presumed in favor of the sentence of such men, so often deliberated. This is supported by what is noted in Digestum, De evictionibus, l. Haeres, § 1. Moreover, it is not fitting for merchants of good faith to dispute on the subtleties of law, but to observe their agreements, as stated in Digestum, De manumissionibus, in l. Si fideiussori, § Quaedam. Hence, they cavil with an improper desire, as noted in Codex, De deposito, l. De fide, and De mutatione patriae professionis. And therefore, I, Baldus de Perusio, Doctor of Law, am of the opinion and advise, as the consuls of the merchants were of the opinion, that their sentence should be executed, notwithstanding the objections raised, which tend rather to quasi-perfidy than to good faith.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 2. Whether an heir who has not made an inventory is bound beyond the assets of the inheritance, both according to canon and civil law.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain man, Masius Vada, who in his will thus disposed, in all his other movable and immovable goods, etc., instituted his nephew Bartolomeo Pauli as his universal heir; and if the said Bartolomeo should die without legitimate children reaching the legitimate age of 25 years, he substituted for himself Lord Andrea Magis, Francis, and Lucanuci, and their descendants, in the portion of the testator’s houses, enclosures, and vineyards situated, etc., and they are bound to make, from the said inheritance and legacy, one seventh for his soul and those of his parents, for each year, consisting of one loaf and one penny for each poor person who shall come to that seventh; but in all his other goods he substituted for himself Matthew and Peter Bonandi, and Peter Lucannutii, in equal shares, and their descendants; and they are bound to make one seventh for each year, of one loaf and one penny for each poor person who shall come to the said seventh, for the soul of the said [testator], should he wish to receive it. And this, etc. Now the said Masius, the testator, has died, the said Bartolomeo, his nephew, being alive, and the heir, being under 25 years of age, having accepted the inheritance of the said Masius imprudently and without the benefit of inventory. Afterwards the said Bartolomeo died, leaving as his heirs Matthew and Peter Bonon. and Lucannutii, who are said to have been substituted to the said Bartolomeo by the said Masius. Now, on behalf of the Lord Bishop, it is said that the said sevenths ought to be made by the said heirs of the said Bartolomeo, and that the inheritance of the said Masius, although insolvent, pertains to them with the burden of the sevenths; because the said inheritance was accepted imprudently. On behalf of the said heirs of the said Bartolomeo, it is said that the said sevenths ought not to be made, because the said inheritance is insolvent, and because they, the heirs of the said Bartolomeo, being minors, on behalf of the said Bartolomeo, before he had reached the age of 25 years, could have obtained the benefit of restitution in integrum against the said imprudent acceptance made by the said Bartolomeo; and having obtained this benefit, they accepted the inheritance of the said Masius with the benefit of inventory. And although it is said on behalf of the Lord Bishop that the said heirs of the said Bartolomeo accepted the inheritance of the said Masius by virtue of the substitution made to them by the said Masius, this is not true; because it was not expedient for them to accept the said inheritance as substitutes, after they had been instituted by the said Bartolomeo, who was the heir of the said Masius in all his goods. Furthermore, it is said on behalf of the Lord Bishop that, even assuming that the said inventory made by the heirs is valid, it nevertheless does not prejudice the Bishop and the poor, who were summoned before the secular judge regarding the said inventory; and the said heirs say that, notwithstanding this, the inventory is valid; and that they are not bound to summon the Bishop and the poor to any other judge than the secular one. Now the question is, what is the law? In the name of Christ.

† On the aforementioned point, it must be said that, beyond the hereditary assets, the heir is not compelled by canon law, even if he has not made an inventory: as is noted in c. Quisque, de usura, lib. 6, and by Hostiensis in his Summa, de testamento, § 1, at the words “Item si bona.” But civil law formerly distinguished between debts and legacies. For debts were due in full, whereas legacies were due only according to the strength of the patrimony. C. de iure deliberandi, l. Si; § Si vero postquam, C. de legatis, l. Si universae. But according to the law of the Authenticae, no distinction is made between debts and legacies, because the law fictions that the inheritance was solvent, and fictions that the heir has defrauded it. Auth. de hereditate et falcidia, § Scimus. Provided that a minor has the benefit of restitution, eod. tit., § Pupillus; and ff. de auctoritate tutoris, l. Pen.; C. si quis ut se ab hereditate abstineat, l. Si. He may invoke either abstention or the making of an inventory, as is clear from the said laws. But by canon law, the heir is never bound, even if he does not make an inventory, except to the extent of the hereditary assets, as I have said above. But since we are here in the canonical forum, and in a case which pertains to the canonical forum, i.e., that of the bishop, canon law must be observed, as is noted in c. 1, de novo vi operis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When the substitute, upon whom a burden has been imposed, dies before the heir instituted, to whom the testator ordered that the burden be performed. And number 2.
body:
In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: A certain man named Paul Grandagni made his last will and testament, in which he disposed as follows: in all his other movable and immovable goods, etc., he instituted Bar. and Guadagnus as his universal heirs; but if there should be a son born posthumously to his wife Pacepta, if it be male, he instituted him as his universal heir; but if it be female, he left to her for her dowry c. pounds of denarii, ordering her to remain silent, etc. And if his aforementioned sons, or any of them, should die without a son or daughter, and with legitimate children not reaching the age of 25 years, he substituted another or others coming afterwards, not per capita, but per stirpes; and if all his sons should die without legitimate children of the said Massius, and if the said Massius should die without a son or daughter, or with legitimate children not reaching the age of 25 years, whoever should die without children, he ordered, willed, and commanded that from the said goods and inheritance one altar be preserved and made in the said church of the priests, in which altar the divine office be continuously celebrated for the soul of the said testator and his parents by one good and honest priest to be bound to the said altar by the discreet blood relatives of the said Massius and Paul, his brother.

Shortly after the death of the said testator, the said Guadagnus died intestate, the said Bart. remaining with the said Guadagnus, who had been instituted and mutually substituted. Afterwards, the said Massius, who had been substituted, died, the said Bart. remaining as instituted heir.

On behalf of the Lord Bishop, it is said that the said altar left by the said Paul ought to be established in the said church of the priests, since it is said that the condition of the said testament occurred after the death of the said Massius. On behalf of the heirs of the said Bart., however, it is said that the said altar ought not to be established, and that the condition of the said testament did not occur; rather, the substitution made concerning the said Massius did not take effect, since the said Massius, the last substitute, died before the said Bart., who was instituted, died; and thus the said inheritance did not come to him. And if it did not come to him, he could not transmit it to the altar. Now the question is asked: what is the law?

In the name of Christ. To me, regarding the aforementioned doubtful question...

† It appears that, since all have died, without regard to the order of death, the said altar ought to be established both on grounds of what is good and equitable and on the subtlety of law; because the testator wished the said altar to be made after the death of all, which case has occurred, albeit in a subsequent order of mortality. And I prove this thus: this testator made a substitution of the instituted heirs first among themselves; secondly, he substituted Massius to them; after the death of Massius, he commanded that the altar be constituted; hence, the burden of this constitution, which preceded Massius, falls back upon the instituted heirs after their death. C. de cad. tol. §. 2. and arg. de condi. et dem. l. Publius. §. 1. For it was not expressly enjoined upon Massius, but the burden was imposed impersonally. And thus it does not obstruct ff. de leg. 2. l. Celsus. §. quod alicuius. And it supports what we note ff. de cond. et dem. l. quae condi. in prin.

And although a burden imposed on the substitute does not appear to be imposed on the instituted heir, this is true unless, by way of caducity or quasi-caducity, the benefit from the caducity remains with the instituted heir, because that benefit then remains with the burden. § pro secundo of the same title. For in our case, the burden is imposed after the degree, and therefore it pertains to all. Argument: Codex, De libertate præstanda, l. 1. And although the substitution, as regards Massius, is in the case of caducity, it is not so as regards the altar: but contrary to the above, it seems to be a quasi-case. Digest, De militum substitutionibus, l. qui habebat, where, upon the substitution becoming caduc, the preliminary substitution expires along with the substitution of the substitution; but there is another case there, namely, the failure of the condition of a future substitution, as noted there by Sisto. Therefore, I rest on the above, by virtue of l. cohæredes in principio, Digest, De vulgari et pupillari substitutione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a substitution expires upon entry into the order of the Friars Minor.
2. Whether a fideicommissum can be claimed while the person who has entered a monastery is still alive.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain man named Pateranus de Matha made a will, in which he made such an institution and substitution: namely, in all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and actions, wherever they are and can be found, and could be in the future, he instituted the aforementioned Matthiolus, his brother, and John, son of the late Cole, once the flesh-and-blood brother of the said testator, as his universal heirs; and if the aforementioned heirs should all die without legitimate children reaching the age of 25 years, or whenever they should die without children, he substituted to himself the aforementioned monastery of St. Angel and the aforementioned hospital in equal portions. And this, etc. Now, the said testator having died, the said Matthiolus, his brother and heir, died; and the said John, his nephew and heir, survived. This John sold all the goods of the said inheritance; and after the sale, he entered religion, namely, the order of the Friars Minor, and there made profession, and lives. Now, on behalf of the said monastery of St. Angel, it is said that the said inheritance pertains to the said monastery together with the said hospital by virtue of the said substitution made in the said will by the said testator to the said monastery of St. Angel and the hospital. It is now asked, in what portion of the said goods does the said monastery succeed; and from whom, and how, and in what manner can the said monastery recover and claim the said goods, since it is said by the buyer of the aforementioned goods that the said goods ought not to be surrendered, and if surrendered, the price ought not to be lost, etc. In the name of Christ. Having seen the said point, I say

† Regarding the entry into the order of the Friars Minor, a substitution made for one entering does not expire; in which substitution pious places are substituted, as in the Authentica *De sanctissimis episcopis*, § *Sed hoc praesenti*.

But there is a doubt whether the fideicommissum could be claimed during the lifetime of this person who has entered religion: and it seems that it cannot, because natural death must be awaited. D. de iure fisci, l. Statius Florus; § Cornelia; gloss C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. Testatoris; and D. de verbis oblig., l. Ex ea parte, § Insulam. On the contrary, see that after the will is made, it is settled, because entry into the order of the Minor Friars is truly equivalent to natural death with regard to temporal goods; nor does it seem that any other death should be awaited, because the effect cannot be increased by natural death, arg. C. de episcopis et clericis, l. Deo nobis, and what is noted there; and l. Res, in principio; and what is noted in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, § Et quid sit tantum. It seems to me that entry into the order of the Minor Friars does not make the right of the purchaser caducous; rather, the purchaser may possess until such Minor Friar is living, arg. D. de legatis 2, l. Peto, § Praedium. And it supports what is noted by Dy. in the said § Cornelia. And it supports and argues from D. quorum bonorum hereditas peti possit, l. Si parte, § Si per fundum. For the act of the tutor, and the change of status of the author, does not prejudice the purchaser, to whom the right had been acquired. On the contrary, it supports: because the right of the author having ended by impossibility of law due to entry [into religion], the right of the successor seems to have ended. D. de pignoribus, l. Vetus. But there the dominion was still with the author, and the same applies to the right of another; and therefore, the principal being removed, the accessory is removed. D. de transactionibus, l. Et post, § 1. And it supports that the death of the Minor Friar must be awaited, although the Minor Friar and the order possess nothing. D. de legatis 2, l. Cum pater, § Ab instituto in ratione sui. Likewise, the same law, § Hereditas; and C. de his qui in potestate sunt, l. Si. For the question is resolved in l. Si, in fine, C. communia de legatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How much of his estate a person who has reached puberty may dispose of, if he and four brothers have mutually substituted for one another, and two of them have died while still in pupillary age.
2. An heir instituted in a specific thing, or in a quantity, to whom transmission may occur.
3. Whether a universal substitution extinguishes the right of legacies.
4. A substitution cannot be made for a person who has reached puberty with respect to the legitime.
body: In the name of Christ. It is said by Nicolutius of Fabriano, because it is alleged that the said Nicolutius had five children, namely: Vannes, Florucia, Lisa, Benedicta, and Angelucia; and that after the death of the testator, first Angelucia died in pupillary age, secondly Vannes in pupillary age, thirdly Benedicta, being of age, who left her rights to her husband; and it is asked, what the said husband of the said lady Benedicta ought to have, and in what he succeeds the said lady Benedicta in the person of the said lady Benedicta? It must be considered that the testator provided for the said Benedicta in three ways, namely: by instituting her to 200 pounds in possessions and the like, secondly by substituting the sisters, and thirdly by substituting her brother among others.

† As to the first point, there is no doubt that Benedicta ought to have 200 pounds in this manner. And if she had them, and so forth, it is well. But if she did not have them, she would have transmitted her right, and it is scarcely transmissible. C. de caducis tollendis, §. si autem, in the newest compilation. For an institution in a certain thing, or in a quantity, because it does not require acceptance, such an institution by the force of law receives transmission, like a simple legacy, as C. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quotiens; ff. de legatis secundis, l. simplex, §. pro parte. For the right of entering upon the inheritance consists in the universal heir: not in the heir in a certain thing: unless his institution were extended to the whole. ff. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. 1, §. si ex fundo; and l. ex facto proponebatur. And especially the said institution receives transmission to an instituted son, as l. ex militari, §. fin.; cum l. se. de militum testamento; de stipulationibus servorum, l. liber homo, §. fin.; and no. in l. apud hostes, cum si.

† As to the second point, concerning the substitution made in favor of the daughters, there is doubt whether Florutia is included in the said substitution: for the said Florutia was separated from her sisters, and a separate disposition was made regarding her; hence, in that mutual or reciprocal substitution, she does not appear to be included, neither in the active nor in the passive substitution, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *Cohaeredi*, § *Qui discretas*, unless in a certain order, namely, so that those first joined seem to be the substitutes. But the contrary view seems correct, because this substitution is derived from the other party, namely, from the person to whom the substitution is made; for it states, “and if any,” etc., from every respect of those who are substituted; and the words are clear, and from the words the intention is certain, as stated in the Digest, *de legibus tertio*, law *Ille aut ille*, § 1, *Unde*. The section *Qui discretas* speaks in cases of doubt; but where there is certainty, there is no room for conjecture, as stated in the Digest, *de verborum obligationibus*, law *Continuus*, § *Cum ita*. Here, however, there is certainty, because the testator’s language and the parity of affection seem to extend to all. I do not see a certain intent expressed by ambiguous words. For here the language can express two types: first, that the wording of the causes refers to the nearest; another way, that it refers even to those more remote; and this in a twofold manner: first, equally; second, in a certain order, so that joint institutions take precedence in the substitution, as if the substitution succeeds in the place of a certain order of accrual. This I hold to be true, saving the advice of a sounder opinion according to § *Qui discretas*. From this it appears that Florutia does not form a part with her sisters, because she does not concur with them. It follows, therefore, that Vannes succeeded to the part of Angelutia for one-half, and Lisa and Benedicta each for one-quarter. Since this succession is by a singular title, and of one’s own, and of a necessary heir, it admits of transmission, as stated in the Digest, *de vulgari substitutione*, law *Sed si plures*, § *Quos possum*; and see the Code, *de iure deliberandi*, law *Quidam elogio*; and the Digest, *de acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Qui patri*, etc.

As to the third point, concerning the substitution made in favor of Vannes, in this all the daughters are equally separated in fact and in words, and the language is universal; and therefore Vannes succeeded to all the sisters in one-third; and this also admits of transmission. Since, therefore, three sisters survived, each succeeds to one-third of the third. Code, *de impuberibus et aliis substitutis*, law *Si*.

But it is doubtful whether a universal substitution extinguishes the right of legacies; and it seems that it does so in the same person. D. 34, 1, *licet Imperator*; and what is said there by Dy. I hold the contrary: because a universal fideicommissary substitution does not extinguish the right of legacies as to those portions which flow to others, D. 44, 3, *quinquaginta*; D. 34, 4, *cum sit institutio in parte*, which does not cut off prelegata, D. 35, 1, *et quid totum*; D. 35, 2, *miles*, § *si*. Behold, therefore, how Benedicta succeeded under the several provisions. It remains to be seen, when she has died, what belongs to the substitutes by virtue of the substitution made in her favor. For that which does not belong to them remains to her husband as heir.

And I premise that, since the said Benedicta died while still a pubes, she could not be substituted in her legitima, nor by a fideicommissary substitution, as is known from C. de inoff. test., l. ex tribus; l. quam in prioribus; and l. sanctius. However, as to what she had above the legitima, this devolves to the substitutes, and the laws speaking of two quarters have no place here: because the said Benedicta was not a universal heir, but the legitima is due to the son, even if he is not a universal heir. In Aut. ut cum de appe. cogno., §. aliud quoque capitulum; ff. ad trebell., l. 1, §. inde Neratius; ff. ad l. Falc., l. lex Falcidia, §. nunquam. And therefore this is the conclusion: that the husband of the said Benedicta must have the legitima by right of the person of the said Benedicta. The remainder is to be adjudged to the substitutes: because the said daughters had a substitution in the first institution, and also afterwards in the universal one. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a concession made by a bishop without the consent of the chapter and of those whose interest is affected is valid? And what is the rule regarding a legate? See no. 2.
body: In the name of Christ. Napoleon, legate of the Apostolic See, at the instance of the Bishop of Camerino, granted and gave the church of Saint Lucy of Fabriano in the diocese of Camerino, together with its tithes, cemetery, courtyards, gardens, and other things adjacent to that church, to the prior and convent of the house of the Friars Preachers of Fabriano; and he did this both in the name and on behalf of the said Lord Bishop, and by whatever other authority he held. However, the will or ratification of a certain Abbot and chapter, to whom the said church of Saint Lucy was subject, did not accede to this grant. After the said Friars Preachers had continuously held the said church for a period of forty-four years, or thereabouts, now the Abbot and chapter of the said place wish to consent; and the Bishop of Camerino, with his chapter, wishes to confirm and, insofar as it may be expedient, to grant anew the said church of Saint Lucy to the said place and convent of the Friars Preachers. The question now arises whether the aforementioned acts suffice for the said Friars Preachers, or not? On these points

† I, the undersigned, having been consulted, say that the concession made by the authority of the bishop did not hold from the beginning for two reasons. First, because the consent of his chapter did not intervene, as in Extra, De donationibus, c. Pastoralis, and at the end thereof. Second, because the consent of those whose interest is involved did not intervene, which is required in such a perpetual concession, as is fully noted in cap. 1, De rerum permutatione, lib. 6, and is proved by many laws.

But it must be considered whether the legate a latere could have done this, or not, in the matter of the legation. And it seems that he could not, to the prejudice of the said Abbot, as in c. Ultro, De confirmatione utili vel inutili; ff. Quod vi aut clam, l. Prohiberem, § Plane. And because, although he is a legate a latere, he nevertheless cannot, upon viewing the inquisition, confer the right of one and give it to another; nor can he transfer possession pertaining to one church to another. I say this with regard to non-sacred things, which here did not accede to the concession, such as orchards. To the contrary, it seems that the legate could have done this, even to the prejudice of the diocesan bishop, since the diocesan bishop granted it, as noted in Speculum, tit. 2, § Nunc ostendendum, ver. Quarto innuit. This confirms the aforementioned, and ancient possession, as in Extra, De praescriptionibus, c. De quarta, Quid sint. I say that if a new concession of the lord bishop and chapter intervenes, and the express consent of the Abbot and his chapter accedes today, there is no doubt that the concession of the church and cemetery will be valid and will obtain full force, as is proved in the said c. Pastoralis and c. Inter deleatur. And it supports what is noted in Extra, De prebendis, c. De monachis; and what is read and noted in c. Si una, De rebus ecclesiasticis non alienandis, in the gloss beginning Non est iste casus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The solemnity required in the delict of a corporation.
2. Solemnity is not presumed from the statement of a witness.
3. Witnesses testifying to public knowledge state that they add the reason through bodily sense.
4. A witness, in that which he has the greatest right, or which consists in the art of law, must testify specifically by individual causes, not implicitly.
body: In the name of Christ. This is a common opinion, and the community of the Castle of Montis Fortini, regarding the reception of certain individuals from the said Castle who are said to be excommunicated, formulated by the most learned man, Lord Marcus: and having considered the content of the inquiry: and having seen the statements of the witnesses: and having seen the constitution of Lord Bertrand: and that of Lord Egidius: it is asked, whether the condemnatory sentence should be followed, or rather the absolving one?

And it appears first that the condemnatory sentence should be followed: because the harboring has been proven by witnesses testifying from what they saw; knowledge seems to be proven by witnesses who state that their bans were publicly notorious; and this seems sufficient, as noted in l. 1, ff. de receptato. And it supports c. 1, de postul. praelatorum. To the same effect is C. de testi. l. 1, ff. ad mace. l. 4, C. ad mace. l. Zenodorus. For each person is presumed to be such as he is commonly reputed to be. C. de seruis expor. l. moueor. extra de probat. c. qui tuas. To the contrary it appears: because the substantial elements have not been proven. This is shown thus: for in order that a corporation may commit a crime in acting, it is required that it assemble at the sound of a trumpet, or bell, or in some other customary manner, and proceed to commit the offense after deliberate consultation; and thus a certain solemnity is required in the crime of a corporation, as noted in ff. de reg. iu. l. alius, §. refertur. ff. quod metus causa. l. metum, §. animaduertendum. But this has not been proven by witnesses.

† Nor is it presumed on behalf of the said witness regarding solemnity, as noted in C. de usuris, l. 1. Nor does it suffice that he stated implicitly that the common council and the universitas received it; for this cannot be the case unless the aforementioned form, which is required by law, was observed. And those matters which are of law are not proven unless witnesses specifically testify to the fact from which that may be inferred, as noted by Innocentius in Extra de testibus, c. Cum causam. The universitas holds the place of twenty persons, ff. de fideiussoribus, l. Mortuo, when it is legitimately assembled; otherwise, it cannot commit a delict, nor contract, nor bind itself, C. de legatis, l. Si, li. 10; C. de venditionibus rerum civicarum, l. Si, cum si. Secondly, this is proven because knowledge was not established, namely that the universitas knew as a universitas. For, in order that the universitas may be deemed to know, it is necessary that notice was given to it in chapter, or by argument. Nor even does the singular knowledge of the citizens of the city suffice, if it is not in the form of the universitas, as noted in ff. de regulis iuris, l. Non potest dolo carere. Or at least the Queen of the City or of the Territory ought to have known, l. 1, in fine, ff. de libellis universitatis. But nothing has been proven which includes knowledge; for neither was the ban exhibited, nor was it published there by the voice of a herald, ff. de deposito, l. Si quis, in fine; de electionibus, c. Causam, in cle.

Thirdly, it is proven, because the witnesses who speak of public knowledge do not add a reason based on bodily sense, as they ought, as in D. de testamento (29.1), l. qui testat., §. si; and noted in C. de testamento (6.23), l. te.; D. de aqua pluviae arcendae (39.3), l. 3, §. 1. Indeed, they do not even speak of public knowledge, but of private knowledge, if one examines it closely. Fourthly, it is proven, because by the constitution of Lord Egidius a certain form of denunciation to be made was added: this denunciation is of the order and form of the new law, from which one must not deviate, as in D. de adulteriis (48.5), l. denuntia; for this is to allege, but not to prove; therefore, and C. de institutionibus (6.24), l. habeat; when the action of peculium is [invoked], Annaeus in l. quaesitum; and this is most aptly supported by D. de incendio, ruina, et naufragio (9.5), l. ne quid in primo, and §. de his autem. Moreover, where one law establishes a form, another law not prefixed is not to be followed; the new law is to be followed, as noted in D. de iustitia et iure (1.1), l. ius civile; D. ad municipalia (50.4), l. constitutio; in the Authenticum, ut factae novae constitutiones, in rubric and black; and the omission of mode or form, not only in a penal act, but also in a favorable act, impedes the legal disposition, as in D. de verbis obligatorum (45.1), l. qui Romae, §. Flavius Hermes. From these it seems to be concluded that what ought to be proven is not proven by the statements of the witnesses. But if bans and notification of the ban made to the said accused community by instruments were produced, then the community would rightly be in a case of condemnation; but if nothing else is proven than what the said witnesses prove, it is a case of absolution; because neither in the form of the universitas is it proven that it received [the accused]; nor that it knew as a universitas; nor that it was named or certified. D. de actione empti (19.1), l. 1, §. 1. For no one is presumed to be banned, D. de probationibus (22.3), l. ab ea parte. And the knowledge of Titius and Seius and of several individuals is singular knowledge, and not universal, D. de iniuriis (47.10), l. si plures. And especially indulgence ought to be shown to the fatherland, which is bound by paternal affection, arg. D. de receptis (47.15), l. si. And if it is said that the witnesses say that the council received [the accused] as such, therefore as such, Ramponus: to this it is adapted that the proof is adapted to that to which the bodily sense, by which the witness testifies, is adapted; unless the proper sense, of which the witness here testifies, is not such a sense by which such knowledge is had. Moreover, the witness does not say of which council. And if there are several councils in such a county, it is not sufficient that even the council having authority to bind, even by way of delict, D. de pactis conventis (2.14), l. 1, §. 1. And the doubtful statement of the witness in fact does not prove, D. de probationibus (22.3), c. in praesentia. And if it is said that the witnesses say that they were received by the community and universitas, and that they saw it, I answer that they ought to have said more, namely, to specify how they knew that the universitas did this as a universitas; otherwise, that if Titius and Seius delayed in the castle.

† For where that which must be proved has the greatest weight of law and consists in the art of law, the witness must testify specifically according to each individual cause, not implicitly and by consent, as noted by Innocentius in the cited chapter *Cum causam*. This is because the witness could be deceived in that which pertains to law; otherwise, he would be more a judge than a witness. Moreover, being banned and not being banned, insofar as it is a quality inherent in the person, does not consist in something visible against one’s will, but in something invisible. Codex, *De edicto diui Adriani*, l. 2. Hence ignorance is presumed, which ought not to be punished. Codex, *De seruis fugitiuis*, l. *Quicunque*; Codex, *De tabulis*, l. *Generaliter*. This applies especially in the case of a university. Codex, *De re militari*, l. *Tam collatores*; Digest, *De decretis ab ordine faciendis*, l. *Si*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that the property of a person convicted of homicide is to be applied partly to the fisc and partly to the heir of the deceased, whether emphyteutic property of the church is subject to confiscation and application to the respective shares.
2. Banished persons are not truly deported.
3. The fisc is not properly an heir.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain statute in effect states that the goods of a person condemned for homicide shall be applied partly to the treasury and partly to the heirs of the deceased.

† It is asked whether the emphyteutic goods of a murderer come to be confiscated or applied [to the fiscus] in this manner? And I speak of an emphyteusis granted by the Church to a certain class of persons up to the third generation. And this question is quite ancient: and there are diverse opinions. Some said that the goods of this emphyteuta can be confiscated and applied to another on account of the delict of the emphyteuta: as in D. de damno infecto, l. si finita; §. si de vectigalibus supports what is not in Speculum, de prebendis, §. 1, ver. 40, quaeritur. And this opinion is confirmed because this alienation is legally necessary, hence it does not seem prohibited. D. familiae erciscundae, l. alienationes. Moreover, it is a universal alienation: hence it passes with the universality. D. de acquirenda re donatione, l. quemadmodum; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis. To the same effect, because, granted that as regards the inseparable emphyteusis no transfer takes place, it ought to take place as regards the benefit and the annual rent. D. de periculis et commodis rei venditae, l. necessario, §. fin.; D. de re iudicata, l. commodis; Extravagantes, de sequestro, c. pervenit. For in the case of a judgment, the annual rents can be seized, although the principal body of the thing itself cannot be alienated. Others distinguished: either it is an emphyteusis of the Church; and this cannot be applied to the fiscus, nor to another on account of the maleficium of the emphyteuta. Hence, although the emphyteuta falls from his right, it is consolidated to the Church; but it is not alienated, as in Auth. de alienatione emphyteuticorum, §. 1. Let it therefore be in principle a penalty, but not a transfer. And thus they understand what is not in C. unde vi, l. si quis in tanta. Or it is an emphyteusis of a private person; and then either it is transmissible to any heir, and it passes to the fiscus, or to his own heirs, and then it does not pass to the fiscus; but it reverts to the lord. And the reason is that the fiscus is in the place of an extraneous heir. Solus, de matrimonio, l. si constante, §. fin.; not in the place of his own heir, as is noted in l. 2, D. de interdictis et relegationibus. And this is the opinion of my teacher, namely, Master Bartolus in §. si de vectigalibus. According to this opinion, the emphyteusis of a banished person returns to the Church, not to the fiscus, nor to the heir of the slain. To this effect it is that this emphyteusis is granted to a certain class of persons almost as a privilege for them: therefore it can pass to another person under no title, neither the thing nor the right; because all other persons seem prohibited. C. ne res divini vel templi, l. universas; D. de legatis 2, l. cum patronus; l. cum pater, §. libertis. And he who cannot alienate ought to take care that it is not alienated. Per me, D. de verbis obligatis, l. si quis seya. Hence the argument from legal alienation ceases here. And the foregoing are confirmed because a person banished to death is held as dead and as deported, as in §. relegati, in the glossa ordinaria and vulgaris. But by death it returns to the Church if there are no children, and D. de capite diminuto, l. tutelae, §. pen., supports this, where it is said that he goes into exile naked; at least as regards the goods of his territory, he ought to be held as deported.

† Although those under ban are not truly deported, because the governors do not have the right to deport, nevertheless, since they are stripped of all their goods, they are regarded as deported with respect to property, although not with respect to diminution of status; and the same judgment applies to similar cases. C. de insti. et subs. l. si iure. Nor does it follow from de iure fisci. l. statius florus. §. Corneli., because with respect to fulfilling a condition he is not considered dead, as stated there. And therefore the fisc does not restore before natural death, but restores afterwards, because he is not regarded as a son; but with respect to losing his goods he is considered dead.

† and the fiscus [treasury] stands in the place of the heir. C. ad l. iu. de vi. l. tutoris. Nevertheless, it is not properly an heir: because a deportatus [person sentenced to deportation] has no heir. It supports what we have stated. ff. de noua. l. nouatio. And by this, a response is given to that which is said, namely that confiscation is useful for the purpose of perception, because, the emphyteusis being extinguished, no perception is due to the emphyteuta: therefore, neither to anyone else in his person. ff. de leg. 2. l. peto. §. praedium. ff. de pi. l. lex uectigalis. Moreover, an alienation of revenues without limitation of term and time is called a certain alienation of the thing itself. ff. de superficie. l. 1. §. quod ait. But this would be done without limitation of time; therefore, it cannot be done. C. de dona. l. sancimus. ad finem. And what is noted by Cynus. de leg. 2. l. eo. §. instrumento. Furthermore, the instrument in which the form of the said emphyteusis resides contains within itself a general pact concerning true alienation, and it is general as regards persons and species of alienations: and therefore it has a general meaning. C. de reb. eccl. non alienan. l. fi. And whenever this pact is appended, no kind of transaction is permitted, in Auth. de alie. emphyteu. §. sancimus. Concluding, I do not think that in the said confiscation and application to be made to the heirs of the slain, the said emphyteutic goods should devolve. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On what grounds is an arrest rendered void? And what requirements must be met for a person to be arrested as suspect?
2. A person is not deemed suspect if he owns immovable property elsewhere in a nearby place.
3. Suspicion of flight is not proven by oath.
4. It must be proven by witnesses, not by oath alone, that someone is insolvent or verging on poverty.
5. Flight is not proven by oath.
6. An oath cannot be tendered when the opposing party has not been summoned.
7. In civil law, it is not found that a person may be arrested for a civil debt or judgment, unless he is in contempt.
8. The case is concluded by the advice of a learned jurist.
9. Whether an arrest may be granted by agreement.
10. A person who has a surety is not judged suspect.
body: In the name of Christ. For there is no need to color the truth, since it stands alone; therefore, assuming the clarity of the factual truth, I shall briefly proceed to the legal arguments. The issue in the case appears to be as follows, speaking concisely: because John and Vannucius bound themselves jointly and severally on account of the purchase of Zuccoco, a legal proceeding was initiated. It is true that this does not appear otherwise, except by virtue of a general citation, whereby the aforementioned John was to appear to answer according to law. Furthermore, this plaintiff obtained a guarantee from the goods of the said John, wishing to be secured that he would be subject to seizure, as stated in the document. Then, the action against the said John was transferred to a new forum, namely to the court of Perugia. While the litigation was pending and after the exceptions had been examined, the judge granted him a sentence, or rather granted it once and subsequently renewed the order for arrest, whereupon the arrest followed. Now the question arises: since there is doubt as to whether he was lawfully arrested, what is the law? And a wise man does not need it to be alleged to him, because the aforementioned issue resolves the question; nevertheless, because custom must be observed,

I state that this arrest was issued irregularly and in a case not previously stipulated; and therefore I conclude that the arrested party ought to be released. And this, first, due to a defect of jurisdiction; second, due to a defect in the alleged suspicion; third, due to the contrary truth of the alleged suspicion being infringed; fourth, due to a defect of proof; fifth, due to disordered procedure; sixth, due to several other reasons supporting this party.

And first I argue: this proceeding was commenced in Camerino; therefore, it must be concluded there. D. de iudicibus, l. Ubi ceptum. For even by a general citation is a proceeding begun. C. de annalibus exceptionibus, l. Si. Unless the plaintiff afterwards pursued only another species, as is noted there, which he did not do here; rather, he is punished, because he drags the same defendant to various places out of malice. C. de assertionibus tollendis, l. 1, in fine. And note this against the arrest, as is now objected here, because we are in the principle, since this arrest was not made as part of the proceeding, but extrinsically for an alleged cause, not only unproven, but untrue.

To the same effect: because since the plaintiff chose one place for judgment, he cannot afterwards vary. D. de eo quod certo loco, l. Non utique, where it is expressly stated. It supports what is noted in a similar authority, Habita, cum si. Nor does it avail if it is said that the instance in Camerino was finished; because in the lands of the Church, an instance is not finished by a three-year period. X. de iudicibus, c. Significantibus. And because the cause was not litis contestata, as in l. Properandum.

From the second I argue: the suspicion was not put forward, nor was it duly alleged, for the said debtor was of the same condition at the beginning of the obligation as at the time of the license; namely, a foreigner, and not having domicile in Perugia. Since therefore the condition has not changed in Perugia, where he is arrested, he cannot be said to be suspect there. D. de privatis creditoribus, l. Si creditores, where it is expressly stated. D. ut ius possidendi, l. Si is, a quo, §. Si, cum l. Se, and there by Dy. So. Ma. l. Si constante, in principio, per doc. Also, being a foreigner does not thereby make one suspect. D. de iudicibus, l. Si haeres absens, §. Si. For he who contracted with such a person from the beginning seems to have approved him as suitable. D. de manumis, l. Inter eas, §. Abesse. D. de fideiussoribus, l. Qui satisdare. Since therefore no new cause of suspicion was alleged, the suspicion was not duly alleged, nor even correctly. D. de re iudicata, l. Qui cum alio. To the same effect, because the plaintiff did not allege that this man did not possess immovables, but said he did not possess them in Perugia; and thus he restricted himself to a certain place,

† But he is not considered suspect if he possesses property elsewhere in a neighboring place, such as the territory of Camerino. This is supported by the rule on damage by infection, l. 4, § si tam vicinum. And thus hold Petrus and Cynus. Otherwise, every newcomer would be suspect everywhere, except in the place of his domicile; and everywhere could his arrest be initiated without the case being examined, which is absurd and ridiculous. From the third point, I say that the allegation of suspicion is not based on truth: for it is established that in the place of contract and domicile, namely Camerino, he possesses immovable property, and the plaintiff has received a leasehold from him; and since the pledge binds for the entire debt, the pledge is presumed sufficient unless the contrary is proven. D. de re iudicata, l. a diuo pio, § si pignori. Behold, that it does not rest on truth from the very facts. Moreover, it does not rest on truth from the person: for it is established that this man was apprehended in court through his own procurator, who was present and residing in the city, after the compromise had been made long after the oath, which was that he was a fugitive and about to flee; he was convicted of perjury by the contrary fact, and truth opposes standing by such an oath. C. de re creditis, l. fi. It supports what is noted in D. de infa, l. Lucius. And although many things are said fabulously about this perjury, one must not deviate from the path of the law.

† From the fourth point, I say that suspicion is not proved by oath, nor could it be deferred when the opposing party has not been cited. Moreover, I prove this because an oath alone is not sufficient to prove that which causes great prejudice, unless it is otherwise fully proved: as in the laws *In bonae fidei* and *Admonendi*. And even in summary proceedings, full proof must be made, that is, by witnesses and instruments: as in law 1, § *Si ea*, *De ventre in possessionem mittendo*. But the arrest of a person is of great prejudice, and greater than the seizure of property: as in the Code, *Ne filius pro patre*, and the constitution *Et omnimodo*. Therefore, it cannot be done on the basis of an oath alone. This is supported by chapter *Legitima*, *De appellationibus*, Book 6. For it is not sufficient that the party suspects, but the judge himself must have at least some indications of flight regarding the suspicion: Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Cum probatio*; and Digest, *De edicto edicto*, law *Quaero*, in the principal part. Likewise, to depart from the common and absolute course of judicial proceedings, an oath is not sufficient, as noted in Digest, *De minoribus*, law 3, § 2.

† It also happens that the fact that someone is not solvent, or is verging on indigence, must be proved by witnesses, as in no. ff. qui satis. cog. l. si vero. §. j. ff. de magist. conuen. l. 1. §. proba. C. quoniam fiscus, vel priuatus. l. 2. C. de iure dot. l. vbi adhuc. non solo iuramento. ff. de excu. tut. l. paupertas. per lac.
† Likewise, to flee is a fraud, which is not proven by oath. See the note in l. 3, § 2, de minoribus.

† That an oath could not even be tendered without the party being cited, is proven in each case. D. de re iudicata and de adoptionibus, l. nam ita divus; and C. de testibus, l. si quinque. But if it does not apply, §. a Barbaris, because there it speaks of a certain oath of excuse or purgation, not of an oath of proof. Moreover, there were indications in favor of the person to whom it was tendered. S. ex qualitate praecedentis iuris. Furthermore, it does not apply to ad exhibendum, l. thesaurus, because there it concerns preparatory matters and those which are of slight prejudice; but standing in bonds is a matter of prejudice and infamy. Furthermore, it does not apply to §. sufficit, because there it speaks of proof of an impediment according to the understanding of Jacobus. Hence the truth is that from the order of law one should not depart by means of the plaintiff’s oath alone; and this is confirmed by the statute which tenders an oath to a certain class of persons, namely, a citizen of the county and one dwelling familiarly there; hence to deny it to others appears to be that which is distributively granted to some as a prerogative. D. de legibus 2, l. cum patronus; D. de iudicibus, l. cum praetor. For when an oath is chosen for a certain person, one does not depart from the person. C. de rebus creditis, l. generaliter; and de dote praelegata, l. Theopompus. Another statute on this matter speaks negatively; and therefore it supports the proposition, rather than opposes it. And if it is said that it contains an implicit affirmative by contrary reasoning, I answer that this argument is not taken from a statute where another statute expressly disposes the opposite, as noted in C. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. cum patrem; and one statute must be understood according to the limitation of another. D. de legibus, l. non est novum and l. sed et postea, and there it is noted from the fifth point. From the disordered procedure it appears that execution was carried out before the debt was liquidated; and while an exception was pending; and before the judge’s pronouncement on the debt; and thus the procedure was wrongly conducted. D. quod metus causa, l. si, in fine; C. de pactis, l. si pacto, quo poenam, in fine. And it is expressly stated in D. de re iudicata, l. si cum nulla. And if it is said that he was not seized for payment, because this cannot be done except in the case of a judgment debt, but for security to desist, see l. sciendum.

I answer that, for this security, there is no place for personal detention: because it is not found in civil law that anyone can be taken into custody for a private debt, or to stand trial, unless he is contumacious, as in the law *Consentaneum*; or unless someone has been condemned, as in law 1, *Qui bona* [creditoris] possidere. And neither of these is the case here: because here security was never requested. Law *Iam tamen*, section *Nunc videamus*, Digest, *De iudiciis solutis*. And the case proceeded to peremptory exceptions, without security being requested: hence it cannot be done in this manner. Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Pomponius*, section *Rati*. Moreover, since the creditor has resorted to the pledge, and has chosen this path, this possession serves in lieu of security. *Ad Carbo*, law *De bonis*, section *Quae pupillo*, where it is expressly stated. This is not obstructed by what is noted in law *Si*, Code, *De feriis*; because the father’s response follows from the foregoing. For where flight is established in the manner it ought to be established, and the debt is clear in the manner it ought to be clear, holidays cannot be alleged; at least not so as to exempt one from giving security to stand trial during a judicial time. Thus says the gloss there. But here the aforementioned matters are not established; rather, the matter is sub judice as to whether anything is owed, and nothing has been alleged regarding flight, nor does it contain the truth of the fact. From chapter 6 and lastly, thus, this person is defended by a legitimate procurator admitted and legitimated. Law *Vita quos*, section *Si alieno*, Digest, *De damno infecto*. Therefore, he cannot be personally arrested. Digest, *De in ius vocando*, law *Neque impuberes*, section *Si*, where it is expressly stated. Furthermore, the plaintiff chose, as I said, the path of providing for himself through the seizure of pledges: therefore, he cannot resort to extraordinary personal arrest, nor revert to it, as in law *Si*, Code, *De pacis conventionibus*, *Confectum*, *Super qua non contumax*. And it supports this, Code, *De curatore furiosi*, law *Cui bonis*, which works very well if understood correctly. Furthermore, the arrest proceeded against one who did not confess and was not joined: therefore, and so, law 1, Code, *De prohibita sequestratione*, and what is noted in law *Prolatam*, and in chapter *Ecclesiae sanctae Mariae*, *De constitutionibus*. Furthermore, judgment should have been pronounced first on the exception: for it is perverse to compel before discussion, and to execute before pronouncement. And it benefits from chapter *Exhibeatur*, Extra, *De iudiciis*, and the judge sitting on the tribunal in the place of the elders. And nothing of these things was done here, which is worse than a delay pending, and a term extended, contrary to law *Si pars*, and contrary to law *A praecedentis*. And it is strange that there is doubt about this among the wise in law, and more so, because even assuming that arrest could be initiated, in execution the arrest should have been justified by subsequent fact. From what is noted, *Operis novi nuntiatio*, law *De pupillo*, section *Meminisse*. And this was by no means done here: nor is anything proven regarding suspicion. It supports what is noted, Institutes, *Qui modis in possessionem*, section *Semel*, and law 3, section *Pe*, Digest, *De bonis possidendis*, Code, *Quorum bonorum*, law 1.

† rather, it has been concluded in the case by the opinion of a learned jurist. C. de dila. l. cum a nobis. C. de relatio. l. 1. Therefore, he who has been captured in a disgraceful manner must be released, de ver. sig. l. qui neque frequenter. and there, note.

But a certain person wishes to defend this matter, saying that capture and seizure of a free man are lawful by virtue of a pact, without any citation or legal process, which is ridiculous, because what is done by a judge must be done in accordance with the order of law, which cannot be set aside, since it pertains to the authority of the law, not to the will and power of the parties, as stated in § sed quia veremur and the glosses thereon, de officio delegati, in the title de causis. Moreover, a pact must be interpreted and understood in a civil manner, as in ff. de servitutibus, l. si cui, and in the rubric seruato ordine iuris, de rescriptis, c. cum causam, according to Innocentius and Compostella. Furthermore, it is not lawful to seize a free man by virtue of a pact, as in l. 2, de libero homine exhibendo, according to Dyther and all the authorities, de regulis iuris, l. non est singulis. For the capture of a person is an exercise of mere imperial power in the case of a free man; in the case of a slave, it is different, as in l. qui furem and l. penultima, de conditionibus ob causam. And it is clear even to the blind that mere imperial power cannot be conferred by a pact of private individuals. Moreover, this course was not pursued here; rather, the judicial process was followed, and one cannot depart from the form of judicial proceedings, as in de rescriptis, c. cum dilecta, and the glosses thereon, de verborum significatione, l. saepe, in the Clementines. Furthermore, even if it were lawful for a private individual, it would not be lawful for a judge, as noted in l. 2, C. de iure emphyteutici, because he acts as a judge, not as a party, and thus the objection based on § si arbiter does not apply. Moreover, it is established there that there was flight, whereas here there is no such debt. From the foregoing, the truth is apparent to any good and expert man. Furthermore, beyond all the above, it is to be noted that when two persons are bound, even if one is solvent, if the other is also solvent, this suffices, since they are deemed to have given surety for each other, as noted in l. vir uxori, § final.

And thus he is not judged suspect, who has a surety. L. Si fideiussor, §. Si, Qui satis cog. and De tut. et cur. datis ab his. L. Romanus Paulus. And he acts well in the reason of his own case. FF. De verb. oblig. L. Si stipulatus, §. Possum, in fine. §. It is so in our question. The gloss on L. Si constan. supports this, if the reason for the gloss’s statement is rightly weighed. Moreover, it was obtained by concealment from the praetor: because no mention was made of the proceedings, and of the tenure accepted at Camerino; which, if he had done, the prudent judge ought first to have examined the tenure of Valentia. Therefore, etc. L. I, §. Haec verba, and L. Cum no., §. Subuentum, De rescriptis. Let him who must see the truth of the letters see it; he who does not wish to see, will not see. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A testament in which a daughter in power is neither instituted as heir nor disinherited is void by operation of law; but then the codicillary clause may have some effect.
2. When it is necessary to cite a party in the exemplification.
body: In the name of Christ. A legal opinion is requested, which is as follows: A general compromise has been made between Lady Tunitia, daughter of Lord Fran. Centius of Orto, Vicar of Lord Egidius, on one part, and Jac. Io. on the other part, in favor of Lord Oliver as arbitrator: who may adjudicate both on matters of law and fact, and likewise on matters of law alone; whereas Lady Tunitia claims to be the heir of her father by intestate succession. Jac. claims to be the heir by testament, producing simply a certain copy of a certain testament, which is sent to you, Lady Consultant, and certain statutes of the City of Orto, which are also sent to you: together with articles of proof regarding the constitution of the province of Patrimonio concerning approval, and a certain confession made by the said Jac. with the consent of his curator, because the defense of the truth is before the aforementioned arbitrator. Now, having examined the aforementioned documents, the following questions are asked in order: First, whether the said testament is null due to the preterition of this daughter, Lady Tunitia, who is under paternal power; Second, whether the said testament is validated by any statute, which I send to you, since the said statutes are found to provide for the exclusion of a daughter when there is a son of the testator, or a grandson through a son: and neither exists; and it has not even been alleged and proven, nor even alleged; the terms have expired; Third, whether the said statutes are valid without confirmation. And regarding the proof of the said statutes, assuming as established that statutes are not valid without confirmation, and regarding the proof of the rector of the province, or of those judges to whom it was committed, and of the commission, which does not appear except in the manner mentioned in the proof sent to you; and thus it appears that those judges could not approve, since the commission does not appear. Indeed, the words in the proof clearly show the statute, which I send to you, to be rather invalidated than approved. Fourth, whether the said copy of the testament, or copy of a copy, which is sent to you, produced against the said Lady Tunitia, proves its authenticity, assuming as established that it was extracted from the books or protocols of a certain notary now deceased, the said Lady Tunitia not having been summoned or cited for this purpose, etc. In the name of Christ.

It does not seem to me to be doubtful that a testament in which a daughter is neither instituted as heir nor expressly disinherited is void by operation of law, as established in C. de lib. praet. l. Maximum vitium; Inst. de exh. lib. in principio; and Auth. Ut cum de appellatione cognoscitur, §. Illud quoque capitulum. This applies with regard to the institution of an heir; but with regard to the codicillary clause, if it is invalid, the gloss in Auth. Ex causa holds that it produces no effect. The same opinion is held by Guillaume in C. de codic. l. Si. Conversely, Dy and Jacobus de Arena in l. Generaliter, §. De testamento, de fideicommissis, lib. 5, where the case appears to be discussed, hold the contrary. And since this case is omitted by the statute, it remains subject to the disposition of the common law, as stated in ff. sol. matr. l. Si cum dotem. Therefore, it is unnecessary to dispute whether the statutes are valid: they have no application in our case.

† As to the last point, I say that in the aforementioned exemplification, if it is made by the authority of the judge, the party must be cited, as noted by the doctors in Auth. Si quis in aliquo and in Auth. Iure pura. But if, by statute, the exemplification were committed to another notary, then it is not necessary to cite the party, because it is not a judicial act; nevertheless, what is done by him does not prejudice the truth. If there is doubt about the truth, the original document or protocol must be produced. This is supported by C. de fide instrumentorum, l. finalis; and by what is noted in de bonis possidendis, l. 3, §. penult.; ff. de edendo, l. quaedam, §. 1; extra de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum P. tabellio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Upon proof of the sale having been made in truth for Titius, with the name of Angelus inserted, the right is acquired by Titius alone from the beginning.
2. A simulated contract may be challenged principally, and it is the duty of the judge to declare it simulated.
body: In the name of Christ. The matter does not require a multiplication of words; therefore, I pass over it briefly and say that, having considered the petition mentioned above and the proofs made regarding it, judgment ought to be rendered according to the form of the said petition; because it has been proven that an agreement was made between the said Turk and Ang., and also that an agreement was made between them and the sellers,

† That the said Ang. truly purchased for the Turk, inserting the name of the said Angel. in the contract, it was rightly acquired from the very beginning that the right to the property belonged solely to the Turk; whereas Ange. merely provided his services. D. de manumis. l. 3. §. si ab ignoto. Moreover, possession of the Turk has been proven: on account of which, dominion is also believed to have been transferred to him. C. si quis alteri, vel sibi. l. in legitimi interest. arg. D. qui mo. pi. vel hypo. sol. l. sicut. §. superuacuum. And thus it seems to me that judgment should be rendered.

† As to that part of the petition in which it is requested that the contract be declared simulated with respect to the said Ange. and genuine with respect to the said Turk. For this matter may be principally litigated, and the office of the judge may be invoked to declare such simulation, just as to declare the nullity of the contract, as in Extra, De restitutione in integrum, c. Constituens. For on any nullity a libel may be offered. It supports what is noted in Quae sententiae sine appellatione remanent, l. 1, ff. De iniusto testamento; l. Filio praeterito, C. De repudianda hereditate; l. Suus, cum si; and c. Ego Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An inheritance not accepted is not transmitted, even though the right of substitution by fideicommissum exists.
2. The legitime, nor the Trebellian portion, nor the heir’s own property are included in the fideicommissum.
body: The facts are as follows: In the name of Christ. Ioli, alone, having appointed his assessor, drew up his testament; in which he instituted his natural nephew, Francis, who was in his power, as his universal heir, under the condition that if the said Francis should die without legitimate children, he substituted for himself Vannutia, daughter of the said testator, and Margaret, and Donna, nieces of the said testator through his son, and the heirs of the said women, in equal portions. The said Vannutia, Margaret, and Donna were in the power of the said testator, as appears from the testament of the said Ioli, which is transmitted to you at present. After the testator died, with the said Francis, his nephew and instituted heir, a minor, and the said Vannutia, daughter of the said testator, and Donna and Margaret, his nieces, the substitutes, still living; after the said Francis died, being more than 25 years of age, with the said Vannutia still living, and with the said Master Francis, her son and heir, and with the said Donna and Margaret still living; after the said Vannutia died, with the said Francis, her son and heir, and with the said Donna Margaret and Donna still living, the said Master Francis took possession of the inheritance devolved to him by virtue of the said substitution; after the said Donna died, without having accepted the inheritance of the said Ioli, nor of the said Francis, with Michelutia, her daughter, still living, who also died without having accepted the inheritance of the said Ioli, nor of the said Francis, with Ruffina, her maternal grandmother, still living; after the said Donna Ruffina died, with Margaret, her daughter, still living, without having accepted the inheritance of the said Donna Ruffina; after the said Margaret died, with her daughter Appollonia still living, without having accepted the inheritance of the said Ioli, nor of the said Francis, in any other way than by inhabiting the house of the said Ioli for three months; after the said Appollonia, a minor, died, with her father Simon still living; after the said Master Francis, as being closer in degree, took possession of the inheritance both of the said Ioli, his uncle, and of the said Francis, his cousin. It is now asked, what is the share in the inheritance of the said Ioli and of the said Francis? Whether the said Master Francis, or the said Simon, heir and father of the said Appollonia, or the heir of the said Michelutia, in what manner and for what portion the aforementioned persons succeed in the said inheritance, having seen the said testament and the point of law. In the name of Christ. Having seen the said point of law, two things must be considered,

First, concerning the transmission of the inheritance of Fran.; second, concerning the transmission of the substitution, or fideicommissum, left in the will of Iolus. Regarding the first, I say that Master Fran. alone has the right, because the others did not transmit, since they did not accept: as in C. de caducis tollendis, §. in novissimo. Regarding the second, I say that all transmitted: as noted in D. de legatis 1, l. tenet filius; and C. de fideicommissis, l. si in persona, with similar authorities. For if a universal fideicommissum is transmitted, even if the deceased had not yet accepted it: as in l. apud Iulianum, §. utrum, and §. an ista, D. ad Trebellianam. Hence, the shares of the others, having been transmitted, do not pertain to Master Fran., but only his portion designated in the will. But it is necessary to examine what comes into the fideicommissum. For that which does not come into it pertains entirely to Master Fran.

† And it is certain that the legitimate portion does not come into play, as held by Franciscus in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. cum quaeritur. Furthermore, the Trebellianic portion does not come into play if an inventory was made, as stated in extra de testamento, c. Rayn. and Ray. Moreover, the own portion does not come into play, according to Franciscus in ff. de vulgari et pupillari substitutione, l. coheredi, § cum filiae, vers. nec fideicommissio. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a mother is excluded from the inheritance of the said son on the ground that she did not immediately, when she could, petition for a guardian for her infant son, but did so within a year.
body: In the name of Christ. A man named Michelictus died, leaving behind an infant son, and the lady Catherine, mother of said infant, did not immediately assume guardianship when she could have done so, but rather in the eleventh month of the year; after which the infant died in pupillary age. It is asked whether said Catherine, the mother and aforementioned guardian, is excluded from the succession of her said son or not. In the name of Christ. In this matter, the laws speak very precisely.

† For the constitution of the divine Severus states that if she did not petition immediately in accordance with the law, she falls from the succession of the minor. D. Qui petant tutorem, l. 2, §. Divus. Another text explains this word "immediately," because it is understood as when first possible both in law and in fact. D. Ad Trebellianam, l. 2, §. Confestim. Another law states that the mother's solicitude is required in obtaining guardians. D. Qui petant tutorem, l. 1. Another states that diligent office is required and demanded. C. Qui petant tutorem, l. Cum a matre. Which, another states, means that the mother is bound to petition for a curator for the womb: therefore she does not have a term of one year. D. Ad Tertullianam, l. 2, §. Quod si cum praegnans. And if she did not petition for the womb, it is not sufficient to petition after the birth, even if the child is born within the year: as is evidently hinted there. This also seems to be held by Ricardus Malus. Therefore, if the mother is in notable delay for several months, she ought to be repelled from the succession. Nor does it avail the mother that she herself managed the affairs in the meantime; because management must be with the title of guardianship: not de facto: as noted in D. Ad Tertullianam, l. 2, §. Confestim, in the gloss Quod potuit. Furthermore, a late petition for a guardian does not benefit the mother, because an act not done in its proper time does not avail the mother, as noted in D. Ad Tertullianam, l. 2, §. Quid ergo. Here the first point is the day, and the penalty: the day, i.e., immediately; the penalty, i.e., deprivation of succession: therefore purification of delay is not admitted: as in l. Magnam and l.
