Traiectitiae, §. De illo, cum si. To the contrary it seems, that whenever she petitions for a guardian within the year, the mother succeeds by disposition of the new law, as in C. De legatis haereditatibus, l. Sciant. Indeed, even by the laws of the Digest, a term of one year is appointed. D. §. Confestim. And I argue thus: either the term of one year is granted to the one who is unable; and this is false, because no term runs for her, arg. D. De re militari, l. 3, §. Si ad diem. Or to the one who is able and negligent; then I have my proposition: because delay can be purified within the year. Hence that text is not understood as referring to an impediment that does not exceed a year: but to the omission of petitioning. And others say that the lapse of a year induces a presumption of law, and a legal presumption against the mother, that she is presumed to be in delay: and yet she can prove an impediment: which is false, by l. Cum a matribus. And therefore it is frivolous that some say that l. Sciant does not speak of the mother, when it speaks generally thus. C. De administratione tutorum, l. Fin., §. Personis. And the mother's delay is not greater than that of others: especially on account of her sex. Furthermore, succession is due to her by quasi-natural law. I therefore say that if the mother in no way petitioned, and the minor died after the legal delay without a guardian, even within the year the mother is repelled. But if the mother purified the delay within the year, she is not repelled by law. C. De fideiussoribus, l. Scimus. Unless perhaps by the delay the right of the ward was made worse, arg. in l. Et si post tres. For example, because on account of such negligence the goods of the ward remained uncultivated or dissipated in the meantime. For on account of enormous damage to the ward the mother is not deprived: but she is considered unworthy by the law itself to succeed to the goods which she neglected: and to the son, whom she did not treat as a son, having set aside maternal charity. D. l. 2, post princ., D. Qui petant tutorem. But if it is not in the interest of the son to have had a guardian petitioned for, she is excused by law. Arg. D. Ad Tertullianam, l. 2, §. Pe. I therefore put that the law Sciant speaks also of the mother: because it tacitly makes mention of a legacy speaking of the mother, insofar as it extends to all successors, and appoints a term of one year not to the beginning of the petition for a guardian, and the beginning of delay. And thus is understood the saying of Ricardus Malus. But the excuse of the mother if she petitioned within the year, and thus is understood what is said about the year: even in petitioning for possession of goods she has a year. L. 1, §. Largius. And thus she is excused by analogy: and in this case according to that law Sciant, if they did not petition for a guardian within the year, sup. or before, when first they can, similar suppletion. C. De petitione hereditatis, l. 1. Which is not well said: but according to this, mention of the year would be made there in vain, and therefore I think more truly and equitably what I said: and if it be said that the mother sinned more: because against maternal piety. I answer, on the contrary, more is due. L. Nam si parentibus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a petition in which both a petitory and a possessory claim are simultaneously sought is admissible.
2. How the payment of a pension, and thus possession, is to be proved.
3. Whether the statutory prescription runs against a son under paternal power who is unable to bring an action.
4. A statute containing an implied condition is not understood to speak indiscriminately.
1. Whether a husband who did not take a wife nor sustain the burdens of marriage acquires a share of the dowry by virtue of a statutory provision.
body: In the name of Christ. These allegations, wisely made, pertain to the ordering of the litigation, namely

Whether the libel could have been formed in law in the manner in which it was formed. The canonists hold without doubt that it could, in c. Querelam, de electione. The civilians vary, for Master Azo, the fountain of the laws, said that a real petitory action, or a corresponding possessory action, was not granted; but that an officium iudicis ought to be proposed, which is similar to a personal action rather than a real one. Whose opinion is reported at length in the Speculum, in the title De restitutione spoliati, in the fourth part, § Nunc dicamus. Jacobus de Ravanallis, Petrus, and Cynus say that in effect it is the same, or rather certainly not the same, by l. Si, ff. Quorum bonorum. And it is proved thus: From a promise there arises neither a real action nor a personal action, as Inst. De obligationibus, § Sequens; and Inst. De actionibus, § 1. Nor indeed an officium iudicis, ff. De actionibus emptae venditae, l. Qui per conclusionem, § 1; Inst. De actionibus, § 1, in principio. But here it is dealt with by expression, as noted in ff. De exceptionibus doli, l. Secundo, scilicet circa. Therefore, etc. Moreover, for personal prestations, a real action does not lie; for insofar as it is a personal action, it is called an actio in personam; thus in the actio communi dividundo, familiae erciscundae, finium regundorum, which are said to be mainly in rem with respect to the division, and in personam with respect to personal prestations, Inst. De actionibus, § Quaedam. Moreover, impersonal rights are most improperly said to be possessed; nor do they pertain to the vigor of a possessory judgment, De petitione hereditatis, l. Si ut pars. But Innocentius and Hostiensis say the contrary in c. Querelam. And all these doctors have a good understanding: for if the prestation is subjective, from which results subjection and a quasi-servitude, then there is room for a quasi-confessory action proceeding in rem, and a quasi unde vi, or officium iudicis, as ff. De donationibus, l. Aquilius regulus; proceeding for recovery, arg. De agro et censu rustico, l. Si coloni. And so it is with a lower church towards a higher church; otherwise, if there were no superior, but it seemed to arise merely from a promise, C. De praescriptione triginta annorum, l. Cum notissimi, § In his. And thus speaks Petrus and Jacobus de Ravanallis, and Master Azo. And this second member, when the prestation is not a sign of subjection, but is simply an annual debt, and a personal judgment is to be brought, then it is not a petitory action; and consequently it does not have a correlating possessory action. Since therefore in our case natural inferiority cannot be denied, because the church is not of the Patriarchal diocese, the judgment is rightly instituted. In that, however, which the friend said, that in l. Cum de in rem verso there is a prescription, he did not speak well; rather, there is a presumption, not a prescription. Which is clear, because there a ten-year prestation suffices, which does not suffice for prescription, because it has a discontinuous cause, as l. Formem, and l. Servitutes, and l. Hoc iure, § Ductus aquae, De aqua quotannis, with similar cases. And it makes for 18 q. 2, c. Servitium. And what is noted, Inst. De iure personarum, in fine. And these are theoretical statements concerning the foundation of the judgment. Now it must be seen regarding the end of the judgment, i.e., concerning victory, whether it pertains to us to win or to be defeated. And because the end of pronouncement is reached through the medium of proof, therefore I saw the attestations and the ancient instrument,

† On this point it should be noted that, although the witnesses do not prove the cause of the performance, nevertheless the performance is considered below to be formal, i.e., the cause which appears to have preceded in the past. C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 2; ff. de solutionibus, l. 1, together with the following law. And therefore, since the cause of origin is established, from this we have certainty regarding the effect. ff. si servitus vindicetur, l. si a te. Moreover, although the witnesses do not prove to the letter the exact measurement of the grain, nevertheless even the non-payment of a part induces an acknowledgment of the debt, and thus quasi-possession was retained and prescription interrupted, as stated in the aforementioned law cum notissimi, by the tacit reference of the performance to its cause: for which reason we must in every way be victorious on this cause, so that we may also be placed in the usual quasi-possession. Furthermore, having examined the statute under the heading “that creditors shall not demand the debt” after 20 years, which has become obsolete by the lapse of time, without any pension having been made by Guiducius, the father and legitimate administrator of Io. Ang. and Ventura, etc., I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, was consulted whether the aforementioned statutory prescription stands as an obstacle. And it seems that it does stand as an obstacle, because the statute speaks simply and indistinctly; therefore, it must be understood indistinctly. l. de pretio, ff. de publiciana actione. Moreover, at least the father loses his usufruct and the right to demand payment over time, as C. de usufructu, l. corruptionem.

† I say the contrary, because the aforementioned prescription does not prejudice the sons under paternal power. C. de ann. excep. l. 1. §. si. And although the father would lose the usufruct, when it merges with the ownership, which belongs to the sons, as stated in the aforementioned l. si. C. de usufr. l. corruptionem. And I say that the aforementioned statute does not hinder the aforementioned Lo. Angelino and Ventura:

And if it is said that the statute speaks indistinctly, I answer that whenever a statute has a tacit condition, it is not understood to speak indistinctly, although it distinguishes. But this one has a tacit condition, namely, from the day on which the action could have been brought in his own name, when he is a filiusfamilias, and therefore the said statute does not obstruct. And this is the truth. I, Baldus.

OPINION.

Furthermore, having seen the point, the tenor of which is as follows: Peter and Martin treated with each other concerning placing in marriage the said Martin with Joan, an affine of the said Peter, the carnal sister of the wife of the said Peter. And a concord having been made on this, the said Peter, by right and in the name of the said Joan, and also obligating himself by a public instrument, promised to the said Martin that he would cause the said Joan to consent to the said Martin; and that he would give and pay to the said Martin, in the name of dowry, that quantity which, and as, and in whatever manner, Joan and Simon should say, into whom, as into arbitrators and arbiters on one part, and the said Martin promised to the said Peter, stipulating for the said Joan, that he would consent to the said Joan by words of the present tense; and that from her, or from another giving for her, he would recover in dowry that quantity, and make that donation, and with those pacts, modes, and tenors, which, and as, and in whatever manner, the said Joan and Simon should say, into whom the said Martin compromised for his part as into arbitrators and arbiters. For the observance of which, one party from the other, and conversely, was confessed to have received, in the name of spousal earnest money, a thousand gold florins, which the aforementioned party, not observing, promised to the observing party, and standing in faith, to return doubled. Afterwards, the said Martin, on account of leading his said wife, prepared certain things and made expenses, and before he led her, the said Joan died, the marriage not being consummated by carnal copulation. Then, with the passage of time, the said Peter restored to the said Martin the said expenses made by him on account of his said wife, and satisfied him regarding the said expenses. Now, the said Martin, saying that he has gained the dowry of his said predeceased wife, demands from the said Peter the said dowries. And it is true that the said arbitrators and arbiters declared, or arbitrated, the quantity of the said dowry. And one of them ceases to arbitrate, since it does not seem to him fitting, things standing thus, that the said Martin should gain the aforementioned dowry. It is asked, and brought into doubt, whether the said Martin has gained, and ought to have, the said dowry in whole or in part, and whether the said arbitrators are compelled, or ought to be compelled, to arbitrate the quantity of the said dowry, having seen the laws tending to this, and especially the statute placed under the rubric that the husband gains the dowry of his predeceased wife, in the second book of the statutes of the commune of Florence. And presupposing that the said Joan was a foreigner, whereas the said Martin is a citizen of the city of Florence.

In the name of Christ.

† That the husband does not acquire the dowry is because he did not bear the burdens of marriage. For the dowry is due on account of the burdens: and before this, the husband cannot claim the dowry, nor does he acquire the fruits of the dowry, as is fully noted in the Digest, *De iure dotium*, law *Dotis fructus*, in the beginning. Thus, therefore, the common law, which simply provides that the husband acquires the fruits of the dowry, is understood to apply after the burdens have been borne; so too must the statute, which speaks of the property itself, be understood, because the same reason for interpreting a statute applies, as stated in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si ante*, with its gloss. Moreover, a husband who has not fulfilled his part of the marriage contract ought not to gain anything therefrom. Digest, *De actione empti*, law *Iulianus*, section *Offerri*. But this man did not fulfill it, because he did not lead away his wife. Argument: Digest, *De rebus nuptialibus*, law *Denique*. Also, this fulfillment of the condition fails by chance, because he cannot fulfill it due to death. And the matter concerns a gain to be captured (*lucrum captandum*); therefore, nothing is owed. Argument: Digest, *De conditione ob causam*, law *Si pecuniam*, at the end.

To the contrary, because this chance event does not seem to release the debtor: just as when the purchased thing perishes after the contract is perfected, the buyer is not released from the price; so here, with the marriage perfected, he is not released from the dowry. Digest, *De periculo et commodo rei venditae*, law *Necessaria*. Moreover, it seems expressly stated that it makes no difference whether she was led away and cohabited with the husband or not. Argument: Digest, *De rerum amotione*, law *Nihil*, and there by Bartolus.

I consider the intent of the statute from its words, for since it makes a distinction regarding children, it speaks of one who can have children; but without carnal copulation, it is impossible to have children; therefore, on account of the mention of children, it seems the sense is that conjugal copulation is required. A similar consideration is made by the gloss in law *Precibus*, *De vino legato*, law *Si*, section *Cui dulcia*. And if it is said that he began to bear the burdens, so that the matter is not intact (*res non est integra*), I answer that these preparatory acts do not cause the matter to cease being intact. Digest, *De conditione ob causam*, law *Si pecuniam*, in the beginning. Also, because he consented to reimburse her for those expenses, and thus it is as if he had not borne them. Argument: Digest, *De arbitrio*, law *Vtique*. For if he were to acquire the dowry, there would be nothing to reimburse her. Also, the dowry contract was conditional. Code, *De contrahenda emptio*, law *Si*. Therefore, in the meantime, the risk is not on the promisor. Also, the cause of the compromise having ended, it does not seem that an award can be made regarding the dowry. Digest, *De suspectis tutoribus*, law *Post finitam*. Also, this was not yet the wife’s dowry, because the wife had not yet acquired a right in it, since it had not yet been declared. Hence, it was not yet in her assets due to uncertainty. I do not say that uncertainty invalidates it, as in law *Cum post*, section *Gener*. But I say that in the meantime she is not properly said to be endowed, since the dowry is not liquid. Code, *De sententiis quae sine certa quantitate fiunt*, law 2. Moreover, that the dowry is fungible and certain, Digest, *De legatis secundis*, law 1, is a certain interpretation which does not apply in statutes, especially when it concerns an unreasonable gain to be captured at another’s loss, because such a statute must be restricted. Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si vero*, section *De viro*.

Having considered all the above, I say that the aforementioned gain does not belong to the husband, unless he had offered himself ready to take the wife, and it had not been prevented by him. Notwithstanding law *Nihil*, *De rerum amotione*, because there it speaks of a favor without injury to another; here, however, it would be with damage and injury to another. A similar solution is given in the Digest, *De furtis*, law *Si quis uxori*, section *Pe*. Certainly, this question is quite doubtful, whether this woman ought to be called endowed by promise. Code, *De pactis conventis*, law *Ex morte*, and law *Rem in praesenti*, section *Accedit*. Although the quantity is uncertain, it must be ascertained. Law 1, *De legatis secundis*. Finally, however, the opinion seems more just to me, that he does not acquire the dowry when the intrinsic and final cause of the gain fails; and since this cause is natural, it is naturally inherent in the contract for both parties, and must be regarded as if it were expressed; and because the statute, by mentioning children, seems to have contemplated marriage with effect, namely, consummated marriage; unless the statute is interpreted differently by custom. Digest, *De legibus*, law *Si de interpretatione*.

And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws. And to the faith of this, I have subscribed and signed with the signs of my name. And I, Rosellus de Rosellis of Arezzo, doctor of law.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Compensation of penalties is admitted.
2. The words placed in the sentence of the arbitrator, namely that the brothers ought to pay all their debts made before the compromise by any one of them, how they are to be understood.
3. Whether intrinsic interest arises from the delay committed by the defendant: and how much it is estimated, or may be claimed.
4. A promise to pay for another is equivalent to a promise of a fact.
5. Interest is taken in three ways, namely, agreed, common, and singular.
6. What interest is.
7. Damage to the substance promised always arises from delay.
body: The question is as follows. Certain Martin, John Peter, and Serrold, legitimate full brothers, while standing together, and each of them having incurred debts for the preservation of the community with creditors, and wishing to come to a division, and so that the debts might be paid equally, submitted themselves to an arbitrator, who was to proceed, pronounce, arbitrate, and amicably compose regarding the division to be made between them, and regarding every question that was or could arise between the said brothers, having made a solemn compromise with a solemn stipulation, and the addition of a penalty, and the addition that the penalty is incurred as often as a contrary act is done, the contract remaining ratified, with appropriate renunciations, and an obligation of goods. This arbitrator, and also amicable composer, first made a division of certain goods: and having arbitrated and amicably composed by sentence, secondly arbitrated, and amicably composed, and pronounced, that all and each debts that appeared to have been made by the said brothers before the said compromise, and by each of the said brothers with a deed and without a deed, and whatever they are, are to be understood as common, and to be paid in common: and condemned all the aforementioned brothers Martin, John Peter, and Girold to pay: and that they ought to pay in common all and each debts that appeared to have been made, as above, under the penalty of the said compromise. After these things, the said sentence having been ratified by the said compromising brothers, above, Girold, one of the aforementioned brothers, notified by legitimate writing the other three of his said brothers, that before the said compromise he had incurred a certain debt of four hundred imperial pounds with his creditor, making proof of the said debt by a public instrument, and how recently he had been condemned to his said creditor for the said debt, and how he had been committed to prison for the said debt: and how he notified his said brothers, that they should pay three parts of his said debt according to the form of the said arbitral sentence. After the said notification having been made, and a month and more having elapsed, and his brothers being in default in paying their part of the said debt, Girold drew up a libel against his brothers in default: in which libel he narrated the said compromise, and the arbitral sentence, and the aforementioned debt, and the condemnation made on account of the said debt, and the commitment made on account of it to prison, and the notification made to the said brothers, and their default committed: and he alleged, since the debt was of four hundred pounds, that they ought to pay 300 pounds for his interest: because thus it fell to them to pay by virtue of the said arbitral sentence. Wherefore he requested that his said brothers be condemned by the judge to give and pay 300 pounds for his interest in one part. Also in another part 100 pounds for the penalty incurred by virtue of the said compromise. After the litigation having been contested by his brothers, and all the aforementioned things having been liquidated by him acting by public instrument, and public acts, and compensation being objected by his co-brothers of a similar penalty, into which the plaintiff had incurred in a certain one observance not made concerning one arbitral sentence, the judge of the cause pronounced first that there should be compensation of penalty against penalty. Secondly, he condemned according to the requests the said three brothers to the said Girold to pay the said debt of four hundred pounds in 300 pounds to the said Girold for his interest according to the said petition. The said sentence is called into doubt: and they say, that the plaintiff himself could not demand in this manner the said 300 pounds for his interest as his interest. Regarding the compensation of penalties, the parties are content with that made by the judge of the cause; it is asked, what is the law.

† And it is shown that the judge of the said case pronounced judgment correctly: first, regarding penalties, because if both parties had incurred penalties up to a concurrent amount of penalties, the judge acts well in admitting compensation, according to the notes in l. si constat, C. de compensa; l. cum alteri; and l. si ambo, near the beginning, with the notes there. Likewise, the judge pronounced judgment correctly concerning the 300 pounds claimed out of a debt of 400 pounds, because only that amount was to be absolved from the said brothers sued by virtue of the said sentence, since the aforementioned matters were liquidated by public instruments and records. And that this was properly claimed and properly condemned is moved by the reasons set forth below: namely, a just convention legitimated; likewise, just proof; likewise, default committed. Proceeding to the first point, it is argued thus: contracts derive their law from convention, as in ff. deposi., l. 1, § si conuenerit. So much so that the parties are bound and obligated to observe the pacts legitimately agreed upon, as in l. 1, in princ., ff. de pac.; and l. iurisgentium, § ait praetor, in princ.; and l. 1, in princ., de consti. pecu., with similar authorities. But the aforementioned parties, by promising as above, appear to have agreed to do for each other reciprocally, according as the said arbitrator should determine, pursuant to l. fi., and the notes there, ff. de contrahen. empt.; and l. si quis arbitratu, ff. de verb. ob. Therefore, if arbitration was rendered between them, they are bound to observe the arbitration by the foregoing. For if such an award is called a transaction, according to the gloss in auth. vt differrentes iudi., § si vero contigerit, colla. 9., and thus they are bound to observe such a transaction made between them, by argument of the aforementioned laws; and also by virtue of the oath added in the compromise itself, by argument of c. quamuis, de pactis, lib. 6., with similar authorities.

† Moreover, the words of the said arbitral sentence, as pronounced, namely that the said debts contracted by the said brothers, and by each of them, are to be paid jointly, can be understood in two ways. In one way, properly, according to the interpretation of the law, so that the said brothers pay the debts they contracted before the compromise pro rata among themselves. For example, one of the said brothers was obligated for four pounds before the said compromise to a certain creditor of his, which obligation the other three co-brothers were bound to pay him in the amount of three pounds for their virile shares; and so conversely. And that the said words ought to be understood thus is proven by: D. de verb. oblig. l. Stipulatio ista, § Sicut, and § Si quis; and l. Si ita stipulatus, § Grisogonus, in the same title. And thus not Cynus, and the doctors in Auth. Si quando, C. de constit. pecul., where the person of the stipulator is understood in the executive word of the stipulation, just as in the dispositive word of the stipulation. For here the brothers are stipulating to one another in the compromise, and thus in the dispositive word of the stipulation they are expressly named, although now in the executive word of the said arbitral sentence, which can be called the executive word of the said stipulation, the persons of the compromitting parties are not expressly named, yet they are understood by the aforementioned laws, as is alleged above, by legal interpretation. But the words of the said arbitral sentence there, “he condemned to pay,” and that they ought to pay all their debts made before the compromise by any one of them: these words, according to what was promised, ought to be understood that each one shall pay pro rata his virile share of the debt of the brother who is the debtor to that brother. And in this way of understanding the said words, the said brother who is petitioning that his said co-brothers be condemned to give him three hundred pounds of the debt of four hundred pounds, has petitioned well; since there are three brothers,

† by claiming for his own interest, understanding interest in the broad sense, as Bartolus takes it in the first broad sense, as in l. unica, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo, quod interest, etc., everyone can stipulate for himself what is in his interest. ff. de verbis oblig., l. stipulatio ista, §. alteri, Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. alteri. Hence, according to the aforementioned laws, it is in the interest of anyone to have what is promised to him. And in this sense, the libel concludes well, by claiming for his own interest the quantity promised to him, as above, and thus the condemnation followed properly. In another way, the aforementioned words of the said sentence can be taken, and that the said debts are to be paid jointly, and the condemnation made against the said brothers to pay the said debts, which are understood in this way, namely, that the brothers themselves reciprocally pay the creditor of the other brother according to the share falling to him, so that they appear to have stipulated with each other through the person of the stipulator, otherwise the arbitrator. And in this way of paying, the stipulation is valid: unless I stipulate that it be given to my creditor. This is proven in §. si creditori, Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus, and l. liber homo, in fine, ff. de verbis oblig., and a stipulation made by a debtor with a third party, that they pay his creditor, operates with the promisor being placed in default, whereby the obligation for interest succeeds, just as in an obligation of fact, as the aforementioned laws recently cited prove: as l. si ita stipulatus, §. possum, ff. de verbis oblig., where Dy. and Pet. say.

† That a promise to pay for another is equated with a promise of an act, and the law *Facit casum*, as noted by Dynus and Bartolus there, and as noted in the twelfth opposition in the law *Stipulationes non diuiduntur*, D. de verb. oblig., and the law *Si pecunia*, in the same title, and as noted by Azo in the Summa, C. de inut. stipul., l. 1, second column, and the great gloss in the beginning, D. de act. empt., l. *Iulianus*, in the beginning, as noted by Cynus according to Petrus in l. *unica*, in the fourth question, according to the opinion of Petrus, C. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest. If, therefore, by stipulation I promise to pay my creditor, I, who am the debtor, am regarded by the aforementioned laws as if I had stipulated for an act; the act must be said to be of this kind, as in an obligation of an act, for in an obligation of an act, after default, an obligation for damages ensues, as in D. de verb. oblig., l. *Stipulationes non diuiduntur*, § *Celsus*, and in the text and gloss, and l. *Quotiens quis*, in the beginning, and there the gloss, in l. *unica*, C. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest, so much so that it is for the plaintiff to choose whether to sue for damages or for the act, as noted by Bartolus in l. *Stipulationes non diuiduntur*, in the seventh question, at the end, in the ninth question, and the text and gloss are in D. de op. nou. nunc., l. *Stipulatio*, § *Sine idem*, as noted by the gloss in l. *unica*, C. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest, under the heading *In alijs*. And it supports what is noted by the gloss in l. 2, at the end, C. de haer. vel act., together with l. *Haereditatem*, D. de donat. Now, in the case previously stated, if the plaintiff, after interpellation by notice given to his brothers, brought his brothers into default, and thus wished to claim damages, and to claim for his own damage only as much as his brothers ought to pay to their creditor, from which he suffered loss, lest he be detained in prison by his creditor, and lest his goods be sold by his creditor, it was permitted for him to claim thus, by l. *Liber homo*, D. de verb. oblig., and § *Si creditori*, Inst. de inut. stipul. And thus the aforementioned laws are understood by Petrus, as cited by Cynus in l. *unica*, C. de sent. quae pro eo quod interest, in the fourth question, where he treats of intrinsic damages, otherwise extrinsic. And thus it appears to be true from the case of l. *Si ita stipulatus*, § *Possum*, D. de verb. oblig., by contrary reasoning. Likewise, the law elsewhere considers as damages only as much as the debtor owes to his creditor for theft committed by the removal of a name from a tablet, namely, of such quantity as the debtor was obligated in that tablet which was stolen by theft: as in l. *Qui tabulas*, in the beginning, D. de furt., and yet the action for theft is granted on account of damages, as in l. *Ei qui*, in the beginning, D. de furt. In a similar manner, the law acts in l. *Locum*, § *Condemnato*, D. de tabul. exhib. And in a similar manner, the law acts in l. *In lege Aquilia*, § *Si deletum*, D. ad leg. Aquil. In a similar manner, the law so estimates in l. *Fina*, § *Fin.*, D. de eo per quem factum est, which, however, is proven. For where the defendant is in default in performing, the act is considered as much as the interest, where in the beginning, where the text and gloss are, D. de act. empt.

† For as the glossators commonly say, D. de actione empti, l. 1, in principio, and in l. unica, C. de sententiis quae pro eo quod interest, interest is taken in three ways, namely, agreed, common, and singular. The same is noted by Innocentius in c. sacro, de sententia excommunicationis. Although Dynus in c. mora, extra de regulis iuris, sums it up in three ways, namely, for damage commonly estimated, or for damage commonly [estimated] by agreement, or for damage singularly estimated. This is held by Bartolus in l. unica, C. de sententiis quae pro eo quod interest. According to the doctors, it is reduced to two species, namely, intrinsic and extrinsic: as noted by the doctors in l. unica, ex quibus nota idem. Among other things, intrinsic interest arises from delay committed by the defendant regarding the non-performance of the delivery of the thing promised: as in l. vnum, D. si certum petatur, and l. sterilis, § cum per venditorem, D. de actione empti, and in l. hac de tritico. That intrinsic interest, which is the common estimation of that which ought to be performed by virtue of the obligation entered into between the parties, as noted in the aforementioned laws, and that such common estimation always applies, is proven in the aforementioned laws cited above, and l. quod si possessor, D. de rei venditione, text and gloss in l. 1, in principio, with the addition of Franciscus in the small gloss, D. de actione empti, and de periculo et commodo rei venditae, as the gloss there makes. l. penultima, D. quibus ex causis in possessionem, eadem, l. 3, § fin., D. qui satisdare cogantur. If, therefore, the common estimation of the thing applies, one should look in the aforementioned [case] at how much the interest of the plaintiff would be estimated: certainly as much as is estimated by the courts: and goods should not be sold by creditors, and this the legislator considered in the laws, also according to the opinion of Petrus cited above. And this by the aforementioned laws, for the judge, to whom it pertains to tax the interest, as in l. si traditio, in fine, with the gloss there, C. de actione empti, and l. unica, vers. in aliis, C. de sententiis quae pro eo, and l. semper, § interdictum, D. quod vi aut clam, would nevertheless tax it, and it ought to be taxed. For the aforementioned laws also introduce cases of last wills. If a legacy made in the person of someone is not valid, unless it is in the interest of the legatee that it be made to him. This is proven, D. de legatis 2, in principio, D. de legatis 1, l. creditor, in principio, and l. fideiussor, with similar cases. And yet if it is left to Titius that he pay my creditor, or if it is left to my creditor on my account, such a legacy is valid, and an action is given to me. And the law has interest in it only to the extent that I owe to my creditor: as in l. fideicommissa, § interdum, D. de legatis 2, and de legatis 1, l. seruo legato, § si testator, D. de liberis legatis, l. non solum, § 1, in fine, and l. Aurelius, § penultima, D. de iure dotium, l. cum pater, with similar cases. Therefore, the plaintiff could say that it is only in his interest to the extent that his brothers will owe to their creditor to pay, and to claim that interest after the delay committed by the said brothers, as cited above. If, therefore, he ought to claim only that, it is proven by the argument from sufficient enumeration of the parties: which is valid in law, as in D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. patre furioso, and l. 1, in principio, D. de actionibus et obligationibus, Inst. de obligationibus quae ex quasi delicto, in principio. For in the case of the aforementioned question, action is brought for non-performance: and where there is no obligation to restore the thing, but to give the thing in the person of the stipulating creditor, delay is committed by the defendant, as said above, action is brought for non-performance, or one wishes to make singular estimated interest apply, and this cannot be done: because it is money which must be paid, in which this interest cannot apply, as in l. nummis, D. de in iurandum litis, and D. de fideiussoribus, l. ita fideiussorem. Or one wishes to make interest estimated by agreement apply, and this cannot be done, because a penal clause would be presumed to be added in fraud of usury, as in l. cum allegas, C. de usuris, with the notes there. Also, extrinsic interest cannot apply here: since action is brought here for non-performance, as in l. si sterilis, § cum per venditorem, D. de actione empti. This is said by the gloss in l. unica, C. de sententiis quae pro eo, in the gloss in the verse dupli, and there by Cynus in the fourth question, where he treats of intrinsic interest. The same is held by the gloss in l. Iulianus, in principio, D. de actione empti, on the word interfuit. Where the gloss and doctors say that where action is brought for non-performance, intrinsic interest does not apply. Therefore, it must be said that in this case intrinsic interest applies, namely, the estimation of this fact, which is this: how much it is in the interest of this plaintiff, and of any other who would be in a similar case: but how much interest ought there to be? Certainly it must be said, as much as his co-brothers will owe to their creditor by virtue of the aforementioned compromise and sentence. By the aforementioned laws, I adduce l. 1, liberum, D. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum, by which law Jacobus de Belvis, in the lecture on the said l. unica, C. de sententiis quae pro eo, says,

† That interest is a monetary quantity arising from what has occurred, which ought not to have occurred, or from what has ceased, which ought to have occurred; although Bartolus in the aforementioned unique law defines it thus: interest is the estimation of some utility not obtained due to someone’s unjust act or unjust omission. From the definitions of these doctors, it appears that the claim was properly made and the condemnation properly rendered in the said case. For, as the learned Jacobus de Belvisio recounts in the aforementioned unique law on sentences given for one party, the gloss thereon in this definition of interest looked to the act of proceeding, because interest proceeds from damage. The doctors who say that interest is the estimation of damage looked to the act of claiming, since interest is the estimation of damage, which is claimed on account of the damage. Ubertus de Foliatis, a doctor of the laws, in the aforementioned unique law, says that even the definition of the gloss, as it will be explained, had regard to the estimation of damage, namely, the substance of the thing and the damage arising from that substance, such as fruits, or by occasion of the substance, such as an inheritance owed to a promised slave, or a debt, as in the law *Venditor hominis* in the Digest on evictions, and in the Digest on the Aquilian Law, the law *Neratius* in the beginning.

For it is always said that the damage to the substance of the thing promised is to be recovered, as is clear in l. si seruum, in principio, D. ad legem Aquiliam; and in l. in actionibus, § 2, D. de in iurandum; and D. de re vendita, l. qui restituere, § 2; and l. 2, § fin., D. qui satisdare cogantur; and l. vinum, D. si certum petatur; and l. si sterilis, § cum per venditorem; and l. ratio, § cum per venditorem, D. de actione empti. Although sometimes the singular interest proceeds beyond the common estimation up to double, as stated in the aforementioned l. unica, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo quod interest, nevertheless the common estimation is the single amount of that double singular interest. A certain sack of ours, as Cynus says in the aforementioned l. unica, is found in the action for violent robbery, § 1, and in the Institutes, de actionibus, § tripli. Thus it is clear from l. quod si possessor, D. de re vendita; and from the gloss and text in l. sicut, C. de periculo et commodo rei venditae; and from l. primam, in principio, D. de actione empti. Hence, concluding from the first to the last, the interest claimed by the plaintiff was only as much as the aforementioned brothers owed to pay their creditor, according to the aforementioned allegations. And since the allegation of the plaintiff is proven, the actor, having proven his claim, deserves condemnation. And it could and should be done according to the demands, as is proven in l. actor, C. de probatis; l. eleganter, C. de actionibus et obligationibus; l. officium, D. de re vendita. Without taking the words of the aforementioned arbitral sentence, pronounced impersonally, to mean that the person stipulating in the compromise is understood in the aforementioned word, the execution of the aforementioned sentence, as the law understands, that the person stipulating is understood to be repeated in the word execution, as is said above, as in the aforementioned § Grisogonus and others cited above, there is no doubt, because anyone can freely stipulate for himself, and a stipulation conceived in his own person is valid, as in the aforementioned l. stipulatio ista, § alteri, D. de verbis obligatorum, with similar authorities. Wherefore, since it was well demanded before God and justice, and well judged, notwithstanding any of the aforementioned considerations, so that it could not have been judged better than it was judged, and that which was judged is entirely consonant with law and truth according to the aforementioned. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It is asked which of two wills is valid, and whether legacies are due, when the first was made with seven witnesses and the second with five, both having been made by the same testator, and in each the intestate heirs were instituted.
2. Those who succeed intestate are said to be so in two ways.
body: In the name of Christ. He made his solemn will in the presence of seven witnesses: in which he instituted his brother’s son as universal heir, and in it he left many legacies; and he added that if at any time it should not be valid by the law of wills, it should be valid by the law of codicils. Afterwards he made a second will in the presence of five witnesses: in which he instituted the aforementioned brother as heir: and in it he left many legacies with the aforementioned clause added. It is asked, which of these wills ought to prevail? and what about the legacies?

† I answer that, as regards the institution of the heir, doubt may arise from the fact that both the brother and the brother’s son belong to the class of those who would succeed intestate, considering the possibility of the contingency of the cause. For the brother might predecease, and thus his son would be among these successors. Hence, since in the first will the person who would succeed intestate is instituted, and this is done with full solemnity, although in the second will the person of the prior degree is instituted, nevertheless the first will ought to prevail, because it is more solemn. The provision C. de test. l. hac consultissima § nisi forte does not stand in the way, because there it speaks of a case where in the first will strangers to the succession were instituted, whereas in the second, so to speak, those within the family, or those who would succeed intestate, were instituted, although not by right of power or of the household; but here both were of the class of those capable of succeeding. Hence, a privilege ought not to be granted to one and denied to the other, arg. C. qui pign. hab. l. assiduis § exceptis. The contrary is true, namely that the second will prevails, because the father precedes his son in intestate succession and excludes him. Therefore, that case remains in which five witnesses suffice to break the first will and the legacies contained therein, because they have been revoked, and the codicillary clause does not operate unless the will of the testator endures. But this does not endure. And thus Jacobus de Aretio determines. The legacies in the second will, however, derive force from their own codicillary nature, but by the special provision of that § si quis autem, where it is said that the second will breaks the institution and reduces the legacies to the state of intestacy, and it is not necessary for that clause to be added, because as regards this it is superfluous. And this is the case in which the intestate case breaks the testate case as regards all things, and the inheritance devolves to the secondarily instituted heirs not by the mere force of the institution, but by the provision of the law. And they are bound to pay the legacies left in the second will, but the legacies of the first will are taken away together with their codicillary clause, because they are revoked, and the legacies being revoked, the clause added in consideration of such legacies is also revoked.

† From these it appears that those coming intestate are said to do so in two ways. In one way, by computation relative to themselves: and then he who is the nearest among them is said to come intestate: as in the question proposed. In another way, by comparison with those entirely alien: and then whether the person instituted in the second testament is prior in degree among those coming intestate, or more remote, the first testament, being more perfect as to solemnity, is broken; because the potential existence of some case suffices, in which, whether from the second testament, or on account of it, although not from it, the inheritance can be entered upon by civil law, as in D. 28, 5, 2 and D. 28, 5, 10; and D. 28, 1, 1, § 1. Otherwise, if the inheritance could not be entered upon by civil law, but only recognized by praetorian law, for then the first testament is not broken. The rule fails if children were instituted in the second: for example, if the mother or father emancipated the son, under the old law he would have made the testament invalid: because in favor of children, on account of the order of nature, the rule fails, which is laid down in the said D. 28, 5, 10. As in D. 32, 1, 1. For nature is the existence of things per se, or that which is always inherent in the things themselves according to their proper being. Moreover, if in the first testament some come intestate, and in the second others come intestate, and not the same persons in equal, namely, degree, the first testament is not broken, even as regards aliens instituted therein, arg. D. 38, 1, 1. Against this, however, could be alleged the sole law, C. 3, 32, and D. 3, 3, 3. And note these, because they are subtle. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that if a wife dies without issue, her husband shall acquire her dowry, if she dies leaving a daughter whom she had repudiated, the husband shall not acquire the dowry.
2. Whether a judgment rendered on a false ground is void.
3. Falsehood is not committed without fraud.
body: In the name of Christ. There are statutes, one of which provides that if a wife dies without children, the husband shall acquire the entire dowry. Likewise, it provides that, conversely, the husband is bound to make to his wife a donation propter nuptias, which they call the ante-nuptial gift, the amount of which shall be half of the dowry, which the wife shall acquire if she survives her husband without children. The following facts are presented: Licus took Berta as his wife, and there appear two dowry instruments made on the same day, in the same place, and with the same witnesses; in one, the properties are stated to have been given in dowry simply. In the other, it appears that they were appraised. It happened in the case that Berta predeceased her husband, leaving one daughter, who repudiated her mother’s inheritance, with or without an oath. Finally, Berta’s blood relatives claimed back the dowry as being unappraised, and by an arbitrator and umpire a sentence was rendered that the said dowry ought to be restored. From these facts arise two doubts.

First, whether the husband ought to have earned the dowry: and it seems that he should, because the daughter who was repudiated is considered as non-existent. For since she is not admitted to the whole, neither is she admitted to a part; but she is regarded as dead, as in the Digest, On Marriage, with the emancipated son, l. 1, §. si pater; Digest, On Inofficious Wills, l. qui repudiant, §. ultimo. On the contrary, it seems that the statute speaks of children, and does not require that they be heirs; and therefore the condition of earning fails; because we must not add to or supplement the statute: for if the statute had intended to speak of heirs, it would have said so, as noted in the Digest, On the Trebellian Trust, l. ex facto, §. fin. And it seems to be the case in the Digest, On Legacies, 1, l. filius, §. cum quis erit. This part is true according to the said §. cum quis, because one must not depart from the form of the statute, as in the Digest, On Marriage Dissolved, l. si vero, §. de viro.

Secondly, it is asked whether the aforementioned sentence is valid? And it seems that it is not, because it was rendered on a false ground and by means of obreption made to the praetor, as in l. 1, §. haec verba, D. ne vis fiat ei; D. de iudicibus; l. si praetor, §. Matcellus, C. si ex falsis instrumentis; l. 2. But the falsity appears from the instrument of the estimated dowry given: for in doubt the estimation which makes the sale is presumed true, as noted in D. sol. mat. l. estimatae; and l. si aestimatus; and C. de iure dotium, l. si inter virum. To the contrary it seems: because these two instruments are said to be reduced to the concordance of evidentia, just as witnesses with some consideration and distinction, so that namely that instrument which does not mention the estimation is understood to refer to unestimated things: because so it sounds. For one thing is the thing, another is the estimation of the thing, as in D. de usufructu, l. si alij, §. rerum. But the other instrument, which speaks of the estimation, is understood to refer to that which is made for the measurement of the previously made fact: for whenever there is another conjecture, the estimation of the dotal thing does not make the estimation, as in the said l. si inter, which is consistent with this. And that the restitution of the estimation was not promised: hence from the convention of the two writings the sense of them appears, nor is it always the case that the estimation is given, as in C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus. Moreover, let it be granted, namely, that it is for the heirs of the woman to choose which instrument they will use. For in this uncertainty favor should be given to dowries, as the rule says in ambiguis iuribus. Moreover, it is not true that here something false was alleged: because it is not established that the contrary is true; but rather from the conflict of writings uncertainty would result: the declaration of which is committed to the discretion of the judge, as noted in C. de edicto divi adriani, l. si. Moreover, it is not false that it is aided by some beginning of truth. And especially if the beginning concurs with the nature of the thing. D. de legatis 2, l. Cum filius, §. heres. Moreover, the good faith of the actor excludes every vice of falsity,

† because in matters of forgery, fraud is required, as C. de fals. l. nec exemplum. And if any remedy were applicable, which, however, is not applicable, it would be restitution in integrum, because the allegation and proof were made in the presence of the parties, and not by taking advantage of the adversary’s absence, as ff. de re iud. diuus and ff. de except. l. Qui agni. Nor is the sentence uncertain, because it refers to a certain instrument, since the arbitrator pronounced his decision after having seen it, as ff. de transact. non est ferendus. Therefore, in the sentences it will be said “visis actis” [having seen the documents], as it is established that the judges had knowledge of the documents, as extra de praesumpt. cap. afferte and no. ff. de fals. l. si quis obrepserit. And this is just and equitable, setting aside cavils. And thus I hold, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When maleficium is said to be consummated, and when it is merely attempted: and by what punishment it ought to be punished.
2. Statutes do not admit of interpretation: but they are to be understood according to the opinion of the common people, and custom.
body: In the name of Christ. It must be sent,

† That a crime is said to be consummated, and that it is said to be attempted: and in this it must be said that it is called consummated when, as regards the offender, it is perfected, so that nothing remains to be consummated by him or his agent, and nothing remains to be done which is of the essence of the crime. That, however, is called attempted which is imperfect and requires after itself the consummation of the crime. As in D. de furtis, l. Si quis praeferendum and l. Si is qui, §. Si tu Titium; D. de iurisdict. omn. iud., l. Si quis id quod, §. Finis; C. de furtis, l. Si quis servo. Nevertheless, sometimes a crime is consummated according to the intention of the offender, and not according to the intention and definition of the law, as in D. de falsis, l. Exemplum; D. de poenis, l. Si quis legatum; D. de testamento, l. Si quis aliquid, §. Testamentum. And then it is distinguished whether it is consummated apparently, although it did not exist in fact: and the full penalty is imposed. Or whether it is neither apparently nor actually consummated, and then, on account of the intent to commit fraud, an arbitrary penalty is imposed on that ground: because the crime is attempted and consummated in counsel, although the counsel did not have effect. This is noted by Cynus, de sepulcro violato, in l. 1; and by modern authors, and by Decius, and by Ricardus Malaspina, and by Bartolus, and their followers in the said l. Si quis legatum. Furthermore, the attempt itself is distinguished: whether it proceeded to an act very remote, and it is punished more mildly; or whether it proceeded to an act very proximate, and it is punished by a more severe arbitrary penalty, as in C. de servis fugitivis, l. Si fugitivi servi; and fully noted in l. Si quis non dicta rapere. Secondly, it must be premised that when an attempted and not consummated crime is held as consummated, this is not according to the nature of things: because it stands in contradiction thereto, but it is according to a legal fiction. And because fiction has no place in statutes, as noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. 3, §. Haec verba.

† Because a fiction is a certain impropriety: for the words of statutes ought to be understood properly, and according to how the common people understand them. And thus naturally, not fictitiously. Argument: Codex, *De his qui vetere aetate impediuntur*, l. *Si*; Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, l. *Ex ea parte*; § *Insulam*; Digest, *De causa dimissionis*, l. *Tutelas*; Digest, *De iure fisci*, l. *Statutis*. The reputation of the neighborhood is: that § *Cornelianus* refers the mind of the speaker to the disposition and interpretation of the common law; for then it refers to matters to be referred, even if they consist in a fiction, as Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*, l. *Gallus*; § *Et quid si tantum*. I therefore say that in full statutory penalties, a fiction has no place; hence, by custom, the full penalty is imposed for attempted offenses; because neither the case of the statute exists, nor the mind of the legislators, which ought to be gathered from the words, as Digest, *De exercitu*, l. 1; § *Si is qui nave*. However, lest a penalty be lacking for delinquents, this case, as if omitted by the law, is committed to the judge’s discretion as an extraordinary case, as l. 1; § 1, Digest, *De effractione et expilatione*. This does what is noted by Cynus, Codex, *Ad legem Cornelianam de sicariis*, l. *Is qui cum telo*. For statutes and customs ought not to be drawn beyond their natural limits, as has been said; however, the diligence of the judging judge ought not to be lacking, as Digest, *De testamento*, l. *Scio quaesitum*. And by the name of statutes, I understand municipal or provincial statutes, which are not enclosed in the body of the common law, as in cap. 1, *De constitutionibus*, lib. 6. Having therefore premised these things, I come to the point: and I say that this maleficium was begun in part, but was not consummated according to the intention of the delinquent; because the citation was not issued, nor executed; and every crime which is carried out through a messenger or letter does not receive consummation unless the messenger explains the mandate. Argument: Digest, *De aqua pluviae arcendae*, l. *Qui absenti*; § 1. Wherefore I think that in our case there is an arbitrary penalty; because the matter was begun in bad faith; and it did not stand by him. I do not think that the penalty of death or mutilation of any member ought to be imposed; because this man wished rather to make a concussion of a small thing, than truly to commit falsehood. Also because without any solemnity, and because what he did ought not to be called an action. Nor ought it to be called a public instrument. And because a harsh interpretation of laws is to be avoided. For even in penalties themselves, a certain humanity is to be observed, as Digest, *De poenis*, l. *Respiciendum*; § *Delinquunt*; and l. *Aut facta*; and l. *Quid ergo*; § *Poena gravior*; Digest, *De his qui non infamantur*; and l. *Hodie*; Digest, *De poenis*. I believe that this is the safer and more humane way, than to impose a corporal penalty; otherwise there is no difference between a great crime and a small one, and between an attempt and a consummation: which is certainly false. Even the words of decrees do not say to be understood in a Jewish manner: as Digest, *De in ius vocando*, l. *Quamvis*; and noted in l. *Damni*, Digest, *De damno infecto*, with the gloss. *Quidam iudaice*. Of these, however, who are Jewish, and although they are not Jews, the world is sufficiently filled: but as a certain ignominy of the world. See in consilia 237, 248, 249.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one can possess in good conscience goods which are alleged to have once been purchased with the funds of the church, even though this possessor himself purchased them from another third-party purchaser or possessor. And see opinion 297.
2. Whether the rumor of the neighborhood is to be considered.
3. If, after prescription is complete, one has a conscience regarding another's property, whether he is bound to restitution.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain prelate purchased certain properties of the church with money from a certain layman, who transferred the rights to certain relatives of the said prelate, who finally sold the said properties to someone for a just price: and the money was converted to the benefit of the said sellers: nor can it be proven that the money belonged to the church, although some say so. The buyer only doubts the forum of conscience. Now, assuming a certain statute that it cannot be alienated to a non-subject, who, however, pays the taxes and collections unless they make the commune secure for payment. And assuming that it was said to the aforementioned buyer by a certain outsider that the goods were thus purchased, as is stated, although it was not protested. Also, assuming that the sellers said, and say, that the goods were purchased with their own money, not the church's. Also, that among the sellers there was a certain woman of good conscience, who had received half of the said goods unpaid for the restitution of the dowry from those obligated to make the restitution to her. And assuming that if the aforementioned buyer had not bought, many others would have bought, and perhaps for a lesser price. It is asked, First Part of the Consilia. what conscience a good man should have

† Father Reverend John, a certain M., etc., responds to the above-mentioned doubt, when it is asked in the forum of conscience what kind of conscience that buyer ought to have, etc. Always reserving your deliberation, to which I rightly submit myself in these matters and in others, I say in the forum of conscience that two things are made against that buyer. The first is that fame, or rumor of the neighborhood; and secondly, that the protestation made to him by that stranger that those things bought were from the money of the church, are made for that buyer, because he did not celebrate the contract of purchase with the administrator of the church; which is sufficiently consonant with the law, because the rule holds that if a thing is bought with my money, dominion is not sought for him whose money it is. This fails in these rectors and administrators, as these are proven in l. si ex pecunia and l. si ut proponis, C. de rei vend.; c. inquirendum, Extra de peculio clericorum; unless it were proven that the rector of the church contracted through an interposed person: as l. multum interest, C. si quis alteri, vel sibi; and l. cui, §. si ab ignoto, ff. de manum.; 12. q. 2. c. Apostolicos; and l. pupillus, §. per interpositum. Also, and it is made for that buyer, a certain contract celebrated with that woman of good opinion; and because the money was turned to the utility of those buyers, or of the buyer. The obligation of the fame of the neighborhood does not obstruct: for the rumor, or fame of the neighborhood, or of the people, is not to be attended to, as the text says in c. super eo, Extra de eo, qui cogit consanguineam uxoris suae.

† there, however, the rumor of the neighborhood is not to be judged so valid that, unless reasonable and credible proofs are added, it can validly invalidate a contracted marriage. The text supports this in c. Ortus, Episcopus, Extra, de electione; C. de poenis, l. Decurionum; c. Illud, in the verse, Extra, de praesumptionibus; 35 q. 6, c. Si duo; C. ne de statu defuncti, l. Si mater; and the note in c. Contra matrimonium, Extra, de officio delegati. And this fame or rumor, the doctors say, ought not always to be taken into account: because it most often contains the contrary truth, as when it arises solely from the voice of the people or the neighborhood: as in c. Veniens, and there in the gloss, Extra, de testibus. Nor ought one to believe that stranger who reports it. For no credit is given to a single witness, however honest and faithful he may be. 4 q. 3, in the verse, Unus testimonio, in the gloss; 1, in c. Prudentia, on the word, Initium, Extra, de officio delegati. Therefore, this good man ought not to have a conscience so scrupulous: rather, he ought to inform his conscience according to what is established in the civil laws and canons, and to lay it aside, as in a similar case the doctors hold in c. Vigi, Extra, de prescriptionibus, and there by John of Lignano.

† But if, after the prescription has been completed, he has a conscience regarding the alien thing, that he ought not to hold such, but rather to relinquish it: although the thing has become his by prescription, the law permitting, nevertheless, if he were to have such a scrupulous conscience and could not relinquish it, it is safer that he restore it than that he retain it, etc. Gualterus de Sazzis of Pavia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one elected to review all the proofs, rights, actions, and acts to be performed in the case may commit the examination of witnesses to another third party.
2. Whether receiving witnesses, or examining them, is an act of an industrial or formal nature.
3. The words placed in the compromise, namely "neither as to law nor as to fact," and what they import.
body: In the name of Christ. And P. Eusebius, etc., having a dispute with each other regarding and concerning a certain inheritance of the late P. and C., submitted themselves to Lord Christopher as their arbitrator, judge, and amicable composer, concerning and regarding the question, difference, and lawsuit, and any matters emerging, incidental, or dependent thereon; granting to the said Lord arbitrator and judge full power and authority over the aforementioned matters, and each of them, to proceed within a certain term according to law and fact, and by any accord, with any judicial order set aside, and as it shall please him and seem expedient. And to render judgment on the aforementioned matters according to law only, etc. They also chose in the said compromise a certain person who could and might receive all proofs and whatever rights, and all acts then to be made, and also to be produced; and attributing to him in proceeding the power and authority granted, as to the aforementioned arbitrator. It happens, however, that the aforementioned chosen one, being unable to attend the examination of certain witnesses existing in another territory, although it is not necessary for the citation, oath, and examination of those witnesses, entrusted Jacob and C., who, according to the commission made to him, having cited the opposing party in due manner, caused the said witnesses to be cited; and received them to oath; and also examined them; and then transmitted their statements, sealed, to the said chosen one, or to the said arbitrator; before whom it is said by the opposing party that the aforementioned attestations are of no value; and by the producing party it is asserted that they are. From which, thus narrated, it is brought into doubt whether the statements of those witnesses are valid or not.

It must be said that the aforementioned witnesses could not be received by anyone other than the person named in the compromise, for several reasons. First, because in matters that are variable according to the judgment of different persons, the trustworthiness and skill of the individual are deemed to have been chosen; hence, such a chosen person cannot delegate his duties to another. As stated in C. de caducis tollendis, §. ne autem, to receive and examine witnesses is a matter requiring skill, as in C. de senatu, quae pro eo, l. 1, §. in aliis.

† except when they are received under the chapter *Forma* concerning the will of the parties: for then it is something formal: yet not industrial, in c. *Praesentium*, de testibus, lib. 6. Moreover, because a compromise is personal, and does not extend beyond the person, as in D. de arbitris, l. *In compromissis*. Furthermore, the law states that an arbitrator cannot delegate his own discretion, as in D. de arbitris, l. *Sicuti*. Moreover, an arbitrator is equated to a delegated judge: for he cannot subdelegate, unless he is delegated by the prince, as in C. de iudicibus, l. *A iudice*. Moreover, that a compromissary cannot delegate either the entire case or a specific act, is clear from D. de arbitris, l. *Non distinguemus*, § *De officio*. Moreover, a certain person is named, and the power falls upon the named person, not an unnamed one, as in D. de arbitris, l. *Item si unus*, § *Si duos*. Moreover, although an arbitrator may choose a messenger, as in D. de arbitris, l. *Sed interpellatur*, he nevertheless cannot delegate his own knowledge: for the form of the mandate is not to be expanded, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. *Qui Romae*, § *Calimachus*, and D. de manumis., l. *Diligenter*.

† Moreover, those words, "de iure, facto," are to be understood in such a way that nothing is done contrary to the law of nations, as in D. de testamento militis, l. 1; but to proceed through another, and without consent, is thus contrary to the law of nations. Therefore, the procedure of the said witnesses does not appear to be valid; nor can a sentence be rendered against written law in this case, whether the error is expressed in the sentence or not, on account of those words, "s. de iure tantum." See D. de conditione indebiti, l. si procurator, § Celsus. And I was of this opinion at first sight, before I had carefully weighed the words of the instrument. But afterwards, upon reading the instrument again and again, and weighing those words attributing power and bailiffship granted in proceeding, etc., I believe the said commission to have been valid; because to commit the reception of witnesses is part of the procedure; and especially in a case of necessity, in which case it also appears that this was done tacitly; because the business cannot be expedited simultaneously, as in Extr. de testibus, c. si qui testium; and C. de fidei instrumentis, Auth. apud eloquentissimum; and Extr. de probat., c. quoniam contra falsam; and in c. unico, de officio delegati, in Clem. And by this I conclude that the reception of the said witnesses is valid; because it appears that the parties named him; because he was declared by the said commissioner-examiner, as in l. item eorum, § si decuriones; and l. cum esse, § fin., D. de servis rusticis praediis; and D. de rebus dubiis, l. vtrum, § cum quidam. And thus I hold, although before I had weighed the said clause, I would have answered the contrary. I, Baldus. That same matter which is treated in Consilium 245. And because Baldus was acting according to his own conscience, he wished it to appear so to other most learned men as well, and having seen his own consilia, he wished afterwards to advise even himself. And here is added, concerning the contract of the prelate, in the following consilia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The reputation of a neighborhood, just as it engenders a good opinion in a favorable sense, so too does it cause bad faith in an unfavorable sense.
2. How the conscience of a purchaser of a thing bought from the goods of the Church ought to be.
3. When a prelate purchases something, whether what he purchases belongs to the Church or to his blood relatives.
body: In the name of Christ. To set one’s hand to the pen, rather by obeying than by abandoning the worm—or, so to speak, the sting of conscience—seems at first sight to consist in this: as is commonly said,

† Just as the reputation of neighborhood induces a good opinion in the good sense, so in the sinister sense this matter, being of greater weight, causes bad faith, as shown by the argument in the Digest, *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Cum quidam*, § *Et quod dicitur*; and as is read and noted in the Code, *De periculo tutelae*, law *Si tutor*, in the gloss, and by Bartolus in *De usucapione*, law *Celsus*, with the common concordances, on which I do not otherwise dwell.

† But although a thing purchased from an outsider, who does not manage the affairs of the church, even with his own money, does not become the property of the church, yet perhaps it is tacitly bound to the same for the price, as appears from the Digest, De rebus eorum, l. 3, in principio. Nevertheless, it seems that a thing purchased by a prelate may be claimed by the church, or at least permitted to be claimed, whether he purchased in his own name, or for himself, or for his blood relatives: as seems sufficiently gathered from 15, quaestio ultima, c. Fixum, where it is said that if he purchased either in his own name or in the name of another, not of his relatives, but of the church over which he presides, the rights shall devolve. And thus note the gloss, and the same cause, quaestio 3, c. 1, in the gloss, nomine suo; and quaestio 2, c. Apostolicos, in the gloss, contraxisse, ad finem; and quaestio 1, c. Res ecclesiae; and Extra, De peculio clericorum, c. Inquirendum, and c. Unusquisque; and where the masters of both canon and civil law follow: to which, although that decretal Inquirendum does not greatly serve, nevertheless Hostiensis, because of the interpretation of the masters so long observed, minimally etc. Most especially because the church ought not to be in a worse condition than a soldier; and a soldier, and a minor, it is best, therefore from the laws, as he himself argues to the point: nor does it matter whether the prelate purchased by himself or through an interposed person. Argumentum, Digest, De manumissionibus, l. 3, § Si ab ignoto; Codex, De secundis nuptiis, l. Hac edictali.

† Therefore, as the case is presented, if a prelate is said to have publicly purchased property for his relatives with ecclesiastical funds through an interposed person, it would seem that the opinion should be that the property belongs to the church, so that it could be held with a good conscience. However, this doubt appears to be removed, even in the forum of conscience. First, because even if the preceding sentence were true, yet assuming a statute prohibiting acquisition by the church, the aforementioned points seem to be able to be set aside, since it cannot rightly be said to be against the liberty of the church. But the statute, enacted for the welfare of the republic, since it does not prohibit alienation absolutely, but only in a certain respect, the relatives rightly became irrevocably owners immediately; for ownership, which cannot in any way be reclaimed by another, etc. But the church was compensated against the prelate in the name of the money. Moreover, those relatives became secure through lapse of time by legitimate prescription; whereby it happens that a purchaser, even having a wounded conscience from the interposition, which has already occurred, can hold those things with a good conscience due to supervening circumstances; and I consider this part to be true. etc. Lord Christopher de Castellione on the matter of conscience. See in consilia 245, 247, and 249. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When a prelate, by contracting, appears to acquire for himself, for another, or for the church; and when his contract is presumed to be simulated.
2. To whom does a thing acquired by a treasurer belong?
3. A thing purchased by a blood relative of a prelate, who lends money: to whom does it belong?
4. Whether a prelate can lend to himself.
5. Whether a prelate can make gifts to blood relatives, just as he can lend to them.
6. A prelate purchasing through an interposed person: to whom does he acquire?
7. Whether a doubtful conscience induces mortal sin.
8. When a contract is presumed to be simulated.
9. Whether prescription requires good faith.
10. Whether a prelate, in case of doubt, is presumed to make a gift or to lend money to a blood relative.
body: In the name of Christ. This is the matter of inquiry, and therefore, for clarity, it must be premised that sometimes a contract is concluded directly, sometimes through an intermediary, and sometimes it is doubtful.

† If indeed a prelate enters into a contract by himself, or in the name of the church: and there is no doubt that he acquires for the church, and afterwards dies, or is removed, or resigns the administration, nevertheless it remains fixed to the church: because the dominion and possession are rooted in the church itself, just as when a slave acquires for his master. For that which is perfected does not cease to be acquired, as in the Institutes, *Per quas personas nobis acquiritur*, throughout. For if the reason of the law is such, which is estimated for the time, as in the Digest, *De stipulationibus servorum*, law *Servus communis* of Mevius, § *Si aut nomine proprio*: and then either the prelate is such that he cannot have property of his own. E.g., because he is a monk, or a regular canon: and then he acquires for the church, just as a slave simply by contracting acquires for his master: and just as formerly a son under paternal power by contracting acquired for his father, so much so that it did not reside even for a moment in the son, as in the Digest, *De conditione indebiti*, law *Frater a fratre*; and *De acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Placet*. For since it cannot be acquired by the contracting party in his own name, it is acquired by him whose place he represents. 18 q. 1, c. *Statutum*; and Code, *Per quas personas*, law *Finis*.

If, however, the prelate, or administrator, is such that he can have property of his own, either he acquires from the property of the church: and then he acquires for the church, Digest, *De procuratoribus*, law *Quod procurator ex re domini*; Extravagant, *De peculio clericorum*, c. *Finis*. Or from his own patrimony: and he acquires for himself and his heirs. Or it is doubtful from which property: then either we speak of a bishop: and it is presumed that from the property of the bishopric, if at the time when he was made bishop he did not have patrimonial goods, as in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, Authentic *Licentiam*, unless it is proved that he acquired from another cause, for example from the succession of relatives, or from another adventitious cause, even if the dignity was removed on the occasion of acquiring, for example simple notice. For we do not care about such an occasion, but about the final cause, as in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, law *Si vero*, § *Item quicquid*; *De hereditatis institutione*, law *Quidam cum filium*; *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Sed si plures*, § *In arrogato*; *Pro socio*, law *Socium, qui in eo*, § *Finis*.

If, however, it is doubtful from which goods, then the burden of proof lies with the plaintiff: because in doubt the possessor is absolved, as noted in the Code, *De bonis quae liberis*, law *Cum oportet*, after the beginning. To this effect is what is noted in the Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, law *Eum actum*.

† The same, which is said in the case of a bishop, must be said in the case of the treasurer of the fisc, as is singularly noted. C. de iure fisci, l. facultas, lib. 10, unless something else is established by fiscal reasons, and the inventory makes proof of the things. C. de iur. delibe., l. si; C. arbitrium tutelae, l. vlti. Otherwise, the inventory would be made in vain, although the inventory itself could be disproved by witnesses and instruments: and domestic witnesses are sufficient, as noted in l. 2, C. quoniam, et quibus quarta pars debetur, lib. 10, concerning a wife, who is compelled to vindicate the things of her husband: nor does it please that, in doubt, anything should be acquired for anyone for a half part, as ff. de neg. ge., l. Nesennius, in fin., although some say this by law. ff. de pet. hae., l. sed si lege, in §. quod autem. But there it speaks of consumed things, here of acquired things. Sometimes a prelate buys for his blood relatives or friends: and then either from the money of the church without doubt, and the money of the church is presumed, if the church was in possession of the money: because in things which are consumed by use, or converted, dominion is presumed from possession, as ff. de usufr. ear. re., l. 2; C. si cer. pe., l. non vnde originem. For since the transition by consumption is easy, as ff. de sol., l. si alieni, it is rightly more easily presumed, ar. ff. si cer. pe., l. singularia.

But what if a prelate lent money to his blood relative? Would the thing purchased belong to the church? I answer: because the ownership of the money had passed to the borrower, the money was not the church’s, but was owed to him by a personal action; and since the price did not belong to the church, the thing is not acquired by the church. Otherwise, the church would have both the money and the thing, which is absurd, as in D. de actione empti, l. bona fides, and l. 1, C. si servus extero. Indeed, it seems even more so, and this is a special rule regarding money,
