† that a tutor and a prelate may lend to themselves and make themselves owners of the money, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. totiens, § sicut, and noted in l. 2, § fuit quaesitum, D. ad Trebellianum.

But whether, just as a prelate may lend to his blood relatives, he may also make gifts to them: some say that he may, by virtue of a general custom which the Pope knows and tolerates, arg. ff. de donat. l. filius. Others say that this custom is abusive and invalid, which the Pope is said to suffer but not to permit. Others say that, on account of piety or merits, he may do so up to a reasonable amount, as in l. unius, ff. si quid in fraudem patroni. For it is not understood to be squandered, that which is expended on account of the good merits of the church or of the prelate, ff. de donat. l. Aquilius, and l. si pater. Likewise, if it was expended on the promotion of the prelate, or on matters concerning the prelacy, if this was expedient for the church, because the prelate is a principal member of the church, arg. extra de accusat. c. ex parte. Others say that he may not make gifts in any way, ff. quod vi aut clam, l. prohibere, § plane; ff. de pactis, l. contra iure civili, § si filius; unless perhaps insofar as he might have expended it in a business-like manner, for example on horses, residences, and banquets. For if he abstained from these, so that he might provide for his blood relatives, the church has not been made poorer by such a gift, arg. ff. de donat. inter virum et uxorem, l. virum, and C. de episcopis et clericis, l. 2. Therefore, regarding revenues to be appropriated to the prelate himself, he may do whatever he wishes while he lives; but not at death, univ. in c. praesenti, de officio ordinarii, lib. 6.

It follows that one must consider when a prelate purchases through an interposed person, for the same things are to be said in all respects, as in D. de auctor. tutor. l. pupillus, § per interpositam; C. quod metus causa, l. si per impressionem; C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali. For sometimes a person is interposed for reasons of propriety, as in C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione, l. optimam; sometimes in fraud, which is sometimes presumed on account of a legal prohibition, as in D. de probationibus, l. qui testamentum. But in case of doubt, fraud is not presumed, but rather a donation or a mandate, as in D. soluto matrimonio, l. quae dotis, together with its subject matter. Furthermore, it must be considered how the instrument is worded, unless the deceiving instrument admits of something else, or something else is proved by witnesses, as in D. de manumissione, l. 4, § si ab ignoto; and C. de probationibus, l. cum precibus, and l. ad probationem. For what the instrument does not state, we ought not to state either, unless we have proof. D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum, § 1.

And if we doubt in our conscience, a doubtful conscience is not a conscience; nor does it oblige to mortal sin according to Archidiaconus, because it lacks a firm foundation for the intellect: and in case of ambiguity, the possessor ought rather to favor himself than to dissuade himself, because he ought to conform to the conscience of the law, or to the legal disposition: since laws are divinely promulgated through the mouths of princes. And these things have been said concerning the first article of conscience: because one ought not to form a conscience for oneself regarding that which one cannot explain according to the reason of truth, and of a perfect and constant judgment. On the matter of simulation in contracts, see Bartolus, Digestum, De donationibus, l. post contractum. And among other things, note.

† That the act is presumed to be simulated on account of the quality of the persons. Behold, a certain Vagnolus of Assisi confessed that he had received a loan of money from a certain filiusfamilias, the money belonging to Guidon, a son in the power of the said Vagnolus. It was said that this was adventitious property; and therefore the son could bring an action. I said that it was not adventitious, but simulated, and something sought under a color through an interposed person, cf. D. de statu liberorum, l. cum haeres, in principio; and C. arbitrium tutelae, l. si defunctus. Moreover, the son was not a person of industry, and the father was rich; hence the money is presumed to be profectitious; nay, not even profectitious, but nothing at all; because in a loan a simple confession does not prove reality. Now this question is pending.

† Now follows the second article concerning conscience, namely concerning the prescription of time. And it should be known that prescription sometimes runs according to the nature of time, without any aid of possession over time and without any act of the debtor; and then, because time prescribes and not the person, it follows that the good faith of the person is not required. But since an act is not required, good faith is not required. And note: D. 41, 3, *De acquisitione rerum dominio*, l. *Bonae fidei*; D. 43, 7, *De servitutibus urbanorum praediorum*, l. *Haec autem iura*; D. 41, 3, *De usucapionibus*, l. *Sequitur*, § *Si viam*; according to Bartolus, when a lying inheritance begins and ends this prescription. Others hold that prescription runs according to the nature of possession; and then civil law differs from canon law, as in X 2, 14, *De praescriptionibus*, c. *Quoniam omne*; c. *Vigilanti*, and I have said this on both sides. Nevertheless, in ecclesiastical matters, canon law must be observed without doubt. And see what is noted in C. 10, 38, *De acquisitione possessionis*, l. *Cum nemo*: know this, that one who doubts is always interpreted as being in good faith, if he has any occasion for doubting; because he is equated with one who ignores that the thing is another’s, as in C. 9, 18, *De furtis*, l. *Manifestissimi*, § *Si autem dubius*.

† Finally, know that a prelate, in case of doubt, is not presumed to donate money to a blood relative; rather, he is presumed to lend it and to conduct the business of the church, unless there are merits deserving of such a gift. And add what is noted in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Cum quid*. And if I have spoken poorly, bear witness to my error. Baldus, however, wrote in his own case; and therefore he did not have confidence in himself alone, because often a man is carried away by his own will and carnal desire. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To whom a prelate or administrator of a church acquires property, if he acquires it.
2. When something is said to be done against the utility of the church.
3. Ordered charity begins with oneself.
4. Whether a wife is bound to work, and to what works she is bound.
5. To whom a prelate or curator of a church acquires property, whether to the church or to blood relatives.
6. And what applies in the case of an administrator, a curator, and a procurator.
7. What is expedient for churches.
8. Whether an emphyteutic heir prescribes against the church.
9. Whether natural possession is lost by not collecting fruits for ten years.
10. When bad faith hinders one who is acquiring by prescription.
body: In the name of Christ. Petrus and Cynus say in C. de rei vendi. l. si vt proponis; Ioannes Andreae in de testa. l. cum in officii,

† that where two things concur—namely, that he is an administrator of the church, and that he buys with the church's money—in whatever name he buys, it is acquired for the church. And I understand an administrator to be even him to whom money has been granted to administer, because he is bound to render an account of his management; therefore he is an administrator. And more strongly so if he, having been appointed to pay the price, merely lends his name, though otherwise acting in the name of the prelate or the church: as in C. de dona. inter vir. et vxo. l. si filii tui. Or he is not an administrator of the church, and he uses the title of his own name, and receives the property by delivery in his own person, and for himself and his heirs: and then the church does not acquire it, ff. de admi. tut. l. Titium, et Meuium. §. altero. And toward this there is a presumption from the character of the instrument: as in ff. de solu. l. et magis. And the same things must be said if credit was extended for the price: because it matters to whom credit was extended and what was done, and the outcome of the matter is governed by the preceding dealing: as in ff. de iudi. l. 1. And if anyone has possessed for a long time and stored it in his granary, he is presumed owner as though he were owner: as noted in l. pe. ff. de condi. insti. and by the argument in ff. de proba. l. procula. Conclude therefore four cases: for either someone administers the affairs of the church only, and acquires for the church; or he conducts his own affairs only, and acquires for himself; or at one and the same time he conducts his own affairs and those of the church, and acquires jointly; or he trades separately, sometimes for himself, sometimes for the church, and then, if it is established that the money itself belongs to the church, in doubt he is presumed to trade for the church itself, because in reality the transaction belongs to the church on account of the price: as noted in ff. de procura. l. si procurator ex re. the small gloss. But if this is not established, he acquires for himself, because he was lawfully able to trade for himself: as noted in C. arb. tutelae. l. si defunctus.

† On another point, however, I say: that a commonwealth, by preferring its own public utility to the utility of the church, is not said to enact against the liberty of the church; for it principally intends its own utility, even though incidentally it touches upon harm to the church—or rather, certainly not harm, but [the church] would not acquire anew: as in ff. de acqua plu. arc. l. 2. §. idem Varus; ff. de dam. infec. l. Proculus; C. de seruitu. l. si manifeste.

† For ordered charity regularly begins with oneself, according to that saying: 'He sings to the bees, who loves anyone more than himself.' And because we must look to what is principal: ff. de condi. indebi. l. qui exceptionem. Finally, relevant to the said matter of presumptions are ff. de priui. cre. l. si ventri. §. fi.; C. de pig. l. fi.; C. ad Mace. l. fi. §. vlt.; ff. de don. inter virum. et vxo. l. quintus. If therefore this is a special rule in the case of a wife, then the common law is to the contrary. I,

† however, think the same in the case of any woman, so that the suspicion of base gain may be avoided—for instance, in a daughter and a granddaughter, if they have no wool-working craft or other craft from which they can honorably earn. For they are not bound to do business for another: as in C. de bo. quae lib. l. cum oportet. in princip. A wife is also bound to her husband for deferential services, but not for manual and craft services, such as painting: as in l. sicut. de oper. liber.; and add what is noted in C. de fide instru. l. scripturę. in a certain example of the gloss. Hence at times a wife is a partner of her husband in some business, and the profit is divided between them. ADDITION OF BALDUS.

† Say that an administrator who is necessary from the beginning and ex post facto, such as a prelate or curator of a church, acquires for the church with the church's money, whether he wills it or not. And I say that he acquires direct ownership if he names himself in the instrument. But if he names a kinsman or friend for whom he wishes to acquire, and the vendor acts to the end that it not be acquired for the church, he acquires a beneficial vindication of the thing—namely, conditionally, not irrevocably, unless the church chooses this: for the church can choose one of two things, namely either the property or the price. For what if the purchase does not please the church? Can it not repudiate the property and claim back its money? Certainly so. Indeed it seems that since the church has the choice of what to seek in this legal alternative, prior to the election of the thing and the ratification of the contract, the vindication of the thing is not acquired for the church, just as it is not in an alternative created by human act: ff. de vsufruc. l. Sempronius Attalus; and note ff. de rei ven. l. si in rem agat aliquis. For where will and choice are required, prior to the will and choice nothing is precisely acquired: as in C. de rei vendic. l. mater. Likewise, the contract of sale is contracted by consent: therefore it is necessary that he for whom it is immediately acquired consent. Or say that if it is more in its interest to have the money than the thing, then it does not seem to accept the contract; although if it is more in its interest to have the property, it seems to accept by the very fact that it does not contradict: as noted in l. quo enim. §. 1. ff. rem ra. ha. And the reason is that where profit is at issue, one easily consents; but where loss and burden are at issue, one dissents: as in l. filius. §. inuitus. ff. de proc.; and ff. ad Tre. l. quia poterat. I say entirely the same things regarding an administrator who is voluntary from the beginning but necessary ex post facto, as in the case of one who undertook from the church a mandate to buy: because he is bound to assign [actions], nor can the church sue without an assignment as can the fiscus, especially in subsidium: as in ff. de vsuris. l. Gaius. And from the quality of the preceding office we judge of the act simply following: ff. de admin. tuto. l. qui nego. in prin.; nor can anything else be determined consistently with good faith and conscience: ff. man. l. creditor. §. fi.

† But there are some who both from the beginning and ex post facto are voluntary administrators, such as unauthorized managers without a mandate; and these are certainly not administrators, nor officials, nor do they wish to administer or approach the act with that intention: as in C. de neg. gest. l. tutori. Hence if these do not wish to administer in the name of the church, but in their own name, they commit no fraud in contracting: because since they buy at their own risk, they therefore contract for their own advantage; for according to nature the advantages follow him whom the disadvantages follow, as in C. de furtis. l. manifestissimi. §. sed cum in secunda. And if the price is evicted by the church, these buyers are held for the eviction of the price. And thus the risk is theirs, and they are not said to be visited with double loss. And supporting this are C. si cer. pet. l. quamuis. and l. si absentis.; as in ff. de admini. tuto. l. cum quaeritur.; ff. de nego. gest. l. sed an vltro. §. pen.

† And among other things that are not expedient for the church is if the pursuit of the thing bought is difficult on account of the power of the possessor, or on account of municipal law, as in extra de feudis. c. ex parte; because that property does not seem suitable which is difficult to possess: l. 2. §. 1. ff. qui satisdare cogantur; or which is burdened with taxes, because the property of the church ought to be free, not subject to tribute. For the church loves liberty, nor does it wish to be under tribute: as in C. de sacrosanct. eccl. Auth. Item praedium; and noted in the Authen. de non alienandis. §. vult enim. And thus what Petrus and Cynus note concerning the administrator must be distinguished. For they do not mean him who does not assume the office of an administrator, nor is bound to assume it: because he is not an administrator who has no administration, nor does he wish to administer: argument from ff. de solu. l. et magis. Behold, in fact, the property was not sold with respect to ownership, because the possessor was unwilling to contract with respect to ownership, since he had only de facto possession, and did not wish to bind himself further: did this buyer have title? I answer: a just title is ordained to the head or to the condition of usucaption, as in ff. de publiciana. l. quaecunque. But the thing that is prescribed is the property, not bare possession, which is acquired and lost by intention alone: C. de acquirend. posses. l. licet. I say by intention alone, that is, without ownership or title. And therefore this contract, about which the question is raised, does not properly give title against the owner. That bare possession can be bought, however, is clear, because he receives the price: as in l. si mulier. in princip. ff. quod metus causa; ff. de acquiren. posses. l. si aliquam rem.

† Suppose a church stood by for 60 years without receiving the rent from an emphyteutic property: could the heir of the emphyteuta prescribe in good faith? Some say that he could prescribe the rent of the past time, but not the ownership of the property itself. Others say

† the contrary: because by not collecting the rent for ten years it lost civil possession, which having been lost naturally accrues to the church; on this see the note in C. de acquiren. possessio. l. cum nemo; C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum. l. vniuersales. It is certain, moreover, that by the negligence of a decade possession is lost, since nothing has been done in the name of the one possessing civilly: ff. quibus mod. vsufruct. amittitur. l. Pomponius. And this makes against the Abbot of Santa Maria.

† Know that bad faith prevents prescription from beginning to run and from being completed, provided however that it is bad faith in truth, not by legal interpretation: as noted distinctly in c. 2. de reg. iur. lib. 6. And it suffices that he have good faith at three times: once at the beginning, once in the middle, and once at the end; indeed, at two times, namely at the beginning and at the end, even for a moment of time. And the same rule of law applies to a successor: extra de praescriptio. c. quoniam omne. But under civil law the beginning suffices, because the beginning is looked to: ff. de vsucapio. l. Celsus; ff. de acqui. pos. l. clam possidere. in prin.; C. de vsucapione transformanda. l. 1. §. 1. Baldus in his own case.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A statute providing that a sold property may be redeemed by kinship within a year, if the property sold was held in emphyteusis by a church, and the church recovered it as pledged to itself: whether kinship may redeem it from the church; this is a beautiful and subtle question, and see number 4.
2. The giving of something in satisfaction of a debt produces the same effect as a sale.
3. Whether a statute concerning the giving of something in satisfaction of a debt applies to a seller.
4. The defect of being a litigious person does not prevent the parties from reaching a mutual agreement.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is provided by statute that a debtor, and others of his kin, may redeem [the property] within a year by paying the price and the expenses. Now, while the creditor was seeking that the property be adjudicated to him for the emphyteutic right that the debtor held, the rector of the church, which held the direct ownership (proprietas), appeared and objected, stating that it could not be alienated on account of a pact included in the emphyteutic contract. Finally, the judge, in the name of the creditor, sold that beneficial ownership (vtile dominium) to the above-mentioned church, consolidating the beneficial ownership with the direct ownership. The question is asked whether the statute on redemption applies.

† And for clarity it must be premised that sometimes a thing is given in payment (in solutum) to the creditor himself in place of money; and that giving in payment produces the same effect as a sale made to him, unless the thing were evicted. For in a giving in payment, especially when made for a dowry, the primary action remains if the creditor wishes to bring it, as in ff. de solu. l. qui res. in prin. and arg. in l. vlti. ff. de condi. ob causam. But if he wishes to sue by a secondary action for damages (ad interesse), because his interest is perhaps greater than the primary action, he can still do so if the thing is of such a nature as to admit damages, as in C. de sen. et interlo. l. libera. For if money were given for money—for example, another's money for money owed in kind—then only the primary action is granted, because satisfaction has not been made, as in ff. de iure fisci. l. deferre. §. fin. But if for money owed to one person, say Titius, the judge, after auctions have been held, sells to another, say Seius, that is a sale and not a giving in payment, as in C. de execu. rei iudi. l. ordo.

† And therefore a statute speaking of a giving in payment would not apply in this case, because this case can in no way be adapted to the words of the statute, by arg. in l. fi. C. de praediis curialium. li. 10. Next, it is asked whether this statute nevertheless is understood to speak of things given in payment to a church. And it seems that it is: because it is deemed tacitly agreed that the form of the statute can be observed, since statutes are inherent in contracts just as if it had been expressly included in the agreement, as in ff. de euic. l. si fundus. For whoever lives under a law is deemed to contract according to that law, as in ff. de pac. l. si vnus. §. quando and in specie. But this could have been expressly included in an agreement, although Innoc. says the contrary and gives the reason: because it has become holy of holies to the Lord, de for. compe. c. verum. But in this argument he commits the fallacy of accident: because it has not become holy of holies to the Lord in such a way, as he says, but rather with its burden, namely of redemption, as in ff. de manu. l. Caius. For although a condition added to a perfected thing cannot properly be a condition after the thing has been brought into existence, as in ff. de arb. l. Ita demum. and C. de preci. impe. offe. l. vniuersa—for the nature of a pending condition is to impede the origin of a nascent obligation, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. interdum. and l. inter stipulantem. §. sacram. ff. de con. et demon. l. 1. in fi. and noted in ff. de pac. l. Item quia tamen—yet when in preposterous order the action arises before the condition occurs, that condition resolves into a mode, as in ff. de manumiss. test. l. Meuia. and l. cum tale. ff. de condi. et demonstra.

† I say that the aforesaid statute does not bind churches from being able to use free law, that is, the ius commune, because laymen cannot legislate this; and their will must be adapted to what is possible, not to what is impossible, because there is no disposition of impossible things, as in ff. de interroga. actio. l. confessionibus. and ff. de legatis. 1. l. si quis inquilinos. §. fin.; whence the mode, mentioned above, does not seem to attach, as in ff. de manumis. testa. l. fin. Moreover, the statute is referred to a time from which it cannot begin: that is, to a time when ownership has already been acquired by the church itself, as in ff. de manumis. testa. l. si ita fuerit, where a liberty executed does not fall under a disposition prohibitive of manumission. So I say in the present case: for it is established that laymen can make no statutes concerning the property of ecclesiastics, as in extra de constitu. c. Quae in ecclesiarum and ca. ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, even if they were to legislate in favor of the church itself by departing from the ius commune; though by not departing, but beyond the law, they certainly could legislate favorably, 10. distinctio. c. si in adiutorium—for example, that violators of churches are ipso facto banished, or that credit is given to the church's account books, even if not public, and similar things. Furthermore, there is no doubt that while the opposition was pending it could be sold to the opposing party, because the opposer can consent and renounce his opposition expressly and tacitly, as in extra de constitu. c. cum accessissent. and c. cum M. Ferrariensis.

† Nor does the impediment of a matter in litigation prevent the litigants from reaching an agreement between themselves, as in ff. de nou. operis nunc. l. 1. §. et post operis. And the aforesaid points are reinforced by another reason: because the emphyteusis that was sold does not exist in the nature of things, but has been suppressed through consolidation and the servitude extinguished, as in ff. de lega. 1. l. si tibi homo. §. fin. ff. ad Treb. l. si haeres. ff. de iure do. l. si proprietati; and therefore that which has been utterly destroyed cannot revive or be restored. It is possible, however, for a destroyed thing to be instituted anew, but it is not the same thing, as in ff. de vsufruc. l. qui vsumfructum areae. ff. de solu. l. qui res. §. aream. ff. de rei vend. l. si nauis. Therefore, since the emphyteusis in question was merged through consolidation, it is utterly impossible for it to be redeemed, and the recipient is freed from the necessity of the statute just as if the thing had perished, as in l. quod te. ff. si cer. pet.; and consider this well, because these matters are subtle. And so I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, if the vassal does not request investiture, the fief reverts to the lord by operation of law within the year, or whether a judicial sentence is required.
2. Whether, after the fatal period for appealing has elapsed, the appeal is considered abandoned by operation of law, or whether a judicial sentence is required.
3. How many cases occur by operation of law, yet, if there is doubt, require a judicial sentence.
4. Whether an argument drawn from emphyteusis to fief is valid.
5. Whether the lord may, by his own authority, enter into possession of an emphyteusis leased after the passage of time.
6. Whether a new investiture is required in the son of a deceased vassal.
7. Whether the son of a deceased vassal is bound to render the oath of fidelity.
8. Whether the investiture of a fief of one brother benefits the other entirely, especially in the third column following.
9. Whether the fief accrues to the other invested brother because he swore fidelity, or whether it reverts to the lord. And number 13.
10. Whether it is necessary that the lord declare his will that the fief has reverted to him.
11. Whether the lord of a fief, who received service from one but not from the other, may take it away from him from whom he did not receive it.
12. Whether the right of accrual has place in contracts and fiefs. And number 13.
14. A legacy made to two tutors jointly: if one accepts the guardianship and the other rejects it, he loses the legacy; and it reverts to the heir, not to the joint legatee.
15. If there are two sons, one of whom was invested because he requested investiture at the proper time: the other is not bound to request investiture; both because it accrues to the invested one, and because the lord cannot [deny it].
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that Peter, who held a fief from the church, died leaving three sons, of whom one sought investiture within the year and obtained it, while the others did not seek it and lost their share.

† The question arises whether they lost it ipso iure, or whether a judicial sentence is necessary? And it seems that a sentence is necessary; for whether we say that this is a deprivation by human act, then—because from the act arises the right of seeking deprivation—a judicial sentence is required, since every right must be claimed in a judicial proceeding, as in ff. quod metus causa, l. extat; C. de iurisdictio. omnium iudic., l. in criminali; C. quomodo, et quando iudex, the Authentica qui semel, at the end; and what is noted in C. de sacrosanct. eccle., l. iubemus, § economus. Or whether we say that he is deprived by the mere passage of time, still a sentence is required—at least a declaratory one—if the one who possesses denies that the property has reverted to the church; for the law does not pronounce upon a question of fact, but rather the judge ought to pronounce upon it. For that lies within the power of the judge, not in the authority of the law, nor can it be resolved through the handing down of any rule, as is expressly held in ff. [de calumniatoribus], l. 1, § calumniatoribus; ff. de vsuris, l. mora; ff. de poen., l. quod ad statum; ff. de iure fisci, l. eius, qui delatorem; and by Bartolus there.

† We see the same in a similar case: although the fatal periods of appeal have run, the appeal is nevertheless not held to be deserted until this has been declared by a sentence, wherefore the deserter must be summoned. And so Bartolus advised on the basis of l. si contra maiorem, C. de appellatio., where he said that this is the case, although the gloss suggests the contrary in the same title, l. eos, at the beginning. Nor is this surprising, because he might have had a just excuse, and he who is not negligent is not harmed by the passage of time, as is noted in the Authentica de appellatio., after the beginning; and it appears express that a delay must be granted to make one's defense, in ff. de re mili., l. 3, § si ad diem. Likewise, if someone is said to be deprived on account of felony, a sentence is necessary; for a claim grounded on custom must be brought to effect deprivation. It appears to be expressly stated that a fief is lost not ipso iure, but by a sentence after observing judicial order, in c. quicunque aduocantiam, de pace tenen. et eius violato., and many of our ancestors say there that this is an express case.

† Furthermore, certain things occur ipso iure, and yet, if there is doubt, they must be declared by a sentence, as appears in cap. prohumani, and de homicid. in the Clementines. So too, infamy is incurred sometimes ipso facto, sometimes by a sentence, and sometimes from the nature of the punishment, as noted in ff. de infami., l. Lucius; and yet, if there is doubt concerning this, a sentence is necessary. In the same way, a testament in which a son has been passed over is void ipso iure; and yet, unless a pronouncement is made concerning the nullity, the son who possesses is not repelled from the inheritance; and this is supported by ff. ad Silla., l. in cogni. and C. de contratabu., l. posthumo. For certain things occur ipso iure, and yet if they are brought into controversy, there is need for a trial and a sentence, because one ought not to proceed to execution without an examination of the cause, as noted by Innocent in c. inter quatuor, de maior. et obedien. To the contrary, it seems that what occurs ipso iure by operation of law removes the necessity of coming before a judge, as in ff. de conditio. institutio., l. quae sub conditione, § fin.; ff. de nou. oper. nuncia., l. de pupillo, § habet autem. Furthermore, a lord can dispose of his own right without anyone's objection; just as he can sell and permit without consulting anyone, provided that the other has no right in the truth of the matter—otherwise it is different, as in C. de contrahend. emptio., l. dubium; ff. de pactis, l. nemo. For as far as another is concerned, he has free buildings, as in l. loci corpus, § competit, ff. si seruitu. vendice.; ff. de aqua pluui. arcen., l. in concedendo and l. proculus; unless another order was prescribed by law, ff. de verborum obliga., l. qui Romae, § cohaeredes—for example, the order of preference, ff. de legat. 2, l. si tamen; ff. de in diem adiecti., l. inesse. This is supported by what is noted in l. tutor si petitus, ff. de tuto. et curato. dam. ab his; ff. de secund. tabu., l. 2, § expectandum; ff. de contratabu., l. si post mortem, § fin.
† Furthermore, that which is lawful in emphyteusis is lawful in a fief, unless it is proven unlawful, as noted in ff. de legibus, l. de quibus.

† But it is lawful to expel an emphyteuta on one's own authority after the passage of time, nor is there need for a judge, as noted in l. 2, C. de iure emphy.; C. de sacrosan. eccle., Authentica qui res iam dictas; for the natural possession of the emphyteuta is consolidated with the civil possession ipso iure; and therefore it is no wonder if the lord and possessor can do as he pleases with the thing possessed by him without the authority of a judge, as in ff. ad l. Aquil., l. quemadmodum; ff. quod vi, aut clam, l. si vitam, § qui ad ianuam; C. quod cum eo, l. si seruus. Furthermore, a deprivation that occurs naturally by the mere passage of time ipso iure opens the way to the grantor, whence it is no wonder if he can make the investiture that has opened up to him; nor is there need for it to be confirmed by a judge, because by the law of the contract it is dispatched without any controversy of trials; and certainly here an action is not necessary, nor a petition, which does not belong to one who possesses fully and peacefully, as in l. 1, § interdictum, ff. vti possi. This is clear from these words, because by the mere passage of time: and nature supplies the act of the judge, by the argument of l. qui fundum, ff. quemadmodum serui. amitta. Nor does c. si quis aduocatis oppose this, because there it speaks of when the fief must be taken away not by the fact of nature running its course, but by the fault of a delinquent vassal. And that side I consider truer, and it is so observed by custom. But now it is doubted

† whether a new investiture is required in the case of the son. And it seems that it is not, because the fief is the same under the name of the father and of the son, and it is the same contract, the same obligation, as Cynus notes in C. de neg. gest., l. siue. Likewise, ownership is said to be continued in the son, not born anew, as in l. nihil, C. de vsucapio. pro haerede. Likewise, although the father and the son are two bodies, they are nevertheless held for one and the same, as in C. de impub. et aliis substit., l. fin. Furthermore, the father received the investiture for himself and his sons; wherefore the son in vain sought an investiture that he already possesses internally; for possession and ownership can be acquired for another through another, as in C. per quas per., l. 1, because this acquisition consists in fact, or in acquisition by the ius gentium, which relies on equity, as in ff. de acqui. re. do., l. ea, quae ciuiliter. To the contrary, the law on the case seems to be that, although it is true that everyone is deemed to have provided for himself and his heirs, that is, his sons, and not for entirely outside heirs—speaking in feudal matters, as in cap. 1, de duobus fratribus a capite inuesti.—whence the penalty for not seeking investiture within a year cannot be understood except of sons, that is, descendants, as in c. 1, quo tem. mil., col. 10, where it also expressly makes mention of sons. Whence there is doubt to no one, because it is a case in the law that a son who does not seek investiture of the paternal fief within a year and a day undoubtedly falls from his right, unless it was agreed that the father's investiture should benefit the son; which is true if mention was made of the son in the corporal or deliverative investiture, because there is no need for that to be delivered again which has already been delivered.

† Nevertheless, he is always bound to perform fealty, that is, to take the oath of fealty, because he has not yet sworn it; for the oath is personal on the part of the one swearing, as in c. veritatis, de iureiu. And this pertains to the essential form, and therefore it must not be omitted. And if it is omitted, the one omitting it shall be deprived of his right; because he who has offended in one point has become guilty of all; and whenever one of the substantial elements fails, the whole collapses, as in ff. de transac., l. cum hi, § si praetor.

† But does the investiture of one brother benefit the other? I answer: no, unless perhaps the brothers are partners, by the argument of ff. de lib. lega., l. si is, qui duos. I do not believe it benefits him, as in ff. de pac., l. si vnus, § ante omnia; because with respect to the lord they have offended and made themselves alien to the fief, as in cap. 1, quae fuit prima causa benefi. amitten. There also appears what I said concerning fealty, in the oath of fealty—unless it is such a fief that does not require an oath of fealty, or in which by special custom it suffices once for all time, as in eod. tit., c. 1.

† Let us assume therefore as established that those not seeking investiture fall from the fief; but then the question is whether it reverts to the lord, or rather accrues to the brother who swore fealty, since the fief is paternal or ancestral. And it seems that it should be said that the right of accrual is more powerful than the right of ownership. Bartolus notes this fully in ff. de ver. obli., l. si mihi, and I have stated this most fully in c. 1, § cum vero corradus, qui feudum da. pos.; for the right of accrual has a place in a paternal fief on account of the nature and connection of the stock. For in fiefs the right of accrual proceeds from a natural connection, although in other inheritances the connection of blood accomplishes nothing, as in ff. de vulga. substi., l. cohaeredum, § qui discretas. Nor is there need for a new oath or a new investiture, by the argument of ff. de pac. dota., l. inter, § cum inter; ff. de inoffi. test., l. qui repudiantis, § vlt.; and C. quando non peten. partes, l. 1. And therefore it seems that the bishop could not invest another. Furthermore, in fiefs any occasion whatsoever suffices for prescribing on account of the services that the lord receives, as in c. si quis per triginta, si de feudo fuerit controuersia. Someone will say: if it accrues, therefore it accrues with its burden; but the burden consists with being deprived; therefore it accrues with being deprived, which is impossible, for since through the corruption of one thing the generation of another occurs, it is impossible to say that through corruption one becomes more corrupt than the other, by the argument of ff. de haer. insti., l. sub conditione, with its gloss. The laws that say it accrues with its burden are understood of a burden that can be discharged by the one to whom it accrues, as in C. de cad. tollen., § ne autem; but a burden from which deprivation has been decreed cannot be repaired, as in ff. de fideicomm. lib., l. thais, § intra. Furthermore, that something has reverted or been removed ipso iure can be understood in two ways: in one way, that is, without the sentence of a judge, as I said above that the sentence of a judge is not required; in the other way, that is, without the aid of man.

† And certainly it seems that it is necessary that the lord declare that he wishes it to have reverted; for even if it has reverted potentially, it has not reverted actually before the lord wills the avenging of his despised injury, as noted in l. 1, ff. si ager vectiga. So too, a testament in which a son is passed over is null potentially, but not actually, unless the one passed over calls it null, as in C. de contratab., l. posthumo. From this it follows that before the lord declares his will, the fief has not reverted to him, but, so to speak, in the meantime remains in suspense, by the argument of ff. si cer. pe., l. proinde.

† Now the question remains: if the lord accepted service from one and not from the other, can the lord take it away from the one who did not serve? And it seems that he can, because the shares are separated essentially and corporally, and of separated things the reasoning is separate, as in C. de dona. inter vir. et uxo., l. si maritus; C. si plures una sententia, l. fi.; C. si in communi causa in integrum restitutio postule., l. 1; ff. de appella., l. si quis separatim, § quod est rescri. To this what is noted in ff. conmuni diui. serves very well; ff. de uerb. ob., l. eadem, § cato, and l. 2, § item si in facto, and l. in executionibus.

† Likewise, the rule is that the right of accrual has no place in contracts, because the right of accrual is a tacit right, as noted in ff. ad Treb., l. apud Iulianum, § 1, and it pertains to amplification; which amplification has no place in contracts of strict law, ff. de uerbo obli., l. quicquid astringendae; ff. de usuris, l. si stipulatus. Furthermore, sometimes someone is impeded in obtaining; and then, in contracts, on account of the joinder of one and the same cause, and the unified and complex tenor of the contract, the right of accrual has a place; and this holds in non-lucrative contracts, as in ff. de contrah. emp., l. fundus ille; or there an incapable person was deemed to be added for payment, and therefore cannot impede the obligation in solidum in the effective person. For you must know that sometimes a person is introduced in an agreement: then either the agreement is formulated in the person of an absent party, and it is not valid, as there; or in the person of a present party receiving on behalf of the absent party, and it is valid. Whence it is one thing for someone to speak in the person of another, and another to speak in his own person on behalf of another, ff. de actio. et obliga., l. quaecunque. But through the intervention of possession and of ownership arising from possession—and not proceeding from mere pact alone—one can speak in any person whatsoever, according to Petrus and Cynus, who so note on l. 1, C. per quas personas, through that singular law ff. de acquere. do., l. ea, quae ciuiliter. If, however, an annihilation arises in what has already been obtained, the right of accrual has no place in new contracts; although by reason of the old contract beginning from a single person it does. And the reason is that that first contract is universal, just as can be said of Adam, who was a universal man, because in his bosom we were all enclosed, and he was the idea, that is, the pattern of the entire human race, just as a single seal by which infinite letters might be sealed. All therefore who have proceeded from one womb enjoy the old grant; and a universality, while the name of the universality stands, admits of increase and decrease, as noted in l. Lucius, ff. de fundo instru., and proved in l. si seruitus, ff. de seruitu. urb. praed.; and that is called universal which by one essence and one signification expresses all things embraced within it, as noted by Petrus and Cynus on C. quae res pigno. obli. pos., l. fi., and C. de serui., l. non modus. Someone will say: if the lord did not revoke it from one, but invested him, therefore by one act contrary to his privilege he lost it entirely, as in Extra, de const., c. cum accessissent, at the end. But that argument would have a place when, between two who are already deprived, he would invest the other who is likewise deprived. But in our case it was not so, because he invested none other than the one whom he was bound to invest; and therefore he did not perform any act contrary to his right. Nevertheless, consider this: for either he invested one of the brothers regarding his share only, and nothing accrues, neither by force of the old investiture—argument from ff. fam. her., l. heredes, § in illa; ff. ad Treb., l. Lucius, § quae habebat; ff. de acquere. do., l. in agris limitatis; ff. de usufructu, l. dominus—nor by force of the new investiture, argument from ff. de neg. gest., l. qui aliena, § libertos. The same applies if he was invested simply, because he is not presumed to be invested with the share of the other, argument from ff. de contrahen. emp., l. qui tabernas; ff. de lega. [3], l. serui electione, § cum fundus; ff. de lega. 2, l. vnum ex familia, § si rem, and l. cum filius, § dominus; C. de lega., l. uxor patrui; ff. de leg. 1, l. domus, § fi. Or the investiture was made of the entire fief integrally and expressly, for instance with reference had to the stock, in which was the integrity of the whole; and then, because he invested him with the whole when he ought to have invested him with a share, then I argue: the other share was or had been returned to the lord by the passage of time; therefore not on behalf of the one receiving investiture, because by the existing or surviving right of the author the right of the recipient is founded and fortified, as in ff. de vsucap., l. cum vir praedium; and in fiefs this is express in c. 1, qui successo. tenean., col. 10. Whence whether you posit the right of accrual from the person of the vassal, or the right of confirming the contract from the person of the lord, or because the one not seeking investiture is seen tacitly to renounce not only into the hand of the lord but onto the property, that conclusion necessarily follows, that the very newest investiture is not maintained, because the fief is not open. And concerning what is not open, an investiture of a certain person cannot be made, as in c. 2, de conces. preben., because it would induce the desire of waiting for the death of another; and from desire one often arrives at a criminal act, because greed is an insatiable wolf, as in C. de pac., l. fi.

† Finally, he did not determine clearly whether the right of accrual has a place when the fief of one co-tenant is lost; where it seems it must be said that penalties under contracts ought to be applied to creditors, whether they are conventional penalties or legal penalties, as in C. de leg., l. fi.; ff. de litigiosis, l. vlt.; C. de sac. san. eccl., the Authentica qui res iam dictas. Since therefore the lord is a creditor, and falling from the fief is a penalty, therefore that penalty is applied to the lord, and not to another.

† And take the example in the case of two guardians to whom a legacy has been left jointly: one embraces the guardianship, the other scorns it, and thus loses the legacy; for it reverts to the heir, and not to the joint legatee, as in ff. de excusa. tuto., l. nesennius. And that is an excellent and most evident example, and so I hold. This is supported by ff. de reg. iu., l. quod a quoquam; and ff. de petitione here., l. auctori, with the following law, at the beginning; and by Bartolus on l. praetor, § quod de fructibus, ff. de bonis auto. iudi. pos.

† Furthermore, it must be known that if there are two sons, of whom one has been invested in solidum because he sought investiture at the due time, the other is not bound to seek investiture, both because it accrues to the one invested, and because the lord cannot invest that other, as in the chapter duo filii, si de feudo fuerit controuersia. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. It suffices to prove a confession made at another time: because by specifying a different time, I do not bind myself to prove superfluous matters.
2. What effect is produced by the clause "saving the right to add and subtract" inserted in the libelli.
body: In the name of Christ. Premise for the sake of clarity,

† that that which does not give or confer substance and quality to a contract or to an action, does not limit the conclusion of the libel; and consequently it does not pertain to the substance of the proof; it would be otherwise if it were to limit the substance or quality of the libel, as in ff. de appe. l. scio, ff. de instito. l. habebat, and as is noted in extra de rescriptis c. inter cęteras. And therefore, if in the libel I plead a contract simply, and to prove it I adduce a confession of a certain time, since a confession is a repeatable act, if I prove it with a confession of another time, it suffices for me: because it concludes the proof concerning the pleaded action. For by the stating of another time I have not bound myself to prove superfluous matters; especially if in the libel there are those words,

† ‘saving the right of adding and diminishing’; as in ff. de noxalibus l. delictis § si detracta. And thus I conclude. Hindered by infirmity, I cannot extend myself further. Concerning the matter, Bar. noted in de re iu. l. diuus; it is also noted in extra de prob. c. licet. However, an addition which restricts a petition does not pertain to the substance of the proof. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What expenses or improvements may one claim for the custody of a pledged thing, or of a thing to be resold, or for improvements made in that thing? And what is the law regarding the fruits of the thing itself in the meantime? And number 2.
3. Whether a pact, by which one may always redeem a sold thing without a fixed time limit, is valid.
4. A possessor in bad faith, although he cannot acquire ownership by prescription, may nevertheless acquire confirmation by prescription.
body: In the name of Christ. For the sake of clarity, it must be premised,

† that a creditor who received a thing in pledge, and on account of fiscal debts contracted beforehand by the debtor was compelled to pay those debts to the treasury, for instance levies and taxes: that the debtor is compelled to reimburse those debts paid to the person paying. For if indeed the treasury ceded its rights to the payer, it is clear that he can sue under the ceded right, as in ff. de sol. l. Modestinus; ff. mandati. l. si procuratorem. §. fin.; C. de procu. l. qui stipendia. Or, if the rights were not ceded to him: nevertheless, because by that very act he managed the affairs of his debtor by freeing him from the treasury and paying on his behalf, restitution ought to be made to him of that which he truly paid out, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. soluendo, with its subject-matter. And although he does not have the goods obligated under that cause for that paid sum, yet since he has possession of the pledge under another cause, he may retain the pledge on account of chirographic money, as in C. etiam ob chirographa. pecu. l. vnica. Nor does it benefit the debtor that in the meantime his goods were confiscated, because he was afterwards restored to his goods by articles of peace; and this restitution restores all reciprocal obligations to their former state and with their burden, as in C. de sen. pas. l. j. and l. fi. From this it is concluded that that which the noble knight, the said Lord Guido of Astiano, paid to the commune of Siena must be restored to him by that noble who pledged to him the fortress (Rocha), which was in the territory of Siena.

† Secondly, it must be premised for clarity, so that we may know what the law is concerning the expenses incurred in the guarding of the said fortress. Because the said Lord Guido says that he expended fifty florins per month for men-at-arms guarding the said fortress pursuant to a decree or statute of the said city of Siena, and I say that the said noble debtor ought not to be enriched through another's loss, as in ff. de condi. indebi. l. nam natura. Likewise, whence he ought not to recover the thing defended from enemies unless he pays to the extent that it was necessarily and usefully expended in guarding the said fortress, as in ff. de pig. actio. l. 2. §. fi.; ff. de fundo instru. l. si ita. §. vtile. For this expense is necessary for the sake of defending the thing against the incursion of enemies, just like the expense of repairing a thing, because such an expense that preserves the thing in being is similar to the expense of repair, as noted in l. 1. ff. de impens. and ff. de lega. 3. l. cum quaereretur per Bar., just as my brother elegantly noted in his consilium. Although, however, the whole matter pertains to the arbitration of an upright man; because those expenses would not be called useful with respect to the debtor which would exceed so much that the debtor would be forced to consider the thing abandoned, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. sed an vltro. §. 1. The aforesaid things are true in a pledged thing. Likewise, consider the case of a sold thing which was to be resold after a time; although as to the custody of the parties this case is doubtful to me, as in l. custodiam and l. necessario ff. de peri. et commo. rei ven., and I say this through l. domus and l. si domus de leg. 1, especially because the seller was in contumacy toward the commune of Siena and was a rebel, and thus was at fault by taking up arms against his own city; although he was not alone, but among many, yet a multitude of wrongdoers does not excuse him, as in ff. loca. l. li. merces. §. culpę; ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. semper. §. si in sepulchro. For here by his own wrongdoing he gave cause for the edict. Yet I think that the fruits are to be set off against these expenses, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. qui aliena. in prin.; ff. de rei ven. l. fundus; and as noted eo. ti. l. in fundo. To the contrary, however, the Gloss seems to determine that fruits gathered from one's own property are not computed against expenses, ff. de rei ve. l. emptor in prin., where there is a singular gloss; but here the property is not strictly his own, because it is subject to restitution under an express pact of reselling. But certainly the case still appears to be that he who must resell gains the fruits unless he gathered them after default, as in C. de pac. inter emptorem, et uendi. l. 2, where it seems express. I say that this man does not recover outlays made for the collection of the fruits; but those for the perpetual existence of the thing, although it passes away in act, is in effect perpetual. And so I conclude, and all this an upright man will allow.

† I ask whether a pact is valid providing that, without a predetermined time, even indefinitely, the buyer is bound to resell the thing to the seller. And it seems that it is, as in ff. de edi. edic. l. quod si nolit. §. si quid ita; and ff. de const. pecu. l. Item ille. §. quod adiicitur; and because the buyer seems to possess in bad faith, since he knows that the thing can be evicted from him, as in C. de furtis. l. apud antiquos; but a possessor in bad faith does not prescribe in any length of time, as in regula possessor. The contrary seems true, so that infinity may be avoided. Likewise, because the prescription of thirty years is odious, and thus cannot be renounced, as noted by Bar. in ff. de leg. 1. l. nemo potest; nor is it true that this man is a possessor in bad faith, because the thing in the meantime is his own.

† Likewise because a possessor in bad faith, although he cannot prescribe ownership, can prescribe confirmation of ownership, as in ff. de captiu. et postli. reuer. l. in libello. §. si quis seruum; and noted in l. 2. quod metus causa. Likewise against a right that belongs to someone by special law and not by the law of nations, even a possessor in bad faith can prescribe, as is apparent in restitution in integrum, as in C. de temp. in integrum restitu. l. fin.; and ff. de actio. et obligatio. l. in honorariis. §. sed cum rescissa; no wonder, because privileges are extinguished more easily than the common law, as in ff. de testamen. mili. l. eius militis. §. militia; and because a thing easily reverts to the common law, which is called nature, as in ff. de pact. l. si vnus. §. quod, and specifically in the case of a dowry. The summary of this consilium is set forth in consilium 260, where he gave an opinion between these same persons.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The partnership said to have been contracted between brothers.
2. Whether faith is to be placed in the books of merchants.
3. Whether the possessions purchased by one of the brothers are to be shared, and what concerning family expenses, and no. 4.
4. How the division among brothers ought to be made.
5. The capital is to be deducted by him who contributed the funds, although the profit is to be shared.
body: It is not new; indeed, in the name of Christ, let the opinion change with the change of fact: for it is not said to be inconsistent, that which ought to suit different cases in different ways, as in C. de edendo, l. si, and C. de transactionibus, l. ut responsum. Since, therefore, different and contrary issues were previously proposed between these brothers, to which the consuls always refer themselves, now, so that all ambiguity on the subject may cease, a new issue has been formulated, partly consonant and partly dissonant with the old points. The issue is as follows: with the father deceased. In which point it is established first, that the father died leaving five sons as heirs. Second, that the mill was sold for one thousand one hundred florins on account of debts. Third, that the entire price was converted into satisfaction of the debts. Fourth, how the guardian and all the sons came together. Also, that the mother and guardian confessed before John that nothing of the said price remained. Also, that the said John said that he did not wish to have partnership with any of the said brothers. Also, that he made a division with the others, except Raphael, who was underage. Also, that certain other goods were sold. Also, that John exercised the spice trade. Also, that the said Raphael, having become of age, and by working hard and applying himself, brought the profits to the said John. Also, that the said John made certain purchases for himself and his heirs. Also, that the said Raphael requested that the said purchased goods be shared with him, after the age of the said Raphael was fit for contracting the said partnership. Also, that the said John does not wish to share the said purchases. Now several questions are asked: and first, assuming that there was a partnership between them, John asserts and explains that at the time when it could have begun, he had much. The said Raphael denies this. Now it is asked, to whom does the burden of proof belong, that the said John had or did not have; and whether faith should be given to the account books of the said John in his favor. Also, if the possessions purchased in the name of the said John, after the partnership could have begun, are common between them, or the custom thereof; and if not the possessions themselves, but the custom thereof, whether the said John is bound for the interest of the money which he put into the said possessions; also, if the expenses which the said John made for his wife, children, and household, and other expenses which are not social, should be imputed to the said John or to the partnership; also, if the said John had something when the partnership was begun, whether he should have more from the money put into the partnership than Raphael, considering that the said Raphael navigated to various parts of the world, and John continuously stayed at home; also, if the said Raphael, from the common money which the said John had before the partnership, should have his share of the profit, or how it should be done?

† It must be premised for clarity that when only one of two brothers engages in business, no partnership is contracted from which an action pro socio arises: because partnership is an express or tacit contract celebrated for the benefit of both parties. For it cannot be celebrated for the benefit of only one party. It is true, however, that in a partnership one may contribute only labor, the other only money, and yet it is a partnership. Likewise, both may contribute only money, when they conduct the partnership through a factor, servant, or agent of either of them. Likewise, when one contributes only labor and the other only money. Likewise, when one contributes both labor and money, and the other only money or only labor, as in D. pro socio, l. si non fuerint; l. coiri; l. mutuis, and similar authorities. Because in our case both contributed principally labor; likewise both contributed money, which accrued to them from their hereditary share; likewise because Raphael Ioan. reported profits by way of communication and partnership, and Ioan. accepted them, a tacit partnership was undoubtedly contracted, and this is presupposed in the point at issue, when it is said that a partnership was contracted between them. But doubt arises because the said Ioan. claims that he had much property at the time the partnership was initiated, while Raphael denies this; the question is upon whom the burden of proof lies. I answer that this proof is made by indications and presumptions, as noted in C. de arbitrio tutoris, l. si defunctus; and C. de bonis quae liberis, l. cum oportet; and the argument in C. de episcopis et clericis, auth. licentiam; and the argument in X. de peculio clericorum, cap. inquirendum; and what is noted by Innocentius in X. de testamento, cap. cum in officiis. And here it must be considered that Ioan. alleges an affirmative, Raphael a negative, whence it appears that the burden of proof lies on the one who affirms, not on the one who denies, as in D. de probationibus, l. uerius. But elsewhere a distinction is made, as in the case of poverty it is said that the burden of proof lies on him who bases his case on an affirmation or a denial, as noted in l. si vero, § 1, D. qui satisdare cogantur; and C. de probationibus, l. ex persona. Whence, because Raphael is the plaintiff, it appears that he must prove his case. For Ioan. himself proves that he was in possession and still is, as in C. si certum petatur, l. non unde originem; and what is noted in l. pen., D. de conditione instituti. Therefore, that which Ioan. possessed at the time the partnership was initiated is presumed to have been and to be his. Likewise, where there is a division of times, the condition of the plaintiff is always more difficult in proving a certain and determined time, as noted in D. de negotiis gestis, l. eum actum; and by Bartolus in D. de novo operis nuntiatio, l. non solum, § sed ut probari.

† solution, it seems to me sufficiently equitable and just that recourse be had to the account book of both parties: namely, as a certain presumption, not as full proof, which presumption suffices to shift the burden of oath-taking in small sums, as in no. ff. de iureiurando, l. admonendi. And according to Bartolus, s. de donationibus, l. nuda ratio.

† On the second point concerning the purchased possessions, I say that they are not common; but they belong to the said John. However, because the said John deceived, he is bound to half of the profit and interest, which he converted to his own advantage, or to communicate the purchased things: as is most fully declared in another opinion, as is noted by Bartolus in the law *Titium et Mevium*, § *altero*.

† On another point regarding expenses, it was previously advised that each person must manage and govern his own household from his own resources, and not from those of his brother; because they were not partners in this matter, but only in the apothecary trade.

† On the fourth point, I say that, having considered what is proposed and having examined the quality of the persons involved, a good man ought to judge that an equal division of the said profits be made, notwithstanding the caution of the said John, unless it should appear that the industry of the said Raphael was slight; for then he ought to receive that share which seems fitting to a good man.

† On the fifth and final point, I say that from the money of John, namely from the capital, the said Raphael ought not to have any share, but only from the profits, as is read and noted in l. 1, C. pro socio. And because I have written more extensively in other consilia, I do not extend myself further. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The interpretation of a constitution pertains to the one who enacted it.
2. Whether a general principle is restricted by the subsequent provisions.
3. What the clause "ex certa scientia, et de plenitudine potestatis" imports.
4. The indulgence of the Prince is not extended to jailers.
body: We say and declare, in the name of Christ, for the declaration of our banished men of Brescia and others, who have committed any crime, whether from such a day or from such another, that they are and ought to be free and absolved from all bans, past and not past, contumacies, and proceedings, as well as from crimes, both hidden and manifest, committed by the banished themselves or by those not banished, and by those who participated in the gatherings and disturbances made within our territory of Brescia, committed and perpetrated anywhere, just as if those crimes, bans, and proceedings, or contumacies, had never been made or done. And this we do by certain knowledge and from the fullness of power, which we order to be cancelled and to be cancelled. Now, Titius killed and robbed someone within the aforementioned time, but not in the disturbances or riots of Brescia, and before the aforementioned decree he was in prison for the said homicide and robbery. It is asked whether he should be cancelled and released from prison or not.

And because the interpretation of a constitution pertains to the one who enacted it, as is stated in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, in the law *Neratius*; in the Code, *De legibus*, in the last law; and in the Extravagant, *De constitutionibus*, in the last chapter, where there is no doubt that if the prince were to interpret it, his interpretation would be followed. But given these circumstances, the question arises: what is the law? It must be considered that either the prince intended only those offenses committed and perpetrated in a mob, that is, among people gathered together; and in that case, the case in question would not be included, because what is provided for in a mob does not include what is done outside of a mob, as is stated in the Digest, *De vi bonorum raptorum*, in the law *Praetor*, section *Docere*. Or the prince intended offenses committed both in the gathering of people and without such gathering; and yet there is no doubt that our case would be included, because general wording leaves nothing untouched, as is noted in the Code, *De mandato*, in the law *A procuratore*; and in the law *In fraudem*, section *Si*, in the Digest, *De militum testamento*; and in the Code, *De fideicommissis libertatis*, in the law *Si quis in suo*, section *Nos autem*. Or there is doubt regarding the mind of the Prince; and then one must resort to the quality of the words. For there is no greater testimony of the mind than the quality of the words examined, as is stated in the Digest, *De supellectili legato*, in the law *Labeo*, section *Idem Tubero*; and in the Digest, *De verbis obligatorum*, in the law *Quicquid astringendae*; and in the Extravagant, *De privilegiis*, in the chapter *Porro*. Let us therefore come to the necessary interpretation of the words. The words state: "those banned and those not banned, who have committed any offense." And this is at the beginning of the sanction. Afterwards it adds: "and also those who were present at the gatherings."

† Now two points must be considered: whether the general principle is restricted by the subsequent provisions. And it must be said that it is not so in this case: because the subsequent enunciative words do not limit the generality of the preceding disposition, as in D. de iure et facto ignorato, l. Regula, §. Si. Secondly, because that conjunction, "and those who were present," by the force of the conjunction, and by the force of the relative with the conjunction, is broadened: and is explained, and for "and" also D. de legatis 2, l. Hoc legatum, and l. Tamen adiectio, and D. de postulando, l. Et qui suis. Moreover, when a conjunction is placed between cases, such as offending in a mob, and not in a mob. For these are two cases: it never has the effect of restricting, as in l. 1, D. de his qui notantur infamia. Moreover, in benefits the words of the principle are to be interpreted broadly, as in D. de constitutionibus principum, l. Beneficium, and Extr. de auctoritate et usu pallii, c. Ex tuarum. Moreover, this harms no one, and the crime is pardoned by the Prince's own motion. Hence from two things a broad interpretation arises: first, from the nature of the indulgence, as in C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano, l. 1; secondly, from the nature of the proper motion, as in c. Si motu proprio, de prebendis, lib. 6. Someone says that a rescript during a pending lawsuit does not hold, unless there is a clause "Notwithstanding" and c. But it is answered in two ways. First, because that is true when it is at the supplication: but here it is by proper motion, as in l. Qui autem, D. si quis cautio, and l. 3, §. Siis, pro quo, D. quod quisque iudicio. Secondly, because that is true when there is no mention of the pendency of the lawsuit: but here there is.

Thirdly, because here there are two clauses, each of which removes the obstacles. The first clause is when it says, "by certain knowledge." The second is when it says, "from the fullness." c. pastoralis. de re iudicata. in the gloss.

† Someone will say that the indulgence of the Prince is not extended to those in prison, as in D. de turpitate ab ecclesia tapi. l. Domitianus. But this does not hinder, because that is true when the Prince grants indulgence for the process; otherwise, when he grants indulgence for the crime, as is the case here, as is clear when it says, as if those offenses had never occurred. For when the offense is abolished, the sword is placed at the root, and a peremptory exception arises, which there is no doubt applies to those in prison, just as to those not in prison; because the evil has been covered and absorbed, and the obligation or penalty has been completely extinguished. Hence, it is impossible that condemnation should follow, as in D. de iniuriis. l. sed si unius. l. sed si ante iudicem. It is supported by C. senatus rescindere non posse. l. peremptorias. Moreover, this rescript of the Prince has as much force as a definitive absolving sentence; because the constitution of the Prince is the sentence of the king, and it gives rise to the exception of res iudicata, just as the sentence of a man does. For on account of which one thing is such, and this more so. But the sentence of a judge gives rise to the exception of res iudicata because of the law; therefore, much more strongly does the law, in this comparison, make it so, as noted in Authen. de incestis nuptiis. in principio. col. 3. and D. de capite diminuto. l. amissione. §. qui deficiunt. and D. ad Silianum. l. Divus. I conclude from the above that, unless otherwise appears from the intention of the Prince, the said prisoner is to be released. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a thing held in emphyteusis can be taken as security: and whether the direct owner must then be summoned, and whether the agreements that the emphyteuta was bound to observe when wishing to alienate the said thing or its improvements must be observed by him.
body: The words of the investiture contain the clause: "In the name of Christ." Furthermore, this act stipulates, namely, that if the above-named Master Angel, or his heirs, shall wish to sell, alienate, or in any manner transfer the said house to another, he is bound and obliged, and the said Master Angel promises, first to request, denounce, and notify the said chapel; and to offer to it, rather than to any other person or place, the said house with its improvements, for two Papian solidi less per each pound of the price or value of the said house than he could have obtained in good faith from another; and this if the said chapel shall wish to buy or acquire the said house within fifteen days next following the said denunciation. But if the said chapel shall not wish to buy or acquire, or shall neglect or refuse within the said fifteen days, then, after these have elapsed, it shall be lawful for the above-written Master Angel to sell or alienate the said house with its improvements or enhancements to whomsoever he shall wish, except to those places or persons prohibited by law as above stated; to whom, nor to any of them, shall it be lawful to sell, alienate, or transfer, without the one who buys, or into whose hands it comes, granting to the said chapel, or chaplain, or his successor then existing, for the investiture of the said house, for each pound of the price or value, as above stated, of the said house and improvements, twelve deniers, or two Papian solidi. And for this investiture the said chaplain, in the said name, confessed and confesses to have had and received one good and sufficient eel, renouncing the exception of non-receipt of the above-written investiture; and the said contracting parties mutually renounced all exceptions and defenses of witnesses and proof of instruments produced, etc.

† Now it is asked, what will be the law if, on account of the debts of the said emphyteuta, the said emphyteutic property is to be given unsold to the creditor, or sold at the instance of the creditor; whether the said pact, which contained the agreement that if he wished to sell or alienate, he ought to notify the chapel and give it for each pound sold two sous less, claims for itself a place: and it seems that it does not, because the said alienation is necessary, as in D. de fideicommissis libertatibus, l. cum fideicommissum; for judgment is rendered against an unwilling party, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. inter stipulantem, § 1; to this effect, D. familiae herciscundae, l. alienationes. Nor is this surprising, because what is prohibited voluntarily is permitted by necessity, as in D. de manumissionibus testamento, l. quia non potuerunt. Moreover, the right of emphyteusis, since it can be taken as a pledge, and sold by the judge through the aforementioned auctions, and given unsold, as in D. de damno infecto, l. si finita, § si de vectigalibus, and § si qua sunt iura, and there noted. But certainly that which is done by the judge is considered to be done by the debtor himself, as in C. de evictionibus, l. si ob, l. si ob causam; and D. de pignoratitia actione, l. eleganter, in principio; and C. de electi arbitrii sententia, l. libera quidem Theodora; and not D. de regulis iuris, l. id quod nostrum. Furthermore, the buyer has recourse against the debtor for defects: therefore the pacts must be observed in this case, just as if the debtor were selling, as in D. de actionibus empti venditi, l. Iulianus, § idem Celsus; D. de usufructu, l. is qui debet. Therefore the said chaplain must be required, and in no way can he be prejudiced in his rights: because the judge cannot derogate from the right of another third person; but whatever he decreed must be understood subject to the right of a third party, as in D. qui potiores in pignore habentur, l. Claudius, and noted by Innocentius in Extra, ut lite non contestata, c. quoniam frequenter. It accords with D. de re iudicata, l. adiuo pio, § si super rebus. Therefore the said chaplain must be specifically required: and if he wishes to accept, the pact must be observed with priority. But if he does not wish to accept, recourse must be had to the second clause of the contract concerning the laudemium, and the laudemium must be paid to him according to the form of the pact, by argument from D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, § cohæredes. And if the judge proceeded otherwise, the proceeding does not hold to the prejudice of the chaplain. Moreover, the debtor is not said to be unwilling, since he can and must observe the pact. For this matter takes its origin from will, as in D. communia, l. in commodato, § sicut; and therefore whatever follows from it is considered voluntary, as noted in l. 1, C. de naturali libertate. This question is much debated in the matter of fiefs: nevertheless, the final conclusion is as I have said. And if it can be sold to another, much more strongly can and must it be sold to the said chaplain in the name of the said chapel, so that he may satisfy the creditor with money. Thus all things concur in one, the vigor of judgments and the tenor of the fact. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether the sentence of two arbitrators, one of whom [awarded] ten, the other five, or two [awarded] five and the other two ten, is valid.
body: Four were in the name of Christ. Simply: two condemned to ten, two to twenty.

It is asked whether a sentence pronounced for ten is valid; and it seems that it is not. And I argue from the proportion of the number. For just as one relates to one, so two relate to two. But if there are only two arbitrators elected, and they pronounce different sentences, neither is valid, as in D. de arbitris, l. diem proferre, § si plures, in the first response. Therefore, so it is in the case at hand. But if they were in an odd number, the sentence of the lesser sum is valid, as is said there. And in X. de arbitris, cap. 1, lib. 6, if the greater part is not in agreement. Otherwise, if it were in agreement, for example, because two condemn to ten, and the third to five. For the sentence of the two prevails: because they are the greater part, and the more concordant part; and their concordance is formally true, and not by legal fiction, as in the said cap. 1. And this was the ancient opinion of Otto, canonized there, and reasonably: because the lesser number is not formally a part of the greater number, when they are pronounced discretively. Hence, if I promise you five, and ten, by formal predication, I do not promise fifteen, as noted in D. de verb. oblig., l. scire debemus, and D. de solut., l. ubi fideiussor. Because they are not joined to one and the same term, but have a divided sense.

On the contrary, it is argued, because rather, when there are only two arbitrators, and one condemns to ten, the other to five, the sentence pronounced for five is valid: because, speaking realistically, both agreed on five: for the lesser sum is contained in the greater sum of necessity: because the lesser sum is extracted from the body of the greater sum, not conversely, as noted in C. de legibus, l. cum quaestio. The said § si plures, in the first response, does not obstruct this, because there it speaks when two entirely disagree with each other, which can happen from the diversity of things. Also from contrary protestation. Also where absurdity would be sought, for example, if there were a compromise concerning the price of a thing, and one declared five, the other ten. For it would be absurd that a thing worth ten should be given for five, as in D. locati conducti, l. si decem. It says in l. quod si apparent duae tabulae eiusdem testamenti, and in one tablet it appears that the testator left me fifty, in the other one hundred simply, or for the same cause, that the lesser sum is owed to me: not because the writings are reduced to agreement by more and less, but because in the greater sum an error in writing is presumed, as in D. de leg. 2, l. Sempronius proculo.

Solution: if the said arbitrators are in agreement in the cause, and there is no contrary protestation, and all absurdity ceases, the sentence pronounced for the lesser quantity holds, as in D. de re iudicata, l. inter pares. And if you say, how is the sentence valid in the curator bonorum, for a part? I answer: rather, the arbitrator understood to judge of the whole debt, not of a part; otherwise, otherwise, as in l. apud Celsum, § Item quaeritur, de doli exceptione. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus. He himself summarizes in the beginning of his own work, and subtly touches upon the matter of the debtor of the lesser sum. C. qui datis tutelis possident.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a curator of the estate, or one for an unclaimed inheritance, can be appointed where a minor child has become an heir by virtue of the existence of his own heir.
2. The judgment conducted with a minor is void, if the tutor appointed to him did not make an inventory as a tutor, nor did he receive administration by decree of the judge.
