3. Whether the Authentica "minoris debitor" in the Code, "Who may be appointed as tutors," has force in a real action, for example, a claim for recovery of property, or public and in number 4.
5. Argument from "tanquam" [as if]. It is good.
body: ...curator of the property,

† Whether a curator can be granted to the property, or as if to a vacant inheritance, where an infant is the 'suus heres' through the existence of a 'suus heres'. I answer, no, because this is not a vacant inheritance, nor is it vacant property; for in this case a curator ought to be given if he does not have a legitimate or testamentary tutor, since the appointment of a tutor is the ordinary remedy of pupils. But the remedy of a curator of the property and of a vacant inheritance is a subsidiary and extraordinary remedy, as in ff. de haered. inst. in l. si quis institutum. And if he is given, the appointment is void by operation of law, because a tutor ought to be given to persons, not to things, as in Inst. de tute. in prin. Nor does it matter whether he who caused that curator to be appointed knew or was ignorant that a 'suus heres' existed; and an error in the factual basis always invalidates the decree, as in ff. de tuto. et cur. da. ab his. l. sed tutor. §. si petitus. Whatever, therefore, was done with that curator of the property is null and void, because it was not done with a lawful person, as in C. qui da. tuto. pos. l. in uniuersis, and as noted in l. iusiurandum, quod ex conuentione. §. fi. ff. de iureiu.; but

† Suppose that a tutor had been appointed to this infant, yet he did not draw up an inventory as tutor, nor did he receive administration by decree of the judge after the preliminaries were observed. I answer that, likewise, the judicial proceeding is null, as in C. de tuto. et cu. qui satis non dedit. l. fi. and C. arbi. tute. l. ult.

† It is asked whether the Authentica Minor debitor, C. qui dari tuto. pos., applies to a real action—for instance, to a rei vindicatio or an Actio Publiciana; for regarding the hypothecary action it is certain that it applies, as in Auth. Ut hi, qui obligatas, in rubric and text. For the hypothecary follows the nature of the personal action, to which it is accessory; and just as the personal action is extinguished, so by consequence is the hypothec extinguished, as in C. de luitione pignorum. l. intelligere, and as noted in ff. de pac. l. si tibi. §. de pignore.

† But I ask about the rei vindicatio. For example: a testator bequeathed his property to me; upon his death I undertook the tutorship of his pupil son, and neither in undertaking the tutorship nor in the inventory did I mention the said legacy to the judge. Now I claim the legacy; it is objected against me that by operation of law I have forfeited the legacy, because I voluntarily accepted the tutorship when the law prohibited it, punished it, and deprived me of my creditor's right. It is asked, what is the law? And indeed, with respect to the action on the testament and the hypothecary action, it seems clear that I have lost them, because no one doubts that the said Authentica applies to a personal and a hypothecary action. But with respect to the rei vindicatio, which is another remedy, as in C. communia de leg. l. j. et 2. and Inst. de leg. §. nostra, the question is great and doubtful. For if we follow the Gloss that is on l. 1. C. de in li. damno tutore, the said Authentica does not apply; and there is a threefold reason. First, because he who is bound by a rei vindicatio is not a debtor, as in Inst. de actio. §. 1. and as noted in ff. si cer. pe. in l. 1; and this is evident, because he can be released not by paying, but by treating the possession as abandoned; whereas if he were obligated, he would have to pay. The second reason is because the rei vindicatio lies against the pupil possessor, not because he is a pupil, but because he is a possessor.

† Whence here lies an argument from 'tanquam', as in l. de eo. §. fi. ff. ad exhibendum. The third reason is because ownership is a full right that does not need addition; but a personal obligation is not a full right, because to transfer ownership it requires delivery, as in ff. de rei uend. l. si ager. Moreover, in no law is it provided that such a tutor forfeits the ownership of his own property; indeed, even if he had placed it in the pupil's inventory, once it was established that it was his, he would not lose it, as noted by Jac. de Are. in l. ult. C. arbitrium tute. Likewise because ownership inheres more firmly than a personal obligation; for in ownership a simple renunciation does not harm, as in ff. de acque pos. l. si quis ui. §. diuersa. Likewise, in penalties we ought to be content with the causes contained in the law, because penalties are to be restricted, especially where they are imposed solely out of suspicion or presumed malice; for in presumptions and conjectures one must act more leniently, according to Innocent in another matter. But certainly, if you understand subtly, rei vindicatio is primarily available for the declaration of ownership, and the restitution of possession annexed to it is comprehended within the office of the judge, according to Cino and other subtle doctors; but in the declaration of ownership the possessor is not a debtor, even in a broad sense; whence by vivid reasoning that Authentica Minoris does not apply to a rei vindicatio. And thus I am accustomed to hold, defending the Glossa Ordinaria. Yet this reason which I have assigned, no one else has weighed, and on my side I also have as witnesses several distinguished men, namely Nicolaus de Matarellis and Thomas de Tolleto, the distinguished Ultramontane, in his lecture on the said Authentica. To the contrary, however, Jac. de Ravan. and Jac. de Belvis. and Cino hold that in a real action, just as in a personal action, the pupil's proofs could be concealed through the fraud of the tutor, and thus the reason is the same, therefore the constitution is the same. But I answer that the reason is not the same, because ownership cannot easily be proved or disproved, as noted in C. de donatio. l. cum res. Likewise, the equity of ownership, which is of the ius gentium and is called primary equity, as in ff. de pub. l. fi., naturally persuades this, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. si me, et Titiu. And I say the same regarding the petitio hereditatis as to its real effect, as in l. haer. C. in qui. cau. cessat longi tem. praes. In conclusion, I hold that the said tutor has not forfeited the rei vindicatio, or the petitio hereditatis as to real effects; but he has lost personal and hypothecary actions. Lord Raynerius de Forlivio holds that the said Authentica applies in a real action. One could distinguish based on equity: either there are movable things, in which fraud and handling could easily be committed by the tutor, and then, to remove the occasion for wrongdoing, the said Authentica would apply even in a real action; or there are immovable things, which cannot be handled fraudulently, and then in the vindication of them the said Authentica would not apply, because the reason of that Authentica ceases, as in C. quoniam, et quibus quarta pars debetur. l. 2. That distinction is true, yet it is not proved by any law, because that Authentica speaks strictly, and the reason of that Authentica is proven by the concealment of proofs, not the concealment of things, because things ought to be put in an inventory. Certainly instruments also ought to be put in an inventory, l. chirographis. in prin. ff. de admi. tuto. It is better, therefore, to proceed by the simple path and to hold the opinion of the Gloss, that if it is clear concerning the tutor's ownership, so that it cannot be concealed by any evasion, the said Authentica does not apply. But that is not to be omitted from consideration either: for I consider that the house of Zurich, about which the exact question arises, is a loan or mutual house, which is called a Casana, in which there are debts and pledges concerning outside debtors; and as to this it is certain that the said Authentica does not apply, because the rights lie against outsiders, as in C. de leg. l. ex legato nominis and ff. de le. 2. l. cum pater. §. mense. Therefore, in these debts and pledges, the tutor about whom the question arises does not lose his right, as in ff. fam. haerci. plane and l. si quę cautiones; and C. per quas personas. l. fi. is relevant, where it is said that the same applies to pledges as to the principal sum. And so I state and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a fief can be bequeathed to one brother only, to the prejudice of the other brothers.
2. Whether a compromise concerning a fief is valid.
3. Whether an award ratified by the parties is valid, even if no prior compromise exists.
4. When a division or separation is said to have taken place.
body: Since there were several brothers, in the name of Christ, who held a noble and gentry fief from the Illustrious Prince of Achaea, one of them, dying without issue, bequeathed his portion, or some item of his feudal portion, because there is no difference between the whole and the part, namely, a certain small house, to one of his brothers, whom he particularly loved, who was named John.

† It is asked whether this could have been to the prejudice of the other brothers? I answer that no disposition of the deceased in a fief is valid to the prejudice of others who succeed by the law of fiefs, unless they consent, as is established in c. 1, in the beginning, on the succession to fiefs; and in c. Feudatarius, on how one could formerly donate or alienate a fief; and in c. 1, on the degrees of succession to a fief. For since the right of this testator, descending without an heir, expires upon death, he rightly cannot bequeath to another that which he ceases to have by operation of law, as argued from the Codex, on the law concerning the uncle’s executor. The objection from c. First, on the alienation of a paternal fief, and in c. First, §. But also the thing, on by whom investiture is made and by whom it is received, does not hold, where permission is granted to agnates, which is not granted to strangers; because that statement is true only to the extent that the fief does not perish by alienation inter vivos; but it is not true to the extent that it does not perish by the death of the grantor dying without an heir, as in c. 1, §. If concerning investiture, on a thing alienated; and in the Digest, on the law concerning the vectigal.

Secondly, it is asked whether, if a compromise was made among the agnates regarding the aforementioned legacy, so that the said legacy was ratified by the arbitrator and by the agnates with special or general words, whether the said award together with the said ratification is valid to the prejudice of those who consented: and it appears that it is so, as in c. Vassallus, Si de feudo fuerit controversia; and in c. 1, §. Praeterea, Qui motus feudorum amittantur et acquirantur; and in l. 3, C. Communis utriusque iudicii; and what is noted in C. Familiae herciscundae, l. Si familiae. And this is true if the brothers themselves, who were also the feudatories, made the compromise among themselves. But suppose that they did not compromise among themselves, but that all of them on one side and the church instituted as universal heir on the other compromised in Titius, and Titius awarded that the said small house belonged to the person to whom it had been prelegated, and the brothers themselves homologated it.

† It is asked whether the said emoluation is valid? And it must be said that it is not, because no compromise with a penalty, or without a penalty, preceded between them: which is necessary to be done, that a compromise without a penalty precedes; or there be a clause, the compromise remaining ratified. As noted in D. de arbitris, l. 2; and C. de arbitris, l. pen.; D. de re iudicata, l. ait praetor. Therefore, between whom no compromise was made, no emoluation takes place: therefore, the assignment of the said house was not valid. But immediately it is asked, whether the penalty is incurred? And it must be said that it is not, because the arbitrator could not judge on a matter not compromised, as D. de arbitris, l. qui tamen, §. si. From the foregoing it is concluded that the said house remains feudal to all the aforementioned, because the legacy was not valid; nor is eviction due, as l. cum pater, §. euictis, D. de legatis 2; and the said l. uxor patrui. Also, because where there is no compromise, there emoluation ceases, nor does the claim for a penalty have place. D. de pactis, l. si unum, §. ante omnia; and D. de arbitris, l. non distinguemus, §. de officio. Because all the authority of the arbitrator is derived from the compromise: and without a compromise they derive neither form nor origin. And it is relevant, D. de auctoritate tutorum, l. accipientis. And what is noted there, certainly there the contrary seems to be noted, namely that if one seeks to be divided from several, the judge may not only divide him from the others, but also the others among themselves. But this applies to a judge, not an arbitrator: for a judge is assumed according to the nature of the judgment; but an arbitrator cannot do more than the form of the compromise dictates. Moreover, consider subtly that to separate proper allodial goods from feudal ones is a kind of declaration, not division.

† That which was previously common in undivided shares is divided. But these goods were never common in undivided shares, as if the castrense property belonged to one heir and the peculium castrense to another heir. For between them there is no legal community: and therefore the action for division does not apply between them, but rather a declaratory action, as noted in D. de rei vindicatione, l. si in rem agat aliquis; D. de separatione bonorum, l. 1, § sciendum; and D. de minoribus, l. denique, § sed utrum; C. de testamento militis, l. 1. And therefore the compromise between the said heir and the said agnates in no way affects the agnates among themselves, because even a true judgment would not affect them. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a woman under the age of 25, accused of adultery, may validly conduct proceedings without a curator.
2. Whether the confession of a minor in criminal cases is prejudicial to her; and whether she may petition for restitution; and within what period of time.
3. Whether credence is to be given to a judge asserting that he acts according to his conscience.
4. When there is doubt as to whether a person is of majority or minority age, the judge is bound to admit all justifiable defenses.
5. Whether a husband who brings an action for public defamation, i.e., for the adultery of his wife, is deemed to have asserted his own knowledge, which is said to imply consent to procuring.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Either the woman concerning whose adultery inquiry is made is under twenty-five years of age, or she is of majority, or it is doubted, or called into doubt. In the first case, if her minority is established, it is certain that, since no curator was appointed, the proceeding conducted against her is null by operation of law, as in C. de autoritate praestanda, l. clarum; C. si aduersus rem iudicatam, l. cum minores; nor does a confession harm her, since the trial was not lawfully initiated, as in C. qui dari tuto. pos., l. in vniuersis.

† For whenever a minor confesses a crime as the foundation of the trial—and no one doubts this—the confession is null by operation of law if a curator was not appointed, because it was made by an illegitimate person. But even if she had a curator who was present at a confession made through the minor's unsteadiness, or through the deceit of the adversary, or through the circumventing blandishments of the judge, restitution in integrum would without doubt be granted to the minor, not indeed against the offense, but against the judgment and the confession, as in ff. de mino., l. si ex causa, §. nunc videndum; and ff. de confessis, l. certum, §. sed an ipsos; and C. de confessis, l. vnica, through Cy., and l. omnes. And it must be noted that time does not run against a minor to seek this restitution so long as the suit is pending and age assists her. Indeed, even if she expressly renounced it, the renunciation does not harm her, nor does a repeated confession or a continuous confession, because she is repeatedly and repeatedly ensnared; rather, the repetition shows greater unsteadiness; C. ad velle., l. si mulier; ff. de nouationibus, l. doli, §. diuersum, and there through Dy.; ff. de min., l. si iudex circunuento, and there through the gloss. And what I have said concerning renunciation is expressly proved in a capital case, ff. de appel., l. non tamen; and there is an ordinary gloss, which I always cite, ff. de pac., l. pactum inter hęredem. And although a confession is presumed to be true and spontaneous in one of majority, it is otherwise in a minor, unless it is clothed in the garment of presumptions and circumstantial evidence; for minors are not of constant mind nor of firmness, but even yield to the rod, as noted in C. ad Syllenianum, l. fi. Or the confession was made by one of majority, and it does not appear that it was made through fear or error, and the conviction of the judge concurs with the confession; concerning which conviction of mind his word must be relied upon, because a judge is not presumed to be unmindful of eternal salvation, as in C. ad legem Iuliam repetundarum, l. fi.

† And therefore, if the other matters were solemnly conducted, reliance is placed upon the judge asserting from his conscience, as uniquely noted by the gloss on ff. de iudiciis, l. si prętor, §. Marcellus. I say, therefore, that reliance must be placed upon the continuous and unrevoked confession of one of majority for a condemnation, if the discretion of the judge is in accord with the confession from the quality of the persons, or from concomitants, even slight ones; because a slight thing added to a heavy thing makes it heavier, as is evident in weights. And because the minds of men cannot be painted upon parchment, the law has committed several matters to the discretion and conscience of the one judging, as in ff. de quaestioni., l. 1, §. si quis vltro, there: prudently, indeed with faithful and eminent reason, etc., and the rest noted concerning this in c. Rom. de appel., li. 6; and C. quorum appellationes non recipiuntur, l. 2; and ff. de appel., l. creditor, §. iussus.

† In the third case, when there is doubt concerning majority and minority, it is necessary that proofs be received upon this; because age defends against a prosecution just as innocence does against punishment, as noted in C. de iuramen. calum., l. 2, §. quod obseruari. Therefore, whether she is a minor or not must first be discussed as a preliminary question of the threshold of the trial, as in C. de pe. hę., l. si putas. For certain things are preliminary questions of the forum, and these ought to be argued at the threshold of trials, as in C. de adulteriis, l. quam Alexandrum; ff. de minor., l. ait prętor, §. permittitur; and ff. de iure codicillorum, l. quidam referunt; extra de appel., c. ex parte M. Certain things, however, are decisive of the dispute, and these do not impede the weighing; but when the merits of the case appear, the weak must be saved through justice, not through circumlocutions. Certain things therefore concern the beginning, certain things the end, from which this conclusion is evident: that the judge ought to admit all justifiable defenses. Otherwise he makes the suit his own, not only if he does not suffer peremptory defenses to be introduced, but also declinatory ones, as in ff. de edem., l. argentarius, §. cum autem; C. de pac., §. pe. in fi.; and with an equal balance in unjustly condemning and acquitting, as in C. ne Sanctum Baptisma, l. fi. Thus, therefore, it is concluded that the defenses about which question is made ought to be admitted for examination and to be judged according as the reckoning of reasons shall have dictated; and especially because defenses that render a judgment null are always deemed to be raised at the beginning, as in C. de procuratoribus, l. licet.

† Since I now come directly to the crime charged, I say that the husband acted imprudently by alleging public fame; because by this he alleged his own knowledge, as noted in l. si tutor, C. de peric. tut.; and consequently he confesses that he committed lenociny by not divorcing her, but keeping her living unchastely, as in extra de iureiu., c. quemadmodum; and ff. de adul., l. 2, §. si publico; whence he cannot object against the woman a fault of which he is himself the patron, as in ff. so. ma., l. cum mulier. Likewise, because by the form of the statute a woman who has committed adultery multiple times with diverse men is public and notorious, whom the husband cannot ensnare in the toils of the law, since the statute says this expressly. Nor does it stand in the way that she confessed she had committed adultery with no other person; for a negative that is proved by mere assertion consists in a fiction; whence an affirmative of the truth, once proved, derogates from it, because it falls more properly into experience and the senses, as noted in ff. de arbi., l. diem proferre, §. si plures. I conclude therefore in accordance with the discerning arguments of the lord Giliolus, my most beloved son of sharp intellect. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether privileges of princes can be possessed without title.
2. Title is presumed for one from the length of possession.
body: It must be premised, in the name of Christ, that the privileges of princes cannot be possessed without a title, as in the chapter *Ad decimas*, *De restitutione spoliatorum*, Title 6. For since privileges are contrary to the common law, it would involve a contradiction to hold that where there is no privilege, there is possession; because there could be no possession without a title for one’s own right, since a title requires good faith without any objection of contradiction, of law, and by law, as in the Digest, *Pro suo*, law *Ancillam*.

† However, from the length of possession, title is presumed in its favor: because that which has been possessed for a long time is presumed to have the will of the Prince, as in the Code, On the Petition of Inheritance, law *Si filius*. Nor should proof of title be sought after very long periods, as noted in chapter *Iudicium*, On Judicial Proceedings, Book 6, and by Cynus in the Code, On Fideicommissary Instruments, law *Emancipatione*. And because from whose sentence no appeal is taken, it is presumed as his testimony, as in the Digest, On the Office of the Praetor, law 1, section *His cunabulis*. In resolving, I say that the Duchess is presumed mindful of eternal salvation for the light of her majesty, and therefore it should not be presumed that she wishes anything unjust. Nevertheless, if a term has been given for justification, it is not presumed that what consists in fact, unless two things concur in fact, as noted in chapter 1, On Proofs, in the Clementines. And that in one’s own fact one speaks assertively, there is no doubt. Moreover, princes are often deceived regarding knowledge of fact, as in chapter 1, On Constitutions, Book 6. And therefore, to remove all doubt, I believe that a second command or interpretation is necessary, as in the Code, On Laws, law *Si*. But if the Prince or Princess does not wish to declare otherwise, one must not usurp regalia, as in chapter 1, *Quae sint regalia*, column 10, and in the Digest, On Rivers, law *Quo minus*, and *Quod vi aut clam*, law *Prohibere*, section *Plane*. Nor is it always presumed in favor of the possessor: because he possesses against common law. Hence, uncolored possession does not create right, as in the Digest, On Minors, law *Minor autem magistratus*. Let him beware, however, lest the Prince act against conscience: for the time will come when the ship is in port, let it go, laden. And with what measure he measures, the same will be measured back to him, as in the Code, On Judges, law *Rem non novam*. Nor let him trust in his power, he who has God as avenger. And by what has been said, I have touched the point of knowledge and conscience, as in the Code, To the Julian Law on Repetundae, law *Iubemus*.

If, however, the question is about mere positive justice, concerning a privilege, it must be established, as in the Extravagants, On Rescripts, chapter *Ex parte controversis*, and in the Code, On Diverse Offices, law *Probatorias*, Book 12. Indeed, it must be established from the sacred decrees, and it cannot be proved otherwise, as in the Code, On Diverse Offices, law *Probatorias*, Book 12, and noted by Johannes Andreae in the prologue to the sixth book, because according to the true opinion, privileges are not established without the recitation of writing: since they are private laws, they require writing more strongly than public laws, because they deviate from common law: unless the precise will of the Prince appears. Because whatever pleases the Prince has the force of law, as in law 1, Digest, On the Constitutions of Princes, and in law *Idem Vlpianus*, Digest, On Excuses of Tutors, and Digest, On the Office of the Praetor, law *Barbarius*, in the final paragraph, Digest, On Judicial Proceedings, law *Quidam consulebat*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
3. That which is more equitable is more tolerable.
4. One is said to overtake.
body: Assuming that the facts stated in the name of Christ are true, I say and advise as follows:

† that those matters which, having been concluded in law, could and ought to have been effected by our Lord the Pope, considering equity, whether written in the laws or unwritten: because I do not see any proof of obreption or subreption,

† because he who possesses the truth and equity is not said to defraud; let them say what they will, especially since the penalty of loss and deprivation of one’s right is highly odious, and it is more tolerable and more equitable, as stated in D. de verb. oblig. l. si servum, § sequitur, and D. quibus ex causis maiores, l. 1. In both special and general clauses, it is not expedient to allege many points, because the laws are well-known. For he does not obtain [the right] fraudulently, nor [is there] counsel. And therefore, the profound allegations and conclusions of the aforementioned doctors please me, and I subscribe to them with my seal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. He resumes that which he advised in opinion 207, because it appears that other doctors have advised the contrary. And there see the summaries.
1. A bona fide possessor profits from fruits already consumed, unless in a universal action.
body: In the name of Christ.

† I do not see that what they have said has been fully weighed: because this wife has nothing in common with the said John. And where there is no joinder, neither real nor verbal, the right of accretion (ius accrescendi) has no place, because the right of joinder does not arise in distinct things. Here, however, the testator disposed separately of the usufruct, inserting the burden of widowhood; and he disposed by itself of the bare estate, not united with the usufruct; and in this respect he did not burden John in anything, but ceased to bequeath to him anything of the usufruct. Moreover, he imposed the burden upon the universal heir; and although he could not burden beyond the form of the statute, nevertheless the heir could renounce the benefit of the statute, because anyone can renounce a benefit introduced in his own favor; and by tolerating possession on the pretext of the judgment of the testator, the heir himself is deemed to consent, as noted in l. 5, C. de vsufructu. Undeniably, if that wife made the fruits her own under the principal title, neither are they to be restored to the said John, because he has no cause, nor did the said John have in the usufruct any title from the testator; and thus he cannot claim the fruits, even if it were established that they still exist, because they are not his. Nor does lex creditor, § si inter stand in the way, because there the restitution arises from the arrangement of the parties; here it does not, because the disposition of the testator and of the heir tends to the contrary. And ff. de don. l. si tibi dederim is supportive. It is therefore nothing to the purpose whether the rental payments were consumed; but nevertheless it must be said that, if after so many courses of years, this is both on account of the aptitude for consuming and the argument from what commonly happens. What the gloss notes in l. 1, C. si aduersus vsucapionem is supportive.

† And after they have been consumed, a possessor in good faith gains them; therefore, they ought not to be restored, as in ff. de vsuca. l. fructus. It fails in the universal action of the petition of inheritance, as in ff. de petitio. haeredi. l. sed si lege, and l. Item veniam, § fructus, and as fully noted in C. de rei vend. l. certum, and this on account of the nature of the petition of inheritance, although some say the same in both. Furthermore, this woman is presumed to be in good faith, because a woman dealing under ignorance of the law, with the will of the testator and the sufferance of the heir; nor can anyone plead regarding the right of the heir, except the heir himself, especially when dealing with the right of a third party. The laws are common. I, Baldus. See regarding this in consilium 129.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether laborers hired to work in another’s possession are liable, or the hirer.
body: The case is as follows: A certain layman, in the name of Christ, exchanged a certain possession of his with a certain abbot of a certain monastery for a certain possession of the said monastery, without observing the form and solemnity required by cap. 2, de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis, lib. 6, because it was not done with the special license of the Apostolic See nor with the consent of the chapter, but only with the license of the bishop, or diocesan, and with the consent of the said chapter. A public instrument was drawn up regarding the said exchange, and in it the oath of the said abbot was included. After some time had passed, the abbot, having been informed that he had been deceived in the said exchange by more than half the just price, first obtained absolution from the said oath in the court of the said lord bishop, and then petitioned for the rescission of the said exchange by means of restitution in integrum. This was done by a definitive sentence, which, having become res judicata, the lord abbot was restored to his right, and the layman was not restored by the episcopal court to the tenure and corporal possession of the said thing exchanged, previously belonging to the said monastery. In this thing, or possession, the said layman Cicholinus, while possessing it, had a reed bed placed. It happens that the said abbot hired with him a certain member of his household to go to the said reed bed, serving him for a certain salary, and living in his house and at his expense; and also two other laborers hired for a certain price. Being present with these laborers, he ordered them to cut the reeds and those growing therein, and to carry them out of the reed bed, so that the said abbot could have them loaded onto carts and exported wherever he wished. And so it was done, that after deducting the portion of the laborer which remained there, the said lord abbot had all the reeds exported by the said laborers out of the reed bed, and afterwards by carts to wherever pleased the said abbot. Afterwards, the said layman Cicholinus, indignant against the said abbot, and because he could do nothing against the abbot, accused the said laborators of theft on account of the said cutting and exportation of the said reeds out of the said reed bed, in the form and manner contained in the said accusation. The laborers, sensing themselves innocent and blameless, lest they be condemned by contumacy, deliberated to appear; and briefly, all were detained and imprisoned; and finally they excused themselves from the contents of the said accusation, etc.

† It is asked, what is the law. The said laborers, hired by the abbot, who, having obtained by sentence to be restored to the possession of the aforementioned woods, which he had previously exchanged less solemnly, after having been absolved from the oath, claiming lesion beyond half the just price, and who cut down the said woods, etc., are in no way to be punished criminally, neither in person nor in money: for they are excused for many reasons. First, because of the probable and customary practice of peasants: for peasants are accustomed to do such things when hired by those who hire them, as noted in D. de rei vindicatione, l. in rem, § tignum; and D. de iniuriis, l. Item apud Labeonem, § si quis astrologus. Second, because they are entirely free from fault: since these laborers were hired by the abbot and lord of the place, as C. de servis fugitivis, l. quicunque, § finalis. Third, because the act in question cannot be punished civilly on account of any fault: for no fault intervened, neither in deed nor in counsel. Nor was anything done for the purpose of gaining profit or of harming anyone: but solely for the purpose of fulfilling a mandate, which is in its nature lawful and honest, and of the class of honest and useful acts, in which fault is not presumed: and where there is no fault, there is no penalty, as D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. si putatur. Moreover, from whom the civil action is removed, the accusation is also removed: indeed, even more strongly, because the civil action under the Lex Aquilia is granted for slight and very slight fault, but not the criminal action, as noted by Cynus, C. de episcopis et clericis, l. si quis non dicam rapere; and in l. ultima, D. de privatis delictis. Moreover, because corporal penalties require dolus, as D. ad legem Corneli de sicariis, l. in l. Moreover, the principal offender, i.e., the Abbot, did not commit a delict: therefore neither did the accessory, as D. de furtis, l. si quis, § si tu Titium; and D. de iuris omnium iudiciorum, l. si quis id, quod, § finalis. Moreover, all penal statutes require fault, as l. quamvis, D. de in ius vocando. Wherefore it is concluded that the aforementioned are to be absolved. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The judgments which are to be passed are enumerated in this opinion of Baldus and in the following opinions of certain doctors.
2. Whether the crime of injury is a public crime.
3. To whom pertains the coercion of Jews transgressing their canons.
body: ...is granted by law, lest Christians...

† Protection is granted to Jews by law, lest Christians insult Jews, as in C. de iudaeis l. nullus. However, it is not permitted to them to plot against the Christian faith, nor to subvert by deceptions and lies, cajoleries or falsehoods, Jews wishing to arrive at the Catholic faith; nor to corrupt their mind, just as it is not permitted to corrupt the mind of anyone’s sons or servants. For all who wish to serve our Lord Jesus Christ, and it does not stand through them, are near to Christ or Christians, just as a recruit, that is, one newly about to undertake military service; he who is about to do something is held as doing it. If anyone, therefore, removes such a holy purpose, he is to be punished: because he who obstructs the way obstructs the end, as noted in l. 1 C. ubi de possessione agi oportet; and an injury is committed on the way just as at the end, as in ff. de condit. et demon. l. quibus diebus in princi. Furthermore, they dragged the Jew away from a safe place, in which he was able to exercise the freedom of his mind, and led him to an unsafe place, in which he could not be baptized; they did not remain within the boundaries of Jewish doctrine, but acted expressly against the Christian faith, and to its opprobrium and dishonor. For it is certainly manifest that this is a public injury, as in ff. de iniuriis l. Item apud labeonem § cum vitium.

† And in this case the crime of injuries is a public crime: because what is committed against divine religion is inflicted to the injury of all, as in C. de haeret. l. manicheos. And since the earth and the fullness thereof, the world and all men belong to Our Lord Jesus Christ, he who takes away his sheep from this Lord ought to be punished as a sacrilegious person, as is read and noted in C. de furt. l. si nondum. Furthermore, that deed is of great rashness and audacity, in which three crimes are involved. The first is the crime of false preaching. The second is the crime of diabolical suggestion. The third is the crime of simony, insofar as money intervened; likewise it is the crime of greater sacrilege, because they stole a sacred thing from a sacred place, that is, a soul from the church of God and from the treasures of Jesus Christ: wherefore justly such persons provoked against themselves the wrath of God. And if this should pass unpunished, it would be a matter of the worst precedent, as in C. ad legem Iuliam repetundarum l. prima. For they said that no one can be saved in the law of Christ. For it would be enough if it were tolerated to them to preach their own faith—which would proceed from forbearance, not from permission. And therefore without doubt the said Jews are to be punished at least by a pecuniary penalty, or another short of blood and the mutilation of limbs, namely imprisonment, as in the twenty-eighth [causa], first question, c. saepe malorum consortium; because public reason urges that penalties be paid for wrongdoing, as in ff. ad legem Aquiliam l. ita vulneratus and ff. de publicanis l. licitatio § quod illicite. And where we are certain of the crime, although we are uncertain of the penalty, an arbitrary penalty ought to be imposed, as in ff. de poenis l. sanctio legum and l. 1 § 1 ff. de effractoribus, et expilatoribus, and noted in C. de sacrosanc. eccl. l. nemo martyres.

† Concerning that matter, however, it can be doubted whether this pertains to the inquisition of heretical depravity; and it seems that it does not, because these men are not heretics, but Jews. It can be said without doubt that it pertains to the ordinary, that is, to the diocesan, who has general jurisdiction over all matters pertaining to business of the faith. And perhaps also to the inquisition, because with respect to the end in which the offense is committed, that is, against the Catholic faith itself, it touches the Catholic faith—just as if a Jew were to strike a Christian cleric, he could be punished by an ecclesiastical judge, as in extra de Iudaeis c. post miserabilem. And because very many points on this matter have been alleged in the consilia of Dominus Ioannes de Lignano and others, not wishing to take the pen from their hand, I rest content with their statements, in conscience, that is, in accord with God. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In which cases Jews are tolerated. And no. 4.
2. What the Church is.
3. What a synagogue is.
4. To whom pertains the coercion of Jews who transgress canon law.
body: and of the Blessed Virgin, In the name of Christ, and of both Johns. Because it is often called into doubt among the prelates of churches, and especially among the inquisitors of heretical depravity,

† In which cases Jews are tolerated, and what is permitted to them among Catholics, therefore I will discuss in order each thing permitted by law: for first it is permitted to Jews to preserve ancient synagogues, and to repair them, but not to construct new ones, as l. fina. C. de Iud. and c. de ciuitate. and c. deinde. and c. consuluit. in that title. Here, however, it must be noted what comes under the name of synagogue. Where it should be known that from the decrees of Pope Lucius, cap. 2. and from sumpturus, and cingendus, one is considered as girded. And who is prepared 2 from the brocard lib. 3. cap. 1. it is held,

† That "church" is a Greek name, and in Latin it means the same as "convocation," because it calls all to itself; and it is called "catholic," as stated in the twenty-first distinction, chapter *Quamvis*, question 1, chapter *Extra catholicam*. This term signifies the same as "universal," although this name has many meanings, as noted in *Ne prelati*, section 6, above, chapter 1, and in *De verbis significatis*, chapter *Cum clericis*.

† Synagogue, however, is a Greek name: and in Latin it means the same as “assembly,” and it is that of the Jews, as Vg. says. For to be summoned is, by a term properly taken from the one who summons, those who use reason. For an assembly is of sheep and of animals lacking reason. Therefore, synagogue is a Greek assembly of sheep: but in the church the people of the faithful are summoned to the true faith. The same judgment therefore applies to the synagogue among the Jews as is said of the Church among Catholics. Note this, by the Archdeacon, Dist. 9, cap. Ecclesia. Collatio 1, quaestio 1, c. Extra catholicam, by John Andreae, Capitulo, deinde consuluit, De electione, Fundamenta, lib. 6, in principio. Just as among Catholics the church is a public place, in which Catholics are summoned to hear divine offices and to receive the sacraments: so synagogue is said among the Jews to be a public place constructed, in which Jews publicly assemble to celebrate their ceremonies: and just as any constructed place among Catholics for praying is not called a church.

† For it is permitted to anyone to have a private oratory, in which he may have seats for sitting, and lamps lit for devotion, and keep certain books for the office to be said, closed in their cabinets, which can be closed and opened, and other rooms of the house in his home, and a place designated for praying, and solely he and his household, which is not called a church, de consecratione, distinction 1, cap. unicuique, and cap. clericos. So too it is permitted to any Jew to have in his own home a private place for praying and contemplating therein for himself and his household, which is not called a Synagogue: where the law permits the preservation of ancient synagogues and their repair, it prohibits the construction of new synagogues. This is understood regarding public synagogues; otherwise, they may have private places notwithstanding the prohibition of the law. Secondly, it is permitted to Jews to celebrate their customary festivals and offices peacefully and quietly, and in their public synagogues. Distinction 45, cap. qui sincera, which was of Gregory to the Bishop of Naples, and there note the gloss how the church permits this, although they sin by doing so, since the worship of the Mosaic Law, from the advent of Christ, does not differ from idolatry. And thus it is resolved that the church merely tolerates their rites, but does not approve them. For if they were prohibited, they would be compelled to the faith, which ought not to be: That which is permitted is not therefore approved, quaestio 31, cap. hac oratione. Therefore, according to Georgius, they have free faculty to celebrate their customary festivals, as their parents had: then, as Jews, and there the text, that no one disturb them with stones or clubs: and whoever contravenes this shall suffer peril to his honor, or be punished by sentence of excommunication, unless he corrects himself. The same is proved by lex nullus, C. de Iudaeis. Thirdly, it is permitted to Jews to attend the processions of Catholics for a cause; to others it is forbidden. De usuris, cap. quanto, and cap. post miserabilem. Fourthly, Jews obedient to the laws are not to be molested by Christians. Quaestio 33, cap. dispar. Fifthly, Jews are not to be compelled to the faith by violence. Distinction 45, cap. qui sincera, and C. de Iudaeis. Sixthly, that Jews shall not be wounded, nor killed, nor stripped of their money without the judgment of earthly power. Seventhly, that the bodies of the dead are not to be exhumed from their cemeteries, as there. Eighthly, in all their rites they are tolerated, provided they are not done to the reproach of the Catholic faith, and those which are prohibited to them. Quaestio 23, 4, 5, and 6, per totum, eodem cap., and quaestio 8, dispositio 28, quaest. 1 and 2, per totum, 41 dis. c. 2 and 4, 46 distinc. cap. Ismael, 11 quaest. 3, cap. ad mensam. Then, throughout, these proceed according to the above-mentioned common law. If any privileges have been granted by the Roman pontiffs besides these, they are to be observed, de privilegiis, cap. porro, cap. accepimus, traditio.

† After the prohibitory decree has been left, so that it may be understood as having been permitted, it remains to be seen to whom pertains the coercion of Jews transgressing these canons. Here it must be observed that the rites of the Jews do not properly partake of heresy, but rather of unbelief with respect to the disposition of the law; for a heretic, strictly speaking, differs from an unbeliever and a schismatic, although any unbeliever, Jew, and pagan may broadly be called heretics. Note. 24. q. 3. §. qui vero. and c. inter schisma. Therefore, if a Jew observes his own rites, he is not properly called a heretic; rather, he is permitted according to the form of the canons. But if he acts against the form of the canons, he is not a heretic strictly speaking, but a violator of the canons. And thus it pertains principally to the ordinary, who is the guardian of the canons. 25. quaestione. 1. c. nulli fas. and cap. violatores. And thus it pertains more to the office of the ordinary than to that of the Inquisitor of heretical depravity the cognizance of the case; therefore, it is the matter of the lord bishop when a Jew acts against the canons. casus de Iudaeis. c. et si iudaeos. and c. postulastis. And he may punish with a pecuniary penalty, and indirectly. d. c. et si Iudaeos. and c. in nonnullis. de rapto. In an archbishopric, where he also punishes corporally, since it already concerns blood. I, John of Lignano. I, Laurence of Primi. I, Egidius of Presbyteris. I, Gaspar of Calderinis. I, John of Fantuciis. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a testament in which diversity is found, provided that solemnity has intervened, but not in its entirety, is valid.
2. The benefit. L. hac edictali. C. de edicto diui Adri. Whether it applies to an intestate.
3. Whether the penalty of one who claims it for himself applies in a nuncupative testament.
4. Two contrary possessory actions, or petitory actions, just as they cannot be cumulated simultaneously: so neither can a possessory action be contrary to a petitory action, or vice versa.
5. The truth of the testament excludes the truth of the intestacy.
body: A testament, that is, once.

† When there is one testament, that is, made once, containing one or many clauses, and a discrepancy is found, the truth prevails which is confirmed by witnesses: provided that the solemnity has intervened, because the authority of law is grounded in solemnity. Whence, if the solemnity had been omitted due to some defect, that defect of omission passed over by the testator would render the testament useless, as in C. de test. l. ambiguitatem and l. si unus. For superfluous things can be removed, but omitted necessary things cannot be supplied by another than by the testator himself. From this follows the conclusion that one must adhere to the truth. Moreover, the truth is an affirmative thing, and therefore what is utterly omitted cannot be true, nor can it substantiate a testament, or any worldly disposition, as in ff. de lib. et posth. l. commodissime and ff. de ver. ob. l. quicquid astringendae. Whence that which is found omitted is deemed null, as in ff. de verb. obl. l. ista stipulatus, the great [gloss] at the beginning, and ff. de fideiuss. l. fideiussores magistratuum, § 1. And this must be premised in the present question, whose conclusion is this: to follow the truth of fact, if it is clothed with solemnity and legal privilege, as in Auth. de testamentis imperfectis, § fi., and C. fam. erc. l. vlti.

† The second point that must be premised is that the benefit of the law hac edictali, C. de edi. di. Adri., does not have a place in intestacy: although some say that it does, provided that a codicil solemnly made in writing appears, so that then, in accordance with the form of the codicil, after summoning the heir, a grant of possession (missio) is made under an equitable condition, on the authority of the said l. edicto. That opinion is equitable, yet the first is safer, as in C. de codicillis, l. fi. in prin.

† Furthermore, there is the question whether in a nuncupative testament the penalty of one writing for himself and the annihilation of the bequest have place; but the first question is not relevant to the matter at hand. As to the second, it must be said that the bequest to the one writing for himself is vitiated, and not to another, as in ff. de falsis, l. filius, § sequens. And therefore, since it appears that the testament was lawfully executed as to the institution of the heir, the case of intestacy ceases, as in C. communia de successionibus, l. antequam, and l. quandiu, ff. de acque hęredi.; and the judge who pronounces the contrary has wrongly pronounced that it ought to be remitted, because under the edict of the divine Hadrian it is null by operation of law, because there is an express error in form and matter, nor is an appeal necessary on account of a defect of the pronouncement, as in ff. de excusa. tuto. l. qui testamento, in princ.

† Likewise, it should be known that just as two contrary possessory remedies, or two contrary petitory remedies cannot be joined together, so neither can a possessory remedy contrary to a petitory remedy, or vice versa, as in ff. de acquiren. possess. l. naturaliter, § nihil commune.

† The final conclusion is that the truth of a testament excludes the truth of intestacy, as noted in l. 1, C. de sec. tab. Concerning a contradiction in the writing, that which is proven to be truer prevails notwithstanding an error, as in ff. de leg. 2, l. cum proponebatur. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an offer discharges one from the penalty of delay, and how such an offer is to be made.
2. It suffices for the protesting party to make the protest; he is not bound to prove his case against the adversary.
3. Whether novation is understood to arise from an assurance, and at no. 4.
4. The interpretation of § quod autem in the Authentica de fideiussoribus.
5. A debtor is presumed to lie who says that he does not have money on hand.
6. A negative is proved by the very fact that the contrary is not proved.
7. A new contract is considered to be observed when it arises from a voluntary compromise.
body: Practica of the City. In the name of Christ. In a case where a creditor summons a debtor to court to recover a monetary debt, so that if the debtor claims he lacks money and offers to give, in lieu thereof, an equivalent amount of his own unsold property, the creditor is compelled to accept it without further judicial inquiry; but if the creditor insists, the debtor is compelled to disclose all his assets so that the creditor may choose. It now happens that the debtor has notified the creditor, and in the notification formal words were used, stating that the debtor lacks money, and so that no delay may be imputed to him, that he is ready and effectively offers to give and deliver to the creditor such of his goods as amount to the sum to which he is bound to the creditor by virtue of a certain judgment, for the creditor to choose as he wishes, according to the valuation by two or more common friends to be chosen between the parties; the said debtor protesting that it does not rest with him that the aforementioned things are not done and executed.

† Now the question arises, given the circumstances as they stand, whether the debtor has incurred the penalty of the compromise: and it seems that he has, because one must not depart from the words of the compromise, as in D. de arbitris, l. Celsus. But according to the words of the compromise, formal satisfaction has not been rendered, as in l. 2, § 1, D. si certum petatur. Therefore, the penalty has been incurred, as in l. Promissor, D. de constituta pecunia. Moreover, the debtor did not disclose his assets, as he is bound to disclose them. Moreover, he did not offer better assets, as he is bound to offer them, as in Auth. de fideiussoribus, § Quod autem. But the contrary is true, provided that the debtor did not have money on hand, so that he could easily offer it, as in C. de solutionibus, Auth. Nisi et quod non haberet pecuniam ad manus. It is presumed that he did not have money on hand, since the contrary is not proven: because no such order preceded, by which he should be presumed to have money, especially ready for payment, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Singularia, and D. de legatis 3, l. Si chorus, § 1. And therefore, the said offer was sufficient, as in the aforementioned § Quod autem. Furthermore, the creditor, who did not object to the protestation, seems to have acquiesced, as in l. Si fideiussor, post principium, D. qui satisdare cogantur.

† Moreover, it suffices for the protesting party to make the protest, and he is not bound to inform his adversary of what he is doing, as stated in l. prima, §. primo, ff. de liberis agnoscendis. Certainly, the rule that one must not depart from the form of the law is not an obstacle, for this is not a departure, but rather proceeding by execution, as in l. miles, §. decem, ff. de re iudicata. Furthermore, this is a certain practice which always appears to be annexed to its theory, because it interprets it and reduces it to practical application, as noted in C. de dolo malo, l. si quis argentum, in principio.

† Furthermore, it is doubted whether, if alimony for the dowry is owed from the first contract, it ceases to be owed for the future time even with respect to a second contract subsequently made. I answer thus: if there has been a complete withdrawal from the first obligation, because it is a voluntary novation, in which the accessories of the first obligation are not seen to be repeated for the future time, as in D. de nov. l. aliam. Otherwise, if there has not been a complete withdrawal from the first obligation, to which the alimony adheres, as in C. de novat. l. finali. C. de iudic. l. 1. and there fully noted. Moreover, because it is not probable that the woman intended to renounce her alimony, which is granted out of compassion from the dowry, and arises solely from natural equity, even without stipulation, as noted in C. rem in praesenti. §. exactio nempe and C. cui ille, who possesses the dowry, is bound to alimony by the passage of time and the use of the dowry: I do not say that he is bound to usury. D. de sol. l. Titia. C. de iu. dot. l. vbi adhuc. and l. in rebus. and noted in Extr. de usur. c. salubriter. Furthermore, if the alimony had been left in a last will, it could not be settled without the praetor, and prior to the examination of the testament, and with certain knowledge, of which it must be established individually, not by general words by which it is provided that he knew. D. de transa. l. de his. and l. cum hi.

And if it is said that a tacit novation has occurred due to a contrary contract, I answer that this does not please me: because although the last agreements prevail, and sometimes they induce novation by operation of law, which requires the expression of words, as in D. de pactis, l. si vnus, §. pactus, in princ., sometimes they induce novation by means of an exception on account of incompatibility, as noted in D. de novatione and D. de verbis oblig., l. qui vsumfructum; or rather, they effect a kind of rescission from the immediately preceding contract, as in D. locati conducti, l. cum in plures, §. lege dicta, and D. de pretoria stipulatione, l. Valerianus, where this is solemnly noted. However, in our case, the facts are otherwise: because there is neither compatibility nor contrariety here, but rather a certain new provision, as argued from D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. si quis ante. And even if the formal alimony were not included in the contract, the discretionary alimony would be, as stated in the aforementioned §. ex tacito, and as argued from C. de actione empti venditi, l. curabit. It may also be added what is noted by the gloss and Jacobus de Arena in D. solutione matrimonii, l. si mora, and D. ad Trebellianum, l. mulier, §. si haeres.

† Furthermore, for the understanding of § quod autem in the Authentica de fideiussoribus, it must be known that this § does not apply in cases in which a general cession of goods is prohibited; because if a general cession does not apply, then neither does a special cession, by the reasoning of that §. And therefore, if the statute of the city speaks on this matter, the words of the statute are to be observed; provided that in a case omitted by the statute, the common law shall be observed. If, however, cession is not prohibited, then those things have place which I wrote in the beginning, and say, as I said there.

† And because no debtor is presumed to lie who says that he does not have money, he has a presumption in his favor, especially because it is something to deny a negative. On this, note in l. ex persona and l. si vero, § 1, and especially if the quantity is large, and people commonly lack money, for example on account of wars, as in l. funus, § puto, ff. de haereditate instituenda. But if the creditor wished to prove the contrary, he would be heard, as in l. magis, § 1, ff. de rebus eorum, ff. de pactis; l. tres fratres, ff. de re iudicata; l. diuo pio, ff. ad legem Falcidiam; l. penultima, ff. de probationibus; l. cum de lege. It accords with what is noted in l. C. quando, et quibus quarta pars debetur, lib. 10, and in Authen. de haeredibus, et falcidia, § sancimus. I say that the debtor is not presumed to have ready money: because this is a mere negative, not restricted, which is not the object of the sense of sight: because it does not terminate in any visible subject.

And therefore the negative is proved by the very fact that the contrary is not proved, as noted in D. de probat. l. verius and C. qui militare non possunt l. super seruis. For this negative is not a substance, nor a quality, nor any of the predicaments, and therefore it is not a natural being; and consequently it is not provable, except by confession, as noted in C. de probat. l. actor and Extr. de confess. cap. 1, lib. 6. From these things it is expressly concluded that this is not necessary to prove. And thus the paragraph quod autem in D. de fideiussoribus is understood. Hence it follows that the debtor incurs the penalty, for there it is not said that any proof is to be made, but only an offer, just as in the cession of goods.

† On another point, since they have voluntarily submitted to arbitration, the contract is considered preserved as a new one, and no question should be raised regarding the old one, as stated in the Digest, title "If someone provides security," law 1, in the beginning. And thus I conclude without further words: nor do I intend to speak further. And this holds unless the custom of the forum, or the general custom, or the interpretation of the common law in the Piacenza forum is otherwise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether he who knows that he owes and does not pay, when not demanded from him, can prescribe; and what in the forum of law, and in the forum of conscience.
body: a testament in which

† It is asked whether one who knows that he is bound can prescribe by the lapse of the longest period of time: and it seems that he can, because in prescription by the longest period of time the intent or act of the prescriber is not required. Hence even one unwilling prescribes, and one ignorant, and neither unwilling nor ignorant, such as one perpetually insane, and an heirless estate lying vacant; therefore in such prescription good faith is not required. For if I owe you ten by a personal action, that which I owe, before I pay it, is mine: or belongs to no one: when I owe in general, it is possessed by no one. And this is what Bartolus holds in the Digest, De usucapione, l. Sequitur, § Si viam. And this is most true according to the subtlety of law and legal disposition. But according to the equity of conscience, it has always been doubted: because good faith ought to be recognized, and prescription by one who knows that he is bound does not extinguish the natural obligation; but if he is ignorant that he is bound, it kills it, and then he would not be bound in the forum of conscience on account of the authority of the law. This happens twice, because he who has acknowledged the debt again prescribes by commencing the prescription of the longest period of time after such acknowledgment; because such acknowledgment has no greater power than to perpetuate. It is said to perpetuate if it extends to forty years: and this is the term of actions, which cannot be exceeded; because it is the term of life and death, as in l. Cum notissimi and l. Si quis emptionis. These words are to be noted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A legacy of one thing was made to a daughter, and a legacy of a decent usufruct until she marries, and afterwards she was substituted together with other outsiders; the case of substitution has occurred. Will she have the inheritance, and the decent usufruct from her co-substituted associates, beyond her share of the inheritance?
body: Ser Peter made his will in the name of Christ. He left to Osanna, his daughter, by way of institution, one piece of land within his boundaries. Furthermore, he instituted the said daughter as his heir to 30 pounds of denarii and 10 [solidi]. Moreover, he left to her suitable food and sustenance until she marries, ordering, wishing, and commanding that she remain silent and content with her portion and the Falcidian share, as contained in the will. In all his goods, however, he instituted as his universal heirs Anthony and John, his sons, who were minors and subject to his paternal power, and he mutually substituted the said sons and his male descendants in the ordinary, pupillary, and fideicommissary ways. And if all his male sons should die in pupillary age, or later at any time without issue, he substituted for the last survivor his female daughters, and Lady Flora, sister of the said testator, and Francischinus de Arlotis aforesaid, and the Hospital of Lepers of St. Lazarus of Certio. Ser Peter, the testator, died after four days, and subsequently all his male sons died in pupillary age, and only the said Osanna remained. It is therefore asked whether the said Osanna, by virtue of the said will, ought to have suitable food and sustenance until she is married from the heirs substituted out of the goods of the inheritance of her said father? And how ought she to have it? Furthermore, it is asked whether, if by law the said substituted heirs are not compelled to give the said sustenance to the said Osanna by virtue of the will, whether those heirs by law ought to be compelled to consign and give to the said Osanna all the fruits of the goods of her father's inheritance for the purpose of sustaining her? Furthermore, if the said substituted heirs are not bound to this, it is asked how the said Osanna, daughter of the testator, ought to have sustenance and be nourished until she marries.

† The example of Dynus is introduced, which states that if a testator instituted his son as a pupillary heir and left the usufruct to his wife, and the son died during his pupillary age, and he substituted the mother and an outsider: if the mother succeeds by virtue of the substitution, she ought not to have the usufruct, as here. And thus Dynus says: which I understand to apply if she had succeeded to the son by tacit vulgar substitution; otherwise, if by pupillary substitution. For then, since she would have received it from the person of the son as a debt, she would deduct it before taking her share, as stated in the aforementioned §. ex quo, commonly cited, and in the Code, On the Goods of Emancipated Sons, l. 1. These are the words of Bartolus in l. licet Imperator, On Legacies, Title 1. This distinction covers the case when the substitution is either vulgar or merely pupillary; but in our case, the testator expressly made both substitutions. And because the inheritance was not expressly accepted, it seems that the vulgar substitution applies, which causes the existence of one’s own heir to cease. Digest, On Vulgar Substitution, l. si filius, with its material. Therefore, it follows that the legacies do not appear to be tacitly repeated by the vulgar substitutes. But if the heir instituted had not accepted the inheritance during the minority of the pupils, all the legacies of the primary wills would be due, and nevertheless, a third part would be due by the vulgar substitution according to Bartolus. However, it may be said, on grounds of equity and natural law, that the daughter ought to have both: because the testator preferred her, and this not by virtue of repetition, but by the pre-existing will of the testator. Also, because the legacy of ownership does not diminish the legacy of usufruct or of alimony, as in Digest, On Usufruct, l. si alij, §. rerum. Therefore, both are due to the daughter by the presumption of piety, which overrides another presumption of law, as in the aforementioned l. licet Imperator. And because the testator so willed, it is so due by the conjunction of both degrees: because in pupillary substitution both degrees concur, as in Digest, On Vulgar Substitution, l. patris, et filii. If, therefore, it is due to the daughter as a prelegacy in the pupillary substitution, argument from Digest, On Legacies, Title 3, l. Paulo chalimaco, §. Pompo. And what is noted there on this point seems to me, as I had previously advised, though I do not recall how; but this my latest opinion seems to me to have equity, considering the natural and ardent love of the father for the daughter, and the favor of alimony. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who are the nearest relatives in the line, or offspring, of the father? What is a line, and how manyfold is it? And similarly, what is offspring, and what is included under these appellations?
body: In the name of Christ.

† By statute it is provided that the instituted heir, if he does not have a legitimate heir descending from him, cannot make a testament and leave the other goods of the said testator, except to his nearer relations from the line, or offspring, of his father Franciscus de Bas. Now two questions are asked. First, whether the said relations are understood to be substituted, and in what order. Second, what is contained under the designation of the line, or offspring, of the said Franciscus. And it must be said that there are two lines, namely the direct line and the bent line, that is, the collateral line; and the direct line is two-fold, namely ascending and descending; and the collateral line is likewise, namely superior, as paternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, and maternal aunt; and descending, or proceeding, as brother, brother's son, sister, sister's son, etc. And that under the designation of offspring only descendants are contained is clear, C. de natu. libe. auth. licet, with similar texts. Likewise, when we make mention of a line, in case of doubt we understand it of the direct line, not the bent or oblique line, on the argument of ff. de vulg. substitu. l. qui liberis, §. haec verba; and this adequately agrees with the words of the testament, when it is said, 'from the line, or offspring, of Franciscus.' For others, that is, collateral relations connected to Franciscus, are not contained under the name of offspring of Franciscus, nor are they contained in those words 'from the line of Franciscus', because this genitive 'of Franciscus', joined with the preposition 'from' (ex), signifies origin, by the argument in l. 1, §. nunc videamus, ff. de coniungendis cum emancipato liberis eius; for that agrees with the preceding words, when it says, 'descending from him,' as is clear in the Institutes, de gradibus, and ff. eo. l. iurisconsultus. I say, therefore, that if any descendants from the said Franciscus are extant, they are included ad infinitum, the order of degrees being observed, especially because the testament says 'to the nearer relations', ff. de leg. 2, l. cum ita, §. in fideicommisso; and it was most prudently and subtly alleged by the lord Angelus de Perusio, my brother, that it does not matter whether this person is male or female, provided that he or she is descending from the direct line of Franciscus, on the argument of C. de condi. inser. in l. 1, ff. de pac. l. tres fratres. From these things it follows that the nearer descendants of Franciscus have a right in the said bequest, because they appear to be tacitly substituted, as was wisely alleged by my said lord brother. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a contract made in fraud of usury can be declared null after thirty years, and before which judge. No. 3.
2. Whether ownership is transferred by a contract made in fraud of usury.
4. Whether a sentence can be declared null after thirty years.
body: years of the contract

† Whether after thirty years a contract of sale made in fraud of usury can be said to be simulated, and before which judge. I answer: this cannot be sued upon before a secular judge, because the cause is ecclesiastical; although when it is established there that the contract is usurious, the secular judge has jurisdiction regarding how the property is to be restored through a vindicatory action (rei vindicatio), and how the fruits ought to be restored, or whether they reduce the principal. Nevertheless, where it is doubtful whether the contract is usurious or not, the secular judge cannot take cognizance, as is noted in 11 q. 1 c. in summa, and in c. dispendiosam de iudic. in Clementinis, and by Bar. and Me. in ff. sol. matri. l. Titio.

† Secondly, it is doubted whether ownership is transferred by a contract made in fraud of usury. I answer: either it was intended to be a true contract, yet in fraud of usury, and ownership is transferred, but it is rescinded because fraud (dolus) gave cause to the delivery; or it was intended that the contract be simulated—namely, a contract of pledge—and then ownership is not transferred, and the property can be vindicated directly, as is noted in C. plus valere quod agitur l. emptione. And thus it appears that it is one thing to contract simulatedly, and another to contract in fraud: I mean in fraud of man, although as a consequence it is done in fraud of the law; for if it were done directly in fraud of the canon, it would be void by operation of law, as in ff. de iure patro. l. si libertus, and likewise in C. de legiti. l. non dubium. Or it is doubtful, and then in doubt I presume fraud and deceit rather than simulation, because the buyer wished to buy, and the seller wished only to sell—not simply, but in fraud of usury. And this is demonstrated by the pact of resale (pactum de retrovendendo) with its accompanying terms. What is noted by Iaco. de Aret. in C. mandati l. per diversas supports this, where he makes a distinction between fraud and simulation; and yet in both cases the fruits are set off against the sum to be restored once the contract is rescinded, because they were perceived unlawfully. Thus is understood what is commonly noted in C. de proba. l. 1.

† Thirdly, it is doubted whether this contract can be said to have been made in fraud or to be simulated after thirty years. And it seems it must be said: not before a secular judge, as in C. de praescript. 30. annorum l. sicut; but before an ecclesiastical judge, because a usurer never prescribes at any time, as in cap. ult. de praescriptionibus.

† A judgment also cannot be declared null after thirty years by an action of nullity, though it may be by way of exception, as in cap. licet de exces. For whoever sues for nullity invokes the office of the judge, as noted in l. 1 § 1 ff. quae sententiae sine appellatio. rescindantur; which office is prescribed by the space of thirty years, as noted in l. pecuniae § 1 ff. de verb. sign., C. de praescrip. triginta annorum l. sicut, and l. querela C. de falsis; and note these words. And note that although a libel of rei vindicatio can be presented before a secular judge by simply vindicating, nevertheless a concluded contract that was made with the addition of the fraud of usury could not be brought before a secular judge, because he is not the competent judge, and because it notoriously exceeds the form and nature of a simple vindicatory libel. Whence, must this be sued upon directly and principally before an ecclesiastical judge? Or perhaps this quality can be remitted to the bishop, so that once he opens the way and remits it, the secular judge could then pronounce on the principal matter brought before him, as in C. de iudiciis l. quotiens and extra de ordine cognitionum ca. tuam. But the first opinion is safer, because a simple libel does not include the quality of jurisdiction under which the action must be brought; therefore, the proceeding was initiated before an incompetent judge. For Innocen. says that whenever a quality establishes jurisdiction, it must always be expressed in the libel, as he notes in extra de foro competen. cap. verum and cap. licet. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The letters of the prince to the judge, that he ought to reconcile the parties, what they import: and what is to be done by the judge, and whether a transaction is necessary from the rescript.
2. When an impediment, or negligence, harms the appellant in the first year, whether in the beginning, in the middle, or at the end.
body: Since a certain person, sent in the name of Christ, had been dispatched to the naval force of the City of Mantua of our Magnificent Duke by the College of Physicians of Piacenza, with a fixed salary appointed to him for one month, it happened that, upon the letters of the valiant and most upright soldier, Lord Galeazzo, called from Mantua, the Lord wrote on behalf of that physician that, if the Pope could in any way do more, satisfaction should be made to him. Later, upon the complaint of the College, the Lord’s counsel declared that, by law, he ought not to be paid for a longer period. Finally, our same Lord wrote to the Podesta of Piacenza that he should strive by good means to reconcile the parties. Hence, the parties were compelled to submit the matter, both in law and in fact, to the same Podesta. This Lord Podesta wishes to know what he ought to do, assuming all the letters issued from both sides to be true.

And it seems that he ought to settle the matter between them, because this is contained in the form of the mandate, as in the Digest, on Mandate, law *Diligenter*. Such a settlement can be made by an arbitrator, even if the other party objects, as is read and noted in the Digest, on Arbitration, law *Si de meis*, section *Recepisse*, and law *Sed si in seruum*, section *Si quis iudex*; and in the Extravagant Decretals, on Prebends, chapter *Nisi esset*; and on Oaths, chapter *Quintauallis*. For this settlement is not conventional by agreement, but necessary by rescript; for even the praetor sometimes settles by his own authority, as in the law *Quid ergo*, section *Poena gravior*, in the Digest, on Those Who Are Notorious Infamous.

To the contrary, it seems that to compose is of voluntary jurisdiction, not necessary, as in the Code, on Actions and Obligations, law *Sicut*. What, then, if the parties do not wish to agree? I answer: let the law and justice agree them. For it must be known that either the law and the fact are certain; and then a settlement does not apply, which ought to be in a doubtful matter. Hence, then the middle way is not to be chosen, but the plain and expedient way according to law, nor would it be a good method to do otherwise against the will of the parties, as in the Digest, on Negotiorum Gestio, law *Nesenn. Apollinaris*, last section.

Sometimes the law or the fact is uncertain; and then the judge ought to compose between the parties, or settle according to his discretion, because this pertains to the office of an arbitrator assumed by fact, as in the Digest, on Partnership, law *Unde si Neruae*, and this accords with the rescript.

Now I return to the point at issue. And because I consider the letters of the opinion of the lord to be juridical on account of the causes and reasons appearing from the acts, therefore I say that the college ought to be absolved from the petition of the said venerable physician; because, although he might deserve something by virtue, nevertheless he does not have the foundation of justice from the merits of the case, which consists in the fact. And especially because he who has a time limitation, since the nature of every term is restrictive, is considered prohibited after the time, as in the Digest, on Legacies, book 2, law *Statuliberum*, section *Stichum*; Code, on Lease, law *Si cum Hermes*; Digest, on Lease, law *Si lege*, in the beginning; Digest, on Peace, law *Epistola*, section *Si*. However, he ought to be absolved from expenses on account of natural equity, which excludes temerity. Hence, from the writings of the doctors, Innocentius, Hostiensis, and others, I find that this should be said in this matter.

† Sometimes total negligence appears in the first year, sometimes a total impediment: and these are clear and undoubted cases; because in the first case I do not swear to him, in the second I do. Sometimes there is negligence in part of the first year, and in part an impediment: and then either the impediment preceded, and negligence followed: and then the last delay harms, as the said law *illud* states. Because he ought to have finished the case in that time of negligence, if there was so much time that he could verisimilarly have finished the case itself: if there was not so much time, at least he ought to have begun. But if first the appellant himself was negligent, and an impediment subsequently supervened, if the time of the subsequent impediment was nevertheless such that he could verisimilarly have finished the case: and then he is not barred from the second year: otherwise, if the other time of negligence was only such that he could verisimilarly have finished the case, and the time of the impediment subsequently followed. Similarly, then, the opinion of Innocentius is to be followed, who wishes that it suffices for the appellant: because, as he says, the appellant begins the appeal at such a time that it is verisimilar that he can finish it within the first fatal year. And if no impediment comes, he could finish it. And thus now the appellant would be impeded for one day, so that he could not finish the case, then he has the second year. And so note Innocentius in *c. ex ratione*, de appellationibus.
