But in our case there was not such an impediment that this Hermeculfus ought to be relieved, as has been said above, therefore, etc. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the Pope can grant secular dignity to any city: and what he can give or alienate, and what he cannot. And no. 3.
2. What is meant by a liege fief.
body: Whether the Pope may in some [city of the Church create a new secular dignity...]

† It is asked whether the Pope can create in some city of the Church a new secular dignity, which may be called and constitute a marquisate, county, or duchy. And it must be said that he can; and that he may confer that dignity thus created, together with the city itself and every kind of beneficial jurisdiction, upon a new marquis, duke, or count as to beneficial ownership and profits, by making a solemn investiture with the swearing of a general and special oath of fealty, provided that it is not manifestly contrary to the estate of the Roman Church and done to its rivalry, or to the ruin and enormous lesion of the subjects, for they must not be ill disposed of.

† And such a fief is called liege, and it cannot be revoked without fault: and these points are proved both by canon law and by civil law, and by both written and customary law, as in extra de re iud. c. pastoralis in Clem., and extra de iureiu. c. veritat., and extra de iudi. c. nouit., and in the 10th coll., de natura feudi, c. 1, and in the title quis dicatur Dux, marchio, comes, the single chapter. For all fiefs subsist by the authority of the prince, as in c. Imperialem, § 1, de prohi. aliena. feu. per Federicum, and in c. 1, quae sint regalia, in the same collation. And to this theoretical principle Innocent reduces the matter in extra de iureiu. c. intellecto, where he says that kings can make all manner of donations of the things of the realm, namely as to the secondary beneficial, emphyteutic, or feudal ownership, provided that also by reason of the benefit that follows from such grants, a greater interest ought to be rendered to the lord himself, such as rents and feudal services. That fief, therefore, comes from him, that is, the Pope, yet remains under him: because in no way can it be alienated from him, as noted in Auth. quomodo oportet episcopos, in princ., col. 1. For the Pope ought to be the preserver of the papal realm and crown, because he is bound to preserve the honor of the crown uninjured, and even if he should swear to the contrary, the oath is invalid. The same applies in a secular ruler: because the honor of the crown is not alienable, nor grantable to another, nor transferable to another, although it is communicable, because even the Emperor can communicate it to his son, and the empress shines and glitters with the rays of her husband, as in ff. de leg. 2, l. quod principi, and l. si augustae.

† Nor does what Bert. notes in the said c. intellecto stand in the way of the aforesaid, where he expressly notes that prelates of churches cannot enfeoff things that belong to the full property of the Church and are its own peculiar assets, such that they were never previously enfeoffed, as is clear in extra de feudis, c. ex parte, and in c. 1, episcopum, vel abbatem, coll. 10; because from every negative or prohibitory rule, the person of the prince and supreme authority is understood to be excepted, as in ff. de fluminibus, l. quominus; ff. de lega. 1, l. apud Iulianum, § fi.; C. de quadriennij praescriptio, l. bene a Zenone; and it is expressly noted in C. de legi. l. humanum. Nevertheless, I say that this ought to be done in the council of the Cardinals or peers, lest it seem done lightly and without deliberation, as is clear there. Likewise, I consider it praiseworthy, and perhaps necessary, that there intervene the consent of the men of that city whose condition is changed, or that they swear fealty into the hands of the feudatory, as I have read and as noted in ff. de fideicom. liber. l. inuitus, and ff. de actionibus emp. l. Titius. Someone will say, nay rather this is necessary, because the Pope is the moderator and arbiter of his own property; and if I hold a fief, I can sub-enfeoff it even against the will of the vassals, as in c. 1, de capitaneo, qui curiam vendidit. But that text speaks of the case where a vassal is transferred to another lord, not when a free man would be made a vassal, which cannot be done without his consent, as in l. fi. ff. de natalibus restituendis, and ff. de contrahen. empt. l. et liberi, and ff. de verb. obli. l. inter stipulantem, § sacram. And the reason for the difference is that in things sharing a common token change is easy, as in ff. de lega. 3, l. pater filium, § quindecim. libertis. Therefore, the said fief could not be revoked without cause, since it is confirmed equally by the authority and the validity of the prince, as says the text in the said c. 1, de natura feudi, and as Cy. notes on C. de legib. l. digna vox. For that which is confirmed by a certain and constant nature ought not to depend upon the momentary impulses of the prince's mind, as in c. debet, de regu. iur., in VI, and in Authen. constitutio, quae de digni., § illud. Indeed, in a prince, speaking according to God and natural reason, and also canonical sanction, what is not fitting is not lawful; nay, a prince sins more deeply than an inferior, as I have read and as noted in extra de iudiciis, c. cum venisset, by Hostiensis; and in the novel rule of a good pastor, it is to shear the flock and not to devour it: he ought therefore to wait for it to regrow its wool. I, Baldus. Statutes pertaining to the following consilium. In the name of Christ. Presupposing the statutes of the city of Cremona of the following tenor, namely: Rubric on those invested, and that the one investing be put in possession once the election has been made or the term of investiture has ended. Likewise, it is enacted that if anyone invested or to be invested hereafter with anything shall have ceased payment of the rent for so long a time that by law an election may be made, and it has been made—which election, or reclamation to oneself, may be made even on behalf of an absent party—or if the time of the investiture to be made, or of that which lasts today, shall have expired in the future, that such investor, or he who in the future shall make an investiture, and their heirs and the heirs of each of them, and those deriving title from them, shall be inducted into possession of the aforesaid thing, in whosesoever possession or detention such thing shall be, without any libel or solemn petition: provided it first appears that the investor and the one who made or shall make such an investiture held and possessed at the time of the investiture, or that the person invested was in possession or detention of such thing concerning which the investiture was or shall be made, after the investiture itself; saving every right in the thing and to the thing to the possessor-detainer against him who was inducted into possession. And that in the aforesaid cases, and in each of the aforesaid, he from whom it has thus been evicted shall have recourse against his grantors, sureties, mandators, and guarantors, and the heirs of each of them and the possessors of the pledges, just as if it had been lawfully evicted, summarily and without any damage, libel, or solemn petition, provided notice has been given once at a suitable time to his grantors, and the goods of such persons shall be obligated just as if the eviction had been lawfully made. Rubric on the penalty of those hiring a thing from two persons, or accepting an investiture. Likewise, it is enacted that if anyone shall have taken any thing on lease from someone, and afterwards shall have hired that same thing or taken it on lease from another without the knowledge of the first lessor, he shall be fined 25 imperial pounds, and nevertheless the first lessor shall be understood to possess, and the things shall be freely restored to him by the office of the judge and without litigation. And let the same be done if the lessee, upon the expiration of the lease term, does not freely restore the thing to the lessor, even granted that he did not lease it from a second party, or if a tenant farmer or lodger has lost or inverted the possession of the house or leased property: provided that first, in the aforesaid cases or in any of the aforesaid, it be proved that the lessor possessed at the time of the lease, or that after the lease the lessee remained in detention of the leased thing. And if the possession or detention in any case is not found with the lessee, but with a third party in any manner whatsoever, let the lessor be placed in possession by the judge upon examination of the instrument of lease, or upon proof of the lease by witnesses, provided it is established that the lessor was in possession at the time of the lease, or that the lessee was in detention of the thing leased by the lease shortly afterwards, summarily, without the clamor and figure of a trial, and without any formal petition. And what has been said concerning a lessee shall have place in an investiture received from two persons jointly and severally, unless the said investiture were made by two present together, or by one investing in his own name and in the name of the other. And also in the case of the same thing received from two persons precariously, as has been said above concerning investiture. And the same in effect was provided in the old statutes made during the investiture whereof mention is made above. Rubric on the possession of goods passing to the heir. Likewise, it is enacted that upon the death of anyone, the possession of the hereditary goods of the deceased passes to his heir without any physical taking. And if anyone who is not the heir should enter into possession of the hereditary goods, the entry is of no effect, and he shall pay as a fine one hundred imperial solidi. And that anyone may repudiate and abstain from an inheritance devolved upon him, whether under a will or upon an intestacy.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the lessor, or his heir, loses the benefit of the statutes mentioned herein and in the following chapter, if the tenant or colonist has interrupted possession, or has transferred it to another by sale and delivery, and thirty years or more have already elapsed.
2. The statutes of princes and of peoples are of civil law.
3. Whether restitution in integrum can be sought by mere words and incidentally.
4. In how many ways possession can be interrupted.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The question was raised, first, whether if a tenant (inquilinus) or a colonus intervened, or delivered possession by selling and delivering it to another, and thirty years and more have already elapsed, the lessor or his heir loses the benefit of the said statutes, given nevertheless that the said inverter or deliverer always paid the annual rent to the owner. And it seems that he does: because whether there arises from the said statutes a condictio ex lege, as in C. de acquir. poss. l. fi., or the office of the judge, as in ff. si mulier ventris nomine. l. 1. §. necessario., it is certain that prescription runs against both of these remedies by the space of thirty years, as in C. de edicto diui Adriani. l. edicto. §. fina. and as noted in C. de praescriptione 30. annorum. l. sicut. and ff. de verborum significa. l. pecuniae. §. 1.; for every complaint, whether civil or criminal, is extinguished by so long a time, as noted in C. de falsis. l. querela. To the contrary it is argued: for it seems that the thing is not prescribed, because the lessor never lost possession, nor did he know of the inversion or betrayal, nor did he suspect that he could be repelled, since this was neither attempted nor proved; therefore, through the continuation of the rent or charge, he retained possession, as in ff. de praescriptione triginta annorum. l. male agitur. and ff. quibus modis vsus fruct. amittitur. l. Pomponius. Likewise, these things seem to pertain to those prescriptions which do not begin to run against a vacant inheritance, nor against an ignorant heir, as in C. de temporib. in integrum restitut. l. ea, quae.; because he who is not negligent is not harmed by the passage of time, as noted in Authen. de app. in princi. Likewise, that office of the judge is praetorian, argum. ff. ne fiat ei. l. si quis missum.; and a benefit of the praetor is never prescribed against an ignorant person, as noted in Inst. de perpetuis, et temporalibus actionibus. in princip. and l. secunda. §. dies. ff. quis ordo in bonorum possessione seruetur. Someone will say: on the contrary, this time runs against an ignorant person just as it runs against an absent person, who is presumed to be ignorant, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum. l. sicut. and l. fina. C. de praescript. longi temporis. And if you say that this remedy is praetorian, I reply: on the contrary, it is of the civil law, because it is municipal.

† For the statutes of peoples belong to the civil law, ff. de iustit. et iure. l. omnes populi., and in the same way the statutes of princes, as in l. i. ff. de constitutionibus principum. and noted in Inst. de actionibus. §. sed iste. For whether a remedy belongs to the civil law or to the praetor's law can be considered in two ways: in one way, as it is in the starting point (in termino a quo) and in him who establishes it, and then the aforesaid remedies are set forth from the civil law; in another way, as it is not in the terminus, that is, in him who brings the remedy, and then every office of the judge is a living praetorian remedy. But as to the time of prescription, it is viewed as it is in the starting point, as in Inst. de perpetuis, et temporalibus actionibus. in princip. Likewise someone will say: granted that it is prescribed, restitutio in integrum is available on account of justifiable ignorance, as noted by Dyn. in ff. de verbo. obliga. l. ad diem. Then I argue thus: the office of the judge is not extinguished by prescription ipso iure, but by aid of an exception (ope exceptionis), as in ff. de act. et obliga. l. actionum fere. §. placet., just as it is not extinguished by an agreement, especially a tacit one; therefore neither by mere negligence, because negligence can do no more than express consent, and therefore prescription can do no more than an agreement, as noted by Cyn. in l. prima. de anna except.

† This being presupposed, then, restitutio in integrum may be sought by way of replication within the four-year period to be reckoned from the day of knowledge, as in ff. de iureiurando. l. nam postea. §. si minor., and it may be sought orally and incidentally, because it needs no other proof, since ignorance is presumed, as that notable law says in ff. de autho. tut. l. descendentem. and the Gloss on ff. de interrogat. actio. in rubrica. Yet I do not find it sought in the proceedings here, and because perhaps the office of the judge is extinguished ipso iure by thirty years' prescription, argumentum C. de iudiciis. l. properandum. §. finali. Consider regarding that which was substantially touched upon above concerning the inversion of possession.

† For there are four cases according to Ioannes. For either the colonus abandons the land, and from this alone the owner does not lose possession, since he does not acquire it for others; or he loses it by arranging to be evicted having negotiated with the evictor, and likewise, as in C. de acquiren. posses. l. exemplum.; also when he loses it is when he not only simply departs, but does so with the intention that another may enter, and another has entered, because he schemes against the owner; or he is cast out against his will and without fiction, and then the owner loses possession as if he himself were repelled, because the colonus and the owner are deemed the same person, and because the colonus is an instrument of the owner, and upon his feet the owner establishes himself, ff. de acquiren. possessi. l. peregre. §. quibus.; or he delivers it to another, and then Ioannes said that the owner loses possession. But the moderns hold the contrary, because a colonus does not possess, wherefore he cannot deliver possession to another, as is fully read and noted in C. de acqui. poss. l. cum nemo. and by Pet. and Cy. in l. fi. Observe here: because, positing that the opinion of Ioan. were true, it must nevertheless be understood to apply when the colonus delivers corporally and in actual fact, for it is otherwise if precariously or fictitiously, because a precarium is of no validity since he does not possess, as in ff. de acquir. poss. l. quod meo., wherefore this is rather a betrayal than a delivery. Then I argue thus: the owner does not cease to possess, therefore prescription does not run against him except after long negligence, as noted in l. 1. C. de fur. and by Dy. in c. sine possessione; whence it follows that thirty years have not run from the day of negligence, and thus it is not prescribed; just as the thing is not prescribed, so neither is the action or the office of the judge, because as long as the principal lasts, the accessory lasts, as noted by Cy. in l. 1. C. de annali exceptione. in the question de communi diuidun. And according to the aforesaid, the Gloss in the said l. cum nemo must be understood, and these points are subtle enough. And in this manner it seems it must be argued that prescription has in no way run against the acting dominus Ugolinus, since he has always been in a possession more than civil, brought about by municipal law, which says that the possession of the deceased is continued into the heir ipso iure. That is certain, that prescription does not run against a possessor, and said lex male agitur. Likewise, according to certain authorities, the said last law C. de acquir. poss. does not have a place in the case of a tenant for a long term, who has the beneficial ownership (vtile dominium) and beneficial natural possession; wherefore, after the manner of a usufructuary, he never prejudices the owner of the property when the owner of the property always possesses civilly, because each person's possession is judged on its own, as noted in ff. vsufruc. quemadmo. caueat. l. 1. in fi. and l. 1. §. deiicitur. ff. de vi, et viar. On these points I do not dwell, because whether the witnesses are true or false, there is nevertheless one witness who is completely truthful, whose testimony has been verified by the statute. And therefore it suffices for victory in the case, at least from the time that they possessed for thirty years. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether acts performed by the King of the Romans are valid, as if he were already crowned.
2. Three things constitute a canonical act: power, will, and mode.
3. God can do all things, but not sin.
4. A vassal of the Empire who is bound by personal allegiance, who is not obliged to swear fidelity unless the Emperor commands that he swear fidelity to another, and whether the nature of the fief can thereby be altered, so that he is obliged to swear fidelity to several persons jointly and severally.
5. Whether benefices that have passed into their perfect state can be revoked and rescinded without cause.
6. What a prince may do.
7. What is the proper nature of words.
8. Territory and diocese: in what they agree and differ, and what they encompass.
9. What general words comprehend.
10. The son is bound by the contract of the Emperor. Add the following opinion.
body:
King of the Romans. In the name of Christ. He created, made, and erected from the fullness of his power and out of certain knowledge many cities of Lombardy, together with all their dioceses, districts, and counties, as well as Marches. Having thus created this most illustrious dignity, he most fully provided for it, titled it, and granted it in fief to the most noble and illustrious Duke, the Serene Prince, Lord John Galeazzo, who held and possessed certain of these cities and dioceses and acknowledged them from the Holy Roman Empire. He ordered that, insofar as it pertains to the supreme jurisdiction of the Holy Roman Empire, all and each barons, marquises, counts, and all other holders of any fiefs, marches, counties, concessions, jurisdictions, rights, and whatever regalia in the aforementioned duchies and dioceses, should henceforth receive and acknowledge them from the said Illustrious Lord John Galeazzo and his successors; with the final clause added, notwithstanding any laws, enfeoffments, concessions, rights, constitutions, etc.

Now it is presupposed that a certain nobleman, by virtue of a vicariate or concession of the Emperor, holds a certain city which is not inserted in the privilege of the said Lord, together with a part of a certain diocese situated in the territory of another city granted to him. It is asked whether those words concerning dioceses refer to the dioceses of cities not granted, so that the diocese in that part remains under the prior lord, as it was accustomed to be held by him? Or whether it has been transferred to the jurisdiction and power of the said glorious prince newly created, so that the holders must acknowledge from him, or relinquish according to his good pleasure and the new custom? First, I will state my opinion; second, I will defend it against obstacles and contrary objections.

† And I say that the King of the Romans, although not yet crowned Emperor, nevertheless possesses the same power as if he were crowned by the imposition of the crown, according to the common opinion of the jurists; because the crown adds nothing to the Emperor except splendor. And this being premised as true: thus obedience is owed to the King of the Romans, just as to an already crowned Emperor, as noted in the law *bene a Zenone*, through Jacobus de Aretino and Cynus. For the crown is a sign of a certain demonstration and glory; but it is not the substance of the essence, which is initiated in the election and substantiated in the confirmation, although in the coronation it receives an increase of majesty and honor; and if the King of the Romans before coronation were to use these words, "Imperial Majesty," it would be a false style. I therefore say that whatever the King of the Romans has decreed, which is not contrary to the status of the majesty of the Empire, is valid and supported by firm power. Hence, if the King of the Romans gave, ordered, and granted to our lord the Duke that obedience be rendered to him as to himself, with the clauses "Notwithstanding" added, no one ought to doubt that the margraves, and whoever is endowed with any power, and much more the peoples, are bound to obey him formally and totally in the chapters expressly mandated. And also in others, if those which are not specified come into consequence, or are reasonable. And although for the same fief one ought not to swear fidelity twice to two persons; nevertheless, if this pleases the Emperor, obedience is owed; and especially on account of the perfidy or negligence of the subjects. And thus I conclude that our Magnificent Prince ought to be obeyed formally and totally in those matters in which obedience would be owed to the Emperor, if his person were principally and personally interested in Italy. To prove which, it follows, as below, and for the difficult understanding of this question.

† Two matters are principally to be considered: namely, royal power and will; certainly also the manner; for these three canonize all acts, namely power, will, and manner. For without power nothing is brought to an act; and without will nothing is perfected by consent; and without manner nothing is directed to its end.

Regarding the first, we can do that which we can do by right, as in D. 50.16 (De verbis significandis), l. Nepos Proculo. Moreover, it is certain that power is the principle of any effect, so much so that where power, in which we inspect the beginning, is lacking, whatever is done is considered incongruous, as in D. 35.1 (De legatis tertio), l. 1, § Si filius; D. 50.17 (De regula Catoniana), l. Prima; D. 45.1 (De obligationibus et actionibus), l. Inter stipulantem, § Sacram; D. 40.1 (De servis exportandis), l. Si minor.

Regarding the second, namely concerning will, it is certain: for consent and will are the roots of human acts; and we call this their substance, because without it there is no subsistence, as in D. 44.7 (De actionibus et obligationibus), l. Obligationum substantiae; D. 2.14 (De pactis), l. 1, § Conventiones. For all acts are without soul, if not formed by consent; and they lack essential spirit, as in D. 34.2 (Si certum petatur), l. Si ego, and § Non omnes.

Regarding the third, namely concerning manner, it is sufficiently clear: for where the ordered manner is not observed, one cannot attain the end; because when the manner is destroyed, the order is destroyed, and the ordered thing becomes nothing, as in Auth. De hereditatibus et falcidiis, § Inordinatum; Extr. De restitutione spoliatorum, cap. Pisanis; Extr. De rescriptis, cap. Cum dilecta; D. 33.7 (De constituto peculio), l. 1, § 1. Hence the verse says: "There is a measure in things, there are certain limits, after all." And as noted in D. 45.1 (De verborum obligatione), l. Si ita quis, § Lege, Aristotle says that there are two things by which it happens well for men: to set the intention rightly, and to assume the modes leading to the end. And these words ought to be written in the hearts of kings. And Boethius says that there are two things in which the effect of intentional things consists, namely power and will. But power is properly said to be to be able legitimately. For we cannot do that which we can do with injury. To be able thus by nature is not power, but a certain deficiency.

And therefore God can do all things, yet He cannot sin: hence it is that a disgraceful condition is not said to be potestative, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. filius. And the law states that those things which refer to a disgraceful cause ought not to be brought to effect, as in D. de annuis et singulis legatis, l. quintus, § Pomponius, and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. quidam suo. Moreover, upon this first evident point rests one substantial element of that which is sought: whence such a question is submitted for the understanding of the foregoing.

† Suppose that I am a vassal of the Holy Roman Empire, such that by the nature of the imperial fief I am not bound to swear fidelity except to the Emperor. Suppose that the Emperor commands me to swear fidelity to another, while retaining for himself supreme fidelity; can he thereby alter the nature of the fief and subject me to a heavier servitude? Can he require that for one fief I swear fidelity to several persons jointly and severally? It is certain that the servitude owed to several is heavier than that owed to one; can the Emperor overturn all feudal customs and all equity of natural reason? Can he, in general, subject all the laws of the world to his will? Can he proceed to infinity, making an immediate vassal of the Empire an immediate vassal of the King of France? And thus can he subalternize vassal to vassal ad infinitum? It is dangerous to hold this view, for to rescind or diminish what has been granted, or to alter it, is the height of injustice. And what you wish to be done to another, let it be done to you, as stated in Codex, De rescindenda venditione, l. ratas. I consider this law to be inviolable, because it teaches morality, which is the supreme principle in the governance of the world, as set forth in the Institutes, De iure naturali, §. ex non scripto. And this King of the Romans, as far as his words are concerned, has revoked all the favors of other Emperors and all benefits granted by them, insofar as they obstruct the present provisions.

Whether, therefore, can benefits that have passed into their perfect effect be rescinded without cause? If we say that they can, we adopt a bad counsel for our lord and his sons; because we see that when one prince dies, another succeeds who has a different will. Moreover, perhaps the same person might change his will and intention. And therefore I believe that rather one should adhere to simplicity and good faith, namely that those who have been legitimately invested cannot be disinvested without cause, as in c. 1, de natura feudi. And if the lord proceeds in a wrongful manner, recourse should be had to the peers of the court. And if this is not sufficient, war may be waged, as in c. 1, de vasallo milite, qui contumax est. I say this by way of motivation, so that the matter is considered not only as to what is right, but also as to what is advantageous. For he who loves his lord should have deep eyes, so that he sees not only the surface of the sea, but the depths, where it is not safe to sail. I speak boldly: because Seneca says that great heights are deprived of this one thing: because out of fear or excessive reverence, no one dares to speak the truth. But before our lord, on account of his clemency, everyone can speak boldly what is good, especially for himself, and for his own status, and for his most serene sons. A certain King said: I do not hand down to my sons a greater kingdom, but a firmer and more enduring one, because it is well founded. Therefore, one must consider the aforementioned matters, what is fitting and what is expedient, without omitting that all things that can be attempted must be tried; because no one should leave his right undiscussed, as in ff. de petitione hereditatis, l. illud. And when it comes to peace, everything must be carefully examined, because those things that are left unresolved in illnesses, after the crisis, are accustomed to cause subversion.

The doctors say that the Emperor cannot impose a law upon himself; hence, the prince who granted his own privilege can revoke it by a contrary imperial decree. And even if not by ordered law, yet by absolute power, as in the Authentica *De defensoribus civitatum*, § *Interim*, so that deprivation proceeds from the same source as the acquisition and grant, especially since privileges depend solely on the will of the prince, and free will cannot be taken away from another or from oneself, as in D. *De fideicommissis libertatis*, l. *Lucius*; in the Authentica *De defensoribus civitatum*, § *Interim*; C. *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, l. 1; D. *De legibus tertio*, l. *Si quis* in the beginning; and what is noted in D. *De regulis iuris*, l. *Quotiens utriusque*. Therefore, the subject must always keep this fear before his eyes, as it is written: “Serve him with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling.” On this point, however, I do not insist, but refer to what Cynus notes in C. *De legibus*, l. *Digna vox*, and what is noted in the Authentica *Quomodo oportet episcopos* in the beginning. But I do not believe that those things which the prince does by the authority of God are so fragile, unless they are made out of ignorance. For a grant of an immunity prohibited by law confers no right whatsoever, as in C. *De agris et censibus rusticis*, l. *Immunitates*, Book 10; and D. *De vacatione munerum*, l. *Sub munere* and l. *His honoribus* in the beginning; and C. *De petitione bonorum sublatum*, l. *Unica*, Book 10; C. *De operibus publicis*, l. *Si quando*; C. *De decurionibus*, l. *Vacuatus*. Moreover, the prince can subject himself to reason, as in D. *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, l. *Est receptum*. Therefore, if he acts to the contrary, he does nothing, because the prince is bound by the subject matter, which can or cannot be done just as it is capable or incapable of being done, as in D. *De legatis tertio*, l. *Quaesitum*, § *Illud*; and note, Extravagant *De iureiurando*, c. *Intellecto*. Finally, I conclude my opinion that he cannot derogate without cause from those things which he or his predecessors did legitimately, because the whole is one Empire; hence he ought not to contradict himself. However, I do not state this as a settled rule, unless it seems so to others who are more prudent. For this is a controversy about which peace has never been made among the intellects. Nevertheless, our principal case stands in a grant that remains in force, and therefore the Magnificent Empire of Our Lord stands in its firmest stability.

† I proceed to the second step, and I presuppose that the proper nature of words is that which reason and the meaning of correct speech encompass. For meaning is drawn by the substantial nature of the thing, without which the intellect is removed from the intelligible, as in D. de acquisitione et amissione possessionis, l. Plautius; D. de supellectili legato, l. Ita Labeo; § Idem Tubero; l. Si quis filium proprium, in fine; C. de liberis praeteritis vel exheredatis, l. 6. And then words are taken properly when they are notably interpreted, as in D. de verborum significatione, l. Nepos Proculo; and l. Quisquis mihi; C. de his qui veniam aetatis impetrent, l. Finis; D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Fideicommissum; D. de iudiciis, l. Statius; § Cornelio; D. de verbis obligatis, l. Ex ea parte; § In insulam.

† Moreover, it is certain that "diocese" and "territory" are universal terms, as in the Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Pupillus*, § *Territorium*; and also "diocese," as in the Decretals, *De rescriptis*, chapter *Rodulphus*. From these I argue that, if the words are to be understood in their proper sense, it is certain that

† That universal words comprehend whatever is within the bounds of the universality, so that no person and no place is excepted, as in D. de officio praefecti urbis, l. 1, § cum urbem, in the word “quicquid” [whatever], where the case appears to be for our lord the king. It does not matter in whose territory, but in whose diocese; because this is not only a mode of being, but a mode of signifying attributed by the intellect, indeed by the very nature of the thing itself, as in D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. 3, § 1; and D. de legatis 3, l. Patronus, § 1; and D. de legatis 2, l. Gaius, § si; and l. Si fundus; D. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1; D. de legatis 3, l. Praediis, § Balneas; and § Qui domum. For when the matter concerns a corporeal thing, nothing is to be diminished from the right, because the whole is one integral and single intellectual entity, and the same thing ought not to be judged under different laws, as in D. de usucapione, l. Eum qui haeredes.

Furthermore, it is certain that in this entire privilege there are general words not restricted by any special words; and therefore they are to be understood as they stand, according to l. Prima, § Et generaliter, D. de legato praestando; and D. de aleatoribus, l. 1, § Quod autem; D. de testamento militis, l. In fraudem, § fin. and § ult.; D. de legatis 3, Hoc legatum; D. de supplemento legati, l. Si.

And if it be said that rather the words of the prince should not be interpreted so as to be drawn to another’s injury or burden, as in D. ne quid in loco publico, l. 1, § Sunt qui putant; this, however, pertains to a burden, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. Impuberi; and D. de testamento militis, l. Cum filius, § si. Where it is said that he who cannot take away another’s right cannot diminish it, as in the same title, l. Dotalem. And there it is expressly noted that a privilege does not abrogate a rooted privilege. For the first privilege is not abolished by a subsequent one. It is answered that this is done by the words of the privilege.

And if it be said that the second privilege does not abrogate the first, to this likewise it is answered by the words of the privilege; for the aforementioned reasons apply well in a doubtful case, that is, when the words are obscure or the intent uncertain; but where we are certain of the words and the intent, there is no question of restrictive interpretation.

Having seen and considered, one thing must be noted, that more specific provisions prejudice more general ones, as is fully noted in Extr. de rescriptis, c. 1; and C. de silentiariis, l. Decurionibus, lib. 12. And therefore it would be necessary to examine the tenor of the other party’s privilege. But unless it appears, the privilege of our prince must be upheld, as in Extr. de privilegiis, c. Porro, always assuming the power of the Roman King.

† If, however, it is not by way of privilege, but a contract, I say that the treasury is bound by the contract of the Emperor. C. de quadrien. praescrip. l. bene a Zenone. This obligation the Emperor cannot rescind, because it is of natural law. And in this case, presumption does not apply against the prince when he acts contrary to the faith due by reason of the contract, as ff. manda. l. dolus. And therefore, what is done under such pretext is not effective, as l. 1. in fi. ff. de exceptione doli. and ff. de decretis ab ordine faciendis. l. ambitiosa. And there, by Bartolus, it is examined whether the promissory cause is presumed true or not, and I say this especially when it contains the statement of another, as in c. 1. Ex quibus casibus feudum amittatur. colla. 10. If the Pope commits jurisdiction to someone, he nevertheless retains the same jurisdiction for himself, and greater. de praebend. c. dudum. li. 6. It is valid, unless for the sake of peace he expressly permits the contrary, de pace constantiae. c. Rex Romanorum. §. super his. Allegations of Lord Baldus of Perugia. To the same effect, as in the preceding counsel, and in consilium 274.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What kind of contract a fief is.
2. Whether a contract made with a prince is valid, and whether the prince can revoke it.
3. Celestine used to grant in the morning what he revoked in the evening.
4. The Emperor cannot change the status, nor diminish the honor, of the old vassals. Likewise in those things which they have leased in perpetuity.
5. Whether the lord can transfer a vassal against his will to another, or delegate him to another.
6. That which is not transmissible is not delegable, nor assignable.
7. The oath of fidelity is twofold.
8. Who is the competent judge in a case concerning a fief.
9. It is natural for men not to make their liberty worse.
10. Who are bound to obey the Emperor.
11. When a city is sold or granted, jurisdiction is deemed to be granted.
12. When a fief is granted to two persons, one after the other, which of them is to be preferred.
13. Whether a prince can do the same as the Emperor.
body: For the day before, the consul, in the name of Christ, advised by the counsel of Lord Christopher, Lord Paul of Artioni, and many other wise men, held that the Lord Pope could not revoke the fief granted to that nobleman of Lucino. And just as he cannot revoke it, so too he cannot burden it, nor impose any adventitious charge upon it; because a perfect donation cannot be torn apart, nor mutilated, nor can anything be added to it, as is stated in the Code, *De donationibus quæ sub modo*, in the law *Perfecta*; and in the Digest, *De fideiussoribus*, in the law *Contractus*.

† Moreover, a fief is, according to some, an innominate contract, or a nominate one according to others, or at least an anomalous one, perfect in its being. And to a perfect act nothing can be added or taken away, except by the common consent of the parties, as is stated in the Codex, On Actions and Obligations; just as also one ought to be aided by benefits, not deceived, as is stated in the Digest, Common to All Titles, in the law On a Loan for Use, § Sicut; and in the Codex, On Those Who Are Impeded by the Emperor’s Pardon, law 1.

† Moreover, there would be no contract with the prince if the revocation were pending and the substance depended solely on his will, as in C. de contrahenda emptione, l. in ementis. And thus one would contract improperly with the prince, and it would be as if contracts were in some way interdicted to him, which is ridiculous to say, as in l. bene a Zenone, with its subject matter. Likewise in c. decet, de regulis iuris, lib. 6. Indeed, the dispositions of princes ought to be free from all malice and diminution, as in Auth. constitutio, quae de dignitatibus, §. illud. What more is needed? The law states that ancient privileges ought to be renewed, not taken away, as in ff. de aqua quotidiana et aestiva, l. 1, §. permittitur. Furthermore, the prince is a rational creature possessing supreme power; but insofar as he is rational, he ought to obey reason, as noted in Auth. de monachis, in principio.

† Moreover, Celestine, because he granted favor in the morning and withdrew it in the evening, was considered an irrational animal and not a human being, as noted in c. 1, de renuntiis, lib. 6, in the Novels. Nevertheless, I readily concede that the Emperor or the Pope can create and suppress dignities, as noted in the Extravagantes, de constitutionibus, in c. Cum accessisset. However, this is true when the dignity is vacant and while the dignity exists in the abstract; but if it exists with substance, it cannot be suppressed without cause, because a right acquired by another cannot be suppressed, although one may freely dispose of a right open to oneself according to one’s will, as in c. 1, Qui successores teneantur, Collatio 10. Moreover, the prince can permanently make something corruptible, but not to the prejudice of another, even though he is the lord of the world; for this is understood with regard to good and natural governance, so that no occasion for injuries may arise, from which laws are born, as in C. Unde vi, l. Meminerint. And especially because, in case of doubt, the prince is not understood to take away the rights of private persons, and especially by general or effusive words, as in C. De emancipatione liberorum, l. Nec auus; D. Ne quid in loco publico, l. 2, § Si quis a principe; C. De precibus imperatoribus offerendis, l. Rescripta; D. De vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. Ex facto. And this is expressly stated in c. Si propter ius, de rescriptis, lib. 6. Furthermore, a diocese is among the appendages of a city, and therefore, if not granted to the city, it does not appear to be granted to the diocese; because what pertains to the principal also pertains to the accessory, as fully noted in Authentica Ingressi, and D. De regulis iuris, l. Cum principalis; C. Communia utriusque iudicii, l. Possessionum. For perhaps a harsh separation would result if one were separated from the other, which seems unjust, namely, that the members should depart from the head. Moreover, no one ought to yield rights to two persons, as in D. De legatis 3, l. Non quocunque, § Qui Gaium. And therefore the Emperor cannot cover one altar and uncover another. And he who is prior in time is stronger in right, as in C. Qui potiores in pignore habeantur, l. Assiduis, § Exceptio.

It therefore appears that one must conclude that the Emperor cannot alter the status nor diminish the honor of ancient vassals. And this is expressly stated in the Authenticum *De referendariis sacri Palatii*, § *Praeterea*, and in the case of those who have leased in perpetuity and similar cases, because they are perpetual, whence their possession ought to be unshaken, even if the Emperor by his own motion should decree the contrary; for he is presumed to have been circumvented, such that the contrary cannot be proven, as in the Code, *De locatione praediorum civilium vel fiscalium seu temporum*, l. *Praedia*, where it is expressly stated. And in the Code, *De diuersis praediis urbanis*, l. *Pen.*, where it is also expressly stated. For the Emperor does not wish his ancient privilege to be abolished by the inconstancy of the prince; whence the purchase of the Castles of Count Ugolino was not valid, although it had been confirmed by an imperial bull, as I read and note in the Code, *De fundis et saltibus rei dominicae*, Book 11. And it supports this in the Code, *De cupressis ex lucro damnensis*, l. *Omnes*, there: "and lest solace," etc., in the same book. For justice ought to be constant, and a perpetual will. And in the Prince, above all, this is required, as in the fountain of justice. For we cultivate justice, and we profess the knowledge of what is good and equitable, separating the equitable from the inequitable. And whence the privilege of the Prince ought to be perpetual, as in the Authenticum *Constitutio quae de dignitatibus*, § *Illud*, and note in the Code, *In quibus causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria*, l. 1. Moreover, variety and vacillation are inimical to the laws and the material of bad faith, as noted in the Authenticum *De religiosis*, § *Si*. Whence it most befits Kings and Emperors that saying: "God has spoken once." And again: "What I have written, I have written." Whence the prince ought to have one pen and one tongue, and not many tongues; for it is written: "What has proceeded from my lips, I will not make void." And therefore he ought to be immovable, like the cornerstone, and like the pole in the sky.

† It must finally be known that an ancient question arose whether a lord could transfer a vassal against his will to another, or delegate him to another, and the truth is that he cannot, because no one is delegated against his will, as in C. de novatione et delegatione, l. 1. This rule fails in the case of a dowry in favor of the woman, if it causes no harm to the husband; otherwise, if it is so likely to be to her detriment, as in ff. sol. matr., l. 2, §. nec cogitur. And this is held by the learned Doctor Dycus in the same place. Likewise, the glossa determines this. ff. de fideicommissis, lib. 1, l. inuitus. Azo held this while disputing. The same is held by Petrus and Cynus in the aforementioned l. 1, C. de novationibus. The objection from ff. de legatis 2, l. si, §. filiae, does not stand. I answer that there is a special rule regarding dowries; indeed, there is a double favor there, namely, of the dowry and of the last will. But it seems to the contrary, because a lord can transfer to another a servitude owed to him, unless such servitude adheres to the person and is extinguished with the person, so that two cannot concur, as in Inst. de usufructu, §. finitur. Because in things separable from the person, true delegation cannot intervene, as in ff. de novatione, l. si ususfructus. For when the person is changed, the being of the thing is changed, and its duration or perseverance of being, as in l. ususfructus, ff. de stipulationibus servorum. Although the convenience of the fact can be alienated, as in ff. de periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. necessario, §. si. Then I argue thus: he can delegate, because it adheres to direct dominion; and vassalage is a certain kind of servitude, as noted in ff. de usufructu, l. si cuius, in principio. And dominion, as a certain real right, seems transferable, as in C. de hereditate vel actione vendenda, l. si. Nor is the absolute consent of the vassal required, because he is compelled to consent by petitory remedies, and also by domestic coercion, as in ff. de furtis, l. servi et filii, in principio; C. de patria potestate, l. congruentius; C. de hereditate instituenda, l. cum proponas. And this opinion is held by some, if it causes no harm to the vassal; but they say it causes harm if the delegation is to an inferior; otherwise, if to a superior, as reported by Cynus in the place cited above. Others distinguish differently, for either the lord wishes to transfer to another and abdicate from himself by transferring to another: and he cannot do so, and thus the glossa in the aforementioned l. inuitus is understood. Or not entirely, and then it matters whether the service owed to him consists solely in reverence and honor: and this he cannot do, as in ff. de conditione indebiti, l. si non sororem, §. libertus.

† because that which is not transmissible is not delegable, nor assignable, as in l. ex pluribus, D. de administratione tutorum, and D. de ritu nuptiarum, l. non solum, §. si puellae. Or, if the service consists in rendering something which another can render with the creditor’s consent, as in D. de pignoris actione, l. solutum, §. solutam, and C. de exceptionibus, l. 1, then they further distinguish: either the service is certain, and delegation may intervene; or it is uncertain, and it may not, because it is formless and obscure, as argued in D. de operis liberto, l. opere in rerum. This fails if the lord could not make use of such service, because it was factually impossible for him, or useless; for then he may assign and delegate it to another, lest such an obligation of service become a mockery, as argued in D. de operis liberto, l. medicus, and l. si libertus artem, and l. patronus. Thus distinguishes the learned Raynaldus. Therefore, what I can do through another, I can have done by another, so that it may be done for another at my command, which is an excellent argument, D. de mandato, l. idemque, §. si cui. Thus is understood what is noted in 10. coll. de capitaneo, who sold the court, c. in generali, and de l. Corad., c. 1, where on this point according to Raynaldus. But this distinction of his applies when the debtor consents to the delegation, not when he is unwilling; because delegation is made by stipulation, and thus requires the consent of the promisor. Moreover, it must be observed that here the lord can make use of the service, indeed he does make use of it, because he receives the census, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur, and D. quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Pomponius, and C. de agris et censibus, l. litibus.

† It is also established that the Emperor cannot abdicate the empire, not even of the smallest part: because through the smallest parts one would arrive at the extinction of the whole by dividing it into fragments, as in D. de legibus 3, l. Nomen, § 1. Nevertheless, if we truly consider our case, the Emperor has not diminished anything from his status, but has increased it, as he himself testifies in the prologue of his privilege, to whom we ought to believe, as in D. de haereditatibus institutis, l. Pacumeius Androtenus. For a similar thing was done in the Peace of Constance, as in c. 1, de pace constantiae. Because there the Emperor had his son swear fidelity while he was still alive: and while the father lived, the son was not the true Emperor; but he ruled in place of the Emperor. And it is certain that other Dukes and Barons obeyed, as the father commanded. But from examples a necessary argument cannot be drawn, as in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. Nemo. Someone will say, therefore, the Marquises, who are of the lands of our lord, will not swear fidelity to him: which is false, for rather they are bound to swear, as in c. 1, de capitaneo, qui curiam vendidit.

Thus, there are two kinds of oath of fidelity: one which a person renders as a vassal, and feudatory, or subfeudatory; and the question concerns whether this ought to be rendered or not. The other is rendered as a subject, by reason of origin or domicile. And this, without doubt, the Marquises and Earls are bound to render to our lord. Moreover, these two oaths differ formally; and they are not of the same species; indeed, they differ greatly; because he who swears as a citizen, although he incurs perjury, does not cease to be a citizen; nor does he lose the rights of citizens. But he who swears as a vassal loses the fief; and reverts to the superior, at least by sentence; for I do not say that he loses the fief by operation of law itself; but only after his guilt has been convicted and pronounced; for this is the nature of fiefs. Concerning these two oaths, it is stated in the 10th Collection, how a vassal ought to swear fidelity to his lord, c. unico. The first chapter cited, concerning the captain who sold the court, is not an obstacle; for there it speaks of when the lord sold the ownership of the community. But the Emperor cannot uproot or sell the ownership from himself, because he does not hold it by his own right, but by the right of the royal law, and it is not transmitted; and therefore it is not alienated. And although the Emperor is the greatest procurator, nevertheless he is not the owner of the property of the Empire, but rather an official by virtue of his elected office, as in ff. de curatore furiosi, l. cuius bonis. Furthermore, a citizen, because he swears fidelity and does not observe it, if he plots against the Prince, may even lose his life; but a vassal cannot lose more than his fief; nor be punished more severely, as noted by Innocentius, extra de iudiciis, c. ceterum. Furthermore

† The fault of the vassal is examined before other judges, and the fault of the commoner before others; for the judge of commoners is the ordinary judge of the place, whereas the judge of the vassal is distinct in himself, because a fief has its own judges, as in c. 1, "De controversia feudi apud pares terminanda" [On the controversy of a fief to be terminated among peers]; and in c. "Si inter," "Si de investitura inter dominum et vasallum lis oriatur" [If a dispute arises between lord and vassal concerning investiture]; and in c. "Si quis miles," "De contentione inter dominum et vasallum" [On the contention between lord and vassal]. It therefore appears from the beginning to the end that the conclusion should be thus: that if any lord made an investiture or exchange of the benefice of his knight or baron without the consent of him to whom the benefice belongs, it is held as void, as in c. 2, "Quo tempore miles," Coll. 10; and in c. j., vers. "Nam si quis," "Qui successores teneantur" [Who successors are bound]; and in c. 1, "De natura feudi" [On the nature of a fief], cited above. And it has already been said that just as the lord cannot take away, so he cannot change the form established in ancient times, as in D. de administratione tutorum, l. "Quidam decedens," in principio [In the beginning]. For when something is added or subtracted, a new right is created, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. "Ius civile" [Civil law]; D. de verbis obligatorum, l. 1, § "Cum adijcit" [When it is added]; and by the intervention of a new person, a certain novation or novatory addition would be made, as in Inst. quibus modis obligatio tollitur, § "Praeterea" [Moreover]. And this would not be without great indignation of the vassal, and especially when he is an ancient noble who despises new servitude.

† Just as it is naturally inherent in men not to make their liberty worse, as in D. 43.12 (Quarum rerum actio non datur), l. 1, § quae onerandae; and D. 35.1 (De legatis 1), l. Plane; and l. 2, § 1; and by argument from D. 38.1 (Familiae herciscundae), l. Quaedam mulier; and D. 37.11 (De iure patronatus), l. Camelia pia; and D. 38.5 (De natalibus restituendis), l. Fin.; and in C. 5.27 (Qui modo natu effici sui), § Generaliter, Coll. 7.

Truly, most serene Prince, I consider that one of two things must be admitted: either the way is open to us against the others, or it is not. In the first case, you are bound by the same rule in your true status and person, because whatever right one establishes against another, one must use the same right oneself, as in c. 1, § Sacramentum, De consuetudine recti feudi. For whether it is equitable, equity is common to all; or if inequitable, it recoils upon the head of the user of the inequitable right. Nor does the text distinguish in fiefs whether the petition is made or not, as in Extr. De constitutionibus, c. Cum omnes.

But in the second case, if the way is not open, you cannot use that word: “Open your gates, O princes, and the King of glory shall enter in.” Who is this King of glory? The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. May the Most High grant this to you and to us, both here and in the future.

† Certain subjects of the Empire are so for a double reason, namely, as citizens of the lands of the Empire, which are entirely surrounded by fiefs, and nevertheless by reason of the fief. And these are bound to obey the Emperor, the fief being saved, and to swear allegiance as pure citizens, and they are compelled by the Emperor himself, or by him who holds his place, without prejudice to a third party who would have this right by prior right, actively I do not say, but passively. Likewise, without prejudice to the fief: because a fief cannot be taken away unless it is taken away by the nature of the fief. Others, however, are subject to the Emperor by reason of the fief alone: and these would be bound to no one else, except that they are bound to render fidelity to the Emperor himself; and conversely, the Emperor is bound to keep faith with them and not to violate it, as in c. 1, de forma fidelitatis, and in c. 2, de noua forma fidelitatis. I speak, however, of the immediate and mediate subjects of the Emperor. For if another had immediate jurisdiction than the Emperor, they would not be judged to be subjects of the Emperor principally, but of him to whom they are immediately subject, unless jurisdiction were devolved to the Emperor for some cause, arg. extra de iudiciis, c. caeterum.

I have made a distinction between active and passive right, and I give a similarity: if two creditors have a hypothec, one prior, the other posterior, the prior is preferred to the posterior; but the debtor does not defend himself on the ground that the one suing is posterior in the hypothec. And the reason for the distinction is that the active right is in the creditor, the passive in the debtor, as in ff. qui potiores in pignore habent, l. Claudius Felix; ff. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. duobus; and l. in operis; ff. locati conducti, unless the prior creditor prohibits him from delivering possession to the posterior, arg. ff. de lege commissoria, l. mulier; l. mulier; C. de servis fugitivis, l. cum servum, per the gloss and Bartolus, C. de novationibus, l. 3; and what is noted for the lord, ff. de pactis, l. si cum emptore. Thanks be to God.

It is for our lord, because the jurisdiction of the territory is separable from the jurisdiction of the city, for it pertains to him, namely, the Emperor, to divide and sell, as in ff. de assessoribus, l. si eadem, and noted in l. 1, C. de metropolitanae urbis, lib. 11; and it pertains to him to assign territories and appurtenances, as noted by Innocentius, extra de rebus spoliatis, c. cum ad sedem, just as it pertains to the testator to assign his thing, ff. de legatis tertio, l. si quid in earum, § 1, and l. hoc legatum. Likewise, truth and the power of sanctioning are always presumed in the Prince, c. 1, de probatibus, in the Clementines; Bartolus in l. rescripta, C. de precibus imperatoris offerendis. Likewise, he can change seats, c. cum venisset, de iudiciis, per Hostiensis, whose soul is in his hand; Hostiensis says the same; Seneca says the same in De Clementia to Nero, in the beginning; the same is said in the Scholastic History in the Gospel of Matthew, in the beginning. Likewise, all kings of the world use this right, that they appoint and depose dukes and counts, and whom they will, in their kingdom. And where they state the cause, the contrary cannot be proved, and especially when it is a Pragmatic Sanction with the counsel of the nobles; because so many and such testimonies are present, and it is not lawful to contradict, as in l. 2, C. de summa Trinitate. However, if the Emperor lies, Satan will purge him and his accomplices. It is written, "The pride of those who hate you has always ascended," and again, "He has put down the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble," etc.

And he can make one office out of two, and suppress and abolish the other entirely, as in C. de frumento Alexandrino, l. finalis, lib. 11, and noted in Auth. ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio, § illud, however, causes being stated, although it is a part and staff of the city, and necessary for aid, and makes a collection under the city, as noted in Auth. qui mores naturales filii esse sui, § si quis igitur. Nevertheless, from any diversity, they are distinct bodies, although joined by a certain contiguity, whether the city is taken for the people or for the site, for it can be taken in many ways, as in c. si civitas, de sententia excommunicationis, lib. 6, and fully noted by Bartolus, ff. de verborum significatione, l. 1. From which it is concluded that the county tacitly follows the city, and there is one and the same jurisdiction, insofar as it adheres to the territory; because it is not fitting for members to be separated from the head. On this, by Cynus in the said l. 1, § cum 11 urbem, in the lecture, where he thus says,

† When a city or castle is sold or granted, jurisdiction is also deemed to be sold, along with whatever else is contained within the territorial boundary, provided that jurisdiction pertains by reason of the thing, i.e., the territory; but if it adheres to the person, it is not included, as noted by Dyonisius in l. ergo, in principio, ff. de acquisitione rei donatae. Moreover, the power of the Emperor is anomalous, because it is not confined by any rule; therefore, anything is permitted, as in l. 2, C. de criminibus sacrilegii. Furthermore, one must adhere to the words of the prince, who is the disposer and arbiter of his own affairs, and it is not permissible to restrict the freedom of his discretion. Add also that if it is restricted in some respect, it is not restricted in all respects, but only in that which is immediately connected to the restricting term, as in ff. de alimentis et cibariis legatis, l. mella, § Titia decedens, and by the doctors in l. concedendo, ff. de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae.

They say that either both concessions are compatible with each other, and both are valid; or they are not compatible, and then the earlier one prevails, because a right acquired in a thing cannot be diminished for the holder without his consent. It is established what is noted in a similar case: § locati, l. emptorem; and D. de iure fisci, l. Valerius; and C. ad Velleianam, l. iubemus; C. de auctoritate praestanda, l. si. For no one ought to be deprived of his right, as l. 2, D. de his, qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt; and D. de adoptionibus, l. si arrogator, § sed an impuberi; and l. in adoptionibus; and D. de regulis iuris, l. id, quod nostrum. To this rule we must adhere as to a firm foundation. Concluding, I say,

† That the same power which the Lord Duke possesses in matters entrusted and granted to him, the Emperor himself possesses; and thus obedience is due to him, because the King of the Romans can command that obedience be rendered to him, just as to himself, both by law, since he is called King from *regimen* (rule); and because he is an Emperor by causation, although not formally constituted in name. Moreover, King is a name of dignity and equity, whence our Lord Jesus Christ is called King, and it is never found that He is called Emperor, but rather He commands. Emperor is a name of supreme power and of inflicting necessity; nevertheless, the King of the Romans has a causal Empire, although not entirely formal, as is shown by his seal and the image of the seal. Since therefore he has dignity and complete administration, obedience is due to him in all respects, just as to an Emperor formally constituted by the crown. Now I will set forth the allegations for and against. I, Baldus. To the foregoing, add also below, Consilium 333.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the King of the Romans can subordinate a Vicar appointed by him in one city with its dependencies and territory to a Duke subsequently created, and so forth, such that the Duke is understood to be superior by virtue of the Empire, and consequently, that an appeal lies from the said Vicar to the Duke. And number 6.
2. Whether the Vicar is extinguished and revoked, on the ground that the Emperor cannot impose a law upon himself.
3. Whether both possess jurisdiction.
4. Whether the parties cause harm to one another through concurrence.
5. What is the difference between a Vicar, and a perpetual office, and a noble fief, and a perpetual one.
6. The Emperor is lord of the world, God on earth, servant of God, etc.
7. In the Prince, no cause is required in matters of discretion: otherwise in matters decided and determined by natural law or the customs of nations. And whether and when his words are to be adhered to.
8. The Emperor can depose Dukes and Margraves, just as the Pope can depose Cardinals.
10. Whether the Emperor, who granted a fief, can add a visitor, if the feudatory or Vicar mistreats the subjects and cities.
11. Whether a Duke is comparable to an emancipated son.
12. Whether an official is punished if he commits a delict: and whether he is liable for his household.
body: It is asked, if the King of the Romans, in the name of Christ, some time ago created a certain nobleman as perpetual Vicar in a certain city of the Empire, and in its pertaining territory and power; and finally, some time later, created a certain Duke in certain lands and provinces, and their dioceses: whether, if the said territory is part of the said dioceses, it pertains to the said Lord Duke newly created, or not? And for clarity, it must be premised that five doubts arise in this matter from the nature of the case and of privileges. The first doubt is whether the said King of the Romans can subordinate the said Vicar to the said Duke, or subject him, so that the said Lord Duke is understood as superior in the name of the Empire; and consequently, whether an appeal can be made from the said Vicar to him, as one cognizant in place of the Prince, or not. Second, whether the said Vicar is extinguished and revoked, because the Emperor cannot impose a law upon himself. Third, whether both have jurisdiction in solidum in the said territory, not dividing it between themselves by concurrence; but rather so that the latter appears added to the former in the same indivisible whole. Fourth, whether they divide it between themselves into equal halves by concurrence. Fifth, whether there is a difference between a perpetual Vicariate and a noble and perpetual fief.

I return to the first point: and it seems that the answer is no, because no one can impose a servitude on another’s property; hence the owner cannot, against the will of the surface right holder, impose any servitude on the surface, as stated in D. de superficiebus, l. 1, § quod ait; and D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. inuitum. But the Perpetual Vicar does not seem to be equivalent to a surface right holder or an emphyteuta; and especially because every perpetual holder has useful dominion, which takes precedence over direct dominion, as stated in D. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticarius petatur, l. 1, § qui perpetuum. Therefore, the holder of direct dominion cannot impose a law upon him, except one that was inserted in the initial grant itself, as stated in C. de donationibus quae sub modo fiunt, l. perfecta. For one cannot alone recede from the form and force of the initial grant, as stated in c. 1, de natura feudi. Moreover, the right against him cannot be novated by another stipulating party, except in conscience, as stated in l. 1, § cum seruus, de stipulationibus seruorum; and there by Bartolus. For what is founded on the consent of both parties is not dissolved by the repentance of one, on account of the mutual obligation contracted on both sides, as stated in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. sicut; D. de commodato, l. in commodato, § sicut; C. ne fiscus rem, quam vendidit, euincat, l. fin.; lib. 10; and in Auth. constitutio, quae de dignitatibus, § illud.

To the contrary, it seems: for if the Pope first creates a Bishop, and afterwards an Archbishop in whose province the said bishopric is located, there is no doubt that the said Bishop is subject to his Archbishop, so that the lower degree does not prejudice the higher, nor the higher the lower. And each degree stands in its own order, as noted in c. Romana, de foro competenti, pars 1, lib. 6. Thus it will be in the case at hand, because the Duke, of whom we speak, is illustrious. But the Lord Vicar is most clear, so that he is in a lower degree of dignity and jurisdiction; therefore, the lower must acknowledge the merit of the higher, as stated in l. 1, C. de officiis praefecti urbi; and thus, by subalternation, no incompatibility follows, as stated in Auth. de defensione civitatis, § interim. Nor is this a servitude, but a degree, mode, and order; for it is within the power of the Emperor to create one who is greater than others, and to whom at least, on account of the Emperor’s absence, an appeal may be made and recourse had, as stated in C. de appellationibus, l. praecipimus. And this is expressly held by Bartolus in l. finali, D. uti possidetis. And there is no doubt in law, if the words of the privilege admit this sense.

It must be considered here that the words of the privilege are very broad, as stated in D. de officiis praefecti praetorio, l. 1, § cum urbem nostram. Moreover, the genus implies and includes all its species, as stated in D. de legibus tertio, l. si quid earum, § finalis. Moreover, in general speech, a species declared or exceeded is not contained, as stated in D. de peculio legato, l. seruo manumisso; D. de legibus tertio, l. uxorem, § felicissime. There it is said that one in number is more a species than several in number. This is supported by the fact that the order of dignities must be observed, as stated in the rubric and text, and in C. de officio rectoris provinciae, l. potioris; and it is read and noted in Auth. ut ab illustribus et qui super eos sunt, in the glossa ordinaria. And not only in appeals, but also in other reasonable and just mandates. I do not say that the superior can impede the jurisdiction of the inferior, as noted by Archidiaconus, Dist. 11, q. 1, c. de persona; nor does an equal have power over an equal: for an equal has no command over an equal. And yet, if an appeal is made to an equal in the same jurisdiction, the superior cognizes the case, if the appeal was made due to an error of law, as stated in l. 1, § penultimus, D. de appellationibus.

† As to the second point, it appears that the said Vicariate was not extinguished by the said chapter *de natura feudi*. For it is not fitting that the honors of others should become the occasion of damage to others. C. *de statuis, et imaginibus, et virtutum*. For a perpetual Vicary cannot be said to be a person of the church or of the territory. I. *per se sonans*, and *per se*, and residing in itself by its own right, arg. ff. *de tutel.* l. *quae sit*. de pręb. c. *extirpandae*. de fide instru. c. *perpetuus*. Moreover, there are certain things which it is impossible to change, as noted in c. *ad apostolicae* in fi. *de re iudi.* lib. 6. On the contrary, it appears that the Vicary is a mere official: and he can be revoked, if he was appointed by a man: for sometimes he is appointed by law: and in neither case does he have the power of the material sword. C. *de officio eius, qui vicem alterius iudicis gerit.* l. *suggerente.* where this is discussed. For behold, the Bishop made for himself a Vicary on this condition, that he could not be revoked, yet certainly he can be revoked, just as a procurator not appointed for his own interest, as ff. *de iudiciis.* l. *iudicium soluitur.* and even when the matter is not yet concluded, the Vicary is revoked. as appears expressly there. makes the last chapter. extra *procuratoribus.* lib. 6. Also, the name of vicariate is the name of an office, not the name of the reality of dominion, and therefore the very reality of useful dominion could be granted and attributed to our lord, saving the office attributed to another: and such should be recognized as it is. this cannot be denied. As to the third point

It appears that both have jurisdiction in solidum: and if indeed they began to take cognizance together, both shall proceed together; but if not, the condition of the one who seized the case shall not be the better, as in the Digest, De officio consulis, l. 1. Just as if, after the Pope had appointed one bishop, he were to appoint another there without revoking the first, as noted in l. unica, Codex, De metropoli berito, lib. 11. If it were said that both were required, we have an argument from analogy in the Authentica, Ut differentes iudices, in the beginning.

† As to the fourth point, it appears that the parties effect a concurrence for themselves, as in C. de legibus, l. si fortidianum; but to the contrary is the provision in the same title, l. cum quaestio, where only the later one is considered: but that applies to a right not yet rooted. But in a rooted right, a different view is held, as in c. duobus, de rescriptis, lib. 6. And this holds when there is the same will; otherwise, when there is an interval. For, so to speak, when there is an interval, two joint obligors are not formed. ff. de duobus reis, l. cum duo; de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, non ad ea.

† As to the fifth point, the similarity of the offices must be considered. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. ex facto. And it appears that a vicar is more akin to a simple procurator than to a feudatory: because no one is compelled to have a vicar; and it is contrary to the nature of vicariate that one should impose one's services upon another against his will, as in the case of a procurator. L. que omnia cum unum sit adiutorium: and in my assistance, one ought not to sit as judge against my will. It should be known that Bartolus says that if someone has temporal jurisdiction, his consent is not required; otherwise, if he has perpetual jurisdiction, as he notes in l. 1, §. et si post operis, D. de novi operis nuntio. And if this can be done by the consent of private persons, much more so by the consent of the prince, because it is in no one's interest, as the glossa says in the aforementioned l. iudicium soluitur.

† The entire question hinges on the first point, in which it seems to be said that the said Duke, in the name of the Emperor, is to be considered superior in the said diocese without prejudice to the said Vicar, not that they are equal, but that the aforementioned Vicar alternates with the said Lord Duke. For what if the Emperor were to create our Lord Duke King of Arles, which he could do, because it is a kingdom long since formed, although it has been vacant for a long time? Would not the counts and barons of the kingdom be bound to recognize him and swear allegiance to him as king? I believe no one would doubt that this is so. Moreover, whether he is called King or Duke, it makes no difference to the matter: for I do not place force in the name, but in the quality of government and the magnitude of power, cf. D. 12.1.1 (Pater Severinam), § conditionum, when specifically there is dispute about this particular subject; otherwise, it would be different, cf. D. 14.3.1 (Cum), § si tamen. However, I believe the Emperor should be consulted and his response awaited, cf. D. 1.3.1 (Neratius), so that everything may proceed with good fortune. Behold, half of the county is within the Florentine diocese, and half within the Fiesole diocese. Does he who has the Emperor’s concession in the Fiesole diocese hold half of the territory of Florence? Cf. D. 7.1.1 (Si alii) and D. 35.1.1 (Sempronio leg.), D. 35.1.1 (Iulianus), for a part of a species is determined by the species itself. Cf. C. 2.12.1 (Si cum tibi) and C. 7.1.1 (Cum quaestio). And thus the parties make themselves distinct by the division of places already made by their situation, not by concurrence as undivided owners; for example, one beyond the river, the other on this side of the river. If our Lord had a general grace and another a special one, it could be argued that the general is restricted by the special. But he has it enumerated individually, cf. D. 14.1.1 (Scire debemus). Hence, enumerated species receive an exclusive restriction, just as a genus does, cf. D. 45.1.1 (I.), D. 45.1.1 (De stipul. serv.), for a species is excluded from a genus, but the same species is not excluded from a species, but is divided, cf. D. 35.1.1 (Quaesitum), § 1, D. 35.1.1 (Si fortidianum).

† He who is Emperor is lord of the whole world. D. ad l. Rhodiam de iactu. L. deprecatio. Moreover, he is God on earth, as in Auth. de consulibus. Hence Seneca, in De Clementia to Nero, in the beginning, describing Caesar, thus says in the person of Caesar speaking of himself: "I, having pleased all mortals, have been chosen to act on earth in the place of the gods; I am the arbiter of life and death for the nations; what fortune each man shall have, what status, is placed in my hand; what fortune wishes to give to each mortal, I pronounce with my mouth; from our response the causes of joy for the peoples and cities arise; no part anywhere flourishes except by my will and with my favor; nor do so many thousands of swords, which our peace restrains, draw themselves except at my nod; which nations are to be utterly destroyed, which transported, to whom liberty is to be given, from whom taken away, which kings are to become slaves, and upon whose head royal honor ought to be placed, which cities are to fall, which to rise, is within my jurisdiction." Thus he. And in the scholastic histories it is read that he is the same who sets up and deposes kings and magistrates, as is stated in the prologue to the Gospel of Matthew. Moreover, the Emperor is the servant of God, as in C. de officio praefecti praetorii Africae, L. quas gratias, in the words "through us his servants." Therefore, the Emperor ought to serve God and obey the apostle saying: "Masters, render unto your servants that which is just, knowing that you also have a Lord in heaven, in whom there is no respect of persons." And again the law says: "We command all violence and all avarice to cease, and justice and truth to be preserved; and thus God is appeased," as the text formally states in the said L. quas gratias, in the word "ergo." And in the Psalm: "Let my judgment proceed from the face of God, and let my eyes see equity." And again in another Psalm: "Judge righteously, O sons of men." These words are impressed on the seal of the Emperor. And if the Emperor writes one thing in the text, namely, that which is unjust and inequitable, and another thing contrary to himself is on the seal, he is sometimes called a twisted serpent, when he is schismatic, De electione, C. venerabilem. Sometimes a dangerous asp, when he does not wish to hear or do that which is equitable for the peace of the world, as in C. ad apostolicae, De re iudicata, Lib. 6. Whatever, however, is done above the law, is absolute power, and it is not for subjects to reprove, because, as Aristotle says, no inferior participates in that which is superior; but it is necessary to obey. For here the good of obedience is most felt, where obedience is rendered with bent knees to wicked masters.

† Moreover, if the Prince speaks in matters of discretion, no cause is required; but if we are speaking of things decided and determined by natural law or by the customs of nations, he must specify the cause: and his words, uttered of his own motion, are to be upheld, so much so that according to the general custom, as says Cynus, the contrary cannot be proved, as he notes in C. de precibus imperialibus, officio, l. rescripta, in fine; for we always suppose his rescript to have been issued for a just cause, according to Cynus.
