But if he speaks in general and uncertain terms, there is a presumption; yet the contrary may be proved, unless he speaks of his own act or of his own mind; because no one is believed when contradicting himself, as in c. 1, de probationibus, in the Clementines, and there noted; hence if the Emperor says that someone was ungrateful, and therefore revokes the benefit granted to him, proof of ingratitude is not required; especially since he has power over his life and death, arg. ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. in suis; and to fall into the hatred of the Prince is a sufficient cause of ingratitude, as ff. de manumissionibus, l. testamento Centurionis; and because all men and all provinces are the peculiar property of the Prince, we can say what we say about peculium: that peculium arises, increases, and decreases as the master wills, as ff. de peculio, l. peculium nascitur. Indeed, under the Emperor all provinces are established, which see the rising and setting sun, and those on the side, i.e., south and north, as in Auth. ut omnes obediant iudicibus provinciarum, in principio; even the Gallican province, C. de officio praefecti praetorio, l. In nomine de beneficiis, in the word, Galliae, seu Francorum. But that was at a time when, while the Roman Republic flourished, the aforementioned provinces were held in their entirety, as in the same law, §. quid autem Dux. But now the dispositions of the world have changed, as says Aristotle in De caelo et mundo: not that the world will be generated and corrupted, but its dispositions; and nothing is perpetual under the sun. For the cause of corruption in itself is time, 4. Physicorum. Although the Empire always exists, in Auth. quomodo oporteat Episcopos, §. fin., yet it does not remain in the same state, because it stands in continuous motion and perplexing tribulation; and this appears in the change of the four principal kingdoms: among which two are established as more illustrious, the Assyrians first, the Romans last, as says Augustine, lib. 10, c. 8, de civitate Dei, which must last until the end of this age: and to be ruled by the Emperor in temporal matters, by the Apostolic See in spiritual matters.

And just as the Pope can without any doubt depose Cardinals, so too can the Emperor depose nobles, and so too barons; and if he can depose them, he can much more strongly subject them to another, because to him who is permitted what is greater, what is lesser is permitted. D. de servis exportandis, l. cui pacto. Hence Seneca in his book On Manners, at the end, says that the age of the ancients produced Gaius Caesar, to whom whatever he wished was permitted; the law makes it so. D. de constitutionibus principum, l. 1. And Virgil speaks of the Emperor: “You, Roman, remember to rule peoples by empire; these shall be your arts: to establish the custom of peace, to spare the subdued, and to war down the proud,” as reported by Augustine in Book 5 of The City of God, chapter 8. The same Augustine says in Book 1 of The City of God, chapters 1 and 6, that Caesar desired to have this said of him, as if inflated by spirit, because these words are fitting for God alone; but Virgil spoke of worldly power, not of the blessed life. Concluding therefore from the first to the last, it is clear that anything is permitted to Caesar. The subjects are bound to obey; yet if he does evil, let him expect the wrath of God, as noted by Hostiensis in Extravagantes, de iudiciis, c. Cum venisset. For He is the one who humbles and exalts, as in the hymn of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and He is terrible, and who can resist Him? as in the Psalm. And many things can be alleged to the same effect.

But whether the Emperor, who granted the fief, may appoint a visitor, if the vassal or perpetual Vicar ill-treats his subjects, and dissipates the cities committed to him, or absorbs them by imposing heavy and unbearable burdens, and adding new taxes. Hear the words of Paulus de Leaza in c. ad apostolicae, § praeter hoc regnum, on the word aestimationem, where he says thus, and so it is noted, that although the vassal has useful dominion, he ought not to dispute; just as a usufructuary can otherwise be recalled, ff. de usufruc. l. si cui, § sicut; and in the Liber Feudorum, de investitura, c. 1, § quid ergo, up to the end, coll. 10. Paulus, for this reason, holds that the Pope can revoke a privilege, arg. da Nicolaus de Ve, dist. 63, § verum, where the Pope revoked a privilege granted to the Emperor, which had been granted so that he ought to attend the election of the Pope. Moreover, the Pope can command the electors of the Empire that they elect within a certain time; and if they do not obey, he can recall the election of the Emperor to himself for that occasion, as noted in the said c. ad apostolicae, in the gloss, pe. and fin. Returning to the proposition, I say that he can appoint a visitor, nay more, give an assistant, without whose consent depopulations and wars cannot be made, nor new impositions laid upon cities, as in c. grandi, de supplendis negligentibus, lib. 6. For it is in the interest of the Emperor that the world not be dissipated, as is clear from his very cognomen; because he is called Augustus, and see C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, auth. qui res iam dictas. But whether he can command the peoples granted to the duke that they go to Prague. To understand this, I make a comparison,

Whether the Duke is compared to an emancipated son, and thus understood to hold the dukedom as a reward for emancipation? I say that he is not emancipated, because he is under the power of the Prince; therefore, he is equivalent to a son retained in paternal power, to whom the father gave [the dukedom] as one deserving well. For, as an outsider, he acquires ownership and usufruct, as in C. de inofficiosa testatione, auth. Unde si parens. Hence, it is like an adventitious peculium, in which, in this case, the father does not have usufruct, because he granted it to the son personally; nevertheless, he is always under [paternal] power. Hence, it is true that the Emperor is Duke, Count, and Marquis, because all dignity resides in him, just as in the Pope; nevertheless, he is naturally bound to the son, ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. Frater a fratre. Moreover, he is also civilly bound, because it is adventitious, and more than civilly bound, because he is bound by the plenitude of power, 12, because he wished to be bound.

† Sometimes an official does something by vigorously exercising his office; then he is to be praised, not punished, unless he greatly exceeds the bounds. Sometimes he proceeds, bound by his own words voluntarily, not by the demand of justice, or to some other illicit act; and then there is no doubt that the official ought to be punished, as in l. ut vim, ff. de iust. et iur., and there fully on this matter by the gloss and the doctors, whether he is a principal official or of his household, for the household itself, if it offends, is to be punished even by the authority himself; but the authority himself is not punished for the household, if the household offends in that which is not committed to it, for example, if it commits wounds and adultery, as in l. 1, § familiae, ff. de publ. The aforementioned are proven in ff. de poenis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What kind and how great damages ought to be restored to lessees of possessions on account of force majeure and on account of incursions by enemies, and how they are to be proved even from presumptions and from the perception of the fruits of neighboring lands. And no. 4.
2. What the word "on account of" signifies.
1. When sterility is said to exist, and how it is to be proved.
2. When a genus is derogated by a species.
3. Whether a promise of law annuls a promise of a person.
body: The case is as follows: Nicolaus, in the name of Christ, leased from Lord Peter of Vicenza certain possessions and rights of the same Lord Peter for a term of five years, which the said Lord Peter held in the district of Verona, for the price of 100 florins to be paid each year on the first day of January, with the agreement that if the said Nicolaus, on account of war, could not use and collect the said fruits, revenues, and rights leased to him, then the said Nicolaus could not be sued for the portion of the time during which the war lasted; rather, a deduction should be made for him pro rata for the said period. There was also an agreement that if the mills, which were included in the said lease, were destroyed in whole or in part on account of war or on the occasion of any war, then they should be repaired by the said Lord Peter, and the rent of the said mills should also be deducted pro rata for the time according to the order of the factory. Now it happens that in the month of March, 1397, during the said lease, a war arose between Verona and Mantua, and during the said war, in the month of January, 1398, the procurator of the said Lord Peter caused the said Nicolaus to be distrained for the fruit of both the possessions and the mills and rights which he had leased, as aforesaid. Nicolaus opposes this and says that he is not bound to pay the entire rent, but he has confessed to part of it and has deposited and consigned it. The remainder, however, he says is not due, because it is offset by the restoration to be made to the said Nicolaus on account of the damage he suffered due to the war and because he could not collect the fruits and revenues of the possessions and rights which he had leased; and thus the agreement contained in the lease applies. On this point, chapters were produced, proceedings were conducted, and witnesses were examined.

† Now it is asked, what is the law against Nicolaus? And for the lord Peter it is alleged that by a special provision appended to the contract he appears to have departed from the legal provision. Thus, where Nicolaus has not proved that he could not use and collect, as is formally written in the contract, on account of war, although he alleges that he has suffered damage, nevertheless he ought not to be restored, and for this the theory of Cynus and the doctrine in l. 2, C. de iure emphyteuticario are alleged, and thus the headings do not avail the one producing them. On the other hand, it is answered that in the whole contract of the said lease nothing is disposed beyond or contrary to the disposition of the common law; and thus the aforementioned argument has no place. Moreover, even if something were found contrary to or beyond the disposition of the common law, nevertheless such a thing would not be found as would cause the provision of the law to cease; although something specially provided were found, nevertheless, since the provision of the contracting parties was not appended with the intention of novating the provision of the law, the legal provision cannot be said to be removed. D. de re iudicata, l. 4, § si ex conventione; and C. de exceptione rei iudicatae, l. penult., from the contrary sense. Furthermore, in the said contract there is no special provision introduced which cannot concur with the legal provision. Therefore, it ought rightly to be said that the legal provision does not fail, nor is it removed, according to the said § si ex conventione. And thus says the learned Cynus in the said l. 2, in the 6th question. What more? Another doubt arises against the aforementioned Nicolaus: what effect do those words appended in the contract have, that Nicolaus is to be restored pro rata temporis, etc. I answer that the deduction which ought to be made from the rent for the lessee must be certain; and it ought to be moderate according to justice, not numerically, but quantitatively, for proportion must be observed. D. de eo quod certo loco, l. ult.; and D. ad legem Rhodiam de iactu, l. 2, § iactura summa. Otherwise it is a rule, for example, that if damage occurs in half of the revenues, half of the rent ought to be deducted. But not if that half of the damage is worth as much as the entire pension, so that nothing is paid from the pension; for that would be inequitable, and would be a captious negligence, which the interpretation of the prudent has broken. D. de transactionibus, l. cum Aquiliana; and this supports the aforementioned. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. fistulas, § frumenta; and D. de publicanis, l. cum te, § qui maximos. Therefore, in the case proposed, since the witnesses say that Nicolaus suffered damage, etc., the fruits which he lost, that is, the quantities, must be considered; and according to these the deduction is to be made, that is, quantitatively according to the number of fruits to be received and not received; but not according to the number of years, or value, or because it would not be an equal proportion. And I consider this to be the mere truth. Furthermore, I say that Nicolaus’s intention is well-founded, and that he is to be restored; because not only by special law, that is, according to the pacts of the contract, namely if he could not use and collect the fruits and revenues of the possessions leased to him, and this lesser point is proved, as I shall say below, for contracts receive law from agreement, D. de deposito, l. 1, § si conveniat; and D. de suis et legitimis, l. ult.; but even by the common law he ought to be restored; because without doubt it is proved that Nicolaus himself suffered damage, and damage occurring to the lessee falls to the peril of the lessor, even if it arises without his act, provided it is without fraud, fault, or negligence of the lessee. The case is D. de locato conducto, l. fundus. Furthermore, force majeure which injures the lessee, if the injury is not slight, falls to the loss of the lessor, especially if the lessee leased for a stated sum of money. D. de locato conducto, l. si merces, § vis maior; and in the same title, l. ex conducto, § si vis tempestatis, which text speaks directly of an incursion of enemies. In the present case, however, Nicolaus is injured on account of the incursion of enemies, that is, on account of war, or on the occasion of war; therefore, etc. War gave cause to the damage,

And therefore this word, "because," must be considered, as signifying the cause, or the immediate occasion, or the remote one, by virtue of a certain generality of its meaning. D. de incendio, ruina, naufragio, l. 1, § ex incendio; Extr. de praebendis, c. nisi; Inst. de excusationibus tutorum, § propter litem. To dispute whether Nicholas has been injured would be superfluous; but as to the extent of the injury, recourse must be had to the statements of the witnesses. I omit not one point, namely, that for the discussion of the mills in the repair of said damage, according to the terms of the contract, recourse must be had to the records of the factory, which, and what they are, is clearly evident due to their notoriety, so much so that, as a permanent fact, they may be called a proved proof. Furthermore, I omit not another point, namely, that the quantities alleged by Nicholas have not been proved in their entirety; but for the greater part, therefore a deduction must be made for the part proved: and in this I see no room for doubt. For if Nicholas has suffered damage, as they prove, it follows that he could not use, demand, or receive; this is a necessary consequence: because if he could have demanded, used, and received, then he would not have suffered such damage as ought perhaps to be remitted or restored. Moreover

† Sterility is said to occur when the crops have not been gathered, or when it is the common opinion that there was sterility in that year; because all commonly doubt going to gather the crops, according to the note by Innocentius in the chapter Propter, Extra, de locato et conducto, and by Johannes and Bulgarus in the law Si uno, in the beginning, Digest, locato et conducto. Therefore, in our case, sterility has been proven; and thus, consequently, without doubt, restitution must be made to Nicholas according to the quantity of damage proven. And regarding the aforementioned matters, it is to be considered and advised what the law is; and so that the truth may more clearly emerge, the articles produced by Nicholas are submitted, along with the witnesses who testified on the articles, together with the entire proceeding. It is therefore necessary first to consider what and of what kind are the stipulations appended in the contract of lease; and according to those stipulations, whether the articles provide relief, and thus whether they provide relief under special law. Likewise, whether they provide relief under common law beyond the stipulations appended in the contract. Likewise, whether the witnesses prove the articles; and finally, what is to be concluded or pronounced upon the proceeding itself. The words of Cynus, in the title Locato et Conducto, in the law Ex conducto, § Si vis tempestatis, in the word "incursus hostium," are these.

† Here the question of fact is raised: certain persons leased from the common body of bakers certain possessions for a fixed term, namely five years. The collector on behalf of the common body demands the rent; the lessees say that they ought not to be held liable, because they were unable to cultivate, or have cultivated, the said possessions on account of the incursions of enemies who reside in the Castle of Saint Luke. The question is, what is the law? I distinguish: either war and the incursions of the said enemies supervened after the contract of lease was made; and then the rent is remitted, as is said here. Or war existed beforehand; and then it is imputable to them, who knew the condition and state of the thing. Hence they are not excused from the rent, by the authority of the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Qui bona*, § *De illo*, and its noted glosses; and infra, in the same title, law *Habitatores*, § *Ultimo*, according to Cynus. I therefore consider that there are two clauses in the said contract: the first, there, "by pact, etc.," which appears general with respect to any fiefs and revenues; the second, there, "and also with the pact, etc.," which appears special with respect to the destruction even of mills.

And it may be doubtful whether the general clause extends to mills, and it seems that it does not: because when a species is placed after a genus, we attend to the species, and not the genus, as in D. de verb. sign. l. si cum fundum, and D. de leg. 3, l. uxorem, § concubinam.

† Moreover, a special provision of a person, which is restrictive of the law, usually restricts an extensive provision, as in l. si cum dotem, in principio, ff. sol. mat.; C. de pact. conuen.; l. fina., C. de procu.; l. maritus. To the contrary it is argued: because when species and genus are set forth in favor of one and the same person, the broader provision of the genus is not excluded by the provision of the species, as in ff. de fundo instru., l. quaesitum, §. fina. And this is the truth, because sometimes between genus and species no conjunction is added; but the phrase "hoc amplius" or the phrase "et etiam" is appended. And then the signification of the genus is not diminished by the species, as in ff. de leg. 3, l. ea tamen adiectio; ff. de auro, et arg. leg., l. pediculis, §. labeo. Furthermore, in this contract there is mention of mills with respect to repair, which was not present with respect to the preceding chapter: not because it would restrict the remission of the rent, which arises from the nature of the contract and from the uniform reason that must be considered in contracts, as in the aforementioned l. si cum dotem, in principio, ff. solu. matr., according to the other, more correct reading; and ff. de condi. ob cau., l. si extraneus. And therefore neither chapter derogates from the other, but adds, namely, the case of destruction and repair. For what has been added in favor should not be converted into injury; because no legal reason permits this, as in ff. de leg., l. nulla; and C. eo., l. quod fauore. The statement of Cynus is not an obstacle, because he speaks where no pact has been appended concerning the case of war, as in C. de euictionibus, l. si fundum sciens. And therefore I conclude that the diminution of the rent must be made at the discretion of a good man, and conjecture may be drawn from the inconvenience that commonly occurs to others, and from the custom of collection, and from the proximity of places, as noted in l. 2, de rescin. vend. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that a lessee, by alienating or delivering the thing, shall not deprive the owner of possession, if the act was directed to possession and not to ownership, whether an appeal may be taken.
2. To what end the title of lease is directed, and whether it proves possession and ownership.
3. Given the statute mentioned above, if the alienated thing remained with the buyer for a long time, whether possession has been lost, such that it may be recovered in that possessory action, even though the lessor continuously received the rent from the lessee who alienated it.
4. Given a statute providing that the heir acquires possession by operation of law, if a pronouncement is made, whether an appeal may be taken.
5. Whether an appeal may be taken in a mixed possessory action, and when an action is said to be mixed. See number 9.
6. When possession is transmitted to the heir, and when it is retained by the tenant farmer.
7. Whether the tenant farmer, by delivering the thing, prejudices the owner today.
8. Whether an appeal lies from a judgment concerning legal possession, and what distinguishes it from mere and mixed possession. See number 9.
body: The statute provides that, in the name of Christ, giving or transferring does not deprive the owner of possession, provided the act pertains to possession and not to ownership. It is asked whether an appeal may be brought. Secondly, it is asked: if the thing remained in the hands of the person to whom the lessee sold it for a long time, and more than a long time, namely for 25 years, although the lessor continuously received the rent from the lessee, whether possession has been lost, such that it cannot be recovered by any possessory action.

† As to the first point, it appears that an appeal may be taken, because the case is not merely possessory, nor mixed with title, according to the doctrine set forth in the sole law of the Code *Si de momento possessionis* and in the *Speculum* under *De appellationibus*, § *Quibus*, verse 6. To the contrary, it appears that the title of lease does not prove ownership, but only possession; and the contracting parties, among other things, do not prove either. As stated in the Digest *De fidei instrumentis*, chapter *Inter dilectos*, § *Si*; and in the Code *De locato*, law *De conductore*. For the title of lease...

† It is not directed to anything else, except to such a possession, or rather detention, and fruits, as long as the pension is paid, as in C. de praescrip. 30. annorum, l. male agitur, and C. unde vi, l. non ab re. Hence, if it is not appealed in the possessory action, nor in the detentory action, where a lesser prejudice is at issue.

† As to the second point, it seems to be said, and first, that possession is lost over a long time due to negligence, as in D. de usucapione, l. furtum, § fundi, and l. quare, and Inst. de usucapione, § quod autem. To the contrary, it seems: because by receiving the pension, one retains possession. For one never lost it, having retained it, and for the purpose of possessing, D. de usufructu, l. quia qui pretio; nor should a clandestine and fraudulent contract harm the owner. For he is said to possess secretly who did not inform the owner, as in D. pro suo, l. si ancillam, because it is presumed that he suspected he could be repelled, since he ought to have suspected this, as in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. clam possidere, in principio.

Thirdly, it is asked: if a statute provides that the heir acquires possession by operation of law, and a judgment is rendered on this point, whether an appeal may be taken? And it seems that it may not, because mere possession is ousted, or rather, mere detention, since two persons cannot possess the same thing jointly, when some conflict would arise between co-possessors, as in Extra, de probat., c. Licet causam. And because between the death of the former possessor and the possession of the heir there is no intermediate period, as in ff., de legatis, l. Quaesitum, § Praesenti. Therefore, the heir is first in possession, and any possession that would be prejudicial to him is presumed to be clandestine, as in the said c. Licet causam. On the contrary, it seems that an appeal may be taken, because this case is not merely possessory, since it does not lie except for the true heir; and since this statute is contrary to the common law, as in l. 1, § Scaeuola, ff., si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit, it must be understood properly and strictly of him who proves himself to be the heir.

† And thus it is a mixed possessory action combined with the right of ownership: because the heir and the owner are the same, as stated in l. his verbis, D. de haereditate instituenda. Moreover, all the doctors hold that in a mixed possessory action an appeal may be taken; namely, because an appeal is also admissible in the actio ad exhibendum, which is a preparatory action, as in D. de appellationibus, l. creditor, § iussus. And this is even clearer in canon law, as fully read and noted in Extravagantes, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. cum ad sedem.

For the solution of this question, certain matters must be premised, and first that a suus and necessarius heir is not said to have a title as heir or as his own, as in C. de usucapione, l. pro haerede, l. nihil. And yet it is remarkable that he is called a suus heir. But nevertheless, this is said with regard to prescription, not with regard to the continuation of ownership, as noted in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. cum heredes, and l. cum miles, in principio, D. quibus ex causis maioribus.

And therefore it seems that there is a difference between a suus heir, in whom there is properly no title, and an extraneous heir: in the case of the suus heir, it is a mere possessory action without title, and an appeal cannot be taken; but in the case of an extraneous heir, the contrary holds, because in the effective cause of this judgment there are two substantial elements, namely, the right of the heir, and this quasi-possession by fiction; and thus an appeal may be taken.

The objection from l. edicto, C. de edicto divi Adriani, does not hold, because there the matter concerns a special case regarding a written last will or one reduced to notarial form. But observe, that here we are in the prior case, that is, in the case of a son who is a suus heir. And thus it seems that an appeal cannot be taken. But certainly another consideration must be taken into account: because at the time of the father’s death, the things were held under a colonus or lessee, through whom the heir of the deceased acquires possession without any other apprehension; and not a fictitious possession, but a real one; because in this case possession is retained by the will and by another’s body, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si id quod, § 1, and l. si de eo, § si forte.

But certainly those laws are of no avail here, because they speak of the death of the colonus, where the possession of ownership is substantiated in itself and in its proper origin. But we speak, on the contrary, of the case when the owner has died, where his inheritance does not take the place of a person in possessing, as in the aforementioned l. 1, § Scevola. For the nature of possession is to begin from an act, that is, from the placing of the feet, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. 1, in principio.

† Consider whether the tenant retains possession in the name of the heir, which occurs when he pays the rent; and then possession continues to the heir; or whether he lacks a just intent, because he did not pay the rent; and then it does not continue, and thus the text, together with the gloss, states in the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, in the law *Qui universas*, § *Quod per colonum*. Furthermore, Bartolus posits this there and says it is very notable; therefore, the payment of the pension operates significantly, which is true when the tenant was in a position to retain possession; but not when he had already delivered it to others, as in the law *Pomponius*, in the Digest, *Quibus modis ususfructus amittitur*, according to Dynus and Bartolus, who likewise note in the Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, in the law *Quamvis*, § *Si conductor*. And Bartolus says that the law *Pomponius* is very notable for this purpose:

† But insofar as he says that the tenant, by surrendering possession, prejudices the lord in his possession, he speaks according to the old law; otherwise according to the new law, as in C. de acquirenda possessione, namely if one follows the common opinion of modern jurists. And this opinion is very equitable: lest the fraud of the tenant harm the lord, for which opinion the following supports it: l. municipalis, cited above in the rubric de poena conducentis, and c. ibi, officio iudicis absque lite. For since it says “absque lite” [without litigation], it seems that one must proceed by way of fact, and thus without appeal, so that whether the case concerns the continuation of possession or its restoration, it must be handled so swiftly that no appeal can be taken; because no litigation can be raised to prevent execution, as otherwise occurs in c. 1, de re iudicata, in the Clementines. For by virtue of the municipal law, one judgment effectively stands for three; and the statutory possessory action takes the place of the common law possessory action. Furthermore, it must be said that if any title were required, it would be required as a kind of preamble, as we say in the possession of goods for the purpose of cognizance of the cause of action, as in ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. quemadmodum. For that does not found the judgment, but rather orders it, ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. exitus controversiae. I do not know whether I have otherwise consulted on this point:

† because an appeal may be taken from a possessory action of law. But this seems to be a possessory action of municipal law: but I answer, one thing is a possessory action, another is a possessory action of goods. And thus it does not obstruct what is noted in l. 1. C. de secundis tab. and because from the conjunction of common law and statute results a mere possessory action of fact: and the statute says that it exists without litigation. joined together at the same time: because the statute comes into play for the purpose of strengthening the possession against appeal, that which is introduced in favor of possession should not be turned back to the injury and delay of the litigation: because the municipal law says immediately, in which word I place much weight: but all things considered making for and against, although the question is very doubtful, it seems to be said that the appeal should not be granted: because the statute wants that the restitution be made without litigation: and the office of the judge, and equity for the actor is sufficiently known, hence the judge does well ex officio if he does not grant the appeal, as noted by Inno. in c. fi. extra de feriis. because illicit possessions should not be fostered, lest material for sinning be given, as l. illicitas. in princ. ff. de offi. praesidis.
On the aforementioned matter, in the name of Christ, having been consulted, I responded that if there is a dispute because an heir is denied, and to this issue is also attached a possessory claim:

† because an appeal may be taken from the sentence, since it is not a mere possessory action but a mixed one. Nor should the question of inheritance be said to be incidental, because rather it is original and principal: just as a plaintiff acting on a contract and obligation is not said to raise the contract and obligation incidentally; for otherwise the action would not arise. An incidental question is that which adjoins another and comes by way of support: not that which gives substance to the libel. And even if it were incidental, it is incidental on the part of the plaintiff, so that an appeal may be taken: as noted in D. de minoribus, l. intra utile. And I adhered to this first branch in the aforementioned counsel of mine: when there is a question of inheritance and possession, if it is declared that the plaintiff is heir and possessor, an appeal may be taken, because that title, if understood as referring to momentary possession, namely mere possession, arg. D. de legatis 3, l. hoc legatum. For if possession alone is not sufficient to bring an action, this is not called possessory: although in it possession greatly assists, as in l. 2, D. si servitus vindicetur. And note, in the same title, l. sicuti, § si quaeratur. And D. de exceptionibus, l. sed si ante. And l. prima, D. familiae herciscundae. But another case arises when the appellant does not raise the question of inheritance, but rather confesses that the plaintiff is the heir, and even in the libel of appeal. In this case, he cannot appeal, because on this ground, since he has confessed and persists in his confession, even in his libel, he cannot appeal. Moreover, although there is a question concerning the possession of things, such controversy resides solely in the possessory action, from which no appeal lies. Hence I consider that sometimes the question is permitted and doubtful by the negation of both heads, namely the petitory and the possessory: and then an appeal may be taken. Sometimes one article is separated from the other by the defendant’s confession: and then if the cause of ownership is established by confession, on this ground an appeal cannot be taken; for if he confesses, it is therefore notorious. Also, if he confesses, he therefore consents. There remains therefore only the possessory article, and there is no controversy about anything else except the possessory. But from this mere possessory action no appeal lies. And therefore in our case, since it is established by the defendant’s confession and libel, both in the principal cause and in the appeal, that Ugolino is the son and heir: which is the foundation of the other foundation: it follows that only the mere possessory action remains: and therefore no appeal may be taken. Nor does it matter that the defendant raised the exception of prescription, because no law provides that an appeal may be taken from a possessory action to which the exception of prescription is objected. For we measure from the person of the plaintiff, nor can the defendant change the nature of the judgment by raising an exception: as in l. 1, in principio, D. si pars haeredi petatur. The conclusion therefore is such that, considering the terms in which we are, the appeal should not be granted: and let no one believe that these counsels are contrary: because each agrees with the reasons of law, as in C. de edendo, l. si. And these are founded on those things noted by Cynus in D. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. si iudex, in the lecture, where he also explains the statement of the Speculum. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A brother of a certain order, who was also of another order, to which order does he acquire, and having become heir or successor to certain goods: and it matters whether he is heir simply, or for the poor.
2. A religious person made executor, to whom does he acquire.
3. The testator permits his wife to sell for her necessity, how this is to be understood.
4. By reason of the death of a near relative, and of an imaginary one, fraud is presumed.
body: In the name of Christ. For evidence that

† It must be premised that the Order of Saint Augustine and the friars of the said Order are capable [of acquiring]. For they can acquire, because they also choose to live [in that manner]; whence, even if they are called mendicants, they are not mendicants to the same extent as the Friars Minor, because they can acquire, namely the Order for itself, and a professed member for the Order, as noted by Iaco. de Are. and Cy. on C. de epi. et cle. l. deo nobis. A distinction must nonetheless be made as to whether a friar of the said Order is instituted as heir, or whether he is left merely as an executor. For if he is instituted as heir, then it makes a difference: either it is for the poor, among whom he must distribute, and then nothing is effectively acquired for the Order, as in C. de epis. et cle. l. si quis ad declinandam; for although he may be called heir as a mark of honor, as noted in l. filium. in princi. ff. de leg. praestan., nevertheless in effect the poor will be the heirs, or will stand in place of the heirs, looking to the effect rather than to the name of heir, as in ff. de vsur. l. in fideicommissi. §. cum pollidius, and ff. ad l. falc. l. cum dotem. there, 'et sane in plerisque ita observatur etc.', and ff. de lega. 3. l. si quis titio. there, 'nisi dumtaxat etc.', and ff. de ali. leg. l. pecuniae sortem, and ff. de ali. leg. l. filio. §. mariti suę, and what is noted in ff. de condi. et demon. l. si quis eum. Or he is instituted heir simply, and not for the poor; and then he acquires for that Order of which mention was made in the testament, because since his status is incompatible, he cannot hold private property, 12. q. 1. c. non dicatis; C. de sac. san. ec. auth. ingressi. Whence, since he cannot hold private property, it is necessary that he acquire for the Order, or the convent, of which mention was made, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. si filio, and noted in capitu. dudum. §. verum. de sepultura. in cle. Nor is a distinction made in this case as to whether he is a blood relative of the testator or not, although in the case of one who could hold private property a distinction would be made, because in a blood relative regard is had rather to the consideration of blood than to another accidental circumstance, by the argument of ff. de excus. tuto. l. tutor petitus. §. quę tutoribus. Thus, therefore, it is concluded that if in our case the institution was made for the poor, no advantage is acquired for the first religious order, nor for the second, but for the poor to be named, and subsequently named. If, however, it were to be acquired for some religious order, the named religious order would be looked to; and if no religious order were named, that one would be looked to which exists at the time of the testator's death, as in the Authen. de ecclesiasticis titulis. §. si quis in nomine; ff. de condi. et demon. l. quae conditio. §. cum ita; this is supported by what Cyn. noted on C. de sacrosanc. eccle. l. 1, because with regard to acquisition, regard is had to the time at which the day of the bequest yields [cedes], as in ff. de lega. 2. l. si alienus, and l. debitor. §. seruo. And even if after the death he changed religious order, nevertheless the religious order in which he was at the time of death is preferred, since the right was acquired for it, 18. q. 1. capit. statutum. Others, however, say otherwise; and it was a question disputed by dominus Fed. de Senis and placed among his consilia. For certain people say that he cannot enter upon the inheritance except by command of the superior; but he cannot command unless he is the superior at the time of the command, because he holds him in his power; and this applies in the institution of an heir, whereas in a legacy the first opinion is without doubt truer. But I do not examine this further, because it is not expedient.

† The other branch follows, when the religious is left as executor. And it must be said that the office of executor resides in the person of the executor and is not acquired for the Order, because it is personal and consists in the will and act of the executor himself. Nevertheless, he must have the license of the superior, namely of that superior who is superior at the time of the license, as in capitu. religiosus. de testa. lib. 6. and ff. de condi. et demon. l. qui hęredi. in princi. From which it is inferred that, since the said brother Iacobus had license and power from the Abbot of the said monastery in which he resided, he was able without any fraud to distribute the said goods to the poor of the hospital; and there is no doubt regarding the goods not sold,

† but there is doubt regarding that clause of the testament in which it is provided that the said Blancha, wife of the testator, may sell for her necessity; and she, weighed down by illness, sold and confessed that she had received the price. For it is asked whether the said sale ought to prejudice the said hospital; and it must be said that it does not. For in order that the said sale be valid, there must be evident necessity. Secondly, that the power was permitted to the seller in that manner. Thirdly, that the amount is not superfluous for the necessary cause. Fourthly, that the opportunity stands out with respect to place and time. Fifthly, that all fraud ceases, as that notable law says, ff. de exerci. l. Lucius. But here none of the four aforesaid points is established. Likewise, nor does the fifth appear, namely that it was done in good faith; on the contrary, it is rather presumed that it was in fraud, by the argument of C. manda. l. per diuersas and l. ab Anastasio, because a confession is suspect, especially when it tends to the prejudice of the soul and of a pious cause. Indeed, just as we say in the case of a ward and the church, it ought to be established by evident proofs, as Gui. de cu. notes on the said l. fi.

† Likewise, because by reason of impending and anticipated death fraud is presumed, as in ff. solu. matri. l. filiae nec emancipatae, and egregiae, and in c. 1. de renunt. lib. 6. Likewise, necessity is understood with respect to the future, not with respect to the past, as in l. cum hi. in princi. ff. de transac. with its gloss. From these things it is clearly evident that the hospital has justice on its side. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the power of the emperor, who made the Duke of Milan his vicar, and granted other jurisdictions, concerning all of which see above in consilia 326, 327, and 328.
2. When princes may enact statutes against the right of a third party.
body: For the understanding of the matter to be sent in the name of Christ, some undoubted [point] is to be [considered],

† namely, that the Roman Prince can assign and confer his castles, jurisdictions, and dignities in fief; and such is the plenitude of his power that he is above the law, as stated in the Digest, *De legibus*, law *Princeps*. And although he is bound by the plenitude of his honor to keep his grants firm and not to go against the faith of his predecessors, because he ought to be a cultivator and author of justice, as in the chapter *Si clientulus*, section *Ecclesia*, and in chapter 1, *De natura feudi*, where it is said that he cannot divest without cause, because faith is of natural law; nevertheless, if any motive, even a slight one, moves the Prince, he can do what he pleases by the plenitude of his power, according to that ancient saying, *Sibi licet* (it is permitted to himself), as in the aforementioned law *Princeps*, Code, same title, law *Digna vox*. For when matters may arise which are to be estimated as good or bad, no one is a better arbiter and declarer than he, as in the Digest, *De annuis legatis*, law *Meuia*, section *Finis*. And it is noted by Cynus, Code, *De precibus imperatoris offerentis*, law *Scripta*. For he himself is the judge of judges, as noted, Code, *De decurionibus*, law *Nemo iudex*, book 10. And he has no one above his head except God, from whom, however, he should expect punishment if he commits injustice; and sometimes, on account of enormous misrule, the Pope deprived him, as in the chapter *Ad apostolicae*, *De re iudicanda*, book 6. For the Pope is more the Vicar of God than the Emperor; for the Pope is equated to the sun, which is greater than the moon in quantity, dignity, office, and sublimity; nevertheless, all his subjects below the Pope are bound to obey. Moreover, promotion and degradation pertain to him, as Seneca expressly states, book 6, *De clementia* to Nero, at the beginning. Hence all dignities are the footstool of his feet; and he can break, remove, and transfer them, since he is God on earth, as in the Authenticum, *De consulibus*. From these follows such a manifest conclusion, that the privilege of our lord must be observed, as it lies word for word; unless the Emperor himself declares otherwise to have been his intention; which is not likely he will do, because it is expedient for the Roman Empire to keep faith with our Illustrious Lord. For then the Roman Empire rose from the dead, if one considers well, when it granted that Magnificent, Illustrious, and glorious grace to our Lord, Duke of Milan, Count of Pavia, and of virtues, etc. For if the Emperor were to create a Lord King of Arles, would not all counts and barons obey him? No one ever doubted this, unless he were insane. For he is foolish who thinks thus, and errs greatly; because a kingdom is a certain whole containing its parts integrally, both in persons and in things, just as every collective name of peoples and territory. For by these names are contained magnates and all nations, which are circumscribed within designated boundaries, as in the Institutes, *De iure naturali*, section 1. Furthermore, if we consider rightly, nothing is diminished to the Marquises, counts, etc., but a certain new form and style is given; just as the Emperor can do by himself, so can he do by another; as he could place a visitation over them, as in the Code, *Qui pro sua iurisdictione*, law 1, at the end, so that noxious appetite may be limited under the rule of law; nevertheless, for the sake of conscience, one must beware, I speak under this power, and insofar as my opinion agrees with justice, and otherwise not. The supreme Empire was given to the Emperor and is continually preserved, because it is necessary for the republic to be consulted by one, as in the Digest, *De origine iuris*, law 2, section *Deinde*. For it is more convenient for matters to be expedited by one, as in law 3, section *Quod in tutore*, Digest, *De administratione tutoris*. Just as in this house there ought to be only one head of the family, who is called the prince of the family, Digest, *De verborum significatione*, law *Pronuntiatio*, section 1. Also, to protect the safety of the republic is believed to suit no one more, nor is anyone else sufficient for that matter, than Caesar, as in the Digest, *De officio praefecti vigilum*, law *Nam salutem*. And this immense power took its origin from wars. For the Roman people subjected to itself the provinces successively, all together, by the power of arms, Digest, *De origine iuris*, law 2, section *Capta*. Then Sardinia, Code, *De Iustiniano codice confirmando*. And it proceeded with the fates consenting and God permitting, so that the world might be ruled under a rule, and untamed peoples might be given and learn to bear the yoke, 23 q. 1, chapter *Quid culpatur*. For the untamed people must be taught and bridled, not followed. And Blessed Augustine treats of this, book 19, *De civitate Dei*, chapter 21. It must therefore be noted that the original intention of the creation of the Empire was the good and utility of the republic, not private, such as that of Emperor Charles. Therefore, if the Emperor were to oppress the republics, it would not be contrary to natural reason to shake off the yoke of such servitude. Nor does it obstruct that the Church approved the Empire; for it is understood in that which is just, not in that which is unjust, argument in the chapter *Cum eterni*, *De re iudicanda*, book 6, and chapter 1, *Per quos fiat investitura, et per quos recipiatur*, collation 10. Thus says Cynus in the aforementioned section *Capta*. Then Sardinia. But whatever he says, we jurists must say that the Emperor is the lord of the world, even if he administers badly; because an inferior cannot correct a superior; although the Pope could depose him for a very great cause, as in the chapter *Apostolicae*, *De re iudicanda*, book 6; nevertheless, while he is in the act of office, he is considered the best and greatest prince, as in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, law *Unum ex familia*, section *Item Imperator Marcus*. He can indeed alienate, saving the majesty of the Empire, law *Observandum*, Digest, *De officio praesidis*. And he can commit this to another, as in the Digest, *De officio procuratoris Caesaris*, law 1, section 1. Also, he can enfeoff, as in the Authenticum, *De pace constantia*, section *Hoc quod nos*, and section *Consules*, and section *Vasalli nostri*, with the following sections. And *De feudo marchiae*, chapter 1. And *Per quos feudi cognitio derivatur*, chapter 1. And *Quis dicatur Dux, Marchio, comes*, chapter 1. And because honor is in the one who honors, the Prince, by giving a fief, makes the kingdom notable; and it is expedient for the republic rather to have just subjects than perverse ones; and thus it is expedient to have rather a subject Duke than a tyrant, Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *Decernimus*. We also see that other great dukes have under them certain counts and barons, and the Count of Savoy, Geneva, etc. And in fact, nothing repugns to order, which consists rather in law than in voice, as in the Digest, *De peculio legato*, law *Quaedam consuetudo*. He also gives jurisdiction and limits it, as in the Code, *De emancipatis*, book 1, law 1, *Cum si*. Moreover, he gives being and status to dignities. He gives orders and prerogatives to dignities, as in the Authenticum, *Ut ab Illustribus, et qui super eos sunt*, and Code, *Ubi senatores, vel clarissimi*, law 1. For he can make dukes greater, medium, and lesser; it is reasonable that the lesser be subject to the greater, as in chapter 1, at the beginning, *Qui feuda dare possunt*. For even among Angels there are found orders and degrees; the lesser serves the greater. For this pertains to good government and the rule of the universe. Where therefore there are many small counts or Marquises, especially rural ones, the Emperor can make one who presides over the others, and to whom the others may resort as to a certain common superior; just as a master makes a master, law 1, section *Magister*, Digest, *De exceptionibus*. For this corrects wars among them and composes peace, and protects subjects, as in the Digest, *De usufructu*, law *Aequissimum*; Digest, *De servitute urbana praedii*, law 1, *In re communi*; and in law 1, Code, *Ut armorum usus inscio Principe*, etc.; and in the Authenticum, *De armis*, column 6; and Code, *De iudaeis*, law *Nullus*. Certainly, no one doubts that the Emperor can commit his vicarious powers to someone; for what he can do by himself, he can do by another; since he, as the First Person, cannot be personally everywhere. Otherwise, therefore, he asserted it in the part of solicitude, but not in the plenitude of power, absorbing nothing for himself of the supreme jurisdiction; which, since it is something perfect, can neither increase nor decrease, as in the chapter *Dudum*, *De praebendis*, book 6. Also in the *Princeps*, because he disposes as if of his own property, his words are believed; and his motive is held for the most certain reason, as in the Digest, *De aliis legatis*, law *Divi Severus*; and Digest, *De manumissione testamento*, law *Testamento Centurio*. Someone will say, Marquises and Counts cannot be divested without fault, as in chapter 1, *De natura feudi*. For since this is of the nature of a fief, therefore it cannot be discerned against nature, as in law *Si peculium*, section 1, Digest, *De peculio legato*; and law *Per servum*, at the end, Digest, *De usu et habitatione*. I answer, this is not divesting; but placing under a certain rule of justice and equity. Certainly, this power also belongs from the birth of any fief; because the Emperor is always excepted. Nor does he seem to impose a law upon himself, as in chapter 1, section *Finis*, *De prohibitione feudorum alienandorum* by Frederick. Also, it does not obstruct, Digest, *De fideicommissis libertatis*, law *Inuitus*; and what is noted by Cynus in law 1, Code, *De novatione*; and Dynus in law 2, Digest, *Solutis matrimonii*. For here we do not inquire about liberty being taken away or diminished; but about jurisdiction; which resides solely in the authority of the community, argument Digest, *De annuis legatis*, law *Quintus*, section *Pomponius*. For jurisdiction is not against true liberty, but against vices. For law and justice restrain vices and crown virtues, law 1, Digest, *De iustitia et iure*. Hence jurisdiction is committed even against a subject unwilling and suffering damage; because by its nature it is rendered against the unwilling, as in the Digest, *De verborum obligatione*, law *Inter stipulantem*, section 1; and Digest, *De officio proconsulis et legati*, law 2; and in the Authenticum, *De quaestore*, section *Super hoc*, column 6. And in the mandates of the Prince, no cause is required, Extra, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Cum parati*; and note Innocentius in chapter 1, *De iudicibus*, book 6. Also, the Prince can grant useful rights without cause, argument Digest, *De liberto legato*, law *Si is, qui duos*. For he and reason are the same.

† What more need be said? Innocentius states that it is lawful for kings and secular princes to enact something, for a cause, to the prejudice of another’s right, as he elegantly notes in the gloss on the extrajudicial chapter *Debitores*, under the title *De iureiurando*. And just as we hold that certain knowledge is deemed a donation in the contract of stipulation—because such liberality is considered a sufficient cause, as in the Digest, title *De operibus libertis*, law *Campanus*; and title *De exceptione doli*, law 2, section *Circa*; and title *De verbis obligatis*, law *Si diuortio*; and title *De donationibus*, law *Aristo*—so much more strongly is it the case with a Prince that his liberality is deemed a cause. Indeed, because in a Prince, certain knowledge is held to be a just cause, as in the law and the note in the law *Idem Ulpianus*, Digest, title *De excusationibus tutorum*; and it is the ordinary gloss, very notable, in the chapter *Ad hoc*, extrajudicial, title *De rescriptis*. And it supports what Cynus and I noted in the law *Rescripta*, Digest, title *De precibus imperatoris offerendis*; and in the final law, Code, title *Si contra ius, vel utilitatem publicam*.

Furthermore, if the Emperor grants his men to someone, he does not thereby seem to alienate them, because he still retains the majority, as argued in the Digest, title *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Talem*, section *Finis*; and as argued in that which is in the law and note, Digest, title *De adicienda lege*, law *Si seruo*, at the end, in the great gloss. Therefore, subjects, both magnates and commoners, should bear this patiently and without indignation. For if magnates must submit, all the more so must commoners, if the King or Emperor wishes their necks to be subject to greater and higher authorities than themselves, because we cannot be equal to the more powerful, as in law 3, at the beginning, Digest, title *De aliena iudicii*.

Moreover, the modern King of the Romans cannot, by himself, due to the distance of the territories, rule Italy. Furthermore, he can appoint someone in his place to administer justice, as in the Digest, title *De officio eius, cui mandata est iurisdictio*, law 1, section *Cuius rei*; and title *De origine iuris*, law 2, section *Post deinde diuus*, words *Quotiens*. Furthermore, the Emperor even delegates matters that are normally non-delegable, as in the Code, title *Qui pro sua iurisdictione*, law 1, at the end.

From these points, it follows evidently that our lord, the Vicar of the King of the Romans, by virtue of his dignity, which is a certain monarchy created according to his own will, can require and command that newly instituted oaths be sworn to him, without derogating from the substance of the dignities of Counts and Barons, and without overturning good customs, which must be entirely observed if they have a certain form, as in the Digest, title *De annuis legibus*, law *Seio*, section *Medico*; and title *De usufructu legato*, law *Sempronio*, section *Si*; there, “and in that manner, etc.”; and title *De communibus praediis*, law *Venditor*, section *Si constat*; and in chapter 1, title *De constitutionibus*, book 6.

For if it is understood that he intends to detract from another’s right, as is clearly stated and noted in the extrajudicial chapter *Ad aures*, title *De rescriptis*, the oath is understood to be in lawful, honest, and customary matters, as in the Digest, title *De auro et argento legato*, law *Pediculis*, section *Argento praetorio*. And it is noted in the Digest, title *De regulis iuris*, law *Non videtur*, section *Cui iussu*. They will swear, therefore, according to the words of the privilege, and saving their other rights, which ought to be reserved for them as far as the law requires, as argued in the Digest, title *De damno infecto*, law *Praetor*, section *Si controversia*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When a contract is said to be perfected through a messenger whom one is accustomed to employ as a messenger, and the confirmation of such a contract.
body: In the name of Christ.

† A creditor, needing grain for himself, his necessities, and those of his household, writes to his debtor named B., who is situated in distant parts, asking that it please the same debtor to give of his grain for a fair price up to the concurrent amount of the debt. The debtor writes back that he is ready at the rate of four ducats per salma. The creditor writes to a certain member of his household in this form: first, that he should not exceed the sum of the price of three ducats and one-seventh per salma; second, he writes in this form: "Concerning the matter of the grain, since the said B. does not wish to give the grain for a lesser price than the previously stated four ducats for each salma, keep it in mind to speak with the debtor himself concerning the matter of the said grain, and to work regarding the business of the said grain at a price, whatever can be done for my convenience and advantage." Finally, the said messenger concluded the bargain for three and a half florins for each salma, to which the said creditor writes that he is not satisfied. The question is whether the said bargain is perfected or not, so that the said creditor is bound to stand by the contract, and what the law is. And it seems that it is not, because these seem to be familiar letters rather than letters of mandate, as in C. quod cum eo l. fi. Likewise, because purchase and sale is a voluntary transaction, and therefore does not bind an absent principal except by mandate or ratification, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. si pupillus § sed si ego. Likewise, because the limits of a mandate must be diligently observed; whence I weigh heavily those words, "not exceeding in effect the price of three ducats and one-seventh per salma"; whence, regard being had to the first letters sent to the said messenger, the said principal would not be bound, as in ff. mandati l. diligenter and ff. de neg. ge. l. qui aliena § libertos. Likewise, because all those words that preceded before the contract was concluded seem to have been certain preliminary discussions and not obligatory, C. de rescinden. vendi. l. si voluntate and noted in l. eleganter around the beginning, ff. de condi. indebi. I premise, however, that coming to the substance of the business, it must be seen whether the said messenger had a mandate to conclude the said contract, or not; and it seems that he did not have a mandate to contract, but only to negotiate and write back as a kind of intermediary, by the argument of ff. de arbi. l. si de meis § recepisse and ff. de institoria l. cuicunque § non omne and ff. de acquiren. haeredita. l. eum, qui duobus § filius. To the contrary, it seems that he had a mandate to complete the transaction on account of the words, because he had a mandate "regarding the business of the said grain," by the argument of ff. de neg. ge. l. ex facto. For the word "regarding" (circa), when placed inclusively, includes its extremes. Secondly, because he had a mandate "to work at a price, whatever can be done"; therefore, he was able to negotiate and work concerning the price, by the argument of ff. mandati l. creditor § Lucius; and the word "can" (poterit) signifies not only the potential but the act, ff. de statu libe. l. 3 § si quis. Likewise, to whom power is given, the effective power is given in law and in fact, de verbo. signi. l. nepos. Thirdly, on account of those words, "for my convenience and advantage"; for the advantage of the principal does not consist in preliminary talk, but in the conclusion and solidifying of the contract; for from this arises the convenience and advantage in effect, because words are to be taken with effect, as in l. 1 § haec verba ff. quod quisque iuris; for advantage is in the substance and in the effect, ff. de neg. gest. l. quae vtiliter, ff. de impen. in rebus dota. fac. l. 1 with l. sequen., ff. de verbo. signi. l. impensa. Furthermore, those words, "not exceeding, etc.," were revoked by the subsequent mandate, l. cum plures § locator ff. locati. Likewise, the first mandate itself is understood to be broadened and extended, l. qui ad certum tempus, especially on account of the necessity of sustenance, ff. de neg. gest. sive haereditaria, ff. de exercito. l. fi. Likewise, the matter was subject to perish in time, because the debtor was about to sell to another; and thus it was permissible for the messenger to interpret the mandate and to anticipate, that is, first to act and afterwards to write back. Furthermore, it is presupposed that this contract was advantageous, and we ought to look to the beginning, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. sed an vltro § 1. But that, too, is not to be omitted, which is presupposed on the point, namely that the principal was accustomed to commit himself to the good faith of the said messenger, and to ratify whatever had been managed by him in good faith, as regards the interpretation of the meaning of the mandate; the case is noted in ff. quod cum eo l. titianus; also to this, ff. de aur. et argen. lega. l. cum quidam libertum. I consider, therefore, that the chosen faith and diligence of the messenger should not be harmful to him; we ought to say that the said transaction, as having been usefully commenced and originating from the principal himself, must be held as ratified by the principal, as in ff. de neg. gestis l. Pomponius scribit, l. si negocium; and I think this part is true and equitable, all the aforesaid having been examined, and because the original mandate, which was limited, was subsequently broadened, and thus it was acted with a mandate. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. 12
2. To transfer a usufruct is one thing, whereas to transfer the right of usufruct is another. The right of patronage cannot be sold unless together with the entire universitas, and number 1.
3. In how many ways the term "totum" (the whole) is used.
5. What is not permitted in a specific case is not permitted in general.
6. What the names of honors contain.
7. Words are to be understood according to how the common people understand them.
body: A certain woman, in the name of Christ, transferred to her husband, by title of dowry, the usufruct of a certain estate, and the rights thereof were appraised to him, on this condition: that the husband, during the subsistence of the marriage, shall hold and receive the fruits for the burdens of the marriage, and that after the death of the husband, the rights and the usufruct shall be restored to the said woman.

It is asked whether, by this, the woman has lost her formal right of usufruct, so that it has reverted to the ownership, or not? And it seems that she has lost it, as in the Institutes, De usufructu, § Finitur. To the contrary, because that is true when it is said, “I yield the right of usufruct”; otherwise, if one says, “I yield the usufruct,” because then it is understood in a broad sense for the benefit [commoditas], not for the inseparable right, as in the Digest, De locato, l. Si quis domum, § 1; Digest, De periculo et commodo rei venditae, l. Necessario, § Finalis.

Solution: She has not lost her right; because it appears that only the benefit [commoditas] was intended. And this for three reasons. First, because the words speak of the burdens of marriage. For the benefit [commoditas] is abandoned by the burdens, not the intellectual right itself. Second, because of the word “to receive the fruits,” which clearly expresses the intention of the contracting parties related to the benefit [commoditas] alone. Digest, De usufructu legato, l. Fundi Trebatiani. Third, because words must be understood according to the nature of the matter. Digest, De usufructu, l. Proculus. And it is expressed in the contract. Code, Si pignus pignori datum sit. Nor is it surprising that the name of usufruct is taken for the benefit [commoditas]. l. 1, Digest, De usufructu legato.

Certainly, it is also to be noted that that which is retained in hope within the body of the marriage, and will return, and is also reserved, is not said to be entirely alienated. Code, De iure dotium, l. In rebus, by the express provision of the disposer, as noted in the Digest, De adiciendo legato, l. Si servo, in fine, great gloss.

Moreover, if there had been an error in law, and especially in the subtlety of the law, the woman would be aided, particularly to avoid damage. Also, by this. Digest, De contrahenda emptione, l. Qui tabernas. Also, one is not presumed to throw away his own [rights]; nor even to choose a way to impugn his own judgments. Digest, De testamento militis, l. 3. Hence, having examined the mind of the contracting parties and the sound understanding of the words, this woman has not lost her right, nor has the usufruct reverted to the ownership in any way.

† Secondly, it is asked, assuming that one sold all honors, and all dignities, and the right of patronage, which he had in such a place, whether the sale and transaction of the right of patronage mentioned for this cause is valid or not? And it seems at first that it is not, because the sale or transfer of the right of patronage does not take place unless with the universality of things to which it adheres, as noted in the chapter *Ex literis*, *de iure patronatus*, and in the gloss on the law *Si operarum*, *ff. de operis liberti*, and in the law *In modicis*, *ff. de contrahenda emptione*. Also, because there was an expression of the right of patronage, which seems to vitiate, etc. On the contrary, it seems from the fact that the universality seems sufficient when it is said "all honors, dignities, etc." Also, it is said that the expression does not seem to vitiate; and if it were vitiated, whether that general clause, namely "all honors and dignities, etc.", supposing the special clause concerning the right of patronage is vitiated, contains within itself the right of patronage, so that the buyer could in the aforementioned case obtain the right of patronage, or not? For clarity, it must be known that the right of patronage of a church is not among goods, nor is it, properly speaking, among the goods of a lay patron, much less than the right of patronage of a freedman, and therefore principally and in itself it cannot be alienated, as noted in *ff. de acquirenda rerum dominium*, law *Quaedam*, and in the aforementioned law *In modicis*, and law *Si operarum*, *ff. de praescriptionibus verbis*, law *Naturalis*, in the end, *ff. de legatis 1*, law *Plane*, in the second place. Hence, principally and specially, it is not subject to commerce, nor can it be separated from the person by way of voluntary alienation. Argument: *ff. familiae herciscundae*, law *Quaedam mulier*, and *ff. de iure patronatus*, law *Carmelia pia*. But it can be alienated accessorially with the universality, that is, as a part with the whole, and as the contained under the container: because with the universality all things pass which are contained in it or under it, as stated in the aforementioned laws, and *ff. de petitione hereditatis*, law *Item veniunt*. Therefore, it can pass as a part in the whole,

† It must be known that one thing is an integral whole, such as a fund, and everything that is contained within its integrity, as in D. 41.1.3 (Eum, qui aedes) and D. 41.2.1.1 (Possideri). Another is a numerical whole, such as ten and twenty, as in D. 2.1.1.1 (Si idem cum eodem) and C. 4.12.1 (Final). Another is a general whole, which is predicated, that is, verified according to the nature of its definition, of any species contained under it, or by reason of the sign, which is called universal, or universal term. But among jurists it is more commonly called general, or general, or common of appellation, as this term animal according to dialecticians, and this term man according to jurists, as in D. 33.1.1 (Si quid earum) § Inter emptum. And note in L. 2, Si certum petatur. Sometimes it is said to be a whole, that is, totally, or in every way, as in D. 1.2.2 (Post originem).

† It must now be observed that the right of patronage does not pass in hope principally and in itself; but it passes with the whole integral, as with the land. For example, if a church is founded in some part of a territory, whether it passes with the whole integral, and it must be said that it passes with the whole universal, and it does not pass with the whole integral. Hence, if anyone were to say, I give you all my patronage: this is a certain general thing, which is predicated of any patronage of his, and which does not pass by number, it cannot pass by genus, because it is not different to say all patronage, than this and that and so on. Nor is genus anything other than species enumerated.

And that which is not permitted in the specific case is also not permitted in the general case, as established in C. de praescrip. 30. anno. l. omnes, and ff. de lega. 3. l. si corus. Therefore, considering the aforementioned facts, since the right of patronage in our case does not come incidentally, nor as something contained within another thing that actually holds it, the general term cannot so subtly include it, as noted by Innocentius in Extra de iure patronatus, cap. ex literis. Moreover, those words, "all honors" and "all dignities," signify nothing regarding the right of patronage; indeed, there is a diversity in the appellation and express designation.

† For the term "honor" includes honor, but not honor coupled with a burden. Because a mixed thing is not contained under simple things, as in the Digest, *De legatis*, Title 3, Law *Hoc legatum*. The right of patronage is principally a burden rather than an honor, *Quaestio* 16, *Prima*, Chapter *Visis*; or at least it is something mixed, and simple things are very different from mixed things, as in the Digest, *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, Law *Imperium*, § *Mixtum*. It is established in the Decretals, *De probationibus*, Chapter *Licet causam*. Moreover, according to common usage, patronage is not called an honorific, that is, if it stands in its own name, argument from the Digest, *De pactis*, Law *Iuris gentium*, § 1.

† and words are to be interpreted according to the understanding of the common people: as in D. de fundo instructo, l. cum delationis, §. Asinam; and D. de legatis 3, l. librorum, §. quod tamen Cassius. It is therefore concluded from the foregoing that the right of patronage was not transferred, nor could it have been transferred by these words. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a husband may leave the usufruct to his wife against the provision of a statute.
2. When a statute or law goes beyond its proper scope in making a provision, whether an act otherwise performed is valid.
3. A husband may remit to his wife a burden that he cannot bear.
body: In the name of Christ. In accordance with the case of that good woman to whom a usufruct was bequeathed in the will of her late husband, whether she remained a widow or entered into second vows, and this notwithstanding any general or special law providing to the contrary, in which case it was asked: whether, because the woman entered into second vows, she fell from the said usufruct? And this by virtue of the said statute. The rubric: that a husband cannot institute his wife as heir, nor bequeath, nor leave anything in any last will to his wife, except a usufruct. Item, we ordain that henceforth no husband may institute his wife, nor bequeath, nor leave anything in any last will to his wife, except a usufruct; moreover, he may not leave the ownership of any thing, but she may not enjoy the said usufruct except honorably, and by remaining in widowhood, and by honorably preserving her husband's bed; however, the husband himself may leave alimony to his said wife, she honorably preserving her husband's bed, but he may not afterwards sell or alienate to his wife or to another during the subsistence of the marriage; and if it shall have been done otherwise, it shall ipso facto neither be valid nor hold.

† For clarity, I premise that where a statute prohibits something from being left, a testator cannot bring it about that the statute does not have a place in his testament. First, on account of the general rule: because a prohibitory law cannot be renounced; as in l. 1 and 2, C. ne fideiussores dotium dentur. Second, on account of another rule: because no one can bring it about that the laws do not have a place in his testament; as in ff. de lega. 1, l. nemo potest.

† Third, on account of the express text of the law in ff. de lega. 1, l. si quis inquilinos, §. fina.; ff. de lega. 2, l. codicillis, §. vltimo; ff. ad l. falcid., l. quod de hominis, §. 1. If, however, the law does not expressly prohibit, but permits, and does not proceed further, there is no doubt that it is valid; as in l. 1, C. de sacrosan. eccle., and l. 2, C. communia de lega., with similar texts. But if the law proceeds further by disposing how the bequest is lost—as is said here, that the usufruct left is lost through entering into second vows, because it says that she cannot enjoy it except in widowhood—

† then the husband can in his testament remit this burden by permitting that she may marry and retain the legacy, because this statute had emanated for the favor of the testator. The text is express in Authen. de nuptiis, §. disponet. For to marry is not shameful, but honorable, as in ff. ad Trebell., l. mulier, §. cum proponeretur; and this is expedient for the commonwealth for the sake of replenishing the city with free persons, as in l. i, ff. solu. matrimo., and ff. de conditio. et demonstra., l. hoc modo; and formerly the condition of celibacy was rejected, ff. eod. titu., l. mulieri et titio, and C. de iudic. viduit., l. 2, and aut. cui relictum, and the notes there. For that she loses the usufruct by marrying is a kind of penalty, which the testator or his heir can remit; as in C. vt in possess. leg., l. scire. I, Baldus. Long case of the following consilium. In the name of Christ. The Count of Beaumont, named by his proper name Longaspada, had from an ancient marriage three castles, which the same count sold to the community of the city of Arles for the price of 10,000 Tours pounds in the years of the Lord 1326, and the said community afterwards gave the same castles to the count in fief for himself and his heirs, a pact having been entered into between them among other matters of such kind, that the said count holds and ought to hold, himself, his heirs, and his successors, the said three castles in noble, straight, and gentile fief from the said commune, and all and singular the castles, villages, and places that the said count, and his sons or any of them, shall acquire, the lord count himself, and his sons, heirs, and successors, making peace and war concerning those castles at the will of the said count against whatever persons, etc., as is contained therein. It happened that in the course of 1334, the said count acquired another castle in addition to those three that he previously held in fief, as above. Which having been acquired, the said count approached the elders of the said city of Arles and notified them how he had newly acquired such a castle; whereupon he offered separately to hold it in fief from the said commune by virtue of the said pact, by which he promised to hold in fief all and singular castles that he shall acquire, etc., as is contained above in the said clause. Which notification and obligation having been made, the said elders accepted the same obligation and invested the same count with the said castle, and the count himself prudently swore fealty and performed it in the accustomed and common form. Which having been completed, the said count afterwards in the year of the Lord 1341 alienated the said castle last acquired by him, without the consent of the commune of the aforesaid city or its garrison, to another count who well knew the condition of the said castle, who is named by his proper name Theodoric. Which alienation the said commune says to be void, asserting the said property to be feudal and that it could not be alienated without the consent of the commune itself or the city; and consequently the said commune infers that the purchaser could not acquire the said property; nay rather, he is bound to return it to the same commune, and this gratuitously and without price, since he knowingly purchased feudal property, etc., according to the notes in the Book of Feuds in the title de prohibita aliena. per Fede., ca. sancimus, §. cacillidis, with similar texts. On the contrary, however, the said counts, both the one selling and the one buying, say, denying that the said castle was feudal: for the said Count Longaspada, the seller, says that although in his ancient investiture he promised to hold in fief from the said commune all castles that he should acquire, even besides the first feudal ones, as above, and although he acknowledged the said castle last acquired by him in fief, and received investiture for it, as above, nevertheless the said castle was not thereby made feudal, since at the time of the said last investiture the said castle in question was not among the goods of the said commune of Arles, nor was the ownership of the said castle ever transferred to the said commune by such acknowledgment and investiture, nor even the possession of the same; wherefore, since the aforesaid acknowledgment and receipt of investiture was not a mode of making the said [property] feudal, the said Count Longaspada infers that the said alienation cannot be revoked. And the said Count Theodoric, the said purchaser, says the same for the preservation of his right, as above, inferring from the premises that therefore he was able to acquire, as above.
