The jurists of the said commune, however, reply to the things alleged by the aforesaid counts, and say: that by the said acknowledgment and investiture, this clause of the said pact especially assisting, the ownership of the said castle in question is feigned by a kind of brevi manu to have been transferred to the said commune, and by the same brevi manu delivered back in fief to the said count as vassal. Now, concerning the premises, it is asked: what is the law? Secondly and principally, it afterwards happened that in the course of 1356 the said Count Longaspada died, many children and grandchildren having been left by him; some of which said grandchildren acquired another castle in the year of the Lord 1370. Which castle the said purchasers held in such a manner that they made no acknowledgment for it to the said commune, nor did they receive investiture. And finally, the said grandchildren also alienated the said castle acquired by them, as above, without the license of the community or city aforesaid. Which alienation the commune of the said city also hastens to challenge, saying that by virtue of the said pact, the said castle newly acquired by the said grandchildren is both ipso facto—that is, by the very fact that it was acquired—and ipso iure feudal, and thus by law a fief subject to the said city, just like the other three castles first granted in fief in the ancient investiture, and consequently it is inalienable, as if it were the outgrowth and property of the said city. On the contrary, the said alienating grandchildren, or the one who bought from them, say, stating that the force of the said pact is not of such efficacy that castles acquired after the times of the said ancient investiture are ipso facto and ipso iure feudal unless the deed of the contracting parties themselves first intervenes; nor would a mere demand or receipt of investiture suffice, as intervened in the preceding case; nay rather, after the said ancient times, etc., there is need of a notification of such new acquisition made by them, as above, or a demand made upon them by the said community that they hold it in fief according to the form of the said pact, etc., and that they not sell, nor donate, nor otherwise deliver the said such castle to the said commune; so that the ownership of such castle is first transferred to the said commune, and once transferred, the said commune delivers back or renders such castle afterwards in fief to such vassal acquiring it. Which things—namely, the aforesaid or similar acts transferring ownership—not having been done, it remains, as the said acquirers say, that the said castle is in no way feudal; nay rather, it could also be lawfully alienated. The said vassals who acquired it, as above, also say further that in the event they are bound by virtue of the said pact to hold in fief from the said commune all castles that they shall acquire, etc., that they are not bound to do this gratuitously; nay rather, it is fitting and due that the said commune pay to the vassal himself the price for which he purchased such castle, or at least give the value of such castle newly acquired, since it does not seem fitting that the vassal himself of the three castles, etc., should buy another besides them, perhaps at a very high price, as was the case in the present instance, and afterwards deliver it gratuitously, and constitute himself the vassal of another concerning that which he acquired unencumbered; otherwise it would follow that the said city would be enriched with another's loss, which ought not to be. But the jurists of the said city reply to the things alleged by the said vassal, saying that so great is the force of the said ancient pact that whatever the said vassal shall acquire, he must hold in fief, and this gratuitously and without another price or valuation or value of the thing; nay rather, the first beneficium transferred to the first count suffices, by virtue of which that Count Longaspada bound himself and also his descendants to hold in fief even things to be acquired. And that things to be acquired fall under the obligation of that ancient pact is just as possible as what we see in one who generally binds his present and future goods, or those had and to be had; for things to be acquired, after they have been acquired, are found to be just as bound as those goods that were already acquired at the time of the obligation. From the premises it is also asked: what is the law? And above all, let the forces of the said pact be diligently considered. And let the consilium of the lord Baldus de Perusio be had in the premises, who not only in the matter of feuds, but indeed in all the peaks of the law, is recognized as the most illustrious and more fruitful than all others. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pact is valid or not, by which whatever anyone, or his heirs, acquires, whether it be castrensia (military fiefs) or similar, is to be a fief of a third person.
2. Fiction does not operate more than truth.
3. When one may donate, sell, or make an agreement concerning future things.
4. We look more to the time in which something is conferred than to the time in which something exists.
5. What effect does the pact, repeated above in the person of the contracting party, have, unless the contracting count acquires for the city or community, and if he sells, does he fall into a forfeiture?
6. A pact is part of the price.
7. When something is granted, it seems that what follows from it in the order in which it could follow is also granted.
8. A penalty is indivisible.
9. Whether the price ought to be returned to the new buyer.
10. He who knowingly trades against the law does not recover the price.
11. Regarding the castrensia purchased by the heirs of the contracting party, mentioned above: whether they have become feudal, so that they cannot be alienated. See the opinion of Irrequisiti.
12. Whether possession passes by contract alone.
13. The denomination and appellation of a fief is threefold.
14. Every fief can broadly be called paternal, which took its origin in the person of the transmitters.
15. Whether ancient instruments prevail without it appearing that there was a mandate of the notary for the instrument.
16. Antiquity gives authority and credibility.
17. Whether a matter begun by one procurator can be pursued by another.
18. Whether the alienation of the father harms the son: and what is the case regarding fiefs.
19. Whether transmission has place in fiefs and royal dignities, and what comes under the name of the son.
body: In the name of Christ. In the first place, it must be examined

† whether that pact—namely, that all and singular the castles, villas, and places which the said Count shall acquire, the Count himself ought to hold as a proper and noble feud from the said community—is valid or not. And it seems that it is not valid by reason of generality and uncertainty, by the argument of ff. de transac. l. cum aquil.; for that is uncertain which is contained within no boundaries, as in ff. de censi. l. forma, and ff. de rei vendica. l. si in rem agat aliquis. Likewise, from a pact so uncertain no possession can be acquired, because there is uncertainty by reason of place and share, as in ff. de acquiren. posses. l. 3. §. incertum, and l. locus. Likewise, from such a pact an inconvenience and absurdity could follow, that is, an enormous lesion beyond half of the just price, if perchance the said Count had acquired a castle improved twofold; but inequity of this kind is to be avoided, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione. l. domum, C. de rescindenda venditione. l. secunda, and by the argument of ff. de legatis tertio. l. offilius. Furthermore, the law says that ownership is transferred from a contract of partnership without delivery, but in present things, not future ones: as read and noted in l. prima. §. in societate, and l. si quis societate, at the end, in the title ff. pro socio; because to future things not yet possessed a true or fictitious delivery cannot be adapted, because what does not exist cannot be delivered: for there must be some body that can be delivered by the deliverer, as in ff. de haeredi. vel actio. venditio. l. quod si nulla.

† Likewise, a fiction ought not to effect more than the truth: as in l. liber homo, de stipulatio. seruo., and de noxali. l. electio. §. si is, and ff. de adoptio. l. adoptio; but in truth no one can deliver what he does not have: therefore neither fictitiously, as in l. cum eo, in the beginning, ff. de acquiren. rerum domi. In doubt, therefore, that is, in what is uncertain, nothing is valid: as in ff. de in diem adiec. l. cum duo serui, with the many concordances cited there. To the contrary it seems,

† because one can well contract regarding future things, and donate and sell them, provided they are in commerce, that is, applied to the uses of man, or fit to be applied or to come into them: as read and noted in C. de pac. l. fina., C. quae res pignor. obligari possunt. l. vlti., ff. de condictio. demonstratio. l. nam ad ea, ff. de actio. emptio. l. si iactum retis, extra de re iudic. capitu. Abbate sane, ff. de verbo. obliga. l. inter stipulantem. §. sacram, ff. de contrahen. emptio. l. nec emptio, in the beginning. Furthermore, that uncertainty or generality is reduced to certainty and species after the fact, whence that which is done is valid just as if it had been certain from the beginning, by the argument of ff. de hęred. institu. l. asse toto, and ff. de rebus dub. l. vtrum. §. cum quidam.

† Certainly we ought to look to the time at which something is conferred, rather than the time at which something is made, as in ff. de contrahen. emptio. l. quod saepe. §. si quis amico, and C. de donatio. ante nupt. l. quod sponsę. The resolution: on this point it must be said that the pact is valid, as in ff. de contrahen. emptio. l. qui fundum vendidit, in the first response, and that uncertainty does not vitiate it, because it was reduced to certainty, as in ff. pro socio. l. coiri, with the following laws, and ff. mandati. l. fina, in the beginning, and ff. de procura. l. Item ad litem, with countless similar texts. Indeed, we have a similar contract, which was formerly called the colonary contract: C. de sacrosan. eccle. l. iubemus. §. fina., and in the Authentica dum alienam. §. uult enim. Therefore, let the validity of the pact be presupposed as constant. But let us proceed further,

† namely, what that pact is able to effect: and first, in the person of the contractor; second, in the person of his heirs. In the person indeed of the contractor and in the person of the heirs the pact was conferred, and it had two heads of persons and two heads of things to be acquired. I take first, therefore, the things acquired by the Count who first receives the feud: whether they immediately became feudal, or at least through the investiture subsequent thereto. And it seems first that immediately, because from the contract of purchase and sale, or from the act set over against that contract, ownership passes to the city without possession, because this is special in a city and in a church, as in C. de sacrosanct. eccle. in the final law. For there are two contracts from which that privilege arises regarding the church and the city, namely the contract of purchase and sale—and I understand this together with its pact and its appurtenances,

† because a pact is part of the price, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione. l. fundi partem, and ff. de actione emptione. l. si sterilis. §. si tibi, and ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium. §. quinimo. Likewise the contract of donation—and I understand this broadly, because privileges ought to be extended, as in l. beneficium, de constitu. princi.—so that it contains also a donation subject to a condition or charge (sub modo), which properly and simply is not a donation, nor mere liberality, since it contains in itself a burden after the fact, as read and noted in ff. de donatio. l. 1, and l. hoc iure, and l. aristo. From these it follows that immediately, because the said first Count acquired the new castle, it was made the city's to such an extent that the city can enfeoff it to him, because that is the tacit order of those contracts, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. certi condictio. §. si nummos, and l. singularia, and ff. de dona. inter virum, et vxor. l. 3. §. sciendum.

† Because when something is granted, that which follows from it seems to be granted, and in that order by which it can follow, as in ff. de seruitu. l. si cui, and ff. de seruitute vrbanorum praediorum. l. seruitutes. §. si domo. Furthermore, even if ownership had not been acquired by the city immediately, it would nevertheless have been acquired through recognition into a feud. For recognition itself includes two things in itself: the first is to be given to the city; the second is to be received from it as a feud, as in ff. si cer. peta. l. si tibi, and by the argument of ff. solu. matri. l. seruos dotalis. Likewise, investiture is a valid proof of transferred possession, as in extra de consuetudine. c. ex parte. Thus this Count has beneficial ownership from the city, and conversely the city has the naked property perpetually alienated to it by the Count himself. Likewise, the Count has natural possession from the city, but the city has civil possession through the quasi-delivery of the Count: for which civil possession services are rendered to the city as the principal mistress, and nonetheless for the natural possession, whose benefit is in the hands of the feudatory. But to the contrary it seems, because here corporal investiture did not intervene, which ought to be done on the thing, or in sight of the thing, as in c. 1. de consuetudine recti feudi, and by the argument of ff. de iure dot. l. si sponsalibus. §. fin., and without corporal investiture a feud is not something perfect unless it is subject to the penalties of feuds, because it does not have in itself the requisite quiddity nor nature, as in c. 1, quid sit inuestitura, collatio 10. The resolution: all things considered, I say that this Count fell into forfeiture (commissum), and perhaps of all the castles:

† because the penalty is indivisible, and by reason of the conjoined part it is incurred in solidum in the person of the contractor himself, by the argument of ff. fami. ercis. l. haeredes. §. si unus, ff. de penu leg. l. 1, at the end, and ff. de verborum obliga. l. eadem. §. Cato. Yet I deem it more equitable that only those castles fall into forfeiture which were alienated without the city having been asked, lest the legal penalty exceed the offense, as in ff. de his, quibus, vt indig. l. rescriptum. And if it is said that, to the contrary, nothing fell into forfeiture because corporal possession was not delivered to the Count: I answer, this was not necessary, because he possessed it; hence fictitious delivery suffices, since the title was true, arising from the principal contract, as fully read and noted by Cynus on C. loca. l. qui rem, and by Bartolus on ff. de acquiren. possessio. l. si aliquam rem; to which serves ff. de rei vendica. l. quaedam mulier, and what is fully read and noted on C. de acqui. pos. l. cum nemo.

† But it is asked incidentally whether the price ought to be returned to the new buyer; and it must be said that the city is not bound to return the price, because it vindicates its own property, as in C. de furtis. l. 2, because an unfair condition could not be imposed upon the owner by the act of a third party, as in de rei ven. l. si mancipium. But whether the said Count, the seller, is bound to return the price to them can be doubted. For it seems that he is, as in ff. de euic. l. si praedium, and ff. de actio. emp. l. emptorem. §. ibidem. To the contrary it seems, because he who knowingly buys a feudal thing loses the price, as in c. imperialem. §. talionis, de prohib. alie. feud. per Fed.;

† for he who knowingly bargains against the laws does not recover the price: first, in order that he may be punished, because he showed contempt for the law, as in C. de sacro sanc. eccle. l. iubemus nulli; second, because unjust purchasers are not permitted to recover the price, as in C. de agri. et cen. l. quemadmodum, book 10; third, because the buyer paid a price which he knew he did not owe, as in ff. de reg. iur. l. cuius per errorem. The resolution: he who has knowingly bargained against the law cannot claim the price which he paid, unless this had been expressly agreed by a pact secured by a stipulation, as in C. de euic. l. si fundum sciens. I come to the second principal point,

† in which it is asked: what about the castles bought by the heirs? Have they been made feudal by the pact of the deceased, such that if they were alienated by the heirs without the knowledge of the said sovereign city, they have reverted to the said city? And it seems that yes, because the heir is bound by the pact of the deceased, and especially if he did not make an inventory, because the heir and the deceased are deemed one and the same person, as in l. haeredes, ff. de regu. iur. Likewise, ownership passes to the city without possession, as in the said l. fi., C. de sacro sanct. eccle. Some say further that even possession passes when it was in the hands of the contracting party. For if ownership passes, which is greater and more strongly rooted in the holder, as in ff. de acquir. pos. l. si quis vi. §. differentia, much more strongly ought possession to pass, as in ff. de acqui. pos. l. 1. §. si vir vxori.

† To the contrary is the truth: because possession does not pass by contract alone, although in the Church it is special that possession passes, by notable title and abusive investiture, as in extra de consuetudine. c. 2, and there by Innocent; and so the Glossa determines that possession does not pass without delivery, or some act that is held for delivery, as noted in the said l. fin. de sac. sanct. eccle., and ff. pro socio. l. cum duobus. §. idem respondit, and ff. de publicanis. l. commissa. Nor is this surprising, because even to an heir possession does not pass unless it is apprehended, because it consists in fact and in a bodily act, or quasi-bodily act: as in ff. de acqui. pos. l. cum haeres, ff. quibus ex cau. mai. l. denique, ff. si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit. l. 1. §. scęuola; wherefore concerning possession there is no question, and he who does not possess, nor quasi-possess, cannot invest another, as in ff. de acqui. rerum domi. l. traditio. From this it follows that the said city has no feudal ownership in the said castles acquired by the heirs, because it never possessed them. Someone will say: granted that those castles are not feudal, nevertheless they belong to the city by the pact, as in the said l. fin.; therefore the city can vindicate them by the same law. I answer: consider subtly that that law equates a contract and a legacy; but a testator, by bequeathing the property of an heir, does not transfer ownership, as noted in ff. de serui. l. Papinianus. Likewise, only the things of the deceased are hypothecated, not the things of the heir, as in C. communia de lega. l. 1 and 2. Likewise, in a general hypothec the goods of the heir separated from the goods of the deceased do not come, as in ff. de pigno. l. Paulus, and noted in C. qui potio. in pigno. hab. l. assiduis, near the end of the Magna Glossa; yet a certain Glossa which is in l. 2, C. communia de leg. says that a testator, by bequeathing the property of the heir, transfers ownership, as though the heir, by entering upon the inheritance, seems to consent to this and ratify it, an excellent argument in ff. quibs mod. pigno. vel hypo. sol. l. sicut. §. venditionis. But consider further that the heir is bound by quasi-contract, and the specialty of the said final law has no place in quasi-contracts, because it is special in four cases; whence, concluding from first to last, it follows that the castles acquired by the heirs cannot be revoked or evicted from the buyers by the city, namely on the grounds that they fell into forfeiture: because there is no forfeiture. Baldus de Perusio. Further, in accordance with the premises, it is asked whether a castle newly acquired by any of the said grandsons—whether it is made a feud by operation of law or by the fact itself, or by the act of man, say by reduction or something else of this kind—is a new feud, such that the right of revocation among agnates has no place in it; say, because if it is alienated to one agnate of a more remote degree, other agnates of a closer degree cannot revoke it or retract it by revoking: or whether it is deemed an ancient feud because of the force of the clause of the said pact. Likewise, because a dispute is pending between the said parties, as above, and one party produces certain ancient instruments of sales in which mention is made, as by a procurator, or in the name of the procurator B., as of whose procuracy appears by a public instrument written by the hand of such notary M., he bought such a castle, etc., and it is not known who the notary was who was to receive the instruments of the procuracy, since there are many of that name, nor does it say whose notary he was, nor is the instrument of his mandate produced, nor does it otherwise appear concerning it. It is asked whether the said ancient instruments of sale make full proof without the instrument of that procurator's mandate appearing: especially since it was denied in court that that alleged procurator ever existed in the nature of things; and if he did exist, it is denied that he had a legitimate mandate to make the said purchase. Likewise, whether an instance of a suit begun by a procurator can be changed to another procurator with the adverse party objecting, but with the first procurator not objecting, without any cession, or without all things being narrated anew by the second, into whom the transition is made, according to what is noted in l. mutari and in l. causę, at the end, ff. de procur., with similar texts; and what ought to be done in such a change, and whether it hinders or helps the aforesaid that in the said suit proceedings are conducted without the formal structure of a trial. As to the first,

† I answer that there is a threefold denomination and designation of a feud: for one is a new feud, another is paternal, and another is acquired by ancestors. For that is called 'new' which proceeds from the very first acquirer and has not yet made a transition to another degree; but 'paternal' is that which descends from the father down to the fourth degree of children; and that is called 'acquired by ancestors' which has already exceeded the fourth degree: for above the fourth degree neither ascendants nor below descendants have proper names, but those, namely ascendants, are called 'progenitors' by an unnamed term, and those begotten are called 'offspring' or 'descendants'. The beginning, therefore, makes a new feud, but derived further into another degree it is not called new, as in c. 1. de succes. feudi, and there noted by the Glossa quid ergo, in the text on the word initium.

† Yet in a broad manner every feud can be called paternal which took its origin in the person of those transmitting it, as in c. 1. de gradi. succedend. in feudum, at the verse quod ita. Moreover, a feud will be understood to begin in that person in whom it first had perfect being through investiture: for before investiture it is not a feud, as in c. 1, in the beginning, quid sit inuestitura, and in c. sciendum, de consuetudine recti feudi. And from these things it follows that if the said first recipient alienated without consulting the city, the collaterals of that feudatory have no right of revocation, as in cap. 1. §. in alio vero, de succes. feudi, and in c. 1. §. cum vero Corradus, qui feudum dare possunt, and in cap. 1. §. nos autem, and §. calidis, de prohibita aliena. feudi per Fredericum; to which serves c. primum. §. sed et res, per quos fiat inuestitura, and in c. Titius, si de feudo defuncti fuerit controuersia, and de alienatione feudi paterni. c. 1. Furthermore, that question does not proceed in the new castles acquired by the grandsons, because, as I have said, the rights of a feud are not deemed to exist, although the personal obligation passes to the heirs, as noted in the said c. 1, in the Glossa that is called de successione feudi, and in the Magna Glossa. For a real acquisition is one thing, a personal obligation another: as in ff. de leg. 1. l. apud Iulianum. §. si Titius.

† As to the second point concerning the ancient instruments, I think there is no place for the denial, but the instrument must be stood by. For whosoever that notary was, it is nothing to the point, because the authority is the same, by the argument of ff. de libe. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. si Caius.

† Likewise, antiquity gives authority and credibility, since instruments have been brought into use and for proof, as in extra de verbo. signific. l. super quibusdam. §. Praeterea, and by the argument of ff. de vsuris. l. cum de in rem verso; and what Cynus notes on C. de fide instru. l. solennibus. Otherwise ancient instruments ought not to be revoked; and many writings are without a title, as is evident in the Book of Psalms, because the author is not known precisely, and yet they make proof. Yet a text says that ancient instruments are weakened in credibility, as in the Authentica vt ecclesia Romana. §. 1, and extra de testibus. cap. Albericus, and C. de falsis. l. si quis decurio serve this. Therefore, proof of the impossible is not to be made; it suffices that it is established that it was so customary in the past: as in ff. de vsuris. l. cum de in rem verso.

† As to the third point, I say that either it is contained in the mandate that one may begin and the other may prosecute, and then a cession of the instance is not necessary, by the argument in l. 1, ff. de officio consulis; or these words are not there, and then a cession of the instance is necessary, as noted in ff. de procurat. l. mutari, and l. quae omnia, or that past matters be narrated anew and things to be done be added, which is done in brief words, that is, by the sole recitation of the fact, and there by Bartolus. Under canon law, I do not think that that superfluity and scrupulous subtlety is necessary, by the argument of extra de electione. c. querelam, especially in administrators who have a public office, as are the syndics of cities, as in ff. de euictio. l. si ideo. §. 1; and the practice of the courts is such that what one has begun, another can prosecute by a direct path without cession of the instance; c. si duo, at the verse nisi dictum, de procura. in the Sext serves this. The conclusion therefore on each of the difficult doubts is clear, just as I have clearly stated, and these points pertain to the summits of the law.

† One thing remains: whether the father's alienation harms the son? And I say that either the father stipulated for the feud for the son as heir, and it harms him; or for the son as son, and it does not harm him; or it is doubtful, and then in a feud he seems to stipulate for the son as heir, in c. 1, an agnatus, uel filius, and in c. 1, de duobus fratribus a capitaneo inuestitis. But if an outsider, say a notary as a public person, had stipulated for the father and the son at the mandate of the father, the same applies; but if as a manager of the affairs (gestor) of the son and the father, the son would not be understood to have been placed in the sequence of succession, but only in rank, that is, upon the father's death; and thus the alienation of the father would not harm him; rather, it would open the feud to the son himself, because the exclusion of the former is the inclusion of the latter. What is noted in ff. de pac. l. si tibi. §. si pactus, and C. de oper. lib. l. liberti, by Petrus and Cynus, serves this.

† This is the nature in a transmissible feud; but in a non-transmissible feud, as in a feud of royal dignity, say of a March and a Duchy, the name of the son is understood for the son simply, not for the heir, as in ff. de verbo. obli. l. stipulatio ista. §. si quis ita. Chapter 1, §. in feudo, de feudi alien., where it says 'it has been usurped', does not stand in the way, because that usurpation ceases where there is an expressly opposing defect, which is the ius commune, and it can be referred as in C. de procu. l. maritus, and the final law, C. de pact. conuentis. For I understand the pact according to the ius commune and according to usurpation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. In how many ways a contumacious person is said to be so.
2. He who does not wish to attend an election renders himself alien to it; and what if he is present but refuses to elect.
3. If two elections are held in discord and at different times, which of them prevails.
4. What are the essential elements of an election, and what are incidental; and when it is valid, and when not.
5. Custom confers jurisdiction.
body: In the name of Christ. For clarity, it must be premised,

† that although one who is summoned and does not come is sometimes truly contumacious, sometimes fictitiously so, and sometimes neither truly nor fictitiously; and when he was impeded by an accident; nevertheless, if having been cited he approaches, and afterwards withdraws, he is always truly contumacious, unless a preceding necessity, which naturally cannot be resisted, naturally compelled him to withdraw: as in ff. de re iudic. l. quaesitum; ff. de publicanis. l. Caesar; extra de dolo, et contu. cap. 1. lib. 6; C. quomodo et quod iud. l. ab eo.

† Secondly, I premise that he makes himself an outsider to an election who does not wish to participate in the election, as in ff. de fideicom. liber. l. si legatario. §. a duobus. Iacob. de Aret. says it must be noted that those who are absent through contumacy make themselves strangers to the election, and the right of electing is transferred to their co-electors, as here, and extra de elec. c. cum nobis olim. The same applies if they are present and do not wish to elect, as infra eo. l. non tantum. §. penu. according to Iacobum de Aret.; and similarly Oldra., saying thus: hence it is gathered that if there be several who have the power of electing, and some are absent through contumacy, the power of electing is transferred to the others. So supra eodem. l. 1. and 4. §. hic, says Oldra.

† Thirdly, it must be premised that when two elections take place in discord, not simultaneously, but at different times, either the first is valid and the second is not valid; or the first is not valid, and it is then notorious that it is not valid, and the second is valid, provided it is otherwise lawful and formal. But if it is doubtful whether the first is valid or not, the second election made in the interim must be quashed, as in extra de elect. c. consideramus. and capit. auditis; undoubtedly because electors must be certain both as to the right of electing and as to the fact. For they cannot elect by mere act, but with full deliberation of mind and certain knowledge, as in l. quaero. ff. de eo, qui pro tuto.; and the rule of law states comprehensively that all things done by determination of the mind cannot be accomplished except with true and certain knowledge; to the same effect, ff. de testamentis. l. de statu; C. de captiuis, et postliminium reuersis. l. nec nos; ff. de condi. et dem. l. multum interest. Having therefore premised these things, I posit two conclusions: the first is this, that the election of Master Antonius was canonical; which is proven thus:

† It was lawful and formal, therefore canonical. I say that it was lawful as to the substance of the consent of the greater and sounder part; secondly, as to the substance of the form. And these two are what canonize an election: namely, the substance of consent and the substance of form. Other matters are accidents or incidentals, as in extra de ele. c. quia propter. and c. in Genesi. And I consider that if we make a comparison of number to number, the voting electors of Master Antonius were the greater part, that is, more than half, as in C. de decu. l. obseruare. and l. nominationum formae. li. 10. If, however, I consider the time, either the smaller part had fallen from the right of electing, because they had made themselves strangers to that right through contumacy, and also they elected after lunch, and thus at an improper hour; for it is noted with this defect, although it may not perhaps belong to the substance. Likewise, although those who withdraw ought to be recalled, as in extra de elec. capi. ecclesia, nevertheless, if when summoned again they do not come, that second summons is held as a peremptory term, as in extra de elec. cap. cum inter vniuersas. Wherefore, concluding from first to last, the first conclusion is that the election of Master Antonius was canonical, and that of Master Felix abusive. To this is added the authority of the party of the Minister General; for that ought to be valid which is confirmed by his authority, because he holds the supreme place in the order, as in l. 1. §. solent. ff. quando appellandum sit; and ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. si praetor; and C. de praediis curia. l. 1. lib. 10. Nor does the contrary appeal stand in the way, because it is frustratory, as in capi. statuimus. de elec. lib. 6; for frivolous appeals, that is, those in which there is evident injustice, are not to be entertained, as the rule of canon and civil law states. This is confirmed especially by the Pope's privilege. For it is presupposed that he proceeded according to the order of the order of the aforesaid Lord General; I say this in so far as the words of the privilege say "according to the custom of the order," as in extra de verbo. significa. capitu. abbate. Likewise, it does not stand in the way if it is said that the Minister General could not substitute voters in the place of the schismatics, even though it is not called into doubt that he could substitute in place of other faithful; for which allegation supports the fact that it does not appear to be expressly found in law, namely, that one may be substituted for schismatics or infidels, and we blush to speak without law, as in Authen. de trien. et semis. §. si consideremus. I respond that this allegation is neither good nor true; for it is provided that another can be substituted in the place of an absent or impeded guardian, as in ff. de tutelis. l. quaesitum. It is doubted whether the same applies if the guardian is banished, because obstinate and pertinacious schismatics are compared to the banished and exiles, as in C. de haeredi. authen. Gazaros; and certainly the law determines that the same applies to the banished and exiles, that in their place another not only can, but ought to be subrogated. And properly speaking this is not a subrogation, but an appointment, because a deportee or a schismatic is held as dead, as in l. 1. in fin. ff. de contratabu.; and ff. de lib. et posthu. l. Gallus. §. et quid si tantum; and therefore without doubt the said Father General was able to appoint notable persons in the manner in which he appointed them. And to this ff. ad Tertu. l. 2. §. non solum. and §. sed quod diximus. and §. si mater. serves very well; and ff. de tu. da. ab his. l. si tutor reipublicae. §. pen.; and ff. de testa. tutel. l. si quis sub conditione. §. plane; for civil and canonical death is equated with natural death, ff. de verbo. obliga. l. ex ea parte. §. in insulam; for schism is similar to death, because schism is a kind of heresy, since he who doubts in faith is an infidel, according to that saying, "he who does not gather with me scatters," as in C. de iudaeis. l. caelicolarum. and the notes there. Nor is it to be doubted that those who condemn the Minister General ought not to remain unpunished, lest public authority become degraded, as in ff. de re iu. l. contumaciae; ff. de his, qui no. infa. l. debuit; ff. si quis iusdicenti non obtemperauerit. l. 1; because he who contemns the magistrate also contemns the commonwealth itself, and contempt of the praetor's majesty must be judged, as in ff. de iuris. om. iudi. l. si familia. And from these things it follows conclusively, as was premised, that the said Minister General was able to substitute voting electors for the schismatic places and for those who are missing. For since guardians can do this in their custodies, and provincials in their provinces through the statutes of the order, much more strongly can the General in general and provincial chapters supply, subrogate, and appoint voters, lest what is conceded to an inferior be denied to a superior, as in C. de offic. praefec. vrba. l. prima; since the Minister General was present, the supplying could rather belong to him, as in ff. de damno infec. l. 4. §. si iam vicinum; I do not say, however, that from this anyone's right should be taken away, as in l. 2. ff. de his, qui sunt sui iuris. Supporting the church and the jurisdiction of the Lord Minister General is the fact,

† that custom gives jurisdiction, and he has this from the general custom of the order, according to what is fully read and noted in l. 1. C. de emanci. libero. by the Glossa and Cyn.; and ff. de iuris. om. iudi. l. more maiorum; and because their custom was approved by the Pope. Whence it has become like a privilege, which is of even greater authority than simple custom, as in extra de verbo. significatio. capitu. superquibusdam. Furthermore, the text says: we deservedly make all things our own, to which authority is imparted from us, as in C. de vete. iur. enuc. l. 1. §. omnia et enim. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Words determined to a certain time, place, or quantity, or to the present time, do not comprehend another time, place, or quantity.
2. Whether a legacy made of goods purchased and ready extends to those which were purchased and prepared afterwards.
3. Words are to be interpreted so that the disposition may be most valid for pious causes.
body: The case is as follows: An indulgence, granted in the name of Christ by the Lord Supreme Pontiff to a certain chapel, which, although it had been constructed some time ago, was recently renamed in honor of the Visitation of the Blessed Mary and Magnificat, and applied to the illustrious and noble Lady, the Duchess; furthermore, after the said application and new naming, the feast of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary was publicly solemnized. Finally, the said indulgence was obtained and secured for the said chapel, or within the said chapel, and the tenor of this privilege contains these words in form. Therefore, desiring that the chapel under the name of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, constructed in the church of Saint John of the house of the hermit brothers of Saint Augustine outside the walls of Novara, be recognized, it is objected that it was not constructed. I answer that, although it was not so named from the beginning, it is now so called.

† It is asked whether the said indulgence is applied to the said chapel, and whether it binds; and it appears that the said indulgence is not applied to the said chapel, because the words state that the chapel is under the name of the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary, constructed in the church of Saint John; but in the said church the said chapel is not found to be constructed. And that which is not found is held as nothing, as in the Digest, *De legatis*, book 1, law *Si quis legaverit*. For since the chapel itself, nor one similar to it, is not found, the privilege does not bind, by argument from the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *In testamento*. For on account of uncertainty the disposition is vitiated, nor is it reduced to certainty in the proper manner: as in the Institutes, *De legatis*, section *Incertum*; and in the Digest, *De testamentis tutoribusque*, law *Duo sunt Titii*. Furthermore, words determined to a certain time do not comprehend another time, as in the Digest, *De servitute urbanae praedii*, law *Si servitus*. Thus, words determined to a certain place do not comprehend another place, as in the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *Damni*, section *Si is, qui*; Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Rutilia*; and law *In l.* Similarly, words determined to a certain quantity do not comprehend another quality. Digest, *De legatis*, book 3, law *Hoc legatum*; Digest, *De noxalibus actionibus*, law *In delictum*, section *Si extraneus*; Digest, *De testamento militis*, law *Titius*. We also have that words determined to the present time do not comprehend the future, as in the Digest, *De auro et argento legato*, law *Si ita*; Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, law *Cum stipulamur*; and law *Si a colono*. Now in our case the words appear to be terminated with respect to place, and with respect to time, on account of that participle, *constructa* [constructed]; therefore, if it is not found to have been constructed from the beginning under that name, the tenor is false, and consequently the privilege is void, as in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Legis venditionis*. And it supports the foregoing, which is fully read and noted in the Extravagantes, *De sponsalibus impuberum*, chapter *Ad dissolvendum*.

To the contrary is the truth. And I premise for understanding, that just as there are certain things which were and are undoubtedly, to these a privilege can be granted; there are certain things which were, and at the time the privilege was given are not in the nature of things; and to these a privilege cannot be adapted, as in law *Apud*, Digest, *De auro et argento legato*; Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Quo loco*, section *Si iam mortuo*; Digest, *De aqua quotidiana et aestiva*, law *Hoc iure*, section *Si aqua*. Although in our privilege I would think that memory and its remains would suffice. These words are understood to be added for demonstration, or for understanding: not for restriction, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda rerum dominia*, law *Insula*, at the end, where it says, "but so that the thing might be more easily understood, you called that field, which had been an island, an island." There are certain things which are now, which were not previously; and to these things a privilege can undoubtedly be granted, as is fully read and noted by Cynus in the Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, law *Placet*, in the penultimate and ultimate questions. But there are certain things which neither were nor are in nature, but the disposer believed them to be; and to these, if there is no hope for the future, a privilege cannot be granted: as in the Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Si mihi Mevii*; for where there is no substance, there cannot be quality. For quality is to be inherent: as in law 2, Digest, *De usufructu*. But if there is hope for the future, a future privilege can well be granted: as in the aforementioned law *Si servitus*, section *Futuro*.

Now let us see in which case our question stands. And the whole question rests on that word, *constructa*; because this chapel was not constructed from the beginning under that name; but I say that it suffices that it is found to be constructed under that name at the time the privilege was given; because the time of the grant is considered, as in the Extravagantes, *De rescriptis*, chapter *Cum te*. And a hospital is said to be constructed, for example under the name of Saint Anthony, although from the beginning it was a profane house, if however the house was reduced to a hospital, as in the Authenticum, *De ecclesiasticis titulis*, section *Si quis in nomine*. For the imposition of a new name makes the construction under that name. Hence, it refers to the beginning of the name that the word *constructa* is verified. And for this I give almost a case of law,

† For if a testator bequeaths to his wife purchased and ready-made items, even those subsequently purchased and prepared fall under the legacy, as stated in the Digest, *De legatis* 2, *Si quid earum*, in the beginning. Another law states that if a testator bequeaths Agatea, and that slave had been alienated, and later another was purchased, to whom the name Agatea was given, this new Agatea is included in the testamentary disposition, although she was not previously so called, as stated in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, *Filiae*, § *A Titia*. Thus I say in the present case that the chapel, which shines with a glorious name, and which bore that name at the time of the grant, was in existence; and in that same chapel is held the privilege of indulgence, because the words of the privilege signify it.

And because they cannot signify anything else, the words ought rightly to be interpreted in such a way that so pious and so fruitful a disposition may be valid and not vitiated, as is argued from the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *In testamento*; and from the Digest, *De fundo instructo*, law *Fundus, qui locatus*; and the Pope would have declared and granted the same, if he had known, as is stated in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Tale pactum*, section *Si*. From which it is evidently concluded, according to what is proposed, that the said indulgence pertains to, or is due to, the said chapel. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A judgment rendered abruptly, without any facts proven, and without any delays being set, is void and deserves no execution.
2. It is presumed in favor of the arbitration, just as in favor of the judge’s sentence.
3. How a negative, which consists in writing, is to be proven.
4. It is presumed in favor of the arbitrator.
5. The term of the litigation is considered as the term assigned to each party.
6. A judgment rendered abruptly, without any facts or proofs, and without any terms being set, is void.
7. For what purpose negative propositions are made, and how one ought to respond to them.
body:
By the statute of Pavia, chapter In the name of Christ: whoever wishes to state or allege that the precepts, awards, or arbitral decisions of an arbitrator or arbitrators are inequitable or unjust, must within thirty useful days from the date of the precepts, awards, or arbitral decisions, and from knowledge thereof, state and demonstrate this, both by way of action and by way of exception, regarding the grievance and inequity, and concerning all his rights; and in this case, proceedings may be conducted extra ordinem, even without observing any legal or statutory solemnity. Once this term has elapsed, execution must be carried out by the judge regarding the said precepts, awards, or arbitral decisions, unless it has been shown within the said thirty useful days that there is a grievance and inequity in them.

Now, an arbitrator and umpire condemned the defendant to a certain, not inconsiderable sum without any proof. This arbitral decision was sought to be reduced to the award of a good man, and no other term being given by the judge for proving, and nothing further being said or done by either party, the useful month has elapsed. Execution of the arbitrator’s award and arbitral decision is sought, because this recourse is said to have been abandoned.

Conversely, it is objected that since nothing lies upon the one seeking reduction to prove, it is understood by that very fact to be proven: that the contrary is not proven. For every condemnatory sentence is presumed to have been rendered against the law when no facts have been proven.
† Now the question arises, what is the law? And it appears that the aforementioned sentence should be executed for three reasons.

First, because it is presumed to be a definitive arbitral award, just as a judge’s sentence is, as noted by Dynus in the counsel beginning “Tholomeus manentis.” Second, because the statute assigns a term of thirty useful days for proof, within which term the party seeking reduction should at least have produced the articles of charge and caused the acts to be shown by the notary of the case to the judge of this quasi-appeal.

† For thus is the negative proved, which consists in writing, namely by the collation of the acts, as in C. si certum petatur, l. fin. and in l. 1, C. de exactionibus tributorum, lib. 10, and ff. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum, § pro Aurelio, and C. de probationibus, l. ad probationem. If, therefore, the one seeking reduction has not done this, let him impute it to himself; because the term of a month, after which no other is expected, is precisely peremptory, nay, even fatal, as in C. de temporibus appellationum, Auth. ei qui. The third reason is, because the statute so provides, when it says that after the lapse of the said month execution shall take place, unless it has been shown that the sentence is unjust and inequitable; but here nothing was said about injustice or inequity, as it ought to have been shown:

† because, as I have said, it is presumed to be at one’s discretion: as noted by Cynus, C. de epis. aud. l. si qui ex consensu. Moreover, this statutory term runs, even if the judge does not assign a term: because Bartolus says that the time of the litigation is considered as the term for proving and producing evidence, as noted by Bartolus, ff. de arbi. l. si de meis. §. fin.

And I say that the term assigned to each party for proving, as far as incumbent upon them, is considered fixed, unless someone argues that this is false because the defendant may prove after the term; and therefore this term is not peremptory for the defendant, but for the plaintiff, as in C. de tempore in integrum restitutionis, l. petendae. To the contrary it seems, because in a condemnatory sentence a cause is required, just as in a contract of promise, as noted in C. de iudiciis, l. properandum, §. illo, and ff. de his qui non infamiantur, l. 2, §. ignominiae; but here no cause was inserted in the condemnation. Moreover, a sentence rendered without any facts being proved, nor with dilations for proving set by the judge or arbitrator, is void by operation of law. And it is noted in extra de constitutionibus, in c. Ecclesia Sanctae Mariae, secunda quaestio, 1, cap. Nos in quemquam, and C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus, l. Inter prolatam. Someone might say that an arbitrator is not bound by necessity to assign any dilation, as noted by Innocentius de iureiurando, ca. Quintavallis, especially because from the form of the compromise he has free power, argumentum ff. de legatis 3, l. Fideicommissa, §. Quamquam. But certainly when he proceeds by condemning and not by compromising, he is not properly an arbitrator, but rather one declaring the law. And although he has full authority, nevertheless he must pronounce according to good faith, as in ff. mandati, l. Creditor, §. Lucius, in fine.

† It is established, however, that to pronounce judgment abruptly is not to pronounce judgment in good faith, as stated in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum his*, section *Si praetor*. Furthermore, common matters cannot be presumed to have been solemnly acted upon when nothing has been acted upon, as stated in the Code, *De sententiis ex peritorum recitandis*, law *Secunda*. Moreover, it must be considered that the period of thirty days is a useful period; but a useful period does not run during negative proof, because by the nature of things one is deemed to prove, and appears to prove, by the very fact that the contrary is not proved, as noted in the Digest, *De probationibus*, law *Verius*. Certainly, the nullity of this arbitration appears without any other proof; therefore, its execution ought not to take place, as is fully noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Quarta*, section *Si ex conventione*.

I also say that negative positions are made for caution, not out of necessity: and they are not properly positions, because nothing is posited; and therefore one ought not to answer them as positions, but as interrogations, as noted in c. 1, de confessis, lib. 6, unless the negation contained an implicit affirmation, as in Extra, de fidei instrumentis, c. Cum Ioannes heremita. From which it is concluded that whether this case is appealable or not, no proof lies upon him who denies that he is bound; because neither the ordinance of man nor the ordinance of law so provides. D. de appellationibus, l. Hi qui ad civilia, and l. Cives et incolae, and there fully by other doctors and by me. And because if nothing is proved against you, I do not condemn you. C. de edendo, l. Qui accusare, and see Innocentius in c. Solet, in fine, de sententia excommunicationis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the husband, or his heirs, can recover from the wife expenses incurred and improvements made to the dotal fief. And no. 4.
2. A donation between husband and wife is not confirmed by death, unless delivery, or quasi-delivery, has intervened.
3. What a donation is.
body: In the name of Christ. Dotally to a certain...

† A husband granted an estate in emphyteusis to Titius, with this pact expressly added, that upon dissolution of the marriage it should be restored to the woman with all improvements that might be made by the emphyteuta, for which the woman should not be held liable in any way, but the husband himself. It is asked whether, upon dissolution of the marriage and restitution of the emphyteusis to the woman, the husband is held liable for the said improvements, or the woman, or the heir of the husband, or neither, or both? And it seems that one must stand by the contract, and one must not depart from its terms, as in ff. de pac. l. 1. §. 1, C. de iure emphy. l. 2, and ff. depositi l. 1. §. si conuenerit. Nor let anyone say that through that pact nothing is acquired for the woman because no one can contract for another unless the other is present, as in ff. de ver. obli. l. stipulatio ista. §. alteri and l. si procuratori pręsen.; because the statute of the place provides that one person may acquire through another. And a statute can dispose this, just as the ius commune disposes in many cases, and especially in a dotal matter, as in ff. solu. mat. l. Caius, as if it were added to the property of the woman herself while it lasts, as in C. de iure do. l. in rebus, ff. depositi l. publia in prin., l. 1 C. de dona. quae sub modo, and ff. de pac. l. in traditionibus. Also because the said pact seems to have been added for the purpose of releasing, from which an exception of fraud (exceptio doli) is acquired, as noted in ff. de libera. l. non solum. §. si liberaturis and ff. de pac. l. rescriptum. §. fi. And on the other hand, it seems that that pact was not valid, because the effect of that pact is a donation made between husband and wife; for since the wife derives a gain from that pact out of the husband's liberality, it follows of necessity that it is a donation, as in ff. de dona. l. hoc iure.

† And a donation between husband and wife is not permitted, nor is it confirmed by the death of the donor unless it was supported by delivery or quasi-delivery, as in ff. de don. inter vir. et vxo. l. Papinianus, and as noted in l. 1 C. de dona. ante nuptias and C. de dote cauta non numerata l. quod de suo. And it is confirmed that this is an intervention (intercessio) of the husband made for a debt on behalf of the wife with the intention of not claiming it back, as in ff. de pac. l. fideiussoris and ff. de usufructu earum rerum, quae vsu consumuntur l. tribus; for had it not been for that pact, the woman was bound to refund the expenses, and having been released gratuitously from this debt, it is said to be donated to her;

† because a donation is a gratuitous agreement regarding any thing whatsoever when no other remedy remains, as in ff. de nouationibus l. si quis delegauerit. I say this on account of a pledge, the renunciation of which is not a donation, as in C. ad vel. l. iubemus and ff. quae in frau. credito. l. si pignus, because the debtor still remains obligated by an action or personal remedy.

† Someone will say, no donation is involved between the emphyteuta and the husband, as in ff. de donatio. l. vt mihi donares. Solution: I concede this; nevertheless, a donation results between husband and wife; whence the husband who paid for the benefit of the wife recovers from her because she was made richer, as in ff. de dona. inter virum, et vxorem l. vxor marito. And I believe this to be true, nor do I find that the instrument says the contrary, namely, that the husband cannot recover from the wife insofar as he paid for her out of his own pocket. Item, one is also said to intervene for someone who is not obligated if the ground of the debt begins from the one who did not bind himself, just as if he had bound himself, even though when he did not bind himself the result—that is, the obligation—is not upon him, as in ff. de dolo l. eleganter. §. seruus pactionis. Wherefore that which was turned to her benefit can be recovered from the woman, even if through an unjust arbitral award rendered upon this matter between others it does not remain turned to her benefit, as in ff. quod met. causa l. quod diximus and by the argument of ff. ad treb. l. debitor. §. fi., unless that loss had been inflicted upon the woman through the fraud of the husband seeking back those expenses, because the husband had brought the case to this unjust arbitration, by the argument of ff. de arbitris l. inter castellianum, and the enacted law 2, C. si mater indemnitatem promiserit. It is no objection if it is said that the expense was incurred with the intention of not seeking it back, because here, by an express pact, recovery was granted against one party, since they are conventional expenses in which the husband obligated himself for the advantage of the wife, as the emphyteuta would not have contracted otherwise. And in this way answer is made to the law in hoc iudicio, ff. communi diuidun., along with its subject matter, and relevant to the aforesaid are ff. de nego. gest. l. siue haereditaria and l. sed an vltro. §. 1. Therefore, conclusion is made on behalf of the heir of the husband against the woman that she is held liable, because she was enriched from that donation, from which no actual or fictitious delivery followed between husband and wife. But against this it seems: because by paying for her, he is feigned to have paid and she to have delivered to the creditor; therefore, it is confirmed by death. Solution: here he did not pay, but promised, and remained solely within the limits of a promise. Item, if not the husband, but his heir had paid, that delivery by the heir would not confirm the delivery of the deceased, which was also rendered void by the death of the donor. The same conversely if the husband had paid when the woman was already dead, for the same reason, ff. de reb. dubiis l. si inter uir. et vxorem. All the above having been set aside, it must be considered that an emphyteusis is a kind of lease, as in the Institutes locati §. adeo. But if the husband leases the dotal land, he is bound to observe the pacts, even if by a certain consequence they tend in favor of the wife, as noted in l. diuortio in prin., ff. solu. mat. Item, if the husband mandates anyone to incur an expense on the dotal property, he is liable under the action on mandate, as if conducting his own business, because the dowry is in his estate; and that mandate can be said to be for his own sake and for that of another, as in l. 1, ff. mandati. Nevertheless, if the expense was for the perpetual utility of the property, upon dissolution of the marriage the husband would recover from the wife just as if he had incurred the expense by himself, because he who acts through another is deemed to act by himself; and the woman is held liable at least to the extent that she was made richer, because the husband by managing the business acts for the wife, and the wife for herself, as in C. de neg. gest. l. quod in uxorem. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether prescription runs against the right of offering. And whether. 7.
2. Whether prescription runs against conditions.
3. Whether prescription runs against a potestative condition.
4. Whether prescription runs against a resolutory condition.
5. Whether prescription runs against emancipated sons for claiming the benefit of the portion.
6. Whether a patron may prescribe against a freedman.
8. Whether prescription may run against a future pledge action. 9. Whether a creditor who lost possession and later recovered it is bound to restore it.
body: The question is asked whether a creditor...

† Concerning that which is asked, whether a creditor possessing a hypothec for an extremely long time can prescribe against the right of tendering, which belongs to a debtor wishing to sue by the action on pledge (actio pignoratitia). The question is an ancient one, and it is seen that he can prescribe, because every right is prescriptible with respect to an exception; but that is a right, and is called a right, and is the right of tendering: therefore it is prescriptible by the longest time. This is stated by the text of C. de praescrip. 30. anno. l. cum notissimi. §. Sed cum illud. And this is a negative prescription, namely that tender cannot be made, and prescription does not run against the action on pledge, because it has not accrued, but it indeed runs against its accrual, lest it be able to accrue; and thus the creditor will retain the pledge for the unpaid debt, and one that cannot even be paid against the creditor's will; nor nevertheless will he become the owner of the thing, because no one ever becomes owner through prescription unless he possessed under title 'as his own' (pro suo) or quasi. But a creditor does not possess pro suo, nor quasi pro sua, as in ff. qui satisda. cogan. l. sciendum. §. creditor; whence he does not prescribe ownership. Nevertheless, he well prescribes against the right of tendering, as has been said. This is confirmed by the gl. on the said §. sed cum illud, and ff. de usuca. l. pignori, and ff. de pign. actione. l. si rem. §. omnis. Furthermore, it is explicitly stated that the right of tendering can be prescribed against, ff. de captiuis, et postliminio reuersis. l. in bello. §. si quis seruum; this is also confirmed by gl. ff. de usucap. l. pignori. But almost all the moderns are to the contrary, saying that either the right of tendering concerns an accrued action, and prescription can run against it—as for example, a second creditor has the right of tendering to a prior creditor in order to prefer or confirm his own already accrued hypothecary action, as in the said §. sed cum illud—or it concerns an action that has not accrued, but depends on the tacit condition of tendering; and then it cannot be prescribed against, as when a debtor wishes to tender to a creditor so that a hypothecary action may accrue to him, for in the meantime there is no formed right; and all prescriptions require some formed right, and the reason is because prescriptions are exceptions, and there is no exception prior to an action. Likewise, privation is not prior to possession (habitus), as in ff. de uerb. obli. l. decem.

† And therefore conditions shall not be prescribed against, but actions. And this is also the reason, because conditions operate in the manner of a certain capacity of fact (facultas facti), and prescription does not run against these capacities: argument from ff. de uia publica l. uiam publicam. Bartolus holds this opinion in the said l. pignori, adding such a reason beyond the other doctors: because a son can be instituted under a potestative condition of giving, if it is a slight condition, as in ff. de haere. insti. l. si ius. §. puto, and noted by Cynthius C. de insti. et substi. l. si pater; and the law says that a son can fulfill it up to the last breath of his life, as in ff. de conditionibus institutionum. l. fi. And then Bartolus argues: if it could be prescribed against, therefore after forty years the son would be found to have been passed over (praeteritus), and as one passed over he would break the testament; which is false.

† He therefore concludes that the prescription of time cannot be raised against a potestative condition, which is in accord with the common rule: for prescription does not run against one impeded from suing, as in C. de annali pręscriptione. l. 1. §. fi. But certainly it could be answered: because it is true if the removal of the impediment is in his power; for then prescription does indeed run.

† Whence prescription runs against a rescissory action that has not yet accrued: because it was in his power to make it accrue by seeking restitution in integrum and obtaining it through victory, as is noted in C. ex quibus causis maiores. l. fi. To this pertains extra de elec. c. eis quibus, and ff. quibus ex causis maiores. l. sed et si per prętotem. §. 2.

† Likewise, the annual prescription runs against an emancipated son for seeking possession of goods under the interdict unde liberi, and yet under the ancient law he cannot seek it prior thereto, unless he first seeks possession of goods for the sake of acknowledging the suit, as in C. de inoffi. testa. l. 2.

† Likewise, a patron prescribes against a freedman, although the freedman cannot sue except after seeking leave (venia). Furthermore, it is explicit that a potestative condition is prescribed by default (mora) of non-fulfillment, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. hęc conditio, scilicet in legacies and fideicommissa, not in the institution of heirs, unless perhaps the institution of an heir is resolved into a legacy, as when someone is instituted in a specific thing, a universal co-heir having been appointed, as in ff. de hęredibus insti. l. si quis instituatur, and C. eo. ti. l. quotiens. He concludes, therefore, that he who was negligent is prejudiced by the lapse of time, and in fulfilling conditions; whence Bartolus's reasoning does not well prove that for which he adduces it, although he speaks subtly.

† But I say through other, new reasons that a creditor who possesses a pledge does not prescribe against the right of tendering: because he cannot prescribe against the right of setting off the debt through the gathering of fruits, as in ff. de solutionibus. l. titia. And when the debt has been diminished, subsequent fruits become stolen, as in ff. si cer. pet. l. si quis nec causam. §. res pignori, and ff. de furtis. l. si quis uxori. §. eum creditorem; and the right of tendering cannot be prescribed against. Likewise, by another reason: because a creditor who gathers fruits acknowledges himself to be a creditor, and moreover himself to be a debtor with respect to the action on pledge; therefore his prescription is interrupted daily, as in C. de pręscrip. 30. anno. l. cum notissimi. §. 1. Likewise, by gathering fruits the debtor tacitly tenders to him, and he accepts, and acknowledges holding from him. Likewise, he cannot change the cause of his possession for himself. Likewise, he does not possess [civilly], therefore he does not prescribe. Likewise, to what purpose would he prescribe against the right of tendering, if he could not gather fruits from another's property without the taint of theft? And every prescription presupposes some end toward which it is ordered, and such an end as obtains legal effect; but here there would be no such end. Furthermore, through this prescription an opportunity for wrongdoing and for detaining another's property while it remains another's, against the will of the owner, contrary to natural law, would be given. But a sufficiently strong reason militates in favor of the gloss's opinion: for the debtor can invoke the office of the judge so that the creditor may be precisely compelled to receive the debt and make a receipt or written instrument for the debtor, as in C. de fi. instru. l. plures apocis publicas. l. 1. lib. 10. ff. de lega. 3. l. 11. §. si rem. For this harms him in nothing, and benefits the debtor, ff. sol. mat. l. 2. §. nec cogitur, C. de liberali causa. l. sicut datum; therefore, prescription runs against this office of the judge, as in C. de pręscri. 30. anno. l. sicut. Furthermore, when the debt has been extinguished, prescription of the thing can begin, and not only the thing may be prescribed, but also against the action on pledge, which is already then accrued: as in the said l. sicut, and what is noted in l. 1. C. de annali exceptione.

† I hold that in the meantime prescription cannot run against the future action on pledge; the argument from de offi. iudicis. l. quia nullę does not stand in the way. The law says this, but only speaks of the right of tendering and depositing, as in C. de vsuris. l. acceptam, and C. de solutionibus. l. oblignationem; and it is noted that the glosses inquired concerning the right of tendering, yet similarly they ought to have inquired concerning the right of depositing and consigning.

† Secondly it is asked: if a creditor lost possession through the violence of a third-party intruder, and afterward the intruder, doing a favor to the creditor, restored it, whether the creditor is bound to restore; and it must be said that yes. For the question is whether he is discharged if he recovers, as in ff. de rei uend. l. nisi malit, with l. si uero. §. Iulia, where it is explicit that he is also bound to give security to restore in the event that he regains the power to restore. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the articles of peace, or of a league, or of a confederation are to be interpreted.
2. In contracts of good faith, unforeseen cases of law are included; otherwise in contracts of strict law.
3. What truth is.
4. Contracts by agreement may receive an accidental form.
5. What interest is.
body: In Christ’s name.

† The chapters of this league must be examined one by one, and a suitable interpretation must be applied, which is always inherent by necessity, by verisimilitude, or from the nature of the matter itself, as in ff. de pac. dotalibus l. inter socerum § cum inter patrem; ff. de verbo. ob. l. igitur ita stipulatus and l. forte; ff. pro socio l. si socius pro filia; and that is deemed to be in the minds of the contracting parties which is beneficial to both parties and burdensome to neither, ff. si quis cautionibus l. 1; ff. de solutionibus l. cum stichus; for ease of fulfillment provides an incentive for contracting, especially when a partnership is contracted by law, so that we look not to what is expedient for this one or that one, but to what is useful to the partnership itself, ff. pro socio l. cum duobus; and toward those things which are easier regarding the manner of performance are the minds of wise men directed, as in ff. de neg. gest. l. diuortio; for since man by nature is a rational animal, he is presumed to be endowed with several rational faculties and a friend of reason itself, ff. de conditionibus institutionum l. filius; and although the letter can sometimes lend itself to several interpretive forms, nevertheless that one must be observed which contains the most humanity and which natural discernment—which is greater than every virtue—suggests to us; and thus mute reason speaks in our hearts, and regulates and governs conditions, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. in cond. primum locum and l. pater Seuerinam § conditionum. Therefore, the best interpreter of pacts is utility and the final cause: because everything that moves naturally tends toward the good, which all seek, as is clear in many principles of the philosophers; nor can there be received in the nature of things a greater light than the light of the intellect. These premises having thus been set forth by way of preface, where the text of the words is clear, we need not labor; but where it is confused or general—because generality breeds obscurity—obscurity must be shunned like a mist before the eyes of our intellect, since light dwells in clarity, not in obscurity. Let us leave these generalities and come to the facts, and what is contained in the first chapter: between whom the league was made and for what purpose, because it was principally for the purpose of defense, but incidentally also by way of offense; and because one cannot be separated from the other, the whole is understood to be permitted, even by divine law, ff. de iusti. et iu. l. ut uim; ff. ad l. Aqui. l. scientiam § qui cum aliter, and l. si ex plagiis § tabernarius; C. vnde vi l. 1; and in clemen. vltima de homicidio; and since the work is lawful, one may associate allies with oneself, as noted in l. culpa est, ff. de re. iur. But it must be noted that the words speak of all those troops whom the said allies are able to keep at their stipend. For this word 'they are able' [possunt] signifies moderation and the judgment of a good man, ff. de verbo. sign. l. nepos proculo; and the expense must be adapted to the emerging necessity, as in ff. de exercitoria l. Luc.; nor indeed ought one to feign necessity, but rather enter into expenses according to the quality of the impending causes: for in a small necessity one ought to expend less, in a great necessity more, argument in l. 1, ff. de alimentis pupillorum. There follows another chapter, which begins, 'Likewise if it should happen' [Item si contingat], in which it is provided that the allies are either attacked at the same time or not at the same time. In the first case, aid must be sent to the needy one; in the second case, to the one attacked, according to the exigency of the necessity; this is a good and equitable chapter, because nature imitates nature: it transmits aid to the sick member, and where it hastens more, there is the danger. Likewise, it hastens more to save a ship than that it perish, and so much more to save men than to save merchandise or animals, as in ff. ad l. Rhodiam de iactu l. nauis onustę. Now follows another chapter, in which Andreas is joined to the other allies and is further specified in several matters, concerning all of which four main doubts principally turn: first, concerning the stipends; second, concerning the damages; third, concerning the promises; fourth, concerning the crossbowmen; about which let us see in order. And I begin at: 'After an interval, etc.' [postquam per interuallum etc.], in which chapter it is contained that the noble man Andreas of Montefauo was received with the first general pacts, and with certain new, special, and specific pacts, it is valid, etc.; and as an introduction to the said pacts, as if to their final and substantial matter—because a substantial form cannot be found except in pre-existing matter, which is sometimes natural, sometimes of the final cause, sometimes contractual, sometimes intellectual. It must be premised that in general chapters we follow the nature of generality; in special and specific ones we follow the nature of speciality, as in ff. de annuis lega. l. seio § medico; nor ought we to depart from specified words because of the difficulty of the promisor, provided that what was promised can be fulfilled by someone else, as in ff. de verbo. ob. l. continuus § illud; ff. si cer. pet. l. quod te; ff. locati l. in naue saufelii; ff. de publicianis l. cęsar. And this therefore is the theoretical disjunction of the articles of the aforesaid questions, which must be distinguished and each adapted to each. Now, some promises are made in a determinate manner, the limits of which must be precisely observed, or at least satisfaction must be made for the interesse, because he who does not observe his promises is not a good man. Nay rather, to breach faith is serious for serious men, more serious for more serious men, and most serious for the most serious and exemplary men, because it is evil in itself and a bad example set externally, as in ff. de constituta pecu. l. i in princip.; nay rather, a good example arising from renowned men is more beneficial to the common people than the substance of a good thing from unknown men; and if it be asked what the substance of a good thing is, I say: that you do not do to another what you would not wish done to yourself, etc., for this is the law and the prophets, as in prin. decretorum; and if the mind of man is compared to that mirror, the key of intellect not erring through the consolidation of the scriptures, the soul is rendered very safe: because if you bear the faith of an innocent man, you have the greatest security; indeed, great security is given by excuse, for 'blessed are they whose sins are forgiven,' great by innocence, but the greatest by an eager conscience, as in C. de iniuriis l. si non conuitii; C. de his, quibus vt indignis l. cum fratrem. Someone may say: therefore in bonae fidei and stricti iuris contracts there ought to be no difference, because bad faith has been cast out from all acts, while good faith is approved in all, as in C. de act. et obli. l. bonam fidem. The solution is: rather, there is indeed a difference, because the laws have established that in bonae fidei contracts unforeseen cases are brought within the limits of the foreseen cases,

† but stricti iuris contracts do not concern unforeseen cases, as in ff. de ne. ge. l. quia tantundem; ff. de eo, quod certo loco l. 3 § Iuli. Nevertheless, in all contracts good faith—that is, a good mind—is looked to, although sometimes fatal impossibility excuses from a penalty, though I do not say from the principal sum, as noted by Inno. in c. 1, extra de offi. dele.; naturally fortuitous events prevent things that are yet to be contracted, but they do not dissolve what has already been contracted in fact and by obligation, as in ff. ad l. Rhodiam de iactu l. sunt vehenda § idem iuris; for that which is perfected and has passed into the bonds of law does not yield to an imperfect event, and although this defense cannot accomplish more, as in ff. de procuratoribus l. Tit., because eyes cannot be plucked from a blind man, as in ff. de dolo l. nam his; nevertheless that is not properly to enter an exception, but to avoid compulsion, as in C. qui bonis cedere possunt l. fina.; and then this allegation turns into the nature of a cession of goods, so that he who alleges this must hand over his goods to his creditors, as if he expressly said, 'I surrender my goods' [cedo bonis]; otherwise such an allegation that one is unable is neither truthful nor lawful, since the retention of goods implies contradictions, namely that one has them and is unable; and a liar to himself can tell the truth to no one: because false imprudence, always in error, cannot change the dignity and high nature of truth, as noted in ff. de neg. ge. l. sed an vltro § fi.

† For truth is nothing other than the very constancy and firmness of things, as noted in ff. de aqua plu. arcen.; and this is the base and foundation of justice, than which virtue none is more renowned; whence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: 'Before all things let a true word go before you,' namely from the heart, from the tongue, and from the fruit of the deed; and whoever has resolved in his mind not to keep faith is immediately a liar.
