Furthermore, although all these contracts can be called bonae fidei on account of the nature of partnership, which demands good faith in the highest degree, even without formal demand [interpellatio]—or say, as I will state below, which is scarcely found in other contracts except where mora is incurred—nevertheless in general contracts, by an express pact to maintain good faith and repel malice, all contracts of the world can be reduced to the likeness and resemblance of those which by nature are bonae fidei contracts, ar. ff. de pac. l. non impossibile; and conversely, contracts which by nature are bonae fidei can, by an express pact, be reduced to the likeness of stricti iuris, if it is agreed that nothing can be added or taken away except what the writing states, argu. ff. de vsufr. lega. l. si alij; C. de fi. instru. l. contractus. Furthermore, strict law consists in precisely observing the words and the writing, whereas broad law consists in supplementation, as noted in ff. de condi. inde. and ff. de triticar. l. in hac; it clearly appears,

† that by an express pact contracts can receive an accidental form, that is, one which does not originally adhere to its own subject; but natural forms cohere unless they have been removed by pact, ff. de contrah. emp. l. pacta conuenta. Natural things cohere naturally; but accidental things, unless expressed, we believe not to be present. We must return to the matter at hand, because it is better to take up one thing than a hundred. I ask whether the act of arguing is among an infinite number of people, the conclusion of responding, and the medicine of healing among few. And I come to the said clause, 'that the said allies during the said time and in time of peace, etc.' And concerning that chapter, what it is and what it says, it is not easy to say, but what the word sounds, that shall be done, ff. iudicatum solui l. iudicatum; nor do we indulge the Gloss where we have the text, ff. de leg. 3 l. ille aut ille § cum in verbis. There follows another chapter, which begins: 'If however it should happen that the said allies and the said Andreas have war with anyone bordering upon or neighboring the said Andreas and/or his territory, or someone who makes manifest war against the said Andreas, not meaning the allied troops, then during the said war the said allies are bound to pay to the said Andreas by way of provision 100 gold florins monthly'; and this chapter seems doubtful, because war was not waged against all the said confederates, but against the said neighboring Andreas and against the commune of Macerata, and therefore the common copula, which arises from a coupled plural number and from the word 'or' [seu], does not seem to have a place in a divided sense, namely when the others would not have war, but Andreas alone; because the nature of the copulative is to require both parts to be true, as in ff. de conditionibus institutionum l. si hęredi plures; but I say the contrary, because a war is common to all partisans and those who assist one another in an act of war, as in extra de postulatione praelatorum c. j. Whence the copula of war applies very well between Andreas and his partisans, as in ff. de arbitris l. cum pęna; whence I conclude that the said 100 florins are owed each month during the aforesaid war. And the same applies to the crossbowmen after formal request; because since this subvention is a kind of service [obsequium], it is not owed except to the one requesting it, just as we have said in the case of vassals. Likewise I say that after formal request, and not before, the interesse is due, which is the restoration of damage.

† For so is interesse defined: the restoration of emerging damage and the replenishment of lost profit; and so forth, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo quod interest l. vnica. To this the commune of Macerata is bound from the nature and form of the partnership, as in ff. pro soc. l. de illo; and because it was so promised, let good faith therefore be observed, that is, without cavillations, as in ff. de verbo. signi. l. est natura cauillationis; and l. pe. ff. ad exhibendum. Bart. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a judgment rendered on an abandoned appeal is to be called definitive or interlocutory. Likewise, generally, which judgments are definitive and which are interlocutory.
body: In the name of Christ.

† Upon the question of whether a sentence whereby it is pronounced that an appeal is deserted, or that a reduction to the arbitrament of a good man, or an action of nullity has been extinguished by the running of the fatal period established by municipal law or by any express or tacit renunciation, is interlocutory or definitive: It would seem to be argued that it is definitive. And this, first, arguing from the general meaning: because it puts an end to the litigation; for it matters not in what words it is delivered, since by whatever words it is entirely terminated, that sentence is properly definitive, and not improper—indeed, most proper—because the definition and the thing defined coincide, as noted in l. omnis diffinitio, ff. de re iud. Likewise, by the argument from effect: because everything is said to be of such nature as is discerned from its effect, ff. de iureiu. l. sed et si possessori, § sed si rerum; ff. de verb. obl. l. 2, § quędam partis, and l. in executione, § pro parte, and l. stipulationes non diuiduntur; indeed, nature yields to effect, and the effect by its predominance unites the nature, as in ff. de postulando l. 1, § bestias, and Instituta de rerum diui. § pauonum. But no one doubts that a sentence declaring an appeal deserted puts an end to the whole lawsuit; and to put an end to and to finish are the same thing. And as has been said, we do not care about the terms, provided the words are equivalent, as is noted in C. de senten. et interlocutionibus l. praeses, and ff. de arbit. l. quid tamen, § Pompo.; for these are not sublime expressions to which one must adhere in the Judaic and Hebrew manner, by the argument in C. de testamentis l. quoniam indignum. Furthermore, that sentence is definitive which has the attributes of a definitive sentence: for example, that it passes into the authority of res judicata; likewise, that the exception of res judicata arises from it, as noted in C. de arbitr. l. prima, and ff. eodem l. 2; likewise, that it is ordered into execution, as noted in C. de appellationibus l. eos, in principio; likewise, that it cannot be delivered against an undefended minor, against whom regularly any interlocutory sentence may be made provided he is lawfully cited, ff. de minorib. l. minor, even if he is quasi-contumacious; but it is certain that an undefended minor does not suffer a sentence of deserted appeal, and the Gloss expressly concludes that it is definitive, C. quomodo, et quando iudex l. si pręses quasi desertam; Jacobus Butrigarius also holds the same there. Likewise, it is assimilated to a definitive sentence in more respects than to an interlocutory one, and thus one looks to that wherein the greater similitude is found, as in ff. de statu hominum l. Quęritur. To the contrary is truth itself, namely that it is interlocutory by natural reason and effect, although it has proximity and affinity to a definitive sentence; and this is proved by its contrary, namely that an appeal is not deserted, which is interlocutory, therefore by conversion the same holds. Upon this reasoning Johannes Andreae grounds himself in ca. fi. de appellationibus in Clementinis. Furthermore, it is not delivered upon the principal cause, but upon the proceedings. Likewise, it is delivered upon an emergent matter. Likewise, it is sometimes delivered solely by the running of the fatal period, and it is rather the period itself that pronounces than the judge, ff. de excusationibus tutorum l. scire oportet, § consequens. Likewise, a sentence upon the instance is interlocutory, C. de iudiciis l. properandum, in fine. Likewise, from this sentence an actio in factum does not arise, ff. de infamibus l. furti, § primo; therefore it does not have those attributes of definitive sentences, just as if the judge were to pronounce that no appeal was made within ten days. Likewise, a vivid reason is that it is delivered separately from the principal cause, ff. de minoribus l. intra vtile. Likewise, it is pronounced without the causes of the cause being discussed; for it is not necessary to discuss the obligation, but the judgment, because the truth of the obligation is of no benefit to the deserter once the process does not support him, as in C. de fideicommissariis libertatibus l. fi.; for he who wishes to fly to the sentence bypassing the process wishes to fly without feathers and allegations, and dashing against the ground breaks his legs. From these things it is expressly concluded that the said sentence is interlocutory; yet because it is of great prejudice, one can appeal from it as from a grievance of the judge, nor can this reporting be justified even from witnesses received afterward, because a judge is not said to have aggrieved if he could not have had cognizance of the grievance, as in capitulo appellant, de appellationibus in Cleme., and as noted by Bartolus in ff. de minoribus l. ait prętor, § permittitur; nor are new allegations of law necessary, and concerning law which needs no other proof other than that the text of the law be seen always and everywhere. Nor does it stand in the way of the aforesaid that it terminates the suit, for a sentence rendered upon a peremptory exception nevertheless perpetually prejudices, as in C. ad l. Fabiam de plagiariis l. pręses; Jacobus Butrigarius delivered this theory to us in the question of Ranaxense. CASE. The words of the privilege state: 'To the said Thomas and to his heirs and successors, male and female, we give, concede, and confer by our own motion, graciously, out of the imperial plenitude of power, and from certain knowledge, the places, castles, and other things noted below, with all and singular honors, mere and mixed imperium, power of the sword, jurisdictions, ranks, vassals, etc., and all rights whatsoever by whatever name they may be designated, with all honors, appurtenances, and profits in any way belonging to the said places and castles and to the Holy Roman Empire in any manner whatsoever. The names of which places and castles are these, namely Ritortum and Saluanum, as well as the mere and mixed imperium, the power of the sword, all manner of jurisdiction, and the right of imposing tallages and any exactions whatsoever, and all rights and usufructs whatsoever belonging to us and to the Roman Empire itself in the said places and castles, from certain knowledge, out of the imperial plenitude of power, and by special grace, we irrevocably give and transfer both to the present Marquis and to his aforesaid heirs and successors; and in the aforesaid and each of the aforesaid we will that he and his heirs and successors, as above, be and hold in our place: giving and granting by special grace and out of the plenitude of our power to the said Marquis and to his heirs and successors, as above, license, power, and authority to enter and take in any manner whatsoever and at any time the tenure and bodily possession and quasi-possession of all and singular the things given and transferred, as above, without the requisition and authority of any superior president, governor, judge, or any magistrate whatsoever, at the entire free will of the said Marquis, his heirs, and successors; notwithstanding in the aforesaid and each of the aforesaid any rights, customs, graces, privileges, investitures, concessions, and confirmations, letters, or rescripts, general or special, made or to be made, conceded, or granting in the contrary to any city, commune, or private person, even if special mention would have to be made of them or any one of them by law. All of which, insofar as they may conflict with our present concession and transfer in whole or in part, we derogate from the said plenitude of power and from certain knowledge by the tenor of the present letters, etc., also supplying by the tenor of the present letters, of our own motion and out of the imperial plenitude of power, every defect in solemnity or otherwise, if any should have perhaps occurred in any way in this transfer, donation, and concession, saving the superior dominion which belongs to us and to the Holy Empire over the aforesaid Marquis, his heirs, and successors.' Afterwards, upon the death of the said late Thomas, and of Isnardus, late son of the said Thomas, to the son of the said late Isnardus, Marquis Malaspina, the Emperor granted in 1382 a certain privilege, in which the aforesaid privilege was inserted, and then in it these words were added, among others: 'as well as the donations, transfers, and all privileges and benefits granted and made by our predecessors the Lords Roman Emperors, and specially by the aforesaid Lord Charles, our lord and most dear father, predecessor of the said Marquis, we have confirmed, ratified, approved, renewed, and granted anew from the clemency of our innate benignity, as well as from the plenitude of Roman Royal power, and from certain knowledge we liberally confirm, etc., notwithstanding in the aforesaid and each of the aforesaid any rights, etc., as above. All of which, insofar as they may conflict, etc., as above, also supplying by the tenor of the present letters, of our own motion and out of the plenitude of Roman Royal power, every defect in solemnity or otherwise, if any should have perhaps occurred in any way in this transfer, donation, concession, and confirmation, saving, etc., as above.'

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A pact, which one may enter into by one’s own authority, may be given in a contract, in a last will, in a donation, and in a sentence; and what in an Imperial rescript, when the clause of plenitude of power and ex certa scientia is present.
2. Imperial rescripts are not valid against matters at rest, if they do not make mention of proceedings and sentences.
3. An executor can be one in his own clear matter.
4. An imperial title suffices for dominion; nor is delivery necessary.
5. A petitory and possessory action arises from a privilege of the Prince.
6. The first privilege prevails over the second; it fails if the first is revoked on account of something inserted in the second.
7. A rescript of the prince that it be permitted to go against a sworn pact of not suing is not valid, and what for heirs and grandsons. And number 8.
body: To the evidence before 11 In the name of Christ. it must be submitted,

That the Emperor, regarding his own right which he grants to someone in a privilege, may impose a law according to his will; and may grant a greater favor to his privilege-holder, so that he may possess by his own authority and by perpetual right, having expelled any unlawful possessor; for the Emperor is the living law on earth. And we see that this license may be given in a contract, provided it does not touch the right of a third person, as in C. de pignoribus, l. 3; and in a last will, as above de legatis 2, l. Titia, § 1; and in a donation, extra de consuetudine, c. 2; and in a sentence, as is noted, ff. de re iudicata, l. miles, § fin. But the Emperor could not give license for anyone to expel by his own authority a just and lawful possessor; because such a license would contain a flagitious act and a delict. C. unde vi, l. meminerint. Indeed, such a rescript would be presumed to be obtained by fraud, as extra de rescriptis, c. 2; and it is sufficiently clear in l. 1, C. de petitione bonorum sublatiorum, lib. 10. Nor does the clause of plenitude of power obstruct this; because that clause is understood as referring to the plenitude of good and praiseworthy power, not of blameworthy or tyrannical power. For the Emperor is not said to be able to do anything except what he can do by right. Likewise, those words “by certain knowledge” accomplish nothing; because rather they are more apt to express a greater delict; and therefore this temerarious and abusive precaution, which princes today use in their rescripts, should be entirely rooted out from its source; nor should it be so frequently used.

† It is secondarily to be premised that imperial rescripts do not hold against matters that have been transacted or settled, especially if they do not mention the proceedings and sentences, as in C. sentent. rescindi non posse. l. fi. And if, by the authority of a rescript, one baron should occupy the property of another, he is bound to restore it to him with its fruits, as in C. unde vi. l. autoritate. As noted in C. de fundis, et saltibus rei dominicae. l. si qua loca. lib. 11, where the ordinary gloss is on the literal text. If the Emperor grants a castle to someone, he can juridically give license to take possession by his own authority. But if he cannot grant the principal thing, he cannot grant the accessory either. Also, because natural and civil reason has more power than the Emperor. Also, because the Emperor himself is a mortal rational animal. To make this evident, it must be premised that the Emperor can grant an imperial castle as to right, that is, as to useful ownership: because sometimes it is a fief, sometimes it is not a fief: because it is not granted for any service, or uncertain service: but it is simply useful ownership: although when fidelity is sworn without the mention of services, it may be called a free fief, as in extra de fide instrum. c. inter dilectos. Nevertheless, the superior ownership always remains with the Emperor: because no inferior can share in it who is not capable, nor is it possible to detach it from the body of the Empire, unless it is transferred to the greater body of the Holy Roman Church: concerning which there is sufficient discussion in the prologue to the Digests. Also, he can grant it as to fact, that is, as to possession. For the authority of the prince is no less powerful than the authority of a presiding praeses, whose authority suffices for the transfer of possession. ff. de acquir. posses. l. qui vniuersas. §. item cum praetor. And there is no doubt that the prince can grant license to remove another unlawful detainer, as is commonly known, and he can also grant this power to the donee himself, as noted in de re iudi. l. miles. §. qui iudicati. C. unde vi. l. meminerint. and l. si quis in tantam.

For nothing prevents one from being an executor in his own case, provided that the right is clear and not doubtful; for he cannot declare himself to have a right to a matter in which a judicial sentence is necessary, as stated in C. *Ne quis in sua causa*, l. 1. It follows from this necessity that he cannot also pronounce judgment for himself in taking possession. However, if it is notorious that he has a right—for example, if it is notorious that a castle belongs to the Emperor and that it has been granted to the one who has obtained possession—then no legal reason opposes that he may acquire possession by any means, even secretly, and retain it once acquired; for what is lawful in taking possession is lawful in retaining it. C. *Quod cum eo*, l. *Si seruus*.

† And it must be known that the Imperial title suffices for dominion; nor is delivery necessary for this purpose, but only with regard to factual use, as argued from ff. de publica, l. commissa; ff. pro socio, l. cum duobus, § idem respondit. For a privilege is the law of the prince; and the law can transfer dominion without instrumental assistance or taking possession by foot. Let it therefore be concluded that if the castle was open to the Emperor, i.e., in his liberty, whether in law and in fact, or in law only, or in fact only, one must adhere to the rescript or privilege; so much so that if he who held it unjustly, and who was secretly expelled, or expelled by armed force, does not care: because the prince can openly yield arms, as in l. 1, C. vt armorum vsus inscio principe, lib. 11, and wishes to act to recover possession, he cannot, because he is expelled by the authority of the great praetor, i.e., the prince. And the same applies if someone were expelled by authority duly formed, and jurisdiction established, and with our legitimate process concurring, as noted in 2. q. i., c. in primis. Secondly, I premise for clarity,

† That from a privilege of the prince arises both a petitory and a possessory action, if it is valid: and a possessory action for acquiring possession is available to one who has not yet possessed, or the office of the judge, which is not properly an interdict of the praetor or of the canon, as noted by Innocentius in c. 1, de officio iudicis.

Thirdly, I premise that either both parties claim a privilege; and then the earlier privilege prevails, whether it be of the same Emperor or not: because there is one Empire, even if the first Emperor had granted it only once, and the second had repeated it ten times, the first letters are stronger, because they have a right founded, as in extra de rescriptis, c. 1, because at the time of the later grant no open right is found in the grantor. It fails in the prince, if he revokes the first privilege for cause: and that cause is expressed in the letters: of this the prince is believed, as in clem. 1, de probationibus. But without any cause or occasion, the Emperor could not lawfully divest, nor strip of his investiture one who has been legitimately invested: unless the investiture had been made at pleasure, just as manual benefices are taken away by the superior at will, that is, by mere will, but never perpetually, unless fault has been proven, although Caesar has no need of proving, yet litigants between themselves so, that he prevails who shows stronger rights. From these is inferred the solution of other doubts, namely whether the said Thomas could expel, etc., say, as above, because the Emperor's rescript did not hold: therefore he granted nothing, if it is proven that which is presupposed in the third point,

† because from a pact not to sue arises a natural obligation not to sue in perpetuity, against which natural obligation a rescript does not hold: especially since it makes no mention of it, as in Extra, de decimis, c. Ex multiplici. Moreover, it is expressly stated that he who has sworn not to act contrary thereto cannot obtain [a grant] from the prince, and by obtaining it he becomes infamous. C. de transactionibus, l. Si quis maior. But if he had granted it of his own motion, it would seem that action could be brought on the ground of supervening right: because it is a new right and a new cause, which was not previously considered, by argument from ff. de evictionibus, l. Si rem, quam a principio. Nor could it have been considered: since it depended solely on the power of the prince, as in ff. de legibus, l. Apud Iulianum, §. Finis; and in cap. Abbate, de re iudicata, lib. 6. Consider that this lord Thomas could not obtain [a grant] for himself: because he was a perjurer.

But whether this applies to his heirs and grandchildren, it seems that it does not: because where there is no beginning, there is no succession, nor derivation, nor transmission. Also, because it proceeds from a tainted root and a rejected cause. To the contrary, it seems: because the term "successor" is not always used for an heir; but sometimes for one to whom something accrues for the time being, without having an origin of transmission from a predecessor, as in the extrajudicial title on prebends, in the chapter *Dilectio*. Hence, I can use the bare ministry of another, who could have been my instrument, and yet not his own. As we see, that through an unworthy minister a worthy one is sought. The rule states: he who uses the aid of another, uses it with his own cause, and with the defects of that aid or act, because from a vitious act an effective right is not sought; but nevertheless this does not occur with the personal defect of incapacity: because the defect in the minister is not considered to the prejudice of a third party. Hence it follows that successors, to whom the order of time gives succession, and not a true transmission of any hereditary body, do not succeed to the judgment; consequently, the privilege is valid, because the right begins with them. This could perhaps be defended if they renounced the paternal inheritance; otherwise not, for if they are heirs, they are bound regarding eviction: and the action which holds one liable for eviction against him and his heirs, repels the same person as plaintiff by way of exception. In support of this is the fact that a necessary heir has the necessity of embracing both, namely the paternal inheritance and the paternal benefit, or of repudiating both, although a voluntary heir could separate them, as in chapter 1, *An agnatus, vel filius*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when the oath of a father is prejudicial to his sons, both in bringing an action and in raising a defense.
body: The Emperor granted it. In the name of Christ. Let us now suppose that Titius had sworn not to obtain it.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned oath impedes the rescript, even though the conjunction joins both Titius and his heirs, namely his son. It appears that for the half part concerning Titius, the rescript is invalid due to the obstacle of the oath; but for the half part concerning the sons, it is valid, because the father’s oath does not bind the sons for two reasons. The first reason is its personal nature, on account of which the oath is placed intransitively, that is, so that it cannot depart from the soul of the oath-taker to another. For it is a sacrament and a character, the form and figure of whose substance is in the soul of the oath-taker, as stated in Extra, de iureiurando, c. Veritas, and in Codex, de rebus creditis, l. Generaliter, in principio. For if at times the heir succeeds to the thing sworn to, and to the communicable bond of obligation arising from contract, nevertheless he does not succeed to the spiritual bond and to the communicable oath. And therefore in fiefs, heirs renew oaths, because the oath of the deceased is one thing, albeit not different in kind, and the oath of the heir is another; although the oath of the deceased is a certain exemplar, and the oath of the heir is taken from it formally. It therefore appears that the perjury of the deceased does not harm the sons.

But then it is objected: the sons make use of the aid of the father who obtained the rescript; therefore, they are said to act with their own fault; and thus the fraud of the petitioner harms them, because it is fraud committed in the substantive right from which the action must proceed, as stated in Digestum, de exceptione doli, l. Apud Celsum, §. Auctoris, and §. Si eam legitima, l. Si procurator agit. But I answer that it is not considered who speaks to the Emperor, but upon whom the effect of the benefit is directed or conferred, by argument from Digestum, de legibus secundis, l. Cum pater, §. Donationis. Since therefore the sons come by the liberality of the Prince, although by the diligence of the father, considering that diligence is a remote cause and not the proximate cause of the benefit, and in the proximate cause itself no fault or defect is found, it follows that for the half part concerning the sons, the said rescript ought to be valid, by argument from Digestum, de legibus secundis, l. Si Titio, et ei.

As for whether the said conjunction is to be understood distributively, namely so that one part is valid for the undivided share and for the sons, and finally, if granted, it seems to be the case in Digestum, de usufructu accrescendo, l. Si quis Titio, et haeredibus. And I argue thus: the word "heirs" is therefore understood there as referring to the sons, because it concerns such a right that cannot be hereditary; for the formal usufruct, of which it speaks there, cannot be transmitted by hereditary right, as stated in Digestum, de verbis obligatis, l. Stipulatio ista, §. Si quis. Thus, therefore, the name "heir" is used for the blood heir, because it cannot be understood otherwise while preserving the reason of law and appropriate and fitting language, as stated in Digestum, de operis libertorum, l. Liberti. Hence, concluding from the first to the last, it appears that at least for the half part of the children, the rescript is valid.

Someone will say: are not the sons liable for eviction? Therefore, they cannot come against the contract of the father, insofar as they are heirs; because the action that holds one liable for eviction repels the same person as a plaintiff by way of exception. I answer: yes, if we were in a lawsuit and an exception were raised. But here the sons are not suing; rather, they are in possession. Therefore, the objection does not stand.

The same person says: it was obtained by concealment (obreptitium) from the Emperor; therefore, the privilege is invalid by law itself. I answer: it was not obtained by concealment by the sons, because they did not command it. The part of the father is indeed void and vitiated, and it does not accrue to the sons, because unjust possession does not accrue to just possession, as stated in l. Pomponius, Digestum, de acquirenda possessione. But if, justice being preserved, it could accrue, then the right of accrual would have place among partners in imperial liberality, as stated in Codex, si imperialis, l. Unica.

Consider that concealment (obreptio) does not render the rescript null, but it must be proven that it was obtained by concealment, and that an exception be raised. Hence, if the one who obtained it by concealment does not sue, but is in possession, he must be protected in possession until it is revoked by sentence. And just as the principal matter holds by mere law, both possess the cause and the license granted by the Prince; but the Prince ought to revoke it.

Furthermore, from the paternal contract, insofar as it is an act to sue, the sons can be sued; and insofar as it is an act to raise an exception, the sons can be repelled by the exception, as stated in Codex, de transactionibus, l. Si pro fundo.

And know that all that I have said, I say by way of allegation, because my inclination is against the petitioner, although the things said are subtle and useful for both sides.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The rescript of the Prince concerning the grounds on which he is not bound.
body: I ask: certain nobles of the Empire divide a castle among themselves, adding an oath not to act against this arrangement. Finally, one of them obtains from the Emperor the entire castle, without mention of the said division, and with the clause added that he may exercise jurisdiction and seize possession by his own authority. He secretly and surreptitiously took possession from his co-owner and ejected him from possession. Now the said ejected party seeks to have the said possession restored to him, together with damages, fruits, and interest. But the ejector, or his heirs, say that they are not bound, because they entered by the authority of the Prince, and by a new title and new cause, and this is one step. Another is concerning a certain other castle similarly granted to him: whether it can be claimed and vindicated by the petitioner by means of a rescript, notwithstanding the said title of transaction and possession in good faith; because it is presupposed that the said transaction was made between the said nobles in good faith, and according to ancient custom. And it must be premised for the weight of the question that it is presupposed that the said castles are of the Empire. Therefore, the question is: what is the law? And to this, what divine grace may provide in truth, let counsel be given.

† And it seems that one must first say that the said rescript does not hold, because it did not mention the composition, as in c. ex multiplici, de decimis. Also, because it was acted against an oath, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si quis maior. Also, because there was no mention of the adversary’s discolored possession, as in cap. quod nostris, de concessione prębendae. Also, because from the said contract arose a natural obligation and an exception of just defense, which cannot be removed by rescript, as in C. de transactionibus, l. causas, et lites; C. sententiam rescindi non posse, l. fina. Also, because the said rescript is injurious, as in C. vnde vi, l. meminerint. Also, because the said license could not have been granted, as in C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. fina, unless the possessor had first been deprived by sentence in a competent judge’s court, as is noted in C. vnde vi, l. si quis intantam, and ff. de acqui. pos., l. iuste. Also, because the use of jurisdictions should not be permitted to private persons, as in ff. de regul. iur., l. non est singulis. Also, because the requested goods have been removed, as in C. de peti. bonorum sublatis, l. 1, lib. 10. Also, because the rescript is ambitious, as in ff. de in ius vocando, l. sed si hac, §. patronum; and such rescripts containing a concession of dominion or another right are null by law itself, as in l. rescripta, C. de precibus Imperatori offerendis. Also, if the grace were valid, because it contains only the right of the grantor, nevertheless possession could not be taken away without knowledge of the cause, as in de pręben., capitu. licet episcopus, lib. 6. Also, the custom of the noble house is similar to the custom of a town, for a large kinship and a town have the character of a small city according to Aristotle; therefore the custom holds among them, so that they may make concord over common fiefs; otherwise they would have to always remain at war, especially when the Empire is vacant, which is to say most unjust, since the contrary is most just, as in ff. de vsufructu, l. ęquissimum. Therefore they may divide and make agreement among themselves, because among those having a common symbol, transition is easy, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. voluntas.

To the contrary it seems, because cities and castles are of the same law, that is, public, royal, and sacred, as in ff. de iustitia, et iure, l. 1, §. publicum ius; but these are not in the commerce of private persons, and therefore a pact of private persons is not valid, at least when revoked by the Prince, as in ff. de legatis primo, l. apud Iulianum, §. finali. Also, it does not belong to anyone to dispose of the right of a third party; therefore neither of the things of the Empire, nor of the things of the fisc; because public right cannot be disturbed by the pacts of private persons, as in ff. de pac., l. inter; instituta, de Bontomeu, de Bonvsucapionibus, §. res fisci; nor can a possessor in good faith say that he purchased fiscal rights and jurisdictions without solemnity, as in ff. de rescin. venditione, l. fundus; C. si aduersus fiscum, l. edicto. Also, the improper possession of the possessor does not bind the hands of the Emperor, who can impose whatever law he wishes on his own thing, not only the Emperor, who is above all earthly things, but any owner of his own thing; for the Emperor possesses his property in its genus, that is, majority and liberty, which cannot be separated from his own bones, that is, jurisdiction; just as the Empire cannot fail, because it is established by God and joined to mortals, as in Auth. quomodo oportet episcopos, §. fin., colla. 1.

Solution: if the castles were fiscal, whether of a free fief, that is, free, or conditional, that is, under a mode, the said concession would not hold, as in ff. de aqua plu. arcen., l. in concedendo, because the prince is not seen to wish to do injury to anyone. The same if they belonged to certain nobles by foundation of the castles, or by perpetual custom, of which the contrary is not remembered. These, however, must be proven by those who say the rescript is not valid; otherwise judgment should be for the petitioner, who has a title from the prince to useful ownership, notwithstanding contrary improper possession; and so I hold, as in capitulo imperialem, §. callidis. Therefore the opinion comes for the lady, if the castles were open to the Emperor, or to the King of the Romans. The nature of the thing operates the same as the expression of words or persons. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The terms of a bill of exchange are interpreted, and words of the future tense create a condition; nor can one depart from these terms, nor is there room for repentance: because they are named contracts. And whether a contract of exchange is permitted, and not usurious. And no. 6.
2. Words of the future tense signify a condition.
3. One must not depart from the letters, nor is there room for repentance, because they are named contracts.
4. The writings of merchants and moneylenders are held as a sentence in a transaction in rem iudicatum.
5. To add or subtract something is not permitted, unless by the consent of the parties.
6. From an innominate contract, I give so that you may give: by what action is it brought.
body: Letters were made in the name of Christ, of the tenor set forth below, namely: paid by this first letter on the 9th day of October to Luca de Goro 45 livres, which are for the value due from Masio Rena at the time he paid them, and entered into my account. And may Christ keep you. Bonromeo de Bonromei, greeting. From Milan, on the 9th day of May, 1325. On the reverse: Alessandro di Bonromei and Dominico de Andrea found first the sum of 45 livres.

† This writing has several parts: the first part contains the mandate, and to whom it is directed, i.e., the name of the writer and of the person to whom it is written, the tenor of the mandate, or the terms of the mandate. And this is clear from these words, “paid by this first letter on the 9th day of October to Luca de Goro 45 livres of grossi.” And this first part lasts until there, namely, “follows.” The second part, in which the cause of the mandate is declared, is there, when he says, “namely, 45 livres are for the value.” And follows with the text, which cannot be separated, nor divided, “for the value.” Then follows the third part of the letters there, “at the time you pay him.” The fourth part of the letters there, “and put it to my account.” Now there is no doubt that this is an epistolary writing: because it contains those things which are of a letter, namely, on the back, to whom it is written. Inside, however, who writes, and what the friend mandates to the friend. Also, these letters sound like a certain commerce. First, between Masiolo Rena and Bonromeo, and this is the present commerce, which is confessed by the counting. Second, it contains future commerce between Bonromeo and Alexander and others, between whom Bonromeo and Alexander and others will then contract business, when it will be accepted, and the mandate will be consummated: because words of the future time signify a condition, as in D. de leg. 1, l. Stichum, qui meus erit. And if this condition in any way fails, even by a fortuitous event, no obligation is contracted, as in D. de verb. sig. l. cedere diem. Because now it is necessary to see three things: first, whether the counting made to Boromeo by Mosiolo Rena induces any contract between Masiolo and Bonromeo. And it seems that it does not, because it was not agreed between them that Bonromeo should be bound to anything, except to write the letters of mandate: namely, with effect, so that they be accepted, and by their force payment be made to Luca named in the letters. Which things being explained, Bonromeo incurs no obligation to the said Mosiolo: because the whole force of this commerce, and the whole tenor is directed to the said Luca. And I argue thus, this could be done in a loan and deposit. D. si certum petatur, l. certi conditio, §. si nummos. D. depositi, l. publia, in principio. Nor does repentance, or variation, or departure from the original form have place, nor in the substantial nor accidental parts of the contract: because it is a named contract, as in l. 1, de rerum permutatione. Indeed, more so, because if these were accustomed to payment for the benefit of both parties, repentance would not have place, hence the counter could not repent, as in D. de solutionibus, l. aliud. And argument. D. de verb. obligatio, l. qui Romae, in principio. And it is expressed. D. de pactis, l. si cum fundum. Nor does it hinder that counting intervened, because not every counting obligates him who received, but only as it was agreed between the contracting parties, as in l. non omnis, D. si certum petatur. And if it is said, this was a deposit, therefore repentance has place. I answer, this was not a deposit, but exchange commonly called: in which the utility of both parties is principally turned, which should not take away the act of one from the other. Nor do contrary protests hinder, which are against the force and authority of the contract. D. de constituta pecunia, l. unde falsa. Otherwise it would follow that Bonromeo could be deprived of the profit of exchange by the sole will of the adversary: which is false. D. de negociis gestis, l. Pomponius. Nor can it be said that Bonromeo is enriched in anything, since he who accepts the mandate has money ready for payment, which he offers, hence he is considered as paying, as in C. de usuris etc. Also, let there be novation by the intervention of the thing, and one obligation goes out, and is torn from the body of another, as is noted. D. si cer. petatur, l. singularia. D. mandati, l. qui negocia. Nor do adventitious cases pertain to consummated contracts, as in C. si certa, peta, l. incendium. And note. D. locati, l. in naue saupheli. Consider, sometimes money would remain with the recipient without cause: and this would be unjust, and therefore then the money should be yielded to the counter from that, as I may say, divine and noble equity, of which it is held. D. si cer. pe, l. si me, et Titium. Which law, as a mirror, should be before the eyes of merchants. And therefore where after counting nothing follows, what was received should be restored. It fails in donation. But where it is transferred to another, it should not be returned except for defect of final cause, for example if he to whom it is written in our matter declines the mandate, or payment: because by declining the mandate, no mandate is contracted: and by declining payment, although he accepts the mandate, the money is not ready for payment, hence no novation is made, as excellently noted by Bart. and I after him in the said l. singularia. Furthermore, it is to be known that an exchanger is sometimes given as paid, sometimes as to be paid, for if it was agreed that by the promise made by the exchanger the old obligation is understood to be removed, and a new one substituted, the pact must be observed: but if nothing is done about liberation, but only about the obligation of a new person, then the first action lasts, as noted by Bart. D. de nouationibus, l. si debitorem. Namely, if it is immediately at the end of the promise, without interposing a contract of transfer and change of writings, D. de praetoriis stipulationibus, l. penul. These promises of exchangers are like liquid sentences: yet by them it is not understood that satisfaction has been made, since the action lasts, and the debt subsists. D. de fun. instru, l. nepoti. C. de confessis, l. 1, per Cy. However, if the exchanger offers from the beginning, or later, for example that it suffices that the money is ready for payment from the interval as to this, so that there be a quasi novation, the first debtor is freed at least by the help of an exception, as noted. D. de nouationibus, l. delegare. D. de pignoratitia actione, l. solutum, §. satisfactum. D. mandati, l. inter causas, §. abesse. Now to the proposed question of Boromeo, for if indeed his letters are formally observed with effect, he cannot be sued, and the injustice of sudden cases, or the fraud of those who cease, harms him who was not at fault. But if the letters were not put into execution, then he should owe back what he received: because the cause ceasing, the effect ceases, as in l. cum quis, and l. si extraneus, D. de conditione ob causam. But what, behold, the said Masiolo wants that Bonromeo transmit to him letters, as there Bonromeo wrote to Alexander, and to the partner let them write, let us say to Seius the merchant: because he says that Alexander and the partner are not good promisors, since they are fraudulent partners: hence if they paid, other creditors could revoke pro rata: and thus with effect it would not be satisfied, hence it cannot be said that the money is ready for payment, since it is subject to eviction. As in D. de excep. do, l. pater §. ex quadrante. But Bonromeo responds, and says, you counter are not named in the letters as creditor, but rather as procurator of the recipient, to whom the letters are written, therefore it does not compete to you to act: for you act by no right, because without action no one experiences, as in D. de neg. gest, l. si pupilli, §. videamus. Note. Not everyone named in an instrument acts from the instrument: but only he to whom the credit is directed, as in D. de ver. obl, l. Iulianus, §. 1. D. de solut, l. verus procurator. Moreover, Bonromeo says, I did everything I am bound to do: because I wrote the letters: and I want that it be put to my account. Also, for one debt I am not forced to make so many writings: thus putting myself in double peril: nor am I forced to change writings, because this does not come from the nature of the contract. For this makes that notable, it suffices once. Hence Bonromeo concludes, and wrote the first letters, and I want the second, and third according to the custom of commerce: nor do I want to oblige myself further, of which there was no sense, nor thought, because it could harm me according to that which is expressly read, and noted. D. so. ma. On the other hand, the other party says, you received, and did not pay out, therefore give back, because the thing is entire, and the mandate still stands at the end of the mandate. And the counter says, this mandate was made for my benefit only, and therefore I can prohibit that it be paid, but returned, as in D. de solu, l. si cum Cormelius. D. de donat, l. sed iure, §. si quis. But Bonromeo responds, that this contract is not a contract of mandate, but of market celebrated for the benefit of both: and therefore repentance does not have place. Because now having seen the reasons for and against the cause, let him decide who has to decide according to the reasons which seem more urgent: especially because the writings of merchants should be stable and firm, to whose faith all recur, as in D. de eden, l. quædam §. nummularios. According to that common saying, I have written, I have written.

† because the writings of merchants and money-changers are held to have the force of a judicial sentence: and, so to speak, by their own credit they pass into the status of res iudicata, that is, into the solidity of firmness and irrevocability, as in the Authentica de fideiussoribus, §. argentariorum. Although in modern times some merchants and some money-changers commit enormities, the mass of them, and the best part, and the fifth element [are upright]. Finally, say that either according to the first agreement and intention of the parties the letters can achieve their effect: and then Bonromeus cannot be compelled to innovate anything; otherwise it would be unjust that satisfaction were not made to the one who paid out the money, or to another on his behalf. For the payment itself made him a creditor by the very fact; at least let it be paid to others, because it is in his interest, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. liber homo, §. si, and l. si ita stipulatus, §. grisogonus.

† Moreover, he who adds to or detracts from a contract appears to create a new contract, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. 1, § cum adijcit. But this is not permitted without the consent of the contracting parties, D. qui satisd. coguntur, l. de die, primo responso. This rule does not apply to praetorian stipulations, which are corrected, altered, and executed at the discretion of the praetor, as in D. de praet. stipul. l. 1, in fine. And if a notary were to record something in the order of the president, the writing would be presumed false, as in C. de testam. l. si vnus, and D. de his, qui in testa. deletur, l. 1; C. de probation. l. iubemus. Moreover, in a written contract it is not permissible to add or alter anything from the original draft or root, as in C. de fid. instr. l. contractus. And therefore a notary may not superscribe or dispose of anything, because every contract is concluded in writing by the notary; for the writing is the substance, and is simultaneously the matter and the form, from which one cannot depart; and therefore protocols are left aside, and original writings are treated as true copies, as in Auth. de tabellionibus, § si. Moreover, what if Bonromeus had transmitted the money, or had confirmed it through those messengers? It would be difficult to withhold that money and entrust it to a new person, because this could not be done without expense and litigation; and therefore he is not compelled to do so, as in C. de novationibus, l. prima. And there it is noted by Peter, Cynus, and others, notwithstanding D. mandati, l. idemque, § si cui, because there the text speaks of a procurator who manages another’s affairs, who is bound to obey his principal; but Bonromeus manages his own business and in his own name, and is not bound by any consequence to make a new promise; otherwise one would proceed to infinity through variable promises, which is absurd. Moreover, it suffices that it has been approved once, D. de fideiuss. l. qui satisdare; C. de testib. l. si quis testibus; D. qui satisd. cog. l. si ab arbitro. But what kind of contract was this? And it appears to be a contract for the purchase and sale of money, for just as a sale consists in money due to the diversity of the subject matter, so if there is added a diversity of place or time where payment is to be made.

† And thus merchants judge that the contract of exchange is lawful in its own nature: because it is a purchase and sale, and by natural equity on account of the dangers which are undertaken in the transmission of moneys. D. de nautico foenore, l. periculi. And thus profit is lawfully compensated, as D. pro socio, l. si non fuerit. Hence it is not usury, because it is not gratuitous, and it is not granted on account of time, which is common to all living creatures; but on account of the danger bought and sold, argumentum D. de emptione et venditione, l. si iactum retis. Furthermore, I do not care whether it is a certain exchange from thing to thing, or from person to person: because it is a firm and solemn contract. Moreover, these letters appear to be letters of constituted money, where the first contracting person is placed as the foundation of the cause; the second person, because after the receipt of the money is appended as the effect, and this can be in two ways: either that it is a certain person appended, and obligation is sought for him; and then Bonromeus has the right, especially if it is his interest, because conversely he could compensate his own account: because they would have with them more cases. D. de negotiorum gestione, l. cum pecunia. D. de edendo, l. si quis ex argentariis, §. rationem. And in constituted money, obligation can be acquired for an absent person by messenger or letter, just as between present persons: because it is contracted by consent. But if the one receiving the money was appended as procurator of Masiolus, and then Masiolus would have the right, as D. mandati, l. idemque, §. si cui. Because the obligation is rooted in him, and not transferred to another: for he who stipulates to his procurator, or to the manager of his own affairs, seems to stipulate for himself. D. de solutionibus, l. si cum Cornelius. In doubt, however, it is presumed that the business principally pertains to him who counts the money: because it is presumed to be his, and the one appended to the solution seems to be added as a simple procurator. D. de verborum obligationibus, l. Iulianus, §. qui fundum. D. soluto matrimonio, l. dotis, with its material. It makes what is noted. C. de constituta pecunia, in Authentica si quando. But where it would be established that Bonromeus, for his own sake and that of Masiolus, had made the said writing on account of some interest, then Bonromeus would have the right, because he would not be bound to do anything except what the writing says, and to the effect for which it speaks. D. commodati, l. commodato, §. sicut. And if the offered libel is well considered, the wise drafter of the libel considered and weighed all these things. And note that in this writing no promise is contained, neither under a personal word nor impersonally, yet it seems to be understood as made personally to the counter, as the said Authentica si quando, namely that the one appended is presumed to be for paying, which whether in this case it is said to be added, or is said to be appended principally for itself, has already been said. And thus whether the business is managed for the absent person by the present one, or conversely to be managed for the present one by the absent one, and with subsequent mandate. Where the counting is the cause of another minister, there it is certain that the bare minister is a procurator. But where the business would principally pertain to him to whom payment should be made, then it would be the contrary, because he who first counted would be the minister, and the one receiving the solution would be the principal and master of the business: which a good man will weigh from the quality of the persons, and from other things customary between them. Furthermore, Bonromeus has a determined benefit, that is, exchange, and just as he ought not to sustain inconvenience, so neither ought he to be enriched: because the subsidy of exchange resolves into the fact of exchange in money counted, as D. depositi, l. dies sponsaliorum. And in l. Lucius. And argumentum de usuris, l. in fideicommissis, §. cum Polidius. For Masiolus it makes, because this one is named first in the letter: therefore he is presumed principal. Furthermore, each one is presumed to contract and agree in his own name. D. de solutionibus, Prima Pars Consiliorum. D. de probationibus, l. si pactum. Moreover, it would be granted that no part, that Masiolus was an institor, yet since he stipulates to act and demand in the name of the mistress: because he has a direct action from his own contract, argumentum D. depositi, l. quod servus. But certainly here he did not act as an institor of another, but as another, his institor: therefore he must prove the mandate, that he was his institor or manager, because mandate is not presumed. D. depositi, l. si quis inficiatus. Turn and re-turn the aforesaid in your brain, that the libel against Bonromeus is ill-conceived, it appears, because from the innominate contract do you, so that you give to another. D. de donatione, l. hoc iure, §. si quis.

It ought to have been proceeded by way of a condictio ob causam on account of repentance, or by an action on agreed terms for damages; the latter mode of proceeding would also apply in a named contract. D. de verb. oblig. l. liber homo, §. si. But here neither of these modes of proceeding was employed; therefore, the action was brought improperly and the bill of complaint was ill-drawn, although it appears to be expressly stated that this is an innominate contract. D. de pactis, l. si cum fundum. One could have resorted to a stipulation. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one prohibited from alienating to a non-citizen may institute him as heir.
2. By statute of law, or of the municipality, it may be provided that a person dies partly testate and partly intestate.
3. Whether strangers may become citizens in their absence, and with no one accepting on their behalf, subsequently ratifying and accepting.
4. Whether a citizen made by statute has the force of natural citizens. And see also at the end of the opinion, under the words “but here arises a doubt.”
5. One who uses an instrument is deemed to ratify and verify it.
6. By a statute prohibiting anyone from alienating by any contract, whether last will is also included: and see also below at the end of the opinion under the words “subsequently it is doubted.”
7. A relative of diversity of substance requires similarity in quality.
8. Whether a statute prohibiting distribution, alienation, or bequest to persons of another territory is valid.
9. Whether the statute mentioned above applies to a citizen made by decree of the elders, authorized or strengthened by the consent of the prince.
10. By a statute prohibiting anyone from acquiring by contract or in any other way, whether he may acquire by way of institution.
body: Statute of Piacenza. In the name of Christ. No one shall dare in any way to alienate any immovable property or jurisdictions located within Piacenza or its district to anyone not belonging to the City of Piacenza or its district. If this is contravened, the alienation shall be void by operation of law.

And it appears that the alienation is not valid, as in l. 1, C. non licere habitatoribus metrocomiae, li. 11, because what the law prohibits, the testator cannot bequeath, as in ff. de leg. j., l. citra, and l. si quis inquilinos, §. fi. On the contrary, it appears that it could come and pass with the universality, as in s. directa institutionis haeredis, ff. de acquirenda rerum dominione, l. quaedam, although it would not come in the substitution of the fideicommissary, as in ff. ad Trebellianum, l. quia perinde. And there is a reason for the difference: because alienation by direct institution necessarily includes this under itself, since one cannot die partly intestate, or be testate for one thing and intestate for another; but a fideicommissum and a legacy can well admit division, as in ff. de heredibus instituendis, l. si quis homo institutus fuerit excepto fundo. But nevertheless, I do not rely on this reasoning.

† because a statute of law or of a municipality may well provide that someone who has died is considered partly testate and partly intestate, as in D. de testamento 28, l. miles ita, §. et quia diximus; and see the note by Cynus and others in D. de iustitia et iure 1, l. cunctos populos; and C. de secundis nuptiis 5, l. 1; and D. de adoptionibus 25, l. si rogator, §. sed an impuberi. Nevertheless, I do not think that by the said statute the institution of a universal heir is prohibited, but rather modified. D. de inofficioso testamento 29, l. posthumus. I come to the second point, which is as follows, namely

Whether strangers can become citizens in their absence, and with no one receiving them on their behalf, even though they subsequently ratify and accept. And it seems that they cannot, because to receive someone as a citizen is to contract, and a contract cannot be made between absent parties unless through an intermediary organ or by letter, as in D. de donationibus causae mortis, l. inter mortis. For in citizenship an obligation is contracted on both sides: it cannot be contracted without the consent of both parties. D. de acquisitione et obligatione, consensu. And it is similar regarding adoption and arrogation, which cannot be done unless both parties speak and are present. D. de adoptionibus, l. 2 and l. post mortem, §. si. By way of benefit and privilege, however, it can be done, because a benefit and privilege can be conferred upon an absent and unaware person, provided that he ratifies it, as in c. si tibi absenti, de praebendis, lib. 6, and it is noted. D. de iureiurando, l. Labeo. For even one legitimated by privilege and by offering to the curia can ratify, as in Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, and §. generaliter. Moreover, this is a kind of choosing and eliciting, or inviting, not contracting, as is noted in l. ciues, C. de incolis, lib. 10.

I come to the third point, which provides that no alienation may be made unless leave has been obtained. For he sufficiently obtains the leave of the citizens, even of those who are natural citizens, who by virtue of their nobility are made citizens by statute; because he is now of the flock of citizens, and a numbered or supernumerary member thereof, and of the same civil body and corporation, both actively and passively, as is stated in the law *Tribunus*, in the Digest, under the title *De militum testamento*. For since he has acquired the rights of citizens, he cannot be regarded as an outsider.

† It is certain that he who uses an instrument is deemed to ratify and verify it, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, in the title *De exceptionibus*, chapter *Cum venerabilis*. Suppose the words of the statute state that no one may alienate by any contract into emphyteusis, or grant in fief, or by any other mode or color devised, etc.

† It is asked whether they contain the last will, and it seems that they do not: because the words "they extracted" do not pertain to the right of making a will. D. de verborum significatione, l. verba gesserunt; and D. de legatis 3, l. pater filium, in principio. The generality of the words, or in another way, does not stand in the way.

† because a relative term denoting diversity of substance requires similarity in quality, as is noted. C. de ser. fugi. l. fugitiui. and arg. ff. de vino legato. l. si. §. cui dulcia. But the last will receives a more liberal interpretation than a contract; nor is it of the same interpretation or nature; nor does it signify by its understanding the same or similar thing, as ff. de regulis iur. l. in testamentis.

† But concerning this kind of dominion, it may be doubted whether a statute can prohibit that property be distrained, alienated, or left to persons of another territory. And it seems that it cannot, if the owners of the things are not subject to the municipal laws of that place. For one cannot impose a law on those not subject, as in the law *Cunctos populos*, with its material. On the contrary, it seems that this law is *in rem*, not *in personam*; because it says that no immovable thing may be alienated outside the district. And even if it were posited that no subject person, etc., may alienate outside the territory, nevertheless, because the outsider, who is prohibited, is subject, the statute holds; because one can impose a law on one's own person, i.e., on one's own subject, as in the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *In quorum*, and law 1, Code, *De cupressis ex luco damnosis*. And where two extremes are required, if one is invalid, what is done does not hold; because the recipient cannot be of the thing without the received, nor can it receive unless it is transferred into it, as in the law *Si ego*, *Si certum petatur*. Solution: If the words of the statute begin with the subject person, because they are directed to him, for example, "No citizen of Piacenza may alienate to a Parmesan," therefore the statute is valid; otherwise, if the words begin with the non-subject, for example, that the non-subject may not acquire, because it is directed to the non-subject; because one cannot be incapacitated by those who enact. Or say that the statute is valid in both cases; because the reason is the same for correlatives, as in the final law, Code, *De indicta viduitate*.

But here arises a doubt: what if a foreigner has become a citizen by a decree of the elders, with the authority of, or the consent of, the Prince? I answer that this foreigner has acquired the use of the toga of Piacenza, and therefore he can acquire and contract, as in D. de iure fisci, l. sed si accepto. And note that this citizenship is a benefit, which is accepted like a legacy: it is not said to be ratified, because it does not proceed from him, but into him; and all its force depends on those who enact it. Ratification, properly speaking, cannot apply unless that which is feigned to have been done by the ratifying party through ratification, as in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. si pupilli, § sed si ego. And there is no doubt that a privilege does not proceed from the privileged person, but from the one granting the privilege, from whom it derives its existence, although through acceptance privileges assume an unchangeable acquisition of benefit, as in D. de conditionibus et institutionibus, l. si quis hereditatem.

† Subsequently, it is doubted that if a statute says that one cannot acquire by contract, or in any other way, whether one can acquire by way of institution of an heir: and it seems that not, because of the general words inserted alternatively, or in any other way: because he who excludes everything, there is nothing that he does not exclude. ff. de rebus dubiis. l. si is, qui ducenta. §. vtrum. de rebus alienis non alienandis. l. sin. Moreover, this prohibition is made in favor of certain persons, namely citizens, whose interest it is because of taxes, levies, and collections, not because of the nature of the thing itself, nor for

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A clerk who is a notary, having been deprived of his notarial office by the bishop on account of the crime of forgery, cannot be restored to the notarial office.
body: A certain cleric was [excluded] on account of some hatred: therefore, it is understood to refer to alienation, even by the institution of another heir, as in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali; and l. si quis prioris, §. certum, C. non licere habitatoribus metrocomii, l. 1; ff. de legatis 2, l. peto, §. fratre. To the contrary, it seems, ff. de acquirendo vel amittendo hereditate, l. quædam. Moreover, lest anyone die partly testate and partly intestate, as is noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, l. 1. It seems to be said, truth being preserved, that the aforementioned statute is not to be understood as applying to the institution of an heir, because it does not apply to intestacy either, in whose place the institution succeeds. The objection from §. fratre does not hold, because there, in the case of alienation, the thing was left to the family, whereas here it is left to no one. Moreover, this mention of contracts, which ought to restrict, so that it may have effect in declaring the quality of the genus, applies unless the testaments of the ancients provide otherwise. I, Baldus.

† It is proposed that a certain person, in the name of Christ, was condemned for forgery by his bishop; and finally, by the same bishop, he was restored in full. After this restoration, he drew up instruments as a public notary. The question is whether such instruments are valid or not, and it seems that they are valid, because one restored in full is regarded as if he had not been condemned. D. de postulando, l. 1, § de qua; C. de sententiis passis, l. 1 and l. si. To the contrary is the truth itself, because a bishop cannot restore an infamous person, since this is reserved to the prince and the senate, as is fully read and noted by Innocentius and others in c. cum te, de re iudicata. Moreover, whether we consider the nature of the crime, because it is the crime of forgery, which is most atrocious and detestable, and repels one from giving testimony, as in c. testimonium, de testibus; D. de infamibus, l. Lucius; or whether we consider the nature of the penalty, or of actual and verbal reproach, D. de infamibus, l. ictus; or the nature of the sentence, eod. tit., l. 1, it is true that Master Dy. says that the nature of the procedure must be examined, because just as one condemned by inquisition is not infamous, as l. 3, § 1, D. de suspectis tutoribus, Bartolus holds that rather he is infamous, D. de publicis iudiciis, l. infames, from which it is clear regarding a crime, especially by confession, to this effect Extr. de actionibus, c. 1, lib. 6. Furthermore, this notary was condemned for breach of faith, and is released from the oath of notary, hence he is said to be extinguished and deprived of authority, as D. de infamibus, l. 2, § miles, and it is expressly stated that henceforth he cannot draw up instruments, in Auth. de armis, in fine, Coll. 6, and l. si aliquid, de successoribus et archariis; C. de dignitatibus, l. iudices, lib. 12; D. de senatoribus, and much less is he admitted to give testimony, D. de testibus, l. 3, § 1, Iulia, l. Cassius. Nor can the praeses prevent infamy from following one condemned for theft or forgery, since this crime is not committed without fraud, as D. de furtis, l. non potest. Likewise, to a soldier condemned for breach of faith, the right to make a will by military law cannot be preserved, as l. si quis in principio, § miles, D. de legatis tertio. But rather it seems that a bishop could restore a fool, as is noted in Dist. 50, in c. Domino sancto, but that gloss is commonly rejected; or by sustaining that he speaks when infamy is contracted for a light cause, as d. cap. cum text., de re iudicata. Moreover, it still seems to stand in the way Extr. de iudicibus, c. At si clerici, where it is said that bishops can dispense, but that must be understood before the definitive sentence, as D. de infamibus, l. quid ergo, § poena gravior, or it speaks there as far as the execution of ecclesiastical order is concerned. Finally, I conclude from a certainty that a bishop cannot restore him to the office of notary, from which he has once been deposed with most grave infamy; for from the clerical order a bishop cannot fully absolve or deprive of authority, except as is contained in c. Degradatio, de poenis, lib. 6, but from the notaryship one can be fully removed, because by the office of notary no character is imprinted on the soul.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. An ancestral and paternal fief passes to the agnates, notwithstanding any disposition of the deceased.
3. Possession relieves from the burden of proof.
3. Whether a confession made in the absence of the opposing party constitutes proof.
4. One must not depart from the glosses.
5. How manyfold is the quality of goods, or of patrimonies.
6. How an ancient fief is proved. And no. 10.
7. A fief is a certain servitude contrary to the nature of things.
8. Whether a married woman may change her domicile.
8. The lord of the fief may invest the daughter of the vassal out of love for the father.
9. How a fief is proved, and by what means. And no. 11.
12. A negative, difficult to prove, induces suspicion against the witness.
13. How prescription of a fief is proved.
14. Those things which the testator held at the time of his death are presumed to be his own.
body: ...foundations... In the name of Christ.

† In the matter of the feudal property of the lords of Scipione, the foundations are, in my view, clear. First, a testamentary disposition has no effect in them; rather, an ancestral and paternal fief passes to the agnates notwithstanding any arrangement of the deceased, extra de success. c. 1 and c. 1 de gradibus succedendi in feudum. Moreover, that the castle of Scipione with the salt wells is an ancient paternal fief is proven: for these men and their forebears are in quasi-possession of the Margraviate and of the fief of the castle of Scipione and of the salt wells, with the knowledge and consent of the prince or of his vicar, as has been proven by witnesses; therefore, without any other showing of the investiture, when they themselves swear that they are vassals, the presumption must be in their favor, as in c. 1 de consuetu. recti feudi; therefore that quasi-possession together with their oath is sufficient without the showing of the investiture.

† Furthermore, when someone is in possession of any status, quasi-possession relieves the quasi-possessor of the burden of proof and transfers the burden of proof to the adversary, as noted by the gl. in l. si solennibus, C. de fi. instru., which gloss lord Jac. and lord Bal. approve through l. circa, ff. de prob. Furthermore, whenever any persons are in quasi-possession of any status that could have inhered in them from their origin, quasi-possession relieves the quasi-possessor of the burden of proof and transfers the burden of proof to the adversaries, as in l. circa, de probat. and noted in l. si prius, ff. de ope. no. nun. Now, these noblemen and their forebears are in quasi-possession of the vassalage of the Holy Empire regarding the land of Scipione and the salt wells, which status could have inhered in them from their origin, since they could have been born vassals of the Holy Empire from an ancestral and great-grandfatherly fief; for that reason, that quasi-possession suffices without any other display of privileges, and it transfers the burden of proof to the adversaries. Since they, therefore, have not proved the contrary: therefore, etc. And even if this quasi-possession of so long a time did not constitute full proof, it would constitute some indication and some presumption. Likewise, there is public fame that they are vassals of the Holy Empire for the land of Scipione and for the salt wells; which, even if it did not constitute full proof, constitutes semi-full proof, or some indication, as in l. 3 § eisdem, ff. de test. and noted in l. de minore § tormenta, ff. de quaestionib. Likewise, there is the confession of lord Giovanni, father of Marchasoto, and of Marchasoto himself, that they were vassals of the Holy Empire for the land of Scipione and for the salt wells, and that the castle and the wells were a fief of the Holy Empire.

† which confession, made out of court, even in the absence of the other party, by force of the statute of this city constitutes full proof. Likewise, according to the ius commune, even if it does not constitute full proof, it constitutes some indication, as noted by the gl. and Bar. in l. capite quinto, ff. ad l. Iul. de adul. and by the argument of l. quaero in fi., ff. de edil. edic. and l. fulcinius § 1, ex quib. cau. in poss. eat. Likewise, there are three witnesses beyond all exception testifying that they heard the privileges of the Emperors Henry and Charles read; because even if they do not constitute full proof, they constitute semi-full proof, so that there is room for the tendering of the oath, as noted by the gl. in l. sicut, C. de fide instru. and

† one must not depart from the glosses in practice. Likewise, there are two witnesses skilled in letters—namely, a notary and a priest—testifying to the tenor of the privileges, to the effect that the castle of Scipione with the salt wells was granted in fief to lord Albertino and his successors, from whom these noblemen descended. Likewise, it is also proven by these men that they do not have a copy of these privileges, since by custom they remained with Marchasoto; and this has been fully proven. Likewise, it has been proven that those of the Rossi first entered the castle, where they had been seen in the possession of Marchasoto, and carried away the writings of Marchasoto from the castle, as appears from their productions; and these men swore in the proceedings that they did not have them in their possession, [First Part of the Consilia,] and thus did not have the means of exhibiting them.

† For the sake of clarity, it must be stated beforehand that there are certain qualities of goods, or things of one's own or adventitious patrimony, which by one not of full age can be sold, donated, alienated, and exchanged, and of which an adult can dispose by testament and codicil. The Institutes de rerum di. § si quis a non domino and § per traditionem, ff. de acqui. rer. do. l. acquiritur and l. traditio, C. comunia dele. l. j. and 1 ff. de rei ven. throughout, and C. man. l. in rem mandata, speak of this patrimony. The second quality of things is castles donated by the Emperor not in fief, but as private property. And the same applies to these as applies purely to other patrimonial goods, even though they may be castrensian: because they were transferred with full right, and they belong neither to the fisc nor to the donor, but to the donee, as in l. bene a Zenone and C. de do. l. si ad ea. The third kind of things is a fief, and if it is ancient, a testament concerning it is not valid, because it belongs to the agnates; and

† it is presumed ancient because it has thus proceeded from many ancestors in the past; and it is so named because antiquity provides a cause for prescribing, as noted by Bar. on usucapion, l. celsus. Likewise, a fief is presumed from the correspondence of services. Nevertheless, these things must be proved; nor does past possession suffice to prove by presumption. Rather, present possession is required, without violence and clandestine servitude, as noted by Bar. and by me in l. pe., ff. de conditionibus institutionum.

† and a fief is a kind of servitude against the nature of things, which once were free, and are today presumed to be so, as noted in ff. de no. ope. nun. l. si prius, ff. si seruitus vendicetur l. alterius, and ff. de usufruc. l. si cuius in prin. Concerning the examination of the records, I cannot extend myself: because I am ill, and afflicted in body, though not in mind, by the grace of God. Conscience in doubtful matters is very good and pleasing to God, as noted in ff. de neg. ges. l. at qui natura § cum me. As to the matter of lady Agnese, who is the prior agnate, it must be said that whoever wishes to succeed into the place of any person must prove that person dead by burial or by other certainty, or by sufficient conjecture of it, as in C. de captiuis l. nec nos. Likewise, the person must be exhibited, as in l. cum si exhibuissent, ff. de publ. Likewise, a confession accords with natural facts, and therefore it is presumed true, and it is valid even among those who are absent, as in l. quoti., C. de naufragiis, book 11.

† Likewise, it is said that lady Agnese was made a foreigner because she was married by me, and thus changed her origin, as noted in l. origine, de municipibus, et originariis. But that allegation is not true: because it speaks there only with respect to judicial forum, not with respect to goods, since by reason of the goods she retains her original domicile, as noted in l. 1, C. de mulieribus, et in quo loco, book 10. And this in non-feudal goods; for feudal goods do not pass to women,

† unless the lord wishes to invest the daughter out of honor and love for the father; which is not proposed here. Likewise, a fief of the prince is not proven by witnesses, but by writing, as in l. bene a Zenone; but inferior fiefs are proven by writing, and likewise by the peers of the court.

† Likewise, if it is an ancient fief, it is proven by other suitable witnesses; what is noted in the proem of the Sext in the Novella supports this. Likewise, public fame has great weight; yet alone it does not suffice, as noted in C. de rei vendica. l. iudicia and the said § cum me. Likewise, under the common law, ownership is not proven between absent persons through enunciative words, as in C. de iur. et fac. ign. l. cum falsum. Likewise, to that which is said, that heirs are presumed to have the writing: it is answered that possession is not presumed, as in l. 1 § Scaevola. Likewise, it is difficult through what is noted in c. 1 de usuris, in Cle.
