Likewise, it is difficult to prove the tenor of the privilege because of the other things that are required, namely regarding the Emperor’s sign and other solemnities, and because it is necessary that they recognize the document by the seal and other things which must be subtly inquired into, as in extra de fi. instr. c. inter dilectos. And note that these castles are commonly accustomed to be fiefs of the Emperor, as in c. 1 quae sint regalia, coll. 10; and from frequency and generality truth is presumed, unless an inconsistent custom is proven. And note that in this country, as in Austria, non-feudal castles are no fewer than feudal ones; and therefore it is uncertain whether they are feudal or not. Furthermore, regarding the Parmese goods, there is no doubt that they belong to these noblemen of the Rossi, where it does not appear elsewhere concerning a substitution made to the said Marchasoto. What I have said—that possession has great weight—understand this to hold unless it is violent, as in C. de probationib. l. si de possessione and l. vis eius; because a favorable presumption is excluded by a crime; what is noted in ff. ad leg. Aquiliam l. in l. Aquilia si deletum, and l. fina., ff. de in litem iurando, and ff. de furtis l. qui tabulas and l. quidam tabularum supports this. I, Baldus de Perusio.

On the matter of fiefs. In the name of Christ. [Certain] qualities, which are called those of nature: but those which it has in common with other contracts are not called the nature of fiefs; but under a general name, as if they stood apart, we say that the nature of a good-faith contract is such, and the nature of a strict-law contract is such, and the nature of the action for dowry is such; and so for each individual one. Now, nature is a certain reason which inheres in the act itself by the disposition of law, or custom, or the equity of the judge, whether principal or accessory; as this is confirmed by various laws, which are commonly [cited]. Among others, those which are attributed to the nature of the fief are the mode of proof. For one mode of proof is by witnesses, another mode of proof is by public or authentic instruments, namely, the bulls of princes or bishops. Furthermore, some witnesses are peers of the court, [and] the same applies to the vassalage of the same lord [regarding] fidelity. Others are outsiders, concerning whom I have spoken in another opinion; and therefore I do not repeat it.

† Now I come to the question asked, whether the fief of the March can be proved by other witnesses than by the peers of the court, or by a privilege of the prince? And on this point we have no law speaking specifically for or against. And therefore it seems that we cannot say anything else, except that the aforementioned general rule holds, that either the fief is new, that is, which is now said to have first taken its origin: and then it must be proved by the peers of the court, or by a tested writ: it is called a tested writ, because formerly instruments were very brief: and the brevity of the charter does not vitiate the instrument. This fails if the lord’s court does not have peers. Likewise it fails in the case of a clerical fief. But if it is an ancient fief, all good witnesses are admitted, even if they are not peers, as in c. 1, *Si inter directum dominum et vassallum de investitura*; and in c. 1, *De feudo guardiæ*; and in C. *Sciendum*, *De consuetudine recti feudum*, cum si. Nevertheless, the possessor may well argue that, just as the collation of an ecclesiastical benefice of notable quantity, quality, dignity, or jurisdiction cannot be proved except by sacred documents sealed with the bull of the granting prince, as in C. *De diversis officiis*, l. *Probatorias*, lib. 12, so too in the case of a feudal benefice to which territory is annexed, l. *Mensuratum spatium iurisdictionatum*: for every perpetual concession of jurisdiction has the character of dignity and the rank of superior excellence, since it presides over a universality. And on this point, sufficiently detailed notes are found in the prologue to lib. 6 in the *Novella Facit*. It is supported by C. *De iure fisci*, l. *Prohibitum*, *De metatis*; l. *Devotum*, C. *De mancipiis principum*; l. j., 96 dist., ca. *Nobilissimus*. To this effect is *Extra*, *De rescindendo*, per totum; and *De præcepto imperatoris officii*, and the following title, per totum; eo. c. *Quæ perscripta concedi solent*. And the meaning of the words requires that what is granted by written decree should not be granted by the oracle of the living voice: for rescripts are so called from being written back, and therefore l. *Bene a Zenone*, in the word *existimare*. Unless it is said that that law speaks when the prince’s rescript tends to derogate from the right of another, namely the lord of the alienated thing. But certainly in our case, since a rescript or privilege is alleged, it must be proved by that species of proof which is alleged for the substance of the concession: for he who produces an instrument seems to bind himself; since only one act is presumed, as in c. *Cum Ioan. hæredi*, *De fide instrumentorum*. Someone might say, here the privilege is proved by witnesses who testify that they have read and seen it, not abolished, not cancelled, nor erased, nor vitiated in any part of it. For visible things are proved by sight, intellectual things by intellect: which intellect, however, must never be absent, as in ff. *De testamento*, l. *Qui in testamento*, §. *Si*. I answer: unless the case is proved which happened against one’s will, such witnesses do not prove: for that is not testimony, but testimony of testimony; and it is from another’s conscience, not from their own and immediate knowledge of the deponents: and the witness is to be examined regarding his own conscience, and not regarding another’s; and therefore testimony from hearing of hearing, and from touch of touch, does not prove: for between the sense and the object there is a certain medium, in which the witness could easily be deceived.

† Moreover, this negative assertion is difficult to prove and remote from the matter at hand; furthermore, a negative plea, being very difficult to prove, gives rise to suspicion against the witness, as stated in the Extravagant Decretals, under the title *De causa possessionis*, chapter *Cum ecclesia*. Likewise, one must not provide material for fabricating falsehoods, as held in the Digest, under the title *De editionibus*, law 1, section *Editiones*. Furthermore, for the same reason that a copy of a copy is not valid, testimony based on testimony is likewise invalid, as I have stated in another opinion.

† But here it is not without use to observe, because prescription is always proved by witnesses: and especially where the length of time induces a tacit concession; in which case it is not necessary to prove the title. D. si serui vend. l. si quis diuturno. Nor indeed is good faith to be proved, nor the truth which arises from the contract of time. C. de apocis publi. l. quicunque. D. de vsu. l. cum de in rem verso. C. communi diuidum. l. pen. and note in c. si quis per 30. si de feu. fue. controuer. But to this I answer, that in that prescription two things are required, namely, the knowledge of the Emperor, and silence. C. de serui. et aqua. l. 2. Also, that the user was using it as if by feudal right, just as in the prescription of servitudes, as l. fi. D. quemadmo. ser. amit. Hence it is concluded, that an imperial fief cannot be prescribed unless with the knowledge of the Emperor, or his deputy, as noted by Bartolus, D. de publi. l. si publicanus. Also, he who has possessed for so long a time is presumed to have the direct dominion, as noted by Bartolus, D. de acque pos. l. rem quae nobis considera. A fief, while it is acquired, is a matter of fact: but after it has been acquired, it is a matter of law. But facts are not presumed: and therefore he who alleges a fief must prove it. Moreover, this is clear from the fact that agnates must prove the fief gradually and so necessarily, that they must prove that the fief descended to them by right of succession from the stock, as noted in cap. 1. §. hoc autem sciendum. qui feu. dare possunt. col. 10. But this proof of such a fief could not be given by anyone by testimony: because although it was in the goods of the vassal while living, it did not remain in his inheritance, just as some things are ours while we live, and when we are dead are not counted among our goods, as noted in c. praesenti. de offi. or. li. 6. C. de leg. l. vexor patrui. But take heed, you who have to judge, and examine the facts so carefully that neither your conscience nor mine may be injured, and thus I protest to you under the threat of divine judgment, knowing for certain that you have a good conscience, which is the mirror and lamp of things to be done. I speak according to what is proposed: but if the truth of the fact were otherwise, it must be followed in all respects. Truth is to be true and to be spoken. Here it happens that

† Those things which the testator held in full possession at the time of his death are presumed to have been his own property, until the contrary is proved, as in l. edicto and l. 3, ne vxor pro marito, with many others. It is also supported by C. de epis. et cle., l. raptores. And natural possession is an instrument and an order, whereas civil possession, if it is the body of the mind, is rational. And therefore one thing is understood through the other, as noted in I. stipulatio ista, §. hi quoque, de ver. obl. From which it clearly follows that a fief is not presumed in derogations of a will; because both general reason and natural equity suggest that wills should be upheld wherever it is possible without derogating from the rights of another. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The Pope has no superior, nor any equal: and in what manner he may enfeoff and ennoble his own.
2. A fief is sometimes regulated according to its nature, and sometimes according to agreements, by which it is lawful to depart from the simple nature of the fief.
3. The usages of good style are to be observed: because they were devised by those more skilled.
body: It is together with the truth

† It must be presupposed and together with the truth that the cities, towns, castles, and dwelling places which the Roman Church holds and possesses in respect of every kind of jurisdiction—whether by the munificence of emperors or kings, or by other lawful titles from which ownership is accustomed to arise—belong to the Church by supreme and free right, so that the Roman Church is greater and sovereign, without recognizing the Emperor or any other as superior or equal in honor, or in jurisdiction, or in any preeminence. For this her prerogative and possession or quasi-possession of countless years claims for itself, as well as the opinion of all nations that possess sound understanding, as is noted in l. 1, § cum urbem, ff. de offi. prefecti ur., and in the beginning of the Feuds, and by Gu. de Cu., Cyn., and others. And it is clear by the most evident reasoning, because in truth the Emperor is a vassal of the Church and swears fealty to her, nor can he otherwise be confirmed or crowned, as in c. venerabilem, de elec., and in c. 1, de iure iu., in Clem. Although by the sufferance of the Church the Emperor might exercise in the lands of the Church certain things that belong to voluntary jurisdiction, such as creating notaries and similar things that harm no one, nevertheless it is impossible and implies a contradiction that the Roman Church could recognize any superiority or even equality from the Emperor. And this having been presupposed as established, it must next be examined—as is asked below—when the Pope with his College wishes to elevate, and still further ennoble and adorn with honors certain Magnificos, who are a great support to the Church in temporal matters, especially in modern times when the lands of the Church suffer slaughters, damages, and countless tribulations: what mode and what form is to be held as more secure, more fitting, and more just, and by what path one should proceed and conclude. Concerning the aforesaid, it must be presupposed that the Pope can do this out of the plenitude of power, with superiority, honor, and the oath of fealty reserved to himself; for even the Emperor can do this, as in c. 1, de feudo marchiae; therefore so can the Pope, who is greater than the Emperor, because what is permitted to an inferior is much more strongly permitted to a superior, as in ff. de offic. praetoris, l. Barbarius, at the end, and C. de adoptio., l. 2.

† Furthermore, there appear to be three ways: namely, by emphyteusis, because nothing is un-infeudable to the Pope, that is, which he cannot grant in feud if he wishes, according to what is noted in extra, de iudi., c. cum venisset. Another way is by feud, and that is a liege feud, and it especially ennobles, as in c. pastoralis, de re iudica., in Clemen., and as is noted there. The third way is that of a perpetual vicariate, which is transmitted to heirs if this is expressed in the grant, through what is noted by Bartol. in l. pater, ff. de serui. lega. But it must be noted that emphyteusis is not a species of dignity, since it is a kind of lease, which does not ennoble the lessee; nor would one become a duke through it, since it is a mercenary transaction, as in Instit. locati, § adeo. Likewise, a vicariate is the name of a certain subordinate office, as in c. extirpandae, de praebendis, although a perpetual vicariate is found in de fide instrumentorum, c. perpetuus; and therefore it does not signify a dignity of this kind. Wherefore it seems that one must arrive at the feud of a duchy, which by its preeminent nobility renders its subject illustrious. Since, therefore, we have regard here not only to utility but also to dignities, the way of the feud is nobler. For the lord is bound to the vassal in the same manner as the vassal is bound to the lord, although the vassal swears fealty to the lord and not vice versa, as in c. 1 and the following title, de forma fidelitatis, colla. 10; whence the vassal can demand the aids of the lord when it is expedient for him concerning the feud, to which the lord would not be bound by an emphyteutic contract or by a grant of a vicariate. And therefore the way of the feud is nobler, loftier, and more useful. And because a feud is sometimes regulated according to nature, sometimes according to pacts, which are a second nature, as in c. 1, § cum vero corradus, qui feud. dare possunt, and in c. 1, de natura feud., and in c. 1, de feudo non habente propriam naturam, it is lawful by agreement to depart from the simple nature of a feud, as in c. 1, de eo, qui sibi, et haeredibus suis masculis, et foeminis. For contracts from an agreement produce the law for the act, ff. depositi, l. 1, § si convenerit; whence by agreement females may succeed to a masculine feud who otherwise would not succeed; in which case they will be able to perform the services through a substitute, because this is understood to have been tacitly agreed, ff. de verbo. obliga., l. continuus, § si ab eo. Likewise, a woman shall not be bound except to those things that befit the female sex, by the argument of ff. qui petant tutores, l. credendum. Likewise, by agreement one can swear fealty to the lord receiving it for himself and his successors, and provided that if he did not swear to a new Pope, he would no longer incur forfeiture; because the oath on the part of the recipient is real, although on the part of the swearer it is personal on account of the exception and nature of the oath itself, which inheres in its own subject, so that they do not communicate alien matters, as in C. de rebus credito., l. generaliter, in the beginning, and elegantly noted by Innocen., extra de iureiuran., c. veritatis. Since, therefore, by agreement or the clauses of a privilege all doubts can be clarified with the consent of the Apostolic See, so that by the clear nature of the words all matter of dispute may be cut away, as in ff. de verbo. obligatio., l. stipulationes, it is most advantageous so to arrange it. Furthermore, regarding the succession of a female, it would not be equitable that she succeed along with male offspring, nor useful to the subjects; and therefore females are accustomed not to be included, or if they are included, they are accustomed to be placed in default of surviving males;

† and good styles are to be observed, because they were invented by the more experienced; and where there is prudence, there repentance is dead, as in C. de divor., l. dubium, and C. de dona., l. si avia. Behold, therefore, what I think concerning the case of my magnificent lords of the glorious House of Malatesta; nevertheless, whichever of the three ways they hold, it is valid in law, because the subject matter is capable of any of the aforesaid three forms, although the more elegant form is the form of a feud, through which the feudatory shines more brightly, as in l. 1, C. de praepositis laborum, lib. 12. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A stipulation made for oneself and for Titius extends to the heirs of the stipulator, but not to the heirs of Titius, by the very nature of the right inherent therein.
body: ...of which, see here...

† Likewise, the form of the words which here appears to be most personal, because it says 'for himself'; but this is no obstacle, because if one stipulates for himself or for Titius, he is understood to stipulate also for his own heirs, but not for the heirs of Titius. For this expression, 'for himself', demonstrates, but does not restrict; and because a personal statement is construed with the principal verb, not with the executive verb, ff. de probationibus, l. si pactum. Whence the expression 'for himself' is an expression of foundation, but not of restriction, ff. de act. et obli. l. quaecunque; ff. de verb. obli. l. eum, qui. §. qui sibi. Whence it signifies the beginning, but not the end, and renders the statement complete in subject and predicate, C. de consti. pec. auth. si quando; which the continuation of real words shows, ff. de iuris, et facti igno. l. regula. §. fi. and by the argument of extra de appella. c. 2. requiris. For statements joined by a copula of identity, and not of diversity, mutually borrow their meanings from one another, arg. ff. de fun. instr. l. cum de lanionis. §. 1. This is referred back in the following consilium where it is marked 'oportet. n. naturam sequi'. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. Whether privileges pass to sons or successors, and when; and in number 5.
3. The cause stated by the prince is presumed to be final.
4. The nature of the thing must be considered in every disposition.
5. Whether a real, personal, or hypothecary obligation passes to heirs.
6. Whether a privilege passes to successors and sons, and when.
7. The prince is bound to renew the father’s privilege for his sons; otherwise, he does them an injury.
8. What the phrase “for himself” signifies.
body: for the evidence that

† It must be premised, for the sake of clarity, that one privilege is personal, another is real, and another is reasonably doubtful as to whether it is real or personal; or there may be found in it an intermediate jurisdiction, disposition, or a diverse one with respect to the extremes—for instance, on the part of the grantor it ends with the person, but on the part of the recipient it passes to the successor; or, conversely, it extends to certain burdens, or to certain cases, and to other burdens or cases it does not. In all of which it is necessary diligently to examine the tenor of the privilege, as in de priuilegiis, c. porro. For all privileges are by nature of strict interpretation, because they impair the common law, and therefore they rely on the words. Moreover, belonging to the words and the tenor is also the cause or reason written in the privilege; for the reason reveals what was said, and discloses and demonstrates its meaning, as in ff. de acqui. poss. l. si is, qui animo, and ff. de haere. insti. l. fi.

† which cause, when posited by the prince, is presumed to be final and true, even though it contains enunciative words, by the argument in C. de testam. mili. l. ex his verbis fortunato, and as noted in c. 1 de probat. in cle. It must also be considered whether it is granted upon a transmissible matter, namely, one which does not naturally and necessarily adhere to the person,

† because we look to the nature of the thing in every disposition, C. de cad. toll. §. ne autem; ff. de ver. obl. l. stipulatio ista. §. si quis ita. For it is necessary to follow nature, ff. de ver. ob. l. ita stipulatus. la granda, because nature itself governs conditions, ff. de cond. et dem. l. pater Seuerinam. §. conditionem. And regarding this it must be considered whether the burdens consist in a personal obligation, or in a real or hypothecary obligation. And I say that if they are attached or imposed upon persons by reason of a poll-tax [munus capitis], there is both a personal and a hypothecary obligation:

† which hypothecary obligation, however, does not consist in all the goods, but only in that affected property; and this hypothecary obligation can exist without a personal obligation, as noted in ff. de publicanis, l. conmissa, and ff. ad Trebell. l. si haeres. And because it consists in possession, as in ff. de euictio. l. si cum venditio in patri, and possession does not pass to the heir by hereditary right, but by apprehension, as in l. 1. §. Scaeuola, ff. si quis testamento liber esse iussus fuerit, it follows that the heir is not bound by such a hypothecary obligation as an heir, unless it had been brought into judgment, as in l. i, ff. de pręto. stipu., and l. de eo, §. fi., ff. ad exhiben. The nature of real actions is to pass to the heir of the plaintiff, but not to the heir of the possessor, unless legal proceedings have been commenced. Moreover, immunities benefit those who possess, but are not necessary for those not possessing, because the latter are not bound by a hypothecary obligation. It can also be said that, although there is no personal obligation, there is nevertheless the office of the judge, to which the hypothecary action adheres; and these points are true, these premises being established.

† It follows to consider whether the privilege passes to successors. Dynus says that either the person is the immediate cause of the privilege, and then the right acquired from the privilege passes to the heir, because it took its form, origin, and perfection in the form of the deceased, as Dynus notes in c. priuilegium personale; but Petrus says that either the privilege is not enclosed in the body of the law, and does not pass, l. 1, §. permittitur, de aqua quoti., and l. 1, de iure immunitatis; or it is enclosed in the body of the law, and then it is granted having regard to natural equity, and it passes to the heir, as in ff. de in integrum restitu., non solum, because of natural equity, and also because the person of the heir is represented by the person of the deceased. Likewise, the condition of the obligation is not changed by the person of the heir, neither as to its essence, nor as to its contestation, as in ff. de verbo. obliga. l. 3; C. de restit. mili. l. qui a patre. Likewise, the office of the judge which arises from a privilege is capable of transmission, ff. de admini. tuto. l. si tutore. Or it is granted not by way of natural equity, but without any root in natural equity, and then it does not pass to the heir, ff. de regu. iur. l. in omnibus; ff. de consti. principum, l. 1, according to Petrus and Cynus, who note this so elegantly, C. ad Velle. l. haeredem. From this theory it would seem concluded that the said immunity was extinguished by death, because a successive and not instantaneous benefit admits of division of time, so that it may endure for part of the time, and for part of the time not endure, ff. so. ma. l. alia; ff. de re iu. l. sed hoc ita; and l. assiduis, C. qui pot. in pig. habeantur, with its subject-matter. But certainly, it rather seems that the said privilege passes to the sons and posterity on the following ground: because whenever children are the cause of the privilege, the privilege passes to them, as in the said l. assiduis; and conversely, if parents are the cause of granting a privilege to children, it ought to pass to the children of the children on account of love and honor for the parents, even if the parents have ceased to be among the living, and thus the merits of the fathers pass to the sons. Likewise, because that privilege seems to have been granted to memory and nobility, which is understood to live on through glory. Likewise, even if those reasons were not sufficient, that other reason nonetheless suffices,

† because the prince is bound to revoke, otherwise he does an injustice; the text is golden and common in the said §. permittitur. Furthermore, granted that a personal privilege is terminated with the person, that is true unless the grantor went further by extending it. But here he went further through an extensive and exemplary similitude; for that which is present in the exemplifying term is deemed to be present in the exemplified term, even by tacit repetition, as in ff. de condit. et dem. l. in testamento; ff. de dote pręlegata. l. Theopompus, there where it says, “knowing my intention with unequal sums.” For since the prince equalized them to other nobles named in the privilege, everything and whatever he granted to those, he is also deemed to have granted to lord Antonius in the same manner, form, and order, as in C. de rei vxo. act. l. rem in praesenti, §. 1, and l. i, ff. de leg. 1. This is supported by what is noted in l. edita act., on the word, as the doctors note: similitudinary words attached to indefinite terms, and not in a determined manner, are deemed to repeat the same form, as in de ver. sig. l. abb. Furthermore, positing that the immunities were terminated once the person was terminated, nevertheless the liberty acquired for the territory would be perpetual, because the nature of liberties, like that of servitudes, is perpetual, ff. de censib. l. forma. §. quiquam; ff. de seruitutib. l. seruit. Likewise, mystical or figurative bodies, such as servitudes are, are not said to die, because to live with the living is to be always in them, found mystically, C. de fructib. et litis expensis, l. fi.

† Nor does the phrase “for himself,” which is in the letters of the lord, stand in the way, for a disposition is not always rendered personal by this phrase; because it is not placed strictly, but for the purpose of enlarging the grace there is added, “and to those written below,” etc. Likewise because mention is made of the heirs of the late Lord Gilbert; thus the intention of the speaker appears, by the argument in ff. de vino legato. l. fi. §. cui dulcia. And this is the virtue of the conjunction: because it has the effect of enlarging, ff. de leg. 3. l. ea tamen adiectio; ff. de fundo instru. l. seges. §. Caio. Bartolus says that a personal benefit is buried with the person, concerning the authority and use of the pallium [...], whether it be a material benefit, as of the pallium, or an intellectual one. From the aforesaid it is concluded in favor of the said noble sons, that they are not to be disturbed in the said privilege, but defended together with the testimonies. And what is noted by Bartolus in l. pater, de ser. leg., and extra de institutionibus, c. cum nouisset, through Innocent, and ff. de pac. l. iurisgentium. §. pactorum, through Guilielmus and Bartolus, serves the aforesaid extremely well. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Given a statute providing that whoever attempts to commit adultery shall be punished by beheading. Now, a certain man made an attempt, but because the woman cried out, he fled. The question is whether he ought to be beheaded, or whether he should be punished by some other penalty, and how the word *nixus* is to be interpreted.
body: it is provided that whoever

† By a statute of Piacenza it is provided that whoever strives (nixus fuerit) to commit adultery shall be beheaded. Now Titius, with the intent of committing adultery, seized Bertha and threw her to the ground, but she resisted and cried out, and Titius, frightened by her cry, fled; he was captured by the podestà of Piacenza, and an inquest was drawn up against him narrating the deed and charging the intention to commit adultery; he confessed the wrongdoing. It is asked whether he ought to be beheaded; and it seems that he should, because this appears to be an abduction of a woman, as in l. 1, C. de raptu virginum. Likewise, even if the abduction was not consummated, it is nevertheless an enormous crime attempted and carried out through a proximate act, as in l. si quis non dicam rapere, C. de epi. et cle. Likewise, because the statute speaks clearly and expressly by punishing the striving; therefore, since we have the law, we ought to follow it, even though it may be harsh and exceedingly rigorous, as in ff. qui, et a quibus, l. prospexit; for it is not ours to rescind the statute, either simply or in a certain respect, because a judge ought not to be more merciful than the law, as in Auth. de iudicib. §. oportet. Likewise, this man committed adultery in his heart and even in his deed, and therefore Divine Scripture judges him an adulterer; and thus by two laws, divine and human, he ought to be punished as an adulterer, and more strongly and expressly under the municipal law. To the contrary seems to be the truth: for either you argue from the ius commune, and then custom, which interprets the ius commune, provides that he should be punished more mildly, that is, with a pecuniary penalty, as Speculator says, and as noted through Cynus on C. ad l. Corneliam de sicariis, l. is, qui cum telo; nor is it true that this is the crime of abduction, for to abduct is to drag from place to place with force, as in ff. ne quis eum, qui in ius vocatus est, l. sed eximendi; or you speak of divine law, and then through indulgence the penalty would be remitted, and we do not use this divine law in court, but it is left to God alone; or you speak of municipal law, and in this lies the whole weight of this question; and to know this, it is necessary to expound this word, 'nixus'. There is the text in l. finali, §. penult., C. de temp. appell., which expounds it as 'having striven with supreme effort' (summa ope nixus); and the Gloss on the chapter ex eo, de regulis iuris, in the Sext, expounds 'nixus' as, namely, with effect, or because he persevered. And I expound 'nixus' as meaning that he did whatever he could, and it was not through him that he failed to arrive, namely, at the proximate and immediate act, as because he wished to open the enclosures of modesty, and it did not rest with him that he did not. For an act is not called proximate if another is more proximate; for example, if someone touches garments or grasps by the clothes. And this is evident from natural reason, for that is called proximate which, being assumed, the other follows continuously and easily: argument from ff. de servitutibus rusticorum praediorum, l. tria praedia, and l. qui sella, §. in rusticis. Moreover, he who flees is not understood to persevere, but rather to abandon what he had begun: argument from C. de falsis, l. qui falsam. From these things it is concluded that this man is not said to have striven (nixus), but to have begun to strive or to have wished to strive, because it is not stated in the inquest that he did whatever he could and that it did not rest with him. From which it follows that this man ought not to be beheaded, but under another chapter of the statute he is to be punished with a pecuniary penalty, as the discretion of the judge shall dictate; for in matters of discretion no fixed form is given, as in ff. de effractoribus et expilatoribus, l. 1, §. expilatores; ff. de poenis, l. hodie; and noted on ff. de infamibus, l. quid ergo, §. poena gravior. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The statute that a woman shall not marry outside the territory with the inheritance, etc., how it is to be understood, is discussed in this most elegant opinion. And no. 3.
2. How the term "inheritance" is to be understood.
4. A father cannot disinherit a daughter from her maternal inheritance.
5. Who is called an outsider.
6. Whether a woman marrying with a maternal dowry is said to have married with the maternal inheritance.
7. The word "with" — what it signifies.
body: In the name of Christ. No woman shall marry with an inheritance outside the jurisdiction of the commune of Milan; and if she has married outside the jurisdiction, she shall not succeed to anyone belonging to the jurisdiction of Milan; but that inheritance shall pass to the nearest agnates or other relatives; and this applies whether it passes by testament or intestate. And in the same manner it shall pass to the nearest agnates or other relatives if any inheritance is deferred or opened to a woman married outside the jurisdiction of the commune of Milan; and the same shall be and be understood in all descendants of such women who are born of one not subject to the jurisdiction of the lord podestà and the commune of Milan.

† One must weigh each individual word of the statute, in which its meaning rests. And first, that word, "se nubat" [she marries]. Second, that word, "cum haereditate" [with an inheritance]. Third, that, "extra iurisdictionem" [outside the jurisdiction]. Fourth, that word, "non succedat alicui de iurisdictione" [she shall not succeed to anyone of the jurisdiction]. Fifth, that word, "sed illa haereditas perueniat in agnatos, vel alios propinquos" [but that inheritance shall pass to the agnates or other relatives]. Sixth, the sixth clause. Seventh, the seventh. I return to the first: the words say "se nubat", which, disregarding grammar, means to marry; where it must be considered whether she who is married by her father appears to marry herself. And it seems that she does, because the substance of marriage comes from oneself, that is, from one's own and immediate consent, without which marriage can neither be initiated nor lawfully consummated, as in C. de nup. l. in copulandis and l. nec filium. To the contrary it seems that the father is the author of these nuptials, and it consists in the father's power and authority—I do not say of the father alone, but together with the daughter, as in ff. de contratab. l. 3. si emancipatus, ff. de iure do. l. adoptiuum; whence this proposition, "she married herself," is not simply true unless there is added "with the father's authority"; but the statute does not speak of that addition, and thus when the words of the statute cease, the statute ceases, because a compound is not contained under simple terms, whether it is distinguished in reality or by difference of cases, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. hoc legatum est; especially since, out of reverence for paternal authority, she seems to have consented rather than to have chosen a husband, as in ff. quarum rerum actio non da. l. 1. §. quae onerandae. Likewise because the father's command, even tacit, excuses a girl remaining in his power from the penalty of inability to succeed and from the statute, as in ff. de regu. iur. l. ad ea, because in such an act there is no fraud, but rather it is a penalty without fault, ff. de actio. et oblig. l. seruus non in omnibus, ff. de his, qui notantur infamia. l. 1.

† Next in the statute is that phrase, "cum haereditate" [with an inheritance]. And indeed, an inheritance is said to belong to a deceased person; when, however, it has been accepted, it becomes the property of the living person and is not properly an inheritance, ff. de vulg. substi. l. sed si plures. §. filio and l. 1. §. sciendum ff. de separatione bonorum. To the contrary it seems: because it is called an inheritance with respect to what it once was, and it is also now a right and an estate body, ff. de verb. sign. l. nihil aliud and C. de peti. haeredi. throughout. Moreover, if these words spoke only of a vacant inheritance [haereditas iacens], they would presuppose an impossibility, because since the right of accepting is a direct and inseparable right, it cannot be ceded, as in l. si mulier. §. ex asse ff. de iure dotium; and therefore this word, "inheritance", here stands for the hereditary patrimony, as in ff. de haereditate, vel actione vendita throughout. But although this is true only to this extent, join the whole phrase together: for it says, "no woman shall marry with an inheritance." Now let us see,

† whether this girl married with an inheritance. And it seems that she did, because she appears tacitly to have given her property as dowry, as noted in ff. de iu. dotium. l. mulier. To the contrary it seems: because there can be a marriage without a dowry claimed by the girl, if it proceeds from the father or a stranger, or from no one, as in C. de dona. l. fi. and quando, et quibus quarta pars debetur. l. vlti. and l. 1. C. de imponenda lucratiua descriptione. book 10. The solution: it must be conceded that this girl did not marry with an inheritance, nor is she bound to ratify what her father did,

† a father cannot abdicate the maternal inheritance from his daughter: because either he does this by way of delict, and the delict of the father does not harm the daughter, as in C. ne filius pro patre in rubro et nigro; or by way of repudiation: and the same holds, as in C. de bonis, quae liberis. l. quod non solum in princip.; or by way of contract and alienation: and it is certain that the father cannot alienate, even though he has the usufruct, as in C. de bonis maternis. l. 1; and because it is not transferred to another, it does not depart from the original ownership, as in ff. qui. ex cau. maio. l. denique; moreover, to bring it about that a daughter cannot transmit nor make a will, but must remain excluded, would be to alienate the daughter from the common law. Moreover, this daughter does not have to claim as an heir, but to sue under the contract of transaction, although this reasoning will not hold for the sons of the daughter, who

† necessarily must claim to be heirs of their mother. Now it is certain that the statute must not be understood absurdly, so that an unjust condition can be imposed upon that girl—and especially a minor under 25 years of age—by her father or paternal uncle, and she be disqualified from succeeding, ff. de haer. inst. l. pater, ff. de iur. et fac. ign.; which is also most iniquitous when they are lawful administrators, because they ought to protect property, not squander or overthrow it, as in l. qui fundum. §. si tutor ff. de vsucap. pro emp. According to the matters submitted, the statute does not speak to our case: because the beginning of the fact does not match the statute, and from the beginning of the title the subsequent event is formed. Likewise, those words, "marries with an inheritance," signify that she is heir and owner, because the prohibition of alienation signifies that ownership precedes, as in l. si ita ff. de manu. testameto; for transfer cannot take place unless ownership precedes, because he who has nothing can transfer nothing, as in Auth. Ingressi and l. traditio ff. de acq. re. do. For it must then be observed that if she is once an heir, marrying does not cause her to cease being an heir, because she cannot cease to be the same person as the deceased, in which identity the fictitious continuation of ownership consists, as in l. si sine. §. sed papi. ff. de mino. and ff. de haer. inst. l. aliquo casu. But what if this woman who married a foreigner dies? Children born of the foreigner do not succeed to her, being in the case of the statute, because they are held as nothing, and those who are held as nothing do not make a degree or an impediment to others, as in ff. de lib. et posth. l. Gallus. §. et quid si tamen and ff. de coniungen. cum eman. lib. l. 1. §. si pater and ff. ad tertu. l. 2. §. obijciatur; for he who has no right of succession in the city is counted among non-entities, as in ff. de vul. sub l. lex Cornelia. Let us clarify the matter with an example, because examples show a matter as with a finger and subject it in a way to touch, as in Inst. de gradibus. §. sed cum magis, as in l. 1. de prescrip. ver. Let the example then be such: of two sisters, one married a foreigner, the other a citizen of Milan. As long as she who married the foreigner lives, there is no question of her succession, as in C. de capti. l. nec nos; no one, while alive, has an heir except in hope, ff. de lib. et posth. l. in suis, ff. de acqui. haere. l. qui superstitis. If she who married the foreigner dies, therefore, with children surviving her, let the sister or another from that stock succeed by the statute, and not the children born of her who married contrary to the statute, because so dictates the statute made in favor of the commonwealth of the enactors themselves, rather than of those marrying; nor is it any wonder, because this occurs elsewhere, that outside the territory succession is not open to be deferred to those who are not of the same territory, as in l. 1. C. non licere arbitratoribus metrocomiae. For that statute has its origin in a subject, although it proceeds to a foreigner; and because a law addressed to the principal and subject extends itself by a certain prejudicial consequence also to a non-subject, because the legislator looks to what is principal, as by way of foundation, as in l. 1 ff. de auto. tu. and ff. de lib. leg. l. si is, qui duos.

† But is he said to be a foreigner who has a domicile in Milan? I answer no, because as to forum and property he is a true citizen of Milan, as noted in c. statutum. §. cum auth. de rescriptis. in VI, even if after contracting the marriage he changes his domicile: because the statute referred to the beginning of the marriage, as in l. quid ergo in princ. ff. de his, qui notantur infa. Finally I conclude that our case must be disposed according to the common law: because the statutory terms cease according to the matters that were proposed, as in ff. de acq. haere. l. si seruum. §. non dixit. But how can the Milanese enact that a foreigner, say a Pavese, cannot claim a maternal dowry consisting in quantity or in kind, for generic things are not in a territory, as in ff. de iud. l. fideicom. §. tractatum and l. vlti. C. de praescri. lon. tem.? Since therefore they are not in the territory, nor of the territory of the enactors, their statute is not valid, as in c. postulasti. de foro com. by Innocent; unless we say that actions are said to belong to that place where they ought to be exercised, as in ff. de solu. l. quem, or where they took their origin by reason of contract or quasi-contract, as in ff. de iudiciis. l. haeres absens. But then l. exigere dotem ff. de iudiciis would seem sufficiently to stand in the way regarding dowry, where it is said that the domicile of the husband is looked to, wherever the contract was celebrated. But I answer that that law can be derogated from by an express statute of the place, just as it could be derogated from by a pact; because statutes and customs have the force of a pact made by the consent of all citizens. But I do not dwell on this, because the practice of Milan so maintains.

† I ask whether a woman who says, "marry me with my maternal dowry," is said to have married with a maternal inheritance, assuming that there is nothing else in the inheritance than the dowry? I answer no, because if a mother testates concerning a dowry, she does not thereby testate concerning an inheritance, but concerning a specific thing or a quantity; and this is fully noted in ff. de transac. l. controuersia and C. de haered. institu. l. quotiens; and the difference is apparent from this, that a dowry and an inheritance are not of the same nature, nor of the same definition: and from this it clearly appears that the girl about whom inquiry is made here, and her sons, and her descendants are not included in the prohibition of the statute, because she did not marry with an inheritance.

† For the word "cum" [with], being a copula, requires the participation of both parts. I, Baldus. As to a statute that for any property alienated to a subject only so much per pound should be paid: does it extend to legacies in a testament to a non-subject and to legacies to the church?

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the term "alienation" includes a last will.
2. A clause placed at the end clarifies all that precedes.
3. A prohibition on alienation does not include a son.
4. Whether immunity can be acquired by prescription, and for what period of time.
body: A certain Lucchese citizen left in his will certain possessions to certain persons who are not subjects. Likewise, from other assets he ordered two chapels to be established and endowed; and a statute is presupposed, wherein it is provided that whoever of the city and district of Lucca shall have wished to alienate in any manner any immovable property unto anyone who is not subject to the jurisdiction of the commune of Lucca, shall pay ten soldi of every pound of the true appraisal of the property that he alienates or transfers unto another who is not subject to the jurisdiction of the aforesaid commune; and if an alienation should happen to take place without payment, it shall fall ipso iure, and be understood to have fallen, into the right and ownership of the commune of Lucca; and the contract shall be null and void ipso iure. It is asked what the law is, and whether the commune can by its own authority seize possession, the prescription of time notwithstanding.

† And for clarity it must first be considered whether the last will is contained under the name of alienation. And it seems undoubtedly that it is, because an alienation is every act through which ownership is transferred, as in l. 1. de fundo dotali. But it is certain that through a last will ownership is transferred, as in l. 1. and 2. C. communia de legatis. Furthermore, that prohibition is general, as in C. de secun. nup. l. hac edictali, and l. si quis iuris, §. certum, there where it says, “it will be seen to be an alienation of property, because it is in a will”; therefore the statute claims application for itself, because the words of statutes are to be observed just as they lie, as in ff. de exerci. l. 1. §. si is, qui nauem, and what is noted there. To the contrary it seems: we shall say either that the testator alienated—and that does not seem true, because during the lifetime of the testator the day of the legacy does not yield [its right], as in C. de cadu. tollen. §. et cum triplici; likewise, the legatee cannot accept except after the testator is dead; likewise, even after he has died, if he repudiates the legacy, it is not said to be alienated, ff. si cer. pet. l. proinde—or we shall say that the heir alienated, and that does not seem true, because since the text of the statute says, “when he shall have wished to alienate,” a certain heir alienates not voluntarily, but out of necessity, as in ff. de lega. 2. l. vnum ex familia, in principio. Furthermore, it seems absurd that the said statute be understood to apply to a last will, which ought to be free with respect to the testator, as in C. de sac.san. eccl. l. 1, and gratuitous with respect to the legatee, as in l. hęredem, ff. mandati. Solution: The words of the statute seem to decide this question, namely that the said statute does not have place except in contracts, because the words of the statute say, “and the contract shall be null and void ipso iure,”

† which clause clarifies the whole statute, ff. de iurisdictio. omnium iudi. l. si idem. cum eodem, §. fina., and extra de appel. c. secundo requiris, and C. de prae. curia. l. fi. lib. 10. And it proves this by such reasoning: for although the beginning of the law seems general, or indefinite, because it says “in any manner,” nevertheless after the genus there follows a restrictive species, because it adds “and the contract, etc.”; whence the species restricts the genus, as in ff. de verbo. signi. l. si cum fundum, ff. de leg. 2. l. legatorum, §. qui plures; and especially because the words “they transacted” and “they contracted” do not pertain to testaments, as in ff. de verb. signi. l. verba gesserunt. Regarding that, however, which is left to chapels of the city of Lucca or outside it, it is less doubtful, because the Gloss says that the church is held in the place of a son, ff. de verbo. obliga. l. si ita quis, §. ea. l.,

† although a son is not included in a prohibition of alienation, as in l. 1. C. de impo. lucra. descrip. lib. 10. Likewise, because under the general word of “non-subjects” the liberty of the churches is not contained, nor does anything appear to have been devised against it, especially because it would induce mortal sin; for he sins mortally who ordains anything in fraud of the liberty of the church, as in c. non minus, and c. aduersus, de immuni. eccle.; and I say this unless by custom and practice the said statute has been extended to last wills, for just as it has been practiced, so ought it to be observed, save where it is against the liberty of the church.

† And then, whether prescription would run against immunity, and of what time, recourse must be had to the determination of the Doctors on l. vlti. C. de sacr. sanc. eccle., as in ff. de diuer. et tempo. prae. l. intra. 4. §. in omnibus, and by Dyn. in l. 2. de regu. iur. lib. 6. For if indeed they have not been incorporated into the fiscus, as is the case here—since they have not been denounced to the fiscus—twenty years are required from the time at which they were acquired through the municipal law for the fiscus or community. But if they had been denounced to the fiscus by some promoter, it would be prescribed by the space of four years; and the statute is no obstacle, because since it disposes nothing concerning prescription, it is left to the disposition of the common law. Furthermore, it must be noted that the said statute does not invalidate anything except contracts, and therefore not last wills, which are more favored, as in ff. de regulis iur. l. in testamentis. But nevertheless, there seem to be things contrary to this reasoning: because concerning property confiscated ipso facto, a testament cannot be confirmed, since the things have departed from the corpus of the inheritance, and have been transferred to the fiscus before to the legatee; which would be true if that statute were interpreted to apply to last wills, and prescription had not run, but the periods of time were elapsing. In what manner, however, the statute has been practiced and customarily understood is not established to me, and therefore upon this article I cannot advise except as upon a doubtful proposition, save by distinguishing as above. And you should know that the opinion of Barto. is that on account of an unpaid tax—which is similar to our case—in things not incorporated prescription runs against the fiscus in four years, as he himself noted in said l. in omnibus, counting from the day on which the fiscus began to be able to act. But the former distinction pleases me more, because a tax does not pertain to immovable things, but to movable things, which are more easily prescribed. And that which is said, that the property of the fiscus is not usucapted, is true in incorporated things, in which usucaption undertaken ceases, as in insti. de vsucap. §. res fisci; and add what I, Baldus, noted in ff. de iure fisci, l. 1. §. an bona.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A rescript of the prince that is ambitious is not to be executed, but rather a response must be written to the prince. And why it is called ambitious, because it contains injustices and vices, with the truth being tacitly expressed.
2. Whether the assertive words of the prince prove anything, and if proof to the contrary is admitted, whether it transfers the burden of proof to the contrary.
3. Restitution does not draw consumed fruits.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that settlements were made, and judgments rendered and confirmed, between the agnates and the spurious sons of a testator; and that, without the said agnates having been cited, when it was asserted to the Emperor that the said agnates had killed the testator, he legitimated the said spurious sons and restored the goods to them, appointing an executor to effect their entry upon the inheritance, notwithstanding any contracts whatsoever and any prescription of time whatsoever. Now, since the said agnates were not cited, nor those deriving title from them, and since also one of the said spurious sons was deceased,

† it is asked whether or not the legitimation by the Emperor harms the heirs of the said agnates and those deriving title from them, considering also that a forty-year prescription has already run. And it is a wonder how such a rescript came out of the chancery, since it contains so many abhorrent inequities and absurdities, as in extra de rescriptis, c. 2; for it is said to have issued upon asserted deceits, with natural and civil defenses removed, especially because it takes away all things that are of the ius gentium, likewise settlements, likewise prescriptions, likewise a testament, and likewise it disposes concerning a person already dead. From all of which I believe it is void, as the prince was circumvented; nor is it probable that the prince willed this, as in c. quamuis, de rescriptis, lib. 6, and as fully noted by the Moderns in l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum, de liber. et posthu. Likewise, legitimation is a kind of regeneration, but after death nothing can be regenerated, as in ff. de oper. lib., l. qui libertinus, §. posthumus. Likewise, it is presumed clandestine, from the fact that the possessor was not cited, as in C. vnde vi, l. meminerint; C. si per vim, vel alio modo, l. fina.; ff. de natali. restitu., l. vlti.; C. si propter publi. pensi., l. si deserta. Furthermore, even if the agnates had killed the testator and were unworthy, nonetheless a judicial sentence is required, as in l. his consequenter, §. 1, ff. fami. herci.; ff. de iure fisci, l. Lucius; which could not be pronounced upon homicide without the party having been cited, as in extra de re iudica., c. pastoralis, in clemen.; and since the rescript is void through grounds of suspicion, the functions of the executor cease, as in l. 4, §. condemnatum, ff. de re iudica. Likewise, he is not a mere executor who has to ascertain whether the petition rests on truth, and therefore defenses, if any are competent, ought to be heard, C. si contra ius, vel vti. pub., l. et si non cognitio and l. fi., and as fully noted by Innocent and others in extra de re iudica., c. de caetero. Furthermore, even a mere executor must not inquire into the substance of the prince's rescript, as in extra de iudiciis, c. cum venisset, because he would make himself superior or equal to the prince and would place his seat in the North by attempting to be like the Most High, as in C. de crimine sacrilegii, l. instar; nonetheless, the prince's rescript appears void by law itself and to contain very many defects, wherefore it ought not to be executed, and he ought to consult the prince himself, a copy of the consultation having been given to the party, and wait for a second transmission, as is read and noted in Authem. de mandatis principum, §. deinde comparationes; nor is an injury thereby done to the prince, since it is done by mandate of the law and not in contempt of the prince, C. de prae. impera. offe., l. rescripta. For the guileless ears of princes, judging others by their own nature, are presumed to be circumvented by the importunity of petitioners, as in C. de petitio. bonorum sublatis, l. 1, li. 10; and such rescripts are called ambitious, as in ff. de decretis ab ordine faciendis, l. ambitiosa; and they induce sin, that is, the plunder of another's goods, and would subvert the just and ancient ownership of things—which is iniquitous and contrary to good morals; and other such rescripts are never accustomed to issue when a just king sits upon the throne, against whom nothing malicious prevails, as in C. de summa trin., l. epistola inter claras. But if the impetrant wished to justify and prove the rescript as contained in the petition, then the rescript ought to be committed to execution, the order of law having been observed against the holders of the inheritance and the goods of the said testator; because the prince can grant effective graces not only for strictly determined causes, but also from just motives and occasions, and can rescind what seems to him unjust, as noted in the prooemium of the Digest; for this occurs either on account of the superabundance of the merits of him to whom it is granted, or on account of hatred of the wrongdoers from whom it is taken away, as in l. 1, ff. de constitutionibus principum. Likewise, consider that here no mention was made of matters judged and arbitrated, except in a perfunctory and uncertain manner, which operates nothing; and see what is noted in l. turpia, de lega. 1.

† Likewise, this is not in the granted matters and the principal verb of the rescript, but in the enunciative clause 'non obstante'; which enunciative words do not dispose, but assist if they can, otherwise not, as in c. 1, de praebendis, in clemen. From which it is concluded, as above, that unless the death is proved along with the other things to be proved, the rescript does not hold. It is therefore doubted—because the prince in the dispositive words seems to declare that he does not do so through error, and to hold the aforesaid causes as true and legitimate—whether proof to the contrary is admitted against this disposition of the prince; and if it is admitted, whether the burden of proving the contrary is transferred to the agnates and nephews themselves, or rather to the spurious sons and those adopted. According to what is noted in clemen. 1, de probationibus, wherein it is said that against the assertive words of the prince, namely those in which the grace is founded, if indeed the prince attests to his own act, proof to the contrary is not admitted; but concerning another's act, such an assertion transfers the burden of proof to the adversary. For this does not hold in that which the prince is probably ignorant of; and such an assertion of the prince does not create law to the prejudice of an innocent person. Furthermore, here a negative could not be proved; hence it would not only transfer the burden of proof, but would totally swallow up the defense of the absent party, which is of natural law, as is the case in the said c. pastoralis. Likewise, those words do not stand in the way, since those deriving title from them would have prescribed at least through just titles, as in C. de praescrip. triginta annorum, l. si quis emptionis. Likewise, the prince claims information through certain letters, which information is a kind of report, and upon that information he founds himself; but that information or report does not prejudice an absent and ignorant person, as in C. de rela., l. 1. Likewise, even the prince ought to cite when he pronounces, as in C. vnde vi, l. meminerint; ff. de adop., l. nam ita diuus. Likewise, the possessor is always to be cited, as in c. licet episcopo, de praeb., lib. 6, and C. si propter publicas pensitationes, l. si deserta. Likewise, concerning the fruits there is no doubt, and especially concerning those consumed, that the said rescript ought not to be understood of them, but especially of those that are extant, not those that are not extant, ff. de vsuc., l. sequitur fructus,

† and restitution does not drag in consumed fruits, as in C. de haeret., Authen. idem de necessariis. And for certain, the said rescript contains many enormities upon inspection; and although the Emperor has fullness of power, nonetheless he can err in law and in fact, and therefore at least a second command ought to be awaited before execution is made, as in Authen. vt iudi. non expectent sacras iussiones and in Auth. in medio litis non fieri sacras formas, col. 8. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The fisc has the moneys collected by its tax farmers from provisions, even if they have come into the hands of a third-party depositary; and a negotiorum gestor must not convert the principal’s moneys to his own use.
2. Utility succeeds in place of the thing.
3. The confession of the treasurer does not prejudice the prince, nor the city.
body: ...seems to be this, the banker...

† The conclusion of the fact seems to be this: the banker first paid himself interest upon his principal before the treasury was paid from its excise taxes and revenues, and thus the said banker undermined the fiscal accounts, and out of the funds of the treasury paid himself, or caused his principal to be paid. The treasury reclaims the interest; the banker reclaims; but the banker, whom they call a discounter, says that he contracted nothing with the treasury, nor did he receive interest—which he calls profit—from the treasury. Likewise, he alleges a certain confession of the treasurer, through which he pretends to be released from the moneys received by him, and from the treasury if he had been bound to it in any way. It is asked, what is the law? The tax collector, after he has collected the revenues or customs, is made owner of what has been collected, as Bartolus notes in ff. de publi. l. cotem. §. qui maximos. Nevertheless, for the amount for which he farmed the customs, those revenues which reached him are obligated to the treasury itself, on the basis of the argument in ff. de acti. emp. l. Iulianus. §. offerri. and l. si ventri. §. 1. ff. de pri. cre., as are also all his own goods, until full satisfaction has been made to the treasury, as in ff. de iure fis. l. aufertur. §. fiscus. And if the tax collector deposited or consigned the said moneys with any money-changer, until the money is consumed, there is no doubt that it is obligated to the treasury, because it still remains among the goods of the tax collector, as in ff. depositi. l. licet. §. rei depositae. But if the money is not extant, but has been consumed by the money-changer, and the money-changer has been made wealthier, without doubt the money-changer is liable to the treasury by an action upon the equity of the law (actio utilis),

† because an economic benefit succeeds in the place of the thing, as in ff. de vsufruct. l. qui precio., ff. de legatis secundo. l. Imperator. §. fin., and ff. de pign. l. cum tabernam. Now in the proposed case I say that the money-changer, or banker, was made wealthier from the fiscal revenues. And I prove this first with regard to the interest which he paid to himself, because to receive interest is indeed an odious gain, as in l. 1. C. de condictione indebit. Therefore, he must restore it, not as interest, but as the principal sum of the treasury, as in ff. de iure fisci. l. deferre. §. fina. and l. Titius; unless the banker himself had lent at interest with the consent of the lord, or the lord had mandated it to the banker himself, or to the treasurer, for the lender could retain what was paid for this reason, because it proceeds from the lord's will, and the lord ought not to make void what has proceeded from the lips of the lord: although to borrow at interest is a sin in the recipient, not in the provider, as in extra de iureiurand. capitu. debitores. And it pertains to the honor of the lord, indeed it pertains to his advantage, to pay agreed interest, otherwise he would rarely find a lender, as noted in l. prima. ff. de pigno. actio. Regarding the principal itself, in the name of Christ, of the two thousand florins converted to the benefit of the lord, there is no doubt that the lord is bound, and that a set-off can be made with him by the said banker. The conclusion therefore is this: that the lord is bound for the principal of the two thousand florins that reached him, and for the agreed interest for the said amount; but for the other sum, which the banker paid to the treasurer, the lord is not bound; rather, it ought to be restored to the lord, because the banker ought not to be enriched by his frauds, as was said, notwithstanding any confessions made in bad faith and extorted, because an administrator of affairs cannot convert the lord's moneys to his own uses to the lord's prejudice: ff. de negotio. gesto. l. qui sine vsuris est. and ff. mandati. l. creditor. §. Lucius. at the end, and the case is there. Likewise, the condition of the lord cannot be made worse by confessions in which fraud and deceit are present, because this does not seem to have been mandated or permitted, as in l. si pater. ff. de priui. credi., and ff. mandati. l. si mandauero. §. qui centum; which paragraph, by its rationale, applies exceptionally well to our question.

† The confession of the treasurer also does not prejudice the prince or the city, as in ff. si certum petatur. l. ciuitas. and Authen. hoc ius porrectum. C. de sacro sanct. eccle., and as noted in l. si pupilli. §. 1. ff. de negost. gest., and by Innocent in extra de deposito. capitulo grauis., and ff. de exercitoria. l. Lucius., and ff. de institoria. l. cuicunque. §. omne. And what has been paid before the due date is not reclaimed when the day arrives, as in ff. de cond. indeb. l. sub conditione. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When one person is killed by several, which of them is liable to the death penalty, and whether all are liable, or one, or two, etc., and whether the attempt is punished when the result does not follow.
body: A certain rumor has already been made in the name of Christ in the land of the Duchy of Milan, in which rumor a certain Vincentius de Taino was wounded with two wounds, namely one in the stomach with a bread knife by Antonius de Turate with great effusion of blood, and by Ambrosius, son of the aforementioned Antonius de Turate, with another wound in the right shoulder blade with a dagger with blood, from which an inquiry was formed by the Lord Podesta of Milan and the judge of malefices against the said Antonius and Ambrosius for the death of the said Vincentius. And let the said inquiry be seen, if it pleases. Afterwards, the aforementioned Ambrosius was captured and consigned to the prisons on account of the contents of the said inquiry, to which inquiry the said Ambrosius responded and denied being guilty of the contents thereof, but Antonius, as one who had absconded, was cited and banned from life. Afterwards, the aforementioned Ambrosius, personally detained as above, given a term by the aforementioned Lord judge for defense, made chapters, wishing to prove that the said wound inflicted in the stomach was not mortal, and thus not to be held liable for death, but to be condemned pecuniarily for the wound only, on which chapters certain witnesses, both physicians and others, were produced and received. And let the chapters and the witnesses produced and received be seen, as above. Now it is asked whether the said Ambrosius should be condemned for the said wound only and not for homicide, or not.

† If several persons struck one individual, and he died, the blow of each must be considered; and if the wound of one was mortal, and the wound of the other was not mortal—which can be assessed from the testimony of physicians regarding the quality of the location, the person, and the quality of the instrument, as in l. semel, C. de re militari, lib. 12; and ff. ad l. Corn. de sicariis, l. 1, §. sed si claua; and extra de utrum copula et homicidio, c. significasti—the law states that he whose blow caused death is liable for the homicide, while the other is not liable for the homicide, but only for the wounding, as in ff. ad l. Aquil., l. item mella, §. sed si plures. The ancients said that either a civil action is brought, and then that distinction is true, or a criminal action is brought under the Cornelian law on murderers, and then both are liable to the penalty for homicide, because one killed, and the other had the intent to kill, as in C. ad l. Corn. de sicariis, l. is qui cum telo. And thus punishment is more severe in criminal law, because it is treated as a completed act, whereas in civil law, in civil punishment, intent is considered rather than effect. Others say that he who strikes in a place where death is not usually caused, for example in the foot or hand, does not seem to have had the intent to kill, and therefore is not punished under the penalty of the Cornelian law, as in the aforementioned §. sed si claua, and there by Jacobus de Arena. Moreover, by custom, the aforementioned law is, who with a weapon, is not observed, as there fully by Cynus, and this is the opinion of the Speculum. Furthermore, the statutes of cities consider the act, not the intent, if the act did not result in death; and thus it is observed. Others say that if the wounding party assisted the murderer, he is liable to the penalty of the Cornelian law; if not, then he is not, as in ff. de furtis, l. qui servo, §. si. And if indeed they deliberately joined together with intent to commit homicide, they are considered to have assisted each other; but if in a brawl, then otherwise, as fully noted by Cynus in the aforementioned §. sed si plures, in his additions. The truth, considering the aforementioned point, is that the son is not liable for homicide, but only for the wounding. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who are said to be joined in fact and in words, who in fact only, and who in words only, and when the right of accretion has place among them, and when it does not.
body: Whether the copula "and" [induces verbal conjunction].

† I am asked whether the copula "and" or another conjunction placed between clauses induces a verbal conjunction from which the right of accretion arises. And it must first be premised that there is a conjunction of words (dictionum), a conjunction of clauses (orationum), and a conjunction of speeches (loqutionum), as is noted in ff. de pecu. legato. l. quaedam in testamento. A conjunction of words occurs when a single act of a verb governs two different words, as in "I bequeath to Titius and Seius such-and-such an estate." A conjunction of clauses occurs when there are two clauses with a copula, as in "I bequeath an estate to Titius; likewise to Seius I bequeath that estate; likewise to Seius a house." I also premise that sometimes one determination determines several determinables, as in "I bequeath to Titius and Seius an estate"; for "I bequeath" determines the determinables, while the determinables are Titius and Seius; then, by virtue of the unity of the utterance, the legatees are joined in words—which is the same as saying by unity of utterance, as in C. de cadu. tol. §. hoc ita tam varie. And this applies when the testator did not speak distributively; for if he had added shares, because of the distribution of shares they would not be joined in the thing (re), but only in words, as in ff. de haere. insti. l. interdum. For where there is a division of the intention distributing shares, there is said to be a real distinction, while the verbal conjunction nevertheless remains; and both proceed from the force of the speech and the intention of the testator, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. re coniucti. in the first and second responses. Therefore, when there are two connected clauses, yet each stands by itself, such a copula does not produce a verbal conjunction, because they are different determinations determining different determinables, as is noted in ff. de hęre. inst. l. liber homo. §. Titius. And where there is a distribution of shares, there is no conjunction in the thing; and this is clear by an argument from the effect, because it does not produce the right of non-diminution. Likewise because to the slave of the testator it does not attribute its force to each in solidum. From these points it is thus concluded that the distribution of parts removes the real conjunction, whereas the distribution of clauses removes the verbal conjunction. And this is the very truth. And two principal verbs make two clauses, which dialecticians call categorical, because each of them has a subject and a predicate as its principal parts, and by itself; hence here there is no copulative, because it connects neither the sense nor the words, since each by itself has its own instrument, and therefore there is no union. And just as the distribution of parts relates to real separation, so the distribution of clauses relates to verbal disjunction. This is expressly proved in institu. de leg. 3. §. si coniunctim. Secondly, I respond that what I said—that a plurality of clauses causes verbal conjunction to cease, so far as pertains to the right of accretion—is true if each clause is complete in noun and verb, for instance, "I bequeath an estate to Titius, and to Seius I bequeath the same estate"; but if one clause is complete in noun and verb, while the other is without a verb, as in "I bequeath an estate to Titius, and to Seius the same estate," then there is a verbal copula, because the verb "I bequeath," placed once, is common, and as it flows over the whole, as in ff. de lega. 2. l. cum pater. §. cum imperfecta. in the word, they are admitted to communion. And in this way the opinion of dominus Raynerius, who said that verbal conjunction exists in connected clauses, could be understood; in this way the opinion of Bar. in l. triplici can be reconciled with the opinion of Raynerius. And from the aforesaid it is evident that a common term is that which induces verbal conjunction, but two terms do not produce a verbal conjunction; and therefore when "I bequeath" is attached twice, they are not joined, because this term, "I bequeath," is placed twice. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether those who purchase in bad faith, or accept in fraud, may be molested, or not, by the true owners of those goods purchased or donated.
2. What a son is, and why he is so called.
3. On the interpretation of the law *bene a Zenone*.
4. A son granting goods generally is not considered to grant those in which a third person has a singular and perpetual right.
body: In the name of Christ. Officials of the chamber [...]

† The question is whether, if any goods have been sold by the treasury of the lord Duke or by the lord Duke himself—presupposing that the said illustrious lord Duke holds all the regalia and fiscal rights of the Empire granted to him by right of ducal and perpetual lordship—the said things sold or donated can be vindicated by anyone to whom they belonged by right of ownership prior to the said sale or donation; or whether they are indeed inevinciable, and the said buyers or donees have been made new owners and perpetual possessors, so that they are secure from all disturbance; and [on the other hand] whether the said officials could not sell the property of another to the prejudice of the true owner, nor even the lord Duke himself, because the general mandate of the said officials does not include things that do not belong to the principal. For a general mandate must be adapted to those things that are lawful, ff. de cond. ind. l. si procurator. §. celsus; nor should the commissions of princes be so interpreted that prejudice is generated to others, as in l. 2. §. si quis. ff. ne quid in lo. public., extra de autoritate, et vsu pallii. c. ex tuarum; because wrongs must not arise from the fountain of justice, as C. vnde vi. l. meminerint. Indeed, the duke himself does not seem to be able to take away the ownership of another, since ownerships are of the ius gentium, as noted in l. quot. and in l. rescripta. C. de precib. Imper., whence the prince is under the natural law, as C. de legi. l. digna vox. To the contrary it seems that the said buyer and donee is perpetually secure, just as if it had been expressly stated, as C. de quadriennij praescri. l. 2. in glo. nunc fortis; and not only if the beneficial prince himself, that same duke, has alienated it, but also his procurator, because he has a general mandate with free administration, as l. 1. ff. de offic. procu. cesa. Bartolus holds this expressly in l. si procur. ff. de iu. fisci, referring the dictum of Bartolus to the text of that law, which speaks of a fiscal procurator selling; for fiscal sales cannot be made except with the intervention of a minister of the treasury, because

† the treasury of itself is a kind of inanimate body not having consent by itself, but simply representing it, so that there is added what is noted in l. 1. C. de contractibus iudicium, and by Petrus and Cynus on C. de sac. san eccl. aut. quibuscunque modis, stating that what is alienated or donated as fiscal or imperial to one receiving in good faith, that is, without fraud, the receiver is secure; but if it is as if in the execution of someone's decree upon another's property, then it can be evicted by him who was not [a party], because a decree is understood to be interposed saving the right of a third party, as noted by Innocent on the title ut lite non conte. c. quoniam; and the same if as from the goods of Seius when they belonged to Titius, because a mistake of the final cause prejudices the grant, and an effective right is not acquired from a surreptitious contract; and these things are true in things incorporated or to be incorporated. If it is a corporeal thing, or at least assigned, if it consists in a right—for an assignment made to officials is held as possession—then the buyer, or donee, or privileged person is perpetually secure; nor is this inequitable, because he who originally had the right has recourse against the treasury within four years, and thus is kept indemnified in effect; therefore he does not suffer loss, because the treasury is always solvent, for it is called fiscus as if fixed. Hither is added what is read and noted in ff. de leg. 2. l. qui solidum. §. praedium, ff. de condi. l. Lucius, ff. de rei vend. l. Item si verberatum, and in the prooemium of the Digest; and it is a common text in l. bene a Zenone and what is noted on C. si aduer. fisc. l. edicto. It is not hindered by ff. de iur. fisc. l. Valerius. §. Trisonio, because there it speaks of a burden which arises from the fiscal contract itself and is inherent to it, similar to if the treasury should sell an inheritance, for under the name of an inheritance are contained active and passive actions, as C. de haere. ven. l. 1. For the buyer is secure from extrinsic and emergent things, not from a burden that comes tacitly from the nature of the contract, because the nature of the contract is that which governs and regulates them, as ff. de vsuris. l. si stipulatus, whether it be of a general nature or of a privileged nature.
