Likewise, it is not hindered if it is said that the privilege of the treasury or of the Emperor belongs to no one else because it is most personal, as l. 1. de consti. principum, because no inferior touches the supreme majesty, as C. de leg. l. fin.; for here a change of treasuries does not take place, because the treasury is the same, since the Emperor granted that very treasury to the magnificent [prince], and when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law take place, extra de constitutionibus. c. translato. It is not hindered by ff. de publicanis. l. licitatio. §. fi., where the privilege of the treasury does not pass to the buyer, because there the treasury itself does not pass, whence by a change of the person it is fitting that the status of the thing also be changed, as ff. de acqui. haer. l. Paulus and l. 1. C. de imponenda lucratiua descriptione. lib. 10. Likewise, in the same way, what is noted in l. 1. C. de bonis vacantibus does not hinder. And the aforesaid are confirmed because we see that through the privileges of the Emperors the treasury is granted to cities as to administration and as to jurisdiction, in the Authenticum de defensoribus ciuitatum. §. nulla; whence cities could establish the same with respect to their subjects if they had full regalia from an Imperial grant, otherwise not, ff. de priui. cre. l. antiochensium, ff. de polli. l. totiens, because not only a city but provinces are assessed by the common law unless they are fortified by an Imperial seal. For the Emperors, on account of distinguished nobility and union with the Roman Empire, are accustomed to grant privileges, as ff. de excu. tuto. l. non solum. §. si libertus, when it says 'on account of distinguished nobility and the union of Roman origin.' Faith and supreme devotion make this union with the Emperor, which may never be absent from a prince, our lord Duke. These things I believe and hold, saving the substance of truth. Certain conditions therefore concurring, namely: that the thing was solemnly sold; likewise, that fraud did not provide the cause of the fraud; likewise, that delivery took place, or that which is held for delivery, and that in that very delivery no lawful objector intervened,

† then the lex bene a Zenone has place, otherwise not, as C. de rebus va. l. fi. lib. 10, C. de priuilegio fisci. l. 1, ff. de rescin. vend. l. fundus, C. si propter publicas praestationes. l. 2, ff. de emptionibus. l. si pignora.

† Likewise, if the treasury grants goods generally, it is not deemed to grant those in which a third party has a singular and proper right, as ff. de euictionibus. l. 1, and in c. 1. de inuestitura. de re aliena facta. colla. 10, ff. de re iud. l. quod nostrum, extra de pignoribus. c. ex literis. But magistrates deputed to these matters and referendaries who have to report to the lord must be truthful, cautious, and discreet, so that subjects are not extorted, as C. de bonis proscri. l. si quis post hac. The conclusion: the lord has the beneficial treasury, and the beneficial is equivalent to the direct in all things and through all things. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Who are called ordinary judges, and who delegated judges.
2. Whether a lessee of a house, who was unable to inhabit it on account of a troublesome wife, is nevertheless bound to pay the full rent.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The Lord Duke of Milan commanded the Elders and the Podestà of Milan to admit a certain citizen of Piacenza as a citizen. Now it is asked whether they are understood as ordinary officials or as delegates. I reply: if they did not otherwise have ordinary power over this matter, then, because they were assigned to this single specific act, they are deemed delegated commissioners; and therefore, without the Podestà of Milan, the admission would not be valid, as Bartolus expressly notes on ff. de decretis ab ordine faciendis, l. ambitiosae, at the end.

† Secondly, it is asked whether a tenant who could not inhabit the entire house leased to him on account of the disturbance caused by a certain woman living there is bound to pay the full rent. I reply: he is liable only for that portion which he inhabited and for that time during which he inhabited it, and not beyond, by the argument of ff. de contrahen. emptio. l. officio and l. dolum, and ff. locati, l. habitatoris. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether ownership of the dowry property, upon the death of the mother during the marriage, passes by operation of law to the children.
1. i
body: when the woman has died in

† It is asked whether, when a woman has died in marriage, ownership of the dotal property passes by operation of law to the heir of the woman. I answer: it is not transferred to the heir by operation of law, because the vacant inheritance represents the person of the deceased woman; and even positing that the transfer of ownership were a privilege, nonetheless, because an acquisition is made for a vacant inheritance from the same causes as it is acquired for anyone, as in ff. si cert. petat. l. eis, qui. §. pen., and thereby the privilege is executed through the transfer of ownership, it deservedly passes to any heir whatever as a hereditary act, in accordance with the theory of Petrus and Cynus which they state at C. ad Velle. l. haeredem. Moreover, that is not properly a privilege, but is a certain exuberance of singular favor toward her, which passes at least to a child of that same marriage, as in C. qui potiores in pigno. hab. l. assiduis. and l. etiam. ff. solut. matrimon.; and therefore the daughter of the said woman has the right of claiming the said dotal property for that share in which she is the heir of the mother, as in C. de iure dotium. l. in rebus., and lex haeredem. ff. de reg. iur. supports this. 1 I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a lessee who withdraws from the leased premises before the expiration of the lease term is bound to pay the entire rent or only a proportional share.
body: In Christ's name. A tenant vacated

† The question is, when a tenant has departed or left before the expiration of the lease term, which had been made for several years, whether he is bound to pay the full rent for the entire time, or indeed only to the extent that he dwelled there, and no further? I respond: either it was due to the tenant, and he is bound to pay the full rent; or it was due to the lessor, and he is not bound except pro rata for the time during which he dwelled, as in ff. de migrando. l. 1. §. si pensio. But I understand it to have been due to the lessor if it was caused by his own act, or by the act of his predecessor, for instance of the testator from whom he derived his title, as in ff. de verborum obligatio. l. stipulatio ista; for the act of the deceased is interpreted as the act of the successor, as in C. de rei vendi. l. cum a matre; and therefore he is equally bound by the act of his predecessor just as if by his own act. Sometimes the tenant vacates by an accidental event, and this is not our subject matter, but that of the lex habitatoris, in §. fina. ff. locati, and the lex Item quaeritur, in §. exercitu, under the same title. Sometimes he is prevented from dwelling by the disturbing act of a third party, and then a remission is granted pro rata for the time during which he could not conveniently dwell, as in ff. locati. l. si fundus. §. 1. The same that I have said regarding a portion of the time, I say regarding a part of the leased property, namely that he is bound to pay rent in proportion to the use, but not for the other part, by an argument drawn from a thing held for a time, and because this belongs to the office of the judge, ff. de contrahe. empti. l. officio, and l. demum; and thus damages (interesse) are owed only in proportion, and therefore it is not usury; and in this contract, if the lessee had the benefits of dwelling and did not pay the rent, after default (mora) he is liable for damages, just as in the contract of sale, because it is a contract of good faith, as in C. de actio. empt. l. curabit; nor is it called usury, but a certain relative recompense. Sometimes he is prevented from dwelling because delivery was not made, and then to the extent that delivery was not made, the rent is not owed, ff. de actionibus empti. l. qui pendentem, and noted in Instit. de suspe. tuto. §. fin., ff. de excepti. l. pater. §. ex quadrante, ff. de pericu. et commo. rei vend. l. habitationum. §. fin., ff. de decre. ab ord. facien. l. ambitiosa. in fin. From these points it is concluded, according to what is set forth, that the lessee must be absolved from the claim for the time during which he did not dwell, and to the extent that he shall not dwell. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether and when execution is to be delayed while an appeal is pending, and whether all things renewed are to be revoked.
body: In the name of Christ.

† For the sake of clarity, it must be premised that nothing may be innovated while an appeal is pending, provided that the appeal is either valid to some extent or, so to speak, capable of having some effect. For if an appeal were manifestly and substantively invalid, or null by operation of law, execution would not be delayed; for that which does not stand by its own strength does not present an impediment. For an impediment must be generated by the obstacle of an opposing reason, since no free and discretionary agent is prohibited except by its superior or an opposing equal. For this is the nature of equals, that one does not have predominance over the other, unless by favor of the thing or by some privilege, as in ff. de manumis. l. Iulia petronia and ff. de re iud. l. fauorabiliores. Hence, in an equal cause, worse is the condition of the exception of him who cannot prevail. For his adversary has two grounds and two ways of prevailing, but the plaintiff has only one narrow way, namely, through the subtleties of proofs or pressing disputation, as noted in ff. de acqui. pos. l. 1. §. ueteres, or through the stable path of equity, as noted in ff. si cer. pe. l. cum fundus. §. 1. I say, therefore, that sometimes an appeal is prohibited or notoriously null, and execution is not impeded, as in l. 4. §. condemnatum. ff. de re iud.; sometimes an appeal is permitted by law, and then execution is impeded, as in ff. nil nouari appet. pen. in the rubric and the text, and in c. quod nobis olim. de elec., and ff. de infamibus. l. 1. §. 1., and ff. de iniusto test. l. si quis filio exhaeredato. around the middle. Sometimes it is doubtful because of the opinions of the doctors, as in the possession of recovering (possessio recuperandae), and then either the appeal is made with the statement of the cause, and one must desist from execution, or it is made without color of right, and then it is otherwise, as in c. uenerabilis. de sen. excom. lib. 6. and by the argument of ff. de in integ. resti. l. et etiam. l. ulti. C. de ordi. cogni., and this is noted in extra de resti. spo. c. cum ad sedem. and 2. q. 6. c. sunt quorum. Furthermore, if the petitory claim is expressed in the sentence, an appeal can be made on the ground of this addition, as noted by the doctors on C. si de momenta. poss. l. 1. and C. unde ui. l. si quis in tantam, because on account of the joinder of the petitory the possessory is altered, since they come to be examined together and determined together, by the argument of ff. de emp. l. non est nouum, ff. de acqui. poss. l. naturaliter. §. nihil commune, and ff. de ui, et ui ar. l. cum fundum. §. fi. From the aforesaid, three conclusions appear in order: first, that an appeal can be made; second, that the execution ought to be revoked, as in c. non solum. de appella. lib. 6.; from these a third is concluded, namely, that all innovations ought to be revoked, because the plaintiff bound himself by proceeding in a converse manner, and these things pertain to the merits of the process. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who has the right of patronage also has the right of a census, and vice versa, and how they differ from each other: and whether he who has a census can summon the goods of the patronage, on which the census is paid, and when the census or pension should be paid, the cause of which is unknown.
2. Whether the right of patronage remains with him to whom it first belonged, if the hospital is demolished and rebuilt.
body: [merits of the principal case]

† Now I come to the merits of the principal case, to the right of patronage, whether it pertains to the abbot or to the prior; and it seems that it pertains to the Abbot, because the hospital was founded upon his territory, and an arrangement that has been made is presumed to have been executed, by whomever the execution was made, ff. de ver. obl. l. cum servus, and l. sin. C. de usuris pupillaribus. To the contrary, it seems not, because it is not established by whom it was built, nor in whose name; and concerning this the proof must be notable, as in ff. de ne. gest. l. eum actum, because the burden of proof always rests upon the claimant, as in l. i. in fi. uti possidetis, and C. de rei ven. l. fi. and l. doce ancillam. Likewise, when the rights of the parties are obscure, the condition of the defendant is always better, as in the rule in ff. de ver. ob. l. si servum. §. sequitur. It must be known that in the foundation the founder can, with the consent of the bishop, reserve a certain census, as in extra de iure patro. Praeterea; secondly, he ought not to exact beyond what has been assessed, as in extra de statu mona. c. in singulis. §. ult.; and that the payment of a census is one thing, and the right of patronage is another, as is gathered and noted in l. 1. §. 1. ff. de publi. And if we consider the case before us, no mention is made in it of any right of patronage established from the beginning, but only of a census; and therefore we ought not to extend it, as in ff. de fideius. l. fideiussores magistratuum. §. pro nihilo. And the things that arise from the right of patronage are very well known, such as honor, emolument, presentation, prelation, defense, and maintenance, which nonetheless are not contained in a censual contract, C. de sac. san. ec. l. placet. Likewise, the right of patronage arises from endowment, the building on the ground, or from succession; but the censual right arises from its own specific articles; therefore they are not the same, since they are generated and extinguished in different ways; whence the Abbot ought to be content with his own bounds and not invalidate another's, as in C. finium reg. l. si constiterit. Someone may say: here he is patron by reason of the ground; but to this I reply that the origin proceeded from another owner, not from the Abbot, because the consignment to the Abbot was made conditionally, arg. ff. de leg. 2. l. unum ex familia, C. de test. tu. l. tutor; nor does he hold it from an heir, ff. de hære. insti. l. si servo fideicom., ff. de manu. vindic. l. pater ex providentia; for he is deemed to act in whose discretion it rests to act, not he who merely executes, as in extra de appel. c. novit. It must also be known that a census or pension whose cause is unknown ought not to be paid, unless it has been paid for a long and continuous time, or by law—namely, because it is censual by its nature or the location of the place—or in the present acts because they contain this, as in ff. de proba. l. census, C. de don. l. censualis, ff. de acqui. rerum do. l. quæ quisque, C. de agri. et censi. l. litibus. lib. 10. 18. qu ulti. c. servitium, de ver. sig. l. super quibusdam. And proof of the receipt of a census, if indeed it is with sufficient time to prescribe the census, proves ownership. But if it is for a lesser time, then if with good faith, it proves quasi-possession; if, however, it is by coercion or deceit, it proves intrusion, extra de appel. c. bonæ. If, however, it is claimed from a promise, it must be shown whether, in what manner, and how much was promised; and we must remain content with the terms of the contract, ff. de ver. obl. l. quicquid astringendæ; whence, if it is asked what right the said Abbot has, let the document speak; but if the second is proved, if it has been necessarily proved how much right of patronage he has to confer: let therefore the said Abbot be content with that right and that payment which has been customarily made, especially in the most recent times, as in ff. de acqui. pos. l. si quis ante, C. ne de statu defunctorum. l. si mater, ff. de ali. leg. l. mella. §. 1, and arg. de pac. l. pacta novissima, ff. de proba. l. procula, ff. de usu. l. quis emisse.

† On the other point, whether when a hospital is destroyed its goods remain to the patrons of the mother church, it must be said that they do not, but it ought to be reformed and rebuilt, unless it has been destroyed by a perpetual sentence of a superior, as noted by Inn. de no. ope. nun. c. cum ex iniuncto, ff. de usus f. l. an ususfructus, ff. de leg. 3. l. pater. §. tusculanus; for although hospitality is in that place deformed in act, nonetheless it subsists by virtue—that is, in capacity; and it is not lapsed because of the hope of repair, as noted in l. sicut. §. fi. ff. quod cuiusque univer. nomine, and by Moder. in l. 1. et ult. ff. de colleg. illicitis. The conclusion is that the Abbot cannot claim possession, but can only demand the census, because the possessions are not his, nor have they devolved to him, as noted by Inno. in ca. constitutus. de reli. domi., and concerning this noted by Barto. ff. de dam. insec. l. si finita. §. si qua sunt iura. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an imperial vassal may submit himself to a certain city.
2. In what manner confederates are said to break a treaty.
3. And whether one who has promised to defend and treat another well may disturb him in his rights.
4. Whether the first party to contravene the pacts of a treaty is said to have broken the pacts of the treaty, and to have contravened alone, so that the other party is not bound to observe the pacts towards him.
5. Whether one making a confederation with one person may confederate with his enemy.
body: Whether a vassal of the Emperor...

† First, it is asked whether a vassal of the Emperor can submit himself to any city and contract an alliance with it. And it must be said that he can, without prejudice to the Emperor, as noted by Archi. in de haereti. c. praesidentes, and Hostien. in de iudic. c. significauit.
† Secondly, whether he who offends a subject of an ally is understood to act against the alliance: and it must be said that he is, as noted by Inno. in c. dilectis. de app.

† Thirdly, whether he who has promised to defend someone and to treat him well can disturb him in his rights and prohibit him from using them. And it must be said that he cannot prohibit nor molest him, as in l. alterius. si seru. vendi. and l. frater a fratre. ff. de cond. inde.

† Fourthly, whether he who first violates the pacts of the alliance is said to have broken the pacts of the alliance, and to have alone contravened it to the effect that the other is not bound to observe the pacts toward him: and it must be said that the one who first offends is the one who acted against it, and he alone incurs the penalty. ff. de transactio. l. qui fidem.

† Fifthly, whether he who made an alliance with one party can ally himself with that party's enemy. And it must be said that he cannot, unless on the occasion of a cause recognized by law upon just grounds, for instance fear, because lawful defense is permitted; nor ought he to wait until he is struck, extra de homicidio. in c. significasti, and ff. de verb. obl. l. quidam cum filium. Furthermore, it must be said that by a simple verbal act or promise neither party is understood to break the alliance, because an agreement must be understood in a case permitted and possible by law, namely for defense or just repelling of force; for such an agreement is favored by natural and common law, and therefore it is not penal, and it aims at defense, which is by natural law, and at removing ambushes on either side, ff. de iustitia, et iure. l. vt vim. Likewise, when one party commits a wrong, or prepares to commit one, it is lawful for the other party to take counsel, aid, and protection so that violence may not be done to him, as in ff. de off. procur. Caesaris. l. fi. and ff. de off. praes. l. illicitas. §. vt potentiores; but to break out into an act of physical force by initiating it is permitted to neither party, and he is said to initiate who first attacks, l. 1. §. cum arietes. ff. si quadrupes pauperiem fecisse dicatur, because he who gives cause to the crime is more criminal than he who pursues it, as in C. de ser. fug. l. quicunquibus. §. fin. and C. de his, qui ad ecclesias confu. l. si seruus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A lease does not extend to things purchased after the lease was made.
body: Magnificent and illustrious, in the name of Christ. The Duchess of Milan, through her officials, made leases of the possessions of Lazelata for a certain annual pension, under or in the name of the territory; afterwards, by sentence, she obtained a certain port within the said boundaries,

It is asked whether the said port is included in the said lease? And it seems that it is: because things acquired after the contract are added to the universality, as in D. de fundo instr. l. Lucius. The contrary is true, because no thought was given to future things, as noted in l. si, C. quae res pignori obligari possunt; D. de verb. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae; and l. cum stipulamur; and l. si a colono; D. de contrah. empt. l. ruptilia; and l. inest; D. de damno infecto l. damni, §. Sabini; and arg. D. de transact. l. cum Aquiliana; and D. de pact. l. tres fratres; D. ad l. Falc. l. si haeres; D. ad Trebell. l. si debitor, §. final. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a lease made of an emphyteutic thing is said to be terminated by law if the emphyteuta renounces the emphyteusis to the lord, and the lord accepts it.
body: Masiolus leased, in the name of Christ, for a certain period, a certain house built for a kiln of lime-burners. This Masiolus was a perpetual emphyteuta; finally, during the term of the lease, this Masiolus renounced the emphyteusis into the hands of the lord, who wishes to eject the said lessee, because he claims that the house has reverted to him by his own right and freely.

† It is asked whether it is possible, and it seems that it is: because when the right of the lessor is extinguished, the right of the lessee is also extinguished, as in D. de pignoribus, l. lex vectigali. Moreover, this seems to be expressly stated in C. quibus modis feuda amittuntur, c. 1, § rursus infidelis, in the word "refutauerit." To the same effect is D. locati conducti, l. si quis domum, § huic, and the entire general rule that when the right of the author ends, the right of the successor ends, as in D. de medicis stipendiariis, non ex masculo, successoris. On the contrary, it seems that the solution of the contract should not remain in the power of the debtor, as in l. si res, D. quibus modis pignus vel hypotheca solvitur. Moreover, this seems to be expressly stated in D. quomodo ad servitutem amittatur, l. si partem, § 1. Moreover, this is not a simple renunciation: because one cannot renounce against the owner, as in l. si quis vi, § differentia, D. de acquisitione possessionis; but it is a certain new pact and a new contract, which does not prejudice another with whom it was not concluded, as in l. finalis, D. de pactis, and noted by Bartolus in l. in diem, D. de aqua pluviae arcendae. Moreover, this renunciation seems to have been made in fraud, therefore it does not prejudice his lessee, as in D. solutionibus matrimonii, l. filiae meae, and D. de bonis libertorum, l. liberto octingenta. Moreover, there is one condition for all the years, and from the beginning the day of obligation has passed, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1, § si pensio, D. de migrando. Moreover, the lessee derives his cause from the first lessor through the first lessee, therefore he cannot be expelled by the first lessor, D. de pignorum actione, l. solutum, § unde si domum, provided that the rent is paid to the owner. This is the case in the aforementioned l. lex vectigali, and this opinion is very equitable. And if we say the contrary, nevertheless the said lessee would have an action ex conducto for his damages.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether legitimated persons have the right of presentation. Add the following opinion.
body: Lord Ambro. In the name of Christ. He maintained that the priest, or chaplain of the church of Saint Bartholomew of Olena, ought to be elected or nominated by the undersigned heirs of his patronage, whom he established or ordained as patrons of the said chapel; and in their default, by their male descendants only. These heirs are, namely, Lord Christopher de’ Medici, archpriest, and the father of the spurious children, Lord Vittore de’ Medici, and Jacopo de’ Medici, legitimate. And while living, he elected the priest Stephen. Now, the illegitimate sons of the archpriest, and therefore spurious and not legitimated, presented one; but Jacopo, legitimately born, presented another.

† Here it is asked whether the legitimated have a voice in the presentation, considering the said testament, and the aforementioned legitimation, and the words and intent of the parties, and other matters to be considered. And it appears that the said legitimated have the right of presentation. And this is shown thus: speaking according to natural truth, there is no doubt that these are male descendants; for nature is immutable, as in the Authentica *Quibus modis natura efficit suos* near the beginning, in the gloss noting the most glorious word. And every descendant is considered substituted for his ascendant. But what shall be said of the voice of him who died without a descendant in the voice of the father? The son succeeds by the testament of the founder of the chapel. If the patrons are equal in number, he to whom the substitution pertains may adhere to whom he wishes, and also provide by himself. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Bastards do not have the name of sons, and they are infamous.
2. The Prince is a god on earth.
3. The Emperor can legitimize bastards, and those born of incest, and he can delegate this power.
4. Whether the Emperor can legitimize bastards with respect to the right of ecclesiastical patronage? And what is the case with the Pope. And number 5.
6. Whether descendants are called bastards.
7. How the word "descendants," uttered by a priest, is to be understood.
8. Who are included under the term "descendants."
9. What the term "to whom" signifies.
body: It must be premised, in the name of Christ, that a woman brings forth a human being, and that a man begets a man. This is so natural, indeed precisely natural; nevertheless, what is not in accordance with honest morals is deemed impossible, as in the Digest, On Conditions and Stipulations, Institution, l. filius.

Hence it is that bastards do not have the name of sons not only in those matters which require excellence, but also in others which require a state of unblemished reputation. For as far as reputation is concerned, all children are legitimate by comparison and in relation to those legitimately born, and they are not to be associated with them; and especially those who are so degenerate that they do not deserve even the name of sons; and those who cannot be named without infamy, such as one born of a nun or of a priest, as noted in C. de modo testandi, apud l. pe. For nature blushes to have begotten such persons, who were born as it were contrary to nature, as in Auth. de incestis nuptiis, in principio. Nevertheless, our Emperor, as if prodigal of his majesty, and under the guise of piety and the simplicity of nature, wishing to mitigate whatever pleases him, has decreed that it should be regarded as law, as in ff. de constitutionibus, principio, l. 1. And thus the will of the prince is the law. And if it pleases the prince, let it be valid as if it pleased God.
† because the prince is God on earth, as in the Authentica de consulibus. and

† Therefore, we must presuppose that the Emperor can legitimize both bastards and those born of incest, and can delegate this power; because this power is his own, and not another's, and is voluntary on the part of the Empire; and no one can contravene his own power, as noted in Auth. quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, §. si, col. 7, provided that no prejudice is caused to others by such legitimation, and the necessary and customary clauses of non obstante are appended, and such non obstantia are those which pertain to the power and the iuris dictum of the Emperor, from which he could not remove the obstacle of canon law, because he who cannot grant cannot remove, as in the rule "eius est nolle, qui potest et velle." Under this consideration hangs this article.

Whether the Emperor can legitimize for the right of patronage of a church: it seems that he can, because he can legitimize for inheritance; but under this universality is contained the right of patronage, because one cannot be an heir unless he is a universal heir; a testator cannot die partly with an heir and partly without an heir. From this it follows that the right of patronage passes with this universality, which is comprehensive of all hereditary rights without exception; because the right of patronage has a burden in itself; and it comes in the passive consequence, that it cannot be separated from the inheritance itself. Moreover, that which comes in consequence is regulated by the principal, as in l. 1, de acquisitione tutelae; and this is by the disposition of both civil and canonical law. Moreover, that which is principal prevails; but the inheritance is principal, and the right of patronage is accessory, or so annexed that it cannot be separated from the universality itself, as noted in cle. plures, de iure patronatus. Therefore, he who is the lord of the inheritance is the lord of the right of patronage; and he who can have one, can also have the rest, extra de iure patronatus, c. ex literis; ff. de acquisitione rerum donatarum, l. quidam; ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. in modicis.

However, the right of patronage is not simply hereditary; because it is specially annexed, and in the power of the church; and therefore the Emperor cannot give or take it away principally and by itself, because principally, indeed totally, it is of ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and presentation must be made to an ecclesiastical judge, and not a secular one, extra de iudiciis, c. quanto; and in cle. dispendiosam; and de re iudicata, c. pastora. And that it is not of the contentious forum, from the fact that a layman is not capable of contentious jurisdiction, certainly he will not be capable of involuntary jurisdiction either, as C. de testamento, l. consulta, in fine. But there is a very strong doubt: behold, the Emperor gives the inheritance, and this he can do without doubt, and canonical law establishes that the right of patronage passes with the inheritance; therefore, by canonical law, these heirs are patrons. And it seems difficult to respond to this reason; but it is responded that this is true, unless the quality of the person of the heir is not capable of this right. It is said that when transmission is made with the universality to one not capable, transmission cannot be made, as l. si alienum, §. in extremis, ff. de hereditate instituenda; and l. 1, §. exigit, ff. de bonis possessionibus secundum tabulas. But bastards do not seem capable, as in c. 1, de filiis presbyterorum, lib. 6; because they suffer a defect of birth, as c. innotuit, de electione; and they are odious to laws and canons, as extra de renuntiatione, c. nisi cum pridem; and they do not follow the father, as ff. unde cognati, l. si spurius; and l. hac parte; and ff. de statu hominum, l. vulgo.

Moreover, because even the patronage of a church is a certain prerogative, preeminence, and honor, which does not befit bastards in the church of God. For it is shameful in the church of God to have such a one above the vertex, and to call persons of dishonesty to an honest place, as in l. si qua, C. de spectaculis, lib. 11.

Furthermore, it was subtly alleged that, inspecting the disposition of the testament, which makes mention of descendants, and does not say "and of the heirs" of him about whom it is inquired, it descends to descendants not as heirs of goods, but of blood. Hence, it is not of the universality of the inheritance, but of a special right of descent. C. de operis liberti; ff. de acquirenda hereditate, l. patre haerede, §. 1; ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si; ff. de legatis 1, l. filius, §. si quis; ff. de pactis, l. si tibi, §. pactus. It makes what is noted by Pe. and Cy. in l. 1, C. de conditionibus insertis. If therefore it is a non-hereditary right: therefore it does not pass with the universality of the inheritance. For since a disposition has been made regarding the right of patronage in descendants specially and by itself, it does not pass to the heirs of the priest; rather, just as a legacy is deducted from the inheritance, so that if the said priest had instituted other heirs than descendants, granted that those heirs had the universality, they nevertheless do not have the patronage. l. proinde, ff. si certum petatur; and ff. de peculio, l. sed si damno; and l. a Titio, ff. de furtis. And by this it seems that the aforementioned allegation is removed, presupposing that in this article the disposition of the testament is valid.

† However, there would be no doubt about this if they had been legitimated by the Pope with regard to the right of patronage of the church: because the Pope can legitimate spiritual matters and those annexed to spiritual matters. Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi, in the chapter Tanto. And immediately, natalium is about the principal jurisdiction of the church, as in Extra, De ordine cognitionis, in the chapter Tuam. Nor does the status, which depends on marriage, pertain to the Emperor, as in Extra, Qui filii sint legitimi, in the chapter Per venerabilem. What is therefore noted: Extra, De fide instrumentorum, Cum P. tabellio. That the Emperor can legitimate just as the Pope can, is true in cases and lands subject to him; in spiritual cases, the Emperor does not legitimate, nor does he put his hand to another's cart, as noted in the Codex, De incestis nuptiis, in the constitution Ex complexu. For, as Innocent says where above, these are almost miraculous, and as if contrary to nature, De infamia, in the chapter Facere bonam famam, and De illegitimis, in the chapter Legitimum, and to subject all things of one's own right to another. Hence, from the aforementioned, it seems to be concluded that, due to the defect of the power of the efficient cause, i.e., the Emperor, the legitimation does not hold with regard to subjecting the church to the patronage of bastards, nor can he oppose the clause "notwithstanding any decree": because canonical statutes cannot be derogated by the Emperor, who is subject, just like any layman. Someone will say that a bastard, not in his own name but in the name of an alien bastard, can be instituted as heir and a legacy can be left to him, as noted in the Authenticum, Quibus modis naturales efficiuntur sui, § fin., Collatio 7. But these former bastards come from transverse providence, because they are descendants from the transverse line,

† Hence, since they come by virtue of the will, and are descendants in the transverse line, and no reason prevents them from coming, certainly even if they were not legitimated, they would come. This reasoning concludes that if something is left to Titius, a friend, and his descendants, the descendants from him come, even if they are spurious. But whether this is true, let us see: and let us proceed further by disputing about the power of the Emperor regarding the words of the will and the interpretation of words; for the words say, "upon whose default" the descendants come. For this addition, "upon whose default," is of the plural number and conjunctive signification: but from the disposition of the conjunction, the truth of both parts is required; but here one remains in the nature of things, and does not default; therefore, the condition is false, or at least not yet verified, as in D. de re dubia, l. Is qui ducenta, § Cum quidam, and § Utrum; and D. de cond. et demonstr., l. Si heredi plures. Moreover, on account of the prerogative of degrees, it seems that he who exists is preferred, D. de leg. 2, l. Cum ita, § Ita, § In fideicom.; and D. ad Trebell., Heredes mei, § Si. Furthermore, when substitution is made by several with a verbal or mental conjunction, and the condition exists in the person of one and not the other, if indeed the person exists who, by the presumed will of the testator, excludes the substitute, there is no place for substitution, C. de impub. et aliis subst., l. Pen. But if such a person does not exist, substitution has place in the share of the one who defaults, as in D. ad Trebell., l. Heredes mei, § Cum ita. But here there exists a true and legitimate agnate, who ought to be preferred in honor of the family or agnation, as in l. 1, § Quamvis, D. de vend. inspi. But against this, it seems to oppose the will of the deceased, who, imitating nature, requested the descendants in the place of his progenitors, following the natural and orderly effect more than the subtlety of law, D. de haer. inst., l. Lucius, in fine. Furthermore

† This word, "descendants," reported by the priest, cannot be understood except as referring to a spurious child: as in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Haeredibus, §. Si. And it can be understood as a matter of law; therefore, we shall understand it of him not only by conjectural interpretation, but by necessary interpretation, having regard to the person to whom the speech is directed. But to this it may be replied that "descendants" refers to those who can have legitimate descendants: because words are to be understood in a civil sense, as in the Digest, de Servitutibus, l. Si cui. Hence, any legitimate qualification being set aside, and even assuming that they repudiated the paternal inheritance by which they were legitimated, they could nevertheless come to the patronage by virtue of the disposition of the law of wills, as in the Authenticum, de Ecclesiis, tit. §. Si quis aedificat, Collatio 9. Moreover, the Emperor can legitimize incestuous children, who can be legitimated both actively and passively: so that they may be subjects of the Emperor, as in l. Qui in provincia, §. 1, Digest, de Ritu Nuptiarum. And if it is said that such children are odious, and therefore are not included in favors, as in the Digest, de Legatis 2, l. Lucius, §. Lucius Titius damas, I answer that, on the contrary, they are not odious with respect to collaterals, nor is it even a new thing,

† That in many cases those who are less legitimate are included under the term "descendants," as when we use natural rather than civil terms, as noted by Bartolus in l. 2, ff. de accusationibus and C. ad Iul. maiestatem, l. quisquis; and by Ioannes Andreas in c. statutum, de haereticis, lib. 6, in the Novella. It seems to be said that the testament should be observed. The case is in d. §. si quis aedificationem, in the Authenticum de ecclesiis, tit. col. 9, because imperial legitimation adds nothing to nor detracts from the testament, as C. de testibus, l. omnium, because it is not the intention of the Prince to alter testaments, but to favor and observe them, and to have them observed as they stand, and without external interpretation: unless where the law interprets, as in c. quia contingit, de religiosis domibus, in the Clementines. Hence, if the testator substituted to legitimate children to be born legitimate, it is not understood to refer to legitimated children, because they are not legitimately born: especially if another dignity or another natural reason does not allow it. ff. ad Trebellianum, l. ex facto, §. si quis rogatus. Hence the Speculum says that in the emphyteusis of the church illegitimate children are not included. in Spec. de locatione, §. nunc aliqua, near the end. Hence it is concluded that legitimation after the making of the testament will not change its meaning: but the natural sense, not the fictitious, is taken, because the mind of man is natural, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. fideicommissum. And therefore the weight of our question rests on the testament, whose words are: "If they fail, to their descendants." For it is alleged, as I said above, that the words of substitution comprehensively should be verified in any of the extremes, as C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. haereditatem. This seems to be held expressly by the Speculum in Spec. de locatione, §. nunc aliqua, vers. 69, vers. quaeritur, pone. But that is on account of presumed providence and charity. But to this it is answered, because that is true in direct substitution, but not in fideicommissary substitution: therefore neither in legacies, because legacies and fideicommissa are equated. And to this see and induce the law haeredes mei, §. cum ita, and in the same title, l. Lucius, §. Caio. But certainly §. cum ita speaks when the condition is in the person of the last dying, but in our case one survives: and he seems to be tacitly called to the whole right, or at least to the voice of him who died without a descendant, as ff. de legatis 2, l. Titia Seio, §. Seia. Hence the one presented by him is to be preferred: granted that these legitimated ones succeed in the paternal right, as d. c. plures. It seems that the condition of the testament has not yet occurred by such theory: because the condition is taken from the whole, if indeed it exists in the person of the last dying, and not the first, fideicommissary substitution has place: but if conversely it exists in the person of the first, with the last surviving, fideicommissary substitution has no place. But so it is in the proposal: therefore the substitution is not verified. Wherefore the aforementioned descendants do not come into the substitution, nor by transmission, because the testator wished the descendants to come, unless the principal ones, who were instituted patrons, failed. For that word, "quibus."

† It is understood to apply to all: because it is taken from the whole; and the indefinite is equivalent to the universal, and especially the collective. This does not constitute an obstacle. §. Caio. Because when each one was asked about his own share, it appears that each one is burdened individually. But this response does not seem sound, because a transfer to descendants appears to be a certain burden on the decedent: because it prevents transmission: unless one says that a legacy divided by time, namely first while alive, and to descendants afterwards, is not properly a burden, because nothing comes to be restored: and each acquires as much as the time allows, as in l. si seruus communis meuii. §. fina. de stip. seruo. Also because it depends on family affairs. Also one thing is ordained: for example by a testator, who in his will provides a dowry. Another is formed, namely by a bishop, who interposes his authority: the former is mine. §. cum ita. tacausale, and of the future: the latter is formal, and of the present, as we say in the dowry of a girl, who is said to be dowered, even before she marries, on account of the hope of the future. ff. de admi. tuto. l. cum plures. And regarding the dowry, he can ordain concerning it. ff. sol. mat. l. quoties. And the right of patronage is indivisible, lest an inconvenience arise: and because it cannot be reduced to the divisible. Other allegations to the two preceding opinions.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. One who does not observe a pact, yet demands that it be observed by the other party, may not bring an action.
body:
The words in the law *Haeredes* are as follows: In the name of Christ. It is said, or it is treated, either of direct substitution or of fideicommissary substitution. In the first case, because the testator said, “I institute Titius and Mevius as heirs: and if both should die in pupillary age, let such a one be heir,” and one dies in pupillary age, the substitute does not claim his place; and thus speak the contrary laws. But if it is treated of a fideicommissum to be restored under that condition which is said in this § *Habet locum*, § *Iste*, and this will be shown below, in l. *Lucius*, § *Caio*, and l. *Si*, § *Filia*, de legatis 2. The reason for this solution might be: and thus it seems to hint in § *Caio*, because when the testator makes a direct substitution under that condition, if both should die in pupillary age, it is the same as if the substitution had been made under two conjunctive conditions; and in that case it is required that both exist, as in l. *Si haeredi*, de conditionibus et institutionibus. Then it seems that the testator appended two conditions separately; hence it suffices that one exists. And thus speaks this text, and the aforementioned l. *Lucius*, § *Caio*. For this is the regular rule, that whenever something is appended conjunctively, it is regarded as if it had been appended separately; and it suffices that one be done: as in l. *Salsa*, § *Fin.*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, and l. 2, de conditionibus et institutionibus, and l. *Qui concubinam*, § *Praestitus*, de legatis 3.

Jacobus Butrinteus said: or the disposition has singular and separate reasons, not commonly referring to the disposition; and then the plural expression is resolved into singularities: as in l. *Falsa*, § *Si*, de conditionibus et demonstrationibus. But when the reasons commonly refer to the disposition, so much so that one suffices without the other, and then it produces one effect and one disposition, it is not resolved into singularities: as here, and in l. *Si servus plurium*, ff. si quis cautionibus. Jacobus Butrinteus and Cynus in l. *Pe.*, de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, in 2, opposite, when speaking of the cause of possession, with *cum ita*, and § *Fides*, that it is a fideicommissary substitution, if the fideicommissary substitution is similar, whether it is made singularly, the faith of each for himself seems to be elected, hence each seems to be burdened for himself: as in l. *Lucius*, § *Caio*. But in direct substitution it matters whether the substitution was made jointly or severally. In the first case, truth is required, at least in the person of the last dying. In the second case, each is referred to each according to Cynus. The aforementioned distinction is confirmed by the gloss in l. *Pater filiam*, § *Duos*, ff. ad legem Falcidiam. The text in § *Cum ita* gives the reason, because just as the whole relates to the whole, so the part to the part, ff. de re iudicata, l. *Quae de tota*. But the text in § *Seio* holds another reason regarding the words of the testament, because in a fideicommissum each is burdened with his own part, and not that of another, therefore the death of the other would be awaited in vain. And this is a living reason of the jurist, and especially because there remains no person who, by the presumed will of the deceased, may exclude the substitute, according to Bartolus. For that § *Cum ita* is based on the presumed consideration of the testator: and he counts two of his precepts: because there remains no person who by any right may exclude the substitute; therefore conjunctive words are taken distributively, as if he had expressly said, “I substitute such a one in his part, and such a one in his,” resolving the plural into its singularities, as in the laws cited above. For just as when the conjunction is placed between those honored, as if I leave to Titius and Seius, so if it is placed between those burdened, the truth of both parts is not required. Thus, since in conditions the conjunction is supposed between different persons burdened with respect to the thing, which receives distribution, the signification is attributed to each part for itself: l. *Cet inter copulativam dispositionem* respectu unius personae, et copulativam conditionem longa sit differentia.

Now I come to our case, because the words say, “them failing.” And first, whether these are words determined in number, or indefinite, or universal. For universals are made not only by three words, as the dialecticians say, but by the mind of the disposer, as the jurists say, who say that from its proper signification the indefinite is similar to the universal. The laws are notable: *aliquan haeredem* [any heir], since any heir would have the same, but *descendente* [descendant] does not equate, when the reason for including them under this heading is not the same, according to Dynus and Oldradus. Moreover, this does not seem to be a proper substitution, but a certain division of time, namely to the parent during life, and to the child after the death of the parent, as in C. de legatis, l. *Fina*. Moreover, if it were a substitution, it seems to be equated to a direct one, that no faith of the parent toward the child is elected, and it is a certain translation rather than a fideicommissum. But the contrary seems true, because legacies and fideicommissa are equated; and because this is a burden on the parent: for he is burdened in this, because otherwise he would transmit the right of patronage with the universality, as in cap. *Ex literis*. Which now he does not transmit in the thing itself, but by the singular disposition of the testator, and by the direct path it passes to the descendant as to a descendant, not as to one not existing and existing. This clause is proven. ff. de operibus libertorum, l. *Ut iurisconsultus*, § *Si liberi*. Nor let anyone say, these cannot take, because they are spurious; for rather they can take from the testament of collaterals, as of any strangers: as noted in Authent. *Quibus modis* naturales efficiuntur sui, § *Fina*, Coll. 7, and ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. *Is qui*. Moreover, these are legitimated by the Emperor, who can confer the true right of legitimation: just as he can confer the true right of Romans. And that which can be induced by truth does not need the aid of fiction, as says l. *Tanquam*, and therefore the text says that the sons are legitimate: that word, *sint* [are], is a word precisely signifying the truth of substance; otherwise the letter would use the word *videri* [to seem] or *haberi* [to be held], as noted in ff. de verborum significatione, l. *Mercis*. Nor does it obstruct that which is noted by Innocentius in cap. *Cum P. tabellio*, de fide instrumentorum, where he says that spurious children are born in a way contrary to nature: for this is true with respect to natural justice and origin, which is a stain of fact. And that which is done cannot be undone. For this alone is denied to God: but because they are reborn, just as baptized persons recover the rights of origin, and then they can succeed in the inheritance, as in l. *Ex facto*, in principio, ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus. From this it necessarily follows that the right of patronage passed to them. For by the sentence of a secular judge, if the inheritance passed, by consequence the right of patronage of the church necessarily passes. And this happens by the disposition of civil and canon law: that by the disposition of the inheritance, which is succession, or the right of succeeding to the universal right which the testator had, this same thing is clear in the testament, which is of civil law: and in intestate succession, and in possession of goods, which is of praetorian law. And this happens, because one cannot die partly testate, partly intestate, as says the rule of law. Or partly with an heir, partly without an heir, as noted in C. de secundis nuptiis, unless this is done by a special and regular law, or by the disposition of the Prince, or by the impossibility of the taker, as if he were a Jew or a Saracen, who is legitimated by the Emperor for other things, except for the right of patronage. And if it is said, the right of patronage is annexed to the spiritual: I answer, it is rather annexed to the inheritance.

All things considered, and sufficient allegations of both parties heard, I say, that these legitimated have one voice of their father: and those legitimately born have another voice. The voice of the dead, namely of him who died without a descendant, is common to both; or of neither as caduc, and because of the discord of the patrons, he who has the right of instituting may adhere, by right, to whom he wishes. And especially to the more worthy, both of the presented and the presented one. And thus there is room for gratification, as in many articles of law.

Beyond the said counsel, I do not omit that Speculator holds, that as long as all have not died, there is no place for substitution, as noted in Speculum de locato, § *Nunc verum aliqua*, verse 69, *quaeritur, pone ecclesia*. And if anyone wishes to hold this opinion, these legitimated would not yet have any right of presentation. Notwithstanding l. *Haeredes mei*, § *Cum ita*, because there it speaks of a divisible thing, but the right of patronage is indivisible, which would be diminished by the concurrence of the instituted with his substitute: which does not seem to have been the mind of the testator. This question is doubtful on both sides, and is disputable: but in a doubtful matter it is safer to observe the words of the testament, because those words, “them failing,” are equivalent to this conjunction A, B, and C failing, because the one named in the institution of the patronage seems to be preferred and placed before by the testator, as in ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. *Publius*, § 1, there, “but it is not probable,” and the aforementioned Sostratus. He who has to institute may, by right, confirm the one elected by the legitimate counsel, as counsel is sought, as noted by Innocentius in cap. 1, in fine, de iure patronatus. The said Speculator in emphyteusis, which is given out of grace and love of the recipient, and according to the right of accretion, the interpretation was given, by the same reason of favor, the division of the will is made in a fideicommissum, otherwise in direct substitution, because to exclude those coming intestate is in a way odious: and for this reason sometimes direct is turned into oblique, as in l. *Precibus*. For he who substitutes directly does not intend to burden anyone, but he who substitutes by fideicommissum intends to burden each with his portion: and in emphyteusis those words, of which the Speculator speaks, do not smell of a burden.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
0. It cannot.
2. The benefit of the second law, C. de rescindenda venditione, also applies in the case of an incantus, or in a sale made by the fiscus.
body: Case, on which, in the name of Christ, it is submitted in terms. The masters of the revenues of our Magnificent Lord sold to Absalom de Sansonis the office of extraordinary treasurer of revenues for two years, and for the price of eight hundred florins, with certain agreements, namely that the said Absalom should receive all revenues, both ordinary and extraordinary, pertaining to the chamber of extraordinary revenue. Also, that the said treasurer might take from anyone paying over certain revenues, if he paid one florin, or less, three imperiali of confession; and if from one florin up to ten, six imperiali; and if from ten up to twenty-five, twelve imperiali; and if from twenty-five florins upwards, three imperiali solidi, and not more, except concerning the denarii of the possessions of Milan, for which he should have two florins and two solidi for confession. And if during the said term anything were diminished on account of some grant, or donation, or restitution, there should be made due restoration, etc. It happens that the Magnificent Lord does not wish to observe the agreements made with him, because he wishes part of the said revenue to be received by other officials, rather than by the said treasurer. And therefore the said treasurer refuses to exercise the said office, and also to pay the price of the said revenue, on the ground that on the part of the said Magnificent Lord that which was promised is not fulfilled. On the other hand, on behalf of the said Magnificent Lord it is alleged that the said treasurer cannot withdraw from the contract.

I answer that the agreements are clear, because if something is diminished, restoration must be made pro rata, as in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. officio. But if the agreement is not observed at all, since such agreements gave cause to the contract, he who does not observe the agreement cannot demand that the contract be observed in his favor, as in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. cum te; and D. de locato conducto, l. quæro, § inter locatorem; D. de actionibus emptoris et venditoris, l. Iulia, § offerri; and l. qui pendentem; D. de exceptione doli, l. pater, § ex quadrante; and C. de pactis, l. cum proponas.

† The same applies if the agreements are not observed and exceed half of the just price, or of the appraised value, as stated in D. de contrahenda emptione, l. domum; C. de rescindenda venditione, l. 2; D. de verbis obligatis, l. si quis cum aliter, which is noted. See also C. locati conducti, l. olei. It supports what is noted by Bartolus in D. de verbis obligatis, l. si quis arbitratu, in the verse “Formo tibi unam quaestionem,” etc. And the same is noted by Bartolus in D. de damno infecto, l. si finita, § eleganter, in the principal question. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a judge’s decree validates a contract in which the ward was prejudiced, and whether a decree gives rise to the presumption that all formalities were observed, examined, and true.
body: Question, upon which, In the name of Christ. is submitted in the terms set forth below. A tutor of a ward, on account of another’s debt, sold the ward’s house for the price of 22 florins, with the decree of a judge. And in the very instrument of sale it is asserted that no other movable goods nor money were present in the assets of the said minor; and thus the judge interposed his decree. Nevertheless, it does not appear that any other excussion was made by the said judge or tutor of the goods of the said minor. But the ward, after the said guardianship had ended, seeing himself deceived, began to claim back the said house, stating that the alienation was null; and insofar as any, he sought the benefit of restitution in integrum. And for his foundation he produced an inventory made before the said sale by the said tutor, in which the tutor placed it as being of much greater value and common estimation beyond the quantity for which the said house was sold. Nor does it otherwise appear that other movable goods were given unsatisfied for the said debt, except the price of the said house. On the other side it is alleged that the interposition of the decree causes it to be presumed that all things were done solemnly. Moreover, although the confession made in the inventory proves against the tutor, it does not prove against the buyer; and therefore, because it is not otherwise proven that movable goods were present at the time of the said sale, it is presumed that all things... what is the law, etc. CASE.

† That all solemnly performed acts are presumed to have been examined and to be true, as narrated in the instrument from which the judge issued the decree, is held by the gloss in l. 1, C. de fide instrumentorum et iure hastae fiscalis, l. 10. The same is held by Speculum in Speculum de emptione et venditione, § nunc dicendum, vers. et breviter scias. And this seems to be proven by the text in l. 1, § 1, ff. de rebus eorum. And the text says that he who alleges obreption must prove it; therefore, if he does not prove it, it is presumed in favor of the instrument. One may be led to the same conclusion by what is noted in l. actor, ff. rem ramm habere. To the contrary, it seems that solemnities which consist in an act separate from the principal one are not presumed; because they are external solemnities, as noted in ff. de verbis oblig., l. sciendum, and ff. de publico, l. quaecunque, § finalis, and by Innocentius in de eo qui furtive ordines suscepit, cap. innotuit. Moreover, the judge is not believed unless it appears from the records. de officio delegati, c. cum in iure; de probationibus, c. quoniam contra falsam. Moreover, in the sale of a minor’s property, inquiry and examination are required, as in ff. de rebus eorum, l. magis puto, § non passim. Therefore, if inquiry was not made, the decree is not valid; because that which ought to be clear to the judge is not clear, as in ff. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor. Bartolus expressly holds this part in the aforementioned l. sciendum, because this examination could not have been made at the place and time of the making of the instrument, nor at the time of the decree; nor is the tutor to be believed, and especially because the judge ought to inform himself from the reasons of the ward and from the inventory, as in the aforementioned l. magis puto, § in primis. And because the inventory is more strongly presumed than the contrary exception of the tutor, as in l. si, C. arbitrium tutelae. And thus, against the presumption of solemnity, there is another presumption, namely, that movables existed; the presumption is not followed. ff. de in integrum restitutione, l. divus. Solution: Although the ward might have had money and movables, nevertheless, at the time of the issuance of the said decree, the said money might have been consumed; and similarly regarding movable things. However, because they are presumed to exist, since the contrary is not proven, as in C. de probationibus, l. ex persona, and ff. qui satisdare cogantur, l. si vero, § qui pro rei qualitate, I say that the said decree and the said sale did not hold. Nevertheless, because the said money was converted to the benefit of the ward, the buyer has the right of retention of the thing bought, until the aforementioned price is returned to him, as noted in C. commodati, l. sub praetextu, by Cynus and others, and in ff. de condictione indebiti, l. si non sortem, § si centum, and in ff. de pignoris actione, l. eleganter, § qui reprobos. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether ownership and possession of a church are acquired through investiture.
2. By whom a hospital building is presumed to have been constructed.
3. Whether the term "buildings" includes the land.
4. How possession and ownership are to be proved.
5. When the confession of a slave is to be believed.
6. The thing itself is determined from the boundaries of the things.
7. Intent is required in the case of interversion.
8. Whether one owing a census or tribute is the useful and direct owner, and whether he loses his right if he fails to pay the tribute.
9. Whether an appeal may be taken from a possessory action.
10. Execution carried out after an appeal has been lodged must be rescinded.
11. Whether the right of patronage endures when a hospital is broken down and completely destroyed.
body: The instrument made by Otto, preceding himself, in the name of Christ, having been invested by the Abbot of Saint Peter with a golden ring concerning four perches of land, refused said investiture in the hands of the said Abbot. And the said Abbot accepted it for the purpose of establishing there a hospital in honor of God, which was to be built by a certain Frater Gandulf, to whom the aforementioned Abbot made a donation of the said four perches of land, the said Abbot retaining for himself, in the name of the said monastery, the right of patronage and of appointing masters in the said hospital, subject to an annual census of one pound of candles. And these matters were solemnly carried out due to the interposition of a decree; from these, contracts were celebrated in 1262.

† Here, first of all, it is asked, since no tradition of possession appears, whether any right has been acquired by the said monastery of Saint Peter: and it seems that not, because dominion and possession are not proved by an instrument made between others: although contract and obligation are proved between the contracting parties, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. predia; and in X. de fide instrumentorum, cap. inter dilectos, §. fin. And this is true if dominion and possession are denied under oath against calumny, as noted in Speculum, de locatione, §. nunc aliqua, vers. 52. The same is asked if someone says under oath against calumny that he is ignorant, because the fact is ancient: because dominion is not proved by title alone. But if dominion were established, it would suffice in the case of a church, as in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. finalis. Indeed, some say that even possession would be presumed, as in cap. 2, X. de consuetudinibus. But there, a tradition made by the custom of the place intervened. Some also say that dominion is not transferred by renunciation, arguing from C. de transactionibus, l. si pro fundo. Bartolus touches upon this passage in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. quae nobis. However, this opinion is rejected by the gloss in C. de probationibus, l. cum res, namely when dominion is disputed directly or principally. For just as the essence of dominion is different from that of possession, so too is the mode of proving possession different, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. naturaliter, §. nihil commune. Therefore, on this first point, I conclude that from the matters narrated no proof arises for the church of Saint Peter, unless it were aided by other instruments: because often that which is not proved by itself is proved by an adjunct, as in D. de re vendita, l. quaedam mulier; and in C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. minus instructus. For the antecedent draws the consequent to itself, and conversely. Likewise, from the beginning of the title, the subsequent event is formed, as in l. 1, C. de impositione lucrativa descriptione. And this is as far as the first point is concerned.

The following is another case, under the heading "In the name of Christ," dated 1319, September 27, in which it is contained that the Abbot of the said church, asserting that the Hospital of Saint Anthony, built on the aforementioned territory, pertains fully by right to the aforementioned monastery both in temporal and spiritual matters, appoints a certain pauper as minister of the said hospital with the burden of paying a census; however, it is presupposed that it does not appear that this pauper administered the said hospital, nor that he paid the said census. Furthermore, it does not appear who built the said hospital, nor that it was built on the said territory, except insofar as this might result from the words of the said instrument. I answer as above, because a transaction between others does not prejudice others, unless he proves that he possessed the said church, as in the rule of law. What must be proved is set forth in the Speculum in the title De locato, § Nunc aliqua, verse 56 and verse 58, Quæritur, and it is clear. Digest, De publicanis, l. Si eum quis, si duobus, and § Fin.

But here it remains to be seen, if it appears that the hospital has been built, by whom it is presumed to have been built; and it seems to be said that it is presumed to have been built by him who was bound to build it, as shown by the argument in the Codex, On the Administration of a Ward’s Property, in the final law. For nature itself proves that the hospital was constructed; and reason dictates that it is presumed to have been made by him who ought to have made it, as Bartolus proves in the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, in the law Cum servus. And this reason greatly favors the Abbot. It is a continuous [clause] with the preceding instruments, and very close to the truth; nevertheless, it does not extend beyond the body of the hospital, and with another territory it has nothing in common.

† because the word "buildings" does not include the land, as stated in the Digest, on the action of sale, law "fundi" 1328, according to the opinion of Nonius, and in the law "granaria" in the Digest, on usucapion, law "eum, qui aedes." Although sometimes gardens connected to the buildings themselves are included, as in the Digest, on urban servitudes, law "Olympico," and in the Digest, on legacies, book 1, law "praediis," section "pe. et fi." This accession is extrinsic, not intrinsic, because it is not contained in the substantial definition, but has its own body and its own substance. To this I add that the said hospital was completely destroyed, about which I will speak below. I, Baldus.

It follows that whether, in the name of the Lord, in the name of Christ, the same Abbot instituted in perpetuity Brother Guidon and the other members of the Order of Saint Anthony, in the name and on behalf of the house and Order of Saint Anthony of Vienne, with respect to forty perches of land, upon which one church had been constructed under the name of Saint Anthony, together with certain houses adjoining it there, subject to a census of nine florins, with the stipulation added that the same investees should cause said investiture to be confirmed both by the Pope and by the General Abbot of Saint Anthony of Vienne. However, no evidence appears of this confirmation; rather, there appears a confession, namely that the said Abbot confessed to having received from Brother Guidon, in the name of the lords of Saint Anthony, nine florins for the census. Furthermore, there appears another instrument concerning another payment of nine florins. Now the question arises whether from these things the right of the said Abbot is proved.
† and it seems that this is so, because whenever something is acquired for the master by the act of the slave,

The confession of the slave is upheld, as in D. de manum. l. Cayus; D. bas. Sancti Anto. Vienensis; and likewise the brothers state that the instruments celebrated between Brother Guidon and the said Abbot of Saint Peter are valid. Moreover, the said confirmation is presumed from long possession, by analogy to D. de acq. haer. l. qui in aliena; C. de pet. haer. l. si filius. And the cause is presumed from the payment of the census, as in D. de usur. l. cum de in rem verso. And from the preceding title, the subsequent possession is understood, as in D. de rei vend. l. quaedam mulier; C. de acq. pos. l. 2; D. si serui vendicentur. l. si a te. l.

† And from the boundaries of things, instruments being placed, the things themselves are declared. D. de censu, l. forma; D. de rei vend., l. si in rem agat aliquis. Moreover, two adjacent things can be comprehended by inspection of the eyes. They are suburban, serving urban properties, without which the principal urban properties do not fare well. And situated within their body, or near their body, or assigned to them: just as we say similarly regarding the suburbs of a city, as fully noted in c. ciuitas, de sententia excommunicati, lib. 6, and l. 2, D. de verborum significatione. Moreover, what the eye has seen, no one easily denies. And what is manifestly apparent from the outside need not be proved, D. fin. reg., l. si irruptione, § ad officium; and C. fin. reg., l. si quis super. Moreover, here certain houses were expressly mentioned as adjacent, and therefore adjacency ought not to be proved otherwise, because demonstration is argued in vain for a thing already demonstrated. D. de legatis 3, l. Patro, § 1; D. de donationibus praeteritis, l. 1, in fine; D. si certum petatur, l. certum.

To the contrary it seems, because from all these things possession is not proved, nor corporeal investiture, as in c. 1, de consuetudine recti feudi; and D. quibus modis ususfructus amittitur, l. Pomponius; C. de donationibus, l. censua; D. de acquisitione rerum dominii, l. quae quisque; D. de finibus, instit., l. inter dilectos, in fine. Moreover, there is no appearance of mandate or ratification, D. de deposito, l. si quis inficiatus; D. de negotiorum gestione, l. si ego. And that it was done without mandate does not prejudice the lord, unless ratification is established: because ratification makes the business ours, which was conducted in our contemplation, as D. de negotiorum gestione, l. si pupilli, § idem ait. Nor is he said to interrupt possession who denies this: since it is never proved that he possessed under this title.

† is required. n. for the interposition of the act to the intent of spoliation, as C. de acquisitione possessionis, l. si; ff. de vi et vi armata, l. colonus; ff. de restitutione spoliatorum, l. olim causam. Let us see, and let us presuppose not only true, but also proven, all that is contained in the said instruments. I ask what right results to each party from the above-mentioned investitures and confessions: and whether the direct dominion, albeit conditional, i.e., censual, or the useful, or emphyteutic dominion, has been acquired by the Order and the Lords of Saint Anthony; for in the said instruments there is no mention of the reservation of dominion made by the Abbot of Saint Peter. Therefore, the said 40 perches of land pertain to the direct and total dominion of Saint Anthony of Vienna, because a perpetual censual contract is a just cause for transferring direct and total dominion, albeit with the burden of tribute or census, as C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. placet. For these things stand together, that one pays tribute, if indeed he has direct dominion, as C. de usucapionis transformatione, l. 1; just as one has dominion, and yet performs a servitude for another. For the payment of census is a certain servitude, arg. extra de electione, c. quaerelam. The doctors say in the said c. olim causam, on the word "three solidi censuales." Note that by the retention of the pension, dominion is not retained; otherwise it would be superfluous that which follows: "dominium nihilominus," etc., de hoc supra in titulo, i. c. si, de re iudicata; c. cum Bertoldus, de religiosis domibus; c. constitutus, de appellationibus; c. bone, etc. And 1. says Bartolus in l. 1, §. hic titulus, ff. de publicanis.

† If, however, a census or tribute is owed to someone other than the fisc, for example to a private individual, a city, or a church, then the one who owes the census is the useful and direct owner; and if he does not pay the census, he does not lose his right, as is alleged in the cited chapter *Constitutus*. It is stated that this is notable, and that an emphyteutic contract is not presumed unless the one who granted it reserved for himself a right in the thing. From these points it is clearly concluded that the Church of St. Peter has no ownership, nor legitimate possession, in the said lands and houses, without prejudice to the truth that a census might be owed, as in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Fideiussor*, section *Tractatum*, subsection *Qui tamen*.

Furthermore, it must be known that those things which are left in consideration of Blessed Anthony, when the testator would not otherwise have made a bequest, are acquired by Blessed Anthony himself. Nor is it necessary that it appear that the one to whom it is left in this consideration is a brother of the said order, as in the Digest, *De vulgari substitutione*, law *Si plures*, section *In arrogato*; Digest, *De annuis legatis*, law *Annua*, section 1. And even to a church can be acquired by any Catholic, as by a subject of the Catholic and universal Church, under whose spiritual power we all are; for the Lord’s is the earth, etc. This is proven by the first question, seventh chapter, *Quotiens cordis oculus*.

Finally, it follows that there is another instrument, in which it is contained that the aforementioned Brother Guido, asserting that the house described below had come to the said hospital by title of legacy, of which, however, there is no evidence, invested certain Jacob the baker in 1337 with the said house, concerning which the question now arises, by a perpetual fictum. Another instrument was drawn up in 1339, in which it is contained that the said Jacob sold the said house to Lord Carbono with the burden of paying the fictum; and that the said Lord Carbono was invested in the name of the said hospital by the aforementioned Lord Guido in the year 1340, on the day, etc.; and that after the said investiture, the aforementioned Carbono paid the said fictum to the said Brother Guido.

Now the question arises: what right results from the said instruments, presupposing the possession of the said Carbono? And there is no doubt that a Publician action results; because Carbono possessed by title and in good faith, as is read and noted in the Digest, *De usucapione*, law *Census*. And if forty years had elapsed, ownership would have been acquired, as in the Code, *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, authentic *Quas actiones*.

Then there is added a certain verbal investiture towards Brother Benedict of the Order of St. Anthony. But I say that from the said investiture no right was acquired to the said Abbot of St. Peter, or to his monastery, because a religious, being a servant of his monastery, cannot prejudice his monastery, as in the Code, *De pace*, law *Servus*. And especially because the last heir of the said Carbono invested Francesco of Florence with the said house; which he could do, even if he could not have had more than useful ownership from the censual contract, as in the Digest, *De contrahenda emptione*, law *Qui tabernas*; Digest, *De legato primo*, law *Si domus*, final section.

Having examined the contracts, let us come to the matter of judgment. And speaking realistically, it does not appear to me to be true that the said Abbot has a right, but rather the said Francesco. And unless I saw something else in the facts, the law seems to me to be most certain there, according to what is proposed. And there remains only to see about the appeal, whether an appeal can be taken from the sentence passed for the said Abbot in the possessory action for recovery of possession; and whether its execution should be stayed; furthermore, out of abundance, whether the right of patronage continues after the destruction of the hospital.

† Regarding the first point, whether an appeal may be lodged, it seems to be said that it cannot under civil law, if the action is purely possessory, as is stated in C. de sen. et interlo. om. iudi. l. post sent. and C. si de momen. pos. l. vnica. But under canon law, an appeal may be lodged, especially if a reasonable cause is expressed in the appeal, as in extra de resti. spo. capit. cum ad sedem and c. ex conquestione, and de testibus capit. significauerunt.
