As for restitution in integrum, there is no doubt that a minor and a church may seek it if they have suffered enormous injury; this is fully debated and noted in the aforementioned l. vnica si de momen. pos. and is sufficiently proven by C. de iudiciis l. properandum in fine, joined with the beginning of the same law, and by the ancient maxim that aid is afforded to a minor, and by the special law of the church; therefore, why is aid not afforded in the same manner under the common law by invoking the assistance of a superior? Moreover, if it were a possessory action for recovery, and the sentence were extracted by the judge according to the constitution of the law si quis in tantam, it would be even stronger and more just to say that an appeal could be lodged, so that no prejudice be done to the property right, arg. ff. de appel. l. creditis §. iussus. This is noted in Spec. de appel. §. in quibus versi. 6 and versi. sed nunquid, although Archi. has written much on this point, 2. q. 6. §. sunt etiam quororum versu, si de possessione.

† Nevertheless, this is the truth, and therefore execution carried out while an appeal is pending must be revoked by way of *attentata*, as is stated by Innocentius in *c. Non solum*, *De appellationibus*, lib. 6, namely that if the entire judgment is annulled, so too is the execution, *De officio delegati*, *c. Pastoralis*. I come

† On the final point concerning the hospital that has been broken and completely destroyed: I say that through it a rector cannot be presented, because it is dry and barren, as stated in the Digest, *De servitutibus rusticorum praediorum*, law *Et Attilianus*, unless for the administration of its goods and in hope of restoration, by argument from the Digest, *De legatis primo*, law *Domos* and law *Si domus*, and from the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Paulus*, section *Domo*. For the emphyteusis endures in those goods which have not perished by chance, as stated in the Code, *De iure emphyteuticario*, law 1, and by argument from the Digest, *De conditionibus indebiti*, law *Qui exceptione*, section *Si pars*. For the remainder retains the name of hospital; and what remains for the sustenance of the hospital will be administered to the poor, or converted to the rebuilding of the hospital, if it is possible to repair it. The text elsewhere states that a house will be leased, in which the hospital is to be maintained in the meantime, in the Authenticum *De ecclesiis*, section *Si quis aedificationem*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one may renounce by agreement the reduction to the arbitration of an upright man.
body:
I premise that this [question] is: whether by agreement one can renounce reduction to the good man’s discretion. And Jacobus de Arena holds that yes, in such a manner, namely that a liberatory agreement be made not to sue and not to exercise such right of reduction in the case where such reduction happens to be applicable, as in a similar case. D. de liberatione, l. Non solum, §. fin.; and l. Si rationes; and D. de pactis, l. Si unus, §. Illud. And in this form Cynus says. Dynus, however, held simply that one cannot renounce such reduction, in c. Scienti, de regulis iuris, lib. 6; and D. de verbis oblig., in l. Quidam cum filium. For he says that a tacit condition is always understood, if he has arbitrated equally. Jacobus Butrinteus held that such renunciation is valid unless fraud proceeds from the arbitrator’s mind; but where injury does not intervene in fact, he says the agreement must be observed and is valid. Nor does Dynus’s reason stand against this, according to him; for it is true that a tacit condition is implied, unless something else is expressed; for by agreement the tacit nature of the compromise is altered, as we see in a similar praetorian stipulation. D. de verbis oblig., l. In conventionalibus. Bartolus holds simply with Dynus, because if the agreement were valid, the arbiter or arbitrator would be induced to commit a wrong. But this reason does not carry much weight, because it would already be the case that if fraud on the part of the arbitrator appears, the agreement would have no effect, as C. de arbitris, l. 3. Whatever the case may be, the common obligation is that whatever verbal caution has been added, reduction may be sought on account of enormous injury; for the compromisers did not truly intend that the arbiter or arbitrator would injure them enormously, arg. D. de mandato, l. Creditor, §. Lucius; and D. de transactionibus, l. Cum Aquilia. Nor do the said laws Non solum, §. fin., and Si quis rationes, stand against this, because they speak of a free act, namely a legacy; but we are dealing with a compromise, in which the parties’ intention is not to make a gift; nor would they come to an arbiter or arbitrator if such had been their intention. Rather, intending to pursue their right, they approach him; and therefore they ought not to be deceived by him, in whom they place their confidence, arg. D. de transactionibus, l. Qui cum tutoribus, §. Qui per fallaciam; and D. de pactis, l. Tres fratres. We see something similar in a free discretion given, and l. Quia in praeiudicium alterius non est trahendum, as D. de testamento militis, l. 1; and l. In fraudem. And it supports what I noted in c. Saepenumero, de verborum significatione.

Secondly, I premise that where an arbitrator injures a party enormously, it is presumed that he did so from his mind and with fraud, as noted in D. de praetoria stipulatione, l. Fin.; and by Bartolus in D. pro socio, l. Si duo societatem, §. Arbitrorum. From the above it follows, whatever opinion we hold, that since the parties here have been enormously injured, the arbitral award, although fully rendered, ought to be reduced. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The license granted to an arbitrator must be understood as full, but with good faith.
body: On the Granting of Arbitration. In the name of Christ. It is to be understood in this manner. Indeed, fully, but based on good faith. Digest, On Mandate, Law: The Creditor, Section: Lucius. And therefore, that which has been done in bad faith and in an excessive manner ought to be corrected by the discretion of the judge, if manifest inequity appears, as in Digest, On Partnership, Law: Hence, if Nerva; Digest, On Freedmen’s Work, Law: If a freedman; thus, On Oaths, Constitution: Quintavallis; and in Constitution: Scienti, On the Rules of Law, according to Dyonisius; Code, On Arbitrators, Law: Pe, according to Cynus. And therefore, if the arbitrator has exceeded the limit excessively, either entirely, or to a great extent, or wholly, it shall either be annulled, or the act exceeding the limit shall be reduced to the limit, whether fraud has intervened, or gross negligence, which is compared to fraud: for example, if a profound error has intervened. Digest, If the Reaper Stated a False Measure, Law 1, Section 1. Someone might say, an award is a species of compromise, as noted in Authenticum: Ut Differentes Iudices, Section 1. Therefore, it must be upheld, even if great injury has intervened. Digest, On the Trebellian Trust, Law: Lucius, Section: If. Solution. There, it speaks of a true compromise, which the parties make by themselves. But if the power to compromise has been granted to the arbitrator, and he compromises improperly, it may rightly be requested that it be reformed, since it was done contrary to the right of the parties bound and contrary to their expectation, as is noted. Digest, On the Signification of Words, Law: Those Words; and Code, On Contracting Sale, Law: Final. I, Baldus. In

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Those condemned to death become slaves of the penalty, but whether they can make a will.
2. A corporal execution carried out contrary to the law of the constitution does not induce slavery of the penalty, nor incapacity to make a will.
3. Whether a sentence passed for death entails execution.
4. Whether a vassal who kills another vassal, both he and his sons, are deprived of the fief by the law itself, or by sentence.
5. Whether a vassal who expelled another vassal loses his right.
6. Whether an impetration made by one who by force expelled his co-heir from a common castle is valid.
7. Whether one accepting an inheritance must be certain of the death: and what certainty is required.
body: condemned to death.

† The law says that those condemned to death become slaves of the penalty, nor can they make a will; ff. de testa. l. eius, qui. §. hi vero. And the reason is two-fold: namely, because they lack goods and the status of freedom; therefore they do not make a will, as being not even the owners of property. For the will of one who has left no goods in the city is not valid, as in ff. de vul. sub l. lex Cornelia; for with his life he loses all his fortunes, as in ff. de bon. pos. secundum tabulas. l. qui ex liberis. §. testameto; the aforesaid points are proved in ff. de iniu. testa. l. si quis filio exhaeredato. §. sed et si quis. Ioan. And. holds that he cannot make a will even for pious causes or concerning the restitution of usury, so that it would be valid by the law of a will or of codicils, as he fully notes in capitu. quanquam. de usuris. lib. 6. in nouel., and it was so determined in disputation. But it must be observed that the reason given in the text in the said §. et si quis, where it says, “for he becomes a slave of the penalty,” has been corrected according to the glossa placed there. For although they are subject to the penalty, they are nevertheless not slaves of the penalty: because today no well-born person, that is, a freeborn person, is made of servile condition by reason of punishment, as in the Authen. de nup. §. quod autem, although the contrary is noted in ff. de pęnis. l. qui vltimo. If therefore we hold the glossa that is on the said §. sed et si quis, the reasoning of those texts having been corrected, the prohibiting law ceases to apply, as in l. adigere. §. quamuis. de iure patrona. and ff. de adulte. l. quod ait lex. But surely, although one reason may be corrected, the other remains: namely, because he left no goods in the city, since upon his natural death the provision of the Authentica bona damnatorum succeeds. But here it must be considered that one who dies while the time for appealing is pending is not said to die without goods; nay rather, by his death while the appeal is pending the judgment is extinguished, just as if an appeal had been made, as is singularly noted in ff. de accusatio. l. ex iudiciorum; because the benefit of appeal while the time for appealing is pending works the same effect as an appeal solemnly interposed, as is noted in l. 1. ff. nil nouari appel. penden. But it is certain that when an appeal has been interposed, whether it was received or not, it is confirmed by death, as in the said l. si quis filio. §. hi autem omnes. Therefore, the will of this man in question, who was beheaded immediately after the sentence, was also confirmed by death. But argue from ff. de don. inter virum, et vxorem. l. sed interim; and confession alone does not take away the right of appeal, because it could be revoked or excused in the cause of appeal, as is noted in ff. de appel. l. creditor. §. iussus; for example, if to recover his possession, when other civil remedy failed him, he used victorious arms in a brawl, as is noted in C. de iudaeis. l. nullus facit; ff. ad l. Aquil. l. ex plagis. §. tabernarius; and C. ad I. Iuliam de vi. l. quoniam multa facinora; and C. vnde vi. l. 1; for wounds must be healed with steel when they do not accept the treatment of soothing applications. If, however, it were a case in which one could not appeal by law, such that an appeal would be void ipso iure, then the common opinion is that the will is not valid; to the aforesaid points supports ff. de appel. l. non tantum; C. quorum appel. non reci. l. 2; C. de appel. i. aditos; with similar passages. Furthermore, he who defends himself unlawfully may be attacked, yet with moderation, if he can exercise moderation, as in C. de his, qui ad ecclesi. confu. l. si seruus. It should also be known that if the sentence were void ipso iure, there is no doubt that the will would be valid, as in the said l. si quis filio. §. quod si quis, and l. 2. ff. de poenis.

† And from the aforesaid it appears that bodily execution carried out contrary to constitutional law does not induce slavery of the penalty, nor the incapacity to make a will; ff. de testamen. l. qui a latronibus; and support is lent by what is noted in l. pe. ff. de condit. ob causam, if the goods were not expressly taken away; and in ca. 1. §. fina. de milite vasallo, qui contumax est; and extra de accusa. capitu. cum dilecti. And note that Barto., following Iaco. de Are. in the said l. ex iudiciorum, says that if the condemned man does not appeal, he must blame himself. But he does not speak the truth, because the benefit of the delay of 10 days must not be taken away from anyone; and this man, up to and including the last breath of his life, has the time for appealing, which he cannot renounce in a capital case, as is noted in ff. de pactis. l. pactum, although by custom assessors do not observe this delay of 10 days for appealing; capit. idultum. de reg. iur. But against the aforesaid it seems,

† because a sentence pronounced to death immediately carries with it execution in capacity (habitu), though not in act; the same holds intellectually, though not materially, because one who is alive is not yet dead, as is noted in l. qui duos. ff. de manu. test. For he still needs food and sustenance; ff. de capi. dimi. l. lectum; ff. de re iud. l. si victum; nevertheless, the sentence immediately takes away the status that consists in law, that is, freedom, as is noted in ff. de pe. l. qui vlt. and there this is fully stated by Bar., who also says that by custom no period for appealing is waited for; which is fortified by the reason that such a sentence is not passed except upon one who confesses, and confession creates notoriety, and against notoriety plaintive libels are not admitted, as is noted in c. Romana. de appel. li. 6. But that is understood, as Spe. there noted says, that within the time for appealing bodily execution cannot take place, and that before bodily execution can take place, it immediately follows that today he will not become a slave of the penalty; and if he dies in the meantime, the will is valid, just as if he had died after an appeal had been interposed; because if he does not lose his goods in the meantime, he therefore does not lose his status, that is, freedom, because he who loses freedom leaves no goods in the city, as in ff. de vul. sub. l. lex Corne. In short, if we wish to believe the glossator, Spec., the will is valid, and the swiftness of death does not pertain to the right of making a will. Bar. says that a delay introduced by the law cannot be renounced in capital cases, as he notes in ff. de pub. iud. l. custodias. in fi., meaning to say: it would be otherwise if they had been granted by man, that is, by the ministry of the judge. But can written instruments be renounced? And it seems that they cannot, unless they are suspected, or denied to be true, as in C. de fi. inst. l. si aduersarius. l. fi. From the aforesaid it appears that the swiftness of execution does not take away the benefit of the delay by law, although it takes it away de facto. As to the second point, it is proposed,

† that one of the feudatories killed the other, who was his full brother, or his paternal cousin. It is asked whether the killer and his sons have thereby fallen from the right of the fief? And it must be said that through a sentence he who killed his brother is deprived of the fief by forfeiture, and it reverts to the lord, as in cap. 1. similiter. quibs mod. feud. amitta.; yet not ipso iure, but through a sentence where fault is joined, as in ca. sanci. quo tempore miles. in the same collation; and in capi. 1. §. denique. quę fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi; and in capitu. si vasallus culpam. Si de feudo controuer. fue.; and in capitu. 1. an ille, qui interfecit fratrem domini sui; and in capitu. imperialem. §. callidis. on the word, amittat. de prohibitio. feu. alie. per Federic.
† It follows to see whether Cabriotus, who had expelled Nicolaus, had fallen from his right. I answer, as I have said, a sentence is required, as noted in C. vnde vi. l. si quis in tantam.

† Likewise it is asked whether an impetration made by him who expelled his co-holder by force from a common castle holds good? And the glossa ordinaria determines that it does not, and gives the example in count Bartolotus; C. de fundis, et saltibus rei dominicae. l. si qua loca. lib. 11.; and it is express in C. vnde vi. l. autoritate.

† Another point follows, because it is not known whether the son is alive or not. I answer: he who enters upon an inheritance must be certain of the death, as in C. de captiuis. l. nec nos; nevertheless, certainty by sight is not always required, because death is proved by an argument from what commonly happens, as is noted in C. so. ma. l. si quidem. and l. qui ex liberis. in prin. de bo. pos. secundum tab. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the sign of the cross is of the substance of the inventory.
2. The solemnity is not slight if the law proceeds further by annulling.
3. Preambles are not of the substance.
4. An inventory is so called from the act of finding.
5. Whether the citation of absentees is required in the making of an inventory.
6. Whether the sign of the cross affixed in any part of the instrument suffices.
7. If the inventory is not begun within a month, but is solemnly completed within the following two months, whether the law is satisfied.
8. Good faith excuses and supplies many defects.
9. In the making of an inventory, the presence of the judge is required, and not his decree.
body: whether the sign of the cross is the beginning

† It is asked whether the sign of the cross is the beginning of an inventory, or rather a certain prelude to it, or a certain preface or exordium; and whether it pertains to the substance of the form of an inventory, so that if this formality is not observed, the inventory is null ipso iure, and the heir is held in solidum just as if he had not made an inventory at all. And on this point there are two opinions: one contains rigor, because it tends toward a penalty; and that rigid opinion holds that the inventory is not valid, because this formality is not insignificant, since it was introduced in honor of God, as in ff. de aur. et ar. le. l. Titia. §. fi. Likewise, the sign of the cross makes God a witness, as in Auth. quibus mo. na. effi. leg. §. quantum. Likewise, he who makes the sign of the cross, by looking upon this terrible sign, has in mind not to commit fraud or deceit, just as the Gospel placed before one's eyes sometimes causes an oath to be deemed sworn with the sacrosanct scriptures having been touched.

† Likewise because the law goes further by declaring nullity: for it says, if they have consolidated the aforementioned observance, that is, if they have observed all clauses in solidum, then let them have the benefit of inventory, and not otherwise, C. de iure deliberan. l. fina. §. et si praefatam. But that is not a trivial formality, where, if it does not intervene, the law goes further by declaring nullity, as in ff. de transactio. l. cum hi. §. si pretor. Likewise Speculator, who had experience of the entire practice of both laws, and who knew well the writings of the ancients, places the sign of the cross in the instrument of the inventory, in Spe. de instr. edi. §. dicto at the end. To the contrary it seems, for that sign of the cross is placed before so that one does not proceed to the inventory with unwashed hands, ff. de orig. iur. l. 1, not that the sign of the cross itself pertains to the inventory;

† and preludes when omitted do not vitiate, because preambles do not belong to the substance, as noted in Authem. in medio litis non fieri sacras formas. §. fi. and by Bart. in ff. de test. l. si quaeramus.

† Furthermore, 'inventory' is named from 'finding' (inueniendo), as in C. de bonis vacan. l. fi., C. arbitrium tutelae. l. vlti., C. de bonis proscriptorum. l. si quis intra., and C. de episco. et cler. l. nulli.; but by the sign of the cross nothing is found, therefore it is not of the body of the inventory, an argument from C. de feriis. l. a nullo and C. de codicillis. l. si idem. Furthermore, in the inventory of a tutor, curator, orphanotrophus, and the like, the sign of the cross is not of the substance; and yet if they do not make an inventory, they are presumed to have embezzled, and to have omitted items in the inventory with the intent of concealing the truth, ff. de administratione tuto. l. tutor, qui repertorium., C. de admi. tuto. l. tutores.; therefore by analogy the same holds in the inventory of an heir. Furthermore, the intention of the law is one, namely that the truth shine forth; and once this is obtained, other superficial matters are not cared about, because they do not pertain to the essence (de esse), though they may pertain to good order (de bene esse), as in C. de fideicom. l. quaestionem at the verse 'lex enim', and this opinion savors of natural equity: for penalties that arise if a formality is omitted, provided that the truth is observed, do not savor of a good or right conscience, as noted in c. quanquam. de vsuris. lib. 6. in the Novella. Cynus holds this opinion in C. de iure deli. l. fi., because although this formality is not light out of fuller reverence for God, nevertheless it is not burdensome, and therefore when omitted it does not vitiate, as in l. 1. in fi. ff. de ven. inspi. and the argument in l. 1. C. de formulis. The Apostle says, 'whatever you do, do in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,' and yet those words, 'in the name of the Lord', are not of the substance, because it suffices to say, 'be my heir,' as in l. 1. ff. de haere. insti. Although notaries include them by common style, nevertheless those who execute the act are not required to utter these words, as noted in 23. dist. c. in nomine domini. Likewise, the benefit of inventory benefits Jews and Saracens subject to the Roman people; and yet they do not make the sign of the cross on account of their superstition; and it would be absurd for them to be in an easier condition than we who catholically profess Jesus Christ the Son of God, as in C. de Iudęis. l. Iudęi Romano.; on the contrary, in many things Jews are in a worse condition than true Christians, since the synagogues of the Jews cannot be alleged by Christians so that their worship may be approved, C. de Iudaeis. l. quod Cornelia., nor with respect to civil honors, as in C. eod. l. fi. From these points it follows that the sign of the cross is not properly the beginning of an inventory, because by that sign one does not proceed to anything substantial of the inventory. And therefore the advocates seem to err who say that such a person made the sign of the cross for the beginning of the inventory. Likewise, they place the heir in great danger: because the heir would believe that he had three months remaining to him—one to begin the inventory, and another two to finish it. For according to the opinion of Speculator, as soon as it is begun, the two months run, as in said §. oneroso, and thus what is completed after two months is of no avail, because when the law proceeds further, delay cannot be purged; nevertheless, the fairer opinion would be that after the first month has elapsed, the other two months should run, because whatever he does within the month, before he completes it, is said to be begun until it is perfected, and a testament is said to be begun until it is consummated, as in ff. de vsuca. l. ceptam. and ff. de leg. 3. l. fideicommissum. §. 1. Now it follows

† to see, since in the beginning of the inventory absentees were not cited, whether the inventory is vitiated by this. It seems that it is, as in Authen. de haere. et fal. §. si vero absunt. Solution: I say that if fraud could have been committed in the begun inventory, the inventory is not valid; but if fraud could not have been committed, as in the setting down of immovable goods, as in C. quando, et quibus quarta pars debetur. l. 2., then citation is not required, because it does not concern, nor can it concern the absentees; and because what can be done against their will can be done without their being cited, as noted in ff. de bo. pos. l. 3. §. pe.

† Next it is asked whether it suffices to place the sign of the cross on any part of the instrument: and it seems that it ought to be placed at the beginning in the manner of a title, as noted in l. 1. C. ne liceat potentioribus. To the contrary, that it should be placed at the end of the inventory in the manner of a subscription, C. qui testa. face. pos. l. hac consultissima. §. fi. Solution: it suffices if it is made on any part of the instrument, C. de insti. et substi. l. pe., de appel. c. secundo requiris.

† Concerning one point it is asked: if the inventory was not begun within the month, but solemnly consummated within the other two months, whether the law has been satisfied: and it seems that it was not, because the first term was not satisfied; and whenever the law requires several things to achieve one effect, one alone does not suffice, but both are required, as in said l. cum hi. §. si praetor. To the contrary it seems, because ultimate diligence is beneficial and supplies what was lacking at the beginning, since the matter is intact, as in ff. de optione legata. l. apud aufidium. and ff. de no. ope. nun. l. praetor. §. si aliquando. Furthermore, the inheritance concerning which the question is raised was for the greatest part, after debts were deducted, in remote parts, since the testator was from Chieri in Piedmont, and there were four thousand florins in the province of Brabant; in which case it suffices for the inventory to be begun within four months, and to be finished within another eight months running continuously, as noted in C. de iure delib. l. fi. §. sinautem a locis; within which four months all formalities were without doubt observed, both concerning the sign of the cross and concerning the citation of absentees, namely of those who could be cited, and through a publicly posted edict, and all the rest, just as the law formally requires. Therefore, the said inventory was solemn, and the heirs have the benefit of inventory. And this is just and equitable, especially

† because good faith supplies many things by excusing, as in ff. de condi. et demon. l. quamuis., especially in the subtleties and snares of the civil law, and l. j. in fi. ff. de abigeis., and as noted in l. eum, qui. §. in popularibus. ff. de iureiu., especially in avoiding penalties. That point is certain: that the time for the inventory does not run against one who is ignorant; whence, as soon as he knows the things to be set down, so soon must he begin the inventory; and for this he shall have at least one month. Furthermore, an ignorant person is not in bad faith, as in C. de incestis nuptiis. l. cum ancillis., ff. de admini. tu. l. quidam decedens. §. ex quo innotuit., ff. de excus. tuto. l. quinquaginta., ff. de edil. edicto. l. cum sex., ff. de infamibus. l. genero., and ff. de calum. l. annus.

† In addition it must be known that in the drafting of an inventory the presence of a judge is required, because he who must cite ought to be present; nevertheless it is provided by no law that his decree is required, as noted in Speculator where cited above, and from the argument in C. qui admitti ad bono. pos. possunt. l. fina., and what Bartolus notes in ff. de dona. l. Modestinus. and C. de testamen. l. omnium. But in the inventory of a tutor a decree is required; and the reason is that a tutor cannot administer unless administration is decreed to him by the judge, as in C. arbi. tutelae. l. fina., but the heir has administration by his own right. Furthermore, in our question a decree was interposed, except concerning things that subsequently came to the knowledge of the heir. And although the nature of a decree does not extend to future things, nevertheless these come as a consequence of what preceded, just as if a tutor supplements his inventory. For it can probably be said that a decree once interposed suffices, because it immediately brought with it the execution of the benefit of inventory. I, Baldus. From the statement of the case it summarizes itself.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A declaration placed in a limitation of a contract does not pass to the heirs.
2. Whether set-off may be pleaded against a deposit.
body: Two points are to be considered: In the name of Christ. The father and daughter made a deposit for the purpose of converting it into the redemption of properties, or into a right of repurchase (retrodatum) to be effected in the person of the father and daughter, or of the daughter alone, by the will of the father; and under this form the depositary bound himself; and the father died without having declared his will; and the daughter repudiated her father’s inheritance. The question is whether the said daughter can bring an action to effect the right of repurchase; and it was adjudicated by arbitrators that she could so act, provided she caused and ensured that the said deposit be returned to the said vendor, who had bound himself to repurchase, and this was rightly approved. Hence, the said purchaser is not bound to repurchase unless he has the price according to the form of the contract and the approval. Now the said daughter brings an action against the said depositary, demanding that he observe the pact; he says that he is not bound, because he bound himself for the cause of repurchase and under the condition of the father’s will; moreover, the said money was presumed to be the father’s property; and that the daughter is not the heir of the father. Furthermore, he raises the exception of compensation from an instrument of loan of a quantity corresponding to the said deposit; moreover, he alleges that the money was sequestered to him and that he was forbidden to pay it on account of the dowry of the late said depositor. Now the question is, what is the law?

† And this question arises between the depositing daughter and the depositary: for it is certain that, the facts being thus, a resale ought not to take place unless the price be paid out, as in l. 2, C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem; ff. de solutionibus, l. si solutus; ff. de actionibus emptoris, l. Iulianus, §. offerri; Instit. de rerum divisione, §. venditae. Other questions therefore arise between the said daughter and the said depositary: because the deposit was made under a certain law, and the father did not declare his will; and a declaration of will placed in a condition or limitation of the contract does not pass to the heir, as in l. 4, ff. locati conducti; Extra de rescriptis, c. si gratiose, lib. 6; and it is commonly noted, ff. solutione matrimonii, l. post dotem; and arg. ff. de verbis obligatis, l. qui Romae, §. augerius. Nevertheless, from this it would follow that, the cause being reduced to no cause, the said deposit ought to be restored to the depositor, if this had been claimed, as in Lo. de Castel in his libellus, as in ff. de dolo, l. si oleum. Nevertheless, it ought not to be restored to the said daughter except for her share: because the obligation is divisible, ff. de verbis obligatis, l. eadem, §. Cato; and l. reos, §. cum tabulis, de duobus reis; and l. si diversa, locati conducti. Even if the entire sum of money had belonged to the daughter: because one who deposits another’s money can stipulate for himself, as in l. 2, C. si certum petatur; and here a stipulation intervenes both truly and presumptively: because a stipulation is presumed when an instrument intervenes, as in Instit. de inutilibus stipulationibus, §. si scriptum.

It remains to consider the exception of set-off: and it appears that it does not obstruct the case of natural deposit, because he who does not observe the law of deposit is considered to have committed spoliation, as noted by the Doctor in the chapter *Qui ad agendum*, On the Rules of Law, Book 6; and in the Code, On Set-off, the final law, in the clause *Accepta actione depositi*. And if it is said that here the action arises from a stipulated agreement, I answer: rather, it is the action of deposit informed by the agreement appended in the same instrument, as in the Digest, On Agreements, the law *Iuris gentium*, section *Quinimmo*. And even assuming that interest succeeded in the obligation, nevertheless the origin and cause must be examined, as in the Digest, On Gifts, the law *Quicquid*.

Furthermore, the sequestration made by the judge, because it was not made formally, nor for a debt to which she would already be bound, does not harm the daughter. See the Code, On a Wife Not Being Sued for Her Husband, the law *Ob maritorum*; because she repudiated the paternal inheritance, as in the Code, On the Right of Delation, the final law, and similarly in the Code, On Deposit, the law *Si*, and the authenticum there placed. Nor is it presumed that this money belonged solely to the father, because the contrary appears from the instrument of loan made to the daughter; and also from other presumptions, as noted in the Code, On Goods Which Are Free, the law *Cum oportet*; and in the Code, On Pledge, the final law. However, he who promised to resell is not compelled to receive part and resell part, as in the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, the law *Stipulationes non dividuntur*.

The solution is that the order of the transaction was in this form, namely: that this depositary first lent to the daughter by simple delivery (*breui manu*), and he received that loan as a deposit from the daughter alone; and thus the said deposit was fulfilled by reason of the loan, or rather, no out-of-pocket payment or natural numeration intervened, although there were two agreements, one of deposit and the other of loan. And thus, because both descend from one source, it can be said that set-off has place, by argument from the Digest, On the Partition of an Inheritance, the law *Meuius*, section *Eum*, because the deposit arose from the loan. And this is dictated by natural equity, because no one ought to be enriched from my thing to my injury, as in the Digest, On the Action for a Certain Thing Demanded, the law *Si et me, et Titio*.

I also say that where deposit does not appear by numeration, but only by the mere convention of the contract, the laws which state that the cause of deposit is privileged in this respect, so that set-off is not admitted, would not have place, by argument to this point, which is excellent: the Code, On Who May Have a Pledge, the law *Assiduis*, in the small gloss which begins *Non ergo in dote confessata*.

I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The case, briefly stating the opinion in effect, declares who are of the family of the rectors, and whether the rectors of the city are liable for their family, and in which cases they are liable, in which not.
body: The case is as follows, in the name of Christ. John is the general vicar in the entire territory of the lord: and by the form of his letters he has provision and salary for himself and his family, which he is to keep in his house. Moreover, he has salary for one vicar, two notaries, and one constable: and these he himself chooses and hires, and sends wherever he wishes, and retains them in his house at his own expense, and to them he himself promises and pays salary, as the powers of cities do. He also has the right to keep a company of Pavia archers exercising the office of bowmen, and the constable himself chooses and hires these bowmen: and those whom he hires write to the true bench: some are to go and care for the territory of the lord: others are assigned to him both for accompanying him and for exercising the office with him, as he may command. Sometimes he has a company of Hungarians, sometimes a company of crossbowmen on horseback: sometimes lances, sometimes 12 horsemen, or riders, who are chosen by the aforementioned lord, and are enrolled for hire as stipendiaries of the illustrious lord of our lord: and they themselves receive the stipend, and stand on their own. Nevertheless, they are assigned with the aforementioned John in the aforementioned modes for accompanying him: and for obeying in his office.

† A doubt now arises: if these horsemen and cavalrymen, as stated, are enrolled, not hired, nor selected by the aforementioned Lord John Ungari, or if the crossbowmen, the *ab aequo* [those paid equally], or the *a lancea* [lance-men] commit a delict or offend, whether the aforementioned Lord John is liable for them, should they flee or fail to pay, as if they were of his household; and whether they ought to be considered or called of his household; so much so that if a statute or decree provides that anyone who apprehends a banned person shall earn 100 livres, provided that if the person apprehended were of the official’s household, he shall nevertheless earn only 50 livres, the aforementioned such Ungari horsemen, *ab aequo* horsemen, or cavalrymen, or *lancea* men, ought to receive 100 livres; yet, as if they were of the household of the aforementioned Lord John, they ought to receive 100 livres, as do those who are not of the household of the aforementioned Lord John.

Lord Dy. says in l. 1, §. *familiae*, D. de publicanis, that the master is not liable for the delict of his household member, according to l. *quotiens*, D. de noxalibus. This fails in the case of the aforementioned §. *sed familiae*. Bartolus distinguishes: for when someone appoints a household member to some office, and the household member offends in that office, then the master is liable, because he is at fault for having selected such a household member, as in D. furti adversus nautas, cauponas, stabularios; or if he offends outside that to which he was appointed, then the master is not liable. This is sufficiently proven in Extravagantes, de restitutione spoliatorum, c. *cum ad sedem*. And the same distinction is said to be used if it is asked whether rectors of lands are liable for the delicts of their household members. For if they offend in the office committed to them, they are liable; if outside the office, they are not liable. Therefore, he who sues against a magistrate for the delict of his household must prove two things: namely, that the person is of the household, and that he was appointed to such an office; and that he offended in that office. That he is of the household is proven because he stood under the name of the household with others of the household, and exercised acts proper to household members, according to Bartolus. However, in effect, these were the words of Lord Dy. in l. *observare*, §. *proficisci*, D. de officiis proconsulis, and the laws which are such are notable, because if a household member of a magistrate wounds someone, the magistrate is not liable to pay the penalty if criminal action is brought against him; otherwise, if he offends by reason of his office, as in Auth. *ut diffinita iudicia*, §. *tantum*, and infra, D. de publicanis, l. 1, §. *familiae*, and the gloss beginning *rationabilis*, and infra, D. furti adversus nautas, cauponas, stabularios, l. 1, §. *servi*.

Moreover, those are properly called household members whom he keeps with him, as in D. de iure omnium iudicum, l. *qui iurisdictioni*. Hence, those who live separately and live for themselves are not properly household members. Also, if he does not select them, but a superior does, it cannot be said that bad selection is his fault; nevertheless, he is liable if he can prohibit and does not prohibit. And this is by reason of the office he holds: for it pertains to the necessity of his office to prevent and also to punish, as in D. de poenis, l. *si quos forte*, §. *si quis*, and in Auth. *iusiurandum quod praestatur ab his*, where it says, “I shall always endeavor to have such a person attending me: and concerning me, all, so that I indeed do not purloin; but those who purloin and offend concerning me.” And in Auth. *ut iudices sine quoquo suffragio*, §. *eos*, where it says, “so that they do not appear to be doing harm through others; or that they offend and purloin, which is more shameful,” etc. Behold, therefore, what is the law regarding household members whom you, Lord John, selected; but regarding stipendiaries and similar persons, whom our Illustrious Prince appoints to you, you are not liable for bad selection, because you did not select them, but received them into your retinue out of necessity by the command of a superior; command excuses, as in D. furti, §. *qui iussu*, D. de infamibus. But you are well liable for bad use, if you command them to do something unjust, or if you do not resist those acting badly according to your ability, as in C. ne sanctum Baptisma, l. *si*, arg. C. de appellationibus, l. *quoniam iudices*, because he who neglects is deemed to consent; indeed, even to foster, as noted in c. 1, de officio delegati, and D. qui sine manumissione ad libertatem perveniunt, l. *Imperator*. And this is regarding delicts; but regarding their contracts, you are undoubtedly not liable, because not even a father is liable for his son, as in C. ne filius pro patre, throughout, unless you were holding someone contrary to the law, or the command of a superior, or a statute; for then you are liable civilly for their fault, as in the aforementioned §. *proficisci*.

It has been seen regarding the penalty; now let us see regarding the profit, whether, as to the profit, these stipendiaries ought to be called of the official’s household; and it must be said that they are not, because they are not of the body of the household, but distinct and separate, and for themselves, as is proven by the theory of Bartolus which I recited above. And it supports this: D. de rei venditione, l. *qui restituere*. These are rather your defenders, who lead you securely on journeys, than common servants. And usage of speech does not call them your officials, nor your servants.

I, Baldus of Perugia.
CON. Prima Pars Consiliorum.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A uterine brother has no right to demand a partition with a brother who is related through both parents; and if a partition has been made between them, it is rescinded. And l. 2, C. de rescind. vendit. applies to the contract of partition.
body: In the name of Christ. It is proposed that a brother divided the fraternal inheritance with his brother, and from both parents [he derives] greater dignity.

† uterine: and that which was made therefrom was a formal instrument. It is asked whether the said division can be rescinded? And truly, that it cannot, because one is not permitted to be ignorant of the law. C. de iur. et fac. igno. l. pe. Moreover, each person is presumed to know the law, as C. de legi. l. leges sacratissimae. And therefore the contract must stand, as C. communi diui. l. si maior. The contrary is true, because relief is usually granted in cases of divisions improperly made among adults: and that which has been shown to have been made unequally is to be reformed for the better, as C. communia vtriusque iudici. l. maioribus. The gloss says there that when one party has been deceived by more than half. Certainly here he was not deceived only in a share, but in the whole: therefore it is of no effect. ff. de contrah. emp. l. domum. Furthermore, a division is a kind of exchange. As fully noted, ff. de verbo. obli. l. qui Romę. §. duo fratres. But an exchange cannot be made unless something is transferred from one side to the other, as ff. de rerum permu. l. 1. But here the uterine brother contributed nothing from his side: therefore he could not exchange. Furthermore, it must be considered that either the matter concerns profit to be sought, or profit already acquired being taken away. In the first case, error of law is not the immediate cause for rescission, if the contract otherwise has its essentials. In the second case, however, error of law excuses, because losing rooted profit is damage, since it is made from the goods of only one person, and from his certain patrimony, as l. 1. §. sciendum. ff. de separa. bono. And thus the law si emancipata does not obstruct. C. de iur. et fac. igno. This is expressly stated. C. eo. tit. l. si post diuisionem. and l. cum falsa. and l. cum testamentum. It is therefore concluded that the said division was not only unreasonable, but also made in an impossible manner, and is of no effect. And this pertains to the office of the judge. ff. de offi. praesi. l. illicitas. in prin. lest Ulpian’s simplicity devour the flock, and that it is a flock, is sufficiently shown: because a curator has been appointed to him by interdiction of his goods. And it would have been good if, after examining some witnesses on these matters, and with the judge sitting on the bench, these things were done: if they have not been done, as ff. de curatore furiosi. l. obseruare. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 2. Which dignity in the church is greater after the bishop, that of the archdeacon or that of the precentor; and from what it may be known which dignity is greater.
body: ...greater dignity.

† The Archdeacon holds the greater dignity after the bishop in a cathedral church, whence his dignity is greater than the dignity of the provostship; the text is common and express in 25. di. capit. perlectis. And this is evident, because he holds a cathedra in the church, and the height of the seat signifies the pre-eminence of dignity, because greater persons ought to sit in a higher place, as is read and noted in instituta de bono. posses. §. aliam vero. at the word altiore loco, where the glossa says: draw from here that the more worthy ought to sit in a higher place; and he is higher who is nearer to the lord, so the glossa notes there. Moreover, it is most well known that the archdeacon of the church of Augsburg possesses in many respects merum and mixtum imperium in his archdeaconry, which is a dignity of the aforesaid church; but there is no doubt that to have merum and mixtum imperium carries excellence in itself, and it is not granted except to greater magistrates, as in ff. de officio eius, cui manda. est iurisdi. l. j. in prin., and ff. de iurisdi. om. iudi. l. Imperium, and ff. de dam. infec. l. 4. §. duas. and §. si tam vicinum, and C. de pedaneis iudicibus. l. placet, ff. de iud. l. pars literarum, ff. de iniuriis. l. nec magistratibus. Similarly, it is also certain that he who presides over more and better persons is greater, as noted in Authem. constitutio, quae de dignitatibus. §. generaliter, where the glossa says: note, more noble on account of subjects. Item, it is clear that among judges many are lesser and few are greater, as noted in Auth. de iudicibus. in rub. colla. 6. Furthermore, it is also the reward of dignity to have subjects, as noted in Auth. vt iudices sine quoquo suffra. §. volumus, where the glossa says: note, the reward of dignity is to have subjects. Item, it is true that each one in his own seat and dignity is greater than any other, as is read and noted in ff. de manumis. l. apud. eum, where the glossa says: are not both spectabiles there? And respond: be it so, but each is greater in his own territory; clearly because one ought not to touch upon the office of another, as noted in C. de executoribus et exactoribus. l. 2. lib. 12. And he who usurps the place of another is deemed guilty of sacrilege, C. vt dignitatum ordo seruetur. l. 2. lib. 12. Item, he is more worthy who has power over another, as in capit. 1. de maio. et obe. per Innocen.; whence by reason of office the son is more worthy than the father, and superior, as in ff. ad treb. l. nam quod. Item, more worthy is he who holds a dignity with administration than he who holds the bare name of a dignity, as in C. vbi senatores, vel clarissimi. l. quotiens, and C. vt dignitatum ordo seruetur. l. 2., and C. de praeposi. et tri. scholarium. l. vnica. lib. 12. there, when it says: when they have earned the provostship, and by chance have not attained to higher things, that is, administration. Noble insignia also make one more worthy, because they signify the investiture of a dignity, although they do not confer full possession of it, as Dyn. fully notes in capitu. 1. de reg. iu. lib. 6.; which insignia are properly called fasces, that is, honors, as is read and noted in Authen. de consulibus. in prin. colla. 4. When, however, there are two dignities of diverse kinds, as in our case is the Archdeaconry and the provostship, then if it should be asked which is the greater dignity, a comparison of the man would decide it; for that is called greater from predominance which can do the most; it is called greater from honor and excellence to which, according to the status of dignity, greater honor is owed and exhibited in sitting, in writing, and similar things, as in l. i. ff. de albo scribendo. Better stipends also indicate that someone is more acceptable to the Prince and of greater virtue, as in l. nemo. C. de officio magistri officiorum, and ff. de lega. 2. l. cum filius. §. pater cum filia, there where it says: you may grant more for honor, etc. Item, the text says that utility is increased through dignity, ff. de iudi. l. si longius. in fin., and elsewhere it says: for his honor has been increased, not his condition changed, ff. de condi. et demon. l. falsa. §. 1. Honor, however, is properly [the accompaniment] of a rank of dignity with administration, and honors ought to be conferred by degrees, ff. de muner. et honoribus. l. vt gradatim; thus rank shows excellence, and custom makes one noble and distinguished, as in ff. de mune. et hono. l. honor. §. 1. Item, that is a greater dignity which is given for a great benefit, and which men generally deem to be greater, as in ff. de infami. l. athletas. §. 1.; and many other things could be noted on this matter beyond those alleged by the distinguished doctors who have made allegations in this matter and have rightly given counsel on behalf of the venerable Lord Peter, provost of Augsburg. Nor can anything be objected against him, except that at one time he was not in possession, ff. de acquirend. posses. l. peregre. §. quibus explicitis, and ff. de vi, et viar. l. cum fundum. §. fin.; because no one loses his right, even if he loses possession; nevertheless the thing easily reverts to its nature, as in ff. de pac. l. si vnus. §. pactusne peteret. at the verse quod in spem dotis. And if it were said that he resumed possession by his own authority, I say that it was lawful, since the possession was vacant; for he who finds his own possession vacant intends to despoil no one of possession, as noted in C. unde ui. l. si quis in tantam; nay rather, the dignity itself was calling its spouse to return to it, and returning to the church is a kind of passive act rather than an active one; indeed, if he did not return as soon as he could, he would be in default, as in capitu. 1. de clericis non residentibus, and C. de sacrosan. eccle. l. qui sub praetextum, and ff. quibus ex cau. ma. l. in prouincia. §. 1., etc. Furthermore, although an elective dignity is not included in letters granting a dignity simply, as in c. cum in illis. §. illis uero. de prębendis. li. 6., nevertheless, because in the letters of Lord Peter mention is made of an elective dignity, there is no doubt that an elective dignity is included, because it is expressed in the text of the letters, as in extra de priui. capit. porro, and ff. de leg. 3. l. ille, aut ille. §. cum in uerbis. But this creates a doubt: because his predecessor, namely Lord Antonius, had not impetrated it as an elective dignity, and thus had had no right; whence the dignity did not become vacant through his death. But I respond that Lord Peter was an expectant and had impetrated generally, whence any calling whatsoever is contained, as in ff. sol. mat. l. si quis sic stipuletur. But now we fall into another doubt, because then it would follow that the collation had devolved to the Apostolic See, of which devolution no mention was made in the letters of Lord Peter; therefore it seems that the letters are to be understood as surreptitious, or at least not to encompass this dignity that had devolved to the Pope. That doubt I do not decide at present. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A rescript is not valid in the face of a tacit truth, and execution is not to be granted.
body: Whether an impetration is valid

† Moreover, it is asked whether an impetration made concerning a dignity or a benefice is valid when no mention was made of the possession of the adversary. I answer: either the possessor cannot allege a just or colorable title, and then the impetration is valid; or the adversary has a colorable title, and then either the title is null ipso iure, or to be annulled by a sentence. If indeed it is null ipso iure existently, but not evidently, then either there is the clause "any unlawful detainer being removed" (amoto quolibet illicito detentore), and then the impetration is valid, because this clause is equivalent to a mention having been made of the colorable possession according to Ioannes de Deo; but if this clause is not present, the impetration is not valid, because that possessor cannot be removed without a definitive sentence delivered principally and not incidentally, and thus he will not have it by executive mode, as in c. cum nostris, de conces. praeben. If, however, the possessor is in possession of law and of fact, even if unworthily, nonetheless before he is removed the benefice is not vacant, and therefore it cannot be impetrated. The Doctors note this in the said c. cum nostris and in c. pro illorum, de praeben. Inno. nevertheless says that that clause, "any unlawful detainer being removed" (remoto quolibet illicito detentore), directed to execution, has no place unless the detention is notoriously unjust; and the reason is because those matters which require a deeper investigation do not pertain to the office of an executor. And this is true, and harmonious with the above distinction. Innoc. de priui. c. cum olim. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In contracts, judgments, and legal proceedings, the place where they are made is always considered.
body: The statute provides that no one shall presume to draw up any instrument before an arbitrator or umpire unless he has been chosen by the parties by their mutual consent; and if another notary, who has been so chosen, performs any act, it shall be void and of no effect by operation of law. Now, a certain notary, who was not thus chosen, drew up certain acts at the command of the aforementioned arbitrator, who was also a layman, between two laymen, as well as their award. The question is whether the said acts are valid or not. And it seems that they are not valid, first

† From the general rule, because in contracts the place of the contract is considered, and in judgments the place of the judgment, and in proceedings the place of the proceedings, because proceedings tend toward the ordering of the litigation. The laws are common. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, while an incidental matter or interlocutory issue is pending, proceedings may be had on the principal issue, and whether the time period runs.
body: First, it is provided by statute, in the name of Christ, that the principal cause shall not endure, nor be able to endure, beyond the space and time of forty useful days, to be computed from the day the litigation was commenced, which is understood to have been commenced when the petition was submitted and recorded in the acts, etc. And in the same statute, it is subsequently provided that all dilatory, declinatory, peremptory, and certain exceptions and replications, of whatever kind they may be, concerning which there has been no cognizance or decision between the parties, shall remain saved to both parties at the end of the litigation, during the time of disputation, so that the progress of the cause shall not be delayed on this account. By another statute, it is provided that between an ascendant, a descendant, or a neighbor, provided that he has been required to do so within the prescribed days, a compromise must be made with a friend or friends. Now, it is alleged that the requirement was made within ten days after the litigation was contested, concerning the principal cause; on which article, because the neighborhood was not established, witnesses were received on both sides; and finally, beyond the forty useful days, it was pronounced interlocutorily that the cause should not be committed, because they were not neighbors. After this pronouncement was made, the plaintiff requested that the judge proceed on his libel. It is opposed that the instance of the principal cause has been extinguished. The question is asked: what is the law?

† I answer briefly that, during the aforementioned disposition, which is the dispute concerning the transfer of the forum to arbitrators, the aforementioned period of forty days does not run. This is supported by three reasons:

First, because a useful period does not run against a plaintiff who is impeded by the act of the defendant. This is an expressly stated case. D. de minoribus, l. inter utile. This law determines this question in precise terms.

Second, because where the order of the statute ceases, the statute itself ceases, as in Auth. de haereditatibus et falsis, §. si quis autem non in plures. But in the article of compromising, or not compromising, the order of the statute providing for declinatory exceptions to be reserved at the end of the time ceases, because the nature of this exception does not permit such reservation, nor does this time permit it, as D. de iudicibus, l. sed et si susceperit, in principio; and Extr. de re iudicata, c. inter monasterium; and noted by Bartolus, D. de re iudicata, in l. quidam consulebant.

Third, because a general statute regarding declinatory exceptions does not apply to this declinatory exception, for which special provision has been made, as D. de verbis obligatis, l. doli clausula; and D. de poenis, l. sanctio legum. And this is confirmed by an express law, for since the last statute speaks of a period of ten days, it is clear that this case is exempted from the general rule expressing another period, as D. de legibus, l. talis scriptura.

Furthermore, it seems to be said that this is not among the exceptions that may be raised after the contestation of the lawsuit. For he who, without protestation before the judge subject to declination, contests the lawsuit, appears to have tacitly renounced his declinatory exception, as in the aforementioned l. sed et si susceperit. And the statute must be understood as not applying to one who renounces tacitly or expressly, because to those who renounce, no access is open to that to which they have renounced, as C. de pactis, l. postquam liti.

Furthermore, that the aforementioned useful period did not run is thus demonstrated. The pendency of the lawsuit operates the same as a judgment, which can be rendered, as D. de exceptionibus, l. fundum Titianum; and l. fundi. Since therefore it was possible to render a judgment that the cause should be compromised, which judgment would impede the running of the aforementioned useful period, so too does the pending lawsuit.

Furthermore, periods of compromise made are subtracted from useful periods; indeed, from continuous periods, as C. de temporibus appellationum, Auth. si tamen; and in c. quandiu, de appellationibus; in Clementina. Therefore, even while this article is pending, as Extr. de restitutione in integrum, c. 2, in fine; and D. de excusationibus tutorum, l. diximus.

Furthermore, when impeded by a legal impediment, the prescription of time does not run, as C. de annali exceptione, l. 1, in fine; and C. de iure deliberando, l. fin., §. donec. But the judge and the parties could not proceed on the principal matter while this article was pending. And if the judge had proceeded, the proceeding would have been null by law itself; or at least temerarious, because he rightly doubts his jurisdiction in the meantime, as noted by Bartolus, D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum interest.

Moreover, it is a useful period; hence days are not counted in which the judge did not sit, nor could sit, on the bench for the principal matter, as l. 2, D. quis ordinarius in bonis possidet servandis; and l. 1, D. de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum, cum si. From which, concluding from the first to the last, it is most clearly evident that the period of forty useful days in the principal cause was not elapsed during the aforementioned time concerning the aforementioned dispute. Nor does the period of forty useful days run concerning the aforementioned incidental matter; because it is not provided for by law, as D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. si servum, §. non dixit. Moreover, the principal matter does not escape the cognition of the judge; therefore, neither does the incidental matter.

Furthermore, while an appeal from an interlocutory judgment is pending, the time of trial pronounced from the beginning nevertheless runs; and much more so if we are within the time for appealing. This is the case, and it is not expedient to proceed by argument. C. de dilationibus, l. a procedente, vers. et si forte. And although it gives the reason there that one cannot appeal from an interlocutory judgment, yet in the same glossa it appears that the same holds if one could appeal, because otherwise the case could not proceed. For whether an interlocutory judgment is rendered on such an incidental matter, or whether proceedings are taken, or whether proceedings are not taken, one can nevertheless appeal, as D. qui satisdare cogantur, l. arbitro.

Furthermore, there is a case in c. non solum, §. 1, de appellationibus, lib. 6, where it is said that before the judge to whom the appeal is made issues an inhibition, proceedings may continue. But he cannot inhibit unless the appeal is issued on a probable cause. Therefore, before the appeal is made, the instrument by which the inhibition will not proceed. The text is expressly stated there. Wherefore, since the judge from whom the appeal is taken was not impeded, the useful periods run without doubt; otherwise they would never run; because interlocutory judgments from which one cannot appeal on just cause are rare.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether witnesses from a university are considered competent, and when they are, and when they are not.
2. Whether a witness who, either directly or indirectly, and who out of necessity or from a contingent cause, perceives some profit, is competent or not.
3. Whether assignment may be made during pending litigation.
body: L.VII. It appears publicly in the name of Christ. The community of the castle of Barutii is bound to a certain nobleman by an uncertain and large quantity of florins, which it cannot pay unless they make among themselves a distributive collection for the payment of this debt, as stated in l. 1, § quibus, ff. quod quisque universitatis nomine. Now, a certain assignee of this quantity, who is the son of one of the creditors and the nephew of another, his uncle, demands this quantity. It is true that this assignment was made during pending litigation with the said uncle and father. However, the said universitas claims to have paid, and to prove this, it introduced witnesses from the universitas itself, to whom, together with the rest of the universitas, the burden of paying the said collection belonged. From this case, it is asked first, whether the said witnesses are competent to prove the said payment? Second, whether the said assignment was valid, considering also that the said assignee is an ecclesiastical person?

† I answer the first point, and I say that the question is most ancient and common, namely whether those belonging to a corporation may serve as witnesses in a case involving the corporation. This question is posed by Cynus in the Codex, in the title *De testibus*, in the law *Parentes*, and he determines that if this controversy concerns the individual utility of each member, they ought not to be admitted to give testimony; nor are they competent witnesses according to Jacobus de Ravanis, Petrus, and many ancient and modern authors. But in the law *In tantum*, section *Universitas*, in the Digest, under the title *De rerum divisione*, in his ordinary lecture, he says that either the case is one of the corporation or college, with respect to name, honor, and advantage; and then those belonging to the corporation may serve as witnesses; nor does it matter that for this reason they will collect less, because this advantage accrues to each person principally, and only in consequence to the whole. Or the case is one of the corporation with respect to name, but with respect to advantage it is that of the individuals; and then they cannot testify, because the cause is considered private. But Johannes Andreae, in his additions to the Speculum, in the title *De testibus*, section *Operis versio*, asks: "But whether..."

† He states that when individual members of a corporation derive benefit from their own testimony, they cannot serve as witnesses. I therefore respond to the question asked: and I say that they are not competent witnesses. To demonstrate this, I observe that there are two obligations here: one of the corporation towards the creditor, for example arising from a loan; the other of the individual members towards the corporation, because the individuals are bound to the corporation for the collection of taxes, as stated in the Digest, *De munere et honore*, law *Rescripto*, section *Si*. Now it is certain that if they could prove payment by their own testimony, they would be immediately released from the obligation by which they are bound to the corporation; because, once the corporation is released, they would necessarily be released as well. Therefore, the outcome of the dispute immediately concerns them. Moreover, it matters greatly whether the benefit accrues to someone by necessity or by casual contingency. In the first case, whether mediate or immediate, one is not a competent witness, as is clear in the case of a guarantor and a seller who is liable for eviction. And wherever the exception of *res iudicata* would apply to a witness, there that witness would not be competent, as noted in the Digest, *De finitis regundis*, law *Eos*, and in the Code, *De testibus*, law *Omnibus*. In the second case, however, the testimony is admitted, as in the Code, *De testamentis*, law *Dictantibus*. Since, therefore, in our case we are dealing with a necessary benefit to the witnesses, it is not in doubt among ancient or modern jurists that a witness who wishes to free himself from obligations and prejudices by his own testimony is not competent. And this concludes the first point.

† As to the point where it is said that the assignment was made to a more powerful party, this is false: because the university is more powerful than a single cleric, as in c. Statutum, de rescriptis, lib. 6. As to the other step, namely that the litigation was pending: certainly a judgment had already been rendered for a larger amount, which included this smaller one. Therefore, the rights could be assigned. And because the assignment was necessary, as is asserted, since it was made in place of the legitimate portion owed to the assignee, and in the division of goods, as in D. de familia erciscunda, l. In iudicio; and l. Alienationes; and l. Finalis, C. de litigiosis. Regarding the statements of the witnesses, I say nothing, because the records speak for themselves. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a son is presumed to know his father’s will, and whether knowledge or ignorance is proved by presumptions.
2. Whether the words added by the notary in the instrument, indicating that he knew the inheritance pertained to him, prove that he knew it pertained to him by virtue of the will.
3. Whether acceptance or intermeddling presupposes knowledge of the will.
4. One who is ignorant cannot renounce his benefit.
5. Whether a son who has renounced his father’s inheritance is thereafter deemed to have intermeddled by possessing it.
body:
In the year 1371. In the name of Christ. Of the most holy father in Christ, and lord, our lord Gregory, by divine providence and clemency, Pope. On the 23rd day of the month of December. Let all know who shall inspect this present instrument, that whereas the wise and learned man, Lord Jacob, formerly of Lord Nerius, was constituted in the presence of me, the notary subscribed below, and of the witnesses subscribed below, he asserted, said, and affirmed that it had recently come to his knowledge that the aforementioned Lord Nerius had died a natural death, with his sons, the aforementioned Lord Antonio and the aforementioned Lord Jacob, his legitimate and natural children, surviving him; and also knowing that one-half of the inheritance of the aforementioned Lord Nerius, formerly his father, pertained to him, and also that it was his will, on account of the death of the aforementioned Lord Nerius, according to the form of law, therefore, not wishing the aforementioned Lord Jacob to act imprudently, in every manner, way, right, and sum by which he could better and more usefully do so, he aided and seized the inheritance of the aforementioned formerly his father, namely for the one-half falling to him: with the benefit of law and inventory, and he wished it to be considered as accepted and seized from the day of the aforementioned acceptance; and making, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the sign of the cross at the beginning, and for the sign of the acceptance and seizure of the aforementioned inheritance with his own hand; requesting me, the notary subscribed below, that I should draw up a public instrument of the aforementioned matters, the act being done in the city of Perugia, in the public way, before the house inhabited by Lord Baldus, in the presence of Lord Baldo, son of Master Francis of Perugia, doctor of law, of the parish of Saint Peter, and of the parish of Saint Lucy; John, son of Master Bartolus of Perugia, of the parish of Saint Peter and of the parish of Saint Andrew; Antonio Colonna of Perugia, of the parish of Saint Peter, and of the parish of Saint Mary of the Hill; and Francis, son of Master Thomas of Assisi, witnesses called, present, and requested for this purpose; and I, Peter, formerly of Thaddeus of Perugia, of the gate of Saint Peter, and of the parish of Saint Sylvester, public notary by imperial authority, and ordinary judge, was present to all and each of the above-mentioned matters; and, being requested to write, I wrote and published, and appended my accustomed sign. In the name of Christ, Amen.

L. in totum. Generally, all things which are to be done in a distinction can be accomplished only if they are true as to their essence, and with certain knowledge as to their manifestation. D. de regulis iuris. L. in totum omnia. Therefore, in things depending on the mind and on the true existence of terms, two things are required, namely truth and certainty of truth. D. de captivis. L. nec nos praeterit. But in things depending on truth, truth alone suffices. D. de conditionibus ob causam. L. si pecuniam. §. si servum. And C. de suis et legitimis. L. apud hostes. But in things depending solely on the mind, essence is stronger than truth. D. de conditionibus ob causam. L. 3. §. subtilius. Therefore, it must be considered in the acceptance of an inheritance whether one wished and knew, or not; but it must be considered whether one said that he knew, or if the notary says so, whether knowledge of the testator or intestate is presumed explicitly, or not. And it seems that knowledge is not presumed unless the words of the testator have been read and understood. D. de transactionibus. L. de his. To the contrary, because the notary asserts that he knew, and the word of the notary is the word of the party, as is noted. D. de verbis obligantibus. L. sciendum. And in things depending on the mind and knowledge, regard is had to his mind; at least in that which obligates him, who asserts that he acts with certain knowledge. Otherwise, our teachers would have been fools, who caused these words to be inserted in instruments: which is the act of a madman, and of madness, for would that we were such as the ancients were. And it is proved. D. si quis cautio. L. sed et si quis. §. fin. And argument. D. de testamento militis. L. qui iure militari. But these matters ought to be discussed more deeply, and subjected to a higher inquiry, etc.

First, it must be seen whether a son is presumed to know his father’s will. Second, whether by those words, “knowing that the inheritance pertains to him,” it is proved that he knew that it pertained to him by will. Third, whether the acceptance of an inheritance presupposes knowledge. Fourth, whether a son ignorant of the will can renounce the benefit of abstention. Fifth, whether a son who has renounced his father’s inheritance, by subsequently possessing it, is said to have intermeddled.

† Regarding the first point, I say that in case of doubt, one must resort to presumptions (conjectures), for by means of a presumption not only is knowledge proven, as if the son was in the house, and the will was made in the house; because household members are presumed to know what we do in the house. C. de repudiando l. consensu. §. servis. unless the will was made under a secret seal, that is, in writing, as in Inst. de pupillari substitutione in principio. Sometimes ignorance will be proven by presumptions, as if the son was in a distant country, such that knowledge of the witnesses could reach him only by messenger and letters. D. si certum petatur l. eius, qui in provincia. l. quidam decedens. §. ex quo. Innocentius D. de administratione tutorum. But if it does not appear from presumptions, ignorance is presumed. C. de periculo tutoris l. si tutor. C. de iure deliberandi l. quoniam sororem. and l. cum antiquioribus. vers. si enim ipse. and l. ulterius. de probationibus with similar authorities.

† Regarding the second point, I say that by entering into possession, one is deemed to contract. L. *Apud Iulianum*, § *fin.*, D. *Quibus causis in possessionem eatur*. And the words which the heir then utters are held to be a lawful confession made in the presence of adversaries, by argument from C. *De pactis*, L. *Post venditionem*; and what is noted in D. *De negotiorum gestis*, L. *Pomponius scribit*; L. *Nesennius*, D. *De solutionibus*; L. *Stipendium*, § *ult.*, D. *De verbis obligatorum*, L. *Sciendum*; or that he caused it to be written, C. *De probationibus*, L. *Cum precibus*. For even a general confession prejudices the party, when one confesses himself to be an heir, although he does not state by what right. D. *De interrogationibus et actionibus*, L. *Fin.* And by this, in our case, it is presumed that he knowingly intermeddled, because so it is provided for in the instrument.

† On the third point, I say that legal commingling does not presuppose knowledge. C. de suis, and the law l. apud hostes. But commingling of mind and act presupposes knowledge of the will, both in the case of a sui heres and in that of an extraneus, as in ff. de libe. leg. l. cum haeres. For a sui heres and an extraneus do not differ in those matters which depend upon will. ff. de acqui. haere. l. cum bonis. If, therefore, anyone in an instrument declares himself heir, he is deemed to confess and state all that is necessary by virtue of implied acceptance, argumen. ff. de acqui. haere. l. illud. Moreover, when a son remains silent, knowledge is not presumed; yet when he performs some other act indicative of knowledge, knowledge is rightly presumed. And what act is clearer than one’s own confession? C. de nonnu. pecu. l. generaliter.

† On the fourth point, I say that one who is ignorant cannot renounce his benefit. D. de inofficiosa testatione, l. mater decedens. For the repudiation of an inheritance and its acceptance require the same knowledge, D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. his potest; D. si pars hereditatis petatur, l. illud, together with similar authorities.

† On the fifth point, I say that, while the matter remains intact, it appears advisable to proceed. C. de repu. diui. l. fin. Whether he performs civil acts, such as selling or promising; or whether he holds natural actions by possessing and collecting fruits, as in Inst. de haere. quali. et diff. §. fin. ff. de acqui. haered. l. pro haerede. If he has performed these acts, this person is undoubtedly deemed to have effectively intervened. ff. de iure deliberan. I. si quis seruus. cum similibus. And so I say, and I, Baldus, advise accordingly.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a person can be punished for a wrong committed elsewhere.
2. From what circumstances a change of domicile is presumed.
3. Whether an inquiry can be made into a wrong committed elsewhere.
body: In the name of the Lord, Amen. The point is as follows, namely: Titius of Siena, having had a lawsuit and dispute with Lady Berta, guardian and mother of the children of Sempronius, formerly her husband and a citizen of Siena, and finally being overcome and convicted in the said lawsuit, the same Titius absented himself from the city of Siena, fearing that on account of the civil proceedings instituted against him he would be personally apprehended; and he delayed and took up residence in the city of Arezzo. Finally, after a certain period of time, the same Titius deliberately and with careful consideration left the said city of Arezzo, in which he then dwelt and had his residence, and went to the said city of Siena; and there he remained hidden and in ambush for three or four days with a certain associate, no words or rumors having initially or at that time been circulating, he made an assault and attack against Gaius, a citizen of Siena, who was related to the said wards; he struck him with many blows and wounds, on account of which the same Gaius died immediately; and the said maleficium was committed by the said Titius and his associate upon the person of the said Gaius near and close to the aforementioned city of Siena. Afterwards, however, after the said maleficium had been done and committed by the aforementioned persons, they absented themselves from the said city of Siena and its county; and on the same day or the following day after the commission of the said maleficium and homicide, they fled into the county and district of Arezzo; and afterwards, after some days, they entered the said city of Arezzo. Now, however, the Captain of War and Guard of the said city and county of Arezzo wishes to proceed by inquisition, and by virtue of his office and discretion, to punish and condemn the said Titius, the offender, on account of the said maleficium and homicide committed by him and his associate upon the person of the said Gaius.
