† It is now asked whether he can be proceeded against and punished, and with what penalty he should be punished, given that he first moved himself and afterwards took refuge in the aforementioned city of Arezzo, as stated above. Having examined the statutes of the commune of Arezzo, the election of the said lord captain of Arezzo, and the common laws, etc.

† The question stands thus: In the name of Christ, whether you have established domicile in the city of Arezzo, or not. For if you were residing there as a fugitive, it is certain that you did not acquire domicile there. D. de servis expug. l. Titius servum. But if it appears with certainty that you chose that place for your permanent residence, and established your household there, then that place became your domicile, and you could be punished there. C. ubi de crimine agi oportet. l. 1. But if there is doubt, then in one who has resided for ten years, the intention to remain permanently is presumed from mere residence alone. C. de incolis. l. 2. But in one who has stayed for a shorter time, the intention to acquire domicile is not presumed from mere residence alone. D. ad municip. l. liberti persona. Unless from other circumstances joined together, such as because you moved with your entire family, and your household goods, and with the greater part of your fortune: then domicile is presumed. C. ubi senatores, vel clar. l. 2. and note, Extr. de foro compet. c. ex parte. according to Innocentius. For where your treasure is, there is your heart. And therefore where one has family and the greater part of his fortune, he is always seen to be there in intention. D. de captivis. l. nihil. D. de pignor. l. debitor. C. de agris et censib. l. fin. lib. 11. From these it appears whether this murderer can be punished in Arezzo: for if he had acquired domicile there before the crime, he can be punished there; if he had not acquired it, he cannot be punished there, although he fled there. Only the law permits him to be captured and remitted to the place of the crime, in Auth. ut nulli iud. §. si vero quis comprehensorum. But cities do not make such remittances by custom, as noted in Cle. pasto. de re iudic. in Cle. si autem dubitatur, recourse must be had to what I said above. I do not omit one thing, that the beginning of the place from which this person, or these persons, moved to commit the crime should not be considered; but the final place of the crime should be considered, according to the note by Bartolus, D. de adulteriis. l. Quia ait. §. fin. And therefore the mere access from Arezzo to the city of Siena does not cause him to acquire the forum of Arezzo; the penalty must also be imposed according to the statute of the place of the crime, because those statutes draw and extend the common law to the place of judgment, as fully noted in l. cunctos populos. by Bartolus and others. C. de summa trinit. I conclude therefore that he does not acquire the forum of Arezzo solely from the fact that he went and returned. But if domicile previously established in Arezzo appears, he properly acquires the forum there, and then the penalty must be inflicted according to the place of the crime:

† And this applies if he is accused. The same holds if by inquisition. The ancients stated that a crime committed outside [the jurisdiction] cannot be cognized. And Johannes Andreeus approves this among the Moderates. But Cynus and Bartolus say that it can, as Bartolus himself reports in the aforementioned law *Cunctos populos*. In Perugia, caution is observed; on this point the matter is still sub iudice, and the ancient practitioners held the negative opinion; but the more modern authorities hold the affirmative. The safer course is the ordinary one, namely by accusation. But the statute of Arezzo seems to declare that wherever homicide is committed, it may be inquired into, which statute is valid. Law *Fin.*, Digest, *De decretis ab ordine factis*; Code, *De eunuchis*; Law 2, Code, *De commerciis et mercatoribus*; Law *Mercatores*.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. †Given a statute providing that those who denounce receivers of banished persons shall earn a certain reward, and another statute providing that syndics are bound to make denunciations, whether syndics who make denunciations ought to receive the reward.
2. Denunciation is twofold, namely private and public.
3. A reward granted by the ordinance of the law is lawful and honest.
body: At Perugia it is provided that

† By a statute of the city of Perugia it is provided that anyone harboring a person banished for wounding shall be punished by a fine of one hundred pounds, which fine the podestà and the captain are bound to exact from the harborer; and of this fine half belongs to the commune of Perugia, and the accuser or denouncer is to have the other half; and that the syndics of the castles and villages of the territory of Perugia are bound to denounce such harborers; but that they are bound and ought to denounce homicides and bloody woundings with a weapon under penalty of 200 pounds. Now it is asked, having seen and diligently examined the tenor of the said statute, whether the syndic of a village who denounces the said crime ought to have half of the said penalty. And it seems that he ought not; for it is provided by law that if a slave avenges the death of his master, he obtains freedom as a reward, ff. ad Sille. l. si quis in graui. §. si ex stipulatione. Now the jurist, for the interpretation of this law, frames this question: what if this slave disclosed the death of this master under necessary compulsion, whether he ought to have the said reward? And it is determined that he ought not, and it is given as a general rule that a reward is not due to an informer unless he informs spontaneously; this is the text in d. l. si quis in graui. §. vtrum. Therefore, since this syndic acted out of the necessity of a public office and through fear of the penalty of the statute, he does not merit the reward. What the statute says concerning the denouncer must therefore be understood of a private denunciation, not of a public one, which is made by virtue of office. And Bar. seems to hold this, adding another reason, namely because he would take money shamefully when he is bound to act gratuitously, as in l. pe. de condi. ob tur. causam. The contrary must be stated, having considered the said statute, and having considered that concerning the same deed, if it is done, a reward falls due, and if it is not done, a penalty falls due; nor is this inconsistent: for it is provided by law that one who fulfills the will of the deceased obtains the reward of the Trebellianic fourth, and one who does not fulfill it suffers a penalty, as in Auth. de hęr. et fal. §. si quis autem non implens. Likewise the good are rewarded, and the bad are punished, ff. de iusti. et iur. l. 1. there: 'the good not only through fear of penalties, but also by the encouragement of rewards.' And it is not novel that, for the sake of rewarding fidelity, both the laws and the statutes confer rewards, C. de statuis, et imaginibus. l. virtutum; ff. de excu. tuto. l. tutor. §. qui tutoribus. If therefore the syndic is faithful in denouncing, because he denounces the crime when it appears to be true, he is deservedly to be praised and rewarded; nor is he less worthy of a reward because he rightly discharges his office, since he brought the truth into public ears and into the light, C. de epis. et cleri. l. nullus. in fi.

† And to make this more clearly evident, it must be considered that denunciation is twofold, namely private—which in civil law has no effect unless it passes into an accusation, according to Bar., and that word 'by denunciation' cannot be understood of this, but rather that word 'accuser'; and denunciation is a kind of accusation without a conclusion, and this can be called a narration, which is a part of the accusatory libel; an accusation is not the whole libel itself with a tacit or express conclusion, as in extra de symo. c. licet hely—and the other is public denunciation, which is made by virtue of office, and this alone is recognized in the civil law, which prepares the way for an inquisition, C. de accusa. l. ea quidem; ff. de custo. reorum. l. diuus; C. de iniuriis. l. 1; and so holds Bart. in extraua. ad repri. on the word 'denuntiatione', in 1. Because therefore the statute confers the reward under a twofold head, under each by itself, it is valid under the head of accusation, which includes private denunciation as its integral part, as in C. de famo. lib. l. 1. §. sane; and under the other separate head, namely of the one denouncing: this is not ultimately of one species, but is public according to Bar. Therefore it necessarily follows that that word 'or denouncer' stands for the syndic who denounces by virtue of public office, because it cannot be understood of any other, ff. de fund. instru. l. fundus, qui locat., and by argument ff. de opt. leg. l. si optimo. Moreover, this word 'denouncer' can be understood in several ways; I say that I understand it in whatever way, since an indefinite proposition is equivalent to a universal one in a favorable cause, as Dyn. notes in Rub. de regu. iu. lib. 6. Moreover, when by the same law provision is made concerning the reward and finally concerning the office, not adversatively, but copulatively and connectedly, by reason of the copula the whole is understood as connected and repeated, as in ff. de fun. instru. l. Seyae. §. Gayo; and so it is here, because the whole belongs to the ordinance of the same law. A similar case: the law says that when in one part of a will mention is made of a posthumous child, then in another part of the same will the word 'children' uttered indefinitely also comprehends a posthumous child, whom otherwise it would not comprehend, ff. de leg. 1. l. qui filiabus; so must it be said here regarding this indefinite word 'denouncer'. Moreover, to restrict statutes to an invalid denunciation, namely to the mere relation and notification of the fact, would mean that one would obtain through an invalid act a reward that a valid act would not yield, which is ridiculous. Moreover, the words of a statute do not admit of a restrictive interpretation except by the tacit rationale of the same statute, or of another statute of the same municipality, ff. de verbo. oblig. l. quicquid astringendae, and l. si mihi, et Titio. §. si stipulatur; and therefore the said statute, as being most useful to the commonwealth, principally for the extermination of the banished, is not to be restricted, but to be aided by an ampler interpretation, ff. ad Sille. l. si quis in graui. §. is quoque, and ff. de condit. et dem. l. hoc modo. From which it is most truly concluded that half the share is owed to such a syndic by virtue of the said statute; and the judge ought to declare this in the sentence, as in ff. de haere. insti. l. testamento domini. The dictum of Bar. does not stand in the way, because the words of the statute remove the contrary; for the reward is conferred under its own appellative noun of this kind, which by special necessity and by its indefinite and general meaning comprehends the denouncing syndic himself. It is otherwise in a reward conferred by the ius commune, because it is not conferred under such a noun, but only as an example of laudable will and fidelity, C. de preci. impe. offe. l. 1; for the will must be in the freedom of choice, not in the necessity of a contribution. But the statute does not consider the act as it proceeds from the will, according to which one merits or demerits, but considers the effect of the act as it is useful to the commonwealth; and thus §. vtrum does not stand in the way. Likewise, the argument of Bar. regarding shamefulness does not stand in the way,
† for a reward that is given by the ordinance of the law is not shameful, but lawful and honorable, ff. ad Sille. l. lege Cornelia. §. praeterea. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A son disinherited without any cause being stated in a will that contains a codicillary clause cannot succeed, except to the extent of his legitime.
body: In the name of the Lord, Amen. The noble and wise man, son of the late Lord Antonio degli Albizzi of Florence, and now resident in Venice in the contrada of Saint Cassian, although afflicted in body, yet sound in mind, considering the case of human frailty, and the disposition of his affairs and goods, by this present nuncupative testament, which he says is without writing, made and procured in the following manner: first, he chose his burial, etc. Also, among other things, he disposed in the following manner, namely: he ordered and willed that Antonio, his son, and Monassola, his daughter, should have nothing at all, jointly or severally, of the inheritance and goods of the said inheritance of the said testator; but he disinherited them and each of them, and deprived them of his inheritance. In all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, and claims of any kind, present and future, he instituted and willed Laurentius and Marianus, legitimate and natural sons of the said testator, to be his universal heirs. And the said testator willed that this be his last testament and his last will, that it may be valid and ought to be valid by the law of testament; and if it could not be valid by the law of testament, that it be valid by the law of codicils; and if it were not valid, or would be valid, by the law of codicils, that it be valid by the law of donation causa mortis. And by every other law, mode, and form, by which it may better be valid and hold according to the custom, and manners, and statutes, and ordinances of the city of Florence. Wishing and declaring from now that if there were anything in the present testament contrary to the form of the statutes, or custom of the city of Florence, or if any clause or solemnity were omitted which would have the effect of invalidating this testament, he willed and commanded that it be reduced to the form of the said statutes and custom; and that every defect be supplied by me, the notary subscribed below, so that the present testament and last will be valid and hold, without changing the substance of those things which he ordained in the present testament. In the name of Christ. Amen.

† It is certain that the said testament was null by law itself as regards the institution of heirs, because he disinherited his son without stating any cause, as in Auth. ut cum de appel. cog. §. aliud quoque capitulum. And therefore the sons are heirs ab intestato in equal shares. But there is doubt, because the testator wished it to be valid by law of codicil. Whether the said Ant. is bound to restore to his brothers his virile share, the legitima being deducted, or whether he is not bound. And we are now in a difficult step. For the gloss in Auth. ex causa holds that that clause operates for nothing, unless when the testament does not avail from defect of solemnity: otherwise if it does not avail from defect of disinheritance. It is believed that the father went mad, who omitted natural charity. ff. de leg. 3. l. filio praeterito. And this equitable opinion of the gloss was held by almost all the ancient doctors, and among the moderns Ol. de Laude and Rich. Malum hold it. Also Gul. de Cu. holds it, l. ultra. C. de codic. For since the law calls the intestate a vitium scarcely differing from madness, that which is denied to the testator by one way ought not to be permitted by another way, since the effect would succeed in the place of the prohibited way. ff. quod cum eo. l. sed filius. But the lord Dy. Ia. Bu. and Bar. say that such a clause is valid, and that those disinherited ought immediately to succeed ab intestato by reason of the fideicommissum, and to restore to their brothers their portion, the legitima being deducted: and this by l. posthumus. §. si paganus. ff. de in offi. testamento. and ff. de testa. l. ex ea. and what is noted, C. de fideic. l. eam, quam. and l. ex testamento. and the argument, ff. si quis omis. cau. test. l. qui autem. And this is expressed according to one reading, ff. ad Tre. l. si quo patroni. in fi. to this also it is specially alleged. ff. de fideic. liber. l. generaliter. §. ex testamento. And this is the truth: and thus it is to be held.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether, after a division of all things among brothers, excepting the house, and after a protestation made in the tenth year concerning the division of the said house, the division may be demanded after another ten years by him who made such protestation.
2. Whether patience is presumed to be a title.
3. Whether a legacy is presumed from time.
4. Whether a division is presumed from time together with possession.
body:
Amen. In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: a certain lord Leo died in the year of our Lord 1354, leaving four legitimate and natural sons, one of whom is called Peregrinus, another Florius, and another Petrus. These brothers, after the death of their aforementioned father, divided among themselves all the hereditary goods that belonged to their said father, except for one house in which their father resided at the time of his death and during his life; and in which the said father had resided for 25 continuous years immediately preceding his death; and this was proven in court. The said Florius, who is one of the aforementioned four brothers, continuously held and possessed the said house, which was truly never divided; and at present he holds the said house; so that after the division made of the other paternal goods, which was made more than 20 years ago, the said Florius has continuously held and possessed the entire said house. It happened that in the year of our Lord 1363, the said Nicolaus, who is one of the said four brothers, was present before the said Florius, his brother, who holds the entire said house, and spoke words, which are mentioned in the chapter written below, or those words which are proven by the three witnesses written below, who testified regarding it and swore upon the entire case; to which words the said Florius responded, as contained in the attestations written below.

Now I ask you, my lord, whether the chapter formulated as it stands, assuming it is proven, removes the presumption of division made regarding the said house, of which presumption the gloss speaks in the law *Si maior*, Codex, *De communi dividundo*, and there by Bartolus. Furthermore, whether, notwithstanding that after the aforementioned confession another 10 years have elapsed, during which, as stated, the said Florius held and possessed the said house, the said Nicolaus, notwithstanding the presumption of division made regarding the said house, may bring an action against the said Florius so that he may divide the said house with him for a fourth part? The advocates of the said Florius, the defendant, say that this chapter does not avail, even if it were proven; because after the said confession of the said Florius, another 10 years have elapsed, during which the said Florius, as stated, continuously held and possessed the said house; and thus another new presumption of division arises due to the possession of the last 10 years. And the said advocates of Florius also say that the said chapter written below is not proven by the three witnesses written below, nor anything that avails; and that in this chapter is not proven that which suffices to remove the presumption of division alleged by the advocates of Nicolaus, which the said chapter written below avails; and that although the chapter is not proven word for word, nevertheless that which suffices to remove the presumption of division urgently arising from the possession of 10 years is proven, especially because the witnesses swore upon the entire case. And the said advocates of the accuser say that it suffices if within the first 10 years, or in the subsequent 10 years, the said Florius made the said confession, which is proven by the witnesses written below; which suffices, whenever he confessed that the division was not made, in the manner of that one who, at the request of another, confessed that he had received in the name of a messenger; after the lapse of two years, he who made the said confession wishes to oppose the exception of non-payment. That after two years he may, according to the common opinion of the gloss, although the burden of proving lies with him who claims that after two years, nevertheless if he proves that his creditor, who received the said confession, said and made the confession in his presence, but never paid before the two years, after the two years, and even if one or two more biennia were to pass, a new presumption of money paid would not be induced, etc.

It is asked from these things, what is the law? Whether the said chapter is proven, so that it suffices to remove the said presumption; and whether, notwithstanding the said presumption of division made, the said Nicolaus may in law demand from the said Florius, his brother, that he divide the said house with him for a fourth part? The chapter written below was made to remove the presumption of division made, of which presumption the gloss speaks in the said law *Si maior*. Furthermore, that in the year 1363 and the month of November of that year, or at that time of which the witnesses spoke, the said Nicolaus, being at the fish stone placed at the porch of the house of the merchants of Verona, said to the said Florius: "Florius, I never had a part of the houses of my father Lord Leo, in which he died, which lies in the city of Verona in the quarter of Saint Zilius: I would wish to divide them with you and with our other brothers." And then the said Florius responded to the said Nicolaus: "You have nothing of the said houses, except what our father and our lady Bellina, our mother, left in their testaments to me, Florius, and to Peregrinus and Petrus, the said brothers." And then the said Nicolaus responded to the said Florius: "I do not believe this, because father and mother would never have done this." And then the said Florius responded to the said Nicolaus: "I have the testament of my father and mother, and I will show it to you; and if it does not appear that my said mother and father bequeathed all the said houses to me, Florius, and to Peregrinus and Petrus, our brothers, I promise you that I will divide with you that which I hold of the said houses." And thus responded the said Nicolaus: "I am content." In the name of Christ, Amen.

There are three cases: either it appears that everything was divided; or it appears that certain things were divided, and consequently others remained undivided; or an express division does not appear, but a division is alleged, and long possession as divided is introduced for proof. In the first and second case, we stand on certainty: nor do we consider the conjecture of time, or we have certainty of the truth. C. de pac. l. si certis annis, and arg. ff. de fid. instr. l. plures apocis. apocis. If therefore it appears by instrument, or witnesses, or confession of the adversary, that there was a division in certain things, the rest, which were not divided, are said to be divided. ff. fa. her. l. inter haeredes. In the first and third case, when a tacit division is alleged from acts, possessions made and held as divided, the gloss says that a division is presumed: for that which cannot be clearly proved by words is proved by conjecture, as ff. pro soc. l. ita. and C. de peti. haere. l. filius. and arg. ff. de proba. l. proculdubio. For those things which do not require the expression of words can also be done tacitly. ff. de pac. l. item. For indeed even the solemnity of words itself is presumed from time with possession. ff. de acqui. haer. l. 6. or with protestation. ff. de vsur. l. cum de in rem ver. and no. 29. q. 2. c. sed vitium. But the transmontani say that from long possession as divided a title by division is not presumed: because from mere patience a contract or title having preceded is not presumed: this appears C. de rei vendi. l. nullo. ff. de serui. vendi. l. si quis diuturno. ff. de aqua plu. arc. l. 1. in fi. The law cum de in rem verso does not obstruct. For there a true act of obligating intervenes. l. praestatio. which is presumed to be made with it. de proba. l. cum de indebito.

† But patience is not a true act of a person: because silence is a certain privation, not an act: and prescriptions, which are founded on mere patience, are not said to be founded with title: although the same effect is produced as by a true prescription, as noted in C. de serv. et aqua. l. 1. I say on this point that reciprocal patience induces a presumption of division: and from it arises a tacit exchange, just as from different things an express one arises. And this is a presumption, against which, however, proof to the contrary is admitted, as in ff. de pac. l. tres fratres. But the patience of one party alone does not suffice to presume a division. For example, if one person alone possesses a common thing, and has possessed it thus for a long time, and says that in the division the whole thing remained to him, and that he gave his share to his brother in money, certainly this is not presumed, because unless possession appears on both sides, a division is not presumed: for it is easier that something be done on both sides, as in C. de transa. l. et de fideic. Thus, therefore, the extremes must appear: and then a division would be presumed, because it has a cause from which it arises, namely, communion. But where patience has no cause, then it is true that it is not regarded as a title. And this passage was not well understood by those who speak otherwise. Let us therefore suppose that the possessor did not possess with the intention of division: but under the pretext of a precept, i.e., a prelegacy, which is outside the division:

† Whether a legacy is presumed from mere passage of time? Certainly not, because here there is only forbearance on one side. Moreover, because such an act, namely a legacy, cannot be established even by the consent of the forbearing party. C. de test. l. non dubium. And therefore, an act of a third party is not presumed from forbearance.

But whether in this case division is presumed from the time with possession: I say that if it is established that he did not possess with that intent, but by a putative right through legacies, the possession does not benefit him; for the intent of the possessor must be inquired into, as in D. 41.2.1. Therefore, just as a true division requires a true consent to divide, so does an interpretative one, by argument from D. 6.1.1. Thus, the mind is proven by the confession of the possessor, D. 41.2.1. And therefore, concluding to our case, because the house was not possessed on the ground of division, but on the ground of the alleged legacy or bequest, of which there is no proof, nor is it presumed unless it is shown, as in C. 5.72.1, and that it was not possessed on the ground of division is proven by two witnesses who testify about the assertion of the possessor, and consequently about the intent, D. 33.7.1. It seems rightly to be inferred that the said house is not considered to have come to him as part of the division; and thus it is established that there is common ownership, which is presumed in the present from the past. Hence, it is rightly ordered to be divided, especially if it is established from the proportion of the other parts that this house should nevertheless fall to one person; for in reciprocal cases, equality and due proportion make a strong presumption, C. 6.23.1. And so.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. During the subsistence of the marriage, if a confession regarding the augmentation of the dowry intervenes, whether the wife may claim such an augmentation from the husband's heirs.
2. A promise made on account of a donation is not confirmed by custom; but a confession is so confirmed.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: a dispute is expected between the aforementioned Bona, woman of Vallexio in the district of Verona, widow of the late Master Martin, a money-changer, and the undersigned heirs of the said late Master Martin. It is true that the said Master Martin received a dowry from the said Bona, his wife, at the time of the marriage contracted between them, as fully appears in the instrument. Thereafter, for a long time, he made an augmentation of the dowry to his said wife. In the instrument of the dowry augmentation, he confessed that he had received a sum from the said lady for the augmentation, and in the name of the augmentation of the dowry of the said lady; he renounced the exception of non-receipt of the quantity, etc. Then the said Master Martin died intestate, no further mention being made of the said confession, nor of its revocation. To this Master succeeded his two full brothers and blood relatives, from whom the said lady wishes to claim her said dowry and the said augmentation of the dowry. Nothing appears regarding the payment of the augmentation of her dowry. The question is whether she may do so, notwithstanding that the said confession was made fictitiously and with the intention of making a gift to his said wife. In the name of Christ. Amen.

† When, during the subsistence of the marriage, the husband confesses that he has received an augmentation of dowry, if indeed a true receipt intervened, the heirs of the husband are undoubtedly bound to the wife. C. de do. cau. l. 1. C. de dona. ante nup. l. aut dos data. de pac. do. l. inter virum. §. cum inter. ver. nec separabiliter portio. C. de iu. do. I. etiam cui consequens. But if no true receipt intervened, but only the hope of receiving, then, if the time for opposing the exception of non-numerated peculium has elapsed, and the confession is clothed in a private or public chirograph, this can similarly be recovered under the name of augmentation. C. de do. cau. l. fin. But if neither a true receipt nor the hope of receiving intervened, then either the confession was issued by way of donation, or for some other cause: if by way of donation, then it is confirmed by the death of the husband,

† Because although a promise arising from the cause of a donation is not confirmed by death, as in D. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. Papinianus, nevertheless a confession is confirmed by death, because he who confesses on behalf of another is deemed to possess or retain for him, arg. D. de pact. l. ab emptoribus; and D. de iur. dot. l. si sponsalibus. But if it is for another cause, for example because the woman is noble, or is to be reconciled to her husband, arg. D. de man. l. creditor § 1, because perhaps the husband had killed the father or brother of the wife, then another matter irrelevant to the question is raised. But if it is doubtful on what cause this confession was made, then if there has been a waiver of the exception of the dowry not paid, some say that it appears to have been made with the intention of making a donation, because he waives the donation, as in D. de nov. l. si quis legauerit. Others say that in that case the public instrument is regarded as a dotal one: and a dowry is presumed, and not a donation, as in the ordinary gloss on C. de do. cau. l. 1 in the addition, which is today beyond the gloss. Nor is it surprising that between husband and wife every contract is effective except a donation. D. de lib. lega. l. Aurelius § fin. But this does not seem true, because a confession between prohibited persons appears to have been made in fraud of the law, as in D. de prob. l. qui testamentum. And if the principal obligation does not bind, the waiver does not bind, arg. C. de non nu. pec. l. fi; D. de nov. l. doli mali § diuersum. And therefore we must say either that it is presumed to have been made in hope of future payment, or on the ground of a donation, or even under the title of a dowry: thus the dowry is simulated, i.e., feigned; but the donation is real; and thus from what is simulated arises something else which is real. And this I believe to be true, because a false designation of a dowry has the force of a donation; and if made after the marriage is dissolved, it is valid immediately. D. de verb. obl. l. si diuortio. But if made while the marriage subsists, it is not valid immediately, as noted in D. si certum peta. l. 2 vers. ueluti, if after the marriage it is confirmed by death. C. de dona. cau. l. quod de suo, and there noted. And therefore for such a confession, which does not create a dowry, the woman does not have the privilege of the dowry, because it is considered as a mere donation, as noted in C. qui potio. in pign. habe. l. assiduis § exceptis in the small gloss. As often husbands, who have lived well with their wives for a long time, wishing to reward the long solicitude of the wife towards the husband, and her chaste affection, do this in honor of the marriage already completed; the words of the law are in another matter. D. de legat. 2. l. unum ex familia § Imperator Marcus loquitur. Where the husband confessed with a waiver of future payment: because no other presumption properly applies here than that of a donation. For from the clauses between the principal statement itself it is presumed whether it is fictitious or real, as noted in D. de condi. institu. l. si quis sub conditione haeredes, as in the gloss. I, Baldus. CON.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The question whether a dowry instrument executed by the wife during the subsistence of the marriage is valid, and whether it is upheld by the wife’s oath, and whether such an oath produces any legal effect.
2. Whether an oath is personal in nature, and its effects.
3. Whether a contract not permitted between husband and wife becomes effective upon the addition of an oath.
4. An assertory oath produces no effect where contrary intent is established. Add consilium 471, part 5, which begins, “super eo,” and the chapter.
body:
In the name of the Lord, Amen. The question is as follows: It arises between John and John, full brothers and blood relatives, on one side, as heirs of the late ser Ameritus, their uncle; and a certain Marcus, heir of the late lady Constantia, sister of the said Marcus and late wife of the said ser Ameritus, on the other side. This is because the said Marcus, in the name of the inheritance of the said lady Constantia, his sister, wishes to claim from the said full brothers and blood relatives a dowry of one thousand five hundred pounds of small denarii. This dowry the said late ser Ameritus confessed to have had and received from the lord Patro, a noble knight of lord Bernard of Creanis, present there, giving, counting, and dowing on behalf of the lady Constantia, daughter of the late lord Bartholomew, and from the same lady Constantia, wife of the said Ameritus, present there, during the marriage between them, which had lasted for ten years and more, recently past. The said ser Ameritus promised to restore this dowry in every event, etc., and renounced the exception of a dowry not counted and not received, and every other aid, as fully appears from the instrument transmitted to you, which you can see at length.

After this, the said lady Constantia, still during the marriage, feeling her conscience burdened and harmed, and clearly knowing that the said ser Ameritus, in truth, had received no dowry from the said Peter, nor from the said lady Constantia, nor from anyone on her behalf, wishing to acknowledge good faith, made to the said ser Ameritus, her husband, a settlement and renunciation of everything and the whole of what the said lady Constantia or her heirs could claim from the said ser Ameritus or his heirs by virtue of the said instrument of confession of dowry. She promised in the said instrument not to use, nor by virtue of the said instrument, to molest the said ser Ameritus or his heirs in any way, by herself or her heirs. And all these things the said lady Constantia did to the said ser Ameritus with certain knowledge, acknowledging good faith; and she promised to keep and observe all the aforesaid things, each and every one, and in no way to contravene or come against them, by herself or her heirs, in law nor in fact. And thus she swore on the holy Gospels of God to observe, etc.

However, the said full brothers and blood relatives, heirs of their said uncle, intend to defend themselves, saying that the said renunciation was simulated and made in fraud of the donation between husband and wife; and they intend to prove the aforesaid by the instrument of settlement made by the said lady Constantia to the said ser Ameritus, her husband and uncle of the said brothers, a copy of which instrument is fully sent to you below. Now it is asked, what is the law regarding the aforesaid: whether the said dowry can be recovered by the said Marcus from the said brothers, or not. In the name of Christ. Amen.

† Regarding the question whether a confession, made by the wife to her husband while the marriage subsists and fortified by the wife’s oath, that the dowry instrument was simulated, is valid or not; and whether the oath has any effect: it must be known that either the dowry instrument has a presumption in its favor, or it has a clear and lucid accounting of the payment in itself. If the woman bases her claim on a presumption, for example on a presumed or fictitious payment: as in C. de dot. cau. l. si, then a confession made in writing to the contrary overcomes such presumption. C. de nonnu. pecu. l. generaliter. And this is true assuming equal standing of the persons and times: and because both occurred before the marriage, or both while the marriage subsists. For when the power of opposites is equal, that which is later prevails. For that which was done most recently takes precedence. ff. de acquiren. pos. l. si quis ante. But if the woman, or her heir, bases her claim on a true payment, then such a confession, which is contrary to the right of dowry, does not bind while the marriage subsists. For the right of dowry cannot be made worse, as in ff. de pac. dot. l. 2, versic. et si cum venisset. For whatever is done during the marriage to the prejudice of the dowry, and so that the woman remains without a dowry, is not valid. C. si dos constante matri. l. 1. Nor can this be brought about even by an oath: for it is considered to have been given against public law; for public law, and public and common utility, are understood to be at stake in dowries. ff. sol. matri. l. 1. And therefore it cannot be infringed by the agreements of private parties: and this is according to civil law, as noted in C. de iur. dot. l. si praedium. But according to canon law, the rule is different, as in extra de iureiur. 6, mulieres.

† And although the oath is extinguished with the person who swears it, nevertheless the effect of the oath is not extinguished. Namely, the invalidation of an act validated by oath, as in the Authentica *de iureiurando a maiore praestando*, after the beginning; and in the Digest, *de legatis tertio*, law *cum quis*, section *codicillos*. And thus, by reason of the oath, it appears that proof is made against the heirs of the one who swore, and firmness is given to the sworn act, so that it may in no way be contravened, neither by the one swearing nor by his heir.

Bartolus also holds that a contract not permitted between husband and wife, such as a donation, becomes effective upon the addition of an oath. D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si quis pro eo, in its first and last members. But with due respect to Bartolus, he disposed of this point too hastily. For when the law prohibits consent on account of the public good, so that marriages may not be venal and temporary, but possess perpetual concord within themselves, an oath produces no effect, as noted by Cynus, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. 1, in the last question, although he does not explain it well. And even assuming it were valid, it ought to be relaxed by the bishop, because natural equity suggests that it should be relaxed. Wherever a relaxation is granted to the one who swore, no relaxation is expedited for his heir, because the oath is personal on the part of the swearer, Extr. de iureiurando, cap. Veritatis, according to Innocentius. And I consider this opinion more correct, in favor of marriages and dowries, arg. l. Assiduis, C. qui potiores in pignore habentur; D. de legatis 1, l. Si quis in quibus, §. Finis; C. ad Velleianam, Auth. Si qua mulier. And this is especially true in the lands of the Empire, in which natural equity and the public good are given more weight than an oath.

Now, applying this to the matter at hand, it must be known that the dowry instrument attests to the payment made at that time; therefore, it does not appear that a true payment of the dowry preceded, one that was not simulated. And thus the contrary confession appears simulated and not true. Nor should one stand in the way of judicial proceedings unless there were presumptions; for sometimes a payment that appears superficially is false essentially and null in effect. D. de solutionibus, l. Qui sic solvit. Nevertheless, in doubt, what appears is presumed to be. C. de dote probanda, l. Cum precibus. For such substance is presumed as the surface is; and such invisible thing is presumed as the visible thing is figured in all things, as l. Pediculas, §. Neratius; and l. Si quando, D. de auro et argento legato. And what is expressly attested to in the payment appears, because it speaks demonstratively to the eye of sense, not enunciatively to the eye of intellect. For an enunciation sometimes falsely states. Often a written statement is made of some act as if it were past, whereas a commemorative script, which demonstrates the thing to the eye, as because the said notary attests to the place and time of the making of the instrument, the payment having intervened, and the delivery, which is also done by sight, D. de solutionibus, l. Si pecuniam, cannot attest except to the truth. Therefore, those ablatives, "giving" and "paying," pronounced with the present tense or present place, as because it says "then" or "there paying," denote a true act; but pronounced absolutely to determine the pluperfect past, as he confessed that he had had and received from such a giver and payer, etc., they do not signify an act to be done, but enunciate a fact done.

The conclusion, unless something else is proved, is in favor of the woman. Probation by presumption to the contrary would not be valid by itself, but because united with the confession, which by itself is invalid; nevertheless, they make faith when joined together, arg. de successionibus ab intestato, c. Cum dilectus. The same applies to the heir of the woman. By this it appears that the said instrument ought to be upheld; and on this I have otherwise advised formally, just as I advise now: proposing, however, that a contrary opinion was procured by a certain doctor, and it is natural that doctors have contrary opinions. And that doctor bases himself solely on the oath, in that part which is assertory, and in that part which is promissory. For he says that an assertory oath is to be believed, because the simple confession of the said woman would be believed with cause, unless fraud or fear were established. He alleges the common laws, which the blind and barbers know. But here it must be considered first that if we attend to the rule, a confession made with cause is valid, unless it appears that that cause is expressly false. Then it is not valid in effect, if such a cause is of the essence of the act itself, as D. de exceptionibus doli, l. 2, §. Circa. But here it appears that the cause inserted in the last instrument is false: for it says that the said Ameritus truly never had nor received, etc. For the dowry instrument says the contrary, and attests to the true payment, there where it says, "there present, giving and paying, and dictating," etc. For these words attest to the true act of payment, and there where it says, "which he also said there in the same number," as noted, C. de non numerata pecunia, l. Si ex cautione.

† And an assertory oath has no effect where the contrary truth is established, as is noted in the Digest, *in fine*, l. Lucius. Secondly, if we consider the exception to the rule, it must be considered that when the truth is not proven by an external act, but is proven solely by an act of words, or by the mere confession between husband and wife, it does not constitute effective proof to the prejudice of the other party, because a confession made even with an oath in favor of one who is capable is not understood to be made in fraud of the law, as in l. qui testamentum, and there the text and the glossa ordinaria, Digest, *de probationibus*, and Digest, *de legibus*, in l. cum quis decedens, §. Titia, and there Bartolus clearly determines this. Therefore, the simulation of a dotal instrument cannot be proven by the mere confession, which is said to have been made while the mother was alive, because the husband is not capable of seeking a right from this confession while the mother is alive. And Bartolus openly states this in the said §. Titia. Furthermore, another said doctor states that an obligation arises between husband and wife from a promissory oath, whether it is appended to a contract or to a disposition. For it does not lead to the detriment of eternal salvation; therefore, it must be observed both by the woman and by her heir, because although the personal nature of the oath does not pass to the heir, its reality, i.e., the validation of the act, does pass, as in the Authenticum *sacramenta puberum* with its material. But here it must be considered that he argues from a rule which holds for capable persons: but the husband is not capable of seeking this right from the mere confession of the wife made during the marriage; for it is that confession which is presumed to be simulated, not the true payment, which appears precisely. And by this, the title C. *plus valere quod egitur* does not obstruct, but rather supports the argument, for the heirs of the woman have in their favor the truth in the true act of payment produced: but her adversary has in his favor the confession of simulation asserted by oath. Therefore, between spouses, the true act of fact should prevail rather than the act of words, because between them it is not strengthened by mere confession, as in Digest, *de liberis legitimis*, l. Aurelius, §. fi. From which it is concluded that one should rather adhere to the oath of the dowry, which attests to the true act, than to the instrument of confession emanating from the simulation: unless that confession of simulation could be aided by other probable indications. And these are confirmed by the Authenticum *sed iam necesse*, Codex, *de donationibus ante nuptias*. For if there is a special favor for other creditors there, that the dotal instrument made during the marriage is not to be adhered to, so that other creditors may not be defrauded: therefore, if there are no other creditors, such an instrument is to be adhered to, since it attests to the true payment, as is noted in the said l. si ex cautione. Otherwise, there would be an easy way for women to remain undowered: since husbands could easily extort such confessions from them. Which is inequitable and absurd, as in Codex, *ad Velleianam*, Authenticum *sive a me*, and Authenticum *si qua mulier*, and what is said there by Cynus. And these things are true in a mere point of law, saving always the truth of fact; however, unless something else appears contrary to what is clothed in law, according to the point of law we cannot depart.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. When several persons are engaged in a brawl against someone, and one of them is mortally wounded, and it is apparent who inflicted the wound, only that person is held liable.
body: In the name of Christ.

† I presuppose that in the city of Fadra not all subtleties of civil law are considered; but rather a certain good simplicity and the way of truth are observed. I say this because, according to law, the said denunciation

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A security granted to someone, that he may not be sued for a debt, must be understood as applying, except in cases of wrongdoing, and see no. 5.
2. A security granted by law, that no one may be arrested in his dwelling house, is not understood to apply in cases of crime.
3. A security granted to someone for a debt does not extend to a tax debt.
4. When a debtor is properly so called.
5. Whether immunity for a debt benefits in cases of delicts.
6. A benefit granted to someone, that he may surrender his goods, does not extend to those who are sued on account of a delict.
body:
It does not proceed: because it does not contain the time, nor the place confined according to the form of the law of libels. D. de accus. et testib. Nor do they even testify about the place or time: as is necessary in criminal cases, and especially in capital ones. Also, because the accuser died during the pending trial, according to the common law the process would be extinguished, but not the crime, because an accusation could be made again. D. de publ. iudic. l. Accusante. C. Si reus, vel accusator. per totum. Also, because it was acted upon regarding the wounding, and death ensued during the pending litigation. Hence many say that a new instance is required, as noted in D. de damno infecto, l. Damni, § Sabini, by the doctors. However, because I consider that in the city of Padua truth is rather considered than solemnity and subtlety of law, I come to the question proposed: and I say that when several are in a brawl against someone, and one mortally wounded, and it appears who did it, he alone is liable for the homicide. D. ad legem Aquiliam, l. Item Mella, § Si plures. And therefore Moses is liable for the homicide of the case: because it is established that he inflicted the wound from which death ensued. Stephen, however, is not liable for homicide on account of such a good kingdom: and let the others fear punishment. Let the Lord Count impose a pecuniary penalty on him, because these brothers were together in the same brawl to participate, as noted in Speculum, de Homicidio, vers. Poenae quatuor homines. Others say otherwise. D. de Sicariis, l. Si in rixa. But I adhere to the Speculator and his reasoning. And thus I say, and I advise, I, Baldus, Doctor of Both Laws, currently lecturing in Padua. In the name of Christ. Amen.

That Jacobus Aboleo, formerly treasurer and steward of the most magnificent Lord of Padua, now resident and inhabitant of the city of Verona, can be sued in the said city for the restitution of the money of the said most magnificent Lord of Padua, which, being the aforementioned official, he stole from the said Lord by departing and fleeing with it, or even without it, notwithstanding the grace, safe-conduct, and promise made to him by the most magnificent Lords of la Scala, is evidently demonstrated more clearly than light by the words first related in the said grace, as in D. de petitione hereditatis, l. Item veniunt, § Praeter haec, and § Sicanda. The words are these, namely: We, B., R., and A., brothers of la Scala of Verona, etc., lords and general captains, wishing to grant grace to the discreet men Jacob and Francis, brothers of the Olearii of Padua, inhabitants of our city of Verona, and to attend to and observe the promises and graces made to them by our most magnificent late father, Lord Causa Signior of la Scala, so that they may be more fervently inclined to the honors and benefits of our cities, by the tenor of the present, by the fullness of our power, we give safe-conduct to them and each of them, and we wish and command them to be secure anywhere in our lands: granting to them that with their sons, household, goods, and things of whatever condition they may freely, securely, and without any molestation or burden stand and dwell in our cities of Verona and Vicenza, and their districts, notwithstanding any direct and suchlike crimes committed: excepting, however, those having a derogatory clause; and we wish and command that the aforementioned safe-conduct and our security have the firmness of strength only for past causes and crimes: so and in such a way that under their occasion or pretext they may not in any way be molested, namely from the time of the third, etc. I say, therefore, that the said safe-conduct does not in any way extend to the case of which we speak. And I demonstrate this by many reasons.

And the first reason is this: security granted to someone, whereby he cannot be sued for a debt, must be understood as excluding cases of wrongdoing; this is proven by C. de his, qui ad ecclesias confugiunt, l. 2, with its gloss, where it is stated that although a person enjoys immunity granted to him by reason of a temple, which is a place of safety and secure refuge, nevertheless he does not thereby have immunity from being sued for a delict. For he may be removed from it for any wrongdoing; nor does immunity protect him, as expressly stated in the law and noted in Auth. de manumis., princ., in §. neque autem. But there is no doubt that the said official committed a threefold crime: perfidy, flight, and theft; hence immunity ought not to protect him. Indeed, one who has committed a delict is excluded from grace, as ff. de legibus, 2, l. Lucius, §. Lucius Titius damnatus.

† The second reason is derived from the law *Datur securitas*, which provides that no one shall be arrested in his dwelling house. Digest, *De in ius vocando*. The law *Plerique* states, however, that this is understood to apply except in cases of crime; because for criminals there should be no place of safety and no refuge, as is noted in the Digest, *De in ius vocando*, law *Sed et is*, and in the Digest, *De re iudicata*, law *Nemo*. This is correct in principle. For fraud is excepted from all security. Digest, *De legibus*, Title 1, law *Si servus vetitus*.

Third reason, because security granted to someone does not extend to the debtors of the fiscal chamber, as is expressed in Auth. de man. prin. §. publicorum. But the chamber of the Magnificent Lord of Padua is a fiscal chamber, because it has been granted rights by the Emperor in Padua by privilege; therefore, the immunity does not extend to our case.

Fifth reason, for either this is a promise, or a favor, or both together, i.e., a promise made out of favor. If it is indeed a promise, it must be restricted according to what is good and equitable, so that it does not include persons whom it would be unjust to include. It must be justified. For every promise, the more it can be justified, the better, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. quidam cum filium. But it would be unjust if it included a thief and a fugitive. For the favor granted to Barbarius did not make him free, because he was a fugitive and a thief, as in ff. de off. praesi. l. Barbarius. And although the people and the prince could have done so, nevertheless it is not presumed that they wished to do so. Moreover, sometimes one can do more than one wishes; sometimes one wishes more than one can. de off. dele. c. cum abbaticis.

If, however, it is a favor granted by rescript, then because the rescript imitates the common law in similar cases, as in ff. de vulg. substi. l. ex facto, and the common law does not wish to grant favor of time or place to fugitive debtors, as noted in C. de feriis. l. fi., and there is no mention of flight in the rescript; therefore, in the rescript there was obreption against the Lords of la Scala. Hence the favor is not valid, as in extra de rescr. c. dilectus filius Abbas §. Stephani.

If, however, both promise and favor are involved, still those things are not included which the lord would not have likely granted. ff. de pig. l. obligatione generali. Nor is an unusual case included. For those things which rarely happen are not included. ff. de contrahen. empt. l. si fistulas. §. frumenta. But the flight of officials is most rare and most deserving of punishment. in Auth. vt iudi. sine quoquo suffrag. §. 1. and §. necesse. In doubt, no one is presumed to have granted against another what he ought to disdain to have granted against himself. ff. de solu. l. 1. And therefore the Lords of la Scala are not presumed to have wished to include under general words the illustrious Lord of Padua, as in c. sedes. de resc. and noted in eo. ti. c. 2. lib. 6. per lo. And. et alios.

† The sixth reason is that a debtor, properly so called, is also a creditor, and a creditor, properly and strictly speaking, is one who trusts the faith of the creditor. D. 6.1.1. Hence, no one is said to be a creditor or debtor properly on account of a wrongful act, but only loosely and abusively. Since, therefore, this security is to be restricted to the strictest meaning of the words, it does not extend to future delicts.

The seventh reason is a certain theoretical one: for either immunity is granted to someone on account of a necessary cause, such as on account of an embassy, and then you should say as in D. 2.50.2 § legatis (Digest, On Judges); or it is granted on account of a voluntary cause, and then it never avails in delicts, according to the laws cited above. The eighth reason is that this rescript is special with regard to the person to whom it is granted; hence it is valid, because there is no non obstante clause, as expressly noted in D. 50.17.3 § suae (Digest, On What Each Has Sworn). And this is not the case, because the lords cannot [grant it], for the Pope and the Emperor have no less power, and yet it is valid because the due form was not observed. The ninth reason is that a thief, by committing the theft everywhere, commits the delict there, and accumulates forum upon forum, D. 47.2.1 (Digest, On Theft), according to Bartolus. Therefore, from a new commission of the theft after the grace, an action arises by reason of the new territory; hence, because he sins today, he can be sued today. The tenth reason is that, in which the grace of the great doctor of Consignorio cannot operate, a second grace made in imitation cannot operate, as in D. 38.2.1 (Digest, On Free Legacies), l. Aurelius. But the grace of Lord Consignorio does not operate in our case, because Lord Jacob, by subsequently submitting to the calculation of accounts and rendering an account to the judge, renounced the declinatory forum, D. 2.11.1 (Digest, On Judges), l. sed si susceperit. Henceforth, the principal rescript was issued under the authority of Amen; consequently, the second one, its confirmatory, as in C. 11.3.1 (Code, On Excuses of Tutors), l. voluntarie; X. 3.32.1 (Decretals, On Constitutions), c. cum M. Ferrar. The eleventh reason is that the concession of the affidavit concerns goods and his own things: in which I consider that either it is established that they are his, and the immunity has place; or it is doubtful, and the same applies, because in doubt, one having the declinatory forum can oppose it; or it is certain that he holds another’s goods, and the declinatory forum avails nothing to him who is notoriously bound by a delict; which a good man does not defend, because in notorious matters, declinatory exceptions of forum, domicile, or origin do not have place by a pretended privilege against the forum, C. 9.22.1 (Code, On Where Criminal Actions Should Be Brought), autem; D. 2.11.1 (Digest, On Judges), l. sed si restituatur, in the first place, and especially after a confession voluntarily made in court. For sacred forms then can operate nothing, as in Auth. in medio (Authentic, In the Middle), lit. non fieri sac. iussiones (in the red and black). Therefore, whether the question is about honesty, the lords of la Scala are not bound to observe it, because they did not promise; or if the question is about law, they do not say so, because they ought not, by the clear reasons assigned above, and thus I conclude firmly. And it supports what is read and noted in C. 4.2.1 (Code, On Where Violence Is Used), l. autoritatem.

† To this is added by analogy that the benefit granted by law to debtors, namely that they may surrender their goods, does not extend to those who are sued on account of a delict or quasi-delict: for every wrongdoing is accustomed to exclude every benefit. D. quae in fraudem creditorum l. si. §. si. and no. X. de usura c. cum tu. and l. 1. C. ubi se. vel clari. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The state of affairs being such that whoever has been condemned may be attacked with impunity: and if he has obtained a remission recorded in the court records, yet has not been erased from the book of those under ban, whether he may still be attacked with impunity. Add also the following opinion.
body:
In the name of Christ. To make clear the points to be discussed, certain statutes must first be set forth. First, a statute and edict of the magnific lords of the House of la Scala provides that whoever is banned for homicide or any other crime punishable by death from the city of Verona shall be understood to be, and is, banned from the city of Vicenza, and vice versa. Furthermore, a statute of the said city of Verona provides that those banned for rebellion, homicide, robbery, or any other crime punishable by death may be attacked and killed with impunity, provided that a condemnatory sentence has first been pronounced by virtue of the ban, and not before. Likewise, a statute of the city of Vicenza provides that those banned for rebellion, homicide, or any other crime where the penalty is death may be killed with impunity, and those who kill them shall be considered immune from punishment, provided that a condemnatory sentence has first been pronounced against the said banned persons by virtue of the ban, and not before. Another statute of the city of Vicenza provides that no one shall be considered banned unless he is written in the common book by name and surname, together with the sign and name of the notary; nor shall anyone be considered exempt from the ban unless he has been notified in the book of the forum of bans, with the sign and name of the notary, in the order of the books of the forum of bans. Another statute of the city of Vicenza provides that whoever causes another to be killed for money shall be punished with the ultimate penalty.

From the aforementioned statutes, the following question arises. A certain John made an agreement in the district of Vicenza with Bertus and Antonius that they should kill a certain Herighetus in the district of Vicenza, and he promised them 100 livres upon the commission of the said homicide against the person of the said Herighetus. This Herighetus was banned and condemned in the commune of Verona for two homicides and two robberies. The said Bertus and Antonius, carrying out the said agreement, killed the said Herighetus in the district of Vicenza. The said John was captured and confessed that he had made an agreement with the aforementioned Bertus and Antonius that they should kill the said Herighetus, and that he would give them 100 livres for the said homicide committed; and that by virtue of the said agreement arranged by him, John, the aforementioned Bertus and Antonius killed the said Herighetus. The Podestà of Vicenza proceeds against this John by inquisition, stating that John ought to die by virtue of the last-mentioned statute, which provides that whoever causes another to be killed for money shall be punished with the ultimate penalty.

In defense of the said John, several arguments are advanced. First, that the said Herighetus was banned and condemned for homicides and two robberies in the commune of Verona; and thus, by virtue of the statute of the commune of Verona, he could be killed with impunity. Furthermore, by virtue of the edict of the said magnific men of the House of la Scala, he was understood to be banned; and he was banned from the city of Vicenza by virtue of the said edict, joined with the statute of the commune of Vicenza, which provides that those banned for rebellion, homicide, etc., may be killed with impunity. Therefore, no action should be taken against the said John in any way. Moreover, by inquisition, by virtue of the statutes of the commune of Vicenza, which are transmitted to you, and especially because the said statute stating that those who kill banned persons shall be considered immune from punishment specifies a certain crime, to such an extent that the judge cannot even proceed by inquisition, as noted by Jacobus de Aretino in the gloss to l. 1, §. quod vero, ff. de aleatoribus, and as noted by the doctors in l. servus, C. de his, qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt.

But against this it is objected that the said Herighetus had received a promise or guarantee from the late magnific lord Consignotus of la Scala that he could remain secure in the district of Vicenza notwithstanding the bans and condemnations he had in the commune of Verona. And so stand the words of the said promise or guarantee, which is produced against the said John. And against the said John, and for the said John, many arguments are alleged and produced on both sides, which are directed and transmitted to you to be examined.

Now the question is asked: whether the said judge may proceed against the said John, and whether the said John ought to be punished with the penalty of the statute punishing those who cause another to be killed for money.

† In the name of Christ, amen. That the said homicide could be committed and ordered with impunity is proven by these reasons. First, from the appearance of the ban, which remains, which appears to excuse those who act, as in D. de interrogatoribus actionibus, l. Etate, §. Ex causa. Second, because since it is in the book of bans, it is found to be in such a quasi-possession: hence it must be regarded as such. C. de testamento, l. 1; D. de servis exponendis, l. Moveor. Third, from just ignorance. For, in order to excuse ignorance, having the appearance of being has the same effect as truly being: but this ban has the appearance of being, therefore it has the same effect as if it had true being, just as a revoked mandate, which has the appearance of being, has the same effect in excusing the ignorant person as if it were not revoked and truly existed, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Eius, qui in provincia; D. de solutionibus, l. Cum quis, §. 1. For one justly ignores that what was formerly the case has changed, nor is it presumed to have changed unless it is proven. D. de institoria, l. Sed et si publicus, §. Proscribere. Fourth, because concerning another’s act, and especially a hidden one, ignorance is presumed unless it is proven that he was informed, as in D. de mandatis, l. Si fideiussor and l. Ultima; D. pro socio. Fifth, because ignorance excuses from corporal punishment, whether just or unjust. D. de abigeis, l. 1, in fine; C. de plagiariis, l. Plagii; D. de liberali causa, l. Igitur. And these are presumed. D. de probationibus, l. Verius. Sixth, regarding this question, the case seems to be D. de adulteriis, l. Peccatum, and this is noted by Cynus in C. de repudiis uxoris. Seventh, because a ban that appears prima facie to be something is presumed to be something. C. de edictis diversorum auctorum, l. 2 and l. Edictum. And even if it is said to be null, the offender is excused, as noted by Decius in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. 3, §. Si servus. Eighth, because the confidence granted to him seems to have expired by the death of the grantor, argumentum in l. Ultima, D. de poenis; and what is noted in l. 1, C. de postulando. Hence, such confidence does not seem to be valid against the successor in office, because a promise and prohibition made without cause seem to expire when the jurisdiction and office of the permitting or prohibiting party end, argumentum from the aforementioned laws. Ninth, because what is lawful to do is lawful to order to be done, as noted in D. de vi et vi armata, l. Cum fundum. And he who cannot be held liable principally cannot be held liable secondarily, as in D. de furtis, l. Fullo, §. Nemo. Tenth, because this determination is general, that it is lawful to kill a banned person, and it does not distinguish how, whether by having him killed for money, or in what manner: hence we cannot distinguish against the general determination of the law. D. de allegationibus, l. 1, §. Quod autem; D. de militum testamento, in l. Fraudem, §. Finis. For since this banned person is an enemy, fraud is not said to be committed. D. de dolo, l. 1, §. Non fuit. Moreover, one statute should be understood with the determination of another, hence a statute that prohibits and imposes a penalty should not be referred to cases in which a special permissive reason is found. D. de legibus, l. Quid ergo, §. Haeres; and D. de verbis obligatis, l. Qui servum mihi. Finally, I say that both Jacobus de Belvis and Bartolus advised in fact that it should be so. Namely, by a ban having the appearance of a ban: although the obligation is extinguished by payment or absolution, of which there is no proof to the one seeing and reading the ban, excuses the offender from punishment, and thus I hold with both Jacobs, namely Bartolus and Baldus. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. To the same effect as the preceding.
2. The cancellation of a ban by one lacking authority is of no effect.
3. It is equivalent not to observe a mandate, or not to have one.
4. An official is not believed when asserting that he has a mandate, unless it is established.
5. One is not believed when asserting that peace has been made, unless it is established.
6. What the clause “if it has been established to you” imports.
7. The assertion of a judge does not prove the fact of the parties.
body: In the name of Christ. Amen.

† Let us bring together the statute and the decree of the lord, and let us state: if anyone has been bannished and condemned, he may be attacked with impunity, provided the condemnation was previously rendered; and these words "condemned" were added from the decree of the Lord della Scala. Let us see whether these words "having been condemned" add anything to the statute. And it seems not, because the same thing was expressed in the statute when it was said "a condemnation having been previously rendered"; therefore, implicitly to say one is equivalent to saying the other, for the participle "condemned" indicates a completed act, that is, it signifies that a condemnation was rendered. The words "a condemnation having been previously rendered" signify similarly; there is no difference where the meaning is the same, arg. C. de test. l. quoniam indignum; C. communia de leg. l. 2 in princ.; ff. de legi. l. scire leges; 1 q. 1 c. Marcion; C. de legi. l. non dubium, and similar texts. To the contrary, it seems that it could be said that the participle "condemned" signifies not only that the condemnation must have preceded, but also that it must endure and remain in force at the time of the attack. For he who has been erased from the book of the condemned is regarded as having paid, not as condemned, as noted in ff. de excep. rei iud. l. si quis cum totum § plene. Thus, he who has been removed from the book of defendants is no longer said to be among them, unless he is newly received among them, as in ff. ad Turpil. l. si interueniens in verbo exemptum reum. But those words, "a condemnation having been previously rendered," denote a completed act in such a way that they do not require its continuing relevance, so long as the ban remains in its form, as in C. de insti. et subst. l. antepenult. For it matters greatly whether the prior elements are required for a single effect principally and causatively, or one as a cause and the other as a condition; for in a condition it suffices that it be true for a moment, but in a final cause of a future effect, in which it has not drawn its execution from the past, it does not suffice unless it endures; and a written bond does not endure when the obligation is extinguished, ff. de leg. 1 l. huiusmodi § legatum; ff. de pact. l. Labeo. It is one thing, therefore, to say: "Let an outlaw and a condemned person be liable to be attacked with impunity," because these two qualities, namely being outlawed and condemned, taken copulatively, must both be true at the same time for this effect, and if one is vitiated, both are vitiated. It is another thing to say: "Let an outlaw be liable to be attacked with impunity, a condemnation having been previously rendered"; because then the cause of the permitted attack is solely the ban in this sequence, namely because a condemnation has followed. Now, that a condemnation has followed cannot be denied, even though it was afterwards canceled, ff. de capt. l. in bello § factae; C. de gener. aboli. l. indulgendum. The fault can afterwards be removed, but the guilt, once contracted from the condemnation, leaves manifest stains. Solution: It must be said, regarding our proposed case, that there is no difference between these phrasings, because in both cases the ban and the condemnation are required not only to have preceded, but to be in force; for through these two things a person is made a public enemy and war is declared against him, not through one alone. But he to whom pardon has been granted is not an enemy, provided that the pardon and reconciliation are established. For pardon is never presumed unless it is proved, l. 3 in fi. ff. de adi. leg., and C. fam. herc. l. in ipsius, ff. ad Syll. l. diuus, Inst. de iniur. § fi. Although I grant, therefore, that the abolition of the condemnation extinguishes the ban, because the principal to which the other is ordered is extinguished—and therefore also its antecedent *iudicatum solui*, when it was sought—

† nevertheless, if the cancellation was made by one lacking authority, it is of no effect, ff. de his quae in testamento delen. l. 1, and fully noted in C. de testamentis l. nostram; ff. si tabulae testamenti nullae ext. l. 1; ff. de probat. l. si chirographum; C. de solut. l. inducens; ff. de pact. l. postquam and l. Labeo. Or if the cancellation is unknown, so that the ban is recorded but the cancellation is not at all, in these two cases the killing is not punished: in the first it is never punished, because it was lawful to attack one who was truly and effectively banned and condemned, even if he had believed it was not lawful for him to do so, ff. de furt. l. inter omnes § recte; ff. de crim. expil. hered. l. fi.; in the second it is not punished because, led by the written record, he believed, since he has notoriety on his side; and if a non-notorious fact is opposed to a notorious one, one must stand by the notorious fact, because that which is held by all is more probably believed, as was fully stated in the first consilium. Let us examine, therefore, in our case, who caused the condemnation to be canceled, and why.

† And it must be considered that not having a mandate and not observing the form of a mandate are on the same footing; and therefore a judge who does not observe the form of his mandate is reduced to the status of a private person, de rescrip. c. cum dilecta; de rest. spol. c. Pisanis; for the given form pertains to the very essence of the thing, just as does the lawful or natural form, ff. de arbit. l. quid tamen; C. de senten. l. prolata and l. diligenter, and similar texts. For the cause of a cancellation must always be investigated to see whether it is true, as must also the authority of the one who examines it, ff. de in integ. restit. l. omnes; ff. de his quae in testamento delen. l. cancellauerat. Nor can anyone cause this cancellation to be made other than the prince, or the lieutenant of the lords della Scala, or their delegate or commissioner, ff. de poen. l. relegati; nor does the abusive decree of the podestà or the vicar of the lords have any force in this regard, ff. de decre. ab ord. facien. l. ambitus, and there fully by Bartolus.

† Nor is his assertion credited regarding a commission directed to him, C. de mand. prin. l. 1; de off. deleg. c. cum in iure peritus; dist. 96 c. nobilissimus; ff. depos. l. si quis inficiatus; and this must be registered in the acts, as noted in C. ad Treb. l. penult.

† Likewise, he is not credited when he asserts that a peace was made, unless it is established, as in l. illicitas § veritas, ff. de off. praes., and c. quam contra, de probat., and C. de arbit. l. ne in arbitris, and as noted in c. innotuit, de eo qui furt. ord. suscep., by Innocentius. But something else is also necessary: when the lord mandates his official, "Cause the condemnation of such a person to be canceled if he has peace," this means "if it shall be established to you that he has peace"; for it ought to be clear and established to him, l. hoc autem in princ., quibus ex caus. in poss. eat.; ff. de condit. et demon. l. multum interesse; nor does the truth suffice without proof. However, it cannot be established to him unless the fiscal proctor is cited, and if a mandate concerning the cancellation is issued without his citation, it is null by operation of law,

† because the clause "if it shall be established to you" always requires judicial cognizance of the cause and the citation of the interested parties, according to what was subtly noted by Innocentius in c. fi. de praesump., and in c. 1 de off. deleg. in Clem. Hence, since the cause is fiscal, the proctor of the fiscal chamber of the lords della Scala ought to have been cited; otherwise the interlocutory judgment was null. Furthermore, the safe-conduct must be considered; for it too contained a condition, concerning the fulfillment of which a declaration ought first to have been made, ff. de condit. et demon. l. qui sub condicione redolendarum; for as often as one arrives from one procedure at another, that procedure must be settled, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1 § praetor habet, ff. de nov. oper. nunt., or at least it must be clear from the acts, C. ad Treb. l. penult. § quum autem. Here, however, nothing appears regarding a completed peace; and those words enunciatively uttered by the judge by way of recital—namely, because it is established to him regarding the peace—do not effect a disposition, because a peace is not made by the judge, nor is the proof thereof;

† because the judge’s assertion does not prove an act of the parties, as in ff. de transac. l. cum hi § si praetor, and said c. quam contra falsam. It is clearly concluded, therefore, that the said homicide was committed with impunity on account of a just error; both because the substance of the condemnation was not lacking, and also because the cancellation appears to be null. And thus I state and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a grandson from an emancipated son, to whom something has been left, can sue for the supplement of the legitime, notwithstanding the renunciation made by his father to his own father and brothers.
2. The devolution of an inheritance occurs in three ways.
3. To cede to another is something different than to renounce simply.
4. One who has ceded a hope cannot, after a condition subsequently arises, renounce to the prejudice of the person to whom he ceded.
5. Today the difference between emancipation and paternal power has been abolished. Add the following counsel.
