body: In the first consultation, let us therefore examine in our case who caused the condemnation to be cancelled, and why.

And it must be considered that it is equivalent not to have a mandate, or not to observe the form of the mandate; for which reason a judge who does not observe the form of the mandate is reduced to the status of a private individual, as stated in the rescripts: c. Cum dilecta, De restitutione spoliatorum; c. Pisanis. For the form is constitutive of the very essence of the thing, just as the legitimate or natural form is, as held in ff. De arbitris, l. Quid tamen; C. De sententiis, l. Prolata; and l. Diligenter. And if the cause of cancellation is always to be sought, it must be inquired whether it is true, and also whether it is just, even on the part of the one who examines it, as stated in ff. De in integrum restitutione, l. Omnes; ff. De his quae in testamento delentur, l. Cancellauerat. Nor can this cancellation be made by anyone other than the prince, or the lieutenant of the Lords of La Schala, or their delegate or commissioner, as held in ff. De poenis, l. Relegati. Nor does an abusive decree of the praetor or of the vicar of the lords avail in this matter, as stated in ff. De decretis ab ordine faciendis, l. Ambitus; and there fully by Bartolus.

† nor is credit given to his assertion regarding the commission directly granted to him. C. de man. p. l. 1. de off. deleg. c. cum in iure peritus. 96. dis. c. nobilissimus. ff. depo. l. si quis inficiatus. and this must be recorded in the records, as noted. C. ad Treb. l. pe.

† Moreover, no credit is given to one who asserts that a peace agreement has been made, unless it is established, as stated in l. illicitas, § veritas, D. de officio praetoris; and c. quam contra, D. de probat.; and C. de arbitris, l. ne in arbitris; and as noted in c. innotuit, D. de eo qui furtum ordinariam suscipit, according to Innocentius. But another requirement is necessary when the lord commands his official: “Have the condemnation of such a person cancelled, if he has peace,” which means, “if it has been established to you that he has peace,” for it must be clear and established to him. See l. hoc autem, in principio, D. quibus ex causis in possessionem eat; and D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. multum interesse. Truth without proof is not sufficient; nor can it be established to him unless the fiscal procurator is summoned. And if the mandate for cancellation is issued without summoning him, it is null by operation of law.

† because the clause “if it has been established to you” always requires a hearing of the case and the citation of those who have an interest, according to the subtle note by Innocentius in c. fin. de praesumptionibus and in c. 1. de officio delegati in 6th; hence, since the case is fiscal, the procurator of the fiscal chamber of the Lords of La Scala ought to have been cited; otherwise the interlocutory judgment was null. It must also be considered regarding security: for he himself had a condition in his favor, concerning the existence of which it ought first to have been declared. D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. qui sub conditione; for whenever from one order one proceeds to another, it is necessary to speak about that order, as noted by Bartolus in l. 1. §. praetor habet, D. de novo operis nuntiando; or at least it must appear from the records. C. ad Trebellianum, l. pen. §. quum autem. Here, however, nothing appears regarding the peace concluded; and those words, enunciated by the judge by way of cause, namely “because it is established to him regarding the peace,” do not induce a disposition, because peace is not made by the judge, nor is it proof:

† Because the assertion of the judge does not prove the fact of the parties, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, § si praetor, and D. C. quam contra falsam. It is therefore clearly concluded that the homicide was committed with impunity due to just error; also because the substance of the condemnation is not lacking; and also because the cancellation appears null. And so I say, and I advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An emancipated son, having made a sworn renunciation, cannot come to the inheritance, nor to the supplement.
2. An emancipated son, who can come to the inheritance, or to the legitime: must collate what he received.
3. To an emancipated son, the grandson remains in the power of the grandfather.
4. The difference between emancipation and paternal power has been removed.
5. The grandfather does not have the right to disinherit or institute as heir a grandson who, at the time of the grandfather's death, is preceded by his father, and whether a legitime is due to one born of an emancipated son.
6. If the son of an emancipated person acquires something from his uncles: those uncles cannot come against the emancipated person, who promised for himself and his heirs.
casus:
In the name of Christ, Amen.

The point is this: the prudent man, Lord John, son of Lord Antonio de Maseis of Verona, had six sons, namely Rolandino, Nicholas, Marcus, Antonio, Criscibenus, and Michael. The aforementioned Marcus died while his father was still living, leaving three daughters. Michael also died while his father was still living, without sons or daughters. Nicholas, however, died after his father’s death, leaving sons. Here, Lord John first emancipated Rolandino, from whom Rolandino was born; at the time of emancipation, there was a certain John. Finally, this Lord John made his will, in which he instituted the said Rolandino as heir in certain things, and also John, the son of the said Rolandino, in 15 pounds, as the series of the will clearly dictates; but he instituted the universal heirs to be the remaining sons, of whom two survive, namely Antonio and Criscibenus. Now John, the son of Rolandino, wishes to exercise his right in his own capacity against his uncles Antonio and Criscibenus. Here several questions arise.

First, whether Rolandino can sue in his own capacity for the supplement of his legitime? Second, if he can, whether that which was left to him, or that which he received from his father, or that in which he was instituted, must be imputed to the fourth part due by natural law? Third, whether John, the son of the said Rolandino, who is sui iuris, because he was already born when Rolandino was emancipated by his father, can sue in his own capacity for the supplement of his legitime, as if his father had been removed from the picture by emancipation, especially since the said Rolandino repudiated the inheritance of the said Lord John, and also of his father after the death of his father, who instituted the said Rolandino, his son, as heir to himself in twenty-five denarii, and ordered him to be content, tacitly, etc., and the said John in twenty-five pounds. Fourth, and lastly, whether by virtue of a certain promise made to John by the said Rolandino to the said Lord John and his sons, if John, the son of the said Rolandino, should take anything from the heirs of Lord John, can the said heirs obtain it from the said Rolandino, or act against him in some way on this account. In the name of Christ, Amen.

It must be premised for clarity that a son sometimes precedes his grandson, born of himself, both in degree and in the right of succession; sometimes he precedes in degree, but not in the right of succession; indeed, he precedes in both ways, that is, in degree and in the right of succession. At times, the son is admitted to the paternal succession and accepts it; then, as regards the grandson, nothing is owed to him in the person of the grandson himself, as is fully stated in the law *Et nunc*, Code, *Unde liberi*; and in the law *Qui se patris*, in the great gloss. This is founded on the rule taken from the order of proximity and of law, Digest, *De liberis et posthumis*; the law *Gallus*, Digest, *De in iustis testamentis*; the law *Si quis filio exhaeredato*, in the first response. For when another precedes, he who follows cannot receive, Digest, *De bonis liberorum*; the law *Filius*. Or because, without doubt, sometimes the son has not yet accepted, but can accept, and then the preceding cause of the grandson’s claim still hangs in suspense, by argument from Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*; the law *Pater filium*. For a doubtful cause of exclusion usually excludes in the meantime, Digest, *De conditione indebiti*; the law *Sufficit*. At times, the son did not accept the succession or legacies devolved upon him, but repudiated them; and then he made room for the grandson, and transfers and devolves that right to the grandson by the successor edict, both intestate and by will, Digest, *De inofficioso testamento*; the law *Si is, qui*; Digest, *De contrahenda tutela*; the law *Non tantum*, section *Si emancipatus*; and noted in Code, *De inofficioso testamento*; the law *Si quis filium*; and by Dy. in chapter *Non debet alteri*. And these laws speak of a will having been made. And noted in the said law *Qui se patris*; and Institutes, *De legatis agnatis succedentibus*, section *Placebat*.

† And devolution is of its own nature in three ways, according to the gloss: from one’s own to one’s own, although others hold the contrary regarding from one’s not own to one’s own, as from an emancipated son to a grandson retained in power; and from one’s not own to one’s not own, as from the maternal line, or from both emancipated, namely the son and the grandson. But among collaterals, or in the legitime, the edict of succession has no place, because the law speaks only of a brother and a sister, not of their children, in the Authentica de haereditatibus et falcidia, §. primum. Therefore, if a son sometimes ceded his legitime to another, then by ceding he is deemed to acknowledge. Codex de iure deliberationis, l. si auia.

† and therefore it excludes the grandson: and thus it is one thing to cede to another, and another thing to renounce simply. D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. fuit quaestionis. And this the son may do after the death of his father. D. de liberis agnoscendis, l. si. Not during the life of the father, unless with the consent of the father: and with the father persevering in the same will until death. C. de pactis, l. si. When the son is removed from the picture while the grandfather is alive: then the succession devolves upon the grandson. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. quid si tantum. Let us therefore see to which member our case pertains: and thus we shall know what is the law regarding the grandson. For sometimes the son dies, sometimes he cedes, sometimes he abstains, sometimes the quality of the act is doubtful. If, therefore, he dies while the testator is alive, his fault does not harm the grandson, because the grandson has this right not by pact, but by the benefit of the law: and therefore he cannot be burdened by the pact of his father. D. de adoptionibus, l. si arrogator. And this is expressly noted by Bartolus. D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. qui superstitis. And this is not our case. But if he cedes his rights, or a species of future right: the cessionary is preferred to the grandson, because the cessionary derives his cause from him who is preferred, as J. qu. J. C. ius.

† nor does he, who cedes the appearance, afterwards, when the condition has arisen, renounce to the prejudice of him to whom he ceded, as is argued from l. si partem, § 1, D. de tutelae aut curatoriae administratione seruorum amittenda; and from the last law, C. de pactis. If, however, he abstains, the grandson succeeds, as I said; but if the quality of the act is doubtful, this seems to be our proper case. For, upon viewing the instrument celebrated between the said son on one part, and the father and brothers on the other, in which instrument there are ambiguous words concerning renunciation to the transfer, or cession, of the legitimate portion as if held by confession, obscurity arises from the ambiguity as to what kind of act this is. For, if one looks at the beginning, from which the discourse starts, when it says “refuting,” for to refute an inheritance and to repudiate are the same thing, because both are privative. And thus, from the beginning of the instrument, it appears that it was an abstention from the inheritance given in a pact; and from this beginning it seems that the sense and understanding of the whole instrument was subsequently formed, as argued in D. de hereditate instituenda, l. si. And this is also followed in the same instrument, when it says “renouncing and remitting”; therefore, the way is open for the great-grandson. But against this stands the text in the instrument in the words “absolving and releasing”; for to absolve and to release is an act which includes preceding knowledge, and it is a dispositive act. He who releases must have the right to do so; and every privation presupposes possession, as stated in D. si certum petatur, l. eius qui in provincia. This is supported by the fact that he confessed to having owed the portion in five hundred florins; hence, this was not an abdication of abstention, but a primitive payment of debt, as in D. ad legem Falcidiam, l. cum quo peculio, § si. Therefore, since the son has the legitimate portion, no place remains for the grandson, nor for any others who might claim a right. For the exclusion of the son, Bartolus holds this openly in D. de contractibus, l. 1, § filius, in the fourth question; and this is the very truth, as stated in the chapter N. nepotis: preceding the son, his father’s grandson has no right; but here the father precedes. For today, an emancipated son is preferred to such a grandson according to the true opinion. For since the legitimate portion is due to the emancipated son just as to his own, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. omnimodo, it is impossible that it should be due simultaneously to the son and to the grandson; therefore, in the legitimate portion, the emancipated son is preferred to the grandson, his son.

† Moreover, because the distinction between emancipation and paternal power has been abolished, even with respect to testamentary dispositions. And if not entirely as regards the mode of succession, at least as regards the effect of succession. Furthermore, because today the title *De coniungendis* has been abolished, and thus the glosses speaking on this matter must be understood. D. *De coniungendis*, l. 1; D. *De minoribus*, l. *Si filius*; D. *De inofficioso testamento*, l. *Si proponas*; and in Auth. *Ex causa*; and in the said § *Quid si tamen*; D. *De iniusto testamento*, l. *Posthumorum*; C. *De collationibus*, l. *Si emancipati*; C. *Unde legitimi*, l. *Certum*; C. *Communia de successionibus*, Auth. *In successione*; and in Auth. *De hereditatibus et falcidia*, § *Exheredatos*, col. 1. From which it is clearly concluded that the right to bring an action for the supplement does not belong to the said son or grandson. And on this matter, one should consider what is more fully treated in C. *De codicillis*, l. *Pactum*. I, Baldus.
body: Diligently having examined the testament of the said Lord John. Having therefore seen the emancipation of the said Rolandino, and a certain oath having been taken by the said Rolandino, and mature deliberation having been had in agreement, we, Argentinus and Paganinus, the undersigned, thus answer the questions put to us. First. On the first doubt, we say and advise,

† that the said Rolandinus can claim nothing in his own right. He himself has closed his mouth by means of a sworn settlement, which he made. C. de pac. l. quamuis. And it is stated in l. pactum. C. de colla. and l. si. de pac. and Bartolus in l. si qui pro eo. ff. de fideius. And there is no room for doubt on this matter: especially since here Rolandinus was then emancipated, for emancipated persons contract as fathers of families. C. de eman. lib.

† On the second doubt, nothing need be said, since we take it as established that Rolandinus cannot claim anything, or cannot sue for a supplement. If, however, someone were to say, albeit incorrectly, that he could sue for a supplement: then it is clear that he must bring into account what has been given to him, according to the doctrine set forth in l. si emancipat. C. de collationibus; and even if this Rolandinus were or had been in power, such gifts are counted towards the legitime, l. omnimodo. C. de inofficioso testamento. As for gifts given as a reward for emancipation, Petrus holds that they are so counted, in l. sancimus. C. de inoff. test., and this is the common opinion of advocates, as Ray. says, who speaks more clearly and explains this in l. ut liberis. C. de collationibus. Let us pass over this point, for it is superfluous to dispute it here.

† On the third doubt, which is more weighty, namely whether Lo., the son of Rolandinus, emancipated and excluded, can sue in his own right for a supplement, we premise certain conclusions for the clearer investigation of what is to be said, through which the truth will appear. The first is that, according to the true opinion of Johannes in l. sed etiam, ff. de adoptionibus, approved in l. liberum, eod. tit., and in l. 3, ff. de capitis diminutione, the grandson remains in the power of the grandfather when the son is emancipated. The second is that, as long as the first degree has place, the subsequent degree is not heard. l. Gallus, in § 1, and in Authent. de haeredibus, quae ab intestato, in principio; for the first cause is that of children, the second that of grandchildren, etc.

† Third conclusion, that today the difference between emancipation and paternal power has been abolished, in Auth. de hær. quæ ab intest. §. multum; for the son does not cease to be an agnate through emancipation. Glossed in l. quem filius, ff. de adop. Nor do we distinguish intestate successions from testamentary successions, as we shall say below; although a certain gloss did so, although it is commonly rejected. The fourth conclusion is, that he alone brings an action for the supplement of the legitime, who, having been passed over, could bring a querel against the will: ad aliud. n. no remedy has been found for the supplement, except to exclude the passed-over heir from the querel. l. omnimodo, l. qui nuper, l. qui in priorib., in l. 1, and in l. cum quæritur, and l. parentibus, C. de inof. testam.

Fifth and final conclusion: that the grandfather is not required to disinherit or institute as heir a grandson who, at the time of the grandfather’s death, is preceded by his father. D. de inoff. testa. l. si quis exheredato; Inst. in the words “cum nec exheredati.” In this case, the opinion of Gallus is superfluous; it applies when the son dies during the lifetime of the grandfather. D. l. Gallus, § 1. For a grandson who is preceded by an emancipated son is not owed a legitime by natural law, as the gloss states in D. l. si, de lib. et posth. And this doubt is now resolved, first, by our late lord, the learned Raymond, in D. l. posthumorum, in the beginning, de iniusto test., where it is asked whether a child born to an emancipated son, if passed over, breaks the grandfather’s testament, and consequently whether a legitime is owed to him; and he says that it does not break it, and consequently that a legitime is not owed to him. D. l. cum quaeritur; C. l. parentib., de inoff. testa. And thus he says he advised in fact at Bologna. The same question is raised by Bartolus, against all others, in D. l. Gallus, § quid si tamen, in the words “ponit quaestionem, quae fuit de facto,” and he follows the learned Raymond, and says that this is the case in C. l. meminimus, § 1, de leg. haer. And he responds to the gloss which is in § et quid si tamen, and in D. l. posthumorum, in D. l. emancipati, and in Auth. ex causa. Since, therefore, the emancipated son precedes the grandson, nothing is owed to the grandson, as the gloss says in D. l. si, non ob. That the son is removed by the end, because he is deemed to have donated his right to his brothers; and thus transferred it to them. D. l. in aedibus, § veluti, de don. Hence such a right is not said to be evoked. And thus we firmly say and advise.

† To the fourth and final doubt, we say that although this John would win something or bring a suit against the universal heirs of Lord John, for this reason the said heirs could not bring the condictio Rolandinum. The reason is clearly apparent, for Rolandus promised by himself and his heirs. But if John were to sue, he would not sue as an heir, but in his own person. For a living person has no heir, as stated in l. 2, ff. de hereditate vendenda. Moreover, he cannot sue except on the basis of a fact; and if he were to win through the imprudence of the judge, l. si per imprudentiam vel iniuriam, which the heirs of Rolandus could not impute to him, they must retain it for themselves, ff. de fideiussoribus, l. exceptio. And thus I say and advise, I, Argentinus, Doctor of Laws of Raynerius. And for the greater firmness of strength, I ordered my customary seal to be affixed, always reserving the counsel and judgment of anyone who may think better, as is written above. I say and advise, I, Paganinus de Salla, Doctor of Laws. For greater strength, I had my customary seal impressed, always reserving the better judgment, to which I willingly submit myself. cON.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How witnesses testifying about usury ought to testify.
2. Whether blood relatives are competent witnesses.
3. Whether reputation can be proven by two witnesses.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. I, Angelus de Castellione Aretino, Doctor of Both Laws, Archpriest and Canon of Padua, and Canon of Arezzo, having been requested to write the truth concerning the article whose tenor is as follows: A legal expert gives counsel concerning the dispute between Vincentius, son of the late Master Azo de Malado, or Vgotio the notary, or Master Bartholomew the furrier, son of the late Daniel, his procurator and in procuratorial name on his behalf, on the one side, and Pax, son of Michael, or Ser Johannes de Moledo, notary, his procurator and in procuratorial name on his behalf, on the other side: whether the said Pax is, and ought to be pronounced, a public and manifest usurer, notwithstanding the oppositions and objections raised on the part of the said Pax, or whether he ought indeed not to be so pronounced. And here, having inspected the proofs of both parties and all the acts and proceedings had between the said parties, etc., I say and advise, saving wiser counsel, that the said Pax ought to be pronounced, and must decisively be pronounced, a public and manifest usurer, notwithstanding the oppositions and objections on the part of the said Pax; and this having seen the sayings and attestations of the proving and reproving witnesses produced on both sides, especially by virtue of a certain synodal constitution which begins *manifestum autem usurarium declaramus*, in that part where it says: "we say it is the same if he is proven a usurer by two suitable witnesses, even if they are singular in their testimonies, provided that public fame labors against him," etc. Now it remains to respond to certain doubts that arise from the process, which at first sight seem to oppose my counsel. The first is whether that witness is to be called suitable who states that Pax is a usurer, and for the reason and knowledge of his statement says that the said Pax lent to him at usury. The second is whether a witness is called suitable who is of the consanguinity of the producer. The third is whether fame can legitimately be proved by two witnesses. Concerning these doubts, although lengthy discussions could be revived, having cast aside all superfluity, I shall state simply what seems to me the truth,

† and concluding briefly, I say therefore to the first, that the witness in question ought to be deemed suitable, because the benefit or disadvantage of the cause in which he deposes does not principally concern him; nor, merely on the ground that the said Pax should be pronounced a usurer in this cause, would any emolument accrue to the said witness, or should any restitution of usuries be made, because a matter conducted between others, etc., as the laws are common knowledge; and because it does not suffice to prove someone a usurer, even if usury was lent by him, unless payment of the usuries is proved, and other matters about which it is held by the Doctors in extra *de iureiu.* c. *ex literis*. This opinion is proved by Inn. in extra *de testi.* c. 3, and in c. *cum nuntius*, where it is clear that prelates and clerics can be witnesses in the cause of their church; and the reason is that the cause of the church is not properly that of the prelate or clerics, even if an emolument redounds to them secondarily. To the same effect is what is held in Inst. *de testa.* §. *legatariis*, and what is noted in Spe. *de instrumentorum edit.* §. *postremo*, otherwise beginning *instrumentorum*, at the word *quid de legatario*. Nor does what the Doctors and the Gloss note on the said §. *legatariis* stand in the way, because that applies when the legacy was of such a kind that it would be due unless the will were valid, and the will being confirmed, the legacy is necessarily due; but in our case it is otherwise, because even if Pax is proved a usurer, nothing is nevertheless due to Benevenutus the witness unless a new demand intervenes, as was said above.

† To the second doubt, I say that, as a rule, all witnesses are called suitable, even though they be consanguineous or domestics of the producer, to whom command cannot be given by reason of paternal or master's power. This is the literal text which is held in C. 4 q. 3 at the verse *item idonei*, and noted by the Doctors in C. *de testa.* l. 2. I concede, however, that between the witness and the producer there could be such great affection, even without kinship, that the said witness would be weakened and not called fully suitable, as I think is noted by Ugo in C. 3 q. 5 c. *in summa*, and in Spe. tit. *de testi.* §. 1 at the verse *item excipitur, quod est domesticus*, and the following verse; but in our case, such great affection is not established from the matters that were presented to me.

† To the third, I say briefly that although fame is not introduced by a few, once introduced it is corroborated by two witnesses. This is proved in extra *de testi.* c. *tam literis*. To the like effect makes what is held in C. *de bon. poss. secundum tab.* l. 2, and C. *de fideic.* l. *fi.* To the same effect is what the Doctors note in extra *de iureiu.* c. *ad nostram*, and ff. eod. tit. l. 3, and it is the ordinary gloss on C. 2 q. 1 c. *fi.* Archidiaconus notes the same in c. *omnibus* C. 2 q. 5, and by reference through the moderns in extra *de accu.* c. *inquisitionis*. And so I, the aforesaid Angelus, say and advise; in truth of which testimony I have affixed my customary seal. And so I, Argentinus [son of the] Lord Raynerius, Doctor of Laws, say and advise; and for the greater strength and firmness, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an episcopal constitution, by which it is proved by two singular witnesses that someone is a usurer, is valid.
2. Whether the singular witnesses in the aforementioned case are singular witnesses in proving reputation.
3. Whether a witness testifying about reputation, because he publicly heard it said, proves it.
1. If a substitution is made by a testator to several sons with the addition of a collective name, and the condition exists in all persons, whether the substitute is called, and what if it exists in only one person. See the distinction.
2. If the testator instituted his sons, and to the first dying without children he substituted by fideicommissum the survivor, and if both die without children, he substituted the poor, and one dies first without true or fictitious children, and subsequently the other without: what the poor substitutes should have.
3. Whether the legitime of sons can be diminished or increased by statute.
4. If the condition fails in the person of the first by legal fiction, and the condition existed in the person of the second, whether the poor come to any part of the fideicommissum.
5. What is imputed to the legitime.
6. Faith is given to writings in the inventory.
7. Whether an alternative libel proceeds: and what in positions.
8. Whether the heir of the one asked after death is sued from his own acceptance, or from the acceptance of his predecessor.
9. Whether a dead person is presumed to be he about whom there is a rumor: and when mention is made in instruments for the word, formerly.
11. Whether an instrument received for husbands in the name of the wife is presumed to be received to the end that the wife's title and dominion be sought.
12. Whether a fideicommissum is diminished by a division made by right of faith, with some reservation made.
13. The condition, if without children: whether it comprehends heirs of law.
14. Whether a statute extends to past events.
15. What this word, born from himself, imports.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the case of Vincentius against peace, it must first be considered,

† whether a constitution of a bishop is valid which provides that a person may be proved to be a usurer through singular witnesses. And it seems that it is not, because where there is singularity, there is variety, and likewise unity, because each one is alone. And it is contrary to divine and human law that credit should be given to the statement of one person alone, and a bishop's constitution directly hostile to civil and canon law is not valid, ff. de off. praefe. praeto. l. normam. To the contrary, to prove a crime in general, singular witnesses suffice, because the genus is proved through the species about which they depose, just as Inno. says concerning heresy, extra de accu. c. generaliter; and thus that constitution does not seem contrary to law; but I omit this, because this is not what is asked.

† Secondly, it is asked whether witnesses who are singular in their statement are seen to be singular as to repute (fama). And say that if they depose concerning absolute repute, as is the case here, they are not singular; and especially because the proof of repute refers also to articles not proved, as is noted in Spec. de notoriis crimin. §. famae. ver. quid si testis.

† Thirdly, it is asked whether a witness who says that there is repute, when interrogated about the cause of his knowledge says that he heard it said publicly, proves repute. And Bar. holds that he does not, as in ff. de quaest. l. de minore. §. tormenta. But what if he says that he heard it said by several (a pluribus)? Still he does not prove it, because he could have heard it from only two, as in ff. de testi. l. vbi numerus; and two do not suffice, as is noted in ff. de accusa. l. ea quidem. What if he says, "because I heard it said by persons knowing the aforesaid things"? I say the same, that repute is not proved, because it can be understood that he heard it from two; and thus he does not prove repute. And this is the truth; wherefore, because our friends have advised poorly, their error is not to be followed, but an agreement should be made with the party, because I do not have at present anyone through whom I may send back the parchment/fur; let us desist from buying. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 10. The inventory shall prove [the case], if the decree concerning the guardianship is invalid.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the question which is pending between the school of Santa Maria and the Lord Desideratus, several doubts arise upon which subtle and very full allegations have been made on behalf of the school. However, to provide a clearer resolution, certain general points must first be laid down.

† And first, when a testator substitutes to several instituted sons with the addition of a collective word—saying, for instance, “and if all,” or “and if both,” or “and if either”—either the condition of the substitution exists in person, and without doubt the substitute is called (C. de impu. et aliis sub.); or the condition exists in the person of one, but fails in the person of the other; and then either the condition exists in the person of the first dying and fails in the person of the second dying, or conversely it fails in the person of the first and exists in the person of the last. If indeed the condition existed in the person of the first and not of the last, it matters whether a person survives whom, by expressly assumed and due affection and the tacit will of the deceased, excludes the extraneous substitute, and then the substitution ceases (ff. ad Treb. l. haeredes mei. §. cum ita; and arg. d. l. pe. in ratione sui; ff. de vul. sub. l. vel singulis; ff. de haer. inst. l. Luc.; ff. de reb. du. l. si is, qui ducenta. §. fi.; arg. ff. de inst. et sub. l. generaliter); or no person survives, and then the fideicommissary substitution, even though it speaks of several, would be made absolutely or indefinitely, and then there is no doubt that insofar as the condition exists, the disposition is seen to be purified, even in the share of the one and first dying (ff. ad Treb. l. Lucius. §. Gayo), because just as plurality is aggregated out of universals, so it is resolved into those very unities or singularities (ff. de condi. insti. l. 2; ff. de condi. et de. l. falsa. §. ult.). If, however, it is made under a collective noun, as “and if all,” or “and if both,” then by the rigor of the words the condition is not divided, but must exist just as the letter lies; but by interpretation of law, and thus a resolution into singularities is now made, arg. d. §. cum ita according to Bartolus; yet this case is not altogether unentangled; and this when the condition exists in the person of the first, but not in the person of the last: then there is room for the substitution. This is properly the case in d. §. cum ita.

† Secondly, it must be seen, if a testator institutes sons, and to the first dying without children substitutes through a fideicommissum the survivor, and if both die without children substitutes the poor; and first one dies without children, true or fictive, and subsequently the other dies without children: what ought the substituted poor to have? Where it must be considered whether in the person of the first dying there is understood to be a twofold subordinated fideicommissary substitution, so that the meaning is that to the first dying he substituted the surviving brother for as long as the brother lived, but after his death without children he substituted the poor to that same first dying, and thus transferred the substitution from the brother to the poor; or rather that to the first dying there was made only a single substitution, namely of the brother, if the brother should survive. And this latter view is true, since in the person of the last dying there is understood only a single substitution; therefore neither in the share of the first, arg. ff. de vul. substi. l. iam hoc iure. §. 1. in ratione sui, and l. Lucius. The poor therefore do not come in as substituted to the first dying, but they do indeed come in as substituted to the second dying. Let us see, therefore, what these poor take. And for this purpose it is necessary to premise that when a testator first honors and afterwards burdens, the whole comes to the fideicommissary, if the words of the testament do not conflict, as in ff. ad Treb. l. Marcellus. §. quidam liberis. Whence in the fideicommissary what the surviving brother takes by reason of the substitution to make, it has been approved that the substitution concerning the first dying is also valid, as in ff. ad Treb. l. Scaevola; so that the meaning is that half of the half of the first dying comes to be restored to the poor, because what the survivor received as heir of his brother—that is, the legitime and the Trebellianic portion—is outside the cause of the fideicommissum, because he takes it not by benefit of the father, but of the brother, and as heir of the brother, extra de test. c. Ray. and c. Ray., and ff. de vul. subs. l. cohaeredi. §. cum filiae. vers. fideicom., and arg. of what is noted in l. polla, C. de his, qui. vt indi. in ratione sui, ff. de adop. l. si arrogator. versi. sed an impuberi; for when the said legitime and Trebellianic portion have once been excepted from the fideicommissum, they do not fall back into the fideicommissary, argu. de remis. pig. l. si solita providentia; which legitime and Trebellianic portion he retains by operation of law, and therefore it can be pleaded against anyone possessing, as in ff. ad l. Fal. l. linea Margaritarum, especially regarding the legitime, in which by operation of law the burden of the fideicommissary does not hold nor extend itself, C. de inof. test. l. quam in prioribus. Concerning the portion of the last dying, however, in which the poor or pious places were instituted by the father, by the ius commune they ought to have two parts, according to the true opinion that the Trebellianic portion is not deducted from bequests to pious causes. But by the statute it appears that if the statute speaks in our case—concerning which I will speak below at the end of the consilium—they ought not to have more than the third part, which is permitted by the ducal statute to be left by ascendants to strangers. Someone will say: that statute is not valid to the prejudice of churches or of the poor, as in Auth. cassa, et irrita.

† But for the understanding of this point it must be known that by statute the legitime of children can be diminished; for although the legitime is owed by natural law, just like aliment, nevertheless its boundary, that is, its measure and form, is of civil law, and therefore it can be altered by statute, as is fully noted by Cynus on C. de nup. l. sancimus. And thus it can be diminished; much more can it be increased, because it is a favor to increase the legitime, as in Auth. de trien. et semis. in prin. Since therefore that increase is legitime, the same rule of law applies to it as to the legitime introduced by the ius commune; for since the father is a debtor of the child in the legitime, and the child is considered a creditor, the father cannot testate in favor of another concerning that which he owes to the child, as is noted in ff. ad l. Fal. l. si quis legatum. §. vlt.; ff. so. ma. l. si cum dotem. §. si pater; extra de testa. c. 1. li. 6. Nor is it an injury to the poor or to the churches if they do not put their sickle into another's harvest, extra de testa. c. filius, argu. C. finium re. l. si constiterit in ratione sui. Furthermore, the statute directs its words to the testator himself, upon whom, as upon a subject, it can impose a law of testating, ar. C. de test. l. fi.; for it does not give form to the church, but to subjects, ar. ff. de mu. et hono. l. rescripto. §. vlt., and as noted in ff. ad muni. l. incola.

† Thirdly, it must be seen: if in the person of the first the condition fails by fiction of law, as by profession in a monastery, and the condition subsequently existed in the person of the second, whether the poor come to any part of the portion of the first deceased. For it is certain that the monastery excludes the surviving brother, as in Auth. sed hoc praesenti, and ex de prob. c. in praesentia, because one who has entered is feigned to have children in favor of religion; yet this fiction does not extend where pious places are substituted, as is clear there. But to the first dying, certainly the poor were not instituted, or in place of his own, as I have said above; because in the person of the first dying only a single substitution is found, namely of the surviving brother, not of the poor. From which it seems conclusively to be said that the poor are in no way called to the substitutions of the first dying. This step is subtle, and to one looking subtly it will appear that the truth is to the contrary. For if the surviving brother is not called because a legal fiction excludes him, then upon the death of the first son in the monastery there does not survive a person who, from the presumed will of the deceased, excludes the substituted poor; therefore they come by substitution, as in d. l. haeredes mei. §. 1. according to the doctrine of Bartolus. Moreover, although the surviving son would be excluded for his own interest by the fiction, nevertheless for the interest of the poor, to whom he is to restore, he ought not to be excluded; for often someone takes what he is to restore which he would not take if he were to retain it, as in ff. ad Treb. l. cogi. §. hi qui solidum; and the middle person being omitted, the final person must be looked to, and his privilege preserved, ff. ad l. Fal. l. cum dotem. And therefore I hold conclusively in our question that the school and the poor ought to have a third part of the whole inheritance; and dividing it between them, it appears that each has a sextans, that is, two ounces out of twelve the school has, and two out of twelve the poor have. Nor is it to be doubted that the school, to which the hospital is united, and which is instituted in contemplation of the hospital and of hospitality, is to be deemed a pious place; for certainly a thing draws its denomination from that to which it is united, as is fully noted in extra ne sede vacante. c. 1.

† It now remains to be seen what regarding the legitime, and concerning the legitime which will be due: by the ius commune it is certain that alienated and dissipated goods are imputed, as in Auth. de rest. et eam, quae parit. §. quamobrem. col. 4; but fruits are not imputed, C. de inof. test. l. Sancimus. §. repletionem. I say the same regarding the statutory legitime, so that the same law applies to the increase as to the principal, as in ff. de pac. do. l. inter. §. cum inter. Furthermore, the statute does not permit an ascendant to testate to an outsider except concerning a third part; whence we doubt in vain, as in C. de nup. l. 1, and in Authenti. de testi. §. 2. colum. 8.

† Therefore, of all things that are described in the inventories—to which faith must be given against those who write them and their heirs, as in C. arbi. tutel. tutel. l. fi. and in Auth. de haere. et falci. §. sancimus, for in vain would they be made if faith were not given, as noted in l. chirographis. §. 1. de admi. tu.—I say that the said school, or hospital, ought without doubt to have a sextans, that is, a sixth part of the entire inheritance; and something more, as below several passages are touched upon in the allegations; and first concerning the alternative libel, upon which

† it must be said that it proceeds, since it accords with the nature of the obligation, the nature of the trial, or the disposition of the law, as noted in l. 2. §. item si in facto, and l. 1. ff. de act. empt.; and the same in a position, de rescr. and c. parte by Innocent.

† Secondly, it is touched upon concerning an heir requested to restore after death, whether he is sued from his own adiation or from the adiation of his predecessor; and it is established that the action begins from the former, but the cause from the deceased, as in C. de act. ab haer. l. 1; ff. ad l. fal. l. pater filium; the causal action begins from the predecessor, the formal from himself. And thirdly, it is touched upon whether these fraternities are an approved collegium; and it must be said that they are, even by the ius commune.

† And fourthly, it is touched upon whether he is presumed dead concerning whom there is common report, and who is also mentioned in an instrument with the adverb 'formerly' [quondam]; and it must be said that he is, as noted in l. eius, qui in provincia. §. 1. ff. si cert. pet.; C. so. ma. l. si quidem.

† Fifthly, it is touched upon: if the decree regarding guardianship is not valid, whether the inventory proves; and it must be said that it does, because although a sentence or decree does not hold on account of the order of law having been omitted, nevertheless a confession holds, as in extra de resti. spo. c. pisanis.

† Sixthly, it is touched upon whether an instrument received by a husband in the name of his wife is presumed to have been received to the end that title and ownership should be acquired for the wife, as in C. si quis alteri, vel sibi. l. multum; or rather that superficially the husband transacted the business for himself, not for the wife. For I am not speaking in the case of the gloss on l. si ut proponis, where the wife buys; but where the husband added the name of the wife. And the gloss speaks truly that simulation of the name is presumed, ff. de do. inter vir. et vxo. l. uxor marito. But here it is not expedient to say this, because it is just as if the woman, by mandate of the husband, had caused herself to be described in the instrument, and therefore the right and business belong principally to the husband, ff. man. l. ideoque. §. si cui. It is more true, however, that an action in rem belongs to the husband and his heirs, where the price which the husband paid is offered to him or his heirs, l. uxor.

† Seventhly, it is touched upon concerning the division made of a fideicommissary right, wherein it must be said that by such reservation the fideicommissary right is not diminished, ff. de transac. l. qui cum tutoribus. in prin.; de ver. ob. l. qui Romae. §. duo fratres, by Dynus and others; nevertheless it is not increased in anything, ar. ff. de lib. leg. l. Aurel. §. testamento, and especially to the prejudice or favor of a third party, as argu. C. ad Treb. l. non iustam; C. de don. ante nup. l. pe. in fi.

† It is also touched upon concerning that condition, 'if without children', which does not comprehend an heir of law unless he is an heir, that is, a descendant, of nature. It fails in favor of a monastery, of the contemplative life, or of a life vowed to God, which, since it is sincere, ought not to be hindered by any temporal matter, even if the testator should expressly dispose to the contrary, according to Ricardus and Bartolus. By this reasoning, not even a statute could dispose to the contrary. But the Lord Iacobus de Belvisio, disputing equally, held the contrary, namely that if it is clear that the father had in mind children of nature, not children of censure, and he said this by name and specifically in the testament, declaring his intention, that he can well do this; because the interpretation of law regarding the will of another has no place where the testator himself interprets it. And this opinion is accustomed to be approved by usage. As long, therefore, as the monk lives, the monastery holds, ff. de iure fis. l. stamus. §. Cornelio. But when the monk is dead, he restores to those to whom it comes by restitution; and thus in our case, even in person, the fideicommissum made from sister to sister did not expire. It is no objection that it is tacitly understood of children of nature, and yet the monastery excludes the substitute; for that tacit understanding is a certain interpretation of law, whence it is taken away by that interpretation, namely by the interpretation of §. sed hoc praesenti. But where the testator expresses 'an heir of one's own body', there is room for no interpretation, as in l. ille aut ille. §. cum in verbis. ff. de lega. 3. And if it is said that that fideicommissum hinders the contemplative life, I will deny that, because he who is led by the Spirit of God and renounces the world and private property manifestly despises the wealth of the world, nor does he bind his mind to the grasping of temporal things, arg. C. de munerum patri. l. professio. And following that opinion, half of the portion of the nun would have come into the fideicommissum of the sister; because the statute concerning the third part does not apply from children to children, just as it also says that in testaments it is not permitted for ascendants to leave to extraneous persons or places what exceeds a third of their goods. The two parts, therefore, which by the legitime are said to be assigned to descendants, since they have the nature of a legitime—because they cannot be burdened—ought therefore also to have the name; for to whatever the nature of a thing is applied, the name itself also seems tacitly accommodated, C. de lib. praete. l. 3. These said two parts have place when an outsider is left, not among one's own similarly, C. de impo. luc. descri. l. 1. lib. 10. To this is also added the ducal decree, which wills that it is always to be understood of children of nature.

† But here another passage occurs: whether that statute, by force of the statute, and insofar as it might be contrary to the ius commune, claims a place for itself in testaments made before the statute. And it must be considered that sometimes the cause and the obligation are before the statute, and then a statute disposing simply does not refer to those things which consist of the past; sometimes both, namely the right and the cause, are of the future, and then without doubt it is included; sometimes the cause is of the past and the effect of the future, as in our case. And then either the statute disposes concerning the form—that is, concerning the law of the form, what form is to be observed in making it—and it has no place in that which has already been made, as in C. de test. l. iubemus. 1. responso; or it disposes concerning something else: then either that other thing is among those that follow the form, that is, declarative and interpretative of the form of the words of the testament, so that it gives to those very words a new understanding not otherwise given by law; and the same, because it does not pertain to things already ordained, which ought to be interpreted according to the interpretation then prevailing—just as if a testator a year ago made a testament and bequeathed to me 10, the law interprets it according to the money then current, not that which afterwards begins to run, because the meaning of words is born at the same time with the utterance of the word itself, nor is the meaning of the testator changed, even though the disposition of the law is changed afterwards; it makes for the aforesaid, ff. de lega. 1. l. si servus plurium. §. fi.; de re. iur. l. semper stipulationibus; and what is noted in c. vlti. de decis. in cle. de testamentis. l. haeredes palam. §. sed si notan.—or that other thing is not of the appendages and annexes of the form, but is something extrinsic, say concerning the paying of some tax, or concerning the earning of execution, or concerning the deducting of a greater legitime, and thus it is indeed drawn to old matters as to the origin of the cause, but not as to the origin of that which is caused, or the effect. And thus is understood the matter of the law leges, C. de fi. instru. l. contractus with similar texts. Wherefore, in the present matter, I think that the said constitution interpreting testaments has no place in testaments made previously as to mere interpretation, but the intention is clear, as is the case in ours, because it is clear that he had in mind children of one's own body,

† on account of the phrase 'born of oneself' [ex se natis]; so that if the statute comes to confirm the testament, then according to Iacobus de Belvisio that is inherent by the ius commune which previously was in force. If, however, it were not of the ius commune, and the testator had also died at the time the statute was enacted, then the statute would not confirm what was invalid at the time of the testator's death, nor would it be drawn backward in this respect, because in this it would be contrary to the laws, l. intervenit, de leg. praest., and by the argument of those things which are noted in l. talis scriptura, ff. de lega. 1. I therefore leave aside the statute in our question, and I rest on the ius commune; and holding the opinion of Iacobus de Belvisio, it follows that half of the half of the nun is owed to the substitutes, and thus in total she ought to have two ounces and a half. And that ounce is that small amount beyond the sextans of which I spoke above; and on these points I rest conclusively as to the point of law, but in fact the acts speak for themselves. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. From the diffuse case, the summary is derived.
2. Whether the daughter of a person condemned to death ought to have her legitime portion in the goods of the condemned, but who has been restored.
3. A slave is said to be subject to the penalty of intestability.
4. What effect is produced by restitution in integrum granted by statute; and also at number 7.
5. Whether a dead man can be, and when, condemned for a delict.
6. Restitution produces the same effect as postliminium.
7. What effect is produced by the words, "we place him in his own position."
8. What is meant by a dowry-giver.
9. We impose the law not by words, but by meanings.
10. When caution is to be given regarding the use of the discretion of a good man.
11. What the term "according to" signifies.
body: A certain citizen of Florence. In the name of Christ. Gregory, as a traitor to the overthrow of the status of the illustrious City of Florence, was condemned to death, with all his goods totally confiscated. And the sentence against him was executed, whereby Gregory left behind two unmarried minor daughters. It is also true that at that time there were alive in the world Nicolaus and Nofrius, his carnal brothers; finally, by the commune of Florence it was reformed [or declared], that the said Nicolaus and Nofrius should be, in full right and entirely, universal successors in place of the said commune of Florence, and for equal parts of all and singular goods and rights which had belonged to the said Gregory. Provided, however, that the said daughters have the right to demand to be dowered, and the amount of the dowry is less than 200 Florins; it may, however, be increased at the discretion of b. and c., who can make such declaration within three months, and in the meantime they shall provide for them, as is provided and stipulated by law and according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the commune of Florence, with the said brothers bearing a certain burden of payment, to which they shall comply. Afterwards, the said Nicolaus married off the said daughters and gave them the declared amount. Then one of the said daughters died. Then the said Nicolaus died, leaving three daughters and having acknowledged the said goods. Now it is asked: what right does the daughter of the said Gregory have, presupposing the statute of the commune of Florence, which provides that no woman may succeed her father intestate when a carnal brother exists.

† For the understanding of this most subtle question, it was alleged on behalf of the said daughter of Gregory: and without repeating the subtle allegations. I premise that the said Gregory did not die intestate,

† but he died intestate. Because a slave is subject to punishment, as C. qui test. fac. poss. l. 2, and there by Cynus. Furthermore, I premise that this Gregorius could not have an heir in any way, because one who left no goods in the city cannot have an heir; this is the text, ff. de vul. subs. l. lex Corne. From which it appears that we are entirely outside the case of the statute placed under the heading "in what manner a woman succeeds intestate." But this must be considered, because by the commune of Florence it was ordained after the death of the said Gregorius, that all and each who until now have been condemned and exiled, or condemned, however, or exiled only by some rector or official of the commune of Florence on account of the subversion or disturbance of the state, are to be understood and are from now on themselves, and any of them, restored in full to the said condemnations as to their first capacity and reputation: and as to goods and rights not actually seized by the commune, either by right or by fact: and all their descendants against any incapacity of whatever kind.

† Now it is asked whether this restitutio in integrum can have any effect with respect to the sons of the said Gregory. And it seems that it cannot, because from whom the words of the law are removed, its province is also removed, as in D. de acquisitione hereditatis, l. si servum, § non dixit. But the words of the law do not seem to speak of those who are extinct, and, so to speak, according to the common and ordinary practice of jurists: because the authority of the senate cannot do what is impossible by nature, as in l. 2, D. de usufructu earum rerum quae usu consumuntur.

† Moreover, the law provides that a deceased person cannot be released, as expressly stated in the text. D. de operis liberti, l. qui libertinus, §. posthumus. Furthermore, no provision of law can take effect unless it falls upon a subject capable of receiving it, i.e., upon a subject. Hence, a decree issued against a deceased person is void. D. qui satisdare coguntur, l. si decesserit; and C. de caducis tollendis, l. 1, §. et cum triplici; and D. de hereditatibus instituendis, l. quo loco, §. si iam mortuo. To the contrary, it seems, considering the crime of lèse-majesty, in which a deceased person can be condemned, i.e., his memory and goods confiscated, as Inst. de hereditatibus ab intestato, §. per contrarium; and D. de accusationibus, l. ex iudiciorum. Just as memory can be condemned, so too can memory be restored in full by the argument from the contrary, and once memory is restored, even the goods are deemed restored, as l. 1, C. de senatus consulto Pegasiano. And in support of this is a certain very notable law, which says,

† That the same effect is produced by restitution and by postliminium. D. de in iustis testibus, l. si quis hereditate, §. si, where Iacobo de Arena says thus: Note that restitution and postliminium produce the same effect; just as through postliminium it is feigned that someone was not a slave in the past, nor lost his goods, so too in our case: because memory has returned through postliminium, or I will equate it to the fiction of the Cornelian law, so that he is understood to have died at the hour preceding captivity; indeed, at the hour preceding the offense, as stated in the aforementioned law, lex Cornelia. Furthermore, for the sake of the remnants of condemnation, absolution is useful, by argument from l. 3, C. si penitentia appellatio mors interuenit. Also, let us observe that an excommunicated person is absolved after death. Also, one accused of heresy, as in c. a nobis, §. et incertis, D. de senatus consulto, and in c. accusatus, de hæresibus, lib. 6. From which it is evidently gathered that by sentence of the statute, a dead person, i.e., his remains, can be absolved; indeed, even by sentence of a judge. Hence, no one will say that there is no subject to be absolved; therefore, the absolution is not valid, because indeed there is a subject, namely memory, good fame, and relatives, as stated in the aforementioned c. a nobis. Also, we say that we absolve such a person. For the word "quodam" (a certain) is often implied, as in l. eius qui, D. si certum petatur. Also, the cancellations of the dead must be cancelled; nor should they be left in the books, just as the condemnations of the living are. Wherefore, acts are cancelled to the end of invalidating them; acts done in the past do not give any faith to the condemnation, as in l. acta, D. de re iudicata. Also, I see that sometimes a favorable decree is interposed concerning a dead person, as in l. cum quasi, in principio, D. de fideicommissis liberis. Also, I do not think anyone would doubt that if the statute expressly said, "we restore to full rights the living and the dead," the words should rightly be understood as referring to memory and to goods with respect to successors. But considering the general words of the statute itself, this must have been the intention of the legislators: because those who suffer from another's fault are more worthy of pardon than those who suffer from their own, as in C. de natura liberorum, l. legem Anastasii, where it says, "they are not unworthy of mercy, who suffer from another's vice." But it is objected to these points that the Commune of Florence had first placed the said brothers in his place, to whom a right had accrued by law and by honor, which they had fulfilled, whence it could not afterwards be taken away from them, as in l. 1, C. ne fiscus rem, quam vendidit, euincat, libro 10. And it is similar to what is said regarding the legitime after the legitime heirs have accepted the inheritance, D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, §. et quid si tantum. To strengthen which, it is added that, by disposing that the brothers succeed in the place of the fisc, it seems to recognize the goods, as in C. de iure delatorum, l. si auia, and Inst. de hæredum qualitate et differentia, §. si.

For to place someone in one’s own place is the same as to transfer one’s rights to him, as in the Digest, ad Trebellianum, l. Qui quadringenta, where it says, “so that he may be constituted in his own place.” For if the fisc were not considered to have transferred its rights, the said brothers could have no right in their own person; but the goods would be vacant, without an heir and without a successor, unless one were to say that they were granted to the occupant as existing in the goods of no one; but this would not be well said. Sometimes, however, one is placed in the stead of another because the first is excluded and the second is subrogated, as when these words are used in a vulgar substitution, as in the Code, de hereditatibus instituendis, l. Si, where it says, “in the place or share of Plotius.”

† What, therefore, shall we say? I answer and state that whether this restoration is understood to apply to memory and to goods, as if she had died intestate, there is no doubt that the said ward, and the dowry, as long as she was in the age of wardship, and afterwards before she was actually handed over in marriage and the dowry was paid, ought and must have had the usufruct of all the paternal goods. And the time of the age of wardship is sufficiently established.

† because in the meantime she could not be considered dowried, as in D. quod falso tutore auctore, l. an etiam in patrem; and D. quando dies leg. cedat, l. quod pupillae. Nor does the statement of Bartolus stand in the way, who says that she is called dowried who is dowried in a will, and who holds the same regarding a ward or another person in l. cum in plures, §. pen., D. de admi. tu., because it would follow that in the meantime she ought not to have maintenance, for which the statute assigns the usufruct of all goods: which is expressly contrary to the words of the statute, and also contrary to the common law, as appears expressly in D. de alim. etci. leg., l. cum vnus, §. si idem et post nubilem aetatem; because "dowried" is understood as one to whom a dowry has been actually given, not one who can bring an action for a dowry, even if a judgment had been rendered concerning the dowry; because it is not said that satisfaction has been made, although an obligation or condemnation has been incurred, as in D. de fun. instru., l. nepoti. If, therefore, this restitution is understood to apply to memory and goods, which I consider most true, these girls ought to have the full usufruct for the said time, as in c. nulla mulier, §. si vero ipse filius, vel filii, Qualiter mulier ab intestato succedat. The above has been alleged. But let us assume that the said restitution in integrum does not touch our case; but that we are simply under the provision of that reform which begins "curam diligenter habentes." And I weigh the words of the said provision there: "and in the meantime let others provide for themselves as is provided and guarded according to law, and according to the form of the statutes and ordinances of the commune of Florence"; for it is certain that nothing is provided by the common law in the crime of high treason, as in C. ad l. Iul. maies., l. quisquis, although it speaks there when against the prince, and even where it only permits daughters to succeed in place of maintenance to the legitime in the goods of an innocent mother, not in the goods of delinquents, as in C. de haeretic., auth. Gazaros, and in auth. bona damnatorum. Also, because the goods were expressly taken away and confiscated. Also, it is certain that nothing is provided by municipal law regarding simple maintenance in the case of an uncle, but only regarding usufruct. Therefore, it is necessary that those words, "as is provided by law, and according to the form of the statutes," be referred to a similar case; because, so that the office of piety may not be lacking, we recur from similar cases to similar cases. And if there are several similar cases, we recur to the more similar one. For the same thing is considered very similar, as in D. de condi. et de., l. in testamento quidam. It is therefore necessary that we either recur to a similarity taken from l. quisquis, §. ad filias, where the legitime is assigned in place of maintenance; and thus these daughters ought to have one-third part of the ownership, and the usufruct not computed with dowries until the actual dotation, or computed afterwards, as in C. de inoffi. testa., l. quam nouella; or it is necessary to explain that in the said reform maintenance is placed for usufruct, i.e., usufruct in place of maintenance; so that the word "according to" is placed by way of similarity, since it cannot be placed demonstratively, as in extra de verb. sig., in c. Abbate. Nor are these things contrary to or against reason; but it is a certain natural interpretation, because otherwise the words cannot be understood; for understanding maintenance without usufruct, we have no law or statute providing anything, which is contrary to the words and the mind of the said reform, and contrary to all natural equity. And therefore, for certain, the said daughters ought to have the legitime, or at least in the meantime the full usufruct of the goods, although the words seem to signify otherwise.

† because we impose the law not by words, but by sense, as in l. 1. in fi. C, communia dele. and ff. de iureiu. l. 3. §. pe. and l. sed et si possessori. §. sed rerum. and what is noted, ff. fam. haer. l. et puto. §. 1. and ff. si cer. pet. l. si tibi. there where it says, not always contained in proper terms. and ff. de usufr. l. proculus. And I incline more towards this last part, because a municipal law ought rather to be drawn to another municipal law than to the common law, since municipal laws are of the same kind: for among municipal laws themselves there is a greater fellowship, or communication of understanding, arg. ff. de coniungendis cum emanci. li. l. nihil.

† Someone might say that these girls did not provide security for the usufruct, etc., and therefore they cannot claim the usufruct, as stated in the Digest, On Usucapion, law *Si homo*. I answer that such security is not required unless the usufruct is being transferred, not when the heir is in default of transferring it, as stated in the Digest, On Usufruct, law *Si usus fructus in biennium*. For these brothers, after acceptance, were always in default, at least irregularly due to the minority of the girls, as stated in the Code, On Those Who Are Restored to Their Rights, law *In minorum*, and in the Digest, On Legacies, book 2, law *Titia seyo*, section *Usurarius*. Now it remains to inquire, for the clarification of the preceding points, by what action these brothers are bound to provide the usufruct in lieu of security. For if the Commune of Florence appears to have made a donation to them on condition, they are bound by law 1 of the Code, On Donations Made Under a Condition. But here a more subtle consideration is necessary, for the Commune of Florence does not act here in the place of a donor, because it would be argued that it is bound by direct actions to the burdens of the property, which is false; rather, it acts in the place of the Prince, who restores someone to property for the purpose of preserving liberties. No one would say that a judge is bound, and from this analogy it is inferred that these brothers are said to be anomalous successors to the property, as noted in the Institutes, On Those To Whom Property Is Added For the Sake of Liberty, and as anomalous successors they are sued for the burdens, because they are substituted in the place of those who would succeed intestate; from which it necessarily follows that the right to the usufruct at least accrued to the said daughters, and that the term "in alimentis" is to be understood as referring to more substantial maintenance, i.e., to the usufruct, as stated in the Digest, On Usufruct, law *Dominus*, section *Si*; and in the Digest, On Compromises, law *Cum hi*, section *Si fundum*; in the Digest, On Gold and Silver Legacies, law *Species*; and law 4 of the Digest, On Aliments and Food, law *Cum si*. It remains to answer what is alleged to the contrary, namely, that the word "alimentis" should rather be considered than the relative word "according to the form of the statute," and thus the phrase "according to the form of the statutes" has no effect, and thus we remain with the obligation to provide simple maintenance; and many things could be adduced to this effect. But it is answered that nothing should be superfluous in the law,

† Hence, the word "according to" should not be superfluous, but rather declaratory of the term "aliments." For sometimes "aliments" are used in place of usufruct, and conversely, usufruct in place of aliments: not according to the proper definition of the words, but according to the intention of the speaker, as in C. si secundo nupserit mulier, l. 1. And if one of these words were to be superfluous, it would rather be the word "aliments" that should be superfluous, rather than the word "according to." And the reason is that the bequest has passed into emphyteusis, for natural reason favors posterity, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi. Furthermore, it does not follow that "he must have aliments, therefore not more," because the phrase "according to the form" is tacitly included, and moreover, because this word "according to" is used in an augmentative sense, denoting a full relation, and it is not novel that a tacit supposition be made, so that the entire disposition of the law may be preserved, as if it said "in aliments, and according to the form of the statutes." Furthermore, we are in a matter favorable with respect to daughters, and in a matter odious with respect to the legislators, who deal with hatred and the severity of punishment, as in ff. de liberis et posthumis, l. cum quidam. Furthermore, it does not object if it is said that aliments are a species, and usufruct is a genus, as if containing more; for this word "according to" has the power to extend the species, or rather to declare it. Furthermore, the argument from l. si alii, ff. de usufructu legato, does not apply. Furthermore, consider this example: my father bequeathed to you the usufruct; therefore, in my will, I say, I bequeath to you aliments according to my father's will. For my will must be understood according to my father's will, so that my favorable disposition is not vitiated. The effect is this: that the father's will is preserved, not that it is derogated from, or anything diminished; for words were not added for diminution or derogation, but for the observance of the father's will. So in the case at hand, the words were spoken for the observance of the statute, and therefore they operate as in l. non omnis, ff. si certum petatur, and ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. obligationum substantia, ff. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. Pater Severinam, § conditionum, cum si. From these, it is concluded that the aforementioned daughter of the said person condemned to death must have either the full legitime or the full usufruct. And for the confirmation of the foregoing, consider that just as there is found a causal and formal usufruct, so here aliments are understood as causal, conjoined with usufruct, and not formal, which are species opposed to usufruct, so to speak. Hence, just as if a testator said, "I bequeath a causal usufruct," he would bequeath the ownership, so in the case at hand, so that the reform is not vitiated in any part of itself. I, Baldus.
A salt was granted in the name of Christ to Mae, and to Manfredo, and to each of them, to come to the city of Asti with, etc. See in part 5, consilium 414, beginning: "A salt was granted," etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an emphyteutic concession made up to the large vineyard and so forth is to be understood.
2. The term "up to": when it stands inclusively, and when not.
body: ...granted in emphyteusis...

† The words state: he granted in emphyteusis up to the great vineyard [usque ad vineam magnam]. Item and of forty-six perches of land planted with vines, in some part uncultivated, situated in the said district, where it is called at the great vineyard, which is bordered by etc. Moreover, the lord Pope gave to the same emphyteuta in noble fief the entire possession which the said district possesses and holds, and revoked the aforesaid investitures; nevertheless, it pleased the Illustrious Lord, the Lord Count of Virtues, to determine whether the said territory is comprehended in the investiture, or not.

† Now it is asked, what is the law? The statement of Bartolus is alleged, who distinguishes: either proof is made regarding the intention, and the word 'usque' [up to / as far as] is posited inclusively or exclusively just as the intention has been proved, because the intention clarifies the ambiguous words of a contract and of a last will, as in C. de fideicom. l. voluntatis and fully noted in ff. de pac. l. veteribus and ff. de regulis iuris. l. semper in stipulationibus; or the intention is not established except through the import of the words, and then either it cannot stand with inclusion, and it is posited exclusively, as happens when the terminus ad quem cannot be comprehended under the preceding generality, as in l. pe. ff. de fluminibus; or the terminus ad quem can be comprehended and not comprehended under the preceding generality according to its proper meaning: and then in last wills it is posited inclusively, as in l. patronus. de le. 3. and l. in testamentis. de re. iu., or in contracts, and then it is posited exclusively, because when words are ambiguous, one must favor the defendant rather than the plaintiff, because he who wishes to bind another ought to speak more clearly, as is noted in the said l. veteribus; for in contracts an extension of the obligation is to be avoided, and nothing is included except that which holds between them, as in ff. de ac. emp. l. fundi nihil. Understand this thus when the words are uttered for the purpose of principally binding; but when the words are uttered for the purpose of excepting—for example, because the seller or lessor excepts something obscurely—then an obscure exception is interpreted against the seller or lessor, because he is understood to utter obscure words who wishes to bring an action or plead an exception based on them, and thus is the law veteribus understood. And the reason for the aforesaid is: either the lessor or seller speaks obscurely for his own benefit and to the harm of the other, and let the interpretation be against the seller and lessor, as in l. 1. in fi. ff. de ac. emp.; or, conversely, the lessee or buyer speaks obscurely for his own benefit and to the harm of his adversary, and then let the interpretation be against the buyer or lessee, as in l. si in emptione. in prin. ff. de contrahen. empt.; for he is understood to utter the words whose interest it was that the words were uttered, not his whose interest it was that the words were omitted, as in ff. de ver. obl. l. quidquid astringendae. Or the words were uttered by a third party, say by a witness or notary, yet they are not entirely obscure, but can admit a probable interpretation; and then they are interpreted toward the lesser part, and this is the opinion of Nicolaus de Mata. Or say that there are certain things which the buyer or lessor himself ought to specify as knowing the fact better, such as the boundaries, servitudes of the property, and the like; and then the obscure word is interpreted against the seller and lessor, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. labeo scribit obscuritatem with the following law, and in l. cum in venditionis quod and l. saepe. §. fi. and ff. de serui. vrba. praedio. l. si arborem. §. fi. There are certain things which the seller or lessor does not need to specify; and then an interpretation is made against the buyer or seller, as in ff. de contrahen. empt. l. si in emptione. From this it is concluded that when the interpretation is uncertain regarding the boundaries, and thus regarding the thing brought into the contract, because the lessor ought to have specified more, the interpretation is made against the lessor—unless someone should say that there is a special rule in the Church in favor of the Church, so that the interpretation would be made for the Church rather than against the Church, by the argument of ff. de iure fisci. l. fi. But that exception is not well proved by any law. Let it therefore be concluded that obscurity of boundaries harms the lessor, so far as it can be comprehended under the words; whence if a lessor says, 'I lease to you such meadows up to one hundred iugera,' I will understand it inclusively, because the boundary can reasonably be included. Item, and by such doctrine, because either that which is placed by way of a boundary is of the essence or content of the same thing, and then the boundary is included as internal; or it is of the essence or content of another thing, and then it is otherwise, for a boundary is twofold, namely, an internal boundary and an external boundary, as noted in C. de euic. l. si fines agri; although as far as the reading of that law is concerned it does not please the gloss, nevertheless in itself it is the very truth. Yet our question is not decided by this. I return therefore to our case, in which I say one must first consider what is likely, as noted in the said l. veteribus; and to this let the amount of the rent be added, for a comparison of the rent having been made to the property in question, a presumption arises against it, as noted in l. 1. ff. de superficiebus; it is true that in deserted places this comparison does not properly apply, as in sands, gravel-beds, and the like. Thirdly, we ought to consider the appellative nouns, or terms, for from a diversity of terms something is not presumed to have been granted, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. praediis. §. balneas and §. qui demum. Fourthly, we ought to consider the present quality of the thing itself at the time of the contract, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. in lege. Item, I say this precisely because it is not called a vineyard where there are no vines, although there once were.
