For this noun, 'vineyard', is a name and a real thing; for no one would call a vineyard that has been uprooted and reduced to the form of plain land—and for that reason call it a vineyard—what was once a vineyard, just as that which was once an island but now is not is not called an island, as in l. insula. §. fi. ff. de acqui. re. do.; for when the form of a thing is changed, its name is also changed, as in ff. de vsus fru. l. qui vsumfructum areae. Whence, because the words do not say, 'up into the old great vineyard', but say, 'up into the great vineyard', which is understood of land currently under vines, bare land is contained up to the place with vines, but the place with vines is not contained except to the extent that it has been expressly assigned from the great vineyard; because the words say, namely: of all lands, meadows, woods, pastures, and gravel-beds situated and lying in those parts, to which in part borders the said monastery from the great vineyard; whence nothing of the great vineyard, which was a vineyard at the time of the contract, is included except those 46 perches of land planted with vines, as in ff. de leg. 3. l. haeres meus. §. duae statuę. Nor do I care if perhaps some roots of the vineyard were still under the ground, because that which lies under the ground is not to be considered, but that which is seen, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. in l. fundi. From which it is concluded that the contract of the said investiture of lease extends up to the bonded boundary of the great vineyard, in such a way that it includes the non-vineyard, but excludes the vineyard. For that vineyards should be included on account of the word 'usque' is impossible, because when an inclusion would include a contrary quality of the thing, the word 'usque' is never posited inclusively, but is posited exclusively. Concerning the matter of this word 'usque', see the notes on C. de nup. l. a calligato by Cynus and ff. de offi. pręsi. l. meminisse. But because our subject concerns solely the interpretation regarding boundaries, no other matter is to be treated here, because it has been fully stated above. From these things it clearly appears that that which has ceased to be a vineyard, from which fruits are not gathered but has become barren, is not called a vineyard, just as, conversely, if a vineyard were made from barren land, it would not be called a barren estate, as in C. de alluuionibus, et paludibus. l. 2. §. 1., ff. de act. empt. l. si duorum. §. fi., and C. de bonis proscriptorum. l. si quis intra, and ff. sol. ma. l. diuortio. §. quod in sementem, and ff. de cen. l. forma censuali. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a statute providing that a non-subject cannot succeed to a subject is valid; and, assuming it is valid, whether one can succeed to a mother who was from the said city where the statute is in force, but who married in another place, and thus, as having lost her origin, is not a subject; and number 2.
body: A certain Mediola, in the name of Christ, had wives: from the first was born Lady Prima; from the second was born Margaret; from the third was born Lady Secunda. It happened that the said Lady Prima was born outside the power and jurisdiction of Milan. And from her there now exist two sons, Christopher and Philip. Now the said Philip and Christopher assert that they are heirs of their mother, the said Lady, and also of half of their grandfather, the said Mediola. To whom the said Lady Secunda opposes herself, saying that they do not succeed to the grandfather nor to the mother; and she alleges the statute of Milan, which provides that no woman married outside the jurisdiction of Milan shall succeed to anyone of the jurisdiction of Milan, even by will. The same is understood regarding the descendants of such women, who were born from [a father] not subject to the jurisdiction of the Lord Podesta and the commune of Milan; it is asked, what is the law.

And it appears that the said statute is invalid, insofar as it entirely excludes descendants from a natural debt, as noted by Dy. in c. indultis. Furthermore, because the said statute cannot impose law upon non-subjects and deprive them of succession, as in l. cunctos populos and in l. extra territorium, with its common material. But since the contrary is observed by common custom, I do not insist on this point: because things should not be changed, and so forth, as in ff. de legibus, l. minime. And therefore, attention should only be paid to the words of the statute. And it must be considered that there are two doubts here. The first is whether the maternal grandfather succeeds, presupposing without prejudice to the truth that the said statute is valid; and it appears that he does not, because if their mother were alive, she would not succeed, since she is married outside the jurisdiction of the community of Milan. But it is so that, if the private stock or parent is deprived, such deprivation extends to the descendants, in whom there is a greater or the same reason for exclusion: nor is this to be demonstrated, but it is the mind and understanding of the statute, as noted by Cy. in l. 1, C. quae sit longa consuetudo, as in c. 1, §. notandum, qui feudum dare possunt, col. 10, and this when the stock is rendered ineligible by law. But this reason does not appear true: because odious statutes do not admit extension; hence, although the statute excludes the daughter, it does not exclude the son of the daughter, as in ff. de contrahenda, l. 3, §. si emancipatus. But certainly, rather, because the statute not only excludes the woman, but grants an accessory right to the agnates and the nearest relatives within the jurisdiction of Milan. Hence, what is granted to one is taken away from all others, as in ff. de legibus, l. 1, l. quod in rerum, §. si quis. This is held by Bar. in l. 2, ff. ad tertium, semper, provided that the words permit this through necessary or probable interpretation. I call it necessary, namely, by a point of reason; I call it probable, by the way of equity, as noted in ff. si certum petatur, l. cum fundus, §. servum tuum imprudens. But if the exclusive words, which come by a certain consequence, would effect nothing. For I say that the principal purpose of the legislator is to include, which is achieved by the means of excluding. Hence, the principal intention is the favor of the agnates: for which the exclusion of the woman is necessary, just as we say that the principal intention of nature is to generate, and secondarily to corrupt. And if it did not have the intention of generating, it would not have the intention of corrupting, as the Philosophers say. But examination is not necessary here, because the wise men who made the statute of Milan spoke cautiously, and it is to be understood that the same applies to all descendants of such women who were born from a non-subject to the jurisdiction of the lord of power and the community of Milan: so that the law declares itself, and therefore there is no question, as in C. de institutionibus et substitutionibus, l. generaliter, §. pen., and C. de fideicommissis, l. acutissimi, with similar cases. Having therefore omitted the preliminaries, it must be considered that in the fact proposed, the father of the said Christopher and Philip had an assessment in the city of Milan. And this can be in two ways: either because he had the greater part of his fortunes there, by which it would be understood that he had domicile and was subject to the jurisdiction of Milan, as in l. 2, C. ubi senatus, or cl. with its material; or because he had some goods, but not the greater part, and then they would not be properly called subjects or subordinates: although by this they would be bound to the burdens of the assessment, nor would they obtain the forum there: as in ff. ad municipalia, l. libertus, §. sola, and l. incola iam. If this is so, the said nephews cannot claim the goods of the maternal grandfather, notwithstanding at least the observance of the said statute in fact, although it is inequitable, as in l. maximum vitium and l. 1, §. 1, ff. quod quisque iuris, and l. perspexit, qui et a quibus. And this, as far as the goods of the grandfather are concerned, let it be said conclusively, that the said nephews are repelled by the said statute, presupposing the observance of the said statute.

† Now it remains to consider the maternal dowry: and I say that they succeed to their mother; because by this they do not succeed to anyone within the jurisdiction of Milan. Here it must be considered that the said first lady, at the time of her death, was not within the jurisdiction of Milan, but within the jurisdiction of her husband’s domicile; and this especially with regard to the right of forum, because she had been transferred from her original forum: and she followed her husband entirely, as regards the right of domicile, as stated in D. de iurisd. omnium iud. l. cum quaedam puella. This is a special rule for a wife, even with regard to origin. This is the notable gloss in C. de incolis, l. mulieres. Since those not subject to the jurisdiction are not prohibited from succeeding to those not subject to it, therefore the said sons are not prohibited from succeeding to their mother. And this is the truth. Regarding the succession to the maternal grandmother, I say that either the said first lady succeeded to her mother before she was endowed; and then the said brothers succeed in the same manner as in the case of the maternal dowry. The same applies if the right to enter into the inheritance had already been acquired by the said lady; because it is transmitted to descendants, as stated in l. 1, de his, qui ante apertas tabulas. But if the said first lady was married before the death of her mother, then the said brothers would not succeed to the said grandmother; since their said aunt was of Milanese origin and domicile. Hence, for the same reason that they are excluded from the succession to the maternal grandfather, they are excluded from the succession to the maternal grandmother by the same statute. I, Baldus. I.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether it is permissible to change one's counsel, or intention, or choice.
body: The words of the testament are as follows: In the name of Christ. If any of the aforementioned sons were disposed to study legal science or canon law, just as at present his son is studying civil law, or if in the future any other of the aforementioned sons were disposed as above, and wished to go to study, the aforementioned books were to be kept for him, as above, so that he might study and acquire the aforementioned science. And if he should prosper well in his studies, he bequeathed to him the aforementioned books and wished that the expenses incurred in study be paid from the portion falling to him. And shortly after it follows: But if any of the aforementioned sons disposed himself to study the arts and medicine, he wished that there remain for him a certain town [or collection] of all books necessary and sufficient for learning the aforementioned sciences; and if he should prosper well in them, he shall have the aforementioned books before the portion. Now it happens that one of the other aforementioned sons disposes himself to study the arts and medicine, and is a master in the arts, and necessary and useful books have been purchased for him. But now, seeing that the aforementioned G., his brother, has legal books of far greater value, he wishes to withdraw from the study of medicine and to hear the laws.

It is asked whether he may vary his choice. At first glance, it seems one should say that he may; indeed, if he were to learn all these sciences, he ought to receive double legacies, as stated in the Digest, *De annuis legatis*, in the law *Qui Marco*; and see the note in the Authenticum *Ut iudices sine quoque suffragio*, § 3, *Illud tamen decreuimus*. This is noted by Cynus in the Code, *De delegationibus*, in the law *Cum quaestio*.

To the contrary, it appears that this is a matter of rare occurrence, that anyone can possess so many sciences perfectly; for scarcely is any length of life sufficient for even one science, since life is short and art is long, as Hippocrates says. Furthermore, because the testator spoke in the alternative, and in alternative statements one part is true, not both, as in the law *Si vero*, in the beginning, in the Digest, *De solutione matrimonii*, and in the Digest, *De mandato*, in the law *Si vero*. Moreover, the same rule should apply to study as to marriage; but in this phrase, "when he shall have married," the first marriage is signified, as in the Digest, *De verbis obligatis*, in the law *Boues*, § *Hoc sermone*. Furthermore, this seems to be expressly stated in the Digest, *Qui et a quibus testari possint*, in the law *Matrimonii*. For it seems the sense is of that principal science, which is not called by any other principal sciences, as seems expressly stated there. And I consider this opinion to be the true one.

Nor do I consider that he is disposed to study the laws from this alone, that he says he is disposed; but from his age and other indications this must be judged, as in the Digest, *De legatis tertio*, in the law *Stichus*. And just as a monk, before he professes, must prove himself for a year, so that it may appear whether he is disposed to observe the rule, he must first test himself for some time; because disposition is not induced in the soul without acts, unless we speak of first potency, which is not properly a disposition. For disposition immediately precedes habit and is a certain principle of habit. Something should be established regarding the disposition itself. But whatever the case may be, as I have said, things being thus situated, I consider that he cannot vary his choice; since it is not honorable to vary, as in the Code, *De modo multarum*, in the law *Eos*, unless when a man changes his counsel for the better without prejudice to another; for it is the mark of a wise man to change his counsel, as in the rule *Mutare consilium*, and what is noted there by Dynus.

For when it is asked whether one may change his counsel, a distinction is made: either from the preceding election some right has been acquired, or a right has been acquired for another, and he would not be deprived; or no one loses anything. In the first case, he cannot change his counsel, as in the aforementioned law *Apud Aufidium*. In the second case, the same rule applies, as in the law *Si*, in the Code, *De codicillis*, and noted in the chapter *Quod semel placuit* by Dynus, Book 6. In the third case, variation is permitted if no one is prejudiced. But in our case, by the election, the right to the books of that art has been acquired, and the right to the books of the other science has been lost by that alternative word, "if, however," as in the Digest, *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, in the law *Titia, si vero nupserit*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether, and when, a notary is counted among the number of witnesses.
body: In a certain town, in a certain town...

† There are two statutes of the town. In the first it is provided that in any instrument at least three witnesses are to be employed, among whom there is to be at least one who knows the contracting parties, and the place in which the instrument is drawn up, and the notary is to write the name and surname of each witness, and the father's name, and whence the testator or the witness originates; and the witnesses are understood to be suitable and to know the contracting parties if this was inserted into the instrument by the notary, unless the contrary is proved; but in the case of those appointing syndics for lawsuits, it suffices if the witnesses know him at whose instance the community was assembled. In the other statute it is provided that if a contract or alienation is made for one hundred pounds of pennies or more, an instrument is to be requested, and two notaries must be present at the contract or alienation, counting the notary who delivered the instrument; otherwise faith is not to be given to the instrument. Posit, then, that two notaries were employed, and three witnesses counting the notary who subscribed; he did not, however, state whence they originate. The question is asked whether the instrument is valid? I answer that it is not valid, because two witnesses are lacking, as in C. de testa. l. si vnus and C. de fideicom. l. si veritas; and it is expressed that two notaries together do not suffice in Authen. de haere. et fal. §. si vero absunt. But although the instrument is not valid, nevertheless the contract and alienation can well be proved by the living voice of three witnesses, among whom there is one who knew the contracting parties. For it must be considered that proof is made either by living voice, or by instrument alone, or both by living voice and at the same time by writing: in the first and third cases the notary is counted in the number of witnesses, as in C. qui test. fa. pos. l. hac consultissima. §. fi. But in the second case, the principal notary is not counted in the number of witnesses, because it would follow that a notary and one witness would suffice, which is false, although some argue to the contrary, and wrongly so. On this, the doctors note in ff. and C. de test. l. domitius and C. de fideicom. l. quaestionem; and this is the truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An arbitrator cannot order one party to sell to the other party; and if he does so, the award is null.
body: The words state that the plain in the name of Christ is to remain with the said Antonio; and in compensation for the price and value of the said plain of the castle, they cancel all excesses and offenses, whatever injuries, etc. The question is whether, as regards this article, the said award is valid?

† And to understand the aforesaid, let us consider the power of the arbitrator, whether he can adjudicate the disputed matter in this manner, namely, for a certain price and with certain compensations to be made? And it seems at first that he can, for several reasons. The first is that the said arbitrator had very full power; hence whatever he did in good faith ought to be considered valid, as in D. 17.1.13 (Creditor) § Lucius. For that which is done in good faith is considered well done, as in D. 12.1.1 (Quamvis) and note D. 12.2.1 (Eum qui) § In popularibus. But there is no doubt that the arbitrator did this in good faith, and for the benefit of both parties, so that the cause of offending might be removed, especially between subjects and their lord, since it is in the interest of subjects not to contend with their superior; for we cannot be equals to superiors, as in D. 2.1.1 (Quia etiam). Moreover, it is certain that an arbitrator can settle between parties regarding a disputed thing, and decree that the thing remain with one party and a certain quantity be given to the other, as in D. 4.8.1 (Si de meis) § Recepisse and D. 4.8.2 (Sed si in servum) § Si quis iudex. For this is a kind of transaction, which an arbitrator can make between parties, or explain and declare what is implicit in the compromise, as noted in Auth. Ut differant iudices § 1, Coll. 9. Moreover, the decretal seems explicit, which says that two were contending over a certain priory: and the arbitrator elected to arbitrate said that one should have the priory, the other should have certain revenues; the text there says that the arbitration is valid regarding the priory: but regarding the revenues it is not valid on account of the defect of simony; therefore, in temporal matters, in which simony is not committed, it is valid in whole, or at least as to the thing itself. This is the case expressly stated in X. 3.4.1 (Nisi esset). To the same effect it is that this can come into a transaction, as in X. 3.4.1 (Nisi esset); X. 2.27.1 (Veniens). Therefore also in arbitration. Moreover, a judge can compensate between parties, as in D. 37.11.1 (Meuius enim). Therefore also an arbitrator, because arbitrations are reduced to the likeness of judicial proceedings, as in C. 2.12.1 (Rem non novam); D. 4.8.1. Moreover, if this were not so, it would follow that the condition of the law Si quis in tantam would still remain for the nobleman Antonio, and the question would remain both possessory and petitory regarding the said plain; for it cannot be that regarding the same chapter the thing is valid on one side and not valid on the other; for just as a contract cannot limp, so as to be valid on one side and not on the other, as in D. 18.1.1 (Iul.) § Si quis colludente. Likewise neither a quasi-contract, nor a judgment, nor an arbitration, as in D. 4.8.1 (Si cum dies) § Unde eleganter and D. 4.8.2 (In sacris) de proximis sacrorum scrineorum, as in X. 3.21.1 (Prudentiam). Moreover, another consequence would follow, namely, if the said Antonio was in possession of the said plain justly or unjustly, he is so today in the same way; or conversely, if his adversaries were in possession, as they were, so they are; for an arbitration which is not valid in law does not merit execution; nor can anything be innovated under its pretext. And thus the principal lawsuit which was between the parties would still remain undecided; which seems to the evidence of absurdity, lest lawsuits arise from lawsuits, as in C. 7.55.1 (Terminato); for lawsuits ought not to be immortal, as in C. 1.1.1. For it pertains to a good prince to cut off the matter of lawsuits, as the letter says there, and therefore the prince could confirm such a transaction, as in d. c. Veniens. Many other things can also be said to persuade that the said award is valid. But the truth is to the contrary: for an arbitrator can well order that something else be given, in the name of a transaction; for this is required by the nature of the compromise. And thus it ought to be understood, as noted by Bartolus in D. 2.27.1 (Cum Aquiliana). But he cannot order one party to sell his thing for a certain price; for selling pertains to a new contract, about which there was no compromise, hence an arbitrator cannot order what pertains to a new contract, as in D. 4.8.1 (Non distinguemus) § De officio and D. 4.8.2 (Qui tamen) § Item si arbiter. That which he ordered here to be sold appears from the name of price, as in C. 10.10.1 (Si). From which it appears that the sentence passed on the said plain was not valid, and if it were valid, it ought to be rescinded; for no one is forced against his will to sell his thing; nor even a thing not his, as in C. 4.1.1 (Sicut). Moreover, from this follows such a conclusion, that since the said award is on the said plain, neither for the said nobleman nor against the said nobleman, that all lawsuits and questions which were between the said lord and the said community, as pending lawsuits, are to be decided anew, C. 2.1.1 (Si ut proponis) with its gloss. And this is my counsel in law, but I advise the parties that they reconcile, for what can be advised cannot be commanded, as in D. 6.1.1.1 § Et post operis. And therefore what I have written, because I have already counseled on this: and the counsel is true, and the allegations. Let the learned one answer to the contrary, their libel proceeds in law, according to what has been said above. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A long-term lease of an emphyteutic thing is invalid if the owner has not been consulted; but the thing thus leased reverts to the owner.
2. An award of an arbitrator is a kind of settlement.
3. When a settlement is said to be an alienation.
4. Ownership is not transferred by the sentence of an arbiter, nor by that of an arbitrator.
body: For clarification,

† it must first be premised for clarification that under title of a simple lease for a not long period, an emphyteuta can lease to another. For even a usufructuary can do this, although the usufruct is terminated by alienation: because that is not an alienation, as in ff. loc. l. si quis domum. §. 1. and ff. de peri. et commo. rei ven. l. necessario. §. fi. But he cannot lease for a long period, even if the words say under title of a simple lease, as Dy. notes with the Gloss, ff. de leg. 2. l. codicillis. §. instituto. And if he were thus to lease without consulting the lord, the emphyteuta would forfeit his right; for the lord ought to be asked whether he wishes to lease for an equal rent, nor is he said to lease his own property, but the emphyteutic right, as in ff. de acqui. pos. l. si aliquam rem.

† Secondly, it must be premised for clarification that an arbitrator's award is a kind of transaction when it disposes something on both sides, as is noted in Authen. ut diff. iud. §. j. But when it is determined on one side only, it partakes more of a pact than of a transaction, as in ff. de transac. l. 1.

† Thirdly, it must be premised that a transaction either contains an obligation to give (dari): and then it is called an alienation once delivery follows. The same holds if it contains an agreement that a right be transferred: because eviction comes into play; it is otherwise if it contains an agreement to retain, as in C. de transac. l. si pro fundo. For there is a difference between an exception and ownership, as in l. sed et sic possessori. in prin. ff. de iureiu. Just as if a lord were to make a pact not to claim his property, he would not on that account be said to alienate ownership; whence he could vindicate it from any other possessor, except the one with whom he made the pact, as in ff. de pac. l. si unus. §. ante omnia. Fourthly, it must be premised that he who establishes a title for a possessor or detainer, by which title ownership is accustomed to be transferred, is understood to deliver and alienate, as in instit. de rerum diui. §. interdum. and ff. de rei uend. §. quaedam mulier.

† Fifthly and lastly, it must be premised that ownership is not transferred by the decree of an arbiter or arbitrator unless the lord delivers or quasi-delivers, as in extra de test. c. Rayn. These premises having been laid down, I come to the question: and I say that by the decree of the arbiter and arbitrators no alienation followed, nor was the cause of possession changed; nor was it indeed of the intention of the arbitrators that the beneficial ownership should be transferred, except with the lord's consent, and therefore they added and arbitrated that the emphyteutae should effectively procure that the canons invest them under the name of a libellus, etc. Nevertheless, whatever the case may be, matters seem subsequently to have proceeded further: namely, that the said emphyteutae held and possessed—one by the will of the other, and the other by the will of the other—the said domiciles, which could not be alienated even between themselves, ff. de transac. l. cum hi. §. si ita., because they were distinct emphyteuses; through which sufferance and mutual consent delivery is said to have occurred in accordance with the preceding personal obligation, as in C. de acqui. pos. l. minus instructus. And thus a certain illicit transfer and alienation seems to have been made. For the words of the award say that they are bound to surrender and release with full right: because words bind personally to surrendering and releasing with full right. But to surrender and release with full right is an alienation when followed by delivery or quasi-delivery, not before, as in ff. de ver. sig. l. alienatum. Nor does it stand in the way that the words say that they are bound to assign the action, and thus concern a future time, because that tacit future time was brought into the present by that delivery. Likewise, it is not necessary to assign rights that cannot be assigned without the lord's consent. But whether they are assigned or not assigned, provided that it arrives at the delivery of possession, even from a preceding cause, a prohibited alienation arises there, and therefore it seems that the emphyteuta has forfeited his right. Nevertheless, in a fief we hold that a vassal can compromise, as in c. vassallus de suo. si de feu. fue. contro. As I have said, the award of an arbitrator is similar to a transaction and comes to the same thing. This question depends sufficiently on the understanding of the said law si pro fundo, because a transaction is not an alienation in retaining, but in giving or transferring it is. But indeed to this it is answered by that expression 'with full right', because that quasi-transfer is in transferring: and thus it is in the form of a future alienation, and in the execution of the award, which execution was de facto completed through the delivery of possession. And therefore, presupposing that the said award was valid with regard to the personal obligation, subsequent delivery having followed, an illicit alienation took place without the lord's consent: concerning which surrender of possession in execution of the said award a public instrument is presupposed to appear; and therefore it reverts to the lord, that is, to the church, as in C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum. l. vniuersas. and C. de iure emp. l. fi. Especially because he who delivers to another against the will of the lord, intending to transfer his right away from that right to the one to whom he renounces, alienates himself, as in insti. de vsus. §. finitur. And thus I hold that the property reverted to the church. However, if the canons made the investiture, approving the award in part, they cannot contravene it in the other part: but they ought to make the investiture of the other house. If, however, in the meantime they alienated it to another, they cannot do this to that person's prejudice, as in ff. de publiciana. l. siue autem. §. si duobus. From which it finally follows that that house remains with that woman who was invested with the open emphyteusis, which cannot be invested in another, as in c. 1. qui succes. tenean. col. 10. To that doubt, whether he who does not take care etc. is bound to the penalty of the compromise, or to damages (interesse), I say yes; nor does this fall within the renunciation that they made mutually: because they did not remit to each other the right of the award. But he who ought to have taken care, and did not take care, is therefore bound to the penalty or damages. For he who is bound to take care is not bound for the act of another, but for his own act, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. si quis alium. and fully noted in ff. de act. et ob. l. quaecunque gerimus. And these are standard legal principles. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Arbiters are bound to render judgment on the whole matter; nor ought they to compel the creditor to accept a partial payment.
2. The phrase, what it signifies.
body: Noble man, Master An. In the name of Christ. [He] received from Lord Philippo de Landulphis two thousand florins, and more; and since the said Lord Philippino did not have ready money, they made between themselves a very full compromise to three arbitrators, concerning the purchase of lands from the said debtor for satisfying himself, the creditor, and others, who arbitrators were to declare the price in agreement, and not otherwise. In Patisio I promised and they did not give the arbitral power of viewing, declaring, and cognizing the manner and price of the said sale with securities and terms nominatively on certain possessions situated in three vocabula and territories. It is proposed that the said arbitrators wished, if they could do so by law, that for eight hundred florins of the said sum the said Antonio should receive a certain part of the said lands: whereas in two of the said territories the said Lord Philippino is said not to have any rights: nor to be able to sell juridically. It is asked,

Whether the said arbitration award can be partially executed: I answer that it cannot, for three reasons. First, because they must either judge the whole matter or nothing at all, as stated in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Quid tamen*, in the beginning. Second, because the words placed in the compromise, namely "for satisfying themselves," import the final cause of the compromise.

† The term "dictio" implies the final cause, as noted in the Digest, title *De peculio legatorum*, law *Dominus Sticho*. This final cause requires fulfillment, just as a condition does, as stated in the Digest, title *De conditionibus et demonstrationibus*, law *Quibus diebus*, section *Si*. The third reason is that, since the entire debt is liquidated, the creditor is not compelled to accept a partial payment, as provided in the Digest, title *De usuris*, law *Tutor*, section *Lucius*. Therefore, if the aforementioned arbitrators were disposed to render an unjust sentence, our lord may command them to consider what they should do; and since they ought not to depart from the path of reason without some mandate from the lord, the foregoing is well supported by the Digest, title *De conditionibus indebiti*, law *Si non sortem*, section *Si centum*, and by what is fully noted in the Digest, title *Si certum petatur*, law *Quidam estimauerunt*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a carrier is liable to the owner of the goods if the goods are lost due to a toll not being paid.
body: A certain carrier, in the name of Christ, was to carry certain bales of cloth, in which were certain silver jewels inside certain closed and sealed boxes, as far as the place of Carpentras; and he promised to pay all ancient tolls and customary ones, which ought to be paid on account of them. When this carrier had brought the said bales to a certain place called Grignani, which is within the boundaries of Paris and Carpentras, in which place a toll of one grossus is paid for each bale, and if the said bales contained silver jewels or anything of weight beyond the cloth, two grossi are paid; that carrier at the place of Grignani did not pay for the toll more than one grossus. For this reason, those two bales, in which beyond the cloth there were those boxes, fell into the hands of the authorities and were lost.

† Now it is asked whether the carrier is liable to the owner of the goods or not: the carrier says that he did not see the said chests being loaded. And even if it were proved that he saw them being loaded, it would not be proved that he saw the things which were inside the said closed and sealed chests. In the contrary, the owner alleges that the said chests were of weight: and that the said carrier saw them being loaded: and although he did not see the things which were inside, because owners do not wish such things to be seen by carriers, he ought to have presumed that there was something inside for which a toll should be paid; but the carrier responds that in the chests there could have been things for which no toll, or only a small toll, namely one grossus, ought to be paid. Now it is doubtful what the parties should be in this matter for the judge to decide. And it seems that the carrier is not liable: because the owner ought to have shown him the goods for which he knew a greater toll ought to be paid: or if he did not show the goods, he ought to have declared: see that you pay a greater toll, for declaration is sometimes necessary, as noted in l. si, in the beginning, ff. naut. caup. stab. Hence the owner, through his own fault, incurred the penalty, because, having knowledge, he did not warn the muleteer. Also, it is not probable that the muleteer wished to undertake for himself a double peril: he ought therefore to have been informed, as in l. 1, §. si, ff. de act. empt. In the contrary it seems, for the law says that he who hired the transport of wine from Campania, if any controversy arises on the journey through his act, is liable to the owner of the wine, as in ff. locat. l. videamus, §. qui vinum de campania. Another law says that the carrier is liable to pay the toll of the vehicle: but it is not true that this is to be understood unless from agreement: but here an agreement intervened, as in ff. locat. l. cum in plures, §. vehiculum. This question is solved in the facts, for if the muleteer knew the things which were carried there, or hidden, without doubt he is liable for the damage. If, however, both were at fault, the condition of the plaintiff is worse, as in the said l. si plures, §. locator horrei. But if he was ignorant, or was ignorant of the chests being loaded, without doubt the peril is the owner’s, as in ff. locat. l. colonus, §. navem. Or if the muleteer knew the chests were loaded: but was ignorant of the things which were inside: and this is the doubtful case as to the disposition of the law. For if we say that fault is imputed to the owner, the muleteer is not liable. But if we say that fault is imputed to the muleteer, because he ought to have looked out, then the muleteer is liable. This distinction is made in the said §. qui vinum, detio actoris. But if the owner was at fault, and the muleteer in bad faith, then the muleteer is liable: because bad faith outweighs fault, as noted in ff. sol. mat. l. si mora. But this bad faith is proved, unless it is proved that the carrier, or muleteer, was warned even by any stranger, as in ff. de pet. her. l. sed si lege, §. scire. Also, if it was the custom of merchants to put precious things in such chests: because contracting parties ought to refer to what is commonly done, as in ff. de edil. edict. l. quod si voluit, §. quia assidua. The conclusion is this, that either bad faith or fault of the carrier is proved: and the carrier is liable, and for this proof true or presumed knowledge is required. Also, he who ought to know is held to have knowledge, as in l. quod te, ff. si cert. pet. But he ought not to inquire into another’s secrets, nor open the chests, as in l. 2, quando, et quibus quarta pars debetur, ff. 10. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A brother cannot seize and imprison his brother, even if the latter bears on his shield the depiction of a traitor.
body: ...nuo de Salutijs ca...

† It was not lawful for that knight of Saluzzo to capture his brother and place him in prison without a formal renunciation of allegiance (disfidatio), because the Doctors say that this is a species of quasi-treason, as noted by Jo. An. in c. pro humani. de homi. li. 6. in nouel. Likewise, since that nobleman was not the Marquess, he ought to have deferred to the lord Marquess, that is, to accuse him before him as the common lord; nor was plundering lawful, as in c. 1. §. fi. de mili. vas. qui contu. est, where plundering is not permitted except when the superior refuses to render justice; this is noted in C. de iude. l. nullus. Likewise, that which is done by private authority through the use of arms is capital, as in C. vt armorum vsus inscio principe. l. 1; and therefore it was not lawful for the said knight by his own authority to capture his brother-in-arms, as he calls him, C. de pac. l. licet; and this is lawful in only one case, namely when a brother commits treason against the other, but not when one commits it against a third party. And these points weigh against the knight of Saluzzo. But against that other party it weighs that he challenged him as a traitor, and bore him depicted upon his shield as a traitor; for this is not lawful, because this is a greater injury than a defamatory libel, concerning which there is capital punishment, as in l. 1. de famosis libellis. For it is lawful for no one to impose an evil name, ff. ad Treb. l. facta. §. si in danda; for it is not found in the law concerning such a painting that it is permitted, except perhaps to those possessing merum imperium, and with the cause having been investigated, and a definitive sentence having been pronounced. And therefore he who wishes to justify this ought to prove it by the custom of arms, and that he did that which the code of arms requires; and ff. de iniur. l. vestem sordidam is relevant. But these matters do not on that account resolve the question, because the question is, since it is a cause of treason, whether they ought mutually to duel, as in Inst. de haere. ab intest. §. per contrarium; and it seems that they should. To the contrary, because these acts of treason do not regard the same subject, for one says that the other wished to betray the Marquess, and attempted this; the adversary says that this man betrayed himself, whose brother[-in-arms] he was, etc. I, Sialdus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Jurisdiction, honor, territory, district, county, natural, real, and perpetual dues, tithes, and tithe collections: how they differ from one another, and which of these are owed to the archbishop.
body: In the name of Christ. For clarity, it must be premised according to that which is proposed: the lord Archbishop of Milan had, and was accustomed to have, in the said great valley jurisdiction, honor, district, and certain real and perpetual prestations, and [the right] of measuring grain under the ancient measure, which was smaller than the new one. For these things differ: jurisdiction is the power of administering justice either by oneself or through another, as in ff. de iuris. om. iu. l. Imperium. §. fi., and that both by way of necessary and contentious jurisdiction, as in ff. de ver. ob. l. inter stipulantem. §. sacram., and by way of voluntary jurisdiction in the agreements of parties that require the judge's decree, as in l. 2. ff. de officio proconsul.

† Honor, however, is when, during the joyful visitation of the lord Archbishop, honors are paid to him, such as guest-gifts and courtesies or blandishments, which are provided for the purpose of visiting him or one sent by him, and the like. To this honor also belong all obsequious and reverential services, as in c. 1. §. similiter. qui. mo. feu. amit. colla. 10. The district, moreover, is the territory in which jurisdiction resides, as in c. vbi periculum. de elec. lib. 6. and noted in l. 1. C. vbi de pos. agi oportet. and inst. de act. §. rursus; and it differs from a county, because a county is properly the district of cities, including those of lords, for a county is a certain accession to a city and its natural appurtenances, de rest. spo. c. cum ad sedem. Real and perpetual prestations, on the other hand, are such as a certain amount of grain each year, or a certain quantity of money in place of grain. Likewise, tithes are most strictly real prestations; and if indeed they derive from special law, they cannot be transferred to laymen at all; but if they derive from temporal law—which are not properly called tithes, but certainly decimationes—they may well fall to laymen, as when the Emperor grants to me the tithes of a certain part of his temporal territory; for just as he can grant the whole, so too a part. But this is of no relevance to our proposition; rather, it should solely be considered that temporal, perpetual, and real, as well as quasi-real prestations, whose collection was initiated by the authority of a king or prince, must be called simply temporal, and pertain to the temporality, not to the spirituality, of the Archbishopric, except insofar as it is an ecclesiastical thing, because holy things are of the Lord, as Inn. says. These premises having been considered, since the lord Archbishop does not exercise temporal jurisdiction in administering justice, the said people of the valley are not bound to undergo the burdens that concern the exercise of that jurisdiction, since they perform them under the Magnificent [Lord], by the argument of ff. de condi. et dem. l. plautius. §. item scinditur. and ff. de alimen. leg. l. alumnae. §. saeia., because when the cause ceases, the effect ceases. Other burdens, however, which regard honors and real prestations, since the territory has not truly been separated from the domain of the Archbishop, but rather he holds the direct universal domain, they are bound to undergo, because the cause does not cease; therefore the effect does not cease. And in these matters the assessment of an upright man must be applied, as in ff. de contrahen. emp. l. officio., where it is said that an abatement must be made by the equitable arbitrament of a judge, and for as long as it is equitable for it to be made, and no longer. Concerning the old and new measure, it must be said that the original one must be observed, unless it has been changed by custom, as in extra de censi. c. olim., or by agreement, as in ff. de fideius. l. si ita fideiussorem accepero. And in short, this question stands relatively, for when one extreme is destroyed, the other is destroyed, and conversely it is constructed and remains intact, as in l. fi. ff. de accep. la. and ff. de transac. l. qui fidem. And therefore it must be examined what is rendered for what, so that justice and humanity may be preserved on both sides. One point must not be omitted: that if the lord Archbishop is in possession of receiving [them], that possession ought not to be taken from him nor inverted by the subjects, except by authority of a superior, as in extra de elec. c. querelam., unless the lord Archbishop willingly chooses to suffer this on account of the poverty of his subjects, with whom the Church ought to sympathize as a father sympathizes with his sons; this is expressly read and noted in C. de annonis, et tribu. l. omnes pensitare. lib. 10.; and this for a time, namely as long as the poverty lasts and extraordinary burdens press, and no longer, as in ff. de vacatione munerum. l. his oneribus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How district and appurtenances are to be proved.
2. Full sovereignty consists in four things.
3. What are the duties of the judge when both parties ground their claim in the same manner.
4. Which documents are better regarding ancient facts.
5. What is included under the name of appurtenances.
6. Whether the inhabitants of a community may testify concerning territory.
7. Whether a vassal may testify for his lord: and household members.
8. In a possessory action, he prevails who proves either older possession or title.
body:
The words of the Prince, in the name of Christ, are as follows: We commit, delegate, to the learned man, our vicar, Lord John, the hearing, cognizance, and summary, simple, and plain termination, without the noise and formality of judicial proceedings, with all delays and cavils ceasing, solely truth being considered, of the question which is being litigated and is expected to be litigated between our beloved vassals, the lords of Gabiano, the commune, and the men of the said place on one part, and the men of Fontaneto on the other, on account of the fields and boundaries of the said places, and on account of whatever depends therefrom; and that he shall not admit an appeal from an interlocutory judgment, except according to civil law, nor shall he grant any right to any of the said parties from present possession. And so forth.

Now, since no petition was offered on behalf of the said Commune of Fontaneto, because they wished to make themselves plaintiffs, chapters were drawn up concerning the boundaries and territories, they asserting that their fields extend as far as the bank of the Po River; and that the territories of the adversaries do not extend beyond the bank of the Po River. But the other party attempted to retain possession together with the assertion of a petitory claim, and with the assertion of notoriety and perpetual fame among the surrounding inhabitants. The chapters were drawn up prudently on both sides; yet more prudently on the part of the said nobles, because they assert possession with the patience of the adversary up to the day of the present controversy. Such patience operates greatly in incorporeal things, as in servitudes, jurisdictions, and the like, as in l. 2, C. de serv. et aqua. And although for the said Commune of Fontaneto, because nothing was claimed, a condemnatory sentence against the opposing party could not be founded, yet because the party of the nobles and the men of Gabiano submitted their petition, the judgment is founded on both sides. And therefore it remains to proceed to the proof of witnesses and instruments.

† I preface, for the clarity of the entire matter, how pertinences and districts are proved: I say that sometimes places and territories are evidently and notoriously distinct: sometimes by royal roads; sometimes by rivers; sometimes by mountains or valleys; sometimes by stones or very apparent signs, and in these ways territories are commonly distinguished, as noted by Johannes Andreae, according to Gozzadinus, in the Extravagant *De probat.*, c. *Cum causam*. Sometimes also the boundaries of jurisdictions are proved by express or tacit assertions of the parties, as noted in the Code *De contrahenda et committenda stipulatione*, l. *Optimam*, and in the Code *De iure deliberandi*, l. *Cum aliquis*. Sometimes they are proved by the opinion and judgment of the common people and those dwelling in the vicinity, who in this matter are more suitable witnesses than others, as in l. 1, § 1, Digest *De flumine*; and the simpler and more rustic they are, the more credible they are, because they do not testify except concerning the possession of fact, as those who always stand with their eyes upon those very places, as noted in the Digest *De verbis oblig.*, l. *Stipulatio ista*, § *Hi quoque*. Furthermore, they are proved by the sentences of judges and arbitrators, as in the Digest *De arbitris*, l. *Inter castellanum*, and in the Institutes *De officio iudicis*, § *Finis*. Sometimes they are proved by the collection of revenues, as in the Code *De finium regundorum*, l. *Si quis super*. Suppose, therefore, that witnesses say that they saw one party possessing from such a river towards the front of such a castle, or from such a large and notable stone, and one that is immovable; is it presumed that that river or notable stone is the boundary, or not? And it must be said that it is presumed, because it is customary to do so. For custom judges a great part of what something is, as in the Digest *De edilitio edicto*, l. *Quod si nolit*, § *Quia assidua*; and in the Digest *De fundo instrato*, l. *Cum delationis*, § *Asinam*; and in the Digest *De legatis tertio*, l. *Si chorus*, § 1. Furthermore, sometimes boundaries are proved by the appointment of custodians, as in the Digest *De fundo instrato*, l. *Si ita*, § *Villae custos*. Also by the exercise of jurisdiction, the collection of tolls, and similar acts; for by these means the district is proved both on land and at sea, indeed in the sky and air, because up to the sky the possession should be free to the owner, as in c. *Ubi periculum*, *De electione*, lib. 6. In this way, gallows signify dominion over the air, because the suspended hang in the air.

† and this is the great significance of the pure Empire, which consists in four things: just as there are four elements in the air, as I said, in fire, as when someone is burned for sorcery; in water, as when someone is placed on the rack and thrown into water or into a river, as in l. 1. C. de patribus, qui filios occiderunt; in earth, as when someone is laid on the ground and beheaded, as in l. 3. C. de epis. audi. cum si. Because, returning to the point, I say that the party which better proved the necessary or probable boundaries ought to prevail in the case, because justice makes the better-proving party stronger for the good, as in C. de edicto diui Adriani, l. edicto, § 1, and there this doctrine is taught magisterially,

† when both parties found their claim, but one does so better than the other. But if they found their claim in an equal manner, the judge may, from the free motion of his own mind, with God alone as witness, and not adhering by way of any carnality, friendship, or other passion, choose which party he wishes to prevail, as is noted in the Digest, De re iudicata, l. Duo iudices dati. But if he does not wish to adhere to either, because his mind does not incline more to one than to the other, then there is room for that dispute concerning two parties proving equally in the interdict *uti possidetis*, of which we have noted in the Code, Uti possidetis, l. 1. But observe that this dispute does not apply in the action for the settling of boundaries (*finium regundorum*): because it is a petitory action, as noted in the Code, De interdictis, l. Incerti. Hence the judge cannot say, “As you have claimed, so let you claim,” because such a sentence would contain nothing, as in l. 3, Code, De sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum. Therefore, he must decide against his own reluctant teeth. But what then? He may avail himself of the aid of surveyors and the counsel of prudent laymen, and especially of elders, who are more credible witnesses in matters concerning the substance of things, as in the Digest, De aqua pluviali arcenda, l. 1, in fine, and Digest, De probationibus, l. Si arbiter.

† Moreover, concerning these ancient facts, better evidence is provided by instruments executed with the consent of the parties who were in place at the time, in whose stead the newcomers have succeeded as shoots from the root, as held in D. 10.1 (finium regundorum), l. eos; and D. 22.6 (de probat.), l. Celsus, and there, no. Having thus premised these theoretical points, the following rules of law must be noted for the practice of our question, and the statements of the witnesses must be carefully examined. Nevertheless, it must also be premised that pertinences consist not only in possession, but also in right and jurisdiction, as held in D. 50.17 (de verborum significatione), l. verbum pertinere; and in the aforementioned c. Cum ad sedem, de restitutione spoliorum, where Innocentius states.

† that only those things are understood by the name of appurtenances which have been established by statute, or custom, or disputed law, so as to accede thereto. And he adds these words: “But nothing is attributed to a castle by law which is its appurtenance; nevertheless, it is customary for men and their statutes to assign a certain territory to a castle, which it ought to have in its jurisdiction, and to respond to others.” But Speculum, in the title De restitutione spoliati, § Quia vero, verse Quid de colligentibus pedagia, says that certain things are not accustomed to be held, nor by privilege of the Prince, such as tolls, passages, or salt duties. And where there is no proof of privilege, possession is required, and that of such time as there is no memory of the contrary, as in Extra, De verbis significandis, chapter Super quibusdam. Yet I do not believe the same applies to the prescription of contentious jurisdiction; because that belongs to municipalities by common law as regards simple jurisdiction and certain small fines, as in Authentica De defendendo civitate, § Et iudicare. They can also prescribe mere and mixed Empire by a very long time, as in Codex, De diversis officiis, law Viros, lib. 12. But not passages, etc., which are reserved to the Prince, as in chapter 1, Quae sint regaliae, Collatio 10.

Furthermore, it must be premised that an older possession, which was peaceful in ancient times, even if it has since begun to be disturbed, is stronger than a new one in quieting adversaries, because the older it is, the more just it is, and the force of disturbance ought not to aid the disturbers, as in Extra, De probationibus, chapter Licet causam.

Therefore, having premised these things, I consider that the witnesses on both sides are very varied and discordant regarding possession and quasi-territory; indeed, some attempt to approve jurisdiction and quasi-possession of jurisdiction. And I begin with the nobles and the community of Gabiano, because they are the plaintiffs, and they prove their territory or appurtenances beyond the Po River up to the place called Vialesco and the place called Canecagna. Moreover, some witnesses say that if beasts were sent within the said boundaries, the lords and men of Gabiano sent men to seize them, and they caused those to whom they belonged to restore the damage and pay the penalty; and thus say Francischinus, Gocerius, and Corradus. Moreover, William de Vbio says that the said nobles and men of Gabiano held, possessed, and quasi-held lands, goods, possessions, and things in the district of Valisio, inclusive, coming towards Gabiano up to the bank of the Po, freely as their own territory and domain, and of the domain and district of Gabiano. Moreover, John, on the fourth chapter. Moreover, Facinus, on the fourth chapter, says that the men of Fontanetto by force and violence sent their beasts to destroy the meadows, etc. Moreover, William de Lorella, on the first and tenth chapters. Moreover, William de Ranerio, on the tenth chapter and on the fifth, although he says he does not know what quasi-possession is. Moreover, Anthony, on chapter 1, who, when asked what territory is, answered that it is lands, meadows, possessions, and woods. Moreover, Angelinus de Monte. Moreover, William de Ranis. However, it must be noted that some witnesses testify fully, others not.

Moreover, it must be noted for the part of these nobles an ancient public instrument, by which it is provided that there was already a lawsuit concerning the said boundaries; and it was declared, to which declaration one must adhere, as in Digestum, De arbitris, law Inter Castellianum.

Now let us see the witnesses, namely for the community of Fontanetto, and certainly their witnesses testify in effect the exact opposite: and there are eight witnesses, or about that many, who testify by sight that the territory of Fontanetto extends up to the river Po. And they seem to testify that it is held in solidum, and consequently that the lords and men of Gabiano have no right in the said territory, as in Extra, De causa possessionis, chapter Cum ecclesia. Now the question arises, what is to be said in this matter? It cannot be denied that the variety of witnesses and disturbances on both sides obscures the lawsuit and makes the possession uncertain, as is the glossa ordinaria in Digestum, Quod metus causa, law Extat.

† Moreover, it cannot be denied that there is a doubt in law as to whether witnesses of a corporation may testify concerning territory; nevertheless, the common opinion is that they may, provided that no benefit or detriment accrues to them; otherwise, if they were to receive an immediate benefit, as noted in the Speculum de testibus, § Opponitur, under the words “But whether in the case of a corporation,” and in the law In tantum, § Universitatis, Digest, De rerum divisione, and according to Cynus and the Code, De testibus, law Parentes, according to Cynus.

† Likewise, regarding a vassal, whether he may testify for his lord, is similarly doubtful in law: nevertheless, it must be said finally, that these persons are not excluded on account of any principal head of any law stating this, but on a general head, because they are domestics: and commands may be issued to them. The Speculum seems to say that they are excluded, in Spec. de teste. §. op. ver. item excipitur. quod est domesticus, but may not a community command one of the community, and yet is he not excluded? Likewise, who is more of a domestic than a citizen of the same city? and yet he is not excluded according to the same Speculum. Hence, if you consider these matters, the Speculum seems to contradict itself. The solution is to say that this is a matter of discretion, for the witness is of good life and reputation, and gives probable testimony: and especially if he is supported by the statements of others, who are not vassals, credit is given to their testimony as though corroborated by good life, reputation, and other external witnesses, as in ff. de lega. 3. §. tu magis. and ff. de eden. l. si quis ex argentariis. §. 2. there, quid enim and c.

Finally, it is necessary to gather all the aforesaid points and arrive at a conclusion: and I say that the matter is entirely doubtful due to the entanglement of proofs and possessions, and the mixture of acts on both sides. He prevails in the case who has the older possession, as stated in the Digest, *De probationibus*, chapter *Licet causam*. And if it is not established which possession is older, and one party has a title while the other does not, he who has the title prevails both in the petitory and in the possessory action. This is expressly determined by Jacobus de Arena in the Code, *De re vindicanda*, law *Quotiens*. And since the nobles of Gabiano demonstrate their title and cause through a compromise and the subsequent award, which has the force of a transaction, and consequently the force of a res iudicata and a definitive sentence, as noted in the Authenticum *Ut differentia*, § 1, insofar as it is contained in their instrument, there is no doubt that they have the right. And if there is doubt whether the same bodies [of land] are involved, let one go to the places and subject the matter to ocular inspection, as in the Digest, *De finium regundorum*, law *Si irruptione*, § *Ad officium*. As for the other matters, the said nobles and the commune prevail by virtue of older possession proven by less suspect witnesses, as in the Code, *De edicto divi*, law *Edicto*, § 1. And since it has been proven that the men of Fontaneto were disturbers, they are therefore the later possessors, as noted in law 1, § *Stipulatio*, *De appellationibus*. It is therefore concluded, and necessarily follows, that these nobles of Gabiano and the commune of Gabiano uphold justice: and judgment should be rendered in their favor, and perpetual silence imposed upon the other party. And thus I hold, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a wife may receive from her husband the restitution of a deposit formerly made to her father, of whom she is not the heir, but rather in the name of her brother, who is the heir.
body: whether the second may receive it, such is the case.

† It is asked whether a wife, in the name of Christ, may repudiate a certain deposit formerly made to her father, of whom she is not the heir, but rather receives it in the name of her brother, who is the heir? And it seems that she may not: because a donation is presumed, which is not valid between husband and wife. Moreover, because it is presumed that she does not have money except from the husband’s goods, as in D. de donis inter virum et uxorem, l. Quintus. And thus the husband has not been satisfied. I say the contrary, for this is not a donation between husband and wife: since the wife does not become enriched by such a release, as in D. de donis inter virum et uxorem, l. Si sponsus, § Concessa. Moreover, the law Quintus does not apply, because it is not presumed that the money belongs to the husband, when the contrary is asserted; rather, it is presumed to belong to the person in whose name it was paid, as in D. de probationibus, l. Cum de indebito. It is also not to be doubted that the release is valid even by reason of childbirth, even if the cause of donation is not specified, as in D. de pactis, l. Tale pactum, in principio. It is also asked, rather childishly, whether it can be proved by an instrument with two or three witnesses described in the instrument? And there is no doubt that it can, as in C. de testibus, l. Testium, and in Auth. de fide instrumentorum, § Oportet, with its entire very common material. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Can one stipulate for another in a dowry and in an ante-nuptial gift? But can a woman bring an action without cession?
body: In the City of Alexandria. In the name of Christ. Gregory confessed that he had received from the brothers of his wife, Francisca, in the name of her dowry, four hundred Imperial pounds as dowry, and in the name of dowry, with his sister and wife, the said Francisca, solemnly stipulating in her name and on her behalf; wherefore the said Gregory gave to the said Francisca, by way of donation propter nuptias and in the name of the antifactum, according to the custom and usage of the city of Alexandria, one hundred Imperial pounds. This dowry, together with the aforementioned antifactum, the said Gregory promised to the said Louis and the brothers, receiving in the aforementioned name, to give and pay, should the case arise for the demand and recovery of the dowry and antifactum. Now the case for the recovery of the dowry and the donation ante nuptias has arisen.

It is asked whether a woman can bring an action without cession? And it seems that she cannot, according to the common laws, which state that an action is not sought for one person by another, unless it is subsequently ceded, as in Inst. de inut. stip. § si quis alii; and fully noted in C. de act. et obl. l. 1; and l. ff. fam. haer. l. plane; ff. mand. l. si procuratorem § si; ff. de leg. 1. l. huiusmodi in princ.; ff. de pact. dot. l. inter socerum § pro se; ff. de leg. 1. l. huiusmodi in princ. For since it is special in certain cases to sue without cession, as in ff. de adopt. l. non alter and l. his verbis, therefore the common law is to the contrary, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. ius singulare.

Friend, consider that a woman, whom an outsider dowers, even without any stipulation, has a direct action on the stipulation, as in C. de rei uxoriae act. l. 1 § 1; much more so from a useless stipulation. The same is expressly proven in the same law, § accedit; and C. de pact. convent. l. ex more. And therefore it is ridiculous to doubt this, because it is a case of law in dowry. But regarding the donation propter nuptias, one might doubt, because no law expressly provides that the woman is deemed to have tacitly stipulated the donation propter nuptias; nevertheless, the same should be said regarding the donation, but for another reason. Namely, because in the contract of donation there is a special rule, as in l. 1 C. de don. quae sub modo. Furthermore, because since the words of the instrument state that the said Gregory gave to the said Francisca propter nuptias, it is presumed that the said Francisca was present; the text is in l. 1 C. de contrahenda et committenda stipulatione. And whether the arbiter or the judge pronounced the contrary, he was in gross negligence, because he ignored the law; and this is not an obscure law, but notorious to all experts in law, as in ff. de verb. oblig. l. sciendum; and Inst. de inut. stip. § si scriptum. And to confirm the foregoing, it serves ff. de verb. oblig. l. si procuratori praesentis. Nor is it expedient here to discuss the matter of the law case only. To the mother, to the mother. And this is the truth. And thus Lady Francisca has instituted a clear and evident action. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a doubtful substitution among children is to be interpreted as a fideicommissary substitution or as a pupillary substitution.
body: The words of the testator state: In the name of Christ. I, Peter, Henry, James, and Francis, in equal shares: so that if one dies without heirs descending from him, another shall succeed to the other, and each to the other. This notary was a very poor grammarian:

† It is doubted whether this substitution is pupillary, such that the mother is totally excluded. And it seems that it is not, because this substitution appears to have been fiduciary on account of those words, “without lawful heirs,” as noted in C. de impuberibus et aliis substitutionibus, l. precibus; and in Extra, de testamentis, c. Raynutius and c. Raynaldus. To the contrary, it seems from the ordinary gloss, which is in Inst. de pupillari substitutione, § qua ratione. That gloss expressly states that in pupillary age this substitution is pupillary. Moreover, this is proved by the following reasoning: where the glosses are contrary, the question is doubtful; but regarding this substitution there are contrary glosses; therefore this substitution is doubtful. Then I argue thus: a doubtful substitution among children is considered direct, as noted in ff. de vulgari substitutione, l. verbis civilibus, where there is a singular gloss. To the same effect, because in wills the more favorable part is to be chosen; but a pupillary substitution is favorable, whereas a fiduciary one is not favorable, as noted in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. ex tribus. Therefore, in doubt, this substitution is to be interpreted as pupillary. Moreover, this is confirmed by the wish of parents, who seem to confer as fully as possible upon their children, as in C. de fideicommissis, l. cum acutissimi; and ff. de bonis liberis, l. nihil, § facilior. Furthermore, a pupillary substitution is fuller than a fiduciary one, and therefore is to be embraced, as in ff. de hereditate instituenda, l. 1. Moreover, these words, “let them succeed one another,” are words of direct substitution; because properly a successor is he who succeeds to the universal right, as in C. de hereditate instituenda, l. si. Moreover, he is said to succeed in dominion and inheritance who succeeds directly, arg. ff. si ager vectigalis vel emphyteuticus, l. 1, § qui in perpetuum. Finally, this is expressed in c. si pater, de testamentis, lib. 6. The objection from the gloss in l. precibus does not hold, because that gloss must be understood when the testator did not proceed further to direct words; otherwise, if he proceeded further to direct words, because then it is a direct substitution, and the mother is altogether excluded, even though that condition “if without children” is added. The text is in de vulgari substitutione, l. centurio. From these it is concluded that the wife of the said testator must have only the legacies left to her, which she could have given to whomever she wished; and that she can claim nothing from the said legacies. ff. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, § sed nec impuberis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is the effect of a derogatory clause containing impossibilities? And is it to be regarded as not having been appended? And does a first will containing a derogatory clause revoke a second will?
body: The words appended in the first testament, under the heading "In the name of Christ," are stated as follows: the said testatrix, protesting that she does not intend, nor wishes, to make any other testament or codicil, nor does she intend to derogate in any way from the said testament; and if any testament should appear after the present testament, it shall not be valid, unless the entire psalter of the church were described therein. Then, after the lapse of almost ten years, the said testatrix made a second testament, prefacing it with these words: namely, she said that she wishes and commands that every testament made by her hitherto, and all her last will, be null and void; and that this present testament, and the contents thereof, remain in full force: instituting the same heir in all her other goods as in the first; and then appending a codicillary clause in the common form. Now the question arises, which of these testaments ought to prevail.

† Consider that the derogatory clause appended in the first will contains certain enunciative derogatory words, namely when it states that he does not intend, nor wishes to make, nor to derogate. Furthermore, it contains certain dispositive derogatory words, namely when it states that it shall not be valid, with a certain addition, namely unless, etc. For now, if you consider the enunciative words, they effect nothing: because intention and will can change; and it happens naturally and necessarily that the human soul does not remain in the same motions. Moreover, this occurs by law, that one can change, as in l. 1, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis; and l. diui, §. licet, de iure codicillorum; ff. de adimendis legatis; l. Quod iterum, ff. de legatis tertio; l. si quis in principio testamenti, ff. de legatis primo; l. si mihi et tibi, §. in legatis. But if you consider the dispositive words, namely the word "shall not be valid," the testator could not do this, that his last will should not be valid: unless it does not refer to the disposition of law, but to his own intention, saying that he protests that he does not wish it to be valid. However, if you join the enunciative words with the dispositive ones, this is the sense of the words: that from now on, just as from then, he does not wish it to be valid, unless that form of the description of the entire psalter is observed. But note this: unless, because this "unless" is impossible, or impossible due to excessive difficulty, and therefore this "unless, etc." is held as not added, as if he said "unless I touch the sky with my finger," as in l. 1, ff. de conditionibus et institutionibus. From which it follows that the derogatory clause remains only within its limits, namely derogatorily. From which it follows that whether we say that the said clause appended in derogation of laws is not valid, or in derogation of will, it has been removed by the subsequent similar derogatory clause as regards the generality of the words of affection and greater power, because later ones derogate earlier ones: and especially as regards legacies and pious causes, as in ff. de testamento militis, l. militis codicillis, §. veteranus; C. de legatis, l. datum; C. de fideicommissis, l. fideicommissum et institutio; de ademptione legatorum, §. Ego Baldus, i. cum similibus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The college consists of two parts out of three parts.
body: By the venerable statute of the corporation and artists of the University of Pavia, it is provided that all statutes are to be understood simply, as they sound; nor are they to be glossed, except according to the sense which they manifestly convey; nor may dispensation be granted regarding anything determined by statute, unless it be with the consent of three parts of the college of doctors. Furthermore, it is proposed that another statute provides that the voting doctors ought to be twelve, who have votes and receive salary; however, some may and ought to be received as supernumeraries in the said college, provided they are original doctors, or from the district, or the bishopric of Pavia, or outsiders, provided they are salaried and lecturing; and these supernumeraries may present and convene. Now it happens that, when the said college was convened, seven and the prior were present; all had been cited there, yet three were absent, while the others did not attend, with the exception of one who appeared after the proposal made by the prior, and objected; the number of all having full vote was thirteen doctors.

It is asked whether the person in question, who was a doctor of arts but not salaried, and was a Sicilian, may and ought to be received by the prior? Furthermore, it is asked whether, if he ought not to be received strictly according to the law, he may nevertheless be received by the said prior under these circumstances, especially since those absent are content that he be received. On these points many things could be said.

First, it appears that he may not and ought not to be received, both according to the common law and according to the form of the said statute. For in the proposed case, in the citation made by the prior, two parts of the college were not present; for eight do not constitute two parts. Therefore, the college was not duly assembled; for two parts publicly assembled constitute a college, and not fewer, as stated in D. Quod cuiusque universitatis nomine, l. Nulli; and C. De decurionibus, l. Denominatae formae; and fully noted in D. De regulis iuris, l. Aliud, § Refertur; and D. Ad municipalem, l. Quod maior.

Furthermore, according to the form of the statute: because the statute requires that three parts of the college of doctors consent; these words seem to denote a number of persons, as in C. Quod circa, De electione, in the Clementina. Hence, even if nine had been present, nevertheless three parts of the total number of the college did not consent; therefore, and as stated in C. Cum debeat stari, the first part is to be understood according to the evident face of the words without any other interpretation.

On the contrary, the truth itself appears to be otherwise: for although at the beginning there were only eight, a ninth person immediately joined them; and he was present in the subsequent act, while the speaker was speaking; and although he dissented, he nevertheless completed the number, as we say regarding arbitrators, since contradiction in presence is less harmful than absence, as stated in D. De arbitris, l. Tres. For the act was not consummated, since the discussion and deliberation on what was to be done were still ongoing. And thus it was not an act of exclusion, as stated in C. De fideiussoribus et instrumentis, l. Contractus; and C. De testamentis, l. Cum antiquitas. Hence it appears that the assembly was solemn and perfect, because more than two parts were present, not counting the prior.

From this it immediately follows that three parts of these two parts, which constitute the full college, could make the said deliberation according to the common laws cited above; moreover, the voices of the absent seem to have receded from the present and joined them, as singularly noted by Jacobus de Arena in D. De fideicommissis liberis, l. Si legatario, § A duobus; and it is expressly proven in Extravagantes, De electione, c. Cum nobis olim.

But assuming, and without conceding, that he ought not to be received by necessity, I say that he may be received by right, and ought to be received by courtesy. Here it must be considered that the form of the statute regarding reception says "may and ought"; thus it establishes a form for both necessity and power simultaneously through the conjunction. But does it not establish a form for power alone? And whatever is not imposed on the judge by necessity, seems also to be denied to his power, as stated in D. De iudicibus, l. Non quicquid; and l. 1, C. Quomodo et quando iudex.

Therefore, it seems to me that it is more advisable to desist from a rash contradictor than to impede the due honor. And especially since perhaps the said statute in some way savors of monopoly, as stated in Extravagantes, De praebendis, in C. Venerabilis, § Nos igitur; and Extravagantes, De constitutionibus, c. Omnes, § Mandamus.

It stands according to the common law that those absent beyond the jurisdiction are not to be cited, nor do those present impede this form of nomination. And this is noted in C. Praesentium, De testibus, lib. 6, in the gloss on the word "ipsorum".

Furthermore, it is certain that when there is doubt about the intent of the statute, the statute must be understood according to the common law, as stated in C. De noxali actione, l. Si servi; and Extravagantes, De consuetudinibus, c. Cum dilectus.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the penalty of the gibbet is a greater penalty than decapitation? and no. 4.
2. Any corporal penalty is greater than any pecuniary penalty.
3. When the law confiscates goods, this penalty arises by operation of the law.
4. To be deprived of burial is the greatest penalty.
5. In the penalty of the gibbet, goods are not included.
body: In the name of Christ.

† For the sake of clarity, it must first be premised that the penalty of the gallows is greater than that of decapitation, although through both penalties the soul is separated from the body.
