And for that reason soldiers who must lose their life on account of a crime are by custom decapitated, but are not hanged on the gallows, even for a crime for which a commoner is hanged. Thus the gloss notably states in l. desertorem, § 1, ff. de re mili.

† Secondly, I premise for the sake of clarity that any corporal penalty is greater than any pecuniary one, as is read and noted in ff. de poenis, l. in seruorum, § fin.; and therefore, when a comparison is made between a personal penalty and a pecuniary one, the personal penalty is always understood to be greater, as in C. de infa., l. et si seuerior, and ff. eo., l. quid ergo, § poena grauior, and it is most fully noted there.

† Thirdly, I premise for the sake of clarity that when the law confiscates goods ipso facto, that penalty occurs by the sentence of the law, although a judge's declaratory sentence is necessary, as in c. pro humani, de homi., lib. 6, and by the argument of ff. de iure fisc., l. eius, qui delatorem; and here it is customarily called a canon of latae sententiae, as noted in ff. de cap. dimi., l. amissione, § qui deficiunt. Fourthly, it must be premised that the decree of the lord speaks of extracting a banned person from a similar, equal, or lesser ban, as appears in the letter of the decree.

† But when a comparison is made between the penalty of the gallows and the penalty of decapitation, the penalty of the gallows is greater in reality, and more ignominious, because the penalty of decapitation is instantaneous, whereas the penalty of the gallows has some duration of time. Hence there is no doubt that it is naturally greater.

† Likewise because the body is not handed over for burial, and to be deprived of burial is the greatest penalty, as in C. de his, qui patrem, vel lib. occi., l. 1. To this two living reasons are added. For the penalty of the gallows here was greater in fact and effect, because it was executed, and he died a slave of the penalty. But the man concerning whom the inquiry is made is alive both naturally and also civilly, that is, de iure and de facto, since he is not within the power of the magistrate, as in c. pastoralis, de re iudi., in Clemen., and l. in laqueum, ff. de acquiren. rerum domi. Furthermore, these are two bans, one on the person, the other on the goods; because a penalty joined by the conjunction 'and' creates two sentences: one against the person, the other against the property; and each is deemed notable in itself. The text is in l. 3, C. si pend. appellatio. mors interuene., and the ordinary gloss in Authen. de armis, § oportet, colla. 6, and it is a very singular gloss. However, as to the capital penalty, there is no doubt that he is to be unbanned from it, even if perhaps he does not recover his goods; because with respect to goods it differs from the penalty of the gallows, in which goods are not included.

† This is the singular gloss in l. 2, C. qui testa. face. poss., since the penalty of the gallows arises from a private crime, not a public one, as the gloss elegantly notes in l. penult., ff. de condit. ob causam. From which it is evidently concluded that the aforesaid persons banned on the occasion of the said homicide, according to the words and intention of the decrees of our lord, and by the rigor of the law, and according to the points of reason, are to be radically freed from the capital ban and also canceled. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A sentence approved by the parties is not called a sentence, if the substantial solemnity was not observed in proceeding, but it has the force of a pact.
body: In the case of the illustrious In Christi nomine. tolini de Mandello, having seen the sentence passed with the consent of the parties by Dr. Bertrandum de Arnessario, etc.

† Considering that the case was not formally joined, nor was an oath against calumny taken, nor was any order observed regarding the substantial procedural steps, it is certain that the judgment was invalid, because although the parties consented to the judgment, they did not consent to proceeding with the substantial requirements omitted. And even if it were assumed that they had consented in all respects and in every way, their consent could not impede the legitimate order, as stated in the Code, *De litibus contestatis*, Authentica *Offeratur*; and expressly noted in the Decretals, *De officio delegati*, chapter *De causis*; and in the Decretals, *De libellis oblatis*, chapter *Primo*. It supports this what is noted in chapter *Saepe*, *De verborum significatione*, in the Clementine Constitutions. Hence it clearly appears that the said judgment does not have the force of a judgment.

But it must be examined whether the said consent is valid by the law of pact; and it must be said that to consent and to make a pact are not properly the same thing, as in the Digest, *De regulis iuris*, law *Aliud est vendere*; and in the Digest, *De manumissionibus vindicatis*, law *Si pater*, at the end. Nevertheless, sometimes consent operates the same effect as a pact; indeed, a pact is inherent when, by consent, delivery or quasi-delivery has taken place. For he who is fortified by a consensual delivery has a just exception, although a pact in itself is naked, as in the Digest, *De pactis*, law *Divisionis placitum*. And therefore, the said judgment, insofar as it is absolving, although the judgment itself is invalid, nevertheless, because the consent has the force of a pact not to sue, an exception opposes the plaintiff, if Dominus Vetolinus is in possession, as in the Code, *Communia utriusque iudicii*, law *1*.

It should not be said that this pact was made in court, because this is not a court proceeding, since the solemnity was not observed. Therefore, the consent remains in the form of a naked pact, from which, by civil law, an exception arises, not an action; but by canon law, an action arises, if nothing has been performed by the plaintiff, as in the Decretals, *De pactis*, chapter *Primo*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When and in what manner may an appeal be taken from execution? And whether execution is delayed by the appeal, even if it has not been admitted.
2. The clause, "we do not admit unless, and insofar as, and we are bound by law": how it is to be understood.
3. The word "unless": what it signifies.
body: In the name of Christ. A papal delegate, concerning the collation and assignment of a priory, after an appeal has been interposed, which appeal he does not receive except in the form which follows, namely: we do not defer, except insofar as we are bound to defer by law; he invokes the secular arm through the execution of the aforementioned collation. It is asked,

Whether, the facts being thus, the secular judge is bound, or may by right, obey the mandates: when the exception of surreption has been raised against the apostolic letters; and whether pronouncement has been made thereon or not: having seen the apostolic letters and the acts conducted in the case, it must be said that if a contradiction appears to the delegate appointed to confer, whether before he confers or afterwards, he who alleges that he possesses jurisdiction should not carry out the execution of the collation, unless he assumes the role of the judge delegate; because cognizance of the cause requires judicial determination, as is the text and the master gloss in chapter 1, *de officio delegati*, in the Clementine. And therefore he is bound to admit a reasonable appeal, which is from the actual execution, and it is valid, even if not formal. For in every executor who executes that which is outside the scope of jurisdiction, an appeal may be taken, provided a reasonable cause is stated, as in C. *quorum appellatio non recipitur*, l. *ab executione*. Although it would be otherwise in an executor who had no cognizance, as in Extra, *de re iudicata*, cap. *de caetero*, and *de appellationibus*, cap. *noverit*, unless he exceeded the limits of the commission in executing; and then it is not properly an appeal, but a certain recourse, since it is made by a non-judge, as in D. *qui satisdare cogantur*, l. *arbitro*, according to one reading.

Furthermore, it is most well-known in law that, pending an appeal from the final end of the litigation, nothing may be innovated. D. *nil novi fieri si appellatione interposita*, throughout; and l. 3, C. *de appellationibus*; and C. *de sententiis et interlocutoribus*, l. *cum solitis*; and D. *de minoribus*, l. *intra utile tempus*; and D. *de infamia*, l. *furti*, § 1. From which it appears that, in our case, since an appeal is pending, execution ceases, as in cap. *non solum*, *de appellationibus*, book 6. But beyond this, it is evident

It must be premised that when a judge states that we do not give credence to an appeal, except insofar as we are bound by law: and that he either grants refutatory apostols only, or mixed ones, namely refutatory and reverential ones. In the first case, it would seem to be said that the said apostols are simply refutatory; yet this is not true: because refutatory apostols are expressly stated, but tacitly included under the phrase "except" are admissive.

And this is due to the nature of the word *nisi* [unless]: because where it has a negative antecedent, it appears to affirm, as noted by the Doctor in the chapter *Peccatis*, *De regulis iuris*, Book Six, together with similar authorities. In the second case, there is no doubt when the apostolic letters are mixed, for the sense of the Apostolic letters is that we do not defer, that is, we ought not defer as a matter of right; but out of reverence we do defer. And the nature of such apostolic letters is that they are such letters of referral, yet modifying the referral, because out of reverence, they nevertheless advocate jurisdiction to you, if you would retain it, as in the chapter *Ab eo*, *De appellationibus*, Book Six. For example, when an appeal is doubtful, whether it holds as a matter of right or not, it must always be deferred; and if it is not deferred by the judge, it is deferred by law, as in the law *Si cuius*, *Digestum*, *De appellationibus recipiendis*. But here one cannot deny that there is doubt: because a question of fact becomes doubtful through negation, until the sentence passes into *res iudicata*, as in the law *Eleganter*, § *Si post*, *Digestum*, *De conditione indebiti*. Moreover, the examination of this truth has been transferred to the Pope by the interposed appeal, as in the *Codex*, *De tempore appellationum*, law *Per hanc*. And it should be observed that those words, "if and insofar as," depend on a future event, which must be declared by the appellate judge, and therefore interim suspension is required, as in the chapter *Secundo*, at the end, *Extra*, *De restitutione in integrum*, and *Digestum*, *De excusationibus tutorum*, law *Diximus*. Wherefore it follows that the invocation of the secular arm is supported by no law. And it must be considered that this impetration has no place except in notorious cases, from which one cannot appeal, and thus they are reduced to harmony, Innocentius and the Archdeacon, who seem to contradict each other, namely Innocentius in the chapter *Significasti*, *De officio delegati*, and the Archdeacon in the chapter *Ut officium*, *De haeresi*, Book Six. And the chapter *Ultra*, *De exceptionibus*, Book Six, supports this in its own reasoning. And this is especially so given the pendency of the aforementioned term of fifty days, which has not yet elapsed, as in *Extra*, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Personas*, and the words *extunc*; and what is noted in the said chapter *Cum appellationibus*, in the penultimate gloss, in the version *Sed elapso termino signato*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether ignorance excuses a vassal who did not request investiture within a year and a day, and what is the case regarding impotence. Numbers 2 and 4.
2. Whether a vassal who has fallen from his fief falls by operation of law itself, or whether a sentence is required.
body: A certain nobleman, by name, possessed a certain ancient and paternal fief for sixty years and more, computing the time of himself and his ancestors; and he died leaving an heir, who did not possess the said fief and who was ignorant that the things were feudal; for which reasons he did not request investiture within a year and a day. Whereupon the Abbot assigned the said fief to another and solemnly invested him. Therefore, a question arising concerning the said feudal things, the heir of the said nobleman alleges two things.

† the most ancient possession, without their ancestors ever having sought investiture: on account of which it is presumed free, unless it is proven that they possessed and prescribed by their own right; because every thing is presumed free, unless the contrary is proven, as noted in l. altius, C. de serv. et aqua, and by Dynus in l. si prius, de novi oper. nunc. Moreover, prescription runs for a period of forty years in good faith against the Church: in which case the intent of the possessor is examined, and not the intent of the person against whom prescription is claimed, as in C. ne rei dominicae, vel templorum, l. universas, and extra de praescrip., cap. de quarta. But if they knew the thing to be feudal, they would not prescribe at any time, as in C. de praescrip. triginta annor., l. male agitur. However, this person, concerning whom the question is asked, had a just cause for ignorance, as in ff. de reg. iuris, l. qui in alterius. Furthermore, it is alleged that even if the things were feudal, ignorance of fact excuses, because it is impossible for one who is ignorant to recognize the fief and seek investiture as of a fief. And thus it is that whenever ignorance of fact renders the act impossible both in law and in fact, no prescription runs, as in ff. de aedil. edict., l. cum sex; ff. de cal., l. annus; C. de capt. et postlim. rever., l. nec nos; ff. de condit. et demonstr., l. multum interest; ff. quis ordo in bon. poss. ser., l. 2, §. dies. And this is expressly stated in cap. primo, quo temp. miles, in the words “nisi iusta causa.”

† Moreover, there is a rule in the matter of fiefs that impotence excuses, as in the final chapter on fiefs, [stating that] without fault [a fief] is not lost; and the gloss there says that this is a notable word, for sometimes equity ought rather to be observed toward the vassal than the strictness of the law; nor does every occasion suffice for taking away a fief, as in the first chapter, § Si quis, [titled] On the causes by which a fief is lost. For one should not act with feudatories as with enemies, but benignly; for the origin of fiefs is a certain benignity and graciousness, as appears in the definition of a fief. And this is the very truth, that an impossible necessity of demanding the institution within a year does not lie against one who justly ignores the fact; because custom does not bind to the impossible, especially since nothing impossible should even be enjoined upon servants. For everything that is impossible falls away by reason of its impossibility, as in the sole law, C. de sententiis, quae pro eo, quod interest.

† Here also arises a certain doubt: namely, assuming that he has fallen from his right, whether he has fallen by operation of law itself, or whether a sentence is necessary: and the gloss determines that it is by operation of law itself, as I said in the aforementioned chapter, *Quo tempore miles*.

But another doubt remains: if the heir does not possess, but the church possesses, whether, if he does not demand investiture within a year and a day, he loses his right. And perhaps it can be said that he does not, because the church is not bound to render services; therefore, it is not bound to promise them to him, since he cannot enjoy them, just as a tenant is not bound to pay the rent if he has been expelled from the holding. Perhaps otherwise if he possesses. Thirdly, because his own negligence, in not pursuing his right, should not harm the lord; but certainly the heir was not here at fault for the loss of possession. And therefore, he who does not have the benefit should not bear the burden, as in C. de fur. l. manifestissimi, § cum in secundo. And it supports what we fully note in ff. loc. l. si uno, § item cum quidam. Therefore, if the lord cannot invest, because a third party possesses, the time for demanding investiture does not run against the vassal for eviction. And this statement is, I, Baldus, say, quite reasonable.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a donation made by a father to a son in his power is valid, even if an oath not to revoke it has intervened; and whether the father can revoke it; and what is the law similarly in the case of a daughter, to whom the father donated on account of a dowry, swearing and constituting himself as holding in the name of the daughter.
body: is for clarity,

† It must first be premised for clarity that a donation made to a son in power, even though the father states that he donates irrevocably and inter vivos, nevertheless is not valid from the beginning, but is confirmed by the death of the father, as in C. de inoffic. donat. l. secunda, C. de donatio. inter virum et vxor. l. donationes; and therefore it can be revoked by the father, because it has the force of a testamentary bequest, as noted in C. de collat. Authenti. ex testamento; for between a father and a son in power an alienation does not hold, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione l. 2, nor a civil obligation, as in ff. ad Trebel. l. Imperator, and ff. de conditio. indebi. l. frater a fratre, and ff. de fide instrumen. l. si quis pro eo §. primo, and ff. de vsu. l. pro donato l. prima §. si pater filio; and had an oath not been interposed, there would be no doubt. But on account of the oath it can be doubted: and first it seems that the oath is not valid, because, as I have said, it has the force of a testamentary bequest: therefore repentance has a place, as in extra de celebra. missa capitulo cum Marthe, and there this oath is customarily treated fully. Furthermore, the law says that it is a special rule regarding a dowry that a filius familias is capable, as in ff. famil. herciscund. l. Pomponius Philadelphus: therefore he is not capable of a simple donation; and an oath sworn to an incapable person is not valid, as read and noted in ff. de legatis tertio l. cum quis decedens §. Titia. Furthermore, the sale which the father later made is a necessary alienation on account of the necessity of the household estate, and by it the donation is not revoked, but the estimated value is owed, if it is equated to a legacy, as in ff. de legatis tertio libr. vndecimo §. si rem. If, however, it is equated to a donation between husband and wife, the donation is revoked, as in C. de don. inter vir. vxo. l. si maritus. To the contrary it seems that, because an oath is a spiritual matter, and in spiritual matters paternal power does not run, as in c. si annum de iudiciis libro sexto, therefore by such an oath, notwithstanding paternal power, the contract is validated, and ownership passes from it, as in capitulo secundo de pactis libr. sexto. Furthermore, a donation between husband and wife with the intervention of an oath and delivery transfers ownership, nor can it be revoked, as noted by Cyn. following Petr. in C. de sacrosanct. eccle. l. prima, in fine. Likewise, from this oath a right has been acquired for the daughter: therefore by the statute mentioned in the point at issue, the right is prohibited from being transferred to another. Wherefore it seems it should be said that the daughter ought to be preferred in the things donated and delivered to her through a constitution of precarium, which constitution of precarium the father cannot overturn, as in C. de acquiren. possessio. l. ex liberis. Furthermore, the father lost possession and transferred it to the daughter, as in ff. de acquir. possessio. l. prima §. si vir vxori. Therefore, all things considered, namely both under the ius commune and municipal law, and because an oath affects not only the person swearing, but also him who derives title from him, as noted in extra de iureiuran. capitulo cum contingat in the novella, the aforesaid daughter, on account of the force of the said oath, ought to be adjudged [preferred]. Yet this question is quite open to doubt, through those things noted by Bar., which can be alleged for and against in the said l. si quis pro eo; I hold what I have said, saving better deliberation: although from an oath no civil obligation arises, nevertheless a canonical obligation arises, which has the force of a civil and natural obligation, even between master and slave, Abbot and monk; thus such is the oath, which can be observed without prejudice to eternal salvation. To this points what is noted in extra de instit. capitulo cum venisset. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment rendered on a hypothecary matter is said to be definitive.
2. Whether a judgment rendered, which annulled a judgment rendered on a hypothecary matter because excussion was not made, is definitive or among interlocutory judgments.
body: The case is as follows: In the name of Christ. Titus brought an action of hypothecary against an outsider possessor, seeking to recover the things hypothecated to him. A final judgment was rendered in favor of this Titus, and the outsider possessor was condemned to release and vacate these pledged things, although an exception of excussion had been raised. An appeal was taken from this judgment, and in the appellate proceedings it was pronounced that the judgment was erroneous and the appeal well-taken, on the ground that a legitimate excussion of the principal debtor’s assets, which ought to have preceded, had not taken place. Furthermore, the parties had been absolved from costs due to the just cause of their litigation. From this judgment, an appeal was taken, with no cause inserted in the appeal. It is doubtful whether this judgment, in which it was pronounced that the judgment was erroneous and the appeal well-taken, on the ground that a legitimate excussion had not preceded, is absolutely interlocutory or definitive. If it is definitive, the appeal interposed therefrom is validly interposed; but if it is interlocutory, the appeal is improperly interposed, because no cause is inserted therein. Now, from the foregoing, it is asked of us whether this judgment, thus rendered, ought to be called interlocutory or rather definitive? Because the arguments on both sides have been touched upon very prudently, I do not repeat the arguments and proceed to the determination of the first point.

And I say that a judgment rendered on a hypothecary claim is definitive, and an appeal may be taken from it as from a definitive judgment. This gloss is ordinary, which generally determines this in any real action, as in D. de rei vend. in the last gloss, a gloss better than which is not found in law. And it is confirmed in D. debitor, § iussus, D. de appellatione. Secondly, I say that a judgment rendered to the contrary by the judge to whom the appeal was made, who pronounced that the judgment was wrongly given and the appeal well taken, is definitive. This ordinary gloss is still among the best that are in law. C. de sententiis et interlocutoribus omnium iudicum, l. praeses. And there the gloss sets forth the reason why it is definitive. And therefore, omitting circumlocutions, an appeal may be taken without insertion of the cause, as noted in C. de his quibus ut indignis, l. minoribus.

† Now I come to the second article, in which it is asked whether the principal defendant is presumed to be absent or present, and why the burden of proof lies upon him. I answer that being present or absent concerns the ease of summoning. And therefore, as the gloss on the Ordinance says, so do I say, that either they are of the same domicile, and this is called presence; or they are of different domiciles, and this is called absence, as is noted in the Authenticum *De fideiussoribus*, § *Sed neque*, in the gloss beginning *Praesens*, and it is noted from the fact that it is read and noted quite elegantly in the chapter *Statuisti*, § *Cum autem*, *De rescriptis*, Book Six. Finally, I was asked about such a doubt: whether, if during a pending appeal the principal debtor began to be absent, a judgment previously ill-ordered would become valid; and I do not believe that this suffices during a pending appeal, because this is a new fact entirely unconnected with the prior ones, the absent party being absent, as in the Code, *De temporibus appellationum*, law *Per hanc*. Although, if this had supervened during the first trial, it might perhaps have sufficed, because Alberico da Galeoto holds that excussion may be made during a pending trial by the confirmation of the judge himself, by the law *Si rem*, § *Fin.*, Digest, *De pignoris actione*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If there are many creditors and the debtor is not solvent to all of them, which of them are to be preferred? And which are to concur pro rata of the debt to the assets of the debtor.
2. A confession made before a judge has the force of a sentence.
body: The case is as follows: A., a citizen of the city of Pavia, debtor to several persons, broke his bank and his credit, and, unwilling or unable to answer or satisfy his creditors, took to flight. While in flight, not daring to enter the city and appear in public, he constituted himself debtor to Gay in the sum of a thousand, on account of a deposit, binding all his goods to the said Gay on account of the aforementioned cause. Then, after some days, having been granted a safe-conduct by the most observant and sufficient our lord, and having returned to the city, in the presence of the judge, the podestà, he confessed that he was, and had been at the times described in his books, a true debtor of Titius in the sum of a thousand, on account of a deposit, binding all his goods to the said Titius on the occasion aforementioned, constituting, etc. From the foregoing, it is asked, first, whether the instrument made by the said banker while in flight is valid in law? Second, assuming that it is valid to the prejudice of the said banker, is it valid to the prejudice of another creditor, to whom, in the second place, in the presence of the judge, he confessed that he was, and had been, a true debtor for another thousand, and to whom he bound all his goods, as is expressed above?

† First, it must be considered whether any obligation had previously existed in the person of the said Gaius at the time when the said money-changer constituted himself a debtor, or not. For if any true obligation had previously existed, say as follows below. But if no obligation had previously existed: then this *constitutum* is understood to have been made in fraud of creditors, and both it and the hypothecation of the goods ought to be rescinded. This is the case in l. 2, ff. *quae in fraudem creditorum*, and in Inst. *de actionibus*, § *item si quis in fraudem*. For if this is so in the case of a confessed dowry, which is privileged, such that the confession is presumed to have been made in fraud of creditors: as noted in l. *assiduis*, § 1, C. *qui potior in pignore habet*, and C. *de donationibus ante nuptias*, Authent. *sed iam necesse*. Therefore, all the more so in other cases. To this point, there are also very strong presumptions: first, flight, as in ff. *de conditione indebiti*, l. *si non sortem*, § *primo*, and ff. *de solutionibus*, l. *fugitivus*. Second, the large quantity, because one thousand, as in ff. *quae in fraudem creditorum*, l. *omnes*, § *Lucius*. Third, because a fugitive is presumed to be acting in bad faith, as in ff. *de suspectis tutoribus*, l. *impuberibus*.

But if a true debt had previously existed, then if this Gaius were the sole creditor, or even with many others, and the assets were sufficient to cover the debts, there is no doubt that the constitution of the debt would be valid: and also the hypothecation. Thus, in a hypothecary action, he who is prior in time is stronger in law, as in the rule *qui prior tempore*. And this is fully explained there by Dynus, with similar authorities.

But if the assets are not sufficient to cover the debts, then the rule is that when all unsecured creditors (*chirographarii*) are so from contract, satisfaction must be made to all pro rata, if they equally watch over obtaining their claims, as in ff. *de privilegiis creditorum*, l. *privilegium*. However, in the case of a deposit, it must be considered whether the deposited things or money still exist: and the depositor is preferred to all others. But if they do not exist, then the depositary is preferred to the lender (*mutuatarius*). But if all are from the cause of deposit, they come pro rata, as in l. *si ventri*, § *in bonis*, ff. *de privilegiis creditorum*. And these statements of mine regarding pro rata distribution are true, except in two cases. The first is when one creditor watched over his claim, and satisfaction was made to him by a willing payer: for he is not bound to share with the other creditors. The second case is when he watched over his claim and gained precedence by a judicial sentence: for by watching, he improved his own condition, as in l. *pupillus*, ff. *quae in fraudem creditorum*. For although recognition of the debt had previously been made to the said Gaius out of favor, nevertheless he who gained precedence by sentence, or its equivalent, seems to be stronger than him.

† for a confession made before a judge has the force of a judgment: and from it arises an action in factum; and therefore one could be persuaded that, if the confession made to the subsequent creditor is true and not simulated, this subsequent creditor appears to have first resorted to the protection of the judge and to have obtained it; and therefore he should be preferred, as having execution ready at hand, as noted by Dynus, Jacobus de Arena, and Bartolus in the aforementioned law *Pupillus*. This holds notwithstanding a hypothec constituted by another in fraud, as stated in the aforementioned law 2, *Digestum*, title *Quae in fraudem creditorum*, in the word *proponant*, as the gloss says, *rem hypothecando*, provided that all press their claims simultaneously; for this matter of preference is doubtful to me; but I have no doubt regarding the rate, according to what is proposed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How are the collected sums to be assessed and levied? And observance and time are held as truth.
body: it was observed to pay

† Just as it has been observed and paid hitherto throughout very long times, so in the future it must be observed by any possessor whatsoever: as in C. de agric. et censibus. l. litibus. libr. 11. where it is expressly stated. For these are real or mixed burdens that follow the things themselves, to whomever they may pass: as in C. sine censu, vel reliquis. l. omnes. C. de mulie. et in quo loco. l. prima. lib. decimo. ff. de impensis in rebus dota. factis. l. neque. ff. de vsufruc. l. si pendentes. §. si quid. For these are real burdens precisely because they are perpetual and ordinary, and they are imposed only upon the possessors, namely on account of the possessions that are in the territory: as in C. de muner. patrimo. l. prima. and l. fina. and C. de decurio. l. vacuatis. and C. de anno. et trib. l. omnes pensitare. and l. omnes omnino. And since the law is administered to the possessions themselves, it is lawful for the one holding jurisdiction in his own territory to use that jurisdiction, and to distrain, and to burden the possessors, and to sequester the fruits, and to do similar things, just as has been accustomed hitherto: as in C. de exactorib. trib. l. missi opinatores. and there is a notable text on this custom; and in Authenti. de mandatis princi. §. coges. Furthermore, if it is doubted whether these estates belong to his jurisdiction or not, the truth is presumed from ancient observance: as in ff. de vsuris. l. cum de in rem verso. For antiquity gives jurisdiction: as in C. de eman. libe. l. prima. and pure and mixed authority (merum et mixtum imperium): as is noted in ff. de iurisdictio. omnium iudic. l. more armorum. C. de diuersis offic. l. viros. by which law our question is sufficiently determined. Moreover, from the fact that payment was made for a very long time concerning these possessions as if within the territory, it is sufficiently proved that they are of the territory: because so many payments made over so very long a time are considered, as it were, to induce possession and prescription: as in extra de electione. cap. queleram. Indeed, time is held for truth, as the law is noted in l. prima. C. de serui. et aqua. From these matters it is apparent that, unless the debt is paid, the civil pledges, or grains, which have been lawfully seized or arrested, ought not to be returned. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The agreements between the lessor and the lessee are to be understood.
body: Agreement between the parties. In the name of Christ. The plaintiff speaks thus: Furthermore, if due to war or a breach of the Po River it should happen that the crops cannot be gathered, it shall be at the discretion of the said lessee to either abandon the crops or pay the rent, provided, however, that with respect to the lands sown with the lessee’s own oxen, the said lessee is bound to give one-third part to the aforementioned lessor. It happened that the said lessee gathered hay, wheat, barley, and spelt, and other crops that were to be harvested throughout the month of August. Then, in the month of September, a breach of the Po River occurred; and due to the flooding of the water, the said lessee could not gather any part of the millet and broomcorn millet existing in certain fields of the aforementioned possessions, nor any part of the re-cut hay, which is cut twice a year. On account of these things, the aforementioned lessee says he does not wish to pay the rent to the lessor, but, feigning a desire to abandon the lease, relies on the aforementioned agreement. The lessor replies that the rent is owed to him, because the lessee gathered the greater part of the crops, and almost all the crops; however, he offers a separate point, that if, according to good faith, he is bound to remit something from the rent, taking into account the damage, he is willing to remit that amount. Now the question arises: what is the law?

† And first, it appears that the lessee should uphold justice. I mean the justice of the agreement, which is greater than any other in contracts, as in D. 16,3,1 § si convenit (De deposito); and in C. 5,21,1 § si id, propter quod (Quae fuit prima causa beneficii amittendi), column 10. This is explained as follows: the final cause of the rent is derived from the whole, that is, from the fruits themselves, not from any particular harvest, because the agreement on the rent was conceived under a certain integral concept. But this final cause ceases; therefore, the promise ceases, as in D. 19,2,1 § inter locatorem (De locato). Moreover, the agreement is indivisible; hence, it suffices that some fruits are prevented, by argument from D. 10,2,1 § idem iuris (Familiae erciscundae). Furthermore, the lessor should impute the loss to himself, because he spoke in ambiguous terms; for he who speaks in ambiguous terms incurs the danger at his own peril, as in C. 8,53,1 (De donationibus promissis). Moreover, one must not depart from the words of the contract, because they are clear, as in D. 46,1,1 § 1 (De fideiussoribus); D. 45,1,1 (De verbis obligatis); C. 4,19,1 (De probationibus). Furthermore, this agreement is lawful, as it provides for future indemnity against fortuitous events, as in D. 18,1,1 § frumenta (De contrahenda emptione); and D. 18,1,2 in principio; and a certain fact in C. 3,31 (De iure emphyteutico). Moreover, fruits are not said to be gathered unless those of the entire year are gathered, because the fruit of the whole year is one, as in D. 24,2,1 § quod in semine (De soluto matrimonio). Moreover, it is lawful, even for one coin, to depart from a contract on account of an agreement, as noted in C. 1,3,1 (De sacrosanctis ecclesiis).

On the other hand, it seems that the judge, by his office, should reduce the rent and not depart from the rent entirely, as in D. 18,1,1 (De contrahenda emptione), unless the damage exceeded one-half, as in D. 18,1,1 (De contrahenda emptione). The words of the contract do not stand in the way, because they are not precise words; hence, they must be understood according to the nature of the contract, or at least according to the nature, so that they do not greatly exceed it, as in D. 9,2,1 (De damno infecto), where Jacobus de Arena says: "Note that the words of stipulations and contracts are to be understood according to the nature of the business being conducted," as here, and above in D. 9,2,1 (De damno infecto); and D. 9,2,1 § haec (De stipulationibus); and above in D. 19,2,1 § sed si verbo (De locato); and D. 10,2,1 § secundo (Familiae erciscundae), Jacobus de Arena. And although we could here entirely depart from the nature of the contract, because on account of excessive damage nothing would be reduced from the rent, nevertheless, a certain middle way should be assumed, and one congruent with the arbitration of a good man, namely, that the rent be reduced to the extent that the lost harvests would have been worth if they had been gathered. For to say the contrary would be very inequitable. It is certain that agreements must be interpreted according to equity, as in D. 17,2,1 (Pro socio). And I embrace this part as the more equitable. For in contracts of good faith, equity prevails more than excessive subtlety or dialectical argumentation. The conclusion is this: on account of particular damage, one departs from the contract to this extent, as in D. 19,2,1 § fin. (De locato); and D. 19,2,1 (De locato). And the aforementioned points are confirmed by convincing reason. For the words of the contract state that it is at the discretion, etc. But by the name of discretion is understood the discretion of a good man. The laws are common, but a good man never arbitrates that one should depart from the whole on account of a slight injury, but that it should be reduced to equity. And therefore, this case falls under the question in D. 18,1,1 (De contrahenda emptione); and D. 39,5,1 (De operis liberto); and C. 2,15,1 (De iureiurando). The counsel of Lord Baldus, and he had ten ducats. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. How the term "pro dimidia" is to be interpreted.
body: It is proposed that it was decided in the name of Christ that Titius should be invested with one half of a certain fief, and Sempronius with the other half of a certain fief.

† It is asked how the word “for a half” is to be understood: suppose, for instance, that the said fief consists in tithes, and thus in an incorporeal right. Furthermore, suppose that certain tithing lands exist and were formerly occupied; now it happens that a certain nobleman has occupied, as his own, half of the said tithing village: Titius says to Sempronius, “I wish to have my half in that part which is not occupied; you, however, Sempronius, must go against the occupier and there pursue your half.” Sempronius, however, says that both ought to have a share of the advantage and the disadvantage, although the renunciation was made for a half, speaking thus simply, since the investiture was made to each for a half in general. It is asked what the law is. I answer that Titius, who wishes to have the good things for himself and the bad things for his partner, has neither law nor equity on his side. And first, from the nature of co-ownership in undivided shares: because every clod of land pertains in undivided shares to each of the partners, as in D. de rei vend. l. Pomp. si ex aequis, and there fully noted; this is also fully noted in D. de ver. obl. l. qui Romae, § duo fratres, and is expressly proved in D. de leg. 2, l. Meuius, § duobus. Since the body [of the tithes] is not distinct between them with regard to the tithes, neither of them can say that he ought to receive more with respect to any particular body than the other. Moreover, these tithes are similar to the Falcidian fourth, which must be deducted from all things, and not from one thing, as is fully read and noted in l. 2, C. ad legem Falcid. Furthermore, this would be a leonine division, which ought not to be, because equality must be observed in dividing, as in l. 2, C. quoniam, et quib. quarta pars debetur, lib. 10, and the law expressly states that equalization must be made by mixing suitable and unsuitable estates; for those who possess or seek useful places must also accept deserted ones, as was decided in C. de omni agro deferto, l. qui utilia, lib. 11. Furthermore, co-ownership is properly in undivided shares; for once division is made, there is no co-ownership, but the things are entirely separated, as in D. commu. praed. l. si quis duas. Also, by the same reason that Titius wishes to be preferred to Sempronius, Sempronius ought to be preferred to Titius; for “what right each has,” etc., as in D. quod quisque iuris, l. 1, and Extr. de constit. c. cum omnes. Also, an equal has no authority over an equal, as in D. de arbitr. l. nam magistratus; hence no one can constrain his partner, especially to choose the worse, as in D. communi divid. l. Sabinus. And if it is said that he renounced half, therefore he must give half: this is not true, because these words induce nothing else than that they make him a partner in undivided shares in that right which the conceding party had, as in D. de contrahenda emptio, l. qui tabernas, and Extr. de donatio, cap. pastoralis. And thus, concluding from the first to the last, it is clear that the said Titius ought to have no prerogative, but ought to be equal in all respects with the said Sempronius, and Sempronius with him. And so I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a prorogated compromise is said to be one and the same as the first, or whether it constitutes something new; and if the oath was not specifically repeated in the prorogation, it is not understood to have been sworn again.
2. By reason of the prorogation, it is understood to be one and the same when both are of the same form and nature; otherwise, the contrary holds.
3. What the word "and" (et) and the like import.
body: The question is,

† In the name of Christ. A promise made with the addition of a certain term and a certain penalty, and with an oath corporally administered not to go against it: and finally, within the term, the said compromise was prorogated, after first narrating the contents of the first compromise, and not specifically mentioning any oath, except by adding the word “etc.” Whether the oath is understood to have been repeated, so that if one goes against the award rendered after the term of the first compromise, the violator may be called a perjurer, or may be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to observe the oath? And it seems that he is a perjurer, or may be compelled to observe the oath: because it is one and the same compromise, as in D. de precario, l. sed si manente. On the contrary, it seems that there are truly two compromises, as noted by the gloss and expressly stated by Master Cynus in l. si cum dies, in principio, D. de arbitris, and in his response to l. sed si manente, he says that the situation is different in a precarium, whose nature involves the addition of time, or at least a tacit understanding thereof. Solution. In our question, it must be said that the oath, since it is to be administered corporally and with express words, and this is the form given to it by law, is not understood to have been repeated, as in X. de iureiurando, cap. clericus. And I apply that chapter to the case thus: the first oath was limited in time, namely, if it should happen that the arbitration is made within the prefixed term; then afterwards, after an interval, the parties prorogated the term. Hence, what subsequently followed is not bound by the bond of the first oath, which was limited. And perhaps even if it were expressly said that he was bound by the same oath, provided that it was not expressly repeated in the form in which one ought to swear: because it is one thing to say “under the same oath,” and another to say “to swear once.” This is the case in the said chapter clericus. Otherwise, if it had been done in the first compromise by determining the prorogation. And the reason for the distinction is evident, because an oath does not extend to matters about which there was no thought at the time of the oath, but it does extend to matters about which there was thought, or which ought to have been considered by the nature of the act, as noted there by Bartolus and Innocentius. Moreover, to swear without having seen or examined the facts would be foolish, as argued in D. de transactionibus, l. de his. And therefore, according to Hostiensis, it should not be presumed to apply to such cases. To the same effect: D. de auro et argenti legato, l. si ita; and what is noted in D. de verbis oblig., l. qui Romae, § duo fratres. Moreover, to swear is something odious and perilous, and therefore should not be extended, according to Ioannes Andreas. Furthermore, if we wish to see whether it is the same compromise or not: either we speak regarding the truth of the terms, or the form, and it is not the same compromise, because whenever something is added or subtracted, it is in some way a new thing, as in D. de iustitia et iure, l. ius civile; D. de locato, l. cum in plures, § lege dicta; D. de praetoria stipulatione, l. Valerianus; and it is expressly stated in C. de nova, l. fin. Or we speak regarding interpretation and extensive fiction: and then it is the same compromise, because it had this capacity for prorogation from the beginning, and therefore, although the pecuniary penalty is understood to be repeated, as noted in l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a Proculo, by Innocentius in X. de appellationibus, c. praeterea, nevertheless the rule is different regarding the penalty of perjury, which is perilous and greater than any pecuniary penalty.

† Moreover, this is confirmed by the following notable doctrine: for, by reason of prorogation, one and the same thing is understood when both are of the same form and nature; otherwise, if they are not of the same form and nature, as is elegantly noted in c. Hi qui, Auth. de prebendis, 6. But here the prorogation was not of the same form, because it was without an oath; therefore, why should not one and the same compromise be understood?

† It is no objection, and I say and so forth, because this wording implies matters that are natural or customary among prudent persons. But to swear upon sutures, and without having seen them, is not the custom of prudent men, as I said above, nor is it of the nature of a compromise; rather, it is contrary to the nature of a compromise, as stated in the Code, *De arbitris*, in the Authentica *Decernimus*. But those things which are done contrary to nature are not understood to be tacitly repeated, according to the common doctrine; therefore, etc. Moreover, those who prorogated the term expressly stated a pecuniary penalty; they said nothing about the penalty for perjury; therefore, it must be considered as omitted, as stated in the Digest, *De fundo instructo*, in the law *Quaesitum*, § *Idem respondit*. From which my conclusion is clearly verified, namely, that here the oath is neither understood nor can be understood as repeated by the words used. And therefore, discussion regarding its observance is in vain. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A daughter dowered by her father renounced the paternal inheritance to her brothers with the consent of her parents: the brothers having died during the lifetime of the father, can she have a share of the inheritance, notwithstanding the renunciation? And whether such a renunciation was valid, even with a thousand oaths.
2. Can a daughter who, after the death of her brothers, renounced to her father accepting for himself and his heirs, obtain a share of the paternal inheritance after the father's death, notwithstanding the said renunciation? And what is the law regarding feudal or emphyteutic property, whether such a renunciation extends to it, no. 3.
4. Whether a division is presumed from ten years' possession.
body: was dowered by her father,

† A certain young woman was dowered by her father, wherefore, with the consent of her parents, she renounced to her said brothers the paternal and maternal inheritance; these brothers died during the lifetime of the father and mother. The question is asked: does the said renunciation harm her? And it seems that it does, because the said renunciation passed into a pact and contract inter vivos, as appears from the form of the renunciation, as in ff. de donat. causa mortis l. cum ita donatur; therefore, it passes to the heirs of the said brothers, as in ff. de probat. l. si pact. and ff. de pact. l. iuregentium § pactorum. To the contrary is the truth, because in the paternal and maternal inheritance the said brothers have no heir: since they died during the lifetime of the father and mother, whence they neither succeed themselves nor make others heirs. Wherefore, the said renunciation and pact is in the condition of a caducary gift (caducum), as in C. de cad. tol. § pro secundo. Furthermore, that renunciation and pact were referred to the time after the death of the parents, because during their life one cannot succeed them, since no living person can have an heir. And even if a thousand oaths were sworn, that which is naturally impossible cannot be made possible by an oath, as in ff. de pact. l. iuregentium § pactorum; and therefore it is impossible that anyone should be excluded by a renunciation from a future succession, except only when the succession is opened, and not before, as in ff. de condi. et demonstra. l. Titius vsufru.; unless one were to say that she renounces the future hope: and such a renunciation is valid, because it is de non succedendo, according to Bartolus; it is otherwise in a pact de succedendo, because it induces the desire to seek another's death (votum captandae mortis); and it seemed to that distinguished doctor, my teacher, that this opinion of his is valid at civil law, as he holds in l. fin. de pact. and ff. de verbo. oblig. l. stipu. hoc modo. But note this, because the aforesaid doctor considers only one extreme, which is on the part of the person renouncing, but he does not consider the extreme on the part of the person receiving the renunciation. For the latter treats of expanding a future succession through the renunciation; and therefore it cannot be denied—since a pact is the consent of two parties—that the person receiving the renunciation acts contrary to good morals, unless those concerning whose succession the agreement is made consent, and persevere in that consent until death, as in the said l. fin. C. de pact. And therefore those err who believe that such an oath is valid, as noted in C. de colla. l. pact., unless it is made between others who contract regarding a future succession with the consent of the parents concerning whose succession the agreement is made, in which consent they persevere until death; but with respect to the parents themselves, a renunciation in their favor would not be binding even with an oath under civil law, though it is otherwise under canon law. But in the former case, where a pact is made concerning the succession of a third party, the oath effects nothing, because it is against good morals; and with this distinction c. quamuis lib. 6 must be understood, joined with c. non est obligatorium de re iu. in the same compilation. And these things are true not only while the father is living, but also if his death is uncertain, as in C. de captiuis l. nec nos. Likewise, an oath made against the force and authority of the laws does not hold, as in ff. de leg. 1. l. si quis inquilinos § vlt. and fully noted in C. de pact. l. pacta, quae contra, where it is remarkably said: the same if a brother acts against other parts of the law. But certainly that interpretation does not please, for the text there says that this pact made to the father by the daughter is one which the civil law disallows. But according to you it does not disallow, but approves it, as in the said l. fina. C. de pact.; therefore your interpretation is not good. The solution is clear from the aforesaid: because either the pact is made with the one to whom succession is to occur—and so that chapter speaks—or with a certain third party; and then either with the consent of the person whose succession is treated of and who perseveres in that consent, and the oath is valid; otherwise not. Now, returning to our case: because the brothers ceased to exist in the nature of things, the principal pact fails, and therefore also the oath, which is its accessory, especially since those things which ought to be considered in a pact cannot be denied, as noted in C. de pact. l. creditori tuo; therefore, when the donee dies during the life of the donor, the pact is dissolved, as in l. non omnis ff. si certum peta. Likewise, the rule is such that that pact is personal which does not pass to the heir; but this pact does not pass to the heir of the said brothers, therefore it is not personal—for the rule is given that what is personal does not pass to the heir, as in ff. de pactis d. § pactorum and l. qui in futurum § si ex altera [and] l. auus in the same title, and C. de rei vxo. actio. l. rem in praesenti § videamus. From which it is clearly concluded that the said renunciation does not prejudice the said young woman who renounced. Nor are we within c. quamuis, because she in no way comes against the oath. The second question follows under these terms:

† because a certain other young woman, after the death of the said brothers, renounced into the hands of the parents—who were receiving for themselves and their heirs—their inheritances both by testament and intestate, with an oath and at the time she was dowered, this cause having been inserted: namely, because she confessed and was content that she was sufficiently dowered and had the legitimate portion due to her; and the words of the renunciation and pact were very broad. Eventually the father, concerning whose succession the matter is treated, died intestate, leaving certain non-dowered sisters; and it is true that this woman who renounced, since she was a minor, did this with the authority of a curator and with a judicial decree. Now this woman who renounced wishes to succeed along with the other sisters and to collate her dowry. It is asked whether she can. And it seems that she cannot, because the case falls under the said c. quamuis, because no one can return to that which they decided to renounce, as in ff. de aedil. edi. l. quaeritur § si venditor; for the said renunciation was referred to after the father's death; hence it accrues to the non-dowered sister just as if the renunciation had been made after the father's death, because the acts of parties operate according to the time to which they are referred, as in C. de don. ante nup. l. quod expensae. To the contrary, the truth seems to appear, for great consideration must be given in such renunciations to whether a person exists who, by the presumed will of the father, excludes the one renouncing, and then the renunciation harms her—for example, if a male son exists, as in ff. de pac. l. tale pactum § fi.; it is otherwise if there does not exist a person who excludes the one renouncing coming from an intestacy based on the father's presumed will: for suppose that neither a son nor a daughter existed, but only the fisc, or some who were not of the children, would the daughter be excluded? I do not think that case was contemplated, because it is the case in the said l. tale pactum § sin. Suppose that at the time the dowry was given the estate was smaller than at the time of death, so that, upon consideration, she does not have the legitimate portion, which was the final cause of the renunciation: surely, when the final cause of the renunciation ceases, its effect ceases, arg. ff. de vacatio. mun. l. his honoribus § auctis. Likewise, this renunciation is odious, and matters that are odious should rather be restricted than enlarged. Likewise, it must be subtly considered here, because either we do not consider the renunciation as a simple renunciation—and then it is not valid, as in l. is potest ff. de acqui. hęr.—or as a pact of not suing (de non petendo), and then it does not exclude the right of entering upon the inheritance. But she can enter upon the paternal inheritance. But what if she assigns as heir, and the exception of the pact would stand against her, except that the father received the renunciation for himself and his heirs, and by dying intestate the law of the Twelve Tables and the tacit will of the father, since she is among the sui and necessary heirs, make her an heir? Therefore, although she was rejected as a daughter, nevertheless, from the tacit will of the parent which supervened after the pact at the time of the father's death—because at that point the father seems tacitly to have instituted her—she is certainly admitted, just as if she had been expressly instituted; not simply as a daughter, but from the supervening will of the parent, as in ff. de iure codi. l. si quis cum nullum; whence it seems to be clearly concluded that the said sister succeeds together with the other sisters by collating her dowry. Likewise, natural equity and the father's equal affection toward his daughters dictate this, argu. l. 2 C. de inoffi. testa.; and the distinguished Doctor, dominus Bartolus de Saliceto, my honored brother, subtly says this in a consilium on the same point. But I also do not omit this: that the said girl was a minor, and that a curator cannot be granted for donating, nor can a judge interpose a decree; and therefore if the statute required a decree and the authority of a curator along with an oath, the statute would not be satisfied; the text is express, C. si maior factus l. fi. § cum autem. But because perhaps the said subtlety might not please many with respect to paternal proper, or allodial, goods, it follows to see concerning the third. Therefore,

† the third doubt follows, namely: what about emphyteutic goods, if the instrument states that he receives the emphyteusis for himself and his descendants? And briefly, without doubt it must be said that the said renunciation does not extend to emphyteutic goods for three reasons tending toward the same conclusion. First, because the said goods are not acquired by hereditary right, although there are opinions on this; nevertheless, Bartolus so confirms in l. Gallus in prin. ff. de lib. et posth. and ff. de ope. lib. l. vt iusiurandi § si liberi. Second, because a new emphyteusis is formed in the person of the children, as in ff. de verb. ob. l. stip. ista § si quis ita and C. de vsufr. l. fi. Third, because this is express: that although someone renounces a paternal inheritance, he does not renounce a fief, unless by the phrasing of the words or interpretation of the law he ought to be an heir; so c. primum an filius, vel agnatus col. 10 is understood. But look subtly at the words of the contract; for in that emphyteusis a legitimate portion is not due, but the whole, not a quota, to all daughters, as noted in l. etiam ff. sol. mat.; and therefore the mention of the final cause, that is, of the legitimate portion, does not pertain to emphyteutic goods, because when the words of a contract are removed, the rights of the contract are removed, as in ff. de contrah. em. l. qui tabernas. Several questions are asked,

† and first, whether a division is presumed from a ten-year possession held as divided? And it must be said that it is, because to possess is an act of fact intervening from both sides. And the ordinary gloss determines this in l. pen. C. communi diui., although some who do not understand say the contrary, stating that a contract is not presumed from mere sufferance, not considering that when sufferance is related to sufferance, a kind of exchange results, in which a division is inherent. From these things the solution to the other doubts depending on the aforesaid is apparent. On the point of the lady de more, who was left as heir, it must be said, matters being as they are, that she was left as mistress (domina), as in l. his verbis ff. de haer. inst. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What remedies are to be pursued for incorporeal rights.
2. Whether the possession of a community can be proven by peasants using the forest.
3. Whether witnesses concerning the community are competent witnesses.
body: It must be premised in the name of Christ.

† Sometimes a petitory action is proposed, and not a possessory one; sometimes a possessory action, and not a petitory one; sometimes both; sometimes the office of the judge is proposed; sometimes a negative action is proposed for incorporeal rights. The first two members are clear, from those things which are fully read and noted in D. de acquirenda possessione, l. naturaliter, §. nihil commune; and D. de iudicibus, l. si de vi; C. de rei venditione, l. ordinarii; and C. de interdictis, l. incerti. The fourth member, concerning the office of the judge, is proved in l. si, D. de officio procuratoris Caesaris; D. de variis et extraordinariis cognitionibus, l. de usu aquae. There is also another mode of proceeding, namely by an action for injuries, as in D. de iniuriis, l. iniuriarum, §. fin.; and D. de actionibus emptoris, l. qui pendente. And the difference lies in whether an interdict or the office of the judge is proposed. For even in the interdict *uti possidetis*, the submission of a libel and the joinder of issue are required, as in Inst. de interdictis, §. hodie. Moreover, in these cases, he prevails who proves that he possessed at the time of the joinder of issue. This may be done either continuously, by continuing the old possession; because he who formerly possessed is presumed in the interdict *uti possidetis* to possess today, unless the contrary is proved, as in Extr. de probationibus, c. licet causam; and noted by Odofredus and by Cynus in C. de probationibus, l. siue possidetis. But in the office of the judge, in this case, a libel is not required; but a simple petition and proof, as noted by Speculum in tit. de petitorio et possessorio, §. pen., versi. in summa not.; and it is expressed in l. liberis, §. vlt., D. de libellis causae, according to Andreas de Pisis. Secondly, it must be premised for clarity, that it is easy to prove that individuals possess, for example Peter or John, because the whole matter to be proved consists in sight; for the land is seen, and the acts of men are subject to sight and are perceived by ocular faith, as in D. de verbis obligatorum, l. stipulatio ista, §. hi quoque; and noted in l. 1, §. 1, D. de itinere, actuque privato. But to prove that a corporation possesses, this is difficult, because a corporation is a name of law, and not of persons, as noted by Innocentius in Extr. de sententia excommunicationis, c. grauem. Moreover, because although individuals possess, nevertheless the corporation does not possess, unless it is proved that they had a mandate from the corporation in council or in assembly, as in l. 1, in fin., and l. 2, D. de acquirenda possessione, according to the gloss and Bartolus; and D. de dolo, l. sed ex dolo, §. 1; and D. de re iudicata, l. aliud, §. refertur. It is true that the gloss...

It raises a doubt whether possession of the universitas is proved by peasants using the forest: and it must be said that yes, if they possessed in the name of the universitas with the knowledge of the universitas, otherwise not, as noted in l. sicut, § 1, quod cuiusque universitatis nomine. And because the universitas can do nothing in its own right, it must be known that the ratification or consent of its administrators proves their knowledge, as is read and noted in ff. ad exhibendum, l. tingi, § Item. Having thus premised these two points, another matter follows. For clarity, it must be premised that in a possessory action, whether for retaining possession or in the judge’s office aimed at removing the injury of the disturber, it is impossible for the universitas to win unless the aforementioned elements representing the universitas are proved: and therefore it is impossible for the Gabiani to win in this possessory action; namely, because what they possess as a universitas is neither pleaded nor proved. Moreover, that individuals possessed is uncertain, and who these individuals are is uncertain, and uncertain proof is no proof; because a person in general does not possess, but a certain person, as in extra de probationibus, c. licet causam. Moreover, because here the matter concerns possession of territory and jurisdiction, it is evident that the territory of a castle cannot be possessed by individuals, nor jurisdiction, since it is of public law, as appears expressly in l. 1, in fine, ff. de acquirenda possessione. Moreover, because nothing has been claimed by the men of Fontaneto, nothing can be adjudicated to them. This is the ordinary gloss and the statement of Azo in l. 1, C. uti possidetis, namely Azo in his Summa and Accursius in the gloss beginning precario tenet, in the verse sed pone. According to the natural rule of judgments, which is that nothing can be adjudicated to one who claims nothing, as in ff. de exceptionibus rei iudicatae, l. si inter me et te. And this is held by Hostiensis and Ioannes Andreae in cap. ex conquestione, de restitutione spoliati, upon deep discussion. Nor do proofs without a libel avail as to the effect of victory as a plaintiff, because they were made without the contestation of the lawsuit, as in extra de lite contestata, cap. primo, and extra de electione, cap. dudum. Having thus shown that the community and the men of Fontaneto cannot win as plaintiffs, let us see whether they can win as defendants. And for clarity, the tenor of the public instrument must be premised, by which it is provided that the commune, universitas, and men of Fontaneto approved and ratified a certain compromise and the award following therefrom, which they made with the lords of Gabiano, namely lords Jacob and Thomas, who were then lords of the said castle, from whom the present nobles, their sons, are known to descend; present and receiving peace, settlement, and a pact not to sue regarding all their right and the remission of the said commune, and regarding everything and whatever the said commune and men of Fontaneto could claim and demand in the island and pasture, etc., concerning which things there is now controversy, as can be seen at a glance, and as appears from the boundaries, as in ff. de censibus, l. forma. In which instrument there is a constitution of precarium: hence the universitas could never interrupt possession, nor did it interrupt the said nobles, as in C. de praescriptione triginta annorum, l. male agitur. And in this matter, the older the possession, the better, as is read and noted in ff. de probationibus, l. census, and extra de probationibus, c. causam. Hence there is no doubt that any possession made by the commune and men of Fontaneto would benefit the said nobles of Gabiano, because he possesses in whose name possession is held, as in ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. quod meo. Moreover, as to the possession of the said nobles, nothing has been proved adversatively, as appears evidently from the premises to anyone not closing the eyes of the intellect. And the said nobles’ possession is certain, and the community of Gabiano has their consent and cause: hence without doubt they are the victors. Nor let anyone say that the libel is ill-formed, because the ordinaries form such a libel in l. Aurelius, § centum, ff. de libellis legatorum, and in the Speculum and all authorities; moreover, it has all the substantial elements of a libel: therefore the libel is well-formed, as noted in l. 1, ff. de edendo. Moreover, it cannot be answered that dominion over the things, territory, and jurisdiction is not proved by possession of so long a time, because more than thirty years have elapsed continuously from the time the said instrument was made until now, as in C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis, l. si. Moreover, he who gives me a title cannot raise a question of dominion against me; nor he who obligates himself to me, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. non unde originem, and ff. communia, l. ita ut si fur, with the common opinion. From which, since the said libel is founded on the substance of truth and on the true strength of proofs, no competent man can deny that the nobles of Gabiano and the men of Gabiano ought to prevail. And this second opinion is the most true.

But neither is it to be omitted regarding the witnesses, whether those who are to be produced on behalf of the men of Fontanet are suitable. And if their syndicate and procuratorship are examined, it must be said that they are not; because the mandate concerns universally all, and individually each one: and the articles are framed in these terms; and therefore the individuals cannot be plaintiffs and witnesses. Nor is it necessary to resort to the statement of the Speculum and others on the question whether individuals of a corporation may testify in a case of the corporation, because this is a mixed case, both in the name of the corporation and of the individuals, as is noted by Bartolus in l. 4, § actor, ff. de re iudicata. Moreover, the statement of the Speculum received a limitation regarding advantage, as is fully noted by Cynus in ff. de rerum divisione, l. in tantum, § universitas. It accords with what is noted by Bartolus in l. deferre, § idem decreuerunt, ff. de iure fisci. Furthermore, he is not a procurator, but an individual plaintiff, as in ff. de procuratoribus, l. filius, § veterani, there: "or he who [pursues] a common cause," etc. I add this, so that nothing concerning contingencies is omitted. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. An arbitrator cannot order either of the parties to sell or relinquish his property for the other.
body: In the name of Christ. Having examined my opinions, in which I said

† that an arbiter and arbitrator cannot order either party to concede its right to the other for a determined or undetermined price, or in exchange for giving or remitting some other thing, because this was not submitted to compromise, nor does it pertain to the sequence of the matter submitted to compromise; and because it is an injury to compel someone against their will to alienate their property or to concede it to their adversary even for the highest price, as in C. de iure delib. l. nec emere, and ff. de rei vendi. l. nec quasi; and such an arbiter not only exceeds the bounds of the submission, as in ff. de arb. l. non distinguemus § quaesitum, because the submission was not made for selling or conceding the property, but for putting an end to the lawsuit, and also because there is an express error in the award, since it is contrary to the said lex nec emere. Finally, a certain confirmatory sentence ensued, in which the said award is pronounced valid, and that it contains no cause among the inserted causes, namely because the said award is equitable, notwithstanding what was said concerning buying and selling, because no mention is made in the award of buying and selling, but only these words are stated: that by way of recompense for the price of the value of the said plain, of the castle, and the value of the aforesaid things, he halts and annuls certain proceedings and remits certain penalties; wherefore this judge pronouncing says that these words do not smack of buying and selling, where a thing and a price are required; and therefore the reasoning alleged in my legal opinion does not hold. One must marvel at that sentence, because I have said, and I say, that he cannot take away ownership from a party to the compromise for any price consisting in a donation or remission, nor even order in any manner that someone abandon their property for another thing, whether this falls under an innominate contract by reason of price, or under an innominate contract. The case is in the said l. nec emere, which the bleary-eyed and the barbers know. Likewise, no one has ever said that an award which exceeds the bounds and nature of the compromise is valid. But even if that award had been rendered for the sake of peace, it would still not be a good peace to work evident injustice and with great detriment; for to say, 'if you wish to have peace, go without your property' is not a juridical statement, even if uttered with whatever contrived intention. Furthermore, the said judge added this new reason in confirmation of the said award: namely, because he said that the said commune, by violently selling the said plain and despoiling the said Antonio of the peaceful possession in which he was, the men and the said commune lost all right that they had—at which reason any intelligent person ought to marvel, because through l. si quis in tantam one does not forfeit one's right ipso iure, but only when a privative sentence has been pronounced, an action having been brought under that lex; which sentence I do not find in the acts, nor even a libel brought upon the said l. si quis in tantam; wherefore it is certain that an owner does not forfeit his right except through a sentence, as is noted there. Secondly, because it has not been proved that the said commune, to which the plain belongs, inflicted any violence, because it has not been proved that this was deliberated in the council of the universitas, nor that any violence was inflicted in the form of a universitas; wherefore a universitas does not forfeit its right on account of the delict of certain persons, as is noted in l. aliud § refertur ff. de re iu., along with the common learning which is known to all. Thirdly, because the said men continued their ancient possession, always held and continued from the time of the predecessors of that nobleman; wherefore it is lawful by one's own authority to enter into possession, as in l. j C. unde vi, and l. sed et si quemcunque ff. ad l. Aqui., and ff. quod vi, aut clam. l. si vitem § qui ad ianuam, and l. si servus C. quod cum eo. Fourthly, because this judge pronouncing is contradictory to himself; for if the community had forfeited its right, therefore nothing ought to have been given to it in recompense, as in the said l. si quis in tantam; therefore the award contradicts the confirmation and the confirmed award, and by reason of perplexity it is invalid, as in ff. de reg. iu. l. ubi repugnantia. Since therefore the aforesaid things are said to be true, and the acts speak to this, there appears not merely an error, but a sufficiently great fault on the part of the said judge pronouncing, or little consideration of the acts. And therefore the said pronouncement ought without doubt to be revoked, and by this the said peasants, standing apart, offer to abide by the opinion of any college that is not suspect. And thus I, Baldus, say and advise.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. A father's promise to his daughters that he will make them heirs is not valid.
body: In the name of Christ. The fact is as follows: Cechinus de Collesimo had three daughters; he married off one, and subsequently married off the others, keeping the youngest born in the house and taking her husband into the house. Then he drew up his solemn testament, in which he instituted two daughters as his heirs in their dowries and beyond; but the daughter remaining in the house, named Federica, he instituted as his universal heir. Afterwards he died, as appears by a public instrument written by the hand of Peter, notary present, and who exercised the office of the notary for thirty elapsed years. After his death, Federica his daughter, instituted as universal heir, entered upon the inheritance of her late father, meddled with it, and possessed it peacefully as time went on. The other two married daughters of Cechinus say that the goods of the late Cechinus their father belong to them pro rata, because they say that Cechinus married off the firstborn, and that he promised to her husband, stipulating in a notarial form, that if he should die without legitimate male children, that very first betrothed bride, together with the other daughters to be married, would succeed pro rata per capita; and they tendered a libel in the action communi dividundo, seeking that the said Federica divide with the other sisters all goods, rights, and actions. On the part of Federica it is excepted that the instrument is null both in respect to the author and drawer, as well as in respect to the form and substance, because he is not, nor can he be, a notary; and he also delivered the instrument to the parties in another form than that which was produced in judgment. It is asked what the law is. It is not
† expedient to allege so many words: because the case falls under l. pactum, quod dotali. C. de pactis., to the effect that the pact is not valid. And therefore the consilium is true. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If a house, leased for the use of a grammar professor, was recommended by the teacher himself to a certain prudent young man, and was subsequently burned down by accidental fire, whether the teacher is liable, or the young man, or neither, for the damage to the house to the lessor.
2. Declaration regarding the fact that fires usually occur due to the fault of the inhabitants.
3. Who is bound to prove that the case was fortuitous, the lessor or the lessee?
body: A certain master, in the name of Christ, having left the school, entrusted to a nephew of his, who was an adult of twenty years of age, yet industrious and discreet according to his age, and his disciple, the charge of diligently guarding the house and the money. This nephew, following the custom of schoolmasters, had beds there in order to visit the chambers of the scholars, just as the master himself was accustomed to do, and to have the lights extinguished at night. He visited the chambers at the appropriate hour and found only one light, which he had extinguished. Finally, during that night, a fire broke out from below and burned down the house and all the master’s goods of great value contained within. Compensation for the damage is sought from the said master. The question is: what is the law regarding the lessor of the said house?

† It must be considered that this claim can be founded on two grounds. First, on the action arising from a lease (ex locato), in which the nature of the contract does not encompass even the slightest fault (culpa levissima), as stated in the Digest, Title on Lease and Hire, Law "If as a certain," Section "This must be seen."
