Second, on the action under the Lex Aquilia, in which the slightest fault is considered when committed by an act (committendo), but not by an omission (negligendo), as stated in the Digest, Title on Usufruct, Law "If anyone's," Section "Finally." We adhere to the text and not to the gloss, because according to the text, that Section is always cited to the effect that the action under the Lex Aquilia is granted for damages caused by an act, not by an omission, according to Doctor Raynerius and others. Therefore, it must be seen whether this master was at fault in any way; and if he was at fault, whether it was slight or the slightest fault. And it appears that he was at fault in a grave manner, or at least in a slight manner, because he should not have entrusted such care to a boy; since naturally such an age is not governed by itself, but by a procurator, because it is established that they do not have full diligence, as stated in the Law and noted in the Digest, Title on Institutions, Law "But if anyone," Section "Pupil." Moreover, one who negligently entrusts his thing to a friend must impute it to himself, as stated in the Digest, Title on Actions and Obligations, Law 1, Section "He also," and in the Institutes, Title on How Obligations are Contracted, Section "Furthermore." But here negligence is proven from the effect, because if he had been diligent, the case of fire would not have occurred; just as it had not occurred previously, as stated in the Digest, Title on the Lex Aquilia, Law "If a slave," Section "If a fornicator." Moreover, in a fire, fault is always presumed, as stated in the Digest, Title on Peril and Loss of the Thing Sold, Law "If the seller." To the contrary, it seems that the age of 20 years is suitable for counsel and prudence of mind, as stated in the Code, Title on Those Who, by Reason of Age, Obtain, Law 2. And such persons are considered in the place of adults, if they are accustomed to do what more diligent persons do, as stated in the Code, Title on Who and Against Whom, Law 1, in the beginning. Moreover, it is customary to entrust the custody of scholars for a short time when some necessity of household affairs arises. And certainly, at such an age, one is fit to govern schools and to be a teacher in grammar and in the arts, and even in the laws, as stated in the Digest, Title on Postulation, Law 1, Section "Childhood." Therefore, much more so for the custody of household goods. Moreover, in this young man, integrity of mind, counsel, and care for the matter appear, which should suffice. He did what any diligent master ought to have done. Moreover, he was the nephew of the lessee, in whom the bond of blood induced confidence, as stated in the Digest, Title on Common, Law "It would be argued." Moreover, one over 17 years of age is considered by law a suitable procurator for business, as stated in the Institutes, Title on Who Cannot Have Power, Section "Once," and in the Decretals, Chapter "Who generally," Section "Not to mention," Title on Procurators, Book 6; and in both places is the case of this question regarding the point of presumed suitability. Moreover, the absence was not improbable. Moreover, the said fire has its cause from an unknown author; it should not be imputed to the master himself, even if one of the scholars had secretly taken it, as stated in the aforementioned Law "If sold," where is the case of this question. Certainly, to use the services of scholars is not to use the services of bad men, but filial services. For we rightly call them our sons, as stated in the Digest, Title on the Signification of Words, Law "To whom the principal." Therefore, from their fault, our obligation is not contracted, unless the origin of the fault proceeded from us, as stated in the Digest, Title on Theft Against the Shipowner, Law 1, Section "In the slave," although the gloss there, solving the contrary from the Law "Let us see," Title on Lease, says that it is one thing when one introduces into his own house, and another when into another's. And he says well, when the alien thing was not prepared for this use. But this house of grammar was prepared for that use, to lead and keep scholars; hence the introduction does not contain fault in itself, as stated in the Digest, Title on Usufruct, Law "Trees," Section "Ship." Moreover, neither does the appointment of a custodian [imply fault]; because the custodian did what a diligent person would do; and what is, so to speak, of the nature and custom of such custody. And we have a similar case with herds of cattle, whose custodians are mostly boys; for by custom, those who entrust custody to them are excused; because they are capable of greater diligence. Hence, if those things proposed in the facts are true, both the matter of fact and of law is determined in favor of the said master of grammar. To which the aforementioned Law 2, in the beginning, Code, Title on Those Who, by Reason of Age, Obtain, makes most optimally and formally.

† As to that which you say, that fires are usually caused by the fault of the inhabitants, as in l. 3, § et quia, de officio praefecti vigilum, I answer as follows: Because it is not established whose fault it is, the lessee is not liable. And because you say "usually," it is evident that sometimes it occurs without fault, as when a spark carried by the wind ignites straw, and the fire multiplies invisibly among the straw, which also happens, just as the cunning of an enemy sneaking in at night, despite the greatest diligence.

† Hence, since the lessor has the burden of proving fault, he fails if he does not prove it. For proof must conclude with necessity, or near necessity: for in matters contingent on either party, we favor the defendant, as in Extra de probat., c. In praesentia, and l. Non hoc, with its subject matter. Moreover, he employed such care as a diligent person would employ in his own affairs. l. Custodiam, de periculo et commodo rei venditae. The sound of the aforementioned law does not intend to say anything other than that no other pact was added in the contract. And it is supported by ff. de nautis, cauponibus, stabulariis, l. Nautae, et caupo. And thus I say and advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A legacy made of debts is to be understood as referring to true and liquidated ones.
2. The word, or what it imports.
body: The words state as follows: "In the name of Christ, within a month, to deliver and hand over to the guardians of Perugia so many and such debtors, and instruments against those same debtors, which shall amount to the sum and quantity of 225 Genoese florins, namely, from those and out of those debtors who are bound and obligated to pay John de Corrado and others, by reason of the bread shop, and from those debtors and names of debts, etc. And let such debtors and quantities of debts be those whom and which the said guardians wished to choose and take, and to retain for themselves in payment of that quantity, which are described in the books of the shop. Now it is asked, what these words import."

And as appears, these words are divided into three parts: in the first, the obligation to give the names of the debtors, or the instruments, up to “namely, those”; in the second, the declaration concerning which debtors, up to “and let them be such debtors”; in the third, the election of those names by the tutors, up to “this being done”. I therefore say, taking the third particle, that the said tutors are not bound to accept, unless the true debtors described in the books of the said pharmacy: because the option of the names of the debtors described clearly has been given to them, therefore it is necessary that those debtors be [true]. And this [follows] from the first part of the writing, and from the mention of the instrument, because it says “so many and such debtors, and instruments”, i.e., that the names must be clear. Therefore, the said Gimetus must prove that the debts subsist and are true, as in l. 1, C. Creditorem euictionem pignoris non debere, where it is held that the creditor must be proved to be that one; otherwise, he is bound to assign the action. There is the text, and there Butrinteus and Bartolus say this.

† Likewise, that word “or” (seu), whether placed in an explanatory or ampliative sense, signifies this, as in the Digest, *De auro et argento legato*, law *Si quis ita*: if placed in an alternative sense, it means that by instrument or otherwise; it is understood and read as referring to another proof, namely one other than by instruments, which is more expeditious and facilitates execution.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a judgment may be rendered subject to a condition.
1. Instruments and contracts differ.
2. Which instruments prove, and which may be challenged as false.
3. That one is bound to prove the falsity of an instrument alleged by way of exception by the debtor...
4. Whether servants of an abbot on behalf of the monastery, guardians on behalf of a ward, and tenants on behalf of their lord may serve as witnesses.
body: In the name of Christ. A certain assessor... Titius, who complains in the syndication process against the judge, stating that he had already paid that debt. Now it happened that in the syndication process that assessor was acquitted, with this reservation: provided that if the said debtor proves that he has paid; and if he proved it, he was condemned. The latter proved that he had paid.

† It is asked whether the said sentence is to be ordered for execution against the said assessor, or not. And it seems that it is, because even though a sentence is conditional, it is valid, and once the condition exists it is executable, as in C. de senten. et interlo. om. iudi. l. cum eorum, and in l. 1. §. biduum. quando app. sit. The truth is to the contrary. And for clarity, it must be premised that sometimes a sentence is rendered against the right of the law, sometimes against the right of the party, and sometimes against the right of the judge; which third member I add for a clearer understanding, although it does not fall under that member 'against the right of the party.' And I take that third member, and I say that a judge cannot be condemned for lack of skill, nor even for fraud, on the basis of things newly to be proved after his sentence, because proofs made after the sentence do not prove the iniquity of the judge, nor can they convict him; rather, he who did not prove can only complain of himself. This is the case in ff. de eden. l. argentariis. §. cum autem. The decretal says the very same thing literally in extra de priui. ca. cum olim. Wherefore, regarding the said sentence there is much to be wondered at. And therefore the useful is not vitiated by the useless; and the said assessor remains acquitted, and in no way condemned; and if there were any condemnation, it ought to be rescinded as evidently iniquitous upon its very inspection. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Instruments and contracts differ.
2. Which instruments provide proof, and which can be challenged for forgery.
3. Who is bound to prove the forgery of an instrument alleged by the debtor by way of exception...
4. Whether servants of an abbot for the monastery, guardians for a ward, and tenant farmers for a master can be witnesses.
body: In the name of Christ. For clarity, it must be premised,

† that a contract and its terms are one thing, while an instrument and the terms of an instrument are another. For the principal contract with all its clauses is the act of the parties; the setting down of the date, consul, place, and witnesses is the act of the notary, as noted elegantly in l. j. §. edi. at the end of the great gloss, ff. de eden. Secondly, certain words of Iac. Bu. must be premised, which at first sight appear in many respects to stand in the way of the monastery, which he posits in C. de eden. on the authentica si quis in aliquo doc., which are as follows:

† "Likewise I ask, which instruments provide proof? I answer: private ones do not, unless solemn, as noted in l. instrumenta. de proba. But a public one—which has three names, namely original, exemplar, and protocol—regularly provides proof, as in l. cum precibus. de proba. This fails if it is rendered suspect, which occurs in one of three ways: in one way, because it is erased, effaced, or cancelled in the place in question, and then that instrument does not provide proof, nor can such a defect be purged, as in ff. de edi. diui Adri. tol. Secondly, it is rendered suspect by reason of the person of the producer, as when he is a vile and abject person and accustomed on other occasions to produce false documents; and this defect is well purged if another reputable person similarly produces it with him, and this is proved, as in l. si quis. §. cogentur. ff. de eden. In the third way, it is rendered suspect by reason of the person of the writer: because he is accustomed on other occasions to write false documents, and such an instrument does not provide proof, l. si aliquid. de susceptoribus, et archa. But although he may be found today to write false instruments, instruments made in the past do not on that account appear false; on the contrary, they shall provide proof, even though some suspicion attaches to them: Iac. Bu." Since, therefore, the instrument produced on behalf of the monastery suffers from two defects—namely, a defect of appearance, because it is cancelled in a suspect place, namely in the person of a witness; and because the notary is thoroughly defamed, and that so much among good and grave men that the governor of the province, on account of his gravity, ought not to believe him—therefore, as well by reason of the form or figure of the instrument as by reason of the person, credit ought not to be given to it; rather, it ought to be rejected as false, as in extra de priui. c. cum olim pp. But on the contrary, I premise

† for the elucidation of what is stated by Spe. in the title de proba. §. 1. at the word sed pone, whose words are these: "But suppose I demand from you one hundred which you owe me; you deny the debt; I produce an instrument to prove it; you except against it on grounds of forgery. Now it is asked, which of us must prove? Iaco. distinguishes, for either the matter of forgery is pursued civilly or criminally. If civilly: either that instrument is suspect on its face—for example, it is cancelled, or effaced in some part of itself, or the notary was accustomed on other occasions to make false writings—and then the producer must prove that it is genuine, C. de proba. l. iubemus; or it is not suspect, and then the party excepting must prove that it is false, C. de eden. l. qui accusare. If, however, the matter of forgery is pursued criminally, then both must prove, yet first the party excepting, and subsequently the producer, as in C. de fal. there." These are the words of Speculator, which contain the very truth, because there is the text in the said l. iubemus. For cancellations and the tarnished reputation of a notary (unless he had been stripped of office) pertain to questions of faith (credibility), as in C. de testamentis. l. si vnus. And therefore, either faith is imparted to the instrument, or not; but it is necessary that this faith be imparted through lawful witnesses, otherwise the instrument is not believed. And if indeed lawful witnesses depose directly concerning the truth of the instrument, because they were present at the transaction, as in C. de testi. l. testium, then it is clear that one relies on the instrument, if the witnesses have been lawfully received and faith has been imparted to it, whether we speak of ordinary or summary proceedings. But before faith has been imparted in summary proceedings, those witnesses ought not to be received who belong to a deeper inquiry in ordinary proceedings; so the lex notes in edieto. Because in that edict it is necessary that the writing does not appear damaged, yet the substance of the question consists in the writing itself; for in that edict the judge must proceed by eyewitness faith, not by the hearing of the ears, as in insti. de gradibus. §. sed cum magis. Likewise I say that indirect proof suffices, as when the debtor has acknowledged the genuineness of the bond, as in l. cum fidem. de non nu. pec. Since therefore in this manner faith has been imparted to the said instrument through two witnesses of good repute, one must, it seems, stand by the said writing; or rather, even more so, by the said witnesses. Likewise, because a suspect writing is not wholly invalid; rather, the writing and the witnesses mutually assist one another, as in the said l. si quis ex argentariis. §. cogentur.

† It does not stand in the way that one witness is a servant of the abbot and the other an old tenant farmer (colonus): because in the cause of a monastery they can indeed testify, as in spe. de teste; otherwise it would be in the power of the abbot to withhold proofs from the monastery by making someone his servant or tenant. Likewise, no one doubts that the servant of a tutor can be a witness in the cause of a ward. Likewise, although a tenant farmer may be said to be a dependent (familiaris) after a fashion, nonetheless he cannot be lawfully commanded; nor are friends repelled from testifying, the text being in ff. de usuris. l. sciendum. And these matters belong to the subtlety of the law; but may God, who is truth, protect the truth, whether for or against, because I do not know it. Rather, I have made these allegations solely according to a conscience informed by the acts of the case. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pact made with a servant appointed to sell his master's goods, whereby he may not sell any goods to another under penalty, is valid.
2. Whether the penalty is incurred each time the agreement is violated.
3. Whether he who promised not to sell may sell through an interposed person; whether an action for the penalty may be brought on the bare pact.
body: In the name of Christ. Titius leased his goods from Matine. He appointed Seyo to sell gold cloth on his behalf in the city of Malo, and promised that the said Titius, whether acting for himself or for another, would not sell gold cloth in the said city of Malo during the term of the said lease, under a certain penalty to be incurred each time a breach occurred; nor did any other stipulation of penalty intervene.

† Now it is asked, first, whether the agreement is valid; and truly, that it is not: because it is against the public utility; for it is in the public interest that there be many merchants in the cities, as l. 1. C. de monopoliis. To the contrary it seems, by the rule: the praetor says, I will uphold agreements. Also, it is a serious matter to break faith, as l. 1. in prin. ff. de consti. pecu. Also, this is an agreement of one single person, which does not derogate from public liberty, because there are infinitely many others who can sell the said cloths. Also, one person does not make a monopoly, but a gathering. Also, it is lawful for an agreement that my servant ought to work for me alone during the time of the works, and not turn to contrary work, and to my motive, as ff. locati. l. in operis. Also, he ought to be solicitous for my benefit, against whomsoever I act, and against himself, as ff. de cond. ind. l. frater a fratre. §. potius. Also, in this special speech is contained the person speaking, as de inquisitionibus veritatis. C. de solu. l. Also, the agreement is valid, nor is it permitted for you to fish where I fish: just as custom and prescription are valid, as l. vt iniuriam. in fi. ff. de feriis. and l. venditor. ff. conia praedio. Also, no. casum expressum. ff. de ope. lib. l. libertus negotiatoribus. a contrario sensu. For this I introduce the saying of spec. in tit. de locato. §. restat. where he says that the lessor of labor ought faithfully and solicitously to do whatever he believes useful to the lessee and his affairs: and to abstain from contrary things. And he puts these words in the form of an agreement. And thus it would be well to the point, that however the agreement in grain, as being against public utility and against the favor of foodstuffs, would be null by the law itself, if anyone were to agree that he could not carry grain to the needy in the street, as l. 1. ff. ad legem Iuliam de annona.

Secondly, it is asked whether the penalty is incurred an infinite number of times. And it seems that it is, for this pact, “as often as, as often as,” etc., is approved by law, as in D. de arbitris, l. si duo. But this appears to be very inequitable, as in C. de sententiis, quam pro eo quod interest, l. 1, in fine, because it ought not to exceed four times the total interest. But the gloss there says that interest is not multiplied in penalties, unless it is referred to interest by means of multiplicative terms, as in D. de verbis oblig., l. si ista, § ante. But you will say, here are multiplicative terms, “as often as, as often as.” Nevertheless, they are not referred to interest according to the wording. But the opinion of the transmontane jurists considers the reality; we, however, commonly follow the gloss. Yet the following does not stand in the way: D. de legatis 3, l. fideicommissa, § si quis decem, because the case there is different.

The third point is whether one who has promised not to sell may sell through an interposed person. And it must be said that this is contrary to the intent of the agreement, as in D. 50.17.129 (Fraus) and D. 35.1.108 (Haeres meus), § Quod in fraudem.

Fourth, and the last point, is whether an action for a penalty can be brought on the basis of a bare agreement. And it must be said that it can, because the accessory is clothed by the principal through the coherence of the contract, as in D. 12.1.10 (l. lecta). This is fully noted in C. 2.15.1 (l. petens). Also, because on account of the writing a stipulation is presumed to have intervened, as is fully noted in D. 50.16.18 (l. sciendum) and in Inst. 3.19.1.2 (§ si scriptum). And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. If the testator provided that all debts, whether contracted by the son who is the heir or by any other heir, are to be paid by the said heirs, is it understood that each is liable for one-half? Or how is this to be construed?
body: The case is as follows: In the name of Christ. Gregory of Ferrara and Galeotto, his emancipated son, purchased certain tolls from the commune of Ferrara for a period of two years, paying monthly in proportion. Finally, the said Gregory, coming to death, made a will, in which he ordered that all debts contracted both by the said Galeotto and by any other of the Marineti of Ferrara, in which debts the testator himself is not bound, shall be paid jointly by his underwritten heirs, namely by the said Galeotto for one half, and by John and Nicholas, his nephews from another predeceased son, for the other half, provided that the said debts were contracted and incurred before the death of the said testator. And there he added these words: “willing and ordering that for this reason no hypothecary action be sought against the said creditors.” And the said testator died after one month of the said lease, or after one year, I do not care, the said contract subsisting and all payments having been made up to that time. After whose death many months successively elapsed, for which nothing was paid. It is asked, how is it to be paid? For they say that from the said contract arose a double obligation, namely against the said Galeotto for one half, and against the said Gregory for the other half; and that the said Galeotto is bound in one half by his own person, and not in the name of the heir. Likewise, the said Gregory was bound in the other half by his own person; which obligation of the said Gregory is divided among the said heirs according to their hereditary portions by the law of the Twelve Tables, as in C. de pactis, l. pacto debitorum, and C. de hereditatis petitione, l. pro hereditariis. From which they infer necessarily that Galeotto is bound by his own person for one half. Likewise, as heir, he is bound for one half of the other half. But on the contrary, Gregory says that this is not true; and this by virtue of the said legatee’s stipulation, that all debts contracted both by the said Galeotto, son of the testator, and by any other of the Marineti, shall be paid by the said heirs, namely by the said Galeotto for one half, and the other nephews for the other half; which legacy, indeed, prelegacy, is valid, as in ff. de legatis 2, l. cum ab uno. Now it is asked, what is the law?

† namely, whether the said Galeotus is liable for three parts, and the said nephews for one-fourth part of the entire said debt; or whether the said Galeotus is liable only for one-half, and the said nephews for the other half of the entire debt incurred after the death of the testator: and there would be no question, were it not for the said legacy and the disposition of the testator. In favor of Galeotus, the words of the testament are alleged. First, because the words state that all debts contracted by the said Galeotus are to be paid for one-half, as above, and he who says "all" excludes nothing, as in D. de legatis 3, l. Iulia, in principio, cum si. Second, because of the word "to be paid" (solvenda). For this word demonstrates the future time occurring, both after the testament but before death, and after the death of the testator, as in D. de verbis significandis, l. verbum oportebat, and l. verbum facere. Third, this seems to be proven openly by those words, "provided that the said debts were made and contracted before the death of the said testator." For there is no doubt that the said contract had its origin and form in the lifetime of the testator; because we say a contract is made on the day it was celebrated: as that day is placed in the instrument, as in D. de editionibus, l. 1, §. editiones. Moreover, "made" (factum) is said of that which cannot be regarded as undone, as in D. de captivis, l. in libello, §. factae. Moreover, we take "contracted" (contractum) to mean a mutual promise, as in D. de verbis significandis, l. Labeo, §. contractio, even if the contract is conditional, as noted in C. de pactis, l. petens. Moreover, the words of legacies ought to be understood broadly, especially between related persons, as in D. de aureo et argenteo legato, l. Quintus, §. si, and C. de legatis, l. cum alienam. Moreover, this is aided by the equality to be preserved among children, as in D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, §. euictis. Moreover, if the said Galeotus had not been emancipated, but had brought his earnings to his father, natural reason, as well as civil law, would suggest this, as if the father had used his labor, not as a co-debtor, but as a minister, as in D. de editionibus, l. Praetor, §. 1. But rightly Sabinus.

On the contrary, it seems that the said testament does not cover our case. And first, because of those words, "in which debts the testator himself is not obligated." For this debt, about which the question is asked, is one and the same debt, if each bound themselves in solidum, as in D. de pactis, l. si plures. For it is thus probable that the instrument contains an obligation with respect to the fisc. But among themselves, each is liable for a share, as noted in l. 1, C. de duobus reis. Moreover, if the instrument did not say "each in solidum," nevertheless those words, "for which debts the testator himself is not obligated," could not be verified, because the proposition "is not obligated" is not universally true, since he is obligated for a share from one and the same contract, as in D. de duobus reis, l. Reos, §. cum in tabulis. Moreover, this is proven because the testator expressly wished the time of death to be considered: namely, that at that time the debts were contracted and made. To this end, all laws agree that the time of death is to be considered, as in l. Mella, §. 1, D. de adimendo legatis, and l. Cesserunt ad iudicem, and D. de verbis obligandis, l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a procuratore, D. de fundo instrato, l. Lucius, with its material. However, it must be seen what is meant by "debts contracted and made," for a debt can be considered in two ways: namely, initiatively, and then it will have been begun before the death of the said testator; and completively, and then it did not exist at the time of the death of the said testator, but rather the action began with the heir, as in C. ut actio ab haerede et contra haeredem, l. 1. For from a lease for a future time, an effective obligation is not born, although several rents are reduced to one stipulation, they are not reduced to one obligation, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. si a colono, and D. de stipulatione servo, l. si servus communis meuii, et castrensis peculii, §. si. Moreover, this contract, as regards the act of the contracting parties, does not have its existence pending the future; but as regards the act of binding effectively, because the final cause is not yet in its act: nor is it possible, as in D. de verbis obligandis, l. inter stipulantem, §. sacramentum, and l. interdum. It is impossible that an effective obligation was born in the meantime, and if it were born, it would not be acted upon to sue. Since therefore the testator considered the effect of the contract according to the time of death, we are no longer in the case of the testament, and for this I adduce three laws and one glossa ordinaria, namely D. de legatis 2, l. si ita scripto, and l. si a colono, and what is noted in d. l. 1, verbum oportebit.

Furthermore, I declare this, because the testator conjunctively joined "contracted" and "made" debts; therefore, so that no word may be superfluous, that term "contracted" refers to the ordering of the contract, and those words "made debts" necessarily refer to the substance of the debt's fact: but there is no debt which is not a certain debt to be paid, as in D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus, l. haeres meus. Moreover, "debt" is a civil term, which signifies not yet done, but of obligation; and "obligating" we must take to mean if he cannot defend himself by exception, as in D. de liberali causa, l. vel obligatus, §. obligatum, D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussor obligari, §. fideiussor, versi. nam licet, and there this is expressed. Moreover, in last wills we must avoid absurdity, insofar as we can, as in C. de conditionibus inserendis, l. 2, and D. de legatis 3, l. Offilius Imperator. Absurdity appears if we suppose that after death the said lease was profitable: for certainly Galeotus would want one-half of the said profit from his own person, and another half of the half from the person of the father, therefore, etc., as in C. de rescindenda venditione, l. ratas. From which considerations, laws, and reasons, I think the said nephews uphold justice, that in effect they are not liable except for one-fourth part of the damage. For as I said, the testator referred himself to the time of death: and words are to be understood effectively according to the time to which they refer. And because they would not have but one-fourth part of the profit, as in C. de furtis, l. manifestissimi, §. sed in secunda. And thus I say, and I advise. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A contract concluded before a judge and sworn to is not presumed to have been entered into with fraud, nor is it deemed simulated. See also nos. 2, 3, and 4.
2. If two notaries are required in a certain place, one does not provide proof in another place, because the statute of the place is considered.
2. Those succeeding by virtue of the Authentica *Bona damnatorum* are not proper heirs.
body: ...approached the judge...

† The contracting parties approached the judge: and concerning their contract, at the time of the contract, they caused a sentence to be rendered that the said contract was true, and not simulated, concerning a true debt: they therefore swore that it was so, and that they would not contravene it; execution of the sentence is sought: an objection is raised against the public instrument that it is not valid, because the asserted notary is not a notary, nor in lawful quasi-possession of the notariate. I answer: this exception does not proceed here, because it is not opposed against the underlying transaction, but rather it is said that it does not furnish proof.

† Secondly, it is asked whether the exception of non-counted money can be opposed; and it seems not, because the confession was made in court, as noted in ff. de interrog. act. l. 1. in the penultimate gloss. Likewise, on account of the oath, because he swore that these things were true; it would be otherwise if he had not sworn to the truth, as noted in C. plus valere quod agitur. l. emptione. Thirdly,

† it is asked whether it can be objected that the contract was entered into through fraud: it seems not, as in l. 1. C. de praediis curialium. lib. 10. and C. de transac. l. actionem. in the second response. Fourthly, it is asked

† whether it can be objected that these things were done simulatedly, because the parties were acting with the intention that it would be a simulated contract. I answer that he could. And ff. de verbo. obli. l. cum stipulatus sim mihi a procuto: because if it was in fraud of usury, this can be objected once absolution from the oath has first been granted by the bishop, capitu. 1. de iureiurando. Likewise, if the contract were simulated in the aforesaid manner, because the party acting upon it sins against his brother, proceeding could be made to absolution by way of denunciation, after evangelical denunciation has preceded, as in extra de iudiciis. capitu. nouit. and extra de iureiuran. cap. ad nostram. On this, note C. plus valere quod agitur. l. emptione. and C. de transactio. l. cum ea.

† It is asked, if in a given place two notaries are required, whether one makes full proof in that place, or elsewhere. I answer: no, because the statute of the place is looked to with respect to the number of notaries or witnesses, since it is a certain necessary solemnity which must be present at the place and time of the contract or last will, for every solemnity must be conjoined with the act just as form is with matter; as in C. de testamentis. l. fina. and noted by Inno. in capitu. dudum. de rebus eccle. non alie. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a cleric condemned to perpetual imprisonment, who died there,
body: he could have made a will. Heirs. A person condemned to death or to perpetual imprisonment made a formal will, and afterwards an informal one; which of them is more valid. Whether an heir can be instituted whose status is uncertain, because some say he is a bastard, etc. Whether a bastard can be instituted as heir to a specific thing. Whether a father, by compromising, prejudices his son in the goods in which he has a usufruct.

† In the name of Christ. The first question is whether the will of a cleric condemned to perpetual imprisonment, who finally died there, is valid. And it seems that it is, because either you say that this person is intestable by civil law: and this is false, because this penalty is rejected by civil law: and such a sentence is null by the law itself, as C. de poenis, l. credibile. And it is certain that a sentence null by the law itself does not make anyone intestable, as ff. de iniusto testamento, l. si quis filio exheredato, §. quod si quis fuerit damnatus. Or you say that everyone is intestable by canon law. And certainly this is not found expressly in canon law: therefore it is understood to be permitted, as ff. de procuratoribus, l. ab ea parte. Moreover, there are certain persons enumerated who cannot make a will, as appears in Inst. quibus non est permissa factio testamenti, per totum, and especially in §. fin., where the gloss enumerates them, and among others is one condemned to civil or natural death. But this person is not condemned to natural death, although he is condemned to the tedium of life. Nor is he condemned to civil death: for imprisonment is not regarded as civil death, as in the aforementioned l. si quis filio, §. eius qui, there, licet in carcere. And although Innocent says the contrary in c. non obstat, because Innocent says that this is a capital penalty, and is the greater penalty that can be imposed by canon law, except actual degradation and delivery to the secular judge, as in c. degradatio, de poenis, lib. 6. Hence, rightly, this condemned person is assimilated to one condemned to the mines, who, although today he does not become a slave of the penalty, nevertheless cannot make a will: because he loses all benefits of civil law, and therefore also the capacity to make a will, which is principally of civil law, as ff. de testamentis, l. eius qui, §. fin., and ff. de legatis 3, l. 1, §. praefectus. For the capacity to make a will is a matter of public law, as ff. de testamentis, l. testamenti factio. And with regard to public law, this person is considered dead, as ff. de bonis possessis, l. edicto, §. rei capitalis, and ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. 1, in fin. What is more true, namely, that this person cannot make a will, if he is finally condemned by his bishop to the penalty of perpetual imprisonment, by those things which Innocent notes in Extra, de accusationibus, c. qualiter. Notwithstanding that this penalty is disapproved by civil law, because in clerics we must adhere to canon law, as Extra, de foro competenti, c. si diligenti. Moreover, there would be no doubt if he were condemned to the penalty of perpetual imprisonment with his goods expressly taken away: because he who left no goods in the city cannot have an heir, as ff. de vulgaribus substitutionibus, l. lex Cornelia.

† And those who succeed by virtue of the Authentica *Bona damnatorum* are not properly heirs; for neither does the fiscus come in on this head, as is stated in the Digest, *De nova*, in the final section, and in the law *Novatio*, under the same title, and there noted. And in persons who cannot make a will, it matters not whether anything has been left for pious causes or not, as is fully noted in the chapter *Quamquam*, *De usuris*, Book 6. Nevertheless, it is true that Speculator, in § *Compendiosa*, *De instrumentis*, where he enumerates the persons who cannot make a will, makes no mention of this person condemned to perpetual imprisonment. But I am of the opinion that he is included under the category of those condemned to death; for even if he does not die immediately, yet on account of the filth of the prison life is necessarily taken away, hence on account of the punishment death is at hand, as in the Code, *De custodia reorum*, law 1, there: "within the confines of the prison to give to death," and afterwards he adds: "to be consumed by long decay." And in fact we see that they live but a short time; therefore this punishment is ordained to death, just as if someone were condemned to undergo perpetual tortures until he breathed his last; and if it is not a brief death, it is a long one. And thus I hold on this point, that this person is neither actively nor passively capable of making a will; nevertheless, because although he is not condemned to sudden death, he is condemned to a shortness of life. There is also another, better reason, because this punishment either finds a slave or makes a slave; since it cannot fall upon a slave, as is stated in the law *Incredibile*, joined with the canons, and in the law *Nam*, *De iure canonico*, it falls upon a vile and abject person, namely the punishment of servitude in prison. And I speak of the case where this punishment is imposed as the term of the punishment by a definitive sentence. Secondly

† It is asked: A cleric, capable of making a will, made a solemn will, in which he instituted friends as heirs; afterwards he made a non-solemn will before three witnesses, in which he instituted his natural brother. It is certain that the first will is not revoked by civil law, because the inheritance cannot be entered upon by virtue of the second will according to civil law, as is noted in the Digest, *De iniusto testamento*, in the law *Cum in secundo*. Furthermore, it is not revoked by the provisions of the Code, which dispose that the first will is revoked in one case, even though the inheritance cannot be entered upon by virtue of the second will according to civil law, namely when in the first will strangers are instituted absolutely, and in the second those who would succeed intestate are instituted before five witnesses. For in that case the first will is broken; and yet the second is not valid so that the inheritance can be entered upon by it. But the way of intestate succession is opened, so that all those who succeed intestate inherit, not only he who is named, and if he repudiates, the way is open to those who follow. And this is what the text says, *iure testati* [by right of the will], in the Code, *De testamento*, in the law *Hac consultissima*, § *Pe*. But now five witnesses were not present, but only three; therefore the first will remains firm, notwithstanding the contrary view, as in the Extravagant, *De testamento*, chapter *Cum esses* and chapter *Relatum*, because they do not speak of the case where a solemn will preceded. To the contrary it seems, because this person is a cleric, and it is not assumed that he is subject to civil law, but only to the law of nations; by which law the consensus of the last will is valid, just as the consensus of contracting parties. And on this is founded the law of the Twelve Tables, as in the Authenticum, *De nuptiis*, § *Disponat*. Therefore, by the law of nations, or by the natural custom of mankind, it is thus observed: although civil and praetorian law dispose otherwise, as in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, in the law *Quaestionem*. Moreover, it is not unjust for a will to be made by a priest, or before a priest, but before two witnesses and a priest, or another cleric in sacred orders, the will is valid, as is noted in the said § *Compendiose*, verse *Item per ius canonicum*. Therefore, since clerics ought to live according to the canons, such a will revokes the first; indeed, more so, because the inheritance can be entered upon by virtue of the second according to canonical law. But because it would be presumptuous to hold this, I adhere to the first opinion, that the first will is not revoked: unless perhaps with regard to castrense property arising from the clerical office itself; as we say in the case of a soldier in active service, for a cleric, who is always engaged in divine offices, as above in the Decretum, *De sacramento sanctae ecclesiae*, in the law *Si qui sub praetextu*, is equated to a soldier in active service, as is noted in the law *Miles*, in the Digest, *De re iudicata*.

Thirdly, it is asked: suppose that it is doubtful whether someone is a natural child or a spurious one, because some say that the mother had another husband, while others say the contrary; whether, in case of doubt, this person, whose status is uncertain, can be instituted as an heir? I answer: yes, because he is presumed capable; and where the law presumes or defines, there is no uncertainty, as stated in the aforementioned law *Si quis filio*, beyond the middle. Fourthly

† It is asked whether a spurious son can be instituted heir to a specific thing? I answer that, if he is in need of support for life, he can be instituted so that he may receive up to the amount of his maintenance; the remainder shall remain with the intestate successors, unless there were an instituted heir, because then it goes to the substitute. First, it is assumed to be true regarding canon law, not civil law, as in the Decretals, in the title De eo qui duxit in matrimonium, chapter Cum haberet. Given this assumption, the other points are also true according to civil law, as in law 2 and law Si pater, Codex, Nunc Papae, sive exsecrabilis vir domi, De haereditatibus instituendis, and Codex, De fideicommissis, law Eam quam. Moreover, it will be estimated how long he can live, as in the Digest, Ad legem Falcidiam, law Haereditarium. And if the legacy does not exceed the value of this uncertain event, he also acquires full ownership, and perpetual; otherwise, if the testator had bequeathed that thing for maintenance, because then the legacy would be extinguished by death, as noted in the Digest, De transactionibus, law Cum hi, section Si uni. It is doubted

† Concerning a certain transaction made by a father regarding property in which he holds the usufruct, whether it prejudices the son; and it appears that it does, if he transacted cautiously and prudently due to the uncertain outcome of the litigation; otherwise not, as in C. de bonis matri. l. 1; C. de pactis. l. pactum curatoris; and C. de transactionibus. l. praeses. Nevertheless, I advise the one transacting with the father to do so with the authority of a judge; because it is always beneficial for a judicial decree to intervene in contracts, as in ff. de solutionibus. l. si stipulatus. §. si lanceam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether an appeal from a judgment rendered by a subdelegate to the subdelegating authority is valid.
body: ... of the lord Pope, or execu-

† A delegate of the lord Pope, or an executor, subdelegated his duties to another simply, with no part of his jurisdiction having been reserved to himself in any other way; he has not yet proceeded to the execution of the adjudicated cause; and in the presence of the parties, one of whom, claiming to be aggrieved, appealed to the subdelegating judge himself. The question is whether the said appeal holds. On this point, a judgment was rendered by order of the subdelegating judge himself, and it was pronounced that the said appeal did not hold, because the said delegate reserved nothing of jurisdiction to himself. For if he had reserved anything of jurisdiction to himself, the said appeal to him would hold, as in c. si delegatus. §. ad eum. de offic. de leg. in VI°; and this Spec. maintains in Speculum de appellationibus, c. nunc tractemus, v. quid si delegatus, and the following verse. But if it had been added in the appeal, "to any competent judge whatsoever," the appeal would indeed hold as if lodged to the Pope, as noted in C. de bonis authem. iudi. pos. l. cum proponas. And for clearer understanding we shall distinguish three cases: for either some part of jurisdiction is subdelegated, and then an appeal is made to the subdelegating judge; or the whole contentious jurisdiction is subdelegated, but not the executive, and the same [applies]; or the whole jurisdiction, both in taking cognizance and in judging, as well as in executing; and in that case, once the sub-executor has begun to take cognizance, the subdelegating judge has discharged his office, and henceforth he can take cognizance of nothing, nor can an appeal be made to him, because he completely lacks jurisdiction. And therefore, when an executor appointed for providing subdelegates the execution for providing—which word is understood comprehensively, as Inno. notes in ca. in literis, de offi. de le.—it is impossible for the subdelegating judge himself to reassume jurisdiction when the matter is no longer whole; and therefore an appeal cannot be made to him. And that is the intention of the Speculator. Someone will say: does he not, by committing the definitive [judgment], seem to commit the execution? Therefore he reserved nothing of jurisdiction to himself, and thus one of the aforesaid limbs is false. Certainly Inno. maintains this in de offi. dele. c. si pro debilitate. But Hostien. says the opposite, and better, because although the pronouncement of the sentence, which belongs to jurisdiction, is committed, the execution, which belongs to mixed imperium, does not seem to be committed, although under canon law it could be expressly committed, as is proven in ff. de re iudi. l. a diuo pio, in prin., ff. de pac. l. tale pactum, §. qui prouocauit, and ff. de iurisdictio. om. iud. l. iubere cauere. And therefore the opinion of Hostien. is better on this point than the opinion of Inn.; but in the case of a subdelegate appointed for providing, the opinion of Inno. is truer. And this, as I think, was the consideration of the Speculator. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The first prebend is not vacant if the one opting for a second has not obtained peaceful possession; it is otherwise in other circumstances, notwithstanding a protestation.
body: In the name of Christ. The case is as follows: the venerable man dominus Johannes, canon of the cathedral church of Piacenza, constituted [proctor/representative?] of a certain abbot, as the senior canon opted for a certain canonical prebend vacant by the death of the late dominus Jacobus Jacobi, formerly canon of the same church, under this form, namely: if and insofar as it is due to the said dominus Johannes, and not otherwise, nor in any other way; a protestation having been premised by him that all right belonging to him to his own prebend should be safe and reserved to him in the event that the present option should not be valid, and until he should have obtained peaceful possession of the present option. Now it happens that he could not obtain possession because the lord of the land was unwilling.

† The question is whether his prebend can be impetrated by anyone? I answer that either he was at some time in peaceful possession of the opted prebend, and then the first is vacant by operation of law, and can be impetrated as vacant, nor does his protestation assist him in these prejudicial matters; or he was never in peaceful possession, having been impeded de facto, and then the first prebend is not vacant, as these points are proved in c. gratiae, de rescrip., in Clem., and what is noted in Extra, de elec., c. cum in cunctis, and in c. de multa, de praeb., and ff. de inof. test., l. si sub hac, and ff. de cond. ob causam, l. 3, § neratius. And what I said regarding when he had peaceful possession, I say the same if it was through his own fault that he did not impetrate it by petitioning the superior, as in ff. de contrah. emp., l. labeo scribit, § si mihi bibliothecam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a father may donate to one of his sons property exceeding the amount subject to insinuation.
2. A father claiming that his son has rendered good service is not believed; rather, it is necessary that the son prove the services rendered.
3. Whether derogation from insinuation may be made by agreement.
4. When a summary accumulation is to be made.
5. A confession is valid, and a payment as unpaid between father and son.
6. The presence of the lord of the fief has the force of insinuation.
7. A father may donate a fief to one of his sons.
body: Noble Marquis. In the name of Christ. Careto made a certain confession against the noble Lord George, his emancipated son, in which he confessed that he was bound to his said emancipated son in the sum of six thousand four hundred and ninety florins, because the said Lord George had paid the creditors of the same Lord Boniface from his own purse, notwithstanding that the name of the said Lord Boniface was contained in the instruments of disturbance and release, and no mention was made of the said Lord George. Wherefore the same Lord Boniface gave to the said Lord George, in payment for the aforementioned quantity, a certain castle with its rights and appurtenances. And because it was worth more by several thousand florins, he donated it by individual sums of five hundred florins, and renounced the laws stating that a donation not insinuated is not valid beyond five hundred gold coins. And he did this saving the right of the Illustrious Lord, the Marquis of Ferrara, because the said castle is feudal to him. The said Marquis ratified the said contract, and invested the said Lord G. with the said castle and rights.

It is asked whether the said contract, thus celebrated between the party and the son, without any other insinuation intervening other than that mentioned above, is valid in law or not; and if the said donation were not valid beyond five hundred gold coins, whether it is to be understood as insinuated before the Lord Marquis, simply because it was produced to him and approved or admitted by him; and whether it is valid and has perpetual firmness in the investiture of the said Lord Marquis, or not; also presupposing that the said Lord Boniface has several other sons who have not been invested with the said fief.

† And it appears first that one should not adhere to the father’s assertion: for the law provides that, although the father may assert that his son is deserving, nevertheless the father’s assertion is not believed unless the son proves that worthy merits preceded, which merits ought to have fostered such affection on the part of the father, as is read and noted in C. de colonis, l. si donationem. And this is proved by l. si forte, ff. de castrensi peculio.

Furthermore, one cannot derogate by agreement from laws providing for insinuation, for insinuation is a certain great solemnity, introduced into the instrument so that no fraud may be devised in instruments of donation, as in C. de don. l. data iam pridem. And no one can act so that solemnities do not have effect in his contract or last will, as in ff. de legat. 1, l. nemo potest; ff. de legat. 2, l. codicillis, §. final; and ff. de pactis, l. ius publicum. Moreover, those words, that there are so many donations, etc., do not operate to make them several donations, since they were made at Mantua under one contract and one context; hence the whole is one instrument, especially because the things are not enumerated individually, arg. ff. de verb. oblig. l. scire debemus.

† Moreover, a cumulative consideration must be made in summary, since it arises from one and the same contract; otherwise, if there is an interval, see the argument in the Digest, On Compromises, law *Si plures*. Also, these words, that there are so many donations, imply a certain divided agreement; nevertheless, the substance of the donation is universal, and if the donation is invalid, the agreement is invalid; for this donation in principle is single and universal: and if that is invalid, the accessory clause is invalid. Also, if the aforementioned clause were effective, so that insinuation would not be necessary, we would act against the reason of the law, because insinuation has been introduced; for fraud could easily be committed here, just as if the clause had been inserted. Also, one who donates all his properties seems to donate them individually, as in the Digest, On Legacies, Book 3, law *Si corus*; and yet the individual items are not considered separately, but the whole is considered universally, as in the Code, On Donations, law *Sancimus* and law *Si quis argentum*. The contrary seems to be the case. And I divide this contract into two parts; the first part contains a dation in payment,

† And this holds without doubt between father and emancipated son: because between them every obligation consists, as is fully read and noted in l. 2, C. de inofficiosis donationibus; ff. de fideiussoribus, l. si quis pro eo, § 1; and ff. de conditionibus indebiti, l. frater a fratre, § quae sit. Hence both confession and the giving of what was unpaid were valid without doubt. l. tantum prout tanto. Nor is it novel that a contract is divided by parts, as ff. si certum petatur, l. nam et si fur, 1, responso. The second part of this contract is a donation. Now it is true that it is not valid beyond five hundred gold coins without insinuation, even if it had been given as a reward for emancipation, as is fully noted by Cynus, C. de collationibus, l. vt liberis. Nevertheless

† I say that it is sufficiently stated to have been insinuated, when it has been insinuated before the lord of the fief who has jurisdiction. For he is the superior, and the cognizance among vassals pertains to him, as in extra de iud. c. certum. Moreover, since he invested the son with the will of the father, he holds as if the investiture had been made by the lord with the consent of the vassal; nor does repentance have place, as in c. 1. §. rursus si fideliter. qui. mo. feu. amit. col. 10.

† Moreover, a father may donate a fief to one of his sons, provided that he does not deprive the other sons of their legitime, just as he could make a prelegatum, as in c. j. an agnatus, vel fi. col. 10. From which is inferred the solution to the aforementioned questions. I conclude finally that the aforementioned instrument is valid as to any of its parts. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given a statute providing that daughters of a dowried woman shall not succeed, may they claim their legitime? And this is a most elegant and subtle legal opinion.
2. The word "ab intestato" placed in a statute: how it is to be understood, and number 5.
3. Who is properly called a successor.
4. The term "cum" (with): what it imports.
5. Subrogation requires two extremes.
6. The disposition of a statute cannot abolish the principles of nature.
7. In statutes, we attend more to the words than to an imaginary intent.
body: In the name of Christ. Statute of the city of Briga concerning intestate successions. It is thus provided that sisters shall not succeed with brothers, or with nephews, in the goods of their father intestate; nevertheless, the brothers are bound to provide dowries for them, if they have not been honorably endowed according to the capacity of the patrimony. Now, a father having male children and a certain daughter, or a granddaughter through a son, named Constance, who has been honorably married and endowed by her father or grandfather, instituted his sons as heirs; and beyond the dowry, he made some legacy to the said Lady Constance. Those instituted entered upon the inheritance by will; and because the dowry and the legacy are not sufficient for the legitime of the said Constance, the said Lady Constance wishes to bring an action for the supplement of her legitime.

† It is asked whether it is possible, and it seems that it is, because he has this right by the common law, as in C. de inoffic. testa. l. et omnimodo and l. sancimus. The statute does not derogate from this common law right, except as regards intestacy; therefore, an action for supplementation may be brought on the basis of a will, either because this is a case contrary to the statute, or because a case omitted by the statute must be regarded as promised, as in ff. de acqui. haere. l. si seruum §. non dixit. Furthermore, just as the correction of laws is to be avoided by another common law, so too by a municipal law, as in C. de noxali. l. si serui vestri and extra de consuetu. cap. cum dilectus. Moreover, statutes are of strict law and therefore do not admit of extension, as in ff. so. ma. l. si vero §. de viro. Also supporting this is C. de insti. et substi. l. generaliter in the beginning, where if someone who is requested to restore an inheritance dies intestate, he causes the fideicommissum to fail by making a will, because there is always a conflict between the testate and the intestate, as in l. ius nostrum ff. de reg. iur.

For in the statute three words contained therein must be weighed, namely: the word "ab intestato," the word "a successione," and the term "cum." From the first, therefore, it is argued that [the heir] is not excluded, because the supplementation of the legitime is by will, since a will has been made. And thus the words of the excluding statute fail; and the words of the common law do not fail; therefore, we adhere to the disposition of the common law, as if the statute expressly stated that we correct the common law by will. A similar question arises in the edict on joining with emancipated children, where many and great modern authorities hold that that edict is not corrected by will. They hold the same regarding the difference between emancipation and paternal power, although the glossators commonly hold the contrary, as discussed by Cynus in Auth. In successione, and by me in l. Gallus, §. Quid si tantum, and in ff. Minorum, l. Si filius, and in Auth. De haereditatibus et Falcidia, §. Exhaereditatio, C. De collationibus, l. Si emancipati, ff. De inofficioso testamento, l. Si proponas, and in l. 1, ff. De coniungendis cum emancipatis liberis. Moreover, the correction of laws is to be avoided, and especially where the correction would involve odium. These are common legal principles.

And secondly, namely from the word "from succession," it is argued as follows: for a successor is he who succeeds to the right; and this is from the proper meaning of the term, as in D. de edendo, l. quædam, § is autem. But he who succeeds only to the legitime is not a successor to the right, since he does not succeed to another's property, as in D. de inofficioso testamento, l. Papinianus, § Quarta. Therefore, although the statute excludes from succession, which properly signifies the universal right, it nevertheless does not exclude from the legitime. And this is confirmed by another reason: for a son is never excluded from the legitime, unless the law or agreement expressly states this, as in C. de inofficioso testamento, l. Si quando, § Sin.

† From the third, namely from the word *cum*, I argue thus: this word *cum* has the force of conjunction when used affirmatively or negatively, as in D. de usufructu accresc. l. Si mulieri cum liberis. And this is what we say elsewhere, that nephews succeed more strongly *cum* (together with) the uncle in stirpes; but if they succeed on their own, they succeed in capita according to Azo. For this word *cum* signifies “together with this one”; therefore the sense of the statute is that a woman cannot succeed together with a male. But she who succeeds in the legitime does not succeed together with a male, but separately and under a different right. Moreover, the latter does so universally, the former particularly; and thus there is no conjunction between them, as in D. de bonis poss. l. Sed cum patrono. It therefore seems good counsel to advise the males that they should repudiate the inheritance under the will and take it as intestate heirs; they do nothing in fraud of the will, as in D. de leg. 2, l. Cum pater, § Si Titio. But if they were to accept under the will, let them blame themselves, because by their own agreement they have bound themselves to the legitime.

† And this opinion, namely that the said woman could claim her legitime from the will, is further proven thus: the ablative “ab intestato” is to be understood conditionally, as in D. de cond. et demonstr. l. a testatore; but from the condition an argument is drawn a contrario sensu, as if it were expressly stated that she is not excluded from the will: as in D. de officio eius, cuius in manibus est ius, l. 1, § eius rei. It is established that this supplementation, once a will has been made, is from the will, not indeed formally, but causally, as we say. C. de collatione, l. ut liberis. Moreover, the statute provides in two ways, namely concerning succession in favor of males, and concerning the dowry of the female. Now, since the condition from the law for providing a dowry applies only in intestacy: therefore neither does her, so to speak, proportional share apply, arg. C. de senatusconsulto et interloquendo, omnes iuvenes, l. cum solutum. For whenever extremes are conjoined, one without the other does not stand; especially because one is the final cause of the other, without which the legislator would not otherwise have acted. Since therefore the dowry is a certain compensation for the legitime, as noted by Cynus in l. sancimus, de nuptiis, where the statute ceases in providing a dowry, it also ceases in excluding; otherwise it could happen in the case of a testator that the woman would have neither dowry nor succession: which is absurd. To the contrary it seems, because the legitime is a third or half of the portion due in intestacy, as noted in C. de inofficioso testamento, auth. l. novissima. But to this woman nothing is due in intestacy except the dowry: therefore there is no legitime. Furthermore, the definition or description of the legitime is this: the legitime is a third or half of the portion due in intestacy to children or parents. Therefore, from whom the definition is removed, the defined thing is also removed. But from the female the definition of the legitime is removed: therefore also the legitime. Likewise, she is repelled from the legitime from the will, because the legitime takes the place of the querela or actio contra tabulas, as in the aforementioned l. omnimodo. But the actio contra tabulas or querela does not lie for this woman, as I have often examined, as in C. de libellis praetextatis, l. maximum vitium, in my lecture. For that which is substituted in the place of another partakes of the same principal nature, and the nature inherent from the beginning of its production, as noted in D. si certum petatur, l. certae condictionis, in principio.

† Moreover, substitution requires two extremes: that which is substituted, and that to which it is substituted; but the latter extreme is not present here; therefore, no substitution takes place; consequently, the substituted action does not lie, as stated in *l. si cum*, § *qui iniuriarum*, D. *si quis cautio*. Furthermore, it is difficult to respond to this point: the action for supplementation was introduced principally in favor of wills, so that they might not be broken by a complaint or by a suit *contra tabulas*; but here, for another reason, they cannot be broken—namely, on account of sex and dowry; therefore, the subsidiary provision of the law regarding supplementation ceases to apply, because it would not be a favor to the will, but rather a detriment. What, then, shall we say in this difficult question?

† First, it must be stated for clarity that, although the statute excludes the daughter from the legitime, it does not appear to exclude the debt due by natural law itself; rather, it does so by means of an exception, as in Inst. de iure naturali, or by means of some appeal. Or we may say that it does not abolish natural law, but its effect, as in D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. cum hic status, §. siue. Hence we say that, in case of intestacy, nothing is owed. I answer: on the contrary, it is owed by natural equity, which cannot be entirely abolished; and the legitime is measured accordingly, as to which the question or the provision of the statute cannot abolish the principle, as in C. de iure dotium, l. in rebus, and l. cum ratio, and l. 2, D. de usufructu earum rerum, and quod non, D. de institutionibus et iure manumissionum. As for the last point, even if the statute stated that the son could not render the will void or bring an action for inofficiousness, nevertheless the disposition would be removed, because it was introduced by a mixed favor of the will and of the children. And although the favor ceases at one extreme, it remains at the other, where it can remain, as in D. de contractibus, l. si post mortem, §. fi. And this is the way by which the aforementioned daughter can be defended in her claim for the legitime, although not without mental strain, especially when the actual intent of the statute is considered, as in C. de interdictis, l. 1.

But what is it in the statutes? We weigh the words more than an imaginary and uncertain intent, as in D. de usufructu legato, l. si alii. Moreover, due to the conflict between common law and municipal law, we ought not to extend municipal law as if it were irregular and anomalous law. It must be premised for clarity that municipal statute does not abolish natural law or civil law in its entirety or in part, but rather removes its effect; this is evident, for if that statute were annulled, it would not be necessary to enact anything new in a second municipality, because common law would immediately succeed, which would not be the case if common law had been extinguished by municipal law. This is stated by the glossa in a similar case, D. de pactis, l. si unus, §. quod, in the specific case of dowry; and these were the words of Razza and Lord Cynus in a similar case, D. de usufructu, ea. rerum quae usu consumuntur, l. 1; and 2 q. 2; and §. 1 in a similar case, Mag. Extr. de consuetudine, c. cum inter; and all the consultees, D. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. cum hic statutum, §. sive. And therefore the legitime of the testate still has its example and origin in the intestate, whose image is not entirely abolished, just as it would not have been entirely abolished by common law. Furthermore, it would seem to be said that the image would not be left, as in C. de litibus, liber. tol., l. 1, in principio; and yet the woman would come generally as in the case of the testate, since no correction is found. Let us therefore conclude that the legitime of the testate is formed by the legitime of the intestate, which would be according to common law; for, considering that the statute disposes otherwise in the case of intestacy, nevertheless, it is not objected that no querela or action contra tabulas would be given; because by that method we arrive at the woman’s right to the intestate cause, or statute, as when one does not reach the head, because she is excluded by law; but rather it confirms the head from which she is not excluded, namely, the head of the testate. Moreover, intestate, so to speak, the law makes a will and provides for it; but in the wills of our Lord, human providence does not provide, as noted in a similar case, C. qui potiores in pignore habeantur, l. assiduis. And therefore the case of the testate and the intestate is different, and therefore I conclude that, since the statute does not exclude her from that head, neither do I exclude her, especially on grounds of equity. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The preceding opinion on the matter of the legitime is by Baldus; this one, concerning the same case, is by Salicetus, who concludes in favor of Baldus’s opinion in the City of Mantua.
2. The Authentica *Sed hodie*, Codex, *De adulteriis*, applies to a husband who brings an accusation but fails to prove it.
3. Whether an excluded person may claim the legitime.
body: In the name of the Savior, in the name of Christ. Our Jesus Christ, from whose mouth all right judgment proceeded, and of his glorious Virgin Mother, and of the entire heavenly court, amen. Having seen the said case, and the question, and also the will, and the statute, of which mention is made above in the said question, I suppose that the said lady Constantia could not succeed to her said grandfather P. intestate, because of the sons of the said Peter excluding her from intestate succession by the force and disposition of the Mantuan statute placed under the heading "On intestate succession" in the verse "But sisters."

† Where any woman is excluded, or repelled, so that she may not succeed, not only with brothers, but also with nephews, etc., having assumed this, I proceed to the question asked, namely whether in the case proposed the said Constantia can bring an action for the supplement of the legitime. And first, that she cannot bring an action by certain means. First, because the legitime is one-third of that portion which this woman would have had with fruits intestate, as is noted in the gloss in Auth. Nouissima, C. de inoff. testa. But Lady Constantia will have nothing intestate on account of the nephews, who exclude her, as in the said statute: therefore there is no legitime, nor is any portion of the legitime due to her; since there is no portion of nothing, as C. de probat. l. Actor, with similar authorities. Second, to the same effect, for a law correcting in one thing is said to correct in another consequent and necessary thing. This is clear in Auth. Ingressi, C. de sac. sanc. eccle. and in Auth. de monachis, §. Illud. Third, because when the matter is removed, that which is derived from it is also removed, as is clear to the sense and is proved. Ff. de legat. 3, l. Quaesitum, §. Illud fortasse. Fourth, because he is admitted to the petition of the legitime who, having been passed over in the will or disinherited, could bring a querel or break the will, as C. de inoff. testa. l. Omnimodo and l. Si quis filium. But given the aforementioned statute, Lady Constantia, having been passed over, could not bring a querel against or break the said will; since no injury was done to her by the testator, inasmuch as she was not called to his succession intestate, and yet it is on account of such injury that they are admitted and called to the querel, as in the said l. Omnimodo, vers. Si tamen, and Ff. eod. tit. l. 2, 3, and 4.

But against this stands the general reason: namely, that what is not changed, is not prohibited from standing, as C. de appellat. l. Praecipimus, with similar authorities. Second, because a correction in one of correlatives is not extended to the other, unless it is stated, as C. de iudic. vidui, l. Finalis, in principio. It supports what is noted in the antepenultimate and ultimate glosses in l. Finalis, C. de rescindenda venditio. Third, for this side it is argued, because the legitime is one-third of the entire substance of the testator, as in Cor. de triente et semisse, §. Primo. Nor is it said to be of the portion intestate; and this is the newest law, because perhaps the legislator so disposed; and according to this, the arguments made in opposition do not stand in the way. Fourth, I assume that the text in Cor. should be understood as referring to one-third of that which he would have had intestate; nevertheless, the legitimate portion, and thus the one-third, is not found by statute, but by common law; therefore it is referred to one-third of that which she would have by common law, not by municipal law; because it was not expected or considered by common law. And for this, see C. de testam. l. Iubemus, in fine, and what is noted in the gloss in a similar case, and Jacobus Butrius, idem in Auth. Quieres huiusmodi, C. de sacrosanc. eccle. Fifth, for this side it is argued, because this correction alleged to the contrary proceeds from a certain extensive and odious interpretation; because it is against common law and nature, therefore it is not to be admitted, as Ff. sol. matr. l. Sit condito testamento, in si vero, §. De viro, de lib. et posth. l. Cum quidam, and Extra de regul. iur. c. Odia.

And in support of this, it is well stated by Jacobus Butrigarius and Cynus in the Authentica *Sed hodie*, Codex, *De adulteriis*, where they say that the penalty arising from the new law, which is now in force, namely that an adulterous woman be confined to a monastery, applies to the husband who accused her but failed to prove his charge; and thus he ought to be subjected to a similar punishment. And they state that this proceeds from equity, so that a milder penalty may be imposed and the severity of penalties restrained; otherwise, if equity and favor suggest the opposite, as is the case in our instance, in which rigor, equity, and favor, by which hatred is avoided, suggest that such a statute should not exclude women from claiming the legitime or its supplement, which is quantified with respect to the portion due by intestate succession under the common law; since the statute does not prohibit them from claiming the legitime or its supplement. Sixthly, because a person is excluded from intestate succession on account of having made a will, as stated in the law *Quandiu*, Digest, *De acquirenda hereditate*.

† Nevertheless, one who is excluded is not prohibited from claiming the legitime, or its supplement, as provided in C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. si, and l. scimus, §. repletionem. Therefore, in the case at hand, one who is excluded from succession by statute without any fault of his own, and to the advantage of another, ought not to be said to be excluded from the claim of the legitime. Seventhly, for this opinion, there appears to be a quasi-case in the Authentica Si qua mulier, at the end, C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, where children who are excluded from succession by the favor of a monastery are not excluded from claiming the legitime. And the same holds in the Authentica Hoc amplius, C. de fideicommissis, and in the Corpus, de hereditatibus et falcidia, §. si quis autem non implens. Eighthly, the text proves this, C. de crimine laesae maiestatis, l. quisquis, where daughters excluded from their mother’s succession are not excluded from claiming the legitime. And if you say that the contrary is stated there regarding a son: I answer that there the son is deprived of succession and the legitime by his own presumed act, and thus by his presumed delict, as the letter of the law proves there. Ninthly, because every impubes who is arrogated, who, or when, is not admitted to the succession of his arrogating father, is not prohibited from claiming his legitime by action under the law, as in ff. de adoptionibus, l. si arrogator, and ff. de collatione bonorum, l. 1, §. si impubere. Tenthly, this is confirmed by reason, because laws speaking in the case of intestacy do not imply the same in the case of testacy, as noted by the gloss in the Authentica Ex causa, C. de libellis prætendis vel exheredationibus. And because this opinion seems founded on stronger reasons than the first, and because it rests on great equity, I follow it. And because from the aforementioned reasons the response to the arguments alleged to the contrary is clear, it is not expedient to respond otherwise. Or distinguish: either civil law or municipal law excludes women from succession in favor of agnate parents, and then, unless it is expressly stated that they are excluded from claiming the legitime, or its supplement, they are not repelled, as in our theme by the laws cited above; or by their true or fictitious delict: and then they are also understood to be excluded from claiming the legitime, as in C. ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, l. quisquis, in that part where it speaks of a male son, who on account of his fictitious or presumed delict is also deprived of the legitime. And for this also add C. de episcopis et clericis, Authentica Si captivi. And this when the reason of the delict is uniform for the deprivation of both, otherwise the contrary, as in the said Authentica Hoc amplius. And although judgments should be made by laws, not by examples, nevertheless I do not omit what I heard, that in the audience of the Lord Cardinal of Albano, brother of Urban V, it was judged among certain nobles, while I was reading at Padua, for this opinion, which I held above. And thus I say, and I counsel, I, Bartholomew de Saliceto, etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the heir of a manifest usurer should be put into possession.
2. How that doctrine is to be understood, namely that it is established today, it is litigated today.
3. The fact of law is stronger than the fact of man.
body: A certain John died in the name of Christ, having instituted Martin as his heir. At the time of his death, his sister was in his house, as was the aforementioned inscribed heir, and thus they remained after his death.
