The said Martin claims that he ought to be confirmed in possession of all the goods of the deceased which were in his possession at the time of death, especially since the statute provides that possession of the deceased and all its effects pass to the heir by operation of law. On the other hand, the said sister states, in the First Part of the Consilia, that the said John was a manifest usurer and provided no security; therefore, the said testamentary instrument was void and empty. She offers to prove this immediately and separately, through witnesses present in the city, so that without delay the witnesses may be received and examined. For this reason, she requests that the said Martin be removed and prohibited from disturbing her, the heir ab intestato. The question now arises: what is the law? And

† It seems beyond doubt that the said sister ought to be heard. For it is certain that the testament of a manifest usurer, who died without having furnished security, does not deserve to be regarded as having the name of a testament; nor does it deserve execution for pious causes, as in c. quamque de usuris, lib. 6. Likewise, it is certain that he who is in possession, if he indeed alleges a similar title, has his rights heard, even if he does not offer to prove it immediately; but if he says the testament is null and states that he will prove it forthwith, he ought to be heard; otherwise not, as noted in l. 2 and l. edicto, C. de edicto divi Adriani. But this sister is ready forthwith to prove her case; therefore, the way of proof ought not to be narrowed nor denied, as in extra de appellatione, c. interposita.

To the contrary, it seems that the right of one showing a testament not cancelled is a proven right; and presumption favors the testament, as noted in C. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. et si post testamentum. Likewise, just as the written heir is presumed, so from the form of the statute possession is presumed to have continued in him; and thus he ought to be defended in that possession. And here it must be observed, for here lies the subtlety of this point: since the written heir is presumed to be the possessor, he holds the part of the defendant; but the unwritten heir, since he is not presumed to be the possessor, holds the part of the plaintiff, as in l. liberis, § ultimo, ff. de liberis causis.

And therefore the heir cannot raise an exception by saying, “It is established today, it is litigated today”; rather, he must bring an action, and that doctrine, “it is established today, it is litigated today,” does not assist the plaintiff, but the defendant. Nor can the sister say, “If you are not the heir, therefore you do not possess”; but I, the sister, possess, and I am the heir. Because the presumptive possession of the instituted heir entails that she must bring an action, but not raise an exception. The case is in the aforementioned law *Liberis*, § *Ultimo*, *De liberis causis*. And therefore the judge’s duty is to defend the instituted heir and to enjoin the sister not to disturb him in possession, until she proves her right by the submission of a libel and the observance of the judicial procedure, as is done in cases of nullity of a will, as in the Institutes, *De interdictis*; the Code, *Commune*; and the Digest, *De damno infecto*, law *A quo fundus*. Consider also that, since the statute makes the heir the possessor immediately, it is impossible for the sister to concur in possession.

† because the act of the law is more powerful than the act of a man: and it operates more immediately, as noted by Innocentius in the Extravagantes, *De appellationibus*, chapter *Praeterea requisiti*. And it is impossible that two persons should possess in solidum, as in the Digest, *De commodato*, law *Si ut certo*, § *Si duobus vehiculum*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. On the matter of varying witnesses: and who are said to be consistent, and who are not.
2. The word of a witness saying “to the aforesaid, I was present,” how it is to be understood.
3. What a variation of a witness induces.
4. Something may be written in the presence of a witness, and without his seeing it.
5. The discrepancy of a witness renders him singular, and he does not prove.
6. Whether a prosoneta is admitted as a witness.
7. In a contract of deposit, we do not rely on confession: otherwise in a loan.
8. Given a statute that instruments not subscribed by two no
body: A. says he made a writing

† A certain person named A. says he made a writing in the form of an acknowledgement of a deposit of one thousand, and subscribed himself; and three witnesses, as it appears, also wrote. By virtue, therefore, of the said writing, in which an obligation of goods is contained, a hypothecary action was brought against an outside possessor, since the principal debtor was insolvent. In this proceeding, the said three subscribing witnesses were examined. The tenor of the subscription of the said debtor is as follows: 'I, A., above-written, wrote with my own hand, and subscribed.' The tenor of the subscription of the first witness is as follows: 'I, Salinus, witness above-written, was present at the aforesaid, and subscribed myself.' The tenor of the subscription of the second witness is as follows: 'I, John, witness, was present at the aforesaid, and subscribed myself.' The tenor of the subscription of the third witness is as follows: 'I, Iacopinus, witness, was present at the aforesaid, and subscribed myself.' These witnesses were examined in the aforesaid cause, and the first witness testified in effect that the said writing and the said subscriptions were genuine, yet he said that he did not see the said acknowledgement of the said deposit being written, but he saw it written, and heard the said debtor then confessing that the said writing was made with his own hand. Here it is first asked whether his statement is contrary to his subscription? And it seems that it is, because in the subscription he inserted these words, namely, 'I, Salinus, witness above-written, was present at the aforesaid, and subscribed myself.' Afterwards, he says that he was not present at the aforesaid regarding the writing of the said debtor, but was present at the subscription of the said security. Likewise, he said that he did not see the aforesaid moneys counted.

† Now it is asked, what is the law? And it seems that that phrase, 'was present at the aforesaid', refers both to the security and to all preceding things, because that phrase, 'at the aforesaid', makes a full repetition, as in ff. de fundo instruc. l. Seya. §. Cao. To the contrary, it seems that the words uttered by the principal debtor state thus: 'I wrote, and subscribed.' But the word 'I wrote' is in the past tense, for he does not say 'I then wrote'; nor does it matter whether he wrote then or before, if that writing was then exhibited to the witnesses, as in C. qui testamenta facere possunt. l. hac consultissima. §. at. cum humana. Likewise, the words of the principal debtor contain nothing other than an acknowledgement, as in C. de arbit. l. ne in arbitris. Therefore, the statement of the first witness is not rendered false, since he was present at the writing, because a writing has in itself a permanent act, by the argument of ff. de iure codicillorum. l. plotiana. and ff. de verbo. signifi. l. verbum oportebit. per di. But to this, the learned jurist with whom I conferred replies that the said aforesaid responses are not valid, because even though it were not of the essence of the writing that it was written then, nevertheless it must be of the form of the testimony, because the writing must agree with the testimony, by the argument of ff. de leg. 2. l. cum pater. §. cum imperfecta. But here the living voice of the witness does not agree with the writing, because he detracts another element from it along with the writing, namely his own presence: for, as Bar. elegantly says in d. l. 1. de auth. tuto., if he speaks of his own presence, he is then understood to speak, as it were, of a certain bodily standing-by, not of knowledge of that matter. Which must be understood thus, namely, not of necessity, but of a presumption both of law and of nature. Likewise, from things that commonly happen, one who is present is presumed to hear and understand, ff. de ver. obl. l. si procuratori. Present. I think that the statement of Bar. does not apply to subscribing witnesses, because subscription necessarily includes knowledge.

† From which it appears that the said witness, in subscribing, spoke from his own knowledge and understanding, which afterwards he seems in some respect to have denied; and a variance of a witness, even if it is not concerning the weight of the cause, nevertheless renders the witness less worthy of belief; but if it were in the substantials of the cause, it would render him criminal, which however in the present case I do not think. But that there is some dissonance, I do not deny, as the records speak; for we cannot speak more or less of the records than the records themselves speak, as in l. fideius. magistratuum. §. 1. ff. de fideius. Now follows the second witness, who testified that the said security was written and subscribed by the own hand of the said debtor and of the above-mentioned witnesses, and in the presence of the said witnesses who subscribed themselves. Furthermore, in that he says 'it was written in the presence of the witnesses who subscribed themselves', he contradicts the statement of the first witness; but to this it is replied that each witness can speak the truth according to his own judgment:

† for it could have been written while the said witness was present, and yet without his seeing it; the gl. ord. says this on C. de testi. l. testium, and dominus Bar. treats this passage in l. 1. in fi. ff. de aut. tu. Or it can be said, so that the witnesses do not fall into a contradiction, that those words, 'in the presence of the said witnesses', refer to that word, 'subscribed', because it is not denied that in the subscription of the security all were present, arg. extra de testi. tu. c. tu fili. Likewise, another contradiction is objected: because the said first witness says that he did not see the money counted, whereas the second witness says that he saw it counted beforehand; but to this it is answered that the adverb 'beforehand' resolves the contradiction, according to that maxim, 'distinguish the times and you will harmonize the writings', as noted in C. de furtis l. apud antiquos. But if the said second witness had expressly said that the money was counted in the presence of the said witnesses, whether then or before, the said witnesses would be contradictory and incompatible, and therefore neither of them would be believed by way of proof, as in ff. quemadm. testa. aperiantur. l. 1. in fi. But to this the said learned jurist responds and says that it is true that they can be distinguished so that they are not contradictory, yet that distinction brings it about that they are not co-witnesses, and therefore they do not prove. For instance, this one asserts that he has that one as a co-witness, who is not; therefore, between them there is no harmony,

† and it is certain that by dissonance a witness is rendered singular and does not prove, as in extra de probac. licet causam. Likewise, it must be noted that the said witnesses, in subscribing, utter one and the same rehearsed statement, but in testifying it is otherwise; and for that reason they are not co-witnesses to each other, and thus their asserted writing is not grounded, because it does not harmonize; and therefore, since the said writing is denied and is private, it does not prove. As to the third witness, that two of them were brokers [prosonetae],

† because a willing broker is admitted to testify, although an unwilling one is not compelled, as in Auth. de testi. §. pen. and in c. mediatores. de testi. lib. 6., although dominus Cy. says that when a witness has been summoned, he is understood to testify unwillingly according to Bar. de Capua—which is not true, nor is it approved by custom, because it is of the nature of judicial proceedings that they be summoned, although sometimes their statements are valid without a summons, as singularly noted in ff. de his, quibs vt indign. l. post lega. §. is vero. and as I have very fully noted on C. de epi. et cle. l. presbyteri. As to that which is questioned concerning the comparison of hands, that it does not appear to have been solemnly made because it was not in the presence of the judge, but by chosen notaries: it must be said that if indeed they were chosen with the parties present and consenting, or with one present and the other absent but solemnly summoned, their said election is valid; otherwise not. Likewise, if these chosen persons make the comparison in the presence of the parties, or with them warned for this purpose, it is valid; otherwise not, arg. C. de secun. nup. l. hac edictali. §. is illud. and in l. 1. in prin. ff. de ven. inspi. and what is noted in Auth. de triente et semisse. §. quoniam saepe. For, so to speak, they perform jointly the office of witness and of judge, because testimony of expertise is, in a certain manner, to judge; and therefore the party must be summoned for it, as in ff. de re iu. l. de vno quoque and C. de testib. l. si quando and ff. de dote pręleg. l. Theopompus. Furthermore, with the parties present, it must not be omitted that what the witness says about the sack proves nothing, because what is inside the sack is neither seen nor counted, and in this the testimony of sight is required, as in ff. depositi. l. 1. §. si cista. Custom, however, is to the contrary, that he is believed to have counted, and it suffices that the sack with the coins is there, and the receiver confesses that so many coins are therein, and one stands by the confession. But that custom is rather abusive, although it is frequently practiced in my homeland; nevertheless, there the notary goes directly to the money-changer, and he never writes that it has been counted unless it is counted immediately at the money-changer's in the presence of the witnesses. From this it follows that those who saw it counted are not co-witnesses with the one who says he saw the sack; but this is little to the point:

† because in a contract of deposit, one does not stand by the confession, as in C. de non num. pec. l. in contractibus. and ff. depositi. l. publica. §. fina., although it is otherwise in a loan [mutuum], because men are readier to confess, for no one takes a loan except under the pressing necessity of domestic affairs, or a greater one, and therefore is readier to confess that he has received. But in a deposit it is not so, because he cannot use the money. The final conclusion is that I would stand by the said subscription, as in C. de non nume. pecu. l. generaliter. and C. de fide instrumen. l. scripturas. and Authen. si quis vult caute deponere, unless there were some kind of variance in the statements of the witnesses; nevertheless, a crime is not to be dealt with here, because I do not consider that there is any crime, nor any fraud, although, proceeding by the strict subtleties of the law, it does not appear to have been lawfully compared to a public instrument according to those things that are set forth above and which the records speak; and this I say, saving the truth of the fact, to which a judge ought principally to look, and strive with all his powers to discover the cause, as in C. de sententiis, quae pro eo proferuntur. l. 1. §. in alijs, whence the Decretum says, 'it behooves one judging to examine all things'; and if the comparison was not duly made once, it can be made again, because the useful ought not to be vitiated by the useless, as in clem. testibus, by the opposite sense, and the notes there. Or more briefly, three things are here to be weighed: namely, the subscription, the deposition of the subscribers, and the comparison of hands. If we weigh the subscription, although it is clean and without blemish, it is a private writing, which of itself does not make full proof. If, however, we consider the statements of the witnesses, they are not entirely conformable with the writing; nor is it a wonder, because the memory of men is slippery. If, moreover, we consider the comparison of hands, the form that is required in comparisons does not seem to have been observed in every respect; nevertheless, if the status of the cause allows it, a comparison can be made again, in the same manner as the witness is impugned or defended. Furthermore, it does not stand unless perhaps the said variation of the witnesses were to vary it; and so I hold, saving the substance of the truth, which any judge ought to have before his eyes, saving whatever cavils. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. A dowry may be constituted during the subsistence of the marriage.
2. A gift may be made by the maternal grandmother and the mother-in-law, and through them, to the grandson and daughter; [and whether] the [prohibitions] of the *Codex* regarding donations between spouses are valid, and to what extent they extend.
4. Of which city a wife is said to be a citizen.
5. The origin of the law confers a right of new origin.
6. What a statute speaking of citizens comprehends.
7. Which days are included under the term "days," given a statute that the arbitrator must render his award within 40 days.
8. If an arbitrator orders that someone not be molested under penalty, whether, upon payment of the penalty, he may be molested.
9. Whether an award rendered in favor of the seller benefits the buyer.
body: Seya's origin: her father, In the name of Christ. Titius, a native of the City of Parma. While in a valid marriage, Titius confessed that he had received, in the name of Seya's dowry, one thousand [units of currency] from her maternal grandmother; and he promised to restore the same to Seya in every case of dowry restitution, with an obligation of his goods, and he waived the exception of non-payment of the dowry, as appears from the instrument executed on that day. Against which instrument the defendant possessor raises a hypothecary defense.

† stating that the said Instrument is presumed to arise from a cause of donation, which cannot exist between husband and wife. And especially because no delivery (traditio) intervened, as in D. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. Papi. Hence, although the donor predeceased, the donation is not confirmed by death. To this effect it is noted in C. qui pot. in pign. hab. l. Assiduis, in the small gloss, which states that the disposition of that law does not apply to a dowry confessed but not paid. To the contrary is the truth itself: because a dowry, during the subsistence of the marriage, can be constituted both by confession and by payment, unless it is constituted to the fraud of other creditors, as in C. de dot. ante nup. l. Si, and Auth. Sed iam necesse. Nor can the exception of non-payment of dowry be raised: first, due to the lapse of time; second, because it was waived, as noted in C. de non num. pec. l. Si executione. This waiver was not made between husband and wife, but between the maternal grandmother and the husband, where a donation is not presumed, but a dowry. For as is the instrument in form, so is it presumed in substance: one must adhere to the words of the instrument, as in C. de probat. l. Cum precibus, and Extr. de usur. c. Naviganti. Simulation is never presumed unless proven, as in C. plus val. quod agi. per totum, and D. de pact. l. Iuris gentium, §. Quod fere, unless the contrary is expressly proven. Moreover, the matter here is not concerning a dowry between husband and wife, because in the contract it is the grandmother who is presumed to have donated to her granddaughter, not the husband to the wife, as in D. sol. mat. l. Gayus, and l. Rem in praesenti, §. Extraneum, and C. de iud. dot. l. Auia. Certainly, it is also not doubtful that a dowry can be constituted for a marriage already contracted, even long ago, as in D. si cert. pet. l. 2, ver. Veluti, and D. de act. et oblig. l. Obligamur, §. 1; otherwise, a dowry constituted before marriage would not be valid unless it were transferred at the time of the marriage, as in C. de don. ante nup. l. 1, and l. Quod sponsae. And on this matter, it is sufficiently noted in the said l. 1, de dot. ante nup., by the gloss and Cynus. It is therefore concluded that the said instrument must be upheld. For even if the husband confessed to having received from the grandmother with the intent to donate, two donations would be seen: one by the husband to the maternal grandmother, and another by the maternal grandmother to her granddaughter; although the swiftness of the acts may conceal one, as in D. de don. inter vir. et ux. l. 3, §. Sciendum, and l. Sulpitius.

† It is established, however, that a mother-in-law and a sister-in-law can make donations to one another, and likewise the former can make a donation to her grandson and daughter: because they are not connected through any paternal power, as stated in the Digest, *De donationibus inter virum et uxorem*, law 1, with its gloss. Moreover, even if it were said that a husband had made a donation to his wife, it would not be a simple donation, but one made in consideration of the dowry; in which case it is not required that the husband make delivery, due to the nature of the dowry, which ought to be possessed by the husband, as stated in the Code, *De dote cauta non numerata*, law 2, although the gloss thereon becomes entangled.

Next follows the second point, for the statute of Parma provides that an instrument shall not be valid unless two notaries are present and requested, even if it is made outside the territory of Parma within a certain distance. Now, a compromise was made between the aforementioned lady and a certain citizen of Parma; and the arbitrator rendered his award outside the district of Parma, of which it does not appear that more than one notary was requested. The question is whether the said instrument of the award is to be given credence in the city of Parma. And it seems that it should, because under common law one notary with witnesses suffices, as noted in the Authenticum *De hereditatibus et falsis*, § *Si vero absunt*. Moreover, the statute of Parma cannot regulate matters outside its jurisdiction, especially by annulling what is lawfully done outside its territory, because outside its territory the city of Parma is regarded as a private person; therefore it cannot make statutes, just as it could not administer justice, as in the law *Cunctos populos* and the law *Extra territorium*, and in the chapter *Ut animarum*, *De constitutionibus*, Book 6.

On the contrary, however, even if we were to say that such an instrument is valid as to the substance of the instrument and proves its contents elsewhere than in the territory of Parma—because the citizens of Parma cannot extend their roots beyond the boundaries of their territory—nevertheless, as regards using it in the city of Parma, it is necessary that the statute of Parma be observed. For concerning those matters which are brought before the court of Parma, they can properly make statutes, as in the law *I.*, D. *De usu*, and D. *De testibus*, law 3, § *Si*. Furthermore, the statute of Parma binds the citizens of Parma in any place, since it specifies the place, as in D. *De decretis ab ordinario faciendis*, law *Si tunc*. Consider that an instrument is not valid unless the notary is requested, as in the Authenticum *De tabellionibus*, § *Nos autem*. But the contracting parties, who are citizens of Parma, cannot, by virtue of the prohibiting statute, order an instrument to be made; therefore the instrument made by the single notary, who is not enrolled, is not valid. I therefore say that the said statute is to be observed among citizens of Parma in the court of Parma; and consequently, credence should not be given to it, as in C. *De testamento*, law *Si unus ex testibus defuerit*. And because a statute which regulates the credence to be given by a judge regulates its own judge, and thus the place of the court is considered, this law alone is called praetorian and binds him; and it is established that the praetor is bound to observe the statutes of his place, as in Extra, *De iure immunitatis*, chapter *Venientibus*.

The third article is whether the aforementioned Seva should be called a Parmesan. And it seems that she should not, even if her origin were proven; because the said origin is causal and momentary; and that which is momentary is not to be considered, as in the Digest, On Judges, the law *Heres absens*. But the contrary is true, for if a woman is captured by enemies and gives birth there, this child is said to have been born among the enemies, although it was born there by chance, as in the Digest, On Captives and Postliminium, law 1. Therefore, if the origin is proven, there is no doubt that this Seva is of proper Parmesan origin; and she is called an original native by reason of the event; and as an original native, she is subject to municipal laws, and conversely enjoys the benefit of municipal laws; because just as one is born to a city, so the city dies to itself, as in the Digest, On Captives and Postliminium, the law *Cum duae*, because these are correlative. Moreover, because this Seva was married to a Parmesan, she ought to be considered an original Parmesan, even while she is a widow.

† because the origin of law confers upon the wife a right of new origin, as is noted in C. de municipibus, et originariis, l. origine, lib. 10, which gloss is not found elsewhere. Moreover, because the statute does not speak in these words, Parmensi, which words signify origin: as is noted in ff. de excus. tuto., l. si duas, in the word communes; but it uses this word, ciuis, or districtualis. But it is certain that one becomes a true citizen and a true districtualis through domicile and perpetual home, as in ff. de incolis, l. ciues, and l. 2, C. vbi senato. vel clari, l. 2, so much so

† That statute, speaking of citizens, is understood to speak properly and truly of permanent inhabitants, and without any fiction, as stated in the aforementioned law *cives*, in the word *domicilium* and in the word *lare*. And this is fully noted by Bartolus in the Digest, title *De usucapione*, law *Si is, qui pro emptore*.

† The fourth article: the statute provides that the arbitrator must render his award within 40 continuous days, to be computed from the time of the compromise; and if he neglects to render the award within the said time, the compromise and the award shall be void. Let us suppose that nothing was notified to the arbitrator at the beginning, but only that 30 days have elapsed. The question now arises: whether, if he did not render the award within the following 10 days, he may subsequently render it. And if we consider the nature of continuous days, his power appears to be extinguished; but if we consider the nature of useful days, it does not appear to be extinguished. Useful days are indicated by the word "neglects," as in D. de excus. tutor. l. quinquaginta and l. scire oportet § consequens. To this I answer that the word "neglects" does not require that all 40 days be useful, but it suffices that some of the said 40 days be useful, within which the arbitrator is negligent in deciding the case, as in D. qui ex causa mai. l. ab hostibus § si.

The fifth article: suppose that in the decree of the lord it is stated that the compromise shall not endure nor extend beyond the term of 40 useful days, to be computed from the day of acceptance made by the arbitrator; whether this contradicts the aforementioned statute regarding continuous days? I answer that it does, as in C. de dolo l. 1 and C. in quibus causis in integ. rest. non est necess. l. superuacuam; and therefore the term for the expiration of the office does not lapse for one who is ignorant, as noted by Bartolus in D. de his qui non infa. l. gest. nero.

The sixth article is whether, if the arbitrator undertakes that the matter shall not be disturbed, the plaintiff may disturb it by paying the penalty or the damages: regarding the penalty, the ordinary gloss states that it applies to a mere arbitrator. In c. quamdiu, de appellationibus; in the Clementina sed considerato, considering that by the form of the statute awards have the force of a definitive sentence, one who is ordered not to sue or not to harass cannot contravene this order, even if he wishes to pay the damages. D. de re vendicata, l. qui restituere. And because we are here dealing with an arbitral award, where execution cannot be taken away from the party to whom it is due against his will, as D. de pactis, l. rescriptum, § si pacto.

The final point is whether an award rendered in favor of the seller benefits the buyer. And on this it must be said that it does, just as in the case of a compromise; for the right to raise an exception passes to the singular successor, as stated in the law *Etiam*, in the Digest under *De iureiurando*, and fully noted by Dyonisius in the law *Filium*, section *Adiciatur*, in the Digest under *De damno infecto*. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Contracts that may be entered into with ecclesiastical prelates.
2. The successor of a prelate to which contracts he must adhere.
3. Monosyllabic terms, namely, what they signify.
4. Where one year begins, another ends.
body: Reverend Father, in the name of Christ... the Lord Bishop, on the 13th day of the month of May, leased to Titius in these words: from the feast of St. Martin next coming until nine years next following, paying each year on the feast of St. Martin 40 florins. And during the term of the said lease, the bishop died. It is asked whether the succeeding bishop is bound to abide by the said contract.

† For the understanding of which, it must be premised that certain perpetual contracts are permitted, such as fiefs and emphyteusis; and these, if celebrated according to customary practice, pass to the successor of the lessor, provided that the contract was valid from the beginning: as in c. *I. qui successores teneantur*, coll. 10. Certain perpetual contracts are prohibited, such as if a prelate wished to newly enfeoff, or to grant in emphyteusis things not accustomed to be held in emphyteusis or enfeoffed; and this neither he himself is bound to ratify, nor his successor: as in C. *de sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, l. *Iubemus nulli*; and in c. *1. episcopus vel abbas*, coll. 10. The same is to be said regarding a lease extending over a long time, because it is a species of alienation: as in ff. *de superficiebus*, l. *1. §. quod ait*; ff. *si ager vectigalis*, l. *1. §. qui in perpetuum*; in Authen. *de alienationibus et emphyteusibus*, §. *locationes*, unless those solemnities intervene which are required in perpetual alienations. And if such a prelate had sworn not to alienate without consulting the Roman Pontiff, the authority of the Pope must intervene if there is a new alienation, as in c. *Si quis*, *de rebus ecclesiae non alienandis*. However, that oath does not extend to things accustomed to be alienated, granted in emphyteusis, or enfeoffed, as in extra *de feudis*, c. *Ex parte*; because custom gives things their nature and the quality of alienability: as in l. *1. §. permittitur*, ff. *de aqua quotannis*; and it is an excellent text in ff. *quod vi aut clam*, l. *Prohibere*, §. *plane*.

It now remains to consider leases for a short term, that is, for ten years exclusively, and whether the successor in the prelacy or administration is bound to stand by the tenant or lessee. For I do not speak of a prebendary, because a prebend attaches to a canonry, which ends with the death of the person; when the actor dies, the act is extinguished, insofar as it is in the process of being performed for a future time, as in D. loc. cond. l. si quis domum § huic; D. de nov. oper. nunt. l. quotiens § si; D. de pign. act. l. lex vectigalis. But I speak of a prelate or legitimate administrator, whose dignity remains in the church itself even when vacant of a pastor, as in D. de leg. 2 l. quod principi. There the distinction is briefly made as follows: either the prelate contracted with the consent of the chapter, and the chapter with the consent of the prelate, and it passes to the successor, because the chapter does not die; and there are two authorities united, and stronger, namely those of the prelate and the chapter, as in c. ut nos, gloss. C. de facult. laic. eccl. eccl. auth. hoc ius porrectum. Or the prelate alone contracted, and then it matters whether he contracted concerning a thing whose administration pertains jointly to the prelate and the chapter, or to the chapter alone; and the contract is void from the beginning, and neither he nor the successor is bound, as in leg. and nos. ex de rescr. c. edoceri, and ex de his quae fiunt a prelato sine consensu cap. quasi per totum. Or it was concluded concerning a thing which pertains to the administration of the prelate alone, and then it matters: either he contracted in his own name only, and the successor is not bound; or he contracted in the name of the church, for example in the name of the episcopate, and then either he converted the money to the utility of the church, and this is established, and the successor is bound; or to his own personal profit, and this is established, and the successor is not bound. So says Bernard, Innocent, and all the doctors in d. c. querelam, ne prelati vices suas. Or it is doubtful, and then it must be proved that it was turned to the utility of the church, arg. D. si cert. pet. l. ciuitas. But some say that there is a special rule in loan contracts; nevertheless, at least this must be proved, that utility could have accrued to the church therefrom, as in D. de exercit. l. Lucius § pen. For what if much more is found than was leased, so that the lease might seem in a way gratuitous? Certainly the successor is by no means bound to stand by the lease; because he is to be considered not as the heir of the lessor, but as the church itself, which does not die, and to him, through his predecessor, no condition ought to be imposed, as in D. de iur. et fact. ign. l. iniquissimum. Otherwise the predecessor could consume that from which the successor has to live, and would appropriate everything to himself, leaving nothing to the successor; which is false and absurd; and especially because the prelate can do whatever he can by virtue of mandate, not by virtue of ownership, because his mandate ends with death, as in c. ult. de procur. in Clem. nisi in rebus perfectis, as in D. de inst. l. si quis mancipii § si impubes. The above are confirmed by what is read and noted in 12 q. 2 c. in summa, and c. alienationes, according to Innocent. Therefore it is concluded that the lease of a bishop does not pass to the successor, unless the contract was concluded for the utility of the church and under a suitable rent, or unless it was concluded with solemnity, as the aforementioned glossators and doctors say. It now remains to consider another point, namely whether by these words, “from the feast of St. Martin next future until nine years from then next future, paying on the feast of St. Martin next future, and thus every year at the beginning of the year,” it is doubtful how these words are to be understood: whether they include the first St. Martin, because the contract was concluded in the month of October, or exclude it; for this is a common question,

Whether the monosyllable "a" denotes separation of time, or conjunction and connection. For in the first case it excludes, in the second it includes. Let us therefore see what is the law regarding this monosyllable "a," or regarding the syllable "ab." Some say indiscriminately that this word "a" and "ab" is placed exclusively, as in D. de actionibus emptoris, l. Ratio, §. Si. Others say it is placed inclusively, as is most fully noted by Arch. in c. Statutum, de praebendis, lib. 6. But Jo. And. says one thing in the gloss there, and pursues another in the novella. But elsewhere he is very laconic in c. Quam sit, de electione, lib. 6, in the novella, in the word "a tempore," where he thus says: "It is clear from this that even that day will be counted," although Franc. Vercellensis argues to the contrary by the decretal Pia, infra de exceptionibus. But an expressly different case is formed: and he solves the contrary. Jo. And.'s words are brief: but the interpretation is not brief. It must therefore be said that either the intention of the law, or of the contracting parties, is established by the words, and we adhere to the words declaring it, whether they precede or follow, as in D. de legibus, l. Si servus plurium, §. Si, and what is noted in D. si certum petatur, l. Cum quid. Or if it is not established by the words, and then either if it were placed inclusively, an absurdity would follow: and it does not include, but excludes. Or an absurdity would follow if it were placed exclusively, and then it does not exclude, but includes, as noted by Cy. in C. de nuptiis, l. Acalligato. Or however it is placed, no absurdity follows. And then it matters whether the word "a" or "ab" is joined at the beginning, and it is placed inclusively: the law says, "I institute as heir my grandson, who shall be born within 10 months from the day of the death of my son": that the day of death is counted in the 10 months. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. Gallus, in principio. It says the oath of fidelity, §. I swear from this hour henceforth to be faithful. Certainly this hour is included: because the act is joined at the beginning of its proper time, as in c. 1, de nova forma fidelitatis. The words of the contract say, "From this day I promise 10." Certainly the present day is included: because it is a certain integrity of time, which does not exclude its first beginning, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Lecta, §. Si. And generally wherever it is joined with its beginning, it includes that beginning. But if it is joined with a time which is not of its beginning, then it is placed exclusively: as if someone is cited to appear within 10 days from today, it is not from the judge's admonition: because it is not from the ordered appearance, as in l. 1, D. si quis cautionem. Similarly if the bishop says, "Unless you pay within 8 days from this day, I excommunicate you." For delay does not begin to accrue from the day of excommunication, but the course of delay begins on the following day, as in D. si certum petatur, l. Lecta, §. Sed cum fortis. From this theory we arrive at the conclusion of our question: I speak by way of motivation, that the word "a" is placed inclusively. First, because the lessee receives the fruits of the first St. Martin's Day, which he could not receive by virtue of another lease: because the second is finished, for the reason of avoiding absurdity, because there ought not to be two festivals in the same year, in which the fruits of almost the whole year consist. For one year has only one fruit, comprising 12 months, as in D. de solutione et mutatione, l. Divortio, in principio, and §. Quod in se mensem. Thirdly, by doctrine, because the word "a" is joined to its beginning, as the script of the contract declares there in the beginning, "of each year," where the disposers wished it to be: as in l. 1, C. quoniam dies legati cedat, and D. eodem, l. Nec semel, §. Si in habitatione, and l. Firmio, and D. quando dies legati cedat, l. Si cum praefinitione, and d. l. Lecta, D. si certum petatur. From which I conclude that the word "a" here is placed continuously and inclusively, not separatively, both from the nature of the beginning uniting with its course of time: and for the reason of avoiding absurdity and duplication: and for the reason of declaration: because, as I said, "a" placed between the beginning and the end of time joins from moment to moment: but where it would be placed between contrary terms, or which could not be joined together, then it would be placed exclusively. And of the first there are many examples. Behold, if I say, "From the rising of the sun until its setting is the day." Also if I say, "From youth age is prone to evil." Also if I say, "From the sole of the foot to the top of the head, there is no spot in him." For in all these, and similar ones, the word "a" is placed inclusively, as is clear to any observer. So in the case at hand, when I say "From the feast of St. Martin until the other feast of St. Martin." If the word "until" is placed exclusively, it is necessary that the word "a" be placed inclusively: and if the contrary, the contrary. Since therefore the first feast, by the law of this contract, and not of another, belonged, as has been said, to the lessee, it necessarily follows that the last feast of St. Martin does not belong to the same person.

† because where one year begins, another ends, and it revolves. For thus it is with days, as in D. de feriis, l. more Romano. Likewise with months; therefore also with years, which are measured by days and months, as in D. de statu liberorum, l. cum heres, §. Stichus; and D. de minoribus, l. 3, §. minorem. And it supports what we note in C. de appellationibus, auth. hodie; and in c. pia, de exceptionibus, lib. 6; and D. de usufructu, l. defuncta; and D. si certum petatur, l. si quis nec cam, §. res pig; and in c. si perpetua, de rescriptis, lib. 6; and Inst. de verborum obligationibus, §. omnis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The contract of sale, as regards its substance, is perfected by consent; it makes no difference whether a small or very small earnest money was given.
2. Whether, upon a completed sale, the seller is bound to execute a deed of sale for the buyer.
body: A certain person bought something for one hundred in the name of Christ, and gave one coin as an earnest. Finally, by the order of the said seller, the said buyer paid the seller’s creditor ten each year for two years. Now the said buyer demands that the said seller make out a deed of sale for him; but the seller says he is not bound to do so. The question is, what is the law?

I answer that this question consists not only in law, but also in fact. As to the law: the contract of sale and purchase, as regards the substance of the obligation producing effects on both sides, is perfected by consent, as stated in the Institutes, "On obligations which are contracted by consent," in the principal paragraph. Nor does it matter, in this respect, whether an earnest money (arra) was given or not; nor whether a small, very small, or large earnest money was given, because the earnest money is an argument of the sale. However, it is not a means of rescinding or establishing the sale, as stated in the Institutes, "On sale and purchase," § 1. But what must be considered here is what was agreed upon between the parties. For if the seller was not otherwise going to sell unless the price was paid to him immediately within a short interval, then the buyer, who proceeds with delays and procrastinations and does not offer the full price, ought not to be heard, nor does he have any justice on his side. But if it was agreed between the contracting parties, including the heir and the strangers, that the price should certainly be paid to certain persons and at certain times, the agreed pact must be observed, as stated in law 1, § 1, Digest, "On pacts."

But it is doubtful whether, once the sale is perfected by reason of consent, the seller is bound to the buyer to execute an instrument of sale. And according to the common opinion, the seller is not bound to do this, but is bound for damages, for as much as it is to the buyer’s interest that the thing be sold and delivered to him, as in l. 1, in principio, ff. de actione empti. But according to the opinion of Martinus, which is more equitable, if someone sells his own thing which he possesses, he is bound precisely to deliver it; but if he cannot deliver it, either in law or in fact, he is bound for damages, as noted in the title of the Institutes, de contrahenda emptione et venditione, in the gloss on the word “tradatur.” From these authorities it appears what is the law in the question proposed. For if the buyer, who bought by words, circumvented the seller, who otherwise would not have sold, he cannot demand that an instrument be made for him. But if it is proved that the aforementioned matters and those following occurred by the consent of the parties, then he is compelled [to execute the instrument], because satisfaction is understood to be given by the very fact that the agreement is observed, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. quod vendidi, and ff. de pignoribus et hypothecis, l. solutum, § solutam. But if the buyer deceived the seller, because it was agreed that the price should be paid immediately, otherwise he would not have sold, then the seller is not bound, as in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. cum te. But if, at the will of the seller, the buyer paid the seller’s creditor, the contract was ratified by consent; and therefore it must be perfected, and a writing drawn up therefrom, if the seller possesses [the thing], as has been said; for concerning those things about which we contract, we ought to make a caution, i.e., a writing, concerning the same, lest the means of proof be taken away by fortuitous events, as in C. de liberationibus cautionibus, l. sicut datam. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. What is the effect of a legacy made to a wife by appointing her as the owner of all his property, while instituting an outsider as heir?
body: with an extraneous heir.

† A certain man, having instituted an extraneous heir, bequeathed to his wife through these words: "I will that my wife be the mistress of all my goods, as long as the said lady Countess shall live, and shall lead a widowed life, and shall live chastely and honestly in my house, and shall not demand her dowry from my said house; to which wife of mine I bequeath the usufruct of all my goods, until etc., as above." Then it follows in this form: "and if she should be unwilling to stay, or unable on account of the burdens of the commune," he made certain other legacies. Now it is asked whether, by staying in the house and living chastely and honestly, as is contained in the first part of the legacy, she ought to have the full usufruct. And it must be said that she does, for when an extraneous heir is instituted, the word "usufruct" has its full meaning. But when a son is instituted, then the custom written in the curia burgari has place, which by universal custom is approved and by common usage of speech, so that she has only maintenance, [which] is understood to have been left, as is noted in l. 2 C. si secundo nupserit mulier and by Dynus in l. Titia cum testamento, § Titia cum nuberet ff. de leg. 2. And from these points it appears that, since here an extraneous heir was instituted, the testator's wife ought to have the full usufruct of all goods, for the condition of a wife ought not to be worse than that of any other legatee, as in ff. de vsufr. leg. l. vxori maritus; nay rather, in a legacy to a wife, the broadest possible interpretation must be made, as in ff. de leg. 3 l. Item legato, § parui, in honor of a well-spent marriage, as in ff. de leg. 2 l. vnum ex familia, § item Marcus Imperator, especially because a widow is feigned to be in the marriage of her husband and to be in his service as long as she perseveres in widowhood and honesty, as in l. sicut de ope. liberto. and noted in C. rem in pręsenti, § exactio. From which it is concluded that the said widow ought to have the intact usufruct, once caution has been furnished concerning using and enjoying according to the arbitrament of a good man, if the universal heir demands that it be furnished to him, as is read and noted in ff. de usufr. leg. l. uxori fructu bonorum; the same if she received [the fruits] in good faith not knowing that she was bound to the said security, as is noted there and in l. 1 C. de usufru., for the burden of providing security can be tacitly omitted, since it is not of the substance of usufruct, as is noted in l. 1 ff. de usufr. and C. ut in poss. leg. l. scire. And it is to be noted that, even if there were some particular legacy of usufruct bequeathed to the said wife, for instance of a certain fief, nevertheless by a particular provision a general provision is not diminished where there is no contrariety of will, as in ff. de fun. instru. l. quaesitum, § ulti., and there fully noted. I, Baldus, have subscribed.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Uterine sisters succeed to all more remote relatives being excluded, and throughout the entire opinion.
1. Whether statutes harm non-subjects in the intestate succession.
3. How many kinds of citizens there are.
4. How a statute providing that statutes are to be understood according to the letter, as they stand, is to be understood.
5. Whether the term "brother" includes a sister.
body: Ganna, who was married to John de Albin, in the name of Christ, died, leaving no agnates, except as follows: she left two uterine sisters only. Also, she left an uncle. Also, she left two sons from another uncle, all of whom were citizens of Albenga by origin. Also, she left an aunt with four sons from Petra. These sons and their mother are foreigners and outsiders to Albenga, because the place of Petra is not subject in any way to the city of Albenga. However, one of the said four sons, namely Peter, became a citizen of Albenga by agreement; but later he withdrew and took up residence in Rimini in the province of Romandiola at his wife’s domicile, along with himself and his sons.

† Now, since it is certain from the law that uterine sisters succeed to all more remote relatives excluded, as in C. de legibus hereditatibus, auth. post fratres, and there noted, and there is no doubt about this, that uterine sisters under the common law are preferred not only to uncles but also to paternal uncles and any other more distant relatives, and in all the goods of the deceased, with all distinction between agnation and cognation removed. Nevertheless, a doubt arises from the statutes of the commune of Albenga: and this question is divided into three parts: presupposing that the statutes of the said commune should be understood literally, as they stand, without any glossation or external interpretation.

† And the question is common: whether statutes harm non-subjects in intestate succession; for if such statutes are understood as real, they affect property within the territory, but not other property. If, however, they are personal, they affect neither. But this is not our point; rather, the contrary: whether they benefit non-subjects, namely whether non-subjects are preferred by virtue of the statutes over those who ought to succeed according to the common law. And it can be plausibly said that they do not benefit them, because municipal statutes are equated with agreements, as noted in C. de decretis decurionum, l. 1, i. 10. But no one can make an agreement for another; therefore, neither can one enact a statute for a person entirely foreign. Moreover, because statutes should not be one-sided: hence, just as they do not bind a non-subject, so too they do not benefit him; for the rule is the same for opposites. And therefore hostages do not use the law of the city, unless they have been admitted to the privileges of the city, as in ff. de iure fisci, l. sed si accepto usu togae. And then they use it only as long as they remain there; and not if they return to their homeland, because domicile can be changed, as in leg. and no. ff. ad municipalia, l. assumptio. Unless someone is a citizen by agreement and permanently attached to the city by pact; because a pact has perpetual strength and firmness, as in ff. de acquisitione et obligatione, l. obligationum fere, § placet.

† Moreover, there are certain honorary citizens, and these endure perpetually. There are some honorary citizens admitted to undertake public offices, and these do not endure unless they undertake such offices, as argued from the Digest, *De solutionibus*, law *Quod si forte*, § 1, and the Code, *De sacris sanctis ecclesiis*, law *Qui sub praetextu*. Furthermore, a citizen is understood to be one who has acquired status with regard to public offices, not with regard to succeeding or not succeeding a private person; because just as a natural son is not legitimated to succeed those who do not consent, nor conversely, so too, so to speak, a person made a citizen through arrogation by a citizen, as in the Authenticum *Quibus modis naturalis effectus sui*, § *Et generaliter*, and as argued from the Digest, *De legatis* 2, law *Si ita quis*, § *Is cui*. And because no one is understood to grant privileges to outsiders against prior natural and true citizens, I understand that neither does the city; because subjects ought to be regarded as sons, since the city is called the mother and the prince the father, as in the Code, *De inofficioso testamento*, law *Si quis filium*. Hence, when the prince writes to his subjects, he writes using the word "sons," as in the Code, *De fideicommissis*, law *Cum acutissimi*. But this point would be quite doubtful when someone has been admitted to full citizenship; because such a person acquires all the favors of citizens, both active and passive, and is held to be a citizen, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, law 1, § *Lex Falcidia*, and noted by Bartolus in the Digest, *De usucapione*, law *Si is qui pro emptore*. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, the statute of Albingaun expressly provides that a citizen elected, or subsequently made, shall have the privileges of citizens if he does not abandon his residence; and therefore the conclusion is true, as in the Digest, *De hereditate instituenda*, law *Ex facto*, § *Rerum autem*, and the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Debitor*. Now remains the third doubt, turning to the words of the statute, which doubt arises among the citizens of Albingaun, excluding, as I said, the outsider citizen from the benefit and interpretation of the statute. Then Alsosia associates the calti.

It must be known, however, that although statutes ought to be understood literally, because so the statute dictates, nevertheless this literal understanding also requires a civil interpretation: first, from the side of those enacting, so that they may have been able to enact; second, from the side of the user of the statute, so that he may be included in it; third, from the side of the matter, so that the matter is not different; fourth, from the side of the form, so that the chapters arising therefrom conform to the form of the statute. And then one must not depart from the letter; otherwise, the contrary holds, as in D. 4.8.1 (prospexit) and D. 10.3.12 § non dixit (si seruum). A similar rule applies in the Rule of the Friars Minor, because the text states that they cannot be glossed, but must be observed literally, as they stand. I therefore return to the point at issue, namely, the statutes. The statute provides that if a person dies intestate, having left behind no father, grandfather, brother, nephews, or great-nephews, or paternal uncle, but having left behind a maternal grandmother and a son of a paternal uncle or of the father’s sister, the son of the paternal uncle or of the father’s sister shall succeed to the whole, namely, the son of the sister equally with the grandmother. It is therefore true that the statute defers the succession to the son of the aunt, because it is true that he did not die leaving behind a father, grandfather, brother, etc. To the contrary, it seems that those words, “having left behind no brother,” ought to be understood as including “nor sister,” because

† The term "brother" includes the sister, as established in the Digest, *de legatis tertio*, law *Lucius*, section *quaesitum*, and in the Digest, *de pactis*, law *tres fratres*. However, this interpretation certainly does not apply, because the statute provides that statutes are to be understood literally; the letter is understood as the common explanation, not as the extensive interpretation of the learned, as stated in law 1 of the Digest, *de verborum significatione*, according to the gloss and Bartolus. But it seems to me to be highly unjust that full sisters are excluded from the son of an aunt, who is in the fourth degree. And although the sons of an aunt are not agnates, because among agnates only the sons of sisters are counted, who have the rights of agnates, yet they do not possess the substance of agnation, which proceeds from the father, as stated in the Code, *de legatis hereditatibus*, law *meminimus*, and in the Code, *unde liberi*, law *qui se patris*. And I prove this by the same statute of the city of Alba, the words of which are as follows: "If, however, one dies intestate, leaving no father, grandfather, brothers, or grandson, but leaving a uterine sister, the uterine sister shall succeed in the maternal property; but in the paternal property, the male agnate up to the fourth degree." But here there is no agnate; therefore, the right of accretion applies, as stated in the Code, *de testamento militis*, law 1. Indeed, one and the same right should be considered as a whole, not from different heads or from different considerations, because there is no person capable of excluding. And there is no doubt about this regarding goods located outside the possession and jurisdiction of the city of Alba, because statutes concerning intestate succession are not extended to goods located outside the jurisdiction of the enacting authority, as I fully stated in the law *cunctos populos*, after Cynus and Bartolus. And thus I hold that uterine sisters are preferred, both by the disposition of law, by natural equity, and by the precedence of degree, also because the words of the statute are suitably adapted, which in the conclusion do not name the uterine sister except by naming agnates. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an obligation without a cause is valid.
2. Whether custom binds strangers.
3. Whether the letters of an official make faith by attesting to the custom of the place where the official is located.
4. If, during a pending compromise, when the instrument has been sworn, a complaint has been lodged before the bishop, who ordered the oath to be kept, whether the complained-against party has incurred the penalty.
5. Whether one can compromise regarding an oath.
6. What the words "each to each" signify.
7. Whether a cession without expression of title is valid.
body: Between John and In the name of Christ. The matter proceeded thus: because they made a precise general release for each other, and confessed to having mutually received complete payment of those things which they had had to claim against one another. Afterwards, however, an instrument of the following tenor was drawn up: the said Aloysius solemnly promised to the said John the sum of 600 florins for restoration, without otherwise specifying what the cause was, or of what kind; and the said instruments were made in the city of Genoa, from which the said John was a native. But the said Aloysius was a stranger there, because he was from Milan. Now it is the custom of Genoa that, notwithstanding a general release, the said subsequent promise is upheld, of which custom the Podestà of Genoa and the Council attest by their authentic letters. From these facts three doubts arise. The first is whether the said obligation of six hundred is valid. The second is whether the said custom extends its roots to the forum of Milan. The third is whether the aforementioned letters make probative proof of the custom.

† Regarding the first point, it seems that the aforementioned obligation of six hundred can be defeated by an exception, because it does not contain a certain cause, as stated in l. 1, §. circa, de doli excep. To the contrary is the truth itself, because rather it does contain a cause, as for the sake of reason, as in ff. de pac., l. emptor, §. Lucius. Moreover, the most recent agreements must be observed, as in C. de pac., l. pacta nouissima. Also, those things which are done immediately are considered to be included, as in l. lecta, §. dicebam, with its subject matter. Also, from the preceding and following, the cause is understood, as noted in ff. si cert. pe., l. cum quid. Also, the instrument of release contains a confession, not a payment: and from a confession one departs by a contrary assertion, as in C. de non num. pec., l. generaliter. Also, the aforementioned promise made with certain knowledge binds effectively, as in ff. de ver. ob., l. si diuortio. And this concludes the first point.

† On the second point, it appears that the said custom is not to be observed, because custom does not bind strangers, as argued from the Digest, *De pignoribus*, law *Debitor*; and by that law, *Ita determinat*, the gloss of the Decretal. Furthermore, because it does not appear that the contract was made in Janua, as in the Digest, *De iudiciis*, law *Haeres absens*, § 1. On the contrary, it appears that the said custom disposes of decisive matters, i.e., regarding the validation of the obligation; therefore, the place of the contract is considered, as in the law *Si fundus*, *De evictione*, with its subject matter. Solution: If the instrument is examined, the words of the instrument determine the question, because the parties intended that where the place was, and the contract was made there, the performance of the payment should be rendered, although they added several other places, and even if this were not the case, the law would be the same. For the question here is not that of the judge, but of the debt itself. On

† Thirdly, it appears that the aforementioned letters make proof, considering the quality of the writers, to whom much faith ought to be given, and auth. 96, dist. c. nobilissimus. Solution: this question is not necessary on account of what I have said above. Now there remains a certain other doubt: namely, that pending the compromise, when the instrument was sworn, the complaint was deposited before the bishop, who ordered the oath to be observed and the promises to be fulfilled.

† It is asked whether this person, who has relapsed, has incurred the penalty: and it seems that he has, as noted in c. Quandiu, De appellationibus, in the Clementines. To the contrary, it seems that he has not, because the debtor scorned that precept, and thus fraud is compensated by fraud, as in l. Quamuis, D. De in ius vocando, and l. Si, §. Sed si stipulator, D. De eo per quem factum erit. Consider: if indeed the compromise is dissolved by going to the judge, then, since it is due to the one going that the arbitrator cannot judge, the penalty is incurred. For this rule is established: that he who prevents the arbitration from being promulgated, either by refusing to appear for the instruction of the arbitration or in some other way, is bound to the penalty, as in D. De verbis obligatis, l. Si quis arbitratus. But if the compromise is dissolved, then either the penalty was attached if one were to act against the compromise, and then he incurs the penalty; or if one were to act against the precept of the arbitrator, and then a distinction must be made as to which matter or clause the penalty is attached, by argument from those things noted in D. De iureiurando, l. Si duo, per rationem, §. 2, in the gloss of the same; and what is noted in the same title, l. Nam et postea, at the end, in the great gloss on that question, when the stipulation is incurred pro rata. For, insofar as that clause refers to the matter adjudicated, it is not incurred beforehand; but if it refers to the simple controversy, then it is not dissolved, as is the case when the controversy is compromised to an arbitrator; for then it is considered that a transaction has been made, as the arbitrator has declared, as noted in Auth. Ut differant iudices, §. Primo. Hence, repentance has no place, as in C. De transactionibus, l. Quamuis.

† Thus, it is no objection that, according to some, one cannot compromise regarding an oath: for this is true as regards the guilt of perjury; nevertheless, as regards the bond of the debt, the compromise is valid, as in D. de iureiurando, l. duobus, §. fina., together with the following law, omnia.

† and each one, that is to say, what has been stated, namely all together and each individually, so that the sense may be divided, not composite. For the word "singulis" (to each) usually attributes the thing to each person in solidum, as in D. de vulgari substitutione, l. vel singulis; or as the context permits, as in l. in singulis, D. ad legem Falcidiam; and in l. singulis, D. de exceptione rei iudicatae. Hence, by the very fact that mention is made of a price, mention is made of a contract, because the estimation serves in place of the name of sale, as in D. de usucapione, Prima Pars Consiliorum, pro empto, l. litis aestimatio; and D. de administratione tutorum, l. cum quaeritur. After the Lateran Council, D. si certum petatur, l. cum fundus, §. servum tuum imprudens, at the end, §. porro factum. The law nemo simulat can be said, because the substance of the law is truth, as in C. de indice libertatis tollendo, l. unica. No objection.

† That the title is not expressed in the assignment, because this is a necessary assignment, which is made by mandate of the law, as is fully known. ff. de mandato, l. Papinia. and ff. de solutionibus, §. Modestinus. and C. de mandato, l. per diversas, §. exceptio. Moreover, where there is a price for the assignment, there is the title of the purchase of the claim, as C. de praediis curialium, l. si, lib. 10. Therefore, the said assignment is valid in law. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a modern enfeoffment made according to a retroactive custom is valid or not.
2. Whenever there is a cause for granting or denying an action, the time must be proven.
3. A custom of 100 years, which proceeds against the Church, also proceeds against the Roman [Church].
body: Assuming that the council of the tithe cannot be granted in a perpetual fief.

† It is asked, if many concessions appear to have been made after the Council, in which it is mentioned that they had previously been accustomed to be enfeoffed, and it does not appear whether this was before or after the Council, nor is the common opinion regarding such a long time, of which there is no contrary memory, proven by witnesses: whether the modern enfeoffment according to the retroactive custom is valid or not: it seems at first that it is not valid: because the validity of this contract is founded on time, namely, that such tithes are those which were accustomed to be enfeoffed before the Council: therefore, this time must be proven. f. quod ante,

† because whenever time is the cause for granting an action or denying a petition, he must prove this to whom the burden of proof lies for bringing the action or raising the exception, as is fully read and noted in D. de negotiorum gestis, l. cum act. and D. de novi operis nuntiatione, l. non solum, §. sed vt probari. Hence, he who alleges a time of which there is no contrary memory must prove this, as in l. 1, in fine, D. de aqua pluviae arcendae; D. de probationibus, l. si arbiter. To the contrary it seems, because he who wishes to prove some fact against the laws must sometimes prove the time. But here he does not prove how the enfeoffments appear after the council: nevertheless it does not follow, therefore not before. Moreover, he who wishes to destroy some fact to be done in order must prove the order, as noted in cap. literas, de rescriptis, in Clementin. Also, since doubt arises from an uncertain time, we must presume in the better part, as C. de probationibus, l. matrem suam; and noted in l. qui iurasse, §. pen., de iureiurando.

† Moreover, a custom of one hundred years prevails even against churches: and not only against other churches, but also against the Roman Church, as in the Authentica "Ut Ecclesia Romana gaudeat praescriptione centum annorum," in the rubric and in black, and in the Code, On Sacred Churches, the final law. Moreover, the emphyteuta is in possession, in which he must be defended, unless it is proved against him, as in the Institutes, On Interdicts, §. commodum. Moreover, those owing to this feudatory cannot demand that he prove his title: since they have already approved him and paid him, because by doing so they would seem to dispossess him, as in the Extravagant, On Elections, c. querelam, and noted by Dy. in c. qui ad agendum, On Things of Right, book 6. Moreover, one should not depart from what has long been considered equitable, as in the Digest, On Constitutions, the first law, in rebus novissimis. Moreover, from three preceding leases it is presumed in infinitum before, as in the Code, On Public Edicts, l. quicunque. Moreover, this is supported by the Digest, On Use, l. cum de in rem verso. Moreover, even if prescription did not run against the church, it nevertheless runs against the guarantors in the space of thirty years, as in the chapter Si quis per 30, If a dispute arose about a fief. Wherefore the toll-collectors must be compelled to pay the tolls in the usual manner: and among themselves prescription is preserved. l. si publicanus, §. in vectigalibus, On Publicans, according to Bartolus. That which is noted in l. sicuti, §. si quaeratur, If a servitude is sold, is to the point, for since dominion comes incidentally, it suffices that good faith was held at first. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. The opinions of the syndics, on what grounds they are said to be null, and at number 3.
2. Arbitrations delegated by law do not endure, unless for one year.
4. Awards are a certain kind of settlement.
body: unless it appears from the aforesaid that the suit subsists
† That the sentence of the judges is not valid, is proved first by the statement of Master Bartolus.

† He states that arbitrations granted by law do not last for more than one year, as he fully notes in ff. de verborum obligatione, l. si quis arbitratu. For the office of a magistrate is accustomed to last for a year, as in Auth. de defensoribus civitatum, §. si, col. 3; and in an arbitration given by law, not by a person, it seems to be expressly stated in l. si, §. 1, communi delegatio. And thus it does not oppose what is noted in l. sed si compromissum, ff. de arbitris, because there it speaks of an arbitrator given by a person. Otherwise, one would have an arbitration in the proposal, which is absurd, unless it were such a matter that could not be completed within a year, either due to the difficulty of the case or due to the uncertainty of the fact. For he is not harmed by the passage of time who was not in delay, as noted in Authen. de appellationibus, in principio, col. 8.

Secondly, it does not seem valid in reason, because, once the matter has been calculated by a definitive sentence, another definitive sentence is not valid, as is fully noted in l. 1, C. de errore calculi. The third reason is that this second sentence was rendered against a transaction which had acquired the force of res judicata from the first.

† For the transaction itself is a matter of praise, as noted in the Authentica *Ut differant iudices*, § 1, col. 9, because where all accounts have been settled, everything is understood to be at rest, as in the Digest, *De pace*, l. *Emptor*, § *Lucius*. The fourth reason is that in a partnership no one ought to be condemned unless the accounts have been calculated on both sides, as in the Digest, *Pro socio*, l. *De illo*. And therefore it appears that in this calculation all interest has been included; and thus no pronouncement could have been made regarding interest on a single item. The fifth reason is the venue, because judgment could not be rendered in the church, as in c. *Decet*, Extra, *De immunitate ecclesiarum*. The sixth reason is that since no proof was received regarding the interest, the sentence rendered was null, as noted in the Code, *De sententiis et interlocutionibus*, l. *Prolatam*, and in the Extra, *De constitutionibus*, c. *Ecclesia S. Mariae*, and *De sententia excommunicationis*, c. *Solet* by Innocentius. Finally, it must also be weighed that the first sentence was rendered with the consent of both parties, and therefore it should be presumed in its favor. I leave the remaining points to be supplied by one who thinks more deeply. The objection does not hold if they say that this is an arbitrament; for this is not true, since it was not rendered in the form of an arbitrament or declaration, but of a definitive sentence. On this, see above in Consilium 396, albeit with different words.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the seal of a certain person is to be relied upon in matters that do not pertain to his jurisdiction.
2. Even writings made by the king himself are not believed.
3. If I permit someone to sell my property, nevertheless, if I do not deliver it, I do not lose ownership: rather, this power is terminated and restored upon the death of the grantor.
4. Whether prescription is permitted in the forum of conscience: and whether by this it pertains to the secular judge.
5. Whether an oath is personal, and passes to the heir of the one who swore.
6. Whether an oath perpetuates an obligation.
7. The bad faith of the deceased does not harm the heir.
8. Whether the good prevails over the equal.
9. Who is said to have bad faith.
10. Whether a contact is said to be usurious, if the creditor enjoys the fruits.
11. Canons prevail over laws in the matter of usury.
body:
A certain document: In the name of Christ. We, John, Marquis of Ferrara, etc., by these present letters make known that, by our will and express consent, the noble B. Guidotto Grassella, in the name and on behalf of his brother Corrado Grassella, appointed in our castle of Calliano the Castellan of that place, and as custodians the noble men Uberto and John, brothers of Coconato, counts. The said nobles Uberto and John, in our presence and in our hands, swore bodily upon the Holy Gospels, with a solemn promise, to guard and keep faithfully and diligently our said place of Calliano, and to render to the aforementioned Guidotto and Corrado and their heirs a good and true account of the fruits, revenues, and profits to be had and received by the said Uberto and John from the said place and on its account. And if we have not satisfied the aforementioned Grassellas concerning the aforementioned sum of florins, to which we are bound by instrument, the said Uberto and John, under the faith of their bodies and the aforementioned oath, promised that the said Guidotto, in his own name and on behalf of Corrado de Grassellis, or their heirs, shall freely, absolutely, and without delay surrender, relinquish, and deliver up our said castle place and the place of Calliano at the request of the said Guidotto and Corrado or their heirs, until we have fully satisfied them concerning the aforementioned sum of florins. We ordered this to be done by T. Gambarino of Ricoboni, our notary, and to be strengthened with the seal of our name. Given at Clauasso on the day, etc.

The case is argued according to the tenor of this document. Two objections are effectively raised: first, that this document does not make full proof, neither of the transaction nor of the delivery of custody; second, that even if it did make proof, the period of forty years has now prescribed. The question now arises: what is the law? For one sentence has been rendered against the parties, absolving them, and another condemning them; and arguments have been adduced, and copiously adduced, both for and against.

† For the reason that it does not make faith, the general rule is alleged: because no law says that the seal of the one sealing is to be relied upon in contracts made between private persons, not pertaining to the jurisdiction of the one sealing. For this does not pertain to their office: although they are public persons in matters pertaining to their office. Now, however, they are reduced to the status of a private person, and are entirely private persons, even if they were letters of the King of the French. For they do not concern public law, which consists in magistrates, according to the noted opinion of Guido and others in l. publicum ius, ff. de iust. et iur., and according to Innocentius, extra de conuer., c. qui dudum. Moreover, this seal does not appear to have been affixed at the request of both parties: but only by the command of that prince. Similarly, the notary does not appear to have been requested by both parties, nor did he subscribe as a notary public: which is necessary, as Auth. de Tabel., §. nos autem. And generally, it is answered regarding all laws that speak of a seal, because they apply to themselves when such is the matter that pertains to the public office of the one sealing, as extra de proba., c. post cessionem, with its material. Otherwise, if it does not pertain to his public office. For from the office and the seal, the seal is said to be authentic; otherwise, if either of these is lacking, as extra de appell., c. significamte. Notwithstanding c. 1, de prob. in cle., because this is special in the letters of the Pope or the Emperor, therefore in the contrary is the common law: I prove this by another reason, because this writing contains the utility of the Lord Marquis himself: and it is made partly by himself, and in his own cause, and is something indivisible from its context: whence it cannot be valid in part, invalid in part.

† It is certain, however, that writings made by oneself are not believed, even if made by the King, as in C. de probat. l. Exemplum and l. Inter chartulas, de conveniendi fisci debito, lib. 10. And therefore the fisc has writings made by notaries and other public officials appointed for this purpose, as in l. 1, C. de apocryphis, lib. 10. And supporting the aforementioned rule is the fact that, as stated in ff. de edendo, l. Quaedam, §. Nummularios, this is true unless custom dictates otherwise, as in extra de fide instrumentorum, c. Cum dilectus. Moreover, the said writing does not mention the delivery of custody, nor does it prove it, since it was not made in the thing itself, but elsewhere, as in extra de fide instrumentorum, c. Inter dilectos, §. Si, and ff. de acquirenda possessione, l. Praedia. Therefore, they are not bound to restore. What was received is not proven, as in ff. si certum petatur, l. Qui pecuniam. It is therefore concluded that such a writing is a private writing, and even if it were public, it would still not be sufficient to prove, because it does not mention delivery, but rather a certain verbal commission, from which no action for recovery arises. Supporting this is c. 1, quid sit investitura, col. 10. It remains to consider the quality of the said instrument of custody: for the Lord Marquis did not entrust custody, but permitted it; nor did he promise, but consented; nor did he impose a law upon himself that he could not revoke the custody, which by its nature is revocable, as in c. 1, de feudo guardiae, col. 10. Moreover, this is such as
