† If I were to permit someone to sell my property, for if I deliver it, the delivery does not follow from my will, I do not lose ownership; rather, this power is extinguished by the death of the grantor and restored, as in D. si certum petatur, l. eius qui in provincia, §. quas vero. Others, however, say, and perhaps not without reason, that since I grant it following my prior obligation, it does not end with death, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. fundum, §. item si amicus. Nevertheless, it is certain that if possession or detention has not been acquired, I do not cease to be the master and arbiter of my thing; because bare consent does not cause the loss of rights of ownership, as in D. de pactis, l. nemo. Since this is not proven by instrument, nor is it said to be proven by witnesses, it follows that what is not proven to have been given is vainly claimed to be returned. It remains to be seen regarding the point of prescription:

† Here it must be considered that we are in the forum of Caesar, in which the laws speaking of prescription of long time must be observed, as is stated by Cynus in the sole law, Codex, "De usucapione transformatione." Furthermore, we are dealing with the prescription of personal actions, since the action arises from a contract, in which the exception of long time prescribes; so much so that the one who prescribes is similar to one who pays, as in the last law, § "Si," Digest, "De rerum amissione et acquisitione." For it is equitable that the delay of the one who does not claim should harm him, lest the law be evaded. For the terms of laws ought not to be a mockery, just as the terms of ministers are not, as in the last law, Digest, "De rerum amissione et acquisitione," and Codex, "De ingenuis et manumissis," law "Diffamari." Hence, omitting the subtleties of canon law, which dispute over the points of conscience, we, who are in the secular forum, must follow the laws, in which the human race lives throughout the world, as in Digest, "De legibus," law 2, and Codex, "De legibus et constitutionibus," law "Leges sacratissimae." For the forum of conscience does not pertain to the secular judge, because the forum of judgment and the forum of conscience are different forums. And thus, if something is sinned against God here, and not against human laws, it will be punished by God alone, as in Codex, "De rebus creditis," law 2. Bartolus, in the following law, § "Si viam," Digest, "De usucapione," says that in the prescription of a personal action, possession is not required; therefore, neither is good faith of possession. And he determines that the chapter "Quam omne" does not seem to speak of the prescription of personal actions. And this I hold in the Justinian forum, following the statement of Lord Cynus. However, in our question, this discussion is superfluous, because here there is no proof of sin, since there is no proof of debt. It is not an obstacle if it is said that an oath intervenes here by those words which are said from the aforementioned oath, by the chapter "Clericus," Extra, "De iureiurando."

† Moreover, the oath is personal on the part of the oath, as Innocentius states in the Extravagantes, De iureiurando, chapter Veritatis. Although it possesses a certain real character, insofar as it confirms the contract, and in that respect it passes to the heir, as provided in chapter 2, De pace, Book 6, and in the Authenticum Sacramenta puberum, together with its subject matter.

† Moreover, neither civil nor canon law provides that an oath perpetuates an obligation beyond the nature given to it by law; otherwise, the interruptions of prescriptions would have been introduced in vain, and through the aforementioned chapter *Quia omne* they would be nullified, which is absurd. Nevertheless, I do not dissuade anyone from following his conscience, if his conscience pricks him. For I am not speaking of conscience, but of the provision of civil law. Furthermore, we are speaking here of an heir: and the said Dyonisius says that the bad faith of the deceased does not harm the heir, as I myself note in the chapter *Malae fidei*, *De regulis iuris*, Book 6. This is also approved by Cynus in the said law *Unica*, Code, *De usucapione transferenda*. Moreover, even if there were an obligation, it is an unliquidated obligation:

† and therefore it is not established that there was bad faith, as in the Digest, On the Interpretation of Words, the law *interdum*. The final conclusion, therefore, is that the first sentence was juridical, and the second sentence, issued against the first, was not juridical, nor does it contain juridical reasons or allegations: because the plaintiff fails at the very roots of the foundations. Moreover, because perhaps someone might say that it would be heretical to hold against the counsel of the said chapter *quam omne*, which is also to be entirely avoided in the secular forum: and from this it follows that the said chapter should be observed in the forum of justice and in lay matters: because there is no doubt about ecclesiastical matters, since all such things are the holy of holies to the Lord, and belong to the forum of the Church, as noted in the chapter *verum* On Competence of Forum; and just as the Church itself ought to be preserved, as in the Code, On Sacred and Sanctified Churches, the law *iubemus*; and just as they are under the power of the Pope and of canon law, notwithstanding that civil law says that something is good law but not equitable:

† and that good prevails over equal, as noted in l. 1, ff. de iustitia et iure, and C. de iudicibus, l. placuit. For to this canonists respond that this is true in those having good faith: but not in those having bad faith.

† It is therefore asked, who is said to have bad faith: and the law says that he who does not consider himself the owner, but believes another to be the owner of the thing, as C. de fur. l. apud antiquos. But if I know that I am bound to give my thing, I do not possess it. Likewise, if I am a debtor in a genus, I do not possess the genus, because a genus is not a thing constituted in a body, as noted in ff. de peti. haer. l. regulariter. And this is the subtlety of Bartolus. But the simplicity of the canonists responds to this, that I do not sin because I possess, but because I do not satisfy my conscience: and because I sin against my brother, as l. dolus. ff. mandati. Because, omitting these intricacies, I come more to the 1st marrow of the matter:

And I say that the said contract is usurious by its very form, because it was agreed that the creditor should enjoy the fruits and make a profit, as appears from the convention of the instrument, which consists of two parts, and of the aforementioned instrument subsequently following the first, and taken from the principal itself. That such an instrument savors of the vice of usury by its very form is expressed in *l. lecta*, § *si*, D. *si certum petatur*, where it is said, "the same can be said of fruits." From this we have a correct conclusion in the way of the forum and of conscience, that the said writing, as contrary to laws and canons and containing an illicit contract, does not support the plaintiff. Moreover, usuries not claimed for a very long time appear to have been remitted, as in D. *de usuris*, *l. qui semisses*. The same applies to the restitution of the custody, which was ordered for the vice of usury and for fostering the money of usuries, by argument of those things noted by Innocentius in X. *de filiis presbyterorum*, c. *Constitutus*, and in D. *de deposito*, *l. bona fides*. And it is made by what is noted in D. *si certum petatur*, *l. rogasti*, § *si tibi*, for fruits joined by pact are usury, by the general rule given there in the gloss: "but if by disposition of the law they diminish the principal, it is not usury." As for the fruits and profits, the petition is to be repelled as contrary to law, and consequently the first sentence was true and just according to God, according to canons, and according to civil laws, as is noted in C. *l. cunctos populos*, and in D. *pro socio*, *l. socium*, which etc., because

† The canons prevail over the laws in the matter of usury. For the canons are so much higher than the laws in this matter, as the steering of the heavens is distant from mortals, as is noted in C. de usuris, aut. ad hoc. And hence it is said that the laws do not disdain to imitate the sacred canons. Likewise, the sacred canons differ from the laws of the world as much as the perpetual differs from the corruptible.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Just as statutes cannot be made against the liberty of the Church, so too can they not be made against pious places, such as hospitals.
2. The poor are equated with wards.
3. The difference between reduction and restitution.
4. Whether congregations, or confraternities, and pious places have restitution in integrum.
body: In the City of Brescia. In the name of Christ. Lawful foundations: one for aiding the oppressed and for feeding the poor; the other is called the Congregation of Saint Francis, under whose care is the Hospital of Mercy of Brescia. These two congregations were instituted as heirs, or legacies were left to them; against which is objected the statute of Brescia, which provides that no one shall acquire, or presume to make, any alienation inter vivos, or in last wills, by which possession or dominion of any immovable thing, which is in the city or district of Brescia, is transferred to any college, or singular person, which does not sustain the burdens of the community, and is not subject to the jurisdiction of the community of Brescia in civil and criminal matters. And that the said statute is, and is to be understood, written in rem; and that those things are rendered vitiated by a real defect, so that they cannot be acquired by prescription. The question is, what is the law.

† And on this point I say as follows: either the said congregations are founded by bishops, and then they are considered pious places, to which a legacy may be left notwithstanding the statute, especially on account of the annexation of a hospital; for just as statutes made against the liberty of the church are invalid, so too are those made against the liberty of hospitals, as stated in C. de episcopis et clericis, l. omnia. But then the statute would not be valid against the liberty of the church, because what may be left to the church is not only a matter of common law, but also a privilege in this regard, such that nothing contrary thereto may be established by municipal law, according to Oldradus, per l. ultima, C. de sacris sanctis ecclesiis. Therefore, such congregations, in the name of the poor,

† Those who are equated with wards: For the poor in general are equated with wards, as in C. de epis. et cler. l. orphanotrophos. They could seek restitution in integrum against a judgment, even if a reduction to the discretion of an honest man could not be sought under strict law.

† For that reduction is a distinct species containing a complaint of inequity, whereas restitution in integrum is the aid of the miserable, as in the Digest, *De minoribus*, l. *Praeses*, and l. 3, in the beginning, *De rerum amissione*. Or these universities, or congregations, are secular: and they exist in fact, not by privileges, as in the Extravagant, *De religiosis domibus*, c. *De synodochiis*. And then they are subject to the common jurisdiction of Brescia in civil and criminal matters. For on account of a crime they can be destroyed and dissolved, which presence, as regards the intellectual body of the university, is a criminal penalty, as is added in the note of Innocentius, Extravagant, *De novo opere*, *Nunquid Episcopus*: *Vec.*, *Cum ex iniuncto*.

† It remains doubtful, however, whether they have the benefit of restitution in integrum under the common law. And indeed they do have it, because they are not governed except by curators, i.e., ministers; since they cannot govern themselves, as is noted in l. ciuitas, ff. si certum petatur. Just as absentees who are undefended or poorly defended are restored, as in l. ultima, ff. de in integrum restitutione; l. pen., tit. generali. For by their end and by their work these colleges are holy, because they serve almsgiving and piety, and by public authority and usage they are regarded as such, as is noted in l. 1, quod quisque iuris. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a vassal who does not possess the fief is bound to seek investiture within a year.
2. Whether a vassal who does not seek investiture within a year forfeits his right by operation of law or by sentence.
3. And whether that sentence has the force of a judicial sentence.
4. Who is the competent judge in a feudal case. See also nos. 5 and 6.
7. The lord of the fief cannot be dragged by his vassals outside the city in which he resides.
body: Andreas Feudata In the name of Christ. ren. renounced into the hands of Peter, Bishop of Verona, a certain fief of his, which he acknowledged from the Bishopric of Verona, before Philip was invested: which renunciation the said Bishop accepted, and invested the said Philip. But the said Philip could never have possession of the said fief on account of the secular power of the lord of the said city of Verona: in the course of time a new Bishop, James, is created. After his creation, the said Philip appeared within a year and a day from the creation of the said Bishop James before the Vicar, and others conducting the affairs of the said James, requesting to be invested as the rightful vassal of the Bishopric of the aforementioned fief. The Vicar and the others responded that they could not invest him, because they did not have the power, and the Bishop was absent. In the subsequent time, the Bishop came to the city, and had edicts made, that everyone should appear to receive investitures of their fiefs, otherwise from then on he pronounced against them a sentence of deprivation. All appeared except this Philip, who did not appear within a year and a day, nor even up to three years. Finally, the Bishop granted the said fief to another.

† It is asked in the first place, whether a vassal who is not in possession is bound to seek investiture within a year and a day: and it seems that he is not, because he is not yet a vassal, since he has not yet been corporally invested, as in c. 1, *quid sit investitura*, col. 10. Moreover, this comparison is made by the debt of fidelity to be exhibited and offered, as in c. 1, *quo tempore miles*; but investiture must precede fidelity, as in the first chapter, *quod precedere debeat investitura, vel fidelitas*. Hence, since he has not yet obtained the benefice, he is not bound to the service of fidelity, as in D. de actionibus empti et venditi, l. *Iulia*, § *offerri*. To the contrary it seems, because the Bishop, by proposing the edict, denounced to him at least tacitly that he should seek investiture: since he could also make it corporal. If therefore the vassal did not obey, he ought to lose the right which he had. For if the right in the thing is lost: therefore much more strongly the right to the thing, as in D. de optione legatorum, l. *mancipiorum*.

Secondly, it is asked whether he who does not seek investiture loses the right by operation of law itself or by sentence; and it seems that it is by sentence, as in the cited chapter *Quo tempore miles*, in the word *damnetur*; and in the cited chapter *Sancimus*, in the word *laudata*. To the contrary it seems, for he who is excluded by time is excluded by operation of law, at least by way of exception, if the excluded party brings an action. For it suffices that knowledge is brought forward by way of exception, because he who does not comply with the terms established by law is deemed to have renounced, as in C. de iure emphyteuticario, l. 2; ff. ad Trebellianum, l. Facta, § Si quis bonorum; and note ff. de negotiorum gestis, l. Si ego. Which opinion I hold to be true, because whether he is already deprived or is to be deprived, the exception stands in his way.

Thirdly, it is asked whether that sentence pronounced has the force of a sentence; and I say that it does not, because it was not rendered in accordance with the order of the law, as is stated in C. communi. vel epistolas, l. interlocutio, and in C. de pac., l. si pacto, quo poenam.

Fourthly, it is asked whether that appearance made before the Vicar was sufficient, and excuses the one appearing? I answer, no, since he did not have authority, nor mandate. For general Vicars of Bishops cannot notify late, nor can they invest by virtue of general vicariate, just as they cannot alienate, as in D. 43.29, l. prohibere, § plane. Moreover, this case is similar to that in which one summoned by law or by a judge appears before an incompetent judge. This similarity is proven by the law D. 2.1, l. et quia.

Fifthly, it is asked whether this controversy is to be determined by the peers of the court; and it seems that it should be, because this is the general rule in matters of fiefs, that when there is a dispute concerning a fief between the lord and the vassal, the peers of the court, that is, other vassals, ought to determine this controversy, as in c. 1, *De controversiis inter vassallum et Episcopum*; and in c. 1, *De milite vassallo qui contumax est*; and fully noted in the extrajudicial collection, *De iudicibus*, c. *Certum*; in c. *Imperiale*, § *Si vero inter dominum et vassallum*, *De prohibita feudorum alienatione*, according to Frederick. To the contrary, it seems that this person is not properly a vassal, since he was not invested corporally; and in c. 1, *De consuetudinibus recipiendis in feudis*, he is rather a certain creditor of the Bishopric. And in cases concerning the Bishopric, the Bishop has cognizance, as in c. *Guillisarius*. The first opinion is the more common one.

Sixthly, it is asked, without prejudice to the rule that peers ought to adjudicate: suppose that this Philip is unwilling to choose peers on his own behalf; how shall the case proceed? I answer that, if indeed Philip does not possess, he shall be repelled from the threshold of the courts, as stated in the Digest, title *Qui ex causa*, law *Sed et si per praetorem*, section *Sed si dum decreto*. But if he is in possession, and thus disregards the hearing, the Bishop shall be put in possession on account of his contumacy, until he purges his contumacy and reimburses the expenses. And perhaps he shall be compelled to give security for not molesting, until he proves his right; because a fief is a certain servitude, as noted in the Digest, title *De usufructu*, law *Si auus*. But in this manner one proceeds in servitudes, as stated in the Digest, title *De novo operis nuntio*, law *Si prius*; title *De damno infecto*, law *A quo fundus*; title *Si serui*, law *Is, cuius*. For it can be said that the said vassal ought to be summoned to the court, to which also the peers are summoned, by general proclamation; and if he does not come upon the third summons, by this very fact he ought to forfeit the fief, unless he purges his delay within a year, as in the cited chapter 1, in the beginning, title *De militibus vassallis qui contumaces sunt ad conveniendum*. Therefore, in one word I say that they shall be summoned by general proclamation, because all the vassals of the Bishop are like a certain universitas, in which individuals are not summoned, but all together, as noted in the law *Non potest videri dolo careret*, Digest, title *De re iudicata*. And according to Innocentius, title *De maiore et obedientia*, chapter *Humilitas*, and Innocentius in the cited chapter *Ceterum*, it is said that it suffices to require two peers; but where ought these two to be?

† It is certain that in a city or bishopric, because it is not equitable that the lord of the fief be dragged by his vassals outside the city in which he resides, or his bishopric. For this is owed to the honor and reverence of lords. This is a singular and unique text in law, in c. Nomine, § Illud, de pace constantiae.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a renunciation of vacation days renders the vacation period useful.
2. Whether witnesses are to be compelled to testify at that time, and the judge to render sentence.
body: renunciation having been made of the holidays,

† It is asked, if holidays have been renounced, whether harvest time is called available time [tempus utile] or continuous time [tempus continuum]: and it seems that it is available, because the judge can render a decision on these days, as noted in l. i. ff. de fer. and ff. de arb. l. si feritatis. To the contrary, it seems that it is not available,

† because just as the renunciation of the parties cannot prejudice the witnesses so as to prevent them from pleading their holidays, as noted in the said l. i., so it ought not to be able to impose a necessity upon the judge, whence the judge is not bound to proceed if he does not wish; and thus it is not available time. Concerning witnesses, the gl. notes this in the said l. 1. de feriis; concerning the judge, however, no doctor touches upon anything. I believe that the judge cannot plead holidays, and thus the time is available, by the said l. si feriatis, because jurisdiction is a power introduced on public authority with the necessity of administering justice at a suitable place and time. But this is a suitable time, since holidays were renounced for proceeding with and deciding the cause; therefore the statute applies which speaks of available time. If, however, an impediment intervened by reason of the witnesses because they could not be compelled, that time of the impediment would be deducted from the middle, as in l. 2. ff. quando app. sit and l. prima. ff. de diuer. et tempo. praescrip. and l. non eum. ff. qui. ex cau. maio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. An heir instituted to the universal estate in the first clause of the institution, if subsequently ordered in a later clause to be content with only such a thing, does not appear to have been revoked from the first institution; but rather is burdened with a fideicommissum.
2. To whom a tacit fideicommissum is to be restored: whether to those coming intestate, whether to the usufructuary, or whether to the poor.
3. How these words, "domina" and "usufructuaria," are to be understood.
body: The status of Sempronius. A certain Titius, in the name of Christ, made a will, in which he said thus: I institute as heirs in my goods two poor Christians to be chosen by my wife and the executors. Furthermore, he subsequently added thus: I ordain that the said two poor Christians shall be heirs in eleven solidi for each, with which they shall be content, and they ought not to have anything beyond that. Furthermore, he ordained that his wife shall be mistress and usufructuary of all his goods, as long as she lives. Furthermore, he left certain executors for the aforesaid matters, and he died.

It is asked whether the aforementioned will contains any universal institution of an heir. And it seems that it does: because in the first chapter of the will it is thus provided, “I institute two poor men as heirs.” To the contrary it seems, because he immediately added, “I bequeath and ordain that they have 11. soli only, and no more”: and thus these two poor men are to be considered legatees: as C. de haered. inst. l. quotiens. And if it is said, rather they have the entire right of accretion, as ff. de haere. inst. l. quotiens. §. si duo. It is answered that to an heir instituted in a certain thing, or a certain quantity, whom it was not necessary to institute by virtue of the disposition of the law, the right of accretion may be prohibited: as ff. de haere. inst. l. quotiens. §. si duo. Wherefore it seems to be said that this will does not contain a universal heir: and thus this man died intestate, because a will cannot be called a will which does not have an heir, as l. proxime. ff. de his, quae in testamento delentur. This question is to me sufficiently doubtful: nevertheless it seems to be determined by l. prudenter alleged by the advocates. ff. de leg. 3. l. peto. in princip. where first, when someone is instituted as a universal heir, although in a subsequent chapter of the will he is commanded to be content with certain things, nevertheless by this precept the institution is not removed: but the instituted heir is burdened with the charge of a fideicommissum. And I hold this on account of the diverse wording of the words: and on account of the diverse clauses.

It remains to be considered regarding this tacit fideicommissum, to whom it appears to have been left: whether to the wife by those words, “mistress and usufructuary during her lifetime,” or to those who would come to the intestate succession of the testator himself; and similarly, there is sufficient ground for doubt concerning this matter. It seems that it should go to those who would come to the intestate succession, because these poor persons do not have any universal coheir, or because it may be understood as written with regard to the restitution of the fideicommissum, as stated in the aforementioned law *Peto*, in the section “there we shall say,” where the text states that the said words are understood to have been added for the sake of the legitimate heir, that is, the one who ought to come to the intestate succession; therefore, this fideicommissum ought to be restored to those who would come to the intestate succession.

On the contrary, it appears that such poor persons are understood to have been substituted by fideicommissum; because, since the executor is appointed in the will without a determined mode, the executor is understood to be left for the purpose of distributing the goods to the poor, as stated in the extrajudicial title *De testibus*, chapter *Cum tibi*. Thus, the wife must receive her legacy, subject to the Trebellian portion; or perhaps the Trebellian portion is not deducted, because she does not have ownership; and the usufruct by itself does not exceed a quarter in value; because the value of ownership is no less than that of the usufruct, as noted in the Digest, title *De usufructu*, law *Uxori meae*.

And those words, “dominam” and “usufructuariam,” are explained: and “domina” of the usufruct, according to the common understanding, is vulgar. Therefore, the ownership ought to be restored by the fideicommissum, but I doubt to whom, for it is probable that the testator wished to dispose of the entire inheritance for pious causes with regard to the class of the poor, as in the cited chapter *Cum tibi*. For the testator does not seem to have had affection for those who would succeed intestate, but rather for the pious cause. Nevertheless, it is difficult to respond to the cited law *Peto*. The chapter *Cum tibi* is not an objection, because the sense of the words uttered cannot in any way be adapted to the poor in general; for the testator, under one structure of words, also said, “I institute as heirs two poor persons, whom the wife and the commissioners shall choose,” and he spoke of nothing concerning the poor in general. Therefore, we cannot depart from the determination of the cited law *Peto*, which states that these words appear to have been added in favor of those who would succeed intestate, and thus it is held, unless it were proven by at least two witnesses that the testator had a different mind on the last day of his life. On this point, the executors themselves and the wife could also testify, if no other reason stands in their way, as in the *Institutes*, *De testamentis*, § *Legatariis*. And if the said wife is the nearest heir intestate, it must be considered whether, by accepting the cession from the poor, she appears to renounce the intestate succession. And it must be said that those who would succeed intestate do not take as those succeeding intestate, but tacitly as fideicommissaries under the will, as if the testator had expressly said, “I beg that you restore [the property] to those who would succeed intestate,” because these words do not signify the cause of intestacy, but the persons to whom succession is deferred intestate. For now the entire cause of intestacy does not exist, because the will is valid, as has been said. Although, therefore, the instituted heir has ceded his rights in the universal fideicommissum, by this the fideicommissary is not said to renounce the fideicommissum, but rather to acquire further the right, if any, which belonged to the cedent under the will, as in the *Digest*, *Ad Trebellianam*, law 1, § *Inde Neratius*. And in that manner, it does not matter if they ceded their rights as to the executor, because for that reason the fideicommissum does not fail.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Who is said to be the closer agnate.
body: that the goods of the deceased from

† It is provided by statute that the goods of one dying intestate shall devolve upon the nearest paternal agnates, and in default of them, that the nearer relatives from the maternal line shall succeed. It happened that a certain lady Catherine died, leaving behind daughters of a uterine sister [sororis carnalis], and leaving behind sons of a certain uncle of hers [annuculi], and leaving behind a certain Tonolinus, a consanguinean on the father's side, and her cognate. It is asked who succeeds. And it seems that the nearer relative does, as in Auth. defuncto. Furthermore, the son of a sister enters into the rank of agnates, as in C. de leg. haere. l. meminimus. §. 1; therefore he, or she, succeeds as a nearer agnate. Furthermore, the son of a sister is related through the root of the mother, and thus through the paternal line, because when he derives from the mother, he savors of the origin of his mother, since the medium through which one arrives at the consideration of consanguinity is founded in an agnate. But I say the contrary, and I premise that he is called the nearest agnate whom no agnate precedes; for here 'nearest' is not taken comparatively in relation to the cognatic line, but electively, because he is preferred, as in institu. de legi agna. suc. §. proximos. And therefore neither the daughters of the sister nor the daughters of the uncle have any right in that inheritance, but only the said Tonolinus, it being established that he is of paternal lineage and the words of the statute being verified; moreover, they are called agnates up to the [first?] degree of agnation, computing the degree according to the civil law. The case makes a summary.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. The first benefice does not become vacant if the person who opted for the second did not obtain peaceful possession thereof, notwithstanding any protestation to the contrary.
body: In the name of Christ.

† It is provided by statute that if the last day of any term established by law or by human act falls on a feast day, the following non-feast day ought to be counted in its place. It happened that a submission to arbitration was made to endure, let us assume, for ten days; now, the tenth day was a feast day in honor of God, and likewise the eleventh; the twelfth was not a judicial day. It happened that this arbiter and arbitrator did not render the arbitral decision on the tenth day, which was the last day of the term, yet a feast day, but rendered it on the eleventh day, also a feast day; on the twelfth day, however, he pronounced nothing. It is asked whether the said arbitral decision is valid? I answer: it is not, because either it was a holiday as far as this matters for an arbitration, and thus it is not valid on account of the feast day in honor of God, as in ff. de arbi. l. si feriatis; or it was not a holiday, and then it is not valid because it was outside the term of the submission to arbitration, C. quando prouo. non est necesse. l. cum non eo die. But if you ask of me whether it was a holiday or not: I answer that a distinction must be made: either the statute expressly proclaims holidays in arbitrations, and then it is a holiday; or it does not bring in holidays, and then it matters whether he pronounces as an arbiter, and it is a holiday, or as an arbitrator concerning the agreement of the parties or by his own equitable discretion, and it is not a holiday:

† because just as a compromise can be made on a Sunday, so also an arbitration can be held, as in C. de fer. l. fi. through Butrigarius. For arbitrations approach closer to a contract than to a judicial proceeding, as noted in Auth. vt diffe. iudi. §. 1. Or he pronounced collectively under both heads: and then it is valid and can be valid; for sometimes something is done in only one way, and then it is not valid in that way where contracting an obligation is at issue, as in l. j. §. j. ff. de const. pecunia; or something is done in a twofold manner, and then if it is not valid under one head, it is valid under the other under which it can be valid, as in C. de codic. l. si quis argentarius.

† Furthermore, consider that those arbiters who are chosen out of necessity are said to be quasi-delegated judges, as in C. de priuil. l. pen., although by reason of the equitable discretion that they possess, they exceed the nature of judges, because judges cannot settle parties except by the will of the parties, whereas these men can do so even against the will of the parties, as in ff. de no. ope. nun. l. 1. §. et post operis; yet whatever quality of discretion they have, they are reduced to the likeness of judges, and therefore it seems that they ought to observe holidays in honor of God if they pronounce simply, and not by way of mere equitable discretion. Concluding briefly: whatever may be said, the truth is that the said arbitral award does not hold, either because it was outside the term, if it was not a holiday for this purpose, or, if it was a holiday, because it was a feast day. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In the recovery of a dowry, which forum we must attend to, whether that of the heir of the deceased husband, or that of the former husband himself.
body: Whether an heir who has his own domicile in Milan can be sued for the restitution of a certain dowry once provided to the deceased, which deceased was not from the jurisdiction of Milan. The motive of this question does not consist in the general rule, because according to the general rule an heir can be sued both in the domicile of the heir himself and in the domicile of the deceased, as in ff. de iudic. l. haeres absens. But the doubt consists in the case of dowry, because in a dowry we measure the forum by the person of the husband, as in ff. de iudic. l. exigere dotem. Solution: I say briefly that as to the decision of the cause, the forum of the husband is looked to; as to the bringing of the libel, the action may well be brought in the forum of the heir himself. If therefore it is asked how much is to be restored in the name of dowry—because this pertains to the decision—the forum of the husband is looked to; but if it is asked whether the judge of the domicile of the heir is the judge or not, and in what order the proceedings are to be conducted, I say that he is a competent judge, and he proceeds according to the statutes which speak of the order of judgment in the city of Milan, as in l. 1 C. de emancipa. libe. and l. cunctos populos with its matter. Nor do I examine here otherwise what Ioan. noted in c. 1 de sponsalibus in the Novella of the Decretals, and Archi. in dist. 12 c. illa. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. In actions for a fixed sum, regard is had to the time at which the day of the obligation and of performance fell due.
2. Whether the obligation for the toll is contracted in the port, or at the gate, when goods are introduced into the city.
3. Whether the obligation for the toll is contracted in the suburbs, or at the introduction through the gates.
4. The practice is to be observed.
5. Whether a proceeding conducted before a judge alleged to be suspect, even if he is not, from whom an appeal was taken, is valid.
6. What are the just causes of suspicion against a judge.
7. He who enters upon the turf of the land where the toll began to be due is deemed to have entered the entire land, even though the toll collectors were not present there.
8. The condition of the finder is stronger than that of him who neglected to seek the thing.
9. When someone succumbs on a point of law juridically without any exception, the vanquished is to be condemned to pay the costs to the victor; nor does the opinion of the learned excuse him, nor does the oath against calumny.
body:
Statute of the commune: In the name of Christ. When certain goods were brought into and out of the city of Pavia, if they were found in the public streets of the suburbs and within the precincts of the sanctuaries, etc., or were stored, governed, and deposited in the said suburbs, from which goods of the said suburbs a written record is made, and ought to be, or can be collected, a certain toll or gabelle is to be levied on all the aforementioned items. Then this is added by agreement, that whoever is bound to pay these tolls according to the aforementioned manner and form must and ought to pay said tolls before the goods enter the city, if they wish to bring them into the city: and this at the gates. But if anyone is found bringing said goods into the suburbs, where he wishes to unload them there, he may well be compelled to make payment before they enter any house in those suburbs: which payment shall likewise be valid regarding what subsequently happens to be done by those buyers in the said suburbs.

It is now proposed that certain goods were unloaded in the said suburbs during the term of the first seven months’ buyers: and from those buyers payment was accepted, and a bond of payment was made or promised on that occasion. Now the gabelle collectors of the subsequent five months wish to open the chest and demand the said gabelle again. Likewise, the owners of the goods wish to introduce them into the city without payment of another gabelle. The question is asked: what is the law?

And it must be observed that this case was committed to the report of a certain upright man, whose report it was promised would be adhered to by both the judge and the parties. Finally, before the said reporter reported, the reporter himself was accused as suspect, being an agnate or affine of one of the parties to the said second gabelle: and this was asserted by the personal oath of the recuser. Then this reporter reported and declared in this form, namely: that the payments of the tolls of said goods, timber, stones, and merchandise, which ought to enter and be brought within the city of Pavia, for example because they were unloaded to the air, by right pertain to and ought to be made to the toll collectors of the subsequent seven months, and not to those of the prior seven months; but the payments of said goods, which were unloaded in the boroughs and within the precincts of the sanctuaries, so that they might remain there, for example because they were unloaded in some house of those boroughs and within the precincts of the sanctuaries established, pertain to and ought to be made to the toll collectors of the first seven months, and not to the toll collectors of the last five months.

It is also to be known that against this report it was proven by certain witnesses of contrary practice: however, not for so long a time that a prescribed custom is proven. Now from all these things the question is asked: what is the law? And this theme is divided into three questions. The first question is: what is the sense of the statute. The second: whether the said recuser could report, and whether his declaration ought to be adhered to. The third: whether the said report is refuted by the said contrary practice, considering the commission made to him.

† For clarity, it must be considered at the time of which payments the obligation of the tax was contracted: I say contracted, in such a way that the day of the obligation and of the payment has arrived; for just as the day arrives for each person, so must the payment be made, in such a manner that one does not usurp the advantages of another, nor enjoy the time of another; for each acquires only as much as the reason of the law and the form of the contract dictate, as in D. de stipulationibus servorum, l. si servus communis Mevii, and Castr. de peculio; D. de iure fisci, l. Valerius; D. de usufructu et de defuncto, l. l.; D. quotiens, D. de solutione matrimonii, l. divortio; D. quemadmodum servus amittitur, l. et si sic; D. si certum petatur, lege si quis nec causam, §. res pignori. To this end, however, it is necessary to know whether this obligation, so to speak, is contracted in the port or at the gate,
I speak by way of analogy.

† For if the port duty is to be paid immediately in the port of Genoa, because the goods are in the port, the obligation is contracted; but if the obligation is contracted at the gate, when the goods are brought into the city of Genoa, then the obligation is not contracted until one has arrived at the gate, as in D. de verb. sig. l. in l. censoria, and D. loca. l. pe. §. nauem.

† Now I make a comparison of the suburbs to the port, and of the city gate to the port gate: hence let us see where and when the obligation of the toll is contracted: whether in the suburbs, or at the entry of the gates. And it seems that a distinction must be made: For either, as he comes from the suburbs, he arrives at the place destined and at the terminus of his journey, and then he ought to pay in the suburbs. Or he does not arrive at the place destined; for although he passes through the suburbs, nevertheless the obligation is not then contracted in the suburbs: because the place through which one passes is not considered, but the place to which one goes, as is commonly noted in C. de aedificiis privatis, l. si quis post haec, which is most apt for this purpose. ff. de pignoribus, l. debitor. and ff. de hereditatibus institutis, l. ex facto, §. rerum autem. But if it be doubtful with what intention the bearer of the goods proceeded, then we must say that that place is presumed to be the place destined where the goods are unloaded and he departs after unloading the goods, arg. ff. de furtis, l. quod destinaverat. Nor does it seem that a distinction should be made whether in the suburbs or similar places he left the goods exposed to the air or not: because whether exposed to the air or not, since the purpose of the one bringing them was not at that time to proceed further, but the terminus of the journey was outside the gate, there the payment ought to be made as the place destined. From this it appears that the right was acquired by the first collectors, and payment could rightly be made to them, and ought not to be made to the later ones: because the statute dictates that one payment made in the due manner and to the proper person suffices. But against this it is objected from the report of the said honest man, to whose report it seems one ought to adhere. First, as a matter of law: Second, as a matter of convention: he proves the first by l. Theopompus, ff. de dote praelegata. But beware, for that law requires the oath of the reporter, just as the oath of a witness is required, concord. C. de secundis nuptiis, l. hac edictali, §. is illud. and in Auth. de non alienando, §. quod autem. For this reporter was not appointed by law, but was chosen as a witness of practice and custom. Second, it does not seem that he ought to be believed,

† because it has been proven by witnesses of contrary practice, which must be given greatest weight by referring to the most recent times, as in D. de alimentis, l. Mella, § 1. Although these witnesses do not prove the right, i.e., the prescribed custom, they nevertheless prove the fact, i.e., a certain observance or practice, which does not accord well with the report of the said honest man. Thirdly, it is said that the said report is refuted because the said reporter was challenged as suspect. But on this point let us consider, since much is argued both for and against, and yet the core of the question is not touched. For if indeed this reporter is rather a witness than a judge, it is clear that although a witness is alleged to be suspect, his testimony is not null; but it is within the discretion of the judge to examine the quality of the suspicion, and if it is slight, he is not rejected, as in C. de testibus, auth. Si dicatur. If, however, we say that this person is a kind of arbitrator, then it is not necessary for him to swear, as in C. de arbitris, auth. Decernimus, and he cannot be challenged except for a grave cause, as in D. de arbitris, l. Licet and l. Non distinguimus, § Cum quidam. We cannot challenge our own judge, as in C. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. Priuatorum. And therefore the laws which speak of the challenge of a suspect judge are irrelevant. Nevertheless, we shall not pass over this lightly, because Innocentius says that the challenged judge does not cease to be a judge, nor is he prevented from proceeding, unless an appeal is made. Bartolus, however, says the contrary, that after the challenge his proceedings are invalid by operation of law; but a distinction must be made, for either the cause of the challenge is notorious, and then his proceedings are invalid by operation of law, as in l. 1, C. si quacunque prędi. potesta.; or the cause of suspicion is not notorious, and then either we are speaking of civil law, and the proceedings are invalid, because in civil law it suffices to allege suspicion, as is read and noted in C. de iudicibus, l. Apertissimi; or we are speaking of canon law, and then either arbitrators have been elected, and the proceedings of the challenged judge are invalid by operation of law, because jurisdiction pertains to the arbitrators as judges prorogated in place of the challenged one; hence jurisdiction is suspended in the meantime, because it has succession, as in C. de iudiciis, l. Pe, in fine; or arbitrators have not been elected, neither in the principal case nor in the case of suspicion; and this point is doubtful: for the judge seems to say that he cannot proceed, even to delegate. But Innocentius says the contrary. On this I say that either he proceeds in matters of jurisdiction, for example by declaring himself judge or by delegating another; and this he cannot do. But if he proceeds in the principal matter, the proceedings are valid, unless an appeal is made, according to Innocentius. But it is strange that they are valid if he cannot determine whether he has jurisdiction; for this is contrary to l. Lex quacunque, D. si quis in ius vocatus non ierit. For the question of jurisdiction is fundamental, as noted by Innocentius in c. Innotuit, de eo qui ordinem furtive suscepit. And according to this, suspicion more strongly undermines jurisdiction than an appeal from an interlocutory judgment; because it more directly affects the person of the judge and prevents joinder of issue, as in C. de sententiis et interlocutionibus omnium iudicum, l. Cum solutum. Finally, I conclude that whatever may be the case in canon law, in civil law, which is to be observed in Pavia, the proceedings of a challenged judge are invalid, if we hold that in civil law the cause of suspicion need not be proven, nor even alleged as a matter of necessity; nevertheless consider that a challenge without cause is more effective than one with an improper cause; because impropriety vitiates the libel of challenge due to an expressly stated error, hence it is more valid to say uniformly than to ineptly assert it in the manner of a certain assertion.

† and therefore it would have to be seen whether the cause, because [the person] is a blood relative or an affine, is this cause of suspicion: and we do not have in law a statute regarding affines, except concerning the husband and wife and their children, as in D. 1.22.1 (*Qui iurisdictioni*). Unless suspicion were gathered from customs: for example, on account of excessive association. Briefly, certain causes of suspicion are expressed in law as legitimate; certain are rejected by law as not suitable; certain are intermediate between these: and these are left to the discretion of the arbitrators, who ought to be chosen in this case, D. 22.5.3 § *Tu magis* and D. 47.10.1 § 1. Finally, reducing all the above to a conclusion, I conclude in favor of the old [ones] and not in favor of the new [ones], according to those things which are proposed.

It must also be considered that he who enters upon a single clod of earth where the toll begins to be due is deemed to have entered the entire land, as stated in l. 3, § 1, D. de acquisitione possessionis. Moreover, the toll is not in anyone’s property before the commencement of entry, because it is owed to no one; but afterwards it becomes the property of the occupier, and the place itself is said to be occupied, even though the toll-collectors were not present there, as in D. quemadmodum servitus amittitur, l. quaesitum. It is true,

† Wherein, when inquiry is required, or discovery takes place, the condition of the discoverer would be stronger than that of the one who neglected to search, as in the Code, on fideiussors, l. si barsatoram. For he is not said to have discovered who did not investigate, as in the Institutes, on the division of things, §. Item lapilli. And it should be noted that this question is more one of law than of fact,

And that when someone in a point of law yields legally without any exception, the vanquished is condemned to pay the costs to the victor; nor do the opinions of doctors excuse him, according to the solution of the moderns. C. de ingenui manu. l. si auam. Hence, the oath against calumny does not excuse from costs, nor does any color of litigation, where someone yields on a point of law, not on account of the aforementioned. C. cum in veteri. and Bartolus with his gloss. and Bartolus in l. si convenit. ff. de re iud. because suspicion removes the contrary, as noted in Auth. de trien. et semisse. §. et quod saepe. coll. 3. I, Baldus de Perusio.
Certain persons purchased, In the name of Christ, the tolls of the city of Genoa by these [terms], etc. See in the 5th part, counsel 41, beginning: "Certain persons purchased," etc.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a successor is bound to abide by the lease of his predecessor.
2. In the alienation of church property, whether it suffices that the authority of the bishop intervenes at a later time.
3. Whether a void contract of alienation of church property can be confirmed by the consent of the parties, the cause being known, through the bishop; and what is required in a donation requiring insinuation.
4. A decree properly interposed is also presumed to have been done correctly.
5. Whether an alienation of the useful domain of a church without the authority of a superior is valid.
6. Whether an ecclesiastical emphyteusis granted for one hundred years is valid at least until nine years remain. See also no. 8.
7. When the useful is vitiated by the useless, and when it is not. See also no. 10.
8. If a church is not capable of reimbursing the expenses of the emphyteuta, it may renew the lease.
11. Whether absentees are to be summoned in the alienation of ecclesiastical property.
12. Whether the time of the contract or the time of its emergence is to be considered.
body: A certain John, by the name of Christ, together with the chapter, having first made certain arrangements, invested A. with a certain possession and the rights of possession, which pertain to the said monastery, for a fixed term of up to nine years, for a certain annual canon, and with the agreement and conditions that all expenses and all improvements were to be made by the emphyteuta himself in repairing the houses, which were much dilapidated, and in bringing barren and uncultivated lands into cultivation, and in doing other necessary things. Upon the expiration of the term of said lease, they were to be restored and compensated to him, the emphyteuta, by the aforementioned Abbot and chapter; otherwise, the emphyteuta himself would retain and enjoy the said possession and its rights until he had been satisfied for the aforementioned improvements, notwithstanding the payment of the usual annual canon. Then, upon the expiration of the time of the aforementioned lease, the said Abbot and chapter, having neither paid nor satisfied the expenses to the said A., invested L. and P., brothers of the said A., with the same for a fixed term of up to nine years, for a certain annual canon, with the agreements and conditions contained in the first investment. After the said investment had ended, the said Abbot, with the consent of the monks residing in the said monastery, having first made certain arrangements, solemnly invested L., brother of the said A., and C., son of the said A., for a fixed term of up to twenty-nine years, under the annual canon contained in the first lease, without having satisfied the expenses or improvements made by the said A., the first lessee, and by L. and P., the second lessees, and with the agreements and conditions contained in the preceding leases; however, no mention was made of past expenses, nor was there any reservation of improvements. To this last lease, or grant of emphyteusis, authority was imposed without decrees, after the contract had been celebrated for a month, by the Vicar of the Lord Bishop of Piacenza, who had a mandate for this from the said Lord Bishop, to whom the said monastery is subject. From the foregoing, it is first asked whether this first lease, or grant in emphyteusis, could have been made for up to twenty-nine years, given that it was not customary to lease for such a long time. Second, it is asked whether the consent, or decree of the superior, which intervened after the contract had already been celebrated for a month, has the effect of vitiating the contract, or whether it rather lends strength and firmness to the contract. Third, it is asked whether it is necessary that monks not residing in the said monastery be present at such contracts, although they are of the same monastery, or whether it suffices that the residents be present. Fourth, it is asked whether such a contract can be rescinded; but it is asserted that it was made for a lesser price than the said possession is currently worth due to the improvements made by the lessees, although before the aforementioned leases it was not worth more. Fifth, it is asked whether the emphyteutae, both the first and the second and third, can hold and enjoy the said possession and rights, paying the usual canon, until they have been satisfied for the expenses and improvements, as appears in the agreements. To

† It is necessary to set forth the evidence. In the name of Christ. The predecessor prelate sometimes contracts in his own name; and then he can never extend his scythe into the harvest of his successor, as in D. loc. cond. l. si quis domum § 1; D. sol. matr. l. diuortio, where the wife is held to abide by the lease of her husband, because that must be understood when it is for no short time. Also, because there the husband had a cause from the wife, as noted there; and C. loc. cond. l. emptorem, according to Cynus. Sometimes the prelate contracts in the name of the church, which is whenever not the prelate alone, but the prelate and the chapter contract together; because in their persons the church is represented. Also, when the prelate alone, as prelate, acts in that which touches him alone: in which case a distinction must be made; for sometimes we speak of the alienation of property; and this he cannot do even with the chapter, unless the due solemnities are observed, as in c. 1 de reb. eccles. non alien. lib. 6; and in c. monasterium and 12 q. 2 c. si qua de rebus; and Extr. de reb. eccles. non alien. c. si quis presbyterorum; C. de sacr. sanct. eccles. l. iubemus nulli; in Auth. de non alien. § vult enim; and § quia vero Leonis.

† And it is of substantial solemnity that the authority of the Bishop intervene; but concerning this there is doubt whether this authority may follow at an interval; and it seems to be said that yes, if there is utility for the Church, because we ought not to care for the subtleties of law, provided that the Church makes its condition better, as noted in the Digest, *De transactionibus*, law *Cum hi*, section *Eam*, and there the glossa ordinaria. To the contrary it seems, because where there is a defect of form, we do not care about the quality of the matter. But here authority is required for form; therefore, if authority is lacking, the contract is not valid: and this is the truth, because the contracting parties are not capable, unless they are made capable by the authority and permission of the superior, or license. For these do not regard the beginning, as in the Digest, *De infamibus*, law *Quid ergo*, in the principle, saving what I shall say below.

† I therefore ask: if, after a contract has been concluded without the authority of a superior, both parties appear before the Bishop and request that the contract be confirmed, and the Bishop, having heard the case, confirms it, does such confirmation hold? I answer yes, as in C. de decurio, l. si quos, lib. 10; and Extra de iure patronatus, c. cura; and l. 1, § solent, ff. quando appellandum sit. For then the parties are deemed to contract anew in the presence of the Bishop, because whenever something substantial is added to a contract, the contract is deemed to be renewed anew, as in ff. de contrahenda emptione, l. pacta conventa, § Paulus; and ff. de pactis, l. iuris gentium, § adeo. And we have a similar rule in the case of a donation, which is not valid beyond the legitimate portion unless it is insinuated before a judge present and interposing his authority, as noted by Guido de Cayellis in C. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis, l. illud. And yet, if a donation precedes and both parties present it to the judge, it becomes valid from that time forward, because what was done in the past is drawn into the present, as in ff. de officio proconsulis, l. observare, § si. And this is the opinion of Bartolus in ff. de donationibus, l. Modestinus. It would be otherwise if only one party sought confirmation while the other party was absent; for that which was done ineffectively does not become valid by the consent of one party alone. And note this according to the Speculum in the title de emptione et venditione.

† Where it has been decreed that [an appeal] was duly interposed, it is also presumed to have been done correctly, according to the concordant passage in the Digest, On Acquiring Possession, l. Iuste. And it is the notable text in l. 1, Codex, On the Property of the Court, Book 10. The first member concerning the alienation of ownership has been expounded: and it does not pertain to our subject matter.

It remains to be considered regarding the alienation of useful dominion, namely of a fief or emphyteusis. Here, distinguish: either this contract was celebrated according to the custom of the church, or against the custom, or beyond it. In the first case, the contract is valid, and the authority of a superior is not required, as stated in the extraneous chapter *Ex parte* on fiefs, and in chapter 1 of the section *Qui feudum dare possunt* in Compilation 10. This is true if the fief is open, or if the emphyteusis is open. However, the concession is not valid if, in the meantime, the prelate dies, as stated in chapter 1 of the section *Qui successores tenentur* in the same compilation. In the second and third cases, when it is precisely against the custom, or beyond it, the concession does not hold, which the custom or the statute of the law disapproves, as stated in the chapter *Ecclesia sanctae Mariae* on constitutions.

† But here it is doubted: what if it is sought to be granted for 9 years, and it is granted for 100 years? Does it at least hold for 9 years? And it seems that it does not, because the rule is that where one acts to bind, if what one does is not valid as done, it is not valid as it could be valid, as in D. de constituto peculio, l. 1, § eum qui. Therefore, the same applies to the alienation of ecclesiastical things, which is more odious than a personal obligation. To the contrary, because the useful is not vitiated by the useless, as in C. de donationibus, l. sancimus.

† Solution. It must be considered that sometimes an addition is made to render something invalid, sometimes to diminish it, and sometimes to specify the type of contract. In the first case, if what I do is not valid in its entirety, it is valid in the part in which it can be, as in D. de precario, l. cum precario. In the second case, it is not valid in any respect. The law states that if a compromise is made regarding a free person and a slave, because the addition of a colleague tends to diminish the right of the other colleague, the compromise is in no way valid, as in D. de arbitris, l. Pedius, § in servum. In the third case, because there is no agreement on the type of contract, the act is not valid, as in D. si certum petatur, l. si ego. It sometimes fails as an exception, as in D. de donationibus, l. si tibi dederim.

† Since our question pertains to the first member, nevertheless it must be distinguished in that member as follows: either the concession was made for a single price, and then it is not valid in any respect; for example, for a thousand for the entire term, because on account of the unity of the price the contract cannot be divided, as in l. cum plura, D. de edicto edicto; and this is not our case. Or, if for each individual year a single pension for that year is paid, then the useful is not vitiated by the useless, but it is valid to the extent that the reason of the law permits, as in D. de stipulationibus, l. si servus communis Mevii, §. si; and D. de locato conducto, l. si quis domum, §. huic; and l. si quis fundum; X. de transactionibus, c. de caetero; X. de praebendis, c. nisi esset; X. de institutionibus, c. cum venisset. And by this our question is determined, that the said contract is valid up to nine years, even without any authority of the Bishop, because a lease for a short time is considered an administration, not an alienation. Beyond nine years, however, it is not valid, unless those things intervene which are required in a full alienation; among which is the authority of the Bishop, not interposed perfunctorily, nor arbitrarily, as in D. de transactionibus, l. cum hi, §. si praetor. It should be noted, however, that if the church was not able to bear the restoration of expenses which were to be made good by agreement, as in D. de minoribus, l. intra utile, §. vendentibus; and l. 1, C. de alluvione et palude, then on account of the burden of debt it would be lawful for the church to renew [the lease] up to twenty-nine years, as in Auth. de alienationibus et emphyteusibus, §. locationes. For the utility of the church is well served if it rather re-leases a thing which will burden the church, than recalls it, as in D. de negotiis gestis, l. sed an ultro, §. si. This, however, pertains to the investigation of fact; hence it is a question of fact rather than of law.

It must be known that there is a certain other contract, which pertains neither to direct dominion nor to useful dominion, but is a contract of mere lease, concerning which see the Digest, title *de locatione et conducto*, law 5, § *die*; the Code, law 2; the Institutes, § *insti.*; and the opinions of Cynus and Decius. And the truth is that, in the case of one who cannot alienate, it is not considered an alienation. Nevertheless, it is not valid except for a short time. And thus it should be understood, as noted by Innocentius and Ioannes Andreas in the Decretals, title *Ne praepositi*, chapter *Vices suas*; and by the Archdeacon in Distinction 12, Question 2, chapter *Alienationes*, chapter 5. And in this contract, the useful is not vitiated by the useless, because they are separate. For there are three cases: sometimes the useful is separated from the useless from the very beginning; sometimes it is separable; and sometimes it is neither separated nor separable. I have written fully on this matter in my commentary on the Code, title *De sacrosanctis ecclesiis*, chapter *Aut ingressi*. And although this is a brocardic method, nevertheless what I have said is very useful. And from these things appears the response to all the questions asked, saving that as for that one,

Whether those residing outside should be summoned, and it is to be said that yes, in alienation, but otherwise in another contract, as noted in c. praesentium, de testibus, lib. 6, and in c. cum in ecclesiis, de prebendis; and it is proven in C. de decurionibus, l. observare, lib. 11, and in C. de vendendis rebus civilibus, l. si, and in Auth. de defensoribus civium, § interim, and in C. de legationibus, l. si quod extraordinarium, and in C. de sacrosancta ecclesia, aut. hoc ius porrectum, in the word ibidem servientium.

† Furthermore, if it is asked whether the time of the contract or the time of the subsequent emergence is to be considered, it must be said that the beginning of any renewal is to be considered for the entire renewal; for that quantity of price or rent is to be assessed according to the time of the contract, as in D. loc. cond. l. hominem; C. de rescind. vend. l. 2 and l. quisquis; D. de nov. operis nunt. l. fundum Cornelianum; D. de min. l. intra utile, § vendentibus. I, Baldus of Perugia.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Having confessed to receiving certain sums of money with a renunciation of the non-payment of the money, and promising to include them, or to have them included, within a month in one voyage, to what is he bound by the force of such a promise.
2. How the word "I promise" is to be understood.
3. Impersonality on the part of the stipulator does not vitiate the stipulation.
4. A penal stipulation novates the preceding one.
5. He who alleges a case is bound to prove it.
6. Whether a private writing, confessed, makes faith. And no. 8.
7. An instrument against oneself, written in one's own hand, which makes faith against oneself, and not for oneself, who can make it.
body: The fact is as follows, 1384. In the name of Christ. Month of April. I, John, son of the late Ser Nicodemus, formerly of Jacopucci of Serzana, have had and received, and confess to have had and received, from the persons written below the quantities of money written below, for the purpose of investing them, or having them invested, in one ship with the appropriate officials therein and their wages, in the presence of the witnesses written below. First, I received from Master Peter the Physician, son of the late John of Serzana, 100 gold florins; from Franciscolus, son of the late Peter of Serzana, 200 gold florins; from Federicus, son of the late Grigolus of Serzana, 300 gold florins, renouncing the exceptions of not having been had, not having been received, and not having been counted of the above-mentioned quantity of money; promising to invest the said quantities, or to have them invested, in one ship, or to give them to the said Master Peter, Franciscolus, and Federicus within the next coming month, under the penalty of double the amount of that which I shall have failed to do; wishing, by express pact, for the quantities written below, at the instance of those written below, without observing the promises, to be able to be sued both in rem and in personam in Genoa, Pisa, Savona, Lucca, Florence, and everywhere, and under any magistrate, both ecclesiastical and secular; waiving my authority to allege any place or judge as suspect. But wishing to be sued both in rem and in personam under and in the same places, as if that place had been specially appointed for the payment; or having made this present promise, renouncing every law and aid of laws introduced against those written below, or any of those written below; in testimony of all the above-mentioned premises, I have here appended my customary notarial sign. Done in Serzana in the apothecary’s shop, which is held by Jacobus, son of the late Thomas of Serzana, in the presence of the said Jacobus, Franchinelus Vanni of Serzana, Jacobus, son of Levi, of the castle of Serzana, witnesses called and requested for this, and Lord Jacobus, son of Cibaldinus, judge, etc. From the above, it is asked: to what is the said John bound by virtue of the said document to the said persons, from whom he confessed to have received the said quantities of money, or to their heirs; and what is the law in the above-mentioned matters. Concerning

† The aforementioned issue must be decided as follows: that it was necessary for the said John, in order to be released from the sums expressed in the said document, to have delivered the said ship to the said Master Peter and Francis Federici, and for their benefit, within one month from the date of the execution of the said document, as he promised, as appears in the said document where it is stated, “promising to load or cause to be loaded the said sums into the said ship.”

† For this word, "promising," is understood as a stipulation, with the intervention of those who were counting out the money; and thus, with a preceding interrogation, as in *l. sciendum*, D. de verb. oblig. and as noted there. For whenever it is found written in any public or private instrument the word "promised," or "became surety," or "promising," etc., it is always understood that all things were done with due solemnity, and that an interrogation preceded, and a promise followed between the contracting parties; and here the said counters were counting out the said money to the said John. This is the text literally in *l. 1*, C. de contrah. et committ. stipul. and it is proved in § *fin.*, Inst. de fideiuss. and in § *si scriptum*, Inst. de inutil. stipul. and in the aforementioned *l. sciendum*, where it is said, "all things done with due solemnity," etc. And even if it is not expressly stated in the said writing that "promising" implies, or causes to be implied, the quantities of the said moneys in one obligation, the persons of the said masters Peter, Franciscolus, and Federicus, nevertheless this does not vitiate the stipulation; since the person is not understood to be extrinsic, as in *l. si stipulaveris*, § *Griseogonus*, D. de verb. oblig. but the persons to whom the promise is made are always understood, which here could be none other than the contracting masters Peter, Franciscolus, and Federicus: as contained in their own persons.

† And the impersonality on the part of the stipulator does not vitiate the stipulation, since the contracting person is always understood to be implied in the stipulation, as from the text noted in l. stipulatio ista, § si quis stipulatus, D. de verb. oblig. and as noted by Bartolus in l. si, § si, in the first opinion, D. si cert. pet. Therefore, in the case at hand, since it does not appear that what has been stated above was done by John himself, the said sums of money can be recovered by the said masters Peter, Francis, and Frederick, and after their deaths by their heirs, by means of the condictio ob causam, since the cause for giving them was to be implicated in the said voyage, which was not done; therefore, due to the defect of cause, the said recovery is available, as in l. dedi, § sed si tibi, and l. si pecuniam, and almost throughout the title D. de cond. causa data causa non secuta, and especially since this is expressed in the said document, where it is said, "or they shall give the said sums to the said masters Peter, Francis, and Frederick within the next coming month, under penalty of double and of all that which has been contracted against." Therefore, the said sums of money can also be claimed in double by virtue of those words, "under penalty of double, etc.," which penalty was incurred upon the lapse of the first month, the said implication in the voyage by the aforementioned John not having appeared.

† for the said penal stipulation novated the preceding one, and was transferred into it, as is the text in l. obligationum fere, § 1, ff. de actionibus et obligationibus, and in l. si pacto, quo poenam, C. de pactis. Therefore, the said moneys can be claimed by the said parties in double, notwithstanding that the said John alleges that he purchased the said ship; because nothing appears to this effect, nor does he prove it; and it is the same whether something does not exist, or exists but does not appear, as l. in l., ff. de contrahenda emptione; l. duo sunt Titii, ff. de testamento tutorum, with similar authorities. Therefore, the aforementioned parties, or their heirs, can claim the aforementioned money from the said John himself, or, if he is dead, from his heirs. Even if the said John were to prove that he purchased it, he was obliged, after the purchase, to deliver it to the said buyers, as l. si pecuniam, § item si quis, de condictione ob causam. And in the case where he claims to have possessed it by using it and conducting it by sea against the will of the aforementioned parties, he is liable, as a pirate, for the valuation of the said ship and for all the moneys that the aforementioned parties could have obtained by letting the said ship, as l. si urbana, de condictione indebiti; and what is noted there concerning ship freight; and l. si navis, de re vendita; and l. Iul., de petitione hereditatis. But if he claims to have used it with their consent and to have rendered an account of the profits, let him prove it; and in the case where

† let him say that he lost it, let him prove the casualty, *instituimus qui mores* con. ob. §. final, and there noted; and in the case where he does not prove the said casualty, he is undoubtedly bound to restore the said ship with all the profits and advantages which the aforementioned parties could have let or derived from the said ship, as in the laws immediately cited. And according to Bartolus in the said law *si urbana*, in the first part of that law. But this doubt arises, whether the said writing makes faith, and for the Pope no cause shall be alleged against the said John. And here it must be seen whether the said writing was public or private. And in the case where it was private, there is no doubt that the said John should first be interrogated whether the said writing was in his own hand. And thus I would advise, and that this should be done before all else to avoid every doubt.

And in the case where he confesses that the said writing is in his own hand, it would undoubtedly make proof of the contents thereof, as in the Authentica *Contra qui propriam*, Codex, *De non numerata pecunia*; and what is noted in the law *Scripturas*, Codex, *Qui potest in pignus habere*. In the case, however, where he denies it, proof would have to be made that it was in his hand by means of the sign appended thereto and by comparison of the handwriting according to the form of the law *Comparationes* and the Authentica there placed, Codex, *De fide instrumentorum*; which proof, once made, makes proof according to the determination there set forth. But what is more, I say that the said writing is not private, but public; and it makes proof against the aforementioned John, because it is a public instrument against him. For there are present all things which are required in a public instrument, namely, the year, the indiction, the day, and the month, the place where the instrument was made, as well as the three witnesses described therein; which are required according to the form of the text in the Authentica *De tabellionibus*, in the beginning, in § *Nos autem*. But here nothing is lacking, except that the *rogatus* [notary called upon] does not appear in the said writing. But I say that in the case of a notary this is not necessary to be required; for the *rogatus* is presumed, as is noted by the gloss in the Authentica *De tabellionibus*, in § *Nos autem*. Although it is otherwise in the case of a witness according to the common understanding, in the law *Haeredes palam*, § *In testamentis*, and there by Doctorus and by Cynus, in the law *Hac consultissima*, in the beginning, Codex, *De testamento*.

But here there is only the doubt whether the aforementioned John could have drawn up an instrument against himself in his own hand, and I say that he could, by the authorities cited by Bartolus in l. 2, ff. de stipulationibus servorum, in the first and second columns, concluding that a notary may draw up an instrument against himself, and that it may make proof against himself, and not in his favor; thus it was in the case at hand, therefore, etc. From these considerations, concluding, I say and advise that the aforementioned Masters Peter, Francis, and Federigo, or, if one of them is dead, their heirs, can demand from the aforementioned John, by right, or, if he is dead, from his heirs, double the said quantity of five hundred florins, unless it is proved that the said sum of money was invested in one voyage within a month from the date of the execution of the said writing, according to the form contained in the said writing; in which case then John himself must be condemned to the said voyage, and execution is to be taken on the valuation of the said voyage, and on all the moneys which the aforementioned parties could have obtained by letting the said voyage; and the said writing is to make proof as a public document against the aforementioned John and his heirs. Ubertus de Lampugnano thus advised. It seems to me that two defects exist: first, because it does not appear that the subscription was in the notary’s hand; second, because there is not the sign required in an instrument, as in C. de assessoribus, l. final, and in Inst. de publicis iudicibus, in the glossa ordinaria; on account of which it seems that one should say that the said

† A document does not prove as a private document, unless it is supported by a solemn comparison of handwriting, although the gloss in l. ad monendi, ff. de iureiur. states that by comparison only half-proof is made; but if it were his sign and subscription, the said opinion is the very truth. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a dispensation can be granted by the Pope for a marriage to be contracted between consanguineous relatives without cause.
2. He who doubts the power of the Pope doubts the Catholic faith: and he is to be regarded as a sacrilegious person.
body: In the name of Christ.

† The question is asked whether the Pope, without adding any cause, can dispense so that blood relatives in the fourth degree may contract marriage with a clear conscience? And it must be said that he can, because this is not one of the degrees prohibited by divine law, as in extra de restitu. spo. c. literas. Nor does it stand in the way that he dispenses without cause, because the supreme authority of the Pope takes the place of a cause, since he is living law on earth, and whatsoever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.

† Whence one who doubts his power doubts the Catholic faith and is to be regarded as sacrilegious; C. de crimine sacri. l. disputari., there, "in the manner of sacrilege"; and ff. de ritu nupt. l. qui in prouincia. §. diuus supports this.
