And I believe that this can be done by that Pope who is reputed as Pope by the greater part of the world, by the argument of ff. de officio praeto. l. barbarius; and even if it were an error, children born from such an error would be legitimate, as in de ince. nupt. l. qui contra. And therefore the Italians impetrate from the Roman, whereas other, indifferent persons impetrate from both, which is permitted according to Ioan. And. in addi. Specu.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a condition appended in a last will or in a contract impedes the essence of the contract when it comes to delivery.
2. Any kind of delivery suffices for the transfer of ownership.
body:
A certain Francis, in the name of Christ, made a will, in which he left to his daughter one thousand [units], and to his heir four hundred. Finally, the same Francis, on the same day that the said will was made, made a certain inter vivos donation to his sister, Lady Antonia, of certain properties, with this condition added, that the said Lady Antonia could not use the donated things until the daughter and wife had obtained the aforementioned legacies. Then, the said Francis, two years later, made another will, in which he revoked and annulled the first will. Subsequently, he bequeathed to his said sister, by way of institution, 10 Imperial livres, and ordered her to be content in consideration of the aforementioned donation made to her of the said goods, which donation he ordered to remain in its force. And the said Francis died, leaving a wife, leaving a daughter, and leaving agnates, who were instituted as universal heirs in both wills.

The question arises between the sister, donee, on one side, and the mother and the aforementioned daughter on the other, concerning the goods contained in the donation. For the sister demands that the goods declared in the donation be released to her. Conversely, the mother and daughter say that she should not have them unless she first pays four hundred florins, which are mentioned in the said first will. For the sister replies and says that the first will was revoked by the second, so that the condition added in the instrument of donation was removed from the donation itself, and that the said donation remains pure, so that she demands not only the donated things but also the fruits collected from the day of the testator’s death by the wife and daughter from the donated things. From the foregoing, it is asked, what is the law?

And it appears at first sight that, the condition of the said donation failing, the said donation does not subsist; and this by the general rule: because whenever a condition is appended in a contract or legacy, unless the condition exists, the contract and the disposition of the legacy fail, as in D. ad Trebellianam, l. iubemus, § 1; D. de verborum significatione, l. cedere diem; D. si certum petatur, l. pecuniam; and noted in the same title, l. lectam, in the great gloss; C. de conditionibus insertis, l. legatum, and noted; D. de pactis, l. Item quia; and D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. non solum. But here the condition fails, because the said one thousand four hundred cannot be received by the wife, nor can they be provided, as in the testament, since it has been revoked by a subsequent testament, as in Inst. quibus modis testamentum infirmatur, § posteriore; l. secunda, § primo; D. de conditione indebiti; D. de iniusto testamento, l. cum in secundo; D. de adimendo legatis, l. quod iterum.

To the contrary, I believe that this is the truth itself. And I consider that sometimes a condition is appended to bring the disposition into existence; and then the aforementioned laws speak. Sometimes a condition is appended not to the beginning of existence, but to the execution of existence; and then, although the condition made by the obligor fails, nevertheless the action, which has already arisen, can be effectively brought; and this by a subtle reason, because such a pending condition gives rise to an exception, but the removal of the condition gives rise to a replication. Therefore, the defendant must plead an exception; but against the exception a replication is made. Place the exception in l. commissoria, as in C. de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem, l. commissoriae; and D. de pactis, l. ab emptione; and D. de donationibus, l. 1, in the great gloss.

Thus it is in the case at hand, because the properties were donated and transferred by the constitution of a precarium, as in D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. cum eo. For

† Any kind of delivery suffices for the transfer of ownership, whether natural and civil possession is transferred, or only civil, or only natural, even if clandestine, not to mention if just, when the delivery is made to the owner, as it is said in l. illa singularis, if the advice follows regarding the fund, ff. de fundo dotali. And furthermore, consider that no condition impedes the beginning of the essence of the contract when it comes to delivery, as in l. quod nisi, ff. de iure dot. and ff. de solut. I. sub conditione, and ff. de usucapio pro dote, I. 1, §. 1, unless the condition is inserted into the delivery itself, as is clear from the aforementioned laws. Moreover, it should be noted that in our case, the condition was not attached to the obligation, but to the enjoyment, and it was attached after the contract was perfected as to its primary essence; and therefore, a condition failing due to the act of the one who attached it in his own favor does not invalidate, as C. quando dies leg. ced. l. ex his verbis, and there noted. Thus, the matter stands: because ownership was acquired by the said sister from the beginning, but she had to refrain from acting until, after the death of the said testator, the said legacies were paid; and if the legacies had not been revoked, the sister would have the action by right, but an exception would stand in the way. But since that condition has been removed, a replication is given to the sister; and this subtlety proceeds from the gloss which is in d. l. lecta, joining contrary opinions and reconciling them. Furthermore, it must be considered that sometimes a condition is attached in a contract by reference to the contract; and then the said gloss speaks. Sometimes it is placed in a last will by reference to the last will; and then there is no doubt that the condition can be removed, as ff. de adimen. leg. l. 3, §. conditio. Sometimes it is placed in a contract by reference to a last will, for example, I promise you ten if you give Stichus to Seyus, my heir; or I stipulate with Titius, my heir, and later another is heir; for it is not necessary that anything be given to Titius, as ff. de pactis, l. tale pactum, §. fina. Moreover, it must be considered that sometimes a condition is placed as a certain event simply, sometimes in place of a final cause; and then, the final cause ceasing, the condition ceases, but the disposition does not expire, as ff. ad Trebell. l. a filia, §. alumno. Since, therefore, this condition was attached here in favor of the daughter and wife, if they cannot obtain this favor, the contract is not thereby invalidated, argumen. ff. de legatis. 2, l. Lucius, §. quis quis, ff. de contrahen. emptio, l. Labeo scribit, Si mihi Bibliothecam, ff. de condi. et demonstra, l. si quis eum. Nor is it to be omitted that in the second testament there were these words, tacitly and contentedly in consideration of the donation. These words express the sense of the testator, as ff. de haere. institu. l. qui volebat, expressly adds, which donation he ordered to remain in its force. Someone will say, these words in its force rather harm the sister, if they can affect, than benefit: for its force is not, unless by antecedent it is conditioned, therefore it seems the condition is repeated, as C. de colla. l. vt liberis, in fin. But to this I respond, that the said condition is impossible with the legacy revoked; and therefore, this impossible condition is not said to be repeated in the testament, as ff. de manu. testa. l. fi, ff. de verborum obliga. l. si ita stipulatus, §. Grisogonus. Rather, I say more, that even if it were expressly repeated, because the impossible would not invalidate the last will, which was that the said sister should receive the donated things, as insti. de haere. instit. §. impossibilis, and fully read and noted in l. 1, ff. de condi. instit. and in l. 1, C. de his, quae poen. nomine. From which I conclude conclusively and firmly, that the said sister can claim the said donated things with the fruits unjustly received from the things of the said donor; nor is it desired to linger here, because fruits pertain to the owner by right of ownership, as ff. solu. matri. l. si mora, and there by Jacobus de Are., and ff. de rei vendi. l. solum, §. meum. However, the possessor in good faith is not bound, except according to the distinction noted. ff. de rei vendi. l. fructus. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. I give you one hundred, so that you may give me ten each year for alimony; what kind of contract is this, and whether it is usurious or not.
2. Whether the day interpellates on behalf of the person, such that interest arises from the day of default.
body: The fact upon which the case turns follows in the terms set out below. And first, for the information of the truth of the case, it is assumed that there is a certain statute of the city of Milan, providing in effect that in cases in which interest arises under canon law, the oath of the claimant shall be held as full proof up to a certain sum. Having assumed the aforementioned statute, the fact, or narration of the question, is assumed. And it is true that a certain Master Mafiolus called Niger of the Aliprandi family, and a certain Mistress Joan of Castellione, were legitimate husband and wife, from whom were born into the light a certain Ambrosius, who was of unsound mind, Mistress Orsina, Perolus, and Mafiolus called Peterenus, all their legitimate and natural children. The said Mafiolus died having made a will, in which, among other things, he bequeathed to the said Mistress Joan certain quantities of grain, firewood, and certain other things to be provided annually for the maintenance of herself and the said Ambrosius, her son of unsound mind, during the lives of the mother and the son. And after this will and bequest, the above-mentioned Mistress Joan, in her own name and in the curatorial name of the said Ambrosius, her son of unsound mind, on one part, and the above-mentioned Orsina, Perolus, and Mafiolus on the other part, by compromise came to certain arbitrators, who pronounced an arbitral sentence between the said parties, condemnatory of the said Orsina, Perolus, and Mafiolus, to the provision of certain annual sums of money to the said Mistress Joan, in her own name and in the said curatorial name, by virtue of the aforementioned bequest, for the entire time of the lives of the said Mistress Joan and Ambrosius. Presupposing the statute of the city of Milan providing in effect that in cases in which interest arises under canon law, the oath of the claimant shall be held as full proof up to a certain sum, it is proposed that a certain Thomasellus, by the will of a certain Mafiolus, assumed upon himself, with the intention of novating the debt, a certain annual provision to be made to a certain Mistress Joan; and therefore he received one hundred gold ducats for the purpose of sustaining the burden of the said annual provision, the obligation of which he had assumed upon himself with the intention of novating, as is stated above. The said Thomasellus promised to pay and restore the said 100 florins to the said Mafiolus whenever the said alimentary beneficiary died; which alimentary beneficiary subsequently died twenty years ago. Now it is asked whether any interest can be claimed from the time of the death of the said alimentary beneficiary, and whether the said interest is believed to be proven by the oath of the said Mafiolus according to the form of the said statute.

† Regarding this question, it must be considered what kind of contract this was, namely: I lend you 100, so that you give 10 each year to the lady Joan for her maintenance; and when she dies, you restore to me the entire amount of the said 100. For if this is a contract of loan (mutuum), the said 10 paid each year reduce the principal; because this appears to have been done in fraud of usury, as is noted in ff. si certum petatur, l. rogastis, §. si tibi. But if this is a contract of deposit, the law is the same, once dominion has been transferred, as in ff. de deposito, l. disponsaliorum. For although the words say, “those who make a loan, expecting nothing therefrom,” nevertheless the same applies to any similar contract, as in extra de usuris, c. naviganti. As to whether this contract was a contract of loan or of deposit, see the glossa ordinaria in ff. si certum petatur, in l. cum quid. From this it follows that, since these 10 annual payments were converted to the benefit of the said Mafioli, who was bound to pay the said annual amount, the said annual amount must be considered usurious wrongfulness; for whatever is added to the principal is usury, and it does not matter whether it is paid to me or to another by my will, as in l. solutum, §. solutum, ff. de pignerationis actione. From this it is inferred that, from this contract made in fraud of usury, interest is not due by canon law, because it is not a lawful contract. To the contrary it seems, because even in a contract of loan interest arises by canon and civil law. This is the glossa ordinaria in l. 1, C. de summa trinitatis, which says that the Pope grants letters under this interest. Nor is this surprising, because the debtor’s delay should not harm the creditor, as in ff. de in libris iuris, l. nummus. For as appears there, it is special in the case of money that interest arises beyond the thing due because of delay; because interest within the thing does not diminish the quantity; nor is it found that a decretal disposes to the contrary; therefore, that law should be followed. Moreover, this contract is not a contract of loan nor of deposit; but it is an innominate contract, from which arises an action for him who paid, because he has fulfilled the contract on his part, as in ff. de condictione ob causam, l. si pecunias, §. 2, with the following. And that this was an innominate contract appears from the form, because I give so that you give, as in ff. de praescriptionibus verbalibus, l. naturalis. But assuming that this contract was valid both by canon law, the doubt here is whether the debtor is bound to pay interest; for interest does not arise except from the time of delay, as in ff. de usuris, l. mora, §. si quidem. Therefore, the debtor was not interpellated; and thus he was not in delay; therefore, interest cannot be claimed, as in l. vinum, C. si certum petatur. But if he was interpellated, holding that this contract was a just contract, see ff. de usuris, l. fideicommissum, §. extraneos, and innsit cum Pollidius. Then interest would arise, and one should abide by the oath, considering the quality of the persons and the custom of the place, as in ff. de eo quod certum locutus est, l. 3, §. fin. On which point, proof by oath according to the form of the statute would suffice.

† It remains only to consider whether, without any other formal demand, the passage of time at the moment of death operates as a demand on behalf of the person entitled to alimony. It appears that it does, because the day demands on behalf of the person, as stated in Codex, On contracting and common stipulations, l. magna. This applies whether the day is certain as to when it occurs, or uncertain, as noted by Cynus in the aforementioned l. magnam, in the final question; but Doctor Bartolus in l. ita stipulatus, ff. On the meaning of obligations, states that a conditional day does not induce delay, because one day should not simultaneously create an obligation and delay, since the existence of the condition serves to purify the obligation. Hence, just as a pure obligation does not demand, neither does the existence of the condition. But to this it might be responded that the statement of Bartolus is understood in the case of a condition uncertain as to whether and when the day will arrive; but when the obligation is certain from the beginning as to whether, but not as to when, then the obligation arises from the beginning and is subsequently declared, and such a day demands on behalf of the person, by the authority of Digest, On conditions and exceptions, l. nam et si cum moriar. And what is noted there is that the debtor must know, or ought to know, that the day has arrived, because this is required for incurring delay from uncertain events, as in Digest, If a certain thing is claimed, l. quod te. This question is very doubtful both on the first point, whether this contract savors of the evil of usury, and on the second point regarding delay, and it is safer to abstain from such contracts; nevertheless, according to civil law, there is no doubt that the contract is valid, as in Digest, On the meaning of obligations, l. qui Romae, in the beginning. To this also contributes Extra, On donations between husband and wife, c. per videtras. But that chapter can be understood differently, as noted there by me, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. 3
2. Whether a testament is void when a prohibition has been made to those instituted in a certain thing, lest they demand more, since they do not have their legitime.
2. Whether the right of accretion in inheritances has place against the will of the testator, and whether such a right of accretion can be prohibited by the testator.
3. Whether the testament of a usurer is valid by law.
4. By whom can an objection be raised when an heir is ordered to restore the inheritance and is incapable.
5. Whether heirs are to be deprived if the legacy for the construction of a chapel was not fulfilled? and to whom the inheritance accrues.
body: The testator instituted, in the name of Christ, that a certain chapel be constructed, and he instituted his nephews from his daughter as heirs in an uncertain city. It is said that he requested the said universal heirs in secret to restore [the inheritance] to one not capable [of receiving it], and that they so gave their faith [to this request]. After the testator died, within the year the chapel was not constructed. From these facts arise four doubts.

The first doubt is whether the will was valid. It is alleged that it was valid, because it was left to the nephews through the daughter by right of institution. To the contrary, it is alleged that it was left for less than the legitimate portion, and they were prohibited from claiming more; therefore, the said singular institution, which prohibits the right of accretion, is reduced to the status of a simple legacy: and thus the will is not valid, as in §. aliud quoque capitulum. In Auth. ut cum de ap. cogn. et no. C. de inof. testa. auth. nouissima. and ff. de vul. sub. l. cu ex filio. in prin. and in l. filium. ff. de le. praest. solu. Notwithstanding the argument of truth, it is held that the said will is valid, because even if the testator had instituted in a single number, the will is valid, nor can the son or nephew be said to have been passed over. And this gloss. singu. ff. ad Tre. l. si quis priore. And the reason is: because just as the testator cannot impose a burden on the debt of the subsidiary portion of goods, so neither can he impose any prohibition, as C. de inof. test. l. Quam in priorib. and l. scimus. Furthermore, there is a demonstrative reason, because the right to sue for the supplement succeeds in place of the ancient querel of the inofficious will, as C. de inoffi. testa. l. omnimodo. and l. si quis filium. §. si sicut. Therefore, just as the testator cannot prohibit the querel of the inofficious will, so neither can he prohibit the right of supplement. From this follow two conclusions: the first, that he who institutes a son in the legitimate portion is not said to die intestate: because if the universal heir repudiates, the whole accrues to him. The second conclusion is that, since he dies partly testate, of necessity he dies wholly testate, because the testator cannot by any of his own arrangements die partly testate and partly intestate.

And therefore, in inheritances, the right of accretion applies even against the testator's will; this is the glossa ordinaria to the Digest, *de acquisitione hereditatis*, law *Si servus communis ab extero*. But in legacies and fideicommissa, the right of accretion can properly be prohibited, as noted in the law *Divus*, § *Fin.*, Digest, *de usufructu*. Lancellus, regarding an heir instituted in a specific thing, distinguishes as follows: either it is such a person who, under the old law, cannot bring an action for nullity of the will (*querela inofficiosi testamenti*), and then it can be prohibited, as in the Digest, *de hereditate instituenda*, law *Quotiens*, § *Si duo*; or it is such a person who can bring such an action, and then the contrary holds. This is the noble case in the Authenticum *Ut cum*, Codex, § *Certum*. And this is my ancient allegation, and one can sufficiently proceed by circuitous arguments. This is the truth:

Secondly, it is asked, for it is said that the testament was invalid because the testator was a manifest usurer, and it is not established that he had been formally cautioned regarding the restitution of usury. For although it is said that caution was given before the Vicar of the Bishop, nevertheless the vicariate is not established, even though the notary inserts these words; for it ought to be established otherwise concerning a manifest fact than by these enunciative words, as in the chapter *Si Papa*, *De privilegiis*, Book 6, and in the chapter *Cum in iure*, *De officio delegati*. But on this point I say that presumption favors the instrument, as noted in law 1, *Codex*, *De fide instrumentorum*, and *Ius hastae fisci*, Book 10; and especially for this reason, because the jurisdiction of a vicar is ordinary jurisdiction, and ordinary jurisdiction is presumed, even if it is not proved otherwise, although the case is different with a delegate, according to Johannes Andreae, *Ad hoc*, *Digestum*, *De officiis praetoris*, law *Barbarius*; and what is noted in law 1, *Codex*, *Qui et adversus quos*, prudently alleged by Master Giliolus, supports what is read and noted in distinction 97, chapter *Nobilissima*. Moreover, this exception, that he is not a vicar, does not apply unless it is added that he was not in possession of the vicariate, according to Compostella. For the exception is not sufficient, since mere quasi-possession of the office suffices, as in the chapter *Consultationibus*, *De iure patronatus*. Furthermore, it should be known that both by law and by custom it suffices to express some quantity, adding a general clause, "all and whatever"; and especially concerning uncertain things, as in law *Statuliber*, *Digestum*, *De statuliberis*. Otherwise, one would have to describe in the caution the entire code of accounts of the usurer, which is ridiculous, unusual, and in a manner impossible; and especially at the point of death, as in *Codex*, *Qui testamento facere possunt*, law *Hac consultissima*, section *At cum humana*.

† The third question is whether someone other than the fisc, for example, those coming in intestacy, can object on the ground of tacit good faith regarding restitution to an incapable person; and it must be said that they cannot. This is the singular gloss. D. 38.2.1, § 1. And the reason is that they are invoking the right of a third party, namely that of the fisc, which is impossible, since they do not have a mandate from the fisc; furthermore, we are not before the judge of the fisc, nor is the patron of the fisc present. Moreover, it is not sufficient that the testator said, "restore to the incapable person," unless they have bound themselves by stipulation or written instrument, because they cannot do what the testator did not speak to, as is stated in D. 32.1.1, § intestato, D. 35.1.1, and D. 22.5.1, and D. 49.14.1, § tacite.

The fourth doubt arises because the chapel was not constructed within one year from the date of the notification of the episcopal constitution. But here it must be considered, first of all, that the said constitution does not bind heirs who lack knowledge of the will; hence, proof of such knowledge must be provided, as stated in C. de epis. et cle. l. nulli, in the words “pro sua conscientia.” This is the opinion of Bartolus in ff. de infa. in l. genero, and it is expressly proven in l. ult. ff. de decre. ab ordi. Secondly, it must be known that a judicial notification is required, with which a stricter course is taken than with a statutory notification, as in extra de testa. §. si heredes, and in Auth. de haere. et fal. §. si quis autem non implens. Thirdly, it must be considered and subtly observed that if the heir were to be deprived not on account of the constructed chapel, the goods should be applied to the chapel itself, as in l. pen. C. de leg. But certainly, for another reason, the goods should not be applied to the said nephews, because the testator, in disposing concerning them, limited them and, with a prohibition against demanding more, excluded them from the benefit of the aforementioned authenticum, and could exclude them. For it is notable that the provision of the said authenticum does not apply to those persons who act against the will of the testator, as in Auth. de haer. et fal. §. exhæredatos, joined with l. qui volebat, ff. de haere. insti., and ar. ff. de condi. et demon. l. mulieri, et Titio. From these it is inferred that the opinion of the eminent doctor, Master Gilioli de Cautellis of Cremona, is verified in every part of it, and beyond the aforementioned points, prudently supported by his own reasons. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. When the article has been committed in its entirety, so that no dispute remains, if the consultant has advised on certain matters and reserved the right to litigate on others, whether such advice is valid, and
1. the sentence passed thereon: and nu. 4.
2. The sentence in a possessory action, when it should be rendered for the plaintiff and when for the defendant, both parties proving their possession.
3. Witnesses of a corporation, when they are admitted or not admitted in a case concerning a corporation.
body: The question being pending in the name of Christ, concerning a certain jurisdiction of a territory, as well as dominion and possession, between the quasi-nobles of Gabiano and the community of Gabiano on one side, and the community and inhabitants of Fontaneto on the other; on which said questions of property, dominion, and possession, there had been prolonged litigation; and witnesses having been received for both parties, and proof or assertions made by the witnesses of both sides for and against, the case was finally committed to be consulted by certain learned men. The article of the commission contained the causes, namely, that the disputes arising from boundaries and territory, etc., and all and each matter should be decided in such a way that no further doubt should arise regarding the sentence rendered. However, the said consultants advised in this form: namely, that the defendant party, viz., the community of Fontaneto, should be absolved from the petition of the said nobles, insofar as it concerns the jurisdiction of the territory, power, and district of Gabiano, of which and in which it was said that the places in dispute are located; saving, however, the right of the plaintiff party, viz., the aforementioned persons of Gabiano, as regards dominion and possession of the things in dispute. And thus was the sentence rendered.

† It is now asked whether the said opinion is valid in law, or whether it is indeed outside the form of the commission; and what is the law regarding the judgment that assumes the said opinion as its foundation; this also being presupposed, that the said judgment was rendered by a delegated judge. And what is the law if he were an ordinary judge. And although the said opinion could be invalidated in law: for it states that the defendant ought to be absolved because the case is not proven. For there are three cases: either the plaintiff proves nothing, and then the defendant ought to be absolved, as in l. quia accusare and l. actor; or both parties prove equally, i.e., the plaintiff for and the defendant against; and then either we are speaking of a petitory action, or we are speaking of a possessory action. In the first case, the defendant is absolved, because possession works in his favor, as in Inst. de interdictis § commodum. Or we are speaking of a possessory or quasi-possessory action, and both parties prove regarding possession and quasi-possession, and prove equally. Then either the proofs are adverse, because each proves that he alone possessed, and the same, unless the plaintiff’s possession is according to common law, and the defendant’s possession and quasi-possession are against common law,

† because then judgment would have to be rendered in favor of the plaintiff on account of the aid of law, or conversely in favor of the defendant, if the defendant had the aid of law and not the plaintiff, as in Extra, de causa possessionis, cap. Cum ecclesia; and in cap. Ad decimas, de restitutione spoliorum, 6. If, however, the proofs are not adverse: and this can happen in two ways, either in corporeal things, and then the judge ought and may render judgment for either party by saying that each possesses as undivided co-owners; because in possessing the parties act together through concurrence, as in Digest, de acquisitione possessionis, l. 3, § ex contrario; and this opinion is held by Bartolus. Or in incorporeal things, for example in jurisdiction, which can belong to several persons in solidum, or in servitude, as in l. fin., Digest, uti possidetis; and then the judge ought not to pronounce for each party pro parte, but for each promiscuously, saying: “As you have possessed promiscuously, so possess promiscuously.” Where one party does not prove better than the other; for if the plaintiff proved better than the defendant, or conversely, judgment should be rendered for him, as in Codex, de edicto divi Adriani Tollendo, l. fi., § 1. Others say that the judge could gratify according to his conscience. This is stated by the notable gloss in Digest, de re iudicata, l. Duo iudices dati, cum igitur. Therefore, according to the records which I have seen, since the nobles and counts of Gabiano proved better both as to ancient possession and as to continuous and new possession, judgment ought to have been rendered in their favor, as in Extra, de probationibus, cap. Licet tamen; and that their witnesses are more credible appears,

† because although members of a university are sometimes admitted in a case concerning the university, this is not true if the benefit of the case is distributed among the individuals, since they are not suitable in their own right or in common right by that reason which savors of proprietary interest in the benefit, just as a partner is not suitable in a case concerning the partnership; nevertheless, when they are admitted with the quality of affection, those witnesses are better who are neither in fact nor in affection participants in the case. First Part of the Consilia. And so in the present case, as the Digest, De testibus, l. Ob carmen, the Marquises, and even those who gave counsel say, that less faith is to be accorded, therefore it necessarily follows that if greater faith is to be accorded to the plaintiff’s witnesses than to the defendant’s, the opinion should have been given for the plaintiff, not for the defendant. And of this I cannot but marvel; nevertheless, out of reverence for such great authorities who have given counsel, I do not pursue the matter further.

But another question follows, whether the said opinion was valid. For if it was not valid, the case ought to have been committed to other consultants, who perhaps will examine the records more thoroughly, as in D. de iureiurando, l. Qui per salutem; and l. Si ut proponis, C. quomodo et quando iudex. I say firmly that the said opinion was null by operation of law, because it was contrary to and outside the form of the commission. For, as appears, the commission was made so that consultation should be given on all matters together, such that there could be no partiality regarding one matter; but they did not consult on the possessory aspect of jurisdiction, nor on the possessory or petitory aspects of corporeal things; rather, they reserved the dispute concerning the aforementioned matters, as in l. Cum fundum, §. Fin., D. de vi et vi armata; and D. de conditione indebiti, l. Eleganter, §. Si post. Hence the opinion was invalid, because the consultant is assimilated to an arbitrator, who cannot divide his judgment, as in D. de arbitris, l. Qui tamen; and D. familiae herciscundae, l. In hoc iudicio; and C. de iudicibus, l. Nulli. The same must be said of the sentence, which follows consequentially from the opinion, or at least it ought to be rescinded by appeal, because it was rendered based on a void opinion, thus without cause, and consequently is unjust, as in C. de appellationibus, l. 1. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an agreement can be made that one cannot acquire from the other party: and if it is valid, whether it can be exchanged.
2. Whether the acquirer or the transferor is said to act against the agreement.
3. Whether a contract can be annulled by agreement, or a penalty claimed. And no. 4.
5. Whether one who acts against the agreement, either by force or fear, is bound to the penalty.
6. Whether repentance has a place in exchange.
7. Stipulation is a named contract, and how a named contract is recognized.
8. In unnamed contracts, repentance does not have a place if an oath intervenes.
9. The vassal lost the fief, and had himself reinvested by the lord without knowledge, whether such investiture is valid.
10. One who constitutes himself to possess for another cannot sell to another: and transfers civil and natural possession.
11. It is more to say I possess for you, than I possess by permission.
12. Whether investiture can be made of castles invaded.
13. Whether license given by the lord of the fief excuses from the penalty of the law if anyone in such a case.
14. The party who does not depose is not heard.
body: To the magnanimous men. In the name of Christ. As they came to the division of certain of their castles, namely for the half held in indivision which accrued to the uncle, and for the other half which accrued to his two nephews from the other predeceased brother, on this condition, that any of the said parties could not acquire anything in the portion of the other; and thus they promised to each other, by themselves and their heirs, and confirmed it by oath. Now it happens that one from one party exchanged a certain castle, and the part of the castle pertaining to him, with the other party, with the consent of one of his co-partners. That co-partner, who did not consent, and to whose injury and damage the said exchange was made, says that the said exchange is not valid, because the other party could not acquire any part in indivision in the said castle to his prejudice.

† It is asked whether in the said Castle, for the undivided share, or other places, he could have acquired. And it is to be said briefly, that by the said pact he could not prevent the acquisition of ownership, because no one can agree that it shall not be lawful for him to acquire, nor does a pact not to alienate hold, unless there is an interest of the party making the agreement. And then the alienation is valid, but an action for damages is brought, as in C. de cond. ob causam, l. ea lege; and ff. de verb. oblig., l. si ita quis, § ea; l. and ff. de pactis, l. nemo; and C. de pactis inter emptorem, l. si; and ff. de verb. oblig., l. qui Romae, § cohæredes; and note in l. si, ff. de cond. ob causam. For there may be an interest, perhaps because he who acquired is a quarrelsome man, so that it is in his interest not to have communion with him, or he is an injurious man, with whom one must come to quarrels all day, for it is expedient not to have such partners, as ff. de serv. urb. prœd., l. in re communi; C. quando et quibus quarta pars debetur, l. 2. For communion in undivided shares usually excites discord, as ff. de legat. 2, l. cum pater, § dulcissimis; and § libertus. And because no one is forced against his will into communion, as ff. de cond. indebit., l. eleganter, § si centum, this interest shall be estimated in this manner, namely, how much it would be in the interest of nobles of the same condition not to have such a partner in communion, as ff. pro socio, l. si convenerit; and l. idem est; and C. de sententiis quæ pro eo, l. unica, § In aliis. Indeed, certainly there are some whom it is not expedient to have as neighboring co-owners: for on account of them property is worth less, and is bought and sold for less, as ff. de contrah. empt., l. quid tamen. And the alienation is valid, but damages are due, for which interest the thing itself is obligated. For in an obligation all present and future things are included, as C. quæ res pignori oblig. poss., l. si. Likewise, for a pact and price we have seen a thing be obligated, or as if obligated, as ff. de act. empt., l. Iulianus, § offerri. And this I say regarding this specific point. Therefore, others who did not alienate nor agree may sue for damages, as ff. de legat. 2, l. cum pater, § libertis. But if all had contravened, no one could sue, as C. de fideicom., l. quotiens.

† It may now be doubted who incurs the penalty, whether the acquirer? And there is no doubt about this, because the words speak for themselves. Or does the transferor also incur it, or that both incur it, because when someone is prohibited from buying, it seems that the seller is also prohibited from selling, as in l. 1, C. de cupressis ex loco damnensi, lib. 11. It is safer to hold that only the acceptor incurs it, because the words of the prohibition are directed against him, as in C. ne fideiussores dotium dentur, l. 2. Secondly, it is proposed that among those who could sell and alienate to one another reciprocally, a certain other division was made with a pact that no party could alienate unless with the consent of the other two parties: and if this were contravened, that from now on, as well as from then, the said alienation or contract should be null and of no value, and regarded as not done and not made, and that the part thus alienated should be applied to and belong by operation of law to the other aforementioned lords, provided that if any of the said parties, when in possession, wished to sell his rights to another party, he could do so and is bound to do so at the same price: and a penalty of five thousand florins was attached if anyone should contravene this.

† Here, it is first asked whether a contract can be annulled by a pact. And it must be said that it cannot, unless one has retained possession for himself, or has transferred ownership on the condition that it not be alienated, that is, until it is not alienated. For then, upon the alienation having been made in fact, the thing falls into the forfeiture according to the form of the pact, as is elegantly read and noted in the Digest, *De acquisitione possessionis*, law *Qui absenti*, section *Si quis*. In this contract, however, there appears no retention of possession, nor does it appear that any condition was attached to the ownership. And since it is a special feature of the pact of the *lex commissoria* and of the addition of a day that the ownership is resolved by operation of law itself, it follows that the rule is different in other contracts, because without delivery ownership is not transferred, as is subtly read and noted in law 1, in the great gloss, in the Digest, *De donationibus*. Furthermore, there is no doubt regarding the penalty, that it can be claimed and is incurred, even if there were no damage: because if one goes against the words and the intent of the contract, and expressly, not tacitly, one goes against it, as in the Digest, *De arbitris*, law *Adversus*; and *De verbis obligationibus*, law 2, section *Si*; and law *Stipulatio ista*, section *Alteri*.

† The second case is this: there were three persons, a, b, and c, who could sell among themselves. It happens that a sold to b, and likewise c sold to b. Now, this b, although permitted to sell to a and c, sold to d, a prohibited person. The question is whether a and c can claim the penalty from b. For since a and c retained no right, by their act the interest ceases; therefore, the stipulation of the penalty is not incurred, because the rule is that when, by the creditor’s own act, the interest ceases, he must impute it to himself, as in D. de cond. furt. l. siue manifestus, §. tandiu. But if b had sold a part to a and a part to c, he would not have incurred the penalty; however, by selling his part to a prohibited person, he incurs the penalty. This is posited almost literally in D. de leg. 3, l. pater, §. quindecim libertis.

† The third point is that he suffered, because the one who exchanged was compelled to exchange, and he was so closely guarded by those lacking arms, that he could not do otherwise without danger to his life. Now the question arises, what is the law? I answer, it is not valid in effect, because he made the exchange unwillingly, as in C. de transact. l. interpositas, and l. si quis maior, by contrary reasoning. And it is fully read and noted in ff. quod metus causa, l. qui in carcerem, and ff. de testam. l. qui a latronibus. Nor does he incur a penalty, as in l. nouissime, ff. quod falso tutoris auctore. Nor is repentance necessary where violence intervenes, provided that he did not later confirm the contract of his own free will, as in ff. de cond. ob turpem causam, l. si ob turpem, and there note, and l. 2, C. quod metus causa, sed si impressione, and l. 1, C. si quacunque praedicta potestate. But if the exchange and delivery, or quasi-delivery, were made voluntarily, or if a stipulation had intervened, repentance would not be available, as in C. de rerum permutatione, l. ex placito. For if delivery, or quasi-delivery, intervenes, ownership has been transferred, and repentance is not available if the other party has observed the contract; but if he does not wish to observe the contract, then it returns.

† either the exchange was made by a bare act, and there would be room for repentance due to the cause not having ensued: because exchange is an innominate contract; or a stipulation intervened on both sides, and there is no room for repentance, and in innominate contracts there is no room for repentance, as is read subtly and noted in l. vlti. ff. de condi. ob causam. and l. si pecunia. eo. titu. in prin. and C. de act. et obli. l. sicut. and ff. de pac. 7. l. iurisgentium. §. 1.

† But that the stipulation is a named contract appears from this rule, because it gives rise to an action without any intervention of a thing. But unnamed contracts do not give rise to an action unless there is an intervention of a thing, where the intervention of a thing is placed as the final cause, as C. de rerum permutatione, l. ex placito. As the text sets forth this doctrine. One

It must be known that, in innominate contracts, if an oath intervenes, repentance has no place, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si quis maior. And this is the small gloss on this in the said l. si pecuniam.

The fourth case concerns this nobleman, who had exchanged a feudal castle without the lord’s permission. Fearing that he might thereby lose his right, he had himself invested anew by the feudal lord. The question now arises: what is the law? I answer: if he had not delivered [the property], there is no doubt, because unless the vassal delivers [it] by mere sale or verbal exchange, he does not lose the fief, as stated in D. de verborum significatione, l. alienationis verbum, and there by Dyonisius. But if he had delivered it, then distinguish: either the lord invested him anew with full knowledge and intent, in which case the investiture is valid; or he did so by mistake, in which case it is not valid, as stated in D. de conditione ob causam, l. 2, § subtilius, and in C. de donationibus, l. nec ignorans.

† The fifth point concerns the case where the one who exchanged, and declared that he held possession on behalf of the person with whom he exchanged, did not state that he held it by precarium, but simply that he held it; whether he can afterwards sell it to another. And it must be said that he cannot, because by these words he transferred all his right, and civil possession, and perhaps even natural possession.
† because it is more to say, I possess for you, than I possess by precarium. D. de aqua pluviae arcendae, l. quod meo. and it is the sole gloss. D. 12 de pace, l. ab emptore.

† Sextus suffered. They came to a certain Magnificent and Illustrious Lord Christopher, and his brother, fearing for their other co-heirs. And from that Magnificent Lord they obtained certain agreements, and from him they received investitures of their castles as fiefs in the name of the city of Asti, which Magnificent Lord gave the said city with all its rights in dowry to his Illustrious daughter. It happened afterwards that, because the said Lord Christopher was attacked by his co-heirs, he by force seized two of their castles, concerning which an investiture is sought based on the agreements made with the said Magnificent Lord. The question is whether an investiture can be made for the said castles seized by force. I answer that things usurped by violence cannot be invested, as stated in Codex, "Unde vi," law "Authoritate," unless that usurpation was permitted by law and carried out by the authority of a superior, as in law 1, § "Si," Digest, "De militibus vassallis qui contumaces," and whatever is observed against one is observed against another, as in Codex, "Rescinden," law 13, "Ratas."

† It is asked concerning one person whether he is excused by the law *Si quis in tantam* because of a sentence given to him by his superior lord, and it must be said that if that sentence was duly given, with knowledge of the case, and in a case of truth, because otherwise he could not have provided for himself except by armed force, it ceases, as in § *Si*, C. 1, *De militibus vassallis qui contumaciter*. Otherwise the license is not valid, as in D. *De regulis iuris*, l. *Non ex singulis*, and he incurs the penalty, l. *Meminerint*, C. 14, *Unde vi*.

† Finally, it is asked: certain nobles are litigating among themselves concerning various castles by way of claim and counterclaim before the Lord Governor of Asten. This Lord Governor ordered each party to deposit the castle it held as a sequestration, so that there would be no subsequent impediment to the execution of the judgment. Neither party appealed from this order; rather, one party deposited [the castle], while the other did not. Should that party which did not deposit be heard if it requests that the case proceed? And it must be said that it should not, for three reasons. First, because the contumacious party is repelled from the threshold of the court, as stated in C. de iudiciis, l. sancimus. Second, because equality must be observed between litigants, as stated in C. de fructibus et litis expensis, l. finalis, and C. de proximis sacris scripturis, l. in sacris. Third, because in a case of claim and counterclaim, what one party does in due order, the other must immediately do likewise, and one should not be compelled to do what the other is not compelled to do, as is read and noted in ff. de iudiciis, l. qui prior appellat. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether a pact by which a superior cannot render justice to his subjects is valid.
2. Due to the defect of justice of the superior, a higher authority is approached.
3. Whether marquises can make war among themselves without the license of their lord.
4. Whether a lord can command his subjects to obey him in exercises and cavalry maneuvers.
5. If two marquises are at war, whether either can order his subjects to go to the land of his adversary, so that the cause of suspicion and provocation may be removed.
6. Whether subjects can send others in their place.
body: In the name of Christ. Magnificent lord. Nannus sold certain castles, villages, and men to the city of Asten for the price of 100,000 pounds, and then by another instrument received from the said city of Asten the said castles, villages, men, and jurisdictions in fief, and solemnly promised fidelity; and among other things there was added one pact, that if any person wished to bring an action against the said lord Nannus or his descendants, the said lord Nannus or his successors could not, nor ought, in any way be compelled or constrained by force to office, nor by any captain or rector of the aforementioned city of Asten, and that he is not bound to stand to the law or answer according to law in the city of Asten in any civil or criminal case. It happens that certain Marquises, successors of the aforementioned lord Nannus, commit many offenses against justice against the persons and goods of the men of the said castles and villages, from which they wish to have recourse to the governor of Asten. The said Marquises say that they cannot do this because of the said pact.

† Now the question arises as to what is the law. And it appears that the said pact should be observed. First, by the general rule, because the praetor says, “I will uphold pacts”: and because it is a serious matter to break faith. Second, because a pact has the force of law, as in C. de donationibus inter virum et uxorem, l. penultima, and ff. de publicanis, l. Caesar. Therefore, regarding offenses committed elsewhere than in the territory of Asti, one cannot be sued in the city of Asti. Moreover, jurisdiction can be extended by privilege, as in extra de iudicibus, cap. Novit, and as in cap. Primo, de privilegiis, libro 6. And also because a pact, as noted in ff. de iudicibus, l. Haeres absens, §. Primo. Furthermore, this pact was appended to the transfer of the thing; therefore, it must be observed, as in ff. de pactis, l. In traditionibus.

To the contrary is the truth, and it is proved by this reasoning: namely, the universality of the said castles and villages, and the inhabitants thereof, before the said enfeoffment, were subjects of the city of Asti by virtue of the said sale; and from this, just as the city of Asti was their lord, so conversely it was bound to administer justice to them and to render their rights, because these are correlative, as argued in cap. I, extra de foro competenti, where it is said that the lord must render justice to his subject and preserve the rights of the subject, otherwise he deserves to lose the name of lord. Moreover, jurisdiction is a power introduced for the public good, with the necessity of exercising jurisdiction and establishing equity, as noted in ff. de iurisdictione omnium iudicum, l. 1. And having premised this, I argue demonstratively as follows: the subjects had recourse to the magistrate of Asti, and they did not lose this recourse by that pact, as I will prove; therefore, they retain it, because jurisdiction and lordship are equated, as in ff. de statu hominum, l. Qui furem. Moreover, he who has jurisdiction cannot refuse to hear due complaints, as in the aforementioned cap. Novit.

The objection based on the said pact does not hold, because the subjects did not consent to the said pact, to whom the right to invoke the jurisdiction of Asti had accrued; hence, such a pact rightly does not harm them, as in ff. de pactis, l. Si, and ff. de contractibus, l. Si post mortem, Prima Pars Consiliorum, §. Ultimo. Moreover, when a feudatory burdens his subjects, it is certain that recourse must be had to the superior magistrate, and all the more so if he commits offenses against them, as in ff. de his qui sui vel alieni iuris sunt, l. 2, and as noted in extra de iudicibus, cap. Caeterum. Otherwise it would follow that justice would perish, because where there is no magistrate, justice is dead, as in ff. de origine iuris, l. 2, §. Post originem iuris.

Furthermore, a pact that a superior cannot render justice to his subjects is invalid, because it is contrary to public law, and contrary to the force and authority of the laws, as in ff. de pactis, l. Ius publicum, and l. Iuris gentium, §. Ait praetor, and §. Si paciscatur; just as a pact not to punish crimes is invalid, as in ff. de fideiussoribus, l. Si a reo. Moreover, whatever is not transferred to another remains with the transferor, as in ff. quibus ex causis maiores, l. Nec utilem. But the power to administer justice in one’s own cause could not be transferred to the said marquises, as in l. 1, C. ne quis in propria causa; therefore, it remained with Asti. Moreover, an unjust condition should not be imposed on one person by another, when he himself has not consented, as in ff. de pactis, l. Si unus, §. Ante omnia, and C. de legatis, l. Si cum heres, and ff. de iuris et facti ignorantia, l. Iniquissimum.

† Moreover, all laws proclaim that, due to the defect of justice in the superior, greater power is added; this is expressly stated in the number in l. prima, §. ultimo, de milite vassallo, qui contumax est. Therefore, subjects who are burdened by their immediate superior may appeal to the mediate superior, proceeding step by step according to civil law; although sometimes canon law permits otherwise, as noted in Speculum de appellatione, §. restat, in principio. And from this three conclusions are drawn: if the said Marquises are debtors to their subjects and wish to pay, or if they commit offenses against them, even within the Marquisate itself and not in the possession of Asten, they can nevertheless be sued in the city of Asten before their governor. However, let the subjects beware of fabricating cases where there are no causes against their lords; for on this account they should be punished more severely than others who are not subjects, both by blows of rods and by other arbitrary penalties as enemies and rebels of their lords, as C. de his, qui ad ecclesiam confugiunt, l. si servus, and argumentum in Auth. de quaestore, §. super hoc. And also the Marquises themselves could correct them at home and in court, as ff. ad Sillam, l. et si percussor, §. finalis, and ff. de furtis, l. servi, et filii, in principio, and C. de patria potestate, l. congruentius, and C. de his, qui ad statuas confugiunt, 3.

Secondly, it is asked whether the said Marquises may make war among themselves without the license of the Lord of Asti or his governor. And it must be said that they cannot, for three reasons. The first is that the use of arms must be granted by the prince, and not by another, as is stated in the Code, in the title "On the Use of Arms Without the Knowledge of the Prince," law 1, book 11. The second is that wars are contrary to natural law, unless the necessity of defense is imminent, as is stated in the Digest, in the title "On Justice and Law," in the law "So that force." Therefore, by the force of all judgments and the protection of public law, it is established in the middle that it is not permitted for anyone to take vengeance upon himself, as is stated in the Code, in the title "On Judges," in the law "No one." The law calls such persons robbers, as is stated in the Digest, in the title "On Wills," in the law "Who by robbers." And this is noted by the Moderators in the chapter "Olim," in the title "On Restitution of Spoliation," and in the chapter "Sicut," in the title "On Oaths." The third reason is most manifest, because wars destroy territories, which belong to the lord of the fief with respect to the direct lord: but vassals cannot do this, because it would be to the prejudice of the lord; indeed, on this account they could be deprived of the fief, just as an emphyteuta could be deprived of the emphyteusis when he evidently makes the thing worse, as is stated in the Code, in the title "On Sacred Churches," in the authority "Who the things already said."

Thirdly, it is asked whether the aforementioned Marquises may command their subjects to obey them in military campaigns and cavalry expeditions. And it must be said that they may not, when the war or cavalry expedition is unjust, and this is established, as in the chapter *Domino guerram*, in the title *Hic finit lex*. Then the customs of the kingdom begin, for a subject ought not to be obedient to his lord in wrongful acts, as in the Digest, *De actionibus et obligationibus*, law *Servus non in omnibus*. But if the war were lawful, the subjects would be bound to assist their lords both with their persons and with their property in case of necessity, this being reserved, that they may serve through an equal substitute, as noted in the Code, *De episcopis et clericis*, law *Quisquis*, especially where there is danger to life. And finally, I say that in this matter the custom must be observed, and that going on campaign is a public duty, and necessary, justice permitting, just as *angaria* and *perangaria*. Fourthly, it is asked,

† If two Marquises are at war, whether either may command his subjects not to enter the territory of his adversary, so that the occasion for suspicion and treason may be removed. For this ought not to be done, because one who has been constituted by the emperor is warned to avoid familiarity with the enemies of his lord, as is read and noted in l. 1, § cum patronus, ff. de officiis praefecti urbis, and in the 10th collection, concerning which witnesses are necessary to prove the cause of ingratitude, l. 1, and noted in the title quibus modis feudum amittitur, in the beginning, and C. de inofficiosis testamentis, l. liberi. The law sciendum, § 1, ff. de legatis, supports this. Without cause, however, they cannot prohibit it: for although they are subjects, they are freeborn, and even to freedmen places and commerce cannot be forbidden, as in ff. de operis libertorum, l. libertus negotiatoris. From the foregoing it appears that the said Marquises, when they have a lawful war and are in need of the constant counsel of their subjects, can compel them to go with them personally and precisely.

But if they do not require their counsel or personal presence, the said subjects may send others acceptable to the lord on their behalf, as is argued in ff. de duobus reis, l. nemo est, qui nesciat; and in ff. de operis libertorum, l. si libertus artem; and l. quod nisi, §. ex prouincia; and l. operę in rerum, §. fabriles. Although it is contained in the usages of fiefs that principal persons must fight in person, as is read and noted in c. si miles rusticum, extra, de pace tenenda, et eius violatoribus, there the matter speaks of when combat takes place as a means of proof, so that judgment may be rendered in favor of the victor; and it speaks of another case: for there the principal persons must also swear, whence that matter is very different from the present one. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether one who has not been promoted to orders, without prior admonition, is to be deprived of his prebend.
body: A certain person, in the name of Christ, held a certain prebend for seven years without any dispensation, nor was he promoted to holy orders, nor yet was he admonished by the diocesan or by any other superior that he ought to be promoted by them. It is asked whether he is deprived ipso iure, or at least ought to be deprived.

† This question depends on the understanding of the chapter Statutum, De electione, Book 6, and on the understanding of c. Cum ex, from the same title, and in the chapter Cum in cunctis, De electione, §. Inferiore, in the old decretal. And it seems to be said that, since the man [is concerned], for in a collegiate church the penalty mentioned in the said chapter Cum in cunctis does not apply unless a warning is interposed, as is fully noted in the said chapter Cum ex. And so it seems to me, saving a better opinion. I, Bal. de Peru.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. Given the statute in question, whether those having express hypothecs are preferred to subsequent creditors similarly having express hypothecs, as being prior in time.
3. A species placed after a genus serves to restrict the genus of predication.
4. In a hypothecary action, a real action is brought, just as in the actions of rei vendicatio and rei publicatio.
5. One bound by a real obligation is not properly a debtor.
5. No provision of the laws appears to abolish an express hypothec.
body: In the name of Christ. Statute of the city of Cuneo, which follows. Furthermore, they have decreed that whatever is found and can be obtained from the goods of any fugitive, or which he held and possessed at the time of his flight, or within six months prior, shall be divided equally among all creditors, whether they are creditors or appear to be so by public instrument or condemnation: as regards the goods of fugitives, there shall be no cause or privilege of time among such creditors. And this statute shall apply solely among public and customary merchants exercising trade, and not to other merchants who are not public and customary merchants exercising trade.

The question now arises whether those who have hypothecs expressly granted to subsequent creditors are preferred over those who likewise have hypothecs expressly granted, as being prior in time; or whether, by virtue of the said statute, all are equal. Here it must be considered that there are two kinds of preference: one is impersonal, the other personal, and the latter does not arise except from a cause or a privilege. For from a cause, the cause of deposit is preferred, as in *l. si ventri*, § *in bonis*, D. de privilegiis creditorum. Likewise, the cause of dowry, as in C. qui potiora in pignoribus habent, *l. assiduis*. From a privilege, however, preference is introduced when the person makes room for the privilege, which is the same as the deprivation of common law. And preference introduced against common law is fully read and noted in *l. 1*, C. de privilegiis dotium, and in *l. 1*, D. soluto matrimonio, and in *l. privilegium*, D. de privilegiis creditorum, and in the chapter *privilegium personale*, Extravagantes, de regulis iuris, book 6. Secondly, it must be considered that the said statute, removing the privilege, reduces all creditors to equality. Now it must be considered what this saying means: for by law it is provided that, removing the privilege, those with privileges are reduced to common law, as in D. de excusationibus tutorum, *l. sed et milites*, in principio; and another law provides that a privilege is more easily removed than common law, as in D. de testamento militis, *l. eius militis*, § *militia*. Also, another law says that the right of a noble, which is by our own act, is stronger than by another’s provision, as in D. de fideicommissis liberis, *l. si filius*, § *erit rubriano*. Also, this is what is said, that the law does not deny you its own aid, but yours, as fully noted in C. qui potiora in pignoribus habent, *l. assiduis*, § *exceptis*. But neither must one thing be omitted, that those words, “as to the goods of fugitives among creditors,” do not restrict the principle of the law as if they had the privilege of time.

† because the species, when placed absolutely after the genus, has the effect of restricting the genus of predication. This is the notable text in the Digest, *De verbis significandis*, in the law *Si cum fundum*. From which it follows that the statute, by the force of its wording, removes nothing other than the privilege of the cause or of the person. But especially, an express hypothec is not a privilege of the cause or of the person, as appears expressly in the Digest, *De pactis*, in the law *Rescriptum* and in the same law, and is noted in the final law of the Code, *Qui bonis cedere possunt*. Wherefore, this statute does not remove the express hypothec, nor its prerogative. Moreover, even if the intent of this statute is doubtful, in case of doubt it ought to be interpreted according to the common law, so that no injury be done to another; because in a state of doubt it is not understood to absorb the right of another, as in the Extravagant, *De consuetudinibus*, in the chapter *Cum dilectus*, and in the Code, *De noxali actione*, in the law *Si servi vestri*. Wherefore, it must be said thus: in personal actions, all are equal. But in hypothecary actions, when goods are expressly pledged, he is preferred in law who is prior in time. And that this is in accordance with the intent of the statute, and not contrary to the intent of the statute, I prove thus:

† because in a hypothecary action a real action, namely the hypothecary one, is brought forth, as stated in D. de pignoribus, l. si fundus, § in venditione, which does not consist in an obligation, but in a real right, as C. de solutione pignorum, l. intelligere, and D. de exceptione rei iudicatae, extante, § Latinus, and as noted in D. ad Trebellianum, l. si haeres pecuniam; although the glossa says that the hypothecary action has something of a personal character, as noted in D. de pactis, l. si tibi, § de pignore, and D. ad Trebellianum, l. debitor, nevertheless the truth is that it is purely in rem, just like the rei vindicatio and the publiciana, when it is brought against any extraneous possessor who in no way is bound, as stated in the aforementioned § in venditione, and as Inst. de actionibus, § item Serviana. Therefore, the plaintiff in a hypothecary action does not come forward as a creditor of the possessor, as D. ad exhibendum, l. tigni, § finalis, and thus the statute mentioned does not seem to speak of an express hypothec, since a creditor is spoken of in relation to a debtor.

But the debtor in a real action is not properly a debtor, as stated in the Institutes, De actionibus, § Omnium, and noted by the doctors in L. 1, ff. Si certum petatur. Therefore, so that we may not correct the common law in doubt, and so that we may adhere to the literal meaning of the words, and so that we may avoid absurdity, and so that we may bring the statute into line with the common law, and so that the species may operate after the genus, it must be concluded that in an express hypothecation, he who is prior in time is stronger in right, as in the aforementioned rule of law, Qui prior est tempore potior est iure. But against this stand two words of the statute. First, because it says “held” and “possessed,” which seem to refer passively to hypothecation. Also, that word “by public deed”: because in public deeds a hypothecation is always added. But these two reasons do not conclude with necessity, because the contrary may be true, and it does not follow that, because he is a debtor by instrument, therefore a hypothecation intervened; for a hypothecation is an addition, which is not presumed to be constituted unless it is proved, even though a public instrument has been made for a personal debt. Therefore, according to the subtlety of the law, and also according to equity, it must be held, as I said above, as in C. De iure deliberandi, L. Si, § Et si praefatam, very strongly. For it would be absurd that prejudice should be brought about by the debtor to the creditor, who had provided diligently for himself,
† Therefore, no provision of the law appears to abolish an express hypothec. The text is noted in the aforementioned law, *Rescripto*. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether an assignment of a thing made by a father to his son, and confirmed at the time of death, passes to the son by right of prelegacy.
2. It suffices for the son to prove that the father was the owner, so that he may have a public action or an action for the recovery of property.
3. What is required in a public action for the recovery of property and in the action on a stipulation.
4. How ownership is proved, and whether ownership is presumed from possession. And number 5.
6. If witnesses state that the father and the son possessed the property, whether they prove half of the case, or how they do so.
body: A certain Lord Brasian, in the name of Christ, namely Bartolomeo and John, to whom he assigned certain goods during his lifetime, an assignment which he later confirmed by will. After the said Lord Brasian died, the aforementioned John had sons, namely Lord Aloisius and Antoniolus. Then, after the said Lord John died, the said Lord Aloisius and Antoniolus sold a certain piece of land to a certain Bernard for a certain price, with the agreement that the said Bernard was bound and ought to pay certain debts to certain creditors of the said vendors, debts for which the said Lord John had formerly been obligated together with certain others to a certain Sempronius, with the agreement and promise that the said buyer would cause the rights of the said credit to be assigned to the said brothers by the said creditor. And in the case that the aforementioned conditions were not observed, it was agreed that the said sale would be null and void, as if it had not been made; for otherwise they would not have made the said sale. Then the said buyer did not fulfill the aforementioned agreements, but rather had the rights assigned to himself and his heirs. Afterwards, the aforementioned Lord Antoniolus died, and the said Lord Aloisius succeeded him. This Lord Aloisius, considering that the said Lord Bernard, the first buyer, had not observed the agreed terms of the sale, brought an action for the recovery of the thing sold against the said Sempronius, the second buyer, and proved that the said property had remained in the goods of the said Lord Brasian, and had been held and possessed by him, or by another in his name, for many years; and that it had likewise been held and possessed by the aforementioned Lord John, father of the said Lord Aloisius, during the lifetime of the said Lord Brasian, and successively until the time of the death of the said Lord John. Now the question is, what is the law? And for clarity, it must be premised that

† that the said assignment, during the lifetime of the said Lord Brasian, was valid by the law of peculium, namely, because it was confirmed in the will, and passed into the force and nature of a prelegacy, as is fully read and noted in C. de familia erciscunda, l. filium, quem habentem, with its subject matter.

Secondly, it must be premised that what is in the father’s assets, whether as owner or quasi-owner, passes to the son and successor: and it suffices for the son to prove that the father was owner or quasi-owner, so that he may have a vindication of the thing, or a Publician action, as is clear, e.g., C. de proba. l. siue possidetis. For here there is no question of an action for the recovery of an inheritance, because such an action would not lie against a possessor who is entirely an outsider and holds a single item by a singular title, as is fully read and noted in l. cogi. C. de peti. haeredi. and in l. haereditatem. C. quibus non obijcitur longi temporis praescriptio. and ff. de peti. haeredi. l. nec vllam. with its subject matter.

Thirdly, it must be premised and investigated whether the pact appended to the said sale is a pact of the *lex commissoria* or not. And it appears that it is not a pact of the *lex commissoria* for two reasons. First, because the *lex commissoria* applies when the price is not paid, but here it was not stated that if the price is not paid to the seller, but to a certain other person, as in D. 50.16.105 (*Liber homo*), § *fin*. Moreover, in the *lex commissoria* a certain day is usually appointed for payment, as in D. 20.1.1 (*Post diem*), almost throughout. But here no certain or uncertain day was appointed; therefore, it is not properly a pact of the *lex commissoria*. Then I argue: if it is not properly a pact of the *lex commissoria*, therefore dominion does not pass by operation of law, and thus the *rei vindicatio* is not available, as is subtly read and noted in D. 39.5.1 (*Donationes*), in the great gloss; and D. 2.14.1 (*Ab emptione*); and C. 4.27.1 (*Ea lege*).

To the contrary it seems, because any pact appended for the seller and in his favor in the very contract of sale is said to be part of the price, as in D. 18.1.1 (*Fundi partem*). Therefore, if a pact is appended that the thing shall be ineffectual, the *lex commissoria* is exercised if the pact is not observed, and by operation of law the thing is ineffectual, and thus the *rei vindicatio* or the *actio Publiciana* is available. And although the new second buyer has a title, such title does not avail him on account of the bad faith of the sale, as in C. 7.33.1 (*Authentica Malaefidei*). Nor does it obstruct if it is said that in the *lex commissoria* the appointment of a day is required, because rather I say that a tacit day suffices, which operates the same as an express one, according to the noted rule in D. 2.14.1 (*Item quia*).

Wherefore I conclude that the said pact was a pact of the *lex commissoria*, and that if it is not observed, the land can be vindicated. Nor do I think that the first buyer can raise the question of ownership, unless he proves that he bought his own thing; for then the contract would be null, and the question of ownership could be raised. But if this is not objected, proof of ownership cannot be demanded from the plaintiff, according to the noted authorities in D. 47.2.1 (*Ita ut si furtum*); D. 9.5.1 (*Indebiti*), § *fin*; D. 39.5.1 (*Si alienam*); and D. 39.5.1 (*Qui alienum*). Because the question of ownership can be raised against the one claiming, but not against the one seeking restitution, as in C. 4.10.1 (*Non unde originem*). The second buyer has no more right than the first, to whom he succeeded with his cause and his defects, as in D. 41.2.1 (*Pomponius*), § *Cum quis*; and the said *Authentica Malaefidei*.

† Moreover, even if it were necessary to prove ownership, or quasi-ownership (which quasi-ownership pertains to the Publician action), it would have to be considered whether the witnesses testifying about property provide no reason for their testimony; and in that case they do not prove it, or whether they provide a reason; and in that case one must examine by what means they provide a reason: whether by possession alone, or by the consequence of titles with possession added. In the first case, they do not prove ownership, nor quasi-ownership, because possession has nothing in common with property, or quasi-property. This rule fails wherever the law presumes ownership from possession, as is fully read and noted in C. de prob. l. cum res. Furthermore

† By legitimate consequence of titles and continuous possession, ownership, or quasi-ownership, is well proven, as noted in the last paragraph of the Code, *Communi diviso*, and in the last paragraph of the Digest, *De conditione instituta*. Let the acts speak in this matter. However, the aforementioned Bartolus states one singular point in this matter: when ancient possession is proven, and it does not appear that another possessed before, that possessor is presumed to have been the owner, and consequently, those who descend from him. For from possession, which was previously in no one’s goods, ownership of things began according to the law of nations, as in the Digest, *De acquirenda possessione*, law 1, in the principle, and law *Rem, quae nobis*, and there by Bartolus and by Nicholas de Tudeschis in the aforementioned law *Cum res*. This opinion resolves many ambiguities and difficulties of proof regarding ownership. From these things, therefore, which have been premised, it appears that by reason of the commissor clause, the thing reverted by operation of law to the ownership of the plaintiff, into whom the entire right of both brothers flowed. But here it must be observed whether the possession was of those assigned to the said Lord John, or not. For if it was of those assigned, what I have said is clear; but if it was not of those assigned, the proof of ownership does not conclude except for one-half part, because the said Lord Brasianus, who is alleged to have been the owner, had two sons and heirs; therefore, ownership would not have devolved upon the said Lord

† John, unless for half of the thing sold, as in D. de acquirenda hereditate, l. Duo fratres. And therefore it must be examined whether it appears from the records that the said Lord Brasianus had two heirs or not; because if the plaintiff framed an article concerning two heirs, he would necessarily infer against himself as the claimant, and could not claim more than half, unless there appeared an assignment of the thing. And although one may sell another’s property and attach the pact of the lex commissoria, nevertheless he could not vindicate the thing if it were established that the thing belonged to another; but he ought perhaps to bring an actio triticaria or an actio de indebito for the possession itself. But this last point I do not determine, because it is not expedient, but I leave subtleties of law to speculators. Finally, it must be known that if witnesses say that the father and the son possessed, it is not understood that each possessed half, but we understand that the father had possession which is a matter of law, and the son had a certain right to go and act. D. de liberis et posthumis, l. In suis. And in that law it is noted, D. qui ex causis maiores, l. Cum Midam instrumenta. And what is noted in l. 2, C. qui aetate, and D. de dolo, l. Cum quis, and l. Cum scimus, C. de agricolis et censitis, l. 11, and D. de acquisitione possessionis, l. Qui iure familiaritatis. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. In what ways, and by what agreements and unusual clauses, a contract is presumed to be fictitious, simulated, and usurious: and especially from the smallness of the price.
body: It appears that, in the name of Christ, the case is as follows: I sold a fund to Titius for ten, and Titius promised to resell it to me for the same amount, the fund being retained for three years, on the condition that this promise would not endure beyond the subsequent two years, and no longer. It is alleged that the thing was worth double, or thereabouts. Now I say that the contract was a *pignus* (pawn) and in fraud of usury. I prove the greater value by witnesses through an instrument; however, I do not prove that Titius was accustomed to lending at interest.

It is asked whether this contract ought to be judged as usurious? And it seems that it should not, because in case of doubt it is better to adhere to the words of the contract, as in D. de fideiussoribus, l. fideiussores magistratuum. For the instrument is presumed true, and not false, as in C. de probationibus, l. precibus. Moreover, the decretal seems to require that it be proven that such a buyer was accustomed to practicing usury, as in X. de emptione et venditione, cap. ad nostram. This view is held by Jacobus de Aretino and by Cynus, C. de probationibus, l. prima.
