On the contrary, it seems that it should be judged usurious, because the stipulations placed in a contract determine its nature and quality, as in D. de donatione causa mortis, l. ubi ita and l. finalis; and D. de conditione ob causam. But the stipulations appended here have greater similarity with a pledge contract than with a contract of true sale; therefore, by argument from signs, this contract ought to be considered usurious. For the stipulation regarding the receipt of fruits for three years, before being obliged to resell, is nothing other than a certain usury while the principal is preserved. Moreover, the stipulation that he may not sell unless after two years is nothing other than a stipulation of a pactum commissorium in pledges; therefore, on account of stipulations which do not plausibly occur in a true sale, we must judge the contract fraudulent, as is read and noted in l. 6, D. de conditionibus institutis.

Furthermore, the smallness of the price is an argument of fraud, as in C. mandati, l. per diversas; and especially if the instrument states that, if it is worth more, it is given by the same title, as in l. ab Anastasio. And note, according to Guillelmus, D. de pactis, l. si tibi, in principio: for the more caution is added in suspicious contracts, the more fraud and deceit are presumed.

Moreover, consider here that a contract is presumed usurious which is not commonly in use among good and reputable persons, and which usurers are accustomed to make. Hence, proving the custom of usurers in general has the same effect in proving a usurious contract as if it were specifically proven regarding that person with whom one contracts, as in D. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. finalis. This is proven by the words of cap. ad nostram, in the word "presertim" (especially). And Innocentius holds this there, and in cap. illo vos, X. de pignoribus. And this is the very truth, because the said stipulations and the said price are not consistent with the reality of a true sale, nor can it fall within the understanding of a just judge that this contract, so bifurcated, is clean from the leprosy of the sin of usury. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
2. A statute requiring consent or the presence of someone in a contract is understood to apply, if the presence of that person can be obtained, and not otherwise.
3. How someone is said to be absent.
3. Whether a woman, because she believes her husband dead due to his long absence, can take another husband without the crime of adultery.
4. Whether prescription applies, if she has received unpaid for her dowry from the goods of her absent husband, whom she believed dead: and whether this prescription is said to be between present parties, or between absent parties. And in number 5.
body: A certain Hector follows the question, in the name of Christ.

† The statute of Pavia provides that a wife may not contract without the presence and consent of her husband. The husband has absent himself, and it is unknown where he is. The question is whether she may contract. I answer that if the husband has been absent for a long time and it is unknown where he is, she may contract, because by thus absenting himself, the husband makes himself alien to presence, as in D. de fideicommissis libertatibus, l. si alieno, § 1. Moreover, this is so in order to avoid absurdity. For the statute must be understood as referring to a husband whose presence can be obtained; that is, one in the same dwelling or in a place where he can be required to exhibit his presence. Furthermore, this statute was made in favor of women; therefore, it ought not to be turned to their detriment, as in l. 2, D. de lege commissaria, and C. de legibus, l. quod favore. For it would be absurd if, when utility or necessity is at hand, the woman could not contract these goods. We have a similar rule in another matter, as appears in D. si certum petatur, l. cum filius; C. de annali exceptione, l. vt perfectius; C. de sententiis passis, l. fina; D. de iure dotium, l. profectitia, in principio; D. de iudiciis, l. si longius; C. de episcopali audientia, l. tam dementis. But if the husband were in a nearby place, his presence should be awaited, as in cap. sciendum, in fine, de consuetudine recti feudi.

Secondly, it is asked: this husband remained absent for a long time and was considered dead; the wife recovered her dowry, or someone having a claim from her did so, and a sentence was rendered; whether it is valid. I answer: yes, because it was sufficient that the dowry be restored in the case, since the husband did not bear the burdens of marriage, as in C. de iure dotium, l. ubi adhuc.

Thirdly, it is asked, because this woman, led by just error, married another, and before the woman assumed the guardianship of the common child, it is certain that the marriage is not valid; however, she is excused from the crime, as in the Digest, On Adulteries, law *miles*, section *penultimo*. And the same must be said regarding guardianship, because since the son was under the power of his father, he could not have a guardian, nor could the inheritance of a living person be entered upon, as in the Code, On Captives and Those Returning from Captivity, law *nec nos*. It is also presupposed that,

† Whether she acquired this unsatisfied claim from the husband's assets, or another having a cause from her, whether this person acquired it by usucaption due to just error? And it seems that not, as in the Digest, on usucaptions, l. iusto, § filius. The contrary is true by the law Celsus, with its subject matter, in the same title. For just error, added to any title, induces prescription therefrom.

But it is doubted whether this prescription should be said to be between present parties or between absent parties. For if you consider the fact, it is between absent parties, as in l. j., ff. quibus ex causis maiores. But if you consider that they are of the same domicile, it is between present parties, as in C. de praescriptione longi temporis, l. fina. And this is the correct view, because the absent party ought to have left a procurator; and if he did not leave one, let him impute it to himself, as in Auth. qua in provincia, and in l. 1, and there it is fully noted, ff. de diversis et temporibus praescriptionum, and in l. quaedam, § 1, ff. de legationibus. I, Baldus of Perugia, Doctor of Both Laws.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How the petition is to be drafted for the remedy of the interdict *unde vi*, for recovery or reinstatement.
2. If spoliation is alleged to have been committed by one person, but now another person possesses the property, who has no title from a superior nor from anyone who succeeded to the defect, whether this person is bound by the action *condictio ex capite canonis saepe* or for reinstatement.
3. Given a statute providing that if, after a complaint has been brought, any rights are acquired by the defendant, they shall not avail him, how is it to be interpreted.
4. The condition of the possessor is the better one when the cause is equal.
body: It is alleged that Hector, in the name of Christ, during his lifetime and until his death, possessed one plot of vineyard and meadow; and that after the death of the said Hector, the said plot of vineyard and meadow was possessed by Antonius and the brothers, sons of the said Hector. And while they were holding it, they were deprived of possession of the said property unjustly and wrongfully; and after the said loss and deprivation of the said possession, possession of the said plot of vineyard and meadow passed to Ioannes Borgognonus and to Hector, son of the said Ioannes. This Hector Borgognonus holds and possesses the said plot of vineyard and meadow. Wherefore, the said Antonius, in his own name and that of his brothers, requested to be reintegrated and restored to possession of the said vineyard and meadow, and that the adversary be condemned to restore it. In the first place, it is asked whether the said petition is valid or not.

† And it must be said without doubt, according to the matters alleged, that the said petition does not proceed, because nothing is alleged from which any legal remedy would result in the said reintegration sought. For the interdict *unde vi* does not arise: because they do not allege that they were expelled by force. Hence, even if the act of a certain person were imputed and action were brought against him, the interdict *unde vi* would not lie: because that which is of the form and substance of that interdict is not alleged, as in l. 1, in principio, *unde vi*. Moreover, the interdict *unde vi* is personal, because the words of the praetor say, "from which force, you by force threw him down." For since it arises from a wrongful act, it does not follow the possessor, because he did not commit the wrongful act, as in D. *de vi, et vi armata*, l. *cum a te*. For wrongful acts hold their authors, not others who have not offended, as in C. *de poenis*, l. *sancimus*. Moreover, nothing is alleged of such a kind that the chapter *supra*, *de restitutione spoliatorum*, would have application. For that chapter intends this, that where the interdict *unde vi* fails, yet the thing nevertheless comes to another with a defect: he to whom it comes with the defect is bound by the condictio from that canon; otherwise, if it comes without defect, as is fully noted there. Extr. *de iudic.*, centesima quaestione quinta. Moreover, because the condictio from the chapter *reintegranda* does not have application. For that chapter requires spoliation at the beginning, namely, that someone was despoiled, as is clear there. For it says, "all things are to be restored to those despoiled." Moreover, it requires a defect in the successor, that he succeeded with that defect, as is noted in the said chapter, *quia*. But here nothing is alleged that there was any defect at the beginning in the possession to be recovered, nor in the course of it, in that which is to be obtained through the defendant. Therefore, the libel does not proceed, as in D. *de dolo*, l. *Item exigit*, and D. *quod metus causa*, l. *si cum exceptione*, § *in hac*, and l. 2, D. *de tritica*, and C. *de agricolis et censitis*, l. *si coloni*. Therefore, it can be said that we have found your petition incompetent and inept, as in Extr. *de iudiciis*, cap. *examinata*. Nor does the condictio l. *conquerebatur*, C. *unde vi*, have application. For that constitution requires other things, which are not claimed here, as is clear there, and is noted in D. *quod metus causa*, l. *taxat*.

† It remains to consider the second point. Suppose that spoliation had been committed by one person, but now someone else possesses the property, who derives his title neither from the spoliator nor from anyone who succeeded to the defect: is this person liable under the action on the canon *sæpe*, or under the canon *reintegranda*? I say that he is not, because he derives his title from the actor’s predecessor. And so it is in the present case, because he derives his title from Lady Clemondina, who was the daughter and legatee of Hector, the rector: by virtue of which title she excludes any possessory action of the plaintiff, as in D. ad Trebellianicam, l. *filia fratribus*. And note, C. de edicto diui Adriani tollendo, l. *edicto*. For the said Lady Clemondina had a hypothecary right by virtue of her father’s will, as in C. communia de legatis, l. *prima*. And if the personal action fails, the hypothecary action is granted, as in C. de actionibus et obligationibus, l. *si in solutum*. And since the cessionary is in possession, he must be protected in it, because to him to whom a claim for recovery is granted, retention is all the more granted, as in D. de superficiebus, l. *prima*, § *quod ait*; and D. de regulis iuris, l. *inuitus*, § *cui damus*. And observe here that this right of defense has been proved in court and is liquidated: in which case, in any possessory action, the exception *dolo facis* (that you act in bad faith) is a bar, since it has been established; and especially in a possessory action brought under the said chapter *sæpe* and the chapter *reintegranda*, because those chapters are founded on equity: but there is no equity for the plaintiff, since the defendant’s defense is liquidated. These points are proved in the said chapter *sæpe*, by a contrary sense in the reasoning of the text. And it is expressly stated in the same title, chapter 1. And note, D. de iudiciis, in l. *si de ui*; and according to Innocentius, X. de filiis presbyterorum, c. *constitutus*.

† Moreover, the statute does not apply, which provides that after the complaint has been filed, if the defendant has acquired any rights, such acquisition shall not benefit him; for that provision must be understood as applying only unless he has acquired rights from the adversary, or from someone acting on the adversary’s authority. For it is certain that the plaintiff may assign his rights to the defendant while the litigation is pending. Likewise, he who claims title from the plaintiff, if this is the case in the present matter, because the assignee claims title from the legatee, and the legatee claims title from the father and from the heir, since by accepting the inheritance he confirmed the legacy and, as it were, contracted with the legatee, so that all are considered one and the same person, as in D. de verb. oblig. l. stipulata, § 1, and there by Bartolus, notably. Therefore, if the heir is barred, who cannot act against his own deed, nor against the pact made by the deceased, as in C. de serv. pign. dato, l. si creditoribus, and D. de evict. l. fundum meum, and as I said above, so it would be in the edict of the divine Adrian, and in any possessory action. Moreover, it is certain that what one acquires by the act of the party while litigation is pending benefits him, especially for defense, whether the act is his own directly, or through his agent, as in D. de cond. fur. l. siue manifestus, § tandiu, and l. si seruus, in princ. To the foregoing also applies most aptly D. de evict. l. si rem, in princ., and C. de mand. l. per diuersas, § exceptis, and D. de cond. ind. l. sub cond. Moreover, the following applies to the foregoing,

†because, when the cause is equal, the condition of the possessor in good faith is the better. For by the very fact that he possesses in person, he has more right than he who does not possess, as is stated in D. 43.17.1 (Uti possidetis), at the end, and noted in C. 7.33 (Quibus non obstat longi temporis praescriptio), l. Haereditas. And therefore I conclude that the defendant should be absolved, according to what is alleged. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. How an assurance made by the lord to the offender, that he may come freely, etc., is to be interpreted, and to which offenses it extends; and if it speaks jointly of the offender and the condemned, whether it is understood to apply to the offender alone and to the condemned alone.
2. Whether a case omitted in a dispensation is to be considered as omitted.
body: It is proposed that N. has a safe-conduct in the name of Christ, in this form: “We, etc., by the tenor of these presents, grant to Nichodemus de Fraconibus, our Alexandrian citizen, full and free safe-conduct and protection; so that, from whatever parts he may come, he may come to us, and there, within our territory, stand, go, and return freely, safely, and without penalty, notwithstanding anything done, said, or committed by him heretofore against us, our state, and honor, which may in any way be imputed to him, and notwithstanding any ban issued on account of homicide, or any other condemnation made against him on any occasion or for any crime; commanding all our officials and subjects that they observe these our letters and cause them to be inviolably observed. Given, etc.” Now, the said Nichodemus committed a certain offense, namely, theft and violation of forests, for which he was not tried and condemned.

† It is asked whether the aforementioned security benefits him. And it seems that it does not, because the said security has two clauses, or parts, and no more. For the first part speaks of non-obstantes against acts done against the status and honor of the lord. These words are understood when the act was principally done against the status and honor of the lord. But the offenses about which inquiry is made are not of this kind. The second part speaks of offenses for which condemnation has been made, or a ban issued. And a provision made for one case does not comprehend another, especially one contrary in fact, as in D. de liberis et posthumis, l. commodissime; and D. de servitutibus urbanorum praediorum, l. si domus. Moreover, that which the word does not signify, certainly it does not intend, and this because the force of speech does not extend to that, as in C. de transactionibus, l. si decreta. Furthermore, bans and condemnations could be known to the Prince, but hidden crimes were not known: and therefore it does not seem that there is a dispensation concerning the uncertain, as in D. de pactis, l. tres fratres; and D. de transactionibus, l. cum aqua. Moreover, this grace is a certain dispensation, which does not extend to suppressed defects, argumentum D. de legatis 2, l. omnia. Moreover, a case expressing one incapacity does not contain another incapacity; hence if the Pope says that one may be promoted to orders notwithstanding a defect of birth: nevertheless he may not be promoted if he has a defect of age.

† Because a case omitted in a dispensation is considered as omitted, the grace is revoked, and the dispensation is declared null as surreptitious, as in cap. 1, *De filiis presbyterorum*, lib. 6, and in cap. *Susceptum*, *De rescriptis*, eod. lib. Moreover, this clause, *non obstante* [notwithstanding], appears to declare the intention of the issuer and to restrict it solely to the cases expressly stated; especially since it seems to be of the substance, as noted in l. *fin.*, C. *Senatus consultum rescindendum non posse*. To the contrary, it seems, because the said writing has three parts: the second, *non obstantibus aliquibus* [notwithstanding some]; the third, *et non obstantibus* [and notwithstanding]. Now, the first part is general, and most general; therefore, the entire grace appears to be general, as in D. *De iuris et facti ignorantia*, l. *Regula*, § *fin*. Furthermore, this grace harms no one, nor does it even pardon a crime. Since, therefore, that clause, *non obstantibus* [notwithstanding], harms no one, it is not of the substance, but rather of a certain style, and for the amplification, and not for the diminution, of the grace, as in C. *De precibus imperatoribus offerendis*, l. *Quotiens*. Moreover, the clause, *de facto contra honorem domini* [of a fact against the honor of the lord], is sufficiently general; for there is no doubt that he who acts against the statutes of the lord does not honor the lord, nor fear the lord, as it is written, "He who does not fear the Prince shall die the death." Supply, or in another manner, as it shall seem to the judge, whose majesty is judged to be injured, as in D. *De iurisdictione omnium iudicum*, l. *Si familia*. Moreover, by those words, *quod possit venire ad dominum* [that he may come to the lord], the grace seems to be granted in favor of the lord; because perhaps the lord wished to be informed by him of many things, and therefore the said grace is to be amplified, and not restricted, as in D. *De constitutionibus principum*, l. *Beneficium*. Moreover, since security has been given by the Prince, it must be observed, nor ought anyone to be deceived who trusts in the principal letters, as noted in D. *De publicis iudiciis*, l. *Is qui reus*, and in l. 1, C. *De his qui vetita aetate impetrant*. And I consider this part to be more humane, and to pertain more to the honor of the Prince, and especially because if the Prince gives fuller security to delinquents and the condemned, who are indeed more odious, much more so for those who are worthy of less odium, argumentum C. *De libertate praeterita*, l. *Maximum vitium*, § *pe*. Moreover, a dispensation in two defects comprehends the case in which there is only one defect, as in D. *De liberto et posthumo*, l. *Si ita scriptum*. Hence, the doctors say that if one can legitimize spurious and incestuous children, much more so spurious children only, as noted by the doctors in D. *De verborum obligatione*, l. 2, and l. *Eadem*, § *Cato*. So in the case at hand, if security is given to delinquents and the condemned, it also comprehends any case per se, that is, delinquents only, and the condemned only; because if a just and mixed disposition favorable disposes not only of the mixed, but of any of the extremes. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If someone obtained a papal familiar's expectative right to a certain benefice, yet at the time of obtaining it was not a familiar, even though he later becomes one, whether such a grace of petition harms a third party.
2. The time of the grant of the grace is to be considered.
3. The pronoun "eis" signifies both substance and quality.
4. A special grace is greater than a general one.
5. A general disposition is not entirely abolished, even though the genus is diminished by a species.
body: Petrus de Sefla, in the name of Christ, obtained a canonry under the expectation of a prebend of the church of Saint Ambrose, dated on the 5th ides of November, in the first year of the pontificate of our lord. Likewise, Ioannes de Nargete obtained a general provision for one, two, three, or more [benefices], etc., in the city of Piacenza and the province of Milan, upon the same date; and at the time of obtaining the provision, the said Ioannes was not a familiaris, nor was he a familiaris at the time of the declaration made on the 3rd nones of January in the first year. But at the time of another declaration made on the 6th calends of July in the sixth year, he was a familiaris. It happens that in the third year of the pontificate of our lord, canonries and prebends of the said church of Saint Ambrose became vacant through the death of Iacobus de Barnagerio, which both of the aforementioned Petrus and Ioannes accepted, and for which they obtained that provision be made to them within the due time. And the aforementioned Ioannes possesses them, wherefore the aforementioned Petrus obtained that the case be committed against the said Ioannes concerning the said canonry and prebend to a certain auditor, before whom all terms were observed and the parties came to court. Now it is asked, which of these has the better right to the said canonry and prebend. It seems that Ioannes [has the better right] on account of the prerogative of familiarity, and this for a twofold reason.

First, because it suffices that the quality be found in existence at the time when the day of the disposition arrives, as stated in the Digest, *De rebus dubiis*, law *Si cognatis*. But here, he was a familiar at the time when the day arrived; therefore, on account of the quality of familiarity, he is to be preferred. The second reason is that the said declaration of the Pope is universal, and therefore it seems that it should be understood to apply even to familiarity acquired after the letters were issued, as is noted in the Digest, *De fundo instructo*, law *Lucius*, and law *Finalis*; and in the Code, *Quae res pignori obligari possunt*. To the contrary, it seems that the said declaration speaks in these words,
† in the expectative graces made by him to them in the concurrent grant, where two things are noted.

† First, note the word "eis," which signifies substance and quality, as in D. de noxa, l. in delictis, § si extraneos. Second, note the phrase "factas in data concurrenti." For since it said "factis in data," it referred back to the beginning, as in D. de testamento militis, l. Titius, and l. quid ergo, in principio, de his qui notati sunt infamia. Therefore, familiarity supervening after the grant does not increase the grant, nor does it induce a prerogative of the grant, as in D. de servis exportandis, l. si minor, and in c. si ex tempore, Extra de praebendis, lib. 6. From these, I conclude that by reason of familiarity, the said John is not to be preferred, because he was not a familiar at the time of the grant. Moreover, the said declaration is a certain Papal interpretation, which does not have the effect of adding in extending grace, but rather in preferring, as in D. de libellis legatis, l. Aurelius, § testamento, and in Auth. de filiis ante dotalia instrumenta natis, § fin.

† Consider moreover, that a special grace is of greater efficacy than a general grace, according to the rule set forth in c. *generi per speciem*, Extra, *de regulis iuris*, lib. 6; ff. *de alimentis*, leg. l. *alimenta*, § *basilicae*; and l. *stichus nutricis*; and C. *familiae herciscun.*, l. *quo*. And the reason is, that if the genus derogated from the species, the special provision would be rendered useless. It is no objection, ff. *de legatis 1.*, l. *si domino Stichus*, because there it speaks when both can be saved by concurrence: but in prebends and canonries this is impossible, as Extra, *de praebendis*, c. *maioribus*. On the contrary,

† Although a species diminishes the genus, as in l. si optio, ff. qui, et a quibus, nevertheless the general disposition is not entirely removed, because it remains in other species in which no derogation is found, as in ff. de conditione indebiti, l. cum is, qui Panphilum, §. qui hominem. And therefore I say that, in our case, all other things being equal, he who has a special grace must be preferred, because he who provides specially is deemed to have made the same choice. Hence this election is Papal, and therefore stronger; on this matter it is noted in c. duobus, de rescriptis, lib. 6, and in c. 1, de rescriptis, in the ancient decretal. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If several persons made an assault against one, and one or two of them struck with a very great shedding of blood, but the others without blood or with slight blood, yet the person struck died, whether all are to be punished as murderers.
2. What the word "as" (tanquam) imports.
body: they made an assault

† It is said that certain persons made an assault against one individual: and one, or two of them struck him with a very great shedding of blood; but the others did so without blood, or with slight blood, and finally the person struck died. It is asked whether all ought to be punished as murderers. And it seems that they should, because those who struck without blood, or with slight blood—and I call slight that which would not of itself induce death or severe suffering—surely even if they were not liable as primary actors, they would be liable as those furnishing aid. For Inno. says that he who stands armed with another is seen to furnish a kind of aid, as he himself notes in c. continentiam, de cle. percusso. But the contrary is true, for in the providing of aid three degrees are found: for some provide small aid, and very remote from the act, as in the case of him who lends ladders; some provide intermediate aid, as in the case of him who stands armed, yet he himself does not wish to pursue the murderer. And these are not punished as the slayers, but with an intermediate punishment, that is, a mitigated punishment and not the punishment of the ultimate penalty, as noted by Dyn. and all the ancient doct. in ff. de fur. l. eius, qui opin. and extra de homici. c. sicut dignum, where the case is found. Some, however, are those who provide substantial aid, as are the strikers who wound lethally, and furnish a cause consubstantial with death; and these are punished as the slayers,

† for then the word "as" is a mark of truth, as in ff. de verborum signifi. l. saepe, ff. ad l. aquil. l. item Mela. §. si plures, ff. de iurisd. omnium iudic. l. si familiae, with similar texts. Since, therefore, it is proposed that from blows without a blade, or with a slight wound, it will not naturally nor from things that commonly happen tend to the outcome of death, as in extra de homicid. c. significasti, with good reason the aforesaid strikers, whose acts are distinct, and consequently their intent, implicitly realized, is likewise divided and separated from the intent of the killer, can in no way suffer the punishment of the ultimate penalty, neither in the whole body nor in a limb: but another punishment, somewhat heavier on account of companionship with the killer, as in ff. de his, qui notan. infa. l. quid ergo. §. poena grauior, and ff. de poenis. l. aut facta. §. fi., and ff. de iniur. l. si plures, and ff. vi bonorum rapto. l. praetor. §. docere. Moreover, the intent is also declared from the quality of the instrument; whence Iaco. de Aretio says that if someone has a lance, and did not wish to strike with the iron point, but with the shaft, since one was as easy for him as the other, he is not liable to the penalty of the lex Cornelia, according to Iacob. de Aretio in l. 1. §. sed et si claud. ff. ad legem Corneliam de sicariis. And on account of this, discretion has been given by the law to governors to punish according to the quality of the deed, as in ff. de poenis. l. hodie. Furthermore, one proceeds more leniently when [it happens] in a brawl, and thus, so to speak, from an inadvertent mind, than when from premeditated and planned design, as in ff. de poenis. l. respiciendum. §. delinquunt. Most especially, therefore, the discretion of this matter rests in the breast of the magistrate, provided however that he leans toward the more lenient side. It fails in l. prima, C. de rapto virgi., in which law, since it is special, the common law is therefore to the contrary, as in ff. de legi. l. singulare, and l. vtrum, ff. ad legem Pompeiam de parricidiis, and l. et si amicis, ff. de adulter. etc. I, Baldus de Perusio.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. What effect do those words have, and he condemned to pay jointly, without specifying to whom.
2. Whether one who is bound to contribute with me towards a certain payment can be sued by me so that he contributes, or so that he contributes to me by paying me.
3. Whether a debt shared in common is a delivery or an act.
4. Whether money receives intrinsic or extrinsic interest.
5. Whether intrinsic interest is included in the claim.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† First, let us consider what effect those words have, namely, “and he condemned to pay jointly.” Since they are expressed impersonally and do not specify to whom payment is to be made, if they are understood as directed to the creditor himself, the award would be null, because an arbitrator’s sentence or arbitral award cannot be formed against persons outside the compromittants. D. de arbitris, l. arbiter impera, certum. But if they are understood as meaning to pay jointly, that is, to contribute for the common contribution, then the partner must be compelled, otherwise he must contribute by paying the other partner, so that the latter may be able to pay his creditor; and then there would be no doubt that the libel proceeds.

For the partner, who is bound, ought to contribute purely, so that he may pay his creditor, and he acts properly in demanding this, as is stated in the Digest, *pro socio*, l. *cum socii sumus*, where it says, "how he ought to pay as present"; and l. *cum duobus*, § *fina.*, in the verse *per contrarium*, where it says, "from the common [obligation] it follows that he ought to perform." And although there it premised regarding him who is nearest to paying, and who is compelled to pay by a necessity as it were precise—otherwise he suffered in his body, while detained in prison—and that he who is bound to contribute with me toward a certain payment can be sued by me to contribute, there is no doubt; but whether he can be sued to contribute to me by paying me, this is our question, sufficiently subtle. Here it must be considered that the award (*laudem*) ought to be understood without defect, so that it may be valid, as in the Digest, *de verborum obligationibus*, l. *si ita stipulatus*, § *Grisogonus*, in the following verse *stipulatio*; Digest, *de legibus primo*, l. *huiusmodi*, in the beginning, with the gloss; and it makes the case better, which is noted in the Digest, *familiae erciscundae*, l. *et puto*. Therefore, he ought to be understood as condemned to contribute, the brother, toward the debt by paying. For this speech could not be directed to another, d. l. *arbiter*.

Secondly, it must be considered whether the sharing of a debt constitutes a giving (datio) or a doing (factum). For he who acts, I condemn to pay jointly, intended that they be co-partners in the same debt. D. 44.1.1 (Reus). § Cum tabulis. Since therefore the original debt was one of giving, it therefore appears here also to be a giving, and not a doing. But to this it is answered that three persons must be considered: namely, the first debtor, insofar as the payment ought to proceed from him; and then it is a giving. And the first creditor, insofar as the payment ought to be made to him; and then the payment is likewise a giving. Furthermore, a new person joined to this obligation by the arbitrator for the purpose of suing may be considered. And this in two ways: either insofar as his intention is directed so that payment be made to another, namely to the first creditor; and then a doing is said to be owed. D. 45.1.1 (Liber homo). § Finali. And there by Bartolus. D. 46.3.1 (Qui res). § Qui stipulatus. By Bartolus. Or insofar as the intention is directed secondarily by reason of delay, that payment be made to him as interest. And then a giving is involved in the obligation, for example, that what is given to another by way of interest is mine, as regards me, a doing. He says, “I give you ten so that you grant freedom to Stichus,” who is my natural son, and thus it is my interest; nevertheless, this contract between me and you is not called a contract of do ut des, but is called ut facias, although the extremity itself consists in giving. D. 19.5.1 (Naturalis). Joined with D. 40.1.1 (Manumissiones). D. 12.2. D. 45.1.1 (Qui Romae). § Flavius Hermes. For since from this the dominion is not transferred to the contracting party, therefore as regards him it is not a giving. And the same is the case if I give you ten so that you give to my creditor, or to whom I wish to make a gift: as regards the superficial resonance of the words, it is do ut des; but as regards the subtlety of the law, it is do ut facias, according to the aforementioned rule. As is evident from the fact that,

† That wherever payment is to be made to a third party outside the contracting parties, we consider that interest is due, as is clear, read, and noted in the Digest, *De donationibus*; in the Code, *Sine sensu, vel religione*, l. 1, in the second gloss at the end; and in the Digest, *De pactis*, l. 1, in the gloss *Dandum, vel faciendum*. It follows from this that after default (*mora*), an obligation for interest arises, which includes the entire valuation of such matter. Thirdly, it must be observed that sometimes money is in performance from the beginning, sometimes in liberation, as is the case here. For if the collation had been made, this person would have been openly liberated from the debt he contracted. I say that the quantity, insofar as it is in liberation, receives all intrinsic and extrinsic interest. Hence, whether I am not bound in ten, or I am liberated in ten, or ten are paid for me, the interest is formally in ten, as in the Digest, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, l. *Quaerebatur*. And therefore the bill of complaint (*libellus*) properly concludes formally to ten as to interest. And on this point is the ordinary gloss in the Digest, *Rem ratam habere*, l. *Si sine*, § *Cum autem*, at the end, the great gloss, verse *Ut firmus probo*. And thus there is no objection in the Digest, *De in litem iurando*, l. *Nummis*. Consider therefore two obligations, namely the primary one, and this concludes as to the fact (*ut facti*); and the secondary one by reason of default, and this concludes as to giving (*ut dandi*). And because the fact has a certain quantity and nature, and therefore in this case the interest is liquid: and by this it follows that the wise man, Lord Catelan, gave excellent counsel. For the bill of complaint was well formed, for since action was taken on account of default, it was rightly that interest was claimed. Code, *De exceptione rei iudicatae*, l. *Si longius*, which properly speaks after sentence; *De actione empti*, l. 1, in the beginning; and l. *Celsus*, with similar laws. For the primary obligation, this bill of complaint responds: I sue that you pay my creditor and keep me indemnified, as in l. *Si mandato*, Digest, *De mandato*; Code, *De pactis*, l. *Ex conventione*, at the end. To the secondary noted obligation, into which there has been a deviation on account of default, this bill of complaint responds: because you ought to have paid ten for me, and you did not pay, but were in default, it is to my interest that I was and am liberated in ten, and therefore I claim in the name of interest, and thus without circumlocution the claim is clearly expedited. And for this the ordinary gloss in the Digest, *Ad legem Rhodiam de iactu*, l. *Secunda*, in the gloss beginning *Scilicet magister*, verse *Melius tamen esset*, is most apt. And that the sense of those words is commonly performed thus, this openly proves: Digest, *De legatis secundo*, l. *Fin.*, § *Lucius Titius*. I conclude therefore that the bill of complaint was aptly formed, and the complainants complained ill against the said consulting doctor; for he counseled rightly, correctly, and optimally. And I say this, adding to another counsel previously given by me in this cause, and to the allegations contained therein, believing and asserting this to be the substance of the truth, and I confirm by a new reason. Whenever a thing or act is owed, and after default it ceases to exist, so that it cannot be performed, it is certain that the quantity can be claimed. Digest, *De conditione furti*, l. *Iur. fur.*; Digest, *De confessis*, l. *Iulianus*. Also, when it is certain that after someone has stood in prison, one cannot liberate him from having stood there. Code, *De obligationibus*, l. *Secunda*; Code, *De appellatione*, l. *Provocatione*. Since therefore he who is bound to care for my indemnity and not to put me in prison cannot do this with intent, and this act is extinguished, having ceased to be possible, it is rightly that action is brought for interest. Digest, *De usufructu legato*, l. *Si usufructum mihi in biennium*. I say for total interest, because this act is indivisible according to the nature of acts, which regularly do not admit division. Digest, *De verborum obligationibus*, l. *Stipulationes non dividuntur*; and l. *Eadem*, § *Cato*. For standing in prison is to detain the person almost as a pledge in place; and the liberation of a pledge is not divided, Digest, *De verborum obligationibus*, l. *In executione*, § *Cum quemadmodum*. There is no objection in what the adversaries of this consultant allege: Digest, *De negotiis gestis*, l. *Si quis mandato*. For the text supports the gloss, which should not be understood if someone strives from the primary obligation, that is, from the contract on account of the contract. But if someone strives from the secondary obligation, if from the contract on account of default, that gloss does not speak anything of this, but other laws cited above speak.

† It is no objection that Bartolus alleges in l. liber homo, §. final, where he states that money cannot be claimed as intrinsic interest of the money itself, because intrinsic interest does not apply to money. For he means to say that if I owe you money, say ten units, these ten units cannot be estimated as anything other than ten; indeed, estimation does not apply here, for estimation requires two extremes, namely the thing and the price. Here, however, there is only one extreme, because the interest is the same as the thing itself; therefore, consideration for estimation does not apply to money for money. But in our case, money is not claimed as an estimation of money, but as an estimation of a certain act: for paying another on my behalf is an act which, as regards me, constitutes my interest in the entire sum by which I am bound. And thus this act admits of both intrinsic and extrinsic interest, because the act is a certain thing which can be estimated. D. de verb. oblig., l. stipulationes non diuiduntur, §. Celsus, where it says that the claim is to be given according to the estimation of the act; similarly, my release from obligation is a certain act, because release is an act, D. de curat. furios., in consil.; D. and note de transact., l. siue apud acta, according to the doctors; and it is a case in l. si vnus, §. pactus ne peteret, where it says, in pacts; l. in pactionibus, in releases, or pacts not to sue, the matter concerns an act. Although therefore an obligation, or otherwise a release, must be made from a certain quantity, nevertheless the quantity is that which is in the release, that is, the release from this quantity admits of all interest, namely intrinsic and extrinsic, namely the estimation according to the nature of the act, which is called intrinsic interest, that is, excused by the proper quality of the thing due, and intrinsic, namely by such an action, and that arising from another accident, extrinsic interest, namely, which is to be considered separately from the principal, and does not arise from the thing, but from outside the thing. Thus I describe it, so that the understanding may be easier. Therefore it is concluded that this payment to be made to another is a certain estimable act, the estimation of which is made from the quantity of the debt, as I have said. And those who say the contrary, if they were asked how they would therefore frame the libel on this total interest, would either have to admit the above, or say that the interest of the release cannot be claimed, which is contrary to all truth. And they say that if they had paid, they could sue, because they paid, and only their own interest; otherwise if they did not pay. But I say that if they paid, they could sue, and without intimation in the libel. If they have not yet paid, but the other party is in default of releasing, then they conclude in the libel by way of default, and otherwise they could not conclude to give themselves, if they must conclude to release and conservation of identity. Since therefore this default is expressly alleged in the libel, it appears that counsel has been well given. And where the act is due after default and contumacy, there would be a sequestration of possession for the aforementioned interest, therefore the aforementioned interest is due in specie. C. de primo decreto, §. videndum, vers. actionum autem; and the ordinary gloss holds this literally by the said l. si quis mandato, C. de rescind. vend.; l. ea quod actine, in the great gloss. And thus I say and advise, I, Baldus de Perusio, doctor of both laws, ordinary lecturer at Padua; and for the faith thereof I have subscribed and signed with the sign of my name. On which matters the most wise man, Lord Aegidius de Ripariis, had full consultation with the above-named eminent doctors and with me; and we examined all the laws of both parties fully, faithfully, and truthfully shown to us by him. I, Angelus de Castellione of Arezzo, doctor of both laws, currently lecturing in the Paduan studio, say and advise in all respects as is written above. And in testimony of this matter, I have subscribed with my own hand and affixed my usual seal. And as is further or previously written, said, and advised by the eminent doctor of both laws, Lord Baldus de Perusio, I, Paganinus de Sala, doctor of laws, say, affirm, and advise without doubt, and for the greater firmness of strength, I have affixed the sign of my usual seal, and on the above premises I consulted with the said Lord Baldus, and was in agreement with him in all respects. And thus I say and advise, I, Argentinus of Lord Raynerius, doctor of laws, and for the greater firmness of strength, I ordered my usual seal to be affixed, the judgment of any better judge always reserved.

In the name of Christ, Amen. It must be known that coin is said to be false for three causes, etc. See in the third part, consilium 37, folio 6, beginning "the case is such."

CASE.

Point, upon which are the following statutes.

Furthermore, that if any rancurator [inspector], or official of any tax collectors, both in the city of Vicenza and in the district of Vicenza, deceives any tax collector in his office or inspection, he shall incur a penalty of ten ducats for every denarius by which he deceived the tax collector, and shall be compelled to restore that by which he deceived him: which penalty shall belong to the tax collector.

Furthermore, that no man, or any person, dare or presume to transport, or cause to be transported, wine or must outside the district of Vicenza without the license and bulla [official permit] of the commune of Vicenza, or of the collector of said tax, under penalty and ban of sixty ducats for every cart, and per cart, and in forfeiture of the carts, ships, and beasts with which he transports said wine, and if they were not the transporter's.

Furthermore, that anyone be understood to go against the ban, if he is found transporting without the aforementioned bulla and license, going towards the borders one mile distant from the city of Vicenza, and two tornae distant from the village from which they extract said wine, going towards the borders, saving that if anyone causes wine or must to be transported during the time of the vintage from the dependencies of any village bordering on another village, or from the territory of the city to the boroughs, or to the city for the purpose of making wine, and this from possessions which he cultivates, and causes to be cultivated by himself or by his laborers, he may freely transport without any bulla and license, saving that in any village situated on the borders it is presumed to transport against the prohibition if he transports outside said village going towards the borders without the aforementioned bulla and license.

Furthermore, that the collectors of said tax are bound and must make a bulla for any citizen of the city of Vicenza wishing to transport wine from the city of Vicenza to any village of the district of Vicenza, or from village to village, without any payment, and the same is understood regarding the inhabitants of the villages of the district of Vicenza, under penalty of twenty solidi parvuli [small coins] for each and every time that any bulla is requested. And if any payment were taken, that they incur a penalty of sixty solidi denarii parvuli, and from the denunciation made to the collectors, or their messengers, or any of them, and payment found by them, if they do not immediately do so, it is believed that the citizen wishing to transport, or the inhabitant of good condition, with one witness, is permitted to transport without a bulla, saving that if any person transports, or wishes to transport, wine from the city, or boroughs, or territory of Vicenza to any village of Vicenza, or of the district of Vicenza, or from village to village for the purpose of selling by the measure, or by way of merchandise, or for the purpose of reselling said wine, he is bound and must pay to the collector of said tax, or to the officials for the commune of Vicenza, ten solidi for every cart of nostrano wine, and twenty solidi imperiales for every cart of sclano wine. And in forfeiture of the cart within the third day from which he transported, under penalty of sixty solidi parvuli for every cart, and in forfeiture of the cart, and nevertheless paying said tax. And he is bound to take the bulla of said wine from said official, or collectors, or his messengers, and rancurators, under penalty to be applied to the transporter of wine against the prohibition.

From the aforementioned statutes, such a case is posed.

A certain John in the village of La Costa of the district of Vicenza sold to Peter one mastello [large cask] of nostrano wine for the price of twenty solidi parvuli, with the agreement to measure and transport said wine with his own oxen and his own cart to the house of said Peter situated in the village of La Mota, distant from said village of La Costa by one mile, and there to receive the price from said buyer, the transport and measurement of said wine having been made. Who John, according to said agreement, transported said mastello of wine thus sold in the village of La Costa to the house of said Peter with his cart and with two of his oxen, without any request for a bulla and license from any official of the commune of Vicenza, or of any tax collector, or of his rancurators. To said Peter he measured said wine, and from him received said price there. Afterwards, after two months and more had elapsed, it became known to Bartholomew, rancurator and official in said village of La Costa and of La Mota, appointed by the tax collectors of the commune of Vicenza, of the aforementioned sale and transport of said wine made by said John to said Peter without any bulla and license, and request of said tax collectors, and of said rancurator. Who John, the seller, fearing to be punished and accused by virtue of said statutes, or any of them, by said tax collectors for said sale and transport of said wine made by him to said Peter without the bulla and license of said tax collectors, or of said his rancurator, gave to said Bartholomew, rancurator, three gold ducats, so that he should keep silent regarding the aforementioned matters, and not reveal them to said tax collectors. Who Bartholomew, rancurator, having the aforementioned matters brought to his knowledge, as above, kept silent, and never wished to reveal them to said tax collectors, of whom he was rancurator. Finally, all the aforementioned matters came to the knowledge of said tax collectors. From which, against said Bartholomew, rancurator, said tax collectors proceed, and ask that he be punished according to the order, modes, and penalties written below. But said rancurator defends himself, as all things are more clearly explained below from the doubts to be elicited, and which arise from said statutes, upon which counsel is requested, or ought to be consulted according to the right truth.

And first, let it be a doubt whether said Bartholomew, rancurator, by virtue of said statutes, has incurred any penalty.

Secondly, if he has incurred any penalty, into which, and to what extent he ought to be punished.

I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Given the statute which provides that if anyone carries away something for the purpose of trade, he shall incur such a penalty, and the carrier shall forfeit his cart, and the rancurator shall be bound to pay the full amount if he has colluded. Now, a certain person sold wine and carried it away, and afterwards colluded with the rancurator; whether he is bound to the penalty and the valuation.
2. A merchant is not said to be one from a single act.
3. To sell is one thing, whereas to resell is another, just as to give is one thing and to return is another.
4. A statute does not apply beyond the cases specified by the statute.
body: In the name of Christ. The vendor does not fall under the law of the forfeited beasts and cart from any provision of the statute. For whenever we are within the proper and very terms of a statute speaking specially, we do not argue from other statutes, as is most fitting, according to the Digest, On Verbal Obligations, law *Stipulationes*. But now we are within the proper terms of that section, *Item, that carriers*. But it must be observed whether we are under prohibitive and penal terms, or under permissive and non-penal terms, or at least whether we are in a case not punishable; for if the case is not comprehended under the statute, it suffices that the statute ceases to apply, so that the penalty of the statute ceases, according to the Digest, On the Dissolution of Marriage, law *Si vero*, section *De viro*, and the last law, Code, On the Interdict to a Mother.

And certainly we are not bound by the penal law, which enumerates only three cases when goods are transported from village to village within the district of Vicenza. The first case is when the sale is made by the smallest measure, that is, by the smallest and least measures. Hence, one who sells by the mastello does not sell by the smallest measure, and this is the common understanding, and it is proven by what is said about selling minutatim and frustatim, and as it were by mouthfuls, the wolf devours the lamb, Extra de praescriptione, c. Transmissa; Extra de poenitentia et remissione, c. Deus qui; and the glosses in both places.

Second, when the matter concerns mercantile trade, where it is noted that a single act is not considered mercantile trade, as stated in the gloss on the Digest, *De tributoria*, l. 1, in the beginning, in the gloss beginning *rerum*, where the ordinary gloss is found in its proper terms. Consider, therefore, that in penal statutes, an action *utilis* has no place, because they do not admit of an interpretation based on hatred; and when this is so, neither is one called a merchant, nor is there mercantile trade arising from a single act, as Bartolus clearly and fully determines in *L. legatis servis*, in the beginning, Digest, *De legatis secundis*. The third case,

† when the cause is for resale, and this is not our case. D. de legatis 2, l. cum pater, § fidei tuae committo uxor, in fine. For one thing is to sell, another is to resell, just as one thing is to give, another is to restore: because the word of repetition signifies several acts, not one act. D. de pactis, l. ab emptione, in fine. Since therefore we are outside the cases specially prohibited, it seems that our case is permitted by contrary reasoning,

And thus it appears that the text of the statute is in our favor by way of a contrary inference, which arises from the very wording of the statute due to the specified cases and the nature of the specification. D. de testamentis, l. qui testamento, §. mulier, and there the ordinary gloss. C. de furtis, l. apud antiquos. But according to the common law, this penalty does not apply; this is supported by what is noted in C. de nauticis foeneribus, l. cum proponas, according to Cynus. For nothing illicit is being transported or sold, and thus the carts and animals are not confiscated, because no law states this. From the foregoing it is clear that if the principal is not liable to the aforementioned penalties, then the curator or accessory is not liable, because in a relative penalty, when the principal is destroyed, the penalty ceases. D. de furtis, l. si is qui, §. si tu Titium, and l. fullo, §. ope. For here it cannot be said that there is deception or a trap based on an irrelevant point of law, by argument from l. qui autem, in principio, quae in fraudem creditorum, in ratione sui, cum si. C. de in integrum restitutione, l. fin. Many other matters have been subtly touched upon by the opposing counsel, which it is not necessary to examine further at present. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. If the father stipulated for himself alone that the dowry be restored upon the dissolution of the marriage, to whom does the action for the dowry accrue? And what if it has been restored solely to the daughter?
2. How can the restitution of the dowry to the daughter, to whom the action arising from the stipulation could not belong, become true and irrevocable?
3. The restitution of the dowry to the mother: how manyfold it is, and which is lawful, which is just, and which is not.
4. Whether the confession of the daughter prejudices the father.
5. What effect an oath produces.
6. Where an obligation is prohibited, there also a confession is prohibited.
body: In the name of Christ. The tenor of the letters transmitted to me by the undersigned most distinguished men is as follows. Most dear lord, between Dominic Angelus of Ancona, in his own name and in the name of the procurator of Lady Pisanella, his daughter, wife of the late Thadeus Nicolaus, or Tolutius Blancutius of Ancona, or Loctorellus Pelegrinus of Ancona, procurator, and in the procuratorial names of the said Dominic and Lady Pisanella, on the one part, and Lady Conta, wife of the late Colutius, and mother and heir, as she asserts, intestate, and with the benefit of inventory of the said late Thadeus, her son, or Thomas Antonius of Ancona, in the procuratorial name of Lady Conta, on the other part: before us as arbitrators and arbiters both in law and in fact in proceeding, and arbitrators in law only in sentencing, specially appointed by the said Dominic in the said names and by the said Lady Conta, certain lawsuits, accusations, and questions are being litigated, which are as follows, namely, that the said Loctorellus, in the said procuratorial names, requests that the said Lady Conta, heir of the said Thadeus, be condemned by us to give to the said Dominic and Lady Pisanella the goods and the Arnensia Corredi of the said Lady Pisanella, held by the said Dominic from the said late Thadeus and the said late father of his, and a certain Bonellus Blaututius, contained and declared in the dotal instrument of the said Lady Pisanella, since the said Colutius, Bonellus, and Thadeus, and each of them, appear to be bound jointly and severally. Also, on another part, all goods, namely, cloths of wool and linen with their supports and ornaments, existing between the chamber of the house of the said Lady Pisanella, the dwelling of the said Thadeus; and this by virtue of a legacy made to the said Lady by the said late Thadeus in the testament, which we transmit to you. Also, on another part, 400 pounds left by the said late Thadeus to the said late Pisanella and Dominic, or to one of them, in the aforementioned testament, for part, as is said, of 1,400 pounds of the dowry of the said Lady. Also, to give and pay to the said Dominic twenty gold ducats left to him in the aforementioned testament. Also, on another part, that the said Lady Conta permit the said Lady Pisanella to peacefully possess a certain house, a certain vineyard land. Also, a certain other vineyard land. Also, a certain field land, which she says pertains to her by virtue of a dation in solutum made for the aforementioned 1,000 pounds to the said Lady Pisanella by the said late Colutius and Bonellus. Also, he requested expenses, as more fully appears in the petition of the said Loctorellus, the aforementioned procurator, which we transmit to you. On the part of the said Lady Conta, it is replied that she is not bound to these things; and the aforementioned testament and dation in solutum are impugned and objected against, as appears from the acts. And on the other side, the said Thomas, procurator in the said name, requested that you condemn the said Lady Pisanella to give and restore to the said Lady Conta, heir, certain goods come, as he asserts, to the said Lady Pisanella from the goods of the inheritance of the said late Thadeus, contained and declared in the petition of the said Thomas. On which, it is responded on the part of the said Lady Pisanella that she is not bound, denying that what is in the petition is true, as more fully appears from the acts, on which petitions, responses, exceptions, proofs of rights, instruments, writings, constitutions, statutes, or legacies; or else productions of allegations, have been produced and made before us, as you will be able to see particularly and distinctly. And we have proceeded on the aforementioned matters summarily, mixed in law and in fact, for the convenience of the parties, considering the power entrusted to us in proceeding, all of which we send by the bearer of these presents to consult with us on the definition of the aforementioned matters and the pronouncement of our sentence, which ought to be given in law; since we are merchants and ignorant of law, we send them to your wisdom, most earnestly beseeching you that, according to the arbitral power granted to us, from the petitions, responses, proofs, allegations, constitutions, statutes, and all acts acted and done in the cause or causes, and produced and alleged; and all that we send, diligently viewed, attended to, and considered, you would wish and please to consult and declare to us clearly and openly by your closed and sealed counsel: and what is the law on the aforementioned requests, and in what form and tenor we ought to give and pronounce by sentences, and terminate the said causes; furthermore, that you would wish to write back to us in a clear form, separately from the said counsel, the form and tenor of the said sentences, namely, beginning from the invocation of the name of Christ until the end. And if we condemn any of the parties in expenses, sending us everything well clear and open, so that we may also be able to understand in effect without the aid of any judge, and that you would wish to send the notes of the sentences enclosed in the said counsel, so that you and we may acquire the fullness of honor from the aforementioned matters. And lest you might have any doubt about the acts, whether they were made less legitimately on our part: we put it before you as certain that the acts were made in the proper places, and citations by the proper messenger, and oaths exacted from the parties and from witnesses by the proper person. For we did everything with the consent of the parties, because we are arbitrators and arbiters in proceeding. Furthermore, since the testament, of which mention is made above, was written by the hand of a certain scribe of the ship, not writing well openly, but obscurely: the testament itself, for the sake of less labor, on a certain sheet of paper beyond the instrument, where it was read by a certain other in a better form of letters, we send to you with the said counsel, and that you would wish to remit the notes of the sentences, and to expedite the bearer of these presents as quickly as you can. Moreover, we send to you by the same bearer for your salary ten gold ducats, begging you that you do not look to the smallness of the salary, but rather to the affection towards you of those sending, always ready for all things pleasing to you. Written at Ancona on the 3rd day of August. And among the statutes is a certain constitution of the Roman Church, and certain statutes which have not been published. Do not attend to them, because they have not been published, because they are not true. Yours, Jacobus Bartoli, and Bona Iuncta Petrolus, merchants of Ancona, to the wise and distinguished doctor of laws, Lord Baldus of Perusia, residing at Padua. Subscription. In the name of Christ, Amen. In the first place, it is necessary to consider the effect of the dotal instrument. Secondly, the dation in solutum made to Lady Pisanella, and its effect. Thirdly, the testament of Thadeus, regarding the person of the testator, whether he could make a will, and regarding the person of the scribe, whether his writing is valid. Fourthly, whether those things requested on the part of Dominic and Lady Pisanella are rightly and correctly requested and proved, or not. Finally, the petition of Lady Conta; and these matters are quite intricate.

† Regarding the first point concerning the dotal instrument, it is certain that the father stipulated for himself without joining the person of the daughter; likewise, it is certain that, since the marriage was dissolved during the father’s lifetime, the action against the heirs of the husband belongs solely to the father, by virtue of the tenor of the stipulation. C. de pac. conuen. l. ex morte; C. de iure do. l. auia; C. communia vtriusque iudi. l. fi. Although he is bound to preserve the dowry of the daughter for conversion into a subsequent marriage, C. de rei exo. ac. auth. rem in praesenti, and auth. sed quamuis, consider therefore the aforementioned dotal contract and to whom it speaks: because it addresses the father, and not the daughter, in the case of the restitution of the dowry, but calls upon the father. Although, if the father had died in the meantime, the action for the dowry would pass by operation of law to the daughter, according to the said Auth. rem in praesenti, §. videamus, according to the gloss, even though others say the contrary on this point, nevertheless, since the father is alive here, it is certain that the action belongs solely to the father. And this concludes the first point.

† But because the restitution of the dowry must descend from the dotal contract, let us see how a true and irrevocable restitution of the dowry of the daughter could have been made, to whom the action for the dowry by stipulation could not belong. For it is certain that what is owed to the father alone cannot be paid to the daughter alone. C. de pact. l. filius. Therefore, the said *datio in solutum* in the person of the daughter was not valid without the consent of the father, from the beginning. For now, by ratifying, the father accomplished nothing, because it was not done in the name of the father. ff. de neg. gest. l. si pupilli. §. nam et si seruum. And thus it is said that the *datio in solutum* did not hold in the person of the daughter, since the stipulation was conceived in the person of the father; for what is owed to one cannot be paid to another. Also, during the subsistence of the marriage, the dowry cannot be restored except for a permitted cause, ff. de iure do. l. mutus. §. 1. or for a just cause, and when the husband misuses his substance not by chance, but by fault, because on account of the debtor’s fault the creditor’s claim is accelerated. ff. de pigno. l. quaesitum. ff. ad Tre. l. Imperator. Also, when the husband verges toward poverty by chance or by fault, as in l. si constante. in prin. sol. mat. because then, in favor of the dowry, we depart from the common law, lest the woman remain without a dowry. Nevertheless, even then, if it can be paid, the thing is not ceasing to be dotal, but the ownership and administration are changed, but not its quality; for the husband was the owner and administrator, now the wife is the owner and administrator. However, the land is dotal and cannot be alienated, and it is freed from the burdens of marriage, as in l. vbi adhuc. For this is introduced in favor of the dowry, which during the subsistence of the marriage ought to be common to the husband and wife with regard to the bearing of burdens. If therefore, during the subsistence of the marriage, restitution is made in another way, i.e., that the land be free to the woman and not remain affected by the burdens of marriage, such a restitution to the father-in-law, and the husband, and the wife is not valid, because it is a species of donation prohibited between them, as in l. 1. C. si dos constante matrimonio. Considering therefore the instrument of *datio in solutum*, which exceeds the limits permitted by law or statute: then, because the father of the husband obligated himself to a pension, and constituted himself by dotal right as a tenant and colonist: then, because the instrument says for selling and alienating, when it ought to have said for holding and possessing firmly for the security and preservation of the dowry. I say that the said *datio in solutum* was not valid in law, nor is it credited to the husband, or his father, who has in his power the confessor, that he himself misuses his substance, or verges toward poverty; for since it is prohibited to make donations to each other, the confession of another cause is prohibited, unless the truth is proved, as in ff. de prob. l. qui testamentum. But here a doubt arises, because not only the father-in-law, but also the brother of the father-in-law gave in *solutum*, who is not prohibited from making a donation. Therefore, for his part, namely Bonelli’s, the donation, otherwise *datio in solutum*, was valid. But it is answered, first, because he did not have a cause, or because a *datio in solutum* cannot be divided, so that it may be valid in part and not in part, as in ff. de condi. inde. l. si non sortem. §. si certum. Also, even if a cause precedes, the form is not observed, which is that it be freed from the burdens of marriage. And therefore, all things considered, it seems to me that the arbitrators ought to rescind the said donation, otherwise *datio in solutum*, because it is ineffective, where I consider that they were not arbitrators and arbiters elected upon formulated petitions; for then they could not judge outside the form of the petitions. And upon the possessory, possession being proved, they ought to judge for the possessor, whatever the contract or the cause of ownership might be; but they were elected upon the disputes and lawsuits which could arise from the said instruments and things. And therefore they ought to follow, as arbitrators, the final effect of the truth; for the arbitrator is not restricted to the form of strict law, namely the petitions; but to the form of broad truth and equity, which he ought to have before his eyes. And this is the second point, which was manifoldly obscure on account of the complication of the facts and persons, whence also it must be considered,

† That the restitution of the dowry during the subsistence of the marriage is threefold, namely, necessary, or just; probable, or permitted; and temerarious, or prohibited. That which is probable is the one of which it is spoken in d. §. manente, and in ff. sol. mat. l. si ideo, and l. quamuis. And it can be made, and the father and the daughter are excluded. ff. sol. mat. l. si cum dotem, §. 1. And it is remarkable, because the father ought to have ratified what was done according to the nature of the dowry, and he is deemed to consent by notice. Since therefore everything that is necessary by law is also probable by law, it therefore seems that the aforementioned restitution held even to the prejudice of the father and the daughter, the contrary of which I said above. For the cause of restitution in our case was probable and necessary, therefore the instrument of the gift remained unpaid. And those words, alienandum, etc.

† are added to enlarge: hence they do not have the effect of invalidating the contract; because that which is ordered to increase does not diminish, nor destroy, as in D. de peculi. legato, l. si peculium in principio. Moreover, this clause, which says “for alienating, etc.,” being vitiated because it is contrary to the nature of the act, should not therefore vitiate the act; because this is an accessory clause; and the accessory does not vitiate the principal, unless it has the character of a final cause. But it must be noted that here the father and the daughter are acting; and thus the person of each is joined, indeed united, because this is not a joint action, but each is brought forward in his or her own right; although the names are described in the same bill, nevertheless the cause of action is not the same. And therefore it must be considered, for first, namely, the dotal instrument is in the person of the father; the middle, namely, the delivery of the unpaid dowry, is in the person of the daughter; the last, namely, the father’s will, because a legacy is inscribed to the father. How, therefore, do these matters proceed, both in law and in fact? How can the father divide his legacy and claim 4 pounds from it, and thus accept in part and not in part? For the said 4 pounds cannot be claimed by any other right than from the legacy; because no contract appears in them, as in D. de libe. lega., l. Aurelius, §. ultimo. Therefore, they must be content either with the contract or with the will. D. de leg. 2, l. neminem; D. de lega. 1, l. legatarius. And if they choose the contract, they cannot claim the four pounds, because they are not contained in the dotal instrument, nor in the testimony of witnesses; and a confession made in the manner of a legacy does not prove a debt, because the last will does not avail for a contract, as stated in the said §. fi. And therefore, all things considered, so that we may avoid all ambiguities, it would follow that the will, from which the action is brought, should be regarded as an arbitrator; I say, not attending to the mode of acting, but to the mode of being. How, if it is the truth of law and fact, and thus I would judge that what is contained in the will should be observed as regards the father himself, who is acting on the basis of the will. Moreover, in the coheir, judgment must be rendered for the part, otherwise for the father, because the father acts on the basis of his own stipulation.

† Hence, the daughter’s confession does not prejudice the father. C. de pactis, l. filius. Nevertheless, since it is established from the daughter’s confession that she has the said goods in her possession, and it is probable that she removed them, I am of the opinion that he ought to order her to produce the said goods, and indeed to restore them. And this would be correct, unless an oath had been tendered and the contrary sworn.

But it must be noted that whether the oath is tendered in this action as decisive of the dispute, and then it decides the case, and nothing else is inquired into except whether the oath was sworn. D. de iureiurando, l. non erit, § dato. Or whether it is not acted upon as decisive, but is tendered for the relief of the burden of proof, and then the rule is different. Hence, the response to the allegations does not have the force of truth except against the respondent, as is fully noted in § quod observari. I did not find in the records that the oath was tendered in a decisive form. Moreover, this would be according to the common law,

But by the form of the constitutions, I believe that no concession is valid where obligation is prohibited, because confession tends toward the same end: hence, just as a son cannot bind himself in a loan, so too he cannot confess. And the same applies to the other persons prohibited, because where the act of obligation is prohibited, its confession also appears to be prohibited. D. de legibus 3, l. cum quis, §. codicis. And thus, in conclusion, in the way of written law and strictly, even in the said case, I indeed believe the naked debt to be saved, with respect to the things which for part have already been restored, and the same regarding the things of the chamber: and the same regarding the twenty florins: and the same regarding the petition of the opposing party, that condemnation be made rather on the things proved, and not on others. Of all these matters you have the effect of law. But make from this opinion, since it is clear, your award be dictated to you, because I cannot attend to all matters. It suffices that I have counseled you in the point of truth and equity of law. And as for the objections raised against the testament, because I consider them unjust, I do not care. For the will of a sane person must be preserved, and just as barbarians can make wills among us, so too can we among them, if we are not captives. C. de Episcopis et clericis, l. nulli. I also consider the person of the scribe to be capable, because he was not publicly excommunicated. D. de testamentis, l. cum lego. And because he was not properly excepted, and because his office is not properly public, and even if he were a slave, the writing would be valid by the form of the statute. I, Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument: 1. Whether a confession against a third-party offender is to be upheld, given a statute that a confession of the offender is to be upheld; and generally, whether the confession of one prejudices another, and thus whether it proves, or only serves for the investigation against others. And no. 2.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen.

† An accessory offense cannot be established unless the principal offense or act is established. D. de furtis, l. is qui opem; D. ad Sillianam, l. 1, § item illud sciendum. Moreover, it is not sufficient that the principal offense is established by the joint action, confession, or condemnation of the principal offender, unless it is proven against the accessory in a judicial proceeding instituted against that very accessory. Hence, for example, if Peter is accused of theft and Martin of aiding, witnesses produced against Peter would not prejudice Martin, nor does Peter’s confession prejudice Martin; because these are equivalent: testimony, confession, and a judicial decision. And that which does not prejudice an outsider who did not participate in the same proceeding, one does not prejudice the other, nor the remainder; but it is certain that a matter adjudicated between others, etc. C. de re inter alios acta, per totum. And this is also evident. For what is more connected in adultery than the adulterer and the adulteress? Yet certainly the confession of one does not prejudice the other. D. de adulteriis, l. denunciasse, § quaeritur; and l. nihil, § si. Again, what is more closely joined than two heirs named in the same will? Yet if one confesses the will to be false, it does not prejudice the other. C. de fidei instrumentis, l. 2. Again, what is more mutually bound together than the party producing a witness and the witness produced? And yet if the producing party confesses that the witness gave false testimony, it does not prejudice the witness, arg. D. de infa, l. Lucius. And conversely, if the witness, after an interval, confesses that he was suborned to give false testimony, it does not prejudice the producing party, according to Bartolus in l. generaliter, C. de non numerata pecunia. It supports what is noted by Cynus in l. 1, in fin., C. qui accusare non possunt.

† It is therefore necessary that the principal offense be proven against this procurator in a manner other than through the confession of him who is said to have principally committed the offense. Namely, the confessions of those who confess, unless made during an inquisition, are not valid against others for true proof. D. de poenis, l. qui ultimo, according to Oldradus. This is not obstructed by the statute which commands that the confession of the offender be adhered to; because it is true against the confessing defendant, not against a third party. For a stranger to the common law is not understood to fall under statutes, which can indeed be interpreted according to the common law, which is the general rule directing every human act. C. de noxa, l. si servi vestri. And what is said above is well supported by the fact that he who confesses that he has lost a wager with someone must prove it. For his own confession is not adhered to, although in a common offense credit is not given against another unless that other is convicted. C. de poenis, in auth. novo iure, where it is expressly stated that a confession does not harm another, even in the crime of baractaria. And thus it properly applies to our case: and this is taught by Bartolus in the said §. si tu Titium. And this is the very truth, if every condemnation, which would be founded on the strength of the said confession, is undoubtedly unjust, and must in every way be rescinded as unjust. I, Baldus.
