consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether one who is asked purely, or conditionally, may deduct the two fourths.
2. The donee may, by virtue of the right of donation, if it does not exceed the lawful amount, or if it was insinuated, deduct the legitime and the trebellianic portion.
3. What will be the legitime of daughters, if the daughters themselves, excluded by statute, acknowledge the legitime, and thus form a part.
4. Whether dowry is called the legitime of children.
5. A prohibition of alienation to a certain person does not include sons among themselves.
casus:
CASE. In the name of Christ, Amen. The fact, upon which counsel is sought, is as follows, namely: a certain Lord Alexander of Negaria, citizen and inhabitant of Verona, during his lifetime had two wives: from the first of whom he had four children, namely: John and Bartholomew, males, and Sapina and Helen, females. From the second he had five, namely, Jacob, a male, and Contessa, Joan, Libera, and Catherine, females. And coming to his last death, he made his last will: in which, among other things which he did and bequeathed, by right of institution he bequeathed to the aforementioned Sapina and Helen, his daughters, as above, the dowries which he had given to them and to each of them at the time when they married him; and beyond those dowries, to them and to each of them, fifty pounds of small denarii, commanding and ordering them to be silent and content, etc., as is contained in the said will. He also bequeathed to the aforementioned Contessa, Joan, Libera, and Catherine, his daughters, as above, by right of institution, 600 gold ducats for each, and 50 pounds of denarii, or Rochati, for each, to be given to them at the time when they or any of them shall have merited it, commanding and ordering them and each of them to be silent and content, as is contained in the said will. But he instituted and wished his universal heirs in the said will to be the aforementioned John, Bartholomew, and Jacob equally, and in equal portions. And among other substitutions which the aforementioned testator made with his heirs and to each of them in his said will, he made such a substitution to the aforementioned John, his son and heir, and major 25 years, namely: and if the said John should die at any time without legitimate sons born of a legitimate marriage, then, and in that case, he instituted the aforementioned Bartholomew and Jacob, or the survivor of them, as his heirs vulgarly and by fideicommissum, furthermore prohibiting, forbidding, and commanding in his said will the aforementioned testator to the same John, his son and heir, as above, that the said John should never be able to sell, nor alienate, nor transfer to any person under any title, any thing or things immovable coming to him from the inheritance of the said testator, both by right of institution and from any of the above-written substitutions, or for those which are to be executed as contained in the said will. And if he should sell or alienate any thing or things immovable, or transfer them to any person under any title, except as above, and in that case he willed, disposed, and ordained that the said thing or things thus alienated or transferred should devolve to the aforementioned Jacob and Bartholomew, or to their heirs: because he willed that the same thing or things should come to his descendants or children descending from them in perpetuity.

After the death of the said testator, the aforementioned heirs divided among themselves all movable and immovable, and hereditary goods: except the fruits of the year of the said division pending, which they divided among themselves in common: and except also a certain house and a certain possession, which fell to the aforementioned John and Bartholomew in undivided share. This division having been made, and many days having passed, the aforementioned John made a donation inter vivos to his brother Bartholomew, of all goods, rights, and actions pertaining to the said John in the goods and inheritance of the said late father, or which might pertain to him in the said goods and inheritance, both on account of the legitime due to him in the said goods by natural law, and on account of the trebellianic portion due or to be due to him by reason of the fideicommissary substitution, etc. Retaining, however, the usufruct and exercise of all the said goods and rights thus donated to himself for the whole time of his life: and also under such condition, namely, if it should happen that he dies without legitimate and natural children born of a legitimate marriage, as is more fully contained in the instrument of the said donation. And the said donation having been made, and many years having passed, the said John died, no legitimate and natural children, otherwise sons, surviving him.

Now, from the said fact or theme, it is asked first: whether the said donation was valid in whole; namely, both in the legitime due by natural law to the said John in the said hereditary goods, and in the trebellianic portion due to him by right of the said fideicommissary substitution, notwithstanding the prohibition made in the said will by the said testator to the said John, or whether it was not valid in whole, or in part, notwithstanding the said prohibition, etc.

Secondly: whether by virtue of the said donation the said Bartholomew, the donee, can, notwithstanding the aforementioned legitime due by natural law to the said John and which was due to him without any burden, deduct from all the hereditary goods; and secondly, from the part to be restored by virtue of the fideicommissary substitution, the trebellianic portion due to the said John by right of fideicommissum, also deduct, and thus have and deduct two fourths, or whether he can only deduct that due by natural law, notwithstanding the said prohibition, and not the trebellianic portion, notwithstanding the said prohibition, or notwithstanding that two fourths cannot be deducted.

Thirdly: if the said donation could in any way or cause be infringed by law, or be invalid, to whom, or to which of the said sons and daughters, and brothers and sisters of the said John, is the legitime due by natural law, and how much trebellianic portion, where it can be deducted by law from the estate, is due.
body: In the name of Christ.

† There are various opinions regarding the deduction of two fourths. Some say that only one Falcidian fourth is deducted; others, both; others, the larger one; and others distinguish, saying that if the request is made purely, one is deducted, but if made under a condition, several are deducted, because they do not merge, since they do not occur at the same time of deduction, as is touched upon by the gloss and others. C. ad l. Falc. l. quamquam. ff. de inoff. test. l. Papi. §. meminisse. in Auth. de rest. et ea, quae pa. §. quamobrem. in Auth. de hær. et Falc. §. si quis autem non implens. ff. si cui plusquam. per. l. Falc. l. licet. §. interdum. C. Falc. et er. l. filium, quem habentem. But it has been determined by the Decretals that a son burdened with restitution may deduct both the legitime and the Trebellianic fourth; indeed, this law deducts the legitime, the heir deducts the Trebellianic fourth, the Falcidian fourth due by natural law is deducted from the body of the goods after deducting debts: but the Trebellianic fourth is deducted from the universality itself, which is a universality, otherwise the inheritance without separation of debts. And if we look closely, they are deducted as if not from the same universality, but from different ones: because one universality is pure goods, another is burdened inheritance, and thus there is a double universality, and a lesser one: but nevertheless the lesser is included under the greater. And therefore in effect both deductions revolve around the same subject, that is, the universal and intellectual body of the patrimony. Whatever the custom of the world may be, it stands in this part on the canons, for the Pope can interpret laws with, and sometimes: for example, during a vacancy of the Empire, the Pope could enact civil laws in place of the Emperor, ar. extra de re iu. c. Pasto. in fi. in cle. whence the opinions of the doctors say that they yield to the authority of Blessed Peter, not precede. It follows therefore in this doubt the Decretal extra de testa. c. Ray. and c. Rayn. and in c. si pater. de testa. lib. 6. and thus I have often advised that it should be observed in fact, and thus it is observed.

† And having premised this, I say that the donee may, by virtue of the right of donation, if it does not exceed the lawful limit, or if it was insinuated, deduct the legitime and the Trebellian portion; because the right to the legitime and the Trebellian portion may be ceded and donated. D. 36.1.1 § inde Nerat. But what is the amount of the legitime? For if we count nine children, it is one-half of a ninth part; but if there are three, it is one-third of a third.

But it seems that daughters should be counted: for although they are not admitted under the name of the legitime, they are nevertheless admitted under the name of the dowry, which is substituted in place of the legitime. And therefore women here are counted among those having the legitime. Also, Bartolus, *Digestum*, *De inofficiosa testatione*, l. *Pater filium*; and thus I heard him holding this opinion in the schools. For she who is admitted to something cannot be said to be deprived, nor to be in the case of lapse. And although her legitime is diminished, it does not increase the legitime of another, for there is no place for the right of accretion unless someone is excluded in whole. And especially among those united only by legal connection, *argumentum* from *Digestum*, *De legatis secundis*, l. *Proculo*. But others say that the legitime is the third part established, which belongs to the person to whom it is devolved as if from intestacy, as if it had been devolved by common law: because the rule of the legitime portion has relation to the cause of intestacy, whence it does not matter whether it is devolved by the old law, or by the new law, namely by statute or custom. *Digestum*, *Ad legem Falcidiam*, l. *I*, § *Lex Falcidia*.

† The question stands thus: whether the dowry is said to be the legitimate portion of daughters, or whether it is not said to be legitimate; but in one case, the first, the opinion of Bartolus is true; in the second case, another opinion prevails, for which the following supports. C. de her. inst. l. quotiens. Ricardus Malus calls it substituted in place of the legitimate portion in the question which he disputed; therefore, the opinion of Bartolus is true, which I believe to be true. Nevertheless, Jacobus Butrigarius disputed it and involved many subtleties. And it is a matter of the niceties of the law. By the death of a male, however, the legitimate portion of daughters is not increased in the father's goods, as is noted by Cynus, C. de adulter. l. publico. I say moreover,

† That a prohibition of alienation to a certain person does not include sons among themselves. C. de fideic. l. voluntas. And therefore a brother could give to a brother the right, and hope. C. de don. l. spen. apparet. It appears that the testator intended that it should not be alienated to outsiders, not among themselves. ff. de leg. 2. l. si pater. §. 15. For he made this prohibition in consideration of persons, so that outsiders should not possess these things, but not out of hatred for their own. And thus the prohibition has a personal cause of prohibition real, and thus it would not obstruct the transaction. l. cum hi. §. sed si in pluribus. I, Bal. Add the following counsel.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether the ancient coinage or the new is to be examined.
2. Custom looks backward.
body:
To the Reverend Father in Christ, and before you, Lord Dino Peter de Mathatatis, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See Archbishop of Lardera, and the Reverend Father Lord John, Abbot of S. Grisogono de Iarda, judges delegated by the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord John, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See Archbishop of Strigonia and Vicar General of the Kingdom of Dalmatia, between me, Simon de Auria of Genoa, Royal Admiral and Count of the islands of Farra, Brachia, and Curzona, on one part, and the men or communities of the islands of Farra and Brachia on the other part: I complain and set forth, I, the aforementioned Simon de Auria, against and opposed to the men or community of the island of Farra, in that the said men or said community of the said island of Farra have defrauded and attempt to defraud the said Simon, as Count of the said island, or rather the Royal Majesty, of the salary due to me from the said community by the said community; inasmuch as the said community, at the time when it was previously ruled and possessed, albeit unjustly and tyrannically, by the Venetians, paid or was bound to pay to each count or rector who was then sent by the said Venetians to govern the said island, six hundred and forty pounds of small denarii of the ancient currency then current, every year, for their salary, calculating each Venetian grosso at thirty-two small denarii. And from the time when the said Royal Majesty granted to me, the said Simon, the county of the said island of Farra, the said community has paid to me only six hundred and twenty-three pounds of small denarii of the currency now current, every year, saving the right of calculation; which amount is much less than the aforementioned six hundred and forty pounds of small denarii of the said ancient currency, calculating the grosso as above, and this to my no small damage and loss, or rather to that of the said Royal Majesty. Wherefore I, Simon the aforesaid, earnestly request through you, the above-named delegated judges, that the men or community of the said island of Farra be condemned and pronounced condemned by your sentence to give, pay, and restore, or otherwise make good to me, the said Simon, that which they have hitherto defrauded me of in the payment of the said salary for the entire time during which I held the said island by Royal concession, calculating the currency as above; and also to give and pay in each year during which the Royal Majesty shall have granted to me the communities of the said island of Farra, keeping, however, the salary quit which the said community was bound to pay to the said counts who were sent by the said Commune of Venice, calculating and multiplying the currency as above, with legitimate expenses incurred and to be incurred. And all and each of the aforesaid I request by every way, right, and mode, usage, and form by which it may better be done according to law, saving to me the right of adding, diminishing, correcting, declaring, interpreting, and otherwise requesting one or more times whenever it shall be expedient, and saving all other right of claiming damages, injuries, expenses, losses, interest, and expenses which I have suffered and which I may happen to suffer in the future on account of the said matter, of which I expressly protest.

Copy of the clause intercluded in the Ducal Letters of Venice.

I, the Potestas of the islands of Farra and Batram, swear and shall stand in the said office from the day on which I enter upon it until two complete years, and so much longer as my successor shall remain before coming, whom the Lord Duke shall send, receiving the full salary for so much longer time pro rata temporis, which my salary is one thousand Venetian small denarii, receiving the true grosso, or one for thirty small denarii. In which said office I must keep two Venetian associates, to each of whom I must give thirty pounds and two suitable robes per year. And for this reason I must also have, beyond the said one thousand pounds, one hundred pounds per year in denarii which are accustomed to be given to the counselors of the said land, although they do not say that there are counselors there; however, I shall cause one of the said associates to stand in Batram continuously, as it shall seem good to me. Furthermore, I am bound to have and must keep one notary, eight shield-bearers, and six horses at my own expense, to which notary I am bound to give twenty solidi per year. Moreover, in the year 1326, indiction 11, on July 7, it was taken in the Council of the Kingdom and the Forty that the commission of the Potestas of Farra and Batram be corrected in such a way that where it says that he must receive his salary at the rate of thirty-two small denarii, it shall be as the currency runs.

† This question, whether one should examine the old or the new coinage, is touched upon by the doctors of civil law in l. cum quid and in l. vnum, C. si certum petatur, and in l. in minorum, in qui causis in integrum restitutio non est necessaria, according to Cynus, and in l. uxorem, §. uxorem, de legatis 3, according to Decius. And it was a question of the ancient Pisans, disputed by Jacobus de Belvisio, who determined that the coinage which existed at the time of the promise must be examined, not that which is current at the time of payment. And the time of the contract is examined according to him for this principal reason, because the obligation is certain from the beginning as to what, as to which kind, and as to how much. l. certum, C. si certum petatur. Therefore, it does not change with the passage of time, because time is not a mode of changing the obligation, nor the state of the obligation, which was certain from the beginning, is changed by a subsequent fact, arg. ff. de verbis oblig., l. insulam inter biennium. And the same applies wherever action is brought based on a disposition of a person: because the time of the disposition is considered, not the time of the incident or of payment, so that we may know what, and of what kind, was sold; because, as I said, certainty is considered with regard to the origin and the beginning of the contract, as ff. de verbis oblig., l. sti, quaedam certe sunt. Secondly, the response there, when it says that the province itself. But this does not truly apply to our case, because here action is not brought based on a promise, but in a constitution or custom. And the Speculum says that when action is brought based on a disposition of the law, the coinage current at the time of payment is considered, not the time when the law was issued or the custom introduced. And this is expressly stated in c. ult., de decimis, in the Clementines. But notwithstanding this, it must be said that only so much must be paid to the Lord Count of the Islands in new coinage as is worth as much as the old, according to the tax given to him at the rate of 30 small coins for each grosso. For when a law fixing a tax remains firm, it remains firm until it is revoked by that law. l. sicut aureus, where the legal gold coin was taxed at 75 per pound of gold, and even if the law now speaks of coinage, it is understood to refer to the taxed coinage, as l. si aliquid and l. quotiens, de susceptis et archis, and noted in l. quicumque, C. de servis fugitivis, and l. si, communia delegatorum.

† Moreover, one must not depart from custom, and custom looks backward. D. de alimentis, l. Mella, § 1, ad hoc; C. de locato, l. Licet. For it is deemed tacitly agreed upon the ancient wage. And custom, according to Iacobus and Rebuffus, is argued from D. de fideiussoribus, l. Si, in fine. Furthermore, this is openly proven in Extravagantes, de censibus, c. Ex parte Compostellani, and c. Olim causam. The first speaks of the old measure being observed; the second of the old weight and number being observed. And conversely, if the small coinage were debased, the performance would not thereby increase, as in Extravagantes, de censibus, c. Cum canonicis. The objection from c. Ultima, de decimis, in the Clementines, does not hold, because there the cause was lucrative, whereas here it is onerous. Wherefore, if the honor, namely the stipend, were diminished here, while the labor and expenses of the committed service have not been diminished. Moreover, when one of correlatives is changed in one respect, the other must not be changed either, otherwise the whole would be vitiated. D. de contrahenda emptione, l. Pacta conventa, § Paulus; D. de acceptilatione, l. Finis. And therefore I am of the opinion in favor of the Lord Count of the Isles. And note that the word “as the coinage runs,” and not “as it will run in the future,” strongly favors the Lord Count. Baldus.

consilium-baldo_cons_print_venice_1575_v.argument:
1. Whether payment in coin should be made according to the valuation of the old or the new currency: and see the preceding opinion.
2. Whether prescription runs against payment in coin. 40 years.
3. Whenever a valuation is legally established by statute, it is always understood to refer to the currency once valued.
body: In the name of Christ, Amen. In the question, in which it is asked whether the communities of Farra and Bracchiana are bound to pay to their communities, appointed there by the Royal Majesty, the amount of salary in the currency now current, or that which was current when they were governed by the Venetians. Having invoked the name of Christ, I say first that the fact, on which counsel is sought, was transmitted to me very obscurely; nevertheless, because I recall having given counsel in such a case in previous years, and I sought that counsel in my notes, and I found it.

† And therefore, adhering to them and adding, I say that in favor of the said counts appointed there, the gloss on the word *duos solidos* in the chapter *Conquerente*, Extra, *De officio ordinarii*, holds that payment is to be made according to the estimation of that coin which was anciently and from the beginning accustomed to be paid; unless by payment of a lesser coin, which is now in use, prescription has been acquired, as in the chapter *Olim*, *De censibus*. And this applies whether a greater coin is in use at the time of payment or a lesser one, as in the chapter *Cum canonicis* and the aforementioned chapter *Olim*, *De censibus*. And this is not the opinion of Hostiensis, in the Summa, title *De censibus*, § *Ex quibus*, verse *Quid si moneta mutetur*.

† saying, that if payment has been made in a certain currency, and each year it was paid in that currency, if afterwards, after 40 years have elapsed, the currency changes, nevertheless the payment must be made according to the valuation of the first currency, unless the prescription for payment in the second currency is complete. And thus it should be understood. Cf. c. Olim and c. Cum canonicis, supra allegatum. What I said regarding 40 years, however, is to be understood in the case of the Church; but in private cases, regarding 30 years, as is noted in d. c. Olim. Add what the glossa says in l. Si, in principio, C. de coniunctione delegationis, in the word "20 solidis." And what I said there in my lecture, that if the gold coin or currency increases or decreases in value, as long as they exist, they must be reduced to the understanding of the value of the old currency. Cf. l. Si aliquid and l. Quo, C. de susceptis et archis; and l. 1, C. de veteris numismatis, lib. 11.

† And whenever a valuation is made judicially by law, it is always understood to refer to that money once valued, as we say in the case of the legal gold coin, which was valued so that 70 of them constitute a pound of gold, as stated in the aforementioned law *quo* in the Code on *susceptis* and in the Archalibro 11. And by these arguments I conclude in favor of the said counts that the payment of the salary ought to be made in the currency then current, when the territory was governed by the Venetians; and thus in the currency which was anciently and from the beginning accustomed to be paid. And so I say and advise. I, Baldus. FLNS. Ornioinat fromRGIDD COMpltIE.
